facts: The Principal and Minor Appellants are Greek citizens; the Associate Appellant held a Greek resident permit valid until 2023 as the spouse of a Greek citizen. She had been outside Greece about 13 months at the hearing date, having given birth to a child in Canada. The Appellants argued it was 'unclear' whether they could re-enter Greece.
rule: Article 1E of the Refugee Convention excludes persons with status substantially similar to nationals of a third country. Once a prima facie case of exclusion is raised, the burden shifts to the claimant to establish they lack such status (Rrotaj, 2016 FC 152, aff'd 2016 FCA 292). Status is assessed at the date of hearing (Majebi, 2016 FC 14, aff'd 2016 FCA 274).
application: The Greek Citizenship Code (NDP item 3.1) did not show the Greek-citizen Appellants' citizenship was or would be revoked; Article 19 did not apply to the Principal Appellant (who naturalized as an adult) and at most allowed renunciation for the Minor Appellant. For the Associate Appellant, the legislation entitled valid-permit holders to re-enter, and expressly protected status during absences for pregnancy and motherhood, with no automatic loss after six or twelve months. Her permit remained valid and she had a child during the absence, so re-entry was more likely than not. A bare assertion that the outcome was 'unclear' did not discharge the shifted burden.
conclusion: The RPD correctly found the Associate Appellant excluded under Article 1E, and the Appellants failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that they could not re-enter Greece.

issue: Did the harm the Appellants fear in Greece rise to the level of persecution, or did it amount only to discrimination not establishing a claim under s. 96 or s. 97?
facts: The Appellants, Turkish-Azari from Iran, alleged difficulty renting housing, anti-foreigner sentiment, the Minor Appellant being shunned at school and in parks, and general xenophobia/Islamophobia and police brutality toward migrants in Greece. They nonetheless secured housing, employment, healthcare and schooling, and were never subjected to violence by state actors.
rule: Discrimination amounts to persecution only where the claimant faces systemic or persistent harm producing an insecure existence (X (Re), 2020 CanLII 24189). Country-conditions evidence must be linked to the claimant's own circumstances; the claimant bears the burden on a balance of probabilities.
application: Evidence of violence against migrants crossing the border or in refugee camps did not apply to the Appellants, who lived in Athens as citizens/resident, not as migrants. Reports about mistreatment of homeless persons, drug users and sex workers, and about the Golden Dawn party (concentrated in Western Thrace, Lesbos and Kos), did not concern the Appellants' region or situation, and Greek authorities were prosecuting far-right racist violence. The housing and schooling difficulties, while discriminatory, did not deprive the Appellants of access to housing, work, healthcare or education, and involved no violence.
conclusion: The harm feared amounted to discrimination, not persecution; the Appellants established neither a serious possibility of persecution nor a s. 97 risk in Greece.

issue: Do the Principal Appellant's military service obligations and the COVID-19 situation in Greece establish a risk under s. 96 or s. 97?
facts: The Principal Appellant said he would face mandatory Greek military service, which he did not want because of a bad experience serving in Iran and a wish not to leave his family; he also testified that persons with two children may be exempt and now has two children. The Appellants also feared COVID-19 in Greece, citing a March 2020 school closure.
rule: Conscription under a law of general application does not itself constitute persecution (Etiz, 2013 FC 308). A claimant must adduce evidence linking a generalized condition to a personalized risk under s. 96 or s. 97.
application: Not wishing to leave family for service does not establish persecution; reserve duty was available; the Greek military was regarded as a trustworthy institution and evidence showed only gender discrimination, not ethnic/religious mistreatment; and on his own testimony the Principal Appellant would now be exempt as a father of two. On COVID-19, the school closure mirrored measures in Ontario and no evidence showed the Appellants faced a particular or discriminatory risk in Greece.
conclusion: Neither military service nor COVID-19 established a serious possibility of persecution or a s. 97 risk.

issue: Does the two-year limitation period in s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act bar the claim against the Lorraine Penna estate, despite the Limitations Act, 2002 transition provisions?
facts: Lorraine Penna, an executor of her husband Paul Penna's estate, died December 18, 2003. A claim seeking to hold her estate liable for losses caused by co-executor Landen's alleged looting was first advanced in a notice of motion for partial summary judgment dated December 4, 2006 \u2014 almost three years after her death and about a year after the two-year mark of December 18, 2005.
rule: Section 38(2) of the Trustee Act allows an action against an executor for a wrong done by the deceased, and s. 38(3) bars such an action after two years from death; Waschkowski v. Hopkinson Estate (2000) holds s. 38(3) is an absolute limitation not subject to discoverability. Section 19 of the Limitations Act, 2002 preserves listed limitation periods (including s. 38(3)) and s. 19(4) gives them priority over 'any other provision of this Act', which the court held includes the s. 24 transition provisions (Kramarz; York Condominium Corp. No. 382).
application: The claim, though framed as breach of fiduciary duty, falls within s. 38(2) (Roth v. Weston Estate). Section 38(3) is listed in the Schedule and preserved by s. 19; under s. 19(4) it prevails over other provisions, including the s. 24 transition rules. Treating s. 38(3) as a 'former limitation period' under s. 24(4) would absurdly leave no limitation period for the few straddling cases, which the Legislature could not have intended. Discoverability does not save the claim, and fraudulent concealment was not shown.
conclusion: Section 38(3) applies and, absent any saving provision, bars the claim; the two-year period expired December 18, 2005 before the December 2006 motion.

issue: Do ss. 43 and 44 of the former Limitations Act exempt the claim as one founded on fraud or fraudulent breach of trust to which the trustee was party or privy?
facts: The allegations against Lorraine Penna were that she failed to review Landen's activities, abdicated her duties, and breached her fiduciary duty; there was no allegation that she committed fraud, held trust property, or knew of Landen's fraud.
rule: Section 43(2) of the former Limitations Act frees actions against trustees from statutory limitation periods where the claim is 'founded upon a fraud or fraudulent breach of trust to which the trustee was party or privy' or to recover retained trust property (Edwards v. Law Society of Upper Canada). Being 'party or privy' requires actual knowledge, recklessness or wilful blindness \u2014 a 'want of probity' \u2014 by analogy to knowing assistance in Air Canada v. M & L Travel Ltd., [1993] 3 S.C.R. 787; mere negligence or constructive knowledge is insufficient.
application: Lorraine Penna may have been negligent in allowing Landen free rein, but negligence does not make her a party or privy to his fraud. There was no allegation of knowledge or wilful blindness on her part, and she held no trust property. The motion judge overstated the effect of ss. 43\u201344 by treating them as exempting all fraud claims from limitation periods.
conclusion: Sections 43 and 44 do not apply; the exemption is unavailable, so it was unnecessary to decide the effect of their repeal.

issue: Does s. 47 of the Estates Act relieve against the s. 38(3) limitation period?
facts: Counsel for the appellant received oral notice of a possible claim on April 20, 2005 and a confirmatory letter, but no affidavit-verified notice with full particulars was filed.
rule: Section 47 of the Estates Act stops the Trustee Act limitation from running only where 'notice of the claim giving full particulars of the claim and verified by affidavit is filed with the executor' before the claim would otherwise be barred.
application: Whether or not the claim fell within s. 47, the required affidavit-verified notice with full particulars was never given \u2014 only oral notice and a letter. The formal statutory notice procedure was never invoked before December 18, 2005.
conclusion: Section 47 does not assist the respondents; it cannot relieve against the s. 38(3) bar.

issue: Did the appellant waive the limitation defence by not appealing orders adding the estate as a party or directing it to pass accounts?
facts: The estate was added as a plaintiff in April 2006 and later ordered to pass accounts; the appellant did not appeal these orders.
rule: A limitation defence is not lost by failing to appeal interlocutory orders that do not adjudicate the claim; s. 49 of the Estates Act does not authorize awarding damages on a statute-barred claim (Simone v. Cheifetz).
application: The appellant had no reason to appeal an order adding the estate as a plaintiff, and failing to appeal the accounting order did not surrender a defence available when the estate is called on to defend. Section 49's broad audit powers do not permit awarding damages on a claim barred by s. 38(3).
conclusion: There was no waiver; the limitation defence remained available.

issue: Should the doctrine of special circumstances permit adding the Lorraine Penna estate as a defendant despite expiry of the limitation period?
facts: By March 2005 the estate's solicitors had the LECG report indicating Landen's questionable transactions; counsel was told of a possible claim in April 2005 with eight months left before the limitation expired, yet no claim or s. 47 notice was made until the December 2006 motion. Lorraine Penna had been incompetent since 1999 and was deceased.
rule: Special circumstances may allow adding a party after expiry of s. 38(3) (Swain Estate; Basarsky v. Quinlan), and the doctrine survives the Limitations Act, 2002 (by analogy to Giroux Estate). The onus is on the party seeking relief (Frohlick), and the doctrine is invoked infrequently; a presumption of prejudice attaches, especially where the deceased was incompetent (Waschkowski).
application: The respondents had legal advice and the relevant facts long before the limitation expired but did nothing to sue the estate or invoke s. 47. The presumption of prejudice was heightened by Lorraine Penna's incompetence and death. That the fraudster (Landen) knew of his own defalcation is no comfort to the estate, the real perpetrator and his company are already parties, and no evidence showed the estate received fraud proceeds. Only ordinary injustice from an expired limitation was shown (Canadian Red Cross Society (Re)).
conclusion: Special circumstances were not established; the estate should not be added as a defendant.

issue: Was the impugned imputation that Simpson 'would condone violence toward gay people' a statement of fact or a comment?
facts: Rafe Mair, a controversial radio talk-show host, broadcast an editorial comparing social activist Kari Simpson (an outspoken opponent of positive portrayals of a gay lifestyle in schools) to Hitler, Governor Wallace, skinheads and the Ku Klux Klan, from which the trial judge found an imputation that she 'would condone violence toward gay people.' The Court of Appeal treated this as a factual assertion lacking evidentiary foundation.
rule: 'Comment' includes a 'deduction, inference, conclusion, criticism, judgment, remark or observation which is generally incapable of proof' (Ross v. New Brunswick Teachers' Assn., 2001 NBCA 62). What is comment and what is fact is determined from the perspective of a reasonable viewer or reader; loose, figurative or hyperbolic editorial language is generally construed as comment (Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada).
application: The pleaded innuendo was framed as an inference ('would condone violence') drawn from a factual premise (that Simpson was deeply hostile to gay people). Mair was a radio personality known for opinion, not a reporter of facts, and his listeners would have understood the 'sting' as comment. The respondent herself did not challenge the characterization of the imputation as comment. The Court of Appeal erred in treating it as a statement of fact requiring proof of truth.
conclusion: The imputation was a comment, not a statement of fact, so the applicable defence was fair comment.

issue: What are the elements of the fair comment defence, and should the 'honest belief' element be an objective test?
facts: Mair testified he did not honestly believe Simpson would actually condone violence; he intended only to convey that she was an intolerant bigot. The gap between his subjective intended meaning and the objective defamatory meaning found by the court raised the question of what 'honest belief' requires.
rule: Per Binnie J. (majority), the defence, adapting Dickson J.'s dissent in Cherneskey v. Armadale Publishers Ltd., [1979] 1 S.C.R. 1067, requires: (a) comment on a matter of public interest; (b) based on fact; (c) recognizable as comment; (d) an objective test — could any person honestly express that opinion on the proved facts? The defence is defeated if the plaintiff proves the defendant was subjectively actuated by express malice. The common law is developed consistently with Charter values (s. 2(b)) and the value of reputation (Hill v. Church of Scientology). LeBel and Rothstein JJ. would eliminate the honest-belief element entirely, requiring only comment, basis in true facts, and public interest.
application: The majority modified the honest-belief element to an objective standard: the comment need not be reasonable or proportional, only capable of being honestly expressed by a person 'however prejudiced, exaggerated or obstinate' in their views. This balances free expression on matters of public interest against protection of reputation and avoids making the defence turn on whether the speaker will swear belief in a meaning he denies intending. The onus remains on the defendant to establish the four elements before the plaintiff must prove malice. Abolishing honest belief entirely would be more than an incremental change.
conclusion: The honest-belief element is retained but restated as an objective test: could any person honestly express that opinion on the proved facts?

issue: Did the fair comment defence apply on the facts to protect Mair's editorial?
facts: The debate concerned inclusion of educational materials on homosexuality in public schools. Simpson's speeches used martial and violent imagery ('this is a war... you shoot, they shoot'). The trial judge found the factual foundation stated or publicly known and substantially true, and found malice was not the dominant motive; Simpson did not appeal the malice finding.
rule: Applying the modified fair comment test, the comment must concern a matter of public interest, be based on a sufficient and substantially true factual substratum, be recognizable as comment, and satisfy the objective honest-belief test, subject to defeat by proof of malice.
application: The schools debate clearly engaged the public interest; the factual foundation was stated or notorious to Mair's audience and substantially true; the sting was comment. Simpson's own violent rhetoric provided a sufficient nexus so that at least some listeners could honestly form the opinion that she would condone violence, meeting the objective test even though Mair denied intending that meaning. Malice was not the dominant motive and was not appealed.
conclusion: All elements of the fair comment defence were met and it was not defeated by malice; the trial judge was correct to allow the defence.

issue: Did the RPD err in finding that the mistreatment the Applicants suffered amounted to discrimination but not persecution, including consideration of cumulative effects?
facts: The Principal Applicant, a Jewish woman from Russia, and her son endured anti-Semitic insults, threats, vandalism of belongings with swastikas, and physical assaults (a broken finger in 1998/1999, a supervisor threatening her with scissors in 2005, and a 2008 beating by nationalists). She argued the cumulative effect of this treatment amounted to persecution.
rule: 'Persecution' is a 'sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights demonstrative of a failure of state protection' (Canada (AG) v Ward, [1993] SCJ 74). Multiple incidents of discrimination can constitute persecution under s. 96 IRPA (Ampong, 2010 FC 35), and the distinction between discrimination and persecution is a mixed question of law and fact for the Board, reviewable for reasonableness; the Court intervenes only if the conclusion is capricious and unreasonable (Sagharichi v Canada (MEI) (1993), 182 NR 398).
application: The RPD did consider the cumulative nature of the attacks and ethnic slurs, referencing the 1999, 2005 and October 2008 incidents. It assessed whether the aggregate gave rise to cumulative persecution and reasonably concluded the incidents constituted discrimination that did not reach the level of persecution. The conclusion fell within the range of acceptable outcomes.
conclusion: The RPD did not err; its finding that the treatment amounted to discrimination but not persecution was reasonable.

issue: Did the RPD err in its assessment of the Principal Applicant's credibility?
facts: The applicant stated in her PIF that the neighbour assault occurred in 1999, but the medical certificate was dated 1998, an inconsistency she corrected only when confronted at the hearing. She also failed to provide a medical certificate for the October 2008 incident, despite her mother having obtained certificates for the 1998 and 2003 injuries.
rule: Credibility findings are questions of fact reviewable on the standard of reasonableness (Dunsmuir, 2008 SCC 9). Where there are valid reasons to doubt a claimant's credibility, a failure to provide corroborating documentation is a proper consideration if the claimant's explanation is not accepted (Singh v Canada (MCI) (2003), 233 FTR 166).
application: The RPD reasonably drew a negative inference from the date inconsistency between the PIF and the medical certificate, though the Court noted the weight given was 'at the limit' of acceptability. The RPD also reasonably drew a negative inference from the failure to provide corroborating documentation for the October 2008 incident, which the applicant considered the decisive event, especially given her mother had provided records for other incidents. Applicants bear the onus of producing relevant corroborating evidence.
conclusion: The RPD's negative credibility findings were reasonable and warranted no intervention.

issue: Did the RPD err in its assessment of the availability of state protection?
facts: The applicant complained to police after the 1999 assault but was told to deal with it herself; she did not report the 2005 supervisor incident. Country evidence showed hate crimes are often prosecuted only as 'hooliganism' and investigations are inadequate, but also showed the government had successfully prosecuted individuals for anti-Semitic activities and a revived Jewish community existed.
rule: There is a presumption that a state can protect its citizens; the more democratic the state, the more the claimant must do to exhaust available avenues (Ward; Hinzman v Canada (MCI), 2007 FCA 171). Local failures to police do not amount to a lack of state protection (Flores Carrillo, 2008 FCA 94). Protection need not be perfect but must be adequate (Villafranca).
application: The RPD reasonably found the applicant should have made additional attempts to seek assistance from higher police authorities or other agencies, as she bore the onus of rebutting the presumption. The RPD acknowledged evidence of impunity but also cited instances of successful prosecutions, presenting a balanced, well-documented picture. The Court declined to reweigh the evidence.
conclusion: The RPD did not err; its state protection finding was reasonable.

issue: Did the RPD err in finding the Applicants had a viable internal flight alternative?
facts: The RPD found the applicants could relocate to another city such as St. Petersburg, where it would be highly unlikely the applicant would be identified as Jewish, noting her birth certificate showed Russian nationality with no indication of Jewish ethnicity. She argued an IFA was inappropriate because her husbands were in Canada.
rule: The two-part IFA test requires (1) no serious possibility of persecution in the proposed area on a balance of probabilities, and (2) that relocation be reasonable given the claimant's personal circumstances (Rasaratnam; Thirunavukkarasu). Reviewable on reasonableness.
application: Whether a claimant has relatives in the asylum country is irrelevant to the IFA test. The RPD's core finding—that it was highly unlikely the applicant would be identified or perceived as Jewish if she relocated to a city where no one knew her—was unchallenged, and no evidence showed she was perceived as Jewish by her behaviour or actions. The IFA finding was reasonable.
conclusion: The RPD did not err; the IFA finding was reasonable.

issue: Did the claimant establish a credible, subjectively-held well-founded fear of persecution based on his Jewish ethnicity in Ukraine?
facts: The claimant, a citizen of Ukraine, alleged repeated anti-Semitic assaults by nationalists (UNA-UNSO) from 2008 to 2011, vandalism of his home and car, and threats. He was deported from the US in 2007, his wife and sister live in the US, and a spousal sponsorship was underway. He decided to leave after a 2011 beating but did not depart until 2012, and after arriving in Canada delayed roughly a month before claiming refugee status.
rule: Testimony under oath is presumed true unless there is valid reason to doubt it (Maldonado); credibility is tested against the preponderance of probabilities that a practical, informed person would recognize as reasonable (Faryna v. Chorny). Delay in leaving the country and in claiming protection is a relevant factor undermining subjective fear (Singh 2007 FC 62; Nijjar 2009 FC 1259; Assadi). A lack of subjective fear alone can defeat a claim (Kamana), and a medical report is only as valid as the facts underlying it (Danailov).
application: The panel disbelieved the persecution narrative, finding the claimant had manipulated publicly available articles on anti-Semitism in Ukraine to concoct a story allowing him to relocate closer to his wife pending US sponsorship. It drew negative inferences from his delay in leaving Ukraine (four to five months after the decisive 2011 attack, and years after problems began in 2008) and his roughly one-month delay in claiming in Canada, finding his explanations unsatisfactory. Medical/forensic reports did not attribute injuries to anti-Semitic motivation, and documentary evidence indicated anti-Semitic assaults are rare, which the panel preferred over the claimant's testimony.
conclusion: The panel found no credible basis for a subjective fear of persecution; the claim failed on this ground.

issue: Did the claimant rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in Ukraine with clear and convincing evidence?
facts: The claimant said he made three police reports but received no help, and alleged a procedure requiring a police report before approaching higher authorities. He produced a police forensic medical report from a 2010 incident and other medical reports that did not state the cause of injuries. Ukraine faced instability in Crimea and the east in 2014 but held a presidential election and retained control of most territory.
rule: States are presumed capable of protecting citizens unless in complete breakdown; the claimant bears the onus of clear and convincing proof of inability or unwillingness to protect (Ward; Villafranca). Protection need only be adequate, not perfect, and the more democratic the country the more must be done to exhaust avenues (Kadenko; Flores Carrillo). A contextual assessment of the claimant's situation, the risk, the agent and country conditions is required (Gonzalez Torres).
application: The panel found Ukraine not in complete breakdown, noting elections and continued territorial control. The forensic report showed police did take action on the 2010 incident. The panel rejected the alleged requirement to obtain a police report before complaining to the prosecutor, finding documentary evidence contradicted it and that complaints could be made directly to the prosecutor's office. It found the claimant failed to exhaust domestic recourses and that documentary evidence, though mixed, showed adequate state protection and legal responses to anti-Semitic offences.
conclusion: The claimant did not rebut the presumption of state protection; adequate state protection was available.

issue: Should ARPA Canada be granted leave to intervene on the public interest ground?
facts: ARPA Canada, a not-for-profit advocating for Reformed Christians, sought leave to intervene in an appeal from Chief Justice Hinkson's judgment (2021 BCSC 512) dismissing a Charter challenge by churches and pastors to public health orders prohibiting in-person religious gatherings during COVID-19. ARPA Canada shares theological convictions with some appellants but claimed to bring a distinct perspective. The respondents opposed, calling it a duplicative 'me too' intervention.
rule: Rule 36 of the Court of Appeal Rules governs intervention. Public interest intervenors must meet the factors summarized in BCCLA v. Canada (AG), 2018 BCCA 282: (a) a broad representative base; (b) the case legitimately engages the applicant's interests in the public law issue; (c) a unique and different perspective that will assist the Court; and (d) whether the applicant seeks to expand the scope of the appeal (Watson and Spratt, 2006 BCCA 234; Carter v. Canada, 2012 BCCA 502). Where Charter issues are raised, a more generous approach is permitted (Canadian Labour Congress v. Bhindi), but intervenors may not raise entirely new issues, and interests aligned with a party do not bar intervention where a unique perspective assists the court (Araya v. Nevsun, 2017 BCCA 402).
application: The respondents conceded and the court agreed that ARPA Canada had a broad representative base and that its interests were legitimately engaged. The remaining question was whether it offered a unique, useful perspective without expanding the appeal. Reviewing the appellants' factum, which focused on case-specific details, the court found ARPA Canada's proposed arguments on institutional pluralism and the intersectional impact of the s. 2 breaches rose above those details and addressed broader constitutional issues the appellants had not raised. There was no indication of strategizing to skirt page limits. However, its arguments on s. 15, minimal impairment and proportionality duplicated the appellants' factum or were points the appellants could themselves make.
conclusion: Leave to intervene granted in part; only the institutional pluralism and intersectional s. 2 impact arguments fell within the acceptable 'Goldilocks' zone.

issue: What conditions and limits should govern the intervention?
facts: Having granted limited leave, the court had to fix terms to prevent duplication and preserve fairness, and the appellants sought an extension of time for their reply factum.
rule: Under Rule 36(1) and (3) a justice may impose terms and conditions and specify factum deadlines; intervenors typically are granted the right to intervene on discrete issues only (Janzen v. British Columbia (AG)), and concerns of partiality may be mitigated by a clear order limiting scope (Araya at para. 18).
application: The court restricted ARPA Canada to submissions on institutional pluralism and the intersectional impact of the s. 2 breaches (subparas. 23(a)-(b) of its written submission), capped its factum at ten pages due March 1, 2022, prohibited new evidence or duplication, and permitted the respondents a ten-page response factum by March 11, 2022. Given the alignment of interests, the appellants' request to extend time for their reply factum was refused; their reply was to follow usual timelines and be confined to the respondents' factum. Whether ARPA Canada could make oral submissions was left to the division hearing the appeal.
conclusion: Intervention allowed subject to strict conditions limiting scope, factum length and timing; appellants' extension request denied.

issue: Did the cumulative discrimination the appellant experienced and would experience as a Roma in Hungary amount to persecution?
facts: The appellant, a Roma citizen of Hungary, alleged discrimination and harassment in education, exclusion from employment, forced eviction and homelessness in Miskolc, denial of adequate healthcare, and intimidation by Guardists and skinheads. The RPD found that his personal circumstances did not rise to the level of persecution and assessed each area of discrimination individually.
rule: Under the UNHCR Handbook (paras. 54–55), differential treatment is not necessarily persecution, but discrimination amounts to persecution where measures lead to consequences of a substantially prejudicial nature (e.g. serious restrictions on the right to earn a livelihood or access education), and a claim is stronger where the claimant has suffered a number of discriminatory measures with a cumulative element.
application: Conducting an independent assessment, the RAD found the appellant credibly testified to discrimination in housing, education and daily life. Country conditions evidence (US DOS 2018 report, Hungarian Ombudsman, European Roma Rights Centre) showed Roma face social and economic exclusion in nearly all fields — a 25.9% employment rate, high poverty risk, segregated housing and education, and denial of medical services. The RPD erred by assessing each area individually rather than cumulatively; taken together the measures produced consequences of a substantially prejudicial nature.
conclusion: The RAD concluded the appellant would experience discrimination amounting to persecution should he return to Hungary.

issue: Was adequate state protection available to the appellant, and did a viable internal flight alternative exist?
facts: The appellant said he was targeted by police, fined for petty offences, and that police failed to protect Roma from attacks by Guardists and skinheads. The RPD found the presumption of state protection was not rebutted because he had not sought protection.
rule: State protection must be adequate at the operational level and reasonably forthcoming; there is no obligation to seek protection that would not be reasonably forthcoming. An internal flight alternative must be a viable, safe place within the country.
application: The RAD's independent review of country conditions showed police prejudice against Roma, ethnic profiling, inadequate response to hate crimes, and over 100 cases of hate-motivated violence against Roma between 2009 and 2013. Government initiatives had not changed the overall situation, and the modest fines against a hospital and the city of Miskolc had not driven change. The appellant's experiences were consistent with this evidence. Because conditions for Roma were consistent throughout Hungary, no IFA existed.
conclusion: The RAD found adequate state protection was not available and there was no internal flight alternative.

issue: Did the Hearing Panel fail to disclose the case Mr. Fountain had to meet by finding him guilty of firing a gun that was 'neither necessary nor justified' when the Citation alleged 'careless and reckless use of a firearm'?
facts: The Citation alleged that on August 22, 2001 Mr. Fountain engaged in the 'careless and reckless use of a firearm by firing it over the heads of his sons'. The Panel found he used the firearm to send a message and that its discharge was neither necessary nor justified. Mr. Fountain argued this convicted him of an uncharged offence.
rule: An allegation of professional misconduct need not have the precision of a criminal charge, but must give reasonable notice and sufficient particulars so the person can prepare a defence: Re Golomb and College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (1976), 68 D.L.R. (3d) 25 (Ont. Div. Ct.). Questions of law are reviewed on a correctness standard (Stuart).
application: The conduct alleged to constitute misconduct — the firing of the gun over the boys' heads — was clearly identified in the Citation, and Mr. Fountain's ability to defend was not compromised. The essential inquiry was whether the identified conduct amounted to conduct unbecoming. Conduct that is 'neither necessary nor justified' falls within the ordinary meaning of 'careless' (per Black's Law Dictionary), so nothing turned on the difference in wording.
conclusion: The Citation adequately disclosed the case to be met; this ground of appeal failed.

issue: Did the Panel fail to consider relevant circumstances, including the totality of the evidence and Mr. Fountain's subjective state of mind?
facts: The Panel mistakenly stated that the criminal acquittal was based on 'more technical evidence' about how and where the weapon was aimed. Mr. Fountain argued the Panel ignored the totality of circumstances and his subjective belief that he fired to send a message, as one scares off bears.
rule: A tribunal's decision must be reviewed as a whole; a mistake not affecting the decision as a whole does not justify intervention: Law Society of New Brunswick v. Ryan, [2003] 1 S.C.R. 247. A reviewing court does not re-weigh evidence but asks whether the assessment can withstand a somewhat probing examination: Dr. Q v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of B.C., 2003 SCC 19.
application: The Court agreed the Panel's characterization of the acquittal was mistaken but found the error immaterial to the outcome. The Panel had in fact considered the evidence of Mr. Fountain's state of mind, made credibility findings, and found facts on the totality of the evidence. Its assessment was not unreasonable.
conclusion: This ground of appeal failed.

issue: Did the Panel apply the correct standard of proof?
facts: Mr. Fountain alleged the Panel failed to apply the proper standard of proof in the disciplinary hearing.
rule: The standard of proof in professional discipline is higher than the balance of probabilities but lower than the criminal standard — 'a fair and reasonable preponderance of credible evidence': Jory v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of B.C., [1985] B.C.J. No. 320. This is a question of law reviewed on correctness (Stuart).
application: The Panel specifically identified and acknowledged the Jory standard. No error was identified.
conclusion: This ground of appeal failed.

issue: Did the Panel apply the correct standard of conduct — that of the reasonable teacher?
facts: Mr. Fountain argued the Panel did not address or apply the reasonable-teacher standard in finding him guilty.
rule: The applicable standard against which a teacher's conduct is measured is that of the reasonable teacher, which is higher than that of the reasonable person (Shewan). This is a question of law reviewed on correctness.
application: The Panel expressly identified and acknowledged that the applicable standard was that of the reasonable teacher, and concluded a reasonable teacher would not have communicated with a gunshot in the circumstances.
conclusion: The Panel did not err on this point; this ground failed.

issue: Was the Panel's ultimate finding of conduct unbecoming reasonable where it did not address whether the off-duty conduct impaired Mr. Fountain's ability to teach or harmed the education system?
facts: The impugned conduct — firing a rifle upward at a 45-degree angle after a physical altercation with his adult sons — occurred off-duty. The Panel found the discharge unnecessary and unjustified and below the reasonable teacher standard, but did not analyze whether the conduct impaired his professional functioning or harmed the school system.
rule: Off-duty conduct can attract discipline only where it negatively impacts the teacher's ability to carry out obligations or harms the school system, e.g., by poisoning the school environment: Ross v. New Brunswick School District No. 15, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 825; Trinity Western University v. BCCT, [2001] 1 S.C.R. 772. Direct evidence of harm is not always required; impairment (direct or in the wider sense) may be inferred: Fraser v. Public Service Staff Relations Board, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 455; Kempling No. 1 and No. 2. Not all off-duty conduct falling below the standard warrants discipline (Shewan). Reasonableness review asks whether there is a line of analysis leading from the evidence to the conclusion: Ryan.
application: The Court found no line of analysis in the Panel's reasons connecting the below-standard conduct to a conclusion that discipline was warranted. The Panel overlooked that not all off-duty conduct, even if below the reasonable-teacher standard, grounds discipline. It failed to address whether the conduct constituted direct impairment or impairment in the wider sense, and disclosed no inferences of harm. Although direct evidence of harm was not required, the Panel had to address these issues; by stopping short, its verdict lacked a tenable supporting analysis.
conclusion: The Panel's finding of conduct unbecoming was unreasonable. Appeal allowed and the matter referred back to the College for reconsideration.

issue: Should the plaintiff's claim against the defendant lawyer (former defence counsel) be struck under Rule 9-5(1) and dismissed as limitation-barred under Rule 9-6?
facts: Mr. Warnett acted as ICBC-retained defence counsel in the plaintiff's motor vehicle accident actions from about 2002 until February 2007. In January 2018 the plaintiff sued him alleging fraud and negligence, including that he substituted the plaintiff's 1996 lumbar spine x-ray. The plaintiff failed to appear at the application he had helped schedule.
rule: Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules permits striking a pleading that discloses no reasonable claim, is unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, prejudices a fair trial, or is an abuse of process. The test under 9-5(1)(a) is whether it is plain and obvious the claim has no reasonable prospect of success (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42, para. 17), with speculative allegations subjected to skeptical analysis (Young v. Borzoni, 2007 BCCA 16). Under Rule 9-6, a statute-barred claim raises no genuine issue for trial (Brown v. Canada (A.G.), 2014 BCSC 357).
application: The court found the allegations amounted to wild speculation; even taken as true, no material facts made out any cause of action, and the pleadings were too fundamentally flawed to be saved by amendment. The claim violated all subsections of Rule 9-5(1). Additionally the action was statute-barred under either the current or repealed Limitation Act, whose limitation periods had long expired, leaving no triable issue.
conclusion: The claim against Mr. Warnett was struck without leave to amend and dismissed under Rule 9-5(1), and in the alternative dismissed under Rule 9-6 as limitation-barred.

issue: Should the plaintiff's claim against the expert medical witness be dismissed under Rule 9-6 on the basis of witness immunity?
facts: Dr. McGraw was retained by the defendants, examined the plaintiff three times, provided five medical-legal reports (2003–2013) and testified at the 2005 trial, opining that the plaintiff's lumbar spondylolisthesis was a developmental condition unrelated to the accidents. The plaintiff alleged fraud and negligence and that Dr. McGraw substituted the 1996 x-ray.
rule: Under Rule 9-6, judgment is granted where it is manifestly clear there is no genuine issue for trial. The doctrine of witness immunity renders witnesses immune from civil liability, extending to expert witnesses for in-court evidence and pre-trial activities including assessments and reports (P.(J.) v. Eirikson, 2015 BCSC 847, paras. 21, 25; 311165 BC Ltd v. Canada (A.G.), 2017 BCCA 196).
application: The court held witness immunity applied to Dr. McGraw's assessments, reports and testimony, so the plaintiff's allegations were bound to fail. The immunity protects the integrity of the justice system by ensuring witnesses are not deterred by fear of retaliatory suits. There was accordingly no genuine issue to be tried.
conclusion: The claim against Dr. McGraw was dismissed under Rule 9-6(5)(a); it was also struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a) as disclosing no reasonable claim.

issue: Do the claimants have a well-founded fear of persecution in Tunisia on the ground of religion under s. 96 of the IRPA?
facts: The claimants, a Tunisian couple and their teenage daughter, converted from Islam to evangelical Christianity beginning in 1999. They faced rejection by family and friends, the principal claimant was occasionally taken to a police station for questioning about his beliefs (though never charged), the wife had complaints from parents at the school where she taught, and the daughter felt isolated at school. They worshipped mostly in private homes and did not proselytize actively.
rule: Section 96 of the IRPA requires a well-founded fear of persecution on a Convention ground, including religion. The refugee definition is forward-looking, requiring assessment of prospective risk rather than past discrimination alone.
application: The panel accepted that the claimants are Christians but found the past incidents amounted to discrimination rather than persecution. The claimant was not shown to have engaged in active proselytizing (which remains restricted), instead engaging in gentle private discussions, and belonged to no organized church, so proselytizing was not a religious obligation. Past mistreatment did not, on its own, establish a prospective well-founded fear.
conclusion: The panel found the claimants' fear of persecution for their religion was not well-founded on a forward-looking basis.

issue: In light of the post-2011 changes in country conditions, is there a serious possibility of persecution or a personal risk under s. 97(1) of the IRPA?
facts: The claimants left Tunisia in August 2011, before the October 2011 Constituent Assembly elections. The adult claimants testified they believed the situation for Christians was worse after the revolution, but the objective documentary evidence (International Religious Freedom Report 2011, Freedom in the World 2012, NDP on Tunisia) described significant democratization, eased restrictions on religious association, freedom of worship for Christians and Jews, and cessation of surveillance and harassment of activists.
rule: Section 97(1) of the IRPA requires that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant would personally be subject to a danger of torture or a risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment. Where objective documentary evidence conflicts with a claimant's subjective assessment, the panel may favour independent, objective sources.
application: The panel preferred the documentary evidence over the claimants' subjective belief because it came from independent, objective sources with no interest in the outcome. The evidence showed Christians now practise their faith without restriction, the government promotes interfaith tolerance, surveillance of the type the principal claimant described had ceased, and merely speaking about Christian beliefs would not disturb public order. Accordingly there was no serious possibility of persecution and no personalized s. 97 risk.
conclusion: The panel found the claimants would not face a serious possibility of persecution nor a personal risk under s. 97(1) upon return to Tunisia.

issue: Did the discrimination and harassment the Roma claimants experienced in Hungary rise to the level of persecution?
facts: The principal claimant, her children and her father, all Hungarian Roma, alleged sustained discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing, verbal and physical abuse by Guardists and Jobbik supporters, a broken arm and leg in a 2006 beating, mistreatment of a hospitalized son, and segregated inferior schooling. The father was demoted from a suit-and-tie position and the husband managed only occasional work.
rule: Persecution is not defined in the Convention but means a sustained or systematic violation of basic human rights demonstrating a failure of state protection (Hathaway; Ward). The mistreatment must be serious and repetitive, threatening basic human rights in a fundamental way (Chan; Sagharichi). Discrimination may amount to persecution, but the mere fact of being Roma in Hungary does not establish more than a mere possibility of persecution (Balogh 2016 FC 426; Csonka; Ahmad); the claimant must link general country conditions to their specific circumstances.
application: The panel accepted that Roma face pervasive discrimination in Hungary but found the country evidence does not establish that all Roma, or Roma as a group, are persecuted. The claimants' personal experiences — sub-par housing, under-employment linked largely to limited education, and school discrimination — affected quality of life rather than fundamental rights. There was no evidence they were denied healthcare or social services, and no proof the children received substandard education. The cumulative treatment did not cross the threshold from discrimination to persecution.
conclusion: The claimants did not face a serious possibility of persecution; the mistreatment amounted to discrimination and harassment, not persecution.

issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in Hungary?
facts: The claimants recounted police failures: no report after the 2006 beating, refusal to investigate the hospital assault on their son, and the 2011 Molotov-cocktail attack on the Roma quarter of Miskolc. The father was told he could report an attack at the hospital but did not do so.
rule: A claimant must rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect (Ward; Flores Carrillo; Villafranca). Protection need not be perfect, only adequate at the operational level; the burden is proportional to the level of democracy (Kadenko; Hinzman). Local failures do not establish national inadequacy unless part of a broader pattern (Zhuravlvev; Racz 2013 FC 702; Mudrak 2015 FC 188).
application: The panel found Hungary a functioning EU democracy with police, the Independent Police Complaints Board, the Equal Treatment Authority, the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights and Roma-specific bodies such as the Roma Affairs Council. The Curia's Gyöngyöspata ruling showed police being held accountable for discrimination. Isolated police failures, including the 2011 attack, and the claimants' own failure to pursue available complaint mechanisms, did not demonstrate operational inadequacy. Credibility concerns (the absent hospital reports) further undermined the claims.
conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection; adequate protection is available to them in Hungary at the operational level.

issue: Did the publicity around their son's death in Canada establish a sur place claim?
facts: After the family reached Canada, their son was killed in a traffic accident; the story was reported in a Hungarian outlet and reproduced on a far-right racist website, eliciting racist online comments identifying the family as refugee claimants. The interpreter translated only selected, self-described 'typical' comments.
rule: A sur place claim requires sufficient persuasive evidence that events arising after departure create a forward-looking risk of persecution on return.
application: The panel found the comments genuinely racist but noted the translation was a selective summary chosen by the claimants' own interpreter, and that the story appeared briefly online years earlier. The principal claimant could not explain how racists would learn of and connect the family to the old story on return, and there were no recent posts. The evidence was insufficient to establish a residual, forward-looking risk.
conclusion: The claimants were not sur place refugees; the sur place element was not made out.

issue: Was the RPD's conclusion that the applicant did not have a well-founded fear of persecution from the Israeli Intelligence Services reasonable?
facts: Salim, an Arab Muslim Israeli citizen and licensed pilot, claimed to fear the Israeli Intelligence Services because his profession made him a perceived security threat. His only encounter was an intense but non-detaining airport interrogation in October 2007, and his brother had earlier been questioned. FOSS notes from a January 2007 entry to Canada showed he had denied any problems in Israel and had discussed claiming refugee status before the alleged persecutory events.
rule: Section 96 IRPA (giving effect to the Refugee Convention) requires an objective basis for a subjective fear (Rajudeen v Canada). Findings of fact and credibility are reviewed on the reasonableness standard (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9), with judicial restraint (Southam Inc).
application: The member found the single airport interrogation was reasonable given stringent Israeli security screening and did not amount to persecution or a violation of freedom of movement. The FOSS notes undermined his credibility because he had contemplated a refugee claim before the alleged persecutory events, negating a genuine subjective fear. The Court found this determination well within the reasonable range of outcomes.
conclusion: The RPD's rejection of this branch of the claim was reasonable and not to be disturbed.

issue: Did the RPD err in law on cumulative grounds of persecution and prospective risk, and was its finding that discrimination did not cumulatively amount to persecution reasonable?
facts: Salim relied on lifelong discrimination against Arab Muslims in Israel—inability to train as a pilot in Israel, employment barriers tied to non-performance of military service, racial profiling in education, employment and housing—and argued these cumulatively amounted to persecution. Country reports documented institutional and societal discrimination against Arab citizens.
rule: Where evidence shows a series of discriminatory acts, the cumulative effect must be considered; failing to do so is an error of law (Canada (MCI) v Munderere, 2008 FCA 84). The persecution/discrimination line is a mixed question of fact and law reviewed for reasonableness (Sagharichi); Hathaway's hierarchy of rights and the UNHCR Handbook (paras 54–55) inform the analysis.
application: The member expressly addressed the cumulative doctrine and conducted a forward-looking analysis. She found Salim had completed high school with excellent marks, worked as a lead technician, enjoyed relative economic prosperity and freedom of movement, and lived in a democracy that generally respected human rights. While acknowledging genuine discrimination (including racial profiling and airline discrimination), she reasonably concluded there was no serious restriction on his right to earn a livelihood and that the cumulative effect did not rise to persecution. The Court found the member did not take the US DOS Report or country conditions out of context.
conclusion: No reviewable error; the RPD's conclusion was reasonable. Application for judicial review dismissed with no question certified.

issue: Was the RPD's finding that the Roma respondents had rebutted the presumption of adequate state protection in Hungary reasonable?
facts: The respondents, a Roma family from Gyöngyöspata, Hungary, claimed refugee protection under s. 96 IRPA based on years of persecution, threats, attacks and discrimination, culminating in the March 2011 far-right occupation of their town, from which some 280 Roma women and children were evacuated. The RPD accepted their credibility, canvassed extensive documentary evidence of anti-Roma persecution and police failure, and concluded they had rebutted the presumption of state protection. The Minister sought judicial review.
rule: State protection findings are reviewed on the reasonableness standard (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9; Carrillo v Canada (MCI), 2008 FCA 94). Claimants must show inadequate state protection on a balance of probabilities, and the burden is proportional to the level of democracy (Canada (AG) v Ward, [1993] 2 SCR 689). Adequacy of state protection must be assessed at the operational level — 'Actions, not good intentions, prove that protection from persecution is available' (Orgona; Hercegi v Canada (MCI), 2012 FC 250); mere willingness to address the situation cannot be equated to adequate protection (Bors, Balogh).
application: Although the RPD used the word 'somewhat' loosely, the Court found it conducted a genuine, balanced state protection analysis. The RPD recognized the heavy burden on claimants and Hungary's democratic status, acknowledged institutional and operational protection mechanisms and government progress, but reasonably found that preliminary investigative measures had not translated into meaningful investigations, prosecutions or convictions, and that a climate of impunity prevailed. The documentary evidence about Gyöngyöspata and police ineffectiveness supported the finding. The Court owed deference to this nuanced weighing of the evidence.
conclusion: The RPD's finding was reasonable and fell within the range of acceptable outcomes; the Court would not intervene.

issue: Did the RPD improperly shift the onus of proving state protection to itself or apply a lower standard of proof?
facts: The Minister argued the RPD reversed the onus and applied a lower standard, pointing to loose language such as the claimants having 'somewhat' rebutted the presumption.
rule: The claimant bears the burden of rebutting the presumption of adequate state protection on a balance of probabilities (Carrillo, paras 18, 25), a burden proportional to the state's level of democracy (Ward; Hinzman; Kadenko).
application: The Court held that despite the careless use of 'somewhat', the RPD's reasons demonstrated it was mindful of the correct legal test, recognized the onerous burden on claimants, and applied it. The RPD stated the key requirements of the state protection test, 'a little loosely, but it did address it'.
conclusion: The RPD did not improperly shift the onus or apply a lower standard; this ground failed.

issue: Did the RPD fail to adequately analyse documentary evidence contradicting its state protection findings?
facts: The Minister contended the RPD's assessment was one-sided and ignored evidence of progress made by Hungary in protecting the Roma.
rule: The duty to consider and explain contrary evidence increases with its relevance to the disputed facts (Cepeda-Gutierrez v Canada (MCI), [1998] FCJ 1425). The RPD, as trier of fact, weighs competing country-condition evidence (Molnar).
application: The Court found the RPD explicitly considered evidence of Hungarian government progress, existing institutional and operational mechanisms, the functioning democracy, independent judiciary and security forces, while also weighing evidence that such measures were not effective at the operational level. This reflected a balanced, nuanced weighing of the evidence as a whole rather than a one-sided assessment.
conclusion: The RPD adequately analysed the contrary evidence; the Minister's argument was rejected.

issue: Should the appellants' proposed new evidence be admitted under s. 110(4) of the IRPA and the Singh/Raza factors?
facts: The Roma appellants from Poland submitted a series of news articles on appeal. Some articles post-dated the RPD decision (concerning judicial control, surveillance of opposition figures, populist leaders, and Polish sovereignty); others pre-dated the RPD decision and had been reasonably available before it. The appellants argued the pre-dating articles could not have been submitted earlier because the documentary deadline had passed and the matter was adjourned awaiting a decision.
rule: Subsection 110(4) IRPA permits new evidence only if it arose after the RPD decision, was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been expected to be presented; admissible evidence must also be new, credible and relevant per Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Singh, 2016 FCA 96 and Raza v. Canada, 2007 FCA 385. RPD Rule 43 permits post-hearing document applications before a decision issues.
application: The post-dating articles met the statutory timing requirement but failed the relevance factor because none addressed the treatment of Roma or of Roma by Polish police. The pre-dating articles failed the statutory requirement because Rule 43 would have allowed the appellants to apply to submit them before the RPD decided, so they were reasonably available; and in any event they too failed the relevance factor.
conclusion: None of the proposed new evidence was accepted.

issue: Did the RPD err in its state protection analysis such that the appellants rebutted the presumption of adequate state protection in Poland?
facts: The appellants, Roma common-law partners from Poland, feared persecution. Neither had ever approached the Polish police about the treatment they or their daughter faced, explaining that it would make no difference or they would be called names. They did not allege the police were agents of persecution. The country evidence contained some references to police misconduct and mistreatment of Roma.
rule: There is a presumption of adequate state protection absent a complete breakdown of state apparatus; the more democratic the state, the more a claimant must do to exhaust available avenues, and the claimant bears the burden of rebutting the presumption with clear and convincing evidence on a balance of probabilities (Ruszo v. Canada, 2013 FC 1004; Poczkodi v. Canada, 2017 FC 956). State protection need not be perfect and local failures alone are insufficient. The RAD assesses correctness on independent review (Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93).
application: The RPD erred by treating Poland as a functioning democracy imposing a 'high' burden, since democracy level is not the sole factor and there was evidence of police misconduct; the panel found the correct burden was 'medium'. However, the appellants still failed to meet it: they made no reasonable effort to seek protection, having never approached the police, and the cases relied on (Kozlowski, Dawidowicz, and a 2019 RAD decision) were distinguishable because those claimants had alleged police as agents of persecution or had actually complained. The independent review of the NDP showed only local failures insufficient to rebut the presumption.
conclusion: The appellants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence; the RPD's determinative finding was upheld.

issue: Should the defendants' Response to Civil Claim (RtCC) be struck in its entirety under Rule 9-5?
facts: Shoppers, a franchisor, sued its former franchisee (Mr. Mang and PMPL) for breach of the franchise agreement and misappropriation of funds. The defendants filed a RtCC that admitted some allegations, denied others, and pleaded the defendants' own version of the facts including reliance on Shoppers' duty of good faith under the Franchises Act. Shoppers sought to strike the whole RtCC as disclosing no reasonable defence and as vexatious, embarrassing and scandalous.
rule: Supreme Court Civil Rules R. 9-5(1) permits striking a pleading that discloses no reasonable defence, is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, may prejudice or embarrass a fair trial, or is an abuse of process. Under R. 9-5(1)(a) a pleading discloses no reasonable defence only where the law affords it no reasonable prospect of success (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Ltd., 2011 SCC 42 at para. 17); no evidence is admissible on that branch. A pleading should be struck only where it is plain and obvious the attack is well founded, and the court must consider the pleading as it is and as it could be with appropriate amendments.
application: The court found the RtCC properly addressed each fact in the notice of civil claim as required by R. 3-3(2)(a), admitting, denying or stating facts were outside knowledge, and then set out the defendants' version of facts. Key paragraphs (e.g. para. 1 admitting parties/agreements while asserting an expectation of good faith paralleling ss. 3(1) and (3) of the Franchises Act, and paras. 6-7 denying the equity shortfall and misallocated-expense allegations) advanced arguable defences. It was therefore not plain and obvious the whole defence lacked merit.
conclusion: The application to strike the RtCC in its entirety was refused; read generously the pleading outlined a defence with legal merit.

issue: Which portions of the RtCC should be struck as scandalous, collateral, or lacking a cogent legal basis?
facts: Shoppers alternatively targeted numerous paragraphs. Some pleaded a malign culture among franchisees, cruel gossip, favouritism, alleged illegal conduct by other Associates, bullying and defamatory comments with restraining orders, the termination of an officer's employment, and heads of legal argument including 'corporate social responsibility', breach of fiduciary duty, and workplace bullying/harassment.
rule: Under R. 9-5(1)(b) a pleading is unnecessary or scandalous if it pleads facts legally irrelevant to the substance of the dispute, threatening collateral trouble and expense, and may be embarrassing under R. 9-5(1)(c). Pleadings must state material facts, not evidence (R. 3-7(1)). A pleading is struck only where it is plain and obvious the attack succeeds.
application: The court held the arguable good-faith/bad-faith defence (assurances of a second store withdrawn, threats of immediate termination contrary to past practice, estoppel) should stand. But paragraphs 6, 9, 10 and 12 of Division 2 (malign culture, favouritism, bullying, defamatory conduct, restraining orders) and paragraphs 1 and 2 of Division 3 were collateral and scandalous, and para. 12 improperly pleaded evidence; para. 16 (officer's termination) was not a material fact. Of the legal-basis heads, items 2 (corporate social responsibility), 3 (fiduciary duty—no factual foundation), and 7 (workplace bullying/harassment) were not cogent defences, while item 4 (duty of good faith under the Franchises Act and common law) was legally cogent and remained.
conclusion: Paragraphs 6, 9, 10 and 12 of Division 2, paragraphs 1 and 2 of Division 3 of Part 1, and paragraphs 2, 3 and 7 of Part 3 were struck; the balance of the RtCC was allowed to stand.

issue: Should the Counterclaim be struck for failing to state a reasonable cause of action, and on what terms may it be amended?
facts: The Counterclaim pleaded only six factual paragraphs, without incorporating the affirmative facts in the RtCC. It advanced a 'breach of promise' claim for a second franchise ($720,000), wrongful termination based on absence of notice of default, punitive damages for bad faith and 'poor corporate social responsibility', and referenced Shoppers' obligation to provide an accounting within 90 days of termination.
rule: R. 9-5(1)(a): a pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action where the law affords no reasonable prospect of success (Imperial Tobacco). A breach of contract claim requires material facts establishing a contract. The court may consider documents incorporated by reference in the pleading (e.g., the Associate Agreement).
application: The breach-of-promise claim was in substance a breach of contract claim, but no material facts established a contract to award a second franchise, so it was bound to fail. The wrongful-termination claim misstated Article 13.00 of the Associate Agreement, which did not require notice of default (s. 13.01/s. 4.01(b) permitting termination without cause on 60 days notice), so it too was bound to fail. Punitive damages for 'poor corporate social responsibility' pleaded no material facts and invoked a cause of action unknown to law. Only the accounting claim (referable to s. 4.02(g) of the Agreement) had potential merit, and Shoppers' counsel accepted a counterclaim seeking an accounting and damages for failure to provide one.
conclusion: The Counterclaim was struck for failing to state a reasonable cause of action, with leave to file an amended Counterclaim claiming an accounting and damages for failure to account; further claims require Shoppers' consent or leave of the court. Shoppers was substantially successful and awarded costs, but not in any event of the cause.

issue: Was the claimant credible in alleging she was a Christian being pursued by the PSB?
facts: The claimant, a Chinese citizen from Shanghai, claimed she attended an underground house church, that the PSB raided it and arrested its members, and that the PSB came to her family home 12–13 times seeking her. She provided no summons, warrant, arrest or sentencing documents, or corroborating evidence, and her family remained safe in China. She had also extended her visitor visa repeatedly, enrolled in college contrary to visa terms, and unsuccessfully sought a work permit before claiming refugee protection.
rule: Testimony under oath is presumed truthful unless there are reasons to doubt it (Maldonado principle referenced implicitly). Credibility is assessed on a balance of probabilities; evidence must be probably true, not merely possibly true (Orelien v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1992] 1 F.C. 592 (C.A.)). The RPD may make reasonable findings based on implausibility, common sense and rationality (Aguebor; Alizadeh; Shahamati), and testimony must harmonize with the preponderance of probabilities (Faryna v. Chorny, [1952] 2 D.L.R. 354 (B.C.C.A.)).
application: The panel found the claimant engaged in a series of dubious actions to remain in Canada, undermining her credibility. She provided no supporting documentation (no summons/warrant, no arrest records, no son's transcripts) despite the alleged repeated PSB visits, and country documentation showed a summons would ordinarily be issued in such circumstances. Her account of the PSB's conduct ran counter to documentary evidence about the PSB's methods. The cumulative negative inferences led the panel to disbelieve her allegation of PSB pursuit, though it accepted she is a practising Christian in Canada.
conclusion: The panel found, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was not credible regarding pursuit by the PSB and that her house church was never raided.

issue: Would the claimant face a serious possibility of persecution as a small house-church Christian if returned to Shanghai?
facts: The claimant is from Shanghai, where she lived and worked all her life, and described a small (about 12-member) house church. Documentary evidence indicated authorities in Shanghai tolerate small unregistered house churches (generally under 25 members), with reported incidents in Shanghai limited to very large congregations such as the 1,200-member Wanbang Church.
rule: Under ss. 96 and 97(1) IRPA the claimant must establish a serious possibility of persecution or a personal risk. Objective fear depends on the laws and the manner in which they are applied, and enforcement varies locally (Chan v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1995] 3 S.C.R. 593, citing UNHCR Handbook para. 43; Valentin v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1991] 3 F.C. 390 (C.A.)). Assessment of documentary evidence guided by Yu v. M.C.I., 2010 FC 310 and Li v. M.C.I., 2010 FC 205.
application: The panel reviewed extensive country-condition evidence and found no persuasive, recent reports of arrests or persecution of members of small house churches in Shanghai matching the claimant's profile. It found that if such persecution occurred it would be documented by the many monitoring organizations and consular presence in Shanghai. It concluded the claimant could worship in a congregation of her choosing in Shanghai without a serious possibility of persecution.
conclusion: The claimant failed to establish an objective serious possibility of persecution or personal risk; she is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

issue: Was the Minister's citizenship-revocation action an abuse of office or process because it formed part of Canada's War Crimes Program?
facts: The defendant argued that the Government's 1995 war-crimes strategy misused the revocation procedure to punish suspected war criminals and purge them from Canada on political grounds, pointing to the program's 'evidence of individual criminality' criterion.
rule: A statutory power must be exercised for the purpose Parliament intended (Roncarelli v. Duplessis; Prince George v. Payne). Canada's interest in not sheltering those who concealed wartime atrocities outweighs foreseeable harm (Canada v. Tobiass). Where multiple avenues are open, the Crown may choose among them (Katriuk).
application: Lemieux J. found the strategy was not restricted to WWII, the 'individual criminality' criterion related to criminal prosecution not revocation, abandonment of prosecution did not automatically trigger revocation, and it was the Minister, not the war-crimes unit, who decided to issue the notice. No reprehensible government conduct or improper purpose was shown.
conclusion: The defendant failed to establish abuse of office; the argument was rejected.

issue: Do the citizenship-revocation provisions violate the Bill of Rights or ss. 7, 12 and 15 of the Charter?
facts: The defendant contended the reference procedure gave no full hearing before an independent tribunal, breached fundamental justice, and discriminated against naturalized citizens, exposing him to cruel treatment given his precarious health.
rule: A reference under s. 18 involves only findings of fact, not decisions determining rights, and does not engage s. 7 (Luitjens; Fast). Stare decisis and finality of litigation bar re-litigation of decided issues (Fast; Danyluk). Section 15 analysis follows Law v. Canada.
application: The s. 7 and abuse arguments had already been dismissed by Nadon J., affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal, with leave refused by the Supreme Court; re-argument was barred. On s. 15, the proper comparison was between those who obtained citizenship by fraud and those who, like the defendant, did not; the defendant met none of the three Law inquiries. The Bill of Rights added nothing beyond the Charter.
conclusion: The constitutional and Bill of Rights challenges failed.

issue: Did the Citizenship Act, 1976 grandfather the defendant's citizenship against revocation?
facts: The defendant relied on s. 3(d) (deemed citizen), s. 10(1) ('citizenship under this Act'), and the transitional/repeal provisions ss. 35-36 to argue his 1955 citizenship was immunized.
rule: Substantive rights on acquisition of citizenship are governed by the law in force when citizenship was granted (Oberlander); s. 44 of the Interpretation Act requires the procedure of the new enactment to be followed for matters arising before repeal.
application: The 1946 Act (s. 19) governed the substantive right and permitted loss for fraud; the 1976 Act supplied only the procedure. Section 3's deemed-citizen status is expressly 'subject to' the Act's revocation provisions, so it created no irrevocable status.
conclusion: No grandfathered immunity existed; the revocation procedure applied.

issue: Was the action prescribed or barred by laches?
facts: The defendant argued the Minister knew of the allegations by July 1993 yet did not sue until February 2000, and that record destruction and his ill health made defence impossible.
rule: A cause of action, if any, arises only when the Minister reasonably discovers the fraudulent acquisition; the defendant bears the burden of proving prescription (per Létourneau J.A.'s obiter in the 2002 FCA decision). Laches is an equitable doctrine inapplicable to a statutory revocation process.
application: The defendant, who was not located in Canada until 1995, offered no evidence to establish a start date for prescription and failed to discharge his burden. The revocation reference is not an equitable proceeding, and the delay issue had already been addressed on the earlier motions.
conclusion: Neither prescription nor laches barred the action.

issue: Must the fraudulent means relate to permanent-residence acquisition, or does concealment at temporary-entry selection suffice?
facts: The defendant argued the alleged misrepresentations concerned his 1946 temporary admission under P.C. 3112, not his 1950 permanent residence, so they were irrelevant to citizenship.
rule: Subsection 10(1) permits revocation whenever citizenship was acquired by fraud or fraudulent means and is not limited by the s. 10(2) presumption to the permanent-residence stage (Canada v. Obodzinsky, 2002 FCA 518).
application: Following the Federal Court of Appeal, Lemieux J. held that fraudulent means at the selection stage in Italy that gave the defendant a port of entry, and hence permanent residence and citizenship, fell within s. 10(1). The concealment in Italy was the operative fraud in the causal chain.
conclusion: Concealment at the temporary-entry selection stage was sufficient.

issue: Did the defendant obtain Canadian citizenship by knowingly concealing material circumstances about his wartime collaboration?
facts: The Minister proved the defendant voluntarily served in the Mir-district auxiliary police (Schutzmannschaft) and the Jagdzug, formations complicit in atrocities against Jewish and other civilians in Byelorussia, and later in the Waffen SS, before deserting to the Resistance and the Polish Second Corps; his Polish military notebook recorded only brief German-Army service, and RCMP screening under P.C. 3112 excluded German collaborators.
rule: The Minister bears the burden on the balance of probabilities (Bogutin). Good character and lawful admission for permanent residence were preconditions to citizenship under the 1946 Act; concealment of collaboration and lack of good character warrant revocation (Baumgartner).
application: On the credible commission and expert evidence, the court found the defendant was a volunteer collaborator and accomplice in atrocities (though not proven to have personally killed). Collaboration was a security ground of exclusion under P.C. 3112; the RCMP would have questioned him and, had his past been disclosed, refused him. His concealment led to unlawful participation in the program, permanent residence, Canadian domicile, and citizenship, and meant he was not a person of good character.
conclusion: The court concluded the defendant acquired Canadian citizenship by knowingly concealing material circumstances.

issue: Should Mr. Stukanov be declared a vexatious litigant under s. 40 of the Federal Courts Act and have his access to the Court regulated?
facts: Mr. Stukanov, a self-represented inventor who self-identifies as of mixed Russian and Jewish identity, had pursued numerous unsuccessful judicial reviews of Canadian Human Rights Commission decisions, multiple patent appeals from the Commissioner of Patents, appeals to the Federal Court of Appeal, a dismissed leave application to the Supreme Court, and an Ontario Divisional Court proceeding. Across all of these he relied on the same 'rigorous mathematical proofs' to allege discrimination based on ethnicity, citizenship and country of origin, and repeatedly alleged bias when decision-makers ruled against him.
rule: Section 40 of the Federal Courts Act permits an order regulating access where a person 'has persistently instituted vexatious proceedings or has conducted a proceeding in a vexatious manner'. The courts have identified indicia of vexatiousness (Canada v. Olumide, 2017 FCA 42; Simon, 2022 FC 1135; Fabrikant, 2019 FCA 198), including re-litigating settled issues, unsuccessfully appealing as a matter of course, and unfounded allegations of bias. Any single indicium may suffice (Hicks, 2022 FC 978 at para 33). Intent is not determinative (Olumide at para 20), and an order regulates rather than bars access (Fabrikant at para 36).
application: The Court reviewed Mr. Stukanov's litigation history and found he repeatedly advanced the same discredited mathematical proofs, which every level of court had unanimously rejected as flawed and based on false premises, and re-litigated the same theory of discrimination (correlation confused with causation). He habitually alleged bias and made intemperate accusations (e.g., obstruction of justice, 'criminal like behaviour') when he lost. The three Fabrikant questions were all answered affirmatively: additional regulation was necessary, consistent with s. 40's purpose, and justified by his un-governability and harmfulness to the court system and to the AGC.
conclusion: Mr. Stukanov was declared a vexatious litigant; he may not commence or continue any proceeding in the Federal Court without leave, ongoing proceedings were stayed, and costs of $500 were awarded against him.

issue: Do appeals and judicial review applications arising from administrative decisions constitute 'proceedings' under s. 40, given Mr. Stukanov's argument that he did not initiate them himself?
facts: Mr. Stukanov argued he could not be vexatious because he had not commenced any proceeding on his own initiative; his appeals and judicial reviews merely responded to administrative decisions rejecting his patents and complaints 'without providing a single valid reason'.
rule: Section 40 uses the word 'proceedings'. Jurisprudence has granted s. 40 orders in relation to judicial reviews and appeals (Figueroa v. Canada (AG), 2019 FC 505 at para 12; Coady v. Canada (AG), 2020 FCA 154 at para 25), and courts may look broadly at a litigant's behaviour (Canada Post Corp v. Varma; Hicks).
application: The Court held the wording of s. 40 is self-evidently broad: a judicial review application, an appeal from a judicial decision, and an appeal from an administrative decision-maker are all 'proceedings'. The legislature's choice of 'proceedings' plainly captures the applications and appeals Mr. Stukanov brought, and this is confirmed by case law. His belief that he was compelled to litigate did not remove his conduct from s. 40's scope.
conclusion: His appeals and judicial reviews qualified as proceedings under s. 40, so his argument was rejected.

issue: Was the claimants' evidence of personal persecution credible given the inconsistencies, omissions and lack of corroboration?
facts: The Roma claimants from Hungary alleged decades of beatings, arson attacks, police abuse and a loss of pregnancy from a 1995 beating. Their oral testimony conflicted with their original narrative (Sept 2010), original hearing testimony (May 2011) and amended narrative (Feb 2013). They offered two blanket explanations: the principal claimant's trauma/psychological "shut down" and errors made in preparing the original narrative with prior Hungarian-speaking counsel. Little supporting documentary evidence was produced.
rule: Sworn testimony is presumed true unless there is valid reason to doubt it (Maldonado v.
