application: The Court held there was no legal requirement to route the matter to the Federal Court where the parties agreed the NSP information would not be disclosed; an assertion of privilege can suffice, as with confidential informant privilege. Mr. Jaser made an informed tactical choice, could have gone to the Federal Court at any time, and consented to the procedure, so no procedural unfairness, no s. 650 breach, and no surprise from step-six use of the summaries arose. On the merits, the trial judge correctly stated the s. 21 CSIS Act standard and reasonably concluded paras. 33-38 alone could support the warrant at step five.
conclusion: No legal or procedural error; the trial judge's step-five Garofoli determination is owed deference. Ground dismissed.

issue: Did the trial judge err in refusing to sever Mr. Jaser's trial from his co-accused Mr. Esseghaier?
facts: Mr. Esseghaier was self-represented, refused to recognize Canadian law, and behaved disruptively, including praying on the courtroom floor during jury selection. Mr. Jaser, whose defence was that he was a fraudster and not a genuine terrorist, feared the jury would view both men as radical jihadists. He brought two severance/mistrial applications, both dismissed.
rule: Section 591(3) Criminal Code permits severance where the interests of justice require; there is a strong presumption in favour of joint trials for co-conspirators, and severance is exceptional, granted only where a joint trial works an injustice (R. v. Chow, R. v. Crawford, R. v. Savoury). A severance ruling is discretionary and reviewed for whether the judge acted unjudicially or the ruling produced an injustice (R. v. Litchfield; R. v. Last).
application: The Court found the trial judge applied the correct factors, gave tailored (not boilerplate) reasons, reasonably predicted Mr. Esseghaier would behave better before a jury, and deployed effective remedies for the jury-selection incident (discharging a juror, a strong caution, an added challenge-for-cause question, prayer accommodation). Esseghaier's later compliance and the jury's split verdicts showed the instructions to consider each accused separately worked. No injustice resulted.
conclusion: Both severance rulings were reasonable and error-free; no injustice. Ground dismissed.

issue: Did the trial judge misdirect the jury on conspiracy, including the feigned-agreement defence, the Carter instruction, and the need for identical verdicts?
facts: Mr. Jaser was convicted of conspiracy to commit murder (count two) but the jury could not agree on count one (train plot); Esseghaier was convicted on both. Jaser argued the instructions confused 'agreement' and 'intention', wove the Carter co-conspirator hearsay instruction into the elements, failed to give an 'all or nothing' instruction, and produced inconsistent verdicts.
rule: Jury charges are reviewed functionally and as a whole (R. v. Daley; R. v. Abdullahi). Conspiracy requires a true consensus to bring about an unlawful object with intent to carry it out; agreement and intention are intertwined (The Queen v. O'Brien; United States v. Dynar). The Carter three-step co-conspirator exception applies even to two-person conspiracies (R. v. Barrow; Bogiatzis; Puddicombe). Verdicts are inconsistent only if irreconcilable on any rational basis (R. v. R.V.).
application: The charge repeatedly told the jury Mr. Jaser must be acquitted if he only feigned agreement and that both agreement and genuine intention were required; the recharge made this even clearer. Bogiatzis was distinguishable because the charged conspiracy and the Carter conspiracy were identical. An 'all or nothing' instruction would have been wrong because different bodies of evidence could support different membership findings. The failure to reach a verdict on count one for Jaser reflected doubt about his probable membership, not acceptance of the feigned-agreement defence, and was reconcilable with Esseghaier's conviction.
conclusion: The instructions were adequate and legally correct; the verdicts were not inconsistent. Ground dismissed.

issue: Did the trial judge's out-of-court 'hero' comment about the undercover agent create a reasonable apprehension of bias?
facts: After the undercover FBI agent 'Tamer El Noury' finished testifying, the trial judge told another agent in a private hallway that El Noury was a 'hero' in both countries and to 'take care of him.' This surfaced years later in El Noury's memoir. Fresh evidence (an agreed statement of facts) was admitted.
rule: Fresh evidence going to trial fairness is governed not by Palmer but by the interests of justice (s. 683 Criminal Code; R. v. Cowan). The test for reasonable apprehension of bias is whether a reasonable, informed person viewing the matter realistically would conclude the judge could not decide fairly; there is a strong presumption of impartiality requiring cogent rebutting evidence (Committee for Justice & Liberty; Yukon Francophone School Board; R. v. Richards). In jury trials, whether conduct occurred before the jury is significant (R. v. Murray).
application: The comment was never heard by the jury, which was the trier of fact; the credibility of El Noury was not in issue and the case rested on the accused's own recorded words. 'Hero' has broad colloquial meaning and reflected the agent's exposure to danger, consistent with earlier in-court remarks to which no one objected. The record disclosed no hint of negativity toward Mr. Jaser, and adverse rulings do not evidence bias.
conclusion: Though the comment should not have been made, it does not meet the high threshold; no reasonable apprehension of bias. Ground dismissed.

issue: Did the trial judge err in finding the co-accused fit post-verdict and in declining to order a mistrial for both accused?
facts: After the verdicts, a psychiatric assessment (Dr. Ramshaw) opined Esseghaier was likely unfit; a second assessment (Dr. Klassen) found him fit. The trial judge accepted the fitness opinion and sentenced. Jaser argued that a finding of unfitness would have required a mistrial for both men.
rule: Fitness under s. 2 Criminal Code applies only before a verdict; the touchstone is a reality-based understanding enabling meaningful presence and participation (R. v. Bharwani). Post-verdict, a mistrial may be declared only in highly restricted circumstances (R. v. Lessard; R. v. Henderson; R. v. Burke).
application: The trial judge did not misapprehend the fitness test; he found Esseghaier had a reality-based understanding but subordinated it to his religious ideology, an autonomy choice protected by s. 7. It was open to prefer Dr. Klassen's opinion. Even assuming Esseghaier was unfit post-verdict, at most his sentencing would be delayed; Burke did not support a mistrial, and nothing suggested Esseghaier was unfit during trial or not criminally responsible, so Mr. Jaser had no claim to a mistrial.
conclusion: No error in the fitness finding; no basis for a mistrial for Mr. Jaser. Ground dismissed.

issue: Did the life sentence reflect an error in principle by failing to account for the undercover agent's role in the conspiracy?
facts: The trial judge imposed life imprisonment on count two (conspiracy to commit murder for a terrorist group) with the presumptive ten-year parole ineligibility. Mr. Jaser argued El Noury's active encouragement mitigated his moral culpability.
rule: Police conduct rationally connected to moral culpability must be considered in sentencing; terrorism offences warrant lengthy sentences up to life imprisonment (R. v. Khawaja; R. v. Khalid; R. v. Hersi). Sentencing findings of fact attract deference.
application: The trial judge found Jaser and Esseghaier had already formed their murderous agreement by September 9, 2012, before El Noury had any knowledge of or role in it; El Noury merely encountered and encouraged a pre-existing scheme. This finding was supported by the record and consistent with the jury's verdicts, so El Noury's involvement could not mitigate Jaser's culpability for entering the agreement.
conclusion: No error in principle; the life sentence stands. Leave to appeal sentence granted, sentence appeal dismissed.

issue: Should the plaintiffs' prolix amended notice of civil claim be struck or the action dismissed under R. 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules?
facts: The action, commenced October 2019, arose from a neighbourly dispute between the Beslers and the operators of the adjacent 'What the Fungus' mushroom business. An amended notice of civil claim filed November 2021 spanned 68 pages, with a 33-page response to demand for particulars, totalling nearly 100 pages. The pleadings alleged negligence (bylaw/zoning violations) and defamation, but failed to clearly plead the core elements of defamation, and merely referenced harassment and conspiracy without seeking relief. The defendants applied to strike the pleadings and dismiss the action.
rule: R. 3-1(2)(a) requires a concise statement of material facts. R. 9-5(1) permits striking pleadings that (a) disclose no reasonable claim, (b) are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, (c) may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial, or (d) are an abuse of process. R. 3-7(21) imposes precise particulars requirements for libel/slander. Under Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, the court assumes the pleaded facts can be proven and asks whether it is plain and obvious the claim is certain to fail; a plaintiff should not be driven from the judgment seat. Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61 sets out defamation elements; E.B. v. British Columbia, 2021 BCCA 47 and Gosal v. Gill, 2018 BCSC 2132 address pleading particulars; Lam v. Macdonald, 2018 BCSC 281 holds the burden is very high and striking is reserved for the clearest cases.
application: The court found the pleadings prolix and deficient, making them challenging for a trier of fact and failing to clearly set out the elements of defamation as required by R. 3-7(21). Harassment and conspiracy were merely part of the factual narrative with no relief sought, so those torts were not actually pled. However, negligence and defamation are not novel causes of action, and material facts supporting those torts could be gleaned from the existing pleadings. Applying Hunt v. Carey and Lam, it was not plain and obvious the claims were certain to fail, and this was not a 'clearest of cases' situation warranting striking.
conclusion: The application to strike and dismiss was refused; the pleadings could not stand as drafted but were curable by amendment.

issue: Should the plaintiffs be granted a further opportunity to amend their pleadings rather than have them struck?
facts: The plaintiffs, though self-represented, were sophisticated litigants who effectively conceded the pleadings needed amending. They had earlier been ordered to amend by Gomery J. and filed the amended claim late (November 2021 instead of June 2021). No draft amended pleading was presented at the strike hearing.
rule: A fundamental consideration under R. 9-5(1)(a) is whether the pleading can be preserved by amendment (International Taoist Church of Canada, 2011 BCCA 149). The discretion to permit amendment considers the degree of deficiency, ease of correction, apparent merit, and prejudice (Jones v. Bank of Nova Scotia, 2018 BCCA 381). Pleadings should be read generously for self-represented litigants (Lam v. Macdonald), though the court will not give legal advice or grant indulgences that interfere with another party's right to know the case to be met (Rodrigues v. Tribe, 2016 BCSC 1233).
application: Exercising its discretion, the court concluded the deficiencies were curable and the plaintiffs should have one more opportunity. It ordered a fresh clean further amended notice of civil claim complying with the Rules (including libel/slander rules) by March 3, 2023, with the existing amended claim attached as Appendix A so the trier of fact understands the pleading history without deciphering a 150-page blacklined document. The matter is not res judicata, and defendants may reapply to strike if the fresh pleading still fails to comply.
conclusion: The plaintiffs were granted leave to file a fresh further amended notice of civil claim by March 3, 2023, with defendants at liberty to reapply.

issue: What costs order is appropriate given that the application to strike was dismissed but the plaintiffs conceded amendment was needed?
facts: The defendants' application was dismissed, but the plaintiffs effectively conceded the pleadings required amending. A request or application to amend could have been brought in advance of the strike application, filed some nine months before the hearing.
rule: Costs are awardable at the discretion of the presiding justice. Special costs or Scale C were sought by the applicant defendants.
application: Although the application was dismissed, the court found the plaintiffs' failure to seek amendment earlier was a concern warranting a costs award to the defendants. Costs were assessed on the basis of ordinary difficulty for a one-day proceeding, payable in any event of the cause but not forthwith. Special costs and Scale C were not granted.
conclusion: The application defendants were awarded their costs of the application in any event of the cause, on the ordinary scale, not payable forthwith.

issue: Where a Quebec statute is challenged under both the Quebec Charter and the Canadian Charter, which instrument should be analyzed first?
facts: Chaoulli, a physician, and Zeliotis, a patient affected by waiting lists, challenged s. 15 of the Health Insurance Act and s. 11 of the Hospital Insurance Act under both the Quebec Charter and the Canadian Charter; the lower courts had considered only the Canadian Charter.
rule: Per Deschamps J., where the provisions of the two charters may produce cumulative effects but are not identical, a court should look first to the rules that apply specifically in Quebec, drawing on Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration and the quasi-constitutional, broader purpose of the Quebec Charter (s. 1 contains no reference to the principles of fundamental justice, avoiding the dual burden imposed by s. 7).
application: Because s. 1 of the Quebec Charter lacks any reference to the principles of fundamental justice, its scope is potentially broader and it imposes no dual burden on the claimant; ruling on the Quebec Charter enhances an instrument specific to Quebec and is sufficient to dispose of the appeal without reaching the Canadian Charter.
conclusion: The case is decided under the Quebec Charter; the plurality (McLachlin C.J., Major and Bastarache JJ.) additionally found a s. 7 Canadian Charter violation, while the dissent held neither charter was breached.

issue: Does the prohibition on private health insurance infringe the right to life and to personal inviolability?
facts: Section 15 HEIA and s. 11 HOIA bar Quebec residents from taking out private insurance for services available under the public plan, effectively confining most residents to a public system with significant waiting times; expert evidence showed delays increase mortality risk (e.g., cardiovascular surgery) and cause pain and loss of quality of life (e.g., orthopaedic patients).
rule: Section 1 of the Quebec Charter guarantees the right to life and to personal inviolability, which per Quebec (Public Curator) v. Syndicat national des employés de l'hôpital St-Ferdinand extends beyond physical to psychological and moral inviolability; s. 7 of the Canadian Charter protects life, liberty and security, engaged by treatment delays causing physical and psychological suffering (R. v. Morgentaler; Rodriguez).
application: The trial judge's findings that waiting lists caused by the prohibition endanger life and cause serious physical and psychological suffering apply fully to the broader Quebec Charter right; access to a waiting list is not access to health care, and the out-of-province safety valve was found inadequate.
conclusion: The prohibition infringes the right to life and to personal inviolability under s. 1 of the Quebec Charter (and, per the plurality, s. 7 of the Canadian Charter).

issue: Is the infringement justified, or is the prohibition arbitrary and not minimally impairing?
facts: The Attorney General of Quebec argued the ban preserves the integrity of the public system; experts on both sides offered largely 'common sense' predictions, and evidence covered other Canadian provinces and OECD countries where private insurance is permitted without destroying public health care.
rule: Under s. 9.1 of the Quebec Charter (Ford v. Quebec) and the Oakes test, the government bears the onus of showing a pressing objective, rational connection, minimal impairment and proportionality; under s. 7 a limit is contrary to fundamental justice if arbitrary, i.e. bearing no real connection on the facts to the legislative goal (Rodriguez; Morgentaler).
application: Preserving the public plan is pressing and substantial and rationally connected to the ban, but the Attorney General failed to prove minimal impairment: the experience of other provinces and OECD countries showed a range of less drastic measures and no demonstrated link between the insurance ban and quality public care; the majority found the prohibition arbitrary. The dissent (Binnie, LeBel and Fish JJ.) found no principle of fundamental justice was breached, deferred to the trial judge's findings that a parallel private system would harm the public system, and held the ban justified under s. 9.1.
conclusion: The majority held the infringement is not justified; the prohibition is not minimally impairing (and, per the plurality, arbitrary and unsaved by s. 1). Appeal allowed.

issue: Which appeals were properly before the Court under section 79 of the IRPA?
facts: Mr. Mahjoub filed appeals from the reasonableness judgment (A-478-14) and from two interlocutory orders refusing permanent stays for abuse of process (A-479-14 and A-313-12, the latter concerning commingling of privileged documents). The Federal Court certified only one question, arising out of the reasonableness judgment.
rule: Section 79 of the IRPA strictly limits appeals: an appeal may only be brought from a 'determination' of reasonableness where the Federal Court certifies a serious question of general importance, and 'no appeal may be made from an interlocutory decision in the proceeding.' Once triggered by a certified question, the appeal encompasses the whole judgment and all issues affecting its validity (Baker; Pushpanathan; Harkat).
application: The two appeals from interlocutory stay orders concerned 'interlocutory decision[s] in the proceeding' and were barred by section 79, so they had to be quashed for want of jurisdiction. However, because the notice of appeal in A-478-14 placed in issue all decisions linked to the reasonableness judgment, the substance of the interlocutory issues was nonetheless properly before the Court within the certified-question appeal.
conclusion: The appeals in A-479-14 and A-313-12 were dismissed for want of jurisdiction, but all underlying issues were considered within the properly-constituted appeal in A-478-14.

issue: Was the security certificate reasonable?
facts: The Ministers certified Mr. Mahjoub, an Egyptian refugee, as inadmissible on security grounds. The Federal Court found reasonable grounds to believe he was a danger to Canada's security (s. 34(1)(d)) and a member of Al Jihad and the Vanguards of Conquest (s. 34(1)(f)), based largely on open-source and open-court evidence, including his top executive role on Osama Bin Laden's Sudanese farm used for terrorist training, his contacts with known terrorists in Canada, and numerous lies and omissions.
rule: Under section 78 IRPA the court must determine whether the certificate is reasonable. Section 33 provides that inadmissibility facts include those for which there are 'reasonable grounds to believe' they occurred — an objective basis of compelling and credible information, more than suspicion but less than balance of probabilities (Mugesera; Charkaoui I). Section 34 grounds are read disjunctively; formal membership is not required for s. 34(1)(f) (Kanagendren). Appellate review applies Housen standards (Harkat): correctness for law, palpable and overriding error for facts.
application: The Federal Court correctly identified the 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard and correctly interpreted 'membership' and 'danger.' Its factual findings were impeccably sourced in admissible open evidence and withstood the palpable and overriding error standard; the appellant's invitations to reweigh evidence were declined. Membership in even one terrorist organization (Al Jihad) sufficed to uphold the certificate.
conclusion: The Federal Court committed no reviewable error; the certificate was reasonable.

issue: Is the security certificate regime constitutional under section 7 of the Charter?
facts: Mr. Mahjoub challenged Division 9 of the IRPA and provisions of the CSIS Act, arguing closed proceedings, Special Advocates, evidentiary standards and detention provisions denied a fair hearing and violated sections 7, 8, 9 and 10 of the Charter.
rule: Charkaoui I struck the prior regime but the 2008 amendments (Special Advocates) were designed to cure the defects; Harkat confirmed the amended IRPA security certificate scheme is constitutional provided the named person is given sufficient disclosure to know and meet the case. The 'reliable and appropriate' admissibility standard (s. 83(1)(h)) and 'reasonable grounds' standard were upheld.
application: The Federal Court, presciently anticipating Harkat, conducted a case-specific inquiry and found Mr. Mahjoub was reasonably informed of the case to meet. The CSIS Act investigative and warrant provisions (ss. 2, 12, 17, 21) were neither vague nor overbroad and complied with section 8. Harkat's general blessing of the regime foreclosed the sweeping constitutional attack.
conclusion: The regime is constitutional; section 7 is not infringed, so section 1 need not be considered.

issue: Did the Ministers satisfy the legal prerequisites for issuing the certificate?
facts: Mr. Mahjoub argued the Ministers had to personally review all evidence before signing and that he should have been entitled to judicial review of issuance. The Ministers had reviewed the detailed Security Intelligence Report, received briefings and supporting documents, and personally signed the certificate.
rule: Section 77 requires the Ministers to 'sign' a certificate but this is not an untrammelled power (Roncarelli; Padfield); text, context and purpose govern (Rizzo; Bell ExpressVu). The Ministers need only review enough cogent, credible material to form the opinion that the person is inadmissible; the reasonableness of the certificate is then tested by the Federal Court. Judicial review of issuance is ousted in favour of automatic referral (J.P. Morgan).
application: Requiring the Ministers to review every document would render the Federal Court's reasonableness assessment redundant. The Security Intelligence Report gave ample basis to form the requisite opinion. Any duty of candour owed by CSIS to the Ministers, if it existed, was met, as the Federal Court found no misleading information or omissions.
conclusion: The prerequisites were satisfied; the certificate was validly issued and judicial review of issuance is unavailable.

issue: Should the proceedings have been permanently stayed for abuse of process?
facts: Mr. Mahjoub alleged numerous instances of misconduct: late/omitted disclosure, destruction of CSIS original notes, unfair interviews, warrant deficiencies, use of hearsay/unsourced and torture-tainted evidence, breaches of solicitor-client and litigation privilege (commingling of documents and interception of privileged calls), and overall delay.
rule: A permanent stay is the most drastic remedy, available only in the 'clearest of cases' (O'Connor; Babos; Regan; Tobiass). The three-part test requires prejudice to fair trial or system integrity, no alternative remedy, and, where uncertain, a balancing of interests. Federal Courts Act s. 50 and Charter s. 24(1) provide the remedial power.
application: The Federal Court found many allegations disclosed no misconduct; where breaches occurred (e.g., destruction of intercepts violating s. 7, the commingling seizure violating s. 8), lesser remedies such as disclosure orders, adjournments and removal of the Ministers' litigation team adequately addressed the prejudice. The cumulative prejudice was 'relatively minor' and the gravity of the terrorism allegations weighed heavily in favour of a decision on the merits (Al Yamani). No error of law or palpable and overriding error was shown.
conclusion: A permanent stay was not warranted; the proceedings properly ran to a decision on the merits.

issue: Was the CJC's decision to close the complaints with a formal expression of concern, rather than constituting an Inquiry Committee, reasonable?
facts: Justice Spiro of the Tax Court communicated with University of Toronto officials about the possible appointment of Dr. Azarova as Director of the International Human Rights Program, after being contacted by CIJA, of which he was a former director. Complainants alleged improper interference in an academic appointment and a reasonable apprehension of bias against Palestinian, Arab and Muslim interests. The Vice-Chair referred the matter to a Review Panel, which found the conduct a 'serious mistake' but not serious enough to warrant removal; the Vice-Chair issued a formal expression of concern and closed the complaints.
rule: On reasonableness review the decision must show an internally coherent, rational chain of analysis justified in relation to the facts and law (Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 85, 100–107; Portnov, 2021 FCA 171; Girouard, 2020 FCA 129). The test for recommending removal is whether conduct is 'so manifestly and totally contrary to the impartiality, integrity and independence of the judiciary' that public confidence would be undermined (Therrien (Re), 2001 SCC 35 at para 147; Judges Act s. 65(2)); a Review Panel may constitute an Inquiry Committee only if the matter 'might be serious enough to warrant removal' (By-laws s. 2(4)). Reasonable apprehension of bias is assessed prospectively from the perspective of a reasonable, informed person (Committee for Justice and Liberty, [1978] 1 SCR 369; Yukon Francophone, 2015 SCC 25).
application: The Court found the Review Panel identified and applied the correct Therrien test and the 'might be serious enough' threshold, distinguished its more searching role from the Vice-Chair's initial screening, and reasonably characterized Justice Spiro's conduct as voicing concern about adverse publicity rather than lobbying against the candidate — a characterization supported by the record and confirmed by the Cromwell Report. The Panel applied the forward-looking bias test and reasonably found that a past CIJA affiliation could not alone ground a reasonable apprehension of bias. The Vice-Chair's issuance of a formal expression of concern was itself a sanction and reflected a balanced weighing of the seriousness of the conduct against Justice Spiro's remorse, early acknowledgment and his Chief Justice's support. The applicants' arguments amounted to a request to reweigh the evidence, which is not the Court's role.
conclusion: The decision was reasonable; both the Review Panel's and the Vice-Chair's reasons disclosed a rational chain of analysis justified on the facts and law.

issue: Did the CJC breach the duty of procedural fairness owed to the complainants?
facts: The complainants submitted detailed complaints, received a standard acknowledgment inviting further information, and were later informed of the outcome by letter from the Executive Director. They were not given the Chief Justice's letter, the Vice-Chair's referral reasons, Justice Spiro's submissions or the Review Panel report before the decision, nor invited to make responsive submissions.
rule: Procedural fairness is variable and assessed on the Baker factors (Baker, [1999] 2 SCR 817) and whether the process was fair in all the circumstances (CPR, 2018 FCA 69 at para 54). The CJC complaints process is investigative, not adversarial; a complainant's only legal right is to make a complaint and be informed of the disposition, so the duty owed is at the low end of the spectrum (Taylor, 2003 FCA 55; Slansky, 2013 FCA 199 at paras 164–65; Tran, 2017 ABQB 337).
application: Applying the Baker factors, the Court found the process investigative rather than judicial, with no internal appeal but judicial review available, no legitimate expectation of greater participation (paragraph 6(a) of the Review Procedures being permissive), and a statutory scheme leaving the CJC to set its own procedures. While the decision was important to the complainants and served the public interest in an impartial judiciary, the complainants' interests were not affected in the same way as the judge's. The CJC followed its By-laws and Review Procedures, allowed detailed complaints, conducted an impartial investigation, publicized the referral and outcome, and informed the complainants of the result. Broader reform of the process was for Parliament.
conclusion: The duty owed was at the lower end of the spectrum and was met; there was no breach of procedural fairness.

issue: Was the Officer's finding that adequate state protection was available to a Roma woman in Hungary reasonable?
facts: The PRRA Officer treated Hungary as a functioning democracy and examined objective country-condition evidence to determine whether state protection was available. He referred selectively to portions of the U.S. Department of State 2015 report and other sources, concluded Hungary was 'taking measures' and making 'serious efforts,' and reproduced verbatim a conclusion that first appeared in RPD decisions from 2011, without reconciling contradictory evidence or assessing operational adequacy.
rule: Whether adequate state protection exists is reviewable on the reasonableness standard as a question of mixed fact and law (Hinzman v Canada, 2007 FCA 171; GM v Canada, 2013 FC 710). A reasonable decision must be justified, transparent and intelligible and fall within the range of acceptable outcomes (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9). The passage of anti-discrimination laws and 'serious efforts' are not equivalent to operational adequacy of protection (Paul v Canada, 2017 FC 687); the taking of complaints is not equivalent to protection (Orgona v Canada, 2012 FC 1438). Local failures do not amount to lack of state protection unless there is a broader general pattern of refusal (Villafranca; Kadenko).
application: The Officer selectively cited reports, omitting facts undercutting his conclusion (e.g. Jobbik's electoral gains), relied on boilerplate criticized in Kohazi, and reproduced verbatim a state-protection conclusion traceable to X (Re), 2011 CanLII 94218 that appears in over 100 decisions, without applying it to Ms. Olah's circumstances. He confused enacting laws with implementing them, ignored DOS 2015's findings of systematic erosion of the rule of law and police failure to investigate hate crimes, failed to assess operational adequacy, treated complaint bodies as sources of protection, and did not examine whether the 'general failure' he acknowledged constituted a Kadenko-type general refusal. The reasons were neither transparent nor intelligible.
conclusion: The state-protection analysis, the determinative issue, was unreasonable; the decision was set aside and returned for redetermination by a different officer.

issue: Did the Officer err by failing to assess the applicant's personal risk and whether cumulative discrimination amounted to persecution?
facts: Ms. Olah's profile was that of an unemployed Roma woman over 50 suffering domestic abuse from her husband, supported by his 12 brothers. She did not report the abuse to police because, as a Roma, she feared protection would not be forthcoming. Her credibility was never challenged. The Officer never assessed the domestic abuse allegation or the combined effect of the discrimination she faced.
rule: The assessment of state protection is a factual, case-by-case exercise (Molnar v Canada, 2012 FC 530). A PRRA is a forward-looking analysis personal to the applicant. Cumulative acts of discrimination may amount to persecution and must be considered.
application: Because the Officer never challenged credibility, he presumably accepted the abuse allegations, yet he failed to assess the personal risk arising from the husband and his brothers, and failed to consider whether the cumulative discrimination against an unemployed Roma woman over 50 — recognized in DOS 2015 as a distinct form of economic discrimination — amounted to persecution. This prevented a proper assessment of whether state protection was actually available to her.
conclusion: The failure to assess personal risk and cumulative discrimination was a reviewable error contributing to the unreasonableness of the decision.

issue: What is the scope of the right to examine the Commission's Registrar and staff under Rule 39.03 on judicial review of a decision not to refer a human rights complaint to a board of inquiry?
facts: Payne complained to the Ontario Human Rights Commission of discrimination and reprisal after her demotion and dismissal from Youth Clinical Services following an on-air anti-Semitic remark. Two Case Analysis Reports recommended referral, but the Commissioners, by majority, declined to refer the complaint and upheld that decision on reconsideration. On judicial review Payne served a sweeping Notice of Examination on the Registrar demanding production of the Commission's entire files and disclosure of all staff communications with Commissioners.
rule: Rule 39.03 permits examination of a witness before the hearing of a pending application; Canada Metal Co. v. Heap (1975), 7 O.R. (2d) 185 establishes a prima facie right to examine on matters relevant to an issue on the application, limited only by relevance and abuse of process. There is no right to examination for discovery on judicial review (Ellis-Don). The record on judicial review is 'the record of the proceedings in which the decision was made' (Judicial Review Procedure Act, s. 10), but the superior court may insist on a full and accurate record of what actually transpired before the tribunal.
application: The majority (Sharpe J.A.) held the proposed examination was far too broad—an impermissible general discovery amounting to a 'fishing expedition'—and that Payne had no right to rummage through the Commission's files. However, a party is entitled to have produced a complete account of the facts, recommendations and considerations actually placed before the Commissioners, since a tribunal cannot immunize its process by filing an incomplete record. Because a fundamental human right was at stake and the only recourse was judicial review, and because the sole legitimate factor for the Commission was the merit of the complaint, a focused examination was warranted. Abella J.A., dissenting, would have barred the examination entirely.
conclusion: Appeal allowed in part: the sweeping examination was refused, but a narrowly focused Rule 39.03 examination was permitted to determine what documents, facts, considerations or recommendations not disclosed in the record were before the Commissioners, whether 'strategic factors' underlay the decision, and whether undisclosed reasons existed.

issue: Does s. 30 of the Ontario Human Rights Code bar examination of Commission members and staff under Rule 39.03?
facts: The Commission argued that s. 30, which protects members and employees from being required to give testimony as to 'information obtained in the course of an investigation,' operated as a complete statutory shield analogous to s. 111 of the Labour Relations Act considered in Ellis-Don.
rule: Ontario Human Rights Code s. 30; contrasted with Ontario Labour Relations Act s. 111 (which broadly protects testimony 'respecting information obtained in the discharge of their duties'). Legislatures may enact codes protecting confidentiality (Glover; Cook v. Ip; Ellis-Don).
application: The majority read s. 30 narrowly: it protects only the product of the Commission's investigative efforts, not a general prohibition on examination. Unlike the far broader s. 111 in Ellis-Don, s. 30's language does not prevent producing before the court a full account of the material actually presented to the Commissioners when they disposed of the complaint; to read it otherwise would circumscribe the complainant's right to fairness. Abella J.A., dissenting, found s. 30 almost identical in effect to s. 111 and thus a complete bar.
conclusion: The majority held s. 30 does not preclude the focused examination; it only supports denying a general production of the entire file.

issue: How do deliberative secrecy and the applicable factual threshold constrain examination of a senior Commission official privy to the decision-making process?
facts: Payne relied on the affidavit of former Commissioner St. Clair Wharton, who described the Commission's practices—staff overriding Case Analysis Reports, reliance on 'strategic' cost considerations, pre-drafted reasons not reflecting actual discussions—and gave his recollection of the September 1996 meeting. The Commission did not cross-examine or contradict the affidavit.
rule: Deliberative secrecy of administrative decision-makers is qualified, not absolute, and must yield where a litigant presents valid reasons to believe natural justice was not observed (Tremblay v. Quebec (Commission des affaires sociales), [1992] 1 S.C.R. 952; Agnew v. Ontario Association of Architects). Staff participation does not automatically taint a decision (Consolidated-Bathurst). The threshold is not a 'heavy onus' or proof of the case; an applicant must present some basis for a clearly articulated and objectively reasonable concern that a relevant legal right may have been infringed, but examinations based on conjecture or speculation are not allowed.
application: The majority rejected the 'reasonable evidentiary foundation'/'heavy onus' standard as inimical to effective judicial review, holding it would force applicants to prove their case before obtaining evidence. Because the Commission conducted deliberations in the presence of and with input from non-members, its process was more exposed to review. The unchallenged Wharton affidavit raised objectively reasonable concerns (staff control, reliance on legally irrelevant strategic/cost factors, inadequate reasons, and an incomplete record) sufficiently connected to Payne's complaint to rise above speculation. Abella J.A. viewed the affidavit as mere conjecture insufficient to meet any threshold.
conclusion: The majority held the threshold was met, permitting the focused examination touching only on facts, recommendations and considerations actually before the Commissioners and on whether strategic factors or undisclosed reasons played a role.

issue: Were the portions of Payne's affidavit setting out material not before the Commission properly struck?
facts: Payne's judicial review affidavit set out at length her own version of events at YCS and her dealings with the Commission—material that had not been before the Commissioners when they decided.
rule: On judicial review the court reviews the record before the decision-maker; evidence not before the tribunal is generally inadmissible.
application: Both Abella and Sharpe JJ.A. agreed that because the struck paragraphs contained information that was not before the Commission when it decided, they were properly struck.
conclusion: The appeal from the order striking those portions of the affidavit was dismissed.

issue: Did Eldon Warman contravene s. 13 of the Canadian Human Rights Act by repeatedly posting internet messages likely to expose Jewish people to hatred or contempt?
facts: Richard Warman, an anti-hate campaigner unrelated to the respondent, compiled numerous e-mail postings, bulletin-board messages and newsgroup entries authored by Eldon Warman, a leading figure in a 'detax'/sovereign-citizen movement. The messages portrayed Jews as an evil conspiracy of 'banksters', used dehumanizing slurs, referenced concentration-camp 'soap and lampshades', and blamed Jewish people for a range of ills. The respondent's name and e-mail addresses appeared on the postings; he refused service and did not participate.
rule: Section 13(1) CHRA makes it a discriminatory practice to communicate telephonically, repeatedly, matter likely to expose persons to hatred or contempt on a prohibited ground; s. 13(2) extends this to internet communications. The provision is a reasonable limit on freedom of expression (Charter s. 2(b)) upheld under s. 1 in Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892. The words 'expose', 'hatred' and 'contempt' bear their ordinary meanings and require a certain gravity; trivial comments are not caught.
application: On a balance of probabilities the Tribunal inferred, from the consistent voice, return addresses and website registration, that Eldon Warman authored the postings. Though some content was political and thus protected, the postings vilified and dehumanized Jewish people, promoting hatred and contempt that strikes at their equality and dignity. The frequency and internet posting satisfied the 'repeatedly' requirement, and the material was well beyond trivial or legitimate debate.
conclusion: The complaint was substantiated. A cease-and-desist order was granted (per Warman v. Kyburz, 2003 CHRT 18); the material was subsequently removed from the internet, meeting the Act's remedial purpose.

issue: Should the Tribunal impose the $10,000 penalty under s. 54(1)(c) of the Canadian Human Rights Act despite unresolved constitutional and proportionality concerns and the respondent's absence?
facts: The Commission sought the maximum $10,000 penalty under s. 54(1)(c). The respondent refused to recognize the Tribunal's authority and did not appear, so no submissions were made on his behalf. Penalty caselaw was sparse (only Kyburz had awarded one, uncontested), and s. 54(1)(c) was added in 1998, after Taylor.
rule: Section 54(1)(c) permits a penalty up to $10,000 for a substantiated s. 13 complaint; s. 54(1.1) lists factors (nature, gravity, wilfulness, prior practices, ability to pay). Taylor upheld s. 13 as remedial, not punitive; the penalty provision is severable and, being inherently punitive, was not addressed in Taylor. The Tribunal must ensure a fair hearing and proper airing of constitutional issues even where the respondent does not appear.
application: The Tribunal found the constitutionality of the punitive penalty unresolved, distinguishing it from the remedial scheme upheld in Taylor and noting the absence of criminal-process safeguards (higher burden, mens rea, strict evidence rules) for what is effectively punishment. Comparison with R. v. Ahenakew (a $1,000 fine on conviction) raised proportionality concerns about a $10,000 civil penalty imposed in absentia. With no submissions from the respondent and no reliable range of precedents, the Tribunal could not fairly fix a penalty.
conclusion: The Tribunal reserved jurisdiction for 30 days, requiring the Complainant and Commission to decide whether to make further submissions and to give constitutional notice under Rule 9(7) before any penalty could be considered.

issue: Was the Refugee Protection Division's adverse credibility assessment of the principal applicant and her son unreasonable?
facts: The principal applicant and her son (the male applicant), citizens of Djibouti, claimed refugee protection. The Tribunal found numerous contradictions between the Basis of Claim forms, port-of-entry statements, and hearing testimony. The principal applicant gave differing accounts of why she was detained (her husband vs. her Jewish/Christian-sounding name), and the male applicant's passport stamps showed he was outside Djibouti during a period he claimed to have been detained there.
rule: Credibility findings are reviewed on the reasonableness standard (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9; Ramirez v Canada, 2007 FC 721). While a tribunal should not base findings on microscopic examination of peripheral issues or impugn credibility solely because port-of-entry information lacks detail (Lubana v Canada, 2003 FCT 116; Cetinkaya v Canada, 2012 FC 8), it may draw negative inferences from significant contradictions and omissions between port-of-entry statements and later testimony (Singh v Canada, 2008 FC 453; Jean-Baptiste v Canada, 2009 FC 1261).
application: The Court distinguished Cetinkaya, noting that here the applicants had not merely added detail but had changed their stories, and there were significant contradictions and omissions on key elements of the claims, including the passport evidence contradicting the male applicant's alleged detention date. The Tribunal did not doubt credibility merely for lack of detail but for genuine inconsistencies.
conclusion: The credibility findings were reasonable; the Tribunal reasonably disbelieved the applicants' account of political activity and being targeted by Djiboutian authorities, and the decision regarding the male applicant was upheld.

issue: Did the Tribunal unreasonably conclude that the record did not support the principal applicant being at risk because of her opposition to her daughter's FGM?
facts: The Tribunal accepted that the minor daughter faced a serious possibility of FGM in Djibouti and allowed her claim, but rejected the mother's claim on the basis that she had not declared she feared for herself over her opposition to the practice. The record showed the mother could not directly oppose the husband's grandmother, who insisted on the excision, and could act only through her husband because of cultural norms.
rule: The Board must consider all grounds for a refugee claim even if not raised at the hearing (Canada (AG) v Ward, [1993] 2 SCR 689; Viafara v Canada, 2006 FC 1526). UNHCR guidance (Guidance Note on Refugee Claims relating to FGM) and Guideline 4 recognize a parent may have a claim in their own right where forced to witness the child's suffering or where they risk persecution for opposing the practice. Reasonableness applies (Dunsmuir).
application: The Court found the mother's opposition and the constraints of cultural norms were evident in the Tribunal's own paragraph 81, establishing a basis for her subjective fear. Given the accepted risk to the daughter, the Tribunal should have assessed the mother's own risk under the FGM Guidance Note and Guideline 4. The risk was not hypothetical merely because she could avoid it by leaving the daughter behind, since a mother is not free to abandon her child. Rejecting a protection need on the basis that a person could avoid harm by acquiescing in the persecutory conduct is unacceptable.
conclusion: The refusal of the principal applicant's claim was unreasonable; that part of the decision was set aside and referred to a different member for redetermination, while the male applicant's determination stood. No question was certified.

issue: Did the discrimination, harassment and criminal incidents experienced by the Appellants in Argentina establish a nexus to a Convention ground (race/Chinese ethnicity) rising to the level of persecution?
facts: The Appellants, ethnic Chinese permanent residents/citizens of Argentina, recounted incidents of racial slurs from customers, a 2009 robbery, a 2015 extortion phone call, and bullying/discrimination of the minor Appellants at school. The panel found them credible but concluded the incidents were random and criminal, experienced by other ethnic minorities as well.
rule: Under s. 96 of the IRPA, a refugee claimant must establish a well-founded fear of persecution linked to a Convention ground. Discrimination does not necessarily amount to persecution. As cited by the Appellants (Hathaway, The Law of Refugee Status), a Convention ground need only be a contributing factor to the risk. The RAD applies a correctness standard per Huruglica (2014 FC 799; 2016 FCA 93), conducting an independent assessment while respecting the RPD's credibility advantages.
application: The RAD independently reviewed the record and country documentation. It accepted that race and foreigner identity generate widespread prejudice in Argentina directed at Chinese and other groups, but found the three harassment incidents over three years, the robbery and the extortion call did not rise to the level of persecution — no one was injured, the incidents passed quickly, and the robbery/extortion were criminal and economically motivated with no evidence of ethnic targeting. School discrimination, while unacceptable, did not deny education and was not escalated to higher authorities. The harm faced was a generalized risk broadly shared across Argentine society.
conclusion: The RAD found the panel did not err; the discrimination and harassment did not amount to persecution, and no sufficient nexus to a Convention ground was established, even cumulatively.

issue: Did the Appellants rebut the presumption of state protection in Argentina?
facts: The Appellants alleged police refused to help them because they were Chinese, demanded bribes, took merchandise, and that the Chinese community knew police would not help. They often chose not to involve police. Police did respond to the 2009 robbery; they did not contact police regarding the 2015 extortion despite embassy advice.
rule: A claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect to rebut the presumption of state protection. Country documentary evidence (NDP: US Department of State, Amnesty International, Freedom House) is weighed against the claimant's evidence.
application: The RAD found the Appellants did not provide clear and convincing evidence they sought and were denied protection; they could have approached higher police authorities and reported bribe demands. Country evidence showed federal authorities investigate, prosecute and convict abusive officers, and that Argentine and Chinese police jointly combated criminal groups preying on Chinese business owners. The RAD rejected the claim that police universally refuse to help ethnic Chinese; the mixed evidence on police conduct reflected a generalized problem, not ethnic-based denial of protection.
conclusion: The RAD held the panel did not err; the Appellants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection.

issue: Are the Appellants excluded under Article 1E, and was the claim against Argentina properly assessed?
facts: The principal, female and minor female Appellants are citizens of China and permanent residents of Argentina; the minor male Appellant is an Argentine citizen. The Minister submitted they were entitled to return to Argentina, triggering the 1E exclusion. The Appellants did not contest their status.
rule: Article 1E of the Refugee Convention, incorporated by s. 98 of the IRPA, excludes persons who have status substantially similar to nationals in a country of residence; the panel first assesses any claim against the 1E country before applying the exclusion.
application: The panel found the Appellants entitled to return to Argentina and, before applying 1E, assessed their claim against Argentina, finding no serious possibility of persecution nor risk under s. 97. The minor male Appellant likewise failed to establish a claim against Argentina, his country of nationality. Only if the Argentina claim failed against China would that be considered.
conclusion: The Appellants were excluded under s. 98/Article 1E and were found to be neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection; the appeals were dismissed under s. 111(1)(a).

issue: Did the Commission's withdrawal, the respondent's Consumer Proposal, or the pre-complaint delay deprive the Tribunal of jurisdiction to continue the inquiry?
facts: One week before the hearing the Commission advised it would no longer participate, citing that the impugned material was off the internet, the website had been sold, and Ouwendyk's Consumer Proposal under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act stayed the financial claims. The respondent Ouwendyk asked that the complaints be dismissed, also on the basis that the conduct predated the complaint by more than a year.
rule: Under s. 44(3)(a) and s. 49(1)-(2) of the Canadian Human Rights Act the Commission's request obliges the Chair to institute an inquiry; s. 51 permits the Commission to decline further participation where not in the public interest but does not undo the request; ss. 41(1)(e) and 44(3) contemplate inquiries into conduct occurring more than a year before the complaint.
application: Once the Commission had requested the inquiry, the Tribunal was statutorily bound to hold a hearing, and the Commission's later withdrawal did not remove that obligation. The Consumer Proposal stayed only financial claims (which the complainant then removed by amending his particulars) and did not bar the inquiry. The one-year timing issue was expressly contemplated by the Act. The complainant was present and prepared to proceed.
conclusion: The Tribunal retained jurisdiction and proceeded with the hearing; the requests to dismiss were rejected, though the Tribunal found the late withdrawal 'troubling'.

issue: Were the impugned messages likely to expose identifiable persons to hatred or contempt under s. 13(1)?
facts: The Northern Alliance Website forum and photo gallery contained numerous posts and images targeting Roma, Eastern Europeans, gays and lesbians, the disabled, Hispanics, Chinese/East Asians, Blacks, Aboriginal persons, and Jews, Muslims and Arabs, portraying them as inferior, dangerous, or deserving of elimination, and denying the Holocaust.
rule: Section 13(1) CHRA; the meaning of 'hatred', 'contempt', 'likely' and 'expose' as set in Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor [1990] 3 SCR 892, Nealy v. Johnston, and the Taylor/Western Guard decision; hallmarks of hate material from Warman v. Kouba, 2006 CHRT 50.
application: The messages expressed that people should be hated because of who they are, deploying stereotypes and the recognized hallmarks (powerful menace, predator, sub-human, banishment, call to violence, trivializing past tragedy). They created conditions for hatred to flourish against the targeted groups on prohibited grounds of religion, sexual orientation, race, colour, national or ethnic origin, and disability.
conclusion: The material was likely to expose the targeted persons to hatred or contempt within the meaning of s. 13(1).

issue: Were the communications made repeatedly by means of a telecommunication undertaking within Parliament's authority?
facts: The material was posted on the publicly accessible Northern Alliance Website, which Warman was able to view and download simply by navigating to the site's forum, with no obstacles to access.
rule: Section 13(1) and s. 13(2) CHRA; Tribunal jurisprudence holding internet material is by its nature a repeated communication (Warman v. Beaumont, Harrison, Kulbashian, Tremaine).
application: Because the material was posted on an unrestricted website accessible to anyone on the internet, it constituted a repeated communication by telecommunication, and s. 13(2) confirms s. 13(1) applies to internet communications.
conclusion: The communications were made repeatedly by a telecommunication undertaking within Parliament's legislative authority, contrary to s. 13(1).

issue: Did Ouwendyk and the Northern Alliance act in concert to communicate the messages?
facts: Ouwendyk admitted being a member, elected spokesperson, webmaster and administrator of the site, and posted some impugned material under the pseudonym 'Jay'; he appeared but gave no evidence. Photos, letterhead, a postal box, e-mail, newsletter and financial account evidenced the Northern Alliance as an organized group.
rule: Section 13(1) CHRA requires a person or group acting in concert; jurisprudence including Smith v. Western Guard Party, Taylor, Khaki v. Canadian Liberty Net, Nealy, Chilliwack Anti-Racism Project, Warman v. Western Canada For Us.
application: The uncontradicted evidence established Ouwendyk's personal responsibility and that the Northern Alliance, though unincorporated, functioned as a group acting in concert when the messages were communicated. Ouwendyk did not rebut the evidence.
conclusion: Ouwendyk individually, and Ouwendyk and the Northern Alliance acting in concert, communicated or caused the messages to be communicated within the meaning of s. 13(1); the complaints were substantiated.

issue: What remedies should be ordered given the complainant's own conduct and cessation of activity?
facts: Warman sought a cease-and-desist order and, against the Northern Alliance, a $7,500 penalty and $6,000 compensation. On cross-examination he admitted posting on similar hate sites under pseudonyms ('Pogue Mahone', 'Axetogrind'), including content quoting antisemitic material. The website had been sold and the activity had ceased years earlier.
rule: Section 54(1)(a) (cease and desist), s. 54(1)(b) (compensation) and s. 54(1)(c) (penalty) CHRA; Tribunal discretion informed by remedial purpose; Chair Sinclair's earlier ruling deferring any order pending the constitutional outcome in Warman v. Lemire.
application: A cease-and-desist order was made as a precaution, but not to be issued until final court determination of the constitutional question in Lemire. The Tribunal declined the penalty and compensation because the impugned activity had long ceased and because Warman's own participation on similar hate sites diminished his credibility and was 'disappointing and disturbing'.
conclusion: Only a deferred cease-and-desist order under s. 54(1)(a) was granted; no penalty or compensation was awarded.

issue: Was there an objective basis for the claimant's fear of persecution in Syria on account of his Christian faith?
facts: The claimant, a 41-year-old Armenian Christian from Aleppo, alleged that Syrian authorities and the Sunni majority persecuted his family, including harassment of his children at school, mistreatment of his wife, non-payment by clients of his auto-electrical business, and general hostility toward Christians.
rule: To ground a refugee claim, discrimination must rise to the level of persecution; per para. 54 of the UNHCR Handbook, discrimination amounts to persecution only where it produces consequences of a substantially prejudicial nature, such as serious restrictions on the right to earn a livelihood, to practise religion, or to access normally available education.
application: Documentary evidence showed Christians in Syria practise their faith openly, are well protected by the regime, face no employment discrimination, and that schools accommodate Christian religious instruction and even liturgical languages such as Armenian. The claimant completed high school, his children attended elementary school without restriction, and he had been gainfully employed for eight years as a technical expert. Non-payment by some clients was a challenge faced by businessmen universally and unconnected to later employment. The panel found the treatment did not reach the substantially prejudicial threshold.
conclusion: There was no valid objective basis for the fear; the claimant would not face a serious possibility of persecution for his Christian faith on return.

issue: Were the specific incidents of abuse alleged by the claimant and his wife credible?
facts: The claimant alleged a 1999 church-window smashing that cut him, a 1995 assault by a printing-factory owner, a mid-1980s car theft later seen driven by a policeman, and repeated assaults on his wife including men grabbing and squeezing her breasts and throwing garbage and water at her.
rule: A claimant must establish the alleged incidents with credible and trustworthy evidence; late additions to a PIF narrative, internal inconsistencies, vagueness, and silence in objective country documentation on significant events may undermine credibility.
application: The alleged church vandalism was unsupported by any human-rights documentation, which reliably reported comparable events (e.g., a Damascus synagogue vandalism in 2000), so its absence indicated the event did not occur. The factory-owner assault was a single isolated event seven years earlier with no recurrence. The car theft occurred over 15 years earlier with no link to faith. The most serious allegations concerning the wife (grabbing and squeezing) were added only at the hearing and in oral testimony, and the couple's accounts were inconsistent and vague; the panel found them to be embellishments.
conclusion: The incidents were not credible or lacked probative value and did not establish a well-founded fear.

issue: Did the claimant face a risk on return to Syria as a failed asylum seeker who left without authorization?
facts: The claimant raised, but led no evidence on, the treatment of failed asylum seekers returned to Syria, and could not recall any such incidents.
rule: Where a claimant raises a risk category, the objective country documentation and available evidence must support a serious possibility of harm; silence in recent human-rights monitoring reports may indicate the absence of serious problems.
application: The claimant put forward no evidence of harm to returnees, and the documentary record was silent on the issue, which the panel took as an indication of no serious problems for those returned.
conclusion: The claimant did not have a well-founded fear of persecution as a returnee leaving without authorization.

issue: Did the dependent claims of the wife and children succeed?
facts: The wife and two minor children based their claims entirely on the principal claimant's claim, which incorporated incidents relating to them.
rule: Where dependents' claims rely wholly on the principal claimant's claim, they stand or fall with it.
application: As the principal claimant's claim failed on both objective basis and credibility, the same analysis applied to the wife and children.
conclusion: The dependent claims also failed; all claimants were found neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

issue: Should the appellant's proposed new documentary evidence be admitted on appeal under s. 110(4) of the IRPA?
facts: The appellant tendered nine documents on appeal, seven published after the RPD decision reporting recent events (including violence and hate speech against the Bamileke community and remarks by a government minister), and two published before the decision but said to illuminate the current context.
rule: Under s. 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the RAD may admit only evidence that arose after the RPD decision, was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected to present; if a document meets a criterion, the RAD must also assess whether it is new, credible and relevant (Canada (MCI) v. Singh, 2016 FCA 96).
application: The seven post-decision documents arose after the RPD ruling and were clearly relevant to understanding the seriousness of the current situation and treatment of Bamilekes; the two earlier documents helped explain the current context in light of the others. All appeared to be from credible sources, being reports by renowned journalists and reputable organizations. An oral hearing was refused as unnecessary to assess credibility.
conclusion: All nine documents were admitted as new evidence and the request for an oral hearing was denied.

issue: Did the appellant establish a serious possibility of persecution by reason of his Bamileke ethnicity, including through the cumulative effect of discrimination?
facts: The appellant, a Francophone Bamileke from Douala, cited three 2017-2018 incidents (an assault while travelling in an Anglophone region, an assault linked to a workplace complaint, and the burning of his daughter's Anglophone school) and pointed to escalating tensions between Bamilekes and the majority Beti group, including a minister comparing Bamilekes to Holocaust-era Jews, assaults at Sangmélima, and hate speech targeting Bamilekes.
rule: A refugee claimant must establish a serious possibility of persecution; discrimination that individually appears minor may, through its cumulative effect, amount to persecution, but there must be evidence that the situation goes beyond isolated incidents.
application: While the new evidence showed heightened tension and verbal and behavioural outbursts between Bamilekes and Betis, it did not establish a political climate producing discrimination or violence against Bamilekes to a significant degree; the incidents remained isolated and society had not descended into collective hatred. The cumulative-effect threshold was not met, the broader Anglophone and Boko Haram conflicts were not shown to affect Bamilekes more than other Cameroonians, and the 2017-2018 incidents disclosed no prospective ethnicity-based risk, particularly in Douala.
conclusion: The appellant failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution as a Bamileke, or on a balance of probabilities a personalized risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment; the appeal was dismissed.

issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption that Hungary is able to provide adequate state protection to Roma citizens?
facts: The principal claimant, half Roma and half Jewish, his Hungarian common-law partner, their four children and his mother sought protection citing incidents including a 2010 Magyar Garda assault, a 2008 car arson, a 2006 car accident, and Facebook threats. In several incidents the police took reports, conducted witness interviews, the arsonist was apprehended and sentenced to 5.5 years, and investigations occurred.
rule: There is a presumption that a state can protect its citizens, absent complete breakdown, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence (Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689). The onus increases with the state's degree of democracy (Kadenko). Protection need only be adequate, not perfect or effective per se; local failures do not establish overall failure (Villafranca; Zhuravlvev). The claimant must exhaust reasonable avenues of protection.
application: The Board found Hungary a functioning multiparty democracy with police, courts, an Independent Police Complaints Board, Minority Ombudsman, Equal Treatment Authority, and Roma anti-discrimination legal services. In each incident authorities responded—reports taken, witness interviews conducted, the arsonist prosecuted, and the Magyar Garda dissolved by the courts. The claimants failed to pursue available recourse and did not take reasonable steps to seek protection. Despite acknowledged imperfections and police corruption, the preponderance of objective evidence showed adequate, serious state efforts.
conclusion: The claimants did not rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence; adequate state protection is available in Hungary.

issue: Were the claimants credible in their allegations of persecution based on Roma ethnicity?
facts: The principal claimant gave inconsistent accounts about returning to police after the 2010 assault, the reason for the 2006 investigation, and whether perpetrators knew he was Roma. He acknowledged not resembling a Roma. He maintained an active Facebook account despite alleged threats and initially had no security settings.
rule: Sworn testimony is presumed true unless there is reason to doubt it (Maldonado, (1994) 23 Imm. L.R. (2d)). Contradictions, omissions and implausibilities can rebut that presumption.
application: The Board found contradictions between testimony and the amended PIF and corroborative evidence regarding the 2010 police contact, concluding he embellished his claim. It found it implausible that racial slurs identified him as Roma while driving. The maintenance of an unsecured Facebook account contradicted his claimed fear. These undermined the ethnicity-based fear, and the wife (ethnic Hungarian) and mother added little substantive support.
conclusion: The Board drew adverse credibility findings and concluded the ethnicity-based fears were not substantiated.

issue: Did the alleged harm to the minor children and other family members amount to persecution or a s. 97 risk?
facts: The claimants feared future discrimination against their children; son XXXX XXXX was traumatized in the 2010 assault but no psychological evidence was filed for him. The mother alleged discrimination and being pushed off a bus but gave scant detail. The wife is ethnic Hungarian.
rule: Fears must be more than speculative; an isolated incident, absent corroboration, does not constitute persecution. Sections 96 and 97 IRPA require a well-founded fear or risk, and the state protection presumption applies to each claimant.
application: The children's fears were largely future and speculative; the one 2010 incident affecting the son, without psychological corroboration, did not amount to persecution. The mother provided insufficient evidence and did not rebut state protection. The wife's claim rested on her husband's allegations, which failed.
conclusion: None of the family members established persecution or a s. 97 risk; all claims failed on state protection and evidentiary grounds.

issue: May a corporation defend a criminal charge by arguing that the Lord's Day Act violates freedom of conscience and religion, even though a corporation cannot itself hold religious belief?
facts: Big M Drug Mart Ltd., a corporation, was charged under s. 4 of the Lord's Day Act for selling goods on a Sunday. The Attorney General for Alberta argued a corporation cannot claim s. 2(a) rights and that the Provincial Court lacked jurisdiction to declare the Act invalid.
rule: Section 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 makes the Constitution supreme, so no one can be convicted under an unconstitutional law. Standing to challenge the validity of a law under which one is prosecuted is the same whether the challenge rests on ss. 91–92 of the Constitution Act, 1867 or the Charter. Recourse to the s. 24(1) remedy is unnecessary where the attack is on the constitutionality of the legislation itself.
application: Big M did not come to court as a public-interest litigant seeking a prerogative declaration; it was compelled to defend a prosecution and sought only dismissal of the charges. Whether a corporation can hold religious belief is irrelevant: it is the nature of the impugned law, not the status of the accused, that is in issue. A law that itself infringes religious freedom is inconsistent with s. 2(a) regardless of whether the accused is Christian, non-believer, individual or corporation. Provincial courts have always been able to hold legislation invalid in criminal cases.
conclusion: Big M had standing and the Provincial Court had jurisdiction; any accused may raise the constitutional invalidity of the law under which it is charged.

issue: Does the Lord's Day Act infringe s. 2(a), and is constitutionality tested by legislative purpose or effect?
facts: The Lord's Day Act, whose historic and consistently recognized purpose is to compel observance of the Christian Sabbath, prohibits work and commercial activity on Sunday under penal sanction. Non-Christians and those observing other days of rest are thereby compelled to conform to a Christian religious observance.
rule: Freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a) means, at minimum, that government may not coerce individuals to affirm a religious belief or manifest a religious practice for a sectarian purpose; freedom is characterized by absence of coercion, including indirect coercion (Hunter v. Southam purposive approach). Constitutionality is assessed first by legislative purpose; effects need only be considered if the purpose is valid. Purpose is fixed at enactment and does not shift with changing social conditions; the 'shifting purpose' argument is rejected. Robertson and Rosetanni (Canadian Bill of Rights) is distinguishable because it concerned application, not constitutional validity, of the legislation.
application: The acknowledged purpose of the Act is compulsion of sabbatical observance, a religious purpose. Binding all to a sectarian Christian ideal works a coercion inimical to the Charter and gives the appearance of discrimination against non-Christians; the protection of one religion with concomitant non-protection of others produces disparate impact destructive of religious freedom, contrary also to the multicultural interpretive guide in s. 27. Since the purpose offends s. 2(a), it is unnecessary to weigh the Act's secular effects; legislation with an invalid purpose cannot be saved by inoffensive effects. (Wilson J. would begin with effect rather than purpose, but reached the same result.)
conclusion: The Lord's Day Act, especially s. 4, infringes s. 2(a) of the Charter.

issue: Is the infringement a reasonable limit demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society under s. 1?
facts: The Attorneys General argued that public convenience and the value of a uniform day of rest justified the Act, citing a UN study and comparable legislation in Britain, Australia and New Zealand.
rule: Section 1 requires the government objective to be sufficiently important to override a Charter right and the means to be reasonable and proportionate (impairing the right as little as possible). Parliament cannot rely on an ultra vires or colourable purpose to justify a limit under s. 1 (cf. Quebec Association of Protestant School Boards).
application: The secular 'uniform day of rest' objective was never found to be the legislation's purpose; the Act's pith and substance is the compulsion of a Christian religious duty. Parliament cannot assert a secular objective under s. 1 to validate legislation that in substance compels religious observance, as this would permit doing indirectly what it cannot do directly and would legitimize curtailing religious freedom for the very purpose of curtailing it.
conclusion: The Act is not justified under s. 1; the infringement cannot be saved.

issue: Was the Lord's Day Act validly enacted under the federal criminal law power in s. 91(27)?
facts: The Act compels observance of the Christian Sabbath through prohibitions backed by summary-conviction penalties. All five Alberta Court of Appeal judges, and both parties before the SCC, treated it as criminal legislation.
rule: Legislation compelling a religious obligation by prohibition and penalty is directed to maintenance of public order and safeguarding public morality, an 'ordinary end' of the criminal law (Reference re Dairy Industry Act; Hamilton Street Railway).
application: Because the Act's purpose is compelling Sunday observance for its religious significance under penal sanction, it is aimed at safeguarding public morality and falls within s. 91(27). Had its purpose been the secular goal of a uniform day of rest, it would have fallen under provincial jurisdiction (s. 92(13)).
conclusion: The Act was validly enacted under the criminal law power, but is nonetheless of no force or effect for violating s. 2(a).

issue: Does the government's ownership of airport property confer an unlimited right to control expression, or does s. 2(b) protect expression on some government property?
facts: The respondents attempted to promote the Committee for the Commonwealth of Canada and recruit members inside Dorval airport, a federally owned property, when they were ordered to stop. The Crown argued that as owner it had the same exclusive rights as any private owner to control activity on its property.
rule: Freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter cannot be defeated merely by the government's proprietary rights, given the 'quasi-fiduciary' nature of government ownership (Hague v. Committee for Industrial Organization). Government property is held for the benefit of citizens, not for the state's own private benefit. The Court divided on the precise test: Lamer C.J. proposed a 'compatibility with the function of the place' test at the s. 2(b) stage; L'Heureux-Dubé J. would treat nearly all expression on public property as protected with balancing under s. 1; McLachlin J. proposed a values-based test drawn from Irwin Toy asking whether the expression in the forum promotes the purposes underlying free expression.
application: All members of the Court rejected the Crown's absolutist property argument. The special nature of government ownership means it cannot alone authorize an infringement of s. 2(b). Freedom of expression necessarily requires physical space; confining it to places owned by the speaker would deny its foundation. However, the Court agreed that s. 2(b) does not extend to all government property (e.g., private offices, control towers, prison cells, judges' chambers). Airport public areas, being modern thoroughfares with large and varied audiences, are appropriate forums for expression.
conclusion: The government's ownership does not authorize unlimited control of expression; expressive activity in the public areas of an airport falls within the protection of s. 2(b) of the Charter.

issue: Did ordering the respondents to cease distributing pamphlets and soliciting members infringe their s. 2(b) freedom of expression?
facts: On March 22, 1984, respondents Lépine and Deland peacefully approached travellers at Dorval airport to discuss the Committee's political aims and recruit members, distributing leaflets and magazines. An RCMP officer and the assistant airport manager ordered them to stop, relying on a policy prohibiting political propaganda activities.
rule: Under Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec (Attorney General), any activity that conveys or attempts to convey meaning has expressive content and prima facie falls within s. 2(b), unless it takes a proscribed form such as violence. Content of the message is irrelevant to whether s. 2(b) is engaged.
application: The respondents' conduct clearly conveyed a political message and took a peaceful form. The distribution of pamphlets and discussion with the public were in no way incompatible with the airport's primary function of accommodating the travelling public, which as a thoroughfare with open and waiting areas can readily accommodate expression. The order to cease these activities limited the respondents' freedom of expression.
conclusion: The respondents' freedom of expression under s. 2(b) was infringed by the airport manager's order to cease their activities.

issue: Did ss. 7(a) and 7(b) of the Regulations apply, and was the limit 'prescribed by law' and justifiable under s. 1?
facts: Section 7 of the Government Airport Concession Operations Regulations prohibited conducting 'any business or undertaking, commercial or otherwise' and 'advertising or soliciting' at an airport except as authorized in writing by the Minister. The airport officials relied on an established internal policy prohibiting political propaganda.
rule: A limit must be 'prescribed by law' to be justified under s. 1 (R. v. Therens; R. v. Thomsen). Legislation open to more than one interpretation should be read consistently with the Charter (Slaight Communications; presumption of constitutionality). A limit that is unduly vague or overbroad cannot be a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 (R. v. Oakes; R. v. Edwards Books).
