conclusion: The majority upheld s. 319(2) as a reasonable limit under s. 1 (question 2 answered 'Yes'); La Forest, Sopinka and McLachlin JJ. dissented.

issue: Does the reverse-onus truth defence in s. 319(3)(a) infringe s. 11(d), and if so is it justified under s. 1?
facts: Section 319(3)(a) provides that no person shall be convicted of wilfully promoting hatred 'if he establishes that the statements communicated were true' — placing the burden of proving truth on the accused on a balance of probabilities.
rule: Per R. v. Whyte, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 3, the presumption of innocence in s. 11(d) is infringed whenever an accused may be convicted despite a reasonable doubt; the characterization of a factor as element, excuse or defence is irrelevant — what matters is the final effect on the verdict.
application: Requiring the accused to prove truth on a balance of probabilities permits conviction even where the trier has a reasonable doubt about the truth of the statements, so s. 11(d) is infringed. Under s. 1, the majority held the reverse onus pressing and substantial and proportionate: harm arises whether or not statements are true, the concession to truth is a caution to free expression, and requiring the state to disprove truth beyond a reasonable doubt would gut s. 319(2); the reverse onus is a minimal impairment, analogous to Whyte. The dissent found no rational connection and no minimal impairment, as the state is better resourced to prove falsity.
conclusion: The majority held s. 319(3)(a) infringes s. 11(d) but is justified under s. 1 (questions 3 and 4 answered 'Yes'). Sopinka and McLachlin JJ. would have struck it down; La Forest J. found it unnecessary to decide.

issue: Are the defendants' registered trade-marks (author's pseudonym, logo, and book title in three languages) valid and registrable?
facts: The Stiftung registered in 1999 the marks ABD-RU-SHIN, an A-encircled-by-a-snake design, and the title "In the Light of Truth" in French, English and German, in connection with literary works. The underlying work of Oskar Ernst Bernhardt fell into the public domain in 1991. Drolet sought expungement under s. 57.
rule: A registered mark is presumed valid but the presumption is weak (Emall.ca v. Cheap Tickets, 2008 FCA 50). A mark must be distinctive (s. 2) and must not fall under s. 12 exceptions, including s. 12(1)(a) (primarily merely a name/surname) and s. 12(1)(b) (clearly descriptive or deceptively misdescriptive). Distinctiveness may be inherent or acquired (Tommy Hilfiger, 2005 FC 10; Philip Morris). U.S. authority (In re Cooper; Herbko International) holds a single book title is inherently descriptive and cannot be monopolized, and trade-marks cannot be used to circumvent the Copyright Act (s. 6).
application: ABD-RU-SHIN is a pen name, not a name/surname, and in any event any s.12(1)(a) effect ended in 1971 (30 years after death); it is inherently distinctive, so registrable. The A & SNAKE logo, while spiritually significant, does not have the universal historical recognition of a menorah (distinguishing Canadian Jewish Congress v. Chosen People Ministries) and is not obscene; it is registrable. The title "In the Light of Truth" is not clearly descriptive of content, but the title of a single literary work is inherently descriptive because it is the only way to identify the book; allowing a trade-mark on it would let the owner circumvent the expiry of copyright and keep a public-domain work out of the public domain.
conclusion: The three title marks (LMC 520 520, 519 477, 519 476) are invalid and struck; ABD-RU-SHIN (LMC 519 470) and the A & SNAKE DESIGN (LMC 519 469) are valid.

issue: Did the plaintiff infringe the valid trade-marks or commit passing off?
facts: Drolet reproduced on his volumes a snake-and-A logo (identical to the registered logo on the title pages) and the author's pseudonym spelled "ABDRUSCHIN". He printed only about 100 mimeographed copies, sold to friends and members at cost, without advertising or deposit at the National Library, and openly distinguished his edition from the Stiftung's.
rule: Section 19 gives the exclusive right to an identical mark for the same wares; s. 20 captures use of a confusing mark. Confusion is assessed under s. 6(5) from the standpoint of the ordinary consumer, and must be likely, not merely possible (Mattel; Veuve Clicquot, 2006 SCC 22). Passing off under s. 7(b)/(c) requires misrepresentation (wilful or negligent) creating confusion (Kirkbi, 2005 SCC 3).
application: The logo used by Drolet was identical to the registered A & SNAKE DESIGN and used for the same wares, so s. 19 was infringed. For the pseudonym, no evidence of likely confusion was adduced; the very different appearance of Drolet's mimeographed volumes, the tiny non-commercial print run, the explanatory foreword, and buyers who specifically sought a different version negated confusion. No misrepresentation was shown for passing off — Drolet actively dissociated himself from the defendants.
conclusion: Drolet infringed the A & SNAKE DESIGN mark (LMC 519 469); he did not infringe ABD-RU-SHIN and did not commit passing off.

issue: Did copyright subsist in Kaufmann's French translation, was the Stiftung the owner, and did Drolet infringe it?
facts: Paul Kaufmann produced French translations of the Grail Message over some forty years; the Stiftung held a licence from the Bernhardt heirs (chain: Maria, then Alexander, then Irmingard, then the Stiftung) and a 1969 sub-licence from Kaufmann assigning all rights. Drolet used diskettes of Kaufmann's translation, reordered chapters and added material to reconstruct the 1931 edition.
rule: A translation is an original literary work (s. 2) if it results from skill and judgment (CCH v. Law Society of Upper Canada, 2004 SCC 13). Copyright includes the sole right to reproduce a substantial part (s. 3(1)); registration raises a (rebuttable) presumption (s. 53(2)); infringement requires copying of a substantial part plus access (U&R Tax Services). Fair dealing (s. 29) requires a research/private study purpose that is fair.
application: Kaufmann's translation showed skill and judgment (a substantial, more literary reworking), so it was original; the title chain and 1969 assignment established Stiftung ownership, and any post-mortem revision of Bernhardt's text did not transform it into a distinct work. Expert comparison showed Drolet's text was a substantial copy of Kaufmann's translation; reordering and additions did not cure the reproduction. Consent, fair dealing and good-faith defences failed — the diskettes were not authorization from the copyright owner, and publication was not research.
conclusion: Copyright subsisted, the Stiftung owned it, and Drolet reproduced a substantial part; infringement was made out on the merits (subject to limitation).

issue: Was the copyright counterclaim time-barred under s. 41 of the Copyright Act?
facts: The Stiftung learned of Drolet's book through Mr. Thivierge in 2001 and knew diskettes of the Kaufmann translation had been given to him. The trade-mark action was filed in September 2004; the defendants only sought to add the copyright counterclaim in October 2007 and registered their copyright certificate on 16 January 2008.
rule: Section 41(1) bars a remedy unless proceedings are commenced within three years after the plaintiff knew, or could reasonably be expected to have known, of the infringement. Justice Pinard's order allowing the amendment was not a final determination on limitation, which is for the trial judge.
application: The defendants knew of Drolet's book and of his access to the translation by late 2001; even allowing that detecting copying in a lengthy book takes time, more than six years (and over three years after the action was filed) was unreasonable. They did not rebut the limitation defence.
conclusion: The copyright counterclaim is time-barred and dismissed; no compensation is available for the infringement.

issue: Did the Board have jurisdiction to entertain the grievor's various damages claims for workplace events (hospitalization, broken toes, alleged assault, discrimination, car damage, sick-leave denial, and the CORCAN position) that were never advanced through the grievance process?
facts: The grievor advanced numerous claims for things he alleged happened during his CSC employment. There was no evidence he filed a grievance about any of them; the only grievance filed was against his termination. Some matters (e.g., broken toes at home, staffing of the CORCAN position) were unrelated to employment or governed by the PSEA staffing recourse process, and he was not represented by his bargaining agent.
rule: Under ss. 208, 209, 225 and 236 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act, the Board's adjudication jurisdiction is limited to grievances presented at all required levels; collective-agreement grievances require bargaining-agent representation; and staffing recourse lies under the PSEA. Section 225 makes presentation through the grievance process a condition precedent to adjudication.
application: The Board found no evidence that the grievor grieved any of these matters or moved them through the process; several were unrelated to employment or fell under PSEA staffing recourse (handled by the former PSST). Absent grievances presented at all levels, and lacking bargaining-agent support for collective-agreement (no-discrimination) claims, the Board could not assume jurisdiction. The conflict-of-interest allegations against the adjudicator were found incorrect, insulting and absurd.
conclusion: The Board held it was without jurisdiction to deal with any of these additional claims.

issue: Should the grievor be reinstated or awarded damages in lieu of reinstatement?
facts: In Gill No. 1 (2018 FPSLREB 55) the Board found the grievor was terminated without cause outside probation. The grievor stated he did not want to return to CSC or live in Edmonton; the employer preferred he not return. Seven years had passed since termination.
rule: Reinstatement is not an automatic right even after unjust dismissal (Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. v. Sheikholeslami; s. 228 of the Act). Pay in lieu is appropriate where the employment relationship is no longer viable (Alberta Union of Provincial Employees v. Lethbridge Community College, 2004 SCC 28; DeHavilland factors), as applied in Lâm and Bahniuk.
application: Given both parties' stated wishes, the passage of time and the broken relationship, the Board accepted the wishes and declined to order reinstatement, leaving only the determination of damages in lieu.
conclusion: Reinstatement was not ordered; damages in lieu of reinstatement were the appropriate remedy.

issue: How should damages in lieu of reinstatement be quantified given the grievor's duty to mitigate?
facts: Within about a year of termination the grievor secured a higher-paying position with the Fond du Lac First Nation (starting August 26, 2013), which also provided housing, exceeding his CSC income. He voluntarily left that position after a few weeks to move to another job, and thereafter held a series of short-term jobs, several yielding no income.
rule: A dismissed employee must take reasonable steps to mitigate and reasonably avoid future income loss (Michaels v. Red Deer College, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 324). Damages are calculated by reference to salary and benefits under the applicable collective agreement.
application: The Board found the grievor fully mitigated his loss when he secured the Fond du Lac position at a salary exceeding his CSC earnings; by voluntarily leaving it he acted unreasonably and failed to reasonably avoid future income loss. Damages were therefore calculated from the last date he received CSC pay (after 30 days' pay in lieu, i.e., from November 1, 2012) until August 23/26, 2013, totalling salary of $60,066.53 plus the Penological Factor Allowance of $1,666.66 = $61,733.19, less EI overpayment ($18,042 remitted to Service Canada) and usual deductions, plus pension contributions and interest under the laws of British Columbia. Claims for costs, financial hardship/divorce, lost opportunity/value of money, and miscellaneous medical/dental expenses were denied for lack of evidence or jurisdiction.
conclusion: Damages in lieu of reinstatement of $61,733.19 (less deductions and EI overpayment), plus pension contributions and interest, were awarded; all other damages claims were denied.

issue: Should the EPS documents and the grievor's income/tax documents be sealed?
facts: The employer entered EPS occurrence reports and related documents (Exhibit E-8) containing unproven allegations and information about uninvolved third parties, plus the grievor's ITRs, NOAs and T4s. Both parties requested sealing.
rule: The open-court principle applies to tribunal proceedings; confidentiality orders are governed by the Dagenais/Mentuck test as adapted in Sierra Club of Canada v. Canada (Minister of Finance), 2002 SCC 41, requiring necessity to prevent a serious risk to an important interest and that salutary effects outweigh deleterious effects (see Basic v. CAPE, 2012 PSLRB 120).
application: The EPS package contained information about persons unaware they were reported on or investigated; the tax documents contained personal financial information largely irrelevant to the proceeding, the relevant portions being reproduced in the decision. In each case the salutary effects of sealing outweighed the deleterious effects on openness.
conclusion: The Board ordered Exhibits G-12, G-15, E-8 and E-12 sealed.

issue: What standard of review applies to the Tribunal's determination on workplace disability discrimination?
facts: Stewart, terminated under the employer's drug policy after testing positive following a workplace accident, argued to the Tribunal, courts, and SCC that his termination was discrimination based on addiction. The appellant urged correctness review, saying legal issues arose regarding whether stereotyping is required for prima facie discrimination and when altering a workplace policy becomes 'impossible.'
rule: Reviewing courts generally approach human rights tribunal decisions with considerable deference; the tribunal's task is to evaluate evidence, find facts, and interpret its statute. Where a case involves applying settled legal principles to facts, reasonableness governs: Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9; Newfoundland Nurses, 2011 SCC 62.
application: The majority held that this case involves applying settled principles of workplace disability discrimination to a particular fact situation; the nature of the disability (addiction) does not change the legal principles. The debates were about facts and inferences, not law, matters within the Tribunal's purview. The alleged legal questions were essentially matters of applying accepted law to facts.
conclusion: Reasonableness is the applicable standard of review; the only question was whether the Tribunal's decision was reasonable.

issue: Was it reasonable for the Tribunal to conclude that addiction was not a factor in the termination, so that no prima facie discrimination was established?
facts: Stewart used cocaine on days off, did not disclose drug use, tested positive after his loader was in an accident, and was terminated under the 'no free accident' rule. Addiction is a recognized disability under the Alberta Human Rights, Citizenship and Multiculturalism Act. Expert evidence found he was addicted but retained capacity to make choices about drug use. The first two elements of prima facie discrimination were conceded; only whether addiction was 'a factor' in termination was disputed.
rule: Prima facie discrimination requires: (1) a protected characteristic; (2) an adverse impact; and (3) that the protected characteristic was a factor in the adverse impact (Moore v. British Columbia (Education), 2012 SCC 61; Quebec v. Bombardier, 2015 SCC 39). Discriminatory intent is not required; the ground need only be 'a factor.' No stand-alone requirement of arbitrariness or stereotyping exists.
application: The Tribunal found, based on the termination letter and evidence, that Stewart was fired for breaching the Policy—failing to disclose and stop drug use—not because of addiction, and that he had the capacity to comply with the Policy's terms. It unequivocally and repeatedly stated addiction was not a factor. The majority held there was evidence capable of supporting this factual finding; whether addiction diminished capacity to comply is a case-by-case, evidence-based question and cannot be assumed. Denial was irrelevant where Stewart had capacity to disclose and decide not to use. (Moldaver and Wagner JJ. and Gascon J. disagreed, finding the connection between dependency and termination made the no-factor conclusion unreasonable.)
conclusion: By majority, the Tribunal's conclusion that prima facie discrimination was not established was reasonable and attracted deference.

issue: If prima facie discrimination were established, did the employer accommodate the employee to the point of undue hardship?
facts: The safety-sensitive coal mine imposed a 'no free accident' policy to deter drug use; it offered pre-incident disclosure without discipline, treatment, and the chance to reapply after six months with partial funding of rehabilitation. Stewart argued he could not access disclosure because he was unaware of his addiction.
rule: Once prima facie discrimination is shown, the employer must justify the standard as a bona fide occupational requirement, showing it cannot accommodate the employee without undue hardship: BCGSEU (Meiorin), [1999] 3 S.C.R. 3; Hydro-Québec, 2008 SCC 43. Accommodation must be reasonable, not perfect (Renaud, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970); workplace safety is a relevant consideration (Central Alberta Dairy Pool).
application: The majority found it unnecessary to decide accommodation because no prima facie discrimination was established. Moldaver and Wagner JJ. held the Tribunal reasonably found undue hardship: given the safety-sensitive workplace, individual assessment or unpaid suspension instead of termination would undermine the Policy's deterrent effect. Gascon J. dissented, finding the offered accommodations either inaccessible (pre-incident disclosure, given denial) or post-termination (reapplication), and thus not accommodation in law.
conclusion: Majority: unnecessary to decide. Concurrence: accommodation to the point of undue hardship was reasonably found. Dissent: no genuine accommodation was provided.

issue: What is the role and standard the RAD must apply when reviewing an RPD decision?
facts: The IRPA sets grounds of appeal and remedies but does not specify the standard by which the RAD reviews the RPD. The appellant relied on Alvarez and Eng, urging that the RAD may intervene only for a palpable and overriding error, while other jurisprudence (Iyamuremye, Malhotra) endorsed a reasonableness standard.
rule: Section 111(1) IRPA; evolving Federal Court jurisprudence, culminating in Huruglica (2014 FC 799), which held the RAD is not to conduct judicial review or apply a reasonableness or 'palpable and overriding error' standard, but must conduct a 'hybrid appeal': an independent assessment of the claim, deferring to the RPD only where the lower tribunal enjoys a particular advantage (e.g. viva voce evidence).
application: The panel reviewed the divergent authorities and adopted the Huruglica approach, undertaking its own independent assessment of the evidence rather than merely reviewing the RPD for reasonableness, while affording deference to the RPD's credibility findings made after hearing the appellant testify.
conclusion: The RAD conducted an independent 'hybrid appeal' assessment, deferring to the RPD only on matters where it had a particular advantage such as viva voce credibility findings.

issue: Did the appellant establish that he is a genuine Christian convert entitling him to protection despite credibility concerns?
facts: The appellant, an Iranian, claimed he converted to Christianity after a relationship with an Armenian Christian, fled to Thailand where he was allegedly baptised, and feared harm from his family and his intelligence-officer brother. He could not name major Christian holidays unprompted, gave a baptism certificate in English naming a pastor different from the one he identified, and gave inconsistent evidence about his relationship and travel.
rule: Sections 96 and 97 IRPA; sincerity of religious belief is the crucial issue for a conversion-based claim; plausibility findings should be made only in the clearest of cases (Valtchev); a church-attendance letter does not itself establish sincerity of belief (Jin; Li).
application: The RAD found the RPD made several errors (misstating testimony about the girlfriend's holidays, the English-church attendance finding, the implausibility finding about leaving the Bible, and failing to address baptism photos/video). Nevertheless, on its own review, the weak knowledge of Christmas and Easter, the unresolved discrepancy in the baptising pastor's name, the English-language certificate, lack of contact or corroboration of the relationship, and inconsistent travel and departure evidence cumulatively showed the appellant was generally lacking in credibility and not a sincere convert.
conclusion: The appellant failed to establish a genuine conversion; he was found generally not credible, so neither his refugee claim nor his appeal could succeed.

issue: Was the RPD required to conduct a separate section 97 analysis?
facts: The appellant argued the RPD erred by not assessing his claim under section 97, where the risk test is objective, contending his profile could establish risk even if not credible under section 96.
rule: A separate section 97 analysis is not required where there is no evidence capable of establishing that the person is in need of protection (Fang, 2008 FC 856).
application: Because the RPD found the appellant entirely lacking in credibility and did not accept that he had converted to Christianity, there was no remaining profile of a Christian convert to assess under section 97, and objective evidence about the treatment of converts was irrelevant.
conclusion: No separate section 97 analysis was required.

issue: Did the Board member err by failing to consider the most recent country condition documentation regarding the treatment of Alevis in Turkey?
facts: The applicants, an Alevi family from Turkey, claimed refugee protection partly on the basis of their religion. The Member relied on a UK Operational Guidance Note that in turn relied on the US State Department 2010 Religious Freedom Report, concluding that Alevis practise their beliefs relatively freely. The decision was issued 70 days after the hearing, by which time an updated 2012 Report (contained in the Board's National Documentation Package) was available, containing substantially different information suggesting Alevis face persecution.
rule: A reviewing court will not undertake a detailed review of undiscussed documents, but must assess whether those documents could have affected the result; the test is whether the court is persuaded that an unreferenced document 'was clearly not material to the application or that it could not have affected the result' (Lee v Canada (MCI), 2009 FC 782).
application: The 2012 Report was a substantial rewrite that deleted passages supporting the Member's finding (e.g. that Alevis freely practised their beliefs) and added new information indicating societal abuse, discrimination, obstacles to establishing places of worship, and a violent attack on an Alevi family. This material was contained in the Board's own documentation package and directly contradicted the basis for the Member's conclusion. The Court was persuaded the 2012 Report was material and could have affected the result.
conclusion: The Member erred; the decision was unsafe to rely upon and the application was allowed.

issue: Did the Member err in giving little weight to the brother's corroborating testimony solely because he was a relative?
facts: The principal claimant's brother, Mustafa, had himself been accepted as a refugee based in part on ODP-related activities. He testified that he and Omer attended ODP meetings and were detained by police following a peace-day planning meeting. The Member asked him no questions and disposed of his evidence in a single paragraph, according it little weight because he 'cannot be said to be a disinterested party' and the claimants' own evidence was found not credible.
rule: It is not a sufficient basis to give testimony little weight only because the witness is a family member (Gonzales Perea v Canada (MCI), 2008 FC 432; Leonce v Canada (MCI), 2011 FC 831; Safi v Canada (MCI), 2005 FC 714).
application: The brother's evidence corroborated attendance at meetings of the very party the claimant said he supported, and his PIF was available to test that evidence given his prior accepted refugee claim. The Member gave the evidence little (in effect no) weight solely because it came from a relative, contrary to the established jurisprudence.
conclusion: The Member erred in her treatment of the brother's evidence, which was deserving of some weight; this reinforced the conclusion that the decision could not stand.

issue: What standard of review does the RAD apply to the RPD's findings of fact and mixed fact and law?
facts: The Appellant made no submissions on the role of the RAD. The RAD was reviewing the RPD's factual and mixed findings on state protection and persecution, none of which turned on the credibility of oral evidence.
rule: Per Canada (MCI) v. Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93, para. 103, the RAD reviews RPD findings of fact and mixed fact and law (raising no credibility of oral evidence issue) on the correctness standard, carrying out its own analysis of the record and providing a final determination.
application: The RAD followed Huruglica and conducted an independent assessment of the entire record, considering both counsel's documentation and the NDP evidence, to determine whether the RPD erred.
conclusion: The RAD applied the correctness standard and undertook its own analysis of the record.

issue: Should the more recent NDP be admitted as new evidence and did the RPD err by relying on the earlier package?
facts: The RPD relied on the 2014/2015 NDP in front of it at hearings held January 13 and February 3, 2016, and rendered its decision May 2, 2016. A new NDP package took effect April 29, 2016. Counsel argued the RPD should have used the newer package and cited pp. 211-286 without identifying material differences.
rule: Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA governs admission of new evidence on appeal; the RPD cannot cite documents not disclosed to counsel before rendering a decision.
application: The RAD found the RPD did not err because it would have had to disclose the new package before citing it. Although no proper application was made, the RAD admitted the document since counsel may have been unaware of its availability, meeting s. 110(4). However, the Appellant failed to point to any change relevant to the religious basis of the claim; the passage cited concerned impunity for law-enforcement abuses, not the religious component, so the newer package had no effect on the material aspect of the claim.
conclusion: The new evidence was admitted but had no bearing on the outcome; the RPD did not err in relying on the earlier NDP.

issue: Did the Appellant rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in Ukraine?
facts: The Appellant, a university-educated citizen of Ukraine, alleged police failed to respond to his concerns on three occasions but never brought his complaints to a higher-ranking office, the prosecutor's office, or any civilian oversight body, explaining only that 'the authorities are all the same in the Ukraine.' He relied on a witness from Crimea and on newspaper/internet reports.
rule: To rebut the presumption of state protection a claimant must provide 'clear and convincing' evidence of the state's inability to protect (Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689); the evidence must be reliable, probative and satisfy the Board on a balance of probabilities (Flores Carrillo, 2008 FCA 94); imperfect protection in a state controlling its territory does not rebut the presumption (Villafranca); the burden is proportional to the level of democracy (Kadenko; Hinzman, 2007 FCA 171); a failure to pursue reasonably available protection is usually fatal absent a compelling explanation (Camacho).
application: The RAD found Ukraine's security forces generally responded to societal violence and civilian authorities controlled and disciplined law enforcement. Reported abuses were tied to the Maidan protests, not to Jehovah's Witnesses, and 2015 reports showed investigations ongoing or before the courts. The Crimean witness was not similarly situated. The Appellant, being well-educated, could have researched and approached higher authorities but did not, giving no compelling explanation and providing no court documents or police reports.
conclusion: The Appellant failed to rebut the presumption with clear and convincing evidence; adequate state protection was available.

issue: Did the Appellant establish a well-founded fear of persecution as a Jehovah's Witness in Ukraine?
facts: The Appellant feared persecution based on his religion (Jehovah's Witnesses). Documentary evidence showed societal abuses were concentrated in Eastern Ukraine and Crimea, mostly against Jewish and Muslim communities; vandalism/arson to Kingdom Halls and assaults were infrequent (under 0.01% for most years); many incidents involved only a broken window with unclear motive.
rule: A claimant must establish, on a balance of probabilities, a well-founded fear of persecution under ss. 96/97 of the IRPA, supported by objective evidence linking harm to the protected ground.
application: The RAD, conducting its own analysis, agreed the government generally respected religious freedom, that abuses were not widespread or systemic and were regionally concentrated, and that the Appellant did not reside in the affected area. His testimony that incidents targeted him for his faith was often speculative, and he provided no corroborative documentation.
conclusion: The Appellant did not establish a well-founded fear of persecution; he is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

issue: Did the claimants rebut the presumption of state protection in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) against threats from an Islamic extremist group?
facts: The Christian claimants from Erbil in the KRI fled after the principal claimant was threatened by Islamic extremists following a workplace altercation, receiving two phone threats and experiencing a suspicious car incident. They never reported any incident to authorities before leaving on existing U.S. visas.
rule: States are presumed capable of protecting their citizens except where the state is in complete breakdown; the claimant bears the burden of rebutting that presumption with clear and convincing evidence. International protection is a last resort where no other recourse is available (Canada (AG) v. Ward, [1993] 2 SCR 689).
application: The panel found the KRI is not in a state of complete breakdown — it has its own elected government, security forces (Peshmerga, Asayish), and functioning law enforcement documented as effective and responsive to ISIS-type threats. While protection may be variable based on personal/political connections and somewhat limited for minorities, the preponderance of evidence showed a functioning police and security system. The claimants had no political connections that would exclude them and, critically, made no effort to seek protection, leaving no personal evidence that protection would be denied.
conclusion: The claimants failed to rebut the presumption of state protection against the threats they received.

issue: Do the claimants have a well-founded fear of persecution as Christians in the KRI, considering subjective fear and objective risk?
facts: The claimants described being called names, feeling afraid to wear certain clothing or attend church, yet continued to attend church, held long-serving government employment from which they retired, and had housing. They stated the discrimination was not serious enough to require leaving, and both had travelled abroad and returned.
rule: Persecution requires a 'sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights demonstrative of a failure of state protection' (Canada (AG) v. Ward). Discrimination must amount to serious harm — denial of a core human right — assessed individually. Sections 96 and 97(1) IRPA require a well-founded fear or risk on a balance of probabilities.
application: The claimants' own statements and their travel and return belied a subjective fear based on treatment as Christians. Objectively, documentary evidence (UNHCR Guidelines, Danish Immigration Service, RIRs) distinguished the KRI, where rights of religious minorities are generally respected, Christians worship freely, hold office, and where displaced Christians have sought refuge, from central/southern Iraq. Discrimination existed but did not deny the claimants core human rights.
conclusion: The claimants do not face more than a mere possibility of persecution as Christians in the KRI, nor a danger of torture or risk to life; no well-founded fear was established.

issue: Were there reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Mahjoub was a member of an organization engaged in subversion or terrorism under paragraph 34(1)(f) of the IRPA?
facts: Mahjoub, an Egyptian national and Convention refugee, worked in Sudan as Deputy Director-General of Althemar, a company owned by Osama Bin Laden, and managed the Damazine Farm where Al Qaeda conducted weapons 'refresher' training. In Canada he maintained concealed contacts (often via aliases) with Mubarak Al Duri, Ahmed Said Khadr and Essam Marzouk, found to be members of the Al Jihad (AJ)/Al Qaeda network, and with a VOC-linked number in Kuwait. His travels to and from Sudan coincided with the movement of AJ/Al Qaeda elements.
rule: Under s. 78 IRPA the designated judge determines whether the certificate is reasonable, applying the 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard (s. 33), which per Charkaoui v. Canada, 2007 SCC 9 and Mugesera v. Canada, 2005 SCC 40 requires an objective basis founded on compelling and credible information—more than suspicion but less than the civil balance of probabilities. 'Member' and 'organization' are given a broad, unrestricted interpretation (Poshteh; Sittampalam; Almrei (Re), 2009 FC 1263), requiring at least an 'institutional link' with or 'knowing participation' in the group's activities (Sinnaiah).
application: The Court found the AJ existed and engaged in subversion and terrorism, and that the VOC existed at least as a faction/military wing of the AJ with overlapping membership. Mahjoub's senior, trusted position in a Bin Laden enterprise where terrorist training occurred, his enduring concealed contacts with established AJ/Al Qaeda terrorists, his repeated use of aliases and untruthfulness with CSIS, the coincidence of his travels with AJ movements, one direct source identifying him as an AJ member, and his intercepted self-identification as a 'member' together supported reasonable grounds to believe he had an institutional link with and knowingly participated in the AJ and its sub-group the VOC. Many broader specific allegations (Mujahideen fighting, recruitment, Shura Council membership, the Islamabad bombing) were not established.
conclusion: The Ministers established reasonable grounds to believe Mr. Mahjoub was a member of the AJ and its splinter/sub-group the VOC; paragraph 34(1)(f) was satisfied, which was determinative of the reasonableness of the certificate.

issue: Were there reasonable grounds to believe Mr. Mahjoub personally engaged in or instigated subversion by force (34(1)(b)) or engaged in terrorism (34(1)(c))?
facts: The Ministers alleged Mahjoub arranged travel of AJ Mujahideen, recruited for the VOC and for training in Hezbollah/IRGC camps, participated in the 1995 Islamabad embassy bombing, and led the VOC's military wing.
rule: 'Subversion by force' means accomplishing change by illicit/violent means with intent (Qu; Oremade); 'terrorism' is defined in Suresh v. Canada, 2002 SCC 1 and by reference to the Criminal Code (Almrei; R. v. Khawaja, 2012 SCC 69). Each fact must be established on reasonable grounds to believe, resting on compelling and credible evidence; conflicting evidence is resolved by which version is more probable (Jaballah (Re), 2010 FC 79).
application: The direct evidence supporting these specific allegations was largely uncorroborated intelligence of questionable reliability that could not independently corroborate itself. The Court accepted Mahjoub was in Egypt until at least 1989 and found insufficient compelling evidence that he fought in Afghanistan, arranged Mujahideen travel, recruited members, or participated in the Islamabad bombing. It declined to infer engagement in terrorism/subversion merely from membership, absent established facts of personal participation.
conclusion: The Ministers failed to establish reasonable grounds to believe Mr. Mahjoub engaged in subversion or terrorism under paragraphs 34(1)(b) and (c).

issue: Were there reasonable grounds to believe Mr. Mahjoub was a danger to the security of Canada under paragraph 34(1)(d)?
facts: Mahjoub arrived in Canada in December 1995 as terrorist elements were scattering from Sudan, and maintained contact from Canada with AJ/Al Qaeda-linked individuals (including Canadian citizens Al Duri and Khadr) during the period the AJ joined the 'International Islamic Front' and issued a 1998 fatwa authorizing the killing of Americans and their allies, including Canadians.
rule: 'Danger to the security of Canada' is given a fair, large and liberal interpretation (Suresh, 2002 SCC 1) and requires proof of a potentially serious threat, direct or indirect, grounded on objectively reasonable evidence; support of terrorism abroad may raise a real possibility of adverse repercussions on Canada's security. The grounds in s. 34(1) are disjunctive, so membership does not automatically establish danger.
application: The Court held membership does not automatically make one a danger, but assessed the evidence in context: Mahjoub, as a member of the AJ/VOC, maintained active concealed contact with terrorists committed to killing Western allies, including Canadians, during a period when such operatives were establishing a presence in Canada. This established reasonable grounds to believe he posed a danger to Canada's security.
conclusion: The Ministers established reasonable grounds to believe that, as a member of the AJ and VOC with continued terrorist contacts, Mr. Mahjoub was a danger to the security of Canada under paragraph 34(1)(d).

issue: Was the security certificate signed under subsection 77(1) of the IRPA reasonable?
facts: The Minister of Public Safety and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration signed a certificate on February 22, 2008 certifying Mahjoub inadmissible on security grounds under s. 34(1)(b),(c),(d) and (f), referred to the Federal Court under s. 77(1).
rule: Under s. 78 IRPA the designated judge must determine whether the certificate is reasonable and quash it if not; the grounds under s. 34(1) are disjunctive, so establishing any one ground on reasonable grounds to believe upholds the certificate (Almrei (Re), 2009 FC 1263). The determination is a de novo, contemporaneous assessment of all open and closed evidence, not a judicial review.
application: Having found reasonable grounds to believe Mahjoub was a member of the AJ/VOC (34(1)(f)) and a danger to Canada's security (34(1)(d)), though not that he personally engaged in terrorism or subversion, and being satisfied he was reasonably informed of and able to meet the case against him, the single established ground under 34(1)(f) was determinative.
conclusion: The certificate was found reasonable; the parties were given time to propose questions for certification under s. 79 of the IRPA.

issue: Does s. 83.18 of the Criminal Code violate s. 7 of the Charter for overbreadth or gross disproportionality?
facts: Khawaja and his companion appellants argued that s. 83.18, combined with the definition of terrorist activity, criminalizes innocent, socially useful or charitable conduct only tenuously connected to preventing terrorism, capturing acts creating no real risk of harm.
rule: A criminal law is overbroad, contrary to s. 7, where the means chosen are broader than necessary to achieve a legitimate state objective (R. v. Heywood); gross disproportionality arises where the law's impact is so extreme as to be disproportionate to any legitimate government interest (Malmo-Levine; PHS Community Services). Statutory provisions must be read purposively and contextually (Ontario v. Canadian Pacific).
application: Purposively interpreted, s. 83.18 requires a high mens rea — the accused must knowingly participate or contribute 'for the purpose' of enhancing a terrorist group's ability to facilitate or carry out terrorist activity, a subjective specific intent that excludes unwitting or professionally legitimate assistance. The actus reus excludes conduct disclosing only a negligible risk: it captures only conduct a reasonable person would view as capable of materially enhancing the group's abilities. So construed, the section reaches only conduct with a non-negligible risk sufficiently connected to terrorism. Weighed against the objective of preventing and prosecuting terrorism, and with deference to Parliament's judgment that all aspects of preparation carry substantive harm, the means are not broader than necessary and the impact is not grossly disproportionate.
conclusion: Section 83.18 does not violate s. 7 of the Charter.

issue: Does the terrorism legislation, particularly the motive clause, infringe s. 2 of the Charter by purpose or effect?
facts: The accused argued the motive clause (requiring a political, religious or ideological purpose) would chill expression of beliefs and legitimize profiling based on religious or ideological views; the trial judge had severed it as an unjustified s. 2 infringement.
rule: A law may infringe a right by purpose or effect. Violence and threats of violence fall outside the s. 2(b) guarantee (Irwin Toy; Greater Vancouver Transportation Authority; Suresh; Dolphin Delivery; Keegstra). A chilling effect can sometimes be inferred, but must be causally attributable to the impugned law.
application: Most conduct caught by Part II.1 concerns acts or threats of serious violence, which are unprotected; s. 83.01(1)(b)(ii)(E), read purposively, is also confined to violence and threats affecting essential infrastructure. Thus the law's purpose does not infringe s. 2(b). On effect, no chilling effect could be inferred without evidence: any chill flowed from the post-9/11 climate, not the clause; a chill from a misreading cannot ground unconstitutionality because s. 83.01(1.1) expressly protects non-violent expression; and improper police profiling is an enforcement problem, not a legislative defect (Little Sisters). The clause is drafted respectful of diversity.
conclusion: The impugned provisions do not infringe s. 2; the motive clause is constitutional and should not have been severed. It was unnecessary to consider s. 1.

issue: Did the severance and re-insertion of the motive clause make the trial and convictions unfair?
facts: The trial proceeded with the motive clause severed; the Court of Appeal restored it and upheld the convictions under the curative proviso. The accused claimed he was convicted of different offences than those tried and that he would have testified had motive been an element.
rule: The curative proviso, s. 686(1)(b)(iii), cannot cure errors compromising trial fairness; generally, adding an essential element on appeal requires a new trial unless no prejudice results.
application: The trial judge made a specific finding that the motive component was proved beyond a reasonable doubt in any event. The evidence of the accused's extremist religious motivation, shared knowingly with the Khyam cell, was overwhelming and essentially undisputed. There was no air of reality to the claim he would have testified to raise doubt on motive, since motive remained a live factual issue at trial regardless. No prejudice flowed from re-inserting the element.
conclusion: The trial and convictions were not unfair; the Court of Appeal properly applied the curative proviso. This exceptional result rests on the overwhelming evidence of motive.

issue: Did the armed conflict exception to the definition of terrorist activity apply?
facts: The accused argued his conduct related to the insurgency in Afghanistan fell within the armed conflict exception and that the Crown had to disprove it beyond a reasonable doubt.
rule: Under s. 83.01(1) in fine, terrorist activity excludes acts committed during armed conflict in accordance with international law. The Crown bears the ultimate burden of proving conduct falls within the definition of terrorist activity, but the armed conflict exception functions as a defence the accused must raise with a prima facie evidential foundation.
application: There was no evidential foundation and no air of reality to the exception. The trial judge found the accused knew the Khyam group's activities extended beyond the Afghan conflict and supported those terrorist objectives; his conduct was not directed solely at an armed conflict. The evidence — including support for suicide attacks on civilians — was fundamentally incompatible with international law and the Geneva Conventions. Judicial notice of the Afghan conflict was proper.
conclusion: The armed conflict exception did not apply; the uncontradicted evidence established beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused's conduct was terrorist activity.

issue: Did the Court of Appeal err in substituting a sentence of life imprisonment and consecutive terms?
facts: The trial judge imposed 10.5 years with 5-year parole ineligibility, finding the accused a lower-level 'willing helper.' The Court of Appeal substituted life imprisonment on count 1, 24 years consecutive on remaining counts (concurrent to life), and 10-year parole ineligibility.
rule: General sentencing principles, including the totality principle (R. v. M. (C.A.)), apply to terrorism offences; s. 83.26 requires consecutive sentences; s. 718.2 makes terrorism an aggravating factor; denunciation and deterrence are important given the seriousness of terrorism.
application: The trial judge made three errors: unreasonably devaluing the seriousness of conduct inconsistent with evidence that the accused was a determined and eager participant building detonators and financing the group; failing to weigh the absence of evidence on rehabilitation prospects and continuing dangerousness; and misapplying s. 83.26 and the totality principle. The heightened gravity of the offences justified consecutive sentences exceeding 20 years without breaching totality, which only requires the sentence not exceed overall culpability.
conclusion: The Court of Appeal did not err; the appeal from sentence was dismissed and the substituted sentence affirmed.

issue: Did the trial judge err in excluding the Crown's expert evidence (Professor Mulé) on anti-gay tropes as unnecessary?
facts: At Mr. Whatcott's judge-alone trial for wilfully promoting hatred against gay men under s. 319(2), the Crown sought to call Professor Mulé to explain how the flyer exploited long-standing tropes of disease, immorality and danger to perpetuate anti-gay discrimination. The trial judge accepted Mulé was qualified, unbiased and relevant, but excluded the evidence as unnecessary (and, alternatively, as more prejudicial than probative), while admitting and heavily relying on the defence's religious-context expert (Professor Farrow) and a medical expert (Dr. Loutfy).
rule: Expert evidence is presumptively inadmissible; admissibility follows the two-stage inquiry in R. v. Mohan, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 9 (relevance, necessity, absence of exclusionary rule, properly qualified expert) and the gatekeeping cost-benefit stage in White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co., 2015 SCC 23. Necessity is not judged by too strict a standard and is met where the evidence provides information likely outside the trier's experience (Mohan; R. v. J.-L.J., 2000 SCC 51). An error in applying the legal standard for admitting expert evidence attracts no deference (Abbey; R. v. D.(R.), 2014 ONCA 302).
application: The court held the trial judge misconstrued the nature and purpose of Mulé's evidence. The question was not whether anti-gay discrimination exists (common knowledge), but how the flyer's text and images relied on tropes of disease, immorality and danger to promote hatred and how the targeted community would perceive them—connections a trier might not make alone (Ward v. Quebec, 2021 SCC 43). Just as expert help was accepted to interpret religious references like 'sodomite', similar assistance was necessary to assess references to HIV/AIDS, pedophilia and 'gay zombies' and the flyer's overall subtext. Admitting Farrow's evidence but not Mulé's produced an asymmetric, one-sided record. The alternative prejudice ruling also erred: Mulé's evidence did not attack the respondent's beliefs and any risk of misuse could be cured by instruction.
conclusion: The trial judge committed a legal error in applying the necessity criterion (and the prejudice balancing) and wrongly excluded the expert evidence.

issue: Did the error warrant a new trial?
facts: The trial judge's acquittal rested largely on an incomplete record that analyzed particular claims and images in isolation rather than the flyer holistically; the excluded expert evidence bore directly on the hate speech determination.
rule: To obtain a new trial from an acquittal the Crown must show with a reasonable degree of certainty that the error might reasonably, in the concrete reality of the case, have had a material bearing on the acquittal (R. v. George, 2017 SCC 38; R. v. Graveline, 2006 SCC 16; R. v. Morin, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 345).
application: Given the contextual nature of the hate speech test under Keegstra, Taylor and Whatcott (SCC), which requires assessing expression in parts and as a whole in context, the missing expert evidence affected the very record underlying the acquittal. With that evidence the verdict could well have been different.
conclusion: The error might materially have borne on the acquittal; a new trial on a complete record is required.

issue: Did the trial judge err on the s. 319(2) hate speech standard and in excluding prior discreditable conduct evidence?
facts: The Crown also argued the trial judge misapplied the hate speech test (missing additional hallmarks of hate) and wrongly excluded evidence of the respondent's prior social media posts and 2001 flyers as more prejudicial than probative.
rule: The objective test asks whether a reasonable person, aware of the context, would view the expression as exposing the target group to hatred (Keegstra; Whatcott (SCC), citing Owens v. Saskatchewan, 2006 SKCA 41); expression must be assessed in parts and as a whole; attacks on conduct integral to group identity can be a proxy for attacks on the group (Whatcott (SCC), paras. 121-124).
application: Because the appeal was resolved on the expert-evidence ground and the record was incomplete, the court declined to decide whether the trial judge erred in interpreting or applying s. 319(2), leaving a full analysis to the new trial. It likewise declined to condone or condemn the reasoning for excluding the prior discreditable conduct evidence, leaving that balancing for the new trial judge.
conclusion: These grounds were not decided; they are left for determination at the new trial on a complete record.

issue: Did the trial judge err in law by requiring the Crown to prove that 'gypsies' and 'Roma' were interchangeable terms rather than assessing the totality of the evidence to determine whether Roma were the target of the hate speech?
facts: The accused participated in a demonstration outside a Scarborough motel temporarily housing Roma refugee claimants. Placards and chants included 'Honk if you hate Gypsies', 'Canada is not a Trash Can', 'You're a cancer to Canada', 'Gypsies Out' and 'White power', with 'Sieg Heil' salutes and Nazi and Confederate flags. The information particularized the identifiable group as 'Roma'. The defence conceded Roma were an identifiable group historically persecuted by the Nazis, but argued there was no evidence linking 'gypsies' to 'Roma'. The trial judge acquitted, finding the Crown failed to prove Roma and gypsies were the same.
rule: Section 319(2) of the Criminal Code makes it an offence to wilfully promote hatred against 'any identifiable group', defined in s. 318(4) as any section of the public distinguished by colour, race, religion or ethnic origin. The constitutional validity of s. 319(2) was upheld in R. v. Keegstra, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697. Particulars define the factual transaction the prosecution must prove (R. v. McCune; R. v. Groot). The gist of the offence is the wilful promotion of hatred against an identifiable group; the trial judge must consider the totality of the evidence and draw appropriate inferences.
application: The relevant questions were whether the accused made some or all of the statements alleged and whether those statements promoted hatred of the Roma. It was unnecessary to prove interchangeability between the hateful terms used ('gypsies') and the group name in the information ('Roma'). The reference to 'gypsies' was but one item of evidence. The ethnic flavour of the demonstration, its location outside a motel housing refugee claimants described as Roma, the Nazi theme (salutes, flags, 'White power'), and the conceded fact that Roma were historically persecuted by the Nazis were all factors to weigh. By focussing entirely on one particularized statement and requiring proof of interchangeability, the trial judge misdirected himself as to the essential elements of the offence.
conclusion: The trial judge erred in law. The acquittals were set aside and new trials ordered.

issue: Should the trial judge have taken judicial notice of dictionary definitions showing a relationship between 'gypsy' and 'Roma'?
facts: The Crown presented five dictionaries, including the New Oxford Dictionary of English, whose definitions linked 'gypsy', 'Rom', 'Roma' and 'Romany'. The trial judge declined judicial notice, finding insufficient uniformity because some definitions referred only to male gypsies and some defence-provided definitions of 'gypsy' omitted reference to Roma, and because the issue was 'vital and highly contentious'.
rule: A court may accept without proof facts that are either so notorious or generally accepted as not to be subject of debate, or capable of immediate and accurate demonstration by resort to readily accessible sources of indisputable accuracy (R. v. Find, 2001 SCC 32, at para. 48). The dictionary meaning of words may fall within the latter category (Sopinka, Lederman and Bryant, The Law of Evidence in Canada).
application: The dictionary definitions showed that 'gypsy' can refer to an ethnic group properly known as 'Roma', 'Rom' or 'Romany'. This meaning was capable of immediate and accurate demonstration by resort to indisputable sources. The Court saw no reason why the trial judge should not have taken judicial notice of that fact and considered it, together with the rest of the evidence, in determining whether the respondents intended to target Roma.
conclusion: The trial judge should have taken judicial notice of the dictionary definitions and weighed them with the other evidence; his refusal was an error contributing to the flawed acquittal.

issue: Do ss. 7 and 10 of the Canadian Human Rights Act cover unintentional and adverse effect discrimination?
facts: CN introduced a rule requiring all employees at the Toronto coach yard to wear a hard hat. The rule was adopted for genuine business/safety reasons with no discriminatory intent, and applied equally to all employees. Bhinder, a Sikh whose religion permits only a turban as headgear, could not comply, and his employment ceased.
rule: Sections 7 and 10 of the Canadian Human Rights Act define discriminatory practices in employment. Following Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd., [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536, human rights legislation is remedial and its prohibitions extend to indirect/adverse effect discrimination, not only intentional discrimination.
application: The Court (per McIntyre J., with the Chief Justice concurring on this point) adopted the reasoning in O'Malley given the similarity of aims between the Ontario Code and the Canadian Human Rights Act. The hard hat rule, though neutral and equally applicable, had a discriminatory effect on Bhinder because compliance forced a compromise of his religious principles, unlike non-Sikh employees. Bhinder thus made out a prima facie case of discrimination.
conclusion: The definitions in ss. 7 and 10 extend to both unintentional and adverse effect discrimination; the majority of the Federal Court of Appeal erred in confining the Act to intentional discrimination. A prima facie case was established.

issue: Where a bona fide occupational requirement is established under s. 14(a), must it be assessed individually and carry a duty to accommodate?
facts: The Tribunal found the hard hat rule was, for non-Sikhs, a genuine, useful, reasonable safety requirement adopted in good faith, but held it was not a bona fide occupational requirement as applied to Bhinder because CN had not accommodated his religious needs short of undue hardship, which the Tribunal found was not shown.
rule: Section 14(a) CHRA provides that it is not a discriminatory practice where a limitation in relation to employment is established to be based on a bona fide occupational requirement. The Etobicoke test (Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Borough of Etobicoke, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 202) asks whether the requirement was imposed honestly and in good faith in the interests of adequate, safe, economical performance, and is objectively reasonably necessary.
application: The majority (McIntyre, Estey, Chouinard JJ.; Beetz and Wilson JJ. concurring in the result) held that an 'occupational requirement' is by nature a requirement for the occupation, of general application to the employee group, not susceptible to individual variation. A working condition does not lose its character as a bona fide occupational requirement merely because it produces consequential discrimination; where s. 14(a) applies, no discriminatory practice exists. To apply the requirement individually with varying results would rob it of its character and ignore the plain language of s. 14(a). Consequently, once established as a bona fide occupational requirement, s. 14(a) forecloses any duty to accommodate. Beetz and Wilson JJ. added that reading a duty to accommodate into 'bona fide' would nullify the section. Dickson C.J. and Lamer J., dissenting, would have held that the qualifying words 'bona fide' require justifying the imposition on the individual, incorporating a duty to accommodate short of undue hardship, consistent with the Act's remedial purpose and with Etobicoke.
conclusion: The Tribunal erred in law: having found the hard hat rule a bona fide occupational requirement, it could not exempt Bhinder from its scope. Section 14(a), once satisfied, leaves no room for a duty to accommodate. Appeal dismissed and matter remitted.

issue: Does conflicting federal safety legislation prevail over the Canadian Human Rights Act?
facts: CN argued the hard hat rule had the force of law under ss. 81, 82 and 84(1)(g) of the Canada Labour Code and related protective clothing and electrical safety regulations.
rule: Human rights legislation is fundamental, quasi-constitutional public law of general application that prevails over conflicting legislation absent a clear legislative exception (Winnipeg School Division No. 1 v. Craton, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 150; Insurance Corporation of British Columbia v. Heerspink, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 145).
application: The dissent (Dickson C.J. and Lamer J.) addressed this, holding that the Canada Labour Code and regulations create no exception to the CHRA and that federal legislation is inoperative to the extent of conflict, so that a rule necessary under the Labour Code is not ipso facto a bona fide occupational requirement under the CHRA. The majority found it unnecessary to reproduce or deal further with this argument, disposing of the case on the s. 14(a) point.
conclusion: The majority did not decide the issue, resolving the appeal on s. 14(a); the dissent would have held the CHRA prevails over conflicting federal safety legislation.

issue: Did the trial judge err in finding that the RCMP entrapped the accused and in staying the terrorism charges on that basis?
facts: Following a months-long RCMP INSET undercover operation involving 28 scenarios, Nuttall and Korody placed inert pressure cooker bombs (containing police-supplied C-4) outside the Victoria Parliament Buildings on Canada Day 2013. A jury convicted them of conspiracy to commit murder for a terrorist group and of making/possessing an explosive with intent for a terrorist group. The trial judge stayed the charges for entrapment on three bases: lack of reasonable suspicion when C-4 was offered, that the average person would have committed the offences (partly because the couple feared they would be killed), and a residual finding that the police manufactured the crime.
rule: R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903 establishes an objective test: entrapment exists where (a) police provide an opportunity to commit an offence without reasonable suspicion or a bona fide inquiry, or (b) having reasonable suspicion, they go beyond providing an opportunity and induce the offence; a residual category applies where police conduct otherwise exceeds propriety and manufactures the crime. Reasonable suspicion is more than mere suspicion but less than reasonable and probable grounds (R. v. Kang-Brown, 2008 SCC 18; R. v. Gingras, 2013 BCCA 293). Findings of fact are reviewed for palpable and overriding error (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33); stays are reviewed deferentially (R. v. Regan, 2002 SCC 12; R. v. Babos, 2014 SCC 16); questions of law for correctness.
application: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge made two errors: she wrongly found the police lacked reasonable suspicion when C-4 was offered on June 16, 2013 (Nuttall's active bomb-planning, downloaded Inspire instructions, shopping list and requests presumptively supplied reasonable suspicion per Gingras), and she wrongly found the average person would have planted the bombs, a conclusion resting on a finding that the couple feared they would be killed—a finding inconsistent with her own self-defence ruling (2015 BCSC 963) and based impermissibly on the accused's subjective beliefs rather than the objective police conduct. However, the Court held the third, residual basis was unassailable: the police knew the couple lacked the ability to commit terrorism, yet pushed them relentlessly, supplied the explosive, tools, transportation, location, and direction, chose the date and target, and manufactured the crime. Balancing fairness against the need to protect the public from serious terrorism offences, the police misconduct amounted to a manufactured crime and a travesty of justice.
conclusion: Appeal from the stays entered on counts 1 and 4 dismissed; despite errors in two of the three bases, the residual manufactured-crime finding supported the stay of proceedings.

issue: Did the trial judge err in directing an acquittal on the s. 83.19 facilitation count on the basis that principals cannot facilitate their own terrorist activity?
facts: Count 3 charged the accused with knowingly facilitating a terrorist activity, particularized as the placing of an explosive device at the Parliament Buildings. The trial judge directed a verdict of not guilty, reasoning that s. 83.19 targets persons on the periphery of terrorist groups and that principals cannot facilitate their own activity, so the Crown's principal-liability theory was not captured.
rule: Section 83.19 of the Criminal Code makes it an offence to knowingly facilitate a terrorist activity. 'Facilitate' means to make a matter easier, or to make it easier for another to commit a crime (R. v. Lindsay, 2009 ONCA 532; R. v. Legare, 2009 SCC 56; R. v. Khawaja, 2012 SCC 69). Where counts overlap, the trier of fact should deliver verdicts on all counts and the judge applies the rule against multiple convictions (R. v. Kienapple, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729; R. v. Provo, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 3).
application: The Court held the trial judge misread the particulars: the terrorist activity that was facilitated was the placing of the devices, so preparatory acts (buying pressure cookers and materials, scouting targets) could constitute facilitation. While a person cannot be convicted as both principal and facilitator of the same activity, and generally facilitation involves aiding another, where two people act in concert each could facilitate the other's act, and self-facilitation is not foreclosed. The count should have gone to the jury; any overlapping conviction would then be addressed by Kienapple. Because count 1 (conspiracy to murder) resulted in a conviction, a guilty facilitation verdict would have been conditionally stayed, and the entrapment finding would apply in any event, so a new trial would be an abuse of process (relying on s. 686(4), (8) and R. v. Hinse, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 597).
conclusion: Appeal allowed to the extent of setting aside the acquittal on count 3 and substituting a stay of proceedings; the trial judge erred but a new trial would be abusive.

issue: Did the trial judge err in instructing the jury not to consider count 2 if it convicted on count 1, and in staying count 2?
facts: Counts 1 and 2 both charged conspiracy—count 1 to murder persons unknown, count 2 to place an explosive with intent to cause death or serious bodily injury—both for a terrorist group and limited by the Crown to placing the pressure cooker devices at the Parliament Buildings. The trial judge treated the counts as one conspiracy with two objects, instructed the jury not to consider count 2 if it convicted on count 1, and entered a stay on count 2.
rule: Where there is one agreement with multiple unlawful objects there is a single conspiracy and the Crown need only prove one object (Cox and Paton v. The Queen, [1963] S.C.R. 500). Overlapping counts should be left to the jury with the judge applying the Kienapple principle and entering a conditional stay on the lesser count (R. v. Provo). On a Crown appeal from an acquittal or stay, the Crown must show a legal error and a reasonable degree of certainty that the result would not necessarily have been the same (Cullen v. The King, [1949] S.C.R. 658; R. v. Graveline, 2006 SCC 16; R. v. Jewitt, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 128).
application: Because the two counts alleged different objects (intent to murder versus intent to cause serious bodily injury), there was a route to acquittal on count 1 and conviction on count 2; the trial judge should have left both counts to the jury and applied Kienapple to any guilty verdicts, staying the lesser. Her instruction removing count 2 was an error. However, the result would be the same—a stay—whether under Kienapple or the entrapment finding, so the Crown could not show a real likelihood of a different outcome.
conclusion: Although the instruction was erroneous, the appeal from the stay of proceedings on count 2 was dismissed because the result remains a stay.

issue: Did the Federal Court of Appeal exceed the scope of its judicial review function by reassessing the IAD's findings of fact?
facts: The IAD (per Duquette) upheld the deportation order based on a detailed interpretation of Mugesera's 1992 speech. The FCTD upheld the incitement findings but set aside the crime-against-humanity finding. The FCA reversed several IAD findings of fact, rejected the reliance on the ICI Report and the rejection of Professor Angenot's interpretation, reweighed witness credibility, and set aside the deportation order.
rule: Judicial review of decisions under the Immigration Act proceeds under s. 18.1(4) of the Federal Court Act: questions of law are reviewed for correctness (para. (c)); findings of fact may be set aside only if made in a perverse or capricious manner or without regard to the material (para. (d)), the standard being patent unreasonableness (Aguebor). At the secondary level of appellate review, the appellate court's role is limited to determining, on a correctness standard, whether the reviewing judge selected and applied the correct standard of review (Dr. Q v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of B.C.).
application: The FCA showed no deference to the IAD's factual findings and conducted its own broad-ranging reassessment of the evidence, effectively applying a correctness standard to questions of fact. Duquette's interpretation of the speech was based on a careful review of all evidence, was well reasoned, and was reasonable. Since no reviewable error on the reasonableness standard had been demonstrated, the FCA should have proceeded on the facts as found by the IAD. By contrast, Nadon J. properly rejected as patently unreasonable the findings of Bourbonnais and Champoux Ohrt that murders resulted and that Mugesera was an Akazu/death-squad member, since no evidence supported them.
conclusion: The FCA erred by exceeding its judicial review function; the analysis must proceed on the IAD's findings of fact, including its interpretation of the speech.

issue: Did the speech constitute incitement to murder, genocide and hatred rendering Mugesera inadmissible under s. 27(1) of the Immigration Act?
facts: On 22 November 1992 Mugesera, a prominent MRND member, addressed about 1,000 people at Kabaya. Using violent language, he urged the audience not to be 'invaded,' to 'exterminate' opponents and Tutsi ('Inyenzi'), referenced sending Tutsi corpses down the Nyabarongo River (the 'river passage'), and warned that 'anyone whose neck you do not cut is the one who will cut your neck.' Roughly 2,000 Tutsi had been massacred between 1990 and 1992.
rule: Under ss. 27(1)(a.1)(ii) and (a.3)(ii) of the Immigration Act the Minister must prove on a balance of probabilities that the act would constitute an offence abroad and in Canada. Counselling murder not committed: s. 464(a) Criminal Code; the actus reus is met where statements, viewed objectively, are likely to incite and are made with a view to inciting the offence (Dionne; Sharpe), with intent to bring about the result. Incitement to genocide: s. 318(1) (incorporating the Genocide Convention); requires direct and public incitement plus specific intent to destroy an identifiable group; no proof of resulting genocide required (Akayesu; Media Case). Incitement to hatred: s. 319 requires promotion of the most intense forms of detestation (Keegstra), assessed objectively in social/historical context and by reference to the target audience (Buzzanga).
application: On the IAD's findings, the speech objectively was likely to incite and was made with a view to inciting murder of Tutsi and opponents; Mugesera intended that result given his knowledge of ongoing ethnic massacres. The 'river passage,' understood by the audience, directly and publicly advocated killing Tutsi with intent to destroy the group in part, satisfying incitement to genocide. The speech's violent language and references to past massacres promoted intense hatred of the Tutsi, satisfying incitement to hatred. The FCA erred by applying an abstract 'reasonable listener' standard (Prud'homme) and ignoring the target audience.
conclusion: All three offences were made out on a balance of probabilities; Mugesera is inadmissible under s. 27(1)(a.1)(ii) and (a.3)(ii).

issue: Are there reasonable grounds to believe Mugesera committed a crime against humanity?
facts: The same speech was alleged to be a crime against humanity. The IAD could not establish that murders actually resulted from the speech. Between October 1990 and November 1992 systematic, government/military-linked massacres and mass arrests targeted Tutsi and moderate Hutu, many in and around Gisenyi prefecture where the speech was given.
rule: Section 19(1)(j) of the Immigration Act requires 'reasonable grounds to believe'—more than suspicion, less than balance of probabilities, an objective basis grounded in compelling and credible information (Sivakumar; Chiau; Sabour)—applicable only to questions of fact; whether the facts meet the legal definition is a question of law. Under s. 7(3.76) Criminal Code, interpreted in light of customary international law (ICTY/ICTR jurisprudence), a crime against humanity requires: (1) a proscribed act with its physical and mental elements; (2) committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack; (3) directed against a civilian population; and (4) knowledge of the attack and that the act forms part of it. Persecution requires a gross or blatant denial of fundamental rights on discriminatory grounds equal in gravity to other enumerated acts, with discriminatory intent (Tadic; Kupreskic; Media Case). Finta is overruled to the extent it required discriminatory intent for all crimes against humanity.
application: Counselling murder could not qualify because no murders were proven to have resulted, as international law requires for instigation. However, persecution by hate speech qualified: the speech, advocating extermination in a volatile, massacre-prone environment, was a gross or blatant denial of fundamental rights equal in gravity to other enumerated acts, committed with discriminatory intent against Tutsi and moderate Hutu. A systematic attack (government/military-sanctioned pattern of massacres and arrests) was under way, directed against the civilian Tutsi and moderate Hutu population. The persecutory speech objectively furthered and fit the pattern of that attack, including geographic proximity in Gisenyi. Mugesera, educated and politically prominent, knew of the attack and that his speech formed part of it.
conclusion: Reasonable grounds exist to believe Mugesera committed a crime against humanity; he is inadmissible under ss. 27(1)(g) and 19(1)(j). The appeal is allowed and the deportation order restored.

issue: Does the MPA permit a 'two primary but equal purposes' hybrid classification of an asset, or must an asset be classified as either a business asset or a matrimonial asset?
facts: Mr. Wolfson owned controlling shares in a group of companies owning 21 rental buildings (257 units), with agreed equity ultimately valued at $13,908,662. He sought exclusion of the shares as business assets under s. 4(1)(e); Ms. Wolfson sought matrimonial classification. The trial judge found the companies were held for 'two primary but equal purposes'—an income-producing vehicle and a retirement vehicle—and split the value 50/50. Neither party proposed this approach and the judge did not alert them to it before releasing her decision.
rule: Under the MPA (R.S.N.S. 1989, c. 275) all property is presumptively matrimonial unless it falls within a s. 4(1) exception; business assets (defined in s. 2(a) as property 'primarily used or held for' a commercial/income-producing purpose) are excepted under s. 4(1)(e). Section 16 permits a declaration whether property 'is a matrimonial asset or a business asset'. Statutory interpretation follows Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes Ltd. (Re), [1998] 1 SCR 27 (words read in context, grammatical and ordinary sense). The classifying party bears the balance-of-probabilities burden (Clarke v. Clarke, [1990] 2 SCR 795; Tibbetts v. Tibbetts). Interpretation of the MPA is a question of law reviewed for correctness (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33).
application: The Court held the judge, while correctly recognizing the need to determine the 'primary purpose', erred by creating a novel category of assets that are equally matrimonial and non-matrimonial. 'Primarily' in s. 2(a) means principal or chief—only one purpose can be primary. The disjunctive 'or' in s. 16(1)(b) and 16(2)(b) links mutually exclusive alternatives, and the standalone structure of s. 4(1)(e) (unlike ss. 4(1)(a),(b),(c)) shows no legislative intent to permit a divisible business asset. Sections 13(f) and 18 presuppose that business assets are not divisible as such. No authority supported a dual-primary classification. Amending the business-asset exemption is for the legislature.
conclusion: The judge erred in law; the hybrid classification cannot stand. The classification was set aside.

issue: Was the finding that the companies were held for the equal primary purpose of a retirement vehicle a palpable and overriding error?
facts: The record contained extensive evidence that the properties were operated to generate income in an entrepreneurial sense and kept separate from family finances. Evidence of retirement intention was sparse—limited to affidavit statements about possibly living in one penthouse unit and contested testimony; Mr. Wolfson denied ever discussing 'cashing out' and spoke instead of a 'legacy' for his children.
rule: Factual findings and inferences are reviewed for palpable and overriding error—an error plain to see that has a material impact on the outcome (Laframboise v. Millington, 2019 NSCA 43). To qualify as a business asset the primary purpose must be income/profit generation in an entrepreneurial sense.
application: The sparse retirement evidence could not reasonably establish a 'primary' retirement purpose. The judge conflated 'legacy' with 'retirement' and over-relied on a discussion about personal use of one of 257 units. The record overwhelmingly showed the companies were owned, operated and managed to generate income; the retirement-vehicle finding was plain error affecting nearly $7 million in classification, hence overriding.
conclusion: Palpable and overriding error established; on the record Mr. Wolfson proved the disputed shares are business assets, excluded from division.

issue: Did the judge err in her s. 13 unequal-division analysis and in quantifying the award?
facts: The judge found equal division would be unfair or unconscionable and awarded $4,477,165 (or $1,000,000 if her hybrid classification stood), crafting the award to preserve the effect of her classification. She relied on s. 13(a) (unreasonable impoverishment) and s. 13(e) (date/manner of acquisition), among others.
rule: Section 13 permits unequal division or division of non-matrimonial property only where equal division would be unfair or unconscionable, proven by strong, convincing evidence (Donald v. Donald; Volcko v. Volcko, 2015 NSCA 11; Young v. Young, 2003 NSCA 63). Section 13 requires a two-step analysis (Donald; Archibald v. Archibald): first whether equal division is unfair/unconscionable, then what division would be fair and conscionable. The purpose is to alleviate unfairness, not redistribute wealth. It is an error to consider irrelevant factors, unenumerated factors, or to misclassify assets affecting the analysis.
