conclusion: S. was found to be, and to continue to be, a child in need of protection under s. 37(2)(b), (f) and (g).

issue: What disposition served the child's best interests — Crown wardship for adoption or return to the mother under supervision?
facts: S. had been in care nearly three years. The mother had completed numerous programs (parenting, anger management, Jean Tweed addiction counselling, Strengthening Families, the Thistletown Interface assessment, dyadic therapy), was compliant with antidepressant medication, had ended the relationship with Mr. RR, secured stable housing, and had consistent, positive, largely unsupervised access. S. consistently expressed a wish to return to her mother and to keep contact with her father and extended family, and did not want to be adopted. Assessors identified insight and capacity for change. The mother had, however, relapsed on marijuana on New Year's Eve 2010 and had not obtained a recent hair-strand test.
rule: The paramount purpose of the CFSA (s. 1) is the best interests, protection and well-being of the child, with best-interest factors in s. 37(3). Sections 57(2)-(3) require the court to consider the Society's efforts to assist and to be satisfied that less disruptive alternatives (e.g. a supervision order) would be inadequate before removing a child. The test is whether the parent has in fact changed and can now meet the minimum standard of care (Children's Aid Society of Winnipeg v. R.); parenting need not be perfect (minimum-standard test). Marijuana use is not in itself a protection concern absent evidence it impairs parenting (CAS of Toronto v. T.R.; CCAS of Toronto v. SS).
application: The court found the mother had made great strides, that a strong, meaningful and beneficial bond existed between mother and daughter, and that her fundamental parenting was adequate. The Society's evidence lacked direct observation of the mother-child relationship in her home and was treated with caution (per CAS of Toronto v. H.(B.)). Marijuana use, without evidence of impaired parenting, did not require removal; the residual risk of occasional use could be managed through a supervision order with drug testing, counselling, safety-plan and monitoring conditions. Crown wardship with no access, given S.'s age and wishes, would leave her in limbo.
conclusion: Crown wardship was refused; S. was ordered returned to her mother under a ten-month Society supervision order with detailed conditions, including a graduated transition and continued father access.

issue: Was an order of Crown wardship justified where less disruptive alternatives existed?
facts: The Society sought the most profound order available, Crown wardship with no access for adoption, on the basis of the length of time in care and the mother's historically sporadic engagement.
rule: Crown wardship is the most profound order a court can make and must be exercised with the highest degree of caution, on compelling evidence, and only after careful examination of alternatives (CCAS of Hamilton-Wentworth v. G.(J.)). The Society bears the onus, on the balance of probabilities but with clear and compelling evidence where access is to be denied (CAS of Oxford County v. D.T.). Section 57(3) bars removal unless less disruptive alternatives are inadequate.
application: The court held the Society had not shown that a supervision order would be inadequate, criticized it for not increasing access to test the mother's parenting and for failing to reassess as circumstances evolved, and found returning S. home with tailored supervision conditions adequately met any residual risk.
conclusion: Crown wardship was not justified; the least disruptive appropriate alternative — return under supervision — was ordered.

issue: Did Rosedale establish just cause for the summary dismissal of Mr. Geluch?
facts: Geluch, hired in 1985 as General Manager and Secretary/Treasurer, was fired on the spot on October 31, 1997 after board members interviewed a former employee (Anne Taylor) who described abusive and belittling conduct. Rosedale later alleged fiscal impropriety (a split salary advance, personal use of the club credit card, an unauthorized clothing allowance, and unadjusted financial entries), theft (furniture built by staff, food and wine taken), and abusive conduct including sexual harassment of staff. Geluch was given no reasons at the time and no opportunity to respond.
rule: An employer bears the onus of proving cause on a balance of probabilities, with heightened scrutiny for allegations of theft/dishonesty (Homer v. Roccha; Havens). Whether misconduct justifies dismissal is assessed by the contextual approach in McKinley v. BC Tel, [2001] 2 S.C.R. 161 — the misconduct must give rise to a breakdown in the employment relationship. Sexual harassment (Janzen v. Platy) may justify dismissal, but employers generally must investigate serious allegations and give the employee an opportunity to respond, and may need to warn before dismissing for lesser or condoned conduct (Wallace; Gonsalves; Simpson).
application: The court found the salary advance and clothing allowance were errors in judgment or bookkeeping, fully recorded and reviewed by auditors over years, not dishonesty; the auditor's credit-card report was unreliable and general ledgers were missing, so personal misuse was unproven. The alleged theft of furniture/food/wine was undesirable practice but not sufficiently serious or proven. Geluch's volatile, sometimes abusive style and the sporadic sexual innuendo toward Ms. Buell (1992) were deserving of a warning but not systematic abuse warranting dismissal. Rosedale ignored its own sexual-harassment policy, conducted no investigation, and never warned or disciplined Geluch, who received regular raises. The incidents did not amount to cause individually or cumulatively.
conclusion: Rosedale failed to prove just cause; Geluch was wrongfully dismissed.

issue: What is the appropriate period of reasonable notice?
facts: Geluch was 54, had served twelve years as General Manager, earned roughly $129,000, and took thirteen months to secure comparable employment in Vancouver.
rule: Reasonable notice is determined on the fact-based Bardal v. Globe and Mail factors — character of employment, length of service, age, and availability of similar employment — adopted in Wallace v. United Grain Growers.
application: Applying the Bardal factors to Geluch's senior position, long service, age, and the difficulty finding comparable work in a small industry, the court set the notice period at 15 months, noting the office manager had received 15 months' severance.
conclusion: Reasonable notice fixed at 15 months, with earnings from his subsequent job deducted.

issue: Is Geluch entitled to Wallace, aggravated, or punitive damages, and to vacation and mitigation compensation?
facts: Geluch was fired without warning, escorted out in front of staff during a colleague's retirement party, offered ten minutes to resign, given no reasons until February 1998, no reference or outplacement, and the President's later letter to members referred critically to former senior management. He also claimed 21 weeks of untaken vacation and moving/mitigation expenses.
rule: Bad-faith or unfair manner of dismissal extends the notice period (Wallace v. United Grain Growers). Aggravated and punitive damages require a separate, independently actionable wrong (Vorvis v. ICBC; Wallace); punitive damages require harsh, vindictive, reprehensible conduct (Whiten v. Pilot). The Employment Standards Act prohibits a 'use it or lose it' vacation policy.
application: The insensitive, hasty manner of dismissal and the negative message to members warranted a two-month Wallace extension. No separate actionable wrong (the only candidate, defamation, was not pleaded) supported aggravated or punitive damages. The statutory bar on forfeiting vacation entitled Geluch to $50,000 for 21 weeks; reasonable relocation/mitigation expenses were allowed at $8,000 (home-sale costs offset against capital gain).
conclusion: Two months' Wallace damages ($24,725) awarded; aggravated and punitive damages refused; vacation pay ($50,000) and mitigation ($8,000) granted.

issue: Is Rosedale entitled to recover on its counterclaim?
facts: Rosedale counterclaimed for the clothing allowance, personal airfare, and $500 for furniture built for Geluch with club materials on club time.
rule: A counterclaiming employer must prove its claim on the balance of probabilities.
application: Only the furniture claim was proven; Rosedale established that Geluch owed $500 for items built on club time using club materials.
conclusion: Counterclaim allowed in the amount of $500.

issue: Should Unrau's Statement of Claim be struck out as an abusive and vexatious proceeding?
facts: Unrau filed a Statement of Claim making bald allegations (defamation, theft of IP, abuse of process) that named none of the eleven defendants in its statement of facts, sought $5 million plus impossible remedies such as 'retroactive licensure', 'more open mindedness' and 'respect'. The Court, via Civil Practice Note 7, gave Unrau 14 days and up to ten pages to show a valid basis for the action. Unrau made no reply.
rule: Rule 3.68 of the Alberta Rules of Court permits striking out pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim, are frivolous/irrelevant/improper, or are an abuse of process. Pleadings composed only of 'bald allegations' (GH v Alcock, 2013 ABCA 24) that leave defendants unable to respond are vexatious and an abuse of process (kisikawpimootewin v Canada, 2004 FC 1426). CPN7 permits a paper-only show-cause procedure.
application: The Court had already found (Unrau #1) that the Statement of Claim was prima facie composed only of bald allegations, failed to identify the defendants, advanced unsubstantiated conspiratorial complaints, and sought impossible and disproportionate remedies. Given the opportunity to rebut, Unrau said nothing. Per CPN7 para 3(c), the pleading was therefore struck.
conclusion: The Statement of Claim was struck out as an abusive, hopeless and vexatious proceeding.

issue: Does the Court possess inherent jurisdiction, independent of statute, to impose vexatious litigant orders extending beyond the current dispute?
facts: The Court needed to determine the source of its authority to restrict Unrau's future litigation. Two competing lines of authority existed: a 'Traditional Jurisdiction' view (statute-only) and a 'Modern Approach' (statute and inherent jurisdiction co-exist).
rule: A superior court of inherent jurisdiction may act to prevent abuse of its processes (Jacob, 'The Inherent Jurisdiction of the Court'; BCGEU v British Columbia, 1988; R v Caron, 2011 SCC 5). Inherent jurisdiction is not ousted by statute unless in clear and unambiguous terms (Rose, 1998; Amato). Judicature Act s. 23.1(9) preserves the Court's authority. The Modern Approach (Ebert v Venvil; Bhamjee v Forsdick (No 2); Tupper; Grenier; adopted in Hok v Alberta #2) holds courts may screen anticipated/threatened litigation under inherent jurisdiction.
application: The Court surveyed extensive Commonwealth and Canadian authority, concluding the historical 'gap' in inherent jurisdiction was an error and that Judicature Act ss. 23-23.1 (with its 'persistence' requirement, no interim-order power, single remedy, and notice requirement) is inadequate for the post-Hryniak 'culture shift'. Section 23.1(9) shows the Legislature intended inherent jurisdiction to co-exist. The Court adopted the Modern Approach, under which prospective, proportionate court access restrictions are available under inherent jurisdiction.
conclusion: The Court's inherent jurisdiction provides a complete, flexible, and superior basis to impose vexatious litigant orders; statutory and inherent authority co-exist.

issue: Does procedural fairness require a separate vexatious-litigant process before restricting Unrau, or may the Court proceed immediately?
facts: Unrau had already been told in Unrau #1 that his pleading appeared abusive and exhibited multiple indicia; he was invited to respond and did nothing; he was also aware interim court access restrictions had been imposed. The question was whether Lymer v Jonsson required a further Hok v Alberta #2 two-step process.
rule: Natural justice requires an opportunity to be heard before an adverse decision (Lymer v Jonsson, 2016 ABCA 32; Kallaba). Procedural fairness is contextual and calibrated to the importance/impact of the decision (Baker v Canada, 1999). A leave requirement is a minimal, gatekeeping imposition, not an extraordinary denial of rights (Wong; Olumide v Canada; Trial Lawyers - no one has a right to abusive litigation).
application: Applying Baker, the Court held that a simple leave requirement only minimally affects rights (it screens, not bars, access), that legislative intent (Rule 14.5(1)(j)) treats such restrictions as proportionate, and that the audi alteram partem principle was already satisfied because Unrau had a full chance to respond in Unrau #1 and declined. A further step would be 'undue process' contrary to Hryniak. Lymer v Jonsson, resting on pre-culture-shift authority, was not treated as binding, and in any event Unrau was not 'surprised'.
conclusion: No separate process was required; the Court could proceed immediately to impose a leave-based vexatious litigant order (though more intrusive restrictions would generally require the two-step Hok process).

issue: Should Unrau be declared a vexatious litigant and subjected to global court access restrictions?
facts: Unrau's litigation record showed a 20-year campaign to practise dentistry without a licence: he had been enjoined (Alberta Dental Assn v Unrau, 2001 ABQB 24), found in contempt twice (2001, 2006), refused to acknowledge the Court's jurisdiction, and used litigation to seek delay. His 2018 claim expanded targets to NAIT, the City of Calgary, the FBI and Amazon, and added IP/hacking complaints, with no discernible pattern.
rule: A vexatious litigant order is appropriate where anticipated abusive litigation extends beyond a single dispute (threshold test). Orders must be explicit and enforceable by Court Clerks; where a narrow scope cannot be reliably enforced, the Court should 'default broad' (Biley v Sherwood; Tupper). Rule 14.5(1)(j) automatically extends restrictions to appeals.
application: Unrau's disobedience of orders, refusal to accept jurisdiction, expanding and unfocused target list, and obsessive objective made future abusive litigation across multiple disputes plausible, satisfying the threshold test. Because his targets were unpredictable, no narrow enforceable order was possible, so a global leave requirement across all three Alberta courts was warranted. A simple leave requirement (no additional intrusive steps) was proportionate; fee waivers were revoked and ancillary clauses added.
conclusion: Unrau was declared a vexatious litigant and made subject to a global leave-based court access restriction order; the interim order was vacated and no costs were imposed as the matter proceeded on the Court's own motion.

issue: What is the fit and proportionate global sentence for the offender's terrorism offences?
facts: Mr. Althorpe pleaded guilty to facilitating terrorist activity (s. 83.19(1)), instructing terrorist activity (s. 83.22), and wilfully promoting hatred as a terrorism offence (s. 319(2)/s. 83.2). Over roughly a decade he was a leading proponent of militant accelerationism, produced three Atomwaffen Division propaganda/recruitment videos, co-authored and published three influential Terrorgram manifestos (Militant Accelerationism, Do It for the 'Gram, The Hard Reset) advocating mass-casualty attacks and genocide against Jewish, Muslim, Black, LGBTQ+ and other groups, and led a neo-Nazi 'Active Club'. At least six attacks or plots, including fatal shootings, were inspired by the Terrorgram publications. He pleaded guilty, expressed remorse, had no record, was 18 when he began, suffered childhood abuse and had borderline personality disorder, but Dr. Iosif questioned the depth of his reform and noted he admitted 'I am the same racist guy.'
rule: Sentencing is governed by ss. 718–718.2 of the Criminal Code, with proportionality under s. 718.1 and aggravation for hate motivation (s. 718.2(a)(i)) and terrorism (s. 718.2(a)(v)). Terrorism cases are not a distinct class (R. v. Khawaja, 2012 SCC 69), but denunciation and deterrence are paramount because of the unusual gravity of terrorism (R. v. Esseghaier; R. v. Khawaja). Where terrorist activity is designed to or likely to result in the indiscriminate killing of innocent people, serious consideration should be given to life sentences, and where life is not called for, to sentences exceeding 20 years (R. v. Khalid, 2010 ONCA 861, para. 34). Rehabilitation is a mitigating factor but rigid ideology may support an inference of ongoing dangerousness. Consecutive sentences are required by s. 83.26 and the totality principle applies (R. v. Ahmed, 2017 ONCA 76).
application: The court rejected defence counsel's characterization of the offender as a mere 'ideologist,' finding his talk and messages actually caused death and injury and that his materials were designed to or likely to result in indiscriminate killing. Aggravating factors included his leadership role, decade-long commitment, recruitment and instruction of others, six documented inspired attacks, and continuing risk. Mitigating factors included the guilty plea, expressed remorse and claimed renunciation, absence of a record, youth at onset, difficult upbringing, personality disorder (no causal link found), family support, and harsh custodial conditions. The court distinguished Ahmed (12 years), Ahmad (16 years) and MacDonald (10 years, no proven consequences) as less serious. It found the starting point and appropriate range to be 20 years to life; a trial conviction would likely have attracted life. It imposed a global 20 years (Count 2: 6 years; Count 5: 10 years consecutive; Count 7: 4 years consecutive), less 48 months' combined Summers and Duncan credit, leaving 16 years to serve.
conclusion: A global sentence of 20 years' imprisonment (240 months) was imposed, reduced by 48 months' pre-sentence credit to 16 years (192 months) remaining, with ancillary lifetime weapons prohibition, DNA, non-communication and forfeiture orders.

issue: Should the mandatory-parole-ineligibility presumption in s. 743.6(1.2) be applied or displaced?
facts: Mr. Althorpe received a terrorism sentence exceeding two years, engaging the presumption that he serve one-half of the sentence (or ten years, whichever is less) before full parole eligibility. He had participated in numerous institutional programs, showed motivation to reintegrate, had no misconduct infractions, and Dr. Iosif opined he was not antisocial, was not without remorse, and would benefit from therapy not yet available to him.
rule: Section 743.6(1.2) creates a presumption of one-half parole ineligibility for terrorism sentences, displaceable where the court is satisfied that denunciation and specific/general deterrence would be adequately served by ineligibility under the Corrections and Conditional Release Act; s. 743.6(2) makes denunciation and deterrence paramount with rehabilitation subordinate. The offender bears the onus on a balance of probabilities (R. v. Khalid; R. v. Ahmed).
application: The court found the offender met the onus. Dr. Iosif's assessment that he was not antisocial, led a responsible lifestyle apart from these offences, was not without remorse, and would do well in therapy, together with his extensive programming and apparent motivation to be pro-social, satisfied the court that deterrence objectives would be adequately met without the extended ineligibility. It reasoned that the Parole Board would be best positioned to assess his rehabilitative progress, noting this did not guarantee early release but only allowed an earlier application.
conclusion: The presumption was displaced; Mr. Althorpe is not required to serve one-half of his sentence before applying for parole under s. 743.6(1.2).

issue: Is the Act respecting the laicity of the State intra vires the province under the division of legislative powers?
facts: Bill 21 affirms the laicity of the Quebec State, prohibits certain state agents (Schedule II) from wearing religious symbols, and requires certain persons to exercise functions and receive services with their face uncovered. It contains no penal or criminal sanctions. Opponents argued it is criminal law (s. 91(27)) or falls under Parliament's residual POGG power.
rule: A statute challenged under ss. 91-92 of the Constitution Act, 1867 must be characterized by its pith and substance (purpose and effects, using intrinsic and extrinsic evidence) and then classified under a head of power (Murray-Hall v. Quebec (A.G.), 2023 SCC 10; References re Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act, 2021 SCC 11). There is no general or inherent connection between religion and criminal law.
application: The Court held the Act's pith and substance is to affirm state laicity as a fundamental principle of Quebec public law, establish its requirements and regulate the conditions for exercising certain state functions. The trial judge erred in characterizing ss. 6 and 8 as criminal-law-like, confusing purpose with means; the Act contains no penalty. The Act connects to s. 92(4) (provincial offices), s. 92(13) (property and civil rights) and s. 92(16) (matters of a local or private nature), and certain provisions to s. 45 of the Constitution Act, 1982.
conclusion: The Act is intra vires; the division-of-powers appeals fail.

issue: Can pre-Confederation statutes or unwritten constitutional principles invalidate the Act?
facts: Opponents relied on the Quebec Act (1774), the Rectories Act (1852) and the Hart Act (1832), asserting they enshrine supra-legislative principles of religious equality and freedom of worship that the Act violates, and on the notions of 'constitutional architecture' and unwritten principles.
rule: The supra-legislative character of imperial and colonial statutes was progressively eroded through devolution (Constitutional Act 1791, Union Act 1840, Colonial Laws Validity Act 1865, Statute of Westminster 1931, Canada Act 1982). Unwritten constitutional principles cannot serve as an independent basis to invalidate legislation; their role is interpretive and structural (Toronto (City) v. Ontario (A.G.), 2021 SCC 34). One part of the Constitution cannot invalidate another.
application: The Court traced the constitutional history and found none of these statutes retains supra-legislative status; they were never used on their own to invalidate legislation and have become obsolete or metamorphosed into ordinary statutes (e.g., the Freedom of Worship Act). Section 129 of the Constitution Act, 1867 is transitional and confers no constitutional status. The vagueness/rule-of-law argument failed because s. 6 provides sufficient guidance for legal debate (R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society).
conclusion: Neither the pre-Confederation statutes nor unwritten principles/constitutional architecture invalidate the Act; these grounds fail.

issue: Were the notwithstanding clauses validly invoked and does Ford remain binding?
facts: Sections 33 and 34 of the Act override, respectively, ss. 1-38 of the Quebec Charter and ss. 2 and 7-15 of the Canadian Charter, using standard wording. Opponents argued the use is subject to substantive requirements, must satisfy s. 1/Oakes, is barred by international law, and that Ford should be revisited.
rule: Under Ford v. Quebec (A.G.), [1988] 2 S.C.R. 712, s. 33 of the Canadian Charter lays down requirements of form only; there is no substantive review of the legislative policy behind the override. Stare decisis may be departed from only for a new legal issue or a change fundamentally shifting the parameters of debate (Bedford; Carter).
application: The trial judge correctly applied Ford. Section 1 does not apply to s. 33; the override defeats judicial declarations of inoperability. The simultaneous 'wholesale' use of both charters, the override of judicial/legal rights, and international-law arguments raise no new legal issue; the presumption of conformity cannot rewrite clear text. Alleged 'populism' and legislative attitudes do not fundamentally shift the debate and would require impermissible political judgment. Section 52 of the Quebec Charter requires only formal expression and is broader in scope than s. 33.
conclusion: Sections 33 and 34 satisfy the requirements of form; Ford remains binding; the challenge to the override fails.

issue: May courts review and declare infringements of overridden provisions and grant remedies despite a valid override?
facts: Opponents sought declarations that the Act infringes freedoms of religion and expression and equality rights, and the Lauzon Group sought damages, notwithstanding ss. 33-34.
rule: A valid override under s. 33 of the Canadian Charter or s. 52 in fine of the Quebec Charter removes the statute from the application of the overridden provisions and exempts it from judicial review of conformity with them; s. 24(1) and arts. 142 and 529 C.C.P. cannot ground a remedy where the underlying rights do not apply. Section 33 operates as a kind of 'constitutional privative clause' limiting s. 96 review. The doctrine of mootness (Borowski; Doucet-Boudreau) bars deciding questions with no practical effect.
application: Because the Act is exempt from the overridden provisions, the Court cannot review its conformity with them or grant declaratory or pecuniary relief; to do so would indirectly do what cannot be done directly. Subsidiarily, the question is moot: a finding of infringement would have no legal effect, and the adversarial context was deficient (the AGQ presented no s. 1 justification), so it is not in the interests of justice to answer. Pecuniary relief is also unavailable against the AGQ for constitutionally valid legislation.
conclusion: No judicial review of conformity with the overridden provisions and no remedy (declaratory or pecuniary) can be granted; these claims are rejected.

issue: Does s. 28 of the Canadian Charter (sexual equality) override s. 33?
facts: Opponents argued s. 28, operating 'notwithstanding anything in this Charter,' shields sexual equality from any override and prevents s. 33 from being used in a manner that disproportionately affects women (mainly Muslim women).
rule: Section 28 is an interpretive provision ensuring that the rights and freedoms in ss. 2-23 are guaranteed equally to male and female persons; it has no standalone normative value and is grafted onto those provisions. Its text, placement under 'General' provisions, and jurisprudence (Hess; Nguyen) confirm its interpretive purpose.
application: Since s. 33 permits the override of ss. 2 and 7-15, and s. 28 attaches to those very rights, once those rights are overridden s. 28 is stripped of its foundation and cannot substitute for them regarding sexual equality. Reading s. 28 as limiting s. 33 would create an insoluble logical contradiction (s. 28 cannot bar an override yet permit justification under s. 1) and would incongruously privilege sex over other s. 15 grounds. Section 50.1 of the Quebec Charter is treated the same way.
conclusion: Section 28 does not limit s. 33; it cannot stand in the way of the full application of s. 34 of the Act.

issue: Does the Act infringe s. 23 of the Canadian Charter (minority language education rights)?
facts: The trial judge held that several provisions, by restricting the recruitment of teachers/principals who wear religious symbols, infringed the English minority's right of management and control over its schools, tied to a 'culture' of celebrating religious diversity. Nothing in the Act affects the language of instruction; the quality and facilities of English schooling remain substantively equivalent.
rule: Section 23 is preventive, remedial and unifying, interpreted generously but faithfully to its text (Mahe; Arsenault-Cameron; Rose-des-vents; CSFCB). It protects the linguistic dimension of culture through the medium of the minority language, not all cultural manifestations; the right of management and control pertains to aspects of education affecting the minority's language and culture.
application: No s. 23 rights holder is deprived of a right; nothing in the Act touches the use of English in schools or the quality of instruction. The asserted 'culture' of promoting religious diversity is unrelated to language and would artificially constitutionalize a recent practice, extending s. 23 beyond its scope. Multiculturalism (s. 27) must be reconciled with s. 23, which protects only linguistic minorities. The trial judge gave s. 23 a scope it does not have.
conclusion: The Act does not infringe s. 23; the Trial Judgment is reversed on this point (making s. 1 analysis unnecessary).

issue: Does requiring members of the National Assembly to have their face uncovered infringe s. 3 of the Canadian Charter?
facts: Section 8 para. 1, read with para. 1 of Schedule III, requires MNAs to exercise their functions with their face uncovered, which would prevent a person wearing a niqab or burqa from sitting once elected. Section 3 is not subject to s. 33. The AGQ led no evidence and made no submissions to justify any infringement under s. 1.
rule: Section 3 protects not only the right to vote and to be a candidate but the right to sit once elected, and contains no internal limits; any restriction must be justified under s. 1 (Harvey v. New Brunswick (A.G.); Sauvé; Frank). A stringent justification standard applies.
application: The combined provisions would prevent a person whose sincere beliefs require a face-covering from exercising the functions of an MNA, negating meaningful participation in the electoral process. A sufficient factual basis existed to decide the issue. The AGQ adduced no evidence and offered no s. 1 justification, so the Court could not undertake a s. 1 analysis on its own motion. By contrast, s. 6 with paras. 1 and 6 of Schedule II (President/Vice-Presidents, Minister of Justice) does not infringe s. 3, as those appointments/elections lie outside the electoral process protected by s. 3.
conclusion: Section 8 para. 1 with para. 1 of Schedule III unjustifiably infringes s. 3 and is of no force or effect; the trial judge's finding is upheld, while s. 6/Schedule II is found not to infringe s. 3.

issue: Did Chester owe and breach fiduciary duties to Morris in connection with the share sale, the bonuses, and the profit diversions?
facts: Morris and Chester built IWS from a horse-and-wagon scrap operation into a multi-million-dollar business as 50/50 partners and later equal shareholders. By long custom Morris ran operations and Chester controlled all financial and legal matters; Morris trusted Chester absolutely, signed whatever documents Chester put before him without reading them, and never monitored the finances. Without telling Morris, Chester declared $6.6M in 1981–82 bonuses (and $250,000 in 1979) largely to himself and his sons, permitted Robert to divert IWS profits to Greycliffe and other related companies, and orchestrated the purchase of Morris's shares.
rule: Partners owe each other fiduciary duties of good faith, disclosure of material facts, and avoidance of conflict of duty and self-interest (Lac Minerals; Hodgkinson v. Simms; MacDonald Estate v. Martin; Norberg v. Wynrib). A fiduciary relationship may also be found outside traditional categories where, given all the circumstances, one party could reasonably expect the other to act in his best interests, the touchstone being vulnerability/dependence.
application: As 50/50 partners and brothers, Chester prima facie owed Morris fiduciary duties, a point his counsel conceded until final argument. Applying Hodgkinson, Morris could reasonably expect Chester to protect his interests in financial matters in which Morris was wholly dependent and vulnerable. Chester breached those duties by declaring undeserved and undisclosed bonuses stripping IWS equity, by permitting and concealing profit diversions to Greycliffe and related companies, and by procuring Morris's signature on share-sale documents without disclosing that Morris was selling his shares or any of the material facts affecting value.
conclusion: Chester owed and flagrantly breached his fiduciary duties to Morris with respect to the share sale, the bonuses, and the profit diversions.

issue: Should the December 1983 share sale and lease be set aside for breach of fiduciary duty, undue influence, and unconscionability?
facts: In December 1983, while Morris was ill, preoccupied with an impending angiogram and open-heart surgery, and unaware that share-sale documents were even being prepared, he was called to the office of the family lawyer Ennis and signed a share sale of all his IWS shares for a nominal $3 million (of which he really received about $1.6M) and a 50-year lease at $2,000/month, far below market. IWS shares were then conservatively worth $8.7–$9M apart from stripped bonuses. Chester funded much of the price with Morris's own money (a gifted dividend and a reallocated bonus).
rule: Contracts may be set aside for breach of fiduciary duty, for undue influence (actual or presumed where a relationship of trust and a disadvantageous transaction exist: Geffen v. Goodman Estate; Barclays Bank v. O'Brien), and for unconscionability (inequality of bargaining power plus an improvident bargain: Morrison v. Coast Finance; Norberg).
application: The deal was manifestly unfair, improvident and one-sided. Morris reposed exceptional trust in Chester, was situationally weak and received no independent legal, valuation or tax advice; a presumption of undue influence arose and was not rebutted. Chester exploited an overwhelming imbalance of power to obtain a grossly improvident bargain, satisfying the test for unconscionability. Chester failed to rebut any of the presumptions.
conclusion: The share sale, lease and ancillary documents are set aside as products of breach of fiduciary duty, undue influence and unconscionability; the deal was patently unfair and manifestly disadvantageous to Morris.

issue: Is Morris entitled to an oppression remedy under s. 248 OBCA, and are Chester's sons liable for knowing receipt of the bonuses?
facts: Chester operated IWS as if he were sole owner, causing the corporation to declare a $1M dividend and reallocate $412,000 of Morris's bonus to fund his own share purchase, to lend him $500,000 interest-free, and to pay excessive bonuses to himself and his sons while excluding Morris and his son Michael from the business. Chester's sons received large 1981-82 bonuses funded by the Laidlaw/Lasco sale proceeds.
rule: Section 248 OBCA permits relief where corporate conduct is oppressive, unfairly prejudicial to or unfairly disregards a complainant's interests, protecting reasonable expectations, especially in closely held incorporated partnerships (Brant Investments; Naneff; Ballard; Ebrahimi). Knowing receipt requires a trust/fiduciary breach, beneficial receipt of property, and actual or constructive knowledge of the breach (Citadel; Gold v. Rosenberg).
application: Morris and Morriston had standing. Chester used IWS's resources to secure control and stripped its equity, conduct that was oppressive and unfairly prejudicial to Morris's reasonable expectation of 50% participation. The sons, active in the business and aware of the sale proceeds, had at least constructive knowledge that the bonuses were an unjustifiable distribution of Morris's equity, so they knowingly received them.
conclusion: Morris is entitled to oppression relief against Chester and IWS; Robert, Warren and Gary are liable for knowing receipt of the 1981–82 bonuses ($622,000; $936,000; $500,000 respectively).

issue: Did Chester, Robert and IWS induce Philip Enterprises to breach its contract with SWRI?
facts: SWRI (owned by Morris's sons) had a well-established subcontracting relationship with Philip. After Morris's dismissal and the litigation, Robert tampered with the Lasco documents to make it appear SWRI had cheated Philip, and IWS refused to release Philip from its counterclaim unless Philip stopped doing business with SWRI, also promising not to compete for the business. Philip terminated SWRI on 7 March 1989, the same day IWS discontinued its counterclaim against Philip.
rule: Inducing breach of contract requires a valid contract, the defendant's knowledge of it, an intentionally procured breach effected by wrongful interference, and resulting damage (Posluns v. TSE; Gainers/369413 Alberta v. Pocklington).
application: There was a valid, mutually beneficial contract of which the defendants were aware. Robert forged documents and, with Chester's involvement, used economic pressure and inducements to procure the breach; but for these acts Philip would have continued. SWRI's revenues collapsed from ~$3M to ~$267,000 the following year.
conclusion: Robert, Chester and IWS induced the breach; damages assessed at large at $2.5 million plus $100,000 punitive damages against Chester and Robert.

issue: Was Morris wrongfully dismissed / oppressively removed from IWS?
facts: On 26 October 1988 Linton handed Morris a termination letter ending his position as President and cutting off all family health benefits (Morris had a heart condition and his wife had just been diagnosed with cancer). No genuine cause was given; the alleged theft of accounts and diversion to SWRI was rejected because Chester/IWS had consented to SWRI's activities.
rule: An employer dismissing without cause must give reasonable notice (Bardal; Wallace v. United Grain Growers). Where dismissal forms part of a pattern of oppression it may also ground s. 248 relief (Naneff).
application: Morris was dismissed without cause; his employment was inextricably tied to his ownership, and the dismissal was part of Chester's pattern of oppressive conduct. Given his 45-year tenure, age, presidency and manner of discharge, a two-year notice period was appropriate; to avoid double recovery only salary (not drawings) was awarded.
conclusion: Morris was wrongfully dismissed / oppressively removed; damages awarded on a two-year notice period (salary only).

issue: Did the solicitor Ennis breach his duties to Morris, and were the auditors Taylor Leibow liable to Morris personally?
facts: Ennis had acted for Morris, Chester and IWS for over a decade. He took instructions on the share sale solely from Chester, never explained the documents or advised Morris to obtain independent legal advice, and obtained a waiver of independent advice only after the documents were signed. The auditors, engaged by IWS, omitted material related-party (Greycliffe) disclosure and prepared Morris's tax returns treating the staged share sale as completed.
rule: A solicitor owes fiduciary and contractual duties of care, disclosure and loyalty and must decline to act, or advise independent representation, in a conflict (Davey v. Woolley, Hames, Dale & Dingwall). Auditors generally owe their duty of care to the corporation collectively, not to individual shareholders, absent a specific assumption of a duty (Hercules Management v. Ernst & Young; Caparo; Roman Corp.).
application: Ennis should have refused to act; he breached his fiduciary and contractual duties by failing to disclose that Morris was selling his shares, failing to advise, and lending the transaction a veneer of normalcy — but for which Morris would not have signed. The auditors, by contrast, owed their audit duty to IWS, not to Morris personally, so policy considerations ousted any prima facie duty; the related-party claims were also barred by an agreement/undertaking, though negligence in the tax filings (had the sale stood) would have been made out.
conclusion: Ennis is liable to Morris for the same amounts as Chester on the share sale; the claims against the auditors are dismissed (they owed no personal audit duty to Morris).

issue: Does Obeah attract s. 2(a) Charter protection, and were the applicants' freedom-of-religion rights infringed by the undercover Obeahman operation?
facts: Police deployed Constable Cooper posing as an Obeah spiritual advisor ('Leon'), who befriended the applicants' circle, performed Obeah rituals, and elicited inculpatory statements by promising protection from the victim's evil spirit and from prosecution. The applicants sought exclusion of the recorded utterances, claiming interference with religious practice.
rule: Section 2(a) of the Charter protects freedom of conscience and religion. Under Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47, a claimant must show (1) a practice or belief with a nexus to religion and (2) sincere belief; courts assess sincerity, not validity. Per Big M Drug Mart and Edwards Books, only coercion/interference capable of restricting religious belief or practice engages s. 2(a), and the interference must be more than trivial or insubstantial.
application: Expert evidence (Drs. Henry and Clarke) established Obeah as a religious belief system meeting the Amselem definition; the uncontradicted opinion of a police officer that it was not a religion carried no weight. On sincerity: Pinnock showed scepticism and disinterest and did not sincerely believe, so his s. 2(a) rights were not engaged; Robinson demonstrated genuine, sincerely held belief, engaging s. 2(a). However, the fake Obeahman did not coerce Robinson to abandon or alter his worship — he encouraged the practice — so any interference was trivial or insubstantial. Seeking spiritual harm to enemies through a deity is protected (unlike Rowe, where secular criminal acts were solicited).
conclusion: Obeah merits s. 2(a) protection; Pinnock's claim failed at the sincerity stage and Robinson's failed because the interference was trivial and non-coercive. No s. 2(a) breach was established.

issue: If Robinson's freedom of religion had been infringed, was the police conduct a reasonable limit under s. 1?
facts: The undercover operation was aimed at solving a firearm homicide amid rising gun violence in the Toronto area, using a customized sting after other investigative avenues (including wiretaps) had been exhausted.
rule: Section 1 requires a pressing and substantial objective and proportionality per R. v. Oakes, 1986: rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality of salutary to deleterious effects (Dagenais; Thomson Newspapers). The Crown bears the onus.
application: Combating gun violence and solving a brutal homicide is pressing and substantial. Casting an officer as an Obeahman was rationally connected to obtaining admissions where physical evidence was lacking; the operation was carefully designed, confined to a few settings, and impaired religious freedom minimally. The salutary community benefits outweighed the minimal deleterious effects.
conclusion: Any infringement of Robinson's s. 2(a) rights would be justified as a reasonable limit under s. 1.

issue: Did the police tactics constitute a 'dirty trick' shocking the community's conscience?
facts: The applicants argued the Obeah impersonation was an abusive trick warranting exclusion of the evidence.
rule: Undercover tactics may be excluded where they amount to a 'dirty trick' that shocks the community and brings the administration of justice into disrepute (cf. Roberts; Unger).
application: Having found the investigation did not violate freedom of religion and was a proportionate, legitimate crime-solving measure, the same reasoning defeated the dirty-trick argument.
conclusion: The police conduct did not constitute a dirty trick shocking the conscience of the community.

issue: Were the applicants' s. 15(1) equality rights breached by an allegedly race-based investigative method?
facts: The applicants, black men of Jamaican heritage, argued the Obeah sting targeted them because of their race, colour and ethnic/religious background.
rule: Section 15(1) analysis (Law v. Canada; Lovelace) requires (1) differential treatment, (2) on an enumerated/analogous ground, (3) demeaning human dignity. Criminality is not an analogous ground.
application: The applicants were targeted because they were suspects in a violent homicide, not because of race; they received the same treatment other suspects would receive. Their Jamaican heritage merely made the Obeah technique feasible. No differential treatment on a protected ground was shown; the analysis failed at stage one, and in any event any breach would be saved by s. 1.
conclusion: No s. 15(1) violation was established.

issue: Were the statements to the Obeahman protected by common law religious privilege?
facts: The applicants claimed their inculpatory communications during the Obeah sessions were confidential religious communications.
rule: Religious privilege is assessed case-by-case under the four Wigmore criteria adopted in R. v. Gruenke, 1991: confidential origin; confidentiality essential to the relationship; a relationship the community should foster; and injury from disclosure outweighing the benefit to litigation (as applied in R. v. Medina). All four must be met.
application: Confidentiality (test one) was arguably present. But the applicants' purpose was to obtain protection from the victim's spirit and to obstruct prosecution, not sincere religious counselling, so tests two and three failed; there is no community interest in protecting statements aimed at evading justice. On the fourth test, the harm to prosecution from suppression outweighed harm to the Obeahman-adherent relationship.
conclusion: Having failed at least three Wigmore branches, the communications were not privileged.

issue: Does s. 93(1) of the Constitution Act, 1867 constitutionally guarantee full funding of Roman Catholic separate secondary schools, and is the Court bound by the Tiny case?
facts: Bill 30 proposed to extend full public funding to Roman Catholic separate high schools through to the end of secondary school. Since Confederation, separate school rights in Ontario had been understood not to include funding beyond the elementary level, an understanding rooted in the Tiny Separate School Trustees v. The King litigation (affirmed by the Privy Council in 1928).
rule: Section 93(1) protects only rights or privileges with respect to denominational schools that a class of persons had 'by Law' in the province at the Union (July 1, 1867); the guarantee is not expandable. The five-part test in A.-G. Que. v. Greater Hull School Board applies. Under stare decisis the Privy Council's Tiny decision remained binding until overruled by the Supreme Court of Canada.
application: Both sets of reasons treated Tiny as binding: the dissent found it conclusively established that s. 93(1) funding rights extend only to the elementary level, so full secondary funding is a matter of government policy, not constitutional right. The majority assumed Tiny binding but reasoned that s. 93 permitted the province to restore to separate schools the funded secondary education they arguably provided in 1867; in either view, providing full funding would not 'prejudicially affect' any pre-Union right and was within provincial power.
conclusion: The Court proceeded on the basis that it was bound by Tiny; the dissent held full secondary funding was not guaranteed by s. 93(1), while the majority held the province could validly provide it under its plenary s. 93 power.

issue: Does s. 29 of the Charter protect Bill 30 from Charter scrutiny as a right or privilege guaranteed 'by or under' the Constitution of Canada?
facts: Bill 30 was to be enacted after the Charter came into force under the province's plenary authority over education in s. 93. Its proponents argued the words 'by or under the Constitution' in s. 29 immunized it from Charter review.
rule: Section 29 provides that nothing in the Charter abrogates or derogates from any rights or privileges guaranteed 'by or under' the Constitution of Canada in respect of denominational, separate or dissentient schools. The Special Joint Committee proceedings were considered as interpretive aids (to be given minimal weight per Reference re s. 94(2) of the Motor Vehicle Act).
application: The majority (Zuber, Cory and Tarnopolsky JJ.A.) held that the words 'or under' (and the French 'en vertu de') extend protection to rights granted by provincial statutes validly enacted pursuant to the constitutional authority over education in s. 93, a reading supported by the Joint Committee record and by common sense; Bill 30, in its basic purpose and overall thrust, therefore received s. 29 protection. The dissent (Howland C.J.O. and Robins J.A.) held that only rights constitutionally guaranteed — the s. 93(1) rights existing at the Union — are protected; ordinary post-Charter statutes are not 'guaranteed,' and s. 32(1)(b) makes the Charter apply to all matters within provincial legislative authority.
conclusion: By majority, s. 29 shielded Bill 30 from Charter attack; the dissent would have subjected it to full Charter scrutiny.

issue: Does Bill 30's provision of full funding to Roman Catholic separate schools alone infringe s. 15(1) equality rights?
facts: Bill 30 conferred legislative grants, tax exemptions and property benefits on Roman Catholic school supporters for secondary education, while adherents of other religions who send children to denominational schools received no comparable support and continued to pay both public school taxes and private tuition.
rule: Section 15(1) guarantees every individual equality before and under the law and equal benefit of the law without discrimination based on religion, interpreted purposively (R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.) and consistently with s. 27 (multicultural heritage). Not every distinction is discriminatory, but the law must not favour one religion with benefits not comparably available to others.
application: The dissent held that funding one religious group's schools, without constitutional compulsion and without funding others, was discriminatory and directly conflicted with s. 15(1). Because the majority found Bill 30 protected by s. 29, it declined to decide the full implications of ss. 15 and 2(a), following Skapinker's caution against unnecessary Charter commentary.
conclusion: The dissent found a clear breach of s. 15(1); the majority found it unnecessary to decide the s. 15(1)/s. 2(a) question given s. 29's protection.

issue: If Bill 30 infringes s. 15(1), can it be justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
facts: The Attorney-General argued Bill 30 redressed a historical grievance, restored pre-Confederation equality between the two branches of the common school system, and served a large Roman Catholic segment of the population, while extending funding to other religious schools could fragment the public system.
rule: Section 1 permits reasonable limits prescribed by law demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society; the party upholding the law bears the onus and must show a sufficiently important objective and proportionate means (Big M Drug Mart).
application: The dissent held the Attorney-General had not discharged the onus: since Tiny established there was no constitutional entitlement, there was no unfulfilled 'Confederation bargain'; no evidence showed Roman Catholics' need was greater than that of other faiths, no evidence established a benefit to society at large, and the multi-party political consensus could not immunize the Bill from Charter review.
conclusion: The dissent held Bill 30 was not saved by s. 1; the majority did not reach s. 1 because it found the Bill protected by s. 29.

issue: Does granting a civil divorce under the Divorce Act, or the Act itself, discriminate against the respondent on the basis of religion contrary to s. 15(1) of the Charter?
facts: The parties married religiously and civilly in 1991 and separated in 2015. Ms. Jewitt, an Evangelical Lutheran, opposed the civil divorce, filing a pastor's affidavit denying dissolution of the marriage covenant and citing biblical passages that marriage is severable only by death.
rule: Section 15(1) of the Charter guarantees equality without discrimination based on religion. The two-part test (Kahkewistahaw First Nation v Taypotat, 2015 SCC 30; Andrews v Law Society of British Columbia, 1989) asks whether the law creates a distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground and whether it imposes a burden reinforcing disadvantage. Canadian law recognizes a distinction between civil and religious marriage/divorce (Divorce Act s. 21.1; Bruker v Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54; Syndicat Northcrest v Amselem, 2004 SCC 47). The claimant bears the onus.
application: A civil divorce dissolves only the civil marriage and leaves the religious covenant intact; secular courts cannot grant a religious divorce without unjustifiably entangling themselves in religion. The Divorce Act draws no distinction based on religion — the criteria apply equally to all. Denying the petitioner a civil divorce to accommodate the respondent's beliefs would instead impose her religion on him. Ms. Jewitt led no evidence of disadvantage to Evangelical Lutherans, and even a religious-freedom impairment would be outweighed by harm to the petitioner and the public interest in equality and autonomous choice (Bruker).
conclusion: No discrimination on the basis of religion; the constitutional challenge on this ground was dismissed.},{}}

issue: Does granting a civil divorce under the Divorce Act, or the Act itself, discriminate against the respondent on the basis of mental disability contrary to s. 15(1)?
facts: Ms. Jewitt asserted by affidavit that a civil divorce would exacerbate her already fragile mental health.
rule: Section 15(1) protects against direct and adverse-effect discrimination (Eldridge v British Columbia (AG), 1997; Adler v Ontario, 1996). A claim of adverse-effect discrimination requires an evidentiary basis linking the law to a disparate impact on the protected group; evidence must amount to 'more than a web of instinct' (Taypotat, paras 21, 34).
application: The Divorce Act draws no formal distinction based on mental disability; divorce is available to all who meet the criteria. Ms. Jewitt offered only her own belief that divorce would worsen her mental state, with no evidence that the Act has a disproportionate impact on persons with mental disabilities. This is insufficient under Taypotat to establish a distinction, and no evidence showed a burden reinforcing disadvantage.
conclusion: No discrimination on the basis of mental disability; the challenge on this ground was dismissed.

issue: If a s. 15(1) infringement were established, would it be saved under s. 1 of the Charter?
facts: Ms. Jewitt sought, as a remedy, that the Court decline to grant a divorce between the parties rather than strike down the legislation.
rule: The Oakes test (R v Oakes, 1986) requires a pressing and substantial objective and proportional means (rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionality). Section 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982 does not permit individualized remedies for unconstitutional laws; s. 24(1) provides remedial discretion.
application: The objective of the Divorce Act — providing a framework for dissolving broken-down marriages and ordering corollary relief — is pressing and substantial. Any infringement is rationally connected, minimally impairing (it legislates only civil marriage and cannot accommodate every religion or mental condition, balancing interests through corollary relief such as spousal support), and proportionate. Further, the individualized remedy Ms. Jewitt sought would not be available under s. 52.
conclusion: Any infringement would be saved under s. 1; and in any event the requested individualized remedy was unavailable.

issue: Does the Divorce Act conflict with the preamble of the Constitution Act, 1982 (supremacy of God) or with the Civil Marriage Act?
facts: Ms. Jewitt argued the preamble's reference to the 'supremacy of God' incorporates biblical permanence of marriage into Canadian law, and that the Civil Marriage Act's recognition of marriage as a fundamental institution conflicts with granting divorce.
rule: The 'supremacy of God' preamble prevents Canada from becoming officially atheistic but does not make it a theocracy or incorporate God's law into Canadian law (O'Sullivan v Canada, 1991; Pappas v The Queen, 2006; Mouvement laïque québécois v Saguenay (City), 2015 SCC 16). Statutory conflict requires actual inconsistency.
application: The preamble does not superimpose biblical scripture onto legislation and cannot favour one religion; so the Divorce Act's dissolution provisions do not conflict with it. The Civil Marriage Act was enacted to extend marriage to same-sex couples and amended the Divorce Act to give them equal access to divorce; it has no bearing on the availability of divorce and does not conflict with the Divorce Act.
conclusion: No conflict with the Constitution Act, 1982 preamble or the Civil Marriage Act; the constitutional challenges were dismissed.

issue: Does the Court have jurisdiction to grant a severed divorce judgment where one party contests the divorce, and has the respondent shown prejudice sufficient to refuse severance?
facts: Mr. Van Burgsteden met the divorce criteria (residency, over one year separation, no collusion, no reconciliation prospect), was living with another woman he wished to marry, and sought to sever the divorce from property and support claims. Ms. Jewitt, having caused numerous delays, opposed severance, alleging possible reconciliation and financial, professional and psychological prejudice.
rule: The Divorce Act (ss. 8, 10, 11) and Queen's Bench Rule 15-43 permit severance, which is discretionary (Rimmer v Adshead, 2002 SKCA 12; Yung v Yung, 2006 SKQB 388; Behnami v Mirakhori, 2013 SKQB 177; Theriault v Theriault, 2014 SKQB 423). Severance requires a genuine and substantive reason; opposition must be reasonable and mere lack of consent does not bar severance. Under s. 10, only a realistic possibility of reconciliation requires adjournment (Winstanley v Winstanley, 2009 MBQB 41; Pires v Pires). Courts assess legal, not general life, prejudice (Al-Saati; Spiring). A wish to remarry is a recognized ground.
application: Neither Rimmer nor Yung requires consent; severance may be granted over opposition where reasons are genuine. There was no realistic possibility of reconciliation given failed counselling and the petitioner's new spousal relationship. Religious opposition is not a bar (Qually, Baxter, Gordon, Acchione). The petitioner's wish to remarry and the lengthy delays largely caused by Ms. Jewitt supplied a genuine reason. Her alleged prejudice — inability to claim spousal maintenance against the estate on his hypothetical early death — was remote and theoretical (Spiring), and she could still pursue family property claims against his estate with priority over a new spouse (Family Property Act s. 51). Psychological, financial and professional harms are not the legal prejudice the analysis requires.
conclusion: The Court had jurisdiction to sever a contested divorce; Ms. Jewitt showed no sufficient legal prejudice. Severance was granted, the divorce judgment issued, remaining issues adjourned sine die, and costs of $3,000 awarded to the petitioner.

issue: Did the WSIB's failure to provide an Arabic interpreter, given the defendant's claimed lack of English proficiency, negate the actus reus or mens rea of the s. 149(1) offence?
facts: The defendant, born in Iraq and Arabic-speaking, listed 'Arabic' as his preferred language on the Form 6 but did not explicitly request an interpreter. He communicated in English with his WSIB Case Manager, Return-To-Work Specialist and health professionals. He used Google Translate and his wife's help to complete forms and answered questions in English at his interview and at trial before translation. He was provided an Arabic interpreter at trial.
rule: The s. 14 Charter right to an interpreter applies to court and quasi-criminal proceedings (R. v. Tran; R. v. Chen; R. v. Saini), and the claimant must prove need on a balance of probabilities. It does not extend to non-court dealings with a government agency. Under the WSIA, 1997 s. 178 only French-language services are guaranteed; the French Language Services Act guarantees French services. A failure to provide an interpreter for non-court services may engage the Human Rights Code (Fiordimondo) but not s. 14. WSIB decisions are governed by procedural fairness (Decision No. 1115/22R).
application: The court found the s. 14 trial right was satisfied and did not apply to the defendant's dealings with WSIB staff or physicians. Both WSIB witnesses credibly testified they had no difficulty communicating in English, rated his English 'very good (3/3)', and recorded 'No' interpreter requested; their contemporaneous memoranda were more reliable than his testimony given 20 months later. His ability to answer English questions without waiting for translation, and his use of Google Translate, showed adequate proficiency. Health professionals are ethically required to document interpreter use and none did, supporting the inference that communication was adequate.
conclusion: The absence of an Arabic interpreter did not negate the actus reus or mens rea and did not raise reasonable doubt; the defence argument failed.

issue: Did the prosecution prove the actus reus of the s. 149(1) offence — that the defendant made a false or misleading statement or representation concerning his functional ability?
facts: Between January 18 and February 28, 2024 the defendant repeatedly told his WSIB Case Manager, Return-To-Work Specialist and physicians that he had no improvement, could not lift more than 2–5 lbs, felt continuing pain and numbness, stayed home, and could not return to work. Surveillance video of February 22, 2024 showed him driving 91 km alone and lifting/carrying objects up to 40 lbs for about 15 minutes without a rest break; he was also observed at Double AA Woodworking Ltd. on several February days. Expert Dr. Krievens opined the observed activities were inconsistent with the documented restrictions.
rule: Under s. 149(1) of the WSIA, 1997 the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt a representation/statement was made concerning functional ability in connection with a benefits claim, that it was false or misleading, and (for mens rea) that the accused knew this and knew it could affect entitlement. 'Misleading' and 'misrepresentation' bear their ordinary/dictionary meanings.
application: The court found the defendant made numerous representations to WSIB staff and health professionals, and that the surveillance video and report (Exhibits 17, 18), corroborated by Dr. Krievens' expert opinion and the 'mild lateral epicondylitis' objective findings, demonstrated functional abilities far exceeding his stated limitations. His statements of no improvement/inability to work were therefore false or misleading and caused the WSIB to continue paying benefits (an overpayment of $12,753.89).
conclusion: The prosecution proved the actus reus of the s. 149(1) offence beyond a reasonable doubt.

issue: Did the prosecution prove the mens rea — that the defendant knowingly made the false or misleading representation?
facts: The defendant initiated the claim by filing Form 6, was granted benefits on February 2, 2024, was repeatedly told (letters of Jan 20 and Feb 2, 2024) that improvement or worsening had to be reported, and continued to represent no improvement while engaging in strenuous activity. He claimed February 22 was a one-time test of his abilities that left him in pain, but did not mention this to investigators on September 12, 2024 and raised it only at trial.
rule: Section 149(1) is a mens rea offence per R. v. Sault Ste. Marie because it uses 'knowingly'; knowledge may be inferred from surrounding circumstances (R. v. Aiello) and wilful blindness may substitute (R. v. Briscoe; R. v. Farmer). A person is presumed to intend the natural consequences of voluntary acts (D.P.P. v. Beard; R. v. Daley; acta exteriora indicant interiora secreta). A mistake of fact must be honest and have an 'air of reality' (R. v. Osolin); a claim first raised at trial may be a recent fabrication (R. v. Stirling; R. v. O'Connor).
application: The court inferred knowledge from the defendant's initiation of the claim, his awareness that continued reports of no improvement maintained his benefits, and the contradiction between his statements and the surveillance. His 'one-time test' explanation lacked an air of reality and was a recent fabrication because he did not raise it with investigators when shown the video, did not perform the test before his physiotherapist, and obtained no medical approval. His testimony was found not credible.
conclusion: The prosecution proved the requisite mens rea beyond a reasonable doubt.

issue: Was the prosecution required to prove the defendant knew of an obligation to report a material change to obtain a conviction under s. 149(1)?
facts: The defendant was charged under s. 149(1) (knowingly making a false/misleading statement), not s. 149(2) (wilfully failing to inform the WSIB of a material change within 10 days).
rule: Curtis v. Ontario (WSIB), 2018 ONCA 441 sets out the elements for the failure-to-report offence under s. 149(2), which requires knowledge of a material change and intention not to report. Section 149(1) is a distinct, positive-act offence and does not contain a reporting-obligation element; ignorance of the law is not a defence (Provincial Offences Act s. 81).
application: Because the defendant was charged under s. 149(1), the court held the prosecution did not need to prove awareness of a reporting obligation or of the eligibility rules; it needed only to prove a knowing false or misleading representation about functional ability affecting the benefits claim.
conclusion: No; proof of knowledge of a reporting obligation was not required, and the defence argument on that point failed.

issue: When may a director or officer of a corporate publisher be named as an individual respondent under s. 2(1) of the Act?
facts: The complaint against Alberta Report named the magazine's owner and three Byfields: Michael (author of the article), Link (editor/publisher who reviewed it) and Ted (founder and board member, who was neither author, editor nor publisher). The Panel asked whether merely holding a directorship or officer position suffices to be named.
rule: Section 2(1) prohibits any 'person' who 'publishes, issues or displays or cause[s] to be published' prohibited material. Human rights legislation is remedial and preventative, not punitive (Canadian National Railway Co. v. Canada (Human Rights Comm.), [1987] 1 S.C.R. 1114; Canada (Human Rights Comm.) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892), and must receive a fair, large and liberal interpretation. The Act does not impose vicarious liability; unlike other Alberta statutes (Business Corporations Act ss. 114(1), 218; Securities Act s. 168(1); Fair Trading Act s. 165(1)), it contains no language extending liability for mere knowledge or acquiescence.
application: The focus of s. 2(1) is on the conduct of the person, not their status or position. 'Cause to be published' must be given a broad reading capturing indirect involvement such as instigating or promoting a publication, so that individuals cannot shield themselves behind a corporation and frustrate remedial orders. However, some causal connection is required; a director cannot be liable simply by virtue of office. Dimmock (N.B.) was distinguished as concerning non-human-rights legislation and different facts. There must be prima facie evidence of the causal connection when the complaint is laid, subject to investigation, and individuals without such evidence should be struck.
conclusion: An individual director or officer may be named where there is prima facie evidence, on the face of the complaint or upon investigation, of a direct or indirect causal connection to the publication, issuance or display of the prohibited material; 'cause' is broadly defined and it is a question of fact in each case.

issue: Must a representation take a particular form to constitute an 'opinion' under s. 2(2)?
facts: Alberta Report relied on s. 2(2) ('Nothing in this section shall be deemed to interfere with the free expression of opinion on any subject'), and the parties disputed whether 'opinion' should be defined by form, by a defamation-law definition, or by content and context.
rule: Section 2(2) of the Act; interpretation of human rights legislation requires a contextual approach. Definitions borrowed from defamation law are too constraining for this remedial statute.
application: The court held that whether something is an 'opinion' turns on the content of the message and the context in which it is made and received, not on any particular phrasing, design or structure. Attempting to define the permutations of an opinion in the abstract would artificially restrict or expand s. 2(2). The near-impossibility of separating fact from opinion (illustrated by the Holocaust-denial exchange in oral argument) confirmed that no formal test could work.
conclusion: No particular phrasing, design or structure is required; whether a representation is an 'opinion' depends on its content and context, and is a question of fact in each case.

issue: Is s. 2(2) a bar to, or a defence or justification for, a breach of s. 2(1)?
facts: Alberta Report argued that once a representation is shown to be an 'opinion', s. 2(2) provides an absolute defence to any s. 2(1) breach. LEAF, the AACL and the Director argued s. 2(2) is not a defence but an interpretive/balancing direction; the true defences lie in ss. 2(3) and 11.1.
rule: Sections 2(1), 2(2), 2(3) and 11.1 of the Act; s. 2(b), 2(a) and 15 of the Charter; R. v. Keegstra, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697; Ross v. New Brunswick School District No. 15, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 825; Canada (Human Rights Comm.) v. Taylor (exemption clauses are best seen as admonitions to balance the eradication of discrimination against free expression); R. v. Mills, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 668 (one Charter right cannot trump another); R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103.
application: Treating s. 2(2) as an absolute defence would render s. 2(1) hollow, since a respondent could evade the Act simply by framing prohibited expression as opinion, and would improperly allow freedom of expression (s. 2(b)) to override freedom of religion and equality (ss. 2(a), 15), contrary to Mills. The genuine defences appear in ss. 2(3) and 11.1, which use markedly different language. Following Taylor, s. 2(2) is an admonition to balance the competing objectives. A two-step process is required: the Panel first determines a prima facie breach of s. 2(1) (proper application of 'hatred' and 'contempt' will itself achieve much of the balancing for s. 2(1)(b)), then directly balances free expression against the particular breach. The Oakes test is required only where the constitutionality of the legislation is challenged; otherwise a full, contextual, Charter-sensitive assessment suffices. The media enjoy no automatic exemption for reporting third-party statements but may rely on s. 11.1.
conclusion: Section 2(2) is neither a bar, a defence nor a justification; it is an admonition to balance freedom of expression against the eradication of discrimination. Defences lie in ss. 2(3) and 11.1. Balancing occurs indirectly through the proper application of s. 2(1)(b) and, after a prima facie breach, directly as a second step.

issue: What standards govern whether a representation is 'likely to expose a person or class of persons to hatred or contempt', and do 'hatred' and 'contempt' differ?
facts: The Panel needed guidance on the meaning of 'hatred', 'contempt' and 'likely to expose', and on which analytical test (the federal unitary test, or the British Columbia two-part test) applies under the Alberta Act.
rule: Section 2(1)(b) of the Act; Nealy v. Johnston (1989), 10 C.H.R.R. D/6450; Canada (Human Rights Comm.) v. Taylor (adopting the Oxford dictionary definitions: 'hatred' = extreme ill will, finding no redeeming qualities; 'contempt' = looking down upon, despising, dishonour or disgrace); Canadian Jewish Congress v. North Shore Free Press Ltd. (No. 7) (1997), 30 C.H.R.R. D/5; Collins v. Abrams (No. 3) (1999), 33 C.H.R.R. D/435.
application: The Taylor definitions of 'hatred' and 'contempt' are settled and ascribe different meanings, so different considerations apply to each. 'Likely to expose' focuses on the impact on the target group, not on whether any listener was persuaded. The court rejected the CJC 'likely to increase the risk of exposure' formulation as inconsistent with the Alberta wording, which uses a balance-of-probabilities 'likely to expose' standard, and rejected the federal unitary 'spark a reaction in listeners' test as focused on persuasion. It preferred a reasonable-person standard: whether a reasonable, contextually informed person would consider it more likely than not that the communication would expose the target group to hatred or contempt. The Abrams two-part test, modified to reflect the Act, provides a suitable analytical framework (not a rigid template), assessing both content and effect, and drawing on contextual factors such as content, tone, images, reinforcement of stereotypes, medium, circulation, credibility and vulnerability of the target group.
conclusion: The settled Taylor definitions apply, with different considerations for 'hatred' and 'contempt'; 'likely to expose' means, on a reasonable-person balance-of-probabilities standard, that the communication makes it more likely than not that the target group will be exposed to hatred or contempt. The test must be highly contextual and treated as an analytical framework, not a template.

issue: Were the impugned blog posts defamatory of the plaintiff, or was their defamatory sting lost because of the defendant's reputation as an outspoken provocateur?
facts: Between 2008 and 2010 the defendant, a lawyer and political blogger, published nine posts on ezralevant.com repeatedly calling the plaintiff, a law student and later lawyer, a 'serial liar,' imputing use of 'taqiyya' (deception), incompetence, unfitness to practise law, conflict of interest, and antisemitism. The defendant argued readers would not take his comments at face value given his reputation for stirring controversy.
rule: A defamatory statement is one that tends to lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of right-thinking members of society: Botiuk v. Toronto Free Press, Color Your World v. CBC. Under Grant v. Torstar the plaintiff must prove the words were defamatory, referred to him, and were published; falsity and damage are then presumed. The test of defamatory meaning is objective (per Binnie J. majority in WIC Radio v. Simpson, not LeBel J.'s minority view).
application: Publication and reference were admitted. Calling the plaintiff a 'liar' plainly cast doubt on his integrity — the most important attribute of a lawyer — and other posts imputed incompetence and antisemitism. The court followed Binnie J. in WIC Radio, holding that plainly defamatory words are not saved merely by the speaker's provocateur reputation. Although some speech might be so widely known to be unbelievable that its sting is lost, that was not this case.
conclusion: The impugned words carried defamatory meanings and lowered the plaintiff's reputation; the defendant's reputation did not neutralize them.

issue: Did the defences of justification, fair comment, and qualified privilege protect the impugned statements?
facts: The defendant relied mainly on fair comment, and to a lesser degree on justification and qualified privilege as a fair and accurate report of the quasi-judicial BCHRT hearing. The posts contained numerous factual errors (mis-describing Porter's questions, wrongly saying the plaintiff had trouble finding employment, calling him 'co-counsel' and a 'stand-in' for Dr. Elmasry).
rule: Justification requires substantial truth (Grant v. Torstar). Fair comment (WIC Radio) requires: matter of public interest; comment based on fact; recognizable as comment; and that any person could honestly express the opinion on the proved facts — with the factual foundation stated or known and true. Qualified privilege for reports of judicial/quasi-judicial proceedings requires a fair, accurate, balanced report (Brown; Hill v. Church of Scientology).
application: Public interest was conceded. The words 'liar' and 'lie' were stated as fact, not recognizable as comment, and appeared in headlines; even as comment they failed because the defendant did not prove the students made prior statements with a deliberate intention to deceive — a mistake or lapse of memory is not a lie. The posts were not fair and accurate reports because no witness said at the hearing that the plaintiff was a liar or deceitful, and the conflict-of-interest and 'co-counsel' assertions rested on untrue facts. However, references to 'shake down,' 'junior Al Sharptons,' bullying by abusing the courts, and 'waging war against our values' had adequate true factual foundations and were protected as fair comment.
conclusion: Most defamatory imputations (lying, deception/taqiyya, conflict of interest, antisemitism, fascism) were not defended successfully; only limited statements qualified as fair comment.

issue: Was any otherwise available defence defeated by malice?
facts: The defendant frankly acknowledged a campaign to 'denormalize' human rights commissions and held strong animus toward Dr. Elmasry, whom he equated with the plaintiff. He did little fact-checking, failed to correct errors (with one exception), and attacked only the plaintiff even though the alleged lies were joint statements of all four students.
rule: Malice is spite or ill-will, or any indirect or improper motive, including speaking dishonestly or in reckless disregard for the truth (Hill, para. 145). Proof of malice defeats both fair comment and qualified privilege even where honest belief exists (WIC Radio, para. 53).
application: The court found malice arose not from the anti-commission campaign but from the defendant's animus toward Dr. Elmasry, visited on the plaintiff, evidenced intrinsically by the eighth post and extrinsically by his failure to fact-check or correct errors. His dominant motive was ill-will coupled with reckless disregard for the truth.
conclusion: Malice was established, defeating the fair comment defence to the extent it would otherwise have applied to certain statements.

issue: What damages and remedies were appropriate?
facts: The action was brought under the Simplified Rules, capping recovery at $100,000. The plaintiff was at a vulnerable early-career stage; defamatory headlines surfaced in Google searches; the defendant published no apology or retraction.
rule: Damages are presumed on publication (MacRae v. Santa). Quantum factors include the plaintiff's standing, seriousness of the statements, mode and extent of publication, absence of retraction, and the defendant's conduct and motive (Barrick Gold v. Lopehandia; Hill). Aggravated damages address high-handed conduct increasing humiliation; punitive damages punish where compensatory awards are insufficient (Hill).
application: General damages of $50,000 reflected the serious attack on the plaintiff's professional integrity, the Internet medium, and lack of apology, while recognizing vindication flows chiefly from the judgment.
