Aggravated damages of $30,000 reflected malice, repeated 'liar' headlines, hyperlinking, uncorrected errors, and the defendant's status as a lawyer purporting to report a proceeding. Punitive damages were refused as the combined award sufficed for punishment and deterrence given the defendant was an individual, not major media. A take-down order was granted.
conclusion: The defendant was ordered to pay $80,000 ($50,000 general plus $30,000 aggravated) and to remove the defamatory words within 15 days; no punitive damages.

issue: Did Mr. Spira's persistent communications and conduct constitute civil faults of harassment and defamation under art. 1457 C.C.Q., and could freedom of religion excuse them?
facts: Over more than a decade Mr. Spira, an Orthodox rabbi, repeatedly wrote to Ms. Engel and her lawyer—including a 71-page 'lettre-fleuve'—insisting that her religious divorce (get) was invalid, that she remained an agunah, and that she was in a bigamist marriage, despite repeated demands and formal notices to cease all contact. He was convicted of criminal harassment by the Municipal Court in 2018. He argued his conduct was mandated by religious duty and protected by ss. 2 and 3 of the Quebec Charter.
rule: Article 1457 C.C.Q. imposes a duty to abide by the standard of conduct of a reasonable person; any injury to reputation, whether public or private, constitutes a fault sanctioned by compensation (Baudouin, Deslauriers & Moore). Freedom of religion (Syndicat Northcrest c. Amselem, [2004] 2 S.C.R. 551) protects sincere practices with a nexus to religion but is not absolute and cannot justify infringing others' rights (ss. 4 and 5 Quebec Charter). Findings of fact of a criminal court are not to be set aside by a civil court save exceptionally (Ali c. Guardian, 1999 CanLII 13177).
application: The Court found Mr. Spira's messages revealed an unremitting obsession; he knew Ms. Engel wanted no contact yet persisted, departing greatly from the conduct of a reasonable person. His freedom-of-religion argument failed: the Charter protects rights, it is not a carte blanche to commit a civil fault or to override Ms. Engel's own sincere belief in the validity of her get and her privacy and reputation. His s. 2 'right to assistance' theory and his claim that the federal Divorce Act was ultimately responsible were rejected as baseless. His relentless assertions that she was an agunah injured her reputation and were defamatory.
conclusion: Mr. Spira committed the civil faults of harassment and defamation; none of his defences succeeded.

issue: Did the Spira parents commit or participate in a civil fault against Ms. Engel?
facts: Ms. Engel alleged the parents encouraged and participated in their son's conduct, promised to stop him, hired and paid his lawyers, attended his trial, discussed the matter with about a dozen people, and that Alexander Spira publicly called her a 'moyser' (traitor) leaving the courtroom.
rule: Article 1457 C.C.Q.; a fault of abstention requires foreseeability of the wrongful act and a duty to intervene. Parents are not liable for the acts of an independent adult child not under protective supervision (Paré c. Bénard, 2017 QCCQ 1625). Where evidence is contradictory, the party bearing the burden of proof loses (De Serres c. De Serres, 2019 QCCA 1727).
application: The Court found Bonnie Spira tried to dissuade her son and sought the rabbi's help; supporting an adult child through litigation is not a fault. Allegations that the parents threatened to 'go public', endorsed the writings, or used a computer to send the letter were unproven (the screenshot P-7 was excluded under art. 2855 C.C.Q. for lack of proof of authenticity). Mr. Spira is an independent 41-year-old adult; his written claims of parental approval were merely his own interpretation. However, Alexander Spira's public insult ('moyser') was established and constituted defamation, though its extent was not proven.
conclusion: The parents did not participate in their son's faults; but Alexander Spira committed a fault by his insult, without associated damages.

issue: Did Ms. Engel establish the damages claimed and the causal connection?
facts: Ms. Engel claimed $25,000 in non-pecuniary damages, $42,001.95 in extrajudicial fees, and $2,312.40 in lost wages. She had assessed moral damages at $5,000 in her 2015 formal notice.
rule: Extrajudicial fees are recoverable only in rare cases such as abusive proceedings; the ordinary remedy is legal costs to the successful party. Non-pecuniary damages for defamation are assessed by the gravity of the act, intent, extent of dissemination, and the victim's circumstances (Baudouin, Deslauriers & Moore). Publication of the judgment can have a rehabilitative effect.
application: The Court awarded $20,000 for the harassment given the persistent intrusion, stress, anxiety and fear, adjusting for the low prospect of extrajudicial fees. For defamation it found only very limited dissemination beyond the Municipal Court judgment and awarded a lump sum of $1,000. No damages flowed from Alexander Spira's insult, which no one else heard. Lost wages of $2,312.40 were proven by employer letters and awarded in full. Extrajudicial fees were refused as the defendants had the right to defend without abuse.
conclusion: Ms. Engel was awarded $23,312.40 (against Mr. Spira only), plus interest and the additional indemnity from December 2, 2016, with costs; extrajudicial fees refused.

issue: Did the Spira parents establish that the action was abusive (art. 51 C.C.P.) or that the pleadings were defamatory, entitling them to their fees?
facts: The parents brought a cross-application seeking $36,159.65 in extrajudicial fees plus $20,000 in moral damages, arguing the suit against them was abusive and its allegations defamatory and designed to harm their reputation.
rule: Under art. 51 C.C.P. (Viel c. Entreprises immobilières du Terroir, 2002 CanLII 41120; Cosoltec c. Structure Laferté, 2010 QCCA 1600) abuse requires a proceeding that is clearly unfounded, frivolous, dilatory, or an abuse of the right to litigate. Defamation in pleadings requires allegations that are false, irrelevant and written with recklessness tantamount to malice (Berthiaume c. Carignan, 2014 QCCA 992). One must avoid finding abuse merely because a thesis is somewhat fragile.
application: The Court held Ms. Engel could reasonably have hoped to establish the parents' participation, so a trial was warranted; dismissal of her claim did not make it abusive. Although some allegations (e.g., the son's mental health, parental neglect) were unproven, she did not act maliciously or seek to defeat the ends of justice, and her pleadings did not amount to defamation.
conclusion: The abuse application and the cross-application were both dismissed, with costs.

issue: Was the purpose or effect of s. 28(4) of Reg. 262 to indoctrinate public school children in the Christian faith contrary to s. 2(a) of the Charter?
facts: Section 28(4) required two half-hour periods of religious education per week in public schools. The provision traced back to the 1944 regulation, whose implementing programme stated its aim as 'the acceptance of the historic Christian faith.' In Elgin County the curriculum was developed with the county Bible club and local clergy and, until the litigation, was taught largely from a fundamentalist Christian perspective. Over 90% of the county population was Christian.
rule: Under R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd. (1985), both the purpose and the effect of legislation are relevant to constitutional validity; an invalid purpose cannot be saved by effects, and the original legislative purpose does not shift with changing social conditions absent major amendment. Purpose may be assessed from historical background, legislative debates and official reports. Section 2(a) protects freedom of conscience and religion, which is characterized by the absence of coercion, direct or indirect, and safeguards religious minorities and non-believers from majoritarian religious imposition.
application: The Court, adopting Austin J.'s dissent below and the findings of the Hope Commission and Mackay Committee, held the regulation's original and continuing purpose was Christian indoctrination. Minor amendments and changed social circumstances did not alter that purpose. State-authorized religious indoctrination imposes majoritarian beliefs on minorities and creates a direct burden on religious minorities and non-believers, which the expert evidence of Dr. Freedman confirmed created real pressure and stress on dissenting children.
conclusion: The purpose of s. 28(4) was Christian indoctrination and it violated s. 2(a); even considered on its effects, the regulation was unconstitutional.

issue: Do the exemption provisions in s. 28 cure the infringement of s. 2(a)?
facts: Section 28(10)–(15) allowed parents to exempt a pupil, and a teacher to be exempt from teaching, religious education. Two appellant families declined to exempt their children for fear of ostracism and stigma; only about 124 of 8,100 pupils were excused in 1986-87.
rule: Following Zylberberg v. Sudbury Board of Education (1988), an exemption provision does not save an otherwise infringing religious provision where it imposes on religious minorities a compulsion to conform and stigmatizes those who use it.
application: The Court accepted Austin J.'s finding of an appreciable degree of coercion and inequality, and held, consistent with Zylberberg, that the exemption penalized pupils from religious minorities by stigmatizing them as non-conformists and setting them apart. The existence of the exemption also confirmed that the object was indoctrination rather than ordinary education.
conclusion: The exemption provisions did not cure the infringement and did not alter the indoctrinating purpose of the regulation.

issue: Is the board's religious studies curriculum governmental conduct subject to Charter scrutiny, and does it violate s. 2(a)?
facts: Three curricula were before the Court: the pre-1986 curriculum (conceded unconstitutional), the 1986-87 'interim' curriculum, and the 1988-89 curriculum. Despite added references to other faiths and stated non-indoctrinal aims, the later curricula retained Christian memory verses, prayers, Bible-story resources, worksheets affirming Christian doctrine, and clergy-led 'opt-in' instruction.
rule: Section 2(a) prohibits religious indoctrination but permits education about religion; the school may study religion but not sponsor its practice. The curriculum is governmental conduct authorized by s. 28(4), so if it infringes s. 2(a) the remedy is under s. 24(1) of the Charter, not s. 52(1). An infringement must not be trivial or insubstantial (Jones v. The Queen).
application: Applying the indoctrination/education distinction, the Court found the pre-1986 curriculum indoctrinating (as conceded), and that both the 1986-87 and 1988-89 curricula, despite sincere efforts to broaden them, continued to teach substantially from an exclusively Christian, devotional perspective and contained sufficient indoctrinating material that it could not be regarded as trivial or inconsequential.
conclusion: The curriculum was governmental conduct subject to the Charter and violated s. 2(a); a general declaration of inconsistency was appropriate and the board was enjoined from continuing to offer it.

issue: Can the infringement be justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
facts: The regulation and curriculum were found to have the purpose of indoctrinating children in the Christian faith.
rule: Section 1 only applies to a 'limit prescribed by law'; a measure whose true purpose is to compel religious observance/indoctrination cannot be justified (Zylberberg). Justification otherwise requires satisfying R. v. Oakes (1986), including rational connection and minimal impairment.
application: The curriculum was not a limit prescribed by law, so s. 1 had no application to it. Because the regulation's true purpose was Christian indoctrination it could not be justified. Even if s. 1 applied, indoctrination was not rationally connected to any legitimate objective such as inculcating moral standards, and the measures failed the minimal-impairment requirement, since moral values could be taught without trespassing on personal religious beliefs.
conclusion: The infringement could not be justified under s. 1.

issue: Does a public school division have public interest standing to challenge the constitutionality of funding non-Catholic students at Catholic separate schools?
facts: GSSD, a public school board, sued after Yorkdale closed Theodore's public school and a Roman Catholic separate school division was created that kept a school open with a majority of non-Catholic students, drawing per-pupil government funding away from public schools. The defendants argued GSSD, not being a holder of s. 93 separate-school rights, lacked standing.
rule: Public interest standing is governed by Canada (AG) v Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45: (1) a serious justiciable issue; (2) a real stake or genuine interest; (3) a reasonable and effective means of bringing the issue to court. Standing does not require the plaintiff to be a rights-holder; being genuinely 'affected' suffices (Protestant School Bd. of Montreal; Moose Jaw School District).
application: The Court found the funding question a substantial, novel constitutional issue never before decided; GSSD had a genuine interest given the loss of students, funding and educational efficiencies flowing from Theodore, and the broader 'mandate question'; and GSSD, backed by the Public Section of the SSBA and with the administrative resources to marshal a well-developed factual record, was an effective plaintiff, particularly since individual parents could not realistically fund such litigation and a proposed reference had been abandoned. None of Cromwell J.'s cautions (busybody, absence of contending views, judicial role) were triggered.
conclusion: GSSD was granted public interest standing.

issue: Is St. Theodore Roman Catholic School a legitimate separate school?
facts: The separate school division was created chiefly to keep a rural school open after the public school closed, with the idea originating from non-Catholic parents; the school has always operated with a majority of non-Catholic students but adopted Catholic attributes and instruction.
rule: The Education Act, 1995 and s. 17(1) of the Saskatchewan Act permit a religious minority (Catholic or Protestant) to petition to establish a separate school division; the Minister 'shall establish' it. Motive for creation is not determinative (Saskatchewan Rivers School Division No. 119 v Saskatchewan).
application: Although unusual, the Catholic minority followed the statutory process, the Minister had no discretion to refuse, and the school operated with a genuine Catholic mandate. The court declined to look behind the community's motives.
conclusion: St. Theodore is a legitimate, properly constituted separate school; GSSD's claim on this point was dismissed.

issue: Is funding of non-Catholic students at separate schools a constitutionally protected right under s. 93 of the Constitution Act, 1867 / s. 17 of the Saskatchewan Act, immune from Charter review?
facts: The defendants argued funding of non-Catholic students was either a right frozen under the 1901 Ordinances (s. 93(1)) or an augmentation of separate-school rights validly enacted post-1905 under the plenary power (s. 93(3)), and thus Charter-immune.
rule: Section 93(1) protects only rights existing at union that engage the 'denominational aspects test' (Greater Montreal; Mahe) — denominational aspects, or non-denominational aspects necessary to give effect to denominational concerns. Charter immunity for s. 93(3) legislation (Reference re Bill 30) likewise extends only to rights furthering the denominational character of separate schools (Hogg; Adler; Reference re Education Act (Que.)).
application: The court held the denominational aspects test applies to both s. 93(1) and s. 93(3), for four reasons: case law supports it; a contrary rule yields absurd temporal distinctions; it would give government carte blanche to evade the Charter (as attempted in Fancy); and the defendants pleaded the right as existing under the 1901 Ordinances, precluding a s. 93(3) 'thereafter established' argument. Examining the evolution of the School Ordinances, changing societal norms and Quebec/Privy Council authority, the court found the 1901 Ordinances neither expressly nor implicitly gave separate schools a right to admit and be funded for non-minority faith students, and any such practice was 'a matter of favour', not a denominational right. The essential purpose of separate schools is to separate minority children to be educated in their own faith, not to educate the majority from whom they separated.
conclusion: Funding of non-Catholic students is not a constitutionally protected denominational right; it is therefore exposed to Charter review.

issue: Does s. 17(2) of the Saskatchewan Act guarantee equal funding of non-Catholic students, disposing of the action?
facts: The defendants argued s. 17(2)'s prohibition on discrimination in the distribution of money among classes of schools required equal funding regardless of students' religion.
rule: Section 17(2) forbids discrimination in funding 'schools organized and carried on in accordance with chapter 29' of the 1901 Ordinances.
application: The provision presupposes schools serving their intended separate purpose; it does not answer the prior question of what funding separate schools are entitled to. Preserving 'separateness' (English Catholic Teachers) is a precondition; s. 17(2) cannot create a second, parallel publicly funded system or convert parental choice into a funding right.
conclusion: Section 17(2) does not guarantee equal funding for non-minority faith students and does not resolve the action.

issue: Does government funding of non-Catholic students in Catholic schools infringe ss. 2(a) and 15 of the Charter, and if so is it justified under s. 1?
facts: The government funds Catholic schools per-pupil for non-Catholic students but funds no other faith-based school for non-adherents; Muslim (Huda) and Jewish schools receive lesser or no such funding. Non-Catholic students are evangelized within Catholic schools.
rule: The state owes a duty of religious neutrality (Big M Drug Mart; Mouvement laïque québécois; S.L.); a law that on its face favours one religion breaches s. 2(a) and, concomitantly, s. 15 (Andrews; Withler). Justice Estey in Reference re Bill 30 held Charter breach 'axiomatic' absent s. 93 protection. Under Big M, where a law is unconstitutional on its face, no individual claimant need prove a personal infringement, and s. 52 renders it of no force. Section 1 is assessed under Oakes.
application: Because the funding is not constitutionally shielded, it must satisfy the Charter. Funding one faith to disseminate its teachings to non-adherents at public expense, while denying equivalent support to Muslim, Jewish and other faith schools, is a non-trivial breach of state neutrality and discriminates on the enumerated ground of religion; the impugned legislation is discriminatory on its face, so GSSD as an institution need not prove an individual's infringed belief. The defendants offered no pressing and substantial objective (equitable education and parental choice were either unconnected or themselves Charter-offending) and could not satisfy proportionality; the funding harmed public boards by thwarting rational rural school closures and did not minimally impair neutrality.
conclusion: The funding infringes ss. 2(a) and 15 and is not saved by s. 1. The relevant provisions of The Education Act, 1995 and Education Funding Regulations, insofar as they fund non-minority faith students at separate schools, were declared of no force and effect, with the declaration stayed until June 30, 2018.

issue: Did the plaintiff's notices satisfy the requirement in s. 5(1) of the Libel and Slander Act to 'specify the matter complained of'?
facts: CUPW complained of a July 24, 2014 Sun News broadcast (approx. six minutes, ~900-word transcript) and a July 28, 2014 Toronto Sun article (over 500 words) that allegedly linked the union to Hamas and terrorism. The notices described the publications generally as containing 'untrue, disparaging and defamatory statements' wrongfully inferring support for terrorists and Hamas, but did not quote specific words, whereas the statement of claim set out the impugned passages in detail.
rule: Section 5(1) of the Libel and Slander Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.12 requires written notice within six weeks 'specifying the matter complained of' as a mandatory condition precedent and absolute bar to a libel action (Grossman v. CFTO-TV Ltd., 1982 CanLII 1768 (ON CA)). Notice must make the defendant 'clearly aware' of the matter and give enough clear information to permit correction, retraction or apology; mere generalities are insufficient (Siddiqui v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp., 2000 CanLII 16920 (ON CA)).
application: The court found the notices identified the general tenor of the complaint (depicting CUPW as supportive of a terrorist organization) but did not sufficiently specify the impugned comments, especially given that the statement of claim was able to set out the precise defamatory passages. The notices were more the plaintiff's interpretation of the words than direct references to them, depriving the defendants of the opportunity to consider a targeted correction or retraction.
conclusion: The notices did not meet s. 5(1); the motion was granted on this issue and the action dismissed.

issue: Does an unincorporated trade union have the legal capacity to sue in defamation, so that the point can be decided on a Rule 21 motion?
facts: The defendants argued a trade union, as an unincorporated association, cannot bring a personal action in defamation. The plaintiff is a national union governed by federal labour legislation.
rule: Trade unions have evolving legal status to sue and be sued 'at least' for the purpose of their labour-relations functions (Berry v. Pulley, [2002] 2 SCR 40; PSAC v. Canada (A.G.), 2002 CanLII 19258 (ON CA)). Some authorities recognize union standing in defamation where words injure its financial position or trade activities (Pulp and Paper Workers of Canada, 1973 CanLII 1119; Ironworkers Local 97 v. Campbell, 1997 CanLII 1379), while others hold an unincorporated association cannot be defamed (Stark v. Toronto Sun Publishing Corp., 1983 CanLII 1789). On a Rule 21 motion the pleadings must disclose no reasonable cause of action on a 'plain and obvious' standard.
application: Reviewing the divergent and developing authorities, the court concluded the capacity of a trade union to sue in defamation is case-specific and unsettled. It was therefore not plain and obvious that the pleadings disclosed no actionable cause, so the question was not properly determinable on a Rule 21 motion.
conclusion: The motion was dismissed on this second ground.

issue: Were the pleadings sufficient to connect the defendant Benlolo to the second (print) publication?
facts: Benlolo was a guest on the July 24 broadcast but the pleadings did not specifically connect him to the July 28 article by way of republication.
rule: Liability in defamation based on republication must be specifically pleaded and cannot be inferred; Rule 5.02(2) governs joinder of defendants but does not create heads of liability, and the Negligence Act does not assist. Under Rule 26 pleadings may be amended.
application: Although the pleadings did not connect Benlolo to the second article, the court held his motion to strike the claim against him on that publication would not succeed, and that the pleadings would in all likelihood be amended at this stage.
conclusion: Benlolo's motion to strike would not have succeeded; leave to amend under Rule 26 was available (moot given dismissal on notice).

issue: Should the amendments to the Counterclaim be allowed, or should the Counterclaim be struck for failing to disclose a cause of action or as an abuse of process?
facts: Elkow, a school principal, sued Sana (a parent whose children attended the school) for defamation. Sana counterclaimed, alleging that Elkow and the Edmonton Public School Board owed her a professional duty of care, discriminated against and harassed her, defamed her by reporting to Children's Services, and abused public authority through trespass bans issued under s. 27 of the School Act. Sana had also filed a parallel human rights complaint alleging the same facts.
rule: Under Rule 129(1) the court may strike a pleading that discloses no cause of action, is scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, or is an abuse of process. On a Rule 129(1)(a) application no evidence is considered and pleaded facts are assumed true (Tottrup v. Alberta; Korte v. Deloitte). Duty of care is assessed under the two-stage Cooper v. Hobart, 2001 SCC 79 framework (foreseeability, proximity, residual policy). Breach of statutory duty is not actionable (Saskatchewan Wheat Pool v. Canada). Discrimination and harassment are not independent civil causes of action and must be pursued under human rights legislation (Seneca College v. Bhadauria; Bogden v. Purolator). School Act s. 27 authorizes bans and s. 144.1 protects good-faith conduct.
application: The court held there is no duty of care owed by a teacher or administrator to a parent (Angle v. Lapierre; L.R. v. British Columbia), and the s. 27 bans were lawful, made in good faith and statutorily protected, so no abuse of public authority arose. The alleged harms (inability to help injured children after a lawful ban) were de minimis and non-compensable. The defamation-to-Children's-Services claim failed for lack of an evidentiary basis and because the reporter's identity is privileged under s. 126.1 of the Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act. Discrimination and harassment claims were not actionable, duplicated the concurrent human rights complaint, and were vague and unrelated to the defamation action.
conclusion: The Counterclaim, original and as amended, disclosed no cause of action and was struck under Rule 129(1)(a) and (b), and portions constituted an abuse of process under Rule 129(1)(d). Sana's application to amend was refused and the strike application granted.

issue: Should the affidavit filed by Sana in support of the application to amend the Counterclaim be struck?
facts: Sana filed an affidavit dated October 13, 2006 in support of her application; several paragraphs contained argument and assertions rather than facts, and matters irrelevant to the issues.
rule: Rules 305, 306 and 307 govern affidavits: Rule 305(1) confines affidavits to facts within the deponent's knowledge, and Rule 307 permits striking scandalous, irrelevant or oppressive matter.
application: Paragraphs 3, 4, 9, 10 and 13 offended Rule 305(1) by containing argument rather than fact, and many offended Rule 307 as irrelevant. It was not practical to excise the offending material.
conclusion: The affidavit was struck from the record.

issue: Should the Alberta Teachers' Association be added as a defendant to the Counterclaim?
facts: Sana sought to add the ATA, alleging it had prejudged her and was covering Elkow's legal costs. The ATA's only involvement was providing member services to the Plaintiff.
rule: A party is properly added only where a genuine basis for a claim against it exists; paying a member's legal costs is no basis to be added as a party (Angle v. Lapierre, [2006] A.J. No. 618).
application: The defamation action was personal to Elkow and did not allege defamation of the ATA. The ATA's provision of member services, even including legal costs, provided no basis to add it as a party.
conclusion: The application to add the ATA was dismissed.

issue: Should paragraphs 22 and 23 of the amended Statement of Claim be struck on the basis of mediation privilege?
facts: Paragraphs 22-23 recounted statements made by Sana at a September 10, 2004 meeting arranged as a mediation. Sana refused to sign the facilitation/confidentiality agreement and refused to agree to the ground rules, so the mediation never proceeded.
rule: Settlement/mediation privilege attaches to communications made within a genuine mediation process; where the process does not commence, no such privilege arises.
application: The court accepted that although a mediation was planned, it never started because Sana refused to agree to the rules, so no privilege attached to the interaction.
conclusion: The application to strike paragraphs 22 and 23 was dismissed.

issue: Did Feldman's communication of allegations that the plaintiffs benefited from looted Nazi gold constitute defamation under art. 1457 C.C.Q.?
facts: Feldman, embroiled in an acrimonious dispute with his former partner Irwin Lande, alleged that Dr. Ludwig Delphiner was an SS officer who brought Nazi gold to Canada, which passed through the Lande family to the plaintiffs (Lande's nephews and their late mother's estate). He communicated these allegations in a 'Long Form Affidavit', letters, texts, a special resolution and to numerous prominent Jewish individuals and organizations. The plaintiffs are descendants of Holocaust survivors deeply attached to their Jewish faith. Feldman admitted at trial he had no proof the plaintiffs benefited from any looted gold.
rule: Defamation is a civil fault under art. 1457 C.C.Q. Per Prud'homme v. Prud'homme, 2002 SCC 85, remarks are defamatory if an ordinary person would believe they brought discredit on the victim's reputation; the plaintiff must also show a wrongful act (malicious or merely negligent conduct). The reasonable person takes precautions to avoid foreseeable injury (Bou Malhab v. Diffusion Métromédia CMR inc., 2011 SCC 9).
application: The Court held that, given the history of the Jewish people and documented instances of persons benefiting from property stolen by the Nazis, an ordinary person would believe the allegations discredited the plaintiffs' reputation. Feldman committed a fault: his allegations rested on a grossly incomplete investigation (disembarkation records showed Delphiner was in Canada in 1940; no records of any return to Europe as an SS officer; no evidence anyone benefited from gold). Even if he believed the story, a prudent person would not have disseminated it, and he had no valid reason to involve the plaintiffs beyond anger that they sided with their uncle.
conclusion: Feldman's conduct constituted defamation; he committed a fault under art. 1457 C.C.Q.

issue: What quantum of moral damages is warranted?
facts: The plaintiffs each claimed $500,000 in moral damages. The only public reporting was two Montreal newspaper articles that essentially repeated allegations already in the plaintiffs' own Originating Application and the Commercial Proceedings. No witness confirmed harm to the plaintiffs' actual standing; both were doing well in their careers. Feldman's principal fault was communicating the allegations to individuals and Jewish organizations, none of whom publicized the story or gave it credence.
rule: Moral damages in defamation are assessed using conceptual, personal and functional approaches and by comparison with analogous cases (Cinar Corporation v. Robinson, 2013 SCC 73). Relevant factors include gravity of the remarks, extent of diffusion, duration, the victim's prior reputation, and the victim's own contribution (Lalli c. Gravel, 2021 QCCA 1549; Gestion immobilière Lafrance). The victim's own testimony of humiliation suffices even absent objective harm.
application: The remarks were serious and hurtful, especially given the plaintiffs' Holocaust-survivor lineage, but diffusion was very limited, its public duration short, and most public exposure was placed in the record by the plaintiffs themselves, raising a causality issue. Distinguishing Hill and Soliman (widespread, orchestrated publication touching professional probity), the Court found Feldman's words more benign and not widely published. Both plaintiffs were subjectively affected, Andrew more than Jonathan.
conclusion: Moral damages of $45,000 to Andrew and $35,000 to Jonathan, far below the amounts claimed.

issue: Are punitive damages available and in what amount?
facts: The plaintiffs claimed $1,500,000 in punitive damages, including for the late Sherry's estate. Feldman's actions were intentionally designed to harm the plaintiffs' dignity, honour and reputation. His wealth was disputed (he had declared assets over $57 million in a family matter but claimed reduced liquidity).
rule: Punitive damages require a specific enabling enactment (art. 1621 C.C.Q.) and, under the Quebec Charter (art. 4 and 49), an unlawful and intentional interference with a protected right (Lalli c. Gravel). Quantum considers gravity of fault, the debtor's patrimonial situation, and the deterrent purpose, with restraint; the typical Quebec range is $5,000–$250,000 (Cinar).
application: The plaintiffs demonstrated an intentional violation of their Charter reputation/dignity rights (including Sherry's estate, of which they are universal legatees). However, the gravity was tempered by the absence of any sustained effort to publish the allegations. Deterrence was warranted, but the real concern was communication about the plaintiffs, not the investigation itself; there had been little activity since 2022 and Feldman did not contest the injunction.
conclusion: Punitive damages of $150,000 awarded collectively.

issue: Should the plaintiffs recover extrajudicial fees for abuse of procedure, and to what extent?
facts: The plaintiffs sought $350,000 in extrajudicial fees, having incurred over $318,000 to the Desfossés hearing, over $84,000 on an unsuccessful contempt proceeding, and at least $228,000 thereafter, with three lawyers at trial. Feldman filed a frivolous $3.75M cross application (later abandoned), failed to disavow a mistaken judicial admission, and sought to disqualify counsel.
rule: Ordinarily each party bears its own legal fees, but an abuse of the right to litigate that forces the other party to incur fees creates a causal link warranting recovery (Viel c. Entreprises immobilières du terroir). The Court assesses whether fees fall within a reasonable spectrum, taking a global rather than line-by-line approach (Bélanger; Sommet Prestige).
application: Feldman committed abuses (frivolous cross demand, failure to disavow, disqualification attempt) that increased the proceedings' length. However, the plaintiffs' own fees were excessive and disproportionate to a matter that was not overly complex; much of the early work related to the commercial dispute, and the risk of further public dissemination was modest. A losing, even abusive, defendant need not pay fees outside the scope of reasonableness.
conclusion: $200,000 awarded as a portion of extrajudicial costs.

issue: What is the appropriate scope of the permanent injunction?
facts: The plaintiffs sought a broad permanent injunction preventing Feldman from communicating any information about the estate or the plaintiffs, plus post-judgment disclosure of all remarks made. Some Long Form Affidavit allegations were already public via the Desfossés judgment.
rule: Injunctions restraining expression are extraordinary and, given freedom of expression, are granted only in the clearest cases where the defamatory character is manifest and unjustifiable; orders must be specific and cannot apply generally to unknown future statements (Forensic Technology c. Pyramidal; Champagne c. Collège de Jonquière).
application: An injunction over allegations already in the public domain (paras 6, 69, 84, 89) or containing no harmful information (para 38) would serve no purpose. Paragraphs 39 and 65 contained harmful, non-public information warranting a specific order. The broad request to bar any remark about the plaintiffs was too imprecise to enforce and offended freedom of expression; the disclosure list had already been ruled on in case management.
conclusion: A narrow permanent injunction issued restraining communication of paragraphs 39 and 65 only; the broad requests refused.

issue: Should certain exhibits be placed under seal?
facts: The plaintiffs sought sealing of exhibits P-10, P-11, P-27 and P-37, largely variations of Feldman's Long Form Affidavit containing detailed and disparaging allegations.
rule: Under Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25 and Sierra Club, an exception to the open court principle may be granted where sufficiently sensitive information striking at the biographical core places an individual's dignity at serious risk.
application: The detailed content of P-10, P-27 and P-37, taken as a whole, could damage the plaintiffs' dignity even though the gist was public, so sealing was justified. P-11 (the special resolution) was already in the Commercial Proceedings record and largely repeated in the plaintiffs' own application, so sealing it was inappropriate.
conclusion: Sealing order granted for P-10, P-27 and P-37; refused for P-11.

issue: Should the required statutory findings under s. 90(2) of the CYFSA be made, and in particular is the child a First Nations, Inuk or Métis child?
facts: At the time of D.'s birth the mother said she had Polish ancestry and some Native ancestry on her father's side but did not identify as Native and had no status; she declined the society's offer to explore this. About 1.5 years later she claimed her paternal grandmother (D.'s great-grandfather) was 'Iqaluit.' The society made a referral to the Native Child and Family Services liaison but the mother refused to consent to or facilitate any information gathering. Her name, date of birth information for D. was undisputed.
rule: Section 90(2)(b) requires the court to determine whether a child is a First Nations, Inuk or Métis child before the protection finding. The definition is in s. 1 of O. Reg. 155/18; 'relative' under s. 2(1) of the Act does not include a great-grandparent. Per Catholic Children's Aid Society v. S.T., 2019 ONCJ 207 (Sherr J.), only a low threshold of reliable and credible evidence is needed and a broad, good-faith view should be taken, but there must be sufficient evidence and self-identification must be made in good faith.
application: The mother never identified as FNIM throughout a lengthy child protection history, expressly said D. was not Native at his birth, and her later claim rested on a great-grandfather (outside the statutory definition of 'relative') without any follow-through with the NCFS liaison to substantiate it. There was no credible or reliable evidence meeting even the low threshold, though findings could be revisited on new evidence.
conclusion: The court made the statutory findings without a trial: the child's legal name and birth date as provided, and that D. is not a First Nations, Inuk or Métis child.

issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to whether the child is in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b) of the CYFSA?
facts: D. was removed at birth and had been in society care about 2.5 years. The mother had diagnosed anxiety, depression and PTSD (and possible undiagnosed disorders), a history of domestic violence and criminal charges, unstable housing, and had never been primary caregiver to any of her five children. During supervised visits she was frequently late or absent, became volatile and verbally aggressive toward workers in the child's presence, and directed frustration and anger at the infant when he cried, unable to read his cues. She refused psychological assessment and did not complete offered services.
rule: Family Law Rules r. 16 (summary judgment) and the Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7 two-step framework, applied with exceptional caution in child protection per Kawartha Haliburton CAS v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316 and L.M. v. CAS of Peel, 2019 ONCA 641; only trial-worthy evidence is considered. Under s. 74(2)(b) a child is in need of protection where there is a real (not speculative) risk of physical harm from a caregiver's failure to care/supervise/protect or pattern of neglect; intention to harm need not be proven; mental-health-related risk assessed per CAS of Toronto v. R.S., 2019 ONCJ 866.
application: Applying the R.S. factors to the undisputed affidavit evidence, the court found overwhelming trial-worthy evidence of real risk: the mother's inability to regulate anger and aggression around and toward the infant, exposure of the child to volatility and threats, untreated mental illness with little insight and refusal of assessment/treatment, risk of violence given her history, and an absence of any successful primary-caregiving record. No expanded fact-finding powers were needed.
conclusion: There was no realistic possibility a protection finding would not be made; the court found D. a child in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b)(i).

issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to any disposition other than extended society care?
facts: The mother filed no answer, plan of care or responding affidavit despite lengthy extensions; her plan was vague, involving possible cohabitation with an online boyfriend abroad and unstable housing (evicted at least three times). D. was a healthy, thriving toddler in the same foster home since birth. The mother had not addressed her mental health or anger over more than two years and was hostile and uncooperative with workers.
rule: Section 101(1) CYFSA requires that intervention by court order be necessary to protect the child in future, with disposition in the child's best interests (s. 74(3) factors); ss. 101(3)-(4) require considering less intrusive alternatives and placement with relatives/community; per CAS of Toronto v. S.P., 2019 ONSC 3482 continuing protection concerns may be considered.
application: A supervision order was not viable given the mother's refusal to cooperate, failure to comply with prior supervision terms, and untreated risk; no kin plan remained (the paternal aunt withdrew and was not approved). Weighing the s. 74(3) best-interests factors, the ongoing high risk, lack of a positive parent-child relationship, need for permanency beyond statutory timelines, and the child's need for stability favoured extended society care for adoption.
conclusion: No less intrusive option met D.'s best interests; the court ordered D. placed in the extended care of the society under s. 101(1).

issue: Is an access order between the mother and the child in the child's best interests under s. 105(5)-(6) of the CYFSA?
facts: When exercised, the mother's access was largely negative: many missed and late visits, volatility and threats toward workers in the child's presence, and no unsupervised access ever. After March 2020 she did not see D. for eight months and missed nearly all later scheduled virtual visits. D. is a highly adoptable healthy toddler; he has four half-siblings not in the mother's care.
rule: Sections 104-105 CYFSA; under s. 105(5) no access order is made for a child in extended care unless it is in the child's best interests, with s. 105(6) factors (beneficial and meaningful relationship; impairment of adoption prospects) and s. 74(3) factors, viewed through a global best-interests lens per Kawartha Haliburton CAS v. M.W. and CAS of Toronto v. J.G., 2020 ONCA 415, which also recognizes access can take many forms (letters, email, calls).
application: In-person access would disrupt the foster placement and impair adoption prospects and had been largely negative for D. However, future considerations—D.'s possible interest in his half-siblings and access to his medical/cultural history and 'his story'—weighed in favour of limited written contact. The court balanced these under the best-interests test.
conclusion: The court ordered limited access three times per year by cards, letters or email with updates, with D. as access holder and the mother as access recipient.

issue: Should the applicant father be granted access to his five-and-a-half-year-old son despite the assessor's recommendation of no access?
facts: Meir, an Orthodox Jew, and Kendra, a convert to Judaism who later returned to Christianity, had a turbulent relationship producing Daniel. After separations, minutes of settlement gave Kendra custody and Meir access on terms requiring a Jewish upbringing. Believing Kendra had breached the terms, Meir fled to Israel with Daniel for a period ('the Hegira'), returned the child, and was acquitted of abduction. Kendra, now in a common-law relationship, sought to exclude Meir entirely from Daniel's life; the child had been conditioned to fear his father, and Meir had seen Daniel only once since April 1990.
rule: In access matters the paramount consideration is the child's best interest, not the parents' interests (Elbaz v. Elbaz (1980), 16 R.F.L. (2d) 336). A child normally benefits from the love and guidance of both parents, and access will be denied only in exceptional circumstances or where compelling reasons dictate (Inwood v. Sidorova; Hart v. Twyne (1988), 17 R.F.L. (3d) 107, where a father's right to access persists even after the mother's remarriage).
application: The court found the assessor's recommendation of no access rested on a limited investigation (a few phone calls, a two-hour interview, a one-hour observation) and a personality conflict with Meir, and that she failed to interview readily available collateral witnesses (Rabbi Burak, the Droris, Esther Greenbaum, Moishe David) who described Meir as a loving, devoted father good with children. There was no psychiatric history, no violence, and no concrete evidence Meir would flee again, especially given his restraint during the year-long reconciliation. The child's fear was found to have been instilled by Kendra, who was untruthful in prior proceedings and determined to erase Meir from Daniel's life. Denying a devoted father all access on this record was inappropriate.
conclusion: Access granted to the father on a carefully structured, initially supervised and graduated basis, with the judge remaining seized of the matter; the father to deposit his passports and an Official Guardian report ordered.

issue: Should the father be permitted to expose the child to the Jewish faith and customs over the custodial mother's objections?
facts: Daniel was born a Jew (his mother having converted while pregnant, considered by Rabbi Burak a 'biblical ordinance') and remains Jewish regardless of later training. The minutes of settlement required that Daniel be raised in the Jewish faith. Kendra now provided essentially no religious instruction, taking Daniel occasionally to a Pentecostal tabernacle and keeping a Christmas tree, and argued Daniel could choose a religion when grown; Meir wished Daniel to observe the sabbath, high holidays, dietary laws, learn Hebrew and attend Hebrew school.
rule: Absent compelling evidence that sharing the access parent's religious beliefs or exposure to two religions is contrary to the child's best interest, the Divorce Act is interpreted compatibly with the access parent's freedom of religion (Hockey v. Hockey (1989), 21 R.F.L. (3d) 105); an access parent may take a child to religious services over the custodial parent's objection where no harm is shown (H. (N.) c. P. (C.) (1988), 15 R.F.L. (3d) 418). Religious and ethical environment is a relevant factor in the welfare inquiry (Re K (minors), [1977] 1 All E.R. 647).
application: The court held it in Daniel's best interest to understand what it means to be a Jew, which he cannot do without his father's guidance and teaching, achievable only through access. Kendra's notion that a child with no religious training could later choose a religion was naïve, and material comforts (a pool and pony) could not replace spiritual and moral values. Exposure to two religions would not harm Daniel; Meir could take him to the synagogue. Meir, however, had to be flexible and tolerate that a young child will inadvertently break Jewish observances, as Rabbi Burak acknowledged.
conclusion: The father is entitled, through structured access, to introduce Daniel to the Jewish faith and customs, including a graduated introduction to the sabbath, with the Hebrew-education question to be reviewed after six months.

issue: Was s. 14(1)(b) of the Code correctly interpreted and applied by the tribunals below?
facts: The Tribunal isolated selected phrases from each flyer and concluded, without further analysis, that they exposed homosexuals to hatred and ridicule; the Queen's Bench judge, applying a correctness standard following Owens, upheld those findings by focusing on references implying homosexuals are child molesters.
rule: Section 14(1)(b) prohibits publications that expose or tend to expose to hatred, ridicule, belittle or affront dignity on a prohibited ground, but under Canada (Human Rights Comm.) v. Taylor and Saskatchewan (Human Rights Comm.) v. Bell, as elaborated in Owens, it reaches only expression involving 'unusually strong and deep-felt emotions of detestation, calumny and vilification'; it must be applied objectively, from the standpoint of a reasonable person aware of the context, and must be balanced against the freedom of expression guaranteed in ss. 5 and 14(2) of the Code. Appeal lies only on a question of law (s. 32), reviewed for correctness.
application: The Court held that both tribunals erred by extracting words and phrases in isolation, offering conclusions rather than analysis, and failing to weigh the wider context or the s. 14(2) freedom-of-expression protection. Context is especially important where complaints concern sexual orientation, because such publications usually engage debate on morality, which attracts a high degree of tolerance in a democracy. The proper approach requires reading each flyer as a whole, objectively, in the circumstances of its distribution, and balancing the s. 14(1)(b) limit against s. 14(2).
conclusion: The Tribunal and the Queen's Bench judge applied the wrong analytical approach; the correct approach requires a contextual, objective reading balanced against protected expression.

issue: Did the four flyers contravene s. 14(1)(b)?
facts: Whatcott distributed four flyers under 'Christian Truth Activists' in Saskatoon and Regina. Flyers D and E addressed the inclusion of information on homosexuality in public school curricula and a university conference; Flyers F and G reproduced classified ads from a gay magazine and criticised its advertising policy, using blunt, crude and pejorative language.
rule: A publication breaches s. 14(1)(b) only if, read as a whole and objectively in its context, it meets the extreme Taylor/Bell hatred standard, with the limitation balanced against the freedom of expression in ss. 5 and 14(2) of the Code.
application: Read in context, Flyers D and E were part of an ongoing debate about teaching about homosexuality in public schools; the single hyperbolic phrase in Flyer E did not taint the whole. Flyers F and G were criticism of a magazine's advertising practices; the ambiguous references (e.g. 'boys') did not objectively convey hatred. Isolated crude or demeaning words did not, alone or combined, reach the level of detestation, calumny and vilification required. Whatcott's expression fell within the protection of s. 14(2).
conclusion: None of the four flyers offended s. 14(1)(b); the appeal was allowed and the decision below set aside, with costs to Whatcott. (Smith J.A. concurred, adding that pejorative expression directed at same-sex conduct in a public-policy or moral debate is not justifiably limited.)

issue: Did the University establish a strong prima facie case for an injunction, and if so on what basis?
facts: Protesters affiliated with Occupy U of T breached a fence and set up an encampment of up to 177 tents on Front Campus on 2 May 2024, excluding others and refusing to leave after a Notice of Trespass. The University alleged the encampment was violent and antisemitic, but the evidence of violence and hate speech was largely hearsay and none of it was tied to the named respondents or occupants; contested slogans ('From the river to the sea', 'glory to the martyrs', 'intifada') were shown to bear multiple contextual meanings.
rule: For a mandatory interlocutory injunction the moving party must show a strong prima facie case (R. v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp., 2018). Trespass arises under s. 2 of the Trespass to Property Act and at common law where a person enters, remains on or places objects on another's land without lawful justification; ejectment requires proof of dispossession and possession by the respondents. Sharpe, Injunctions and Specific Performance, notes a strong presumption favouring injunctive relief for deliberate, continuing trespass.
application: The court found no strong prima facie case that the encampment itself was violent or antisemitic, as the incidents were hearsay, isolated and unconnected to the respondents, and the slogans had indeterminate meaning. However, the University clearly established trespass and ejectment: the protesters entered Front Campus, erected structures, excluded others, and refused to leave for over 50 days after being directed to. Exercising freedom of expression is no defence to trespass.
conclusion: A strong prima facie case was established in trespass and ejectment, placing the University at the strong end of that spectrum, though not on the violence or antisemitism grounds.

issue: Did the University suffer irreparable harm?
facts: The University incurred unrecoverable security, sanitation and repair costs, lost the use of a recently $100-million-refurbished Front Campus for over 50 days (including graduation ceremonies and summer camps), and faced ongoing exclusion from and damage to the space, plus reputational effects.
rule: Irreparable harm is harm that cannot be quantified or cured, or that cannot be recovered because the defendant is judgment-proof (RJR-MacDonald Inc. v. Canada, 1994); the loss of the very use of one's property through trespass is itself irreparable harm (1465152 Ontario Ltd. v. Amexon Development).
application: The continued inability to use and control Front Campus was the largest component of irreparable harm; unrecoverable expenses supported the finding; escalation risk from past altercations and hate speech near the encampment amounted to some, but limited, harm; safety hazards and most reputational claims did not qualify. Deprivation of property use for over 50 days, with protesters vowing to stay until demands were met, effectively held the University to ransom.
conclusion: The University established irreparable harm, principally from its continued inability to use Front Campus.

issue: Does the balance of convenience favour the injunction given the protesters' expressive rights?
facts: The injunction would still allow protesting anywhere on campus from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m.; it only barred camping, erecting structures, blocking entrances and protesting between 11 p.m. and 7 a.m. The protesters characterised occupation itself as expression and asked that the dispute be left to negotiation.
rule: The court weighs the harm to each side and may consider the public interest (RJR-MacDonald). Courts have consistently held protesters have no right to occupy or camp on others' property, public or private (Batty v. City of Toronto, 2011; Weisfeld v. Canada; Hamilton (City) v. Loucks), and freedom of expression does not protect tortious conduct such as trespass (RWDSU v. Pepsi-Cola, 2002). There is no legal duty to negotiate before invoking legal rights.
application: Because the injunction preserved the full legal right to protest and only restrained activity in which protesters had no legal right to engage, it did not limit protected expression. Allowing one group to seize a quasi-public space to the exclusion of others (including counter-protesters who had tried to set up their own encampment) would invite a 'tragedy of the commons.' The property owner, subject to Charter values and its own free-speech policies, is entitled to manage competing demands on space. The overnight restriction reasonably balanced protest rights against residents' need to sleep.
conclusion: The balance of convenience favoured the University; the injunction was granted.

issue: Does the Charter apply to the University's conduct, and if so is the limit justified under s. 1?
facts: The respondents framed the case as a Charter matter but served no notice of constitutional question under s. 109 of the Courts of Justice Act. The University is a statutorily autonomous, self-governing institution.
rule: Section 109 requires notice where the constitutional validity or applicability of a statute or common-law rule is challenged. Under s. 32 and McKinney v. University of Guelph, Eldridge, Lobo v. Carleton University and CFS v. Ontario, Ontario universities are not government actors and their decisions on non-academic use of property are not Charter-governed; York Region (2024 SCC 22) is distinguishable as turning on school boards' governmental nature. Even so, courts apply Charter values (Dolphin Delivery).
application: The court declined to decide Charter applicability given the absence of s. 109 notice and instead applied the University's policies interpreted consistently with Charter values. In an alternative analysis it held the Charter does not apply to the University in this context, that in any event the Charter does not protect trespass, and that if it did apply the trespass enforcement would breach s. 2(b) but be justified under s. 1 (pressing objectives of managing shared space, minimal impairment since protest continues, and proportionality).
conclusion: The Charter was found not to apply; alternatively any limit on expression would be justified under s. 1. The result was the same either way.

issue: Was the City's approval of the Palestinian flag-raising beyond its statutory jurisdiction under the City of Toronto Act, 2006?
facts: The City adopted a Flag Policy under By-law No. 4-1999 permitting community members to request the raising of the flag of any nation recognized by the federal government on a courtesy flagpole at City Hall. The ICJP requested that the Palestinian flag be raised on November 17, 2025 to mark Palestine's Independence Day, and the Chief of Protocol approved it. Applicants argued flying a foreign political flag was not a proper municipal purpose under s. 8(2)6.
rule: Sections 8(1)-(3) of the City of Toronto Act, 2006 grant broad authority to provide services and pass by-laws respecting public assets (s. 8(2)4.), well-being of persons (s. 8(2)6.) and authorized services (s. 8(2)7.). Like any property owner, a municipality may set policies for use of its property.
application: The Court held the City had ample authority under s. 8(2)4., 8(2)5. and 8(2)7. to adopt the Flag Policy and administer requests. The real question was not vires but whether the Approval was reasonable under the Policy's terms. No serious issue arose regarding jurisdiction.
conclusion: No serious issue was raised that the City acted beyond its statutory jurisdiction.

issue: Did the applicants raise a serious issue that the Approval was unreasonable — for breaching the Flag Policy, breaching the duty of neutrality, or lacking justification, transparency and intelligibility?
facts: Applicants argued Canada's recognition of Palestine was conditional, that the requesting/affiliated organizations espoused hatred, violence or racism (citing a violent Nov. 5 protest at Toronto Metropolitan University), that raising a politically charged flag breached the duty of neutrality in Saguenay, and that the decision lacked transparency given public safety concerns.
rule: Reasonableness review under Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, requires focus on whether the decision bears the hallmarks of justification, transparency and intelligibility; the burden lies on the challenger. The state's duty of neutrality under Mouvement laïque québécois v. Saguenay (City), 2015 SCC 16 is a duty of religious neutrality flowing from freedom of conscience and religion.
application: The Prime Minister's September 21, 2025 statement and Global Affairs Canada's confirmation showed unconditional recognition of the State of Palestine, so the 'recognized nation' criterion was met. The ICJP was the sole requesting organization; there was no evidence it espoused hatred, violence or racism, and endorsement by other groups did not make them applicants nor was there evidence of their involvement in violence. The Saguenay duty is one of religious, not political, neutrality; the Policy and Approval did not engage religion, and politics is not a relevant Policy consideration. The Chief of Protocol adequately explained the rationale; public safety is not a Policy criterion but was separately addressed with police coordination.
conclusion: None of the grounds raised a serious issue to be tried; the Approval was not shown to be unreasonable.

issue: Did the applicants establish irreparable harm if the injunction were refused?
facts: Applicants asserted the flag-raising would exacerbate division, cause fear among the Jewish community, embolden antisemitic organizations, risk counter-protests and disorder, and cause psychological/dignitary harm; Mr. Epstein described increased harassment since October 2023 near demonstrations displaying Palestinian flags.
rule: Irreparable harm is defined by its nature rather than magnitude (Ahmed v. Abdelmoaein, 2025 ONCA 618); the evidence must be clear, go beyond speculation and meet the balance of probabilities (Muslim Association of Canada v. AG Canada, 2022 ONSC 7284). Where a private applicant asserts a public interest, the harm must be demonstrated (RJR-MacDonald v. Canada (AG), [1994] 1 S.C.R. 311).
application: The Court found the asserted risks of demonstrations, disorder and normalization of antisemitism to be speculative, with no cogent evidentiary basis. The claim that the flag-raising would permanently signal municipal endorsement ignored the Policy's express statement that raising a flag neither implies nor expresses support for a nation's politics or policies.
conclusion: The applicants failed to establish irreparable harm on the balance of probabilities.

issue: Did the balance of convenience favour granting or denying the injunction?
facts: Applicants said the City suffered no material prejudice from deferring a discretionary symbolic event; the City and NCCM argued that enjoining the ceremony would deprive the Palestinian, Arab, Muslim and allied communities of a publicly available resource and produce a chilling and exclusionary effect.
rule: The court must weigh which party would suffer the greatest irremediable prejudice; public interest considerations apply to society generally and to identifiable groups (RJR-MacDonald).
application: Because the applicants established no irreparable harm, while enjoining the event would deprive the ICJP and Palestinian community of a regularly available public resource and impose the harms identified by the City and NCCM, the balance tipped against the injunction.
conclusion: The balance of convenience favoured dismissal of the motion.

issue: Did the plaintiff's conduct justify an elevated costs award beyond the 15% cap in s. 29 of the Courts of Justice Act or a penalty under Rule 19.06?
facts: The plaintiff's $35,000 action against his former employer law firm and one of its former partners was dismissed after trial. The defendants sought $10,500 in costs, relying on a January 7, 2026 offer to settle ($1,000), allegedly unsubstantiated and defamatory statements in the Plaintiff's Claim, and a series of racist, antisemitic, homophobic and sexually charged emails the plaintiff sent during the litigation (including a July 9, 2024 email refusing an adjournment over Rosh Hashanah and referencing Gaza, and October 2024 and October 2025 emails).
rule: Section 29 of the Courts of Justice Act caps costs at 15% of the amount claimed unless the court finds it necessary in the interests of justice to penalize unreasonable behaviour. Rule 14.07(2) permits up to double costs where a defendant's offer is served at least seven days before trial, is not withdrawn, and the plaintiff obtains a judgment no more favourable. Per West End Tree Service v. Stabryla, 2010 ONSC 68 and 10.1 Inc. v. 2248951 Ontario Inc., 2018 ONSC 381, elevated costs must correlate to additional costs actually caused by the unreasonable behaviour.
application: The offer to settle was served only five days before the January 12, 2026 trial, failing the seven-day requirement of Rule 14.07(2) (and possibly not qualifying because the claim was dismissed rather than resulting in a 'judgment'). The pleadings did not rise to unreasonable behaviour. Although the emails were plainly offensive, the costs of the July 2024 and November 2024 motions had already been determined, and none of the offensive emails related to the January 12, 2026 trial or its preparation, so there was no correlation between the misconduct and the recoverable trial costs.
conclusion: No basis existed to award elevated costs under the s. 29 exception or to impose a penalty under Rule 19.06.

issue: Was each defendant self-represented under Rule 19.05 or represented by counsel entitling it to a reasonable representation fee under Rule 19.04?
facts: Both defendants were represented at trial by Mr. Kapoor (lawyer) and Mr. Mardirossian (paralegal), who both work at Mr. Horlick's current firm, Horlick Condominium Law. The recoverable trial fees (items (a) and (b)), after the proposed 47% discount, totalled $5,103.90. The defendant law firm was sued on an employment agreement to which Mr. Horlick was not a party; the claim against Mr. Horlick personally rested mainly on alleged Human Rights Code violations.
rule: Rule 19.04 allows a reasonable representation fee where a successful party is represented by a lawyer or paralegal; Rule 19.05 limits a self-represented successful party to $500 for inconvenience and expense. Per Vardalas v. 1455358 Ontario Inc., 2014 CanLII 40443 and Fanaken v. Bell, Temple, a lawyer who defends his own firm appears as litigant, not counsel. Under Fong v. Chan, 1999 CanLII 2052 (ONCA), and Primeau, a self-represented lawyer may recover above the $500 cap only on proof of an opportunity cost (foregone remunerative activity).
application: Because Mr. Horlick was represented by members of his own firm, he was effectively self-represented, and no evidence of lost billable opportunity was provided, so he was confined to the $500 cap in Rule 19.05. The defendant law firm, by contrast, was a distinct party defended by members of a different firm (Horlick Condominium Law) and was therefore entitled to a reasonable representation fee under Rule 19.04. Splitting the $5,103.90 in recoverable trial fees 50/50 yielded $2,551.95 per defendant, subject to the Rule 19.05 cap for Mr. Horlick.
conclusion: Mr. Horlick was awarded $500 as a self-represented litigant; the defendant law firm was awarded a representation fee of $2,551.95, for a total of $3,051.95 payable within 30 days.

issue: Did the plaintiff establish grounds to believe his defamation proceeding had substantial merit under s. 137.1(4)(a)(i) of the Courts of Justice Act?
facts: Lemire sued Burley in defamation over 2018–2019 tweets and a memorandum describing Lemire as a racist, former neo-Nazi/Heritage Front leader, anti-Semite, homophobe, national security threat, and someone unqualified for and misusing his City of Hamilton IT position. Burley moved to dismiss under the anti-SLAPP provision; Lemire conceded the expression concerned a matter of public interest, shifting the onus to him.
rule: Under s. 137.1(4)(a)(i) and Pointes (2020 SCC 22), the responding party must show the claim has 'substantial merit' — a real prospect of success, being neither frivolous nor merely technically valid, and legally tenable and supported by evidence reasonably capable of belief. Defamation requires (1) words that would tend to lower the plaintiff's reputation in a reasonable person's eyes, (2) reference to the plaintiff, and (3) publication to at least one other person: Grant v. Torstar, 2009 SCC 61.
application: The court found Burley's words were on their face defamatory, tending to lower Lemire's reputation, that they referred to Lemire, and that they were communicated to others. On the limited motion record the court engaged in limited weighing and concluded the claim was neither frivolous nor merely technical and had a real prospect of success.
conclusion: Lemire satisfied the substantial-merit branch; the claim was legally tenable and supported by evidence reasonably capable of belief.

issue: Did the plaintiff establish grounds to believe the defendant had no valid defence under s. 137.1(4)(a)(ii)?
facts: Burley raised the defences of qualified privilege (as to the memo given to the City), fair comment, and justification. His information came from public sources including the Zündel decisions, Warman v. Lemire, mainstream media (the VICE, CBC and Spectator articles), and researcher Richard Warman. Lemire's own admissions confirmed extensive past association with the Heritage Front, Zündel and Droege, his eulogy of Droege in 2005, and his continued hosting of freedomsite.org until 2019.
rule: Once defamation is made out, the burden shifts to the defendant to put defences in play, and the plaintiff must show the defences have no real prospect of success (Pointes, paras. 58–60). Fair comment requires: public interest, a factual basis, recognizability as comment, that any person could honestly express the opinion on the proved facts, and absence of express malice (Simpson v. Mair, 2008 SCC 40; Chernesky). Qualified privilege attaches to a reciprocal duty/interest communication but is lost on wider publication (RTC Engineering; Hill v. Church of Scientology). Justification requires proof of the substantial truth of the 'sting' (Bent v. Platnick, 2020 SCC 23).
application: The court held qualified privilege covered the memo given to the City but was lost when Burley published part of it; Lemire failed to prove malice defeating the privilege. On fair comment, public interest was conceded, the tweets had a factual underpinning, were recognizable as comment (directed at the City's conduct in hiring and shielding Lemire), reflected opinions any person could honestly hold on the proved facts, and were not actuated by malice — Burley's dominant motive being to hold the City accountable. Justification was also supported, the 'sting' (that the City employed someone with a public association with groups whose values conflicted with its own) being substantially true, reinforced by the City's own statement ending the employment.
conclusion: Lemire failed to show that Burley's defences had no real prospect of success; on this basis alone the motion would be granted under s. 137.1(4)(a)(ii).

issue: Did the plaintiff show that the harm was sufficiently serious that the public interest in permitting the proceeding to continue outweighed the public interest in protecting the expression under s. 137.1(4)(b)?
facts: Lemire claimed loss of his City employment, inability to obtain comparable employment, and safety fears for himself and his family. Burley's tweets spanned about four months; Lemire's neo-Nazi/Heritage Front associations had been publicly documented in media, legal reports and the internet for over a decade, including on websites Lemire himself hosted. The City ended the employment after its own two investigations, found no misuse of data, and gave Lemire a letter of recommendation. Lemire's counsel candidly stated he sought to 'erase' his past.
rule: Under s. 137.1(4)(b) and Pointes (paras. 67–81), the plaintiff must show harm and a causal link to the expression, and that the public interest in continuing the proceeding outweighs the public interest in protecting the expression, weighed against core free-expression values (search for truth, political participation, self-fulfilment) and factors including the quality of the expression, chilling effects, the defendant's history of public-interest advocacy, and protection of vulnerable groups.
application: The court found no evidence reasonably capable of belief linking the loss of employment (a decision the City made after its own investigations) or the difficulty obtaining comparable work to Burley's tweets, and found the safety concerns vague and speculative. Burley's tweets were 'merely a drop in the bucket' compared with decades of public material, much of it kept in the public eye by Lemire himself. Weighing the interests, there was strong public interest in encouraging citizens to speak out about municipal government conduct, and Burley was a known activist and member of a vulnerable community; this outweighed any public interest in permitting the proceeding.
conclusion: Lemire failed to meet his burden under s. 137.1(4)(b); the public interest in protecting Burley's expression prevailed.

issue: Is the undertaking in the consent to corollary relief to appear before rabbinical authorities to obtain a get a justiciable civil obligation or a non-enforceable religious/moral one?
facts: On divorcing in 1980, Marcovitz and Bruker signed a Consent that included paragraph 12, by which the parties would appear before the Montreal rabbinical authorities to obtain the traditional religious get immediately upon the Decree Nisi. The Consent was ratified by the court. Marcovitz refused to grant the get for some 15 years. The expert evidence established that participation in the process leading to a get is religious in nature and requires a voluntary, religiously intended act; any prior consent must be renounced before the Beth Din.
rule: Quebec civil law looks to the substance of an obligation, not its form (art. 1425-type analysis; Baudouin & Jobin; Pineau & Gaudet on the distinction between civil and moral obligations). Canadian courts traditionally decline to adjudicate internal religious disputes (Morris v. Morris; Kaddoura v. Hammoud; Levitt's Kosher Foods). Freedom of religion protects sincerely held religious practice and the State should not become the arbiter of religious dogma (Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem). Section 21.1 of the Divorce Act offers only limited relief and only where the recalcitrant spouse initiates a proceeding.
application: Hilton J.A. held that although paragraph 12 was cast in the form of a term of a secular consent ratified by the court, its substance was religious: obtaining a get requires a voluntary religious act that cannot be coerced, and any prior consent is irrelevant and must be renounced before the Beth Din. The Superior Court could never have ordered specific performance of such a term as corollary relief under s. 17 of the Divorce Act, so the parties could not consensually confer such jurisdiction. Adjudicating the claim would improperly draw the court into assessing religious doctrine and Bruker's religiosity. At most the undertaking was a moral obligation, enforceable only in a religious forum.
conclusion: The obligation was religious/moral in substance and not justiciable by secular courts; it could not ground an action in damages.

issue: Can the former wife recover damages for the alleged breach of the get undertaking?
facts: Bruker claimed damages (originally $500,000, later $1,350,000) for being unable to remarry within her faith and to have legitimate children during the 15 years before the get issued in 1995. The trial judge had awarded $47,500.
rule: Damages for breach of contract require a valid, enforceable civil obligation. A moral obligation is not sanctioned by law and cannot be enforced before the courts (Baudouin & Jobin). To condemn a party to damages for failing to perform a religious act would be inconsistent with freedom of religion.
application: Because the underlying obligation was religious and non-justiciable, no enforceable civil obligation supported a damages award. Additional reasons independently undermined the trial judgment: the trial judge wrongly assumed a get would have issued in 1980 as it did in 1995 despite dramatically changed circumstances, mischaracterized the obligation as civil, and Bruker's alternative theory would have required Marcovitz to be untruthful about the voluntary nature of his appearance.
conclusion: No damages could be awarded; the appeal was allowed and Bruker's action dismissed, and her incidental appeal to increase damages was necessarily dismissed.

issue: Was a publication ban warranted in this civil damages action?
facts: The trial judge, after seven days of trial conducted in public, imposed a ban on publishing the parties' and children's names, relying on art. 815.4 C.C.P. and the family-law origin of the matter and the personal nature of the evidence.
rule: Court sittings are public (art. 13 C.C.P.; s. 23 Quebec Charter); publication bans require a two-step analysis (necessity to avoid a compelling risk of an unfair trial, and beneficial effects outweighing harm to free expression), applications must be made in limine litis (D.J.L. v. Vallée; B.B. v. Procureur général du Québec).
application: This was an action in damages for breach of contract, not a family law case; the trial had proceeded in public and the application was not made in limine litis. Embarrassment to the parties was insufficient, and the reasons made little reference to medical, psychological or child-related matters. The Vallée-type exceptional circumstances were absent.
conclusion: The publication ban and the accompanying recommendation were vacated.

issue: Are the writings and communications of the National Alliance illegal and/or contrary to Canadian public policy?
facts: The testator left the residue of his estate to the National Alliance, a Virginia-based neo-Nazi organization founded by William Luther Pierce (also the named executor). Extensive affidavit evidence — the NA's foundational document 'What is the National Alliance?', bulletins by Pierce advocating killing of racial enemies, chairman Erich Gliebe's 2011 Holocaust-denial broadcast, and website postings — showed the group promotes white supremacy, eugenics, racial cleansing, antisemitism and hate-motivated violence.
rule: Public policy embodies the interests of society expressed in the morals of the time, the common law and legislation (Re Millar, [1938] SCR 1; Canada Trust Co. v. Ontario Human Rights Commission (1990), ON CA). Section 319(2) of the Criminal Code makes wilful promotion of hatred against an identifiable group a criminal offence, held constitutional in R. v. Andrews, [1990] 3 SCR 870. Public policy against discrimination is gleaned from federal and provincial statutes, the Charter (ss. 15, 27, 28) and international conventions ratified by Canada.
application: The court found the NA's publications 'racist, white supremacist and hate-inspired,' as 'malodorous, malicious and evil' as the material in Andrews. It rejected the respondent's argument that the writings were 'dated' or protected under the US First Amendment, noting Gliebe's recent antisemitic broadcast and that on the internet national boundaries are meaningless for spreading hate propaganda. The material offends s. 319(2) of the Criminal Code and contravenes Charter values, the New Brunswick Human Rights Act and international anti-discrimination conventions.
