conclusion: The court held that the National Alliance disseminates hate propaganda that is illegal under the Criminal Code and violates the public policy of Canada.

issue: May a court void a testamentary gift because the beneficiary's very purpose is contrary to public policy, even though the bequest attaches no unlawful condition?
facts: The bequest transferred the residue outright to the National Alliance with no stated conditions. The respondent and CAFE argued that courts void bequests only for repugnant conditions, not for the character of a beneficiary, and that bad character or criminal record does not disqualify a beneficiary; they warned of a floodgates of estate litigation and invoked freedom of expression.
rule: Generally bequests are not denied because a beneficiary is of bad character (Bolianatz Estate v. Simon, [2006] SJ No. 64; Jake Estate v. Antleman, 2006 NBQB 371). However, courts may intervene on public policy grounds (Egerton v. Brownlow (1853); Fox v. Fox Estate, 1996 CanLII 779), and the law of wills gives effect to the testator's intent.
application: The court distinguished ordinary beneficiaries from the NA, which has foundational documents declaring its raison d'être. Unlike a drug dealer who does not 'stand for' dealing drugs, the NA exists to promote white supremacy through hate propaganda that is criminal in Canada. From leaving his entire estate to the NA, the court inferred the testator intended it to further those illegal purposes, rendering the gift comparable to a trust for an unlawful purpose. The Attorney General's intervention supporting invalidity reinforced that voiding the bequest served public policy; the floodgates concern was minimal given the unusually strong factual record and litigation costs.
conclusion: The court held the residual bequest void as contrary to public policy, declared an intestacy as to the residue to be distributed to next of kin under the Devolution of Estates Act, and permanently enjoined any transfer of the residue to the National Alliance.

issue: Was a conditional discharge appropriate for two young first offenders who wilfully promoted hatred contrary to s. 319(2) of the Criminal Code?
facts: Kroeplin and Wasikiewicz, both 23 and without criminal records, posted posters on public buildings in Burlington depicting a Jewish man being shot and likening Jewish and Black people to vermin. They pled guilty. Defence sought conditional discharges with lengthy probation; the Crown sought three to four months' imprisonment.
rule: Section 730(1) of the Criminal Code permits a discharge where it is in the best interests of the accused and not contrary to the public interest. Under Sanchez-Pino, Fallofield, Meneses and Carson a discharge normally presupposes good character and that deterrence of others does not preclude its judicious use, but Swierszcz confirms that professional or personal consequences cannot justify a sentence outside the appropriate range, and the more serious the offence the less likely a discharge is not contrary to the public interest.
application: The judge found this a serious hate-promotion offence targeting historically victimized communities, as reflected in the Community Impact Statements, and one where denunciation and deterrence were paramount. A conditional discharge would not send the required message and would be contrary to the public interest, notwithstanding the offenders' youth, guilty pleas and lack of record.
conclusion: A conditional discharge (and equally a suspended sentence) was refused as contrary to the public interest and insufficient.

issue: Should the offenders be sent to jail or receive a conditional sentence of imprisonment given the paramountcy of denunciation and deterrence?
facts: The offence occurred on a single night at two nearby locations; the offenders did not create the images, used low-tech means, and the posters were quickly removed. Both had no record, pled guilty, expressed remorse, had family and (for Wasikiewicz) mental-health and police support, had been ostracized, and had lived under a curfew for 15 months. Wasikiewicz had been hospitalized for a Major Depressive Disorder and had completed 80 volunteer hours; Kroeplin had donated to B'nai Brith. COVID-19 made jail harsher.
rule: Sections 718 to 718.2 of the Criminal Code, with s. 718.2(a)(i) deeming hate motivation an aggravating factor and s. 718.2(d)-(e) restraint principles (Gladue). Section 742.1 sets the prerequisites for a conditional sentence; Proulx confirms a conditional sentence can be a punitive sanction achieving denunciation and deterrence, and Wismayer/Sears confirm it may be available even for serious offences. Proportionality (s. 718.1; Hamilton, Priest) and the COVID considerations in Hearns and Vigon-Campuzano apply.
application: The four statutory prerequisites for a conditional sentence were met, the offenders posing no danger to the community. Jail was within range and three months (rounded to 90 days intermittent) would have been fit, but current jail conditions meant an intermittent sentence would be served in temporary-absence programs. A six-month conditional sentence with full home confinement, a substance prohibition, and probation with a curfew, counselling, no-contact terms and community service (credited for existing volunteer hours/donation) provided the necessary punitive, denunciatory, deterrent, rehabilitative and restorative components.
conclusion: A six-month conditional sentence of imprisonment served in the community, followed by two years' probation, was imposed on each offender.

issue: Did the trial judge err in granting Good Spirit public interest standing to advance Charter claims and to contest separate-school rights?
facts: Good Spirit, a public school division, sued the Government and Christ the Teacher (a separate school division) after St. Theodore School was reconstituted as a Catholic separate school, seeking a declaration that funding non-Catholic students in Catholic schools breached s. 2(a) and s. 15. Good Spirit's stated concerns were financial and administrative (loss of enrolment, funding, and rural-school viability), and the Charter arguments relied on evidence from private religious school representatives who wanted more, not less, funding.
rule: Public interest standing is governed by Canada (Attorney General) v Downtown Eastside Sex Workers, 2012 SCC 45: a serious justiciable issue, a real stake or genuine interest, and a reasonable and effective means of bringing the matter to court. A public school division has no Charter rights of its own and depends on provincial law for its authority; the 'rights holder' principle (Calgary Board of Education; CA Home Builders) limits a public board's ability to attack rights conferred on separate schools.
application: The Court found a disconnect between the Charter issues and the economic/policy issue Good Spirit actually pursued. Good Spirit had no real stake in the Charter rights it asserted; the affected non-minority-faith adherents (who wanted equal funding, not reduced separate-school funding) had not come forward, and success could jeopardize their interests contrary to Adler. As a public division without Charter rights and with no entrenched right under s. 93 or s. 17(2), Good Spirit was also the wrong entity to contest the boundaries of separate-school rights.
conclusion: The trial judge erred in granting public interest standing on both bases; either error alone would dispose of the appeal.

issue: Did the trial judge apply the wrong approach to constitutional interpretation of s. 93 and s. 17(2)?
facts: The trial judge developed eight of his own interpretive principles, treated the 'solemn pact' as diminished, relied on extraneous texts not in evidence, and applied the denominational aspects test to s. 93(3).
rule: Minority-rights guarantees must be interpreted purposively and consistently with their preservation and development (Beaulac; Mahé; Reference re Bill 30; Greater Montreal). Under s. 29 of the Charter, separate-school rights are themselves constitutional and cannot be read down by reference to changing social attitudes. The denominational aspects test (Greater Montreal) applies to s. 93(1), which curtails the plenary power, not to s. 93(3), which merely permits augmentation of denominational rights and is insulated from Charter review through the guaranteed plenary power.
application: The trial judge gave the provisions a restrictive interpretation, wrongly treating the 1905 compromise as weakened and importing the denominational aspects test into s. 93(3). Reference re Bill 30 (Wilson, Estey and Lamer JJ.) holds that legislation augmenting separate-school rights under the plenary power and s. 93(3) is immune from Charter attack without any denominational aspects qualification. Reliance on extraneous, non-peer-reviewed texts without allowing submissions was also an error; fresh evidence (the Waiser affidavit) was admitted.
conclusion: The trial judge erred; the proper purposive approach was applied afresh, and the denominational aspects test does not govern s. 93(3).

issue: Is the Legislative Framework protected by s. 93 and s. 17(2) and immune from Charter scrutiny?
facts: The Education Act and Regulations fund public and separate school divisions on the same basis, primarily by enrolment, without any religious distinction; it is an effect that non-Catholics attending separate schools are funded, just as Catholics attending secular schools are funded.
rule: Section 17(2) of the Saskatchewan Act prohibits discrimination against schools of any class in the appropriation or distribution of moneys, guaranteeing fairness and proportionality (Alberta Public Boards, 2000 SCC 45). One part of the Constitution cannot invalidate another (Reference re Bill 30; Adler). Legislation validly enacted under the plenary power and s. 93(3) is insulated from Charter review.
application: The dispute could and should have been resolved under s. 17(2): funding both systems identically, without religious distinction, is the antithesis of discrimination and is exactly what s. 17(2) protects. Good Spirit sought to introduce a religion-based distinction that s. 17(2) prohibits. The framework is also a valid exercise of the plenary power and s. 93(3), and, so far as engaged, is consistent with s. 93(1).
conclusion: The Legislative Framework is a valid exercise of s. 93 and s. 17(2) and is immune from Charter scrutiny; Good Spirit's claim fails.

issue: If not immune, does the funding infringe s. 2(a) or s. 15(1), and is it justified under s. 1?
facts: No individual testified that funding of non-Catholics in Catholic schools infringed their religious practice; Good Spirit's witnesses (a Muslim and a Jewish school representative) sought equal full funding for their own schools. The framework is neutral on its face and funds all public divisions the same way.
rule: A s. 2(a) breach must be personal and proven (S.L. v Commission scolaire des Chênes, 2012 SCC 7; Mouvement laïque québécois, 2015 SCC 16); the state's duty of neutrality requires proof that the state favoured one belief and interfered with a complainant's freedom. Section 15(1) requires a distinction that perpetuates disadvantage, prejudice or stereotyping (Withler, 2011 SCC 12; Andrews). Section 1 requires a pressing and substantial objective and proportionality (Oakes; Frank, 2019 SCC 1).
application: There was no axiomatic Charter breach and no proof of personal infringement; the neutral framework funds both public systems equally. No evidence showed the funding perpetuated prejudice or stereotyping—the witnesses wanted more funding, not less. Even assuming a breach, the objective of providing equitable, choice-based funding within s. 93 without a public body adjudicating religious affiliation is pressing and substantial, rationally connected, minimally impairing (the alternatives all raised serious problems, including compelling religious tests and running against Adler), and proportionate.
conclusion: There is no infringement of s. 2(a) or s. 15(1); and in any event the framework would be justified under s. 1.

issue: Was the alleged error jurisdictional and what standard of review applied?
facts: TWU and the BCCT agreed the Council had authority to render its decision, but the BCCT conceded a question of law arose over the proper interpretation of the Teaching Profession Act — specifically whether the statute entitled the Council to consider TWU's discriminatory policies.
rule: Under U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault, [1988] 2 SCR 1048, a pragmatic and functional analysis determines whether an error is jurisdictional; an error in interpreting a provision limiting jurisdiction results in a loss of jurisdiction, and the decision is quashed (Bibeault at 1086). Per Nipawin, [1975] 1 SCR 382, basing a decision on extraneous matters, failing to consider relevant facts, or misinterpreting the Act to answer a question not remitted takes a tribunal outside its jurisdiction. A decision based on no evidence, or a patently unreasonable one, is a nullity (Dairy Producers).
application: The Court accepted that the central question — whether the Act empowered the Council to weigh TWU's community standards and its graduates' religious beliefs — was a matter of statutory interpretation going to jurisdiction. If the Council relied on irrelevant considerations or an improper purpose, or acted without evidence, its decision would be a nullity.
conclusion: The error was jurisdictional; the Court examined whether the Council correctly interpreted its mandate and whether an evidentiary basis existed, an error on either warranting quashing the decision.

issue: Did the BCCT exceed its jurisdiction under s. 4 of the Act by considering TWU's religious community standards concerning homosexual behaviour?
facts: TWU, a religiously-founded private university, requires students and faculty to sign Community Standards that condemn 'homosexual behaviour' as biblically condemned. The Council denied approval of TWU's teacher education program because it believed the program 'follows discriminatory practices which are contrary to the public interest and public policy', relying on s. 4 of the Teaching Profession Act.
rule: Section 4 makes it the object of the College to establish, 'having regard to the public interest', standards for the education, professional responsibility and competence of teachers. The phrase 'public interest' must be construed in the statutory context and does not confer unlimited discretion (Lindsay v. Manitoba; Prince George (City) v. Payne, [1978] 1 SCR 458; Roncarelli v. Duplessis, [1959] SCR 121). A body acting for a purpose external to its constitutive legislation abuses its discretion.
application: The Court held that only aspects of the public interest bearing on teachers' education, professional responsibility and competence fall within the BCCT's jurisdiction. The Council conceded TWU graduates were academically qualified and 'eminently suitable' to teach in Christian schools; the Court reasoned they were therefore equally qualified for public schools. Freedom of religion requires societal neutrality and tolerance rather than exclusion of those holding religious beliefs; refusing to certify an otherwise qualified teacher because of a religious belief that homosexual behaviour is sinful went beyond the College's mandate. The community standards were not per se irrelevant — the Council could examine graduates' actual conduct — but could not be used to deny approval absent a link to inappropriate conduct.
conclusion: The Council could consider conduct but could not refuse approval merely because of the religious beliefs reflected in the Community Standards; treating those beliefs as disqualifying exceeded its jurisdiction.

issue: Was the Council's decision made without any evidence and therefore patently unreasonable?
facts: The Council assumed TWU graduates would be biased against homosexual students because of the code of conduct, yet offered no evidence to support that inference. Meanwhile, the Program Approval Team had recommended accreditation, roughly 70% of TWU graduates taught in public schools with favourable reviews, and there was no evidence of intolerance by any graduate.
rule: A tribunal decision resting on a premise that cannot withstand rational analysis, or based on no evidence, is patently unreasonable and loses jurisdiction (Dairy Producers Cooperative; Hicks v. Langley Memorial Hospital).
application: The Council's premise — that requiring students to refrain from 'sinful' homosexual behaviour would produce intolerant teachers — rested on unfounded assumptions and ignored the evidence actually before it, including the Approval Team's report and TWU's detailed record of successful, tolerant graduates. Further evidence could readily have been obtained from the many TWU graduates already teaching. The Council failed to consider the contrary evidence before it.
conclusion: The decision was made without any reasonable evidentiary foundation, was patently unreasonable, and had to be quashed.

issue: What remedy should follow?
facts: The Council denied the application solely on the ground that the program followed discriminatory practices contrary to the public interest and public policy; the Teacher Education Programs Committee had earlier recommended approval subject to conditions.
rule: Where a tribunal acts without jurisdiction, the reviewing court may quash the decision and, where appropriate, direct the outcome by way of mandamus.
application: Because the sole stated ground was beyond the Council's jurisdiction and the Committee had recommended approval on conditions, the Court did not merely remit for redetermination but directed approval.
conclusion: The matter was remitted with a direction that the Council approve TWU's Teacher Education Program for accreditation, subject to the conditions recommended by the Teacher Education Programs Committee.

issue: Does an unincorporated trade union have standing to sue in its own name for defamation?
facts: CUPW is an unincorporated trade union representing mostly federally regulated Canada Post employees, plus about 50 provincially regulated members in three Ontario bargaining units. It sued in its own name for defamation over statements linking it to Hamas and terrorism arising from its political activism.
rule: At common law an unincorporated association traditionally had no legal personality and could not sue (Taff Vale Railway v. Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants). The law has evolved: Berry v. Pulley, 2002 SCC 40 recognises unions as legal entities at least for discharging their labour relations functions; PSAC v. Canada (A.G.), 2002 CanLII 19258 (Ont. C.A.) holds federally regulated unions may sue in their own name and that s. 3(2) of the Rights of Labour Act does not bar them. Fullowka v. Pinkerton's, 2010 SCC 5 and other authorities confirm the broadening juridical status of unions, including protection of reputation.
application: The court reviewed the evolving jurisprudence recognising that a union's ability to defend its reputation is central to its function, and that defending reputation supports its labour relations role even where the impugned comments arise from the union's broader social/political activism. As a federally regulated union CUPW could sue under PSAC without depending on the Ontario statutes; it would be absurd to deny standing because 50 of over 55,000 members are provincially regulated. Section 3(2) of the Rights of Labour Act was therefore not a bar.
conclusion: CUPW has standing to bring the defamation action in its own name.

issue: Were the impugned statements defamatory of and about CUPW?
facts: On 'The Source' broadcast and in a Toronto Sun article, Mr. Agar and Mr. Benlolo made statements and inferences associating CUPW with supporting terrorism, partnering with Hamas, and being terrorist sympathisers, following CUPW representatives' attendance at an Ottawa pro-Palestinian demonstration where a Hamas flag was flown near CUPW flags. Mr. Benlolo said his comments targeted CUPW leadership.
rule: A defamatory statement is one that tends to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of ordinary, right-thinking members of society (Color Your World Corp. v. CBC, 1998 CanLII 1983 (Ont. C.A.)); natural and ordinary meaning includes reasonable inferences (Lewis v. Daily Telegraph). Meaning is assessed in the context of the publication as a whole. Publication to a third party was conceded.
application: Words associating the union with a terrorist organisation and supporters of terrorism were capable of injuring its reputation, even for a politically vocal union. Mr. Benlolo's assertion that CUPW supports a designated terrorist organisation, and Mr. Agar's inferences in the broadcast and article, were defamatory in context. Because the union's leadership is elected to act on members' behalf, comments directed at the leadership were comments about the Union.
conclusion: The impugned statements were defamatory and were about CUPW, satisfying the elements of the tort.

issue: Did the defence of justification (truth) succeed?
facts: Mr. Benlolo argued his words were substantially true, relying on facts including that Hamas is a designated terrorist organisation, that Hamas and CUPW flags flew in proximity, CUPW's support for the Gaza boat and George Galloway tour, attendance at the Brazil World Social Forum, and CUPW's failure ever to condemn Hamas by name.
rule: Truth is a complete defence; the defendant need only prove the words are substantially true (Libel and Slander Act, s. 22; Sidorsky v. CFCN). Justification requires proof of the substantial truth of the 'sting' of the defamation (Bent v. Platnick, 2020 SCC 23).
application: While many underlying facts were true or accepted, the court found CUPW did not knowingly march with Hamas supporters, did not support Hamas, and did not willingly fly its flag next to Hamas's. The proven facts did not establish the truth of the sting — that CUPW supports a designated terrorist organisation.
conclusion: The defence of justification failed.

issue: Did the defence of fair comment succeed and was it defeated by malice?
facts: The defendants argued their statements were opinion that CUPW supported terrorism, based on CUPW's extensive public activism and its failure to disavow support for Hamas when given the opportunity. A banner reading 'Supporting terrorists?' (a question) ran during the broadcast.
rule: Fair comment requires: (1) a matter of public interest; (2) recognisable as comment; (3) based on fact; (4) satisfying the objective test 'could any person honestly express that opinion on proved facts?' (WIC Radio v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Grant v. Torstar, 2009 SCC 61; Hansman v. Neufeld, 2023 SCC 14). Comment need not be reasonable or proportionate. Malice — spite, ill-will, or knowing/reckless disregard for truth — defeats the defence (Hill v. Church of Scientology, 1995 CanLII 59), but a finding of subjective honest belief negates malice (Hansman).
application: The Middle East conflict was plainly a matter of public interest. The statements were recognisable as comment (the banner posed a question; loose/hyperbolic language in editorial context). A sufficient factual substratum existed — CUPW's public activism, BDS support, the demonstration, and CUPW's refusal to deny support for Hamas. The objective honest-belief test was met, and both Agar and Benlolo genuinely held their opinions. Their pre-existing 'angle' and criticism did not amount to the high bar of malice, and their honest belief negated malice. The court also accepted responsible communication and statutory privilege under s. 3(2) of the Libel and Slander Act.
conclusion: The defence of fair comment succeeded and was not defeated by malice; the action was dismissed with costs.

issue: Was there a material change in circumstances since the final Paisley order sufficient to permit variation of the parenting order?
facts: After Justice Paisley's October 22, 2018 order granting the mother sole custody and the father unsupervised overnight access, the Jewish Family and Child Service pursued a protection application; Justice Sager placed the child in the mother's care with the father's access at the Society's discretion, and Justice Spence found the child in need of protection under ss. 74(2)(f) and (h) of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act. Justice Paisley had no knowledge of the Society's involvement or the father's conduct.
rule: Section 17(1) and 17(5) of the Divorce Act require the court to be satisfied of a change in circumstances of the child before varying a parenting order. The threshold under Gordon v. Goertz, 1996 CanLII 191 (SCC), requires a change in the condition, means, needs or circumstances of the child and/or the parents' ability to meet the child's needs, that materially affects the child, and that was not foreseen or reasonably contemplated by the judge who made the initial order.
application: The finding that the child was in need of protection, the ongoing exposure to emotional harm from the father's uncontrolled conduct, and the father's demonstrated inability to safely exercise unsupervised access all post-dated the Paisley order and could not reasonably have been contemplated by Justice Paisley, who was unaware of the concerns. These developments materially affect the child.
conclusion: The threshold for variation was met; the court proceeded to a fresh best-interests inquiry.

issue: Should the father's parenting time be supervised or terminated in the best interests of the child, given the family violence?
facts: Over years of Society involvement the father engaged in relentless harassment, denigration of the mother, vulgar and threatening language, excessive phone calls, breaches of court orders, threats against Society workers, refusal of a court-ordered mental health assessment, and use of the Get as a bargaining tool. His harmful conduct continued even during supervised access and led private supervisor Brayden to terminate services; he was charged with criminal harassment. The child showed emotional distress and expressed both love for and fear of his father.
rule: Sections 16 and 16.1 of the amended Divorce Act require the court to consider only the best interests of the child, giving primary consideration to the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, and to weigh enumerated factors including family violence (ss. 16(3)(j), 16(4)). Jennings v. Garrett (2004), 2004 CanLII 17126 (ON SC) sets out factors for terminating or supervising access, treating termination as an extreme remedy to be considered only after supervision options are weighed.
application: The father exposed the child to a pattern of coercive, controlling and threatening behaviour, had no insight into the harm caused, took no responsibility and refused to comply with orders including the s. 98 mental health assessment. Trained Society workers could not control him. The court found supervised access alone might not protect the child, but ordered professionally supervised virtual parenting time with a built-in safety net: if the supervisor cannot maintain a safe environment and terminates services, the father's parenting time ends permanently. Had the mother been required to remain in Toronto, the court would have terminated parenting time.
conclusion: The father's parenting time was ordered to be professionally supervised, to be terminated on a final basis if the supervisor cannot maintain a safe environment; his request for full, unsupervised parenting rights was denied.

issue: Should the mother be permitted to relocate with the child to Israel?
facts: The mother is Israeli-born with parents, siblings and their children in Israel; she and the child visit for a month most summers, the child is closely bonded to the family, speaks Hebrew and attends a Hebrew immersion school. The mother has good teaching prospects and free accommodation in Israel and fears the father's escalating conduct in Toronto, where the Society's protective safety net would disappear once its file closed.
rule: Following the March 2021 amendments to the Divorce Act, ss. 16.9, 16.92, 16.93 and 16.95 govern relocation; where the child spends the vast majority of time with the relocating parent (s. 16.93(2)), the parent opposing relocation bears the burden of proving relocation is not in the child's best interests, assessed with the factors in s. 16 and s. 16.92 (reasons for the move, impact on the child, notice, compliance history, reasonableness of proposal).
application: The mother gave adequate notice in her application and complied with court orders; the father, who bore the burden, failed to prove relocation contrary to the child's interests. The court found the father's harmful conduct would continue and the mother could not shield the child alone once the Society withdrew. The relocation to the Tel Aviv area (outside the Government of Canada travel advisory's high-risk zones), with family support, secure housing and schooling, would provide stability and reduce the risk of harm. Supervised parenting time by video, or in person if the father travels to Israel, was reasonable.
conclusion: The mother was granted permission to relocate with the child to Israel; the father's opposition and travel-advisory argument were rejected.

issue: Did the defendant satisfy the threshold under s. 137.1(3) of the Courts of Justice Act that the proceeding arose from expression on a matter of public interest?
facts: Gharagozloo, a human rights activist with IOPHR, presented and narrated videos at and about an international religious freedom summit alleging that agents of the Iranian government conspired to assassinate and replace the Gonabadi Sufi spiritual leader Dr. Noor Ali Tabandeh; a fleeting image showed the plaintiff standing beside an alleged conspirator.
rule: Under s. 137.1(3), the moving party bears a not-heavy threshold burden to show the proceeding is causally related to its expression and that the expression relates to a matter of public interest, viewed expansively (1704604 Ontario Ltd. v. Pointes Protection Assn., 2020 SCC 22; Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61). The topic of the expression is determinative, not its merits, manner, or the speaker's motive.
application: Although some of the surrounding feuding was petty, Gharagozloo's expression concerned the human and religious rights violations of the Iranian government and a conspiracy to assassinate and replace a spiritual leader — a matter of profound public interest to a world community. The defamatory or motivated character of the expression is irrelevant to the threshold.
conclusion: The threshold was met; the onus shifted to the plaintiff under s. 137.1(4).

issue: Were Videos #3, #4 and #5, not expressly enumerated in the Statement of Claim, relevant to and encompassed by the defamation action for the anti-SLAPP analysis?
facts: The Statement of Claim expressly enumerated only Videos #1 and #2 but pleaded a 'series of false and defamatory statements' and a 'campaign of defamation' on 'various online platforms.' Gharagozloo featured in Videos #3, #4 and #5, produced Video #4, and used them to invite the lawsuit.
rule: A defamation claim must be fully particularized (what was said, that it was defamatory, publication, and audience) (Catalyst Capital Group v. Veritas, 2017 ONCA 85; Guergis v. Novak, 2013 ONCA 449). Section 137.1(6) restricts amendment of pleadings on an anti-SLAPP motion unless the judge orders otherwise.
application: The pleaded material facts (a campaign of defamation on various platforms) already encompassed the additional videos; enumeration is an incidental, non-material fact, so no amendment was needed. Gharagozloo, prominently featured in the videos, knew the case he had to meet. In any event, the videos were part of the narrative and relevant to each branch of the test, and the court would have exercised its s. 137.1(6) discretion to allow amendment if necessary.
conclusion: All of Videos #1–#5 were engaged in the action and relevant to the motion.

issue: Were there grounds to believe the plaintiff's proceeding had substantial merit, including whether an unnamed but identifiable person can be defamed by an image?
facts: A polished documentary (Video #2, echoed in Video #1) twice displayed for about four seconds an unobscured image of the identifiable plaintiff standing beside a named alleged conspirator under a caption identifying 'main co-conspirators to murder' the Gonabadi Sufi leader; Videos #3–#5 named the plaintiff as a devotee/advisor of the alleged conspirator.
rule: Defamation requires a defamatory statement referring to and published about the plaintiff that would lower his reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person (Grant v. Torstar; Botiuk). Images/photographs can be defamatory depending on context (St. Pierre v. Pacific Newspaper Group, 2006 BCSC 241; Chopra v. Hodson, 2001 ABQB 380). On a s. 137.1 motion the claim must have a real prospect of success — more than a possibility and more than an arguable case (Pointes).
application: A reasonable person, especially within the close-knit Gonabadi Sufi community, would understand the unobscured captioned image as identifying the plaintiff as a co-conspirator; the brief four-second display was immaterial. The case resembled St. Pierre (misidentification implying terrorism) rather than Chopra. The plaintiff did not need to be named to be defamed, and Videos #3–#5 defamed him expressly by words.
conclusion: The plaintiff established a strong case with a real prospect of success; substantial merit was shown.

issue: Did the plaintiff show that the defendant had no valid defence of justification or qualified privilege?
facts: Gharagozloo asserted the images only truthfully showed the plaintiff standing beside Dr. Reza Tabandeh, that his summit presentation was an occasion of privilege, and claimed the statements were true. He offered no evidence linking the plaintiff to any assassination or to the Iranian government.
rule: On the 'no valid defence' prong, once the defendant puts a defence in play, the plaintiff need only show reasonable grounds to believe a trier could reject it (Pointes; Subway v. CBC, 2021 ONCA 26). Justification requires proof of substantial truth; qualified privilege requires a duty/interest to communicate to a reciprocally interested audience, made without malice, and may be defeated by malice (Bent v. Platnick, 2020 SCC 23).
application: The defamatory meaning went well beyond the plaintiff merely standing beside Dr. Reza Tabandeh; Gharagozloo would bear the formidable burden of proving a conspiracy and the plaintiff's complicity, and it was reasonably possible a trier would find that unproven. Qualified privilege might fail because it must be exercised responsibly and could be defeated by a finding of malice.
conclusion: The plaintiff met the onus of showing reasonable grounds to believe neither defence was valid.

issue: Did the public interest in permitting the proceeding to continue outweigh the public interest in protecting the defendant's expression under s. 137.1(4)(b)?
facts: Gharagozloo is a genuine human rights advocate exposing Iranian government abuses; the plaintiff, a devout Gonabadi Sufi, alleged serious physical, emotional and reputational harm from being labelled complicit in the assassination of a spiritual leader, likened to a 'blood libel.' Videos were viewed tens of thousands of times.
rule: The weighing exercise is the crux of the analysis: the responding party must show harm sufficiently serious that the public interest in continuing the proceeding outweighs the public interest in protecting the expression (Pointes). Harm to reputation is presumed from publication and grave imputations (e.g., terrorist supporter) permit inference of serious harm; the court weighs the quality and motivation of the expression.
application: Both parties advanced compelling public-interest arguments and, as between them, the balance was even. The tipping point was the public interest in truth and justice: an anti-SLAPP motion is not a final determination, and only a trial could fairly resolve whether the plaintiff was innocent or whether Gharagozloo's serious accusations were true. Serious accusations warranted allowing the action to proceed rather than a preliminary determination of merits.
conclusion: The public interest favoured permitting the action to continue; the motion was dismissed with costs in any event of the cause.

issue: Is it plain and obvious that the applicants have no reasonable prospect of satisfying the Bedford/Carter test to revisit Adler, so that their Charter challenge to Ontario's failure to fund independent faith-based (Jewish day) schools must be struck?
facts: Members of the Jewish community and Grassroots for Affordable Jewish Education Inc. applied for declarations that Ontario's Education Act scheme, which publicly funds Roman Catholic separate schools and secular public schools but not other independent faith-based schools, discriminates and violates their s. 2(a) and s. 15 Charter rights. They did not seek to affect Roman Catholic funding, only equal per-student funding. Ontario and Canada moved to strike on the basis that Reference Re Bill 30, Adler and Bal render Ontario's funding decisions immune from Charter scrutiny under s. 93 of the Constitution Act, 1867 and s. 29 of the Charter.
rule: A pleading may be struck under r. 21.01(1)(b) only where it is plain and obvious the proceeding has no reasonable prospect of success (R. v. Imperial Tobacco, 2011 SCC 42). Motions to strike should not frustrate potential developments in the law (Tanudjaja). Binding precedent may be revisited where a new legal issue arises from significant developments in the law, or where a change in circumstances or evidence 'fundamentally shifts the parameters of the debate' (Canada (AG) v. Bedford, 2013 SCC 72; Carter v. Canada, 2015 SCC 5; R. v. Comeau, 2018 SCC 15), consistent with the 'living tree' doctrine of constitutional interpretation.
application: The court found only Adler (which extended Reference Re Bill 30 to immunize funding decisions regarding non-Catholic religious schools) needed revisiting; Reference Re Bill 30 (protecting Roman Catholic funding) did not. Considering the combined effect of pleaded changes — the s. 93A amendment by which Quebec and the federal government arguably abandoned the Confederation compromise; the developed principle of state neutrality (S.L. v. Commission scolaire des Chênes; Mouvement laïque québécois v. Saguenay); the growing recognition of minority rights and diversity; the possible positive-obligation argument from Vriend; increasing existential threats to the Jewish community; and, notably, the now firmly-established presumption of conformity with international law (Quebec v. 9147; Hape) and treaties/decisions such as the ICCPR, ICESCR and the UNHRC's Waldman decision holding Ontario's scheme discriminatory — the court held there was a reasonable chance an application judge could find the Bedford/Carter threshold met. Divergent reasons in Adler showed the wording could bear more than one interpretation. The court stressed it was not deciding the threshold was actually met, only that it was not plain and obvious it could not be.
conclusion: Not plain and obvious the applicants are bound to fail against Ontario; the motion to strike was dismissed as against Ontario and the application allowed to proceed to a full evidentiary record.

issue: Does the application disclose a reasonable cause of action against Canada?
facts: The applicants also named the Attorney General of Canada. Canada argued education and its funding fall exclusively to the provinces, that it had taken no action or enacted no law regarding funding of Ontario schools, and that unincorporated international treaty obligations are not domestically enforceable.
rule: Making laws in relation to education is exclusively provincial. International treaties not incorporated into Canadian law are not directly enforceable in Canadian courts (Capital Cities Communications v. CRTC; Baker v. Canada); implementation of treaty obligations is for the political authorities, not the courts (McVey v. United States).
application: Canada undertook no action or law regarding funding of Roman Catholic or other religious schools in Ontario. While Canada's international obligations may aid in interpreting s. 93 and s. 29, they cannot be enforced against Canada domestically through this proceeding, and the impugned scheme is a provincial statute.
conclusion: It is plain and obvious the claim against Canada has no reasonable prospect of success; the application was struck as against Canada.

issue: Should the appellant's extensive further (fresh) evidence be admitted for the purposes of the child protection appeal?
facts: D.M. sought to file 7,864 pages of further evidence (much of it uploaded on the day of the hearing) in support of her appeal from Justice Fraser's summary judgment. The material was diverse: some redundant, some inadmissible hearsay or expert evidence, some argument, and some containing admissions against her own interest.
rule: Section 134(4)(b) of the Courts of Justice Act and rule 38(29) of the Family Law Rules empower an appellate court to admit further evidence; s. 121(6) CYFSA allows evidence of events after the appealed decision. The general Palmer test (R. v. Palmer, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 759) applies but is applied more flexibly, liberally and less technically in child protection cases to give the court current information on the child's circumstances (L.M. v. Peel CAS, 2019 ONCA 841), though evidence must still comply with the law of evidence (Kawartha Haliburton CAS v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316).
application: Perell J. granted the motion, giving D.M. the benefit of the doubt on due diligence, relevance, credibility and potential effect on outcome, while admitting the documents only in accordance with the law of evidence and giving them the weight they deserved. Admitting the corpus in fact confirmed rather than undermined Justice Fraser's findings. Kristjanson J. concurred in the result but would have dismissed the fresh evidence motion, finding none of the material met the s. 121(6)/Palmer criteria and that dumping a new record on appeal was an unwarranted burden.
conclusion: The majority admitted all the further evidence for the appeal, subject to it being weighed according to the law of evidence; the evidence did not change the result.

issue: Was the child protection status review an appropriate case for summary judgment against a self-represented litigant?
facts: The children had been in the father's care since February 2019 due to concerns about D.M.'s mental health. On a status review, the Society sought summary judgment for a custody order; D.M., self-represented at the motion, opposed and cross-moved for sole custody. Justice Fraser found no genuine issue requiring a trial and granted summary judgment.
rule: Summary judgment in family matters is governed by Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules, in pari materia with Rule 20 of the Rules of Civil Procedure, applying the framework in Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7. In child protection cases the court must proceed with caution, apply the best-interests objective of the CYFSA, carefully screen evidence, and assist self-represented litigants per the CJC Statement of Principles (Kawartha Haliburton CAS v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316; Pintea v. Johns, 2017 SCC 23). Appellate review is deferential (palpable and overriding error), with correctness for pure questions of law (Housen v. Nikolaisen).
application: There was ample admissible evidence that the children remained in need of protection and that a custody and restraining order served their best interests. D.M. had indicated she was ready for trial, knew the case to meet, had had counsel in the run-up, and was not a 'special party.' The hearing was fair, and a full trial would inevitably have reached the same result. The further evidence confirmed the fact findings.
conclusion: The case was appropriate for summary judgment; Justice Fraser made no reviewable error, and this ground of appeal failed.

issue: Did the doctrine of federal paramountcy based on the Divorce Act preclude a custody order under the CYFSA?
facts: D.M. and J.K. had stayed matrimonial proceedings under the Divorce Act; the Society obtained a custody order under s. 102 CYFSA. D.M. argued the federal Divorce Act was paramount and ousted the provincial order.
rule: Federal paramountcy renders provincial law inoperative only where there is an operational conflict (impossibility of dual compliance) or frustration of a federal purpose (Multiple Access Ltd. v. McCutcheon; Canadian Western Bank v. Alberta; Alberta v. Moloney). Section 102(6) CYFSA itself provides that no order may be made where a decision-making-responsibility order has been made under the Divorce Act.
application: The CYFSA was intra vires; no decision-making order had been made under the Divorce Act; the divorce proceedings were stayed. Both statutes prioritize the best interests of the children, so there was no conflict of purpose and no operational conflict. Section 102(6) showed the province had guarded against operational conflict.
conclusion: Paramountcy was not triggered; the custody order was validly made and the ground of appeal failed.

issue: Did giving the father discretion over the mother's access constitute an unlawful delegation of the court's access jurisdiction?
facts: Justice Fraser granted custody to the father with access to the mother 'at the father's discretion.' D.M. argued this improperly delegated the court's access-determining authority.
rule: A court cannot delegate discretionary access decisions to a non-judicial actor in child protection matters (J.S.R. v. CAS of Ottawa, 2021 ONSC 630). However, ss. 102, 104-106 CYFSA and s. 28/34 of the Children's Law Reform Act provide that a custody/access order made under s. 102 is deemed a parenting/contact order under the CLRA and remains subject to the ongoing supervision and variation jurisdiction of the court.
application: The J.S.R. principle applies to extended society care orders that terminate court oversight, not to a custody order that ends the Society's involvement while leaving the matrimonial court with continuing oversight to determine and vary access. The parties could return to the (stayed) matrimonial proceedings for access/parenting determinations.
conclusion: There was no impermissible delegation; the ground of appeal failed.

issue: Should the Canadian Jewish Congress be permitted to intervene, and does the relaxed public-interest intervention standard apply rather than the traditional direct-interest requirement?
facts: Ten Jewish students, members of the Concordia Hillel club, sued the Concordia Student Union over resolutions that allegedly banned Hillel and suspended its funding, alleging a broader context of anti-Israel and anti-Jewish harassment and intimidation on campus. The Canadian Jewish Congress, an organization existing since 1919 whose objects include combatting anti-Semitism and acting on matters affecting the Canadian Jewish community, sought to intervene in support of the plaintiffs. The C.S.U. contested the intervention, arguing the dispute was purely private and governed by its by-laws, the Student Clubs Manual, University policy and the accreditation statute, so the relaxed public-law intervention approach should not apply.
rule: Courts have discretion to receive interventions, and the strict approach has been relaxed in cases involving human rights legislation and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (Rothman's, Benson & Hedges v. A.G. Canada, [1997] R.J.Q. 2786). The test weighs whether the third party can make an appreciable contribution to resolving the dispute against the risk of dissipating judicial resources and unduly prolonging the debate; the interests of justice govern. In traditional private/delictual matters a party must have a personal, real and direct interest (Soterm inc. v. Terminaux Portuaires; Jeunes Canadiens pour une civilisation chrétienne).
application: Although the C.S.U. ably argued the case was a private dispute governed by its internal instruments, the Court could not ignore the context of ongoing harassment and intimidation in which the plaintiffs said the offending resolutions were adopted. It is precisely in that context that the C.J.C. has a genuine interest and could assist in resolving the plaintiffs' claim. On balance the C.J.C.'s presence would be valuable and, if adequately narrowed, would not unduly prolong the trial or the interlocutory hearing nor dissipate judicial resources.
conclusion: The intervention was received, but only for the limited purpose of establishing the effect on the Canadian Jewish community of the incidents and events described in the plaintiffs' declaration.

issue: What should the permissible scope and conclusions of the intervention be?
facts: The C.J.C. sought wide-ranging orders, including that the C.S.U. issue an apology to the Jewish community in Canada, cease harassment, repeal its resolutions, and pay symbolic damages, and that the University be declared obligated to provide a safe, discrimination-free environment and to revoke the resolutions.
rule: An aggressive intervenor's role must be circumscribed so as not to duplicate the plaintiffs' claim or seek relief that is of doubtful legality or not properly justiciable; the court may limit witnesses, examination, cross-examination and argument (following the circumscription approach in Rothman's, Benson & Hedges).
application: The Court found the C.J.C.'s requested conclusions went far beyond what is appropriate: many merely restated the plaintiffs' demands, and others—such as ordering an apology to the Jewish community or symbolic damages—were of doubtful legality or improbably justiciable. The intervention was therefore confined to demonstrating the effect on the Jewish community, and the Court reserved to the trial or interlocutory judge authority to limit the number of witnesses, examination and cross-examination, and the duration of oral argument.
conclusion: The C.J.C. was ordered to file an amended intervention limited to seeking that its intervention and the plaintiffs' action be maintained, with the Court reserving broad powers to control its participation.

issue: Was the assault on Ms. Moscoe motivated by bias, prejudice or hate under s. 718.2(a)(i) of the Criminal Code?
facts: A few weeks after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, the victim, a Jewish woman, was placing posters of Israeli children taken hostage on poles on Yonge Street. Mr. Elkhodary approached confrontationally, tore down the posters, swore at her ('I don't give a fuck' when told they were of hostages), pushed her and struck her forehead. He testified he fundamentally disagreed with the posters, considered them fabricated propaganda, and had a Palestinian stepfather and family in Gaza. The defence argued hate was not proven beyond a reasonable doubt because there were no antisemitic words and the victim was not shown to have been sought out.
rule: Section 718.2(a)(i) makes it aggravating where an offence is motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on, inter alia, race, national or ethnic origin, religion, sex or any other similar factor. Case law (R. v. Ingram and Grimsdale (1977); R. v. Lelas (1990); R. v. Soles; R. v. Simms; R. v. Abed) holds that offences targeting a person because of membership in a racial or religious group are more heinous, attack the fabric of a pluralistic society (Charter s. 27), and call for denunciation and general deterrence.
application: The court found antisemitic words are not required for an offence to be hate-motivated. The only reason for the intentional assault was to intimidate the victim and silence her expression of support for the Jewish/Israeli hostages, given the context set out in the reasons for judgment. The assault was aimed at undermining her freedom of expression (Charter s. 2(b)) because she was expressing views related to Jewish people, and Mr. Elkhodary fundamentally opposed the posters' content. The circumstances paralleled R. v. Abed.
conclusion: The court found beyond a reasonable doubt that the offence was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate under s. 718.2(a)(i) and treated this as a statutorily aggravating factor, along with the unprovoked nature of the assault, the victim being a smaller, lone woman, and the significant victim and community impact (s. 718.2(a)(iii.1)).

issue: What sentence is proportionate — a discharge, a suspended sentence, or a conditional sentence?
facts: Mr. Elkhodary, 34, a first offender with no record and no bail breaches, expressed genuine remorse in court, had support from family and friends, and suffers from anxiety, ADHD and past anger-management issues; a GPS-monitoring assessment found him suitable. The Crown sought a five-month conditional sentence plus 12 months' probation and ancillary orders; the defence sought an absolute discharge, alternatively a conditional discharge.
rule: Proportionality is the fundamental principle (s. 718.1; R. v. Parranto; R. v. Lacasse; R. v. Nasogaluak; R. v. Suter). Denunciation and deterrence are paramount for hate-motivated violence. Judicial restraint for first offenders requires considering all sanctions short of incarceration (R. v. Priest; R. v. Proulx; R. v. Batisse). A conditional sentence under s. 742.1 is available where the term is under two years, there is no minimum, and community service of the sentence would not endanger community safety and is consistent with ss. 718–718.2; a conditional sentence can satisfy denunciation and deterrence (Proulx; Wismayer).
application: Given the aggravating hate motivation and impact, an absolute or conditional discharge, or a suspended sentence, would be contrary to the public interest and disproportionate. However, as a first offender who had complied with bail and posed no danger, community service of the sentence was appropriate. A conditional sentence would express society's condemnation, achieve deterrence, allow continued employment efforts and rehabilitative anger-management counselling.
conclusion: Held: a five-month (150-day) conditional sentence was imposed — 50 days house arrest, 50 days restrictive curfew, 50 days lighter curfew, with GPS monitoring — followed by 12 months' probation, a five-year s. 110 weapons prohibition, a DNA order for the secondary designated offence, and the victim fine surcharge.

issue: What standard governs the 'appearance of right' criterion where the requested injunction may indirectly affect freedom of expression?
facts: McGill sought a prohibitory injunction restraining the blocking/obstruction of buildings and paths, excessive noise, and the intimidation/harassment/threatening of persons associated with McGill's policies. Union interveners argued the order would chill picketing and expression and therefore engage the heightened free-speech standard.
rule: Under art. 511 C.C.P. and Groupe CRH Canada Inc. v. Beauregard, the appearance-of-right criterion is normally low (claim neither frivolous nor vexatious). A heightened standard — issuance only in 'the most manifest and rare cases' — applies where an injunction seeks to restrain free speech (Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Canadian Liberty Net; Association étudiante de l'Université McGill v. X, 2025 QCCA 475).
application: The Court found McGill did not seek to enjoin any specific message, protest, banner or slogan; it sought to prohibit physical blocking, excessive noise, and intimidation/harassment. These orders may indirectly affect expression, but are not comparable to injunctions restraining defamatory or hateful speech. The chilling effect is properly weighed at the balance-of-convenience stage, not through a heightened first-step standard. Universities have a right and duty to ensure access to classes and to control their property (multiple prior Quebec authorities), and McGill's apparent right had been recognized four times in prior proceedings.
conclusion: The ordinary prima facie standard applies, and McGill satisfied it — a serious question to be tried was demonstrated.

issue: Did McGill demonstrate that the injunction is 'necessary to prevent serious or irreparable prejudice' under art. 511 C.C.P.?
facts: McGill relied on a series of past violent events (2024 blockades, encampment, building occupation, April 2025 strike disruptions, property damage) and on SPHR Instagram posts vowing 'no business as usual until divestment.' However, those posts were over a year old and SPHR had published nothing since April 2025. Professor Campbell's vague reference to a possible second-anniversary mobilization lacked specifics.
rule: Art. 511 C.C.P. requires that the injunction be 'necessary to prevent' the harm. For a quia timet/precautionary injunction, courts must adopt a cautious approach requiring 'a high degree of probability' that the harm will occur (Sharpe, Injunctions and Specific Performance; Operation Dismantle; Association générale des étudiants... v. Roy Grenier, 2016 QCCA 86).
application: Past events undoubtedly caused serious and irreparable harm, but the issue was likelihood of recurrence. The record contained no evidence of who is behind SPHR or their intentions, no post since April 2025, and no probative evidence of imminent action. There was no 'forte probabilité' or 'probabilité sérieuse' of recurrence in the short or medium term. Nor was there evidence that the injunction would alleviate the antisemitic/harmful campus climate, since McGill expressly disclaimed any intent to restrain expression. Urgency is not required at the interlocutory stage, but an injunction cannot rest on hypothetical harm.
conclusion: McGill failed to demonstrate that the injunction is necessary to prevent serious or irreparable prejudice.

issue: Does the balance of convenience favour granting the injunction?
facts: The order would apply to 'any person having knowledge of' it, cover the entire lower campus and any building used for McGill's operations, and remain in force indefinitely. Unions feared it would chill picketing and mobilization (e.g., the April 2024 AMPFA gathering that 'pretty much blocked' an entrance).
rule: Balance of convenience must always be assessed (Groupe CRH; HRM Projet Children). Courts must consider an injunction's overall impact including its chilling effect, must be reluctant to enjoin conduct unrelated to the claims advanced (Re Brake, 2019 NLCA 17), and must not bind non-parties who act independently (Sharpe; Aetna Financial Services v. Feigelman).
application: Three features tipped the balance against McGill: (1) no identifiable defendant — SPHR is a non-existent entity and the order would apply indiscriminately to anyone on campus regardless of motivation, though McGill could likely have identified individuals; (2) the vast geographic scope (all of lower campus, and no geographic limit for the harassment orders); and (3) the indeterminate temporal duration, which magnifies the inconvenience and chilling effect. McGill's laudable narrowing of the wording did not resolve the uncertainty. Unlike short provisional injunctions where overbreadth is tolerable, the indefinite duration made the inconvenience substantial.
conclusion: The balance of convenience does not favour granting the injunction.

issue: Should the respondent mother's Answer be struck out for failure to obey court orders in a child protection proceeding?
facts: Over almost two years and 25 court appearances, the self-represented mother repeatedly disobeyed orders: she was found to have participated in the disappearance of both children, published prohibited material contrary to s. 45(8) CFSA, was found in contempt and incarcerated 30 days, boycotted the court, and stopped filing material or attending. The children were already found in need of protection.
rule: The Family Law Rules, O. Reg. 114/99 (Courts of Justice Act), permit a court to strike out pleadings where a party fails to follow the rules, obey a court order, or where the pleadings disclose no reasonable claim or defence. Rule 14(23) allows striking a party's Answer where a party does not obey an order made on motion. Courts are reluctant to strike pleadings in child protection matters because it forecloses a parent's ability to assist in determining best interests.
application: The court found the mother was not influenced by court orders, had been found in contempt and punished yet continued to defy directions, and conceded the school and health concerns. It weighed the prejudice to the mother against the prejudice to the children of further delay, emphasizing the need for permanency and finality in child welfare disputes. The court preserved her affidavit material to keep her viewpoint before the court, but struck the Answer as the litigation itself was harming the children.
conclusion: The mother's Answer was struck out (though her affidavits were not), and the matter was allowed to proceed by summary/uncontested trial.

issue: Should the court grant summary judgment making disposition orders without a full trial?
facts: The younger child C. (13) had been missing over seven months, not in school, at risk of inappropriate medication; the older child T. (16) had attended only two days of school in seven months under an interim supervision order. Psychiatric and clinic assessments documented the mother's delusional belief system and its serious harm to the children. The mother filed nothing and did not oppose the motion.
rule: Rule 16 (Family Law Rules) allows summary judgment; Rule 10(5) provides that where an Answer is struck the respondent is not entitled to further notice or participation. The moving party (the Society) bears the burden of showing no triable issue (Children's Aid Society of Halton Region v. K.L.A., 2006 CanLII 33538 (ON CA)), and the jurisdiction must be exercised with caution, taking a 'good, hard look' at the full evidentiary record (Children's Aid Society of Waterloo v. R.S., 2000 CanLII 22902; F.B. v. S.G.). Disposition is governed by ss. 57, 57(2), 57(3), 57(4) and 70(1) CFSA, requiring decisions in the child's best interests, consideration of less disruptive alternatives, and observance of wardship time limits.
application: The court reviewed the voluminous record and found compelling, credible, uncontradicted evidence of overwhelming protection concerns. Community placement for T. had been tried and failed through the mother's interference; no less restrictive plan existed for C.; the mother's prognosis for change was bleak and statutory time limits were running. The relief sought was temporary and less intrusive than the assessor's recommendation of Crown wardship. The court found no genuine issue requiring a trial regarding the children's health and educational needs.
conclusion: Summary judgment granted: C. made a ward of the Society until the later of June 29, 2007 or three months after his return; T. placed with the mother under a three-month supervision order with detailed conditions.

issue: Should the child protection file be transferred from Kingston to Brantford?
facts: The mother had relocated to Brantford and both parties now appeared to consent to a transfer. However, the younger child C. remained missing, and his assessments, medical resources, lawyer, foster home, school and familiar workers were all in the Kingston area.
rule: A court may transfer a proceeding where appropriate, but the governing consideration in child protection remains the child's best interests and the balance of convenience.
application: Despite the unopposed request, the court found the substantial convenience remained in Kingston and that transfer while C. was still missing would be counterproductive to his security. His support network and resources were all in Kingston, and the mother's non-cooperation and disregard for the legal system made transfer inappropriate at this time; the motion could be renewed by C.'s counsel once he was returned to care.
conclusion: The motion to transfer the case to the Ontario Court of Justice in Brantford was dismissed.

issue: On a statutory appeal on questions of law, how much deference is owed to the Board's interpretation of the Human Rights Act?
facts: The Pioneers appealed the Board's decision under ss. 26(3)-(4) of the Human Rights Act, which permit appeals on questions of law only. The Board's task involved statutory interpretation and evidentiary questions it was addressing for the first time.
rule: Sections 26(3)-(4) confer a statutory right of appeal on questions of law and make appeal the only means to set aside a Board decision. Where a legislature grants an appeal on "law or jurisdiction," the patently unreasonable standard does not apply; the court must correct all errors of law (Jones & de Villars; Bell Canada v. Canada (CRTC), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1722). Curial deference is limited to matters squarely within the tribunal's expertise.
application: The court held that appellate jurisdiction is broader than judicial review. Matters of statutory interpretation and evidence do not fall squarely within the Board's expertise, especially on its first occasion addressing them; the court was therefore entitled and obliged to determine the law and correct errors of law without deference.
conclusion: The court would review the Board's legal and evidentiary determinations for correctness and correct any error of law.

issue: Was the exclusion of Gould "discrimination" under ss. 6/11, and did the Board fail to balance equality against freedom of association?
facts: Gould was refused membership solely because she is female. The Pioneers is a century-old male-only fraternal order whose primary objects are the mutual protection and brotherhood of its members. The Yukon Human Rights Act expressly protects, in its Bill of Rights (s. 5), the right to form associations of any character.
rule: Discrimination under ss. 6 and 11 must be assessed by effect, not intent (O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536; Andrews v. Law Society of B.C., [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143). Human rights legislation is quasi-constitutional and given a fair, large and liberal interpretation, but no right is absolute and competing rights (including freedom of association, expressly guaranteed by the Act and s. 2 Charter) must be balanced in their social, political and legal context.
application: The Board declared discrimination "in the abstract" had been established without properly determining whether the conduct fell within ss. 6 or 11 in context, and without recognizing that not all differential treatment is discriminatory. Critically, the Board failed to weigh the Pioneers' countervailing right to associate against Gould's right to equality. The genuine membership screening, congeniality, absence of commercial activity and private character all had to be considered.
conclusion: The Board erred in law; the membership policy may not be discriminatory within the meaning of the Act, and the failure to balance the competing rights was an error requiring a rehearing.

issue: Did the collection and preservation of history amount to providing "services to the public" under s. 8(a)?
facts: The Pioneers' historian, Mr. Cyr, a volunteer, gathered and preserved records about members and provided historical information to anyone in the public who requested it. The intervener conceded there was no discrimination in the distribution of information but argued the male-only preparation of history was inherently discriminatory.
rule: Section 8(a) prohibits discrimination "when offering or providing services, goods or facilities to the public." The word "services" is unqualified; "public" modifies to whom services are offered, not the nature of the services. Legislation must be given the meaning its words can bear (Action travail des femmes).
application: The court held the Board wrongly used "public" to modify "services" and confused "public services" with "services to the public." Even if the historical activity were a service, it was offered to all members of the public without discrimination in distribution. Creating information, however one-sided, shared freely with all who request it, is not conduct caught by the Act; the activity was also expressive conduct protected by freedom of expression under the Act and s. 2(b) of the Charter.
conclusion: The Board erred in law; the creation of information provided without discrimination to the public is not prohibited discrimination under s. 8(a).

issue: Did the Board err by not considering the s. 9 defence and the s. 10 group exemption?
facts: The Pioneers is fairly characterized as a social organization. The Board did not consider s. 9 at all and applied a narrow, restrictive construction to s. 10, concluding the people the Order exists to serve was the whole community.
rule: Section 9 provides that treatment based on factors establishing reasonable cause is not discrimination. Section 10 provides that a religious, charitable, educational, social, cultural or athletic organization may give preference to its members or those it exists to serve. Group-exemption provisions confer and protect associational rights and are not to be read restrictively like BFOR defences (Caldwell v. St. Thomas Aquinas; Brossard (Ville) v. Québec (CDP)).
application: The court held s. 9 should have been considered (freedom of association and expression may be reasonable cause). Section 10 is not a mere BFOR-type limit but a provision integral to defining the Act's scope, establishing the primacy of group rights in specified circumstances, and should be given the ordinary meaning of its words. The Yukon provision, unlike Quebec's, requires no showing that the exclusion is "justified." The Pioneers likely fit within s. 10 as a social organization, and "the people the organization exists to serve" is arguably its members.
conclusion: The Board erred in law in failing to consider s. 9 and in its restrictive treatment of s. 10; both must be considered on rehearing.

issue: Could the Board find history is distorted when recorded only by males without sufficient evidence?
facts: The Board accepted "from a common sense standpoint" that history recorded solely by males would be distorted, while acknowledging the evidence on that point "could not be accorded much weight." This finding grounded its conclusion of prohibited discrimination.
rule: A complaint must be proven on a balance of probabilities (s. 23), and hearings must accord with fundamental justice (s. 22). While the Board may receive relevant evidence beyond strict court rules (s. 11 Regulations), a finding must rest on material with probative value (R. v. Deputy Industrial Injuries Commissioner, Ex p. Moore; Blanchard v. Control Data). A finding of fact with no evidence is an error of law; social/legislative facts require more than common-sense reasoning.
application: The court held the Board reached a critical factual conclusion in the absence of evidence, relying on unsubstantiated opinion and academic writings whose excerpts may not support the propositions urged. Distinguishing admissibility from weight, and cautioning about the danger of over-broad legislative facts in narrowly focused litigation, the court found the complainant had not proven her case even under the relaxed evidentiary standard.
conclusion: The Board erred in law by finding distortion of history without sufficient probative evidence; this independently justified setting aside the decision.

issue: Should the plaintiff be permitted to litigate anonymously under a confidentiality order despite the open-court principle?
facts: The plaintiff, a McGill student who chaired the anonymous online 'No' campaign against the SSMU's Policy Against Genocide in Palestine, sought a confidentiality order. She adduced social-media messages branding 'No' campaigners as 'pro genociders' and 'genocide supporters', an anonymous user boasting of belonging to an 'evil gang', and newspaper articles and a McGill affidavit describing rising tensions and antisemitic incidents in Montreal after October 7, 2023. The SSMU argued her fears were subjective, that the newspaper articles were inadmissible hearsay, and that she had renounced anonymity.
rule: The open-court principle is constitutionally protected under s. 2(b) of the Charter and s. 3 of the Quebec Charter, and codified in arts. 11 and 12 C.C.P. A confidentiality order may issue only where the applicant establishes the three cumulative Sherman/Sierra Club prerequisites: (1) court openness poses a serious risk to an important public interest; (2) the order is necessary because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; and (3) the benefits of the order outweigh its negative effects. Physical safety is an important public interest and serious risk may be established by logical inference from objective circumstantial facts, not mere speculation (Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25; J.C. c. Douville, 2022 QCCA 958).
application: The court found the social-media messages were thinly veiled threats designed to harass, intimidate and silence the plaintiff, and that it was not fanciful to infer she could be further threatened or harmed if named; this was more than negligible or speculative and beyond mere discomfort. Newspaper articles were admissible only to show a broader climate of disquiet, and the McGill affidavit corroborated the tensions. She had not renounced anonymity by filing the injunction application or by disclosing her name in an exhibit filed in support of confidentiality (Exhibit P-2 ordered sealed). Anonymity was preferable to in camera hearings or sealing orders, but the requested order was too broad, so the court adopted Douville-style non-publication/non-dissemination orders while requiring disclosure of her name to instructing SSMU members through counsel.
conclusion: The confidentiality application was granted in part; the plaintiff may litigate anonymously with non-publication and non-dissemination of identifying information, Exhibit P-2 sealed, and her name disclosed only to authorized SSMU members through counsel.

issue: Should an interlocutory injunction be granted restraining the SSMU from ratifying and implementing the Policy pending trial?
facts: A referendum adopted (by roughly 25% of members) the Policy Against Genocide in Palestine, which condemned Israel and demanded that McGill and the SSMU cut ties, divest and take pro-Palestinian positions for five years. McGill's Deputy Provost warned that adoption would breach the SSMU Constitution and constitute an event of default under the Memorandum of Agreement, and that the Policy invoked antisemitic tropes. The plaintiff sought to enjoin ratification and implementation, alleging violations of the Constitution, the Equity Policy and the Antisemitism Motion. The SSMU argued the application was premature (the Board had not yet ratified) and that the Policy was mere political expression protected by student democracy.
rule: Under art. 511 C.C.P. and Groupe CRH Canada inc. c. Beauregard, 2018 QCCA 1063, an interlocutory injunction requires: (1) an appearance of right (a serious question to be tried, neither frivolous nor vexatious); (2) serious or irreparable harm; and (3) a balance of inconvenience favouring the applicant. Sufficient interest is governed by art. 85 C.C.P. Freedom of expression is fundamental (Pepsi-Cola, R.W.D.S.U. Local 558), and courts are reluctant to interfere in the internal affairs of student associations (Presch v. AMS of UBC, 2017 BCSC 963).
application: The application was not premature or moot: its gravamen was the unconstitutionality of the Policy tied to the referendum itself, and the SSMU had undertaken only not to ratify pending the hearing, distinguishing Fried where the Board had refused to ratify. On appearance of right, the court distinguished Presch (a mere 'loaded question' on procedural/contractual grounds) — here a detailed 'loaded policy' omitting October 7 arguably breached constitutional principles requiring the SSMU to facilitate interaction among all communities and respect human dignity regardless of national, ethnic or religious origin; the claim was serious. The court found no appearance of right on the Equity Policy (the plaintiff failed to use the available complaints procedure) or the Antisemitism Motion (not a policy). It found serious harm: the Policy's cascading call to action would exacerbate division and, if antisemitic and unconstitutional, would violate the human dignity of Jewish students with no rescission mechanism until 2028. The balance of inconvenience favoured the plaintiff, as ratifying a possibly unconstitutional four-year policy was more prejudicial than delaying it.
conclusion: The injunction application was granted in part; an interlocutory injunction issued restraining the SSMU from ratifying or implementing the Policy until trial on the merits, without security, and not declared executory notwithstanding appeal.

issue: Was the case appropriate for disposition by summary judgment under Rule 20 of the Rules of Civil Procedure?
facts: Soliman moved for summary judgment in his defamation action. Bordman resisted, arguing numerous genuine issues required a trial, particularly whether his statements were hate speech and whether he was a racist. The record was extensive: video recordings, examinations for discovery, cross-examinations and two factums; Bordman had abandoned the justification defence.
rule: Rule 20.04(2)(a) directs summary judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; Rule 20.04(2.1) permits weighing evidence, assessing credibility and drawing inferences unless it is in the interest of justice to reserve those powers for trial (Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7). In defamation matters availability of summary judgment requires a case-by-case analysis (Skafco Ltd. v. Abdalla, 2020 ONSC 136).
application: Perell J. found a fulsome evidentiary record allowing fair and just determination of defamation, the fair comment and responsible communication defences, and remedies. Credibility concerns evaporated on close review of the evidence. Only the collateral questions of whether Bordman's speech was hate speech and whether he was a racist raised genuine issues requiring a trial, but Soliman did not need those findings to succeed.
conclusion: Except for the hate-speech/racist allegations, the case was appropriate for summary judgment; a trial was not required to determine liability, defences and remedies.

issue: Did Bordman's statements defame Soliman?
facts: Bordman, an alternative-media journalist, published Internet videos and posts asserting that Soliman, a prominent lawyer and Conservative campaign chair, was a supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood and extremist/terrorist Islamic organizations, a closet anti-Semite and Al Quds Day supporter, and a covert advocate of Sharia law in Canada. Publication and reference to Soliman were admitted.
rule: Defamation requires: (1) the defendant made a statement; (2) the words were defamatory (would lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person); (3) the words referred to the plaintiff; and (4) they were published (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61). Grave imputations such as being a terrorist or terrorist supporter are so obviously harmful that harm and general damages may be inferred.
application: Bordman's many statements synthesized into three assertions, each of which would lower Soliman's reputation.
