Once established, falsity and damages are presumed (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61).
application: The statements were posted online worldwide to thousands of followers (publication); they expressly named and depicted Mr. Fakih and Paramount (reference); and they associated the plaintiffs with terrorists, rapists and child killers, which would lower their reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person (defamatory). Justice Nakatsuru had already found the event videos to be facially defamatory and to bear the hallmarks of hate speech, and the other statements were substantially similar.
conclusion: The impugned statements are defamatory; all three elements are met.

issue: Are any defences available to the Johnston defendants?
facts: The Johnston defendants filed no responding materials and provided few particulars in their defence, alluding to 'satire', and relied primarily on freedom of expression under s. 2 of the Charter. They led no evidence of any factual basis for their remarks.
rule: Particulars of justification/truth must be pleaded and the defendant bears the burden of proving truth. Fair comment and responsible communication require the statements to concern a matter of public interest and are defeated by malice (WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Grant v. Torstar). The Charter does not apply to litigation between private citizens; violent, threatening and hateful expression falls outside s. 2(b) protection (R v. Keegstra; Whatcott v. Saskatchewan HRT, 2013 SCC 11).
application: No factual basis for justification was offered, and the defendants called their comments 'satire', which by definition is not fact. Hate communication raises no public-interest subject matter, defeating fair comment and responsible communication, and any such defences are further defeated by malice. The Charter does not apply to private litigation, and even if it did, the defendants' violent, threatening and hateful expression would fall outside protected expression.
conclusion: No defences are available to the Johnston defendants.

issue: What quantum of compensatory (general, aggravated, and special) damages is appropriate?
facts: The plaintiffs are prominent, philanthropic public figures whose reputation was central to Paramount's mission to destigmatize halal food; the internet-based hate campaign caused lost employees, customer concern, family distress, and the loss of a UAE master-franchise deal worth roughly $2.6 million per year. The defendants never apologized and bragged about the harm caused.
rule: General damages are presumed once defamation is made out; factors include the plaintiff's standing, seriousness of statements, mode/extent of publication, absence of apology, and the defendant's conduct and motive (Barrick Gold Corp. v. Lopehandia). Internet defamation is aggravated by its ubiquity and reach. Aggravated damages arise where the defendant's conduct is high-handed, malicious or oppressive (Hill v. Church of Scientology). Special damages compensate for proximate, measurable business loss.
application: The allegations of terrorism and rape were among the most serious possible, published widely online with no way to measure reach; the defendants refused any apology, continued the campaign, and accosted Mr. Fakih and his children, all supporting aggravated damages. The lost UAE deal alone exceeded $2.6 million per year, more than the compensatory damages claimed. The court awarded a global sum encompassing general, aggravated, and special damages.
conclusion: Substantial compensatory damages (general, aggravated and special) are warranted, forming part of the $2.5 million total award.

issue: Is an award of punitive damages warranted?
facts: The defendants evaded service, lied to process servers, breached multiple court orders and cost awards, publicly maligned the court and the 'white woman judge' as being 'in on' a conspiracy, and persisted in hate speech targeting Muslims solely on the basis of religion.
rule: Punitive damages punish rather than compensate and express the court's outrage at egregious conduct (Focus Graphite Inc. v. Douglas, 2015 ONSC 1104). Hate speech is a special category of expression deserving of sanction given its grave psychological and social harm (Whatcott v. Saskatchewan HRT).
application: The defendants' repeated contempt for the court process, breaches of orders, and unrelenting hateful campaign, combined with the pressing societal harm caused by hate speech that marginalizes a vulnerable group, justified punishment beyond compensation.
conclusion: Punitive damages are warranted and form part of the $2.5 million award.

issue: Are permanent restraining orders (injunctions) appropriate?
facts: The defendants continued their defamatory and harassing campaign for nearly three years without abatement, ignored and breached court orders, refused to pay costs awards, harassed the plaintiffs' family and counsel, and gave no indication they would stop.
rule: Permanent injunctions may be granted in defamation actions where (a) there is a likelihood the defendant will continue to publish defamatory statements despite a liability finding, or (b) there is a real possibility the plaintiff will not receive compensation because enforcement of a damages award may be impossible (Sustainable Development Technology Canada v. Sigurdson, 2018 ONSC 7320).
application: Both grounds were met: the defendants' persistent campaign made continued publication highly likely, and their history of ignoring orders and refusing to pay costs made non-payment of any judgment a real possibility. The court therefore restrained contact with, recording of, and defamatory publications about Mr. Fakih, his family, the plaintiffs, and their counsel, including proximity restrictions.
conclusion: Permanent injunctions were granted against the Johnston defendants.

issue: Did the Bucks fraudulently or wrongfully pay themselves vacation pay upon termination?
facts: Under s. 10 of the Agreement the Bucks were entitled to three weeks' paid vacation per year with carry-over, and Oakwood Towers did not dispute the contractual or statutory entitlement. The Bucks took only 5 working days' vacation, had the corporation's accountant calculate the payout, and presented the calculation and cheques to the two designated board members (Roberge and Bigelow) who reviewed, initialed and signed them in accordance with the established practice. Oakwood Towers alleged the Bucks 'paid themselves' $8,094 fraudulently and threatened criminal charges.
rule: Civil fraud/deceit requires (1) a false representation by the defendant; (2) knowledge or recklessness as to its falsity; (3) that the representation caused the plaintiff to act; and (4) resulting loss (Bruno Appliance and Furniture Inc. v. Hryniak, 2014 SCC 8; HSBC Bank Canada v. Lourenco, 2012 ABQB 380). The plaintiff bears the onus and must prove fraud with clear and convincing evidence. The Employment Standards Code, RSA 2000, c. E-9, ss. 34–44 and 42(2) require an employer to pay out vacation pay on termination and to keep vacation records.
application: The Court found no false representation: the Bucks were both contractually and statutorily entitled to vacation pay, the accountant's unchallenged calculation was accurate, and payment was made by the two designated board members following the same approval process used for all Oakwood Towers expenses. Stenzel's evidence that the Bucks took more vacation was vague, unreliable and inconsistent with the documentary record; Oakwood Towers failed to keep or produce vacation records as the Code required. The board president had confirmed to Service Canada there was 'no fraud'. Oakwood Towers suffered no loss by paying an entitlement.
conclusion: Oakwood Towers proved no element of civil fraud; its claim for fraud and for 'wrongfully' paid vacation pay was dismissed in its entirety.

issue: Did the Agreement create an employment relationship, and were the Bucks each individual employees?
facts: Oakwood Towers 'appointed' the Bucks as resident managers, paid them a monthly gross salary subject to statutory withholdings, controlled the work, and retained the power to dismiss under s. 13. The Agreement referred to the Bucks collectively as 'the Manager' but was signed by both and contained an express plurality clause (s. 14). Oakwood Towers argued they should be treated as a single employment unit.
rule: An employment relationship is assessed on four indicia: authority to select, payment of wages, control over the method/what work is done, and ability to suspend or dismiss (Levitt, The Law of Dismissal in Canada). Contracts are interpreted to give effect to the parties' intention, reading the contract as a whole with surrounding circumstances (Sattva Capital Corp. v. Creston Moly Corp., 2014 SCC 53). Employees must be individuals; a full-time worker who is not a partner/shareholder is presumed an employee; 'employee' is defined in the Employment Standards Code s. 1(1)(k).
application: All four indicia were met, so the Agreement created an employment relationship. The 'single employment' argument ignored the express plurality clause and the evidence of Stavropoulos that Mr. Buck insisted Mrs. Buck be a party and that they were intended to be joint managers. Both signed the Agreement, which contemplated more than one employee.
conclusion: Oakwood Towers was the employer; Mr. and Mrs. Buck were each individual employees entitled to the common law and statutory protections owed to employees.

issue: Did Oakwood Towers have just cause to terminate for insubordination?
facts: Oakwood Towers terminated the Agreement about 13 months before its fixed term expired, relying on either a pivotal act of insubordination (Mr. Buck's second July 6, 2016 email after a 'cease and desist' direction) or cumulative minor acts (September 2015 board meeting, December 2015 tenant letters, January 2016 roofing invoice/reserve fund transfer, June 2016 reserve fund report). Much of the friction stemmed from an interpersonal dispute between Mr. Buck and board member/Treasurer Stenzel, arising from a separate suite-management agreement.
rule: The employer bears the onus of proving just cause on a balance of probabilities. Cause is assessed contextually under the three-step McKinley v. BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38 framework (nature/extent of misconduct; surrounding circumstances; proportionality of dismissal). Insubordination requires either willful and deliberate disobedience of a clear, authorized, lawful and reasonable work order (Karmel v. Calgary Jewish Academy, 2015 ABQB 731; Amos v. Alberta) or behaviour amounting to a deliberate challenge; usually more than one instance is required, and cumulative cause requires clear warnings and a chance to improve (Dawson v. Bridge Brand Food Services Ltd., 2007 ABQB 15; Kokilev v. Picquic Tool Company Inc., 2010 BCSC 1412). Employers owe a duty of good faith and fair dealing (Bhasin v. Hrynew, 2014 SCC 71).
application: Working through each incident, the Court found no willful disobedience and no deliberate challenge. The September 2015 conflict ended with an accepted apology and no warning; the December 2015 communication directives were unauthorized, unlawful and unreasonable because they interfered with the Bucks' duties under s. 4 and arose from Stenzel's uninvestigated complaint about a separate contract; the January 2016 work orders were all completed; the June 2016 reserve report was partially completed with no deliberate disobedience; and the July 2016 'cease and desist' order was unclear, unauthorized, unlawful, unreasonable, and not disobeyed, since Mr. Buck's reply addressed legitimate board business. Stavropoulos' evidence was found unreliable and unbalanced. The two weeks' working notice given was itself inconsistent with a genuine claim of just cause.
conclusion: Oakwood Towers failed to prove insubordination or just cause; the termination was wrongful and the Bucks' counterclaims for wrongful dismissal succeeded.

issue: What damages are owed for wrongful dismissal under a fixed-term contract, and was there a duty to mitigate?
facts: The Agreement was a fixed-term contract running May 1, 2014 to August 31, 2017. The Bucks were terminated effective July 31, 2016. Each filed a separate counterclaim. Oakwood Towers did not challenge the damages calculation and did not raise mitigation.
rule: An employee under a fixed-term contract is entitled to the full contractual amount to the end of the term, and has no duty to mitigate (Lovely v. Prestige Travel, 2013 ABQB 457; Bowes v. Goss Power Products Ltd., 2012 ONCA 425). Counterclaims are independent actions (Baig v. Guarantee Co. of North America, 2007 ONCA 847). Vacation pay of 6% applies under the Employment Standards Code.
application: The Bucks had no duty to mitigate, and Oakwood Towers led no evidence on mitigation. The unchallenged calculation (salary to August 31, 2017, gas and laundry allowances, and vacation pay) totalled $85,989.30, divided equally between the two independent counterclaims. Statutory deductions were reserved.
conclusion: Judgment for $42,994.65 to each of Mr. and Mrs. Buck, with pre-judgment interest from July 31, 2016 under the Judgment Interest Act; costs awarded to the Bucks, with enhanced-costs and statutory-deduction issues reserved.

issue: Does the Child Welfare Act contain ambiguity permitting an order for birth-parent access to continue after adoption by foster parents?
facts: Two children apprehended in 1981 had lived with the same foster parents since infancy. The foster parents wished to adopt but opposed continued access by the birth parents. The reviewing judge (Nasmith Prov. Ct. J.) held the statute was ambiguous—particularly because s. 69(15) conflicted with s. 38—and that no physical 'placement' was needed since the children already lived with the prospective adopters, so a 'deemed placement' allowed adoption with continuing access.
rule: Child Welfare Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 66, ss. 38(5),(7),(8)(d), 69(15), 86(1) (and concordant provisions of the Child and Family Services Act, 1984). Section 38(7) bars an access order once a Crown ward is placed and residing in an approved adoption home; s. 38(8)(d) and s. 69(15) require any outstanding access order to be terminated before placement; s. 86(1) provides that on adoption the child ceases to be the child of the birth parents.
application: The court held s. 38 is paramount and requires a choice between continued Crown wardship with access or adoption without access. 'Placement' is an abstract concept and includes a 'deemed placement'; it occurs when the decision to adopt coincides with the child's residence with the prospective adopters, so the fact the children already lived with the foster parents did not create ambiguity. The primary purpose of terminating access is family stability, not merely secrecy: granting access after adoption would put the adoptive relationship on an unequal footing with a natural family because access would be controlled by a judicial or administrative official rather than within the family unit.
conclusion: No genuine ambiguity exists; the legislation requires termination of birth-parent access by the time the children are placed for adoption. Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. erred in law; Lissaman D.C.J. was correct.

issue: Do provisions requiring termination of birth-parent access upon placement for adoption violate ss. 2(d), 7 or 15(1) of the Charter?
facts: The birth mother argued that terminating her access to prepare for adoption violated her freedom of association, her liberty/security of the person, and her equality rights.
rule: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1, 2(d), 7, 15(1); Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143; Reference re Workers' Compensation Act, 1983 (Nfld.), [1989] 1 S.C.R.; Reference re s. 94(2) of the Motor Vehicle Act, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 486.
application: Section 2(d): freedom of association is public and collective in nature and protects associations pursuing common economic, political, religious, social or similar goals; the desire of a parent to be with a child has no such purpose and family relationships fall outside the guarantee, consistent with Re White, Shingoose and Nova Scotia (Minister of Community Services) v. S.(M.K.). Section 7: barring access to a particular person is not confinement; the existence of places one may not go and people who may refuse contact does not deprive another of liberty or security of the person. Section 15: under Andrews, recourse requires that the claimant's situation be analogous to the enumerated grounds; the situation of birth parents is 'in no way analogous' to those listed, following Reference re Workers' Compensation Act.
conclusion: None of ss. 2(d), 7 or 15(1) is infringed, so it was unnecessary to consider s. 1. The statutory provisions are constitutionally valid.

issue: Could the appellate judge overrule the reviewing judge and find that adoption without access was in the children's best interests?
facts: On appeal from the status review, Lissaman D.C.J. received the review-hearing evidence plus a follow-up assessment and further testimony, and concluded adoption without access served the children's best interests.
rule: Child Welfare Act, ss. 37, 43(8) (further evidence on appeal), 1(1)(b) (definition of 'best interests of the child'); Children's Aid Society of Renfrew County v. L.P.W. (appellate function, not a hearing de novo).
application: Because the reviewing judge erred in law by assuming adoption could be combined with continued access, the appellate court could review the decision. All expert witnesses, including the birth parents' expert, favoured adoption, and any value ascribed to continuing access was hypothetical and lost relevance once combination was legally impossible. The best-interests factors in s. 1(1)(b)—the parent-child relationship, disruption of continuity, the merits of the adoption plan, and delay—all favoured adoption; the foster parents had become the children's psychological parents over nearly six years, and imposing unwanted relationships threatened family stability.
conclusion: Lissaman D.C.J. was entitled to and correctly found that Crown wardship with a view to adoption and no birth-parent access was in the children's best interests.

issue: Can a litigant escape the jurisdiction and authority of a superior court by advancing OPCA theories (admiralty court, 'God's Law', freeman-on-the-land, 'I have not consented', etc.)?
facts: In a divorce and matrimonial property action, the respondent Dennis Larry Meads denied the Court's authority, asserting it was an admiralty court, that he was a 'flesh and blood man' subject only to 'God's Law' or the 'Maximus of Law', that legislation did not apply to him, and that he had not consented to the Court's jurisdiction; he left the hearing before it concluded.
rule: Provincial superior courts are courts of inherent jurisdiction descended from the English Royal Courts; where a justiciable right exists there must be a court to vindicate it, and only an explicit statutory ouster removes jurisdiction (Board v. Board; Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Canadian Liberty Net). Inherent jurisdiction cannot be defeated even by privative clauses (Pasiechnyk; Dunsmuir). Belief-based immunity is not a Charter defence and religious belief is subject to reasonable limits (Charter s. 1; Hutterian Brethren).
application: Every OPCA 'magic hat' (exempt group, self-declared immunity, misidentification, different law, admiralty/military court, defective oaths, God's Law) fails because the Court's inherent jurisdiction reaches every Alberta matter not assigned to another tribunal. No Canadian court has ever accepted an OPCA concept; a litigant may argue he is in the wrong court but cannot claim no court has authority over him.
conclusion: Such arguments cannot succeed; they are intrinsically frivolous and vexatious, may be struck without further analysis, and may amount to contempt of court. Mr. Meads is subject to the Court's authority regardless of his assertions.

issue: Do foisted unilateral agreements — fee schedules, copyright/trademark notices, appointments of fiduciaries — bind their recipients?
facts: Mr. Meads served a 'fee schedule' purporting to charge officials $2,000,000 per 'occurrence' of conduct such as arrest or 'disrespect'; a copyright/trademark notice claiming $100,000,000 per use of his name; and documents purporting to appoint a court clerk and Justice Rooke as his fiduciaries, all stating that silence constituted agreement.
rule: A binding contract requires consensus ad idem and communicated acceptance; one cannot foist a contract on another without consent, and silence generally cannot constitute acceptance (Silver's Garage Ltd. v. Bridgewater; Felthouse v. Bindley; Ron Ghitter Property Consultants v. Beaver Lumber). Liquidated damages must be reasonable and not a penalty in terrorem (Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre; H.F. Clarke).
application: None of Mr. Meads's documents could bind their recipients; failure to rebut does not create obligation, and the sums claimed were grossly disproportionate penalties. Such 'fee schedules' are tools of intimidation and may satisfy the actus reus/mens rea of intimidation of a justice system participant (Criminal Code s. 423.1) and the criminal interest rate prohibition (s. 347).
conclusion: The foisted agreements have no legal effect; they are evidence of vexatious conduct and may attract punitive damages, elevated costs and criminal sanction.

issue: Does the 'double/split person' concept relieve a litigant of legal obligations?
facts: Mr. Meads asserted he was two entities — the 'flesh and blood' Dennis-Larry: Meads and a state-created 'corporate' persona DENNIS LARRY MEADS — and executed intra-personal contracts assigning all property to one and all debts to the other, arguing that the support obligations attached only to the corporate persona.
rule: Canadian law recognizes only one legal identity per person; a purported second capacity or entity is a pure fiction not sanctioned by law (Canada (MNR) v. Stanchfield; R. v. Lindsay). A person wishing to add a legal layer must incorporate.
application: Whatever nomenclature Mr. Meads adopted, it is the person before the Court who is bound. The split-person contracts, powers of attorney and indemnities were 'rubbish' with no legal effect.
conclusion: The double/split person strategy fails; Mr. Meads is one legal person fully subject to the Court's orders.

issue: Can an 'Accept for Value' / A4V scheme discharge child and spousal support obligations?
facts: Mr. Meads claimed a secret government bank account linked to his birth certificate and social insurance number, and instructed the Court and the Bank of Canada to pay his support obligations and $100 billion in gold or silver from that account.
rule: The A4V 'money for nothing' concept has no basis in law and has been rejected (Underworld Services Ltd. v. Money Stop Ltd.; Mercedes-Benz Financial v. Kovacevic).
application: There is no secret account and no mechanism by which the Court could discharge obligations in this way; the A4V documents are 'legal alchemy'.
conclusion: The A4V scheme is rejected as absurd; any litigation or defence based on it is inherently frivolous and vexatious.

issue: Was it appropriate to appoint a case management justice and order financial disclosure?
facts: Ms. Meads's counsel could not meaningfully communicate with Mr. Meads because of his OPCA documents and sought a case management justice; Mr. Meads had generally paid interim support ordered by Veit J. but had not disclosed his financial records.
rule: Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, s. 4.11(c) authorizes appointment of a case management justice; family law proceedings carry mutual and reciprocal disclosure obligations, enforceable including by contempt.
application: OPCA-inflected litigation warrants close single-judge supervision; the requested disclosure (tax returns, earnings, investments, precious metals, sworn statement of income/assets) was routine and had not been provided voluntarily.
conclusion: Case management was appropriate and Justice Rooke appointed himself; Mr. Meads was ordered to provide the specified disclosure by 31 August 2012, failing which the Court's powers, including contempt, could be exercised.

issue: Is public education a 'service available to the public' under s. 5 and is a school board a 'person' under the Act?
facts: David Attis, a Jewish parent of children in School District 15, complained that the Board of School Trustees breached s. 5 in the provision of educational services. Preliminary objections questioned whether public education was a covered service and whether the School Board qualified as a 'person'.
rule: Section 5 of the Human Rights Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11 prohibits denial of or discrimination in accommodation, services or facilities available to the public on grounds including religion and ancestry. Human rights legislation receives a broad, purposive interpretation (O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears; Interpretation Act s. 17). 'Person' includes the extended meaning under the Interpretation Act, s. 38.
application: The New Brunswick Court of Appeal had already held that public education under the Schools Act is a service available to the public within s. 5. The Board of Inquiry followed that direction and found a school board established under the Schools Act is a 'person'; the use of 'employer' in s. 3 alongside 'or other person' confirmed employers fall within the general term 'person' used in s. 5, consistent with Memorial University v. Rose.
conclusion: Public education is a service available to the public and the School Board is a 'person' capable of discriminating under s. 5.

issue: Did Ross's off-duty anti-Semitic writings and statements create a discriminatory poisoned environment breaching s. 5(1), and do s. 6(2) or s. 3 shield the conduct?
facts: Between 1978 and 1989 Ross, a teacher in District 15, published books (Web of Deceit, The Real Holocaust, Spectre of Power, Christianity vs. Judeo-Christianity), letters to the editor and gave a television interview alleging an international Jewish conspiracy and denigrating Judaism and the Holocaust. There was no recent evidence of classroom remarks, but Jewish students including Yona Attis experienced name-calling, swastikas and 'Heil Hitler' salutes and felt fear and isolation.
rule: Section 5(1)(b) prohibits discrimination in a public service; discrimination is assessed by effect, not intent (Simpsons-Sears). Teachers are role models and off-duty conduct having a negative effect on the employer's operation is disciplinable (Peterson; Etobicoke Board of Education; Abbotsford v. Shewan; Fraser). Section 6(2)'s free-expression clause applies only to 'this section' (s. 6), not s. 5. Freedom of religion does not entitle attacking or condemning another religion (Boucher; Taylor v. CHRC; Dufour).
application: The Board found Ross's writings were prima facie discriminatory against persons of Jewish faith and ancestry, not scholarly discourse, and that the extensive publicity contributed over years to a poisoned educational environment interfering with the complainant's children's right to non-discriminatory education. The reasonable-effect test, applied from the perspective of a reasonable child/parent, was met; the students' evidence was credible. Section 6(2) was confined to s. 6 and could not exempt s. 5 conduct; there was no evidence Ross's religion required his writings, and even if s. 3 were engaged, a reasonable balance favoured protection from discrimination since attacking another religion exceeds legitimate religious freedom.
conclusion: Ross's off-duty conduct violated s. 5(1) with no reasonable cause to excuse the discriminatory effect; neither s. 6(2) nor s. 3 provided a defence.

issue: Is the School Board liable for Ross's conduct and did it also directly discriminate by failing to discipline him?
facts: The School Board became aware of controversy over Ross's publications as early as 1978, monitored his classroom, established a Review Committee in 1987, but took no disciplinary action until March 1988, then removed the record in September 1989 and gave only a severe reprimand after his 1989 television appearance.
rule: Under s. 5, employers are statutorily liable for discriminatory acts of employees related to employment (Robichaud v. Canada (Treasury Board)); the word 'indirectly' in s. 5 imports employer liability. A school board must maintain a positive, non-discriminatory environment and take a proactive role.
application: Because Ross's off-duty conduct breached s. 5, the School Board as employer was liable. Separately, the Board's reluctance and slow, ineffectual response—failing to act until 1988 despite established authority to discipline off-duty conduct, an inadequate Review Committee that ignored Jewish community submissions, and defensive resistance to the Commission—created the effect of condoning Ross's views, which a reasonable person would anticipate would injure the complainant and his children. Two failed motions were not shown to be discriminatory, and there was no evidence of intent, but effect governs.
conclusion: The School Board discriminated against the complainant contrary to s. 5(1), both indirectly through Ross and directly through its own inaction, with no reasonable cause to excuse the effect.

issue: What remedy is appropriate?
facts: Ross remained committed to publishing his views even after School Board direction. The complainant indicated he would not oppose Ross being placed in a non-teaching position.
rule: Human rights remedies aim to remove discrimination and provide relief, not to punish (Simpsons-Sears). Section 20(6.2) permits an order against any party found to have violated the Act.
application: The Board found monitoring, apology, or restricting Jewish students' access inadequate; the only viable relief was to remove Ross from the classroom while minimizing punitive effect. It ordered systemic measures for the Department of Education and directed the School Board to place Ross on an 18-month unpaid leave, appoint him to a non-teaching position if available, terminate him if none arose, and terminate immediately if he published or distributed the identified anti-Semitic materials.
conclusion: Comprehensive remedial order made, including leave of absence, possible non-teaching reassignment, and conditional termination; the Board reserved jurisdiction over implementation.

issue: What is the applicable standard of review of the board of inquiry's finding that the advertisement violated s. 14(1)(b)?
facts: A human rights board of inquiry found Owens contravened s. 14(1)(b) and the Court of Queen's Bench upheld that result. The Code (s. 32) provides an appeal on questions of law. Boards were ad hoc, staffed by private-practice lawyers without full-time human rights expertise, and operated without a privative clause.
rule: The functional and pragmatic analysis (Pushpanathan; Dr. Q v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of BC) governs standard of review even on statutory appeals: privative clause, tribunal expertise, purpose of the scheme, and nature of the question. Questions of statutory interpretation and general legal reasoning attract correctness (Gould v. Yukon Order of Pioneers; Mossop; Berg).
application: No privative clause and a statutory right of appeal on questions of law; boards had no special expertise; the adjudicative process was not polycentric; and the meaning of 'hatred,' 'ridicule,' 'belittlement' and 'affronts to dignity' are legal concepts informed by constitutional values of equality, freedom of religion and expression. Whether the advertisement offended the Code is not a purely factual question warranting deference.
conclusion: The correctness standard applies; the Court is free to make its own assessment of whether the advertisement offended s. 14(1)(b).

issue: What is the proper meaning and scope of s. 14(1)(b) read consistently with the Charter?
facts: Section 14(1)(b) prohibits publications that expose or tend to expose to hatred, ridicule, belittle or otherwise affront dignity on a prohibited ground; s. 14(2) preserves freedom of expression. The provision directly constrains expression and the dissemination of religious belief.
rule: Statutes are read consistently with the Charter where possible (R. v. Zundel; Rizzo Shoes). In Canada (HRC) v. Taylor the Supreme Court read comparable hate-speech language as reaching only 'unusually strong and deep-felt emotions of detestation, calumny and vilification' of an 'ardent and extreme nature.' Saskatchewan (HRC) v. Bell applied this same threshold to s. 14, including its 'ridicule, belittle or affront dignity' language. Freedom of religion is not absolute (Amselem; Multani; Ross) and religiously motivated speech that harms others is subject to reasonable limits.
application: To be constitutionally valid, s. 14(1)(b) reaches only genuinely extreme expression meeting the Taylor/Bell standard, not merely offensive, distressing or belittling speech, which a robust democracy must tolerate. The provision must be applied objectively—from the perspective of a reasonable person aware of the context—not by the subjective reaction of complainant or publisher. Freedom of religion does not alter this, since s. 14(1)(b) limits religious speech in the same justifiable way it limits speech generally.
conclusion: Section 14(1)(b) captures only speech reaching the extreme threshold of hatred/detestation described in Taylor and Bell, assessed objectively in context.

issue: Did the advertisement, objectively characterized in context, contravene s. 14(1)(b)?
facts: The 1997 ad, published during gay pride week amid an active national debate over sexual orientation rights, cited four Bible passages and depicted two stickmen holding hands overlaid with a 'not permitted' symbol, offered as a bumper sticker. Sexual orientation had only recently become a prohibited ground and an analogous Charter ground.
rule: The objective Bell standard: whether a reasonable person aware of context would understand the speech as exposing the target group to hatred etc. of an ardent and extreme nature; human rights legislation receives a generous, purposive interpretation, and courts must not authoritatively interpret sacred texts.
application: The stickmen were neutral, unlike the demeaning caricatures in Bell, and the 'not permitted' symbol was ambiguous. The Bible citations, though strongly worded, are part of a larger work also associated with love and forgiveness, are open to varied interpretations, and were understood by many to condemn conduct rather than identity. The Board and Chambers judge erred by taking the passages at face value as equivalent to a modern statement that homosexuals should be killed and by ignoring the wider public-debate context. Read as a whole, the ad reads as a position in an ongoing public policy debate, not a message of extreme detestation.
conclusion: The advertisement did not meet the Bell threshold and did not contravene s. 14(1)(b).

issue: Did the tribunals err by failing to consider Mr. Owens' freedom of religion?
facts: All parties accepted Owens published the ad from a sincere, bona fide religious conviction, engaging s. 2(a) of the Charter; the Board said nothing about freedom of religion and the Chambers judge gave it minimal attention.
rule: Freedom of religion includes the right to disseminate belief (Big M) but is not absolute and may be limited where religiously motivated speech harms others (Amselem; Multani; Ross).
application: Although the tribunals gave freedom of religion little or no attention, the validity of s. 14(1)(b) does not change once religion is added, since it justifiably limits religious speech the same way it limits speech generally. The failure did not alter the outcome because the advertisement, properly characterized, did not offend the Code in any event.
conclusion: The tribunals gave freedom of religion inadequate consideration, but the appeal succeeds on the characterization of the advertisement rather than on a distinct religious-freedom ground.

issue: Were the impugned statements capable of, and did they bear, a defamatory meaning?
facts: Ms. Lane, terminated as Superintendent of School District 68 after issuing a 'Christmas Notice' renaming seasonal school concerts, sued in defamation over six statements by trustees and the Board (the First and Second Harrison, Cowling, Montgomery and Saunders statements, and the Board's press release).
rule: A defamatory statement tends to lower a person in the estimation of right-thinking members of society (Salmon on Torts; Vander Zalm v. Times Publishers). Words injuring one in one's calling must impute a quality detrimental (or the absence of a quality essential) to one's office or profession (Gately on Libel and Slander). The judge decides first whether words are capable of a defamatory meaning, then whether they in fact defamed the plaintiff, construing words in their natural and ordinary meaning as understood by an ordinary person.
application: The court held that the First and Second Harrison, Cowling, Montgomery and Saunders statements merely criticized a single decision or expressed disagreement without imputing any detrimental personal characteristic, and so were not capable of defamatory meaning. The Board Statement, by contrast, went beyond criticism of one decision and implied Ms. Lane was responsible for low staff morale, lack of cooperation and instability, imputing a quality detrimental to her as an education administrator; it was capable of and did defame her.
conclusion: Only the Board Statement was defamatory; the other five statements were not capable of a defamatory meaning.

issue: Were the statements published on an occasion of qualified privilege?
facts: Trustees are elected officials; several statements were made to local newspapers, at a public Board meeting, and (Montgomery) to the National Post; the Board Statement was a press release announcing the search for a new superintendent.
rule: Qualified privilege arises where the maker has a duty or interest to communicate and the recipient a reciprocal interest to receive (Adam v. Ward; Hill v. Church of Scientology). Publication to the world may exceed the privilege absent proper reason (Moises; Parlett v. Robinson). A person answering an attack has privilege limited to matters germane to the attack (Douglas v. Tucker; RTC Engineering).
application: Elected trustees had a duty to keep constituents informed on the publicly controversial Christmas Notice and Ms. Lane's employment; the First and Second Harrison, Cowling and Saunders statements were made on privileged occasions to local media/meetings. The Montgomery Statement to a national newspaper exceeded the privilege as the matter was not of national interest. The Board Statement was not a trustee responding to attack but the employer announcing a termination and was not privileged.
conclusion: Qualified privilege applied to the First and Second Harrison, Cowling and Saunders statements, but not to the Montgomery Statement or the Board Statement.

issue: Were the statements fair comment on a matter of public interest?
facts: Some statements were letters to the editor or comments on the Christmas Notice controversy; others (Second Harrison, Saunders, Board) were statements of fact without stated underlying facts.
rule: Fair comment requires (1) recognizable comment on true facts, not a bare statement of fact, (2) a matter of public interest, and (3) an honest expression of the maker's real view (Vander Zalm v. Times Publishers; Brown, Law of Defamation).
application: The First Harrison and Cowling statements were recognizable comment on true public-interest facts and honestly held, so fair comment applied. The Second Harrison, Saunders and Board statements contained no indication of the facts commented on and were treated as statements of fact, failing the first requirement.
conclusion: Fair comment protected the First Harrison and Cowling statements but not the Second Harrison, Saunders or Board statements.

issue: Were the statements made with malice?
facts: Ms. Lane alleged the defendant trustees harboured personal spite, relying on long lists of prior events; Chair Montgomery and the trustees testified their motives were to inform constituents or express genuine disagreement.
rule: Malice defeats qualified privilege and fair comment. For privilege, malice means a dominant improper motive—desire to injure, or speaking dishonestly or with reckless disregard for truth (Hill; Horrocks v. Lowe). For fair comment, the defence fails only if the maker did not genuinely hold the view expressed (Cheng v. Tse Wai Chun).
application: The court found each defendant's dominant motive was to express genuine disagreement or inform the public, not to injure Ms. Lane; relationships were poor but the evidence did not establish ill-will as the dominant motive for any statement.
conclusion: Malice was not proven for any statement; the applicable defences were not defeated.

issue: Were the statements justified as substantially true?
facts: The defendants pleaded justification for all statements except the Second Harrison Statement, providing extensive particulars (Appendices A and B) regarding poor morale, lack of cooperation and instability during Ms. Lane's tenure.
rule: Truth (justification) is a complete defence; the defendant bears the burden of proving the 'sting' substantially true (Brown, Law of Defamation). The defendant may justify its own pleaded meaning (Miller v. CBC) and is confined to its particulars.
application: The court found it was not inappropriate or an error for Ms. Lane to issue the Christmas Notice, so the First Harrison, Cowling and Montgomery meanings were not proven true. However, on the proven particulars, Ms. Lane did cause poor morale, a lack of cooperation and instability, so the Saunders Statement's poor-morale meaning and the Board Statement were substantially true.
conclusion: The Board Statement was justified as substantially true and the poor-morale sting of the Saunders Statement was true; justification failed for the other statements.

issue: Was the plaintiff entitled to Wallace damages for the manner of her termination?
facts: Ms. Lane was dismissed without cause under an employment contract permitting termination on 12 months' notice or pay; she was informed by telephone on a weekend and claimed the manner was callous, seeking six additional months' salary.
rule: Wallace v. United Grain Growers Ltd. permits an extension of the notice period for bad-faith conduct in the manner of dismissal, but only where the employee was wrongfully dismissed and no express contractual notice term governs; employers must be candid, reasonable, honest and forthright and not unduly insensitive.
application: Ms. Lane was not wrongfully dismissed; her contract expressly fixed 12 months' notice/pay, which she received, precluding an implied reasonable-notice term (Barnard v. Testori). Further, the Board acted honestly and, though telephoning on a weekend was somewhat insensitive, it was not unduly insensitive given the circumstances and prior warning.
conclusion: No Wallace damages were available; the claim failed on all three grounds.

issue: Did the respondent establish genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to give the Get, so as to bar relief under s. 21.1(3)?
facts: The parties married in 2012 and separated in 2020. Ms Sabbah requested a Get in May 2021 and complied with the s. 21.1(2) affidavit procedure. Mr. Sabbah refused to grant the Get until the civil divorce was granted, asserting deeply held religious beliefs, citing passages from Exodus, Deuteronomy and Maimonides and alleging his wife's adultery. However, he provided no independent or expert evidence of the objective content of Jewish law, and his correspondence repeatedly threatened to make the Get 'more expensive' and conditioned it on the outcome of the civil proceedings.
rule: Section 21.1 of the Divorce Act gives the court discretion to refuse relief to a spouse who fails to remove barriers to the other spouse's religious remarriage; under s. 21.1(4) the court may decline to strike pleadings where the refusing spouse establishes 'genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature'. Bruker v Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54 holds that a mere ability to refuse under religious law differs from being prevented by a genuine tenet of belief, and that withholding a Get as leverage is contrary to public policy. Zoughaib v El-Mokadem, 2024 ONSC 292 and S(K) v B(S), 2015 QCCS 3717 apply the same analysis, and H(K) v S(J), 2000 CanLII 18733 (QCCS) treats willingness to give the Get only after civil divorce as evidence of using it as a negotiating weapon.
application: The court found Mr. Sabbah's March 15, 2024 affidavit did not assert religious or conscientious grounds, and his June 11, 2024 affidavit raised them only after being served with the s. 21.1 application. He offered no independent or expert evidence establishing the objective content of the scriptural passages he cited, so his stated beliefs appeared only subjectively binding. Following Zoughaib, the court found the refusal had less to do with genuine religious belief than with anger and leverage: uncontroverted correspondence showed Mr. Sabbah threatening to increase the Get's 'cost', linking it to legal fees and the civil outcome, and stating he might die without signing it. He never denied or addressed this leveraging evidence, and made clear he would give the Get only bundled with conclusion of the civil divorce.
conclusion: The court held Mr. Sabbah failed to establish genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature; his position amounted to using the Get as a bargaining tool contrary to the purpose of s. 21.1.

issue: What remedy should the court grant under s. 21.1(3) given the respondent's failure to remove the barriers?
facts: Ms Sabbah sought an order striking Mr. Sabbah's pleadings and prohibiting further applications until he agrees to give the Get. She also sought significantly enhanced costs.
rule: Section 21.1(3)(c) and (d) of the Divorce Act allow the court to dismiss applications and strike pleadings and affidavits of a non-compliant spouse, subject to appropriate terms; H(K) v S(J) modelled a conditional order allowing refiling once barriers are removed. Costs follow Schedule C of the Rules of Court absent authority justifying enhanced costs.
application: The court allowed the application but abeyanced the actual striking until February 14, 2025 to give Mr. Sabbah an opportunity to file an affidavit confirming all barriers to the religious divorce were removed. Meanwhile no existing or new applications could proceed. On costs, the court was not persuaded the case resembled DN v BN, 2022 BCSC 2029, and found no authority justifying enhanced costs.
conclusion: Application allowed; pleadings to be struck if no compliance affidavit filed by February 14, 2025, with no further participation permitted thereafter; costs awarded per Schedule C, Column One.

issue: Is the child in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b) CYFSA because of a risk of physical harm?
facts: The father, subject to a criminal harassment/assault charge, resides with paternal grandparents who have long-term opioid addiction (crushing and sniffing medication) and recent cocaine use; a drug-using paternal uncle lives in an unsecured basement; there are firearms and an unverified gun safe in the home; the father would not permit the CAS to fully tour the home and showed no insight into the risks, refusing to complete recommended programming.
rule: Under s. 74(2)(b) CYFSA a child is in need of protection where there is a risk the child is likely to suffer physical harm from the person's failure to adequately care for/supervise/protect, or a pattern of neglect. The risk must be real and likely, not speculative (Children's Aid Society of Rainy River v. B.(C.), 2006 ONCJ 458); intention need not be proven (Jewish Family and Child Service v. K.(R.), 2008 ONCJ 774, aff'd 2009 ONCA 903); a child may be at risk even if conduct is not directed at that child; limited parental capacity may create risk (CAS of Hamilton v. O.(E.), 2009 CanLII 72087).
application: The court found the home unsafe: nascent-at-best recovery from long-term addiction, recent cocaine use by the paternal grandfather, contaminated surfaces accessible to a child, an unsecured area occupied by a drug-using uncle, and unverified storage of medications and firearms. The father, despite parenting strengths in supervised settings, showed no insight into these hazards and failed to complete programming to build capacity, creating a real and likely risk of physical harm. The court declined to find a risk of emotional harm under s. 74(2)(h), holding the specific enumerated harms were not established, and rested the finding on s. 74(2)(b) alone.
conclusion: The child is in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b)(i) and (ii) CYFSA.

issue: What disposition is in the child's best interests?
facts: All parties agreed the child should live full-time with the mother, whose parenting was not in question. The father sought a return to the February 20, 2019 CLRA order (permitting immediate overnight access) or a supervision order so the CAS would remain involved and afford him more access.
rule: Sections 101 and 102 CYFSA govern disposition; s. 101 permits a supervision order (3–12 months), s. 102 permits a custody order deemed made under s. 28 CLRA. Section 101(8) allows no disposition order where unnecessary. Best interests under s. 74(3) govern placement.
application: A supervision order was unnecessary because the mother's parenting required no supervision and continued CAS involvement would unduly burden her; the father did not seek a supervision order to address his own issues and had not complied with the prior temporary supervision order's programming terms. Simply returning to the CLRA order was inappropriate because it imposed no limits on the location of parenting time and would trigger immediate overnight access while the father still lived in the unsafe home. A custody order to the mother with tailored terms best served the child's needs, developmental stage, security within a family, and ties to her mother.
conclusion: The child is placed in the mother's custody under s. 102(1) CYFSA, with protective terms; no supervision order is made.

issue: Should the father's access be supervised at a third-party facility?
facts: The father had only ever parented in supervised settings since May 2019, missed numerous visits, could identify no suitable alternative access location or supervisor, resides in an unsafe home, has anger-regulation difficulties and made inappropriate communications to and about the mother, and did not complete recommended anger/parenting programming.
rule: Access must be determined in the child's best interests under s. 74(3) CYFSA, consistent with the protection concerns underlying the finding.
application: The father's lack of insight into home risks and appropriate access locations, absence of any alternative location or supervisor, history of unsupervised care being non-existent, failure to complete programming, and difficulties regulating emotions all favoured supervised access; direct exchanges risked exposing the child to inappropriate conduct toward the mother. The court ordered weekly two-hour supervised access at Dalhousie Place where accommodable, noting supervision need not be long-term if the father addresses his housing, anger and communication issues.
conclusion: The father shall have weekly (two-hour) supervised access at a third-party facility (Dalhousie Place), subject to availability.

issue: Did the BCCT exceed its jurisdiction by treating TWU's Community Standards (including the requirement to refrain from 'homosexual behaviour') as discriminatory practices contrary to the public interest under s. 4 of the Teaching Profession Act?
facts: TWU, a private evangelical university, requires students to sign Community Standards forbidding conduct 'biblically condemned,' including homosexual behaviour. It applied for approval of its teacher education program. The BCCT Council denied approval on the ground the program followed 'discriminatory practices which are contrary to the public interest and public policy,' relying on its s. 4 mandate to set standards 'having regard to the public interest.'
rule: An administrative body must interpret its enabling statute correctly; a decision based on irrelevant considerations, an improper purpose, or a misinterpretation of jurisdiction-limiting provisions is a nullity (U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault, [1988] 2 SCR 1048; Nipawin, [1975] 1 SCR 382; Roncarelli v. Duplessis, [1959] SCR 121; Prince George v. Payne, [1978] 1 SCR 458). 'Public interest' must be construed in the context of the statute (Lindsay v. Manitoba). The Wednesbury principle requires exclusion of irrelevant matters.
application: The Court held that s. 4 limits the BCCT to those aspects of the public interest bearing on the education, professional responsibility and competence of teachers; it does not confer unlimited authority to promote all public policy. If an applicant meets the BCCT's standards, the College cannot refuse certification merely because of a teacher's religious belief that homosexual behaviour is sinful. However, the Community Standards were not per se irrelevant: the BCCT was entitled to examine the actual conduct of TWU graduates and to consider whether any inappropriate conduct was tied to those Standards.
conclusion: The BCCT was entitled to consider the Community Standards, but only in connection with evidence of graduates' conduct; it could not deny certification based simply on the beliefs expressed in those Standards.

issue: Was the Council's decision patently unreasonable because it rested on no evidence that TWU's Community Standards produced or could produce intolerant teachers?
facts: The BCCT concluded it was 'entitled to anticipate' that graduates who promised to refrain from behaviour labelled sinful might be biased against homosexual students. No evidence supported this. In contrast, the Program Approval Team found TWU graduates competent, roughly 70% taught in public schools, many taught in multicultural, First Nations and other diverse settings, and there was no evidence of problems with pupils.
rule: A tribunal's decision must have a factual basis; a decision based on no evidence, or resting on a premise that cannot withstand rational analysis, is patently unreasonable and made without jurisdiction (Dairy Producers Co-operative v. Teamsters (1993) (Sask CA); Hicks v. Langley Memorial Hospital (1992) (BCSC)).
application: The Council's premise—that TWU graduates would be intolerant because they promised not to engage in homosexual behaviour—required unfounded assumptions. Evidence actually before the Council (the Approval Team report and TWU's submissions on its graduates' successful public-school placements) contradicted the conclusion of intolerance, and further evidence was readily obtainable given the many TWU graduates already teaching. The Council failed to consider the evidence before it and reached a conclusion it could not have reached had it done so.
conclusion: The decision was made without any reasonable evidentiary foundation, was patently unreasonable, and was quashed; the Court declined to address the remaining Charter and natural-justice issues.

issue: Was the Application for Revocation served within the strict 30-day time limit of article 347 C.C.P.?
facts: The divorce judgment was rendered March 13, 2024 and emailed the same day to the defendant at an address she confirmed was hers and used regularly; she admitted receiving it that day but deletes all emails. A bailiff later served it personally on March 26, 2024, after she initially denied being herself. She served her Application for Revocation on April 22, 2024.
rule: Article 347 C.C.P. requires the application for revocation to be served within 30 days after the party became aware of the judgment; these are strict ('de rigueur') time limits.
application: The preponderance of evidence established that the defendant became aware of the judgment on March 13, 2024 when it was emailed to her and acknowledged received. Serving the application on April 22, 2024 was beyond the 30-day limit; her denial of identity to the bailiff showed she attempted to avoid service.
conclusion: The application was time-barred, and for this reason alone it had to be dismissed.

issue: Was the defendant prevented from defending on the merits by fraud, surprise or any other sufficient cause under article 346 C.C.P.?
facts: The defendant was repeatedly and duly notified of the March 12, 2024 trial date (by court staff, by opposing counsel, and by two judges), had earlier been represented and filed a defence and cross-demand, then ceased to follow her file. She did not attend the trial, which proceeded by default. She alleged a physical illness but produced only old medical documents predating the trial by over a year and gave no testimony or expert report on incapacity.
rule: Article 346 C.C.P. permits revocation of a default judgment where the party was prevented from defending by fraud, surprise or any other cause considered sufficient; carelessness, negligence or laxity is not a sufficient cause. Where health-based incapacity is alleged, expert testimony is generally required (Luft v. Greif; Olivier v. Canada).
application: The evidence showed the defendant knew of the trial date but chose not to attend; her medical documents did not establish any incapacity on the trial date and no expert evidence was adduced. Her failure resulted from her own negligence and carelessness, which cannot ground revocation.
conclusion: No fraud, surprise or other sufficient cause was proven; article 346 was not satisfied.

issue: Does maintaining the divorce judgment bring the administration of justice into disrepute under article 345 C.C.P. because of the defendant's religious beliefs against divorce, or its alleged unfairness?
facts: The defendant claimed deeply held religious beliefs prohibiting divorce prevented her attendance and made the judgment unfair. Yet she had earlier filed an answer, case protocol and cross-demand herself seeking a divorce and partition, never raising religious objections. The judgment partitioned the family patrimony and partnership of acquests equally, based on the plaintiff's full disclosure, while the defendant filed no statements.
rule: Article 345 C.C.P. allows revocation only where letting the judgment stand would tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute; the flaw must be serious and irreparable (Allianz v. SNC-Lavalin; Fabrikant). Marriage and divorce fall under federal jurisdiction; every Canadian has the right to obtain a civil divorce under the Divorce Act. Bruker v. Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54 confirms religious belief cannot defeat the public interest in equality and the right to divorce; s. 21.1 of the Divorce Act prevents using religious-divorce refusal as leverage.
application: The plaintiff had a fundamental right to obtain a divorce notwithstanding the defendant's beliefs. Her belief could not prevent that right and, since she still holds the same belief, revocation would be futile (a new trial would again proceed by default). Her past conduct in seeking a divorce herself undermined the credibility of her religious objection, which was a pretext. The judgment conformed to the public-order partition rules of the Civil Code, and she failed to show any unfairness.
conclusion: Maintaining the judgment does not bring the administration of justice into disrepute; the basis of the judgment is not seriously or irreparably flawed.

issue: Did the sentencing judge commit errors in principle that produced a demonstrably unfit sentence?
facts: Sandouga firebombed the Beth Shalom Synagogue in Edmonton with a Molotov cocktail to express anger and take revenge against the Jewish community for events in the Middle East. He pled guilty to arson under s. 434 of the Criminal Code and received 12 months' gaol plus three years' probation. The trial judge found the conduct reprehensible but found no 'moral turpitude', characterized it as an act of anger, and did not treat it as a hate crime.
rule: Under s. 718.1 a sentence must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender. Section 718.2(a)(i) deems an offence motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on religion or ethnic origin to be an aggravating circumstance. Appellate courts may intervene where a sentencing judge errs in principle, fails to consider a relevant factor, or imposes a demonstrably unfit sentence.
application: The Court held the judge misapprehended culpability: the crime was planned, deliberate and revenge-based (gathering equipment, dark clothing, waiting until 12:50 a.m., intending to hurl a second Molotov cocktail and having poured gasoline), not merely an impulsive drunken outburst. The judge failed to recognize serious aggravating circumstances — the offence was a hate crime under s. 718.2(a)(i) targeting an identifiable religious group, an attack on a place of worship undermining freedom of religion (Charter s. 2(a)), and an act of religious intimidation with widespread effects on the Edmonton Jewish community and inter-community relations. The judge also failed to emphasize denunciation and general deterrence, the paramount objectives for terrorist acts (Ingram and Grimsdale, Lelas, Soles, Atwal).
conclusion: The sentencing judge made errors in principle that resulted in a demonstrably unfit sentence, warranting appellate intervention.

issue: What is a fit sentence for revenge-based arson of a synagogue that constitutes a terrorist act and hate crime?
facts: The maximum for arson is 14 years. Mitigating factors were Sandouga's youth (20), lack of criminal record, guilty plea and payment of roughly $1,100 restitution; but he accepted only partial responsibility and the presentence report suggested he might pose a threat. The Crown sought two and one-half to three years.
rule: Sentences in comparable cases guide the determination of a fit sentence. Planned, revenge-based property destruction attracts substantial terms, and where a terrorist or urban-intimidation aspect is present these crimes consistently attract penitentiary terms despite strong mitigation (Etmannski, Bettger, Thurston).
application: A one-year sentence sits at the low end for arson over a private grievance, but Sandouga's act was simultaneously revenge-based arson, a terrorist act, a hate crime and an act of religious intimidation. Comparable terrorist/intimidation arson cases yielded penitentiary terms of two and one-half years and more even for first offenders. The mitigating circumstances did not outweigh the need for denunciation and deterrence.
conclusion: The one-year sentence was demonstrably unfit; the Crown's appeal was allowed and the sentence increased to two and one-half years' imprisonment in a federal penitentiary, while Sandouga's appeal was dismissed. The Court declined to set a starting-point sentence.

issue: Did the content of Your Ward News amount to 'hatred' against Jews and women under s. 319(2) of the Criminal Code, or was it merely distasteful or satirical expression?
facts: The defendants published and distributed 22 issues of the community newspaper Your Ward News to over 300,000 homes, with an online readership claimed to exceed one million. The material repeatedly depicted women as chattel, sub-human, deserving of sexual and physical violence, and Jews as satanic, blood-drinking conspirators controlling global finance, while denying the Holocaust and glorifying Hitler. The defence argued the writings were unfocused, contradictory, satirical, anti-Marxist ramblings that stopped short of hate, and that they did not target all Jews or all women.
rule: Section 319(2) of the Criminal Code criminalizes wilfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group. In R. v. Keegstra, 1990 CanLII 24 (SCC), the Supreme Court held that 'hatred' connotes 'emotion of an intense and extreme nature that is clearly associated with vilification and detestation', implying that group members are to be despised, scorned, denied respect and subjected to ill-treatment based on group affiliation. The publication must be read as a whole and contextually.
application: After reviewing the entire body of Exhibit 2, the court found that although the paper was at times contradictory, satirical, and professed 'love' for some Jews and women, the overwhelming and consistent message was hatred. Women were represented as immoral, inferior and not human, with celebration of sexual and physical violence against them; Jews were consistently demonized as satanic, reptilian, blood-drinking conspirators, with glorification of Hitler and Holocaust denial. The 'not all Jews / not all women' argument failed because the publication as a whole dehumanised both entire groups. Expert evidence, though impressive, was found unnecessary given the plain content of the exhibits.
conclusion: The content rose well beyond distasteful or satirical expression and constituted hatred of Jews and women within the Keegstra meaning of s. 319(2).

issue: Did the defendants wilfully promote the hatred contained in Your Ward News?
facts: Mr. Sears was the editor writing under the pen-name 'Dimitri the Lover'; Mr. St. Germaine, the publisher, admitted awareness of the content and distribution and told police he had the final say. The paper cost $50,000–$70,000 per issue, financed by donations, and contained calls to action such as urging men to 'SHUT HER DOWN with extreme prejudice', jury nullification to acquit men of sexual assault, and conversion campaigns against Jews.
rule: Section 319(2) requires that the promotion of hatred be 'wilful'. Wilful blindness can supply the requisite intent, and the Crown need not prove that any actual harm resulted from the communication.
application: The court found abundant evidence of intent within Exhibit 2 itself, without needing the admitted prior discreditable conduct evidence. The scale of distribution, the fundraising to spread the message, and the repeated, unmistakable calls to action demonstrated an intent to pass the message of hatred on to others. No other intent could be inferred from a complete reading.
conclusion: Both defendants wilfully promoted hatred against Jews and women; the mens rea of s. 319(2) was established.

issue: Was the s. 319(3)(c) defence of reasonable belief in the truth of the statements available to the publisher, LeRoy St. Germaine?
facts: St. Germaine argued through his police statement that he fact-checked before publication, read all articles, did his own research, trusted Sears's ability, and reasonably believed the statements about Jews and women were true.
rule: Section 319(3)(c) provides a defence where the accused, on reasonable grounds, believed the statements communicated were true.
application: The court held that a belief that one should celebrate Hitler and deny the Nazi Holocaust of Jews has no basis in reason, and that advocating rape and proclaiming women to be less than human likewise has no basis in reason. Such beliefs could not be held on reasonable grounds.
conclusion: The s. 319(3)(c) defence was not available; St. Germaine's asserted belief was not reasonable.

issue: Should prospective court access restrictions under ss. 23-23.1 of the Judicature Act be imposed on Belanger?
facts: Belanger is a long-time promoter and user of Organized Pseudolegal Commercial Arguments (OPCA) through the fabricated Church of the Ecumenical Redemption International. He had inserted himself as purported amicus curiae in the Dimsdale debt proceeding, was already barred from acting as a litigation representative and from entering Alberta courthouses, and, when invited to respond to ATB's application, provided only a rambling 78-minute YouTube video rehashing Strawman Theory and racist conspiracy claims, filing no responsive affidavit or argument.
rule: Judicature Act, RSA 2000, c J-2, ss 23-23.1, as applied in Weidenfeld v Alberta, 2023 ABCA 353 and Unrau v National Dental Examining Board, 2019 ABQB 283: court access restrictions are a backward-looking, last-ditch step requiring persistent abusive conduct identified in s 23(2) and the case law, supported by focused evidence (Canada v Olumide, 2017 FCA 42), imposed only where less intrusive management fails. Use of Strawman Theory raises a presumption of bad faith (Fiander v Mills, 2015 NLCA 31; Rothweiler v Payette, 2018 ABQB 288).
application: The Court accepted ATB's affidavit evidence and its own prior findings in Dimsdale #1 documenting Belanger's decades-long, Canada-wide abusive litigation, harassment of courts, lawyers and officials, abuse of private information processes, and victimization of vulnerable people. Belanger's own video confirmed he would continue to defy Canadian law and court orders and use pseudolaw, proving the case against himself. His persistent Strawman Theory use triggered the bad-faith presumption. No lesser management step could control him because he rejects all authority.
conclusion: Belanger is a vexatious litigant; global prospective court access restrictions requiring leave are warranted.

issue: What should be the scope of the litigation and litigant management restrictions?
facts: Belanger's abuse spanned civil and criminal matters, multiple courts and jurisdictions, and included boasting of directing harassing pseudolaw communications to the Alberta Court of Justice clerks and abusing Criminal Code ss 504, 507.1 private information processes.
rule: Judicature Act s 23.1(6) permits restrictions binding the Court of Justice; the Court has inherent jurisdiction to control its processes, including pre-filing review of criminal appeals (R v Tican, 2024 ABCA 163); a lawyer-representation requirement may be imposed on private informations (Unrau #2), and there is no constitutional right for a private person to initiate criminal proceedings.
application: Because Belanger's abuse extended across subjects, both courts, and criminal as well as civil matters, the Court consolidated the earlier Dimsdale restrictions and extended the leave requirement to criminal appeals, to the Alberta Court of Justice, and required legal representation before laying any private information. Communication and courthouse-entry restrictions were continued.
conclusion: Comprehensive leave, representation, communication and courthouse-access restrictions binding both the Court of King's Bench and the Alberta Court of Justice were ordered.

issue: What costs should be awarded?
facts: ATB was entirely successful and sought full solicitor-and-client indemnity costs after submitting detailed materials.
rule: Against abusive litigants a lump sum award is appropriate to bring the litigation to a conclusive endpoint (Fiander v Mills, 2015 NLCA 31; Uhrik v Barata, 2023 ABKB 517).
application: Given ATB's complete success and substantial materials, and to avoid Belanger exploiting costs processes to prolong litigation, the Court fixed a lump sum rather than assessing solicitor-client costs.
conclusion: Belanger ordered to pay ATB $8,000 in costs forthwith.

issue: Were the impugned Instagram posts (the July 6 repost and the two July 30 posts) defamatory of the plaintiff in law?
facts: Ms. Hawkins, proprietor of Foodbenders, used the eatery's public Instagram account to make pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist statements. On July 6, 2020 she reposted a third party's post calling the plaintiff, a Cityline design expert and former IDF soldier, an 'IDF SOLDIER (aka terrorist)' who aimed a 'sniper rifle at Palestinian children' and was gathering 'whining Zionist friends' to attack Foodbenders. On July 30, 2020 she posted that he was a 'racist', 'viciously' hated Palestinians, a 'killer', and was trying to 'cancel' her.
rule: To establish defamation a plaintiff must prove the words referred to the plaintiff, were published to at least one other person, and would tend to lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person: Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61; Hill v. Church of Scientology, 1995 CanLII 59 (SCC). All circumstances, including reasonable implications, context, audience and manner of presentation, are considered (Botiuk; Skafco). Allegations of terrorism are 'about as serious and damaging an allegation as can be made': Lascaris v. B'nai Brith Canada, 2019 ONCA 163.
application: It was undisputed the posts referred to the plaintiff and were published. The July 6 post's natural and ordinary meaning was that he was a terrorist by his IDF association, pointed a sniper rifle at Palestinian children, was a hypocrite in his BLM advocacy, and had attacked/planned to attack Foodbenders (a criminal). The First July 30 post implied his failure to deny killing Palestinians in his BT interview meant he had done so. The Second July 30 post called him a racist, vicious Palestinian-hater and killer. Given the primary audience of engaged Foodbenders followers and the wider public who could not readily dismiss the claims, each post could and would tend to lower his reputation.
conclusion: All three posts satisfied the test for defamation.

issue: Did the defendants make out the defence of fair comment, and if so was it defeated by malice?
facts: The plaintiff conceded the posts concerned a matter of public interest as he is a public figure. The only fact stated in support of the July 6 post was that he 'is' an IDF soldier, when in fact he had served 30 years earlier for three years as a combat engineer, never as a sniper. Ms. Hawkins abandoned the justification defence, admitted she did no investigation, said her 'primary motive' was that DeLuca was 'harassing' her (unsupported by evidence), and stood by the posts through trial.
rule: Fair comment requires: (a) a matter of public interest; (b) comment/opinion not fact (though inferences of fact count); (c) based on true facts; (d) objectively fair, i.e. any person could honestly express it on the proved facts: WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Torstar. The comment must indicate the facts on which it is based, which must be true. Fair comment is defeated where the dominant motive is express malice — ill will, spite, dishonesty, reckless disregard for truth, or a motive unconnected with the defence's purpose: Hill; Bent v. Platnick, 2020 SCC 23; Foulidis.
application: Most July 6 statements were recognizable comment tied to his IDF association, but the defence failed because the sole supporting fact — that he 'is' an IDF soldier — was untrue and the sniper implication false, so readers could not judge for themselves; the 'attack' allegations were statements of fact. The First July 30 post's innuendo had no honest basis in the BT interview. In the Second July 30 post the 'racist/viciously hates Palestinians' and 'cancel' comments could qualify as fair comment based on his embedded 2019 Facebook post and the contemporaneous interview, but 'killer' was a statement of fact. In any event, malice defeated the defence: the 'whining Zionists' language, Ms. Hawkins's admitted dominant motive to 'stop' and 'expose' him, her animosity toward the IDF and Zionism, and her reckless failure to verify serious allegations.
conclusion: The fair comment defence failed for all posts, being defeated by malice (spite/ill will and recklessness) even where its elements might otherwise have been met.

issue: What quantum of general, aggravated and punitive damages, and what injunctive relief, was appropriate?
facts: The plaintiff sought $375,000–$500,000 in general and aggravated damages. The July 6 post was up ~24 hours and the July 30 posts ~2 hours; Foodbenders had ~16,000 followers. The plaintiff, a professional relying on reputation, testified to emotional distress, death threats and weight loss, but led no evidence of lost clients or earnings and required no counselling or time off. His prominent platform (BT interview, 26,000 Facebook followers) and swift condemnation of Foodbenders by political leaders mitigated harm. The defendants never apologized, ran a justification defence, and stood by the posts.
rule: Defamation damages aim to restore reputation, address injured feelings, and provide consolation and vindication: Hill; Botiuk; Lascaris. Relevant factors include the plaintiff's standing, seriousness of statements, extent of publication, absence of retraction/apology, and the defendant's conduct and motive (Barrick Gold Corp. v. Lopehandia). Malice involving spite, dishonesty or recklessness grounds aggravated damages. Punitive damages are awarded where conduct is so high-handed it offends the court's sense of decency and where general/aggravated damages are insufficient to punish and deter (Hill). A permanent injunction may issue where there is a real risk of repetition.
application: The comparators (Soliman $500,000; Paramount over $1M; Sommer $400,000) involved far more extensive, sustained campaigns and were not comparable. The posts were brief and the plaintiff substantially mitigated harm through his BT interview and continued high profile, with causation problems on the reposted July 6 content and little evidence of lasting reputational or financial loss. Nonetheless the contents were abhorrent, there was no apology, the statements were effectively republished through trial, and his suffering was real. Given the ongoing public concern about hateful comments (Whatcott) and the defendants' failure to be deterred by prior case law, punitive damages were warranted, and the risk of repetition justified a permanent injunction.
conclusion: General and aggravated damages of $75,000 and punitive damages of $10,000 were awarded jointly and severally against both defendants, together with a permanent injunction.

issue: Is the anti-SLAPP screening mechanism in s. 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act engaged?
facts: Warren Kinsella, a political commentator, published tweets, blog posts and comments during the run-up to the 2019 federal election branding Maxime Bernier, leader of the People's Party of Canada, as a racist, anti-Semite, misogynist and bigot. Bernier sued in defamation; the defendants moved to dismiss under s. 137.1.
rule: Section 137.1 CJA requires dismissal of a proceeding arising from expression relating to a matter of public interest unless the plaintiff satisfies the saving test in s. 137.1(4). The moving party first bears the burden of showing the expression relates to a matter of public interest (1704604 Ontario Ltd. v. Pointes Protection Association, 2020 SCC 22).
application: Bernier conceded that commenting on the opinions and positions of a political party leader is a matter of public interest, so the first-stage burden was met and the section was engaged. The burden then shifted to Bernier to satisfy s. 137.1(4).
conclusion: Section 137.1 was engaged; the plaintiff had to clear the statutory threshold to proceed.

issue: Did the plaintiff show grounds to believe the action had substantial merit and that the defendants had no valid defence?
