rule: Damages require a causal link between the defamation and the loss (art. 1607 C.c.Q.) and the plaintiff must mitigate (art. 1479 C.c.Q.). Moral damages repair humiliation, contempt and the psychological/social consequences of reputational harm (Hill v. Church of Scientology). Punitive damages under art. 49 of the Quebec Charter are reserved for malicious, high-handed conduct and only where compensatory awards are insufficient to punish and deter (Hill).
application: Although the termination flowed from the article, the loss-of-income claim could not be properly ascertained: Herman accepted a negotiated severance, the five-year period was excessive, and no evidence of his actual post-2020 revenues (he had started his own company) was adduced. For moral damages, the Court weighed the heinous nature of unfounded sexual-assault allegations, the relationship-driven nature of Herman's work, exposure of his family, easy internet availability of the article, and the repetitive campaign, fixing $200,000. On punitive damages, although Zajdel's conduct was malicious, the compensatory award was sufficient to deter.
conclusion: Loss-of-income claim dismissed for insufficient proof; $200,000 in moral damages awarded; no separate punitive damages.

issue: Should a permanent injunction be granted requiring removal and cessation of the defamatory statements?
facts: Herman sought a permanent injunction to remove all social-media postings alleging drugging/assault, to cease disseminating the allegations in any manner, and to remove the self-published book from sale. Zajdel repeatedly refused demands to remove the statements, insisting on her right to tell her 'story'; the book also contained material unrelated to the Herman allegations.
rule: An injunction is an extraordinary remedy (arts. 33, 509 C.c.P.). A permanent injunction restraining defamation may issue only in the clearest and rarest cases where the defamatory character is evident and unjustifiable and where the evidence shows, on a balance, an intention to repeat; the order must target precise statements to avoid an undue chilling effect on expression (Saputo inc. v. Pekov; Prud'homme c. Municipalité de Rawdon).
application: The evidence clearly showed Zajdel would continue posting the false accusations, having refused demand letters. The injunctive relief was justified and sufficiently precise regarding the postings and dissemination. As to the book, because it contained matter beyond the Herman allegations, the order was tailored to require removal only until references to Herman and his family (and any identifying reference) were removed.
conclusion: Permanent injunction granted, with the book order limited to references identifying Herman and his family.

issue: Does a public-school teacher have a s. 2(b) Charter freedom-of-expression right in his teaching capacity, and was it breached by the prohibition on showing the film and carrying out the project?
facts: Morin, a probationary grade-nine French immersion/Language Arts teacher, showed a BBC documentary, 'Thy Kingdom Come, Thy Will Be Done', as the basis for a project entitled 'What Religion Means to Different People'. After some parental complaints, the vice-principal and principal prohibited him from showing the film or carrying out the project; on internal appeal the Board decided the project could proceed only if its preparation and presentation satisfied the principal and superintendent. The respondent advanced no s. 1 justification.
rule: Section 2(b) of the Charter guarantees freedom of expression. The analytical framework from Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec (A.G.), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 927 asks (1) whether the activity is expression (an attempt to convey meaning, in content and form) and (2) whether the purpose or effect of the government action was to restrict that expression; any restriction must be justified under s. 1 (R. v. Big M Drug Mart; R. v. Keegstra; Ford v. Quebec). Higher administrative 'purposes' belong to the s. 1 analysis, not the definition of the right.
application: The majority (Webber J.A.) held the appellant's choice of film and project was clearly an attempt to convey meaning and thus protected expression; Keegstra confirmed even a teacher's classroom expression falls within s. 2(b). The purpose of the principal's and Board's actions was to control the content the appellant wished to present, and its effect implicated the underlying values (search for truth, participation, self-fulfilment), so freedom of expression was restricted. Since the respondent advanced no s. 1 argument, the limitation could not be justified. McQuaid J.A. dissented, holding that classroom expression in the teacher's professional capacity does not further the values underlying s. 2(b) and, following Walker v. P.E.I., overshoots the guarantee's purpose; the restriction was an employment matter for the grievance process, not a Charter breach.
conclusion: By majority, the appeal was allowed on the s. 2(b) issue: the teacher's freedom of expression was breached and, absent any s. 1 justification, the breach was established; damages were remitted to the trial judge.

issue: Was the appellant's s. 7 liberty interest engaged and breached?
facts: The appellant argued that being prevented from working in his chosen profession, and being pressured to abandon his expression, breached his s. 7 liberty interest, but raised it only in the alternative and conceded it was unnecessary if s. 24 remedies flowed from a s. 2(b) breach.
rule: Section 7 of the Charter protects life, liberty and security of the person; it does not generally extend to purely economic interests such as the right to pursue a particular occupation (Walker v. P.E.I.; Reference re ss. 193 and 195.1(1)(c)).
application: The majority found the appellant had not established any legal foundation for a distinct s. 7 claim, and the claim was essentially subsumed in the s. 2(b) analysis. McQuaid J.A. rejected the argument that Godbout v. Longueuil expanded s. 7 to convert a Charter breach into a liberty deprivation, and held s. 7 does not include a right to employment.
conclusion: The s. 7 ground of appeal was dismissed.

issue: Was there a collateral employment contract, and was the court's jurisdiction over the employment/wrongful-dismissal issues ousted by the collective agreement?
facts: The appellant claimed recruiter Linda Lowther guaranteed him at least two years of employment plus permanence, forming a collateral contract; he also challenged his involuntary paid leave as wrongful dismissal. Each written contract was for a one-year term incorporating the collective agreement and ss. 42-43 of the School Act.
rule: Collateral contracts must be proven strictly, including each party's intention to be bound (Crawford v. Cashin). Where a dispute arises from the collective agreement, jurisdiction lies with the grievance review board and the court's jurisdiction is ousted (prior Appeal Division ruling in Morin (1995); Weber v. Ontario Hydro). Appellate review of factual findings requires palpable and overriding error (Housen v. Nikolaisen).
application: The trial judge found Lowther's statements were general inducements, not contractual, and there was evidence to support that finding; the majority saw no reviewable error and McQuaid J.A. agreed a strict-proof burden was not met, especially given a second one-year written contract in 1987. The wrongful-dismissal/leave issue had already been found by the Appeal Division to fall within the collective agreement's grievance process, ousting the court's jurisdiction.
conclusion: These grounds were dismissed; no collateral contract existed and the employment issues were within the grievance board's exclusive jurisdiction. (McQuaid J.A. held the Charter issues nonetheless remained within the court's jurisdiction because the grievance board could not grant the s. 24 remedy sought.)

issue: Was the defamation claim established?
facts: The appellant alleged servants/agents of the respondent defamed him in conversations with a Quebec school board where he sought employment, and sought post-trial to add three further defamation incidents.
rule: Defamation requires proof of the words spoken and, where applicable, may be met by the defence of qualified privilege; damages must be shown. Amendments to pleadings are governed by Rule 26.01 and may be refused for prejudice.
application: The trial judge found no proof of what was said, no proof the statements were defamatory or spoken by an agent, a valid qualified-privilege defence, and no causation of damage; there was evidence to support these findings. The refusal to allow post-trial amendment of new defamation incidents was a proper exercise of discretion given prejudice. Both the majority and McQuaid J.A. found no reviewable error.
conclusion: The defamation ground of appeal was dismissed.

issue: Should the motion to adduce fresh evidence about the letterhead of the March 7 meeting notes be granted?
facts: The appellant sought to introduce evidence that the letterhead on John MacDonald's notes of the March 7, 1988 meeting did not exist until 1989, to undermine the credibility of witnesses who said the meeting (concerning his future) occurred.
rule: Fresh evidence on appeal is governed by the Palmer v. R. criteria (due diligence, relevance to a decisive issue, credibility, and capacity to affect the result); in civil cases the due-diligence and impact standards are applied more strictly (Varette v. Sainsbury; Dormuth v. Unetreiner).
application: The notes had been in the appellant's possession for years and the letterhead discrepancy could have been discovered by diligence before trial. The evidence went only to credibility on a point not decisive of the Charter, collateral-contract or defamation issues, and so could not reasonably have affected the result.
conclusion: The motion to adduce fresh evidence was dismissed.

issue: Does the Charter compel the province to provide and fund denominational religious schools for minority faiths within the secularized public school system, or does the secularization policy infringe freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a)?
facts: Following Zylberberg and the Elgin County decision, which struck down majoritarian Christian religious exercises and instruction in Ontario public schools, the Ministry issued Policy Memorandum 112 and amended ss. 28-29 of Reg. 298 to require that teaching about religion be non-indoctrinational and give no primacy to any faith. Parents from the Sikh, Hindu, Muslim, Mennonite and Christian Reform communities, including some involved with existing alternative religious schools (SCAP, Eden) whose religious instruction was thereby ended, argued the secular regime coerced them because they could not afford private religious schools.
rule: To found a breach of s. 2(a) of the Charter there must be state coercion that denies or limits the exercise of one's religion (R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.; Adler v. Ontario (C.A.)). Section 2(a) protects freedom to pursue religion without government interference but does not entitle a claimant to state support for its exercise. Government inaction/failure to fund is generally not subject to a Charter challenge (Adler).
application: The court held that secularism is neutral, not coercive: unlike the majoritarian Christian regime struck down in Zylberberg and Elgin County, Policy Memorandum 112 prefers no religion and imposes no indoctrination. The applicants' true objective, evidenced by the relief sought, was to bring minority religious schools under the public board to obtain public funding — precisely the claim rejected in Adler, where the Court of Appeal held there is no obligation to fund private religious schools and that inability to afford private schooling flows from religious choice, not government action. The 'opt-in' alternative-school characterization was a misnomer, since such schools were indistinguishable from the majoritarian schools already found unconstitutional.
conclusion: No infringement of s. 2(a). The failure to establish and fund minority religious schools within the public system does not violate freedom of conscience and religion.

issue: Do the policy memorandum and regulation restrict freedom of expression under s. 2(b) by limiting religious teaching in schools?
facts: The applicants argued that teachers and students could no longer express religious views, display religious posters, or provide indoctrinational instruction because Policy Memorandum 112 and ss. 28-29 limited classroom content. Teachers were not parties; the applicants were parents.
rule: Under the Irwin Toy framework, expression conveying meaning is prima facie protected; a court then asks whether the law's purpose or effect is to restrict protected expression. R. v. Keegstra was invoked for the proposition that a teacher's expressive freedom is engaged when confined to a curriculum.
application: The court found the purpose of the policy was to secularize the public school system, not to restrict protected expression, and its effect was to promote secularism, not to curtail expressive activity. No party's expression was in fact restricted: students remained free to voice their beliefs and teachers could express beliefs outside the curriculum; only indoctrination and giving primacy to a religion were limited. Keegstra, involving a teacher charged under the Criminal Code, was inapplicable and did not establish that a teacher may teach anything free of a set curriculum.
conclusion: No infringement of s. 2(b).

issue: Do the policy memorandum and regulation infringe s. 15 equality rights by forcing minority-faith parents to fund their own religious schools?
facts: The applicants said certain minority religious communities cannot in good conscience use the secular public system and, unlike the majority who benefit from public schooling, must bear the cost of religious education, and that some communities had no private religious schools at all.
rule: A s. 15(1) breach requires (1) a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground and (2) that the distinction be discriminatory by imposing burdens or withholding benefits (Adler; Simpsons-Sears on adverse-effect discrimination). Section 93(1) of the Constitution Act, 1867 and s. 23 of the Charter define the extent of denominational and minority-language education obligations (Bill 30 Reference), foreclosing s. 15 claims in those protected areas.
application: The court held the Education Act draws no distinction based on religion: the public system is secular and funds no private school of any faith, providing universally accessible education. Any distinction arises from the applicants' own religious choice, not from the statute, so there is no adverse-effect discrimination. Members of the former majority are likewise now denied religious exercises. The prohibition was just, fair and constitutional.
conclusion: No infringement of s. 15. Having found no Charter breach, the court did not need to consider s. 1 justification.

issue: Should a conditional stay be entered on one of the two guilty findings under the Kienapple principle where both threats arose from the same conversation?
facts: Mr. Akbari was found guilty of uttering a threat to damage synagogues (s. 264.1(1)(b)) and of uttering threats to kill Jews (s. 264.1(1)(a)), both arising from the same conversation with car salesperson Cameron Ahmad on March 4, 2024, indeed within the same sentence.
rule: The Kienapple principle (R. v. Kienapple, 1974 CanLII 14 (SCC), [1975] 1 SCR 729) bars multiple convictions for the same criminal act.
application: Although the words were uttered in a single conversation and even the same sentence, the focus of each was distinct: the threat against synagogues targeted Jewish communal infrastructure, while the threat to kill Jews targeted Jewish people directly. These are separate offences with different targets. Registering two findings of guilt had little impact on the global sentence but properly reflected the two distinct crimes.
conclusion: The court declined to enter a conditional stay of either count; both findings of guilt stand.

issue: What is a fit sentence for hate-motivated threats to bomb synagogues and kill Jews, and is a conditional discharge available or is a custodial sentence required?
facts: Akbari, a 41-year-old Afghan-born Ismaili Muslim, Canadian citizen with a dated 2013 impaired driving conviction, told a stranger he would plant bombs in every Toronto synagogue and kill as many Jews as possible. He took no material steps to act on the threats and did not publicize them beyond the conversation. He had strong family and community support, expressed shame and some insight, but continued to deny making the threats. Five community impact statements described profound fear in the Jewish community; the Crown sought 4-6 months jail plus probation, the defence sought a conditional discharge.
rule: Sentencing principles under s. 718 of the Criminal Code (proportionality, denunciation, deterrence, rehabilitation); hate motivation based on national origin and religion is a statutory aggravating factor under s. 718.2(a)(i). A conditional discharge requires that it be in the offender's best interests and not contrary to the public interest. The court referenced R. v. Gobin, 2025 ONCJ 266, on the priority of denunciation and deterrence for hate-motivated offences.
application: The most serious aggravating factor was the hate-motivated bias against Israelis and Jews, contributing to a community already under siege by rising antisemitic hate crime. A conditional discharge failed both prongs: Akbari already had a record with no obvious collateral consequences, and a discharge would be contrary to the public interest given the highly aggravating hate-motivated circumstances demanding denunciation and deterrence. The threat to bomb synagogues to kill 'as many Jews as possible' placed the offence near the extreme end. However, mitigating factors — no steps to act, empty threats to a single stranger, significant personal consequences (loss of business, four days pre-trial custody, harassment), compliance with bail, and steps toward rehabilitation — meant community safety was not endangered by service in the community.
conclusion: Probation alone was insufficient; a custodial sentence of 60 days was imposed to be served conditionally (house arrest) plus credit for pre-sentence custody, followed by three years probation, with counselling, weapons and no-contact conditions, a DNA order, and a 10-year s. 110 weapons prohibition.

issue: Is Bill 21 within provincial legislative competence, or ultra vires as criminal law?
facts: Bill 21 prohibits designated state employees from wearing religious symbols (s. 6) and requires certain functions to be exercised with the face uncovered (s. 8). Applicants argued that ss. 6 and 8 are in pith and substance criminal law, regulating religious observance for a moral purpose, and therefore fall under s. 91(27).
rule: Validity is assessed by qualification (pith and substance) then classification. A valid criminal law requires a prohibition, a penal sanction, and a valid criminal law purpose (Siemens v. Manitoba; Renvoi relatif à la Loi sur la non-discrimination génétique; R. v. Big M Drug Mart; Edwards Books). Stare decisis binds the court to Supreme Court statements requiring a penal sanction.
application: The Court held that Bill 21's true character is legislation dealing ontologically with religion, historically tied to the criminal-law heads of public peace, order and morality, and that both its object and effects are religious. However, Bill 21 contains no fine or imprisonment—only administrative and disciplinary sanctions (ss. 12, 13, 16). Bound by Siemens' reference to a 'penal' sanction, the Court could not classify it as criminal law. Absent a federal connection, the law falls under ss. 92(4), 92(13) and 92(16), while the Quebec Charter amendment flows from s. 45 of the Constitution Act, 1982.
conclusion: Bill 21 is intra vires the National Assembly; the ultra vires argument fails.

issue: Does the pre-emptive use of the notwithstanding clauses shield Bill 21 from Charter review of the derogated rights?
facts: The legislature invoked s. 33 of the Canadian Charter (ss. 2, 7–15) and derogated from ss. 1–38 of the Quebec Charter before any judicial ruling. Applicants urged that substantive conditions, informed by international law, be read into s. 33.
rule: Ford v. Quebec holds that s. 33 imposes formal requirements only, with no substantive review of the legislative policy. Ontario (AG) v. G confirms the override may be used for purely political reasons. Stare decisis applies; international instruments have only interpretive, non-binding value (Québec v. 9147-0732 Québec inc.; Kazemi).
application: The Court found no new legal question or changed circumstances justifying departure from Ford, and rejected the proposal to graft s. 1-type conditions onto the override. It observed that the sweeping, pre-emptive use of the clauses—suspending rights bearing no apparent connection to laicity (e.g., solicitor-client privilege, right to counsel, independent tribunal)—appears excessive and cavalier, but remains legally unassailable in the current state of the law; the sanction lies at the ballot box.
conclusion: The override was validly invoked; recourse to the derogated fundamental freedoms and equality guarantees is foreclosed.

issue: Does s. 28 of the Charter operate as an autonomous guarantee capable of invalidating Bill 21 despite the override?
facts: The evidence established that Bill 21's effects fall disproportionately on Muslim women who wear the hijab. Section 28 is not listed among the provisions subject to the s. 33 override.
rule: Section 28 provides that 'the rights and freedoms referred to in it are guaranteed equally to male and female persons.' Interpretation must give primacy to the text (Renvoi Motor Vehicle Act); s. 28 reinforces and informs the interpretation of s. 15 (SFPQ v. Quebec).
application: The Court held that the words 'the rights and freedoms referred to in it' confine s. 28 to the rights actually guaranteed by the Charter. Where the legislature validly uses s. 33 to suspend those rights, there is no remaining substrate of rights on which s. 28 can operate to guarantee equal enjoyment. Although Bill 21 impairs Muslim women's religious freedom and engages s. 15, the override removes any basis for invoking s. 28.
conclusion: Section 28 does not operate autonomously to invalidate Bill 21; this ground fails.

issue: Does s. 8 (with Annex III) infringe the right to be eligible for the National Assembly under s. 3, and is it justified?
facts: Section 8's first paragraph, read with Annex III paragraph 1, applies to members of the National Assembly, requiring them to sit with an uncovered face. A person who covers her face could stand for election but could never take her seat.
rule: Section 3 cannot be overridden under s. 33 and any derogation attracts a stringent justification standard (Frank v. Canada; Sauvé). Parliamentary privilege applies only where necessary to the legislature's constitutional function (Vaid; Chagnon).
application: The Court found that the combined effect inexorably prevents an elected person who veils her face from sitting, thereby negating the very purpose of s. 3. The PGQ's parliamentary-privilege argument, raised only at closing, was not established, and no s. 1 justification was advanced or demonstrated.
conclusion: The combined effect of s. 8's first paragraph and Annex III paragraph 1 unjustifiably violates s. 3; Annex III paragraph 1 is declared inoperative under s. 52.

issue: Do the impugned provisions infringe s. 23 minority-language education rights, and can the infringement be justified under s. 1?
facts: English-language school boards (EMSB) wished to hire and promote staff wearing religious symbols to reflect the cultural diversity of their communities; Bill 21 prohibits this. Section 23 is not subject to the s. 33 override.
rule: Section 23 confers on the linguistic minority the exclusive power of management and control over education affecting its language and culture, including hiring and assignment of personnel (Mahe; Arsenault-Cameron; Conseil scolaire francophone de la C.-B.). Any derogation attracts a strict justification standard; the s. 1 Oakes analysis applies (RJR-MacDonald).
application: The Court held that culture, which s. 23 protects alongside language, encompasses religious diversity; the evidence (including expert reports of Dee and Hehman) showed English boards genuinely value and promote such diversity, and that Bill 21 nullifies their hiring, retention and promotion choices, violating s. 23. On s. 1, the PGQ led no justification; the intervenors (MLQ, PDF) failed to discharge the burden—the deleterious effects on affected persons and minority students are grave while the salutary effects are tenuous and unproven.
conclusion: The first paragraph of s. 4, ss. 6, 7, 8, 10, the first and second paragraphs of s. 12, ss. 13, 14 and 16 (read with the specified Annex provisions) unjustifiably violate s. 23 and are declared inoperative for any person or entity benefiting from s. 23.

issue: Was the requirement of urgency for a provisional injunction established?
facts: The plaintiff, a Jewish law student of Israeli origin, sought to stay implementation of a student-body referendum endorsing an academic and cultural boycott of Israeli institutions. She claimed imminent loss of academic opportunities and exposure to a discriminatory framework within the next 10 days.
rule: Provisional injunctions under arts. 510 and 511 C.C.P. are reserved for urgent situations; urgency must be real, 'immediate and apparent,' not artificially created, and requires diligence (Gestion Solodarmo inc. c. Sawatzky, 2019 QCCS 3567; Pettenon Cosmetics c. De Michele, 2020 QCCS 421).
application: When asked repeatedly what was to occur in the next 10 days, no party could articulate a concrete answer. Exchange programs with Israeli institutions (e.g. Tel Aviv University) were already suspended due to governmental travel restrictions. The plaintiff and the JLSA had already engaged the SSMU Judicial Board's internal process, which was set to be heard within weeks; courts must exercise restraint before internal remedies are exhausted (Association étudiante de l'Université McGill c. X, 2025 QCCA 475).
conclusion: Urgency was not established, which alone was sufficient to dismiss the application.

issue: Did the plaintiff meet the elevated appearance-of-right threshold applicable when the injunction sought would restrict freedom of expression?
facts: The plaintiff argued she sought only to stay the operational consequences of the referendum (severance of exchange agreements, creation of the PACBI committee, constitutional entrenchment), not to restrict expression.
rule: Where injunctive relief touches on any limitation of freedom of expression, the traditional 'serious issue' threshold is displaced by an elevated test: an injunction issues only in the clearest, rarest and most exceptional cases where the expression is so manifestly wrongful the action would almost certainly succeed (Association étudiante de l'Université McGill c. X, 2025 QCCA 475; Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec (A.G.), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 927).
application: The Court held freedom of expression lay at the core of the application. Protection of expression extends to every stage—from formation of ideas to their concrete implementation—and cannot be surgically divided. Boycott is itself a protected form of expression. The referendum and its measures fell at the implementation end of the expression spectrum and were not so clearly defamatory or impossible to justify as to warrant intervention.
conclusion: The elevated test applied and was not met; the application presented no rare, exceptional or manifest case.

issue: Did the plaintiff establish serious or irreparable harm?
facts: The plaintiff alleged loss of academic opportunities, violation of her rights to dignity and to be free from discrimination and harassment, and diminution of the value of her eventual McGill law degree.
rule: An applicant must provide clear and convincing evidence of harm that cannot be compensated by damages; the harm must be specific and personal, not that of a broader collective (RJR-MacDonald Inc. c. Canada (A.G.), [1994] 1 S.C.R. 311; Association étudiante de l'Université McGill c. X, 2025 QCCA 475).
application: There was no evidence the plaintiff intended to pursue an exchange, and the Tel Aviv program was already suspended; as an Israeli citizen her access to such opportunities was doubtful in necessity. The alleged discriminatory impact was not supported by concrete, precise evidence of imminent materialization. The claimed reputational harm to McGill did not translate into personal prejudice to the plaintiff's future degree from a world-renowned institution.
conclusion: Irreparable harm was not established on any of the grounds advanced.

issue: Did the balance of inconvenience favour granting the provisional injunction?
facts: The plaintiff argued refusal would subject her to a discriminatory framework with permanent constitutional consequences, while granting would merely temporarily stay the severance of partnerships.
rule: The balance of inconvenience assesses which party faces greater prejudice from granting or refusing the order, considering the constitutional protection of expression.
application: Granting the injunction would deprive the members who voted in favour of the referendum of the ability to give effect to their political and social expression. The measures were not permanent: a subsequent referendum or the merits judge could reverse them, and no permanence could be inferred from the evidence.
conclusion: The balance of inconvenience favoured the defendants.

issue: Should McGill be granted leave to adduce evidence (Exhibits R-1 to R-10) at the class action authorization hearing?
facts: The applicant seeks authorization to institute a class action against McGill on behalf of Jewish students for damages suffered during pro-Palestinian protests on campus after October 7, 2023, alleging antisemitic and anti-Zionist activity and McGill's failure to take disciplinary action. McGill requested leave to file evidence of court proceedings (injunctions it initiated or supported) and of a public arbitration involving QPIRG after McGill notified it to cease supporting SPHR. The applicant left the matter to the Court's discretion; the applicant had filed only partial evidence of McGill's proceedings.
rule: Under article 575 of the Code of Civil Procedure, at the authorization stage a respondent may be permitted to adduce appropriate evidence to clarify and complete factual elements essential to the application, provided the evidence is not susceptible of being challenged as to scope or probative value and does not open a debate as to its sufficiency (Lachaine v. Air Transat AT inc., 2021 QCCS 256; Lord v. Netflix International, 2018 QCCS 1275; Desjardins Financial Services Firm Inc. c. Asselin, 2020 SCC 30, para. 72).
application: The proposed evidence was directly linked to the allegations against McGill and allowed the Court a full picture of McGill's intervention, given that the applicant had filed only partial evidence. The documents were public proceedings and exhibits filed by McGill, submitted not to prove the truth of their contents but to show McGill's position and the context of its interventions. Accordingly the evidence was not susceptible of challenge as to scope or probative value and did not open a debate on sufficiency.
conclusion: The Court granted the application and authorized McGill to file Exhibits R-1 to R-10, without costs.

issue: Do the claims against the Victoria Symphony Foundation (VSF) and its directors disclose a reasonable cause of action?
facts: The plaintiff, a former principal trumpet, sued the VSF, a registered charitable foundation that raises money and manages an endowment supporting the Victoria Symphony Society (VSS). The VSF had no contract with the plaintiff and did not administer or manage the VSS or its employment relationships. The employing entity, the VSS, was not named as a defendant.
rule: Under Rule 9-5(1)(a) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules a pleading may be struck where, assuming the pleaded facts to be true, it is 'plain and obvious' the case discloses no reasonable cause of action and is destined to fail (Young v. Borzoni, 2007 BCCA 16). Vicarious liability requires the requisite control over the actor (Speckling v. Kearney, 2006 BCSC 506, aff'd 2007 BCCA 145).
application: The VSF was a separate legal entity from the VSS with no contractual relationship with the plaintiff and no responsibility for the VSS's administration or management, and lacked the control needed to be vicariously liable for the VSS's acts. There was therefore no basis for any claim against the Foundation or its directors.
conclusion: It was plain and obvious the claims against the VSF and its directors disclosed no reasonable cause of action and were struck.

issue: Are the claims against the VSS's former directors and staff barred by issue estoppel or abuse of process?
facts: After being dismissed for cause in 2009, the plaintiff grieved and an arbitration panel found (May and August 2012) that he was dismissed without just cause but could not be reinstated due to permanent disability, awarding him $18,000 less an overpayment. He did not appeal or seek judicial review. His duty-of-fair-representation complaint was dismissed by the Labour Relations Board and leave to reconsider was refused; an earlier civil action was dismissed by Leask J. and a human rights complaint was out of time. He then sued individual directors and staff, attacking the legitimacy and jurisdiction of the grievance process and re-raising the exclusion of an audiologist report.
rule: Issue estoppel requires that the same question was decided in a prior proceeding, the earlier decision was final, and the parties or their privies were the same (B.C. (WCB) v. Figliola, 2011 SCC 52; Danyluk v. Ainsworth Technologies, 2001 SCC 44). The doctrine of abuse of process (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63) allows a court to prevent relitigation that would undermine judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the administration of justice, even where issue estoppel is unavailable. Section 139 of the Labour Relations Code gives the LRB exclusive jurisdiction over questions such as whether a person is a dependent contractor or bound by a collective agreement.
application: The action raised the same questions decided in, or that could have been raised before, the final arbitration and LRB proceedings; the defendants sued in their capacity as VSS directors and staff were privies of the VSS, satisfying mutuality. Alternatively, relitigating the jurisdiction, procedure and result of the grievance process, and the already-adjudicated exclusion of the medical report, was an abuse of process. Any new allegations (harassment, unlawful business practices, damage to reputation) were arbitral issues that should have been raised in the grievance procedure, and any jurisdictional concerns about the collective agreement or dependent-contractor status fell within the LRB's exclusive jurisdiction under s. 139.
conclusion: The claims were barred by issue estoppel and, alternatively, constituted an abuse of process; they were struck as frivolous and vexatious.

issue: Does the plaintiff disclose a cause of action against the employer's solicitor, Marcia McNeil?
facts: The plaintiff alleged that Ms. McNeil, counsel for the VSS, withheld or suppressed a 2011 medical report from the arbitration board. The plaintiff himself possessed the report, and it was his union's tactical decision not to adduce it. No allegation was made that Ms. McNeil stepped outside her role as counsel or assumed any obligation to the plaintiff.
rule: No action lies against a solicitor for the actions of her client in which she did not participate, and none lies unless the solicitor is alleged to have stepped outside her role and undertaken an obligation to the plaintiff. Rule 9-5(1)(a) applies where it is plain and obvious no cause of action is disclosed.
application: Ms. McNeil acted within her role as solicitor for the VSS, owed no duty to the plaintiff, and was under no obligation to present his case. The decision not to tender the report was the union's tactical choice, and the plaintiff had the report himself.
conclusion: It was plain and obvious the plaintiff disclosed no cause of action against Ms. McNeil; the claim against her was dismissed.

issue: Is the funding of Roman Catholic separate schools a relevant consideration, or is the challenge foreclosed by the Bill 30 Reference (res judicata)?
facts: Public and Roman Catholic separate schools are fully funded through property taxes and provincial grants, while Jewish day schools and OACSS Christian schools receive no direct funding. The applicants sought equivalent funding by reference to the treatment of Roman Catholic schools; the Attorney General argued the matter was settled by the Bill 30 Reference.
rule: A constitutional reference does not involve a lis inter partes, so res judicata does not technically apply (Bill 30 Reference, upheld [1987] 1 S.C.R. 1148). Roman Catholic separate school funding is guaranteed by s. 93(1) of the Constitution Act, 1867 and, per s. 29 of the Charter, is immune from Charter review.
application: The Court accepted that res judicata did not bar the claim, but refused to let legislation held to be a valid exercise of the provincial education power serve as the fulcrum for an argument that it is unconstitutional in effect. The Bill 30 question had invited full Charter scrutiny and was dealt with accordingly. Roman Catholic funding was characterized as a constitutional anomaly rooted in the 1867 Confederation compromise.
conclusion: Roman Catholic separate school funding is not a relevant consideration and is given no weight in disposing of the applicants' claims.

issue: Does non-funding of Jewish and independent Christian schools infringe s. 15(1) equality rights?
facts: Parents whose religious convictions preclude sending children to public schools must pay tuition (averaging 77% of elementary and 51% of high-school costs at Jewish day schools), whereas public-school parents bear no direct education cost.
rule: Section 15(1) of the Charter; the Andrews/Turpin/Swain framework: (1) has an equality right been denied by a distinction based on personal characteristics, and (2) does the distinction impose a burden or withhold a benefit amounting to discrimination, considering the larger social context.
application: The Education Act creates a distinction whereby those who cannot attend public schools for religious reasons do not receive free education. Looking at the larger historical context, the Court found this to be a distinction based on religion, even if an ironic and indirect consequence of a system designed to be free of religious bias.
conclusion: The applicants' s. 15(1) right to equal benefit of the law is infringed.

issue: Does the non-funding combined with mandatory attendance infringe freedom of religion under s. 2(a)?
facts: The Education Act (s. 21) makes school attendance mandatory; parents whose faith prevents public-school attendance can comply only by paying tuition at independent religious schools.
rule: Section 2(a) of the Charter; R. v. Big M Drug Mart, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295; R. v. Edwards Books, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713 (all coercive burdens on religious exercise, direct or indirect, are within s. 2(a)); Zylberberg v. Sudbury Board of Education (1988), 65 O.R. (2d) 641.
application: Though the Court's initial view was that parents remained free to educate children as they wished, the authorities established that indirect coercion suffices. Government action (mandatory attendance) imposes a cost/burden on those precluded by religious belief from using the free public system, analogous to the exemption-with-cost situation in Zylberberg.
conclusion: The applicants' s. 2(a) freedom of religion is infringed.

issue: Is the infringement of ss. 2(a) and 15 saved by s. 1 of the Charter?
facts: The government's objectives included a tuition-free, secular, universally accessible public education fostering a pluralist democratic society; it argued funding independent schools would jeopardize the public system.
rule: Section 1 and the R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103 test: a sufficiently important, pressing and substantial objective, plus proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality of effects); the legislature need not adopt the absolutely least intrusive means (R. v. Chaulk).
application: The objective of a broadly based secular public system was pressing and substantial. Non-funding was rationally connected to protecting that system, the risk of harm to public schools (Shapiro Report, Lawton affidavit) being a legitimate concern. Impairment was minimal (parents remain free to educate as they choose, with limited indirect support such as tax exemptions), and the proportionality of effects was largely a matter of opinion better suited to the legislature; the effects were not out of proportion to the objective.
conclusion: The limits are justified under s. 1; the legislation is saved.

issue: Does denial of School Health Support Services to independent-school students breach the Charter, and how should it be characterized?
facts: Three children (with hearing impairment, spina bifida/hydrocephalus, and developmental disability) attend independent schools that fall outside the Education Act definition of 'school' and so do not receive school health support services delivered in the school setting.
rule: Reg. 452, R.R.O. 1980 (Health Insurance Act); standing principles from Borowski, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 575 and Finlay, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 607; the ss. 2(a), 15 and 1 Charter analysis already applied.
application: All applicants raising the issue were granted standing. The Court characterized the services as educational rather than purely health services (the services are otherwise available to the children as health services; it is delivery in the school setting that is contested), so the same infringement and s. 1 analysis applied.
conclusion: The health-support claim is disposed of as the education claims were: infringement found but saved by s. 1; relief refused.

issue: What is the fit and proper sentence for an offender convicted by a jury of wilfully promoting hatred against Jews contrary to s. 319(2) of the Criminal Code?
facts: Travis Patron, 31, leader of the Canadian Nationalist Party, posted a written document and a professionally-produced recorded speech titled 'Beware the Parasitic Tribe' on his personal and party websites, describing Jews as parasites and calling to 'remove these people, once-and-for-all, from our country.' The material remained online for a lengthy period (June 2019 to February 2021). He was found guilty by a jury on the indictable offence, which carries a maximum of two years. He has a recent criminal record and expressed no remorse.
rule: Sections 718, 718.1 and 718.2 of the Criminal Code govern sentencing purposes and principles, requiring proportionality to the gravity of the offence and the offender's degree of responsibility. Deterrence and denunciation are primary objectives for hate-promotion offences (R v Topham, 2017 BCSC 551; R v Keegstra, 1996 ABCA 308; Saskatchewan v Whatcott, 2013 SCC 11).
application: The court found deterrence and denunciation to be primary objectives given the serious nature of hate speech, which undermines tolerance and can lay the groundwork for broader attacks on vulnerable groups. Aggravating factors included the planned, deliberate and prolonged nature of the offence, the wide reach of the internet, the harm caused to the Jewish community, and the offender's criminal record and lack of remorse. Mitigating factors included his previously good life. The court adopted the Crown's proposed one year of imprisonment but reduced the probation to one year.
conclusion: The court imposed one year imprisonment (365 days) followed by one year of probation.

issue: Does the seriousness of the hate-promotion offence generally warrant a custodial sentence, and how do proportionality and parity apply?
facts: There is no established sentencing range or starting point from the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal for s. 319(2)(a). The court reviewed numerous s. 319(2) sentencing decisions across Canada, none from Saskatchewan.
rule: Section 718.2(b) requires parity — a sentence should be similar to those imposed on similar offenders for similar offences in similar circumstances. Appellate authority (Keegstra; Lelas) emphasizes imprisonment to denounce hatemongering.
application: From the case survey, the court concluded that a custodial sentence will normally follow conviction under the indictable form, s. 319(2)(a), while non-custodial sentences (typically prosecuted summarily under s. 319(2)(b)) are reserved for less serious offences involving no record, very young or old offenders, or isolated impetuous acts. It is the serious nature of the offence rather than the offender's circumstances that generally supports custody. Patron's offence was serious, planned and prolonged.
conclusion: A custodial sentence was warranted; one year imprisonment was proportionate and consistent with parity.

issue: Is a probation term restricting the offender from publishing information about persons of Jewish religion or origin an appropriate condition?
facts: The Crown sought a probation term modelled on R v Topham prohibiting the accused from publishing or posting online any information about persons of Jewish religion or origin readable by the general public.
rule: A court may impose reasonable probation conditions to protect the community; such a term was imposed in R v Topham, 2017 BCSC 551 at para 60.
application: The court found the purpose of probation was to provide protection for the community after release and adopted the Topham-style prohibition on publishing information about persons of Jewish religion or origin as a probation condition.
conclusion: The condition was imposed as term 3 of the one-year probation order.

issue: How should credit for time served on remand be calculated?
facts: Patron had spent 131 days in jail that the Crown agreed should be treated as time on remand attributable to this charge; the remainder of his 2.5 years on remand was credited to other sentences.
rule: Enhanced credit of 1.5 days for each day served on remand.
application: 131 days at 1.5:1 yields 197 days of credit, deducted from the 365-day sentence, leaving 168 days to be served.
conclusion: 197 days credited; 168 days remaining to serve.

issue: What standard of proof applies on an anti-SLAPP motion under s. 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act?
facts: The defendant moved to dismiss a $200,000 libel action as a strategic lawsuit against public participation. The legislation, enacted in 2015, does not define the standard of proof, and Superior Court decisions had split between a relaxed 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard and the ordinary civil standard.
rule: Section 137.1 CJA sets a burden-shifting analysis. Case law was divided: Able Translations Ltd. v. Express International Translations Inc., 2016 ONSC 6785 favoured 'reasonable grounds to believe' (per Mugesera v. Canada, 2005 SCC 40), while Rizvee v. Newman, 2017 ONSC 4024 and Bondfield Construction Co. v. The Globe and Mail, 2018 ONSC 1880 favoured the balance of probabilities. McDougall v. F.H., 2008 SCC 53 holds there is one civil standard of proof.
application: Recognizing the law was unsettled and pending appellate guidance, the Court adopted the reasoning of Morgan J. and Fitzpatrick J. that there is no reason to apply a standard less stringent than the ordinary civil standard, consistent with McDougall.
conclusion: The applicable standard is proof on a balance of probabilities.

issue: Did the impugned publications arise from an expression relating to a matter of public interest under s. 137.1(3)?
facts: B'nai Brith published an article (August 4, 2016) and a tweet (April 3, 2017) stating that Lascaris, the Green Party's Justice Critic, had used social media to advocate on behalf of terrorists who murdered Israeli civilians. The publications concerned the Israeli–Palestinian conflict, the BDS movement, and a policy resolution before the Green Party convention. Lascaris himself publishes extensively on these matters.
rule: Under s. 137.1(3) the moving party must show the proceeding arises from an expression relating to a matter of public interest. 'Public interest' is assessed by considering the subject matter of the publication as a whole: Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61 (some segment of the community must have a genuine interest in the subject); see also Baglow v. Smith, 2015 ONSC 1175.
application: The communications were plainly expression. Their subject matter — the Middle East conflict, the conduct of governments, the BDS debate and the views of a federal party figure — invites public attention, affects the welfare of citizens and attracts controversy. Like Dr. Baglow, the plaintiff himself publishes in the area, confirming the public interest. The plaintiff's argument that the articles were merely personal attacks was rejected.
conclusion: The moving party met its onus; the expression related to a matter of public interest, shifting the burden to the plaintiff.

issue: Did the plaintiff satisfy s. 137.1(4) by showing substantial merit and that the defendant has no valid defence?
facts: The plaintiff alleged the article falsely characterized him as a supporter of terrorists, damaging his reputation. The defendant pleaded justification, qualified privilege and fair comment, and argued the plaintiff proved no damages. The underlying facts — Lascaris's meeting with Muhammad Alayan, Bahaa Alayan's death, the call to return the body, the BDS motion, Lascaris's candidacy — were grounded in fact.
rule: Under s. 137.1(4) the responding party must show grounds to believe the claim has substantial merit and the moving party has no valid defence, and that harm outweighs the public interest in the expression; the requirements are conjunctive. Fair comment succeeds where the comment is on a matter of public interest, based on fact, recognizable as comment, and one any person could honestly express: WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; s. 23 Libel and Slander Act. The test is not whether the opinion is reasonable but whether anyone could honestly hold it (Baglow); the defence is defeated only by proof of malice as the dominant motive (Grant v. Torstar).
application: The Court assumed the claim had merit despite scant evidence of reputational loss. On defences, the fair comment analysis was decisive: the comment was on a public-interest matter, based on proven facts, arguably recognizable as opinion, and one a person could honestly hold — someone knowing Bahaa Alayan was allegedly involved in a terrorist attack could honestly believe Lascaris's support for the Alayan family amounted to supporting terrorists, even if not a reasonable belief. Mr. Mostyn's evidence showed the defendant was genuinely seeking to influence public opinion against BDS, with no evidence of malice. The plaintiff therefore could not show the fair comment defence could not succeed.
conclusion: The plaintiff failed to establish that no valid defence exists; the s. 137.1(4) test was not met and the action was dismissed.

issue: Does Bill 160's removal of the local property-taxation power from separate school boards prejudicially affect Roman Catholic denominational rights under s. 93(1) of the Constitution Act, 1867?
facts: For over 150 years separate school boards could levy local property taxes (a power rooted in s. 7 of the Scott Act of 1863) to supplement provincial grants. Bill 160 repealed the boards' independent power to set and levy school taxes, centralizing all revenue in the province while guaranteeing proportional per-pupil funding.
rule: Section 93(1) protects rights or privileges affecting denominational schools enjoyed by a class of persons by law at Union that are prejudicially affected (Greater Hull; Bill 30 Reference; GMPSB). Protection extends to the means necessary to achieve denominational education (GMPSB), and the right to levy taxes without limit is itself a 'right or privilege with respect to denominational schools' protected by s. 93(1) (Greater Hull).
application: Section 7 of the Scott Act conferred a stand-alone, unqualified right to tax, separate from the s. 20 proportionality right. Though facially non-denominational, that independent financing power was constitutionally guaranteed at Union. Bill 160's proportional funding does not exhaust that right; it leaves the Catholic community hostage to provincially-imposed funding ceilings without any independent means to enhance resources. A 'separate' system implies a means of financing from within the community, so eliminating the taxing power impinges a constitutional right.
conclusion: The taxation power is constitutionally protected; Bill 160, insofar as it removes the taxation power from the Roman Catholic educational community, is unconstitutional as a violation of s. 93(1) and of no force and effect to that extent.

issue: Are Bill 160's Division D supervision and vesting-order provisions unconstitutional under s. 93(1)?
facts: Division D allows the Minister to investigate boards' financial affairs and seek vesting orders where there is a deficit, default, or likelihood thereof, with mandatory revocation where no deficit exists, and a statutory clause protecting denominational aspects.
rule: The test is whether authority to withdraw a right or privilege necessarily operates to the prejudice of the class affected (Ottawa Separate School Trustees v. Ottawa; Re Ottawa Separate Schools). Sufficiently defined standards for imposition and removal of supervision save such provisions.
application: Unlike the indefinite, standardless power struck down in the earlier Ottawa case, Division D imposes supervision only on defined financial grounds and mandates revocation once no deficit exists; it also statutorily reiterates s. 93(1) protection of denominational aspects. The absence of an express court-review invitation is not fatal, and any attempt to preclude review of a s. 93(1) violation would itself be invalid. A separate factual foundation is unnecessary where prejudice would be per se.
conclusion: Division D is, on its face, constitutionally valid; the applicants' submissions are rejected.

issue: Does Bill 160 contravene s. 93(1) as applied to the public school system through a doctrine of 'mirror equality'?
facts: OPSBA argued that because the separate system's rights are measured against the public system, the public system enjoys reciprocal constitutional protection that Bill 160 infringes.
rule: Section 93(1) is protective legislation for the denominational minority (Re Calgary Board of Education; Alberta Public School Boards' Assn.). Adler v. Ontario holds the public system is 'impliedly contemplated' by s. 93 only as a backdrop, immune from Charter attack, but public school rights are not themselves constitutionally entrenched.
application: The 'reciprocity/mirror equality' argument rests on a false syllogism: shared constitutional recognition does not confer identical rights. The public system is contemplated only as a reference point/means to preserve the separate system's Catholicity, not as an independent constitutional goal; the majority may protect itself through the ballot box. Adler is a shield, not a sword to win denominational rights for public schools (following Campbell J. in Fewer School Boards).
conclusion: The mirror-image argument is rejected; the public school system enjoys no entrenched rights under s. 93(1) (except perhaps a right of existence, not necessary to decide).

issue: Can the applicants rely on a constitutional convention to preserve the boards' taxing power?
facts: The applicants argued a constitutional convention protects boards' power to levy and determine property taxes and that Bill 160 breaches it.
rule: Constitutional conventions are not enforced by the courts and cannot invalidate express legal rules (Reference re: Amendment of the Constitution of Canada); s. 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982 did not make conventions justiciable; implicit powers (New Brunswick Broadcasting) are distinct from conventions.
application: Even if such a convention existed, it could not strike down clear legislation. The distinction between non-justiciable conventions and implicit but justiciable constitutional powers defeats the argument; a convention expanding s. 93 against the province's plenary education power is highly unlikely to exist and, in any event, unenforceable.
conclusion: The constitutional-convention submission is rejected.

issue: Do Bill 160's broad delegation and regulation-making powers offend the rule of law through excessive delegation or vagueness?
facts: Bill 160 confers extensive regulation-making powers on the executive, including the Minister of Finance's power to set tax rates, across numerous enumerated subjects.
rule: Wide legislative delegation is constitutionally permissible provided it is explicitly set out (Hodge v. The Queen; Re Gray; Chemicals Reference; A.G. Nova Scotia v. A.G. Canada). A provision is unconstitutionally vague only if it provides no adequate basis for legal debate (Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society).
application: The enabling provisions specify the subjects of regulation with defined headings, satisfying the requirement of explicit delegation. The tax-rate power identifies its object (school purposes) and the collecting bodies, providing an ascertainable basis for legal debate; it is not vague.
conclusion: The rule-of-law/delegation submission is rejected; the delegation is valid and the provisions are not vague.

issue: Does the Minister of Finance's power to set tax rates by regulation offend ss. 53 and 54 of the Constitution Act, 1867?
facts: Section 257.12(1)(b) empowers the Minister of Finance to prescribe school tax rates by regulation without a money bill; the applicants said this is taxation without representation contrary to ss. 53-54 (applied to provinces by s. 90).
rule: Bills imposing taxes must originate in and be recommended to the legislative chamber (ss. 53-54). Case law (National Fish Co.; Chemicals; Canada Assistance Plan Reference) suggests taxing power may not be delegated casually; implicit repeal of constitutional provisions is rejected (R. v. Mercure; Manitoba Language Reference).
application: The court rejected the implicit-repeal theory but held ss. 53-54 are satisfied where the delegation of the taxing power in a legislature-approved bill is clear and explicit, as here. Municipalities and school boards have always validly exercised delegated taxing powers, reinforcing that express delegation suffices.
conclusion: The ss. 53-54 challenge is rejected; the express delegation satisfies those sections.

issue: Does the six-month procedural maximum for a summarily prosecuted hybrid offence operate as the ceiling, or must the court first determine the fit sentence and then apply the procedural cap?
facts: Wilful promotion of hatred under s. 319(2) is a hybrid offence; the Crown elected summary conviction, capping the maximum at six months per count. The Crown argued the fit sentence should be determined independently, then limited by that procedural maximum.
rule: Section 718.1 requires proportionality to the gravity of the offence and the offender's responsibility. R. v. Cheddesingh, 2004 SCC 16, holds a maximum sentence need not be reserved for the worst offender. R. v. Solowan, 2008 SCC 62, holds a fit sentence for a summarily prosecuted hybrid offence is neither a function nor a fraction of what could have been imposed on indictment and should not be 'scaled down' from the summary maximum.
application: The Court accepted the Crown's position, concluding it must first determine the appropriate sentence under s. 718.1 and then apply the procedural limitation truncating that sentence. The fit sentence per count (18 months) far exceeded the summary maximum, so the six-month cap applied.
conclusion: The court determines the fit sentence first and then applies the six-month summary procedural cap per count.

issue: Should the two counts of wilful promotion of hatred be served concurrently or consecutively?
facts: Over three years, YWN promoted hatred against two distinct identifiable groups—women and Jews—through many issues, not a single incident. Defence argued the hate publication was 'one continuous transaction' warranting concurrent sentences.
rule: R. v. Grummer, 1983 CanLII 5286 (ON CA): although offences from the same transaction are normally concurrent, that rule does not apply where the offences invade different legally-protected interests.
application: Women and Jews have separate, legally-protected interests; the defendant could have promoted hatred against one and not the other but chose both, repeatedly over three years. Each group's interest was separately invaded.
conclusion: The sentences on the two counts are to be served consecutively.

issue: What is the fit sentence for James Sears, and may publication-restricting probation terms be imposed consistent with his Charter freedom of expression?
facts: Sears, in his mid-fifties, edited YWN over a lengthy period, reaching a purported readership over one million with an online presence, glorifying Nazism, denying the Holocaust, demonizing Jews and dehumanizing women. He authored post-trial editions continuing the same themes. The Crown sought the maximum plus three years' probation prohibiting publishing activities.
rule: Section 718.1 (proportionality); s. 718(2)(a)(ii) (hate-motivation as aggravating). Appellate guidance: R. v. Keegstra, 1996 ABCA 308 (one-year term appropriate) and R. v. Lelas (ONCA) (six months increased to one year for anti-Semitic vandalism). Probation terms must not unduly infringe the Charter right to freedom of expression.
application: Given circumstances far more serious than Lelas, the fit sentence was 18 months per count, but truncated to the six-month summary maximum per count, consecutive, totalling one year. The Court found the proposed publication ban too broad, infringing freedom of expression; Sears remains free to publish lawful content, risking re-charge only if he again promotes hate.
conclusion: Sears sentenced to one year (six months per count, consecutive); no probation imposed.

issue: What is the fit sentence for Leroy St. Germaine given the Gladue factors and his personal circumstances?
facts: St. Germaine, nearly 78 and in poor health, published YWN but did not create the hateful content authored under Sears's editorship. He is Metis, cooperated with police via a videotaped statement, expressed regret, and had a history of positive community work. Gladue report was unavailable; restorative justice proved unhelpful.
rule: Section 718.2(e) and R. v. Gladue, 1999 CanLII 679 (SCC): sanctions other than imprisonment reasonable in the circumstances should be considered, with particular attention to Aboriginal offenders. Section 742.1 conditional sentence preconditions; s. 718.1 proportionality.
application: Gladue factors (intergenerational trauma, institutional discrimination), cooperation, regret, age and ill health reduced his moral blameworthiness, though the gravity of the offence remained high. Denunciation and deterrence could be met by a conditional sentence with a punitive component; he posed no danger serving it at home.
conclusion: St. Germaine sentenced to a 12-month conditional sentence (six months per count, consecutive) served under house arrest with conditions; no probation.

issue: Should the action against the individual officers be struck out because officers are not personally liable for acts done within their authority on behalf of the corporation?
facts: Watson sued his former employer TrojanOne for constructive dismissal and also named its President/CEO Harrison and Chief Creative Officer Lee. The Statement of Claim alleged that over nine months the two officers subjected him to bullying, racially insensitive, homophobic and sexist remarks, a public physical/verbal altercation, and a poisoned work environment causing anxiety and depression. The officers moved to strike the claim against them personally.
rule: A corporation is a separate legal person; at common law officers are not liable for acts done within their authority on the corporation's behalf. Under the Rule in Said v. Butt, [1920] 3 K.B. 497, and Normart Management, ScotiaMcLeod and Schembri v. Way, an officer may nonetheless be personally liable where there is conduct on the officer's part that is tortious in itself or independent misconduct from that of the corporation; the pleading must specifically address the cause of action asserted against the officer. The elements of intentional infliction of mental distress (Piresferreira v. Ayote; Correia v. Canac Kitchens) are flagrant/outrageous conduct, intent or knowledge of harm, and a visible and provable illness.
application: Perell J. read the Statement of Claim as suing TrojanOne for breach of the employment contract, but suing Harrison and Lee not for inducing that breach but for their own conduct that was tortious in itself or independent misconduct. Although not named, all constituent elements of intentional infliction of mental distress were pleaded: flagrant and outrageous conduct, intent or knowledge of harm, and a resulting visible and provable illness (anxiety and depression requiring treatment). Independent wrongdoing by the officers was therefore alleged.
conclusion: The claim against Harrison and Lee disclosed independent actionable wrongdoing and should not be struck out; the motion to strike was dismissed.

issue: Are the defendants entitled to an order requiring the plaintiff to deliver further particulars?
facts: The defendants served a Demand for Particulars with roughly 100 questions, deemed the response inadequate, and continued to demand more, seeking, for example, all facts 'supportive' of specific allegations about Harrison's and Lee's own conduct.
rule: An order for particulars is discretionary and must be just (Fairbairn v. Sage). Particulars are normally ordered only if they are not within the demanding party's knowledge and are necessary to enable a response (Fairbairn; Physicians' Services Inc. v. Cass). The court takes a realistic, pragmatic approach (Ontario v. Rothmans Inc.), the standard is the same in simplified procedure (Big Green Property Services), and the motion usually fails unless supported by an affidavit that particulars are not known and are needed to plead, unless the allegations are so bald that particulars are obviously necessary (Steiner v. Lindzon).
application: The defendants filed no affidavit deposing that they needed the particulars to plead, and since the allegations concerned the conduct of Harrison and Lee themselves, they could not claim the facts were outside their own knowledge. Most demands sought facts supportive of allegations, which are matters for examinations for discovery, not proper demands for particulars. The objection that the claim exceeded the monetary limit for simplified procedure was answered by Rule 76 and had no bearing on the motion.
conclusion: The defendants failed to make out a case for particulars; the demand for particulars was dismissed.

issue: What is the governing default rule for documentary discovery under the amended Rules of Civil Procedure — 'broad and liberal' relevancy or proportionality?
facts: The action was commenced under the simplified procedure (Rule 76) for an apology and damages capped at $50,000, yet one of ten defendants delivered a 145-paragraph defence and moved for an extensive forensic analysis of the plaintiff's hard drive, raising the question of what discovery is proportionate.
rule: Rule 1.04(1.1) requires orders proportionate to the importance and complexity of the issues and the amount involved; Rules 29.1 (discovery plan), 29.2 (proportionality in discovery) and 29.2.03 set out the considerations; the Master adopted the eight-factor proportionality test from Rowe Entertainment, Inc. v. William Morris Agency, Inc. (S.D.N.Y. 2002) supplementing U.S. Federal Rule 26(b)(2)(C), and endorsed the Sedona Canada Principles and the analysis of Netzorg and Kern.
application: The Master held that the amendment from documents 'relating to' to those 'relevant to' a matter in issue signalled the abandonment of 'broad and liberal' discovery. Proportionality must be the starting point, not an afterthought, with relevancy remaining only a threshold requirement rather than a licence to unlimited production. He applied the eight Rowe factors and the Rule 29.2.03 considerations to the request.
conclusion: The default rule of discovery is proportionality; the 'broad and liberal' standard is abandoned, so that relevancy is part of, but not the starting point of, the test for permissible discovery.

issue: Is a defamation defendant who pleads justification entitled to production of a mirror image of the plaintiff's computer hard drive?
facts: Levant sought a mirror image of Warman's personal computer hard drive (or examination by an expert) to test his theory that Warman authored the 'Hateful Posting' and used false personas; Warman produced an expert report stating his computer was not on when the posting was made and denied authorship.
rule: A 'document' includes electronic data (Rule 1.03, Rule 30.01(1)(a); s. 31.8 Canada Evidence Act). Case law (Nicolardi v. Daley; Vector Transportation v. Traffic Tech; Northwest Mettech; Innovative Health Group v. Calgary Health Region) requires convincing evidence of a real likelihood of undisclosed relevant documents before a hard-drive inspection; a mirror image is generally not producible, and any examination must be tightly circumscribed to protect irrelevant/private data.
application: Applying proportionality and the Rowe factors, and mindful that the plaintiff had deliberately limited his claim to a simplified, economical proceeding and that Levant appeared to seek the data for collateral uses, the Master refused sweeping access. He allowed only very limited, defined searches (specified personas, IP addresses, related metadata) of a mirror image by an independent, mutually acceptable expert bound by a non-disclosure agreement and Form 53 undertaking, with Levant to fund the expert initially.
conclusion: No mirror-image production or broad access was granted; only a narrowly circumscribed forensic examination of very limited areas of the hard drive by an independent expert was ordered.

issue: To what extent may a defamation defendant use discovery to support justification or to establish the plaintiff's bad character in mitigation?
facts: Levant pleaded a broad justification with detailed particulars and sought documents about Warman's false personas and reputation, arguing his knowledge of Warman's conduct predated the pleading; Warman argued this was a fishing expedition to found new defences and attack his character.
rule: Longstanding defamation-discovery limits (Care Canada v. CBC; I.B.E.W. v. Pacific Newspaper Group; Kent v. Kehoe; Pizza Pizza v. Toronto Star adopting Polly Peck; Scott v. Sampson; Di Poce v. Simpson; Cameron v. Pacific Press; Brown, The Law of Defamation): a defendant pleading justification bears the onus to prove substantial truth, may not use discovery to find a defence unknown at pleading, cannot justify by proof of other reprehensible conduct, and in mitigation may adduce only general bad-reputation evidence, not specific acts of misconduct; the court retains discretion to protect the plaintiff from oppression.
application: The Master declined to treat a broad, generalized plea of justification with particulars as equivalent to a properly particularized specific defence, refusing to let a party 'pry open Pandora's box (or hard drive)' through mitigation-based pleading. Documents concerning Warman's other complaints, litigation threats, employment, funding, and reputation were held irrelevant or of marginal relevance, and most requests were answered as 'no such documents' or requiring no further response.
conclusion: A defendant is not entitled to sweeping discovery by virtue of a broad, generalized plea of justification; discovery was confined to material relevant to whether Warman authored the posting, and character/mitigation-based requests were refused.

issue: Was the infant A.D.Y. a child in need of protection under s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
facts: A.D.Y. was apprehended three days after birth. The mother, T.Y., had a lengthy history of aligning herself with physically and emotionally abusive men (M.S., L.B., E.P.), was assaulted by her co-tenant E.P. days after the baby's apprehension, made unverifiable claims about previously deceased twins, refused a fresh psychiatric assessment initially, and had a very weak personal support system. Dr. Sudermann's parenting capacity assessment found no strong attachment, poor conflict-resolution patterns, and a real risk the child would be exposed to unsafe or problematic people.
rule: Section 37(2) CFSA defines a child in need of protection to include a child who has suffered or is at risk of physical harm, or is at risk of emotional harm, resulting from the parent's failure to care for, supervise or protect the child, or pattern of neglect. Risk of harm must be real and not speculative (Jewish Family and Child Service of Toronto v. R.K., 2008 ONCJ 774, aff'd 2009 ONCA 903; Children's Aid Society of Ottawa-Carlton v. T. and T.). A pervasive pattern of exposing a child to domestic abuse is sufficient. Expert evidence may support a finding of risk of emotional harm (N.V.C. v. CCAS of Toronto, 2017 ONSC 796).
application: Relying on Dr. Sudermann's assessment, the court found the risk of harm to A.D.Y. was real and not speculative. The mother's demonstrated pattern of forming relationships with violent, unpredictable men exposed the child to a real risk of physical harm, and her instability, poor judgment and absence of a stable support network created a risk of emotional harm. The court found strong similarities to Jewish Family and Child Service v. R.K.
conclusion: A.D.Y. was found to be a child in need of protection.

issue: May the court consider post-apprehension evidence on the protection (finding) phase of a child protection hearing?
facts: Much of the evidence supporting protection concerns arose after the apprehension, including the E.P. assault days after the baby was taken and the mother's continued conduct during access and parenting programs. Counsel objected to certain hearsay paragraphs in the social worker's affidavit.
rule: Following Children's Aid Society of Hamilton-Wentworth v. K.R. and C.W., [2001] O.J. No. 5754, and the reasoning approved in Children's Aid Society of Brant v. J.A.T., 2005 ONCJ 302 and Catholic Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto v. C.M., [1994] 2 S.C.R. 165, the relevant time period for facts on a finding of protection is flexible; only facts related solely to disposition are statutorily excluded. The child-centred, best-interests purpose of the Act supports admitting accurate, updated information.
application: The court adopted the flexible approach, permitting post-apprehension evidence to be assessed alongside pre-apprehension evidence. Hearsay paragraphs in the affidavit were admitted for the limited purpose of showing the statements were made and formed the basis for the Society's investigation and action.
conclusion: Post-apprehension evidence was properly admissible on the protection phase and was considered in reaching the finding.

issue: Was a supervision order returning the child to the mother adequate, or was a s. 57.1 custody order to the father and paternal grandparents warranted?
facts: The Society, joined by the father J.M.1, sought a s. 57.1 custody order placing A.D.Y. with J.M.1 and his parents. The child had thrived in the paternal family's care since July 2016. The mother had shown inconsistent parenting, resisted coaching, and had a weak support system; Dr. Sudermann remained guarded about her prognosis. J.M.1, though diagnosed with stable long-term schizophrenia, was stable, medication-free, symptom-free and provided attentive care with grandparental support.
rule: Section 57(3) CFSA requires the least disruptive alternative; the court must not remove a child unless satisfied less disruptive alternatives would be inadequate. Per Windsor-Essex CAS v. T.B., [2012] O.J. No. 4481, a s. 57.1 custody order may not be considered until the court is satisfied that leaving the child with the pre-intervention caregiver under supervision would be inadequate. Principles of fundamental justice apply (New Brunswick (Minister of Health) v. G.(J.), 1999 SCC), and courts must avoid imposing middle-class standards (Re Brown; CAS of Hamilton v. E.O., 2009 CanLII 72087).
application: The court found a supervision order returning A.D.Y. to T.Y. inadequate because her impulsivity and poor judgment could result in quick, sudden risk to the child leaving no time for Society intervention, and because supervision depends on willing acceptance of monitoring which T.Y. resisted. Having found supervision inadequate, the court proceeded to the custody request and found joint custody with J.M.1 and grandparents best met A.D.Y.'s needs, ensuring continuity, safeguarding his settled family placement and obviating the risks identified by Dr. Sudermann.
conclusion: A supervision order was rejected; a s. 57.1 order placing A.D.Y. in the joint custody of J.M.1, J.M.2 and B.M. was made in the child's best interests.

issue: What access order to the mother was in the child's best interests?
facts: There was significant antipathy between T.Y. and the grandparents, who wished to avoid contact with her. T.Y. lived in London while the paternal family lived in Woodstock; she was willing to bus to Woodstock and stay with W.E. Dr. Sudermann recommended supervised, biweekly access at the Merrymount facility, cautioning against overnight/weekend access and over-frequent exchanges.
rule: Section 58(1) CFSA authorizes an access order with conditions following disposition; the test is the child's best interests (Children's Aid Society of Haldimand & Norfolk v. D.(R.), 2011 ONSC 4857).
application: Adopting Dr. Sudermann's recommendations and weighing the parties' commitments, the antipathy between T.Y. and the grandparents, and the distance between cities, the court ordered supervised biweekly access for three hours at the Woodstock Merrymount centre (or Oxford CAS), with costs shared, and endorsed a gradual relaxation of supervision over time upon successful visits.
conclusion: T.Y. was granted supervised biweekly access of three hours, with conditions and provision for future relaxation of supervision in the child's best interests.

issue: Do the defendant's acts constitute civil faults and unlawful interference with the plaintiff's rights under the Civil Code and Quebec Charter?
