conclusion: The court overturned the 'no access' order and substituted a contact order in favour of the mother, the father and the child, though it stayed enforcement pending an openness hearing.

issue: How could the conflict between s. 59(2.1) and s. 37 of the CFSA be resolved?
facts: The child wanted both contact with her parents and adoption by M., but M. stated unequivocally she would not adopt if any access/openness order were made, effectively creating a 'veto' under s. 59(2.1)(b).
rule: Sections 59(2.1) and 37 (best interests) of the CFSA, read with the openness/adoption provisions ss. 141–146, including s. 145.1.1(2) notice of intention to place and s. 145.1.2(1) applications for an openness order.
application: Finding the legislation internally inconsistent with no priority between the sections, the court adopted the 'Pathway Plan' proposed by counsel: by granting each of the mother, father and child a contact order, each becomes entitled to notice of the intended adoption placement and may apply for an openness hearing, allowing best interests to be reconciled through the openness process while M. retains her position. The court made the contact order but stayed it pending an openness application, seizing itself of that hearing under its dual UFC jurisdiction.
conclusion: The court acceded to the Pathway Plan, granted staying contact orders, and directed a four-day openness hearing to commence May 15, 2017, with detailed procedural directions and a costs process to follow.

issue: Do the plaintiffs have standing to seek an oppression remedy when they were not shareholders or appropriate persons when the alleged oppression occurred?
facts: Mr. Hong never personally held EPL shares; 253 Ont. Ltd. was not incorporated until September 2016 and became a shareholder only in September 2017. The alleged oppressive conduct (failure to enforce a confidentiality agreement, giving competitors an advantage in the 2016 proxy battle) occurred in July–August 2016, before 253 Ont. Ltd. held shares.
rule: Under s. 227(2) of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, only a shareholder (including a beneficial owner and 'any other person whom the court considers to be an appropriate person') may seek an oppression remedy. Oppression protects wrongs suffered qua shareholder (Yen v. Ghahramani, 2023 BCCA 403; Dubois v. Milne, 2020 BCCA 216), reasonable expectations are assessed at the time shares were acquired (Ford Motor; Hollinger), and harm to the company as a whole must be pursued derivatively under s. 232 (Tassone v. Smith; Pasnak v. Chura).
application: The reasonable expectations alleged pre-dated 253 Ont. Ltd.'s acquisition of shares, so it had no standing as a shareholder. Ninth Square Capital did not assist because there the claimant was a beneficial shareholder under a binding contract, unlike the plaintiffs. The asserted 'continuing' oppression was unpleaded and, in any event, alleged share-value diminution is a derivative harm. As an unsuccessful bidder for control, Mr. Hong did not fall within the narrow class of 'appropriate persons', and the plaintiffs offered no substantive answer despite notice.
conclusion: The plaintiffs lack standing; the oppression claim raises no genuine issue for trial and was struck under R. 9-6, a defect that cannot be cured by amendment.

issue: Do the conspiracy pleadings raise a genuine issue for trial?
facts: The plaintiffs alleged that Horizon, Ka An and EPL's officers acted in concert to acquire control of EPL and that Horizon breached a January 2016 confidentiality agreement, unfairly defeating Mr. Hong in the proxy battle. Ka An was not a party to the agreement, which did not prohibit acquiring EPL shares and permitted purchases from named entities (Invesco, Harrington), from whom Ka An acquired shares.
rule: The elements of unlawful act conspiracy are combination, an unlawful act, conduct directed at the plaintiff, knowledge of likely injury, and resulting injury (LeRoy v. Timberwest, 2021 BCCA 326). Conspiracy must be pleaded with heightened precision and full particulars (H.M.B. Holdings, 2021 BCCA 142; Gong v. O'Neill). On R. 9-6 the defendant must show beyond a reasonable doubt the plaintiff is bound to lose (Beach Estate v. Beach, 2019 BCCA 277).
application: The pleadings offered only a bald conclusory assertion that conduct was directed at Mr. Hong, with no material facts. More fundamentally, the confidentiality agreement did not prohibit share acquisition and Ka An was not a party, so no unlawful act was made out. The court declined, however, to strike on the privity ground alone, finding the law on whether breach of a third-party contract can constitute unlawful means (Latifi; XY, LLC) insufficiently settled.
conclusion: The conspiracy claim raises no genuine issue for trial and was struck under R. 9-6 (and, being bound to fail, also under R. 9-5(1)(a)).

issue: Is the alleged loss non-recoverable pure economic loss?
facts: The plaintiffs claimed loss of the opportunity to acquire a controlling interest in EPL, allegedly caused by misuse of confidential information; Mr. Hong conceded 253 Ont. Ltd.'s loss arose from diminution in share value after it became a shareholder.
rule: There is no general right in tort protecting against negligent or intentional infliction of pure economic loss; loss from ordinary marketplace competition is damnum absque injuria (1688782 Ontario Inc. v. Maple Leaf Foods, 2020 SCC 35; A.I. Enterprises v. Bram). Recovery is confined to recognized categories (negligent misrepresentation/service, shoddy goods/structures, relational loss), and courts are reluctant to extend tort protection to failed commercial negotiations (Martel Building v. Canada, 2000 SCC 60).
application: The loss of opportunity to control EPL is pure economic loss; Mr. Hong had no right to acquire control and the pleadings disclosed no facts showing the loss arose from anything other than market competition. The claim fell within none of the recognized categories and the plaintiffs advanced no policy basis for a new one.
conclusion: The alleged losses are non-compensable pure economic loss, reinforcing that the claim is bound to fail.

issue: Does reviving the withdrawn Union Goal allegations constitute an abuse of process?
facts: By a June 2021 consent order (deemed adjudged on the merits) the Union Goal allegations were removed from the Oppression Action; leave to bring a derivative action over the Union Goal Transaction had earlier been denied (2019 BCSC 1446, aff'd 2020 BCCA 313). Mr. Hong nonetheless re-asserted the Union Goal Transaction in his response materials, and Ms. Hu's role in that transaction is being litigated in the ongoing Ren Derivative Action.
rule: Relitigation may be an abuse of process where the prior decision is final, the second proceeding seeks to relitigate a decided issue, and relitigation would impugn the finality and integrity of the earlier judgment (Skender v. Farley, 2007 BCCA 629; Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., 2003 SCC 63). Courts have inherent jurisdiction to prevent abuse and protect judicial economy, consistency and finality.
application: Reviving the Union Goal allegations circumvented the consent order and was an 'end run' around the Smith Decision denying leave (cf. Daum v. Gorrell). It would also duplicate the Ren Derivative Action. Despite an opportunity to withdraw them, Mr. Hong did not, supporting an inference the conduct was intended to vex the defendants and continue his retribution campaign.
conclusion: Raising the Union Goal Transaction in response to the strike motions was an abuse of the court's process.

issue: Are the Great Wall Proceedings in substance a derivative claim requiring leave, and are they vexatious and an abuse of process?
facts: 253 Ont. Ltd. framed the Great Wall matter as an oppression claim after EPL, on advice, declined to sue over the 2022 Great Wall transactions and after Mr. Hong had threatened a derivative action. The pleadings alleged share-price depreciation, diversion of assets, and failure to disclose related-party transactions, repeating the proxy-battle and Union Goal allegations. Mr. Hong admitted he chose oppression to avoid the cost of counsel and the 'uphill battle' of the good-faith leave requirement.
rule: A shareholder seeking oppression must show particular prejudice beyond diminution in share value (1043325 Ontario Ltd. v. CSA, 2016 BCCA 258); harm to the company generally must be pursued by derivative action with leave under s. 232 (Pasnak; Robak Industries v. Gardner, 2007 BCCA 61; Foss v. Harbottle). Directors owe fiduciary duties to the company, not shareholders, absent a special relationship (BCE Inc., 2008 SCC 69; Yen). Pleadings may be struck under R. 9-5(1)(a)–(d) where they disclose no reasonable claim, are vexatious, or are an abuse of process.
application: The harms alleged—loss of share value, Ka An's increased shareholding, non-disclosure—were suffered by EPL and shareholders generally, not uniquely by 253 Ont. Ltd.; the corporate-opportunity claim failed because Ka An was not pleaded as a majority shareholder on adequate facts. The claim was therefore derivative and required leave. The conspiracy, fiduciary and negligence claims rested on the same corporate loss and bald allegations. The repetition of failed allegations, the improper choice of oppression to avoid leave, and threats to sue advising law firms established a vexatious, retributive proceeding.
conclusion: The Great Wall Action and Petition disclose no reasonable oppression claim, are derivative claims requiring leave, and were struck in their entirety as vexatious and an abuse of process.

issue: Are the impugned provisions void for vagueness or overbreadth?
facts: Pawlowski, leader of Street Church Ministries, was ticketed for placing 'material' on a street, operating an 'amplification system' in a park, causing 'loud and unnecessary noise' from a motor vehicle, and 'stunting' while ministering to homeless and impoverished people in downtown Calgary in 2007.
rule: A law must be sufficiently precise to give fair notice and to constrain enforcement discretion; overbreadth and vagueness offend s. 7 and may prevent a provision from being a 'limit prescribed by law' (R. v. Heywood; Prostitution Reference; Osborne v. Canada; R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical). A law is void for vagueness only where it fails to provide an 'intelligible standard' or 'sufficient guidance for legal debate'; 'stunting' had been judicially narrowed in R. v. Jones and R. v. Tremblay.
application: The Street Bylaw definition of 'material' ('any object or article') was so broad it could capture a shoe sole or briefcase, providing no intelligible standard. 'Unnecessary' noise in s. 82 of the Regulation gave no intelligible standard and was overbroad, especially applied to a parked vehicle used only as a speaker stand. By contrast, 'amplification system' in the Parks Bylaw gave adequate notice (the accused had previously held permits), and 'stunting', as interpreted in Jones, provided a workable standard.
conclusion: 'Material on a street' and 'loud and unnecessary noise' were unconstitutionally vague/overbroad; the amplification-in-a-park and 'stunting' provisions were not.

issue: Did enforcement infringe the accused's freedom of religion under s. 2(a)?
facts: Pawlowski sincerely believed his ministry — preaching with amplified sound and distributing food to the poor — was a religious obligation drawn from his personal reading of the Bible, and the tickets interfered with these activities.
rule: An s. 2(a) infringement is established where the claimant sincerely believes in a practice with a nexus to religion and the impugned measure interferes in a more than trivial or insubstantial way (Alberta v. Hutterian Brethren; Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem; Multani). The court assesses sincerity, not validity or mandatory nature.
application: The Court accepted the accused's sincere belief that using amplified sound and feeding congregants had a nexus with his faith. Enforcement of the City bylaws (permit requirements, ticketing while saying grace) more than trivially interfered with his religious practice. The provincial provisions (noise/stunting) had only an indirect, trivial effect and, given the Jones interpretation of 'stunting', the accused conceded no s. 2(a) breach arose from that charge.
conclusion: The City bylaw provisions infringed s. 2(a); the provincial provisions did not.

issue: Did enforcement infringe freedom of expression under s. 2(b)?
facts: The accused's amplified preaching, banners, and a cross conveyed religious and political meaning; all charges arose from activity on public parks, streets and sidewalks.
rule: Activity that attempts to convey meaning is protected unless violent in form (Irwin Toy). Expression on government property is protected only where the form is compatible with the principal function of the place (Committee for the Commonwealth of Canada v. Canada).
application: The accused's activity conveyed meaning tied to social and political participation. On the sidewalks pedestrian flow was not significantly impeded, so his expression was compatible with the space; Triangle Park had ceased to function as a general-public space (dominated by drug activity), so amplified preaching was not incompatible with its function. The noise provision infringed expression through overbreadth; properly interpreted 'stunting' did not affect expression.
conclusion: The Street Bylaw, Parks Bylaw and the noise Regulation infringed s. 2(b); the 'stunting' provision did not.

issue: Could the infringing provisions be saved under s. 1?
facts: The City relied on interests in safe, accessible streets and parks and reducing noise; a permit regime existed but the City had refused to accept the accused's permit applications and applied no clear standards.
rule: R. v. Oakes: the limit must serve a pressing and substantial objective and be proportionate (rational connection, minimal impairment, and net proportionality); the state bears the burden on a balance of probabilities.
application: Although the objectives were pressing and substantial and rationally connected, the vague/overbroad 'material' and 'unnecessary noise' provisions were not minimal impairments. The Parks Bylaw permit scheme became arbitrary once the City applied no known criteria and refused to consider the accused's applications, so it failed minimal impairment; deleterious effects outweighed benefits.
conclusion: None of the infringing provisions was saved by s. 1; each was of no force or effect in these circumstances.

issue: Did the officials' conduct amount to an abuse of process?
facts: Enforcement escalated from noise complaints (for which the accused was never charged) to numerous tickets and an increasing officer presence, culminating in the City refusing even to accept the accused's permit applications.
rule: Abuse of process (R. v. Scott; R. v. O'Connor) permits a stay only in the 'clearest of cases' where proceedings are oppressive/vexatious and offend the community's sense of fair play and the integrity of the justice system.
application: The Court found the accused acted in good faith to comply while continuing his ministry, and that the City's intransigence, including refusing his applications, fell 'precariously close' to an abuse of power, but did not reach the 'clearest of cases' threshold.
conclusion: Abusive conduct was found but did not warrant a stay; it could bear on penalty if the accused were convicted.

issue: Was the accused guilty of 'stunting' beyond a reasonable doubt?
facts: On June 18, 2007 the accused preached with an amplified public-address system and a cross at a street corner; the officer testified drivers slowed but no photograph showed distraction, and the Court rejected the claim of danger or distraction.
rule: Section 115(2)(e) of the Traffic Safety Act, interpreted in R. v. Jones/Tremblay, requires a 'stunt' or other activity likely to distract, startle or interfere with highway users — more than merely attracting attention.
application: The accused's conduct was not a 'stunt', and the Court rejected the officer's evidence that drivers were distracted or endangered, finding such a gathering unlikely to distract, startle or interfere with users of the highway.
conclusion: The Crown failed to prove an essential element; the accused was found not guilty of stunting.

issue: Did the Commission exceed its jurisdiction by taking into account the tradition and role of denominational hospitals in Ontario?
facts: The Commission ordered the closure of the non-denominational Pembroke Civic Hospital and the restructuring of the Pembroke General Hospital, a Roman Catholic institution operated by the Grey Sisters. Of 209 Ontario public hospitals, 32 are denominationally owned. The applicant argued the Commission wrongly considered preservation of denominational health care.
rule: Under ss. 6 and 9(10) of the Public Hospitals Act, the Ministry of Health Act and O. Regs. 87/96 and 88/96, the Commission stands in the Minister's shoes with virtually unfettered powers, with no right of appeal to the court. On the political/judicial spectrum it sits near the political/legislative extreme (Knight v. Indian Head School Division No. 19; Whitley v. United States). The court reviews only whether the Commission acted according to law, not the wisdom of its decisions.
application: The Commission was required to consider the public interest in local health systems, including the appropriate role of denominational providers. Considering representations from the Roman Catholic Health Association and accepting a role for Roman Catholic hospitals was a policy decision within the widest area of non-reviewable discretion. Ontario's long tradition of denominational hospital governance was a reality the Commission was entitled to weigh.
conclusion: The Commission did not exceed its jurisdiction by considering denominational health care; the jurisdictional argument failed.

issue: Did the Commission deny the applicant procedural fairness in disclosure, notice of the case to meet, its consultations, or through prejudgment or bias?
facts: The Commission invited public and group submissions but refused to produce lists and copies of all submissions. The applicant said it was not told the case to meet, that a parallel undisclosed process with Roman Catholic interests existed, and that the Commission prejudged and was biased (relying partly on staff drafts and the executive director's statement that the Commission did not analyze the by-laws).
rule: The content of fairness depends on the nature of the body. A policy-making and implementation body is not an adversarial forum and need not adopt court procedures of discovery and production; it must give affected parties a fair opportunity to make their views known. The 'case to meet' principle (Webb, Nicholson, Downing, Consolidated Bathurst) applies fully to adversarial lites but far less to complex polycentric decisions.
application: The Commission's December 3, 1996 notice expressly set out the option of sole governance by the Grey Sisters with the Civic directed to close, clearly disclosing the case to meet. The Civic engaged repeatedly and in a face-to-face meeting with the very denominational-governance issues it now raised, so there were no undisclosed 'new grounds.' Consultation with the Roman Catholic Health Association was the Commission's duty and was proper. Staff discussion drafts did not evidence a closed mind; the Commission rejected the General's governance proposal and required a representative board, showing an open mind. The by-law point disclosed no bias.
conclusion: There was no procedural unfairness, prejudgment, bias or wrongful exercise of discretion; these grounds failed.

issue: Were the Charter challenges under ss. 2(a), 7 and 15 premature and unsupported by evidence?
facts: The applicant alleged the restructuring would infringe freedom of conscience and religion, security of the person and equality, focusing on health services involving sexuality, reproduction and abortion, and on the presence of crosses/crucifixes and a requirement that elected board candidates respect the hospital's values. No present infringement was alleged.
rule: A Charter challenge is generally to be brought when there is an actual infringement, not on speculation of future infringement; standing of a corporation and of a person without a demonstrated need for the services is doubtful. To succeed on adverse-effect claims a claimant must prove the alleged effects will occur or are highly probable. Silent religious symbols do not compel religious practice and do not infringe s. 2(a).
application: The challenge was premature and speculative as no present infringement existed. On the merits, uncontradicted evidence (including Dr. Sharma, Chief of Obstetrics and Gynaecology) showed no religious interference in care; crosses and crucifixes did not coerce anyone; no abortions had been performed in Renfrew county for at least 14 years for reasons unrelated to the closure, so future availability effects were speculative; equality claims lacked any showing of disproportionate disadvantage to a disadvantaged group; and requiring board candidates to respect (not adhere to) the hospital's values infringed no Charter right.
conclusion: The Charter challenges were dismissed on prematurity and, in the alternative, for want of any evidentiary basis.

issue: Does the six-month summary-conviction ceiling function as the 'maximum sentence' to be reserved for the worst cases, or must the appropriate sentence be determined first and the procedural cap applied afterward?
facts: Wilful promotion of hatred under s. 319(2) is a hybrid offence; the Crown elected to proceed summarily, so the statutory maximum was six months per count. The Crown argued this procedural maximum is not the 'maximum sentence' engaged when weighing all sentencing factors.
rule: Under s. 718.1 of the Criminal Code the fundamental principle is proportionality to gravity of the offence and degree of responsibility. R. v. Cheddesingh, 2004 SCC 16, rejects reserving the maximum only for the worst offender/worst offence. R. v. Solowan, 2008 SCC 62, holds a fit sentence for a hybrid offence prosecuted summarily is neither a function nor fraction of what could have been imposed on indictment and must not be scaled down.
application: The court held it must first determine the appropriate sentence on ordinary sentencing principles and only then apply any procedural limitation that would truncate that sentence, rather than treating the six-month summary cap as a benchmark to be discounted.
conclusion: The court determined the fit sentence independently, then applied the six-month procedural maximum per count.

issue: Should the two counts of promoting hatred (against women and against Jews) be served consecutively or concurrently?
facts: Over three years YWN promoted hatred against both Jews and women through many issues; the defence argued the publication was 'one continuous transaction' warranting concurrent sentences.
rule: R. v. Grummer, 1983 CanLII 5286 (ON CA): offences from the same transaction are normally concurrent, but that rule does not apply where the offences invade different legally-protected interests.
application: Women and Jews are identifiable groups with separate, legally-protected interests; the defendant could have promoted hatred against one and not the other but chose both, repeatedly and consistently over three years, through many incidents rather than one.
conclusion: The sentences on the two counts are to be served consecutively.

issue: What is the fit sentence for wilful promotion of hatred in these circumstances?
facts: Sears, in his mid-fifties, edited YWN, a publication with a purported readership over one million and an online presence, glorifying Nazism and Hitler, denying the Holocaust, demonizing Jews, and dehumanizing women while counselling violence against them. A Winter 2019 issue continued these themes after trial. He had 1992 sexual-assault convictions (not appearing on his CPIC record) given little weight. Seven community impact statements were tendered.
rule: s. 718.1 (proportionality); s. 718(2)(a)(ii) (hate motivation as aggravating); s. 722.2 (community impact statements); R. v. Keegstra, 1996 ABCA 308 (one-year appropriate for anti-Semitic hate-mongering by a teacher); R. v. Lelas (ON CA 1990) (one year for anti-Semitic vandalism).
application: Aggravating factors included the vast breadth and online reach of the material and its continuation after trial; the 1992 convictions were given little weight. The community impact statements complied with s. 722.2 and reflected real harm, though harm to the community was in any event universal and obvious. Compared to Lelas (one year in 1990) and Keegstra, Sears's conduct was significantly more serious, warranting at least 18 months on each count. The procedural maximum, however, capped each count at six months.
conclusion: The fit sentence was 18 months per count, but limited by the six-month procedural maximum, served consecutively, for a total of one year's incarceration.

issue: Should probation with terms restricting the defendant's publishing be imposed?
facts: The Crown sought three years' probation prohibiting all publishing, including editing or publishing YWN, to reduce recidivism. The defence argued this infringed the Charter right to freedom of expression.
rule: Charter freedom of expression; probation terms must not unduly curtail lawful expression.
application: The court agreed the proposed prohibitions were far too broad. Sears remains free to publish whatever he wishes, even if unpopular or objectionable, so long as it does not offend the Criminal Code; if he again promotes hatred he risks re-prosecution.
conclusion: No probation was imposed.

issue: Would the proposed amendments permitting marriage commissioners to decline to solemnize marriages contrary to their religious beliefs infringe s. 15(1) equality rights based on sexual orientation?
facts: Following recognition of same-sex marriage, some Saskatchewan marriage commissioners refused to solemnize same-sex unions on religious grounds. The Lieutenant Governor in Council referred two possible amendments to the Court: a 'Grandfathering Option' (for commissioners appointed on or before November 5, 2004) and a 'Comprehensive Option' (all commissioners). Marriage commissioners are public officials and the only route to a non-religious civil marriage, which many same-sex couples must rely on since many faiths will not marry them.
rule: Section 15(1) of the Charter guarantees equal protection and benefit of the law without discrimination. Per Andrews, Kapp and Ermineskin, a claimant must show (1) a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground, and (2) that the distinction creates a disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping. Sexual orientation is an analogous ground (Vriend, Hislop). A facially neutral law can violate s. 15(1) by its effects (Andrews, Eldridge).
application: Neither Option's purpose was to deny rights, but their effect would be to allow commissioners to refuse same-sex couples, drawing a negative distinction on the analogous ground of sexual orientation. The majority rejected the 'someone else will help you' argument, analogizing to refusing service to a person because they are Black, First Nations or Jewish, and noted the significant personal hurt, geographic obstacles, and risk that many commissioners would opt out. Given the historical marginalization of gays and lesbians (Egan), the distinction perpetuated disadvantage and stereotyping.
conclusion: Both Options would, by their effect, create a discriminatory distinction based on sexual orientation contrary to s. 15(1).

issue: Can the s. 15(1) infringement be justified under s. 1, balanced against the marriage commissioners' s. 2(a) freedom of religion?
facts: Compelling commissioners to solemnize same-sex marriages engages the sincerely held religious beliefs of at least some commissioners (s. 2(a)). The amendments were aimed at accommodating those beliefs. During argument the Court raised a 'single entry point' system as a less restrictive alternative, which counsel conceded was less restrictive and operates in Ontario.
rule: Section 1 permits reasonable limits demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society, assessed under R. v. Oakes: (1) a pressing and substantial objective, and (2) proportionality — rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality between salutary and deleterious effects. Charter rights are reconciled at s. 1, with no hierarchy of rights (Dagenais). Freedom of religion is broadly defined (Big M, Amselem) but is not absolute.
application: The majority accepted accommodating commissioners' s. 2(a) freedoms as a pressing and substantial objective and found rational connection, but held the Options failed minimal impairment because a 'single entry point' system could accommodate beliefs behind the scenes without any couple being refused. On final proportionality, the deleterious effects — perpetuating recently-overcome discrimination, genuine harm to same-sex couples, and undermining the principle that the state serves everyone equally — outweighed the limited salutary benefits, since the religious interest concerned acting on beliefs in public office rather than the core of religious freedom. Smith J.A. (concurring) would characterize the objective more narrowly and doubted it was pressing and substantial, stressing that the unprecedented notwithstanding clause would strip gays and lesbians of Human Rights Code protection.
conclusion: The infringement is not justified under s. 1. Both Options would be unconstitutional and of no force or effect.

issue: Is the identity of the employees who supplied the plaintiff with the non-solicitation policy and donor names relevant to a matter in issue under Rule 31.06?
facts: In a wrongful dismissal action against Jews for Jesus (JFJ), JFJ counterclaimed that the plaintiff solicited its donors after termination in breach of contractual and fiduciary duties. Two JFJ employees had emailed the plaintiff a copy of the non-solicitation policy and a list of donors the plaintiff had cultivated. JFJ moved to compel the plaintiff to identify those senders (discovery questions 695 and 893), relying on Rule 31.06(2).
rule: Rule 31.06(1) requires answers to any 'proper question relevant to any matter in issue'; the 2010 amendments replaced the 'semblance of relevance' test with a stricter simple relevance test (Justice Reform Project; Noble v. York University Foundation, 2010 ONSC 399; Brand Name Marketing v. Rogers Communications, 2010 ONSC 1159). Rule 31.06(2) permits disclosure of names of persons who might reasonably be expected to have knowledge of transactions or occurrences in issue. Pleadings determine relevance (Noble).
application: The Master held the new stricter relevance test applied. The transactions or occurrences in issue were the plaintiff's sending of solicitation letters to former JFJ donors and any resulting breach of duty — facts flowing from the plaintiff and documents held by the plaintiff and CPM. The senders of the policy and the donor names could not be expected to have knowledge of what the plaintiff did after receiving that material. Whether an employee independently breached a duty to JFJ was not an issue framed by the pleadings.
conclusion: The identity of the senders is not relevant to any matter in issue; questions 695 and 893 need not be answered.

issue: May identifying information be redacted from a produced relevant document where the information is irrelevant and disclosure could cause harm?
facts: The plaintiff produced (at Tab 13) the email enclosing the non-solicitation policy but redacted the sender's identity. The sender was a current JFJ employee; the plaintiff feared JFJ would discipline that employee for assisting him, and JFJ refused to give a written undertaking not to do so.
rule: The whole of a relevant document must ordinarily be produced and irrelevant portions cannot simply be redacted, except where clearly irrelevant material is of a nature giving good reason for non-disclosure and disclosure could cause considerable harm while serving no legitimate purpose in resolving the issues (McGee v. London Life, 2010 ONSC 1408; North American Trust v. Mercer International).
application: The identity of the policy sender was already found irrelevant; disclosing it would in no way help resolve the issues. There was a genuine risk of discipline of the employee, reinforced by JFJ's refusal to undertake not to discipline and its factum's stance. Although the deemed undertaking rule (30.1.01) offered some protection, that protection could cease if the evidence were filed or used at trial, or upon relief from the undertaking.
conclusion: The redacted identifying information may remain redacted; disclosure could cause considerable harm and serve no legitimate purpose.

issue: If relevant, would the Wigmore case-by-case privilege protect the informants' identities?
facts: The plaintiff sought to withhold the senders' identities on grounds of confidentiality, but filed no affidavit of his own establishing that the communications were made in confidence.
rule: There is no free-standing privilege for confidential information; the four-part Wigmore test (Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254) applies on a case-by-case basis, the first condition being that the communication originated in a confidence that it would not be disclosed (see Cadillac Fairview v. Standard Parking).
application: The plaintiff provided no evidence that either communication originated in confidence; a mere fear of reprisal is not evidence of confidentiality. Without proof of the essential first condition, the remaining conditions could not be assessed, though the Master noted that on the fourth condition disclosure would have little benefit to the litigation.
conclusion: Had the identities been relevant, the plaintiff failed to establish confidentiality under Wigmore; the point was academic given the relevance ruling.

issue: Did the moving parties establish a strong prima facie case on the merits of their counterclaims, including the personal liability of Mr. Glassman?
facts: West Face and Boland allege Catalyst and Glassman hired Black Cube and Psy Group to conduct covert 'sting' operations and defamation/harassment campaigns against them and against former Justice Newbould. Glassman created a handwritten 'Bonus Legend' offering up to US$11.5 million in success fees, and personally directed dissemination of false material. Glassman claimed he acted only as officer/director and that Tamara Global retained the operatives.
rule: A strong prima facie case is more stringent than a serious issue to be tried; the moving party must be 'clearly right and almost certain to succeed at trial' (Lee v. Chang, 2018 ONSC 930; Quizno's Canada Restaurant Corp., 2009 CanLII 20708). Officers/directors are shielded from personal liability for acts under a corporate name unless their conduct is itself tortious, fraudulent, deceitful or dishonest, exhibiting a separate identity or interest (ScotiaMcLeod Inc. v. People's Jewellers Ltd., 1995 CanLII 1301; Khursheed v. Benedig Capital; Guru Eak Transport).
application: The court found the Catalyst Parties' conduct 'despicable' and rooted in deceit. Glassman could not hide behind his corporate capacity because his direction of the false social-media campaign and creation of the Bonus Legend constituted independent tortious, deceitful and fraudulent activity, consistent with prior findings by Boswell J. and McEwen J. that he was the directing mind. The 'dollar for dollar' damages argument was rejected because the counterclaim pleaded conspiracy, breach of confidence, inducing breach of contract/fiduciary duty and unlawful means, not merely defamation, and no authority requires dollar-for-dollar proof.
conclusion: The West Face Parties established a strong prima facie case, including against Glassman personally. Mr. Langstaff, however, did not meet this threshold, his claim's prospects being less clear cut.

issue: Does the Mareva test require proof of intent to remove or dissipate assets to defeat creditors, and did the moving parties meet it?
facts: Glassman relocated to the Bahamas (property first purchased there in 2014, before litigation), listed his Ardwold Gate house on MLS in 2024, and Catalyst surrendered its OSC registration. However, Catalyst renewed its 181 Bay Street lease for five years in 2021, retains over US$1 billion in assets, and Boland admitted on cross-examination he could not identify any asset Catalyst had moved out of Ontario. Glassman retains a house and cottage in Ontario.
rule: The six-part Chitel v. Rothbart test governs (1982 CanLII 1956). On the removal/dissipation element, the majority in R. v. Consolidated Fastfrate Transport Inc. (1995 CanLII 1527) per Galligan J.A. holds the decisive question is the purpose of the arrangement: relief lies only where assets are arranged with intent to defeat creditors. Intent to put assets beyond reach is the 'sine qua non' (10390160 Canada Ltd. v. Casey, 2022 ONSC 628; RBC Dexia; Ghaeinizadeh; Di Menza; Aetna Financial Services Ltd. v. Feigelman, 1985 CanLII 55).
application: The court held the preponderance of authority, including recent cases, requires intent to defeat creditors. There was no evidence Catalyst had moved or intended to move assets; the lease renewal contradicted removal. Glassman's relocation reflected a longer-term plan predating the litigation, and substantial Ontario assets remained. The house had long been on the market and its MLS listing was not revelatory. The court refused to infer intent from Glassman's general bad character, which would lower the high threshold and encourage mudslinging. Ms. MacDonald's evidence about the cottage was contradicted by uncross-examined affidavits (e.g., Mr. Scully) and could not be relied on.
conclusion: The moving parties failed to show a real risk of removal or dissipation, and failed to show the requisite intent to defeat creditors; this element was not met.

issue: Did the moving parties establish irreparable harm and that the balance of convenience favoured the injunction?
facts: Expert evidence indicated Ontario judgments can generally be enforced in the Bahamas and Cayman Islands. The moving parties argued enforcement would be a 'whack-a-mole' exercise. Considerable Catalyst assets remain in Ontario; the moving parties sought to enjoin only $50 million of assets worth multiples of that.
rule: The need to pursue normal means to enforce a judgment abroad is not the type of irreparable harm contemplated for an interlocutory injunction (Khan v. Coloma, 2019 ONSC 7202); mere difficulty or expense enforcing outside Ontario does not entitle a party to Mareva relief absent a genuine risk of disappearance of assets (Aetna).
application: Because ample assets remain in Ontario to satisfy any judgment and there was no clear evidence of intent to shield assets, the difficulty of pursuing hypothetical foreign assets did not meet the stringent irreparable-harm threshold. Tying up Catalyst's assets pending judgment would inappropriately inconvenience the Catalyst Parties; the balance of convenience favoured the status quo.
conclusion: Irreparable harm was not established and the balance of convenience favoured the Catalyst Parties.

issue: Did the delay in bringing the motion defeat the claim for Mareva relief?
facts: An August 23, 2022 letter from West Face counsel already asserted the same risk that Glassman would have insufficient assets and referenced the house sale and asset removal. The motion was not delivered until March 1, 2024. The purported new triggers—the MLS listing and OSC deregistration—were either already known or independently explained (OSC surrender advised by counsel, unrelated to relocation).
rule: Mareva injunctions must be pursued with dispatch; delay may itself show the risk is not significant enough to warrant relief, and injunctions are not awarded to parties showing no sense of urgency (Original Traders Energy Ltd. (Re), 2024 ONSC 325, citing Sharpe, Injunctions and Specific Performance; Lee v. Chang, 2018 ONSC 2091).
application: The court found the same items and conduct relied on now were enumerated in the August 2022 letter; Boland confirmed he held the same view of the risk then. The purported new triggers were unpersuasive—the house-sale efforts were already known and the OSC surrender was explained by unchallenged evidence (Foster affidavit). The over-18-month delay with no compelling explanation was fatal.
conclusion: The lack of demonstrated urgency was a second significant, independent reason the motions failed.

issue: Did the tribunal reasonably characterize the students' request and the services/facilities customarily available to the public under s. 4 of the Alberta Human Rights Act?
facts: Two Sunni Muslim students sought to perform brief (5-10 minute) private prayers involving bowing and prostration during school hours. Webber Academy, a non-denominational private school, framed the request as one for 'prayer space' that it never customarily provided, while the complainants characterized it as being allowed to pray privately somewhere unobtrusive.
rule: Section 4 prohibits denying or discriminating in respect of services or facilities 'customarily available to the public.' Berg v. UBC, [1993] 2 SCR 353 and Moore v. British Columbia (Education), 2012 SCC 61 hold that the 'service' is education generally and includes incidental facilities providing meaningful access; discretion over incidental services cannot be exercised on prohibited grounds. Factual characterization is reviewed for reasonableness.
application: The tribunal reasonably found the students were not seeking dedicated prayer space but permission to pray privately for a few minutes in whatever unobtrusive location was available. Following Berg and Moore, the court held the relevant service was Webber Academy's non-denominational educational programs and supportive facilities that give meaningful access to education. Equating the service with the specific thing requested would render s. 4 meaningless (e.g., a school could refuse wheelchair access because it had never provided it).
conclusion: The tribunal correctly characterized both the request and the customarily available services; Webber Academy had no unfettered discretion to refuse in a discriminatory way.

issue: Did the tribunal correctly find prima facie discrimination based on sincerely held religious belief?
facts: The students testified their Sunni beliefs required prayer during school hours; Webber Academy relied on expert evidence (Dr. Ahmed) that majority Sunni schools permit delaying prayer while at school, and on alleged inconsistencies in the students' practices.
rule: The Moore test requires (a) a protected characteristic, (b) an adverse impact, and (c) that the characteristic was a factor in the impact. Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47 holds a claimant need only show sincerity of belief, not that the belief is objectively mandated by doctrine; courts do not arbitrate scriptural validity. The prima facie test is reviewed for correctness.
application: The tribunal reasonably found the students sincerely believed prayer at prescribed times was mandatory, supported by their evidence, their mothers, coreligionists, and their continued practice at another school. Following Amselem, expert evidence on doctrinal content was of limited relevance and did not defeat sincerity. Being barred from praying and refused re-enrollment was an adverse impact tied to religion, and the students were treated differently from those whose head coverings and facial hair were permitted contrary to school policy.
conclusion: The tribunal correctly identified and applied the Moore test; prima facie discrimination was established.

issue: Did Webber Academy establish under s. 11 that its no-overt-prayer standard was reasonable and justifiable?
facts: Webber Academy's unwritten evolving standard was 'no overt prayer or religious activities on school property,' asserted to foster a non-denominational, religion-free learning environment. It led no evidence of financial or logistical hardship.
rule: Section 11 deems no contravention where the respondent shows the standard was reasonable and justifiable. The Grismer test (BC (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles) v. BC (Council of Human Rights), [1999] 3 SCR 868) requires a rational connection, good faith, and that the standard is reasonably necessary in the sense that the respondent cannot accommodate without undue hardship. Reviewed for reasonableness.
application: The first two branches were conceded/uncontested. On the third, the tribunal reasonably found no undue hardship: the prayers were brief and private, staff had already easily facilitated them for over two weeks, other overt religious observances (turbans, facial hair) were permitted and even advertised, allowing two of 900 students to pray privately was insignificant to non-denominational identity, and Webber Academy had conducted no hardship assessment. Its promotional materials welcomed all faiths and did not signal exclusion of all religious expression.
conclusion: Webber Academy failed to justify the standard; the tribunal's finding of no undue hardship was reasonable.

issue: Were the tribunal's credibility findings on the pre-enrollment meeting and tour reasonable, and did any error affect the outcome or damages?
facts: There was sharply conflicting evidence: the mothers said Ms. Lever assured them prayer would not be a problem and pointed out a library spot; Ms. Lever testified she clearly refused, corroborated by Ms. Grenier.
rule: Reasons must display justification, transparency and intelligibility (Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9; Syncrude Canada Ltd v. Saunders, 2015 ABQB 237). Human rights are matters of public policy that cannot be waived (Etobicoke; Renaud; Dickason). A decision must fall within a range of acceptable outcomes; not every reasoning element must independently pass review.
application: The court found the tribunal unreasonably disregarded Ms. Grenier's corroborating evidence and gave unintelligible reasons for rejecting Ms. Lever's testimony. However, because s. 4 prohibits discrimination whether by denying or discriminating with respect to the service, even a clear pre-enrollment warning could not save Webber Academy, and rights could not be waived. On damages, the tribunal placed little weight on the pre-enrollment communications and focused on the compensatory effect on the students; the awards ($12,000 and $14,000) were within the acceptable range.
conclusion: Although the fact findings lacked transparency and intelligibility, this did not affect the finding of unlawful discrimination or the reasonableness of the damages awards.

issue: Does the omission of 'sexual orientation' from the prohibited grounds in the IRPA constitute governmental action drawing a distinction that violates s. 15(1) of the Charter?
facts: Delwin Vriend was dismissed from King's College in Edmonton in January 1991 after the College learned he was homosexual. His complaint to the Alberta Human Rights Commission was rejected because the IRPA does not list sexual orientation as a prohibited ground. He challenged the IRPA as under-inclusive and contrary to s. 15(1). After Egan v. Canada, sexual orientation was recognized as an analogous ground; the trial judge (Russell J.) held the IRPA infringed s. 15(1) and read the ground in.
rule: Section 15(1) of the Charter guarantees equality without discrimination on enumerated and analogous grounds; s. 32(1)(b) makes the Charter applicable to provincial legislatures in respect of matters within their authority. Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia requires that a law create, directly or by adverse effect, a distinction on a prohibited or analogous ground. Authorities canvassed include Egan v. Canada, Miron v. Trudel, Thibaudeau v. Canada, Symes v. Canada, Eldridge, Haig v. Canada, McKinney and Lavigne.
application: McClung J.A. held that the Legislature's failure to enumerate sexual orientation was legislative inactivity, not 'law,' and did not amount to governmental action for s. 32(1) purposes; the IRPA was neutral, drawing no distinction between homosexuals and heterosexuals, and any inequality existed independently of the statute. O'Leary J.A., assuming s. 32 applied, held the IRPA created no distinction on the basis of sexual orientation because it was silent on the matter, distinguishing Andrews and Blainey where a benefit was expressly extended and then limited. Hunt J.A., dissenting, adopted a 'purpose and context' approach: given the IRPA's remedial purpose and the Legislature's repeated deliberate refusal to add the ground, the silence encouraged and supported the distinction between protected and unprotected victims of discrimination, denying Vriend equal benefit and protection of the law in a discriminatory manner.
conclusion: By a 2–1 majority, no infringement of s. 15(1) was established; McClung and O'Leary JJ.A. found no governmental action/distinction, while Hunt J.A. would have found a discriminatory distinction.

issue: If the omission infringed s. 15(1), was it a reasonable limit justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
facts: The Crown led no evidence directed at s. 1 justification, relying on Hansard and legislative history showing the addition of sexual orientation had been considered and repeatedly declined by the Alberta Legislature.
rule: Section 1 requires a pressing and substantial objective and proportionality per R. v. Oakes (rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionality of effects), with the government bearing the onus.
application: McClung J.A. found it unnecessary to address s. 1 extensively but considered Alberta's response reasonably balanced competing social demands. Hunt J.A. (dissent) found no evidence of a pressing and substantial objective; the omission contradicted rather than advanced the IRPA's purpose, the impairment was total, and Egan's 'incremental/socio-economic' reasoning did not apply because extending human rights protection carried no significant budgetary implications, so the limit could not be justified.
conclusion: The majority did not need to decide s. 1 (having found no breach); Hunt J.A. would have held the limit unjustified under s. 1.

issue: If the IRPA were constitutionally defective, what is the appropriate remedy?
facts: The trial judge ordered that 'sexual orientation' be read into ss. 2(1), 3, 4, 7(1), 8(1) and 10 of the IRPA. The Crown argued reading in was an improper judicial intrusion, and the legislative record showed the omission was deliberate.
rule: Schachter v. Canada sets out the remedial options (striking down, striking down with suspension, reading down/severance, and reading in), with reading in reserved for the clearest of cases and subject to concerns of remedial precision and respect for the legislature.
application: McClung J.A. held reading up was an extravagant judicial intrusion into a deliberate legislative choice; if a violation existed, the proper remedy was a declaration of invalidity stayed for a grace period. O'Leary J.A. agreed reading in was inappropriate. Hunt J.A. (dissent) also rejected reading in because 'sexual orientation' could not be inserted with adequate precision (e.g., the s. 7(2) pension/insurance exclusion), and would instead have declared ss. 7(1), 8(1) and 10 of no force and effect to the extent they failed to protect homosexuals, suspended for one year.
conclusion: All three judges agreed reading in was inappropriate; the majority set aside the trial declaration entirely, while Hunt J.A. would have substituted a suspended declaration of invalidity limited to the employment provisions.

issue: Did the Society establish reasonable grounds to believe the child would likely suffer harm if returned to the mother under terms of supervision?
facts: The newborn was apprehended two days after birth. The father has prior sexual-assault convictions involving children (1995 and 2003) and faces serious current charges including accessing/producing child pornography, voyeurism and extortion. The mother repeatedly refused to release her surety for the father, told workers she did not understand the risk because the child is a boy, refused workers full access to her home, and sent a hostile email stating the Society's rules meant nothing to her and that she would not take the child outside without the father present.
rule: On a temporary care hearing the onus is on the Society to establish on credible and trustworthy evidence reasonable grounds to believe there is a real possibility that returning the child makes it more probable than not the child will suffer harm, and that the child cannot be adequately protected by a temporary supervision order (s. 94(4) CYFSA; Children's Aid Society of Ottawa v. L.(M.), 2017 ONSC 2284; C.A.S. of Ottawa-Carleton v. T., 2000 CanLII 21157). The court may act on evidence it considers credible and trustworthy viewed in its entirety (s. 94(10); Jewish Child and Family Services of Toronto v. A.K., 2014 ONCJ 227).
application: The court found the father posed a real, not speculative, risk given his two prior sexual convictions involving children and serious current charges of a sexual nature. The mother's statements confirmed she did not appreciate this risk and would not act protectively, and her refusal to grant full access to her home and her hostile August 29 email undermined any confidence she would comply with a supervision order. Although the mother had secured independent housing and the child gained weight despite feeding-plan concerns, these positives did not overcome the protection risk. Alleged power imbalance was largely hearsay and given little weight.
conclusion: The Society met its onus: there were reasonable grounds to believe the child would likely suffer harm if returned, and this risk could not currently be mitigated by a supervision order.

issue: What placement is least disruptive and in the child's best interests pending final resolution?
facts: A kinship assessment of the paternal great-grandmother was incomplete and no other kin options were offered. The Society sought continued care with access to the parents in its discretion; the mother sought placement with her under supervision; the father supported the mother's position. The Society expressed willingness to revisit transition once the mother demonstrated cooperation and assigned a new worker.
rule: The court must choose the least disruptive placement consistent with adequate protection of the child (s. 1(2), s. 73, s. 94(5) CYFSA; Children's Aid Society of Hamilton v. B.D. and F.T.M., 2012 ONSC 2448). Before placing a child in Society care the court must consider placement with a relative or extended family member.
application: Because a supervision order could not adequately protect the child and no available kin placement existed (the kinship assessment being incomplete), continued Society care with parental access in the Society's discretion was the least disruptive option consistent with protection and the best-interests factors in s. 73. The court noted the Society was not saying 'never' but 'not yet' and encouraged the mother to acknowledge the risk and prioritize the child.
conclusion: Continued placement in the temporary care of the Society, with access to the parents in the Society's discretion, was ordered as least disruptive and in the child's best interests; the May 13, 2019 order was made temporary.

issue: Should the defendant's counterclaim and statement of defence be struck under Rule 3.68?
facts: Proctor added Chocolate Bikini Company Inc (a.k.a. Surfco) as a party to both her statement of defence and counterclaim, though it was not named by the plaintiffs. The counterclaim sought to relitigate the seizure and sale of Surfco's inventory (already validated by a final, unappealed court order), alleged fraud unsupported by fact, sought impossible remedies (closing all Triple Five malls, freeing captive animals), and claimed $35M with no cause of action.
rule: Rule 3.68 permits striking pleadings that are frivolous, improper, disclose no reasonable claim/defence, constitute an abuse of process, or contain a fatally prejudicial irregularity. A counterclaim by a non-party is a nullity (Lil Dude Ranch Ltd v 1229122 Alberta Inc, 2014 ABQB 39). A non-lawyer cannot act for another litigant (908077 Alberta Ltd v 1313608 Alberta Ltd, 2015 ABQB 108). Relitigating a matter finally decided is an abuse of process (Reece v Edmonton (City), 2011 ABCA 238; Toronto (City) v CUPE, 2003 SCC 63).
application: Chocolate Bikini Company Inc had to be struck as it was improperly added. The counterclaim was a nullity insofar as it advanced a corporate claim; it also amounted to an abuse of process by attempting to relitigate the validated seizure, sought remedies beyond any court's jurisdiction, and pleaded a damages claim with no legal foundation. The statement of defence, read generously in favour of a self-represented litigant, dimly disclosed possible defences of truth and responsible communication, so it was not struck but dealt with on the merits at summary judgment.
conclusion: The counterclaim was struck under Rule 3.68; the statement of defence was preserved to be addressed on the merits.

issue: Were the impugned statements defamatory of the plaintiffs?
facts: Proctor ran a sustained internet campaign across many platforms calling WEM and the Ghermezians 'criminals' who 'stole' her inventory and 'terrorists' practising 'financial terrorism', releasing a 'Thunderstruck 9/11' video, associating the family with Middle Eastern terrorism, and depicting family members' heads on snakes and on bikini-clad bodies.
rule: Defamation requires that the statements be defamatory (tending to lower the person in the estimation of right-thinking members of society), that they refer to the plaintiffs, and that they were communicated to third parties (Grant v Torstar, 2009 SCC 61; WIC Radio Ltd v Simpson, 2008 SCC 40). A false imputation of criminality is defamatory (Knorr v Ibrahim; Hall v Kyburz). Internet publication constitutes publication to the world (Fort McKay Métis Community Association v Morin, 2019 ABQB 185).
application: No evidence showed any charge or conviction; the seizure occurred under legal process, so calling the plaintiffs 'thieves/criminals' was prima facie defamatory. In context, 'terrorist' carried its ordinary sense given the deliberate 9/11 and Middle Eastern associations, and was prima facie defamatory. Because Proctor grouped the Ghermezians as a single 'crime family' and the malls as one evil whole, vilification of any one referred to David and WEM. The material was published globally online.
conclusion: All three elements were established; the statements were defamatory of David and WEM.

issue: Did the record disclose any triable defence, or was any defence defeated by malice?
facts: Proctor raised truth/justification, US copyright/fair dealing, that she is not a racist, responsible communication, qualified privilege, fair comment, satire, freedom of expression, and emulation of Donald Trump. She admitted hating the Ghermezians, sought revenge (a 'revenge' T-shirt video), and posted 'THEY GOTTA GO THEY GOTTA DIE OUT EVENTUALLY'.
rule: Truth is an absolute defence but requires proof of substantial truth (Hall v Kyburz). Responsible communication requires diligence to verify and seeking the other side (Grant v Torstar). Fair comment applies only to opinion, not fact. Qualified privilege requires a reciprocal duty/interest (Hill v Church of Scientology). Malice defeats fair comment, qualified privilege and responsible communication (Daboll v DeMarco, 2011 ONSC 1). Charter rights cannot be used as sword or shield between private parties (Hill).
application: Proctor offered no facts proving the plaintiffs were criminals or terrorists; sincere belief does not establish truth. She made no attempt to verify or seek the plaintiffs' side, defeating responsible communication. 'Criminal' and 'terrorist' are assertions of fact, not opinion, so fair comment did not arise. No reciprocal duty/interest existed for global publication, defeating qualified privilege. Satire is not itself a defence and requires the elements of fair comment. Free speech is circumscribed by defamation law. Emulating Trump conferred no licence. Above all, the record established beyond doubt that Proctor acted with malice — hatred, ill-will, revenge and veiled threats — which independently defeated the privilege, fair comment and responsible communication defences.
conclusion: No triable defence existed; summary judgment was granted for the plaintiffs, the temporary injunction was extended and broadened, and the plaintiffs were left free to apply for a permanent injunction.

issue: Should the plaintiffs' pleadings be struck as an abuse of process for re-litigating matters already decided?
facts: The plaintiffs' 47-page amended statement of claim complained against government agencies and individuals who had not supported L.H. in her long-running custody dispute over her daughter S.T. Morrison J. had repeatedly found no substance to the abuse allegations against the father A.T., a related Judicial Review Petition had been dismissed as an abuse of process, and L.H. had pleaded guilty to breaching the custody/access orders.
rule: Rule 19(24) of the Supreme Court Rules permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim, are scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or are otherwise an abuse of process; the applicant must show it is 'plain and obvious' the pleading offends (Hunt v. Carey). Res judicata bars re-litigation of matters conclusively determined (Angle v. MNR; McIntosh v. Parent) and collateral attack bars attacking a valid order in other proceedings (R. v. Wilson); both may constitute abuse of process under Rule 19(24)(d) (Wayneroy Holdings).
application: The court found that virtually the entire pleading was founded on events already litigated in the Custody Action, the South African proceedings, the criminal proceedings and the dismissed Judicial Review Petition. Vague assertions of conspiracy, discrimination and Charter breaches sought to overturn Morrison J.'s findings and the guilty plea, offending res judicata and constituting an impermissible collateral attack. The pleadings were also so confusing and lacking in causal links that they were irrelevant and embarrassing.
conclusion: The bulk of the claims were struck under Rule 19(24)(c) and (d) as vexatious, embarrassing and an abuse of process.

issue: Do the allegations against the government defendants disclose a reasonable cause of action?
facts: The plaintiffs alleged the Attorney General failed to intervene, the Ministry failed to investigate abuse reports, the Central Authority wrongfully facilitated S.T.'s return from South Africa, Crown Counsel maliciously prosecuted them, and the police failed to investigate A.T.
rule: The Attorney General's discretion to intervene under s. 18 of the Family Relations Act is not subject to judicial review. The Central Authority's duties flow from the Hague Convention (given force by s. 55 Family Relations Act). Malicious prosecution requires proceedings initiated by the defendant, terminated in the plaintiff's favour, absence of reasonable and probable cause, and malice (Nelles v. Ontario). Police forces are not legal entities capable of suing or being sued (Doern v. Phillips Estate).
application: The Attorney General's intervention was discretionary and unreviewable. The Central Authority was obliged to accept the return application founded on Holmes J.'s order and breached no duty. The malicious prosecution claim failed because the charges were founded on L.H.'s failure to return S.T., she pleaded guilty rather than pursuing her stay/abuse-of-process argument, and there was reasonable and probable cause with no malice. The police forces were not suable legal entities, and pre-July 2003 allegations were collateral attacks.
conclusion: Claims against the Attorney General, Central Authority, Crown Counsel and police forces were dismissed; most Ministry claims were struck, but post-July 2003 Ministry claims were stayed pending the variation reasons.

issue: Can opposing counsel, a child advocate, a court-appointed expert and witnesses be sued for their conduct or testimony in the litigation?
facts: The plaintiffs sued A.T.'s lawyers (Sheppard, Hayward) for 'litigation harassment', S.T.'s court-appointed advocate (Fuchs), the court-appointed s. 15 assessor (Dr. Eirikson), and numerous witnesses, alleging essentially perjury.
rule: A solicitor owes an actionable duty only to his or her client, not to an opposing party (Jensen v. MacGregor; Lawrence v. Sandilands). Witnesses, including expert witnesses and court-appointed experts, enjoy absolute privilege for statements made in judicial proceedings (Fabian v. Margulies; Kravit v. Dilli; M.A. v. I.A.S.M.A.). There is no civil cause of action for perjury (Hanson v. Canada).
application: Opposing counsel owed no duty to the plaintiffs, so the claims were frivolous and an abuse of process; the same applied to Fuchs as S.T.'s lawyer. Dr. Eirikson, as a court-appointed expert providing no therapy, was protected by absolute (and qualified) witness privilege. The witness defendants' liability rested solely on alleged perjury, for which no civil action lies. Additional claims (dental care, frostbite) belonged only to S.T., who was not properly joined.
conclusion: All claims against opposing counsel, the child advocate, the expert and the witnesses were dismissed under Rule 19(24)(a) as disclosing no reasonable cause of action.

issue: Should the defamation, former-counsel negligence, and post-July 2003 Ministry claims be permitted to continue subject to particulars?
facts: L.H. alleged that a CLE Society synopsis of Morrison J.'s judgment stating 'it was the wife herself who was guilty of abuse' was defamatory; she alleged her former lawyer Schwartz breached his duties; and continuing allegations against the Ministry post-dated Morrison J.'s July 17, 2003 order.
rule: Rule 19(12) requires defamation to be pleaded with particularity; a lawyer owes a duty of care to his client in contract and tort. Claims should not be struck where they could be saved by proper amendment and where the underlying matters remain live (the pending variation proceedings).
application: It would be inappropriate to dismiss L.H.'s defamation claim before she could particularize it; V.H. had no basis for such a claim. Schwartz's alleged negligence lacked particulars but a solicitor's duty to a client is recognized, so the claim was stayed pending particulars. The post-July 2003 Ministry allegations overlapped with the variation proceedings still to be decided, so it would be wrong to strike them yet.
conclusion: L.H.'s defamation claim against the CLE Society was adjourned, the Schwartz claim was stayed, and post-July 2003 Ministry claims were stayed, each subject to delivery of full particulars within two months, failing which they would be dismissed.

issue: How should decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the parties' young son be allocated in his best interests, given the Mother's allegations of family violence?
facts: The son (3½ at trial) was born post-separation and has always lived primarily with the Mother. The Mother sought sole decision-making and restricted, essentially supervised, involvement by the Father, alleging control, isolation, stalking and a single pushing incident, largely centred on the paternal grandparents' household. The Father sought joint or shared parenting and denied the allegations. By trial's end the parties had agreed to an expanded schedule (alternate weekends and Tuesday overnights).
rule: Section 16 of the Divorce Act mandates that the sole focus be the best interests of the child, with primary consideration to the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being, weighing a non-exhaustive list of factors including family violence (ss. 16.1–16.4). Kaplanis v. Kaplanis (2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)) confirms that conflict between parents does not by itself preclude joint decision-making; a reasonable measure of achievable communication suffices (L.B. v. P.E., 2021 ONCJ 114).
application: The court found family violence present but at the low end of the spectrum, consisting mainly of a single pushing incident and an ever-present tone of control reflecting the paternal family's generational and cultural norms, producing a power imbalance. Post-separation communication was now civil and child-focused, so collaborative decision-making was achievable but full equality was inappropriate. The maximum-contact principle favoured continuing the expanded schedule to give the child stability in both homes.
conclusion: Decisions are to be made by joint consultation, but the Mother has final decision-making authority in the event of disagreement; the son resides primarily with the Mother with the existing expanded schedule (alternate weekends and Tuesday overnights), Father to receive information directly from professionals.

issue: Should the child's given name be changed to add the name the Father proposed?
facts: The Mother registered the child's birth as 'J.A.' on August 1, 2019 without the Father's input and omitted the Father's name. The Father, who believed names were still being discussed and that the Mother had agreed to 'Y.A.', later softened his request from a complete change to adding 'Y.A.'. The child has come to be known as 'J.A.' at daycare and in the world.
rule: The court's authority is exercised in the best interests of the child, balancing the child's established identity against the Father's legitimate interest in participating in naming.
application: The court accepted the Father's sincere evidence and rejected the Mother's explanation for omitting his name, but recognised that 'J.A.' is the name the child knows. Adding 'Y.A.' rather than replacing the existing name was a reasonable accommodation of both.
conclusion: The child's name is changed to 'J.Y.A.'; the Father may complete the necessary documentation without the Mother's consent and may call the child 'Y.A.' in his household.

issue: What child and spousal support, including any retroactive amounts, should the Father pay?
facts: The Father earned $41,292 (2020) and $50,941 (2021); the Mother was financially dependent throughout, has $NIL current income while studying and caring for the child, but strong future earning prospects. The Father had paid $370/month since March 2021; the Mother had refused earlier support offers post-separation.
rule: The Federal Child Support Guidelines set table amounts by income; section 15.2 of the Divorce Act and the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines govern spousal support, with the four statutory objectives (recognizing advantages/disadvantages, apportioning child-care consequences, relieving economic hardship, promoting self-sufficiency).
application: Table child support was $373 (2020) and $469 (2021 onward); the Father was found to have discharged Aug–Dec 2019 support, and arrears from January 2020 totalled $7,889. For spousal support the court chose the 'High' SSAG figure ($978/month) so the child's primary household received a financial boost, but limited it to a defined term while the Mother pursued education, declining a large retroactive award because she had refused earlier payments.
conclusion: Child support of $469/month payable from April 1, 2023; arrears fixed at $7,889; spousal support of $978/month from May 1, 2021 to April 30, 2028, reviewable May 1, 2028 at the 'Mid' range; expenses shared 77%/23%.

issue: Is the Mehr an enforceable contract obliging the Father to pay the deferred sum to the Mother?
facts: The Mehr was a traditional Islamic marriage contract; the Certificate of Marriage recorded a 'deferred' figure of 10,000. The Mother was not present at the negotiations, did not read or have her signature witnessed on the document, and the currency and total (and which jewellery formed the 'agreed upon' portion) were disputed. No expert evidence was led on the Mehr.
rule: Following Bruker v. Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54, a religious contract is enforceable only if it meets the requirements of an ordinary contract. Under ss. 52 and 55(1) of the Family Law Act a domestic/marriage contract must be in writing, signed and witnessed, and the parties, content and obligations must be certain. Judicial notice cannot resolve disputed facts or validate opinion evidence.
application: Without expert evidence the court could not take judicial notice that the Certificate documented a firm and binding Mehr consistent with the practices of the Ontario Syrian Muslim community. Even if it could, the essential terms (parties, currency, amount, whether the Mother assented, and the witnessing of her signature) were uncertain or disputed, so the contract failed for uncertainty.
conclusion: The Mother's claim to enforce the Mehr is dismissed.

issue: Should an equalization payment of net family property be ordered?
facts: The parties were students with minimal assets; the marriage was short (18 months) and cohabitation only about 8 months. Excluding Mehr jewellery, the Mother's net family property was $1,917.85 and the Father's was fixed at $NIL because his student loans drove his separation-date net worth below zero, so in theory the Mother owed him $958.92.
rule: Sections 4 and 5 of the Family Law Act govern net family property and equalization; s. 4(5) fixes NFP at not less than zero; s. 5(6) permits a discretionary variation where an equal division would be unconscionable, including for short cohabitation, depletion (5(6)(d)), a written non-domestic-contract agreement (5(6)(g)) and other property circumstances (5(6)(h)); s. 5(7) treats child care, household management and financial provision as joint responsibilities.
application: The student loans reflected an investment in the future rather than benefit to the family, and the parties were students throughout a short marriage; the disputed Mehr and the joint-responsibility principle under s. 5(7) made any equalization payment contrary to the intent of ss. 4 and 5.
conclusion: The equalization payment is varied to zero; no equalization is owed by either party.

issue: How should the costs of the trial be allocated?
facts: Success was divided: the Mother retained primary residence and final decision-making but failed to prove family violence severe enough to restrict the Father; the Father paid 'High'-range spousal support but only for a defined term; the Mehr claim was dismissed and no equalization was ordered. Neither party behaved inappropriately.
rule: Per Mattina v. Mattina, 2018 ONCA 867, costs are discretionary and governed by reasonableness and proportionality, serving to indemnify successful litigants, encourage settlement, sanction misconduct and ensure just resolution under Rule 2(2) of the Family Law Rules.
application: With both parties partially successful and no misconduct, the most just outcome enabling co-parenting was for each to bear their own costs.
conclusion: Each party bears their own costs of the litigation.

issue: Are the defendants in civil contempt for breaching the orders of Akbarali J. and Myers J. concerning vegetation removal and defamatory/harassing videos?
facts: The Golds leased residential premises next to the plaintiffs. After disputes, Akbarali J.'s interim order (May 10, 2021), continued by Myers J. (July 2, 2021), restrained them from cutting trees/vegetation except by a set protocol and from publishing defamatory or harassing videos about Shane Baghai, his family or agents, and required removal of prior offending videos. The defendants continued cutting trees without following the protocol (including on a Jewish Sabbath weekend when counsel did not reply within 24 hours), continued posting crude, vulgar, threatening and defamatory videos on Ms. Gold's YouTube channel referring explicitly or implicitly to the landlords and the litigation, and failed to remove the earlier videos. Ms. Gold posted a video titled 'The Miracle' inviting the judge to treat it 'as proof of my defiance.'
rule: Under Rule 60.11 of the Rules of Civil Procedure, contempt may be found to enforce an order to do or abstain from an act (other than payment of money). Civil contempt requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt of three elements (Carey v. Laiken, 2015 SCC 17, paras. 33-35): (i) the order states clearly and unequivocally what must and must not be done; (ii) the alleged contemnor had actual knowledge of it; and (iii) the party intentionally did the prohibited act or failed to do the compelled act. A party must comply with both letter and spirit of the order (Chirico v. Szalas, 2016 ONCA 589); motive is irrelevant.
application: The orders were clear, detailed and unambiguous; the defendants advanced only excuses, not confusion. They had actual knowledge, having been represented by counsel on the earlier motions and having acknowledged the orders in affidavits and transcripts. Intention was established: Ms. Gold videotaped tree/vegetation removal in breach of the protocol, posted the videos (some only briefly, but posting even briefly breached the orders), left earlier offending videos online, and expressly announced her defiance. The court rejected the excuse that the videos referred to a 'phantom secret lover' rather than the landlords, finding they implicitly targeted the Baghai family, agents and litigation.
conclusion: All three elements were satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt; the defendants were found to be in contempt of both the interim and interlocutory orders.

issue: What remedy or sanction should follow the finding of contempt?
facts: The plaintiffs sought orders compelling adherence, imprisonment, vacant possession of the leased premises, and relief under Rule 60.12 (stay/dismissal/striking of pleadings). The defendants had shown flagrant, concerted defiance and had also failed to comply with Landlord and Tenant Board rent orders and the costs order of Myers J. (though monetary defaults could not ground contempt).
rule: Rule 60.11 permits any just order, including imprisonment, fine, compliance orders and costs; the four penalty options are no penalty, suspended sentence, fine, or incarceration (Niagara (Police Services Board) v. Curran). Rule 60.12 allows staying or dismissing a party's proceeding or striking a defence for non-compliance with an interlocutory order. Precedents on possession orders: York Condominium Corp. No. 82 v. Singh, 2013 ONSC 2066; Etobicoke (City) v. Whitty (1998).
application: Emphasizing that the rule of law is the bedrock of a free and democratic society and that flouting court orders is an affront to it (citing Mercedes-Benz Financial v. Kovecevic), the court gave the defendants a chance to purge their contempt: full compliance with the prior orders, no vegetation removal except by protocol, and removal of all offending videos (before and after the orders) from YouTube and the internet by January 10, 2022, with no brief re-posting. The defendants' counterclaim was stayed under Rule 60.12 pending full compliance. Failure to comply would bring the parties back for further sanctions, potentially incarceration and/or removal from the premises.
