issue: Did the trial judge err in finding the children were not Métis children under the CYFSA, and did the non-joinder of the EWMNNS render the trial a nullity?
facts: The children's mother (the appellant) and maternal grandmother were Métis women and members of the EWMNNS. The children, aged under five, could not self-identify and had not been registered with the EWMNNS at trial. Both trial counsel directed the trial judge to s. 2(4) CYFSA and the appellant's counsel conceded the children were not Métis. The EWMNNS Grand Chief testified it would not participate and did not facilitate placements.
rule: Under s. 90(2)(b) CYFSA the court must determine, before a protection finding, whether a child is First Nations, Inuk or Métis. The governing criteria are in s. 1 of O. Reg. 155/18 (including s. 1(a): a parent identifying the child as Métis), not s. 2(4) (which addresses a child's bands/communities). 'First Nations, Inuit or Métis community' is defined in s. 2(1) as a community listed by the Minister in a regulation under s. 68; no such regulation listing the EWMNNS was in force. Standard of review for this extricable question of law is correctness (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33).
application: The trial judge applied the wrong provision (s. 2(4)) and erred: the appellant, a parent, had identified the children as Métis, satisfying s. 1(a) of O. Reg. 155/18, and a connection to the EWMNNS was established. However, because no s. 68 regulation listing the EWMNNS as a Métis community was in force, the trial judge correctly declined to add the EWMNNS as a party under s. 79(1)4. Even if joinder had been required, any nullity would run only against the EWMNNS (per CAS of London and Middlesex v. E.M.E.E., 2017 ONSC 5292), which never moved to set aside the order, not against the appellant.
conclusion: The trial judge erred in finding the children were not Métis, but the error did not render the proceeding a nullity and did not require a new trial; the disposition remained the only one adequately protecting the children.

issue: Did the trial judge err in finding the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(c) CYFSA?
facts: A 31-second video on the appellant's phone showed the father, T.E., with an erect penis while the one-year-old child touched it; the appellant recorded and encouraged the activity. She was convicted of possession of child pornography and sexual interference (appeal pending). The appellant conceded the accuracy of the criminal judge's description of the video and admitted her conduct posed a risk to the child. Protection was also grounded on the children's exposure to repeated domestic violence.
rule: Section 74(2)(c) CYFSA: a child is in need of protection where sexually abused or exploited by a person having charge, or where that person fails to protect. Section 93(1)(b) CYFSA permits admission of findings or reasons from an earlier civil or criminal proceeding. Intent to cause harm need not be proven (Jewish Family and Child Service v. K.(R.), 2008 ONCJ 774, aff'd 2009 ONCA 903). Findings of mixed fact and law are reviewed for palpable and overriding error.
application: The trial judge properly admitted Douglas J.'s reasons under s. 93(1)(b); the pending criminal appeal challenged only the legal sufficiency of the facts, not the accuracy of the video's description, which the appellant accepted. The recorded sexualized conduct in the presence of, and involving, the child, coupled with the appellant's failure to stop it and her acknowledged risk of 'early sexualization', supported a protection finding. The concepts of sexual abuse/exploitation are broad enough to capture this conduct. The protection finding was also independently supported by exposure to domestic violence.
conclusion: No error; the protection finding under s. 74(2)(c) (and on the domestic-violence ground) was reasonable and well supported.

issue: Did the trial judge err by failing to admit the appellant's documentary exhibits?
facts: The appellant sought to file certificates of completion and correspondence from service providers as proof of her acquisition of skills. Except for one unsigned, undated letter, the documents were in fact admitted, and were the subject of submissions and expressly addressed in the disposition reasons.
rule: Evidentiary rulings attract deference; an error must be shown to have affected the result. Section 93(1)(b) CYFSA governs admissibility of relevant statements.
application: The record showed the impugned documents were admitted, not excluded. The trial judge found them of little help because they established only attendance, not the depth of participation or insight gained, and did not address the appellant's profound long-standing issues. The appellant's own viva voce evidence (accepted on the point of participation) and the Society's evidence rendered the documents merely corroborative.
conclusion: No reversible error; the asserted exclusion did not occur and could not have affected the result.

issue: Should fresh/further evidence be admitted, and does it warrant a new trial or different disposition?
facts: Both parties moved to adduce affidavits about post-trial developments: the children's registration under the mother's EWMNNS membership, the appellant's continued counselling and education, her problematic relationships (C.M., roommate M.G.), and the Society's cultural services to the children and foster parents.
rule: Section 121(6) CYFSA permits further evidence of post-decision events. Fresh evidence is assessed under a flexible Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 test as adapted for child protection (CCAS of Metropolitan Toronto v. M.(C.), [1994] 2 S.C.R. 165): relevance, potential decisiveness to best interests, and credibility.
application: Most evidence was admitted (with portions excluded as argument, hearsay opinion, or matters that could have been led at trial). The registration evidence merely confirmed the connection to the EWMNNS already found. The Society's evidence showed active cultural programming. The appellant's post-trial self-improvement, while commendable, restated her rejected trial evidence, did not resile from her sworn denial of any domestic violence, and her renewed abusive relationships (C.M.) raised continuing concern. Given the children's ages and time in care, they could not be left in limbo (CAS of Waterloo v. V.L., 2007 ONCA 113).
conclusion: The admissible fresh and further evidence did not alter the factual matrix so as to justify interfering with the disposition or ordering a new trial.

issue: Did the Attorney General establish a serious colour of right that the Act respecting Private Education applies to the Académie operating without a permit?
facts: The Académie, a Satmar Chassidic yeshiva operating since 1952, dispenses primarily Talmudic religious instruction plus about six hours of secular English and math per week to 163 boys, without a Ministerial permit under s. 10 A.P.E. Its programs do not match the Basic School Regulation or Quebec Education Program.
rule: Under s. 752 C.C.P. and Brassard v. Société zoologique de Québec, the applicant must first show a colour of right, which may be clear, doubtful or non-existent; the Supreme Court sets a low threshold (143471 Canada Inc.). Section 10 A.P.E. prohibits operating a private educational institution 'to which this Act applies' without a permit; ss. 1 and 2 A.P.E. define elementary/secondary instructional services as preparing students for further studies in the continuum.
application: The Académie plainly operates a private institution without a permit, but the evidence showed its education is not aimed at preparing students for studies in the elementary/secondary/post-secondary continuum; it is a religious school preparing boys for advanced Talmudic study, the secular classes being a 'survival tool'. This cast doubt on whether the A.P.E. even applies. Given the low Supreme Court threshold, a colour of right existed but was doubtful.
conclusion: A colour of right was established, but it was only doubtful, heightening the scrutiny required for the remaining tests.

issue: Would refusing the injunction cause irreparable harm or render the final judgment ineffective?
facts: The A.P.E., a public-order statute, is said to be violated during the proceedings. The Académie has operated since 1952 (and under the A.P.E. since 1993) with no charge or conviction; it raises freedom-of-religion arguments and the unjustified refusal of a s. 22 Regulation exemption.
rule: Section 752, para. 2 C.C.P.: an interlocutory injunction avoids serious or irreparable harm or a situation rendering the final judgment ineffective. The weaker the colour of right, the greater the irreparable harm required.
application: The Court was not convinced that mere continued operation caused irreparable harm, particularly given the doubtful colour of right, the exceptional circumstances and the long unchallenged operation. However, a final judgment could not retroactively restore compulsory educational services the 163 children may have missed, so the second branch (rendering the final judgment ineffective) was engaged as to the children.
conclusion: No irreparable harm to the Attorney General was shown, though the situation could render the final judgment ineffective as regards the children.

issue: Does the balance of convenience favour granting the injunction?
facts: On one side the public interest in enforcing a public-order education statute; on the other, the children's and community's fundamental Charter rights and the impossibility of placing the boys elsewhere for religious reasons; none of the children were heard or represented.
rule: Where the colour of right is doubtful the Court weighs the balance of convenience; case law (Solski) holds public interest generally takes priority over private litigants' interests.
application: Public interest favoured the Attorney General while fundamental Charter freedoms favoured the defendants. Because public interest takes priority, and doubtful colour of right could not tip the scales to the defendants, the balance of convenience favoured the Attorney General.
conclusion: The balance of convenience favoured the Attorney General.

issue: Should the Court nonetheless exercise its discretion to refuse the interlocutory injunction?
facts: The school has operated over half a century without prosecution; 163 children were neither heard nor represented; the A.P.E. provides penal sanctions (ss. 128, 136); compulsory school attendance was dejudicialized (ss. 14-18 E.A., Youth Protection Act); the injunction would even bar the six hours of secular instruction; the Supreme Court's pending S.L. v. Commission scolaire des Chênes could affect the issues.
rule: An injunction is a discretionary, exceptional common-law remedy (Trudel v. Clairol; Manitoba (A.G.) v. Metropolitan Stores; Pharmascience v. Binet) to be exercised judicially and judiciously (Sharp v. Wakefield); relevant factors include delay, existence of another remedy, and the injunction's usefulness, effectiveness and enforceability. R. v. Jones requires reasonable accommodation of religious convictions in education.
application: The Court identified five reasons: the delay since 1952; the unrepresented rights of the 163 children; the availability of penal remedies specifically enacted for s. 10 breaches (with no evidence of their ineffectiveness); the improper attempt to re-judicialize compulsory school attendance that the legislature had dejudicialized; and the injunction's lack of usefulness, effectiveness and enforceability (it would end even the secular instruction and there is no Quebec analogue to Ontario's 'private school' definition). A full trial was needed to weigh the competing State, parental and child interests, and the pending S.L. decision counselled prudence.
conclusion: The Court exercised its discretion to refuse the interlocutory injunction; the motion was dismissed with costs in the cause.

issue: Should the prosecution be stayed as an abuse of process or a breach of fundamental justice given the prior Quebec acquittals and Quebec's non-prosecution policy?
facts: Dr. Morgentaler had been acquitted by Quebec juries on three occasions on similar s. 251 charges roughly ten years earlier, after which the Quebec Attorney-General adopted a policy of not prosecuting physicians performing abortions. The three accused were now charged in Ontario with conspiracy to procure a miscarriage and argued the Ontario prosecution was oppressive, amounted to 'Crown-shopping', and constituted prosecutorial estoppel.
rule: Assuming the abuse of process doctrine survives Rourke v. The Queen, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 1021, intervention requires exceptional circumstances giving rise to harassment, oppression, prejudice or manifest hardship caused by the Crown (Re Regina and Currie). Section 7 of the Charter's guarantee of fundamental justice does not bar a fresh prosecution differently situated.
application: The prior proceedings occurred ten years earlier, in a different province, arising from different facts and commenced by a different Attorney-General; this was neither exceptional nor oppressive. Forbearance by one province's Attorney-General does not crystallize into a defence or estoppel in another province, and the provincial Attorneys-General operate independently of the federal government. A prosecution based on a different indictment, time and place cannot breach fundamental justice.
conclusion: The abuse of process / s. 7 argument failed; no stay granted.

issue: Is s. 251 void for vagueness at common law or under s. 7 of the Charter?
facts: The accused argued the standard in s. 251(4)(c) ('would or would be likely to endanger her life or health') and the word 'miscarriage' were too vague, and that committees applied inconsistent standards across the country.
rule: There is scant authority that a statute (as opposed to a by-law) can be struck down for uncertainty at common law (Fawcett Properties). The void-for-vagueness component of fundamental justice, if it exists, serves to let a person know whether his conduct is prohibited, not to ensure uniform committee standards.
application: Adopting Laskin C.J.C.'s reasoning in Morgentaler v. The Queen (1975), the committee standard is a manageable one addressed to a professional panel and is not vague on its face. In any event, an accused always knows whether a certificate was obtained, so there is no uncertainty as to criminal culpability under s. 251(1) or (2). 'Procuring a miscarriage' is synonymous with 'performing an abortion' and is not uncertain. Courts are not to supervise the administrative efficiency of legislation.
conclusion: Section 251 is not void for vagueness at common law or under s. 7.

issue: Does the therapeutic abortion committee scheme invalidate s. 251 because the committees do not observe natural justice / fundamental justice?
facts: The evidence showed committees did not permit applicants or counsel to attend, gave no reasons, and applied varying criteria. No specific committee decision was being challenged because the accused had never applied for a certificate.
rule: Natural justice principles are annexed to legislation to bring it into conformity with common law justice (Martineau v. Matsqui). A challenge to a decision-making body's duty to act fairly requires a specific impugned decision.
application: Because no committee decision was actually impugned (no certificate was ever requested), there was no basis for an administrative-law fairness challenge, and the possible failure of committees to follow natural justice could not affect the validity of the prosecution. The same reasoning applies whether framed under common law natural justice or the s. 7 guarantee of fundamental justice.
conclusion: The natural justice / fundamental justice argument failed.

issue: Is s. 251 ultra vires Parliament, an unconstitutional delegation, or a conferral of s. 96 judicial functions?
facts: The accused argued s. 251 was really health legislation within provincial jurisdiction, that it delegated federal criminal power to provincial Health Ministers and committees, and that committees exercised judicial functions reserved to s. 96 courts.
rule: Valid criminal law requires a prohibition with penal sanction directed at a public purpose (Margarine Reference, per Rand J.); Parliament may create exemptions. Delegation between Parliament and legislatures is impermissible (Nova Scotia Interdelegation), but conferring decision-making powers on provincial bodies with criminal-law consequences is not delegation. The s. 96 test (Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979) asks whether a judicial power is being exercised.
application: Following Laskin C.J.C. in Morgentaler (1975), Parliament decreed that interference with the ordinary course of conception is socially undesirable conduct subject to punishment, a valid exercise of the criminal law power; the improved safety of abortion is immaterial. Section 251 does not permit provinces to legislate on abortion but only to establish hospitals and committees that provide a defence; issuing a certificate is not a delegation of federal power (Carruthers v. Lions Gate Hospital). The committees exercise no Criminal Code powers and no judicial function, so no s. 96 problem arises.
conclusion: Section 251 is intra vires, involves no unconstitutional delegation, and does not confer s. 96 judicial functions.

issue: Does s. 251 violate equality before the law under s. 1(b) of the Canadian Bill of Rights?
facts: The accused argued that unequal availability of committees and services, and harsher treatment outside Quebec, denied equality. They also argued ss. 26 and 28 of the Charter entrenched the Bill of Rights.
rule: Section 1(b) is not a charge to supervise the administrative efficiency or regional organization of legislation absent a touchstone of prohibited discrimination in the legislation itself (Morgentaler (1975); Drybones). Sections 26 and 28 of the Charter do not entrench non-Charter rights.
application: Section 251 does not on its face discriminate by race, national origin, colour, religion or sex; any uneven administration is for Parliament to correct, not the courts. The Quebec situation results from prosecutorial forbearance, not the law itself; the contrary view would let any Attorney-General render a law inoperative nationally by non-enforcement. Sections 26 and 28 do not constitutionalize s. 1(b).
conclusion: Section 251 does not violate s. 1(b) of the Bill of Rights.

issue: Does s. 251 infringe the right to liberty and security of the person under s. 7 by denying a right to choose abortion?
facts: The accused relied on U.S. authority (Roe v. Wade; Doe v. Bolton) to argue s. 7 protects a woman's privacy right to choose abortion and the doctor's best medical judgment.
rule: The rights in s. 7 begin with the legal rights Canadians have at common law or statute; if a claimed right is not so protected, the court asks whether it is 'so deeply rooted in the traditions and conscience of our people as to be ranked as fundamental' (Palko v. Connecticut). American privacy jurisprudence is not controlling; the narrower reading in Operation Dismantle (Fed. C.A.) treats liberty and security as protection against arbitrary State interference with the person.
application: A review of the history shows abortion has been prohibited in Canada for over 100 years; the availability of a necessity defence or a certificate does not create an unfettered legal right to abortion, nor is such a right deeply rooted in Canadian traditions. The patient-physician relationship operates within legal prohibitions, so a doctor's best medical judgment cannot strike down the law.
conclusion: Section 7 does not contain a right to abortion; the argument failed and it was unnecessary to consider fundamental justice or s. 1.

issue: Does s. 251 infringe freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
facts: Expert evidence indicated some 'women-centred' denominations (e.g., the United Church) hold that the abortion decision belongs to the woman's informed conscience, and that s. 251(4) transfers that decision to a committee.
rule: Following R. v. Big M Drug Mart (Alta. C.A.), a breach of freedom of religion requires a law with a compelling religious purpose that takes one side of a sectarian controversy; protection attaches to a tenet or fundamental doctrine, being a belief held to be self-evidently true, not to a denomination's debated policy position on a secular issue.
application: Section 251 does not single out any religious group on its face. While rooted in Judaeo-Christian values, no denomination holds an absolute right to abortion as a tenet of faith; positions on abortion are debated policy positions, not articles of faith. Evidence of non-religious 'conscience' would not suffice, as such a reading would be boundless. The proper forum for such debate is the political one.
conclusion: Section 251 does not breach s. 2(a).

issue: Does s. 251 subject women to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment under s. 12?
facts: Evidence showed compliance with s. 251 causes delay making abortions more hazardous, forces women to travel great distances, and sometimes results in women bearing unwanted children.
rule: Section 12's phrase 'subjected to treatment or punishment' implies a conscious State decision to impose treatment or punishment on individuals (analogous to Morgentaler (1975) on the Bill of Rights guarantee).
application: Women who suffer hardship or are denied access are not being subjected to State-imposed treatment because they choose to seek an abortion; the State is not wilfully subjecting them to a course of conduct. The word 'subjected to', like 'impose', connotes a State decision, not the consequence of the individual's own choice.
conclusion: Section 251 does not breach s. 12; the motion was dismissed in its entirety.

issue: Does the Anthony-Cook framework for joint submissions apply where the recommendation follows a guilty verdict rather than a guilty plea?
facts: After Sohier-Chaput was found guilty following trial of wilfully promoting hatred against Jewish people, Crown and defence jointly recommended a three-month sentence with probation. There had been no guilty plea; the offender exercised his right to a full trial.
rule: R. c. Anthony-Cook, 2016 CSC 43 and R. c. Nahanee, 2022 CSC 37 set a stringent 'public interest' test protecting joint submissions arising from guilty pleas. Quebec Court of Appeal authority (Blondeau, 2018 QCCA 1250; Baptiste c. R., 2021 QCCA 1064; Obodzinski c. R., 2021 QCCA 1395) holds the framework applies even where the joint submission follows a verdict, though the benefits of certainty and efficiency are diminished.
application: The Court noted that Anthony-Cook and Nahanee centred on the guilty-plea context and that here none of the usual benefits (avoidance of a trial, saving of judicial time and resources) were realized. Nevertheless, following the binding Court of Appeal jurisprudence, the Court accepted that the objectives of maintaining confidence in negotiated resolutions and avoiding contested sentencing hearings remain important, so the rigorous public-interest test still governs.
conclusion: Yes. The Court held it was bound to apply the Anthony-Cook public-interest test even though the joint recommendation followed a guilty verdict rather than a guilty plea.

issue: Would the joint recommendation of three months' imprisonment bring the administration of justice into disrepute or be contrary to the public interest?
facts: The offender, under the pseudonym 'Zeiger', authored an article on the neo-Nazi platform The Daily Stormer mocking a Holocaust survivor and promoting Nazi ideology and extermination of Jews; he was a prolific contributor (800–1000 articles over two years) to a site receiving some three million visits monthly. The pre-sentence report was unfavourable, risk of recidivism was 'moderate', he expressed no genuine remorse, and a community-impact statement by the CIJA described serious harm to the Jewish community. The recommended three months sat at the bottom of the applicable range (roughly 2–18 months).
rule: Under Anthony-Cook, a joint submission may be rejected only where it is so 'unhinged' from the circumstances of the offence and offender that acceptance would lead reasonable, informed persons to conclude the justice system had ceased to function properly (a high threshold). The judge remains the ultimate protector of the public interest (Reyes c. R., 2022 QCCA 1689).
application: The Court found numerous aggravating factors (premeditated, structured hate messaging incitement to violence, prolific dissemination, no remorse or introspection, ongoing danger, serious harm to the community, mockery of the Holocaust, the s. 718.2(a)(i) hate-motivation aggravator) and only two minor mitigating factors. Comparing the recommendation to comparable cases such as Rochefort (12 months), the Court concluded that a well-informed, reasonable member of the public — reflected in the CIJA statement — would be shocked by so lenient a 'candy sentence' and would lose confidence in the justice system. Counsel's additional submissions failed to dispel these concerns.
conclusion: Yes. The Court held the three-month recommendation was contrary to the public interest and would bring the administration of justice into disrepute, and departed from it.

issue: What is the fit and appropriate sentence for the s. 319(2) offence in these circumstances?
facts: The offence is objectively grave (maximum two years on indictment), attacked fundamental Quebec/Canadian values, was committed deliberately and repeatedly online to a wide audience, and the offender showed no rehabilitation six years later while maintaining his hateful ideology.
rule: Sentencing principles under ss. 718, 718.1 and 718.2 C.cr., emphasizing proportionality, denunciation, deterrence, isolation and protection of society; the s. 718.2(a)(i) hate-motivation aggravator; parity within the established range (roughly 2–18 months); the principle that maximum sentences are not reserved for the abstract worst case (R. c. Friesen, 2020 CSC 9); and restraint in resorting to incarceration (ss. 718.2(d)-(e); Proulx; Parranto).
application: Prioritizing denunciation, deterrence and isolation given the offender's high moral culpability, ongoing danger and lack of introspection, the Court found the maximum could be justified but, applying restraint, concluded a shorter custodial sentence would meet the sentencing objectives. Non-custodial alternatives were rejected as unreasonable.
conclusion: The Court imposed 15 months' imprisonment together with a three-year probation order, including conditions barring access to social media, publishing, association with hate groups, and contact with The Daily Stormer, plus a 10-year weapons prohibition under s. 110.

issue: Was there a material change in circumstances since the 2013 consent (Corkery J.) custody order sufficient to open the order to variation?
facts: The November 2013 consent order, based on Howard Hurwitz's s. 30 assessment, provided for parallel parenting and roughly equal time with each parent. By the time of trial the children resisted spending time with their mother, police enforcement had become necessary, and there had been over 30 police occurrences and constant Children's Aid Society involvement. Both parents brought motions to change, each alleging a material change.
rule: Under s. 17(5) of the Divorce Act (and s. 29 of the Children's Law Reform Act) a court must first be satisfied there has been a change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances of the child. Gordon v. Goertz, 1996 CanLII 191 (SCC) requires (1) a change in circumstances or in the parents' ability to meet the child's needs, (2) which materially affects the child, and (3) which was not foreseen or reasonably contemplated when the original order was made.
application: Both parties sought variation and agreed the current order was not functioning. Independently, the court found overwhelming evidence of material change: the children's entrenched resistance to their mother, the need for police enforcement to secure her parenting time, and a breakdown that could not have been anticipated at the time of the consent order despite early warning signs.
conclusion: The court held there was, without question, a material change in circumstances, permitting it to proceed to the best-interests inquiry.

issue: Did the respondent father engage in parental alienation of the three children against their mother?
facts: The father repeatedly denigrated the mother in front of the children, made excessive daily phone calls interfering with school routines, enrolled the children in hockey to displace skiing they enjoyed with their mother, used a no-trespass order and equipment exchanges to marginalize her, bought floor tickets to take the daughter to a Taylor Swift concert the mother had gifted, and enlisted his 12-year-old daughter to spy on the mother's text messages 'for evidence' while asking the Society not to alert the mother. The children physically assaulted and verbally abused the mother without the father correcting them.
rule: There is no need for expert opinion to find alienation; whether alienation occurred is a conclusion of fact for the judge based on the evidence and credibility (Figliano, per Mesbur J.), applying the indicia described in the parental-alienation literature (Gardner's eight behaviours; Kelly and Johnston's 'alienated child'; Warshak's three traits; naïve/active/obsessed alienators). Credibility of the parents is central.
application: The court preferred the mother's credible evidence over the father's 'polished' but implausible explanations. Measuring the father's conduct against the recognized indicia, the court found the behaviours 'textbook,' escalating from naïve alienation to that of an obsessed alienator, with the Taylor Swift incident and the iPod spying being clear proof. The children's idealization of the father, baseless contempt for and abuse of the mother without guilt, extension of hostility to her friends (C.T.) and normal relations when outside the father's orbit all confirmed severe alienation, not justified estrangement.
conclusion: The court found the respondent had engaged in severe parental alienation, for which he alone (and those under his control) was responsible.

issue: What variation of custody, residence and access is in the best interests of the children, including whether a custody transfer, a temporary no-contact period and the Family Bridges program are warranted?
facts: The children (aged 10, almost 12, and 14) were functioning well in all spheres except their relationship with their mother, whom they refused to see. The mother remained dedicated despite abuse; the father was otherwise a good parent but incapable of supporting the children's relationship with their mother. 'Cooling off' and 'do nothing' options were canvassed.
rule: Once a material change is shown, the sole consideration is the best interests of the child determined by reference to that change (Divorce Act s. 17(5); Gordon v. Goertz), with the maximum-contact principle (s. 17(9)). In severe alienation cases a change of custody, a temporary suspension of contact with the favoured parent, and a structured reunification program may be the only effective remedy; a 'cooling off' period or doing nothing is generally inappropriate (Fidler, Bala, Hurwitz; Warshak).
application: The court rejected the father's 'cooling off' proposal and the 'do nothing' option, finding intervention likely to help, no trauma from placement with the mother, and no justified estrangement. Because the children's relationship with their mother could not be repaired while the father continued his controlling, manipulative interference, the court ordered sole temporary custody to the mother, enrolment in Family Bridges, a post-workshop vacation, and a minimum 90-day no-contact period with the father and his circle, with continued police enforcement, contempt sanctions available, and single-judge case management.
conclusion: The court varied the orders to grant the mother sole temporary custody with the children in her residential care, ordered the Family Bridges reunification program and a no-contact period of at least 90 days, and retained case management of future motions.

issue: Should the child support order be varied?
facts: The April 2014 Wildman J. consent order set child support at $259/month based on disclosed incomes of $105,703 (father) and $89,227 (mother). The father's disclosed 2016 income was $143,897, and with the change in residential care the children would now live with the mother.
rule: A variation of child support is made in accordance with the applicable Child Support Guidelines (Divorce Act s. 17(6.1)); variation requires a material change in circumstances.
application: Given the change to the mother having sole custody and residential care and the father's increased income of $143,897, table support was recalculated. Arrears were fixed and ongoing table support ordered, with annual income disclosure required.
conclusion: The court ordered the father to pay arrears of $6,734 and $2,521/month in child support commencing July 1, 2017, based on his 2016 income, enforceable through the Family Responsibility Office.

issue: Is the proposed expert evidence on anti-gay discrimination necessary to assist the jury in a wilful promotion of hatred prosecution under s. 319(2)?
facts: Whatcott distributed a flyer at the 2016 Toronto Pride Parade warning of the dangers of the 'homosexual lifestyle' and condemning homosexual sex. The Crown sought to qualify Professor Mulé to explain the history of anti-gay discrimination and the 'tropes' (religion/morality, law/criminality, health/sickness) and to opine whether the flyer invoked those stereotypes, focusing on the health trope.
rule: Under R. v. Mohan, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 9, expert evidence must be relevant, necessary to assist the trier of fact, not subject to an exclusionary rule, and given by a properly qualified expert. Per R. v. K.(A.) (1999), evidence is unnecessary if the trier of fact can form its own conclusions without help; necessity means information likely outside the experience and knowledge of the jury. Hate under s. 319(2) is assessed from the standpoint of a reasonable person in context: R. v. Keegstra, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697; Mugesera v. Canada, 2005 SCC 2.
application: The judge held this was not a technical case but one about human behaviour. The jury, instructed on the Keegstra/Mugesera definition of hatred and applying the reasonable-person standard, could determine from the face of the flyer and surrounding circumstances whether it vilified gay people. The well-known history of discrimination against gay people based on religion, health and law is within the experience of a reasonable Toronto juror; the detailed academic linkages need not be spelled out. R. v. Sears, 2019 ONCJ 104 (aff'd 2021 ONSC 4272; leave refused 2021 ONCA 522) showed such expert evidence, while helpful, was not necessary because the impugned publications provided a complete factual foundation. North Shore Press and Mugesera were distinguishable as administrative tribunal proceedings not applying Mohan or a cost-benefit analysis.
conclusion: The evidence was not necessary; the jury could decide from the flyer itself and the surrounding circumstances.

issue: Is Professor Mulé a properly qualified expert?
facts: Professor Mulé is a tenured associate professor of social work, cross-appointed to gender, sexuality and women's studies, who has studied and published on LGBT2-SQI issues, but the defence argued he had never studied the history of discrimination against gay people and was not a theologian, health expert, or lawyer.
rule: An expert is one 'shown to have acquired special or peculiar knowledge through study or experience' (Mohan, para. 27); deficiencies go to weight, not admissibility (R. v. Peng, 2009 ONCA 921; R. v. Marquard, [1993] 4 S.C.R. 223; R. v. Béland). An expert need not be the leading authority and may review literature to shore up knowledge (R. v. Russell).
application: Although discrimination as such was not Mulé's principal research topic, themes of discrimination figured prominently in his work and teaching, giving him knowledge beyond that of an ordinary person. It was unrealistic to require expertise in every subset (theology, law, health) touching the main area; he need only be expert in how the flyer's themes relate to historic anti-gay discrimination.
conclusion: Professor Mulé was properly qualified; any deficiencies would go to weight, not admissibility.

issue: Is Professor Mulé so biased or partial that his evidence is inadmissible at the threshold?
facts: The defence argued Mulé was an advocate whose queer-liberation views and report's tone showed an inherent bias, including passages denigrating Whatcott's religious beliefs.
rule: An expert owes a duty of fair, objective and non-partisan evidence to the court; independence and impartiality go to threshold admissibility, but exclusion should occur only in very clear cases where the expert is unable or unwilling to comply. Once the expert attests to understanding the duty, the burden shifts to the opposing party to show inability/unwillingness, which is a high bar: White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co., 2015 SCC 23. An advocate can be an expert (R. v. Shafia, 2016 ONCA 812; R. v. Sadiqi, 2013 ONCA 250).
application: The judge detected a problematic tone in parts of the report denigrating Whatcott's religious beliefs and an assumption of the superiority of 'progressive' over 'fundamental religious' views. However, in his viva voce evidence Mulé was candid, non-argumentative and did not exhibit that tone; his candour reflected a genuine effort to give unbiased evidence, and defence could cross-examine before the jury. This was not one of the rare cases warranting exclusion for bias.
conclusion: Professor Mulé could give unbiased opinion evidence; bias did not render it inadmissible.

issue: Does the cost-benefit gatekeeping analysis favour admission or exclusion of the evidence?
facts: The Crown's proposed evidence concerned tropes of anti-gay discrimination and analysis of a flyer laden with religious and political content.
rule: The trial judge performs a gatekeeper function, weighing the probative value against costs such as time, jury deference to a credentialed expert, and undue complication (R. v. Abbey, 2009 ONCA 624). Evidence that is not necessary has no benefit (Abbey, para. 93).
application: Because the evidence was unnecessary, it had no benefit. Even if necessary, it carried significant costs: it risked turning the trial into a debate about the merits of Whatcott's religious and political beliefs and about competing values, distracting the jury from whether the Crown had proven each element of the offence beyond a reasonable doubt.
conclusion: The cost-benefit analysis favoured exclusion; the application was dismissed.

issue: Did the respondent establish genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to remove the barriers to the applicant's religious remarriage under s. 21.1(4) of the Divorce Act?
facts: The parties married in Lebanon under Jaafari Shari'a authority and were civilly divorced on January 3, 2024. The applicant needs the respondent's consent to obtain an Islamic religious divorce (talaq) to remarry within her faith and to travel safely to Lebanon. The respondent filed an affidavit under s. 21.1(4) asserting that granting talaq while the civil resolution did not accord with Sharia would compromise his religious beliefs. On cross-examination he admitted his religion permits him to grant talaq, that he had done so in two prior marriages, that his young children were not the reason, and ultimately that he refused because the applicant had sued him in civil court; he also refused leverage-seeking evidence about offering consent in exchange for sole custody.
rule: Section 21.1(4) of the Divorce Act permits a court to refuse to strike pleadings where a spouse establishes genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to remove barriers to remarriage. Under Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47, a court does not assess the validity of a religious belief but may inquire into the sincerity of the belief. Bruker v. Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54, held that where a party is not in fact prevented by a tenet of faith from acting, refusal grounded in anger rather than conviction is not a genuine religious objection.
application: The court found the respondent's affidavit reasons unclear and unsupported by expert evidence. Applying Amselem's sincerity inquiry and the reasoning in Bruker, the court noted the respondent admitted his religion allowed him to grant talaq and had granted it twice before, disavowed the children as a reason, and gave shifting explanations before conceding his real reason was that the applicant had sued him civilly. His angry text messages and evasive, non-credible testimony about offering consent for sole custody confirmed the refusal was rooted in anger and bargaining leverage, not sincere religious conviction.
conclusion: The respondent did not present credible evidence of a genuine religious or conscientious belief; the court declined to refuse its powers under s. 21.1(3)(c) and (d).

issue: Can the court compel the respondent to consent to a religious divorce, or is the available remedy limited to striking his pleadings and affidavits?
facts: The applicant sought both an order compelling the respondent to attend the Imam and consent to talaq and an order striking his pleadings under s. 21.1(3). She argued that striking alone was insufficient to free her from the respondent's control over her ability to remarry and travel.
rule: Sections 21.1(3)(c) and (d) of the Divorce Act authorize dismissing an application and striking pleadings where barriers are not removed. Salehi v. Tawoosi, 2016 ONSC 540 (obiter) drew a distinction between striking pleadings and a mandatory injunction compelling a religious act, the latter engaging Charter freedom of religion. Kariminia v. Nasser, 2018 BCSC 695 ordered a party to obtain a religious divorce where the refusing party had not put his religious rights in issue. Bruker (including Deschamps J. dissenting) affirmed that courts should not enforce purely religious obligations.
application: The court accepted it clearly had authority under s. 21.1(3)(c) and (d) to strike the respondent's pleadings and affidavits. However, it found no binding Ontario authority permitting an order compelling a religious divorce; Kariminia was distinguishable (the party there had not participated or raised his Charter rights) and non-binding, and the civil courts should not enforce religious rules. The court gave the respondent 60 days from the Divorce Order to file an affidavit confirming removal of barriers, failing which his pleadings and affidavits would be struck and he could not further participate.
conclusion: The request to compel consent to a religious divorce was dismissed; the remedy was limited to striking the pleadings and affidavits if barriers were not removed within 60 days, though the court strongly encouraged the respondent to grant talaq.

issue: Was the television broadcast defamatory of each plaintiff, and did it sufficiently identify them?
facts: Westcom's 'Okanagan Magazine' broadcast, produced by reporter Blaine Gaffney, depicted the Presslers' Salmon Arm property as a fortified 14,000-square-foot compound with bunkers, perimeter fences and paramilitary potential, portrayed Claus Pressler as a co-founder and active participant in the anti-Semitic Council on Public Affairs, and implied the couple were deceiving municipal officials. In truth they built a 3,165 sq. ft. retirement home with a barn and honey house in full compliance with permits; Claus was only a passive Holocaust revisionist and minor supporter of his wife's activities.
rule: Defamation protects reputation; the test is whether the imputation tended to lower the plaintiffs in the estimation of reasonable, right-minded members of the community (Lewis v. Daily Telegraph Ltd., [1963] 2 All E.R. 151 (H.L.); MacDonald v. Mail Printing Co. (1901), 2 O.L.R. 278). For television the whole thrust and overall impression—words, images, tone, juxtaposition and editing—must be assessed, not merely the literal words (Colour Your World v. CBC; Grossman v. CFTO T.V.; Vogel v. C.B.C.).
application: The court found the broadcast clearly identified both plaintiffs and, through manipulative editing and juxtaposition of rumour with images of the property, conveyed false defamatory meanings: that Claus was a co-founder and active racist participant in the CPA and that both were building a defended paramilitary/convention compound while deceiving officials. These imputations were untrue and lowered the plaintiffs in the community's estimation. Some alleged meanings (portrayal of Lethbridge as credible; the son ordering reporters off; the 'sole watchdog' overstatement) were not defamatory.
conclusion: The broadcast defamed both plaintiffs, particularly through the false land-use/deception imputations and, as to Claus, the false attribution of active CPA involvement.

issue: Is the repetition of rumours actionable and could the defence of justification succeed?
facts: Both Gaffney and Lethbridge spoke partly in terms of 'rumours' about bunkers, a carpeted barn with a spiral staircase, and paramilitary use, while conveying that a defended compound was being built. None of the property rumours had any factual basis, and the building inspector had confirmed compliance before broadcast.
rule: Repeating a rumour is actionable if the rumour is defamatory; it is no defence to prove the rumour existed—the defendant must prove the substance of the rumour true (Cookson v. Harewood, [1932] 2 K.B. 478n; Tucker v. Douglas, [1950] 2 D.L.R. 827 aff'd [1952] 1 S.C.R. 275; X. v. Y., [1947] 2 W.W.R. 1011; Trafton v. Deschene, [1917] 36 D.L.R. 433).
application: The defendants did not prove the truth of the property/deception imputations—there was 'not a jot of evidence' to support them. The overall effect of the broadcast, despite Lethbridge's denial of paramilitary training, was that a defended compound was being built for possible paramilitary use. Lewis was distinguished because there the underlying fact (an actual fraud-squad inquiry) was true; here it was not.
conclusion: The defence of justification failed.

issue: Could the defendants rely on qualified privilege and fair comment?
facts: Westcom argued community concern created a duty to ventilate the rumours; the program was broadcast in the Okanagan, then on CBC Vancouver, and nationally on CBC Newsworld. Lethbridge argued civic duty to oppose racism and anti-Semitism justified wide publication.
rule: Qualified privilege permits honest statements on an occasion of duty/interest, but is lost by malice or non-bona fide use, and excessive publication exceeds the privilege. Fair comment requires (1) a recognizable comment on true facts, (2) a matter of public interest, and (3) that the comment be fair—an honest expression of the speaker's real view (Van Der Zalm v. Times Publishers (1980), 109 D.L.R. (3d) 531; Cherneskey).
application: Although a duty/interest existed in the Okanagan community, the broadcast was neither honestly presented nor believed by Westcom, and its national rebroadcast was too wide to be privileged absent urgent need. Lethbridge's zeal, unfair tarring of the whole family, and deliberate campaign removed the privilege. Fair comment failed on the first and third tests: the imputations were not recognizable as comment on true facts, were not presented as opinion, and were not honest fair views—true of Eileen as racist/anti-Semite but false as to Claus.
conclusion: Both qualified privilege and fair comment failed.

issue: Did the plaintiffs establish express malice?
facts: The raw footage showed Gaffney used ambush interviews, told interviewees the recorder was off, edited and rearranged statements, omitted exculpatory interviews, and used trick photography (a single concrete brick made to look like a trench). Lethbridge orchestrated hate calls, physically struck the Presslers' car at a demonstration, boasted his objective was to ruin the family breadwinner's pharmacy, and recklessly repeated rumours he knew or ought to have known were baseless.
rule: Malice is any indirect motive other than a sense of duty; producing a sensational story at the expense of truth constitutes malice (Vogel v. C.B.C.; Colour Your World v. CBC; R. Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada, 2d ed., at 1049–1051).
application: Westcom's dominant motive was to enhance ratings by producing a sensational, deceptively edited program rather than a balanced one—express malice. Lethbridge acted with an improper motive to drive the family out of town and was reckless as to truth or falsity, including fabricated attributions to municipal official Nash—also express malice.
conclusion: Express malice was established against both defendants, defeating any privilege and fair comment.

issue: Was a conspiracy to defame established?
facts: Lethbridge had no role in editing the broadcast beyond giving his interview; there was no evidence of any agreement between him and Westcom.
rule: Conspiracy requires an express or implied agreement to commit the tort.
application: Nothing in the evidence showed the defendants acted together pursuant to any agreement to defame.
conclusion: No conspiracy was established.

issue: What damages should be awarded?
facts: Eileen was in fact a well-known racist and Holocaust revisionist whose reputation was already low, but was defamed as to land use/deception. Claus lost his lifelong pharmacy career, partly due to the broadcast though other market factors also contributed.
rule: Damages must relate to the plaintiff's actual pre-libel reputation—the closer the libel to the truth, the lower the damages (Neeld v. Western Broadcasting Co. (1976), 65 D.L.R. (3d) 574); courts must not award sums that stifle free expression (Westbank Indian Band v. Tomat (1992), 63 B.C.L.R. (2d) 273).
application: A nominal 'one cent' award was rejected as it would signal that defaming holders of unpopular views is acceptable. Given Eileen's low reputation, modest general damages were fixed; Claus, a comparative innocent whose career was destroyed, received substantially more. Exemplary/punitive damages were declined despite the malice.
conclusion: Eileen Pressler awarded $10,000 against Westcom and $1,500 against Lethbridge; Claus Pressler awarded $50,000 against Westcom and $10,000 against Lethbridge, with ordinary costs on Scale 3 to the plaintiffs.

issue: Does the court lack jurisdiction over the subject matter of the action because the dispute, in its essential character, arises from the collective agreement?
facts: The plaintiff and defendant were unionized teachers at a Catholic secondary school employed by the Durham Catholic District School Board and represented by OECTA under a collective agreement. The defendant made written reports/complaints about the plaintiff's workplace conduct in accordance with the Board's workplace harassment policy; the plaintiff filed his own reciprocal harassment complaint. The plaintiff then sued in tort for defamation, intentional interference with economic relations, and intentional infliction of mental and emotional distress, claiming the statements damaged his reputation as a teacher and OECTA representative.
rule: Rule 21.01(3)(a) of the Rules of Civil Procedure permits dismissal where the court has no jurisdiction over the subject matter. Section 48(1) of the Labour Relations Act, 1995 requires final and binding arbitration of all differences arising from the interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation of a collective agreement. Under Weber v. Ontario Hydro, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 929 and St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. CPU Local 219, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 704, the court must look to the 'essential character' of the dispute, on the facts, not its legal characterization; where the dispute arises from the collective agreement, jurisdiction lies exclusively with the labour arbitrator. Giorno v. Pappas, Sloan v. York Region DSB, De Montigny v. Roy, and Ciulla v. Toronto Catholic DSB confirm that defamation claims between unionized co-workers concerning workplace conduct fall within the collective agreement even where the defendant is a co-worker rather than the employer.
application: The court found the essential character of the dispute was a workplace dispute. The allegedly defamatory statements were written and circulated in the workplace pursuant to workplace policy, made to the common employer, supervisor and union president—persons expected to be informed—and related to the plaintiff's performance and conduct as a teacher. The plaintiff filed a reciprocal harassment complaint, OECTA grieved the surplus/transfer under Article 1.04, and an HRTO application was pending, all reinforcing that the dispute was workplace-related. The Statement of Claim itself described statements about the plaintiff's 'behaviour, conduct, teaching performance and professionalism'. That the fallout allegedly extended beyond the employment context went to severity and remedy, not to essential character.
conclusion: The essential character of the dispute arose from the collective agreement, so the court lacked jurisdiction; the plaintiff's recourse lay in the grievance/arbitration process.

issue: Does the unavailability, inadequacy or delay of arbitration remedies, or a union decision not to grieve, create a remedial gap permitting the court to assume jurisdiction?
facts: The third-party investigation into both complaints concluded in December 2020 with findings partly substantiating each party's allegations, but no follow-up action was taken. The plaintiff argued the harassment process was unfair, stalled, and left him without adequate remedies, and that an arbitrator might lack jurisdiction to award tort damages.
rule: Under Weber (paras. 54-57) and St. Anne Nackawic, courts retain a narrow residual discretion to grant remedies an arbitrator cannot, only to prevent a 'real deprivation of ultimate remedy'. What matters is whether the arbitrator is empowered to remedy the wrong, not whether the remedies mirror court remedies (De Montigny v. Roy, 2018 ONCA 884; Cherubini Metal Works; Greenlaw v. Scott, 2020 ONSC 2028). A union's decision not to pursue a grievance is irrelevant to the court's jurisdiction; the remedy is a duty of fair representation complaint under s. 74 of the LRA to the OLRB. Nor-Man Regional Health Authority, 2011 SCC 59 confirms arbitrators' broad remedial powers, and arbitrators have awarded damages for injury to dignity, harassment and punitive damages.
application: The court held the plaintiff's real complaint was dissatisfaction with the outcome, which does not create a remedial gap. An arbitrator is empowered to remedy the wrong; that lesser or different damages might be available is not determinative. If OECTA declined to arbitrate, the plaintiff could bring a duty of fair representation complaint to the OLRB, which could order a grievance be initiated. The court noted the older Seneca College decision limiting arbitral tort jurisdiction had been called into question by later authority (Greater Toronto Airports Authority).
conclusion: No remedial gap arose; the residual jurisdiction exception did not apply, and the court would not assume jurisdiction.

issue: Should the court instead stay the action, or permit amendment of the pleadings or the addition of OECTA as a party?
facts: The plaintiff sought, in the alternative, a stay pending resolution of the harassment complaints or grievance, or leave to amend to particularize his tort claims and add OECTA as a party. The investigation had concluded over a year earlier with no follow-up; both parties agreed at the hearing that the Board and Union had taken all the steps they would take.
rule: The court has authority to stay under Rule 37.13(1) and s. 106 of the Courts of Justice Act and inherent jurisdiction. Rule 26 governs amendment of pleadings; Rule 5 governs addition of necessary parties. A two-year limitation period applies under the Limitations Act.
application: Because the Board and Union had exhausted their steps, there was nothing to wait for, so a stay was inappropriate. Further particularization would not change the essential character of the claims—the plaintiff had already pleaded all particulars available to him. Adding OECTA was improper: OECTA had not been served or participated, the action had commenced more than three and a half years earlier and the two-year limitation had expired, and compelling OECTA to grieve would be unwarranted interference.
conclusion: The court declined to stay the action or permit amendment/addition of OECTA.

issue: Is the defamation counterclaim statute-barred, or saved by s. 4(1) of the Limitation Act as related to the subject matter of the original action?
facts: The alleged defamatory statements were made March 19 and 29, 2009; the counterclaim was filed March 25, 2015, nearly six years later. Defamation carries a two-year limitation under s. 3(2)(c) of the Limitation Act. Ms. Pour argued the counterclaim was untimely and unrelated to her claim for unpaid food services.
rule: Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 3(2)(c) (two-year limitation for defamation) and s. 4(1), which provides that lapse of time is no bar to proceedings by counterclaim relating to or connected with the subject matter of the original action. ASM Capital Corp. v. Mercer International Inc., 1999 BCCA 353, and Lui v. West Granville Manor Ltd., 1987 CanLII 164 (BC CA), interpret s. 4(1); the 'relation back' theory was rejected in Lui.
application: The court found the counterclaim's theory—that Ms. Pour and the other family members conspired to pressure the Amnis defendants through defamatory statements and an improper action—was related to and connected with Ms. Pour's action, given the interrelationship of the claims and the plaintiffs' decision to advance them together against all 12 defendants. The 'relation back' argument was rejected per Lui, since s. 4(1) eliminates the limitation defence entirely for related counterclaims.
conclusion: Section 4(1) applies; the limitation period does not bar the defamation counterclaim. The first two arguments failed.

issue: Do the pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action against Ms. Pour under Rule 9-5(1)(a)?
facts: The defamatory emails were sent by Amir Yashar Shoolestani, not Ms. Pour, and related to engineering work; her own claim was for food services. The counterclaim alleged she concurred in and was equally responsible for the emails and conspired with the other plaintiffs in bringing the action.
rule: Rule 9-5(1)(a): a claim is struck only if, assuming pleaded facts to be true, it is 'plain and obvious' the claim cannot succeed; novel or complex claims should not be struck (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., 1990 CanLII 90 (SCC); R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada, 2011 SCC 42; Watson v. Bank of America Corporation, 2014 BCSC 532).
application: Taking the pleaded facts as true—that Ms. Pour participated in a conspiracy involving publication of defamatory statements and improper litigation for an improper purpose—the counterclaim raised a triable issue. Complexity or novelty is not a basis to strike. No affidavit merely contradicting the pleadings could displace this on a 9-5(1)(a) application.
conclusion: It was not plain and obvious the claim could not succeed; the counterclaim disclosed a triable issue. This argument failed.

issue: Does the failure to quote the defamatory emails accurately render the pleading fatally defective?
facts: The counterclaim paraphrased rather than quoted the March 2009 emails; counsel conceded the emails were not accurately quoted but said this was done for conciseness and was a fair reading.
rule: Striking is a draconian remedy that should not be granted where the deficiency can be cured by amendment or a less severe order (Sahyoun v. Ho, 2015 BCSC 392, aff'd 2017 BCCA 96; Royal Bank of Canada v. Roberts, 2014 BCSC 1797).
application: The court agreed the emails should have been quoted accurately but held the deficiency was not fatal and could be cured by a more proportionate remedy—leave to amend to properly quote the emails.
conclusion: Pleading not struck on this ground; leave to amend granted.

issue: Can a malicious prosecution claim stand where the underlying proceeding has not terminated in the claimant's favour?
facts: Ms. Pour's claim for monies owed was ongoing when the counterclaim was filed and remained extant. She had discontinued her action against some corporate defendants but continued against Mr. Ichikawa.
rule: Nelles v. Ontario, 1989 CanLII 77 (SCC), sets four elements for malicious prosecution, including that the proceedings must have terminated in favour of the plaintiff. Abuse of process, by contrast, does not require termination (311165 B.C. Ltd. v. Canada (A.G.), 2017 BCCA 196).
application: When the counterclaim was filed the Amnis defendants had no cause of action for malicious prosecution because Ms. Pour's claim was ongoing. Her discontinuance against related corporate entities—done to clarify her claim was against Mr. Ichikawa—was not a 'termination in favour of the plaintiff'. The defect was not cured.
conclusion: No cause of action for malicious prosecution existed; paragraph 4 of the prayer for relief (damages for malicious prosecution) was struck against Ms. Pour.

issue: Did the plaintiff establish that Mr Veck published defamatory statements of and concerning Mr Warman?
facts: Mr Veck, a WAIS website member, posted an article in March 2009 that reproduced the entire text of a retracted National Post article and amplified it, stating in effect that Mr Warman was 'corrupt', 'surreal', 'strange', a 'radical anti-racist' who had fabricated a racist article about Senator Cools and manufactured 'phony-racism', asserting the National Post allegations were true.
rule: To make out defamation the plaintiff must show the words were defamatory, referred to the plaintiff, and were published; posting on the internet constitutes publication (Barrick Gold Corp. v. Lopehandia, 2004 CanLII 12938 (ON CA)). Repetition is not a defence — one who repeats a defamatory statement is answerable as if he had started it (Associated Newspapers Ltd. v. Dingle, [1964] A.C. 371).
application: The court found the article clearly imputed dishonest and quasi-criminal conduct to Mr Warman — creating hate speech to advance anti-hate complaints — which was obviously defamatory, was clearly of and about Mr Warman, and was published by posting to the WAIS website. That much of the content was drawn from Mr Kay's National Post article did not assist Mr Veck.
conclusion: The three elements of defamation were established; the article was defamatory of Mr Warman.

issue: Did Mr Veck have a legal defence of fair comment, qualified privilege, or responsible communication?
facts: Mr Veck argued his post was fair comment on a matter of public interest, was made on an occasion of qualified privilege, and was responsible communication. He was not a journalist, had read only the National Post article, did not learn it had been retracted, did no further research, and did not contact Mr Warman.
rule: Fair comment protects statements of opinion, not assertions of fact, and comment must appear as comment (WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40). Qualified privilege attaches to an occasion where the publisher has a legal, moral or social duty to communicate and the recipient a corresponding interest (Hill v. Church of Scientology, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130); publication to 'the world' on the internet is generally overpublication (Vigna v. Levant, 2010 ONSC 6308). Responsible communication generally applies to journalists acting professionally (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61).
application: The post was a statement of facts, not opinion; the epithets were rhetorical responses to defamatory facts rather than distinguishable comment, so fair comment failed. There was no reciprocal duty/interest and publication to the entire internet was overpublication, so no occasion of qualified privilege arose. Mr Veck was not a journalist, there was no urgency, he did not seek Mr Warman's side, and the matters were already public — responsible communication did not apply.
conclusion: None of the defences succeeded; Mr Veck was liable.

issue: What quantum of general damages should be awarded?
facts: The article was posted to the entire internet but remained on WAIS for about 18 months without Mr Warman, who vigilantly monitored statements about himself, becoming aware of it. Mr Veck was a lawyer but not identified as such in the post; there was no claim for economic loss or special damages, and no malice.
rule: General damages in defamation are assessed on all the circumstances, including extent of publication; a lawyer's defamatory statement can aggravate damages only where professional status lends credibility, and aggravated damages require malice or egregious conduct.
application: The court inferred from the lack of detection that few persons actually read the article. Mr Veck's status as a lawyer was immaterial since he was not identified as one. He acted without malice, reacting to a reputable newspaper article he believed true, so aggravated damages were not warranted.
conclusion: General damages of $10,000 were awarded; no aggravated damages.

issue: Did Mr Veck's retraction and apology reduce the damages?
facts: After receiving the libel notice Mr Veck removed the article and posted a statement noting that Mr Warman said the allegations were false and retracting and apologizing on that basis, without acknowledging the article was without foundation.
rule: Under the Libel and Slander Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.12, s. 9, a full and effective retraction and apology may mitigate or eliminate damages; the adequacy of the apology is assessed on its substance.
application: The retraction amounted only to a withdrawal because Mr Warman disagreed, and stopped short of acknowledging the article lacked foundation. Mr Veck could at least have stated that the source article had been withdrawn by its author and that he had no personal knowledge of the matters, but did not. The apology fell so short of a full and effective one that no reduction was warranted.
conclusion: The apology and retraction did not reduce the damages; judgment for Mr Warman for $10,000.

issue: Did the testator have the required capacity to make the November 12, 2010 will?
facts: Professor Boss, an intellectually distinguished McGill historian, suffered a series of medical incidents (prostate cancer, a June/July 2010 bout of pancreatitis causing encephalopathy and delirium, gall-bladder surgery) and was later diagnosed (2011-2014) with Lewy Body/Parkinson's dementia. He nonetheless continued teaching two courses in fall 2010 and gave the will instructions directly to the notary.
rule: Art. 703 and 707 C.C.Q.: every person with the required capacity may make a will, capacity assessed at the moment of execution. There is a presumption of capacity; the contestant bears the initial burden and, on prima facie proof of a serious (not merely simple) doubt on the balance of probabilities, the burden shifts to the proponent (Paquin v. Trottier; Succession de Charette, 2017 QCCS 1381). Capacity requires the power to hold the essential field of the mind in appreciation as a whole (McEwen v. Jenkins; Thibodeau v. Thibodeau).
application: The Court rejected the plaintiff's expert (Dr. Brock) for bias and accepted the neurologist Dr. Verret, who concluded that the delirium was transient and reversible, that Lewy Body disease was diagnosed only a year later, and that Boss was near his pre-delirium cognitive state in November 2010. The notary Rapp and numerous affiants confirmed his lucidity, though the Court found some cognitive diminution had occurred by then.
conclusion: Professor Boss had the requisite capacity to execute the will; the incapacity argument was rejected.

issue: Was the will the product of undue influence (captation) by Milica?
facts: The will effectively disinherited Sylvia (Boss's only child, whom he loved despite her bipolar illness), leaving essentially the whole estate to Milica. Independent witnesses described Milica's hostility toward Sylvia, statements that Sylvia deserved to inherit nothing, her control of Boss's social contacts (lawyers' cease-and-desist letters, supervised final visit), her management/censoring of his correspondence, and Boss's growing physical and emotional dependence on her amid some cognitive decline.
rule: Captation requires fraudulent manoeuvres (improper schemes, lies, deceit) that were determinative of the testator's dispositions (Succession de Charette; Brusenbauch v. Young). Capacity does not preclude coercion where weakened faculties reduce the testator's resistance (Brière; Tewkesbury v. Ouellet; Thibault v. Auger). Proof may rest on serious, precise and concordant presumptions (arts. 2846, 2849 C.C.Q.; Longpré v. Thériault), the precision test being one of probability, not near-certainty (Ducharme).
application: The Court found the near-total exclusion of a beloved daughter unexplained and out of character; Milica's antipathy, sense of entitlement to the whole estate, control over Boss's contacts and correspondence, and his dependence and diminished cognition together formed a concordant pattern. Milica's credibility was rejected as she contradicted eight independent witnesses. These facts founded a serious and precise presumption of undue influence.
conclusion: Undue influence was established; the will was annulled and the succession devolves ab intestat under art. 666 C.C.Q.

issue: Should the plaintiff's expert report be excluded?
facts: Dr. Brock's reports lacked the art. 235 C.C.P. declaration initially, he had not been recognized as an expert, and he attended trial acting as a coach/advocate for the plaintiff, speculating on Milica's motives and overstepping the Court's limits.
rule: Art. 22 C.C.P. requires experts to act objectively and impartially; the acid test is whether the opinion would be the same regardless of who retained the expert (White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co., 2015 SCC 23). Arts. 235, 293 C.C.P. govern the declaration and recognition of experts.
application: The declaration defect was cured by refiling; Brock was recognized as an expert in medicine for the aged but not on delirium. However, his manifest bias and advocacy destroyed his usefulness and credibility.
conclusion: All evidence authored by Dr. Brock was rejected except where corroborated by Milica's expert; the exhibit filing objection (P-81.1-.3) was maintained.

issue: Should Milica's cross-demand for defamation succeed?
facts: Milica claimed damages for allegedly false, outrageous and malicious allegations in Sylvia's pleadings (that she abused, controlled and manipulated Boss) and for counsel's use of the word 'greedy' in a case-management conference.
rule: Allegations consistent with and supportive of a genuine claim, made in the context of legal proceedings, are not actionable defamation.
application: The impugned statements were neither outrageous nor malicious but were consistent with a supportable claim of coercion; moreover, para. 110's allegation of manipulation was found proven. Milica's exaggerated claim bordered on abuse.
conclusion: The cross-demand was dismissed with costs; Helen would not have been liable in any event.

issue: Should the plaintiff be compelled to produce the unredacted 12,000+ page appendices to the ICE Report, or were relevance redactions justified under the protocol and proportionality?
facts: In a defamation action alleging Warman authored a 'Hateful Posting', the Court had earlier ordered an Independent Computer Expert to examine a mirror image of Warman's hard drive to determine whether he authored the posting. Single-word searches generated over 12,000 pages of raw data in appendices, which Warman's counsel vetted and heavily redacted for relevance and privilege. Levant moved to obtain the unredacted appendices.
rule: Rule 76 (Simplified Procedure) and Rule 29.2 of the Rules of Civil Procedure require proportionality in discovery; the court must consider time, expense, prejudice, interference with the orderly progress of the action, and overall volume of documents (r. 29.2.03). Parties need only produce relevant documents (Rule 30). Privacy interests in personal computers are heightened: R. v. Vu, 2013 SCC 60; R. v. Morelli, 2010 SCC 8.
application: The Master found the single-word searches produced an enormous, unforeseen volume of raw data, most of it irrelevant to the narrow question of authorship of the Hateful Posting. The protocol, though silent on relevance, was implicitly intended to narrow, not expand, production. Ordering disclosure of 12,000+ pages, requiring further multi-party review, would defeat the Simplified Procedure's goals of economy and speed, was disproportionate, and would sweepingly invade Warman's heightened privacy interest in his personal computer. The core purpose of the order had been achieved: no evidence of the Hateful Posting existed on the drive.
conclusion: Production of the unredacted appendices was refused; relevance redactions were permitted and proportionality favoured denying the motion.

issue: Must the plaintiff provide fuller particulars of his solicitor-client and litigation privilege claims?
facts: Warman redacted appendices citing solicitor-client privilege, litigation privilege and irrelevancy, providing a revised list of objections that did not always identify document type, date, or the related proceedings. Levant argued he could not assess or challenge the claims.
rule: Schedule 'B' privilege claims must identify the privilege, the parties to the communication, its author, and a description sufficient to show relevance (Shibish v. Honda of Canada Inc., 2010 ONSC 3770); factual information in privileged documents that would otherwise be disclosable is not shielded. Litigation privilege endures only to the end of related litigation and yields more readily than solicitor-client privilege (Kaymar Rehabilitation Inc. v. Champlain CCAC, 2013 ONSC 1754).
application: The Master accepted that counsel had reasonably established that all relevant files—those establishing whether Warman authored the Hateful Posting or relating to other issues—had been produced. Requiring Warman to re-review 12,000+ pages to further particularize privilege claims over predominantly irrelevant material would be wasteful, delay the action, and serve only the 'fishing expedition' Levant had sworn he was not pursuing. Levant's own Schedule B was itself devoid of particulars.
conclusion: The request for full particulars of the privilege claims was dismissed.

issue: Had the plaintiff satisfied the ICE Protocol and the Court's original production order?
facts: The ICE Report and earlier Digital Wyzdom reports confirmed no evidence on Warman's hard drive of the Hateful Posting, the pseudonym used, or the registering email address.
rule: An order must be complied with according to its spirit and intent, applying common sense and logic where the literal outcome was unanticipated.
application: The order's purpose—a second opinion on whether Warman could have authored the Hateful Posting—had been fulfilled; the redactions to the appendices did not affect that conclusion. The order was designed to limit, not expand, Levant's access; handing over 12,000+ pages of raw data was contrary to its intent and to the Simplified Procedure Rule. With discoveries now available under amended Rule 76, Levant's original justification for computer access no longer held.
conclusion: The order's spirit and intent had been satisfied; the motion was dismissed with costs to Warman on a partial indemnity basis.

issue: Was the 2020 Will the product of undue influence (captation) by Boris Zalac, rendering it null?
facts: After a 35-year loving relationship, the testator made mirror wills with his spouse Ms. Bouchard in 2015, naming her sole universal legatee. In 2019-2020 his health collapsed (legally blind, hip pain, hearing impairment, depression, isolation, heavy drinking). During the COVID lockdown Boris Zalac, his son, retained his own notary, booked and followed up on appointments, reviewed the draft will and mandate, brought his father to sign, chose his own spouse as witness, and became sole heir and liquidator under the 2020 Will. Ms. Bouchard was never informed; she even unknowingly paid the notary's invoice.
rule: Under the Civil Code of Quebec and Stoneham and Tewkesbury v. Ouellet, [1979] 2 SCR 172, captation consists of fraudulent maneuvers that determine how a testator bequeaths; currying favour is not illegal but seizing the testator's will is. Per Brusenbauch v. Young, 2019 QCCA 914, the party alleging undue influence must prove fraud, defect in consent and causation on a balance of probabilities (arts. 2803, 2804 C.c.Q.), often through serious, precise and concordant presumptions of fact (art. 2849 C.c.Q.). Section 48 of the Quebec Charter protects aged persons against exploitation.
application: The Court found the testator vulnerable, isolated and dependent, and rejected Boris Zalac's portrayal of a 'toxic' marriage as unsupported (all corroborating texts postdated 2019). Numerous indicia from M.P. c. F.D. were present: the heir chose the notary, drove the process, approved drafts, selected the witness, and became sole heir/liquidator, with a complacent notary who missed the testator's impairments. The powerful and only reasonable inference was that Boris exploited his father's weakened state to redirect the estate to himself, contrary to s. 48 of the Quebec Charter.
conclusion: The Plaintiff discharged her burden; the 2020 Will was declared null and void and the estate devolved under the 2015 Will, with Boris ordered to reimburse amounts he paid himself and his lawyers from the Estate.

issue: Should Boris Zalac be declared unworthy of inheriting under arts. 621-623 C.c.Q.?
facts: The Plaintiff added a conclusion in her Modified Application of July 22, 2022 seeking a declaration of unworthiness against Boris Zalac; the succession opened on the testator's death on March 5, 2021.
rule: Articles 621-623 C.c.Q. allow a successor to apply, within one year after the opening of the succession or becoming aware of a cause of unworthiness, to have an heir declared unworthy.
application: Because the 2020 Will was nullified and the 2015 Will (which does not name Boris as a legatee) governs, the unworthiness question is moot. Additionally, the conclusion was added more than one year after the succession opened, so it was time-barred under art. 623.
conclusion: The Court declined to declare Boris unworthy; the conclusion failed as both moot and out of time.

issue: Should the mother have sole custody of the children and what residential/access arrangement serves the best interests of the youngest child, A.E.S.?
facts: The parties are highly conflicted; the four oldest children have no or minimal relationship with the father, and the father consented to the mother having custody of the three girls.
