The plaintiffs alleged no personal dispute existed between them and Douek (the conflict being between a trust/companies), and Jacques Glecer was neither a trust beneficiary nor a company member.
conclusion: The motion to dismiss was rejected; a trial is necessary to dispose of the defamation claim.

issue: Does the fact that the disseminated document was a true (accurate) rabbinical judgment preclude defamation fault, defeating the action?
facts: Douek argued he did no more than relay an authentic ruling of the Beth Din of Geneva; the content circulated was the accurate translation of the tribunal's decision (P-8).
rule: In Quebec civil law the communication of true information may nonetheless constitute a fault (Prud'homme c. Prud'homme, 2002 SCC 85). Where statements are true, liability still arises if the author had no serious and legitimate duty or interest in reporting them (Piquemal c. Cassivi-Lefebvre, [1997] R.R.A. 300 (C.A.)). Defamation can consist in devaluing a person or diminishing their respectability.
application: Because truth of the reported content does not automatically negate fault, and because the choice of recipients and the alleged intent to injure the plaintiffs' reputation within their community were central and unresolved, the defendant could not obtain dismissal merely by pleading he reported a rabbinical judgment. These questions require the full evidentiary record.
conclusion: Truth of the ruling does not render the action bound to fail; the fault question must be determined at trial.

issue: What threshold of unreasonable conduct must be shown to obtain a costs order between parents in a child protection case where one parent breaches an access order and the society takes no position?
facts: The father moved to enforce a December 17, 2019 access order after the mother refused to resume his in-person access to the two younger children and imposed unreasonable pre-conditions. The Children's Aid Society of Toronto took no position on the access order; the dispute was strictly between the parents.
rule: Under subrule 24(2) of the Family Law Rules there is no presumption that a successful party is entitled to costs in a child protection case (Mattina v. Mattina, 2018 ONCA 867). Case law generally requires a very high threshold of extreme or excessive unreasonable conduct before ordering costs between parents (CAS of Toronto v. S.T., 2018 ONCJ 573; Children and Family Services for York Region v. S.(A.), 2010 ONSC 1287). Clause 1(8)(a) permits a costs order where a person fails to obey a court order, without differential treatment for protection litigants.
application: The court reasoned that the high 'extreme/excessive' threshold protects parents from being deterred from vigorously litigating against a well-resourced society. Where the dispute mirrors a Children's Law Reform Act access dispute and the society takes no position, that rationale does not apply. The closer such a dispute resembles a custody/access dispute, and given the harm caused by breaching access orders and the cost of enforcement, ordinary unreasonable behaviour (not extreme conduct) should suffice for entitlement.
conclusion: The court held that a parent who successfully moves to enforce an access order against the other parent need only demonstrate unreasonable behaviour, not extreme or excessive unreasonable conduct, to establish entitlement to costs.

issue: How should the COVID-19 pandemic affect entitlement to and quantum of costs where a parent refused to comply with an access order out of health concerns?
facts: The mother declined to restore in-person access for over two months after the father's May 19, 2020 request, imposing conditions that the father take all children if she contracted the virus or permanently if she died, citing pandemic health and safety fears.
rule: A parent may not engage in self-help or treat public health directives as a licence to terminate parenting time; specifics must be provided and a motion to change brought (Ahmadi v. Kalashi, 2020 ONSC 2047; Catholic CAS of Toronto v. C.P.I., 2020 ONCJ 304). Courts may still order costs for pandemic-era access denial (Smith v. Smith, 2020 ONCJ 219; Medu v. Medu, 2020 ONSC 3159) but may discount costs given pandemic pressures (Winiarz v. Anderson, 2020 ONCJ 238).
application: The court accepted that some delay was understandable while the mother consulted counsel and sought health-protocol assurances, but her unilateral imposition of pre-conditions and refusal for over two months was unreasonable. Following the Winiarz approach, the court recognized the difficult health decisions parents face during the pandemic and the mother's subjective fears, using these to discount rather than eliminate costs.
conclusion: The pandemic did not bar a costs award; the mother's conduct was unreasonable, but the difficult pandemic circumstances and her subjective fears justified reducing the quantum of costs.

issue: Is the father entitled to costs of the enforcement motion, and in what amount?
facts: The father repeatedly and reasonably sought resumption of access, moved to enforce only after being refused, and promptly served an offer to settle that (with minor amendments) formed the basis of settlement. His actual bill was just over $2,300. The mother is of very limited means and had already failed to pay a prior $1,000 costs order made by Justice Paulseth.
rule: Costs are discretionary and governed by reasonableness and proportionality (Beaver v. Hill, 2018 ONCA 840), the factors in subrules 24(12), 24(4), 24(8) and 18 offers to settle (Berta v. Berta, 2015 ONCA 918), and ability to pay (MacDonald v. Magel; Snih v. Snih), though limited means is not a shield. Receipt of legal aid is irrelevant (Ramcharitar; Alvarez).
application: The father acted reasonably, was successful, and was unnecessarily put to the expense of the motion; his time and rates were reasonable. Costs orders serve to change behaviour and discourage future breaches, particularly given the mother's developing pattern of non-compliance. The court discounted the award for the pandemic, the mother's reasonable counter-offer, and her limited means, allowing payment in installments.
conclusion: The father was entitled to partial indemnity costs of $900, payable at $50 per month from October 1, 2020, with the full balance becoming due if a payment is more than 30 days late.

issue: Did the mother establish the Article 13(b) defence that returning the child to Perú would create a grave risk of harm or place her in an intolerable situation?
facts: Shelli, age 5, was habitually resident in Perú when the mother, permitted to visit Canada under a Peruvian order, refused to return her. The mother conceded the retention was wrongful under Articles 3, 5 and 12, so she bore the onus under Article 13(b). The evidence showed sustained psychological and physical abuse and intimidation of the mother by the father and his family — death threats, implicit gun intimidation, a violent SUV confrontation with the child in the back seat, a physical altercation in which the grandmother bit the child, unlawful withholding of the child, and Peruvian psychological reports finding the child was affected by family violence.
rule: Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention (incorporated by s. 46 of the Children's Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12) permits refusal of return where there is a grave risk that return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm or otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation. The threshold is high: Thomson v. Thomson, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 551 (harm must amount to an intolerable situation; source of harm is irrelevant from a child-centred view); Pollastro v. Pollastro (1999, ONCA) (returning a child to a violent environment is inherently intolerable and the harm to the parent on whom the child depends is relevant); Re E (children), [2011] UKSC 27 (a situation this particular child should not be expected to tolerate). Focus is on immediate risk, not a broad best-interests inquiry (Eliassen).
application: Following a full trial, Perkins J. preferred the evidence of the mother and her witnesses, finding the home was one of oppression and abuse and that the father and his family repeatedly used threats and force, disobeying court orders. Applying the high but humane Re E standard, the court found Shelli, now more aware of her surroundings, should not be expected to tolerate the situation she left and would face again, and that any child returned to it would likely suffer serious psychological harm; there was also a real risk the mother would be arrested on entry, suddenly severing the child from her sole reliable caregiver.
conclusion: The mother met the Article 13(b) onus; a return would expose Shelli to a grave risk of psychological harm or an intolerable situation.

issue: Could undertakings or protective/temporary orders alleviate the risk so that return should still be ordered?
facts: The father offered undertakings that the mother would keep custody until a Peruvian court decided otherwise, that he would pay return costs, would not contact the child except as directed, and would try to arrange with the Peruvian liaison judge to make the mother comfortable. He could not, however, bind his parents (who had their own defamation suit against the mother) nor the Peruvian prosecutors and courts handling criminal and enforcement proceedings against the mother.
rule: Courts must consider mitigation through undertakings, temporary orders, or judicial cooperation with the requested state's liaison judge before refusing return (Thomson; Re E; Hoole v. Hoole, 2008 BCSC 1248). There is a presumption the child's home jurisdiction can protect the child, rebuttable by the abducting parent (Ireland v. Ireland, 2011 ONCA 623; Finizio).
application: The court found none of the four options adequate. Direct communication with the Peruvian liaison judge was hampered by language and terminology barriers experienced in the case. Undertakings or orders could bind only the father, not his family or Peruvian authorities, could not be effectively enforced by contempt across jurisdiction, and — most importantly — the father and his family had shown they would not obey court orders. The presumption of home-jurisdiction protection was rebutted.
conclusion: No undertakings or protective measures could eliminate or alleviate the risk; option four (refusal of return) was the appropriate remedy.

issue: Did the mother's parallel litigation in Perú and Ontario constitute forum shopping or an abuse of process?
facts: The mother actively litigated custody, access, support and domestic-violence issues in Perú before and after coming to Canada, with appeals still pending at the Supreme Court of Perú, while also defending the Hague application and advancing a custody claim in Ontario.
rule: Attornment and abuse of process principles; a party who defends and asserts a custody claim in response to a Hague application does not thereby engage in improper forum shopping where continued participation in foreign proceedings is necessary to protect existing rights.
application: Until November 2010 the mother properly pursued her only available remedies in Perú. Afterwards she launched no new proceedings save appeals and a travel-extension request; her Ontario custody claim arose only because the father sued here and a Peruvian chasing order stripped her of enforceable custody rights. Continuing to defend her Peruvian rights was prudent, not abusive.
conclusion: There was no attornment, forum shopping, or abuse of process; the father retains his defences to the mother's custody claim.

issue: When a defendant pleads justification, what test governs the grant of an interlocutory injunction to restrain alleged defamation, and did the plaintiffs satisfy it?
facts: The plaintiffs sought an interlocutory injunction to force Brent Hillier to remove and stop posting internet statements describing Hutchens as a conman running a mortgage/advance-fee scam. Hillier admitted posting under his own name and pleaded justification, pointing to Hutchens' fraud convictions, a Law Society disbarment of a lawyer for assisting Hutchens, adverse court comments, a TD Bank disclaimer letter, and multiple foreign lawsuits alleging an advance-fee scam.
rule: An injunction to restrain alleged defamation where the defendant pleads justification will not be granted 'unless the plaintiff is able to satisfy the court at the interlocutory stage that the words are both clearly defamatory and impossible to justify' (Sharpe, Injunctions and Specific Performance; Rapp v. McClelland & Stewart; Canada Metal Co. v. CBC). The American Cyanamid balance-of-convenience test does not apply (Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Canadian Liberty Net).
application: The court found the motions judge in March 2009 wrongly applied a balance-of-convenience analysis. On the extensive record — Hutchens' fraud record, the Ross lawyers' fraud conclusions, the disbarment reasons, the Murad decision, the TD disclaimer, newspaper articles and foreign advance-fee-scam actions — the court held it was impossible to say Hillier's words were clearly defamatory and impossible to justify. This was not one of the rare and clearest of cases warranting prior restraint of speech.
conclusion: The test was not met in March 2009 and was not met on the current motion; the injunction against Hillier was refused.

issue: Did the plaintiffs' misuse of the ex parte orders disentitle them to equitable relief under the clean hands doctrine?
facts: The plaintiffs represented to the court that 'mavman' was an anonymous poster requiring the extraordinary relief, when they knew mavman was Brent Hillier and how to reach him since September 2008. They then enforced the SCAM.COM orders against Hillier (who had no connection to SCAM.COM), brought a misleading contempt motion, and asserted the orders bound other internet sites such as tdotballers.com, Jewish Whistleblower and Google.
rule: Injunctions and Anton Piller orders are equitable remedies; a party seeking them must come with clean hands, the misconduct relating directly to the transaction in issue (Sherwood Dash Inc. v. Woodview Products; City of Toronto v. Polai).
application: The court found the plaintiffs did not come to court with clean hands: they misled the court about Hillier's identity and anonymity, used the orders as a sword against a non-target and against unrelated websites, and pursued Hillier without notice or an opportunity to be heard.
conclusion: The plaintiffs' extensive misuse of the equitable relief supported denial of the further equitable relief they requested.

issue: Did the plaintiffs' delay in moving the action to trial justify dissolving the interlocutory injunction?
facts: The March 2009 orders had been in place for 20 months. Aside from pursuing Hillier and other websites, the plaintiffs took no meaningful steps to trial and did not add the identified anonymous posters as defendants. Hutchens' health accounted for at most six months, and his own affidavit showed he was content to let the action sit dormant once the postings quieted.
rule: A plaintiff who obtains an interlocutory injunction must proceed expeditiously to trial; unexplained inordinate delay leads to dissolution (Bourganis v. Glarentzos; Ciba-Geigy Ltd. v. Novopharm Ltd.; IGM Resources; Levert Personnel Resources v. LeClair).
application: The court found the delay inordinate and inexcusable with no credible explanation, and that the plaintiffs treated the interim relief as a final determination, silencing Hillier while the action languished, prejudicing his access to his computer and his free-speech rights.
conclusion: The delay independently required the March orders to be dissolved.

issue: Did the March 2009 Anton Piller order apply to Brent Hillier, and were its conditions met?
facts: The Anton Piller order authorized entry and seizure of 'Evidence' from SCAM.COM, its officers/agents and persons in charge of its premises. Hillier had no connection to SCAM.COM other than posting on the site. Authorized persons, a supervising solicitor and police attended his home; on adjournment of the contempt motion he was ordered to surrender his computer.
rule: An Anton Piller order is a draconian remedy for extreme cases requiring four conditions: a strong prima facie case; very serious potential or actual damage; convincing evidence the defendant possesses incriminating material; and a real possibility that material will be destroyed before discovery (Celanese Canada Inc. v. Murray Demolition Corp.).
application: No reasonable reading of the order extended it to Hillier, and none of the Celanese conditions had been established against him because the plaintiffs never disclosed any intention to target him. The April order directing him to surrender his computer was merely a term of an adjournment based on a misleading motion and did not bind him.
conclusion: The Anton Piller order did not apply to Hillier; his computer and other items held by the supervising solicitor were ordered returned immediately.

issue: Did the article contain statements capable of, and in fact bearing, a defamatory meaning of the plaintiff?
facts: Lyn Cockburn, an editorial writer with The Winnipeg Sun, published an article on June 17, 2000 headlined 'Stow your sympathy for maligned prof', responding to a column supportive of Henry Makow, a stipendiary University of Winnipeg lecturer whose contract was not renewed after student complaints. Makow pleaded 12 statements as defamatory, alleging they portrayed him as irresponsible, immoral, bigoted, dishonest, intimidating and incompetent, and unfit to retain his position.
rule: Per Laufer v. Bucklaschuk, 1999 CanLII 5073 (MB CA), a trial judge first decides as law whether the words are capable of the pleaded defamatory meaning and relate to the plaintiff, then (as trier of fact) whether they are defamatory. The test is objective and one of reasonableness (Jones v. Skelton; Capital and Counties Bank v. George Henty), giving words their ordinary and natural meaning in context and reading the article as a whole (Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada; Leenen v. CBC).
application: Sitting as both gatekeeper and fact-finder after the jury was excused, Monnin J. examined each statement in context. He found statements 1–6 and 8–12 capable of and bearing defamatory meanings (imputing beating a girlfriend, sexually loaded questioning of students in and out of class, bigoted remarks about religious Jews and Muslims, shouting, discussing his sex life, intimidation, unprofessional conduct, unfitness). Only statement 7 (that Makow 'twisted the situation') was found incapable of a defamatory meaning.
conclusion: The article contained numerous statements that were, in their ordinary meaning and context, defamatory of Makow and would tend to lower his reputation; statement 7 was not defamatory.

issue: Could the defendants establish justification (substantial truth) for the defamatory statements?
facts: The defendants called five student witnesses; the plaintiff called himself and seven students. Cockburn drew most of her information from a single student, Ms Feuer, and did not verify all allegations with Makow or others. Evidence differed on whether Makow 'beat' his girlfriend, questioned a student about losing her 'innocence', asked about arousal from a novel, disparaged religious dress, shouted, discussed relationships, and whether complainants had reason to fear him.
rule: Once words are defamatory they are presumed false and the defendant must prove they are substantially true, meeting the 'gist' or 'sting' of the charge; slight inaccuracies do not defeat the defence (Gatley on Libel and Slander; Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada). Truth is measured at the time of publication; a defendant cannot justify by proving the plaintiff engaged in other equally reprehensible conduct, nor by honest belief in third-party information.
application: Monnin J. found justification proven only for statement 1 (physical violence against his girlfriend), statement 3 in respect of comments made in class (the 'innocence' question to Ms Rauscher, whose direct evidence he preferred), statement 6(b) (out-of-class inquiries about relationships, per Ms Dean and Ms Sampson) and 6(c) (discussing his own sexual conduct), and statement 10 (a signed, non-anonymous letter of complaint, the seven/four discrepancy being immaterial to the sting). Justification failed for the out-of-class portion of statement 3, statement 4 (arousal question to a specific student), statement 5 (bigoted remark about Jews/Muslims), the shouting element of 6(a), and statements 8–9 (fear/intimidation). Web-site writings post-dating publication did not establish that Makow was unfit at the time of the libel.
conclusion: The defence of justification succeeded only for statements 1, 3 (in-class), 6(b), 6(c) and 10; the remaining defamatory statements were not justified.

issue: Could the defendants rely on fair comment for the statements of opinion?
facts: Certain statements (2, and 11–12) expressed opinion — that the dispute was about 'unprofessional conduct' and that a professor making inappropriate remarks should be removed. The matter had attracted public attention through prior articles and Makow's own interviews and human-rights complaint. Qualified privilege had been abandoned at trial.
rule: Fair comment protects honest opinion on a matter of public interest, provided the words are comment not fact, and are based on facts truly stated (Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada; Hunt v. The Star Newspaper; Digby v. The Financial News; Winnipeg Steel Granary v. Canada Ingot Iron Culvert). If the underlying facts are not proven true, the comment cannot be fair; malice defeats the defence.
application: The court accepted the matter was of public interest and that statements 2 and 11–12 were capable of being comment. However, statements 11–12 rested on the premise that Makow had made all the alleged inappropriate remarks; because only some were proven true, the factual foundation was not established, so the opinion that he should be removed could not qualify as fair comment.
conclusion: Fair comment did not save the unjustified defamatory opinion in statements 11 and 12 because the facts underpinning them were not substantially true.

issue: What damages flowed from the unjustified defamatory statements?
facts: The Sun was widely circulated and the article was republished in the corporation's London and Toronto papers. Cockburn admitted her purpose was partly to present the complainants' side and to stimulate debate, and that she did not put all allegations to Makow. No special/pecuniary damages were claimed. Defendants adduced Makow's own web-site writings and self-published book to attack his reputation and support justification.
rule: Damages for defamation are primarily compensatory and, for damages at large, assessed by reference to the nature of the publication, the victim, its effects and the defendants' conduct (Hill v. Church of Scientology; Leenen v. CBC). A failed or partial justification can aggravate or, where partly proven, mitigate damages (Pamplin; Burstein). Bad reputation may reduce damages but the defendant bears the onus, and reputation is presumed impeccable absent proof (Plato Films v. Speidel; Wiley v. Toronto Star). Aggravated damages require high-handed or malicious conduct (Hill; Walker v. CFTO).
application: Makow was defamed by unproven imputations (out-of-class questioning about losing innocence, the arousal question to a specific student, the bigoted remark about religious dress, and intimidation). His reputation was, however, partly blemished by statements proven true, so his loss was reduced. There was no proof his reputation was already destroyed before publication. The court declined aggravated damages, finding no malice: Ms Feuer's information was substantially what was published and prior articles gave grounds for the opinion.
conclusion: General damages of $5,000 were awarded for loss of reputation; costs could be spoken to if not agreed.

issue: Did De. P. have the required capacity on October 3, 2011 to execute the Power of Attorney and Mandate in case of incapacity?
facts: De. was diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia (FTD) in November 2010; by October 2011 she was largely anarthric, could only answer simple yes/no questions by nodding, and needed help with daily living. Her sisters secretly took her to notary Hristova, who took no notes, was told the condition was undiagnosed, and had De. answer through her sister C.
rule: Consent may be given only by a person capable of binding himself and must be free and enlightened (arts. 1385, 1398, 1399 C.C.Q.); a mandate is a contract requiring capacity (arts. 2130, 2166 C.C.Q.). Capacity to grant such a mandate is assessed on the same test as testamentary capacity; capacity is presumed but a prima facie showing raising a serious doubt or 'suspicious circumstances' shifts the burden onto those asserting validity to prove a lucid interval (C.H. v. R.G.; G.D. v. Ge.D.).
application: The medical evidence of neurologists Sidani and Chertkow and geriatrician Ferrier established progressive, irreversible incapacity, with MoCA scores falling from 20/30 (Nov 2010) to 8/30 (2012). The circumstances of execution were troubling: the notary took no elementary precautions, never met De. privately, accepted a lie that the condition was undiagnosed, and could not recall her verification questions. The sisters, who knew of the FTD diagnosis, exploited De.'s vulnerability and were shown able to make her mimic text they wrote. The burden shifted to R., C. and T., who did not testify, and the family doctors' contrary opinions and Dr. Nowakowski's retrospective 75-80% estimate (with a large error margin) did not discharge it.
conclusion: De. was incapable as of August 1, 2011 and lacked capacity to give free and enlightened consent on October 3, 2011.

issue: Should the Power of Attorney and Mandate be revoked and declared null, and did the Public Curator have standing?
facts: The Curator sought revocation and nullity of the October 3, 2011 Mandate; the substitute mandataries' counsel objected that the Curator had no legal interest in a private matter and that the mandate could not be attacked before homologation.
rule: Article 2177 C.C.Q. permits any interested person, including the Public Curator, to seek revocation of a mandate where it is not faithfully executed or for another serious reason, even before homologation (R.S. v. J.B.).
application: The Court dismissed the standing objection, holding art. 2177 explicitly authorizes the Curator to act and that revocation may be sought before homologation. Having found De. incapable at the time of signing, the Mandate was vitiated by lack of valid consent and had been used by R. to cut off De.'s husband.
conclusion: The Power of Attorney and Mandate were revoked and declared null and void ab initio; R.'s homologation motion became moot.

issue: Were the divorce proceedings De. signed on November 10, 2011 null for want of capacity?
facts: One day after R. denied J. access, De. signed a divorce petition with an affidavit alleging J. forced her to take drugs and that she feared for her life; the lawyer Liebman prepared it within 24 hours, was not told of the FTD diagnosis, and De. could barely communicate.
rule: Capacity to consent (arts. 1398, 1399 C.C.Q.) and art. 2167.1 C.C.Q. context; an incapable person cannot give free and enlightened consent to institute proceedings.
application: The Court found the allegations were false and 'planted' by the sisters; De. could not, weeks after being able only to nod yes/no before the notary, have produced the detailed affidavit and handwritten letter. Tingley J., the only judge to see De., had doubted she was competent to sign. The preponderant evidence showed De. lacked capacity to make such an important decision.
conclusion: De. was legally incompetent to consent to the divorce proceedings, which were declared null and void ab initio.

issue: Should a protective supervision be instituted and should all documents signed since November 1, 2010 be annulled?
facts: De.'s condition had deteriorated to total, permanent incapacity by 2013 (Dr. Ferrier); social worker Souaid recommended protective supervision; all parties eventually accepted an appearance by De. was not warranted.
rule: Protective supervision is established in the person's interest to protect her person, administer her patrimony and ensure exercise of civil rights (arts. 256, 257, 269 C.C.Q.); art. 878 C.C.P. allows dispensing with examination where manifestly unreasonable by reason of health.
application: The Court was satisfied De.'s incapacity warranted protective supervision. However, it declined to declare void all documents retroactive to November 1, 2010, as a dementia diagnosis does not automatically render one legally incapable and no other suspect documents were identified; incapacity was fixed as of August 1, 2011.
conclusion: Protective supervision instituted; documents executed on or after August 1, 2011 (Mandate and divorce proceedings) declared null, but no blanket retroactive nullity to November 2010; form of supervision reserved to a second phase.

issue: Should the plaintiff, an individual, be ordered to post security for costs, and the action stayed pending compliance, under the court's inherent jurisdiction?
facts: Following the breakdown of an accounting partnership, Higgins sued his former partner Willis and related corporations seeking division of partnership assets, an accounting, damages and winding-up of various companies. Willis defended, counterclaimed for essentially the same relief, and applied for an order that Higgins post security for costs (estimated at about $47,000) or face a stay. Because Higgins is an individual rather than a corporation, the motion was brought under the court's inherent jurisdiction. Higgins is an employed chartered accountant who asserted he recently bought a home for $314,000 with $100,000 in equity.
rule: The court has inherent jurisdiction to order security for costs against an individual (Tordoff v. Canada Life Assurance Co., 1985 CanLII 492 (BC SC)), a power to be used 'with great caution' (Gray v. Powerassist Technologies Inc., 2001 BCSC 1208) and 'sparingly' (Tordoff). Poverty alone is no bar to a litigant (Pearson v. Naydler; Cowell v. Taylor). By analogy to s. 205 of the Company Act (which governs corporate parties), the applicant must show at least on a prima facie basis that the plaintiff would be unable to pay the defendant's costs if the action fails; a plaintiff may resist by showing sufficient exigible assets or no arguable defence (Fat Mel's Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co.; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress). If the threshold is met, the discretion is exercised only in very limited circumstances, considering the Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd. factors.
application: The court was not satisfied that Willis had shown on a prima facie basis that Higgins would be unable to pay costs: Higgins is an employed chartered accountant likely to remain so, and his uncontradicted (though undocumented) evidence of $100,000 home equity was sufficient to warrant dismissal. Alleged references to financial difficulties in an earlier related-action application, made over six months earlier and unsupported by evidence, were of little assistance. Even had the threshold been met, discretion would not be exercised: requiring Higgins to post security or face a stay while Willis remained free by counterclaim to pursue essentially the same relief would work an injustice.
conclusion: The threshold was not met, and in any event discretion would be exercised against the order; the application for security for costs was dismissed, with costs left to the trial judge.

issue: Does the Court have jurisdiction to adjudicate alleged Code infractions pleaded as an independent cause of action outside the Code's own complaint process?
facts: The plaintiffs' amended statement of claim advanced two independent parallel claims — one that s. 31(2) of The Vital Statistics Act, 2009 breaches the Charter, and a separate one that it breaches The Saskatchewan Human Rights Code — seeking distinct Code remedies. The Action was not brought as a hearing referred to the court by the Chief Commissioner under s. 29.6 of the Code. Saskatchewan applied to strike all portions seeking relief founded solely on the Code.
rule: Human rights codes foreclose any common-law or public-policy cause of action for violation of the rights they guarantee; the only means of enforcement is the complaint procedure in the statute (Seneca College v. Bhadauria, 1981 CanLII 29 (SCC)). This approach has been consistently applied in Saskatchewan (Lawless v. Conseil Scolaire Fransaskois, 2014 SKQB 23; Cadillac Fairview; Kodellas). Court jurisdiction over Code complaints arises only after a s. 27 complaint and a s. 29.6 application by the Chief Commissioner.
application: The Court found conflicting authority — the Seneca/Lawless line versus the Manitoba cases (Parkinson, Billinkoff) which distinguished Seneca on statutory differences. Although the Saskatchewan Code lacks an exclusive-jurisdiction clause and its s. 38(3) injunction power resembles the Old Manitoba Code, the Court held that Seneca has always been applied in Saskatchewan and has never been overruled. Whatcott was distinguished as involving a defence, not a remedy sought under the Code. Authorities permitting mere reference to a code to bolster an independent claim (L'Attiboudeaire, McKinley) were irrelevant because the plaintiffs asserted the Code as a free-standing cause of action, which Saskatchewan alone challenged.
conclusion: The Court has no jurisdiction to adjudicate alleged Code infractions outside the Code's process. The Code-based claims (paras. 49(5)-(8) and related references) were struck as disclosing no reasonable action.

issue: Does s. 38(3) of the Code confer jurisdiction to grant injunctive relief for alleged Code contraventions absent jurisdiction over the underlying complaint?
facts: Having struck the substantive Code claims, the Court had to decide whether it could still entertain the plaintiffs' interlocutory injunction application founded on the Code. Saskatchewan argued s. 38(3) should be read restrictively in light of s. 38(1), limiting injunctions to cases where a person has been convicted of an offence under the Act.
rule: Section 38(3) allows the commission 'or any person' to commence an action by statement of claim for an injunction restraining deprivation of Code rights; the judge may make any order considered fit. Its plain meaning has been applied by Saskatchewan courts (Bell (1991); Grant (1995); Lawless, paras. 60-61), which confine the court's jurisdiction in such cases to granting injunctive relief only, subject to the established injunction test.
application: Although the Court acknowledged the apparent incongruity of a broad s. 38(3) power following the narrower s. 38(1), and the interpretive approach in Committee for the Commonwealth of Canada, it held the provision is not genuinely ambiguous and its plain meaning has been historically accepted. Section 38(3) therefore confers jurisdiction to hear injunction applications stemming from alleged Code contraventions even without jurisdiction over the underlying issues. This mattered because the plaintiffs had not given notice under s. 13 of The Constitutional Questions Act, 2012 and so could not seek interlocutory relief under the Charter.
conclusion: Section 38(3) confers jurisdiction to adjudicate the injunction application under the Code, so the earlier striking of the Code claims did not bar consideration of the interlocutory application.

issue: Should the requested interim injunctions be granted?
facts: The plaintiffs sought (1) an interim order staying the 'at least 18 years of age' requirement in s. 31(2), and (2) an interim order removing the male/female gender/sex designation requirements throughout the Act and regulations, arguing gender designation infringes freedom of expression.
rule: Interlocutory injunctions require assessment of (i) a serious issue to be tried, (ii) irreparable harm, and (iii) the balance of convenience. A court will not grant interlocutory relief that effectively amounts to mandatory relief, grants the ultimate remedy without trial, or effects legislative change.
application: The Court found both requested orders were effectively mandatory and potentially permanent. The first would strike the age limitation and compel the Director of Vital Statistics to issue amended birth certificates to underage plaintiffs, granting the ultimate relief without a trial and creating unresolved reversal problems. The second was premature and overly broad, requiring elimination of long-standing province-wide gender data collection without a full trial of the sweeping consequences; even successful plaintiffs might obtain a different remedy (e.g., expanded options or a transition period). The plaintiffs offered no authority for an interlocutory injunction effecting legislative change.
conclusion: The injunction application was denied. Costs in the cause.

issue: Did the trial judge err in fixing a 24-month reasonable notice period for the disguised dismissal?
facts: C..., a director-level IBM executive earning about $327,000/year, supervising some 250 people, over 50 years old with roughly 12 years of service, was disguised-dismissed. The trial judge awarded 24 months' notice; IBM argued this was excessive and that she wrongly considered the absence of serious cause.
rule: Articles 2091, 2092 and 2094 C.c.Q.; the notice must be reasonable given the nature of the employment, circumstances and length of service (Standard Broadcasting Corp. c. Stewart). Appellate courts intervene only for error as to applicable criteria or a clearly excessive duration (Transforce c. Baillargeon).
application: IBM was right that absence of serious cause is not a factor going to the duration of notice, but the judge relied primarily on the proper Stewart criteria—seniority, importance of responsibilities, age, and difficulty of finding comparable work. Although generous and at the upper end of the range, the award was not unreasonable, and the incidental reference to absence of cause did not vitiate it.
conclusion: No reviewable error; the 24-month notice period was upheld.

issue: What is the proper starting date for calculating the notice period?
facts: IBM argued the notice should run from September 20, 2006 (or January 12, 2007), when C... learned of the substantial changes. C... continued working and negotiations continued; IBM had insisted throughout that no dismissal had occurred and that C... had resigned.
rule: The determination of when an employee must understand he has no choice but to seek other employment is a highly factual question reviewable only for palpable and overriding error.
application: IBM never gave, expressly or implicitly, any notice of termination; it maintained C... remained employed. The judge found the dismissal crystallized on May 25, 2007, when IBM insisted he take the inferior position. IBM showed no palpable and overriding error.
conclusion: The starting date of May 25, 2007 was upheld.

issue: Did the employee satisfy his duty to mitigate?
facts: C... refused the offered inferior position and, after job-searching, started his own consulting business in early 2008. IBM argued he should have kept looking and that his actual income was understated, seeking a larger deduction ($102,579.75 rather than $60,281.51).
rule: Mitigation is a highly factual question; a reasonable person is not required to accept a humiliating demotion. Appellate deference applies to the trial judge's assessment of the evidence.
application: The judge accepted C...'s testimony and evidence of a thorough job search showing he could not find equivalent work; refusing the degrading post was reasonable. IBM merely asked the court to reweigh the evidence without demonstrating error.
conclusion: Mitigation was satisfied; the deduction of $60,281.51 stood.

issue: Was C... entitled to the employer's virtual SERP contributions accrued before the age-55 vesting condition?
facts: C... participated in a notional SERP retention plan requiring continuous employment until age 55 to receive benefits. He was 51 at dismissal and 53 at the end of the notice period. IBM ended the plan in 2008. The trial judge awarded $52,333.12 for IBM's contribution; C... claimed the full $257,191.62 arguing the age-55 clause was abusive.
rule: IBM could terminate without cause subject only to reasonable notice (art. 2091 C.c.Q.). A clause is not abusive (art. 1437 C.c.Q.) where it pursues a legitimate retention objective known and accepted by all.
application: The age-55 condition legitimately aimed to retain key executives and was not abusive. Even had C... remained employed to the end of the notice period he would not have reached 55, so he never acquired any right to the SERP funds; his situation was identical to any employee leaving before 55, and no proof showed the dismissal was aimed at depriving him of SERP.
conclusion: Appeal allowed on this point; the $52,333.12 award was set aside.

issue: Was C... entitled to compensation for stock options—both the forced exercise of vested options and the RSUs/BFOs that would have vested during the notice period?
facts: Vested options had to be exercised within 90 days of the alleged resignation; C... realized over $70,000 and claimed the difference against the stock's peak price during the notice period. He also claimed for RSUs and BFOs that would have vested during the notice period; the trial judge awarded $18,702.70 (BFO) and $31,243.05 (RSU).
rule: Loss on securities must be assessed without speculation, typically using the average trading price over the relevant period (Nurun c. Deschênes); loss of chance is not compensable in Quebec (Laferrière c. Lawson). Incentive award clauses that are not abusive apply according to their terms.
application: Using the ~$105 average price, C... would have earned less than he actually realized, so no compensable loss existed. As for RSUs/BFOs, they were discretionary retention incentives; had IBM given proper notice it would have ceased offering incentives designed to retain him, so no injury flowed from the insufficient notice or abusive termination.
conclusion: Both option claims failed; appeal allowed to strike the $18,702.70 and $31,243.05 awards, incidental appeal dismissed.

issue: Was the award of $35,000 in moral damages justified and appropriate?
facts: The trial judge found IBM, particularly Ms Keating, engaged in humiliating, degrading and hurtful conduct over many months (perverted performance evaluation, mishandled harassment complaint, later interference with C...'s new business), coinciding with his cancer diagnosis, and awarded $35,000.
rule: Moral harm that is merely the ordinary consequence of dismissal is not compensable; damages are available only where faulty conduct aggravates the normal negative consequences (Stewart, Hoeckner, Saulnier). Care must be taken to avoid duplication with the notice indemnity.
application: The majority (St-Pierre, Gagnon JJ.A.) held the abusive, insidious conduct caused injury beyond the ordinary consequences of termination, and $35,000 was consistent with the jurisprudence and warranted deference. Pelletier J.A., dissenting on this point, would have reduced it to $20,000 as partly duplicative of the large notice indemnity.
conclusion: Majority upheld the $35,000 moral-damages award (Pelletier J.A. would have reduced it).

issue: Could exemplary damages be awarded under s. 49 of the Quebec Charter, and in what amount?
facts: IBM declined to transfer C... to a U.S. post, and the trial judge found IBM used his cancer to justify imposing an inferior position—unlawful, intentional discrimination based on handicap—awarding $300,000, based essentially on IBM's ability to pay.
rule: Section 49 (para. 2) of the Quebec Charter permits punitive damages for unlawful and intentional interference; intentionality exists where the actor acts with knowledge of the immediate and natural, or at least extremely probable, consequences (Curateur public c. St-Ferdinand). Quantum is governed by art. 1621 C.c.Q. (gravity of fault, patrimonial situation, other reparation already owed) and must not exceed what suffices for the preventive purpose (Cinar c. Robinson).
application: The majority held the finding of intentional, unlawful discrimination affecting C...'s dignity was reasonably supported and that Honda c. Keays (a common-law case) should be treated cautiously and applies only at the quantum stage. However, the trial judge erred by fixing $300,000 almost solely on IBM's ability to pay, ignoring gravity of fault and the substantial other reparation owed; $300,000 was disproportionate. Pelletier J.A. would have struck the award entirely.
conclusion: Majority reduced exemplary damages to $25,000; compensatory indemnity reduced by $117,278.87 to $684,488.44; incidental appeal dismissed.

issue: Should the court grant an interlocutory injunction ordering the Fédération CJA to lift the access ban imposed on Hazan?
facts: Hazan, a member of Montréal's Jewish community and a former Jewish General Hospital employee, waged a prolonged campaign of harsh, accusatory correspondence against hospital and CJA figures, notably Steven Cummings, invoking comparisons to Hitler, the Holocaust, Nazis and Valery Fabrikant. In mid-September 2001, upon Cummings becoming CJA president, administrator Cantor banned Hazan from the Cummings building over safety fears. Hazan sought an interlocutory injunction to lift the ban.
rule: On an interlocutory injunction the court applies the three-part test: appearance of right (serious question), irreparable harm, and balance of convenience; where the right is doubtful the balance of convenience becomes decisive. At the interlocutory stage the court must avoid resolving contested factual and legal questions reserved for the trial judge and generally preserves the existing situation.
application: The court found numerous serious, contested legal questions (whether the premises are public, whether freedom of movement was validly restricted, whether the ban was reasonable) that must be left to the trial judge. Granting the injunction would substitute the court's view for Cantor's assessment of a sufficient fear, which was not manifestly unjustified. The court noted objective grounds for fear reinforced by Hazan's conduct at the hearing (pulling opposing counsel's hair, keeping a knife at the witness stand). It preferred to preserve the status quo and prioritize security.
conclusion: The court granted the request only in part, preserving the ban but carving out limited access.

issue: Did Hazan establish a sufficient appearance of right?
facts: Hazan claimed the building housed public services and that his exclusion trampled truth, freedom of expression and democratic rights; the CJA is a private Jewish philanthropic organization owning the Cummings building, with security controls at entry.
rule: To succeed the applicant must demonstrate a sufficient appearance of right; where the right is seriously contested, the court proceeds cautiously and weighs the balance of convenience.
application: The public character of the premises was not proven — non-members' access appeared to be a privilege, not a right. Granting relief would improperly substitute the court's opinion for Cantor's genuine and not manifestly unjustified fear. The court assessed fear on an objective standard and found Hazan's own conduct inspired objective fear.
conclusion: The appearance of right was insufficient given the serious contested questions, favouring preservation of the ban.

issue: Would Hazan suffer irreparable harm and does the balance of convenience favour the injunction?
facts: Hazan sought access to social services, the Gelber Centre, the not-yet-open Holocaust Museum, and the library. He was not a library member and used another library; the museum was not open.
rule: Irreparable harm and balance of convenience components of the interlocutory injunction test; caution favours security over unrestricted access.
application: The court recognized Hazan would suffer irreparable harm if denied social services, and that he might wish to attend Gelber Centre events. It fashioned limited access: social services by appointment, and Gelber Centre conferences with written authorization from Cantor, whom the court found to be acting in good faith. The balance of convenience favoured caution and security.
conclusion: The court ordered partial lifting of the ban: access to social services by appointment only, and to Gelber Centre conferences upon written authorization from Cantor.

issue: Should the amended claim against Lande and Pion be dismissed on the basis of res judicata and lis pendens under art. 168 C.C.P.?
facts: Feldman's accusations that Lande inherited a fortune from Nazi-stolen gold, submerged him in litigation, and caused the liquidation of jointly owned properties had already been the subject of judgments (including Feifer v. Feldman, 2024 QCCS 643, and Feldman c. Succession de Lande, 2021 QCCS 2949) and of a pending defamation action set for trial in 2025.
rule: Under art. 168 C.C.P. an application may be dismissed for lis pendens or res judicata; art. 2848 C.C.Q. requires identity of persons, object and cause. For res judicata the court examines the prior judgment; for lis pendens it compares the pleadings, taking allegations as proven, exercising caution (Rocois Construction Inc. v. Québec Ready Mix Inc.).
application: The court found identity of persons, object and cause between the amended application and the numerous prior and pending proceedings, concluding that Feldman was relitigating claims already decided or before another court, save the false-arrest allegations.
conclusion: The court would dismiss most of the claim against Lande and Pion under art. 168(1) C.C.P., but chose to dispose of the entire claim under art. 51 C.C.P.

issue: Is the claim prescribed under art. 2929 C.C.Q. or s. 586 of the Cities and Towns Act?
facts: Feldman's damages flowed from arrests on December 20, 2019 and June 24, 2020; he sent a demand letter and pursued disciplinary complaints in 2020-2021, but filed his originating application only in December 2022 (and January 2022 against the City).
rule: Art. 2929 C.C.Q. imposes a one-year prescription for defamation, to be read restrictively (Desbiens c. Standish, 2024 QCCA 725, holding that a claim founded on false denunciation attacking liberty falls under the three-year prescription of art. 2925 C.C.Q.). S. 586 of the Cities and Towns Act imposes a six-month prescription for claims against a municipality except for bodily injury.
application: Given the restrictive scope of art. 2929 and Desbiens, the court could not conclude the claim was purely defamatory and thus prescribed as against Lande, Pion and the lawyers. Against the SPVM and Leclerc, however, the six-month municipal prescription applied and had expired well before filing, with no bodily-injury exception.
conclusion: The defamation-based prescription argument was not retained for most defendants, but the claim against the SPVM and Leclerc was found prescribed (and also unfounded and abusive).

issue: Does the amended application constitute an abuse of procedure under art. 51 C.C.P.?
facts: Feldman, a lawyer, claimed 39.5 million dollars against nine defendants over 89 paragraphs, describing a conspiracy led by his former partner Lande, with the lawyers, a business associate (Alavi) and the police cast as enablers; the allegations were largely opinions and conjecture, contradicted by prior civil, disciplinary and criminal outcomes, including his own guilty plea to criminal harassment.
rule: Arts. 51 and 168 C.C.P. permit declaring a proceeding abusive; abuse includes clearly unfounded, frivolous, vexatious or excessive pleadings and disproportionate claims (Bohémier; Gravel c. Orlup; Boggia c. Maiello). Once abuse is summarily established the burden shifts to the plaintiff to justify the proceeding. Lawyers enjoy relative immunity and can be liable only for an independent fault marked by recklessness or bad faith (Chionis c. Gaudet).
application: The exorbitant, unexplained quantum, the recycling of dismissed accusations, and the absence of pure facts establishing fault, causation and damage against the lawyers, Alavi, and the police (mere secret recording and handing it to police being no fault) all pointed to abuse. Feldman offered no substantive rebuttal, merely repeating his allegations.
conclusion: The court held the amended application abusive against all defendants, dismissed it, and condemned Feldman to reimburse Alavi's extrajudicial fees (rectified to $17,978.57) with costs.

issue: Does the grandfather have a recognized cause of action under the Family Law Act to terminate or obtain guardianship of grandchildren who are under a Permanent Guardianship Order to the Director?
facts: The children were placed under a Permanent Guardianship Order (PGO) to the Director under s. 34 of the Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act by Judge Shaw on October 22, 2014. The grandfather filed a Family Law Act claim purporting to terminate guardianship, and at the leave hearing stated he was actually applying for guardianship of the grandchildren; his earlier guardianship application had been dismissed.
rule: Section 25(1) of the Family Law Act permits termination of guardianship only where there is a guardian in place under that Act and either the guardian consents or the court considers it necessary or desirable. Guardianship of children subject to a PGO is governed by the Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act, not the Family Law Act.
application: The children are not subject to guardianship under the Family Law Act; the Director holds permanent guardianship under the CYFEA. The grandparents had already been repeatedly denied access under s. 34(8). It is therefore not possible to use the Family Law Act to terminate the Director's PGO, so no cause of action exists.
conclusion: There is no cause of action available to the grandfather under the Family Law Act.

issue: Does the doctrine of res judicata / issue estoppel bar the grandfather from re-litigating the guardianship question?
facts: The grandparents' guardianship applications were dismissed at a 20-day trial before Judge Shaw; their appeals to the Court of Queen's Bench were dismissed by Justice Dario, an application to reinstate was denied after a substantive review of over 2,000 pages of transcript, and a final appeal to the Court of Appeal to reinstate was denied.
rule: Res judicata makes a final judgment on the merits conclusive between the parties as to matters litigated or that could have been litigated (CAG v. SG, 2012 ABQB 529; Hill v. Hill, 2016 ABQB 49). Issue estoppel (Angle v. MNR, [1975] 2 SCR 248; Toronto (City) v. CUPE Local 79, 2003 SCC 63) requires the same question decided, a final decision, and the same parties or privies.
application: The same guardianship question, involving the same children and the same parties, was decided and exhaustively reviewed on the merits by Justice Dario, whose decision was final after appeal avenues were exhausted. The grandfather's assertion that the merits were never heard was rejected; the reinstatement proceeding was a thorough substantive review of every ground of appeal.
conclusion: Re-litigation is barred; the matter has been conclusively decided and finality applies.

issue: Should the grandfather be declared a frivolous and vexatious litigant and prohibited from bringing further applications without leave?
facts: There had been 54 Family Law Act and 57 CYFEA appearances in Provincial Court, plus Queen's Bench and Court of Appeal proceedings. The grandparents made repeated defamatory accusations (calling various agencies and individuals anti-Semitic, comparing Child and Family Services to Nazi Germany, alleging conspiracy), attempted to locate the children in foster care causing a placement to break down, and published the children's identities contrary to the CYFEA.
rule: Section 91(1) of the Family Law Act allows the court to prohibit a person who has made frivolous or vexatious applications from further applications without leave. Indicia of vexatious conduct include re-litigating decided issues and abuse of process (Kavanagh v. Kavanagh, 2016 ABQB 107; Gauthier v. Starr, 2016 ABQB 213; 420093 B.C. Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal; s. 23 of the Judicature Act).
application: The grandfather persistently pursued applications on matters already decided, engaged in bizarre, inflammatory and defamatory conduct in and outside court, breached publication restrictions, and tried to locate the children. This course of conduct constitutes abuse and misuse of legal process.
conclusion: The grandfather is a frivolous and vexatious litigant; he is prohibited from further applications without leave and ordered to pay $5,000 costs.

issue: Does Parliament have jurisdiction under s. 91(26) to redefine marriage to include same-sex couples?
facts: Marriage predates the Constitution Act, 1867, which conferred exclusive authority over 'marriage and divorce' on Parliament (s. 91(26)) while leaving 'solemnization of marriage' to the provinces (s. 92(12)). Neither the common law nor the C.c.B.C. ever expressly defined marriage, but both understood it as the union of one man and one woman.
rule: Sections 91 and 92 of the Constitution Act, 1867 are attributive of legislative competence over classes of subjects. The Constitution is a 'living tree capable of growth and expansion within its natural limits' (Edwards) to be interpreted broadly and dynamically to meet new social realities.
application: The Court disagreed with Egale (Pitfield J.) that redefinition would require a constitutional amendment. Applying evolutive interpretation—used for 'banks', telephony and 'Indians'—the Court held the meaning of 'marriage' in s. 91(26) can be modulated without amending the Constitution. Section 5 of the Harmonization Act (2001) shows Parliament actively legislating on a substantive condition of marriage.
conclusion: Parliament has the legislative competence to modify the original meaning of marriage to include same-sex couples.

issue: Does the opposite-sex requirement for marriage infringe s. 15(1) of the Charter?
facts: Hendricks and Leboeuf, a same-sex couple in a nearly 30-year conjugal relationship, were refused a marriage licence because the law confines marriage to a man and a woman. Recent federal and Quebec laws extended benefits and (in Quebec) civil union to same-sex couples, but not access to marriage.
rule: The three-part analysis in Law v. Canada: (1) differential treatment; (2) based on an enumerated or analogous ground; (3) that is truly discriminatory by offending human dignity. Sexual orientation is an analogous ground (Egan; M. v. H.).
application: Excluding same-sex couples from marriage imposes differential treatment based on sexual orientation, an analogous ground. Considering the contextual factors—historical disadvantage of homosexuals, the fact procreation is not a condition of civil marriage, and the fundamental importance of the institution—the exclusion sends a message that such unions merit less respect, undermining the couple's dignity. Civil union and economic benefits do not cure this ('separate but equal' rejected, per Linden J. in Egan).
conclusion: The definition of marriage in s. 5 of the Harmonization Act discriminates against same-sex couples contrary to s. 15(1).

issue: Is the s. 15(1) infringement justified under s. 1?
facts: The Attorney General of Canada argued the law preserves traditional marriage, an institution with social, historical and religious roots that the State merely recognized. Interveners argued redefinition would threaten religious freedom.
rule: Oakes test: a pressing and substantial objective, plus proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality of effects); the government bears the burden.
application: The State failed at the first step. Preservation of the traditional/religious conception of marriage cannot justify denying equality; a religious majority cannot impose its conception of marriage on a civil institution (Big M Drug Mart). Complementarity of the sexes and procreation are not conditions of civil marriage. Religious freedom (s. 2(a)) is not threatened, since no minister of religion can be compelled to celebrate a marriage contrary to his faith (art. 367 C.c.Q.). No pressing objective was established; the harmonization exercise was not urgent.
conclusion: The infringement is not justified under s. 1.

issue: Is art. 365 C.c.Q. ultra vires or the source of the discrimination?
facts: The registrar refused the licence citing art. 365 C.c.Q., which requires marriage between a man and a woman. The Attorney General of Quebec conceded a province cannot enact substantive conditions of marriage, which fall to Parliament.
rule: A substantive condition of marriage (capacity, impediments) is within exclusive federal competence; a province may only legislate on solemnization. Section 15 does not alter the division of powers (Haig; s. 31 of the Charter).
application: If art. 365 al. 2 imposes a substantive condition it is ultra vires; if it merely obliges the celebrant to verify the federally-imposed condition it is intra vires. Either way, since the opposite-sex requirement now flows from s. 5 of the Harmonization Act, art. 365 is not the true legal source of the discrimination, and the province cannot grant the remedy sought. The Quebec Charter (art. 10) argument likewise fails.
conclusion: Art. 365 al. 2 is not the source of the discrimination, but its 'man and a woman' portion, being merely a verification of the federal condition, is declared inoperative to follow the fate of s. 5.

issue: What is the appropriate remedy?
facts: The impugned provisions were found to violate s. 15 and be unjustified. The reform of a fundamental social institution engaging strongly divergent values was at stake; Ontario's Halpern judges had adopted differing remedies.
rule: Section 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982. Courts act as guardians of Charter rights (Vriend) but must show restraint before radically changing established law (Watkins v. Olafson), leaving major reform with ramifications to the legislature.
application: Although the Court could simply read in 'two persons', it held the choice of remedy for so profound a reform belongs to Parliament, which has consultation mechanisms to weigh social, religious and cultural impacts. A legal vacuum cannot be left, so the declaration of invalidity is suspended for 24 months.
conclusion: The application is allowed; s. 5 of the Harmonization Act, s. 1(1) of the Modernization Act, and the 'man and a woman' part of art. 365 al. 2 C.c.Q. are declared inoperative, with the declarations of invalidity suspended for two years, costs against the co-respondents.

issue: Was the letter from the Jean Tweed Centre admissible on the summary judgment motion?
facts: The mother sought to rely on a letter from Marcie Pekar of the Jean Tweed Centre, attached as an exhibit to her affidavit, offering opinions from Ms Pekar and unnamed staff about the mother's parenting and attachment. The Society did not object but urged limited weight; the mother urged considerable weight.
rule: On a summary judgment motion the evidence presented must be 'trial worthy' (Children's Aid Society of Ottawa v. J.B. and H.H., 2016 ONSC 2757; Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. B.B., 2012 ONCJ 646). The same admissibility standard applies to parents and to the Society; a court acts as gatekeeper and should not admit inadmissible evidence merely to give it no weight.
application: The letter contained hearsay opinions from unidentified staff, no explanation why an affidavit could not be sworn, no information on the author's qualifications to opine on attachment or parenting, and facts contrary to both the Society's and the mother's own evidence. Admitting it would deprive the opposing party of cross-examination. Even if admitted it would carry no weight, being nearly a year old and predating the mother's termination of involvement with Jean Tweed.
conclusion: The letter was inadmissible; exclusion was not unduly prejudicial since there was no dispute the mother attended the programs and other admissible evidence showed positive interactions.

issue: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial, or could the matter be decided summarily?
facts: The Society moved for summary judgment on its status review application; the mother argued there were triable issues about returning the child to her care, but pleaded no specific facts and largely admitted or did not dispute the Society's evidence over 17 months of involvement.
rule: Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules: the moving party must show no genuine issue requiring a trial (r. 16(4)); the responding party may not rest on mere allegations but must set out specific facts showing a genuine issue (r. 16(4.1)) and must 'put its best foot forward.' Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, as applied to child protection in Kawartha-Haliburton CAS v. M.W., 2018 ONSC 2783 and L.M. v. CAS of Peel, 2019 ONSC 1566, governs; summary judgment is granted sparingly in protection cases but the pre-Hryniak higher-threshold jurisprudence no longer applies.
application: The judge found she could make the necessary findings of fact, apply the law, and reach a fair and just determination on the record without the expanded powers or oral evidence, and that doing so was proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive. The mother identified no specific triable issues and offered no description of evidence she would call; merely advancing a plan does not entitle a parent to a trial.
conclusion: There was no genuine issue requiring a trial; the matter was properly determined summarily on its merits.

issue: Does the child continue to be in need of protection, and is extended society care in his best interests?
facts: The child was apprehended at six days old in November 2017 after a safety plan failed; he had been in care 17 months, exceeding statutory timelines. The mother had persistent unaddressed issues: mental health/depression, inability to meet her own medical and financial needs, keeping her home clean, safe and bug-free, lack of supports, and sporadic access. Alternative plans were her care with supervision or placement with Ms JD.
rule: Status review under ss. 113-114 CYFSA; the original order is presumed correct and the court assesses whether protection concerns persist (CCAS of Metropolitan Toronto v. M.(C.), [1994] 2 SCR 165) and the best interests of the child under s. 74(3), from the child's perspective (CAS of Niagara Region v. B.P. and B.W., 2018 ONSC 4371). Section 122 limits interim care duration; extensions only if in the child's best interests. A parent's plan must be plausible on the whole record (CAS of Sudbury and Manitoulin v. T.S., 2011 ONCJ 745).
application: The same concerns that led to apprehension continued; the mother showed no insight and no sustained improvement despite 17 months of Society and Jean Tweed support. Her plan merely restated what she had consistently failed to do and lacked reality and detail. Ms JD's plan was last-minute, ill-conceived, and already showing tension on the first visit. No evidence supported extending timelines.
conclusion: The child continues to need protection; the only viable plan in his best interests is placement in the extended care of the Society, with a view to adoption.

issue: Should access be ordered, and can an order be 'silent' as to access?
facts: The Society sought an order silent as to access for adoption flexibility; the mother sought access. She had attended roughly one-fifth of offered visits by early 2019, with lengthy absences.
rule: Following CAS of Toronto v. D.P., [2005] O.J. No. 930, a court cannot make an order 'silent' as to access to circumvent the statutory scheme; it must decide the access question. Under s. 105(5)-(6) CYFSA the court shall not order access to a child in extended care unless satisfied it is in the child's best interests, considering whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and whether access would impair adoption; the onus is on the person seeking access (CAS of Niagara Region v. B.P. and B.W.).
application: The court had to decide access rather than remain silent. Applying s. 74(3) best interests factors, the mother led no evidence that access was beneficial and meaningful from the child's perspective; that visits were pleasant and the mother loved the child was insufficient. The young child needed permanency; access would delay and impair adoption, and severing ties would be minimally disruptive given no distress over her long absences.
conclusion: No access was ordered; the child is placed in extended society care with no access to permit prompt permanency.

issue: Did the defendants establish that the action arises from an expression relating to a matter of public interest under s. 137.1(3)?
facts: Between February and December 2021, coaches David Spinney and Ahmed Shamiya, and Mara Schiavulli (mother of wrestler Madison Parks), sent numerous emails to figures in the wrestling and amateur-sport communities and to government officials criticizing Dr. Fowlie's conduct and suitability as Complaints and Appeals Officer (CAO) of Wrestling Canada Lutte (WCL), a largely publicly funded national governing body. The emails concerned his handling of complaints, alleged breaches of confidentiality, and his prior public record.
rule: 'Expression' is broadly defined in s. 137.1(2). Under s. 137.1(3) and 1704604 Ontario Ltd. v. Pointes Protection Association, 2020 SCC 22, the moving party need only show that some segment of the community would have a genuine interest in receiving information on the subject; 'public interest' is given a broad, generous interpretation with no qualitative assessment of the expression (Buttar, 2023 ONCA 539; Sokoloff, 2020 ONCA 730).
application: All the impugned emails related to Dr. Fowlie's decision-making, conduct and suitability as CAO. The CAO role was central to WCL's independent complaints and discipline process created after the 2018 Bennett Report found systemic abuse in Canadian wrestling. Athlete safety in a publicly funded Olympic sport, and confidence in the complaints system, are matters in which the wrestling community and the broader public have a genuine interest. Dr. Fowlie himself conceded on cross-examination that the emails related directly to his CAO role and that the public has an interest in athlete safety.
conclusion: The defendants met their burden under s. 137.1(3); the action arises from expression relating to a matter of public interest.

issue: Did Dr. Fowlie show grounds to believe the proceeding has substantial merit and that the defendants have no valid defence under s. 137.1(4)(a)?
facts: Dr. Fowlie's statement of claim reproduced emails from all three defendants describing him as, among other things, abusive, deceitful, a bully, a misogynist, and racist, and referencing a Canadian Transportation Agency finding against him. The defendants pleaded qualified privilege, fair comment and (for Spinney and Schiavulli) justification.
rule: Substantial merit requires a real prospect of success (Pointes, para. 49). Defamation requires publication to a third party, reference to the plaintiff, and words tending to lower reputation in a reasonable person's eyes (Bent v. Platnick, 2020 SCC 23). The plaintiff must show the defences have no real prospect of success; a defence that 'could go either way' is not defeated (Buttar; Bondfield). Qualified privilege attaches to a reciprocal duty/interest occasion and is defeated by malice or exceeding scope (Bent; Thatcher-Craig, 2023 ONCA 96). Fair comment requires public interest, factual basis, recognizable comment, an objective honesty test, and can be defeated by malice (WIC Radio v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Hansman, 2023 SCC 14).
application: Some emails from each defendant contained words that would tend to lower Dr. Fowlie's reputation, so the defamation claim had substantial merit. As advocates for wrestlers and, for Schiavulli, a parent, the defendants had an interest/duty to communicate their concerns to recipients with a corresponding interest, establishing qualified privilege. However, some record evidence of ill-will (Spinney's threat that Fowlie would 'feel some lasting effects'; Shamiya's threat to bring protesters to Fowlie's IRB workplace) meant the qualified privilege and fair comment defences of Spinney and Shamiya could go either way. There was no evidence of malice by Schiavulli, and her factual bases and the justification defence (supported by admissions and the record) were not shown to fail. The abandoned internet-harassment and false-light claims were found meritless.
conclusion: Dr. Fowlie showed grounds to believe the defamation claim had substantial merit and that Spinney and Shamiya had no valid defence, but failed to do so as against Schiavulli, whose motion was granted at this stage.

issue: Did the public interest in permitting the proceeding to continue outweigh the public interest in protecting the expression under s. 137.1(4)(b)?
facts: Dr. Fowlie claimed over $800,000, asserting the emails cost him his WCL contract, tarnished his reputation and caused health problems. WCL's executive director testified the contract was terminated for WCL's own reasons based on Fowlie's own conduct, not the defendants' emails. Dr. Fowlie continued as an IRB member and held other sports roles; he relied only on the presumption of general damages and led no medical evidence (a supporting affidavit was struck).
rule: The weighing exercise is the crux of the analysis (Pointes, para. 18, 53). The plaintiff must show harm that is 'serious' and causally linked to the expression; presumed general damages and bare assertions are insufficient (Hansman, 2023 SCC 14; Gill v. Maciver, 2024 ONCA 126; Park Lawn, 2023 ONCA 129). Harm is assessed against any pre-existing blemishes on reputation (Levant, 2022 ONCA 79). Quality of and motivation behind the expression, and the chilling effect, are weighed (Pointes, paras. 73-74; Hansman, paras. 76-77).
application: Dr. Fowlie provided no evidence permitting an inference of serious harm; the loss of the WCL contract was attributable to his own performance, not the defendants. His reputation was already blemished by the 2010 CTA decision and a 2019 SDRCC decision, both public. The expression addressed important issues of athlete safety and integrity of a complaints process in a publicly funded sport, and the defendants had no history or animus toward him. Allowing the suit would chill others from speaking out. Fowlie's numerous retaliatory steps (RCMP complaint, complaints to regulators, employers and Ministry of Labour) indicated the action bore the hallmarks of a SLAPP seeking retribution.
conclusion: Dr. Fowlie failed to show serious harm outweighing the public interest in protecting the expression; the balance favoured the defendants and the action was dismissed in its entirety.

issue: What access order is in the child's best interests, given the father's lengthy history of fraud convictions and repeated incarcerations?
facts: The father sought roughly equal 'week about' parenting time, or liberal overnight access, to the child Wolf (born 2004). The mother had sole custody (unappealed 2012 order) and sought to maintain the existing alternate-Sunday daytime access with supervised exchanges. The father had been repeatedly incarcerated for fraud, spent significant portions of Wolf's early years in custody, faced a possible further two-year default sentence, showed no remorse, and had emotionally harmed the mother's older son Denzil by posing as his biological father and then abandoning him. Wolf was thriving in the mother's stable home; he enjoyed his father and paternal grandparents.
rule: Access is determined by the best interests of the child under ss. 24(2), (3) and (4) of the Children's Law Reform Act, with past conduct considered where relevant to ability to parent. Maximum contact with both parents is encouraged where consistent with best interests (Gordon v. Goertz; Young v. Young); a non-custodial parent's regular access is presumptively beneficial and forfeited only in extreme circumstances (Jafari v. Dadar); the party seeking to restrict normal access must justify the restriction, and access may be limited to minimize risk from a parent's conduct or lifestyle (M.A. v. J.D.; W.(B.H.) v. W.(S.M.)).
application: Weighing the statutory factors, the court found Wolf lived in a stable home with the mother as primary caregiver and was doing well. The father's incarcerations and risk of future imprisonment (including a possible default sentence when Wolf would be about 15) made a shared or greatly expanded schedule potentially traumatic and disruptive. The court preferred the mother's credible evidence over the father's grandiose, evasive and contradictory testimony, and found the profound harm the father caused Denzil, his lack of remorse, and his beginning to tell Wolf he was wrongfully convicted, all counselled caution. Nonetheless Wolf loved his father and grandparents and the existing order had gone well, so modest expansion was warranted.
conclusion: Access was modestly expanded to include a Saturday overnight on alternating weekends (plus specified holiday, summer and telephone access), with supervised exchanges, conditional on the father residing with the paternal grandparents; the father's request for equal/50% parenting time was refused.

issue: Should income be imputed to the father and what should the ongoing table amount of child support be?
facts: The father claimed no income and inability to work owing to incarceration, bail conditions, lack of identity documents and his criminal record. However he was a beneficiary of a substantial trust set up by his grandfather (from which he testified he had accessed up to $3.5 million and bought a $1.8 million New York apartment), had funded a comfortable lifestyle and over $500,000 in legal fees, and disclosed nothing about the trust. His CRA assessments showed prior income up to $146,000. He was intelligent, educated and, at the time of judgment, not incarcerated and free to work.
rule: Under ss. 19(1) and (2) of the Child Support Guidelines (O. Reg. 391/97) the court may impute income, including where a payor is intentionally under-employed (s. 19(1)(a)) or is a beneficiary receiving benefits from a trust (s. 19(1)(i)). Drygala v. Pauli sets the test for intentional under-employment; adverse inferences may be drawn for failure to disclose (Smith v. Pellegrini; Maimone v. Maimone).
application: The court found the father was a beneficiary of and had access to the grandfather's trust under s. 19(1)(i), and had failed entirely to disclose it. He was also intentionally under-employed given his capacity, education and freedom to work. Considering trust access, earning capacity and the pre-separation lifestyle funded by the trust, income of $75,000 per year was reasonably imputed. The prior $1,000 temporary figure (on imputed income of $66,900) was unexplained and appeared simply incorrect.
