conclusion: Income of $75,000 was imputed; ongoing child support was set at the Ontario table amount for one child ($782/month, commencing November 1, 2015), with annual disclosure including the trust settlement and financial statements.

issue: Should the father's accumulated child support arrears be reduced or rescinded?
facts: The father had paid only one $1,000 payment since the December 22, 2009 temporary order and nothing for years before, leaving arrears of roughly $70,000. He asserted inability to pay; his father testified he avoided depositing funds because accounts would be seized by the Family Responsibility Office. The mother had struggled financially, relied on social assistance and her parents, and had her credit destroyed by the father's identity misuse.
rule: The discretion to reduce arrears must be exercised judicially per DiFrancesco v. Couto (nature of obligation, ongoing capacity, ongoing need, delay in enforcement, delay by payor, and undue hardship). Mere accumulation without proven past and future inability to pay does not justify relief (Haisman v. Haisman); the D.B.S. factors also inform reduction/rescission (Galloway v. Cassino; H.F. v. P.F.).
application: Applying the DiFrancesco factors, the court found a court-ordered obligation never followed, no payments for years, prompt enforcement efforts by the mother, apparent avoidance of enforcement by the father, genuine financial need of the mother and child, and no evidence that payment would cause hardship given the father's trust access. The father was willing to fund private school and gifts but refused table support. Arrears were recalculated on the corrected table amount for imputed income of $75,000 over five years and ten months, less a $1,000 credit.
conclusion: Relief was largely refused; arrears were fixed at $53,740 (exclusive of interest), payable within 30 days, reflecting the corrected table amount rather than any rescission for hardship.

issue: Should the court adjourn the trial or extend the statutory time limit under s. 122(5) of the CYFSA to allow the grandmother's plan to be assessed?
facts: T.K. had been in the society's continuous care since December 6, 2019 (from about two weeks old), 18 months by trial — six months beyond the 12-month limit in s. 122(1)(a) for a child under six. The maternal grandmother advanced her plan only about three days before trial, after the great-grandmother's kin plan had been withdrawn months earlier.
rule: Section 122(1) of the CYFSA caps interim society care at 12 months for a child under six; s. 122(5) permits a single six-month extension only if it is in the child's best interests. Extensions require 'unusual, exceptional, or equitable considerations' and should not be routinely used (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. LU, 2008 CanLII 26661 (ON SC)). Delay in child protection is measured from the child's perspective (CAS of Toronto v. T.(L.), 2016 ONCA 146).
application: Family relationship is only one of the s. 74(3) best-interests factors and does not trump the effect of delay on a toddler. The grandmother came forward at the eleventh hour despite knowing no other kin plan existed; permitting a last-minute relative to halt trial 'is not the law.' Adding another six months to 18 months of litigation limbo was contrary to the Act's permanency objectives (ss. 1(2), 122(1)).
conclusion: The adjournment motion and any s. 122(5) extension were refused; the trial proceeded.

issue: Does T.K. continue to be a child in need of protection?
facts: T.K. was found in need of protection on August 26, 2020 under s. 74(2)(n) (mother unable to care) per a signed statement of agreed facts. At trial the mother had no stable housing, was transient, had cognitive limitations (mild intellectual disability, suspected FASD), had not taken a parenting program or COVID test, and conceded she could not parent alone; no community supports were proven.
rule: On a status review under ss. 113–114, the court applies the two-step test in Children's Aid Society of Oxford v. W.T.C., 2013 ONCA 491: it must first determine whether a court order is necessary to protect the child in future, considering present circumstances and any new concerns (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S.P., 2019 ONSC 3482), guided by the paramount best-interests purpose in s. 1(1).
application: The parties agreed protection continued. The mother's situation had not materially changed since the SAF: no stable housing, no demonstrated supports, continuing cognitive limitations and transiency. She remained unable to care for T.K.
conclusion: T.K. continues to be a child in need of protection.

issue: Which disposition is in T.K.'s best interests — grandmother supervision, further interim care, or extended society care?
facts: The grandmother lived in a shelter, had had virtually no contact with T.K. for about nine months, missed the Family Group Conference, declined virtual visits, never returned the worker's calls, was in unresolved conflict with the mother, and knew little about the child. The mother's alternative was six more months of interim care to assess that plan.
rule: Section 101(1) requires the court to select the order in the child's best interests, after considering efforts to assist (s. 101(2)), less disruptive alternatives (s. 101(3)) and community/relative placement (s. 101(4), s. 102), applying the s. 74(3) best-interests factors and the paramount purpose (s. 1(1)); relative placement is weighed like any other factor (CAS of Northumberland v. D.P.).
application: The grandmother's proposal was 'little more than a plan to make a plan,' revealing little insight and a serious lack of commitment. Further interim care would require an unwarranted s. 122(5) extension absent the 'unusual, exceptional, or equitable' circumstances described. The society had made reasonable efforts, considered less disruptive alternatives and pursued kin placements up to trial, leaving extended society care as the only option consistent with T.K.'s need for permanency.
conclusion: T.K. placed in the extended care of the society; the supervision and further interim-care requests were dismissed.

issue: What access should be ordered after extended society care, and who should be the access holder?
facts: In-person visits ceased in March 2020; virtual visits were sporadic and short, and the mother chose to stop all visits after April 8, 2021, two months before trial. T.K. was 18 months old with only minor special needs and good adoptive prospects.
rule: Under s. 105(5)–(7), access to a child in extended society care is ordered only if in the child's best interests, considering whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and whether access would impair future adoption (s. 105(6)); the new CYFSA removed the presumption against access and makes best interests predominant (CAS of Toronto v. J.G., 2020 ONCA 415), with access meant only to preserve an existing beneficial relationship (CAS of Toronto v. Y.M., 2019 ONCJ 489). Only the access holder may apply for an openness order (ss. 195–196).
application: There was no meaningful relationship to preserve given the thin, discontinued contact; in-person visits and video calls would confuse rather than benefit T.K. Written/photo contact preserved his ability to know his story without impairing adoption. Making the mother a joint access holder risked, given her lack of insight, an openness application that could unduly delay adoption.
conclusion: Ordered non-visit contact (letters, cards, photos, videos by email), with T.K. as sole access holder and the mother as access recipient.

issue: Was summary judgment appropriate under rule 16 of the Family Law Rules, given the exceptional caution required in child protection cases?
facts: The matter had twice been set for trial but was adjourned when the parent was hospitalized and later when he refused to participate. The parent was found a special party and the PGT appointed. The society moved for summary judgment relying on trial affidavits, joint document briefs, medical/police records and a psychological assessment; the material facts were largely uncontested. The parent did not attend the motion.
rule: Rule 16 Family Law Rules and the two-step test in Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7: there is no genuine issue requiring a trial where the judge can make necessary findings of fact, apply the law, and do so in a proportionate, expeditious and less expensive way. In child protection, exceptional caution is required and the objectives of the CYFSA and the child's best interests govern, per Kawartha Haliburton CAS v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316; L.M. v. CAS Peel, 2019 ONCA 841. The moving party bears the burden; the court must still be satisfied on the evidence even if the respondent fails to raise a genuine issue.
application: The court screened out inadmissible evidence and found the record comprehensive, with material facts either undisputed or not meaningfully contested. It could make the necessary findings without weighing evidence or assessing credibility, and cross-examination would add little. Given the child had been in care over 26 months, summary disposition was not merely efficient but necessary to achieve the Act's objectives.
conclusion: There was no genuine issue requiring a trial; the society established a prima facie case and the parent failed to show any triable issue. Summary judgment was granted.

issue: What disposition order is in the child's best interests — supervised return to the parent or extended society care?
facts: The six-year-old child has Autism Spectrum Disorder and Intellectual Disability with significant special needs. The parent has a primary psychotic disorder with two major involuntary hospitalizations, delusional and aggressive behaviour, criminal charges and convictions (including threatening society workers), and shows little insight or engagement with treatment. The child showed neglect (not attending school, matted hair, dirty) when apprehended. A prior supervision-order return in 2023 broke down.
rule: CYFSA ss. 101(1) (menu of orders), 101(2)-(4) (efforts to assist, least disruptive alternatives, community/family placements), s. 1 (paramount purpose — best interests, protection and well-being), and best-interests factors in s. 74(3). Mental illness alone does not establish need for protection (CAS Toronto v. R.S., 2019 ONCJ 866); court assesses severity, insight, treatment compliance and impact on parenting. A supervision order requires confidence the parent will comply (Windsor-Essex CAS v. L.H.).
application: The court found the risks of physical/emotional harm remained unacceptably high; the parent's severe untreated mental health, lack of insight, hostility and inability to work with the society made a supervision order unworkable. No family/community plan materialized. The child needs stability and a caregiver able to collaborate with service providers. The statutory two-year care limit (ss. 122(1),(3)) had been exceeded, leaving only return or extended society care.
conclusion: Extended society care is the least disruptive alternative consistent with the child's best interests; the child is placed in extended society care.

issue: What access order is in the child's best interests for a child in extended society care?
facts: Since April 2025 the parent has had weekly virtual access, generally positive and beneficial, though visits often end early due to the child's attention span and the parent has recently missed some. In-person access is problematic due to the parent's mental health, aggression and refusal to engage with the society. The society sought a minimum of six visits per year in its discretion; the PGT sought weekly in-person and weekly virtual visits.
rule: CYFSA ss. 105(4)-(6): once extended society care is ordered prior access terminates; access may be ordered only if in the child's best interests, considering s. 74(3) factors, whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful, and (if relevant) impairment of adoption opportunities. Kawartha (2019 ONCA 316) removed the presumption against access and the burden shift. Access discretion may be delegated to the society only if significantly circumscribed by minimum rights (J.S.R. v. CAS Ottawa, 2021 ONSC 630; CAS Toronto v. J.G., 2020 ONCA 315).
application: The court found access beneficial and meaningful, and that the child became dysregulated when visits lapsed, so the society's proposed six visits a year was insufficient. But the parent's untreated mental health, aggression, lack of transparency, missed visits and the need to preserve a limited adoption pool weighed against frequent access. The court balanced these by ordering a minimum of once every other week, with the society given discretion over location, duration, supervision and method, and safeguards (early termination; reduction to monthly if four visits missed in two months).
conclusion: Access is ordered at a minimum of once every other week, supervised, with defined society discretion and safeguards.

issue: Should the parent be an access holder or only an access recipient?
facts: The parent loves the child and has not undermined the foster placement, and had not been dysregulated at a virtual visit since October 2025. However he has anger/aggression/impulse-control problems, a conviction for threatening two workers, serious untreated mental health, a chaotic life, non-transparency, and his condition had repeatedly delayed the proceeding (vacated trial dates, refusal to participate).
rule: CYFSA s. 105(7) requires identifying access holder vs recipient; only an access holder may bring an openness application on a Notice of Intent to place for adoption. Impairment of adoption opportunity (including undue delay) takes heightened importance; attributes suggesting impairment include aggression/anger, lack of support for alternate caregivers, dishonesty, litigiousness, and mental health/chaotic lifestyle (CAS Toronto v. A.F., 2015 ONCJ 678; CCAS v. A.P., 2019 ONCJ 631; affirmed CAS Toronto v. R.E., 2025 ONCA 623).
application: Weighing the A.F./A.P. attributes, the court found the parent's aggression, lack of transparency, ungovernability and chaotic mental health likely to deter a limited pool of prospective adoptive parents and to delay any openness application, outweighing the factors favouring holder status. Protection was provided by ordering that any Notice of Intent be served on the PGT (and the Office of the Children's Lawyer), and the child, given his age and bond, would likely bring an openness application.
conclusion: The child is the access holder and the parent is the access recipient; any Notice of Intent to place for adoption must be served on the PGT.

issue: On an application to strike under Rule 19(24), which of the challenged paragraphs of a petition and affidavit filed in support of judicial review of a labour board decision are inadmissible because they are irrelevant, unnecessary, or amount to argument rather than fact?
facts: Remond Jones sought judicial review of an LRB decision (and its reconsideration) dismissing his s. 12 Labour Relations Code complaint that the Union had failed to represent him fairly against his employer, Canfor. The Union applied to strike paras. 59, 60 and 62 of the petition and various paragraphs of Jones's affidavit, arguing they disclosed no reasonable claim, were scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, or contained argument rather than fact. Much of the impugned material described the personal/reputational impact of the events on Jones and characterized the LRB's findings in inflammatory, adjective-laced terms.
rule: Rule 19(24) of the Rules of Court permits striking pleadings (and, per Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860, affidavits) that disclose no reasonable claim, are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, may prejudice or delay, or are an abuse of process. Rule 51(10) confines affidavits to what a deponent could state in evidence at trial. Affidavits must state facts only, not adjectival opinion or argument (Creber v. Franklin; Kennedy v. Kennedy, 2006 BCSC 190; Chamberlain v. Surrey School District No. 36). On judicial review the materials are generally restricted to the record before the tribunal; evidence going to procedural fairness may be admissible but must not amount to a reinterpretation of the record or a rehearing on the merits (Kinexus Bioinformatics Corp. v. Asad, 2010 BCSC 33). The court cannot award damages on judicial review (Judicial Review Procedure Act, s. 2; McLean v. British Columbia).
application: The live issues on the judicial review were whether the LRB decisions met the standard of review and whether Jones was denied procedural fairness. Measured against these, the court struck material dealing only with the personal, emotional and reputational impact on Jones (paras. 59 of the petition; 29-33 of the affidavit) as irrelevant and, in the case of para. 59, argument for which no damages could be awarded. Paragraphs mixing fact with argument were partially cured: 'incorrectly' was deleted from para. 19 and an argumentative phrase from para. 21, preserving the relevant factual allegations about the fairness of the LRB process and absence of cross-examination. Paragraphs 23 and 24 were struck entirely as predominantly argumentative and inflammatory, seeking to re-argue inferences from the record. Paragraph 60 (nature of the employer's conduct as disciplinary) and para. 62 (the 2005 internal Union report) of the petition, and paras. 26-28 of the affidavit (alleged bias/improper purposes of Union officials, already before the LRB), were held potentially relevant to the standard-of-review question and were not struck.
conclusion: Application granted in part: para. 59 of the petition and paras. 23-24, 29, 30-33 of the affidavit struck; 'incorrectly' struck from para. 19 and the specified phrase from para. 21, with the balance saved; the applications to strike paras. 60 and 62 of the petition and paras. 26-28 of the affidavit denied. Given divided success, each party bears its own costs.

issue: On what legal basis must the court resolve a dispute between parents over the choice of their child's secondary school?
facts: The divorced parents share custody of their 12-year-old daughter X and have amicably resolved past disagreements, but they are at an impasse over whether she should attend [School A] (arts focus) or [School B] (strong academics with Jewish studies).
rule: Under art. 604 C.C.Q., where difficulties arise in the exercise of parental authority, the court decides 'in the interest of the child' after fostering conciliation. Art. 33 C.C.Q. requires all decisions concerning a child to be made in light of the child's interests and rights, considering the child's moral, intellectual, emotional and physical needs, age, health, personality and family environment.
application: The choice of school ordinarily falls under parental authority and is best left to the parents in consultation with the child, but because the parents remained deadlocked despite court-fostered conciliation, the court had to decide. It applied the sole criterion of the child's best interest under arts. 33 and 604 C.C.Q.
conclusion: The court proceeded to determine, on the evidence, which school placement was in X's best interest.

issue: How much weight should be given to the child's previously expressed preference for [School A]?
facts: Between February and June 2015, when she was 11, X expressed a preference for [School A], including in a letter (GK-1). By July 2015 she stepped back, saying she would be happy at either school, and by 2016 she told her lawyer she had no preference and wanted the judge to decide.
rule: An informed wish freely expressed by a child aged 12 or more, without undue influence, is a largely determining factor because it often corresponds to the child's interest (Droit de la famille – 1883; Droit de la famille – 07832; Droit de la famille – 15754). Art. 34 C.C.Q. requires giving the child an opportunity to be heard where age and discernment permit. However, the court is not bound by the child's choice where other factors show it is not in her best interest, and parental authority is not transferred to the child.
application: The court found X's 2015 preference was not fully informed or grounded: she was only 11, her enthusiasm shifted after each school visit, she chose [School A] before visiting [School B], her motivation was limited to the arts program, and she was influenced (unintentionally) by her father's enthusiasm; part of the GK-1 letter was written in defiance and frustration toward her mother. By 2016 she expressed no clear or definite preference. Allegations that the mother had bribed or coerced X rested on inadmissible hearsay and, in any event, were outweighed by the mother's credible denials.
conclusion: X's wish could not be a determining or decisive factor, as it was neither fully informed nor currently clear and definite; the decision had to be made on best-interest grounds.

issue: Which school best serves X's best interest?
facts: Both schools are private, government-accredited and follow the Quebec curriculum. X is a bright, hardworking student interested in sciences and maths, passionate and talented in the arts, and aspires to become a neuroradiologist. She attended a Jewish elementary school; both parents are Jewish, the mother being more observant. [School B] offers high-standard secular studies plus Jewish studies as one of four pillars, along with arts opportunities; [School A] has an excellent arts program but is non-denominational.
rule: The best interest of the child under arts. 33 and 604 C.C.Q. governs, assessed on the child's abilities, character, needs and family environment.
application: The court found [School B] a step above academically and better suited to X's needs, based on the school officials' testimony and the mother's carefully considered understanding of her daughter. X could continue developing her artistic interests at either school, as arts is a pillar at [School B] and the mother would continue supporting her artistic pursuits. The evidence showed X's Jewish education, begun in elementary school, was incomplete and important to her (interest in her Jewish identity, kosher eating), and Jewish studies at [School B] would complete it in a balanced, non-insular environment; the father's proposed after-school program was not equivalent. Attending [School B] would also facilitate continued joint custody between a secular father and observant mother.
conclusion: It was in X's best interest to attend [School B]; the father's motion to modify was dismissed and provisional execution ordered.

issue: Should custody be joint with equal parenting time, or sole custody to the mother?
facts: After a 3.5-year marriage the parents separated. The father sought joint custody and guardianship with alternating weeks; the mother had held sole interim custody since 2001 and sought to keep it. The parties were locked in high-conflict relations, generating nine prior court orders, repeated frightening scenes at access exchanges, and an inability to communicate without rancour.
rule: Under s. 16 of the Divorce Act and s. 24 of the Family Relations Act, the best interests of the child govern custody; the analysis is wide-ranging and free of any presumption for or against joint custody (Robinson v. Filyk; Gordon v. Goertz). Joint custody requires a degree of consultation and cooperation between parents (Lucken v. Hopkins; Ness v. Ness), though it can be ordered even where communication is difficult (P.Y.Y.M. v. D.M.; Carr v. Carr).
application: The Court found the parties consistently unable to prevent tension and strife over access exchanges, causing trauma to the children, and unable to cooperate or agree on a schedule without recourse to the courts. A joint custody order would increase opportunities for conflict and expose the children to greater stress. The mother had been the primary caregiver and provided a stable home; the father, though a good parent to the children directly, showed uncontrolled, frightening behaviour at exchanges and lacked insight into it.
conclusion: Joint custody was refused; the mother was granted continued sole custody and sole guardianship with the children's primary residence with her.

issue: What access arrangement is in the children's best interests?
facts: Dr. Elterman recommended alternating-week care (Wednesday to Monday). The children (ages 7 and 5) attended school in Langley, while the father lived in Vancouver, requiring 45–90 minutes of driving each way. The father's outbursts at exchanges risked psychological harm, though he posed no risk of physical harm.
rule: Access is intended to facilitate a meaningful, continuing post-divorce relationship between children and the access parent, to the extent consistent with the children's best interests (Young v. Young; Anson v. Anson).
application: The Court declined the expanded alternating-week arrangement, citing the burdensome travel from Langley to Vancouver on school days and, more importantly, concern about the father's emotional stability and the risk of psychological harm from his outbursts. The current arrangement, with adjustments, was found optimal to allow the children to know their father while preserving their stable environment.
conclusion: The father was granted alternating weekend access (Friday to Monday), specified Jewish-holiday days (up to seven), birthday, Father's Day, long-weekend Mondays, summer weeks, half of spring break, and daily telephone access; the restraining injunction and police-clause order were continued.

issue: What amount of child support should the father pay?
facts: The father, a manufacturer's representative, ran nearly all expenses through his company and had been paying only $7 per month. The defendant calculated his average income plus 75% of operating expenses at about $39,925; his business had suffered from market conditions and an uncollectible receivable.
rule: Child support is set under the Federal Child Support Guidelines according to the payor's income; a reasonable portion of business expenses may be reallocated as personal income where the evidence supports it.
application: With little evidence distinguishing personal from business expenses but agreement that some reallocation was warranted, the Court imputed a total income of $25,000, yielding a guideline amount of $375 per month for two children.
conclusion: The father was ordered to pay $375 per month in child support effective the first of the month following judgment.

issue: Is either spouse entitled to spousal support?
facts: The parties cohabited about 3.5 years. Neither showed substantial means; the father expected to rebuild his business once litigation ended, and the mother was a fitness trainer with a private clientele about to marry a capable, comfortably situated man.
rule: Spousal support turns on the conditions, means, needs and other circumstances of each spouse, the length of cohabitation and each party's obligation to become self-sufficient (Divorce Act ss. 15.2(4) and (6); F.R.A. s. 89). Marriage alone does not entitle a spouse to support (Moge v. Moge; Bracklow v. Bracklow); a new relationship does not automatically disentitle (Boudreau v. Bradbury).
application: Given the short marriage, the absence of compensatory economic loss, the modest means of both parties, and the mother's successful business and impending marriage providing a comfortable lifestyle, the Court found neither party had substantial means or great need for support.
conclusion: No spousal support was ordered to either party; each party to bear its own costs.

issue: Should the proposed interveners (IJV and NCCM) be granted leave to intervene as parties or friends of the court under Rule 13 in the anti-SLAPP motions?
facts: IJV and NCCM sought, at the eleventh hour after all evidence and 100-page factums had been exchanged, to intervene in defamation anti-SLAPP motions concerning statements that the plaintiff, a former Chief Commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, was a 'terror supporter' and 'Jew-hater'. Both wished to file affidavits and make submissions on the meaning of anti-semitism (NCCM also on the impact of such accusations on Muslims). The plaintiff consented; the defendants opposed.
rule: Rule 13.01 requires a proposed party-intervener to show they may be adversely affected by the judgment or share a common question of law or fact, subject to considering undue delay or prejudice; Rule 13.02 allows a friend of the court to render assistance by argument. The overarching question is whether the applicant can make a useful contribution without causing injustice to the parties (Animal Justice v. Ontario (AG), 2024 ONCA 941; Bedford v. Canada (AG), 2009 ONCA 669; Solmar Inc. v. Hall, 2025 ONCA 570; Peel v. Great Atlantic & Pacific). Intervention is granted sparingly in private disputes, even those with public-interest components, and anti-SLAPP motions under s. 137.1 CJA are meant to be a limited, expeditious screening exercise decided on a limited record (Pointes Protection, 2020 SCC 22; Benchwood Builders, 2025 ONCA 171; Hamer v. Jane Doe, 2024 ONCA 721).
application: The court held these were private defamation actions between two parties each, not constitutional or public-interest litigation, so the intervention test applies more rigorously. Neither intervener had a legal interest at stake; IJV's concern about being called anti-semitic in cross-examinations was collateral and it had not sued. Their submissions on the meaning of anti-semitism would constitute a 'deep dive' into factual issues inconsistent with the limited anti-SLAPP weighing exercise, would augment an already extensive record, and were brought too late for the defendants to respond, risking prejudice and injustice. The plaintiff was well-represented and had already filed extensive evidence on the same issues.
conclusion: The motions to intervene were dismissed.

issue: Does s. 137.1(5) of the Courts of Justice Act bar interventions in an anti-SLAPP motion?
facts: The defendants argued that s. 137.1(5)'s stay on further steps in the proceeding once an anti-SLAPP motion is made prohibits interventions.
rule: Section 137.1(5) provides that once an anti-SLAPP motion is made, no further steps may be taken 'by any party' until the motion and any appeal are finally disposed of.
application: The court disagreed: the provision restricts only parties, and potential interveners are not parties; there is a distinction between steps in the underlying proceeding and steps within the anti-SLAPP motion itself (Catalyst Capital, 2021 ONSC 125); and interveners have participated in anti-SLAPP motions and appeals before (Rainbow Alliance Dryden v. Webster, 2023 ONSC 7050; 40 Days for Life v. Dietrich; Buttar; Hansman v. Neufeld, 2023 SCC 14).
conclusion: Section 137.1(5) does not prohibit interventions; the argument was rejected, though the motions were dismissed on the merits of the Rule 13 test.

issue: Which party should present oral argument first on the anti-SLAPP motions?
facts: The defendants (moving parties) argued the plaintiff should go first because he conceded the expression concerned a matter of public interest, shifting the burden to him under s. 137.1(4). The plaintiff objected, noting the defendants are the moving parties.
rule: On an anti-SLAPP motion, the moving party need only establish that the proceeding arises from expression on a matter of public interest, after which the burden shifts to the plaintiff; ordinarily the party bringing the proceeding argues first even where it bears the persuasive burden, as in defamation trials.
application: The court found that although the plaintiff bears the persuasive burden, the defendants are the moving parties whose materials and submissions address all issues and were delivered first, with the plaintiff responding; there was no reason to alter that order.
conclusion: The defendants proceed first and address all issues.

issue: What parenting time and supervision arrangement serves the children's best interests in light of alleged family violence?
facts: The mother alleged years of physical, sexual, coercive and controlling abuse; the father admitted only to striking the older child A once (verified by the CAS) but denied all violence toward the mother. Reports from CAS/JF&CS and supervisors documented continuing volatility, poor boundaries and impulsivity, though the children love and crave time with the father.
rule: Under s. 16(1) and (2) of the Divorce Act the court considers only the best interests of the child, giving primary consideration to the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being; ss. 16(3)–(6) enumerate best-interests factors including 'family violence' (broadly defined to include coercive and controlling behaviour). McBennett v. Danis, 2021 ONSC 3610.
application: After detailed credibility analysis (applying Kinsella v. Mills factors) the court accepted the mother's account of repeated violence and coercive control during the marriage, and found abuse of A. Although the father's conduct had improved and the children benefit from time with him, ongoing volatility and lack of judgment created continuing risk within the home.
conclusion: Parenting time was expanded (alternate weekends and a weekday evening plus holidays) but must be supervised by the father's mother or aunt while inside the home; supervision is not required for outside-the-home daytime activities, while all overnights must be supervised. The mother remains primary caregiver.

issue: How should decision-making responsibility be allocated?
facts: The father sought joint decision-making but conceded he simply wished to be consulted; the parties had difficulty agreeing (e.g., counselling for A), and there was a history of the father's coercive and controlling conduct toward the mother.
rule: Decision-making is a parenting order governed by the best-interests test; joint decision-making requires evidence the parties can communicate effectively about the child: Kaplanis v. Kaplanis, 2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA); Berman v. Berman, 2017 ONCA 905.
application: Given the family-violence history, it was neither reasonable nor appropriate to require the mother to negotiate consent with the father; however, to foster the father's relationship the mother must consult him (via a third party) on major non-urgent decisions and take his input in good faith before deciding.
conclusion: Sole decision-making to the mother, subject to a consultation process; she may obtain passports and travel during her parenting time without the father's consent.

issue: Should the s. 35(1) CLRA restraining order be continued?
facts: Criminal and then family-law restraining orders had been in place continuously since August 2019; the mother reasonably feared for her safety though no incident had occurred since the charges were laid.
rule: Section 35(1) of the Children's Law Reform Act permits a restraining order where a person has reasonable grounds to fear for their safety.
application: Given the serious proven violence, the mother had reasonable grounds to fear for her safety; the absence of recent incidents was attributable to the standing orders.
conclusion: The restraining order was continued permanently: no direct/indirect contact except through an agreed third party and no approach within 250 metres.

issue: Should income be imputed to the Respondent and what child support is owing?
facts: The father reported net rental losses from a multi-unit investment property, but a spreadsheet he had prepared showed substantially higher gross income, and he gave shifting explanations under cross-examination.
rule: Section 19(1) of the Federal Child Support Guidelines permits imputing income, including where a spouse has failed to provide accurate income information (s. 19(1)(f)).
application: The court found the father not credible and under-reporting rental income, adopting the mother's use of the spreadsheet's actual/projected figures.
conclusion: Income imputed to bring total income to $160,859; arrears of $28,238 fixed and ongoing table support of $2,207/month ordered.

issue: Which claimed expenses qualify as s. 7 special or extraordinary expenses?
facts: The mother claimed retroactive contributions for A.'s private school, M.'s daycare, orthodontics and extracurriculars; the father disputed the private school and complained receipts were provided only before trial.
rule: Section 7(1)(d)/(f) and s. 7(1.1) of the Guidelines govern extraordinary education and extracurricular expenses, assessed for necessity to the child's best interests and reasonableness relative to means; consultation is one factor but not a prerequisite: Titova v. Titov, 2012 ONCA 864; Park v. Thompson, 2005 CanLII 14132 (ON CA); Ondrejech v. Markham, 2021 ONSC 787.
application: A.'s private school was not necessary or reasonable (she thrived in public school, the father had not agreed, and costs pressed the parties' means), but M.'s daycare until grade one was a legitimate expense, as were orthodontics and dance/gymnastics; the delayed-receipts objection was dismissed given the restraining order and violence context.
conclusion: Reimbursement of $842.48 ordered, plus $545/month (33%) toward continuing s. 7 expenses; the private school claim was refused.

issue: How should equalization and post-separation adjustments be determined?
facts: Numerous NFP items were disputed, including a Subaru, a $50,000 transfer, settlement proceeds, cryptocurrency purchased with the mother's credit card, notional capital gains, an OSAP loan, and an Ally Bank date-of-marriage balance.
rule: Equalization under the Family Law Act; s. 14 FLA presumption of resulting trust on transfers between spouses; date-of-marriage and valuation-date assets/debts are tallied on the evidence.
application: The court resolved each item (excluding the Subaru and the $50,000 transfer, adding the BitCoin to the father's side via resulting trust valued at $10,482.72, crediting the father $27,172.49 for the Ally funds, neutralizing the OSAP loan against an RESP), and accepted the mother's post-separation adjustment claim.
conclusion: Equalization payment of $29,928.94 and a post-separation adjustment of $3,054.00 ordered payable to the Applicant within 30 days.

issue: Is Lacombe's action prescribed?
facts: The impugned conduct of Fine and Langenauer began around 2003 but continued through to the seizure of Lacombe's bank accounts in early 2008. Lacombe filed his action on 18 May 2008. Fine argued that if the action was in defamation, the one-year prescription applied.
rule: Defamation's characteristic injury is harm to reputation (Bou Malhab c. Diffusion Métromédia CMR inc., 2011 SCC 9). Under arts. 2925 and 2926 C.c.Q., the general prescription is three years running from when the injury first manifests. Prescription only begins once all elements of liability—fault, damage and causation—are present (Daigle c. Mathieu, 2010 QCCA 1612). A distinction is drawn between gradual and continuous/perpetual injury (Foyer du sport inc. c. Coop fédérée, 2008 QCCA 381): for continuous injury caused by ongoing fault, prescription runs with each new wrongful act.
application: The Court found this was not a defamation action, as Lacombe alleged no harm to reputation among third parties. The alleged abusive proceedings and inappropriate conduct formed part of a continuous process generating alleged injury up to early 2008. The three-year prescription therefore applied and the culminating incidents (the July 2007 notary meeting and the early-2008 seizure) fell within the period.
conclusion: The action was not prescribed.

issue: Were Fine's proceedings and communications abusive?
facts: It was Lacombe who first launched litigation against Langenauer in 2002. Fine, retained by Langenauer, sent demand letters, communicated with the Royal Bank about suspected diverted funds, resisted certain requests, and executed seizures. An error in the notice to defendant (30 days instead of 10) led to a default inscription, but Fine consented to relief from default at the hearing.
rule: To hold a lawyer liable for abusive proceedings, the plaintiff bears a heavy burden: he must show bad faith and that the proceedings were brought without legal foundation and solely to harm (Languedoc c. Martin et Damiani, 2003 CanLII 71989). The conduct must be so reckless, outrageous, scandalous or reprehensible as to constitute a civil fault (Chionis c. Gaudet, 2006 QCCS 2928). Uncommon vigour in exercising rights is not a fault (Foyer du sport).
application: The Court reviewed each complaint—the demand letters, the failure to consent earlier to relief from default, communications with the bank (justified by legitimate fears that Lacombe was diverting funds, which Lacombe partly admitted), reluctance to conciliate, contesting homologation, and the seizures. In each instance the Court found Fine acted with vigour, sometimes more aggressively than necessary, but committed no fault; several of his positions were vindicated by other judges.
conclusion: Fine's proceedings and written communications were not abusive.

issue: Did Fine commit a fault by insulting Lacombe?
facts: Lacombe alleged Fine called him 'stupid frog', 'Your house will be mine', 'embezzler and thief', and 'dick-head et fucking cocksucker'. Some words were spoken with no witness, some before witnesses. Fine denied them; both men were credible.
rule: Where two credible witnesses conflict, testimony affirming a fact is preferred over testimony denying it (Royer, La preuve civile). Where words are spoken before witnesses, the Court assesses whether their existence is more probable than not. Fault engaging liability arises under art. 1457 C.c.Q.
application: The Court preferred Lacombe's evidence on 'stupid frog' / 'Your house will be mine' (spoken privately) and on the notary-office insults ('dick head', 'fucking cocksucker'), the latter corroborated by Ms. Myre. It rejected the alleged Court of Appeal hallway insults, which were uncorroborated and contradicted by Langenauer, and found the 'embezzler' reference was a description of the litigation, not a fault.
conclusion: Fine committed a fault by uttering certain inappropriate/insulting remarks, particularly as a member of the Barreau.

issue: What is Langenauer's liability?
facts: Langenauer retained Fine, followed his advice, believed legitimately that Lacombe was diverting funds (Lacombe sent accountant reports late and signed some leases solely in his own name), and was willing throughout to transfer the buildings on payment of his share. Langenauer allegedly said he would spend $100,000 on a 'hard ball Jewish lawyer', which he denied.
rule: A party has the right to defend himself, retain counsel of choice, and follow that counsel's advice; authorizing non-abusive proceedings is not a fault (art. 1457 C.c.Q.).
application: Since Fine's proceedings were not abusive, Langenauer could not be faulted for authorizing them. His suspicions about diversion were legitimate. There was no evidence Langenauer uttered inappropriate remarks or behaved improperly; the alleged comment about spending money on a lawyer, even if said, was a legitimate expression of intentions within the litigation.
conclusion: Langenauer bears no liability; the action against him is dismissed with costs.

issue: Did Lacombe suffer compensable damages?
facts: Lacombe claimed $525,500 including $300,000 for lost time and income, $50,000 moral damages, and $150,000 punitive damages. He proved lost income only through tax returns showing low incomes 2003-2007 but $320,870 in 2008. He first consulted his doctor in September 2005 (anxiety noted) but was never placed off work.
rule: Damages must be assessed by reference to the reasonable person's perception (T…N.. c. C…V…, 2011 QCCS 2560). Moral injury includes loss of enjoyment of life, pain and suffering (Québec (Curateur public) c. Syndicat national des employés de l'hôpital St-Ferdinand, 1996 CanLII 172). Compensation is personalized (art. 1611 C.c.Q.). Exemplary damages under s. 49 of the Quebec Charter require an unlawful and intentional interference (Augustus c. Gosset, 1996 CanLII 173; St-Ferdinand), distinct from reckless or negligent interference.
application: The Court found Lacombe's reaction disproportionate; a reasonable person would have kept working. The income drop was more likely caused by his own choice to devote his energies to litigation and his disciplinary complaint. The $300,000 material loss claim was unproven for lack of transaction details and market evidence. Moral damages were warranted but minimal given the limited impact and absence of third-party audience beyond his spouse—assessed at $2,500. Punitive damages were refused because Fine's words were reckless and negligent, not intentional in the sense required. Abusive-proceedings-related legal fees were rejected given the finding that Fine's proceedings were not abusive.
conclusion: Lacombe was awarded $2,500 in moral damages; all other heads of damage were rejected.

issue: Is Lacombe's action abusive toward Langenauer?
facts: Langenauer counterclaimed $50,000 alleging Lacombe's action was abusive. The Court found Lacombe's claim against Langenauer ill-founded on the facts.
rule: An abusive proceeding is one that is or may be manifestly ill-founded, frivolous or dilatory (Agence du revenu du Québec c. Groupe Enico inc., 2012 QCCA 479); an ill-founded proceeding is not the same as an abusive one.
application: Although the action against Langenauer was ill-founded, some of Langenauer's conduct could have given Lacombe the conviction he had a cause of action. It was not frivolous, dilatory or manifestly ill-founded.
conclusion: The counterclaim was dismissed with costs.

issue: Are the children TMA and LCA in need of protection under ss. 74(2)(b) and (f) of the CYFSA?
facts: While the family lived together the father imposed rigid controlling household rules (limiting water and hydro use, forcing hand-washing of dishes and laundry, restricting garbage), engaged in ongoing verbal, emotional and physical abuse of the mother (name-calling, twisting her arm, slapping her, a 'hairdryer incident' in which he punched their son TMA who was shielding her), and was physically and emotionally harmful to the children (locking them in a chair, dragging TMA down the stairs, spanking, threats). The children were repeatedly exposed to domestic violence. TMA was later diagnosed with PTSD and separation anxiety, missed school, vomited from an emotional condition, and had flashbacks; LCA became fearful and anxious.
rule: Under s. 74(2)(b) a child is in need of protection where there is a real and likely (not speculative) risk of physical harm from a person's failure to care for or a pattern of neglect (Children's Aid Society of Rainy River (District) v. B.(C.)); verbal abuse and exposure to inappropriate situations can constitute risk of physical harm (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Hamilton v. S.(L.)). Under s. 74(2)(f) a child in need of protection is one who has suffered serious emotional harm (anxiety, depression, withdrawal, self-destructive/aggressive behaviour, delayed development) resulting from a parent's actions; the harm must be more than minor unhappiness and must be 'serious' (Jewish Family and Child Services v. Ki. Sl.). The Society bears the onus on a balance of probabilities (CAS of Niagara Region v. P.L.R.); a court may consider past conduct (s. 93(1)(a)).
application: The court found an overwhelming evidentiary basis. The children were exposed to and directly subjected to the father's controlling and abusive conduct. The mother's evidence was credible and reliable while the father's was not; where evidence conflicted the court preferred the other witnesses. The children were emotionally harmed (TMA's PTSD diagnosis, school absences, flashbacks; LCA's fear and anxiety) and placed at risk of physical harm.
conclusion: The children are in need of protection under ss. 74(2)(b) and (f) of the CYFSA.

issue: Is court intervention through a protection order required to protect the children in the future?
facts: The circumstances triggering the protection findings (the father's abusive, controlling conduct and the resulting trauma) persisted, and the father had gained no insight. The children continued to have significant mental and emotional needs.
rule: Under s. 101(1) the court must satisfy itself that intervention through a court order is necessary to protect the child in the future; the need may arise from the existence or absence of the triggering circumstances or from subsequent circumstances (CAS of Toronto v. S.A.P.).
application: Given the facts underlying the protection finding and the disposition analysis, ongoing protection was required.
conclusion: Intervention through a protection order is required to protect both children in the future.

issue: Should the mother be granted sole custody rather than the joint custody sought by the father?
facts: All parties sought a custody order; the Society, the Office of the Children's Lawyer and the mother sought sole custody to the mother, while the father sought joint custody. There was no history of appropriate communication between the parents. The father continued to blame the mother, denied any wrongdoing, refused to gain insight, had a poor record of cooperation with professionals, did not pay child support regularly and failed to pay propane bills leaving the children's home without heat. The mother had engaged in counselling, cooperated with the Society, and the children were thriving in her care. The children (15 and 13) clearly wished to have no relationship with their father.
rule: Under s. 102 the court may grant custody where it is in the child's best interests, deemed to be an order under s. 28 of the Children's Law Reform Act; best interests factors are set out in s. 74(3). Joint custody requires evidence of historical and appropriate communication and should not be ordered where communication is poor or where a parent seeks it to control the other (Kaplanis v. Kaplanis; Graham v. Bruto; S.(S.) v. K.(S.); Izyuk v. Bilousov).
application: The children's mature views were given significant weight; they had no emotional tie to their father and their positions were reasonable. Joint custody would be 'a recipe for disaster,' providing the father a mechanism to reassert control and re-expose the mother and children to abuse and derail their progress. The mother could meet the children's needs and provide stability, while the father would approach joint decision-making with the same misguided mindset.
conclusion: Sole custody of both children is granted to the mother.

issue: Should the mother be permitted to obtain/renew passports and travel with the children without the father's consent?
facts: The mother sought authority to apply for and renew the children's passports and to travel for vacation without the father's consent. The father opposed, wanting consent rights, and had difficulty signing routine consents in a timely manner and interacting appropriately with the mother.
rule: Under s. 102(2)(a) CYFSA the court may make orders it could make under s. 28 of the Children's Law Reform Act, including regarding passports and travel as incidents of custody, applying a best interests analysis.
application: Given the father's struggles to identify the children's best interests, his delays with consents, and his inability to interact appropriately with the mother, any involvement in the passport/travel process would give him a means to exert control. As sole custodian the mother could make such decisions in a child-focussed manner.
conclusion: The mother is permitted to obtain/renew the children's passports and travel with them for vacation purposes without the father's written consent.

issue: Should the father have access, including through a court-ordered reunification/therapeutic plan?
facts: The father proposed a three-step reunification plan but led no evidence about the proposed service providers despite being told how to present it. The children, aged 15 and 13, were clear, consistent and adamant that they did not want any relationship with their father or to work on repairing it. Dr. Ashbourne testified the children's voices should prevail and warned of risks of forcing adolescents (poor school performance, attempted suicide, running away, loss of the primary relationship).
rule: Under s. 104 and s. 105(2) the court shall order access unless satisfied continued contact would not be in the child's best interests; access should only be forfeited in the most extreme and unusual circumstances, being a remedy of last resort (Jennings v. Garrett). Therapeutic/reunification orders are of uncertain jurisdiction and, even if available, engage the Health Care Consent Act and remain discretionary, to be made sparingly (Leelarantna; Testani v. Haughton; Barrett v. Huver).
application: The father failed to provide the evidence needed to consider his proposal. Even with jurisdiction and dispensing with consent, the court would not make the order: the children's mature reasonable wishes, their significant needs, the father's lack of insight and comprehension of the reunification process, and his poor record with professionals all pointed against it. The children were thriving without their father and deserved closure.
conclusion: There shall be no access to the children by the father, and his request for a reunification plan is dismissed. The father's related requests for report cards, photographs, and children's projects, and to renovate the matrimonial home, are also dismissed (the latter for lack of jurisdiction over property).

issue: Should a restraining order be made against the father?
facts: The mother feared for her own and the children's safety. The father had complied with the temporary no-contact order but had accepted no responsibility, gained no insight, showed disregard for court orders except those enforceable by police, displayed obsessive persistence over reunification (forgoing employment for 5.5 years), and the children recently demonstrated fear of him. The judge was concerned about how he would react to the decision.
rule: Under s. 102(3)-(4) CYFSA the court may make a restraining order deemed to be under s. 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act. Principles from C.(D.) v. C.(M.T.) and Catholic CAS of Toronto v. I.A. require reasonable grounds to fear for safety, considering the onus, caution, psychological as well as physical fear, the passage of time, and the link between past and possible future aggression.
application: Examining the intervening period, the court found the father's continued lack of responsibility and insight, disregard for orders, obsessive persistence and the children's recent fear established a link between his past behaviour and the mother's present fears. The court found he had refrained from contact only because he treated the temporary order as a restraining order, and it was extremely likely he would seek out the mother and children if none were made.
conclusion: A restraining order was granted: the father is restrained from contacting the mother and children and from coming within 500 metres of their home, schools, or other places he knows they may be.

issue: Does the Warsaw Convention govern the claim and, if so, bar punitive damages?
facts: Mr. Chernack was a passenger on an international Air France flight from Montreal to Paris when the incident occurred; he sought $150,000 in punitive damages for interruption of his morning prayers.
rule: The Warsaw Convention (Act to give effect to a Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules Relating to International Carriage by Air, c. C-26) applies to international carriage for reward and, under Art. 17, provides compensation only for 'damage sustained' in the event of bodily injury. Authorities (Shawcross and Beaumont; Naval-Torres v. Northwest Airlines; Surprenant v. Air Canada; Ville de Verdun v. Doré) hold the Convention's damages are purely compensatory and do not include moral or punitive damages.
application: The claim was solely for punitive damages, which the Convention does not provide, whether measured against its objectives or against Quebec law as lex fori. Since the claim did not fall within the compensatory scheme, the Convention could not serve as the basis of the Court's competence under Art. 28.
conclusion: The Court held the Convention does not apply and its competence could not be founded on Art. 28 of the Convention.

issue: Can the Quebec Charter ground the claim, or is it inapplicable because air transport is a federal undertaking?
facts: The alleged violation occurred aboard an aircraft during flight, in the context of managing the aircraft.
rule: Section 55 of the Quebec Charter limits it to matters within Quebec's legislative authority. Under Irwin Toy and Air Canada v. Ontario (Liquor Control Board), aeronautics and the operation of aircraft fall within exclusive federal jurisdiction, forming the 'basic, minimum and unassailable content' of the federal power, so provincial law cannot apply to the essential and vital elements of a federal undertaking.
application: The interruption occurred during the management of the aircraft in flight — an essential and vital element of a federal undertaking — so the Quebec Charter could not apply to it.
conclusion: The Quebec Charter was held inapplicable and could not serve as the basis for the plaintiff's action.

issue: Does the Superior Court have jurisdiction over a claim founded on the Canadian Human Rights Act, or does the Tribunal have exclusive jurisdiction?
facts: Air France argued the Canadian Human Rights Commission and Tribunal had exclusive jurisdiction over any claim under ss. 8 and 14 of the Code.
rule: Per A.G. Ontario v. Pembina Exploration and A.G. Canada v. Law Society of British Columbia (and Art. 31 C.C.P.), provincial superior courts are presumed competent over the full range of cases, whether the applicable law is federal or provincial, unless jurisdiction is exclusively assigned elsewhere by a specific provision. The Code contains no provision granting the Tribunal exclusive jurisdiction.
application: The Code did not confer exclusive jurisdiction on the Tribunal; the Commission and Tribunal share jurisdiction while superior courts remain competent. Mr. Chernack was entitled to choose to seize the Court rather than file a complaint with the Commission.
conclusion: The Court held it had jurisdiction to hear the matter.

issue: Did the defendants discriminate against and intentionally violate the plaintiff's right to practise his religion, warranting punitive damages?
facts: The chief steward, Corneloup, tapped Mr. Chernack on the shoulder during his morning prayers and invited him to return to his seat while preparing for breakfast service; the lighting was dim, Chernack faced the window with his back to the aisle, and the shawl and phylacteries were not noticed. Air France had no policy prohibiting prayers, and Chernack had prayed on prior flights; he completed his prayers, though nervously. Corneloup and the instructor apologized.
rule: Under the Canadian Human Rights Act (ss. 2, 3) and R. v. Big M Drug Mart, freedom of religion protects sincere religious practice from coercion or constraint. Discrimination requires a distinction, exclusion or preference based on an enumerated ground causing prejudice to human dignity (per Quebec Court of Appeal, Egan, Law). Punitive damages require proof of intent to cause damage (Syndicat National des employés de l'Hôpital St-Ferdinand v. Curateur public).
application: There was no Air France policy against prayer, and the interruption arose from routine breakfast preparation, not from any distinction based on religion. Corneloup did not see the shawl or realize Chernack was praying; he did not insist and likely invited other standing passengers to sit as well. No discriminatory conduct, adverse-effect discrimination, or intent to cause harm was established; Chernack was not compelled to abandon his religious ritual.
conclusion: The Court found no discrimination and no intent, so no basis for punitive damages; the claim was dismissed with costs.

issue: Was there sufficient urgency to justify issuing a provisional injunction against the defendant's conduct?
facts: Lande and Pion, who had sued Feldman for defamation in December 2019, sought a provisional injunction to stop Feldman from communicating information about their private lives, from using the media to disseminate defamatory statements, and from contacting their relatives and associates. Feldman had for over a year spread claims that Lande's wealth came from Nazi gold stolen from Holocaust victims and inherited via Ludwig Delphiner; he had made videos, sent a defamatory affidavit, been arrested, and, most recently, a Journal de Montréal article titled 'L'or nazi autour d'une querelle judiciaire' was published on October 31, 2020, which the plaintiffs said was the last straw.
rule: Under art. 510 C.C.P., a provisional injunction requires urgency in addition to the three interlocutory criteria (art. 511 C.C.P.). Per Gervais, L'injonction, urgency must be 'immediate and apparent', reserved for extremely urgent cases where even the delay to obtain an interlocutory injunction would irreparably prejudice the applicant's rights; a merely hypothetical or uncertain prejudice does not suffice.
application: The Court found the defamatory and privacy-related conduct had been known since September 2019 and detailed throughout the Application and Amended Application, including videos and the March 2020 affidavit. While the October 31 Article escalated the dispute into the public eye, it was largely based on extracts from judicial proceedings. Without deciding whether reputation was harmed, the Court held that the Article, even combined with prior facts, did not create a situation where an unforeseeable illegal act by Feldman was imminent so as to establish the immediate, apparent urgency required for provisional relief.
conclusion: The Court held that no urgency existed warranting a provisional injunction.

issue: Were the interlocutory injunction criteria met so as to grant relief at the provisional stage?
facts: The plaintiffs relied essentially on the facts already alleged in their prior proceedings, seeking sweeping orders without new evidence being adduced at the provisional stage.
rule: The three criteria for an interlocutory injunction (appearance of right, serious or irreparable prejudice, balance of inconvenience) must all be satisfied save exceptional circumstances (art. 511 C.C.P.; RJR-MacDonald; HRM Projet Children inc. v. Devimco Immobilier inc., 2020 QCCA 1123).
application: Because the threshold requirement of urgency for a provisional injunction was not met, the Court declined to issue orders of the kind sought without evidence being adduced, notwithstanding the plaintiffs' understandable exasperation.
conclusion: The Court declined to grant the injunction; the motion was dismissed with costs.

issue: Do individual divided co-owners have the legal interest under arts. 55 and 165(3) C.p.c. to sue their own vendor for a latent defect affecting a common portion, or is that interest reserved to the syndicate?
facts: Twenty units at the Jardins de Toulouse II in Boucherville were built and sold by Classique with defective fireplace chimney shafts (missing fire separations), a latent defect. Corrective work was done in both common and private portions; the syndicate acted only as a 'courroie de transmission', imposed no levy and drew nothing from the contingency fund, and each co-owner with a fireplace individually chose and paid its own professionals. Co-owners each sued their vendor for reduction of the sale price and damages.
rule: Arts. 55 and 165(3) C.p.c. require a sufficient legal interest. Arts. 1038, 1039, 1046, 1047, 1063, 1077 and 1081 C.c.Q. govern divided co-ownership; art. 1081 provides the syndicate 'peut' (may) sue for latent/construction defects. Arts. 1726–1729 C.c.Q. govern the legal warranty against latent defects. The leading authority is Belcourt Construction Co. c. Creatchman, [1979] C.A. 595, confirmed by Société d'habitation et de développement de Montréal c. Bergeron, [1996] R.J.Q. 2088, holding nothing restricts each co-owner's individual right to sue its vendor in reduction of price/annulment; followed in Parent c. Daniel, Éthier c. Robson, Bourret c. Brixi and Delorme c. Immeubles 1880 inc.
application: The dominant jurisprudential current, following the Court of Appeal, holds that the syndicate's recourse under arts. 1077 and 1081 C.c.Q. is optional ('peut', not 'doit') and additional to, not exclusive of, each co-owner's own recourse. The co-owner (not the syndicate) owns the indivisible share of the common portions acquired with the private portion and alone can dispose of it. Since the syndicate imposed no levy and each co-owner paid individually, collective and individual interests never opposed, so each co-owner retained interest to sue its vendor in reduction of price and damages under arts. 1726/1728 C.c.Q. A co-owner cannot sue the syndicate for reduction of price since the syndicate is not party to the sale.
conclusion: Each divided co-owner possesses the legal interest required by art. 55 C.p.c. to sue its vendor individually in reduction of the sale price for a latent defect, even one affecting a common portion; the preliminary exception is dismissed.

issue: Does each co-owner filing a separate individual small claims action constitute a prohibited division of a claim under art. 955 C.p.c.?
facts: The total corrective cost for the whole co-ownership exceeded $7,000, and each of the twenty co-owners filed an individual small claims claim of roughly $3,000–$4,000 against Classique.
rule: Art. 955 C.p.c. prohibits dividing, even indirectly, a claim exceeding $7,000 into several claims not exceeding that amount, on pain of dismissal.
application: Because each co-owner holds its own distinct, individual claim against its vendor (as determined on the interest question), there is no single claim being artificially split. The two grounds were intimately linked and interdependent, as Classique's representative acknowledged; Classique did not plead this ground separately or with distinct authorities.
conclusion: There is no prohibited division of a claim under art. 955 C.p.c.; the exception is dismissed.

issue: Which corporate entity is the proper defendant/warranty party given the builder-vendor's numerous name changes, mergers and share buybacks?
facts: The units were sold in 2003 by Habitation Classique 2000 inc. Through a maze of name changes, a 2000 merger, a reversion to 'Habitation Classique inc.', and a 2011 change to 9232-6941 Québec inc. (with borrowed names), plus late-2011 buybacks of its own shares and share transfers, the corporate identity became confusing. Ordered documents were produced late by Classique.
rule: A condemnation can only be pronounced against a legal person that still exists at the time of judgment; the Court has a duty (art. 977 C.p.c.) to verify the lien de droit and propose amendment after checking the REQ. Each vendor in the chain of title, including the builder, is bound to the warranty against latent defects (arts. 1442, 1730 C.c.Q.; Hay c. Jacques).
application: After tracing all corporate transformations through the REQ and corporate registers, the Court concluded that Habitation Classique inc. and Habitation Classique 2000 inc. no longer exist under those names and that the surviving entity carrying the contractual obligations is 9232-6941 Québec inc. The Salomon-Mercier vendors, though in good faith, remain liable under the warranty and may call Classique in warranty.
conclusion: The contractual lien de droit of the plaintiffs and warranty claimants lies against 9232-6941 Québec inc., which is the proper defendant/warranty party.

issue: What amount should be awarded for loss of enjoyment, trouble and inconvenience?
facts: From January to April 2011, in heating season, co-owners could not use their fireplaces; they lost time attending inspections and corrective work, faced an increased fire-propagation risk until November 2011, and experienced stress. No individualized evidence of harm was led for each co-owner.
rule: Art. 1728 C.c.Q. entitles the buyer to damages where the professional vendor is presumed to know the defect; the court arbitrates a reasonable amount in the absence of personalized proof.
application: The Court accepted that sensitivities vary between co-owners but, lacking personalized evidence, awarded a reasonable minimum base compensation. In the Turgeon file, since the Salomon-Mercier vendors were in good faith and unaware of any defect, no such damages were allowed.
conclusion: $700 is arbitrated for each owner or owning couple in file 505-32-029574-127, added to the admitted quantum; no such damages in the Turgeon file.

issue: Should the Court grant the remedies sought to halt the Provincial Court criminal proceeding, or does the application offend the rule against collateral attack?
facts: Fearn, facing weapons and customs charges in Provincial Court (the 'Border Action', trial set for March 2014), applied to the Court of Queen's Bench for prohibition, a stay, a non-suit, an order vacating Canada Customs' decisions, and compensation for false imprisonment.
rule: A court cannot review or vary the decision of another court except in the proper procedural context such as an appeal; any other attempt is a prohibited 'collateral attack' (British Columbia (Workers' Compensation Board) v Figliola, 2011 SCC 52; R v Litchfield). Prohibition is an exceptional judicial-review remedy requiring proof of a lack of jurisdiction or prejudice (R v Anson; R v Song). A stay requires the tripartite RJR-MacDonald test.
application: Fearn's proper course was to complete the Border Action and appeal if dissatisfied. He offered no legal basis for lack of jurisdiction or prejudice; a non-suit belongs at the close of the Crown case; challenges to Canada Customs belong in Federal Court judicial review; and compensation was premature and sought in the wrong form. His stay application failed at the first RJR-MacDonald step because it had no basis in law and was frivolous.
conclusion: The application was an impermissible collateral attack and was dismissed; the Provincial Court proceeding was not halted.

issue: Do Mr. Fearn's OPCA theories provide any legal basis to escape the jurisdiction of the CBSA and Alberta courts?
facts: Fearn, a Sovereign Citizen/Man litigant named in Meads v Meads, argued he was a 'sovereign living soul' subject only to a 'mutant' common law, that governments are corporations, that legislation was 'pretend legislation', that a plea entered on his behalf was void, that judges must produce oaths, and that the courts were part of a Vatican/Masonic conspiracy.
rule: All persons present in or entering Canada are subject to Canadian law (A.N.B. v Hancock; Meads v Meads, 2012 ABQB 571). A not-guilty plea entered by the court is authorized by Criminal Code s 606(2). Legislation is presumed validly enacted (Kruger v R). Foisted unilateral agreements have no legal effect; there is no right to demand a judge's oath; the Magna Carta has no super-constitutional status.
application: Each argument was rejected: Fearn cannot opt out of statutory law, the plea conformed to s 606(2), he offered no evidence that any statute was invalid, the corporate-registry/SEC arguments are irrelevant, conspiracy claims lacked any proof, and the Provincial Court had statutory jurisdiction over the Criminal Code and Customs Act offences. Meads applies squarely to him.
conclusion: The OPCA arguments were legally incorrect and pseudolegal; this was a second and independent basis to dismiss the application.

issue: Is the application frivolous and vexatious, warranting restrictions on Mr. Fearn's access to the Court?
facts: Fearn had a history of three Canadian and seventeen US actions, all dismissed or abandoned, habitually failing to pay fees, suing judges and court staff, and using intemperate, conspiratorial and threatening language.
rule: Frivolous pleadings are factually hopeless or in bad faith; vexatious conduct is synonymous with abuse of process (Wong v Leung; R v Scott). The Judicature Act, RSA 2000, c J-2, ss 23-23.1 and Dykun v Odishaw set out indicia of vexatiousness, including persistently relitigating decided issues, pursuing hopeless proceedings, and rolling grounds forward into new actions against lawyers and judges. All OPCA schemes are inherently frivolous and vexatious (Meads).
application: Fearn's application and litigation history displayed nearly every indicium of vexatiousness. The only logical explanation was a desire to break the rules and tie up court resources.
conclusion: The application was frivolous and vexatious (a third basis for dismissal); Fearn was barred from filing anything relating to the Border Action without leave, and the decision was referred to the Attorneys General for possible broader Judicature Act restrictions.

issue: Can costs be ordered against an accused who advances OPCA arguments in a criminal-related proceeding, and should they be here?
facts: The Crown sought $4,000 in costs. The Court treated the application as criminal rather than civil in character.
rule: In the criminal context, costs are exceptional and flow from the court's inherent jurisdiction (R v 974649 Ontario Inc.; Attorney-General of Quebec v Cronier). The Charter s 7 right to full answer and defence militates against costs. The Court set out four criteria for costs against OPCA accused: the accused initiates the process; relies on a clearly illegal/rejected OPCA basis; is entirely unsuccessful; and the process is ancillary to, not part of, the trial itself.
application: Fearn's application met all four criteria, so costs could have been awarded. However, because the remedy was new and unannounced, fairness required declining it so that Fearn would not be taken by surprise.
conclusion: Costs were not awarded, but Fearn was warned that future frivolous OPCA applications may attract costs.

issue: Does Mr. Fearn's conduct and 'Notice' constitute contempt of court, and can OPCA arguments and guru activity attract contempt?
facts: Fearn's 'Notice' and attachments accused judges of being murderers, thieves, part of a Vatican/Masonic conspiracy, and threatened extrajudicial action and 'hanging'; but in court on January 13, 2014 he was respectful and the hearing proceeded without disruption.
rule: Contempt requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt (Bhatnager). Civil contempt involves disobedience; criminal contempt adds public defiance calculated to depreciate the court's authority (United Nurses of Alberta). Under R v Kopyto, insulting speech is contempt only where it creates a 'clear and present' or 'real and imminent' danger to the administration of justice; the effect or intended effect, not the substance, is decisive (R v Cram; R v Prefontaine; R v Gillespie). Certain OPCA tactics (foisted unilateral agreements, fee schedules, threats of extrajudicial sanction, liens) directed at courts are prima facie civil contempt; commercial OPCA 'guru' promotion may be criminal contempt.
application: Although Fearn's written materials were extreme and obnoxious, they were only peripheral to the hearing and did not disrupt or impede the court process, and he was respectful in court. Had such statements been made in the hearing, sanction could follow. The Crown had not sought a criminal contempt finding.
conclusion: Fearn was not found in contempt, but the Court held that OPCA tactics targeting courts can constitute civil contempt and that OPCA guru activity may be prosecuted as criminal contempt.

issue: Is the youth a child in need of protection under ss. 74(2)(b) and (e) of the CYFSA?
facts: The 17-year-old youth has cerebral palsy, is non-verbal, incontinent and requires full-time care. Living in shelter accommodation with his father, the youth's medical, developmental and dental needs were neglected: he had no family doctor, no dental care (needing surgery since 2020, causing pain), was not in school, and lived in a filthy, roach- and bedbug-infested room. The father repeatedly refused services offered over three years by shelter staff and C.A.S.T. and missed appointments. The evidence was essentially undisputed as the parents largely did not participate at trial.
rule: Under s. 74(2)(b) and (e) CYFSA a child is in need of protection where there is a risk of physical harm from a caregiver's failure to care for or pattern of neglect, or where the child requires treatment to cure, prevent or alleviate physical harm that the parent does not provide. The society need not prove intent to harm; it must prove causation by act, omission or pattern (Jewish Family and Child Service v. K.(R.), 2008 ONCJ 774, aff'd 2009 ONCA 903).
application: The father was overwhelmed and unable to meet the youth's high special needs, resisted and refused services, left the youth alone despite his dependence, provided no medical or dental care, and kept him in an unhygienic and unsafe home. This established both a pattern of neglect and a failure to provide required treatment. The evidence was overwhelming and undisputed.
conclusion: The youth was found to be a child in need of protection under ss. 74(2)(b) and (e) of the CYFSA.

issue: Is a court order necessary to protect the youth and is extended society care the disposition in his best interests?
facts: The father had made no progress in acknowledging or addressing the protection concerns and had no history of cooperating with the many professionals who tried to help. The parents' plan was simply to have the youth returned and taken to China, with no detail on how his needs would be met. The youth was thriving in a specialized Safehaven placement receiving extensive medical services. Placement in extended society care on his 18th birthday would give him priority, lifetime access to funded adult services (the wait list otherwise exceeding 10 years).
rule: Section 101(1) CYFSA lists available orders (supervision, interim society care, extended society care) once a court is satisfied intervention is necessary; the choice is governed by the best-interests criteria in s. 74(3), and ss. 101(2)-(4) require inquiry into prior efforts, less disruptive alternatives and community/family placements. An extended society care order is the most profound order a court can make and requires compelling evidence and examination of alternatives (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Hamilton-Wentworth v. G.(J.); CCAS v. C.M., [1994] 2 S.C.R. 165). Good intentions are insufficient; the question is whether the parent has in fact changed.
application: A supervision order depends on the supervised parent's cooperation and reliability, which the father wholly lacked over three years; it would be an ineffective risk-management tool. Interim society care was inappropriate given the youth's imminent 18th birthday and the need for permanency planning. No family or community alternative was identified. Only extended society care would allow access to the lifetime services the youth needs, making it the least disruptive option consistent with his best interests.
conclusion: A court order was necessary and the youth was placed in the extended care of C.A.S.T.

issue: Should access to the parents be ordered and on what terms?
