facts: All parties agreed access was in the youth's best interests. The youth reacts positively to the father, who knows and loves him; the mother also knows and loves the youth and had cared for him in China. Continued contact maintains the youth's connection to his language and heritage.
rule: Section 105(5)-(6) CYFSA permits access to a child in extended society care only where it is in the child's best interests, considering whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and whether access would impair adoption prospects; s. 105(7) requires the court to specify access holders and recipients.
application: The father-youth interaction is positive, loving and familiar; the mother has a caring history; adoption impairment was not a concern as the youth will only be in care until 18. A detailed joint access proposal met the youth's need for frequent contact, and the youth was designated the access holder and the parents the recipients.
conclusion: Access was ordered on the terms proposed, with the youth as access holder and the parents as access recipients.

issue: Does the plaintiff have a claim in wrongful dismissal and/or constructive dismissal?
facts: Mr. Kushner was hired by FNNND as Communications Officer on August 8, 2023 and terminated on November 21, 2023. The Amended Statement of Claim states FNNND 'unjustly terminated' his employment alleging poor work quality, conflict of interest and failure to be a role model. It does not allege he quit or that his status was ambiguous.
rule: Wrongful dismissal turns on whether the employer had just cause to terminate (Reber v Lloyds Bank International Canada, 1985 CanLII 153 (BC CA)). Constructive dismissal arises where the employer's conduct shows it no longer intends to be bound by the contract, e.g. making continued employment intolerable, typically without a formal termination (Potter v New Brunswick Legal Aid, 2015 SCC 10 at para. 33).
application: Because the pleading alleges FNNND formally terminated (fired) Mr. Kushner rather than that he quit or that his status was ambiguous, the factual matrix supports wrongful dismissal only. Constructive dismissal, which presupposes no formal termination, does not fit the facts pleaded.
conclusion: Mr. Kushner has a claim for wrongful dismissal, but not constructive dismissal.

issue: Should portions of the pleading be struck as not supporting the wrongful dismissal claim or as vexatious?
facts: FNNND sought to strike numerous paragraphs alleging mistreatment by employees/supervisors, criminal records of others, and misfeasance, arguing they were relevant only to constructive dismissal or to nothing.
rule: Under R. 20(26)(a),(b) of the Supreme Court of Yukon Rules, a court may strike a claim that discloses no reasonable claim or is vexatious; allegations must be taken as true and read generously, with striking only where the action is certain to fail (Grove v Yukon, 2021 YKSC 34; Beaugie v Yukon Medical Council, 2012 YKSC 96). Vexatious pleadings include allegations not supporting the claim (Sidhu v Canada (AG), 2015 YKSC 53). Manner of dismissal can encompass pre- and post-termination conduct and courts should not parse too narrowly (Matthews v Ocean Nutrition, 2020 SCC 26; BC v Taylor, 2024 BCCA 44; Wallace v United Grain Growers, 1997 CanLII 332 (SCC) on aggravated/punitive damages).
application: Some mistreatment allegations were retained as potentially relevant to the manner of dismissal or to aggravated/punitive damages (paras. 15, 23, 25, 54-56, 60, 73 with a phrase struck). Others—alleging others' criminal records, third-party misfeasance, character, bald statements or evidence—were struck as irrelevant (paras. 12-13, 16 except 16(c), 22, 38-42, 45, 53).
conclusion: Some paragraphs struck, others retained; the claim reads generously in the plaintiff's favour on the manner-of-dismissal allegations.

issue: Should the claim of negligent misrepresentation be struck?
facts: Mr. Kushner alleged FNNND represented that employment would be long-term and the environment pleasant (later included in the contract), and made representations about Mayo living conditions (transportation, dealerships, utilities, a rental unit).
rule: Negligent misrepresentation requires: a special relationship/duty of care; an untrue, inaccurate or misleading representation; negligence in making it; reasonable reliance; and detrimental reliance producing damages (Queen v Cognos, 1993 CanLII 146 (SCC)). A representation incorporated into the contract sounds in breach of contract, not misrepresentation; an entire agreement clause may defeat the claim.
application: The long-term-employment/pleasant-environment representations were incorporated into the contract, so the proper claim is breach of contract (paras. 5-6, 71, 75, 77 struck). The Mayo living-conditions representations lacked pleaded detrimental reliance and timing, failing to plead all material facts, though the entire agreement clause did not preclude them; para. 47 struck with leave to amend.
conclusion: Negligent misrepresentation claim struck, with leave to amend the living-conditions aspect (para. 47) within 30 days.

issue: Should the claim of unconscionability be struck?
facts: Paragraph 74 alleged the employment contract was unconscionable.
rule: Unconscionability requires (1) inequality of bargaining power from weakness or vulnerability and (2) an improvident transaction; the contract itself must be unreasonable and the unreasonableness must arise from the inequality (Uber Technologies v Heller, 2020 SCC 16 at paras. 62-63).
application: The pleading did not allege that the contract itself was unreasonable, so the essential element of an improvident/unreasonable transaction was absent.
conclusion: Unconscionability claim struck (para. 74).

issue: Should the claim of assault and battery be struck?
facts: Paragraph 57 alleged Mr. Kushner was criminally harassed, accosted and assaulted at a December 2023 community event in Mayo by named individuals, but also included non-parties, irrelevant details and evidence.
rule: A pleading is struck only where certain to fail; specific factual allegations supporting a cause of action are retained while irrelevant material, evidence and references to non-parties may be struck (R. 20(26); Grove; Beaugie).
application: The specific assault allegations against named defendants were retained; the surrounding irrelevant details, evidence and non-party references were struck.
conclusion: Assault and battery claim retained; paragraph 57 partially struck.

issue: Should the plaintiff be ordered to pay security for costs?
facts: FNNND sought $20,000 security for costs because Mr. Kushner is not a Yukon resident and, it argued, advanced frivolous/vexatious claims.
rule: R. 60(44)(a) of the Yukon Rules. No Yukon case law exists; comparable Ontario jurisprudence holds a defendant has no prima facie right to security merely because the plaintiff resides elsewhere—the court weighs factors and the plaintiff may show merit or impecuniosity (Zeitoun v Economical Insurance Group, 2008 CanLII 20996 (ON SCDC), aff'd 2009 ONCA 415).
application: The applicable factors and burdens were not argued before the court, leaving an insufficient basis to order security; the defendant may renew the application, with a case management conference to follow.
conclusion: Security for costs declined at this stage, without prejudice to renewal.

issue: Should the father's access to the three-and-a-half-year-old child remain supervised rather than becoming unsupervised?
facts: The parents separated shortly after the child's birth; the mother had sole custody by consent. Since the application began the father had only ever had supervised access, exercised faithfully. The mother raised concerns about the father's volatile temper, manipulative and controlling personality, possible sexualized behaviour toward the infant, and heavy alcohol and drug use. Justice Katarynych had earlier continued supervision, and the Office of the Children's Lawyer recommended the father undergo a psychological/parenting-capacity assessment, address concerns about sexualized behaviour, and complete a fathers' program before access became unsupervised. The father had not completed any assessment.
rule: Access is determined by the best interests of the child; access is the right of the child, not the parent. The court must focus on the child's safety and well-being in fashioning an access regime.
application: The court accepted evidence of the father's extreme and uncontrolled temper (a startlingly abusive recording, independent witnesses at Service Ontario and the Jewish Community Centre, incidents with counsel), his emotional abuse of and attempts to control the mother, and his failure to address the concerns identified by the earlier judge and the Children's Lawyer despite three years of supervised access. While concerns about sexualized touching and substance use might be resolved through phallometric testing, random testing and supervised exchanges, the father's volatile temper and manipulative, controlling behaviour posed the greatest risk. Because he refused or was unable to address these concerns, unsupervised access was not an option.
conclusion: Access must remain supervised at a government-operated supervised access centre; supervised access is in the child's best interest at this time.

issue: What terms and protective conditions should govern the supervised access and the parties' interactions?
facts: The father had repeatedly harassed the mother's counsel (filing numerous Law Society complaints, threatening emails, posts under assumed names), written improperly to the case-management judge, threatened the mother (prompting police caution), and attempted to control the litigation by intimidation. The mother feared continued abuse once the case ended and she no longer had a lawyer as a buffer.
rule: The court may impose access terms and non-harassment/no-contact conditions and restrictions on further motions where necessary to protect the child and custodial parent and serve the child's best interests.
application: To protect the mother and child while allowing the child to know her father safely, the court ordered supervised access three of four weekends for two hours, allowed the mother to cancel some visits and to obtain the child's passport and travel without the father's consent, imposed a 100-metre no-approach condition, required communication through a monitored program (Family Wizard) limited to civil, child-focused messages, and required the father to obtain leave before bringing any motion to change.
conclusion: The court granted supervised access on defined terms with protective, non-harassment and leave-to-vary conditions.

issue: Is long-term supervised access consistent with the child's best interests?
facts: Supervision had already been in place for over three years, and the father was faithful in attendance; the mother sought its continuation until her concerns were resolved.
rule: Per M.(B.P.) v. M.(B.L.D.E.) (1992), 1992 CanLII 8642 (ON CA), supervised access over the long term is generally not in a child's best interest and is meant to be short-term; however, C.A.M. v. D.M., 2003 CanLII 18880 (ON CA) recognizes supervised access as a longer-term solution where the alternative is no access and access remains in the child's best interest.
application: Although supervision is inherently impermanent and long-term supervision is normally disfavoured, here supervised access was the only alternative to no access given the unaddressed risks, and it allowed the child to build a safe relationship with her father and his family. The court made the order expecting the father to address the identified issues, failing which supervised access remained the only alternative to no access.
conclusion: Supervised access, though ordinarily a short-term measure, was in the child's best interest in this case and was ordered to continue subject to the father addressing the concerns.

issue: Did the wife's abortion without the husband's knowledge or consent, alone or with her other conduct, amount to cruelty rendering cohabitation intolerable under s. 3(d) of the Divorce Act?
facts: The wife, without the husband's consent or knowledge, obtained an abortion in New York in July 1978, arranging it under the guise of a reflective trip to Montreal. The husband, of orthodox Jewish faith, regarded this as an affront to the spiritual conception of marriage. He also alleged frequent unexplained absences, the wife's change of mind about accompanying him on sabbatical, and her withdrawal from the matrimonial bed. The court found the wife's travel was driven by genuine professional duties and that both spouses shared blame for the deteriorating, incompatible marriage.
rule: Section 3(d) of the Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. D-8 permits divorce for physical or mental cruelty 'of such a kind as to render intolerable the continued cohabitation of the spouses.' Per Knoll v. Knoll, [1970] 2 O.R. 169, cruelty involves wanton, malicious or unnecessary infliction of pain or suffering; per Lauder v. Lauder, [1949] P. 277, it is a question of degree turning on the temperament, circumstances and health of the particular parties. The test is subjective and cumulative: was this conduct by this spouse to this spouse cruelty?
application: The court found the abortion, though a weighty and non-trivial act, had only some emotional impact on the husband and did not significantly affect his physical or mental health. The wife's absences were dictated by professional obligations, not neglect, and both parties were at fault in the incompatibility that eroded the marriage. Considered alone or cumulatively with the other complaints, the conduct did not reach the threshold of rendering continued cohabitation intolerable.
conclusion: The wife's conduct did not amount to cruelty within s. 3(d); the petition for divorce was dismissed (no decree nisi granted), despite no reasonable prospect of reconciliation.

issue: Which parent should be awarded custody of the two children?
facts: The two children, aged ten and six at trial, had been in the father's interim custody since a November 1978 consent order and remained in the former matrimonial home they had known since 1974. The father had been an excellent parent and could organize his work hours around the children; the children were happy, healthy and doing well at school. The mother had laudable maternal instincts and a good, loving relationship with the children but her employment required travel necessitating a substitute caregiver.
rule: Custody is determined not by adjudicating parental rights but by making the best disposition for the welfare of the children, the pre-eminent consideration to which parental interests must yield (citing Re K (Minors), [1977] 2 W.L.R. 33).
application: The court found the children thriving in the father's care, benefiting from continuity in their home and schooling, and that the father's flexible schedule allowed personal day-to-day care whereas the mother would need a substitute mother during work travel. Nothing in the mother's conduct warranted censure, but the children's total welfare favoured stability with the father.
conclusion: Custody of both children awarded to the husband.

issue: On what terms should access be granted to the mother given the children's orthodox Jewish upbringing?
facts: The children were being raised in the orthodox Jewish way of life, which the father strongly observed and wished to continue. The mother, though Jewish by conversion, was not committed to every aspect of orthodox observance and had on occasions shopped with the children on Shabbat and proposed weekend visits to Montreal potentially inconsistent with Shabbat. Expert psychological evidence indicated children cope with parents holding different values provided mutual respect and no loyalty conflict.
rule: Access is granted where it serves the child's welfare; religious and ethical views prevailing in the family environment are a significant but not determinative factor, the ultimate question always being what is best for the welfare of the child (Re K (Minors), per Pennycuick and Ormrod L.JJ.). The best interests of the child govern.
application: The court concluded it was in the children's best interests to continue their orthodox upbringing while enjoying liberal, including overnight, weekend access with the mother. To avert chronic litigation, the court set out a detailed access schedule and directed that, when the children are in her care, the mother ensure they eat kosher food and observe the Shabbat 'as far as reasonably possible,' avoiding exposure to influences conflicting with orthodox Jewish spiritual values, subject to reasonable exceptions.
conclusion: Liberal, structured access granted to the mother on specified terms, coupled with a direction to maintain the children's orthodox religious practices so far as reasonably possible; child support fixed at $160 per month per child plus one-half of the Hillel Academy fees, each party to bear own costs.

issue: Did English-speaking Roman Catholics in Griffin's municipality have s. 93(1) denominational-school rights, and is the court bound by Hirsch?
facts: Griffin, an English-speaking Roman Catholic, sought a declaration that the transfer agreement between C.S.R. Blainville and the Protestant-related Laurenval School Board was ultra vires and that he had a right to Catholic education controlled by English-speaking Catholics. In 1867 his municipality was in a 'rural area' outside Montreal and Quebec City where Roman Catholics were the overwhelming majority (17,875 Catholics vs. 532 Protestants in Deux-Montagnes County) and had no dissentient Catholic school.
rule: Section 93(1) of the Constitution Act, 1867 protects rights or privileges with respect to denominational schools that a class of persons had 'by law' in the province at the Union. 'By law' means by statute in force at Confederation (P.S.B.G.M. — 1989). Per Hirsch v. Protestant Board of School Com'rs of Montreal, [1928] 1 D.L.R. 1041 (JCPC), and confirmed in A.-G. Que. v. Greater Hull School Board, [1984] 2 S.C.R. 575, outside Montreal and Quebec City common schools were non-denominational and only dissentient schools of the religious minority were denominational; de facto religious character does not create a legal right (Maher v. Portland; Mackell). The Superior Court is bound by Hirsch under stare decisis.
application: The court rejected each of Griffin's attacks on Hirsch, holding that s. 93(1) must be given the 'specific direction provided by the legislator' rather than a broad Charter-like reading. Under the 1861 Act, the Roman Catholic school in Griffin's area in 1867 was a common school, not a dissentient one, because Catholics were the majority and could not establish a dissentient school. Only the religious minority (Protestants) constituted the protected 'class of persons.' Post-1867 statutes (1971 c. 67) and de facto denominational practice could not alter the 1867 benchmark, and the Superior Court could not depart from Privy Council authority.
conclusion: Griffin and his family, being Roman Catholics in a rural-area municipality, had no s. 93(1) rights or privileges; the first conclusion (ultra vires) was dismissed and it was unnecessary to consider whether any such right was prejudicially affected.

issue: Does s. 23 of the Charter give English Catholic parents a right to minority-language facilities controlled by English-speaking Roman Catholics?
facts: Griffin's children were in fact receiving English-language instruction: two older children attended the Catholic-related Chomedey-Laval school, one attended an English Catholic school, and Amanda had earlier attended the Protestant-related L.T.M. High School under a permissive transfer agreement. Griffin argued s. 23(3)(b) guaranteed him control over the minority-language facilities and that they reflect his Catholic faith.
rule: Section 23(1)(b) (admitted) grants English-language secondary instruction; s. 23(3)(b) grants, where numbers warrant, the right to minority-language educational facilities out of public funds. Case law (Reference re Education Act of Ontario, 1984; Mahe v. Alberta, 1987) recognizes an implied management/control right, but the entrenched right is to minority-language, not minority-denominational, facilities; s. 23 makes no distinction between denominational and non-denominational systems.
application: The court found the children were already educated in English and largely in Catholic-related schools controlled by English-speaking Roman Catholics. Even the Protestant-related Laurenval facilities were controlled by English-speaking ratepayers forming the linguistic minority, satisfying s. 23(3). Section 23 protects language, not the denominational character of facilities. The requested declarations were general and theoretical, unsupported by concrete facts, and courts should not issue abstract rulings (Bérubé v. Benoit).
conclusion: The court declined to decide whether s. 23(3) confers a control right and dismissed the fourth and fifth conclusions as accessory and unsupported by the evidence.

issue: Do the s. 450 transfer agreements discriminate against English-speaking Roman Catholics under ss. 2(a) and 15(1) Charter and s. 10 Quebec Charter?
facts: Griffin complained that his children could be required to attend Protestant-managed schools over which he had no control, whereas French Catholics and English Protestants could attend schools of their own faith. However, no child was forced into a Protestant school; the Laurenval agreement was permissive, Griffin never seriously sought an English Catholic transfer before litigating, and after proceedings began C.S.R. Blainville signed a transfer agreement with the English Catholic Chomedey-Laval board that his children took up.
rule: Section 15(1) requires proof of a distinction based on personal characteristics that imposes a discriminatory burden, considering the actual effect of the law (Andrews v. Law Society of B.C., [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143); justification is assessed under s. 1. A court may decline to decide moot or hypothetical questions where its decision will have no practical effect on the parties' rights (Borowski v. Canada (A.-G.), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 342).
application: The court held the alleged discriminatory situation no longer existed and may never have existed had Griffin made a serious effort to obtain an English Catholic transfer before suing. His inability to vote at Chomedey-Laval arose from a domicile requirement he did not challenge. The serious s. 15 questions were now moot, no adequate reason justified departing from the mootness practice, and the new Education Act (Bill 107) was before the Court of Appeal. The same reasoning applied to s. 10 of the Quebec Charter and to s. 2(a), for which Griffin cited no supporting authority.
conclusion: The discrimination claim was not decided as moot; the second conclusion and dependent third conclusion were dismissed.

issue: Which parent should have custody of the four children on the best-interests test?
facts: The mother had been the primary caregiver of all four children (three girls fathered by the respondent and one boy, J.A.P., whom the respondent treated as his son) since birth, meeting their physical, financial, educational and emotional needs largely alone after the 2012 separation, receiving support from the Jewish community. The father paid little or no support, was chronically abusive and vitriolic toward the mother by text and email, refused to feed the children on access days, breached orders, pulled the boy from class, bought iPads to circumvent an order, and could not control his anger, including a fixation that the mother's new husband (Rabbi P.S.) was a 'child abuser'.
rule: Under s. 24 of the Children's Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12, custody is determined solely on the best interests of the child, considering love and emotional ties, the child's views, stability of the home, ability to provide guidance and necessaries, the proposed plan, permanence of the family unit, ability to parent, blood relationship (s. 24(2)), and past conduct including violence or abuse (s. 24(3)-(4)).
application: The mother's strengths as a stable, child-focused primary parent far outweighed her faults (unilateral school change, excessive without-notice motions, poor preparation of the children for Rabbi P.S.). The father demonstrated instability, financial evasiveness, disregard for court orders, an inability to shield the children from his conflict with the mother and his campaign against Rabbi P.S., and a tendency to bully those who supported the mother. Joint custody was unworkable given his abusive, uncompromising conduct.
conclusion: Sole custody of all four children was granted to the mother, with authority to make all decisions and to keep the father informed of major matters.

issue: Should the custodial mother be permitted to relocate the children to England?
facts: The mother had religiously married Rabbi P.S., who lives and operates his charity business in Edgware, England, and who would not move to Canada and would assume full financial responsibility for the family. The community subsidies she relied on as a single mother were no longer available. The father opposed the move; the boy J.A.P. was adamantly opposed; the Children's Lawyer opposed it, citing disruption, the children's dislike of and poor relationship with Rabbi P.S., an open child-protection file, and unresolved immigration/financial details.
rule: The mobility test in Gordon v. Goertz, 1996 CanLII 191 (SCC), requires a fresh inquiry into the best interests of the child, with no presumption in favour of the custodial parent but with 'great respect and the most serious consideration' given to the custodial parent's views; relevant factors include existing custody/access arrangements, maximizing contact, the child's views, and disruption from the move (also Bjornson, Woodhouse, Burns v. Burns).
application: The court weighed the advantages (economic security through Rabbi P.S., a more peaceful home away from the toxic conflict, the mother's respected decision to relocate) against the disadvantages (loss of frequent in-person contact with the father, disruption, J.A.P.'s opposition). Because the father's contact had been reduced to supervised access and was not currently healthy, and the mother would facilitate extended summer/holiday visits and Skype contact, the benefits of a fresh start outweighed the reduced contact.
conclusion: The move was approved, subject to three conditions: obtaining a custody/mobility order in the divorce file against the biological father Mr. D.P.; proof of English immigration approval; and JFCS satisfaction that Rabbi P.S.'s relationship with the children was no longer a protection concern.

issue: What access to the father is in the children's best interests, and should it be supervised?
facts: The father repeatedly breached orders, exposed the children to his anger, encouraged them to lie and to disparage Rabbi P.S., returned them late, and showed no insight or willingness to compromise; his access had already been reduced to supervised visits. He nonetheless loves the children, and they, especially J.A.P., love him.
rule: Access orders must be made in the best interests of the child under the Children's Law Reform Act; the maximum-contact principle applies only so far as consistent with the child's best interests.
application: To protect the children's emotional health while preserving the relationship, the court ordered a therapeutic first visit, followed by supervised visits, with a graduated path back to unsupervised and overnight access conditional on the father attending counselling and demonstrating he could avoid exposing the children to negativity. After the move, weekly Skype contact and extended summer/holiday visits in Canada were ordered.
conclusion: A staged access regime was imposed, beginning supervised and capable of progressing to unsupervised/overnight and, post-move, block access in Canada plus Skype, with the mother empowered to revert to supervised access if abuse resumed.

issue: How is the father's income to be determined and does the relocation justify a departure from the Child Support Guidelines?
facts: The father failed to comply with disclosure orders, was dishonest about his finances, admitted receiving over $50,000 in undisclosed cash from two contracts, yet claimed poverty. The mother sought to impute $60,000; the father's counsel had admitted $18,000 (2014) and roughly $30,000 (2015-2016). Relocation would create substantial access travel costs, and Rabbi P.S. would provide a higher standard of living.
rule: Income may be imputed under the Child Support Guidelines (O. Reg. 391/97); s. 10 permits departure from the table amount on grounds of undue hardship, and s. 7 gives discretion over special/extraordinary expenses.
application: The mother did not establish $60,000; the court imputed $18,000 for 2014 and $30,000 for 2015-2016, fixing arrears at $11,125 as of January 15, 2016. After the move, requiring full table support plus access travel would cause undue hardship and a lower standard of living for the father, so support was reduced to $600/month with the father bearing all access travel costs in lieu of s. 7 expenses.
conclusion: Support was ordered at $340/month (2014), $725/month (2015-16 and ongoing until the move), reduced to $600/month on relocation with the father responsible for all access transportation costs; arrears set at $11,125.

issue: Should spousal support be ordered and the restraining order continued?
facts: The father had been the family breadwinner and the mother was entitled to spousal support on compensatory and non-compensatory grounds, but the father was functioning poorly and could barely support himself; the mother had survived on her own and did not seek ongoing spousal support. The father had a history of abuse and of intruding into the children's schools.
rule: Spousal support depends on entitlement and ability to pay; a restraining order continues where warranted for protection.
application: Although the mother was entitled to spousal support, the father lacked the ability to pay it without compromising child support; retroactive spousal support would serve no practical purpose. Given the father's ongoing threatening and abusive conduct, the restraining order was warranted.
conclusion: No spousal support was ordered (all claims dismissed); the existing restraining order was continued and made final with additional communication restrictions.

issue: Is the child in need of protection under the CYFSA by reason of a risk of emotional harm caused by the mother's conduct?
facts: Since January 2017 the mother made repeated unverified allegations that the father sexually and physically abused their son G; three police investigations and multiple society investigations verified nothing. The child, closely aligned with his mother, refused all contact with his father and extended family, adopted bizarre and inconsistent abuse narratives mirroring the mother's own texts and a traditional healer's history of abuse, and repeatedly frustrated court-ordered access and reunification therapy. On January 9, 2019 Justice Paulseth had already found G in need of protection under s. 74(2)(h).
rule: Section 74(2)(h) of the CYFSA provides that a child is in need of protection where the child has suffered or there is a risk of emotional harm. The best-interests test must be applied from a child-centred perspective; good intentions are insufficient — the question is whether the parent has in fact changed (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. P.N.S.). Expert evidence is not required to make a factual finding of alienation (A.M. v. C.H., 2019 ONCA 764).
application: The court found the mother's evidence evasive, dishonest and incredible, and that she systematically convinced the child of false abuse allegations, alienated him from his father and maternal family, sabotaged reunification counselling with Ms Urbas, Millan & Associates and Ms Polak, and disobeyed numerous access orders. Even after removal, she breached visit expectations, secretly taped the therapist and failed to bring the baby. The child's views were found not to be independent. The court adopted Justice Paulseth's findings and found ongoing short- and long-term risk of emotional harm.
conclusion: The child G was confirmed to be in need of protection under s. 74(2)(h) of the CYFSA on the ground of risk of emotional harm.

issue: What disposition is in the child's best interests?
facts: The society sought interim society care for four months followed by placement with the father under a six-month supervision order; the OCL and (ultimately) the mother sought return to the mother under strict supervision; the mother alternatively proposed placement with the godmother NL. The father, a member of the military, would relocate to Toronto, had family support and had worked cooperatively with the society; the mother had been ungovernable and untrustworthy.
rule: Section 74(3) of the CYFSA sets out the best-interests factors, including the child's views (weighted by age and maturity), physical/mental/emotional needs, and the importance of a positive relationship with a parent. Section 101(3) requires consideration of less disruptive alternatives (supervision) unless inadequate; s. 101(4) requires consideration of community/family placements. A supervision order is effective only where the parent meets a minimum threshold of cooperation, reliability and trust and is not ungovernable (Jewish Family and Child Services of Greater Toronto v. A.K.; Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. P.N.S.).
application: The child's stated wish to return to his mother was given no weight because his views were not independent and had been poisoned by the mother. The mother met none of the preconditions for an effective supervision order, having repeatedly defied orders even after the child was removed. The godmother was too aligned with the mother to be a neutral caregiver. The father's plan, with society assistance, was found viable and capable of meeting the child's needs and supporting his relationship with the mother in time.
conclusion: The court ordered interim society care for four months followed by placement with the father for six months under a supervision order; return to the mother and placement with the godmother were rejected.

issue: Does the child qualify as a First Nations, Inuk or Métis child under the CYFSA?
facts: The mother, of Trinidadian descent, repeatedly demanded transfer of the file to Native Child and Family Services, claimed native Caribbean ancestry (the 'Paseas tribe' in Trinidad) and used Anishnawbe Health Centre services. She raised the FNIM issue only on the last day of trial; the children had been raised Christian and attended a Christian school.
rule: A finding of FNIM requires an evidentiary basis (Bruce Grey Child and Family Services v. A.B., 2018 ONCJ 516; Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S.T., 2019 ONCJ 207), assessed under O. Reg. 155/18 s. 1; self-identification must be made in good faith. Section 90(2) requires statutory findings to be made as soon as practicable.
application: The mother could not identify any band, community, cultural practices or spiritual beliefs, and no relative or child was affiliated with any native community. NCFS declined the transfer because the mother lacked Canadian Indigenous roots. The court found the claim was not made in good faith but was a manipulative attempt to derail or delay the proceeding. Although the statutory finding had been overlooked, its timing did not affect the outcome.
conclusion: The child was found not to be a First Nations, Inuk or Métis child; sections 74(3)(b) and 101(5) therefore did not apply.

issue: Was the surreptitious recording of the reunification therapist admissible, and should an order barring further surreptitious recording issue?
facts: The mother secretly recorded her intake meeting with therapist Diana Polak (and had covertly recorded society workers, another therapist and the child) and sought to play the recording to impeach Ms Polak. All other counsel objected.
rule: A court has discretion to admit surreptitious recordings by balancing probative value (including reliability) against prejudice, including trial unfairness and the systemic harm of discouraging illegal or covert conduct. Recordings of third-party professionals are strongly discouraged (Fattali v. Fattali; F. (J.) v. C. (V.)) as they undermine the willingness of helping professionals to assist families.
application: The recording concerned a third-party professional taped without knowledge or consent; the godmother was present and could testify to the meeting, so the recording added no probative value. The systemic harm to the administration of justice from admitting covert recordings of professionals outweighed any probative value. Given the mother's demonstrated practice and lack of insight, and the need to rebuild trust with the society and therapists, a prohibitory order was necessary.
conclusion: The recording was ruled inadmissible, and the court ordered the mother not to audio or video record the child, the father, any society worker or third-party professional without prior express consent.

issue: Should the plaintiffs be granted leave to amend their pleadings, in particular to amend paragraph 51 and to add a claim of unjust enrichment against Babcock?
facts: The plaintiffs sought leave to amend various paragraphs and to add an alternative claim in unjust enrichment against Babcock, a shareholder/investor in VW Hotels, first raised almost four years after the action commenced and three days after Babcock filed a summary trial dismissal application. No material facts alleged that Babcock personally received or benefitted from diverted funds.
rule: Amendments are governed by Rule 6-1(1)(b)(i) and the principles in Victoria Grey Metro Trust Co. v. Fort Gary Trust Co. (1982) and Teal Cedar Products (1996): amendments to determine the real issues are generally permitted but not useless amendments or those unsupported by material facts (Salico 2009 BCSC 1489); the court weighs delay, reasons, limitation, prejudice and connection. Unjust enrichment requires enrichment, corresponding deprivation, and absence of juristic reason (Garland v. Consumers' Gas Co., 2004 SCC 25); the corporate veil (Salomon; Malik 2007 BCSC 739; XY, LLC v. Zhu 2013 BCCA 352) protects shareholders. Withdrawal of admissions is governed by Rule 7-7(5)(c) (Kamei Sushi 1996).
application: The court allowed most amendments, and the amendment to paragraph 51 because it did not amount to withdrawing a deliberate, unambiguous admission and raised a triable issue of mixed fact and law causing no significant prejudice to Servus. However, the unjust enrichment claim against Babcock failed to plead an enrichment of Babcock personally, was foreclosed as an unpleaded attempt to pierce the corporate veil, had no reasonable prospect of success and was therefore useless. There was lengthy unexplained delay and Babcock would be prejudiced by defending a poorly pleaded, more complex claim raised almost four years in.
conclusion: Leave granted for all amendments sought except the addition of the unjust enrichment claim against Babcock, which was denied without liberty to re-apply.The plaintiffs had already twice amended their claims against Babcock.

issue: Should the plaintiffs obtain an order for substituted service on Ostrander?
facts: Ostrander, the alleged directing mind of the dissolved corporate defendants, had not filed a response; a 2012 substituted service order via his father's Saskatoon residence had already been used. The plaintiffs sought the same alternative service for the further amended and second further amended pleadings.
rule: The court may order alternative service where personal service is impracticable and diligent, reasonable efforts to locate and serve the defendant have been made.
application: The court was satisfied the plaintiffs had made diligent efforts to serve Ostrander personally and reasonable efforts to locate him, and that personal service was impracticable, on essentially the same terms as the 2012 order.
conclusion: Order for alternative service granted, applying to the amended pleadings and any further process issued against Ostrander.

issue: Should the time for Servus to file its counterclaim be extended?
facts: Servus was added as a defendant on about May 1, 2012 and sought to file a counterclaim against Colter for fraudulent/negligent misrepresentation relating to Colter's statutory declarations, filing its application February 12, 2015 (about two years and 10 months later). No trial date was set and discoveries of Servus were incomplete.
rule: Rule 22-4(2) permits the court to extend time where just and convenient, applying the factors from Squamish Indian Band v. Canadian Pacific Ltd. (1998), summarized in Smith v. British Columbia, 2010 BCSC 928: length of and reasons for delay, limitation bar, connection to the plaintiff's claim, and prejudice to each side.
application: Although Servus was responsible for delay after May 2013, the counterclaim was not time-barred, was closely connected to the plaintiffs' claim (both turning on Colter's statutory declarations and Servus's role as lender), avoided a multiplicity of proceedings, and Servus could suffer prejudice to its full answer and defence if denied. The passage of time was neutral and, with no trial date set and discoveries outstanding, permitting the counterclaim would not delay resolution.
conclusion: Leave granted; time to file the counterclaim extended to March 25, 2015.

issue: Should the corporate plaintiffs be ordered to post security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act, with a stay pending posting?
facts: All plaintiffs were BCA companies; several were dissolved or in receivership, none held real property, and all had their assets charged by registered security interests. Colter and Mustang (85% of the total claim) tendered evidence of 2014 profits but no financial statements or lists of exigible assets. The plaintiffs claimed breach of trust and knowing assistance against Servus, the perfected secured lender.
rule: Section 236 BCA allows security for costs where it appears a corporate plaintiff would be unable to pay the defendant's costs if the defence succeeds. The applicant must make a prima facie case of inability to pay; the plaintiff may resist by showing sufficient exigible assets or no arguable defence (Devocht 2015 BCSC 149; Fat Mel's 1993; Kropp v. Swaneset Bay 1997 adopting Keary Development). Equitable trust/knowing-assistance claims require the funds to be impressed with a trust, knowledge, and participation (PricewaterhouseCoopers Inc. v. Flash & The Boys 2014 BCSC 1093); statutory priorities and reasonable commercial expectations may furnish a juristic reason denying constructive trust relief (Caterpillar Financial Services 2007 BCCA 14; Pacific Shores 2013 BCSC 480; Sabihi 2013 BCSC 1571).
application: Servus made out a prima facie case that no plaintiff could pay costs; the plaintiffs' bare evidence of 2014 income, without financial statements, failed to establish exigible assets. Servus had arguable defences to the trust and knowing-assistance claims, including reliance on the draw-request documents, its perfected priority security, and authorities suggesting equitable trusts should not defeat statutory priorities in the commercial construction context. Neither Colter nor Mustang argued security would stifle the litigation.
conclusion: Security for costs of $40,000 ordered, payable within 30 days; the action against Servus stayed until posted, failing which it is dismissed as abandoned without prejudice to the counterclaim. Babcock and Servus awarded costs at Scale B.

issue: Does the exception to solicitor-client privilege for communications in furtherance of unlawful conduct extend to communications made to perpetrate tortious conduct that may become the subject of civil proceedings?
facts: Dr. Dublin, the former head of the defendant Jewish day school, and his son sued the school and board members for wrongful dismissal, breach of contract, breach of trust, breach of confidence, negligence and intentional or negligent infliction of emotional harm, alleging malice, dishonesty and subterfuge. An e-mail from board chair Ms. Nashman to the school's lawyer was inadvertently disclosed during litigation; the plaintiffs said it evidenced the defendants' malice and intent to inflict emotional harm. The Master found it privileged and ordered its return, without the 'in furtherance of unlawful conduct' exception having been argued before her.
rule: Solicitor-client privilege is a fundamental substantive rule of law (Solosky; Descôteaux v. Mierzwinski; McClure; Lavallee) that approaches an absolute right, subject to strictly limited exceptions. The classic crime/fraud exception (R. v. Cox and Railton; R. v. Campbell) denies privilege where the client seeks advice to facilitate conduct the client knew or ought to have known was unlawful. Sopinka, Lederman & Bryant and Goldman, Sachs & Co. v. Sessions extend the exception beyond crime and fraud to communications made to perpetrate tortious conduct or other breaches of duty; a prima facie case of the unlawful purpose, supported by convincing evidence, is required (Re Whitworth; Sperry Corp.).
application: Perell J. held there was no reason the exception should not include communications perpetrating tortious conduct that may become the subject of civil proceedings, as recognized in the Sessions line of authority and by K.J. Smith J.'s reading of Campbell. The pleadings asserted intentional torts (including infliction of emotional harm, breach of trust and breach of confidence) against the plaintiffs. Having read the e-mail, the judge found it 'may' show that the defendants, or at least its author, intended to inflict emotional harm on Dr. Dublin and his family — enough to bring it within the exception, notwithstanding more benign readings.
conclusion: The e-mail fell within the exception for communications in furtherance of unlawful conduct, so it was not privileged; being relevant, it had to be disclosed and the appeal was allowed on this ground.

issue: Did the inadvertently disclosed e-mail otherwise qualify as a privileged solicitor-and-client communication?
facts: The plaintiffs argued the communication with the lawyer concerned non-legal operational advice about the school's infrastructure, and that it was not intended to be confidential (or confidentiality was waived) because Ms. Nashman used her husband's e-mail account and third parties were involved in its composition.
rule: A privileged communication must be (1) between a client and a lawyer acting professionally, (2) made in the context of obtaining legal advice, and (3) intended to be confidential (Descôteaux; Campbell; Wigmore). Legal advice privilege covers the continuum of advice as to what should be done in a legal context, not only interpretations of law (Reid v. B.C. (Egg Marketing Board); Samson Indian Band). Appellate interference with a master's discretionary findings requires clear error or misapprehension of fact.
application: But for its tainted content, the communication with the lawyer would have qualified as one for the purpose of obtaining legal advice. The Master made factual findings against the plaintiffs' contentions about intent and confidentiality, and did not err in refusing the Turner affidavit, which appeared to be a fishing exercise. The board-member argument also failed: since the plaintiffs alleged malice, they could not claim there was no conflict, and a director's normal entitlement to board communications is qualified where the advice concerns the director's own relationship with the corporation (Re Livent).
conclusion: On these grounds the appeal would have been dismissed; the e-mail otherwise met the requirements of privilege and the Master committed no reviewable error, but it was nonetheless disclosable under the unlawful-conduct exception.

issue: What standard of review applies on an appeal from a master's order concerning privilege?
facts: The plaintiffs appealed the Master's discretionary order that the e-mail was privileged and be returned.
rule: On appeal from a master's discretionary order, a court interferes only if the master was clearly wrong, acted on wrong principles, or misapprehended the facts (Bank of Nova Scotia v. Liberty Mutual; Marleen Investments; Woodheath). Where the order turns on a question of law vital to the disposition, the court interferes if the master errs (correctness).
application: Perell J. found the privilege question of sufficient importance to the possible outcome of the litigation that correctness was the appropriate standard for that legal issue, while the master's discretionary findings on confidentiality and inadvertent disclosure attracted deference.
conclusion: Correctness applied to the determinative privilege question; the master erred in law by not applying the unlawful-conduct exception.

issue: Should the plaintiff's entire statement of claim be struck under Rule 19(24) for confusing and improper pleadings?
facts: Isaac sued a group of BC and Ontario defendants over alleged contracts to establish a securities brokerage business, pleading breach of contract, negligent misrepresentation, defamation, wrongful and constructive dismissal, quantum meruit and unjust enrichment. The claim referred to the defendants collectively, mixed defined and undefined 'agreement' terms, failed to specify parties to the contracts, pleaded inconsistent alternative positions unclearly, and used open-ended particulars ('including but not limited to').
rule: Pleadings must clearly define the issues of fact and law and set out the material facts for each cause of action (Homalco Indian Band v. British Columbia; Troup v. McPherson). Rule 19(24) permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim (19(24)(a)), are unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious (19(24)(b)), may prejudice/embarrass/delay (19(24)(c)), or are an abuse of process (19(24)(d)). Under Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, a claim is struck under 19(24)(a) only if it is 'plain and obvious' it discloses no reasonable cause of action, with doubt resolved in the plaintiff's favour (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress).
application: The court found the statement of claim so confusing and replete with problems that the defendants could not properly respond: it was unclear which terms belonged to which agreement, how they were breached, and who the parties were, and alternative positions were not properly framed. Editing it further was beyond what could be expected of the court. However, it was not plain and obvious the contract-based claims would fail if properly reorganized.
conclusion: The entire statement of claim was struck, with leave to file a new (essentially fully amended) statement of claim advancing breach of contract, unjust enrichment and quantum meruit, but not the claims for which leave was refused.

issue: Do the negligent misrepresentation claims disclose a reasonable cause of action where the representations concern future conduct?
facts: The representations in paragraphs 21, 22 and 24 (that the defendants would take steps to establish WS Securities, and terms about compensation) all referred to intended future events, and the same allegations were also pleaded as breach of contract.
rule: A negligent misrepresentation must relate to existing facts, not future occurrences (MacMillan v. Kaiser Equipment Ltd., 2003 BCSC 672, citing Taylor v. Netron Inc.; Williams v. Saanich School District No. 63).
application: Because all the pleaded representations referred to future events, they could not ground negligent misrepresentation. The plaintiff could rely on the same matters as breach of contract instead. The use of 'recklessness'/'wanton' was clarified not to advance fraudulent misrepresentation, making the pleading additionally embarrassing under Rule 19(24)(c).
conclusion: The negligent misrepresentation claim was struck in its entirety with no leave to amend; the plaintiff was limited to pleading breach of contract for those matters.

issue: Does the defamation claim disclose a reasonable cause of action where the statement communicated was true and the precise words were not pleaded?
facts: Isaac alleged that communication of his employment termination to the IDA was defamatory. He did not plead the precise words complained of, and the fact of his termination was true. He had made no apparent effort to obtain the exact words from the IDA.
rule: A defamatory statement is a false statement to a person's discredit (Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada); truth is an absolute defence. The precise defamatory words must be pleaded or the claim may be struck under Rule 19(24)(a) (Shannon v. King), unless the plaintiff genuinely cannot ascertain them (Bulkley Nechako Cable Vision Ltd. v. CKPO Television Ltd.), but not where he could discover them by investigating. Evidence is inadmissible on a 19(24)(a) application (Rule 19(27)).
application: The statement that Isaac was terminated was true and therefore not defamatory, making it plain and obvious there was no reasonable cause of action. He had also failed to plead the precise words, which he could have obtained from someone at the IDA. The defendants' affidavit evidence that a Ms. Richard sent the letter was inadmissible.
conclusion: The defamation claim was struck with no leave to amend, unless Isaac could plead some other untrue statement alleged to be defamatory.

issue: Do the unjust enrichment and quantum meruit claims disclose reasonable causes of action?
facts: Isaac allegedly worked to start the business, drew up a business plan, organized office space and tried to recruit staff, benefiting WS Securities. He did not plead that he was not properly or at all compensated, nor did he specify which contract underlay the quantum meruit claim.
rule: Unjust enrichment requires (1) an enrichment, (2) a corresponding deprivation, and (3) the absence of a juristic reason (Peter v. Beblow, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 980; Pettkus v. Becker). Quantum meruit awards reasonable remuneration where a valid contract exists but no express consideration term is spelled out (Dictionary of Canadian Law; Gill v. Grant).
application: For unjust enrichment, benefit to WS Securities was made out but the corresponding deprivation was not pleaded because Isaac never alleged he was uncompensated — a significant gap. For quantum meruit, he neither identified the underlying contract nor pleaded lack of adequate compensation. Both were alternatives to the breach of contract claim.
conclusion: Both the unjust enrichment and quantum meruit claims were struck with leave to amend, the required detail (lack of compensation) to be added by amendment rather than particulars.

issue: Can the court determine its jurisdiction over the ex juris Ontario defendants before the pleadings are reformulated?
facts: The Ontario defendants were served ex juris without leave and challenged jurisdiction under Rule 14(6) and (6.1). The joint-liability theory (agency, employment, joint venture, partnership) was pleaded unclearly, and the statement of claim had been struck.
rule: On a Rule 14(6) jurisdiction application the court must determine whether the plaintiff has a 'good arguable case' against the ex juris defendants.
application: It was impossible to assess whether Isaac had a good arguable case against the Ontario defendants on pleadings that had been struck and had yet to be reformulated. He might or might not join them, and his joint-liability theory might acquire a legal basis once properly pleaded, so deciding jurisdiction now would be premature.
conclusion: The jurisdiction application was deferred; it would be considered after a properly drafted amended statement of claim was delivered. The judge remained seized of the matter for that purpose, and the Ontario defendants were not penalized in costs for having reasonably brought the application.

issue: Was there a material change of circumstances justifying modification of the accessory measures and custody arrangements?
facts: Since the December 13, 2011 divorce judgment ratifying the parties' amended agreement, the mother lost her IVAC indemnities and works only on call, the father is approaching permanent college-teacher status with a flexible schedule, X was diagnosed with ADHD, global developmental delay and dyspraxia in July 2014, and Y is now attending high school.
rule: Modification of accessory measures requires proof of a material change of circumstances since the earlier judgment.
application: Both parties admitted a material change had occurred, and the Court found the changes in employment, the father's availability, and X's diagnosis constituted a significant change from the situation existing in December 2011.
conclusion: The Court declared that there had been a change of circumstances since the divorce judgment, opening the door to modification.

issue: Is homeschooling by the mother in the best interest of the child X, or should he remain in the regular school system?
facts: X, aged 9, has severe ADHD, global developmental delay and dyspraxia, and needs resource support. The mother proposed homeschooling him in the morning with external homeschooling socialization; the father wanted him to stay in his current school. The psychologist Dr. Hardoon recommended a small, structured, specialized classroom (10–15 students) and said a one-to-one educational relationship was not appropriate.
rule: Article 604 C.C.Q. permits the court to decide difficulties relating to the exercise of parental authority in the interest of the child; decisions concerning a child's education must serve the best interest of the child (art. 33 C.C.Q.).
application: The Court found no expert recommendation supporting homeschooling; the expert contemplated a small teacher-to-pupil ratio, not one-on-one instruction. Homeschooling by the mother could compromise X's best interest, and there was no necessity to remove him from his school given a possible medication trial and the father's involvement.
conclusion: The Court refused the homeschooling request; on the balance of probabilities the evidence did not show homeschooling served X's interest.

issue: Is the mother entitled to spousal support based on her decision to reduce her working hours to care for X?
facts: The mother, young and previously able to work (she received an IVAC lump sum in 2012 and worked a 6–8 week hospital contract in 2013), claimed she could not work full-time because she spends lunchtimes and hours of homework help with X. Her spousal support claim was tied to her planned homeschooling contribution.
rule: Spousal support must be grounded in a genuine need rather than a unilateral personal choice; a claimant is expected to make reasonable efforts toward self-sufficiency.
application: With the homeschooling request dismissed, the basis for support fell away. The mother's reduced availability stemmed from a unilateral personal choice ('to calm X for the rest of the afternoon'); her efforts were no greater than those of any parent in similar circumstances, and given her young age she should seek full-time work.
conclusion: Spousal support was not granted.

issue: Should shared (joint) custody be granted in place of the mother's sole custody?
facts: The children are 12 and 9. The mother, the custodial parent, made unilateral decisions (keeping X home for lunch, announcing homeschooling, giving medication) over the father's objections. Both are loving, capable parents; communications are workable; the residences, though separated by a 25–40 minute train commute, are not an obstacle.
rule: Custody is governed by the best interest of the child and respect for the child's rights (art. 33 C.C.Q.); relevant criteria include the child's interest, parental abilities, communication between parents, the child's relationship with each parent, and the physical distance between residences (Droit de la famille – 091541, 2009 QCCA 1268). Both parents continue to exercise parental authority jointly (arts. 600, 605 C.C.Q.).
application: The Court found the criteria largely met: both parents are capable and empathic, communication is respectful, there are strong emotional ties, and distance is not an obstacle. Sole custody had allowed the mother to impose unilateral decisions; shared custody would enhance the children's ties to both parents without compromising stability.
conclusion: Shared custody was granted on an alternating weekly basis, replacing the mother's sole custody.

issue: Should the Court grant the father's requested order restraining the mother's alleged defamation campaign?
facts: The mother alleged she was raped by the father in 2008, filed an IVAC application, told friends, and reported to police in 2012, but no criminal charges were laid. The father denied the allegations, said they harmed his career (forcing him to resign from a PhD committee), and sought an order to stop her 'defamation campaign.'
rule: An order to cease defamation is tantamount to an interlocutory injunction, governed by arts. 751 and 752 C.C.P.: the order must describe a particular act (art. 751), and the applicant must appear entitled to an apparent right (art. 752).
application: The requested order was vague, imprecise and not susceptible of execution, contrary to art. 751. Further, the father did not appear entitled to an apparent right under art. 752; the merits could only be decided after a full hearing.
conclusion: The Court declined to grant the order and reserved the father's recourse on the defamation issue.

issue: Was the child in need of protection under the CYFSA, and on what basis?
facts: The child, born prematurely in July 2018, had been cared for by the mother from October 2018. The paternal grandmother and father alleged the mother abused drugs, neglected and injured the child, and led an unstable lifestyle, and repeatedly reported minor bumps and bruises to police and medical professionals. Society workers, doctors and police never verified any abuse or neglect. The paternal grandmother waged a sustained campaign of surveillance, denigration and 'inspections' of the child, and consistently disparaged the mother.
rule: Under s. 74(2)(b) CYFSA a child is in need of protection where there is a risk of physical harm from the person having charge of the child; risk must be 'real and likely, not speculative' and 'more likely than not' (Children's Aid Society of Rainy River v. B.(C.); Algoma v. J.B.). Under s. 74(2)(h) a child is in need of protection where there is a risk of emotional harm (anxiety, depression, withdrawal, self-destructive/aggressive behaviour or delayed development) resulting from parental conduct. High parental conflict and behaviours that estrange or alienate a child from a parent can ground risk of emotional harm (CAS of Waterloo v. A.(B.); CAS of Toronto v. L.R.; A.M. v. C.H.), and expert evidence, while helpful, is not required (A.M. v. C.H.; CAS of Toronto v. R.M.).
application: The court found the allegations of physical harm unsubstantiated: no drug use was ever observed, the injuries were ordinary childhood bumps and bruises never requiring treatment, and housing/employment instability was 'good enough' and not a protection concern. Any early risk was speculative or resolved. However, the paternal grandmother and father displayed 'utter disdain' for the mother, denied the mother-child bond, subjected the child to 'inspections' and clothing changes, engaged in relentless surveillance and negative messaging, and portrayed the mother as dangerous without credible evidence — hallmarks of parent-alienating behaviour. Although the four-year-old had not yet been 'successfully' alienated, the high conflict and conduct created a real and likely risk of emotional harm.
conclusion: The child was not at risk of physical harm under s. 74(2)(b), but was in need of protection under s. 74(2)(h) based on risk of emotional harm.

issue: Did the paternal grandmother have 'charge' of the child and was she a 'parent' under the CYFSA, such that no protection finding could be made?
facts: The mother asked the paternal grandmother to babysit for several days in January 2019; the grandmother then refused to return the child and withheld her, denying the mother any access until April 2019. A temporary order of April 10, 2019 placed the child with the grandmother; the society's amended application was brought in October 2019.
rule: 'Charge' of a child cannot be established through a self-help remedy such as withholding a child (CAS of Toronto v. R.A.; CAS of Toronto v. A.(S.)). Charge/parent status is determined at the time proceedings are initiated (CAS of Hamilton Wentworth v. D.(E.); Durham CAS v. J.S.). The CYFSA definition of 'parent' includes a person with custody or access under a court order; where a society brings an amended application after such an order, that person is a parent (Kawartha-Haliburton CAS v. S.(B.)).
application: Because the grandmother was unlawfully withholding the child and the mother actively sought her return, the mother, not the grandmother, had charge when proceedings commenced in April 2019. The grandmother nonetheless became a 'parent' when the society brought its amended application in October 2019, by which time she had access/care under the April 10, 2019 temporary order. Thus a protection finding under s. 74(2)(h) was available, and the court had jurisdiction to make a dispositional order.
conclusion: The argument was rejected: the mother had charge at commencement, the grandmother was a 'parent' by the amended application, and the court had jurisdiction to make a finding and disposition.

issue: What disposition was in the child's best interests?
facts: The society ultimately supported the mother's claim for custody with limited access to the father and grandmother. The mother sought custody with Sunday and a mid-week visit to the father; the paternal grandmother and father sought custody with only supervised access to the mother. The mother was found loving, capable and willing to foster the paternal relationship; the grandmother and father recognized no benefit the mother brought.
rule: Once a protection finding is made the court must determine whether a court order is necessary and, if so, order the least disruptive disposition in the child's best interests under ss. 101, 102 and 74(3) CYFSA, with best interests being highly contextual and forward-looking (Barendregt v. Grebliunas), including the 'friendly parent' principle and s. 24 CLRA factors. Conduct that would estrange a child from a parent reflects an inability to adequately parent (Malhotra v. Henhoeffer). A s. 102 custody order requires a protection finding.
application: A dispositional order was necessary because, absent one, conflict would continue and there was no underlying parenting order. A supervision order would be neither necessary nor beneficial, as years of society involvement had failed to curb the paternal family's behaviour. Applying best interests, the mother provided loving, adequate care, was developmentally supporting the thriving child, and was a 'friendly parent' willing to support the paternal relationship, whereas the grandmother and father would not nurture the mother-child bond and were steering toward alienation. Custody to the mother with primary residence, sole major decision-making (after consultation), and reduced but regular parenting time to the father (Sundays, one weekday evening, holidays) best served the child's long-term interests. A restraining order was declined, but communication/contact terms were imposed to curb surveillance.
conclusion: The child was placed in the custody of the mother under s. 102 CYFSA with primary residence with her and specified parenting time to the father (organized with the grandmother); no restraining order was made.

issue: Should the court grant shared custody of the young child?
facts: The parents separated in August 2018; the four-year-old son had, through consensual arrangements and an interim December 2018 judgment, been spending alternate weekends and Shabbat suppers with his father, plus week-long vacations. The mother opposed shared custody, arguing the child was too young, emotionally attached to her as a 'figure d'attachement', and that the father's parenting philosophy and poor communication were problematic. The parents live 2.7 km apart.
rule: Custody is determined solely by the child's best interest, considering his moral, intellectual, emotional and physical needs, age, health, personality and family environment (art. 33 C.c.Q.); s. 16(10) of the Divorce Act favours maximum contact with each parent consistent with best interests. There is no presumption for or against shared custody. The Court of Appeal factors in Droit de la famille — 16261, 2016 QCCA 224 apply: parental capacity and availability, need for stability, proximity of residences, age and wishes of the child, minimal capacity to communicate, absence of systematic disagreement, and comparable educational/spiritual values.
application: The court found both parents equally available and loving; the father had been omnipresent in the child's life since 2018 and remained in the family home. A transition to increased access had already occurred, so the child was well prepared to adapt. Different parenting philosophies (martial arts, diet) were not inherently problematic and the mother's criticisms were not warranted. The residences are close, with the ordered school at the midpoint. A minimum of communication existed (agreement on appointments, vacations, daycare). Excessive FaceTime calls were curtailed. An alternating-week schedule was preferred over a 2-5-2-2-5 arrangement to reduce friction.
conclusion: Shared custody was granted on a seven-day alternating basis, with defined additional access for Jewish holidays and restricted FaceTime contact.

issue: In which school should the child be enrolled where the parents disagree over religious (denominational) schooling?
facts: The father sought enrolment in the private Jewish denominational A School (approx. $10,000 fees, Hebrew instruction, Kashruth, kippah dress code, Shabbat early dismissal, numerous holiday closures), asserting the parties had agreed to raise the child in the Jewish tradition. The mother preferred the public B School (part of the A School Board, walking distance, subsidized daycare) or costlier private schools, objecting to A School on linguistic and organizational grounds and religious dogma.
rule: The choice of school must be decided solely on the child's best interest, considering transportation, parental presence, stability, proximity and costs (Droit de la famille — 141229, 2014 QCCS 2417). Freedom of religion is the right to hold and manifest beliefs and not to be coerced (R. v. Big M Drug Mart, [1985] 1 SCR 295); in family matters parents' religious freedoms must be exercised in the child's best interest. Denominational schools are an integral, provincially regulated part of Quebec's educational landscape (Loyola High School v. Quebec (AG), 2015 SCC 12).
application: The court found the parties had clearly intended to raise the child in a setting where Judaism and Judaic rites played an important role, making the mother's reticence somewhat incoherent with her prior conduct (Jewish wedding, establishing Jewish lineage, circumcision, holiday celebrations, request for a get). However, the court accepted the mother's legitimate linguistic and organizational concerns: the child already struggled with English and French, adding eight hours of Hebrew weekly was unrealistic, frequent holiday closures and Friday early dismissals with no guaranteed daycare posed problems, and Kashruth requirements conflicted with the mother's dietary preferences. B School was in walking distance of both homes, strengthening community attachment.
conclusion: The court ordered the child to attend the public B School starting 2020-2021, while taking act of the parties' agreement to enrol the child in an after-school Hebraic program (Free B program at the CPE of the Y) to maintain integration in the Jewish faith and community.

issue: How should child support be adjusted given the shared custody arrangement?
facts: The parties agreed their respective revenues for support calculation were $171,648 for the father and $55,000 for the mother.
rule: Child support is calculated under the applicable Quebec child support determination rules based on the parties' respective incomes and the custody arrangement.
application: Applying the agreed incomes to the shared custody arrangement, the court determined the appropriate monthly amount payable by the father.
conclusion: The father was ordered to pay alimony of $347 per month to the mother for the benefit of the child.

issue: Do the doctrines of res judicata / issue estoppel bar the plaintiff's civil claims against Scott Safety given the prior final WorkSafeBC decision?
facts: The plaintiff worked as a standby medic for Scott Safety at a Storm-operated remote worksite, reported harassment, was moved sites, and was not offered further work. She filed a WCB complaint alleging discrimination and unpaid wages; the WCB dismissed it in a written decision dated November 28, 2018, finding no suitable jobs were available and no discrimination. She then brought a civil claim for constructive and wrongful dismissal and personal injury.
rule: Rule 9-5(1)(a),(b),(d) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim, are frivolous/vexatious, or are an abuse of process. Issue estoppel, a form of res judicata, prevents re-litigating matters by relying on a different theory or 'spin' on the same facts (Rivet v. British Columbia, 2007 BCSC 731) and can apply to administrative tribunal decisions (The Queen v. Bugbusters Pest Management Inc., 1998 CanLII 6467). The three requirements are: same question decided previously, final earlier decision, and same parties or privies (B.C. (WCB) v. Figliola, 2011 SCC 52). Under s. 96(1) WCA, WCB decisions are final and conclusive.
application: The court found the issues raised in the civil action—centred on the loss of further work and treatment at the worksite—were the same issues already decided by the WCB. The WCB decision was final and had not been overturned on appeal or judicial review, and the recourse available was through the WCA appeal processes or judicial review. Allowing the plaintiff to re-frame the same matters as wrongful dismissal amounted to putting a different spin on decided issues.
conclusion: Res judicata applies to the action against Scott Safety; the claims are barred and struck.

issue: Is the plaintiff's civil action an abuse of process as a collateral attack on the WCB decision?
facts: The plaintiff had already litigated her grievance before the WCB and lost; she sought to advance the same underlying facts as a civil wrongful dismissal/personal injury claim rather than pursuing the statutory review or appeal routes.
rule: It is an abuse of court process to use a civil action to collaterally challenge decisions of an administrative tribunal that are otherwise subject to a statutory right of appeal or review (Stephen v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2008 BCSC 1656; Young v. Borzoni, 2007 BCCA 16 at paras. 65–66; Cimaco International Sales v. B.C. (A.G.), 2010 BCCA 342).
application: Because the plaintiff's recourse lay in the WCA appeal mechanism or judicial review, re-litigating the same issues by civil action constituted a collateral attack on final WCB decisions and would cause the vexation the abuse-of-process doctrine guards against.
conclusion: The civil action is an abuse of process; the pleadings are struck.

issue: Does s. 10(1) of the Workers Compensation Act operate as a complete statutory bar to the action against Scott Safety and Storm?
facts: The plaintiff's claims arose out of and in the course of her employment at the worksite, alleging personal injury and dismissal against her employer (Scott Safety) and the site operator (Storm).
rule: Section 10(1) WCA replaces any right of action founded on breach of duty or other cause of action against an employer or worker in respect of personal injury, disablement or death arising out of and in the course of employment; s. 96(1) grants the Board exclusive jurisdiction over such matters.
application: The court read ss. 10(1) and 96(1) as placing the matters in issue within the exclusive jurisdiction of WorkSafeBC and rendering its rulings final and conclusive, so no civil action lay against either defendant in respect of those employment-arising claims.
conclusion: Section 10(1) WCA is a complete bar to the action against both Scott Safety and Storm.

issue: Did El Al commit the tort of unlawful interference with business/economic relations by warning or pressuring travel agencies not to employ or deal with the plaintiff?
facts: After the bankruptcy of the plaintiff's travel agency (which left El Al owed some $688,000 in misappropriated trust monies), El Al on numerous occasions told agencies that were 'plated' to issue El Al tickets that retaining or employing the plaintiff would jeopardize their plating privilege, and declined to participate in events where the plaintiff or his daughter would attend. El Al's plating agreements permitted termination at any time for any reason.
rule: The emerging tort of wrongful interference with economic/business relations requires: (1) intention to injure (the act being directed or targeted at the plaintiff, per Reach M.D. Inc. v. Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada, 2003 CanLII 27828 (ON CA)); (2) interference by illegal or unlawful means — 'unlawful means' being acts the defendant 'is not at liberty to commit' (Torquay Hotel Co. v. Cousins; Reach); and (3) consequential economic loss. Restraint of trade alone cannot supply the unlawfulness element.
application: The court found the intention element met: El Al's actions, though predominantly self-protective, were clearly directed at the plaintiff with knowledge of the foreseeable injurious effects. Several alleged incidents (the Catholic Register article, the Reverend Cantalon and Yad Vashem ticketing, the YYZ telephone allegation) were not factually made out. On the unlawful-means element, El Al was contractually at liberty to terminate the plating agreements at any time for any reason, and it acted to protect a legitimate financial interest, not out of malice as in Gershman. Restraint of trade itself could not constitute the required unlawful act. Economic loss was assumed for the last six complaints.
conclusion: The plaintiff failed to establish that El Al's acts were unlawful; the tort of unlawful interference with business/economic relations was not made out.

issue: Did El Al's direct pressure on YYZ Travel and Payless Travel to end their dealings with the plaintiff amount to actionable interference with contractual relations, and was El Al justified?
facts: El Al told YYZ Travel it would terminate its plating agreement if YYZ continued to employ the plaintiff; after negotiation the plaintiff remained with a minimized profile for the balance of his contract, which was not renewed.
