El Al similarly told Payless Travel it would be better not to deal with the plaintiff, though he apparently continued to work there. No actual breach of the plaintiff's contracts resulted.
rule: Liability for inducing breach of contract extends to interference that prevents or hinders performance even without a breach (Torquay Hotel Co. v. Cousins). Where interference is direct, unlawful means need not be shown; but the defence of justification remains available (Quinn v. Leathem; Posluns v. Toronto Stock Exchange (1964); Thermo King Corp. v. Provincial Bank of Canada (1981); Edwin Hill Partners v. First NFC). Justification turns on the grounds (statutory/contractual/social basis), purpose (good faith vs. malice; genuine financial interest), means used, and the nature of the contract and consequences.
application: El Al's steps toward YYZ and Payless were direct interference, so no unlawful means needed to be proven. However, El Al held a contractual right to terminate the plating agreements at any time for any reason, acted in good faith to protect a real and reasonable financial interest given the plaintiff's prior misappropriation of trust funds, informed the agencies of its precarious position without attempting to blacklist the plaintiff industry-wide, and did not resort to illegal means. Since the acts were lawful as to both purpose and means, they were also justified (per Posluns).
conclusion: El Al was justified in acting as it did; the claim for interference with contractual relations was dismissed. The claims against the individual defendants fell with the claim against El Al. Had liability been found, damages at large of $25,000 would have been awarded, but no injunction would issue given the plaintiff's unclean hands.

issue: Did the cancellation of the applicant's marriage commissioner registration, following his refusal to marry same-sex couples, infringe his freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
facts: The applicant, a Christian minister appointed a marriage commissioner in 2003, refused to solemnize same-sex marriages on religious grounds after a 2004 VSA direction (issued the day of Vogel v. Canada) required all commissioners to marry all legally eligible couples. His registration was cancelled in 2005. Manitoba conceded the applicant sincerely believed he could not marry same-sex couples.
rule: Under R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295, freedom of religion protects against coercion contrary to belief. The test from Mouvement laïque québécois v. Saguenay (City), 2015 SCC 16 requires (1) a sincere belief and (2) interference with the ability to act on that belief that is more than trivial or insubstantial. The Saskatchewan Marriage Reference, 2011 SKCA 3 held that requiring commissioners to perform same-sex marriages could infringe s. 2(a).
application: Sincerity was conceded. The court accepted that requiring commissioners to perform same-sex marriages may impinge on s. 2(a), but found the actual impact on this applicant was not more than trivial or insubstantial: he had only ever performed marriages for people within his ministry or known to him (about five outside couples), did not conduct marriages for the public at large, and would only perform limited Christian ceremonies.
conclusion: The court did not find the impact of the Decision on the applicant to be more than trivial or insubstantial, though it accepted such a requirement could impinge on s. 2(a) rights generally.

issue: Assuming a non-trivial infringement of s. 2(a), did the cancellation reflect a proportionate balancing of the applicant's religious freedom against the s. 15 equality rights of same-sex couples under Doré?
facts: The applicant argued allowing him to remain a commissioner would not harm same-sex couples because others could marry them, and there was no evidence he ever had to turn a couple away. Manitoba argued the clash was real given his stated refusal, and that permitting refusals could leave same-sex couples (especially in rural/remote areas) facing rejection and difficulty finding a commissioner. Manitoba offered two alternatives: registration as a religious official via a recognized denomination, or temporary single-ceremony appointments.
rule: Doré v. Barreau du Québec, 2012 SCC 12 and Loyola High School v. Quebec (A.G.), 2015 SCC 12: a discretionary administrative decision limiting a Charter protection must reflect a proportionate balancing of the Charter value against the statutory objectives. The state need not adopt the least intrusive alternative. The Marriage Reference emphasized the significant and offensive impact on gay and lesbian couples of being refused service.
application: The court found the effect of a commissioner refusing a same-sex couple would be significant and offensive, and that permitting refusals could cascade to non-Christian and divorced couples and burden couples in small communities. The Decision's impact on the applicant was limited because he retained alternative avenues: applying to have his ministry recognized as a religious denomination (he meets 20-30 bikers weekly), or obtaining temporary appointments (as he did six times between 2007-2011, issuable within 24-48 hours in exceptional cases). Manitoba need not choose the least intrusive measure.
conclusion: The cancellation reflected a proportionate balancing of the s. 2(a) and s. 15 protections and the statutory objective of governing access to marriage, meeting the Doré test.

issue: Was a marriage commissioner 'government' subject to the Charter, and did the VSA have statutory authority to cancel the applicant's registration?
facts: The applicant argued he was not a civil servant, was not obliged to perform any services, and that the VSA lacked statutory authority to cancel his appointment.
rule: Eldridge v. British Columbia (A.G.), [1997] 3 S.C.R. 624: a private entity implementing a specific government policy acts as 'government' under s. 32 of the Charter. Nichols v. M.J., 2009 SKQB 299 characterized a marriage commissioner as 'government'. Section 3(3) of The Marriage Act permits the minister to cancel a registration where continued registration would not be in 'the public interest'.
application: Applying Eldridge and Nichols, a marriage commissioner performs an authorized governmental function and must do so without breaching others' Charter rights. Section 3(3)'s public-interest power provided a proper basis for cancellation, since permitting discriminatory refusals was contrary to the public interest.
conclusion: A marriage commissioner is 'government' subject to the Charter, and the VSA had statutory authority under s. 3(3) to cancel the registration in the public interest.

issue: Did the deputy judge deny natural justice by disposing of the claim on an unpleaded defence of qualified privilege without affording the plaintiff an opportunity to respond?
facts: The defamation claim arose from messages exchanged within 'Reunion', a password-protected Yahoo! Group founded and moderated by Dojc for persons of Slovak/Czech and Jewish descent. The trial judge, on his own initiative, found the impugned e-mails protected by qualified privilege and dismissed the claim. Qualified privilege had not been pleaded by the defence, was not raised by either party, and was not discussed in submissions; the appellant had no chance to lead evidence of malice to rebut it.
rule: The opportunity to adduce evidence and make submissions on an issue is fundamental to the right to be heard, and denying it may constitute a denial of natural justice (CIBC v. Prasad, 2010 ONSC 320). Per Brighton Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd. v. Savoia (2006 CanLII 1667 (ON SCDC)), Small Claims Court pleadings are treated liberally and unpleaded relief or an unpleaded defence may be allowed only where no additional evidence beyond what was or should have been adduced is needed and it is not unfair; where a party had no opportunity to respond, the unfairness may amount to a substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice warranting a new trial under ss. 134(1)(b) and 134(6) of the Courts of Justice Act.
application: The trial judge decided the case solely on qualified privilege, which was neither pleaded nor argued. The appellant was deprived of the chance to call evidence of malice, which would defeat the privilege. This mirrored Brighton and constituted an unfairness rising to a substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.
conclusion: Yes. The reliance on the unpleaded defence denied natural justice, and prima facie the appropriate remedy was a new trial before a different judge.

issue: Was it clear from the record that the elements of defamation were not established, making a new trial unnecessary?
facts: The respondent argued no new trial was needed because publication and defamatory meaning were not proven. The material was circulated within a closed, password-protected group; the appellant had regained access after being banned, viewing content as an 'unauthorized eavesdropper'/'trespasser'. Impugned statements included references to the appellant as 'not normal in the head', a 'psychopath', 'score settler', 'Mafioso' and 'harasser'.
rule: Defamation requires (1) words referring to the plaintiff, (2) publication to a third party, and (3) words defamatory of the plaintiff; once established, falsity and general damages are presumed (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61). A statement is defamatory where it tends to lower the plaintiff's reputation among reasonable persons. Publication is an essential element and the burden lies on the plaintiff (Gaskin v. Retail Credit Co., [1965] S.C.R. 297).
application: Reference to the plaintiff was not disputed. Some statements appeared innocuous, but the epithets in para. 29 plainly met the test of defamatory meaning viewed through the reasonable person's eyes. On publication, the law of internet defamation is developing and fact-dependent; whether circulation to a closed password-protected group amounts to publication, and whether the appellant's 'trespasser' status bars reliance on the material, could not be resolved without a full factual record. There is no case law that the manner of becoming aware of the publication affects the analysis.
conclusion: No. The court could not conclude on the record that publication was absent or that the trespasser point defeated the claim, so a new trial was required to determine these issues on a full record.

issue: Does a taxpayer of a minority religion have the right to have his children admitted to the commissioners' public school where no dissentient school exists?
facts: Chabot, a ratepayer of Lamorandière and a Jehovah's Witness (a Protestant for public-education purposes), had two school-age sons. The municipality's only public schools were those under the Roman Catholic commissioners; there was no dissentient school. The commissioners would admit the children only if they submitted to the regular Catholic program.
rule: Section 69 of the Education Act, R.S.Q. 1941, c. 59, obliges commissioners or trustees to admit 'every child domiciled in the municipality' between ages six and sixteen. Section 113 merely exempts a taxpayer from tax if he sends his children to a neighbouring municipality; it does not remove his right to the local school. Section 103 qualifies s. 69 only as regards trustees' (dissentient) schools.
application: Because there was only one school corporation, all ratepayers—Catholic or Protestant—were subject to it, paid its taxes, and must be able to send their children there. Section 113 does not deprive a minority taxpayer of the right to the local school; the option of a dissentient or neighbouring school is not one he is obliged to exercise. Following Hirsch v. Protestant Bd. of School Com'rs of Montreal, rural commissioners' schools (as opposed to trustees'/dissentient schools) are non-denominational and open to all children of the district regardless of faith.
conclusion: Chabot had the right—and indeed the duty under compulsory-attendance provisions—to have his children admitted to the respondents' school.

issue: Are minority-faith children admitted to a commissioners' school obliged to follow the Roman Catholic religious instruction and devotions their father opposes?
facts: The Catholic program included daily prayers and about four hours of weekly religious instruction. The children were initially exempted informally, then ordered to kneel for prayers; on refusing they were expelled, the stated reason being their failure to follow the Department of Education's Roman Catholic program.
rule: The right of a parent to direct the religious education of his children and freedom of conscience are anterior to positive law (natural law; Re Agar-Ellis; Re Meades; Summa Theologica). The Freedom of Worship Act, R.S.Q. 1941, c. 307, s. 2, guarantees free exercise of religion without discrimination. Section 221(3) of the Education Act (duty to have the authorized course of study 'followed') must be read with s. 221(4) (priest/committee chooses religious books for pupils 'of his religious belief'), s. 23 and s. 588 (Jewish pupils exempted).
application: Section 221(3) is capable of two readings; the interpretation conforming to the general spirit of the law and to natural law is that commissioners need only ensure the teachers give the prescribed instruction, not that every child follow the religious portion. The right of Catholics and Protestants to teach their faith in their schools does not include imposing that instruction on children of another belief. The Catholic Committee's regulations, though valid for Catholic children, cannot be applied so as to compel Protestant children to receive Roman Catholic instruction or take part in Catholic devotions.
conclusion: The children are not obliged to follow the religious instruction or participate in the Roman Catholic devotions to which their father objects; the commissioners must accommodate them.

issue: Are the Education Act and the Catholic Committee's Regulations ultra vires insofar as they would compel non-Catholic pupils to receive Roman Catholic religious training?
facts: Chabot gave the Attorney-General notice under art. 114 C.C.P. attacking the constitutionality of the Act and Regulations; the Attorney-General intervened to uphold them. The relevant regulations (Reg. 73(5),(6), Reg. 75(3), Reg. 102) required pupils to follow the whole program, including religious examinations, with no exemption comparable to Reg. 9 of the Protestant Committee.
rule: Provincial jurisdiction over education under s. 93 of the B.N.A. Act is exclusive subject to protected denominational-school rights; regulations may not exceed the enabling statute or override freedom of worship. Approach in Saumur v. Quebec City (per Kerwin J.): a measure need not be struck down if it can simply be declared inapplicable to the claimant.
application: The majority split on remedy. Pratte and Casey JJ. held the Act intra vires and the regulations valid for Catholic children but simply inapplicable to Protestant children—no declaration of invalidity being necessary. Hyde, Martineau and Owen JJ. held the Education Act intra vires when properly construed, but that Reg. 73(5)–(6) and Reg. 75(3) exceeded the Catholic Committee's powers and violated religious freedom because they contained no exemption for non-Catholic pupils. Rinfret J., dissenting, held the constitutional question was not properly before the Court (the appeal not having been taken against the intervenant within the delays) and, in any event, that the Act and Regulations were constitutional and the mandamus should fail for want of proof that the other statutory options were unavailable.
conclusion: The Education Act was held intra vires; a majority found the impugned regulations either inapplicable to, or ultra vires as against, non-Catholic children. The appeal was allowed.

issue: Does the applicant have standing to challenge s. 28 of the Vital Statistics Act and ss. 171–174 of the Child and Family Services Act?
facts: The applicant's birth was never re-registered after her adoption, so her original birth registration was never sealed; she was given a certified copy. She had never been refused information under CFSA ss. 171–172 (identifying information was withheld because there was no ADR match and the putative father refused consent), and she had not engaged the s. 172 review mechanism. Section 169 had been repealed.
rule: Public interest standing under Canada (Minister of Justice) v. Borowski, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 575, requires: (1) a serious issue as to validity; (2) that the applicant is directly affected or has a genuine direct interest; and (3) no other reasonable and effective way to bring the issue before the court. Charter determinations must rest on an evidentiary foundation from those directly affected (Canadian Council of Churches v. Canada, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 236).
application: The applicant was not directly affected by the VSA re-registration provisions because her registration was never sealed; her disdain for the legislation was not a sufficient direct interest, and the roughly 60% of adoptees actually affected were better placed to challenge s. 28. As to CFSA ss. 171–174, she had never been denied information under those provisions and had not engaged the s. 172 review, so their constitutionality could not be assessed on any factual footing. She conceded standing existed for ss. 162–168.
conclusion: The applicant lacked standing to challenge s. 28 of the VSA and ss. 171–174 of the CFSA; she had standing only to challenge the disclosure provisions in CFSA ss. 162–168.

issue: Do the CFSA secrecy/disclosure provisions violate the applicant's s. 7 rights to liberty and security of the person?
facts: The applicant was adopted as an infant in 1956; her birth mother had died before she began searching. She received extensive information about her birth mother and a maternal uncle, but the man named by her mother as her father denied paternity and refused consent to disclosure of his identity. She claimed the non-disclosure devastated her life and health.
rule: A civil s. 7 claim requires (i) a deprivation of life, liberty or security of person and (ii) that it be contrary to a principle of fundamental justice (R. v. Beare, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 387; Blencoe, 2000 SCC 44). Liberty is not synonymous with unconstrained freedom; security of the person requires serious state-imposed psychological stress assessed objectively against a person of reasonable sensibility (New Brunswick v. G.(J.), [1999] 3 S.C.R. 46). A child's best interests is not a principle of fundamental justice (Canadian Foundation for Children, 2004 SCC 4).
application: The applicant failed to establish an evidentiary basis that access to a putative father's name lies at the core of individual dignity; her freedom was constrained by that man's privacy interest, and there is no liberty right to identifying information about someone who has expressly refused consent. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child did not create such a right, does not supersede legislation, and she had no standing to assert children's rights. Objectively, she had not suffered serious state-imposed psychological stress: no treating therapist testified, her problems flowed from childhood abuse and family secrecy rather than the legislation, and the s. 168 discretion (subject to review, which she never invoked) was inconsistent with any deprivation. She identified no principle of fundamental justice.
conclusion: The impugned provisions did not violate s. 7 of the Charter.

issue: Do the CFSA secrecy/disclosure provisions violate the applicant's s. 15(1) equality rights?
facts: Adopted persons obtain birth-parent information only with consent under the CFSA scheme, whereas non-adopted persons know their origins through personal circumstances. The applicant claimed the scheme demeaned adopted persons and reinforced shame surrounding their births.
rule: The Law v. Canada, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 497 framework asks whether the law draws a distinction on an enumerated or analogous ground and whether it is discriminatory in substance, harming human dignity, assessed from a subjective-objective (reasonable person) perspective, considering pre-existing disadvantage, correspondence to actual needs, ameliorative purpose, and nature of the interest.
application: The distinction (adoption assumed analogous without deciding) did not, in substance, demean dignity. The information sought is available to non-adopted persons through personal circumstance, not law; there was no credible evidence the scheme rests on stereotypes about adopted persons. The scheme reasonably balances the competing interests of the adoption triad, offers individualized access, and served an ameliorative purpose. The applicant had already received considerable information; the interest affected was a single withheld name, not complete exclusion. A reasonable person in her position would not find the provisions demeaning.
conclusion: The provisions did not violate s. 15(1); the application was dismissed and s. 1 and remedies need not be addressed.

issue: Had there been a material change in circumstances under s. 29 of the Children's Law Reform Act since the consent orders of February and March 2008?
facts: After a highly detailed 61-clause consent access order made by Justice Spence on 12 March 2008, the mother, within days and continuing for over a year, cancelled roughly 25% of access visits, refused make-up visits, obstructed exchanges, made repeated unfounded abuse allegations against the father, changed the child's clothing and undermined the child's relationship with the father, and breached numerous clauses of the order. The father brought a second motion to change on 12 May 2009 seeking custody.
rule: Section 29 of the Children's Law Reform Act provides that a court shall not vary a custody or access order unless there has been a material change in circumstances that affects or is likely to affect the best interests of the child; the change is a threshold that must be crossed before a fresh best-interests inquiry.
application: The court found overwhelming evidence that the carefully crafted access regime had broken down: the mother consistently, continuously and intentionally interfered with and obstructed access, breached many clauses of the consent order knowingly, and engaged with her partner in a deliberate campaign to alienate the child from the father. This deterioration since the 2008 orders was harmful to the child's psychological and emotional well-being and readily met the threshold.
conclusion: A material change in circumstances was established, permitting the court to proceed to a fresh best-interests determination.

issue: Did the best interests of the child require transferring sole custody to the father and restricting the mother's access?
facts: The five-year-old child had always lived with the mother, her husband P.P. and siblings, but the mother repeatedly obstructed access, ignored medical advice regarding the child's care, made unverified abuse allegations, and undermined the father's role; the father, though rigid and self-righteous and having himself breached some order terms, offered a calm, stable, affectionate household and committed to fostering the child's relationships with both parents and stepparents.
rule: Section 24(1)-(2) of the CLRA requires custody and access to be determined on the best interests of the child, weighing the enumerated factors; the determination is discretionary and child-specific (Van de Perre v. Edwards, 2001 SCC 60; S.G.B. v. S.J.L., 2009 CanLII 24230; Jackson v. Jackson, 2008 CanLII 3222). A court will not gamble with a child's long-term well-being where the status quo is clearly detrimental (A.A. v. S.N.A., 2007 BCCA 363).
application: The court concluded the status quo was harmful and that the mother, a manipulative and intransigent parent blind to the child's interests, would not change despite years of litigation, warnings, costs orders and professional recommendations. Every less drastic remedy (detailed order, police enforcement, supervised exchanges, parenting coordinator, therapy, costs sanctions) had failed. The father's plan, though imperfect, best ensured the child a loving relationship with both parents; his concerns were outweighed by his willingness to comply with orders and facilitate relationships.
conclusion: Custody was transferred to the father immediately; the mother's access was limited to one supervised two-hour visit every other week, with future variation conditional on proof of completed counselling and parenting programs.

issue: Should the British Columbia Supreme Court decline jurisdiction and stay the plaintiff's defamation action on forum non conveniens grounds because Ontario is a clearly more appropriate forum?
facts: David Irving, a British author resident in London, England, sued Gerry Weiner, the federal Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship (resident in Quebec with a temporary residence in Ottawa), for defamation over a press statement condemning Irving's cross-Canada speaking tour. The statement was released through Canada Newswire in Ottawa and distributed to hundreds of media outlets and ethnocultural organizations across Canada, the majority in Ontario and eastern Canada. The tour began in Victoria, where Irving learned of the statement. The defendant's witnesses and documents were said to be in Ontario/Quebec or abroad; the plaintiff pointed to one B.C. witness (Richard Lewers of Sooke) and to his choice of counsel, Mr. Christie, who had expertise in Holocaust-related litigation.
rule: On a forum non conveniens application the court exercises discretion under the principles in Avenue Properties Ltd. v. First City Development (1986) 7 B.C.L.R. (2d) 45 (per McLachlin J.A.) and Ecco Heating Products Ltd. v. J.K. Campbell and Associates Ltd. (1990) 48 B.C.L.R. (2d) 36, applying the 'modified English rule' from MacShannon and Spilada: the court must determine which forum has the most substantial connection to the parties and the transaction, weighing costs, the presence of juridical advantage or disadvantage, the governing law, and other relevant factors, balancing any advantage to the plaintiff against any disadvantage to the defendant. The plaintiff's choice of forum is not lightly denied, but a stay follows where another forum is clearly more appropriate and justice does not require otherwise.
application: The court found Irving had no connection to British Columbia other than being present when the statement came to his attention, and Weiner's most substantial connection was to Ontario/Quebec. Publication originated in Ottawa and most publication occurred in Ontario and eastern Canada; the defendant's witnesses and documents were in Ontario, so costs and inconvenience would be substantially greater in B.C., and Irving's travel from London to Ontario would cost less than to B.C. Trying the action in Ontario deprived Irving of no juridical advantage—Professor Brown's affidavit established no significant differences between B.C. and Ontario defamation law, and the Ontario two-year limitation period had not expired. The sole personal advantage claimed (retaining Mr. Christie) was not lost, since Christie had litigated Holocaust cases in Ontario and local procedure could be handled by an agent. Balancing these factors, Ontario was clearly the more appropriate forum.
conclusion: The court declined jurisdiction and directed that the proceedings be stayed.

issue: Was the will invalid because the formal requirements for a will made in the presence of witnesses were not met?
facts: Joseph Cohen signed the will in intensive care before two witnesses, both colleagues of the liquidator Mtre. Gozlan. Jules alleged one witness (Mtre. Schrier) was not present and that the pages were not initialled.
rule: Arts. 727, 728 and 714 CCQ: a will made before witnesses must be signed before two witnesses of full age; the pages must be initialled, but a will that does not fully meet the formal requirements is nonetheless valid under art. 714 if it meets the essential requirements and unquestionably contains the last wishes of the deceased.
application: The Court found the three defence witnesses (Gozlan, Zuker and Schrier) consistent and credible, so Jules failed on a balance of probabilities to prove Schrier was absent. The absence of initials on each page is a non-essential formality; the will was only three pages, consecutively numbered, and the testimony showed it reflected Joseph's genuine last wishes developed over years of discussions.
conclusion: The will was valid; neither alleged irregularity rendered it invalid.

issue: Was the universal legacy leaving the estate to 'charitable causes in Israel', with the liquidator to choose the charities, valid?
facts: Paragraph 4 of the will bequeathed the entire estate to unspecified charitable works in Israel, leaving the choice of charities to the discretion of the liquidator, Mtre. Gozlan.
rule: Art. 706 CCQ (public order): the power to designate a legatee belongs to the testator alone and cannot be delegated. Delegation is possible only within a trust (arts. 1260, 1261, 1282 CCQ), which requires transfer of property to an autonomous patrimony and an established intention to create a trust (Groupe Sutton-Royal inc. (Syndic de), 2015 QCCA 1069). A bequest to vague objects such as 'charitable causes' is invalid.
application: The legacy was too vague to identify the legatees, like earlier invalid bequests to 'charitable causes' or 'assorted charities'. Delegating the choice of beneficiaries amounted to abdicating a power reserved to the testator, contrary to art. 706. No trust was created: none of the essential requirements were met, no separate patrimony was constituted, and the evidence that Joseph intended to finalize the charity list himself was inconsistent with an intention to create a trust.
conclusion: The universal legacy in paragraph 4 was declared invalid; the estate remained in intestate succession, making Joseph's brothers the heirs (art. 736 CCQ).

issue: Should Mtre. Gozlan be removed as liquidator?
facts: Jules sought Gozlan's removal because of the animosity between Gozlan and Joseph's surviving brothers.
rule: Art. 791 CCQ: a liquidator may be removed when unable to assume his responsibilities, when he neglects his duties, or fails to fulfil his obligations. Removal is not an appropriate remedy merely to resolve conflict with heirs (Vachon c. Riopelle; Bélanger c. Bélanger).
application: The Court found no evidence of any failure by Gozlan. The requested removal was based only on personal animosity, which had not affected the administration of the estate. Removing a liquidator specifically appointed by the testator is an extreme step not justified by anticipated friction.
conclusion: Gozlan remained as liquidator.

issue: Was Jules entitled to damages for defamation and other slights?
facts: Jules claimed $15,000, alleging Gozlan excluded the brothers from Joseph's final months and funeral arrangements, chose a lesser funeral home, accompanied the body to Israel himself, and humiliated the family by spreading rumours that Joseph died penniless, notably through a Facebook post by Gozlan's wife soliciting funds.
rule: General civil liability principles requiring proof of fault, injury and causation; defamation requires disparaging statements harming reputation.
application: There was no evidence Gozlan excluded the brothers or that Joseph had left instructions or funds for a costlier funeral. None of the brothers were able or willing to accompany the body to Israel, and Gozlan's decision was motivated by respect and duty, not profit. The Facebook post was neither disrespectful nor defamatory; Gozlan made no statements disparaging Joseph.
conclusion: The damage claim was dismissed as without merit.

issue: Did the plaintiff sexually abuse his daughter so as to disentitle him to custody or unsupervised access?
facts: The mother alleged sexual abuse based on the child's reddened vagina, a red 'erythema' ring around the anus, excessive masturbation, disclosures of 'playing doctor', and complaints of a sore bottom. Medical examinations were normal; Dr. Mitchell listed multiple innocent causes for the redness. A police interview (Det. Pranzl) with the three-year-old was inconclusive and, per Dr. Elterman, poorly conducted with leading questions. Crown declined to lay charges. Dr. Elterman opined abuse was improbable and that innocent behaviour had been systematically misinterpreted.
rule: In custody/access matters the paramount consideration is the best interests of the child; where sexual abuse is alleged the court will not determine the matter simply on the balance of probabilities but will 'err on the safe side' by denying custody or unsupervised access if the evidence raises a reasonable suspicion of abuse.
application: The trial judge found the medical evidence equivocal and consistent with innocent causes, the police videotape did not establish abuse, and the child's complaints occurred both before and after supervised visits. She accepted Dr. Elterman's opinion that abuse was improbable and found that the mother had planted suspicion in the child's mind by reminding her of incidents that never occurred.
conclusion: There were no grounds to conclude the plaintiff had abused or was likely to abuse Samantha; the abuse allegations were groundless.

issue: Should sole custody be transferred from the mother, the long-time primary caregiver, to the father?
facts: The child had lived with her mother since birth. The father had developed a warm, loving relationship confirmed by access supervisors and family witnesses. The mother had been the primary caregiver and was deeply bonded to the child, but the household exhibited conflict and the mother persistently obstructed access.
rule: The court's primary and paramount concern is the best interests of the child (Family Relations Act framework), weighing stability, each parent's capacity, and the maintenance of the child's relationship with both parents.
application: Weighing the groundlessness of the abuse allegations, the well-founded protection concerns in the mother's home, and the mother's continuous interference with access against the father's ability to provide a stable home and extended family, the judge concluded the father could offer the peace and security the child lacked, while insisting the child maintain contact with both parents.
conclusion: Sole custody transferred to the father, with supervised access to the mother for three months and a review thereafter; the court remained seized for one year.

issue: What effect did the mother's persistent denial of and interference with access have on her fitness as custodial parent?
facts: After March 1990 the mother systematically restricted access, denied it on several dates in 1992, was found in contempt by Warren J., attempted to unilaterally change supervisors, took the child to Ontario in breach of a restraining order, and coached the child to make abuse disclosures.
rule: A parent who refuses access (without proper cause) raises serious questions about that parent's fitness (Tremblay v. Tremblay (1987), 10 R.F.L. (3d) 166 (Alta. Q.B.)); the right of access belongs to the child. Discussing adversarial litigation with a young child further undermines fitness.
application: The judge found the mother confused her own relationship with the father with the child's relationship with him, and that her anger drove her to thwart the father-daughter bond and to discuss the litigation with the child, contrary to the child's interests.
conclusion: The mother's conduct weighed strongly against her as custodial parent.

issue: Did protection concerns arising from the step-father's conduct affect the custody determination?
facts: The child disclosed to the access supervisor and Dr. Elterman that the step-father, Mr. Gidley, hit her, locked her in her room, and hit her mother; a supervisor observed the child cower. Gidley misrepresented his prior marriage to Dr. Elterman; his ex-wife testified to an escalating pattern of physical abuse ('battered wife syndrome'), and Gidley had contacted her during trial telling her not to testify.
rule: A child who witnesses domestic violence suffers consequences akin to a child who is directly abused; protection concerns bear directly on the best-interests analysis.
application: The judge accepted the supervisor's and Dr. Elterman's observations, found Gidley had deliberately misrepresented his history and that the ex-wife's evidence substantiated a pattern of abuse, and concluded the conflict and stress in the Tingren-Gidley household was an equal or greater source of harm than the custody battle.
conclusion: The protection concerns were well-founded and jeopardized the child's physical and psychological well-being, supporting transfer of custody to the father.

issue: Did the society meet the two-part test under s. 94 of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017 to justify a temporary order removing the child from the mother?
facts: On June 12, 2019 the mother, maternal grandmother and the two-year-old child were found unconscious from insulin overdoses; the child suffered profound long-term brain damage. The mother was charged with attempted murder, aggravated assault and administering a noxious substance, was denied bail, remained in jail, and was prohibited by the criminal court from any contact with the child.
rule: Under s. 94(2), (4) and (5) of the Act, on an adjourned hearing the court must make a temporary care and custody order; it may remove the child only where satisfied there are reasonable grounds to believe the child is likely to suffer harm and cannot be adequately protected by a supervision order. The society bears the onus of showing, on credible and trustworthy evidence, a real possibility of harm and that supervision terms would be inadequate (Children's Aid Society of Ottawa-Carleton v. T., 2000 CanLII 21157 (ON SC)). Evidence may be admitted under s. 94(10) if credible and trustworthy in the circumstances.
application: The mother is in jail on serious charges, is legally barred from any contact with the child, and is simply unavailable to care for her. No supervision terms could protect the child if placed in the mother's care. The two-part test was therefore met with respect to the mother.
conclusion: The society met the test as against the mother; the child could not be returned to her care and a temporary order placing the child elsewhere was warranted.

issue: Was it in the child's best interests to be placed in the temporary care and custody of the father or the maternal grandparents?
facts: The child now has exceptional special needs (seizures, tube feeding, developmental delays, vision loss) requiring intensive coordinated services in Hamilton. The father, previously a stranger to the child, had since June 2019 been her primary caregiver, living at the hospital, following professional recommendations and assembling a detailed service plan. The maternal grandparents, with whom the child had lived from January 2018 to June 2019, sought placement but made numerous baseless and malicious allegations against the father, resisted medical direction, and rejected offered counselling.
rule: The court must apply the best interests considerations in s. 74(3) of the Act, choosing the least disruptive placement consistent with adequate protection (s. 1(2); Children's Aid Society of Hamilton v. B.D. and F.T.M., 2012 ONSC 2448) and proportional to risk (CCAS of Toronto v. J.O.1, 2012 ONCJ 269). Section 94(5) requires consideration of placement with a relative before a society placement. The parties agreed no s. 94(2)(a) priority should be given, so the court assessed best interests directly.
application: The evidence overwhelmingly favoured the father: he provided excellent care, made sensible medical decisions, cooperated with providers, had a comprehensive plan, secure accommodation and strong support from the paternal grandmother, and had addressed his past conduct through therapy and courses. The child's closest bond was now with him and her services were established in Hamilton. The maternal grandparents' plan lacked detail, they resisted medical advice, exposed the child to adult conflict and were unlikely to support the father's role, whereas the father supported their continued relationship with the child.
conclusion: Placement in the father's temporary care and custody, subject to society supervision, was in the child's best interests.

issue: What access should be ordered for the mother and the maternal grandparents?
facts: The mother, in jail, was prohibited by the criminal court from contact with the child and no party sought access for her. The maternal grandparents sought generous access including in their home; the child is medically fragile with limited ability to travel, and the grandparents had at times acted inappropriately and resisted medical direction.
rule: Sections 94(8) and 104(1) authorize the court to order access on terms it considers appropriate, guided by the paramount best-interests purpose and the least-disruptive-action principle (ss. 1(1), (2)) and the s. 74(3) factors (Jewish Family and Child Services v. H.B.S., [2012] O.J. No. 5055 (OCJ)).
application: No access was ordered for the mother given the criminal prohibition and her incarceration. For the maternal grandparents, the child's medical fragility, the logistical difficulties of Hamilton visits, and the grandparents' conduct made a fixed extensive schedule unworkable; access was placed in the society's discretion but structured by minimum terms (at least twice weekly for three hours), with power to suspend for inappropriate conduct and a requirement that the father be absent and the society keep the grandparents medically informed.
conclusion: No access to the mother; maternal grandparents' access left in the society's discretion subject to guiding conditions, representing an increase in their time with the child.

issue: Has the society established reasonable grounds to believe the children would likely suffer harm if returned to either parent?
facts: The society apprehended M.S. (9) and J.S. (7) amid extensive protection concerns: sexually inappropriate conduct by the mother, sexually suggestive photos taken and withheld by the father, the father's undisclosed 1980s Utah rape conviction and sexual-offender diversion program, a criminal harassment conviction, an Extradition Act matter, pending sexual/assault charges against the mother, disturbing sexual comments reported by the father's former surety, aggressive behaviour toward school staff and relatives, and the children's exposure to ongoing domestic conflict.
rule: Under ss. 51(2) and (3) CFSA, at a temporary care and custody hearing the society must show, on credible and trustworthy evidence, reasonable grounds to believe there is a real possibility that returning a child to a respondent would more probably than not result in harm, per Children's Aid Society of Ottawa-Carleton v. T. (2000). Section 37(2)(d) and (g) define a child in need of protection where there is a risk of sexual molestation/exploitation or emotional harm. Both branches apply separately to each person who had charge of the children (CAS of Toronto v. A.(S.) and R.(M.)).
application: The court found the evidence 'overwhelming' that the first branch was met against both parents. The mother crossed sexual boundaries and failed to protect the children by not disclosing the father's history; the father either participated in or failed to protect against sexual misconduct, minimized and concealed a documented history of violent sexual offending, and exposed the children to domestic conflict. Together this established a real possibility of emotional and sexual harm under s. 37(2)(d) and (g).
conclusion: The first branch of the test was satisfied against both parents; there were reasonable grounds to believe the children would likely suffer emotional and sexual harm if returned to either parent.

issue: Are supervision terms adequate to protect the children if returned to a parent, applied separately to the mother and the father?
facts: The mother had crossed sexual boundaries but stopped when warned, acknowledged the inappropriateness, cooperated fully after apprehension, had a suitable plan, appropriate housing and supports, and a warm relationship with the children; the bail terms separating the parents addressed domestic-violence exposure. The father showed no insight, externalized blame, concealed and minimized his criminal/therapeutic history, and posed profound unresolved risk concerns.
rule: The society must also show the children cannot be adequately protected by the terms of an interim supervision order (s. 51(3); CAS of Ottawa-Carleton v. T.). The court must choose the least disruptive placement consistent with adequate protection (s. 1(2); CAS of Hamilton v. B.D.), and intrusiveness must be proportional to risk (CCAS of Toronto v. J.O.1).
application: For the mother, the residual concerns were offset by her compliance, insight, cooperation, suitable plan and the protective effect of the parents' separation, so society supervision terms were adequate. For the father, his complete lack of insight, concealment of a violent sexual history, and the many unanswered questions meant supervision terms could not safely protect the children.
conclusion: Supervision terms were adequate for the mother; the children were placed in her temporary care under society supervision. Supervision was not adequate for the father, and the children were not returned to his care.

issue: What access order for the father is in the children's best interests?
facts: The father had a warm relationship with the children and had complied with access to date, but posed unresolved protection concerns, showed no insight, and the foster parents reported the children returning unsettled after supervised visits; more information about the father's risk was required.
rule: Section 51(5) CFSA permits the court to order access on terms it considers appropriate where a child is placed under clause 51(2)(c) or (d), guided by the paramount purpose of the children's best interests, protection and well-being (ss. 1(1), 1(2), 37(3)).
application: Given the protection concerns, the father's lack of insight, and the need to consolidate the children's placement with the mother against the risk the father might undermine it, access in the society's discretion (currently supervised) best served the children, allowing the society to relax terms if the father mitigated the risks.
conclusion: The father's access was ordered to remain in the society's discretion, not less than once weekly, with the society determining the level of supervision.

issue: Should the father be ordered to produce his full criminal and therapeutic records under s. 74 CFSA and Rule 19?
facts: The society sought the father's Utah criminal, sentencing and diversion-program records, Ontario criminal harassment records, Extradition Act records, and current charge records. The father produced only his current criminal record and a summary letter, resisting fuller disclosure and asserting privacy and irrelevance.
rule: Section 74(3) CFSA gives a discretionary power to order production of records that 'may be relevant' — a low threshold (a 'semblance of relevance'; CAS of Algoma v. P.(D.); NS (Community Services) v. B.L.C.) — and applies despite privacy interests except solicitor-client privilege. Where best interests are engaged, the court has a positive obligation to ensure relevant information is before it. Rule 19 requires disclosure of documents relevant and in a party's control or available on request; possession/control includes documents obtainable on request from third parties (Michaud v. Cormier).
application: The father's history of violence with sexual overtones made his entire criminal and therapeutic history relevant, easily meeting the 'may be relevant' threshold; the children's protection trumped his privacy claims. Section 74(3) speaks of 'any person' and can be applied to a party, and the father could obtain the Utah and Ontario records on request, so he had control of them. The Mental Health Act s. 35(6) procedure was not triggered as no harm to treatment was asserted. Rule 19 provided an alternative basis.
conclusion: The father was ordered to request the records directly and sign releases so the society could obtain them, subject to the s. 74(5) confidentiality safeguards and additional restrictions to address his privacy concerns.

issue: Should the court proceed de novo rather than treat the application as a renewal of the earlier safeguard/injunction orders?
facts: Justice Urbas (Dec. 9, 2024) and Justice Larocque (Mar. 5, 2025) had each suspended a vote ratifying the SSMU Policy Against Antisemitism 2024-11-07 on procedural/notice grounds. The present application targets a revised Policy (2025-04-03) and is founded on an alleged lack of appropriate consultation, a different basis than the earlier orders. The parties did not consent to treating the matter as a renewal.
rule: A revised subject matter and new facts require the court to decide the application afresh rather than sitting in review of the prior order (citing Droit de la famille – 20393, 2020 QCCA 435; Publications TVA Inc. c. Transcontinental Inc., 2005 QCCA 1549).
application: Because the December 9 and March 5 Orders concerned the 2024-11-07 Policy while the present application concerns the revised 2025-04-03 Policy, and because there were new facts and a different legal basis (consultation), the court was not reviewing the March 5 Order.
conclusion: The court proceeded de novo and applied the ordinary tests for a safeguard order.

issue: Did the plaintiffs satisfy the criteria for a safeguard order to suspend ratification of the revised Policy?
facts: Plaintiffs, McGill students and SSMU members, sought to suspend the April 8, 2025 board vote ratifying the SSMU Policy Against Antisemitism 2025-04-03, alleging lack of meaningful consultation contrary to the SSMU Consultation Policy and bad faith contrary to arts. 6 and 7 C.C.Q., and that ratification would legitimize hate, intimidation and harassment of Jewish students. The evidence (Solomon's affidavit, Exhibits R-6, R-7, HVS-10) showed extensive consultation since September 2024, invitations to Jewish groups (including Chabad and Hillel), general assembly and legislative council debates, and integration of feedback.
rule: A safeguard order is a discretionary conservatory measure requiring the same criteria as a provisional injunction: appearance of right, serious or irreparable harm, balance of convenience, and urgency (arts. 49 and 158 C.C.P.; McGill University c. Kahentinetha, 2024 QCCA 1050). It must not amount to a judgment on the merits.
application: Urgency was met because ratification was imminent on April 8 and plaintiffs acted timely (though urgency stemmed from the defendant's scheduling). Appearance of right was not established: the SSMU Consultation Policy sets best practices, not firm rules, defines consultation as dialogue/exchange, and the record showed thorough consultation of members and Jewish groups; Chabad, a plaintiff, declined to participate and could not complain. The 2018 comparison was unpersuasive. Serious/irreparable harm was unsupported by the affidavits — plaintiffs did not show how allowing the vote would legitimize hate or harassment. Balance of convenience favoured neither party.
conclusion: Except for urgency, the criteria were not met; the application for a safeguard order was dismissed.

issue: Should the court decide the defendant's oral SLAPP/abuse motion?
facts: The defendant orally sought a declaration that the application was abusive and a SLAPP, referring in part to its pending Motion to Dismiss (filed Feb. 25, 2025) being triaged by special case management judge Justice Éric Dufour.
rule: Abuse/SLAPP arguments should be determined by the assigned case management judge or at the merits stage where they can be properly argued and answered.
application: Since the SLAPP motion was already before Justice Dufour and required a full response from plaintiffs, it was not for this court to decide it on an oral motion.
conclusion: The oral motion was deferred to Justice Éric Dufour or to the merits.

issue: Should the appellants be granted leave to adduce new evidence (legislative facts and fresh affidavits) on appeal?
facts: After the first-instance refusal, women teachers wearing the hijab were denied teaching positions once the Act came into force; the appellants sought to file briefs, debate journals and new affidavits describing these effects.
rule: New evidence on appeal is admissible where it is genuinely new (could not have been filed below), indispensable to the outcome, and admission serves the ends of justice; courts may take judicial notice of legislative facts such as Hansard, and complete evidence is required in Charter cases (MacKay v. Manitoba).
application: The affidavits concerned facts arising after the trial judgment and showed the concrete effects of s. 6 on hijab-wearing teachers, capable of influencing the stay analysis; the legislative materials were proper subjects of judicial notice.
conclusion: Leave to adduce the new evidence was granted unanimously, without costs.

issue: Could the Court raise the previously unargued issue of the interplay between s. 33 and s. 28 of the Canadian Charter at the stay stage?
facts: Before the trial judge the appellants had abandoned Charter arguments and relied on division of powers, rule of law and constitutional structure; during case management the panel invited argument on whether s. 33 can override s. 28.
rule: An appellate court has discretion to raise a new issue where failing to do so would risk an injustice, subject to jurisdiction, a sufficient record, and absence of procedural prejudice (R. v. Mian; R. v. Quan). At the stay stage only the seriousness of the argument need be assessed, not its ultimate merit.
application: The s. 28 question was legally and factually distinct, potentially decisive for the stay because s. 28 may be immune from the s. 33 override, and had a sufficient evidentiary basis; the new evidence allowed a preliminary assessment. The parties were given notice, avoiding prejudice.
conclusion: The Court accepted the new issue as relevant and admissible for purposes of the appeal, without deciding it on the merits.

issue: Should ss. 6 and 8 of the Act be provisionally stayed pending the constitutional challenge, notwithstanding the invocation of the notwithstanding clause?
facts: The Act prohibits certain public employees (including new-hire teachers) from wearing religious symbols and requires uncovered faces; ss. 33/34 of the Act and s. 52 of the Quebec Charter shield it from Charter review. Hijab-wearing teacher candidates were refused employment, causing financial, psychological and career harm.
rule: Metropolitan Stores and RJR-MacDonald tripartite test: (1) serious question to be tried; (2) irreparable harm; (3) balance of convenience, where legislation is presumed enacted for the public good and stays of statutes issue only in 'clear cases' (Harper v. Canada). Appellate intervention in the discretionary stay decision is limited (R. v. CBC).
application: All three judges accepted a serious question and that hijab-wearing teachers suffer irreparable harm. On balance of convenience the majority (Bélanger and Mainville, JJ.A.) held that, because the legislature validly invoked the notwithstanding clause and the presumption of validity applies, a stay could issue only if it were clear that s. 28 defeats the s. 33 override and that the Act unequally affects women — neither being clear given the nebulous, embryonic state of s. 28 jurisprudence, possible s. 1 justification, and comparative practice. Duval Hesler, C.J.Q., dissenting in part, would have suspended s. 6 for the teachers in Schedule II, para. 10, finding the public interest not outweighed given the existing grandfather clause.
conclusion: Appeal dismissed (2-1), without costs; ss. 6 and 8 remain in force pending the merits, to be heard in October 2020.

issue: Are the issues raised by the plaintiff's application moot given that the SSMU Board of Directors decided not to adopt the Palestine Solidarity Policy?
facts: Jonah Fried, a Jewish McGill student and self-described Zionist, challenged a 'Palestine Solidarity Policy' promoted by the SPHR club and approved by 71.1% of voters in a March 2022 SSMU referendum, seeking declarations that the referendum and Policy were contrary to the SSMU Constitution, discriminatory and antisemitic. On April 25, 2022, before the action was filed on July 22, 2022, the SSMU Board of Directors resolved not to adopt the Policy because it did not conform to the SSMU Constitution, equity policy and Quebec law. McGill's Deputy Provost had likewise condemned the Policy.
rule: Article 10, para. 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that 'the courts are not required to decide theoretical questions.' Borowski v. Canada (Attorney General), [1989] 1 SCR 342, establishes a first step of asking whether the required tangible and concrete dispute has disappeared so that the issues have become academic. Courts also will not answer purely hypothetical questions lacking a factual basis (Mackey v. PGQ, 2022 QCCS 5018).
application: Because the SSMU Board declined to adopt the Policy, it produced no real or concrete consequences for any McGill student; indeed the issue was moot from the very outset since all parties—the plaintiff, McGill and the SSMU—agreed the Policy contravened the Constitution and Quebec law. The Court rejected the plaintiff's argument that the Policy was 'in force' by virtue of the referendum/plebiscite distinction, noting the incoherence of asking the Court to treat the Policy as having legal effect only to declare it void ab initio. The added conclusion seeking to condemn future 'like' policies was even more clearly non-justiciable as hypothetical.
conclusion: The issues raised by the application in respect of the Policy are moot.

issue: If the issues are moot, should the Court nonetheless exercise its discretion to hear the case?
facts: A parallel injunction proceeding (No. 500-17-127703-232) concerning a similar 'Policy against Genocide in Palestine' was pending before the Superior Court, argued by the same counsel acting for the plaintiff. The plaintiff had graduated in 2023, and the issues were characterized as more political than legal.
rule: The second Borowski step requires weighing (1) whether an adversarial context remains, (2) concerns of judicial economy, and (3) the courts' proper law-making function. Courts are also reluctant to interfere in the internal affairs of a university or student association absent demonstrated illegality (Presch v. Alma Mater Society of UBC, 2017 BCSC 963).
application: There was no genuine adversarial context because all parties agreed the Policy was illegal and non-existent; judicial economy favoured leaving the virtually identical legal issues to be argued in the pending injunction case; and the essentially political nature of the dispute counselled against judicial interference in the internal affairs of the student association where the impugned policy created no concrete consequences.
conclusion: The Court declined to exercise its discretion to hear the moot case; it granted both motions to dismiss and dismissed the re-modified application with costs. The plaintiff's legal interest need not be decided.

issue: Does Regulation 304's designation of Christmas, Good Friday and Easter Monday as school holidays infringe freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
facts: Regulation 304 under the Education Act designates a Christmas vacation, Good Friday and Easter Monday (and Saturdays/Sundays) as school holidays. The applicants argued these holidays have a religious purpose recognizing Christian holy days, contrary to Muslims' s. 2(a) rights.
rule: Following R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713, Peel (Regional Municipality) v. Great Atlantic & Pacific Co. (1991), 2 O.R. (3d) 65 (C.A.), and CSR de Chambly v. Bergevin, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 525, days such as Sundays, Christmas and Easter, though of religious origin, have become secular common pause days; a calendar including them is secular and neutral on its face. Section 2(a) is engaged only where a state-imposed cost is capable of interfering with religious belief or practice.
application: The court found no evidence that the impugned holidays were chosen for a religious rather than secular purpose; Easter Monday is not a holy day and Good Friday is not a day of obligation in the Roman Catholic Church. The holidays are secular common pause days chosen to coincide with community-wide rest days. Moreover, s. 21(2)(g) of the Education Act excuses a child from attendance on a day regarded as a holy day of the child's religion, so Muslim students may be absent on their holy days without penalty. Any embarrassment flows from the student's own religious obligations, not from the secular legislation.
conclusion: Regulation 304 does not infringe s. 2(a) in purpose or effect.

issue: Does Regulation 304 create adverse effect discrimination contrary to s. 15 of the Charter?
facts: Muslim students must miss two school days each year for Eid-al-Fitr and Eid-al-Adha, while Christian holy days fall on existing school holidays. There was no evidence about how many Christian students actually observe Christmas or Good Friday religiously.
rule: Section 15 equality guarantee; adverse effect discrimination requires a comparator group receiving a significant advantage (per Peel and Bergevin). Absent evidence of real advantage to Christians, discrimination is not established.
application: The court doubted discrimination could be found on the record, noting the absence of evidence that Christian students observe these days religiously, but was prepared to assume adverse effect discrimination arose from Muslim students having to miss school while Christians did not.
conclusion: No adverse effect discrimination was proven, but the court proceeded on the assumption that it existed.

issue: If Regulation 304 infringes s. 15, is the limit demonstrably justified under s. 1?
facts: The legislature chose school holidays coinciding with secular common pause days enjoyed by the wider community, including those in the Retail Business Holidays Act.
rule: Section 1 Oakes-type analysis as summarized in Edwards Books: the objective must be pressing and substantial, and the means proportional (rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionate effects).
application: Providing school holidays is a pressing and substantial objective. Choosing holidays coinciding with community-wide pause days minimally impairs religious rights; the only alternative—making every holy day of every student a holiday—was impossible and would itself be unconstitutional by favouring religion over atheists, agnostics and the non-affiliated (more than 12% of Canadians). Christmas and Good Friday must remain school holidays for Ontario to align with the rest of the western world.
conclusion: Any infringement is a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1; Regulation 304 does not offend the Charter.

issue: Did the Board have a duty to close schools on Muslim holy days or to study the request, and did it fulfil any duty to accommodate?
facts: The applicants asked the Board to make one or both Muslim high holy days school holidays (or professional-activity days) and to study accommodation. The Board had permitted absences on holy days, distributed multi-faith calendars, directed teachers not to schedule tests on holy days, provided prayer rooms and make-up tests, and operated a Multiculturalism Advisory Committee. In 1994 it delayed the school start by two days for Rosh Hashanah as a one-time event.
rule: Assuming adverse effect discrimination, there is a duty to accommodate by reasonable means short of undue hardship (Bergevin). Accommodation need not extend to closing schools; professional activity days are not throw-away days.
application: The court held closing schools for religious observance would itself breach the Charter, and there were too few available days for the many holy days of all religions. The Board had already taken numerous reasonable steps to relieve the disadvantage. The Rosh Hashanah delay was a rare, non-precedential accommodation of an orientation problem, not recognition of a holy day. The Board considered and rejected the applicants' request and communicated its decision.
conclusion: The Board had no obligation to close schools or study the request, and it had already provided reasonable accommodation; the application was dismissed with costs of $7,500.

issue: Do the debate and passage of a censure motion, and the resulting censure of an MPP, fall within parliamentary privilege so as to oust the court's jurisdiction?
facts: Sarah Jama, MPP for Hamilton Centre, was censured by the Legislative Assembly of Ontario after Motion 19, moved by Government House Leader Paul Calandra, was debated and passed, authorizing the Speaker not to recognize her until she retracted and apologized for social-media statements about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. She sought judicial review to quash the Speaker's decision to allow the motion, to have the motion ruled out of order, to quash the censure, and a declaration the measures were unconstitutional.
rule: Courts have no jurisdiction to review matters falling within parliamentary privilege, which is a rule of curial jurisdiction conferring immunity from judicial review (Canada (House of Commons) v. Vaid, 2005 SCC 30; Chagnon, 2018 SCC 39; Duffy v. Canada (Senate), 2020 ONCA 536). Control over debates and proceedings and disciplinary authority over members are established categories of privilege. Motions to dismiss for want of jurisdiction proceed under rr. 21.01(1)(b) and 21.01(3)(a) of the Rules of Civil Procedure; s. 52.1(1) of the Legislative Assembly Act affirms the Assembly holds the same privileges as the U.K. House of Commons as of 1867.
application: The relief sought targeted steps taken within the Legislative Assembly — allowing, debating, voting on and adopting Motion 19 and its disciplinary consequences. These squarely engaged the categories of control over debates and proceedings and disciplinary authority over members. Once a category of privilege is recognized, the court cannot examine the merits or exercise of the privilege; the starting point is the existence and scope of the category, not the fairness of the censure.
conclusion: The subject matter fell within parliamentary privilege; the court had no jurisdiction and the application was dismissed.

issue: Do the categories of control over debates and proceedings and disciplinary authority over members remain necessary in the contemporary context?
facts: The applicant argued Motion 19 and the censure were not necessary in the contemporary context and relied on Chagnon, an employment case about dismissed National Assembly security guards.
rule: Under Vaid, at para. 29, necessity is read broadly and tied to the autonomy legislative assemblies require; the test is what the dignity and efficiency of the legislature require. At the provincial level the court may consider whether a category continues to be necessary. The activity must be so closely connected with the assembly's functions that outside interference would undermine its required autonomy (Vaid, para. 46; Chagnon, paras. 29-31).
application: The correct question was not whether the specific censure was necessary but whether the categories relied on remain necessary. Control over debates and proceedings has been recognized since 1689 and remains central to legislative autonomy; disciplinary authority over members likewise remains necessary, as confirmed in Duffy. Chagnon did not involve a legislative motion or discipline of an elected member and was distinguishable. External intervention would create delays, disruption and costs holding up the legislature's business.
conclusion: Both categories remain necessary in the contemporary context; privilege applied.

issue: Does the location of the statements outside the legislature or the invocation of Charter rights remove the matter from privilege?
facts: The applicant made her impugned statements on X (outside the chamber) and argued her political speech and her Charter freedom of expression, plus impacts on her constituents, warranted judicial review; she also invoked the Legislative Assembly Act and Members' Integrity Act.
rule: Parliamentary privilege is not confined to conduct within the legislature (Harvey; Michaud; Zundel; Saunders). Where privilege applies, the legislature has exclusive competence to adjudicate alleged Charter breaches; judicial review even for Charter compliance would nullify the immunity (Chagnon, para. 24; Vaid, para. 30; Duffy, para. 110). Privilege is as much part of the Constitution as the Charter, and one part cannot abrogate another.
application: The privilege extends to sanctioning conduct occurring outside the chamber, and the applicant had captioned her post by referencing her role as a politician. The Members' Integrity Act was not a comprehensive code waiving privilege, and s. 46 authority over criminal matters is additional to, not a limitation on, privilege. Impact on constituents was considered but, as in New Brunswick Broadcasting where s. 2(b) did not prevail, did not displace privilege. The Charter arguments presumed privilege did not apply; since it did, the court lacked jurisdiction.
conclusion: Neither the extramural location of the statements nor the Charter claims removed the matter from privilege; the applicant's remedy lay with the Legislative Assembly and, ultimately, the electorate.

issue: Is the Village of Burns Lake vicariously liable for the alleged torts of RCMP officers policing a municipality with a population under 5,000?
facts: Burns Lake had a population of approximately 3,649 in 2006 and played no role in hiring, training, supervising or disciplining the defendant RCMP officers. Policing was provided by the RCMP acting as the provincial police force under a 1992 federal-provincial agreement to which Burns Lake was not a party.
rule: Under s. 3(1)(b) of the Police Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 367, the provincial government must provide policing for municipalities of up to 5,000 persons; s. 14 allows the RCMP to serve as the provincial police force. Municipal joint-and-several tort liability under s. 20 applies only to municipalities over 5,000 with municipal constables; liability for provincial constables lies with the Province (s. 11; Quinn v. Dubnyk, 2011 BCSC 792; Roy v. British Columbia (AG), 2005 BCCA 88).
application: Because Burns Lake had fewer than 5,000 residents, the officers were provincial constables, not municipal constables. Burns Lake had no statutory or contractual role in their policing and thus could not be vicariously liable; any such liability rested with the Province.
conclusion: The plaintiff had no basis for a claim against Burns Lake and the action against it was dismissed under Rule 9-6(4).

issue: Are the plaintiff's tort and Charter claims statute-barred, and was the two-year limitation period postponed?
facts: The impugned conduct occurred on October 19-20, 2006; the notice of civil claim was filed April 29, 2011. The plaintiff had already commenced two Vancouver actions (November 2006 and December 2008) advancing mirror allegations. He claimed postponement due to periods of psychiatric hospitalization and incarceration and medication effects, but tendered no expert evidence of incapacity.
rule: The Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266 imposes a two-year period running from when damage was sustained and the tortfeasor is known (Levitt v. Carr; Craig v. ICBC, 2005 BCCA 275). Postponement under s. 6(4)/(6) requires, per Ounjian v. St. Paul's Hospital and Novak v. Bond, [1999] 1 SCR 808, that a reasonable person with the known facts and appropriate advice could bring an action; the onus is on the plaintiff. Trespass, forcible confinement and defamation are not among the s. 6(3) categories capable of postponement.
application: There was no discoverability issue: the plaintiff knew of his injuries and could readily have learned the officers' identities, as shown by his earlier Vancouver actions naming the RCMP and John Does. He unreasonably declined to seek legal advice despite being urged to do so. Even if incapacity or incarceration were established, commencing the action in 2011 would still fall outside the limitation period.
conclusion: The claims for assault, kidnapping, forcible confinement, trespass, illegal search and seizure, defamation and cruel and unusual punishment (and related Charter breaches) were statute-barred and dismissed.

issue: Should the pleadings alleging sexual assault and malicious prosecution be struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of action?
facts: The 18-page, 67-paragraph notice of civil claim quoted the Magna Carta and religious material, described the RCMP as a 'standing army' and used scandalous invective. The sexual assault allegation was based only on being struck on the 'stomach, ribs and genitals'; the malicious prosecution claim was pleaded without its constituent elements. Malicious prosecution and sexual assault claims were not time-barred (s. 3(4)(k); D.E. v. British Columbia, 2005 BCCA 134).
rule: Under Rule 9-5(1) a pleading may be struck where it discloses no reasonable claim or is scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, assuming pleaded facts are true (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 SCR 959; R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42). Sexual assault requires conduct of a sexual nature violating sexual integrity (R. v. Chase, [1987] 2 SCR). Malicious prosecution requires four elements: proceedings initiated by the defendant, terminated in the plaintiff's favour, absence of reasonable and probable cause, and malice/improper purpose (Miazga v. Kvello Estate, 2009 SCC 51; Nelles v. Ontario, [1989] 2 SCR 170).
application: The sexual assault pleading alleged an assault but no facts establishing a sexual context or motive; this was not a mere drafting deficiency. The malicious prosecution claim failed to plead the four required elements. The overall pleadings were prolix, embarrassing and largely incomprehensible.
conclusion: The sexual assault allegation was struck; the plaintiff was granted 60 days to file an entirely new notice of civil claim particularizing malicious prosecution, failing which that claim would also be dismissed.

issue: Did the defendants breach the obligation of good faith in negotiating and cooperating toward completion of the acquisition set out in the Letter of Intent?
facts: Ryer and his partner Greenspoon negotiated to buy Potten's seasonal barbecue company. A Letter of Intent signed December 22, 2010 set a $11.75M price, a $7.7M minimum Net Book Value at closing, and a February 22, 2011 closing. Potten cancelled a February 17 meeting, and the parties then deadlocked over ownership of the strong 2011 profits, with Potten later proposing revised terms the buyers rejected before walking away.
rule: Arts. 6, 7 and 1375 C.C.Q. require good faith in the exercise of rights and in contract formation and performance. The duty to negotiate in good faith is not an absolute obligation to conclude a contract; a party may terminate negotiations over a material disagreement provided it does so reasonably and not abusively (Greenberg v. Capital d'Amérique CDPQ inc., 2011 QCCA 958; Friedman v. Ruby, 2012 QCCS 1778; Pegasus Partners Inc. v. Groupe Laurem inc., 2007 QCCS 476).
application: The Court found Potten cooperated in good faith with due diligence—giving access to his consultant, bankers and auditors and supplying extensive financial documentation sufficient for the buyers to obtain two financing offers; Ryer himself wrote that due diligence was 'progressing well with no surprises.' The failure resulted from a genuine, material disagreement over ownership of the 2011 profits, an issue the ambiguous NBV Clause did not unequivocally resolve (the three protagonists each read it differently). Potten flagged the profit issue early, and both sides made reasonable good-faith attempts to bridge it before the buyers walked away. Delaying closing legitimately affected the deal's economics.
conclusion: No breach: the defendants acted in good faith throughout; the deal failed because of a legitimate, unresolved disagreement, not bad faith. The main action is dismissed with costs.

issue: If there were a breach, are the claimed damages proven?
facts: Ryer's damages claim shifted from $3.24M to $6.24M to $3.69M, comprising lost 2011/2012 profits, consulting fees, and loss of time.
rule: A claimant must prove damages with a causal link and account for offsetting obligations; parties bear their own transaction costs where the contract so provides.
application: Even though the action failed, the Court noted the lost-profits claim ignored the $9M–$11.75M purchase price the buyers would have had to pay, and improperly incorporated alleged unreported cash sales raised only at trial. Consulting fees were payable by each party under the LOI, were partly unpaid, were partly incurred for optional renegotiations, and were billed to a non-party holding company. The loss-of-time claim was overstated—Ryer would have earned about $67,000 over the four relevant months, not $200,000, and he showed no lost future earnings.
conclusion: The damages were unproven and overstated; obiter, they would not have supported recovery in any event.

issue: Can Ryer recover Greenspoon's share of the alleged losses?
facts: Ryer and Greenspoon were to be equal (50/50) partners through a holding company for the acquisition. Greenspoon chose not to sign the LOI and is not a party; the holding company was never incorporated.
rule: A party cannot advance a claim belonging to another who has chosen not to sue; standing requires the claimant hold the right asserted.
application: Greenspoon, for his own strategic reasons, declined to sign the LOI and to bring a claim, and must bear that choice. The intended holding company never existed and is not a party, distinguishing Pegasus Partners Inc. v. Groupe Laurem inc.
conclusion: Ryer cannot claim Greenspoon's share of the alleged losses.

issue: Was Ryer's action abusive, or did his litigation conduct give rise to extracontractual liability entitling Potten to damages on the cross-claim?
facts: Potten sought $350,000 in moral and punitive damages, alleging an abusive suit and a lengthy series of emails Ryer personally sent him during the litigation (invoices, invitations, articles, Holocaust survivor pictures, Jewish New Year wishes, health links) apparently intended to annoy.
rule: An unfounded action is abusive only where brought in a manner 'so patent, or so frivolous or dilatory as to be an abuse of process' (Acadia Subaru v. Michaud, 2011 QCCA 1037); extracontractual liability requires proof of fault, damage and causation.
application: Although weaker than the defence, Ryer's claim was not so frivolous as to be an abuse of right.
