facts: The complainant filed a human rights complaint after being terminated from unionized employment; the applicant challenged the Adjudicator's assumption of jurisdiction, arguing the dispute fell within labour arbitration's exclusive jurisdiction.
rule: Under Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, reasonableness generally applies where a specialized tribunal interprets its home statute, but questions regarding the jurisdictional lines between two or more competing specialized tribunals are reviewed on a correctness standard (Dunsmuir para. 61; Smith v. Alliance Pipeline; Regina Police Assn.).
application: The Court accepted that reasonableness normally governs a tribunal interpreting the Code, but found this case turned on drawing jurisdictional lines between labour arbitration and human rights adjudication. That threshold jurisdictional question attracts correctness; the balance of the decision would be reviewed for reasonableness.
conclusion: The correctness standard applies to the jurisdictional line-drawing issue; reasonableness applies to the remainder of the Adjudicator's decision.

issue: Did the Human Rights Board of Adjudication have jurisdiction over the complaint, or did the essential character of the dispute fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of labour arbitration?
facts: Horrocks, a unionized health care aide, was terminated for alleged breach of an abstinence condition in an MOA negotiated with the Union under the collective agreement to resolve a grievance. She did not grieve the second termination but instead filed a human rights complaint alleging disability discrimination based on alcohol addiction. The collective agreement contained comprehensive grievance and arbitration procedures and an anti-discrimination clause.
rule: Where two administrative bodies could claim jurisdiction, the court must examine the essential character of the dispute in its full factual context and the two legislative schemes to determine which body the legislature intended to resolve it (Weber v. Ontario Hydro; Regina Police Assn.; Morin; Charette; Bisaillon). Mandatory arbitration clauses (e.g. s. 78(1) Labour Relations Act) generally confer exclusive jurisdiction on labour arbitrators over disputes arising from the collective agreement, and arbitrators must apply the substantive rights of the Human Rights Code (Parry Sound; Tranchemontagne). Section 58 of the Code makes its substantive rights paramount but does not make its adjudicative procedure exclusive.
application: The Adjudicator wrongly focused on the legal characterization of the complaint as a human rights violation rather than the essential character of the dispute in its factual context. That essential character was whether there was just cause to terminate a unionized employee with an alleged addiction, and whether breach of the MOA (a last chance agreement forming part of the collective agreement process) constituted just cause. These are matters routinely decided by labour arbitrators, who must apply the Code's substantive rights. Morin was distinguishable: here the question does lend itself to characterization as a grievance, no evidence showed the Union was opposed in interest, an arbitrator would have jurisdiction over all parties, and the applicant conceded it would not raise a timeliness defence. A labour arbitrator was the 'better fit'.
conclusion: The Adjudicator erred; the dispute fell within the exclusive jurisdiction of labour arbitration. The decision was set aside and the complainant is entitled to file a grievance under the collective agreement.

issue: Were the statements complained of defamatory of the plaintiff?
facts: Rabinowitz conducted an internet campaign on the GigPark review site and through impersonating emails, calling accountant Ronald Rutman a 'thief,' 'crook,' 'tax cheater,' 'swindler' and 'master of tax fraud,' using multiple fake identities to simulate many complainants. He admitted authorship and abandoned his justification defence mid-trial.
rule: Defamation is established where the words: (1) are defamatory, tending to lower the plaintiff's reputation in the estimation of reasonable people; (2) are about the plaintiff; and (3) were published to a third party. The defamatory 'sting' is assessed from the plain and natural/ordinary meaning in context (Cusson v. Quan, 2007 ONCA 771).
application: The statements plainly tended to lower Rutman's reputation, were about him, and were published to third parties on GigPark and through emails that affected his Google profile and reached hundreds of family, friends, and community members. The only substantive defence (justification) was abandoned during trial.
conclusion: The statements were defamatory of Rutman; liability for defamation was established (and admitted by Rabinowitz).

issue: Are Bergman and Artcraft jointly and severally liable for the defamation?
facts: Bergman, Rabinowitz's business partner, claimed he only learned of the campaign in April 2009 and told Rabinowitz to stop. Evidence showed Bergman exchanged jocular emails with the fake Rutman account, changed his discovery evidence mid-trial, deleted emails, failed to preserve his Blackberry, and used the threat of a CRA report/end of the campaign as settlement leverage. Artcraft's computers, servers and IT employee were used to run and conceal the campaign; Rabinowitz and Bergman were its directing minds.
rule: Joint tortfeasor liability arises through agency, vicarious liability, or concerted action in furtherance of a common design (Botiuk v. Toronto Free Press, 1995 CanLII 60; Hill v. Church of Scientology, 1995 CanLII 59). A corporation is vicariously liable for acts authorized by its directing minds; the 'sufficient connection' test (Bazley v. Curry, 1999 CanLII 692) only applies where the act was not authorized.
application: On credibility findings, Bergman knew of and was willing to exploit the defamatory campaign for leverage by at least April 2009, bringing him within concerted-action liability. Rabinowitz and Bergman, as controlling minds of Artcraft, authorized use of company equipment and personnel to perpetrate and conceal the campaign, so Artcraft was vicariously liable; the identity doctrine was unnecessary.
conclusion: Rabinowitz, Bergman and Artcraft are jointly and severally liable for the defamation.

issue: What general and aggravated damages should be awarded?
facts: Rutman, a prominent chartered accountant, suffered sleeplessness, embarrassment, and altered his religious attendance; the posts were widely known in Toronto's Orthodox Jewish community and affected his Google profile (5,000+ views). No pecuniary loss was proven. Rabinowitz acted with admitted malice, used pseudonyms mimicking Rutman's family and associates, and abandoned a plea of justification mid-trial.
rule: General damages in defamation compensate for distress/hurt, repair reputational harm, and vindicate the plaintiff's name; damages are presumed (Brown on Defamation; Hill, supra). Internet defamation is a particularly egregious form warranting higher awards (Barrick Gold v. Lopehandia, 2004 CanLII 12938; Cairns v. Modi). Aggravated damages require actual malice increasing injury (Hill, para 190), and a maintained/abandoned justification plea aggravates damages.
application: Given Rutman's excellent reputation, the serious and sustained nature of the falsehoods going to the core of his professional integrity, the insidious internet dissemination, and the paramount need for vindication, substantial general damages were justified. Rabinowitz's malicious methods and aborted justification plea aggravated the injury, but Bergman's and Artcraft's involvement did not reach that threshold.
conclusion: General damages of $200,000 against all three defendants; additional aggravated damages of $200,000 against Rabinowitz alone.

issue: Should punitive damages be awarded and against whom?
facts: Rabinowitz installed IP-masking and data-destruction software to evade detection and breach the Anton Piller order, perjured an affidavit, showed no remorse, and both defendants destroyed evidence and used the campaign and a bluffed CRA voluntary-disclosure threat as coercive leverage in litigation over released claims.
rule: Punitive damages are appropriate for especially egregious, high-handed, malicious or reprehensible conduct, assessed proportionately to harm, misconduct, vulnerability and any advantage gained, and only where compensatory damages are insufficient to achieve retribution, deterrence and denunciation (Estate of Pate v. Township of Galway-Cavendish, 2013 ONCA 669).
application: The defendants' conduct was malicious, aimed at profit/leverage, contemptuous of court preservation orders, and required denunciation and deterrence against similar misuse of the internet. Rabinowitz was far more culpable, but Bergman also engaged in censurable conduct.
conclusion: Punitive damages of $250,000 against Rabinowitz and $50,000 against Bergman.

issue: Are the defendants liable for the assault and the car fire?
facts: Rutman was assaulted outside his office on May 26, 2009 (days before a disclosure motion) and his car was destroyed by fire on June 8, 2009 (shortly after the Anton Piller search). There was no direct evidence linking the defendants; the plaintiff relied on suspicious timing and spoliation of evidence.
rule: An inference must be grounded in proven facts and shown to be probable; drawing an inference without a factual foundation is impermissible speculation. Liability in tort must be proved on a balance of probabilities.
application: The timing and evidence-destruction raised suspicion, even strong suspicion, but too many equally plausible explanations existed; there was an unbridgeable gulf between the proven facts and the conclusion that the defendants caused the assault or the fire.
conclusion: Both the assault and property-destruction claims were dismissed.

issue: Does the conspiracy claim afford additional relief?
facts: The plaintiff alleged conspiracy to injure by unlawful means (defamation, identity fraud, extortion) on the same facts underlying the defamation claim.
rule: Damages for conspiracy to injure are subsumed within the damages already awarded where they arise from the same wrong.
application: Since joint and several liability in defamation was established, no additional damages could flow from the conspiracy claim and no purpose would be served by deciding it.
conclusion: No finding was made on the conspiracy claim; it yielded no additional relief.

issue: Was there a material change in circumstances warranting variation of the final orders in the father's favour?
facts: The father sought sole or joint decision-making, relying on three asserted changes: suspected physical abuse of the children, the mother's alleged parental alienation by refusing his gifts, and the mother's alleged breach of the caregiver-restriction provision. The abuse allegations had been raised and investigated (by Family and Children's Services and police) before the 2017 and 2018 orders and were unverified; the gift-refusal conduct predated the orders.
rule: Variation of a decision-making/parenting order requires the two-stage inquiry from Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27. The threshold is a material change: a change in the child's condition/means/needs/circumstances (or parents' ability to meet them) that materially affects the child and that was not foreseen or reasonably contemplated when the prior order was made and, if known, could likely have led to a different order (L.M.L.P. v. L.S., 2011 SCC 64; F.K. v. A.K., 2020 ONSC 3726; Litman v. Sherman, 2008 ONCA 485). Without a material change the court lacks jurisdiction to vary.
application: The physical-abuse concerns were pre-existing, investigated and unmerited, with the court finding no supporting evidence; the alienation/gift argument concerned conduct known before the orders and was immaterial; and the alleged breach of the caregiver provision was not made out (see below). None of the three asserted matters was a new, unforeseen change materially affecting the children. The court also found no evidence the children were sexually or physically abused and none thriving concerns.
conclusion: No material change in circumstances was established; the father's motion to change failed at the threshold stage and his request for sole/joint decision-making was dismissed.

issue: Where would the children's best interests lie had a material change been shown?
facts: The father has had no contact with the children for about two and a half years, has never had unsupervised access to the son, missed visits, has no realistic childcare plan (proposed caregivers barely know the children), is not meeting his support obligations and shows general instability.
rule: Under Gordon v. Goertz and s. 24 CLRA, the second stage is a fresh best-interests inquiry with no presumption favouring either parent; maximum contact applies only where consistent with the child's best interests, assessed from the child's perspective.
application: The court found no cooperation between the parties, the father's lengthy absence from the children's lives, no realistic care plan, and concerns about his ability to meet the children's material needs, such that even had the threshold been met, sole or shared decision-making could not be awarded to the father.
conclusion: Best interests would not support transferring decision-making to the father; the mother retains decision-making, with a duty to advise of major decisions via My Family Wizard.

issue: Should the father's parenting time be terminated entirely as the mother requested?
facts: The mother pointed to the father's 2017 abduction of the daughter, long-term harassment, denigration, unpredictable behaviour and lack of relationship with the children. However, the harmful conduct predated the final orders, there was no restraining order, supervised visits were largely happy and interactive, and the father expressed a wish to rebuild the relationship.
rule: Denial of parenting time is a remedy of last resort to be imposed only after other options fail (Jennings v. Garrett, 2004 CanLII 17126; Van v. Palombi, 2018 ONSC 6228; Byrne v. Hann, 2020 ONSC 7116; Jordan v. La Russa, 2021 ONSC 8281), assessed against the Jennings factors.
application: Applying the relevant Jennings factors, the court found no post-order harmful conduct, no evidence the children suffered stress/fear, no restraining order, and positive supervised-visit records, so a no-contact order was not warranted; but liberal unsupervised time was also inappropriate given the need for readjustment and monitoring.
conclusion: The mother's request for a no-parenting-time order was dismissed; a graduated regime of supervised then unsupervised parenting time was ordered.

issue: Should the passport-consent and travel-consent provisions be varied to remove the requirement of the father's consent?
facts: The father was required to sign passport applications within three weeks and consent to extended travel; the mother said he failed to cooperate. The court found the father needs to control situations and was not satisfied he had timely provided the necessary forms; it found no risk the mother would relocate given her job, home and family support in Ontario.
rule: Parenting/travel terms may be varied where the best interests of the children and the practical realities so require under the CLRA framework.
application: Given the father's controlling behaviour, doubts about his past cooperation, and the absence of any relocation risk, requiring his consent served no protective purpose and hindered the children's travel.
conclusion: Variation granted: the mother may obtain passports and travel outside Ontario without the father's consent, but may not reside outside Ontario without court order.

issue: Did the mother breach the May 16, 2018 order prohibiting her from leaving the children with her parents pending Family Services approval?
facts: The order barred the mother from using her parents as caregivers until Family and Children's Services approved them in writing. The mother repeatedly contacted Family Services (May–November 2018) seeking approval, but the agency declined to act, saying the matter was outside its eligibility spectrum, and never provided a letter.
rule: A party is not in breach of an order where compliance is rendered impossible by circumstances beyond her control; the court must determine whether the order was in fact breached.
application: The mother did all she reasonably could to obtain the required approval; Family Services simply would not act, making the provision incapable of fulfilment. The court declined to resolve the historical sexual-abuse allegation as unnecessary and found no evidence the children were at risk.
conclusion: No breach was established; this asserted change did not assist the father's motion, and the unworkable provision was effectively removed by the variations.

issue: Does SORA bar all COVID-related causes of action against LTC operators except negligence amounting to gross negligence, precluding certification of the other pleaded causes of action?
facts: Estates and family members of residents who died of or were infected with COVID-19 in Ontario LTC homes pleaded negligence, breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, breach of the Occupiers' Liability Act, and breach of s. 7 of the Charter. The Ontario legislature enacted SORA mid-pandemic to shield those acting in good faith from COVID-related liability absent gross negligence.
rule: Section 2(1) of the Supporting Ontario's Recovery Act, SO 2020, c. 26, Sched. 1 bars any cause of action arising from COVID-19 infection where the defendant made a good faith effort to comply with public health guidance and law, unless the conduct constitutes gross negligence; SORA applies retroactively (ss. 2(4), (5)) and despite conflicting enactments (s. 2(2)). 'Gross negligence' requires a 'very marked departure' from applicable standards (McCulloch v. Murray, [1942] SCR 141; Khanna v. Canada, 2022 FCA 84). Cause of action is assessed on the 'plain and obvious' test (Cloud; McCracken).
application: On a plain reading of s. 2(1), good faith not being contested, the only surviving question is gross negligence — a species of negligence. Breach of fiduciary duty, contract, and occupiers' liability are strict-liability-type claims requiring no proof of fault; adding negligence turns them into 'doctrinal fantasy' duplicative of the negligence claim (Del Giudice; Rotary Drum). Since they cannot be pleaded to require gross negligence, they are eliminated by SORA. Strict liability (Dr. Zautman's theory that any infection proves IPAC failure) is contrary to SORA, which requires proof of a marked departure and does not permit presuming fault from injury.
conclusion: Negligence rising to gross negligence is the only viable cause of action; breach of fiduciary duty, contract, and the Occupiers' Liability Act, and the associated common issues, cannot be certified.

issue: Can the negligence claims be certified where certain independently-owned defendants have no legal nexus (lis) with the bulk of the class and where representative plaintiffs are missing (the Ragoonanan problem), particularly in the municipal and independent-homes actions?
facts: Six actions target corporate LTC groups (Chartwell, Extendicare, Responsive, Revera, Schlegel, Sienna) on a top-down systemic-negligence theory. Five of them also name independently-owned homes merely managed under contract by the corporate group. Two further actions (McVeigh v. Toronto; McDermott v. ATK) sue six unrelated municipalities and 34 unrelated independent operators respectively, grouped only by similarity.
rule: A negligence claim requires correlativity/a lis — an injured plaintiff owed a duty by the defendant (Donoghue v. Stevenson). Enterprise/joint-enterprise liability can bind members of a single corporate family (Downtown Eatery; Kent v. Stop N' Cash; Bazley v. Curry). Systemic negligence requires an 'immediately identifiable single institution' (Carcillo v. Canadian Hockey League, 2023 ONSC 886). In a class action there must be a representative plaintiff with a claim against each defendant (Ragoonanan; Hughes v. Sunbeam).
application: The corporate groups form cohesive enterprises, so the class has a lis against each group and one representative plaintiff per group suffices. But the independently-owned homes only engage in enterprise with the corporate group as to their own single home; the vast majority of the class has no claim against them, and subclasses/new reps cannot cure this mismatch. In McVeigh and McDermott the defendants are legally unrelated — similarity is not commonality; there is no top-down enterprise and thus no systemic-negligence lis, and there are grossly insufficient representative plaintiffs. The court declined to order defendants to find plaintiffs (distinguishing Aphria; following Singh, Azar).
conclusion: Claims against the independent owners in the five corporate actions cannot be certified for want of a lis; McVeigh v. Toronto and McDermott v. ATK are not certified and must be disaggregated into standalone actions with a representative plaintiff for each defendant.

issue: Do the private and municipal LTC operators perform government functions such that a s. 7 Charter claim can be certified against them?
facts: Plaintiffs pleaded breach of residents' s. 7 Charter rights, arguing constitutional rights cannot be extinguished by SORA and that health/elder care is a core government responsibility. The essence of the complaint was that defendants delayed and failed to implement adequate IPAC policies.
rule: The Charter applies to government action, not private enterprise merely because it is regulated (Dolphin Delivery; McKinney; Stoffman; Canadian Blood Services v. Freeman). Municipalities are bound only when exercising governmental/law-making authority (Godbout; Greater Vancouver Transportation Authority). The Charter generally applies to action, not inaction (Rogers v. Faught), and s. 7 imposes no positive obligation (Robertson v. Ontario, 2024 ONCA 86). Negligence cannot be 'dressed up as Charter breaches' (J.B. v. Ontario).
application: LTC homes, though heavily regulated and publicly funded, are not carrying out governmental functions; government is regulator, not operator. Municipally-owned homes operate as licensees running a (mostly non-profit) enterprise, not as government. The core allegations concern omissions/delay in IPAC, which are not amenable to Charter scrutiny, and are in substance negligence claims. Following Robertson v. Ontario, the 'too little, too late' framing is inaction not caught by s. 7.
conclusion: No s. 7 Charter cause of action lies; the Charter common issues cannot be certified.

issue: Should the class be defined to include all residents/visitors during the class period, or limited to those who actually contracted COVID-19?
facts: The proposed Resident, Visitor and Family classes covered all persons in the homes between January 25, 2020 and May 5, 2023 regardless of infection. The evidentiary record (expert reports of Drs. Zautman and Sharkawy, inspection reports, family affidavits) overwhelmingly concerned IPAC and COVID transmission, with only passing anecdotal evidence of non-COVID hardship (e.g., isolation, long waits), some of which flowed from proper IPAC measures.
rule: There must be a rational relationship between the class, causes of action and common issues (Fischer v. IG Investment; Pearson v. Inco); the moving party must identify a class that 'sticks to reality' and the magnitude of the problem (Aéroports de Montréal). Exposure-to-risk classes are possible in some cases (Anderson v. Wilson; Healey v. Lakeridge) but require an evidentiary foundation.
application: Extending the class to all residents regardless of infection inflates the claim disproportionately to a record devoted to COVID/IPAC — a 'tail wagging the dog.' Non-COVID harms were ground-level and largely attributable to the pandemic and to proper IPAC measures (e.g., isolation causing distress, as with Ms. Robertson), not to top-down systemic negligence; expert opinion on staffing/pay was inadmissible outside the physicians' expertise. Staff-shortage harms lacked a factual basis tying them to corporate negligence.
conclusion: The Resident and Visitor classes are narrowed to persons who contracted COVID-19; the Family Class remains as a derivative class.

issue: Is causation of harm a certifiable common issue, or must it be tried home-by-home?
facts: Plaintiffs' experts said any LTC COVID case traces to an IPAC failure; defence experts said individual causation is virtually impossible. Infection/death data varied dramatically between homes within the same corporate group (e.g., Aurora vs. Ballycliffe; Extendicare Guildwood vs. Tri-Town), and IPAC implementation occurred at the home level with divergent results shown in Ministry inspection reports.
rule: Common issues must be answerable in common and not require individual inquiry (Hollick; Western Canadian Shopping Centres v. Dutton; Carcillo). Causation uses the 'but for' test applied with common sense (Clements v. Clements); 'material contribution to risk' is a rare exception (Athey; Snell). A workable methodology for class-wide causation must be shown (Andriuk; Kibalian); statistics/infection rates may serve as a proxy where the record supports it (Levac v. James). Overly general systemic-breach framing is impermissible (T.L. v. Alberta; Massie).
application: Standard of care (IPAC formulation at the corporate apex) is common and certifiable, supported by Mr. Tuttle's and Dr. Zautman's evidence. But causation cannot be presumed from infection (contrary to SORA) and no workable class-wide methodology was offered; the wide home-to-home variance shows causation depends on local implementation. The Aurora/Ballycliffe comparison illustrates that identical corporate policies produced very different outcomes, so causation must be assessed home-by-home, separately for Residents and Visitors.
conclusion: Duty and standard of care are certified as common issues against the corporate groups; causation and damages are not common issues and must be determined in home-by-home mini-trials following the common issues trial.

issue: Is a class proceeding the preferable procedure and are the representative plaintiffs and litigation plan suitable?
facts: The alternative to certification was thousands of individual actions. Six corporate actions have numerous proposed representative plaintiffs (mostly estate executors/family). Defendants challenged all of them, including three whose residents never contracted COVID-19 or who lacked executor standing.
rule: Preferability is assessed through judicial economy, behaviour modification and access to justice (AIC v. Fischer; Hollick); under the pre-October 2020 CPA (transition s. 39(1); David v. Loblaw) common issues need not predominate. A representative plaintiff must be competent and committed but need not know the case's details (Coulson v. Citigroup); must have a personal cause of action against the defendant (Sankar). Litigation plan must match the complexity (Carom v. Bre-X).
application: For the six corporate groups a class action is preferable over unmanageable individual litigation and serves systemic assessment, access to justice and behaviour modification. Most representative plaintiffs qualify; three do not — Allison Gaanderse and Patricia Korchuk (residents never contracted COVID-19, now outside the narrowed class) and Stephen Hannon (no proof of executor standing). The litigation plan meets s. 5(1)(e), to be revised for home-by-home mini-trials.
conclusion: Class proceedings are the preferable procedure for the six corporate actions (not for the independent owners or municipal/independent actions); all representative plaintiffs approved except Gaanderse, Hannon and Korchuk; litigation plan accepted.

issue: Did the flyer promote hatred against gay men within the meaning of s. 319(2) of the Criminal Code?
facts: Whatcott, a self-described 'Christian Truth Activist', infiltrated the 2016 Toronto Pride Parade under a false identity and distributed a flyer warning of the alleged dangers of men having sex with men, using graphic images, medical assertions about HIV/HPV and other diseases, and statements that homosexuality is contrary to natural law and God's plan. The Crown argued the flyer portrayed gay men as diseased, dangerous and sinful through inflammatory lies.
rule: 'Hatred' under s. 319(2) connotes emotion of an intense and extreme nature associated with vilification and detestation, covering only the most intense form of dislike (R. v. Keegstra, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697; R. v. Andrews). The test is objective: whether a reasonable person aware of the context would understand the speech as exposing or tending to expose the target group to hatred (Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission v. Whatcott, 2013 SCC 11). The hallmarks of hate identified in Warman v. Kouba assist the analysis. Borderline cases attract no criminal liability.
application: The court found few, if any, hallmarks of hate: the flyer did not call for violence, segregation, or dehumanize gay men, portray them as a menace to society, or use scripture (e.g. Leviticus 20) to justify violence, unlike Keegstra, Andrews, Harding, Popescu and Sears. Expert evidence showed the medical assertions were largely exaggeration, hyperbole or debatable rather than inflammatory lies, and it is not a crime to communicate falsehoods unless they promote hatred. Read as a whole the flyer expressed disdain and dislike, sitting in the 'grey zone' between legitimate expression and hate speech.
conclusion: The court had a reasonable doubt that the flyer promoted hatred.

issue: Did Mr. Whatcott wilfully promote hatred, satisfying the mens rea of s. 319(2)?
facts: The Crown relied on the flyer's content, Whatcott's subterfuge in gaining admission, his blog describing a 'truth assault' and 'Christian Commando' operation, disparaging language ('Homosexual Shame Parade'), and an alleged lie to police about the source of a photograph.
rule: The accused must have as his conscious purpose the promotion of hatred, or foresee such promotion as certain or morally certain to result (R. v. Buzzanga and Durocher (1979)). Wilful blindness suffices but recklessness does not (R. v. Harding). The word 'wilfully' imposes a difficult burden on the Crown (Keegstra). Intent to create controversy, furor or uproar is not enough.
application: Since the court was not satisfied the flyer promoted hatred, the strongest evidence of intent fell away. The blog, disparaging language and any lie to police were more consistent with an intent to create controversy and provoke than to promote hatred. It was puzzling that Whatcott distributed the flyer to the very group he was said to hate. The conduct amounted to an offensive stunt.
conclusion: The court had a reasonable doubt that Whatcott intended to promote hatred; the mens rea was not established.

issue: Do the Sunday closing provisions infringe freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter with respect to Saturday-observing retailers?
facts: Section 121 of the Urban Municipality Act, 1984 and Saskatoon bylaw 6665 require most retail stores to close on Sundays. Persons of the Jewish and Seventh Day Adventist faiths observe Saturday as their Sabbath and, if they close for religious reasons on Saturday, are compelled to close on both days.
rule: Following R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713, Sunday closing legislation with a valid secular purpose (a common pause day) nonetheless infringes s. 2(a) where its effect places Saturday observers at a disadvantage relative to Sunday observers in practising their beliefs. A court may take judicial notice of society's makeup and, per s. 27, of Canada's multicultural heritage (Jones v. The Queen).
application: The Court agreed with Wimmer J. that the enactments had a valid secular purpose (a common day of rest) but that their effect burdened Saturday-observing retailers by requiring closure on two days. Even absent Saskatchewan-specific evidence, it would be judicial blindness not to recognize the existence in Saskatoon of Jewish and Seventh Day Adventist retailers whose day of rest is Saturday.
conclusion: Assuming such retailers exist in Saskatoon, the Sunday closing provisions infringe s. 2(a).

issue: Are the Sunday closing provisions saved by s. 1 despite the lack of a Sabbatarian exemption?
facts: Unlike the Ontario statute in Edwards Books, neither the Saskatchewan Act nor bylaw 6665 contained a Sabbatarian exemption for Saturday-observing retailers at the time of the charges (an exemption was later enacted by Bill 37 in 1987).
rule: Under R. v. Oakes and Edwards Books, a limit must serve a pressing and substantial objective and be proportionate; a legislature enacting Sunday closing laws must seriously attempt to alleviate their effects on Saturday observers.
application: The Court was inclined to agree with Wimmer J. that the absence of any Sabbatarian exemption was fatal at the minimal-impairment stage, but found it unnecessary to decide the point definitively, proceeding on the assumption that the measures failed s. 1 for want of an exemption.
conclusion: The Court proceeded on the assumption that the provisions were not saved by s. 1, without a final ruling.

issue: Where inconsistency lies only in incidental effect, is the law of no force generally under s. 52(1) or should relief be limited to an individual exemption under s. 24(1)?
facts: Wimmer J. had declared the Sunday closing provisions wholly inoperative, considering an individual exemption for Saturday observers too uncertain and problematic.
rule: Section 52(1) renders inconsistent laws of no force 'to the extent of the inconsistency.' Where a law's purpose and universal effect are valid and only incidental effects are unconstitutional, and a viable way exists to confine the invalidity, the court should confine it; individual remedies under s. 24(1) can protect Charter rights (Reference Re French Language Rights; R. v. Big M Drug Mart; R. v. Seaboyer).
application: The difficulties Wimmer J. identified—inquiry into religious belief and unequal enforcement—do not necessarily bar an exemption; Edwards Books confirms judicial inquiry into sincerity of belief is permissible, and s. 15 permits differentiation to achieve true equality. Striking the whole law where only incidental effects offend would be excessive, unrealistic, disrespectful of the legislature, and doubtfully within s. 52(1). A limited exemption—allowing retailers who close Saturday for religious reasons to open Sunday (but not both days)—is preferable.
conclusion: The provisions are inoperative only to the extent they infringe the religious freedom of retailers who in fact close on Saturday for religious reasons; relief is by way of s. 24 exemption, not general invalidity. The accused's argument on this point fails.

issue: Do the enactments' classifications violate s. 15 equality, and if so are they saved by s. 1?
facts: The Act and bylaw distinguish between retailers and non-retailers, between retailers selling different kinds of goods, and by store size (only stores exceeding 1100 square metres must close under the bylaw). The corporate accused did not claim s. 15 rights but argued the classifications rendered the laws wholly inoperative so that no charge could be grounded.
rule: The three-step Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia / R. v. Turpin framework governs s. 15, with justification assessed at step three under s. 1 and Oakes: sufficiently important objective plus proportionate means (rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionate effects).
application: Assuming without deciding that the classifications denied an equality right on a discriminatory ground, the Court found the objective—securing common pause times for working people—pressing and substantial (Edwards Books). The retailer/non-retailer distinction is rationally connected because retailing is the most visible, vulnerable sector; the exempt-goods distinction serves necessity/convenience and need not be tuned with precision; store-size classification is generally rational, and the courts should not substitute their view for the legislature's choice of the 1100-square-metre line. Because the interest is merely economic and the classifications rest on impersonal commercial grounds, and the laws regulate rather than abrogate market activity in a limited way, they impair equality minimally and proportionately.
conclusion: Even assuming a s. 15 breach, the classifications are reasonable and demonstrably justified under s. 1; neither the Act nor the bylaw is generally inconsistent with the Constitution on equality grounds.

issue: Do the amended statements of claim disclose a reasonable claim, or are they barred by the prior dismissal of substantially identical claims, warranting striking under Rule 19(24)(a)?
facts: The self-represented plaintiff alleged that the RCMP, with the assistance of Telus, Google, Microsoft-certified individuals and others, had implanted microchips in his brain and neck during covert surgery and used advanced communications technology to monitor and control his thought processes, causing physical and psychological harm. In an earlier action (S53706), Wilson J. in 2008 BCSC 1661 struck substantially similar claims against many of the same defendants and dismissed that action.
rule: Under Rule 19(24)(a) a pleading may be struck where it discloses no reasonable claim; the test is whether, assuming the pleaded facts can be proved, it is plain and obvious the action is certain to fail (Carey Canada Inc. v. Hunt, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959). No evidence is admissible on this ground (Rule 19(27)). Issue estoppel prevents re-litigation of matters already decided.
application: The court compared the pleadings and found the main allegations substantially the same as those Wilson J. had found to be 'wild speculation' incapable of proof. Renaming 'the defendants' as 'the RCMP' and adding conspiracy-type allegations against other parties did not materially distinguish the actions. Wilson J.'s unappealed finding that the earlier pleadings disclosed no reasonable claim operated as an estoppel against the common defendants, and the court invoked its inherent jurisdiction to reach the same conclusion regarding the new defendant General Dynamics-Itronix and the individual 'Microsoft Certified Professionals.'
conclusion: The statements of claim disclosed no reasonable claim and were struck under Rule 19(24)(a) as against all remaining defendants.

issue: Are the pleadings vexatious and an abuse of process under Rule 19(24)(b)?
facts: The plaintiff brought fresh actions raising issues either identical to, or that could have been raised in, the earlier action dismissed by Wilson J.
rule: Rule 19(24)(b); parties may not bring in a subsequent action points related to the subject matter of previous litigation that, with reasonable diligence, could have been raised earlier (Dempsey v. Envision Credit Union, 2006 BCSC 750). Re-litigation can constitute a collateral attack.
application: The court accepted that Mr. Rose honestly believed his allegations and was not acting for an improper purpose, so it rejected the improper-purpose argument. Nonetheless, the second action re-raised issues decided against him, and any slight differences could and should have been raised in the first action, making the proceeding an unintentional abuse of process and a collateral attack on Wilson J.'s order.
conclusion: The pleadings were struck under Rule 19(24)(b) as vexatious and an abuse of process.

issue: Are the pleadings embarrassing under Rule 19(24)(c)?
facts: The lengthy, prolix pleadings mixed irrelevant facts and argument and made it difficult for individual defendants to answer specific allegations.
rule: Rule 19(24)(c); pleadings are embarrassing when 'so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is being pleaded' (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC); McNutt v. Canada (A.G.), 2004 BCSC 1113).
application: The court agreed with Wilson J.'s prior finding and held that much of the confusing pleading in both actions fit the definition of embarrassing.
conclusion: This constituted a further ground for striking out much of the statements of claim under Rule 19(24)(c).

issue: Should leave to amend be granted to cure the defects?
facts: Mr. Rose filed an affidavit asserting CAT scans, MRIs and x-rays would corroborate the existence of implanted microchips, and that he could produce evidence of a Telus-RCMP relationship, relying largely on his own opinions and without expert evidence. Superintendent Lott's affidavit stated the RCMP had no knowledge of and did not use such technologies.
rule: A court will not order amendments which serve no useful purpose (Young v. Lort, 2007 BCSC 1152). Wilson J. had held the earlier pleadings incapable of amendment.
application: The court found the allegations were incapable of proof and, more fundamentally, that the actions raised issues already decided against the plaintiff, so amendment would serve no useful purpose.
conclusion: Leave to amend was refused; both actions were dismissed as against all remaining defendants, and the plaintiff's default-judgment application was dismissed.

issue: What is the fit sentence for wilful promotion of hatred against the Jewish people under s. 319(2), and is the offence aggravated by hate motivation under s. 718.2(a)(i)?
facts: Mahr, an 83-year-old man who grew up in Germany and fought in World War II, pled guilty to wilfully promoting hatred against the Jewish people by writing genocidal messages ('Kill All Jews', 'Exterminate Jews', etc.) on walls in parks, mall washrooms, Wal-Mart and businesses in Guelph on 19 occasions over an eight- to nine-month period. He had no prior record but a pre-sentence report and police interview suggested he saw himself as a victim and expressed ongoing antisemitic views.
rule: Section 319(2) of the Criminal Code makes wilful promotion of hatred against an identifiable group an indictable offence punishable by up to two years. Section 718.2(a)(i) deems an offence motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on race, national or ethnic origin or religion to be an aggravating circumstance. R. v. Keegstra recognized the substantial harm flowing from hate propaganda and Parliament's objective in suppressing it; R. v. Lelas (1990), 58 C.C.C. (3d) 568 (Ont. C.A.) held that racially or religiously motivated conduct causing emotional injury calls for a far more severe penalty and general deterrence.
application: The court found the offence obviously and manifestly promoted genocide and was motivated by hate based on race and national or ethnic origin, deeming it aggravated under s. 718.2(a)(i). The messages evoked the Holocaust and victimized every living Jewish person, especially survivors living nearby. Drawing on Keegstra and Lelas, the court emphasized denunciation and deterrence. Mitigating factors were the guilty plea, absence of a record and advanced age, but the court found the accused's professed remorse to be remorse only for being caught, given persistent antisemitic statements in his police interview.
conclusion: The court imposed six months' imprisonment followed by two years' probation with conditions including counselling and 40 hours of community service, treating hate motivation as an aggravating factor requiring a denunciatory custodial sentence.

issue: Should the court accept the joint submission for a conditional sentence (house arrest), or reject it in favour of actual incarceration?
facts: Both Crown and defence jointly submitted that a conditional sentence would meet the ends of justice. The judge had signalled at the pre-trial that a conditional sentence would likely be inappropriate and gave counsel the opportunity to persuade him otherwise and to be heard before rejection.
rule: A sentencing judge should accept a joint submission unless it does not satisfy the ends of justice, would bring the administration of justice into disrepute, or offend the public conscience; the judge must also give counsel notice and an opportunity to make submissions before departing from the joint recommendation (avoiding 'blindsiding' counsel).
application: The judge determined he had satisfied his procedural obligations: he had flagged his concerns at the pre-trial, told the Crown his mind would need to be changed, and confirmed neither counsel would be genuinely surprised by rejection. On the merits, he concluded denunciation demanded real jail — potentially the last opportunity for a Canadian court to condemn to a former World War II German soldier's face conduct springing from the same mindset that led to the Holocaust. A conditional sentence would send the wrong message and be wrong morally and legally.
conclusion: The court rejected the joint submission for a conditional sentence and imposed a term of actual imprisonment of six months plus probation.

issue: Did the court have jurisdiction to hear the privilege motions despite the s. 137.1(5) CJA stay arising from the pending anti-SLAPP motions?
facts: Catalyst asserted privilege over documents generated in 'Project Maple Tree'. West Face and other parties moved for production. The privilege motion was first launched in 2018, went to failed mediation, and was revived as an interlocutory step to anti-SLAPP motions initiated in November 2019 and scheduled for March 2021. Black Cube, a non-party to the anti-SLAPP motions, argued the stay in s. 137.1(5) barred the privilege motions.
rule: Section 137.1(5) of the Courts of Justice Act provides that once an anti-SLAPP motion is made, 'no further steps may be taken in the proceeding by any party' until it is disposed of. Per United Soils Management Ltd. v. Mohammed, 2017 ONSC 904, the stay is non-discretionary but a distinction may be drawn between steps in the proceeding (stayed) and steps within the motion (permissible in the court's discretion). Interlocutory steps within an anti-SLAPP motion must be proportionate and consistent with the legislation's goals of efficiency and economy (Pointes Protection, 2020 SCC 22). Zoutman v. Graham, 2020 ONCA 767 addressed motions commenced before the anti-SLAPP motion.
application: Boswell J. held the privilege motions were legitimate interlocutory steps within the anti-SLAPP motions, not further steps in the proceeding at large. They had been case-managed by a Commercial List judge, the parties actually engaged in the anti-SLAPP motions treated the documents as relevant, and no participating party raised the jurisdictional bar—only Black Cube, a non-party, did. Given this is a $450 million 'Goliath v. Goliath' fight with voluminous materials, the motions were not disproportionate and did not undermine the legislative goals of efficiency and economy. He read Zoutman narrowly, declining to hold that any motion commenced before an anti-SLAPP motion may simply continue.
conclusion: The court had jurisdiction; the privilege motions were permissible steps within the anti-SLAPP motions and were not disproportionate.

issue: Were the Project Maple Tree documents protected by solicitor-client privilege?
facts: Catalyst, through counsel Brian Greenspan, retained Tamara Global, which subcontracted Black Cube and Psy Group to conduct investigations and public-relations operations described as 'litigation support'. The documents in issue were communications among Psy Group employees, between them and Mr. Elwood and Ms. Jamieson, retainer letters, and notes of a witness meeting (the Schedule 'C' Document authored by lawyer Naomi Lutes).
rule: Solicitor-client privilege, a class privilege (Solosky v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 821; Pritchard, 2004 SCC 31), requires (a) a communication between lawyer and client, (b) entailing the seeking or giving of legal advice, (c) intended to be confidential. It may extend to a third party only where the third party is a channel/conduit of communication or performs a function essential to the existence or operation of the solicitor-client relationship (General Accident Assurance Co. v. Chrusz (1999), 45 O.R. (3d) 321). A mere information-gathering investigator is not essential (LCBO v. Lifford Wine Agencies, 2005). Privilege belongs to the client and may be waived expressly or impliedly.
application: None of the Elwood, Tamara, Black Cube or Psy Group documents were communications between solicitor and client, and none of the third parties acted as a conduit or performed a function essential to the solicitor-client relationship—they were investigators/PR operatives. The only document involving a lawyer, Ms. Lutes' Schedule 'C' notes of a witness meeting, was not a solicitor-client communication and, in any event, privilege was waived when the memorandum was deliberately sent to Tamara on Mr. Riley's instructions and then circulated to Psy Group and Mr. Elwood. Genuine solicitor-client communications in the brief (e.g. Moore/Greenspan emails on the Moyse appeal) remained privileged and were not sought.
conclusion: None of the Project Maple Tree documents, including the Schedule 'C' Document, was protected by solicitor-client privilege.

issue: Were the documents protected by litigation privilege?
facts: The documents were created in 2017 while the Moyse and VimpelCom actions were pending (and appealed) and the Wolfpack and Veritas actions were extant/contemplated. They included investigation retainers, target spreadsheets, transcripts of a pretext 'sting' on former Justice Newbould, and communications about a media campaign and pretext investigations of West Face employees.
rule: Litigation privilege (a class privilege) protects documents/communications whose dominant purpose is preparation for litigation (Blank v. Canada, 2006 SCC 39; Lizotte v. Aviva, 2016 SCC 52). It is temporary and expires when the litigation ends, continuing only for 'closely related' proceedings involving the same/related parties and cause of action (Blank). It does not apply where the dominant purpose is not litigation, and under the Blank misconduct exception disclosure may be ordered on a prima facie showing of actionable misconduct or, more broadly, to prevent the privilege shielding improper conduct (Moore v. Getahun, 2015 ONCA 55). Waiver applies as with solicitor-client privilege.
application: The Moyse and VimpelCom actions were finally concluded, and the Wolfpack action—centred on defamation and market manipulation—was not 'closely related' to those WIND-deal actions, so any privilege in documents relating to them had expired. Most Project Maple Tree documents had public-relations or pretext-investigation purposes that were not litigation, and where litigation was only a substantial (not dominant) purpose, privilege failed. The court found only two documents privileged: a September 1, 2017 email and a September 14, 2017 Lutes/Tanuri email dealing solely with the Wolfpack litigation, plus any direct counsel-Tamara communications relating solely to Wolfpack/Veritas. Crucially, the Blank exception defeated any privilege over Black Cube documents: baiting a retired judge into appearing anti-Semitic and using deceit to extract West Face's confidential information were improper 'corporate espionage' and an affront to justice; the court refused to shield such conduct, and misconduct by an agent (not just the client) engages the exception.
conclusion: With the narrow exceptions identified, none of the documents was protected by litigation privilege; the Black Cube documents were also disclosable under the Blank misconduct exception. Catalyst, Tamara, Black Cube and Psy Group were ordered to produce revised affidavits of documents within 30 days.

issue: Should the court permit Black Cube to redact information identifying its agents from documents ordered produced?
facts: Black Cube, whose business model depends on covert pretext investigations conducted by former Israeli intelligence agents, sought to redact any identifying information, invoking privacy and the viability of its operations.
rule: Any discretion to permit redactions must be exercised in the interests of justice; relief amounting to a publication ban requires a formal Notice of Motion and notice to the media under the Superior Court's Consolidated Practice Direction.
application: Black Cube failed to establish the court's jurisdiction for such redactions and adduced no evidence that agents' safety was at risk—at best its business model would be affected, the very model that produced the improper conduct. It had shown no concern for the privacy and dignity of Justice Newbould or the West Face employees it deceived. The request effectively amounted to a publication ban brought without the required formal motion and media notice.
conclusion: The redaction request was denied.

issue: Should parts of Mr. Mason's notice of civil claim be struck under Rule 9-5, and with or without leave to amend?
facts: Mason, a shareholder-leaseholder in a strata-like Business Corporations Act company, sued Mansion House and directors alleging breach of a 2018 settlement agreement, oppression, trespass and conspiracy. Mansion House sought to strike a lengthy 'Procedural History' section (paras. 14-40), certain breach allegations, the oppression claim, the trespass claim, argumentative 'Legal Basis' paragraphs, and abandoned defamation/abuse-of-process/fiduciary-duty claims. A draft amended notice was considered.
rule: Rule 9-5(1) permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim, are unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, may prejudice/embarrass/delay, or are an abuse of process; no evidence is admissible under 9-5(1)(a). The test is whether it is 'plain and obvious' the claim cannot succeed (Hunt v. Carey; Imperial Tobacco), reading pleadings generously (FORCOMP; Nevsun). Pleadings must concisely state material facts and legal basis (Rule 3-1(2)) and contain no argument (Mercantile Office Systems). Trespass must be direct, intentional/negligent and physical (Shaman v. Meek); conspiracy requires the elements in Alexis v. Drury / Harris v. GlaxoSmithKline; oppression under BCA s. 227 is normally sought by petition.
application: The court assessed the draft amended notice as Mason's most recent effort. Paras. 14-40 were an irrelevant, scandalous/embarrassing distraction and struck with leave to plead a concise description of the dispute. Breach sub-para 43(a) was struck with leave (to plead the 'best efforts' term) and 43(b) struck without leave (no supporting term); damages were adequately pleaded. The word 'wrongful' in the oppression heading was struck without leave; the oppression claim (paras. 44-47) was struck with leave to bring it by petition, except subparas relied on for trespass. The trespass and conspiracy claims were held adequate as pleaded despite imperfect drafting. Argumentative Legal Basis paragraphs were struck with leave to replace. Abandoned claims were not struck.
conclusion: The application to strike was granted in part: several sections struck, most with leave to amend, the trespass and conspiracy claims allowed to stand.

issue: Should Mansion House's Commercial Tenancy Act petition be converted to an action and placed on the trial list?
facts: Mansion House petitioned under s. 19 of the Commercial Tenancy Act to confirm termination of Mason's lease based on May/June 2019 directors' and shareholders' resolutions arising from House Rules breaches and unpaid fines. Skolrood J. had set the matter for a s. 19 hearing. Mason argued his oppression/harassment allegations raised triable issues warranting conversion to a trial.
rule: A petition is referred to the trial list only where a bona fide triable issue of fact or law exists; the test is akin to summary judgment under Rule 9-6 — the respondent must not be 'bound to lose' (Saputo; Robertson v. Dhillon; Montroyal Estates). The court conducts a limited review of evidence without weighing it (Richter Estate); a self-serving affidavit without detailed supporting evidence does not create a triable issue (Ghag v. Ghag; Guarantee Co. v. Gordon Capital).
application: Triable issues are defined by the petition itself, not the related oppression proceeding. Most of Mason's allegations did not address the validity of the terminating resolutions. The one relevant allegation (that shareholders were not told of the campaign against him) was undisputed on the record and did not require a trial. There was no evidence beyond bare assertion that the House Rules/fines were improperly motivated, and it would be improper to send the matter to trial merely to permit a fishing expedition, since pre-trial procedures remain available on the petition. Mason was therefore 'bound to lose' on his fairness argument as it bears on the petition.
conclusion: No triable issue was shown; the petition was not converted to an action or placed on the trial list. Mason may still raise the board's conduct in resisting the petition (per Ocean Park).

issue: Should the petition and action be heard together, and should the implied undertaking as to prior proceedings be waived?
facts: Mason sought to have the converted petition heard together with his action and sought waiver of the implied undertaking over discovery, documents and admissions in earlier settled proceedings to support his oppression claim.
rule: Joinder requires common claims/disputes/relationships and interwoven proceedings outweighing prejudice (Raymond James v. Clyne; Hui v. Hoa; Merritt). The implied undertaking (Juman v. Doucette; ICBC v. Titanich) confines discovery material to the originating litigation; waiver requires a superior public interest and is granted only in exceptional circumstances, though prejudice is minimal where the same parties and issues are involved.
application: Because the petition was not converted, joinder was strictly unnecessary. In any event, although some common parties and issues existed, the petition was at a far more advanced stage and Mason could raise the board's conduct within the petition hearing, making the risk of inconsistent decisions minimal, so delaying the petition was inappropriate. The waiver issue accordingly did not need to be decided.
conclusion: Joinder was refused (and rendered moot); the implied-undertaking waiver was not addressed.

issue: What standard of review governs judicial review of the Manitoba Human Rights Commission's screening decision to dismiss a complaint?
facts: The applicant sought judicial review of the Commission's October 2, 2019 decision dismissing her complaint under s. 29(1)(c) of The Human Rights Code. All parties and the intervenor agreed on the applicable standard.
rule: Following Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 (paras. 23–32, 33–52), reasonableness is the presumptive standard of review absent circumstances rebutting that presumption.
application: The parties and the intervenor took the position that the presumptive reasonableness standard applied because none of the conditions rebutting it were present. The court agreed.
conclusion: Reasonableness is the applicable standard of review.

issue: Was the Commission's decision to dismiss the complaint reasonable, given the brevity of its reasons and its rejection of the investigator's recommendation to refer the matter to adjudication?
facts: After a two-year investigation, the Commission's investigator produced a forty-page report recommending referral to adjudication under s. 29(3). A majority of the Board instead dismissed the complaint under s. 29(1)(c) for insufficient evidence, communicating its decision in a one-page letter that relied on the 'broad nature' of the curriculum framework and used the phrase that the curriculum did not, 'in and of itself', create a discriminatory learning environment.
rule: Under Vavilov, a reasonable decision must be both justifiable and justified by transparent and intelligible reasons; reasons that merely repeat statutory language, summarize arguments and state peremptory conclusions, or that do not reveal the decision maker's reasoning on a critical point, are unreasonable. Where the Commission dismisses a complaint at screening contrary to the investigator's findings and recommendation, particularly careful review is warranted and 'convincing' reasons should be provided (Johnstone v. Canada (AG), 2007 FC 36; Sketchley v. Canada (AG), 2004 FC 1151), while deference is owed to the Commission's gatekeeper function (Korsch; Jewish Community Campus of Winnipeg Inc.; Northern Regional Health Authority).
application: The court accepted the deference owed to the Commission but found that where its own investigator had performed a lengthy analysis recommending adjudication, convincing reasons were required. The one-page decision referred to categories of evidence but gave no meaningful examples, and the limiting phrase 'in and of itself' lacked clarity. Read against the record, the decision resembled cases found unreasonable for merely repeating statutory language and failing to convey reasoning on critical points. It may have been justifiable but was not sufficiently justified by transparent reasons.
conclusion: The decision was unreasonable and was quashed; the Commission was directed to reconsider the complaint.

issue: What records constitute the 'transcript' of a questioning on an affidavit under Rule 6.7 that must be filed for a summary judgment application?
facts: Sproule filed the 504-page court-reporter transcript of its questioning on the McDonald Affidavit but excluded marked exhibits, documents referenced but not marked, and undertaking responses and their attached records. The parties disputed what had to be filed, and the term 'transcript' is undefined in the Rules.
rule: Rules 6.7, 6.11(b), 6.20 and 6.23 of the Alberta Rules of Court govern questioning on affidavits; Rules 5.26(3), 5.30 and 5.32 (Part 5 discovery) apply by analogy under Rule 1.7(2). The sufficiency of the record is critical (Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7; Weir-Jones, 2019 ABCA 49).
application: The Court held that marked exhibits form an integral part of the transcript and must be filed. Documents merely referenced but not marked as exhibits are not part of the transcript unless the parties agree or the court orders. Undertaking answers are part of the transcript (subject to the oath), but records produced with undertaking responses need only be filed where integral to a substantive factual answer, not where produced in response to a procedural production request. Applying this, only records for Undertakings #4 and #8 were integral.
conclusion: The Court set out the governing interpretation and directed Sproule to file McDonald's undertaking answers and the records for Undertakings #4 and #8 as part of the transcript.

issue: Did the employer raise a genuine issue requiring a trial on its just cause defence?
facts: McDonald, hired in 2003 and CFO from 2010, was terminated for cause in February 2016 without notice. Sproule alleged incompetence, insubordination, insolence and after-acquired cause. McDonald did not question on the Sproule affidavits; the Court assumed Sproule's evidence true and screened out inadmissible/bald assertions.
rule: Weir-Jones two-stage burden and Hryniak 'genuine issue' test; McKinley v BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38 contextual framework (nature/extent of misconduct, surrounding circumstances, proportionality); incompetence/insubordination/insolence and condonation principles (Baker v Weyerhaeuser, 2022 ABCA 83; Haack, 2021 ABQB 82).
application: Even assuming Sproule's evidence, McDonald received an 'above average' performance review, a significant FY2015 bonus, a title change to Controller, and only vague, conditional advice in January 2016 tied to a possible future presidency of Gunnewiek. There was no clear warning that his employment was at risk, no documented performance expectations, and his conduct was largely condoned. Applying McKinley, dismissal was not a proportionate response to either performance or attitudinal issues, and after-termination conduct could not support cause.
conclusion: There was no merit to the just cause defence and no genuine issue requiring a trial; McDonald was wrongfully dismissed.

issue: Can the reasonable notice period be determined summarily, and what period is appropriate?
facts: McDonald was 56, a chartered accountant since 1983, with 12 years' service in a senior finance role, terminated during the Calgary oil and gas downturn. He claimed 24 months; Sproule argued 12-13 months (one month per year of service).
rule: Reasonable notice is an implied contractual term (Matthews v Ocean Nutrition, 2020 SCC 26; Keays, 2008 SCC 39); its determination is a question of mixed fact and law (Carroll v ATCO, 2018 ABCA 146; Sattva, 2014 SCC 53) applying the Bardal factors. The Court declined to follow Coffey v Nine Energy, 2018 ABQB 898, holding notice can be determined summarily under Weir-Jones/Hannam.
application: With sufficient undisputed evidence on character of employment, service, age, and availability of alternative work (harder given the oil and gas downturn), the notice period could be determined summarily. Rejecting the outdated month-per-year rule and considering comparator authorities (Rice, Cordeau-Chatelain, Stanley), the Court fixed the period.
conclusion: Summary determination was appropriate; McDonald was entitled to an 18-month notice period.

issue: Did the employer discharge its onus on the mitigation defence?
facts: McDonald did not find replacement employment; he applied to 25 jobs over two years and declined one offer significantly below his salary. Sproule adduced no evidence that comparable employment was available and asked the Court to take judicial notice that controller jobs are 'almost always available.'
rule: The employer bears a two-part onus: that the employee failed to make reasonable efforts and that comparably similar employment could have been found (Evans v Teamsters, 2008 SCC 20; Red Deer College v Michaels; Christianson v North Hill News, 1993 ABCA 232). Efforts are not weighed with hindsight; evidentiary gaps benefit the plaintiff.
application: Sproule adduced no evidence on the second branch and the judicial-notice request failed both branches. McDonald reasonably mitigated; he was not required to accept a significantly lower salary. No credibility findings were needed to resolve mitigation.
conclusion: Sproule failed to discharge its onus; no genuine issue for trial existed and McDonald reasonably mitigated.

issue: Is the employee entitled to additional damages for bad faith in the manner of dismissal?
facts: McDonald claimed additional damages equivalent to three months (pleaded as Wallace damages), citing shock and disappointment at being terminated before a long weekend. He provided no medical or other evidence of mental distress.
rule: Additional/moral damages require proof of actual damage flowing from unfair or bad faith conduct in the manner of dismissal under the Hadley v Baxendale principle (Wallace, 1997; Honda v Keays, 2008 SCC 39; Matthews, 2020 SCC 26; Bhasin duty of honest performance); they are not an automatic enhancement (Gerling, 2022 ABCA 210; Elgert, 2011 ABCA 112).
application: McDonald's claim was not properly pleaded as manner-of-dismissal damages, and in any event he adduced no evidence of compensable mental distress beyond ordinary hurt feelings. Even treated as a distinct breach claim, he failed his threshold burden.
conclusion: No entitlement to additional/bad faith damages; the claim was dismissed with no trial directed.

issue: Were the regulations made by the Board and the local Board within their delegated statutory powers?
facts: The Farm Products Marketing Board delegated to the local Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers' Marketing Board powers to make regulations respecting refusal of licences and refusal and reduction of quotas for tobacco production. The appellants challenged the validity of those regulations.
rule: A delegate board may make regulations within the scope of the powers delegated to it under the Farm Products Marketing Act, R.S.O. 1960, c. 137, read as a whole, including the broad powers of delegation conferred on the Board.
application: Reading the statute as a whole and given the unusually broad powers of delegation conferred on the Board, the Court found the regulations of both the Board and the local Board to be within their respective powers and in conformity with the Act.
conclusion: The regulations were validly within the delegated powers; the challenge failed.

issue: Did the 1963 legislation and regulations apply retrospectively to the 1963 tobacco crop?
facts: The dispute concerned the 1963 tobacco crop. The 1963 legislation and the regulations enacted by the Board and local Board purported by their terms to apply to the 1963 crop.
rule: Legislation may operate retrospectively where the wording clearly manifests that intention. Section 18 of the Farm Products Marketing Act (enacted in 1963) defines 'producing,' and 'planting' therein means planting of tobacco plants in the fields, not propagation of seeds in greenhouses.
application: The Court agreed with Grant, J. that the 1963 legislation, by its very wording, was intended to apply to the 1963 crop, and the regulations clearly purported to apply to it. The legislation was thus retrospective with sufficient clarity as to matters concerning the 1963 crop; further, given that 'planting' meant field planting, a licence for the 1963 crop was required.
conclusion: The legislation and regulations validly applied to the 1963 crop with retrospective effect.

issue: Was a specific regulation required to refuse acreage allotment or fix marketing quotas where a licence had been refused?
facts: The applicants had been refused a licence to produce tobacco. They argued the local Board could not refuse to allot acreage or fix quotas without a specific regulation.
rule: Where a licence to produce is required and has been refused, no additional specific regulation is necessary to withhold acreage allotment or marketing quotas.
application: The Court held that a licence for the 1963 crop was required and, since the applicants had been refused a licence, a specific regulation to deny acreage or quotas would be superfluous with respect to them.
conclusion: No specific regulation was required; the refusal was valid.

issue: Did the skeletal 'plan' satisfy the requirements of the Act?
facts: The appellants argued that the purported plan was not a plan as contemplated and required by the statute because it was merely skeletal in form.
rule: A plan, even if skeleton in form, may satisfy the statutory requirements, as established in Reference re Farm Products Marketing Act, 1957 CanLII 1 (SCC), [1957] S.C.R. 198.
application: The Court found that the plan, though skeletal, was a plan as contemplated by the Act, supported by the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in the Reference re the Farm Products Marketing Act.
conclusion: The plan satisfied the requirements of the Act.

issue: Should the plaintiff's Second Further Amended Notice of Civil Claim be struck under Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules?
facts: Ramadan was removed from UBC's PhD program and brought an action against UBC and related entities. Over nearly a decade his pleadings were struck twice (by Loo J. in 2011 and Affleck J. in 2012), each time with leave to amend and repeated warnings and encouragement to obtain legal advice. His latest 20-page Second Further Amended Claim continued to mingle multiple causes of action (negligence, negligent and fraudulent misrepresentation, conspiracy, breach of contract, breach of trust, defamation, forgery) without pleading material facts for the elements of each, and sought to void a master's degree and attack the Senate Appeal Committee's decision.
rule: Rule 9-5(1) permits striking pleadings that (a) disclose no reasonable claim, (b) are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, (c) may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial, or (d) are otherwise an abuse of process. The principles were summarized in Sahyoun v. Ho, 2015 BCSC 392 (test of 'plain and obvious' from Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.; abuse of process from Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63). Elements of fraudulent misrepresentation (Bruno Appliance and Furniture Inc. v. Hryniak, 2014 SCC 8), negligent misrepresentation requiring detrimental reliance (Queen v. Cognos Inc.), and conspiracy (Pro-Sys Consultants Ltd. v. Microsoft, 2013 SCC 57) were identified. Academic disputes are generally to be resolved through internal appeals and judicial review (Jaffer v. York University, 2010 ONCA 654).
application: The Court found the claim so confusingly drafted that it was impossible to know which facts supported which claim, which causes of action were pursued, or who committed them; elements of the various torts were repeatedly mixed. No material facts were pleaded to support trust, defamation, breach of contract, misrepresentation (no detrimental reliance), negligence (no standard of care) or conspiracy (no agreement to injure). Forgery is not itself a cause of action. The claims also amounted to a collateral attack on the Senate Appeal Committee decision, for which reconsideration or judicial review was the proper route (Chandler; Zutter). The plaintiff had been told of these defects repeatedly by the Court and counsel yet made no progress in remedying them, having merely reduced the page count. The Court rested its decision on abuse of process, finding the pleadings ran afoul of every subsection of Rule 9-5(1).
conclusion: The Second Further Amended Claim was struck as an abuse of process.

issue: Should the plaintiff be barred from filing further claims against the defendants without leave of the Court?
facts: This was the third successful application to strike in under a decade, following express warnings—including Affleck J.'s warning that a further successful application could result in the plaintiff being required to obtain the Court's permission before amending—and repeated persistence in advancing the same defective claims.
rule: The abuse of process doctrine under Rule 9-5(1)(d) permits the court to prevent claims that violate judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the administration of justice; a court may impose a leave requirement where a litigant persists in advancing the same deficient claims after being told of the defects (Sahyoun at para. 63).
application: Given the repeated strikings, express warnings, encouragement to seek legal advice, and the plaintiff's continued failure to remedy the fundamental defects, the Court concluded a leave requirement was warranted to protect against further abusive litigation.
conclusion: The plaintiff is required to seek leave of the Court before filing any further claims against the defendants.

issue: Was AWD/NSO a 'terrorist group' within the meaning of s. 83.01(1) of the Criminal Code?
facts: AWD, founded in 2015, adhered to a violent white supremacist ideology promoting 'accelerationism' and a race war to establish a white ethno-state, targeting Jews, minorities, gays and Muslims. AWD was designated a terrorist entity in Canada in February 2021. According to expert Dr. Garth Davies, NSO is a rebranded version of AWD sharing the same Nazi symbolism and ideology. The accused used AWD and NSO interchangeably.
rule: Section 83.01(1) defines a 'terrorist group' as an entity that has as one of its purposes or activities facilitating or carrying out any terrorist activity, or a listed entity. 'Terrorist activity' includes acts done for a political, religious or ideological purpose with intent to intimidate the public and that intentionally cause death or serious bodily harm by violence. In R. v. MacDonald, 2025 ONSC 1939, AWD was found to be a terrorist group even before its 2021 listing.
application: The court accepted Dr. Davies' evidence as credible and reliable despite gaps and one conceded overstatement, noting IMVE groups operate secretly. AWD/NSO's founding on James Mason's Siege, its Nazi symbolism, accelerationist race-war ideology, and application reading list (Siege, Mein Kampf, Iron March publications) all met the definition of terrorism. NSO was found to be effectively the same organization as AWD.
conclusion: The Crown proved beyond a reasonable doubt that AWD/NSO is a terrorist group.

issue: Did the accused know that AWD/NSO was a terrorist group?
facts: In a recorded conversation with undercover officer 'UCO Eric', Bertrand referred to AWD as a 'domestic terrorist organization' and described it as 'weaponized'. His application espoused white-supremacist, antisemitic and homophobic ideology. After arrest he told Sergeant Schedewitz that AWD 'weren't really registered as a terrorist organization' at the time he applied.
rule: Under s. 83.18(1) the accused must know the group is a terrorist group. Per R. v. Hersi, 2014 ONSC 1217, the trier must be satisfied the entity engages in terrorist activity and that the accused knew this.
application: The court relied on Bertrand's own words to the undercover officer, admitting AWD was a terrorist organization, and his interchangeable use of AWD/NSO. His post-arrest minimization to Sergeant Schedewitz was rejected as an attempt to minimize responsibility, contradicting his candid statements when he did not know he was recorded.
conclusion: The court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Bertrand knew AWD/NSO was a terrorist organization.

issue: Did the accused participate in or contribute to the activities of the terrorist group directly or indirectly?
facts: Bertrand completed and submitted an application to join NSO, pledging his loyalty, offering his skills as a self-taught mechanic and his cadet/military experience, invoking his publicized mischief offences as proof of worthiness, and using AWD symbols such as the siege mask.
rule: Section 83.18(3)(b) includes 'providing or offering to provide a skill or an expertise for the benefit of... a terrorist group.' Section 83.18(4) lists factors such as use of the group's symbols. Per R. v. Ansari, 2015 ONCA 575, the offence is made out even if participation does not actually enhance the group's ability. R. v. Khawaja excludes innocent or socially useful conduct.
application: Bertrand's application offered a skill (mechanic), pledged loyalty, shared the group's ideology, boasted of criminal conduct to prove worthiness, and used AWD iconography. This was neither innocent nor socially useful conduct and a reasonable person could view it as capable of materially enhancing the group's abilities.
conclusion: The Crown proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused participated in or contributed to the activities of the terrorist group.

issue: Did the accused act for the purpose of enhancing the ability of the terrorist group to carry out a terrorist activity?
facts: During the indictment period Bertrand committed multiple mischief offences against a same-sex couple's property and the WETrans Centre using swastikas, boasted of these acts to gain acceptance in extremist chat groups, sought to join AWD/NSO, the Folkish Resistance Movement and the Minutemen (which was arming itself), and stated in his application he wanted to be part of a group 'actually doing things to help save/protect the white race'.
rule: Section 83.18 requires a high mens rea: per R. v.
