Khawaja, 2012 SCC 69, the accused must specifically intend his actions to have the general purpose of enhancing the group's ability to carry out terrorist activity; intent may be inferred from knowledge and the nature of the acts. Per Hersi, the Crown need not prove knowledge of the specific terrorist activity.
application: The court found Bertrand was entrenched in white-ethno-state ideology, evidenced by his hate-motivated mischief, his pursuit of multiple extremist groups, and his application statements espousing antisemitic, anti-Black and anti-LGBTQ views. His post-arrest disavowal acknowledged that at the time he held that ideology. The court inferred the specific purpose of enhancing the group's capacity to carry out terrorist activity.
conclusion: The Crown proved this element beyond a reasonable doubt; the accused was found guilty as charged.

issue: Did the trial judge err in the meaning attributed to the Goebbels cartoon by construing it literally as depicting Ross as a Nazi who would advocate extermination of Jewish people?
facts: During a professional-development workshop on Jewish history and the Holocaust, freelance cartoonist Beutel presented editorial cartoons, including a two-panel 'Goebbels cartoon' asking 'What's the Difference Between the Views of ... Josef Goebbels and Malcolm Ross?', with the word 'CONSPIRACY' across it and the answer that one writes in English and the other wrote in German. The trial judge found the cartoon meant Ross was a Nazi who would advocate extermination.
rule: In defamation, whether words/cartoons are capable of a defamatory meaning is a question of law, but the particular meaning is a question of fact for the trier of fact (Vander Zalm v. Times Publishers; Baxter v. C.B.C.). The natural and ordinary meaning is what a reasonable ordinary viewer would infer, including inferences (Lewis v. Daily Telegraph). Cartoons are not to be read literally; they use caricature, allegory, satire and exaggeration (Vander Zalm; Hustler Magazine v. Falwell). Context, medium and audience must be considered.
application: The Court held the trial judge drew too literal a meaning. The word 'Nazi' does not appear and Ross is not shown in uniform; the word 'CONSPIRACY' and Ross clutching his own books show the subject is the similarity of views on the conspiracy theory, not that Ross is a Nazi advocating extermination. The extermination inference was 'an inference from an inference'—implausible and unsupported by Ross's writings or Beutel's pleadings. Since the finding rested on an inference drawn from undisputed, proven facts (not credibility), the appellate court was in as good a position to redraw it and could intervene where the inference was unreasonable.
conclusion: The trial judge erred; the proper meaning is that Ross and Goebbels hold substantially similar views on the Jewish conspiracy theory, not that Ross is a Nazi advocating extermination.

issue: Was the Goebbels cartoon and commentary, bearing the corrected meaning, defamatory of Ross?
facts: The cartoon compared Ross's published conspiracy views to those of Nazi propagandist Goebbels before an audience of fellow NBTA teachers.
rule: A defamatory statement is one tending to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society or expose him to hatred, contempt or ridicule, judged objectively (Salmond on Torts, adopted in Vander Zalm; Color Your World v. CBC).
application: Even on the corrected meaning—that Ross held views comparable to Goebbels on the Jewish conspiracy theory—the cartoon would adversely reflect on Ross's reputation among his fellow teachers and right-thinking members of the community.
conclusion: The cartoon was defamatory of Ross, though liability still depended on the fair comment defence.

issue: Did the trial judge err in rejecting the defence of fair comment?
facts: Beutel pleaded fair comment (not justification), relying on Ross's published works (Web of Deceit, Spectre of Power), the quotations read during the presentation, and some 45 particulars of Ross's views. The trial judge treated the cartoon as comment but rejected the defence because Beutel had not proven as a fact that Ross is a Nazi.
rule: Fair comment protects opinion on a matter of public interest that is recognisable as comment, based on true facts, that any person could honestly express on the proved facts, absent malice (Cherneskey v. Armadale, adopting Duncan and Neill; London Artists v. Littler; Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers; Reynolds v. Times Newspapers). The commentator must prove the truth of the substratum of facts, not the truth of the comment; justification, by contrast, requires proving the comment true (Sutherland v. Stopes).
application: The imputation (similarity of views on conspiracy) was comment—a value judgment based on Ross's identified published views—not a bare statement of fact. The underlying facts (Ross's authorship of and views in his writings on an international Jewish conspiracy) were established and undisputed and provided a sufficient substratum to warrant the comment. The trial judge erred by requiring Beutel to prove the comment true (that Ross is a Nazi), effacing the fact/comment distinction; had he proven that, he would have had justification and no need for fair comment. The trial judge had found the cartoons an 'honest expression of the real view' of Beutel, made on a matter of public interest and without malice, so the defence should have succeeded.
conclusion: The trial judge misapplied the fair comment defence; the defence prevailed and the action should have been dismissed. Appeal allowed and damages set aside.

issue: Did the trial judge err in failing to make separate findings on five additional cartoons alleged to contain distinct defamatory statements of fact, warranting damages for each?
facts: On cross-appeal Ross argued cartoons B, C, E, I and L each conveyed a separate defamatory statement of fact (e.g., that Ross committed a crime distributing hate literature, taught his views in class, was insincere, was mentally disordered, distributed his books to children) that was untrue.
rule: Pleadings define the issues and each alleged defamation must be treated as a separate cause of action; the trial judge must determine the meaning as a threshold matter (Laufer v. Bucklaschuk). Cartoons are not read literally. An appellate court may draw necessary inferences of fact (Rule 62.21) where no substantial wrong results, rather than order a new trial.
application: The trial judge failed to make specific findings on each cartoon, but Ross did not seek a new trial and the underlying facts were on the record. Applying the non-literal approach to cartoons, the Court held each cartoon would be understood by the ordinary reasonable viewer as satirical comment on Ross's racist and anti-Semitic views—not as literal statements that Ross was convicted, taught in class, was paranoid, etc. Given the trial judge's supported finding that Ross was a racist and an anti-Semite, the substratum of fact was true and the comments were honestly held. No substantial wrong resulted.
conclusion: The five cartoons were fair comment based on true facts; this ground of the cross-appeal failed.

issue: Did the trial judge err in finding Beutel acted without malice?
facts: Ross argued Beutel showed reckless disregard for truth, admitted hatred for Ross's writings, and used a savage cartoon before Ross's peers, evidencing a dominant motive to injure.
rule: Fair comment is defeated by express malice—a dominant motive to injure rather than to comment on a matter of public interest (Horrocks v. Lowe; Hill v. Church of Scientology). Incidental ill will, annoyance or resentment does not defeat the defence if it is otherwise exercised for a proper purpose (Brown, Law of Defamation).
application: The trial judge found the presentation reflected Beutel's honest belief and found no malice. Although parts of the presentation were hostile and injurious, Ross failed to prove that a desire to injure was Beutel's dominant motive; a person expressing offensive views could not expect deferential treatment. The finding of no malice was reasonable.
conclusion: No error; the malice ground of the cross-appeal failed and the cross-appeal was dismissed.

issue: Does the residual judicial discretion recognized in Neve to decline a dangerous offender designation survive the 1997 amendments to the Criminal Code?
facts: The Crown argued that after the 1997 amendments the only question on a dangerous offender application is whether the statutory criteria in s. 753 are met, and that the final 'residual discretion' step in Neve no longer applies. It relied on Moore and Carleton for the view that the first 'may' in the provision is imperative.
rule: R. v. Neve (1999 ABCA 206) and R. v. Lyons ([1987] 2 S.C.R. 309, per La Forest J.) hold that even where all statutory criteria are satisfied the sentencing judge retains a discretion to decline the designation; s. 11 of the Interpretation Act construes 'may' as permissive; that residual discretion is part of what renders the scheme constitutionally compliant.
application: Brooker J. found La Forest J.'s statement in Lyons was not obiter but integral to upholding the provisions against Charter challenge. The heavier consequences of the 1997 amendments (automatic indeterminate sentences, seven-year review) make the discretion more, not less, important. Parliament changed the second 'may' to 'shall' but left the first 'may' intact, indicating an intention to preserve the discretion; this accorded with R. v. M.B. and the Interpretation Act.
conclusion: The Crown's argument was rejected; the Neve residual discretion continues to apply after the 1997 amendments, and Neve governs the analysis.

issue: Does one of Tremblay's convictions constitute a 'serious personal injury offence' under s. 752?
facts: Tremblay was convicted of assault causing bodily harm against Monilaws involving over 20 separate incidents, including choking to unconsciousness and banging her head on cement, causing extensive bruising and a possibly permanent thumb injury plus psychological harm.
rule: Section 752(a) defines a serious personal injury offence as an indictable offence involving violence or conduct endangering or likely to endanger life or safety, or likely to inflict severe psychological damage, punishable by ten years or more; per Neve the violence or endangerment must be objectively serious with a likelihood of material harm.
application: Assault causing bodily harm (s. 267) carries up to ten years. The number, nature and frequency of the assaults met the objective seriousness threshold, and both physical and psychological harm to Monilaws were realized.
conclusion: The assault causing bodily harm conviction is a serious personal injury offence; once one predicate offence qualifies, the dangerous offender gate is open.

issue: Has the Crown established, under s. 753(1)(a)(i) or (ii), a pattern showing Tremblay is a threat to others?
facts: Over roughly a decade Tremblay engaged in a consistent pattern with successive female partners and roommates (Daigle, Beaudoin, Fontana, Cariolato, Nikiforuk, Hallson, Monilaws): misrepresenting himself, moving in via a 'hard luck' story, then asserting escalating control and inflicting violence and threats, much of it while on probation or release. Five experts assessed him as a high risk to reoffend.
rule: Section 753(1)(a)(i) requires a pattern of repetitive behaviour showing failure to restrain and a likelihood of future death/injury/severe psychological harm; s. 753(1)(a)(ii) requires a pattern of persistent aggressive behaviour showing substantial indifference to consequences; Neve requires the pattern to include a relatively high degree of intractability and a threat assessment.
application: The court found beyond a reasonable doubt a pattern of persistent violent, controlling conduct toward cohabiting women, of which the predicate offence formed part, showing failure to restrain and substantial indifference (lack of remorse, blaming victims). Without treatment the conduct showed a relatively high degree of intractability, and all experts agreed he was a high risk, establishing that he constitutes a threat.
conclusion: Both thresholds under s. 753(1)(a)(i) and (ii) were met and Tremblay was found to constitute a threat.

issue: Should Tremblay be designated a dangerous offender in all the circumstances?
facts: His most serious offence ever was assault causing bodily harm; his longest prior sentence was six months; no killing, torture, sexual assault or life-threatening injury occurred. He had never received meaningful long-term treatment, and treatment had been imposed only once and never enforced.
rule: Neve's final step requires the judge to ask whether the offender falls within the small group of highly dangerous criminals for whom preventive indeterminate incarceration is warranted, weighing seriousness/moral blameworthiness, treatment prospects, and the offender himself; a dangerous offender designation carries the most severe non-life consequence in law.
application: Comparing Tremblay's conduct to prior dangerous offender cases (L.C.W., J.Y., McArthur, Imming, Gaudry), his offending was not at or near the extreme end. The psychological harm evidence was found unreliable (Crown presence at victim interviews, no treating physicians called). Treatment had never genuinely been attempted, and community control had not been tried. His difficult childhood did not materially reduce blameworthiness but the overall picture placed him outside the targeted small group.
conclusion: The court exercised its residual discretion and declined to designate Tremblay a dangerous offender.

issue: Should Tremblay be designated a long-term offender under s. 753.1, and what sentence is appropriate?
facts: Experts unanimously found a serious risk to reoffend; Drs. Hashman, Weston and Baillie considered treatment could benefit him if intensive and coupled with controlling his access to relationships, while Drs. Nesca and Dutton were pessimistic. The court gave most weight to Hashman and Baillie.
rule: Section 753.1 permits a long-term offender finding where (a) a sentence of two years or more is appropriate, (b) there is a substantial risk of reoffence, and (c) there is a reasonable possibility of eventually controlling the risk in the community; s. 753.1(3) requires a minimum two-year sentence plus community supervision up to ten years.
application: The predicate offence warranted more than two years; the substantial risk was established; and given untried treatment and the possibility of controlling external factors (barring relationships with women) there was a reasonable possibility of eventual control. The court imposed four years for the Monilaws offences and one and one-half years consecutive for the Hallson offences (global five and one-half years, less seven months credit), a s. 743.6(1) order to serve half before parole eligibility, a ten-year long-term supervision order, and a firearms prohibition; the restitution application was dismissed as more properly a civil matter.
conclusion: Tremblay was declared a long-term offender with a net sentence of four years eleven months plus ten years' community supervision; the dangerous offender and restitution applications were dismissed.

issue: Is the debtor's passenger vehicle exempt from seizure as necessary to obtain the care required by her state of health?
facts: Me Teixeira, holding a homologated arbitration award of $78,186.22 for legal fees, seized Ms. Pantazopoulos' vehicle. Ms. Pantazopoulos, who remained guardian and continued using it, claimed she needed it for medical appointments and, prospectively, to care for children if she regained custody. She submitted six medical notes from the Jewish General Hospital, two merely stating she needs her vehicle, and lives at her parents' home in Brossard.
rule: Seizability is the rule and exemption the exception, which must rest on a clear legal provision, with the burden on the party seeking exemption (Gouin v. Boucher, 2020 QCCQ 2758; arts. 2644, 2645 C.C.Q.). Under art. 695 C.C.P., a passenger vehicle cannot be seized if necessary to meet the debtor's basic needs or to ensure care required by their health, but may be seized if essential travel needs can be met by public transit or another vehicle. Caselaw requires convincing evidence that the vehicle is necessary, unavoidable and essential, not merely useful (Deschênes v. Deschênes, 2022 QCCQ 4383; Syndic de Beaudoin, 2023 QCCS 3102; Larose v. Gauvin, 2020 QCCS 429).
application: The Court disregarded the hypothetical regaining of custody. The medical notes largely confirmed diagnoses and did not explain why her condition made a vehicle necessary or why public transit was unsuitable; the sole note on avoiding public exposure dated from the 2020 Covid period. Public transit from Brossard to the Jewish General Hospital was readily accessible. Utility was not shown to be necessity.
conclusion: The vehicle is not exempt from seizure; the debtor failed to meet her burden of proof.

issue: Is the seizure of the debtor's bank and TFSA accounts valid?
facts: TD Canada Trust confirmed a positive statement on the notice of execution: a bank account with $195.07 and a TFSA account with $179.75. Ms. Pantazopoulos claimed the seizure prevented her from paying creditors and that she was being harassed by collection measures.
rule: Seizability is the rule and exemption the exception (arts. 2644, 2645 C.C.Q.; Gouin v. Boucher, 2020 QCCQ 2758). A creditor holding an enforceable judgment may seize the debtor's property (art. 656 C.C.P.).
application: Collection letters were unrelated to the account seizure, and the debtor held accounts at other institutions through which she could pay creditors. Access to these particular accounts was not a condition of paying her debts, and her arguments were insufficient to displace the presumption of seizability.
conclusion: The seizure of the bank and TFSA accounts is valid.

issue: Can the court compel the creditor to be paid solely from the earlier seizure before judgment on the notary's trust account, or cancel the seizure after judgment on the basis of the debtor's withdrawal of a competing opposition?
facts: Before the homologation judgment, Me Teixeira obtained a seizure before judgment; the notary's trust account held $210,907.37 from the sale of the family residence, but Goldwater Dubé had first served seizure proceedings (Superior Court file 500-17-106548-194). Me Teixeira and Goldwater Dubé agreed on distribution ($33,267.06 to Teixeira, balance to Goldwater Dubé) leaving part of the debt unpaid. At the hearing the debtor sought to withdraw her opposition to Goldwater Dubé's seizure and asked the Court to order Teixeira to be paid entirely from the trust account and to cancel the other seizures.
rule: Grounds to cancel a seizure after judgment are limited to those listed in art. 735 C.C.P. Acts of execution are performed by a court bailiff, who distributes the seized sums to creditors and may seek instructions (arts. 658, 680, 762 C.C.P.). A contract binds only the contracting parties (art. 1440 C.C.Q.).
application: The debtor's proposed withdrawal of her opposition was not a ground under art. 735 C.C.P. to cancel a seizure after judgment. It is not the court's role to rule on distribution of the seized property among creditors; that responsibility, including the collocation scheme, lies with the bailiff on the creditor's instructions. The Teixeira–Goldwater Dubé agreement binds only its parties and becomes relevant only when the bailiff distributes the trust-account sums in the Superior Court matter. The Court's role was limited to determining whether a valid reason existed to oppose the seizure.
conclusion: The Court declined to order exclusive payment from the trust account or to cancel the seizures; the debtor's opposition and application to review the bailiff's decision were dismissed with costs.

issue: Did the Attorney General establish a strong prima facie case justifying a quia timet injunction in the public interest to prohibit the Al Quds Day rally?
facts: The AG applied hours before a 3:00 p.m. rally on Al Quds Day, relying on an affidavit from an Assistant Deputy Minister describing the global rise of antisemitic and other violence, the history of the rally, and remarks by an organizer from 2016. There was no evidence of criminal charges or nuisance arising from prior Toronto Al Quds rallies over some 30 years, and no evidence from any police service.
rule: Where the Attorney General seeks an injunction in the public interest, the first stage of the RJR-MacDonald test is modified to require a strong prima facie case (R. v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp., 2018 SCC 5): the applicant must show a strong likelihood on the law and evidence of success at trial. Protest activity that attracts or encourages violence may constitute a nuisance (Dieleman).
application: The Court found no evidence of any prior criminality, hate speech or public nuisance at past rallies, no operational police evidence (contrasted with the detailed record in City of Waterloo v. Persons Unknown), and the AG's own evidence showed organizers were committed to a peaceful, police-coordinated gathering. Decade-old remarks by an organizer and the conduct of unrelated persons could not supply the required strong case; the AG came dangerously close to holding some persons responsible for the conduct of others.
conclusion: The Attorney General failed to establish a strong prima facie case; no quia timet injunction was warranted.

issue: Can a civil injunction be granted to restrain anticipated Criminal Code offences?
facts: The AG argued the rally would constitute mischief, nuisance, unlawful assembly, intimidation, rioting and incitement of hatred within the meaning of various Criminal Code sections, and sought to enjoin those offences.
rule: Per Robinson v. Adams, the equitable jurisdiction of a civil court cannot properly be invoked to suppress crime; unless a right to property is affected, civil courts should not enjoin acts already forbidden by Parliament.
application: The Court held that a civil injunction will not issue to restrain anticipated Criminal Code offences, and noted police already possess ample powers to arrest and charge for illegal behaviour without any court order.
conclusion: The court declined to use its injunctive power to restrain anticipated criminal conduct.

issue: Did the balance of convenience favour a blanket injunction banning the assembly given the s. 2(c) Charter freedom of peaceful assembly?
facts: The primary order sought would ban the Al Quds Day protest in Toronto entirely, on March 14, 2026 'or on any other day,' and authorize police arrests.
rule: Section 2(c) of the Charter protects freedom of peaceful assembly (Hillier v. Ontario, 2025 ONCA 259). Blanket bans that exclude or restrict an assembly because of its message or purpose are 'presumptively disproportionate' and an excessive restriction; political assemblies warrant heightened protection. Violent assemblies do not attract the same protection.
application: The requested ban targeted the assembly because of its message or purpose and could not be minimally impairing on the record. Because the AG had not shown any prior rally was violent or that this one would be, the blanket ban was excessive and disproportionate, and could not survive a proportionality review.
conclusion: The balance of convenience favoured permitting the rally to proceed; the injunction was refused.

issue: Was the alternative relief enjoining criminal, tortious and hate-speech conduct necessary or appropriate?
facts: The AG alternatively sought an order enjoining participants from violating the Criminal Code, committing property crimes, blocking access to buildings, causing a nuisance or engaging in hate speech, with police enforcement authority.
rule: Courts do not direct police to enforce orders arising from civil proceedings (Ogden Entertainment Services), and no court order is required for police to enforce existing law.
application: No one is permitted to break the law or engage in hate speech, and no police officer needs a court order to arrest lawbreakers; the court expects the police to enforce the law and preserve the peace. Ordering the obvious added nothing.
conclusion: The alternative relief was unnecessary and inappropriate; it was refused.

issue: Is a claim founded on a past Charter infringement capable of being waived, and did the release Ms. Horner signed bar and estop her action?
facts: Ms. Horner, a 'pre-Charter widow', lost her workers' compensation survivor's benefits on remarriage in 1980 under s. 68(1) of the 1978 WCB Act. Remedial legislation did not restore her benefits. In 1999, under The Special Payment (Dependent Spouses) Act, she applied for and received an $80,000 lump-sum gratuity, executing a prescribed release discharging Saskatchewan and the WCB from all actions and claims, expressly including claims under the Saskatchewan Human Rights Code and the Canadian Charter, and covenanting never to commence any proceeding arising from the termination of her benefits. She did not allege unconscionability, duress, fraud, or misunderstanding.
rule: In Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47, the Court left open whether Charter rights can be waived, but held any valid waiver must be voluntary, freely expressed, explicit, clear and unequivocal, with full understanding of the consequences. Cases refusing to recognize waiver (Heerspink; Etobicoke; Green Bay; Parry Sound) all concerned contracting out of prospective human-rights protections. Chow v. Mobil Oil Canada, 1999 ABQB 1026 holds that a release of past acts of discrimination is not impermissible contracting out. Korponay v. Canada (A.G.), [1982] 1 S.C.R. 41 recognizes waiver of procedural safeguards where clear and unequivocal, and criminal cases (Rahey, Askov, Richard, Tran, Evans, Smith, Borden) recognize waiver of existing Charter rights. Section 33 of the Charter permits, but does not require, governments to override Charter rights.
application: The Court distinguished Amselem: it turned on the Quebec Charter, did not definitively permit or bar Charter waiver, and the cases against waiver all involved prospective rights. Ms. Horner's release concerned a past infringement (termination of benefits in 1980) and included a covenant not to sue; it settled Charter litigation rather than waiving a prospective right. Unlike Amselem and Godbout, her alternatives were not so stark as to negate choice — she could refuse the payment and litigate (as Ravndahl did) or join a claim; there was no evidence of financial compulsion, so her acceptance was voluntary and tactical. The waiver was explicit, clear and unequivocal, expressly capturing Charter and Human Rights Code claims arising from the termination of benefits, and the s. 52 declaration she sought fell squarely within the 'released matters'. The argument that the government had to invoke s. 33 was rejected: there is no requirement to use the override, and doing so would have foreclosed her claim entirely. Policy favoured enforcing settlements with public bodies.
conclusion: The release is a valid and enforceable waiver and covenant not to sue; Ms. Horner's claim is estopped and barred, and must be dismissed on this ground alone.

issue: Are Ms. Horner's claims for personal relief, including retroactive reinstatement of survivor's benefits, barred by The Limitations Act?
facts: Ms. Horner's cause of action was the alleged unconstitutionality of the benefit-terminating legislation. Her fresh amended statement of claim (para. 41) sought reinstatement of her survivor's pension retroactive to April 17, 1985, plus interest and costs, framed as 'a remedy pursuant to s. 52(1) of the Constitution Act'. The action was filed in 2007, more than twenty years after 1985.
rule: Ravndahl v. Saskatchewan, 2009 SCC 7 holds that a pre-Charter widow's cause of action arose on April 17, 1985 when s. 15 of the Charter came into force, and that personal, in personam monetary remedies are subject to the limitation statute, while a s. 52 declaration of invalidity yields only in rem remedies from which an affected person may benefit. Section 52 provides global, prospective remedies for unconstitutional laws, distinct from personal s. 24(1) remedies (R. v. Ferguson, 2008 SCC 6; Roach, Constitutional Remedies in Canada). The Limitations Act, S.S. 2004, c. L-16.1 imposes a two-year period.
application: Following Ravndahl, Ms. Horner's cause of action arose April 17, 1985, yet her claim was filed in 2007, far outside the two-year period. Her request for reinstatement of survivor's benefits was a personal, quantifiable monetary (in personam) claim, and attempting to attach it to a s. 52 declaration could not insulate it from limitation. Because her pleading did not permit severance of the personal portions, the Court declared all personal remedies statute-barred.
conclusion: Ms. Horner's claims for personal (in personam) relief are statute-barred by The Limitations Act and are dismissed.

issue: Is public education a 'service ... available to the public' within s. 5(1) of the New Brunswick Human Rights Act?
facts: David Attis, who is Jewish and had three children in District No. 15 schools, complained that the School Board discriminated with respect to a public service by employing Malcolm Ross, author of antisemitic and Holocaust-denying writings, and by condoning his views, thereby creating a discriminatory atmosphere depriving Jewish and minority students of equal educational opportunity. The complaint was framed under s. 5, which bars denial of or discrimination in 'accommodation, services or facilities available to the public.'
rule: Section 5(1) of the Human Rights Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11, prohibits discrimination in 'accommodation, services or facilities available to the public.' In Gay Alliance Toward Equality v. Vancouver Sun (1979), 1979 CanLII 225 (SCC), Martland J. held that 'service' in this composite phrase refers to matters such as restaurants, bars, service stations, public transportation and public utilities. Re Winnipeg School Division No. 1 and MacArthur (1982), 1982 CanLII 2975 (MB QB) held a public school is not within such a phrase.
application: The Court traced the phrase to the Fair Accommodation Practices Act and held that although recent case law (e.g., Re Singh; Saskatchewan (HRC) v. Saskatchewan (Social Services)) has broadened 'service' to reach many public services, the word does not stand alone in s. 5(1). Coupled with 'accommodation' and 'facilities,' its meaning remains limited as described in Gay Alliance, which had not been reversed. Extending protection to the educational system was a matter for the legislature, not the courts.
conclusion: The provision of school facilities and an educational program is not within 'accommodation, services and facilities' in s. 5 of the Act; the complaint fell outside the section.

issue: Was David Attis an 'aggrieved person' able to complain under s. 17 where neither he nor his children had contact with Malcolm Ross?
facts: Attis complained about Ross's classroom conduct in 1976–77 and the Board's failure to sanction him, alleging deprivation of equal opportunity for 'Jewish and other minority students.' The evidence was that neither Attis nor his children had ever had contact with Ross as a teacher, and the alleged 1976–77 statements were never identified to the School Board.
rule: Section 17 permits 'any person claiming to be aggrieved' to complain; 'aggrieved' means suffering from an infringement or denial of legal rights. Discrimination, per Re Saskatchewan HRC and Canadian Odeon Theatres Ltd. (1985), 1985 CanLII 183 (SK CA), is exclusion, restriction or preference based on a protected characteristic impairing the exercise of protected rights. A complaint must be expressed in clear terms so the tribunal and the respondent know the allegations (Mackin v. Judicial Council (N.B.) (1987), 1987 CanLII 138 (NB CA)).
application: The Court found no suggestion of discrimination by the School Board in the Odeon sense, and that Attis, having no contact with Ross, was expressing dissatisfaction with the Board's failure to discipline Ross rather than a personal infringement of rights. The complaint was also imprecise, failing to identify the alleged statements or communicate them to the Board.
conclusion: Attis was not an aggrieved person and the complaint did not meet the required standards; even had education been a 'service,' the inquiry could not properly proceed.

issue: Was prohibition by way of judicial review an appropriate remedy to halt the Board of Inquiry?
facts: The School Board and the Teachers' Federation applied for prohibition before the Board of Inquiry held its first scheduled meeting, raising a pure question of law about the Board's jurisdiction.
rule: A court may prohibit an administrative board from acting, but only with extreme caution and where a matter of law is clearly engaged (Bell v. Ontario Human Rights Commission, 1971 CanLII 195 (SCC); Re CIP Paper Products Ltd. and Saskatchewan HRC (1978)). A party need not await the board's decision on a jurisdictional issue before seeking prohibition.
application: The Court held Bell remained good law and binding: since the applicants raised a genuine issue of law (whether education is a 'service' and whether a proper complaint by an aggrieved person existed), they properly sought prohibition rather than awaiting the Board's ruling.
conclusion: Prohibition was an appropriate course; the applications were entertained on their merits.

issue: Should the plaintiffs' statement of claim, or parts of it, be struck out or amended under Rule 19(24) on the basis that it discloses no reasonable claim?
facts: The statement of claim jumbled together particulars of breach of trust, negligence, bad faith, malice and abuse of public office in a single paragraph, pleaded inconsistent theories (negligence and intentional misfeasance), and failed to state material facts distinctly for each cause of action. New counsel conceded deficiencies and proposed a draft amended pleading.
rule: Under Rule 19(24)(a) a pleading may be struck where it discloses no reasonable claim; on such an application the pleaded facts are assumed true (Rule 19(27)). Pleadings must state material facts for each cause of action (Homalco Indian Band; Canadian Bar Assn. v. British Columbia). The governing test is whether it is 'plain and obvious' the claim is bound to fail (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.). The court must consider how the pleading might be amended to state a proper claim (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc.).
application: The court found the existing statement of claim offended basic pleading principles, was confusing and contradictory, and failed to define the issues. It ordered all paragraphs struck. The proposed amended pleading was an improvement but still contained irrelevant allegations (misleading the Ombudsman, misleading affidavit) and an untenable breach of trust claim (Costello). Because viable causes of action could nonetheless be pleaded, striking with leave to amend, rather than dismissal, was appropriate.
conclusion: All paragraphs of the existing statement of claim were struck; plaintiffs were given 60 days to file an amended pleading confined to nuisance (against Wilson), negligence (all defendants), and misfeasance in public office/bad faith (defendants other than Wilson). The action was stayed pending the new pleading.

issue: Is it plain and obvious that the negligence claim against the trust bodies and trustees is bound to fail?
facts: HILTC obtained court orders (1998 and 2008) requiring Wilson to remove waste and authorizing HILTC to clean up if he failed; the plaintiffs alleged the defendants acted, but negligently, in relation to the Wilson property, and interfered with or failed to complete the cleanup.
rule: Mere breach of statutory duty does not constitute negligence (Holland v. Saskatchewan). Policy decisions attract no liability, but once a decision to act is made a public authority may be liable for negligent implementation; implementation of a judicial decree is an 'operational' act (Holland; Kamloops; Just v. British Columbia). Proximity is assessed against the statutory scheme (Cooper v. Hobart; Syl Apps; Broome). Trustees have statutory immunity under s. 287(2) Local Government Act, subject to the s. 287(3) exception for dishonesty, gross negligence or malicious/wilful misconduct.
application: The court noted the law of negligence for statutory public authorities is unsettled and characterized the alleged conduct as operational (failure to implement/complete court-ordered cleanup). The proximity analysis in Costello was fact-intensive following a 28-day trial and could not be conducted on a strike application. As to trustees, s. 287(2) provides protection, but plaintiffs could plead facts falling within the s. 287(3) exception.
conclusion: It was not plain and obvious the negligence claim was bound to fail; the claim, including against the individual trustees, was allowed to proceed by way of a properly drafted amended pleading.

issue: Is it plain and obvious that the claim in misfeasance in public office / bad faith is bound to fail?
facts: The plaintiffs alleged the trustees and trust bodies acted in bad faith and with malice, concealed facts, held secret votes not to proceed against Wilson, and misled agencies, in the exercise of their public functions.
rule: Misfeasance in public office is a recognized intentional tort requiring deliberate unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions plus awareness that the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff (Odhavji Estate). A municipality may be liable in tort for enacting a bylaw in bad faith (Entreprises Sibeca Inc. v. Frelighsburg).
application: Although similar claims failed on the facts in Costello, that was after trial. Given Odhavji and Sibeca, the court could not say it was plain and obvious that claims against either the individual office holders or the municipal corporate bodies grounded in bad faith were bound to fail.
conclusion: The misfeasance/bad faith claim was allowed to proceed against the defendants other than Wilson.

issue: Is the Islands Trust an entity capable of being sued?
facts: The Islands Trust was constituted a corporation by 1975 amendment. The 1989 Act and current Act 'continue' the trust but do not expressly restate its corporate status, while expressly conferring corporate status on the trust council, local trust committees and trust fund board.
rule: Statutory interpretation of the Islands Trust Act; s. 2(1) provides 'the trust known as The Islands Trust is continued.' Islands Trust v. Pinchin Holdings Ltd. previously held the Islands Trust 'is a body corporate.'
application: The court interpreted 'continued' to mean continued in the same corporate form in which it existed under the 1975 legislation. The legislature did not abolish the trust or say it was no longer a corporation, and the court declined to infer removal of corporate status by implication merely because corporate status was expressly conferred on the constituent bodies.
conclusion: The Islands Trust remains a corporation and is capable of being sued; the claims against it were not struck on that ground.

issue: Was the National Assembly's motion denouncing Michaud protected by parliamentary privilege and therefore beyond judicial review, and are those privileges limited to legislative or executive-supervision functions?
facts: After Michaud made controversial remarks about ethnic communities and the Jewish community before a government-created Estates-General commission on the French language, the National Assembly unanimously adopted a motion without notice denouncing those remarks. Michaud sought a declaration that the Assembly lacked power to censure a private citizen for his opinions.
rule: Parliamentary privileges of provincial legislative assemblies enjoy constitutional status and are immune from Charter review (New Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova Scotia (Speaker of the House of Assembly), [1993] 1 S.C.R. 319). Recognized necessary privileges include freedom of speech of members and exclusive control over internal proceedings. Courts may examine the existence and scope of a claimed privilege, applying the test of necessity, but not the propriety of a particular exercise of a valid privilege.
application: The Court found the two privileges invoked—freedom of speech of members and control over internal proceedings—clearly exist and are necessary. It rejected Michaud's argument that privilege attaches only to the legislative and executive-supervision functions, holding the Assembly's business extends beyond bills and government oversight. Even on the narrower view, the motion fell within the Assembly's supervision of a government body (the commission before which Michaud, then attempting a political comeback, testified) and was an exercise of members' freedom of speech expressed by roll-call vote. Once a valid, applicable privilege is recognized, the Court cannot review how it was exercised without dragging the judiciary into a political debate.
conclusion: The privileges applied; the Court had no jurisdiction to review the merits of the motion. The claim that the motion was ultra vires was rejected.

issue: Does section 21 of the Quebec Charter oblige the National Assembly to rule on Michaud's petition, and can a court compel it to do so?
facts: Michaud filed petitions at the National Assembly (notably December 13, 2001) seeking redress for the censure motion. The Assembly never placed the petition on the order paper; a proposed rule on censure motions lapsed with the dissolution of the 36th legislature in March 2003.
rule: Section 21 of the Charter of human rights and freedoms (R.S.Q., c. C-12) provides that every person has a right of petition to the National Assembly for the redress of grievances. Charter rights are interpreted broadly but within their language, structure and history (Reference re Public Service Employee Relations Act (Alta.), [1987] 1 S.C.R. 313). Absent clear Charter language, longstanding curial deference to privileges necessary to legislative functioning is not displaced (New Brunswick Broadcasting Co.).
application: The right of petition long predates its 1975 entrenchment and has always been circumscribed by the Assembly's privileges. Section 21 merely codifies the pre-existing right; it is silent on how petitions are submitted and followed up, and the parliamentary debates show the provision was not even discussed. The word 'petition' denotes a request to enter the Assembly, not a command imposing a duty to adjudicate. Handling of petitions falls within the Assembly's inherent privilege over its internal procedure, a conclusion shared by Brun and Tremblay, so a court cannot order the Assembly to rule.
conclusion: Section 21 does not impose an enforceable obligation on the Assembly to rule on the petition; the requested declaration was refused.

issue: Should the plaintiffs' writ and statement of claim be struck under Rule 19(24)(a) for disclosing no reasonable claim?
facts: Paragraph 16 alleges the defendants attempted to take over Technovision through slander, intentional interference with economic relations, self dealing and abuse of process, and that Mrs. Urquhart breached her fiduciary duty; paragraph 23 alleges breach of fiduciary duty in paying $600,000 for a worthless option. The pleading was awkwardly worded and not fully particularized.
rule: On a Rule 19(24)(a) application it must be 'plain and obvious' that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action (Hunt v. Carey Canada, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959); doubt is resolved in favour of letting the pleading stand; all pleaded facts are assumed true; a weak claim is not a ground to strike; no evidence is admissible (Rule 19(27)), as summarized in Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160.
application: Although the mere attempt to take over the company is not actionable, the facts pleaded, taken as true, are capable of grounding claims in slander, intentional interference with economic relations, self dealing, abuse of process and breach of fiduciary duty. The lack of particulars did not make it plain and obvious that no cause of action existed.
conclusion: The court declined to strike the claim; it disclosed triable issues.

issue: Is the action an abuse of process because it duplicates the earlier oppression proceeding decided by Lowry J. and the Court of Appeal?
facts: Mrs. Urquhart had earlier brought an oppression petition under s. 200 of the Company Act (dismissed and upheld on appeal) and an Ontario action (permanently stayed). This action, brought by writ, alleged tortious conduct by her as a director.
rule: An action is an abuse of process where it seeks to relitigate matters already decided or that ought to have been raised in prior proceedings; a party is not obliged to consolidate a distinct claim with an existing proceeding.
application: The oppression proceeding was commenced by petition and focused on Mrs. Urquhart's reasonable expectations as a shareholder, while this action, by writ, concerns her conduct as a director. The plaintiffs could not have folded these tort claims into the petition (which Mrs. Urquhart herself resisted converting to a trial), and the issues were only superficially similar. The reputational-damage claims and other specific allegations were not before Lowry J. and were not decided.
conclusion: The action was not an abuse of process.

issue: Is the action vexatious as a suit brought to harass or distract the defendant?
facts: The action was filed about two months after Mrs. Urquhart launched her oppression petition; she characterized it as a 'SLAPP' suit brought to distract her. The action had lain largely dormant for eighteen months apart from discovery.
rule: A vexatious proceeding includes one brought for an improper purpose such as harassment or oppression (Re Lang Michener and Fabian (1987), 59 O.R. (2d) 353, adopted in Ebrahim v. Ebrahim).
application: There was no evidence the action was brought to distract Mrs. Urquhart from her other claims, which had proceeded to completion. The mere fact of timing shortly after her oppression petition was insufficient to establish that the suit was vexatious.
conclusion: The action was not vexatious.

issue: Should the defendants be granted leave to advance a counterclaim?
facts: The notice of motion did not seek leave to file a counterclaim; the request was raised only on the hearing day, supported only by a document outlining the relief sought, with no other material.
rule: Leave to file a counterclaim requires a proper evidentiary basis and appropriate notice.
application: There was no material before the court to support granting the order and the plaintiffs had no proper notice.
conclusion: Leave was refused, with liberty to reapply on proper notice.

issue: Should the non-party Friends of Shalom (FOS) be granted leave to intervene as an added party under Rule 13.01(1)?
facts: FOS is a non-profit formed in April 2025 comprising about 155 people (roughly 36% parents of current campers, plus alumni and former staff) to represent the Camp community's interests in an action in which the Plaintiffs seek declarations and orders concerning TZC's governance, membership and use of its Charitable Property, including the Camp and Camp Property. The Plaintiffs consented, the Individual Defendants did not oppose, but TZC opposed, arguing FOS was seeking its own relief and would expand the scope, cost and duration of the litigation.
rule: Rule 13.01(1) permits a non-party to move for leave to intervene where it claims an interest in the subject matter, that it may be adversely affected by a judgment, or that it shares a common question of law or fact; the court must consider whether intervention would unduly delay or prejudice the parties (Rule 13.01(2)). Leave is discretionary and only one of the three grounds need be met (Conti v. Duca; Clublink). The court weighs the nature of the case, the issues, and the likelihood of a useful, non-duplicative contribution without injustice to the parties (Peel v. Great Atlantic & Pacific; Jones v. Taige; De Longte). In a private dispute the threshold is more stringent (Jones; Clublink).
application: The court found FOS satisfied all three grounds. Two primary issues in the action—TZC's governance/membership structure and its use of the Charitable Property (which includes the Camp, Camp Property and camp-derived funds)—overlapped with FOS's concerns about the Camp community having a voice and about camp revenues being diverted to non-Camp purposes contrary to the Objects. The court rejected TZC's characterization of FOS's interest as merely sentimental or ideological, noting current camper families' tuition forms part of the Charitable Property. FOS would be adversely affected if the Plaintiffs failed to obtain governance relief, shared common questions of law and fact, and would make a useful, non-duplicative contribution by bringing the Camp community's perspective. Applying the more onerous private-dispute threshold, the historical, religious and cultural importance of the Camp to the Jewish and Zionist community supported intervention, and TZC's asserted prejudice (added trial length, cost) lacked evidentiary support and could be managed by terms and the trial judge.
conclusion: Leave to intervene was granted; FOS met all three categories under Rule 13.01(1) and its participation would not cause injustice or prejudice.

issue: On what terms should the intervention proceed to balance the interests of FOS and the existing parties?
facts: FOS proposed terms including being added as a party, leading a day of evidence, no discovery, and exemption from costs and security for costs. TZC sought denial or, alternatively, security for costs of $100,000.
rule: Rule 13.01(2) empowers the court to make such order as is just and to guard against undue delay or prejudice; an intervenor cannot add new issues and its participation must serve its proper purpose (Clublink). Rule 1.04(1) requires the just, most expeditious and least expensive determination of proceedings.
application: The court narrowed FOS's proposed terms: FOS was added as a party but may not seek any relief; its evidence and submissions were confined to TZC's governance/membership and use of Charitable Property in accordance with the Objects, excluding day-to-day Camp operations and security issues as beyond the scope of the action. Time limits were imposed on opening/closing statements, evidence in chief and cross-examination. FOS was made subject to costs in the trial judge's discretion and its intervention was without prejudice to a future security-for-costs motion, which was premature on the present record.
conclusion: Leave was granted on amended and narrowed terms designed to minimize additional trial time and balance the parties' interests, consistent with Rule 1.04(1).

issue: Was the deputy judge's failure to give reasons an error of law, and what is the appropriate remedy?
facts: Deputy Judge Sabol dismissed the plaintiffs' action on a motion to strike/dismiss by circling '9(a)' on the endorsement record and awarding $1,000 costs, giving no oral or written reasons. The motion sought two distinct remedies (striking the claim and dismissing the action) on several distinct grounds, making it impossible for the litigants to discern the basis of the order.
rule: Reasons for judgment are the primary mechanism by which judges account to parties and the public (R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26). The duty is met by reasons intelligible to the parties and permitting meaningful appellate review. Where reasons are clear from the record their absence is not a ground for review (R. v. Barrett, 1995 CanLII 129 (SCC)). Where the trial decision is deficient but the appeal court can itself explain the result, its own reasons suffice (Sheppard).
application: The court accepted that in these circumstances the absence of reasons was an error of law, distinguishing Vuong (where dismissal turned on facts external to the pleading such as res judicata and abuse of process, requiring a rehearing). Here the motion turned entirely on legal principles determinable within the four corners of the statement of claim, so the Divisional Court could adequately explain the result itself and exercised its discretion not to remit.
conclusion: The absence of reasons was an error of law, but the court declined to remit the matter and instead determined it de novo.

issue: Do the pleaded claims disclose a reasonable cause of action, or are they defeated by judicial immunity?
facts: The respondent, a judge of the Ontario Court of Justice, presided over a family court application, refused to allow H.K. to represent R.M. as agent, made in-court statements about H.K., and later edited the transcript of the proceedings (for which the Ontario Judicial Council found him guilty of judicial misconduct). The appellants sued for $10,000 alleging injurious falsehood, misfeasance in public office, obstruction of justice and fabricating evidence.
rule: Obstruction of justice and fabricating evidence do not give rise to civil causes of action. Judicial immunity, part of the common law since the early 17th century and inextricable from judicial independence, absolutely insulates judges from civil liability for acts done in the exercise of or in connection with their judicial functions, even if malicious, mala fides, in excess of jurisdiction, or illegal (Morier v. Rivard, 1985 CanLII 26 (SCC); Tsai v. Klug, 2006 CanLII 4942 (ON CA); Bradley v. Fisher; s. 82 Courts of Justice Act). A collateral attack on a judicial ruling outside the appeal process is an abuse of process.
application: Every act complained of — the in-court statements, the refusal of leave, and the editing of the transcript — was done qua judge. H.K. had no status to appeal and no cause of action from the discretionary refusal of leave; R.M.'s complaints about the ruling and transcript were properly matters for appeal, so pleading them collaterally was abuse of process. Judicial functions extend beyond open court to ancillary tasks; the Judicial Council's misconduct finding confirmed the transcript editing occurred in the discharge of judicial duties, and exceeding jurisdiction does not remove an act from the realm of judging. The recognized torts of injurious falsehood and misfeasance therefore could not succeed.
conclusion: The pleading disclosed no viable cause of action; the respondent is absolutely protected by judicial immunity. The dismissal below was correct and the appeal was dismissed with costs of $3,500 to the respondent.

issue: Can a claim in negligence succeed against complainants who reported suspected child abuse to child protection authorities?
facts: Unidentified 'Jane Doe' hospital staff allegedly made false reports to police and the MCFD that the plaintiff sexually assaulted his seven-year-old daughter, leading to her removal from his care for 72 days. The plaintiff pleaded the Jane Does were negligent in making false reports, breaching a duty to be accurate and professional, and that Fraser Health was vicariously liable.
rule: Under Rule 9-5(1)(a)/(b), a pleading is struck where it is plain and obvious it discloses no reasonable claim (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42). No duty of care is owed to the parent of a child in the child protection context because of the serious conflict between parental rights and the statutory duty to protect children (Syl Apps Secure Treatment Centre v. B.D., 2007 SCC 38; C.R. v. Ontario, 2020 ONCA 198; C.D. v. Cunningham, 2014 BCCA 180; Quinn v. British Columbia, 2018 BCCA 320; E.B. v. British Columbia, 2019 BCSC 2200). Section 14 CFCSA mandates reporting by anyone with reason to believe a child needs protection.
application: The plaintiff was not the Jane Does' patient and there was no proximate relationship between him and the complainants beyond his being the subject of their report. Following Syl Apps and B.K. v. Chatham-Kent Children's Services, 2016 ONSC 1921, imposing a duty of care on a mandatory reporter toward the person alleged to have abused the child would create an untenable conflict. The pleadings did nothing beyond asserting the complaint was false, which is immaterial since it is the MCFD's mandate to investigate.
conclusion: It is plain and obvious the negligence claim cannot succeed; it is struck against all defendants without leave to amend and dismissed.

issue: Do the pleadings disclose reasonable claims in defamation and intentional infliction of emotional distress?
facts: The NOCC alleged defamation and intentional infliction of emotional distress, referring to a 'pattern of malice' and a conspiracy among hospital employees, and claimed reputational and emotional harm including public stigma, nightmares and relapse. The defamatory statements identified in para. 11 were said to have been made by the MCFD, not by the Jane Doe defendants.
rule: Pleadings must plead material facts, not bald conclusory assertions, telling the defendant 'who, when, where, how and what' gives rise to liability (Young v. Borzoni, 2007 BCCA 16; Kindylides v. Does, 2020 BCCA 330; Owimar v. Stewart, 2019 BCSC 1198; Mancuso v. Canada, 2015 FCA 227). Intentional infliction of emotional distress requires flagrant/outrageous conduct causing provable injury.
application: The NOCC made only a bare assertion of a 'pattern of malice' without material facts, never identified the 'other hospital employee' as the Mother nor a factual basis for the Jane Does' participation in a joint enterprise, and attributed the defamatory words to the MCFD rather than the defendants. The pleaded harms of 'relapse and nightmares' and unspecified reputational harm were too vague and unconnected to a specific cause of action.
conclusion: The remaining claims are struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a) as failing to disclose a reasonable claim, but the deficiencies are curable, so leave to amend follows.

issue: Is the action bound to fail because of a defence of absolute or qualified privilege?
facts: The impugned statements were reports made to the police and to the MCFD. The applicant argued absolute privilege attached as a first step toward court proceedings, alternatively qualified privilege defeated by no pleaded malice.
rule: Absolute privilege attaches only to statements made to a judicial or quasi-judicial body (Hung v. Gardiner, 2003 BCCA 257; Hamouth v. Edwards & Angell, 2005 BCCA 172). A complaint to an investigative agency such as police is not so protected (Rajkhowa v. Watson, 1998 CanLII 3273 (NS SC); Caron v. A., 2015 BCCA 47). The test is whether the recipient exercises attributes similar to a court of justice. CFCSA s. 101 bars damages actions against persons acting under a duty unless in bad faith; qualified privilege is rebutted by malice.
application: The MCFD is an investigative agency akin to police, not an adjudicative body like a law society or disciplinary college; Division 4 of the CFCSA shows the Provincial Court adjudicates the legality of investigations and apprehensions. Absolute privilege therefore does not apply. Qualified privilege and s. 101 immunity can be displaced by malice/bad faith, but the NOCC pleaded only a bare assertion of malice.
conclusion: The absolute privilege defence does not warrant striking; however, because only a bare assertion of malice is pleaded, the claim is struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a) subject to leave to amend.

issue: Is the claim vexatious or an abuse of process warranting striking and denial of leave to amend?
facts: The plaintiff's harm flowed from a child protection investigation that ended with the Child returned to his care. The applicant argued the action re-litigated child protection proceedings and was brought to harass hospital employees.
rule: Abuse of process (Rule 9-5(1)(d)) prevents claims offending judicial economy, finality and integrity of justice (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63; Chernen v. Robertson, 2014 BCSC 1358). Claims that are substantive challenges to a child protection outcome resolvable within the CFCSA framework may be struck as abusive (Quinn v. British Columbia, 2018 BCCA 320; E.B. v. British Columbia).
application: Unlike Quinn and E.B., the plaintiff does not challenge the MCFD or the reasonableness of the apprehension; he targets the allegedly malicious originating complaint. There was no evidence about the presentation hearing, and the plaintiff learned further details after it, so the claim is not merely a 'rolling forward' of prior proceedings. The plaintiff's efforts to identify the complainants, and his framing responding to prior court direction, did not establish an improper harassing purpose.
conclusion: The applicant did not establish the claim is vexatious or an abuse of process; it is not struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b) or (d).

issue: Should the self-represented plaintiff be granted leave to amend?
facts: The plaintiff's oral submissions set out a much fuller factual matrix (the Mother as an alleged instigator, acrimonious family litigation, the complainants' relationship to the Mother) than his pleadings, and this was his first application to strike.
rule: Courts take a liberal approach to amendment and refuse only where it is plain and obvious the amendment is bound to fail (E.B. at para. 84). A finding of abuse of process or vexatiousness weighs against leave.
application: Because the claim was not an abuse of process and the plaintiff advanced a conceivable factual basis for inferring malice/bad faith, and given his self-represented status and that this was his first opportunity, leave was appropriate for all claims except negligence. He was put on notice to bring proposed amendments to any future application.
conclusion: Leave to amend granted (a fresh claim may be filed) for all claims other than negligence; disclosure orders deferred; costs to the defendants on the ordinary scale.

issue: Were the trial judge's reasons insufficient or the product of a misapprehension of evidence, rendering the hate-promotion verdicts unreasonable?
facts: Both appellants were convicted under s. 319(2) for content in 22 issues of Your Ward News (YWN) targeting Jews (count 1) and women (count 2). The appellants argued the reasons were contradictory (relying on expert evidence the judge said was unnecessary), failed to consider innocent/provocative interpretations, and treated the material as circumstantial evidence without excluding other inferences.
rule: Reasons must be reviewed functionally, asking whether they respond to the live issues in light of the whole evidence and counsel's submissions; intervention is warranted only where deficiencies foreclose meaningful appellate review (R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26; R. v. Dinardo, 2008 SCC 24; R. v. R.E.M., 2008 SCC 51). 'Hatred' in s. 319(2) means intense, extreme emotion of vilification and detestation, not merely distasteful expression (R. v. Keegstra, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697). A verdict is unreasonable only if not reasonably supportable on the evidence (R. v. R.P., 2012 SCC 22; R. v. Yebes).
application: Cavanagh J. found the trial judge used the expert evidence only for historical background, expressly relying on the 22 issues themselves as a complete factual foundation. The judge correctly directed himself per Keegstra on the distinction between distasteful and hateful expression. The YWN issues were direct, not circumstantial, evidence, so Villaroman did not apply. An appellate court should not re-analyse each excerpt in Appendix A; the trial judge was entitled to find an overarching message of hatred dehumanizing Jews and women and to infer the requisite intent, and ample evidence supported those findings.
conclusion: The reasons were sufficient, no material misapprehension of evidence was shown, and the verdicts were reasonable; this ground failed.

issue: Did the trial judge err by not addressing s. 319(3) defences for Mr. Sears, which Sears' counsel did not advance at trial?
facts: Sears' counsel did not rely on s. 319(3); only Mr. St. Germaine raised s. 319(3)(c). On appeal Sears argued the judge should have considered various s. 319(3) defences (e.g., that satirizing 'rape culture' or calling for cultural conversion was permissible).
rule: Section 319(3) provides defences (truth, good-faith religious opinion, statements on matters of public interest reasonably believed true, and good-faith identification of hatred for removal). A trial judge is generally not required to adjudicate a statutory defence not raised at trial.
application: The judge had addressed s. 319(3)(c) for St. Germaine and rejected it. Cavanagh J. held the judge was not required to address defences Sears never advanced, and in any event the result would not have differed from the s. 319(3) analysis conducted for St. Germaine.
conclusion: No reversible error; ground dismissed.

issue: Did Mr. Sears receive ineffective assistance of counsel warranting setting aside his convictions?
facts: Sears complained that trial counsel (Mr. Embry) failed to bring a constitutional challenge, call expert/defence witnesses, advance s. 319(3) defences, effectively cross-examine, and that he was pressured into the agreed facts. Both testified at the appeal; email correspondence showed Sears repeatedly approved counsel's approach.
rule: To quash for ineffective assistance an appellant must establish the facts, that counsel's conduct amounted to incompetence (judged without hindsight against a strong presumption of reasonable professional assistance), and that it caused a miscarriage of justice (R. v. Archer, 2005 CanLII 36444; R. v. G.D.B., 2000 SCC 22).
application: The complaints concerned tactical decisions Sears agreed with or acquiesced in; counsel explained his reasons (including that Keegstra had already upheld s. 319's constitutionality) and Sears praised the closing submissions at the time. The strong presumption of competence was not displaced, and hindsight regret about self-representation did not establish incompetence or an unreliable verdict. The trial judge's summary dismissal without cross-examining Embry, exercising the Cody gatekeeper function, was reasonably open on the affidavits.
conclusion: Ineffective assistance was not established; ground dismissed.

issue: Did the trial judge err in refusing to re-open the defence to raise abuse of process, apprehension of bias, and a Charter s. 2(b) challenge to s. 319(2)?
facts: After conviction Sears sought to re-open, alleging the Crown's summary/two-count election was an abuse of process, that the judge showed bias, and that s. 319(2) unjustifiably limited freedom of expression.
rule: Post-conviction re-opening requires meeting the fresh-evidence test (R. v. Arabia, 2008 ONCA 565; R. v. Kowall; Palmer v. The Queen). Prosecutorial election is discretionary with a presumption of impartiality (R. v. St. Amand, 2017 ONCA 913). Bias requires clear evidence assessed on the informed-reasonable-person test (R. v. S. (R.D.), [1997] 3 S.C.R. 484). Keegstra upheld s. 319(2) against a s. 2(b) challenge.
application: There was no evidence the Crown acted in bad faith in electing summarily or in laying two counts for two distinct groups. An informed person would not conclude the trial judge lacked impartiality. Since Keegstra had already upheld s. 319(2) and nothing had changed, the constitutional argument had no merit and failed the Arabia/Palmer test. The judge also properly declined to re-open sentencing where fulsome submissions had already been made while Sears was represented.
conclusion: The refusals to re-open were not reversible errors; grounds dismissed.

issue: Did the trial judge err in principle by imposing consecutive six-month sentences and in setting the sentence lengths?
facts: Sears received consecutive six-month terms (one year total); St. Germaine received consecutive six-month conditional sentences, with mitigating factors (Métis/Gladue, age 78, poor health, cooperation). Appellants argued the counts arose from the same conduct and should be concurrent.
rule: Sentences attract deference absent an error in principle or demonstrable unfitness (R. v. Ramage, 2010 ONCA 488; R. v. McDonell, [1997] 1 S.C.R. 948). Consecutive sentences are appropriate where offences invade different legally protected interests (R. v. Gummer, 1983 CanLII 5286). Proportionality governs (s. 718.1).
application: The judge reasonably found that hatred against Jews and hatred against women engaged separate legally protected societal interests, justifying consecutive sentences per Gummer. The different sentence for St. Germaine reflected legitimate mitigating factors. The judge considered comparable cases (including Topham) and applied proportionality; no error in principle or unfitness was shown.
conclusion: The sentences were upheld; grounds dismissed.

issue: What is a fit sentence for the mischief and s. 319(1) offences committed by spray-painting hate messages on public and private property?
facts: On December 3, 2015, Mr. Mackenzie spray-painted swastikas and messages calling for the killing of Syrians and Muslims on cars, the Tuscany LRT station, and a C-Train car, causing roughly $20,000 damage to City property. He pleaded guilty to mischief and to communicating statements in a public place likely to incite hatred against Syrians and lead to a breach of the peace (s. 319(1)). He had a related record for mischief and assaults, was on probation, and psychiatric assessment rated his risk of re-offending as very high with limited genuine remorse.
rule: Sentencing objectives of deterrence, denunciation and rehabilitation; s. 718.1 proportionality (sentence proportionate to gravity of offence and degree of responsibility); s. 718.2(b) parity. Section 319(1) requires incitement of hatred by communicating statements in a public place likely to lead to a breach of the peace, a lesser mens rea than the 'wilful' promotion under s. 319(2) (R. v. Buzzanga; Mugesera v. Canada). Comparable hate-crime sentencing precedents (Lelas, Presseault, Nicholson, Harding, Mueller, Mahr, Noble, Andrews and Smith, Castonguay) were reviewed. Per R. v. Lelas, a court must not punish the offender for his beliefs.
application: The court weighed aggravating factors (related record, offence committed while on probation, references to violence in the messages) against the mitigating guilty plea, giving little weight to courtroom protestations of reform contradicted by Dr. Metelitsa's assessment. It found the conduct highly offensive and hurtful but primarily immature and juvenile 'acting out' rather than the ideologically vicious conduct in cases like Mahr and Noble, making Mackenzie less morally blameworthy. His mental difficulties were not treated as mitigating but informed the rehabilitative components. The Crown's proposed 18-month global sentence was found unsupported by precedent and disproportionate, and community service was seen as unrealistic.
conclusion: On Information 160233375P1, 3 months for mischief (count 1) and 5 months consecutive for the s. 319(1) offence (count 2), fully credited to pre-sentence custody leaving 1 day each, plus 2 years' probation; a further 3 months concurrent for the second mischief/breach on Information 151473410P1, consecutive to the first set.

issue: Does the 'worst offender/worst circumstances' principle limit the sentencing analysis and the availability of the maximum penalty?
facts: Defence argued that the 2-year maximum should be reserved for the worst offenders and worst circumstances, relying on R. v. Noble.
rule: The Supreme Court of Canada in R. v. Cheddesingh, 2004 SCC 16 and R. v. L.M., 2008 SCC 31 held that terms like 'stark horror', 'worst offence' and 'worst offender' add nothing and should be avoided; a maximum penalty is imposed rarely but is appropriate whenever the offence is of sufficient gravity and the offender sufficiently blameworthy, assessed case-by-case under s. 718.1.
application: The court respectfully declined to follow the 'worst possible circumstances' reasoning, holding it had been firmly rejected by the Supreme Court, and instead applied the case-by-case proportionality inquiry mandated by Cheddesingh and L.M.
conclusion: The 'worst offender' framing was rejected; sentencing proceeded on individualized proportionality principles.

issue: Can a mandatory s. 109(1)(a) firearms prohibition be imposed on a mischief conviction where the painted messages threatened violence?
facts: The Crown sought a s. 109(1)(a) prohibition; a question arose whether such an order could attach to the mischief charge under s. 430(3). The painted messages called for the killing of, and bodily harm to, Muslims, Syrians and Syrian refugees.
rule: Section 109(1)(a) mandates a firearms/weapons prohibition where a person is convicted of an indictable offence in the commission of which violence against a person was used, threatened or attempted and for which imprisonment of ten years or more is available. The prohibition is not automatic on mischief but is triggered where violence is used, threatened or attempted against a person.
application: The court held that by the content of the painted messages Mr. Mackenzie threatened violence against a person—namely any person who is Muslim, Syrian, or a Syrian refugee—so the violence element of s. 109(1)(a) was satisfied and the order remained available on the mischief conviction.
conclusion: A mandatory 10-year firearms/weapons prohibition under s. 109(1)(a) was imposed.

issue: Does the defendant lack the capacity to consent to the requested psychiatric evaluation?
facts: Ms. A.T., 52, had a decade-plus history of paranoid delusions, was brought to hospital after a car collision, refused all interviews, medication and evaluation, and had no insight into her condition. Dr. Chan, a psychiatrist of 40+ years, concluded she was unable to appreciate the purpose, risks and benefits of an evaluation or that she is sick. Her husband gave equivocal evidence and she did not appear in court.
rule: Articles 10, 11 and 16 C.C.Q. require consent to care; the court may substitute consent only if the person is incapable of consenting. Capacity is a question of fact assessed using the criteria from Institut Philippe-Pinel c. G.(A) and Starson v. Swayze (2003 SCC 32): whether the person understands the nature of the illness and treatment, appreciates the risks/advantages and consequences of refusal, and whether incapacity is affected by the illness. No presumption of incapacity arises merely from mental illness. Onus is on the applicant on the balance of probabilities.
application: Dr. Chan's expert report and testimony, corroborated by Drs. Looper and Kronick, showed persistent paranoid psychosis with no insight. The husband's nuanced, non-committal evidence did not displace this. With no evidence from Ms. A.T. and no opportunity to observe her (she failed to appear despite the court's request), the only reasonable conclusion was that she lacked capacity to consent.
conclusion: The court found Ms. A.T. lacks the capacity to consent to the psychiatric evaluation.

issue: Has the defendant categorically refused to undergo the evaluation?
facts: Ms. A.T. refused a psychiatric evaluation while confined for 30 days, refused formal interviews and medication, left hospital against medical advice, sent a demand letter through counsel, and twice failed to appear in court despite specific requests.
rule: Under art. 16 C.C.Q. and F.D. c. CUSM (2015 QCCA 1139), court intervention requires both incapacity and a categorical refusal of a specifically offered treatment.
application: The medical reports and Ms. A.T.'s conduct, including her repeated refusals and non-appearance, made it implicitly clear she does not approve of and refuses the requested evaluation.
conclusion: The court found categorical refusal established on the balance of probabilities.

issue: Should the court authorize the evaluation and appoint a new psychiatrist?
facts: There was a breakdown in the therapeutic alliance with Dr. Chan, who had been formally put on notice by Ms. A.T.'s lawyer. Dr. Biskin, an experienced McGill psychiatrist, was proposed with no objection.
rule: Article 12 C.C.Q. requires that substituted consent be given in the sole interest of the person, ensuring the care is beneficial, advisable and that risks are not disproportionate to the anticipated benefits.
application: The court found the evaluation beneficial and advisable, with benefits significantly outweighing any risks. Given the breakdown with Dr. Chan, appointing Dr. Biskin was appropriate; the court set out attendance, cooperation and enforcement terms and ordered provisional execution notwithstanding appeal.
conclusion: The application was granted, Dr. Biskin appointed, and the evaluation ordered with provisional execution.

issue: Does the Chief Justice's letter refusing authorization to a vexatious litigant to file a claim constitute a judgment?
facts: Following a 2000 prohibition order barring Fabrikant from instituting proceedings in the Superior Court without prior leave, he sought authorization from Chief Justice Rolland to sue Astral and Pixcom in defamation. The Chief Justice, by a letter dated January 5, 2005, refused ex parte, finding the claim unfounded in law.
rule: A court has inherent power (and under art. 46 C.C.P.) to curb abuse of process by vexatious litigants; a request for authorization should be made by motion supported by affidavit (arts. 88, 564 C.C.P.; arts. 86-87 R.P.C.(S.C.)). The Superior Court is a court of record (Courts of Justice Act, s. 21) whose proceedings must be recorded. A refusal that amounts to a summary dismissal must be reasoned per the rules of natural justice (Baker; R. v. Sheppard).
application: Rolland, C.J. denied authorization without a hearing or notice to the proposed defendants. The Court held this response constituted a judgment rendered after the application was taken under advisement, which had to be recorded in the file where the prohibition order was issued, and which had to be reasoned given its consequences (extinction of the claim).
conclusion: The refusal letter constituted an appealable judgment.

issue: Was leave to appeal required to challenge the refusal of authorization?
facts: Fabrikant filed an inscription in appeal on January 19, 2005 without seeking leave, arguing the refusal was a final judgment disposing of a claim near one million dollars.
rule: Where a decision is rendered in execution of an earlier prohibition judgment, any appeal is assimilated to a judgment in matters of execution under art. 26(2) sub-para. 3 C.C.P. and requires prior leave (Morency c. Commission des affaires sociales). Failure to obtain leave under art. 523 C.C.P. goes to the jurisdiction of the Court and is fatal (Selig c. Chrétien).
application: Fabrikant's request was made pursuant to the May 30, 2000 prohibition order, so the refusal was rendered in execution of that judgment and could be appealed only with leave, which he never sought. The Court added that even had leave been sought it would have been refused.
conclusion: Leave was required; its absence was fatal to the appeal.

issue: Did Astral and Pixcom have standing to move to dismiss the appeal?
