rule: Interim costs/disbursements require the claimant to show inability to fund the amounts, that the disbursements are necessary and reasonable, a clear need for the expert's services, and a meritorious claim on the balance of probabilities (Stuart v. Stuart; Biddle v. Biddle).
application: The mother did not demonstrate a clear need for forensic accountants or out-of-town counsel or document their services and costs. As the father lacked resources to fund the litigation himself, ordering him to pay would in effect order the grandfather to pay. The court instead directed an early settlement conference.
conclusion: The request for interim disbursements and fees was denied.

issue: How and where should the paternal grandfather, who resides in Switzerland and swore an affidavit, be questioned?
facts: The grandfather, resident in Geneva, agreed to be questioned but refused to travel to Toronto; the mother sought his attendance in Toronto or funding of her counsel to question him in Geneva. The father proposed Skype/video-conference.
rule: Rule 20(14) of the Family Law Rules allows the court to set the date, place, presiding person and recording method for questioning a person outside Ontario, but the court cannot order a non-resident to attend in Ontario (A. v. B., leave to appeal refused).
application: Balancing the imperfections of video technology against the need to keep costs reasonable, and given the court could not compel the grandfather to attend in Ontario, the court directed that if he would not appear in Toronto he be questioned by Skype or other video-conference, in English.
conclusion: The grandfather may be questioned by video-conference in Switzerland, in English, if he will not attend in Toronto.

issue: Where the plaintiffs are not named, were they nonetheless identified as the persons of and concerning whom the defamatory words were published?
facts: None of the 25 correctional-officer plaintiffs was named in any article. The 26 October 1978 Denhoff column used general references such as 'his jail guard boys' and 'his gang of bumbling yo-yos at the Fort Saskatchewan jail'. The guards at the centre numbered about 200 and wore a distinctive uniform. Most plaintiffs testified that friends, relatives and strangers linked them to the articles.
rule: A plaintiff must prove the words were published of and concerning him. The test (David Syme & Co. v. Canavan (1918), 25 C.L.R. 234; Knupffer v. London Express Newspaper Ltd., [1944] A.C. 116) is whether the words would reasonably lead persons acquainted with the plaintiff to believe he was the person referred to; language referring to a limited class may reasonably be understood to refer to every member. The author's intention is irrelevant if the words used include persons he did not intend to include.
application: The Mayer article and the second Denhoff article referred only to specific, ascertainable guards involved in the photographer incidents, none of whom were plaintiffs, so those did not identify the plaintiffs. The bulk of the 26 October Denhoff column, however, applied generally to all guards at the centre. Despite Denhoff's stated intention to refer only to those involved, the ordinary sensible reader would take the comments as referring to all Fort Saskatchewan guards; a reader who knew a plaintiff or recognised the uniform would identify him. The group (~200) was not so large, nor the claims so exaggerated, as to prevent identification.
conclusion: The 25 individual plaintiffs were identified by the 26 October 1978 Denhoff column; the actions based on the Mayer article and the second Denhoff article failed on identification, and the action against Mayer was dismissed.

issue: Was the plaintiff union (AUPE) itself defamed?
facts: AUPE was the bargaining agent for the correctional officers but nothing was published about it as a union and no attack was made on its conduct.
rule: A plaintiff, including an entity, must show the defamatory words were published of and concerning it.
application: Mere association as bargaining agent for the guards was insufficient; nothing in the articles referred to or attacked the union.
conclusion: The action by AUPE was dismissed.

issue: Were the impugned words in the 26 October 1978 column defamatory of the plaintiffs?
facts: The column called the guards a 'gang of bumbling yo-yos ... goons ... a joke' and ended 'They haven't got the brains to be Nazis, the discipline to be jackboots or the mentality to philosophically endorse either of the above.'
rule: Defamation is a communication that tends to lower a person in the estimation of right-thinking members of society, exposing him to hatred, contempt or ridicule, or causing him to be shunned or avoided (Linden, Canadian Tort Law, 3rd ed.).
application: 'Goons' connoted lack of intelligence, incompetence and brutality; 'yo-yos', 'bumbling yo-yos' and 'a joke' suggested stupidity and incompetence; the closing statement imputed stupidity, incompetence and lack of discipline. These exposed the plaintiffs to contempt and ridicule and lowered them in their communities' estimation.
conclusion: The statements were defamatory of the plaintiffs.

issue: Were the words fact or comment, and was the defence of fair comment made out?
facts: Denhoff, a hired political columnist, said he intended only to comment on and ridicule the specific individuals and the Journal's coverage, portraying bumbling 'keystone cops' behaviour; he asserted no honest belief that guards generally were incompetent, brutal or unintelligent. No effort was made to prove the truth of the statements.
rule: Fair comment protects honest expression of opinion on a matter of public interest, but the words must be recognisable as comment, not fact (Jones v. Skelton; Cherneskey v. Armadale Publishers Ltd., [1979] 1 S.C.R. 1067; Gatley on Libel and Slander). The defendant bears the burden of proving each ingredient, including an honest belief in the opinion actually conveyed to the reasonable reader; the intended meaning is irrelevant.
application: Some passages were comment/inference, but the closing statements (from 'The Sun doesn't take these guys seriously — Farran or his goons') could reasonably be read only as statements of fact whose truth was not proven. Even assuming all were comment, Denhoff asserted no honest belief in the meaning actually conveyed — a general attack on the intelligence, competence, discipline and violent tendencies of all Fort Saskatchewan guards. The comments descended into personal abuse and invective, which is not protected. Section 9(1) of the Defamation Act was not relied on and would not assist since Denhoff was employed as a columnist.
conclusion: Neither justification nor fair comment was established; the defence failed.

issue: Did the plaintiffs give sufficient notice under s. 13 of the Defamation Act?
facts: The notice named AUPE and certain officers, and referred to 'members of Division 3 (being Correctional Officers)'; only one of the 25 plaintiffs (Albert Heuft) was named, and only as a trustee/representative.
rule: Section 13 requires timely written notice specifying the defamatory matter. Alberta follows the substantial-compliance approach (Paletta v. Lethbridge Herald Co. (1977), 2 Alta. L.R. (2d) 166); the notice need only identify the intending plaintiff with reasonable certainty and bring home the matter complained of (Grossman v. CFTO-TV Ltd. (1982), 39 O.R. (2d) 498; Sentinel-Review Co. v. Robinson, [1928] S.C.R. 258).
application: Although not named individually, the intent to sue on behalf of Division 3 correctional officers was clearly specified and the defamatory material clearly identified, apprising the defendants of the category of plaintiffs intending to sue.
conclusion: There was substantial compliance; valid notice under s. 13 was served.

issue: How should damages be assessed and could they be mitigated by the prior Edmonton Journal publication?
facts: The defendants argued damages should be reduced because the Journal, with larger circulation, had earlier published similar expressions; no action was ever commenced against the Journal, and no settlement or judgment existed.
rule: Section 15(2) of the Defamation Act allows mitigation only where the plaintiff has already sued, recovered or received compensation for defamation to the same effect (Snider v. Calgary Herald (1985), 41 Alta. L.R. (2d) 11). At common law, mere prior publication of a similar libel by another does not mitigate damages (Assoc. Newspapers v. Dingle, [1964] A.C. 371).
application: Section 15 did not apply as no action was brought against the Journal. There is no common-law right to mitigation from another's similar defamation; Denhoff borrowed O'Callaghan's expressions but applied them, with his own additions, generally to the guards, creating a new context and a fresh, searing attack. Damages were awarded in three tiers reflecting the degree of harm: $1,500 to minimally affected plaintiffs, $2,500 to seriously affected plaintiffs, and $3,500 to two who suffered extraordinary anguish (Luke Rusk and Terry Kosack). No damages were awarded for the deceased plaintiff Robert Hatfield. Interest was awarded under the Judgment Interest Act at 4% from 1 April 1984.
conclusion: Damages were not mitigated; substantial damages were awarded to the individual plaintiffs on a three-tier basis.

issue: Was intervention through a court order necessary to protect the child in the future?
facts: The 11-year-old special-needs child was found in need of protection in 2017 and placed with the father under society supervision. The high-conflict relationship between the mother and the father/his wife persisted; the mother repeatedly made unverified abuse allegations, involved the child in the conflict, and showed little insight into the protection concerns. The child had thrived in the father's stable home since supervision of the mother's visits resumed in May 2019.
rule: Under s. 101(1) CYFSA the court must be satisfied that intervention through a court order is necessary to protect the child in the future before making a disposition; if not necessary, s. 101(8) requires the child be returned to the pre-intervention caregiver. The paramount purpose (s. 1(1)) is the best interests, protection and well-being of children (Children's Aid Society of Oxford v. W.T.C., 2013 ONCA 491; C.A.S. of Toronto v. S.P., 2019 ONSC 3482; Catholic C.A.S. of Metropolitan Toronto v. C.M., [1994] 2 S.C.R. 165).
application: The court found this remained a high-conflict case in which the child had been emotionally harmed and would be again absent a structured order. It had significant concerns about the mother's ability to meet the child's needs and her pattern of allegations that worsened the child's behaviour, and it found a protection order necessary to preserve the child's stable placement with the father.
conclusion: Intervention through a protection order was necessary to protect the child in the future.

issue: What dispositional order was in the child's best interests?
facts: The father and his wife had provided a highly structured, stable home for over three years, working closely with the school and professionals, and the child had markedly improved. The mother had many strengths and a loving bond but showed lack of insight, poor judgment, unreliable memory, and an inability to separate her needs from the child's; she had minimized his needs while in her care.
rule: On a status review under s. 113–114 CYFSA the court may make an order under s. 101(1) or a custody order under s. 102, in the child's best interests, applying the criteria in s. 74(3), and preferring the least disruptive course consistent with the child's best interests (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S.B., 2014 ONCJ 518).
application: Weighing the s. 74(3) factors — continuity, stability, the child's needs and the unacceptably high risk of a move to the mother — the court found the evidence overwhelming that placement with the father best served the child. Shared decision-making was rejected because of the entrenched high conflict and poor communication (Kaplanis; Graham v. Butto), and the father was made the decision-maker. Incidents of custody (documentation, travel) were granted given the mother's past non-cooperation.
conclusion: The child was placed in the custody of the father under s. 102, with the father as decision-maker and the requested incidents of custody, and the mother granted access to the child's information.

issue: What parenting-time order for the mother was in the child's best interests and should it be supervised?
facts: The mother's parenting time had been fully supervised since May 2019, during which time it was consistently positive and the child's functioning improved dramatically; earlier attempts at unsupervised access had coincided with escalating allegations and deterioration in the child's behaviour. The child wanted more time with his mother, and the family friend (C.H.) was willing to supervise indefinitely.
rule: Section 104 CYFSA governs access, determined by the child's best interests (s. 74(3)) and the maximum-contact principle (Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27; applied in child protection in C.A.S. of Algoma v. S.P., 2011 ONCJ 93). The party seeking to restrict or supervise access bears the burden of justifying it (Klymenko v. Klymenko, 2020 ONSC 5451); supervision is usually temporary and aimed at repairing deficits (Izyuk v. Bilousov), and equal parenting requires a high level of communication (Bokor v. Hidas).
application: The court rejected leaving parenting time to the father's discretion (making one high-conflict party arbiter of the other) and rejected equal time (communication too poor for a special-needs child). It balanced the risk of the mother repeating past behaviour against her 18 months of positive supervised visits and therapeutic progress, crafting a phased plan increasing frequency to two of every three weekends and transitioning to unsupervised time by April 2021, with third-party exchanges to reduce conflict.
conclusion: A phased parenting-time order was made increasing the mother's time and moving from supervised to unsupervised access by spring 2021, without leaving discretion to the father and without equal time.

issue: Should Dr. Collins's psychological assessment of the mother be admitted as expert evidence?
facts: Justice Zisman had ordered a psychological/psychiatric assessment of the mother. Dr. Collins, agreed to be qualified, conducted it co-authored with Dr. Rokeach, who was completing his first adult assessment while under a 'Supervised Practice' designation. The mother objected that Rokeach lacked adult-assessment expertise and that the opinions were too intermingled to be reliable.
rule: Expert evidence is governed by the two-stage framework in White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co., 2015 SCC 23: the four Mohan threshold requirements (relevance, necessity, absence of an exclusionary rule, properly qualified expert) plus a discretionary gatekeeping cost-benefit analysis, with reliability at the core; judges must act as gatekeepers (Goudge and Motherisk reports).
application: The assessment was logically relevant, necessary, subject to no exclusionary rule, and authored by a duly qualified expert (Dr. Collins), who participated throughout, scored the testing, wrote the opinion sections, and took ownership of the conclusions. The case was distinguished from C.A.S. of London and Middlesex v. C.D.B. (multiple unqualified authors, editing by non-professionals, faulty memory). The probative value exceeded any prejudice, and Rokeach's limited experience went to weight, not admissibility.
conclusion: The assessment was admitted as Exhibit #22, and largely confirmed the court's independent findings about the mother.

issue: Were the injunction proceedings instituted against Ariella Elmaleh abusive under arts. 51 ff. C.C.P.?
facts: Dvir Bitton, son and liquidator of the late Samy Bitton, and Samprêt Plus inc. brought an injunction application against the widow Daniella Damary, notary Znaty and Elmaleh, an occupational therapist at the Jewish General Hospital who had tutored Damary's children. Elmaleh was accused of conspiring to alter the deceased's will and of twice 'removing' the deceased's cell phone. The 176-paragraph application named her in only 9 paragraphs, contained no specific conclusion against her, rested on unproven suspicions, and her sworn affidavit with exhibits showed she took the phone only once (14 May 2020) at the hospital's and Damary's written instruction, without accessing its contents, and was not even at the hospital on the alleged second date.
rule: Articles 51 and 54 C.C.P. permit a court to declare a pleading abusive, without regard to intent or bad faith, where it is manifestly unfounded, rests on no identifiable legal or factual basis, reveals no plausible cause of action and is merely exploratory or vexatious (Choquette c. Quenneville, 2021 QCCS 1936; characteristics per Greenstone Realties, 2020 QCCS 3057: conduct contrary to the aims of the justice system, recklessness through absence of objectively identifiable legal foundation, allegations not withstanding attentive analysis, and escalation out of proportion with the real dispute).
application: The Court found Elmaleh a total stranger to the succession/family dispute, dragged in without any specific conclusion against her, on vague allegations founded only on conjecture. The plaintiffs' strategy of taking allegations 'as proven' to then examine her and 'build' a non-existent case was rejected. Her role could at most have made her a witness. The relentless insistence on keeping her as defendant, coupled with disciplinary complaints and the 'shoot first, talk later' monetary conclusions, satisfied every hallmark of abusive, malicious pleading.
conclusion: The proceeding was declared abusive as against Elmaleh and dismissed in her regard.

issue: Should the proposed amendments to the injunction application be admitted, and did they cure the abuse against Elmaleh?
facts: Nearly six months after Elmaleh's dismissal motion and one week before the hearing, the plaintiffs filed an amended application converting the estate into co-plaintiff, changing the second phone-removal date from 6 June to 6 July 2020, invoking Charter arts. 5 and 9, and adding solidary and unquantified damages conclusions. Damary's counsel formally opposed the amendment.
rule: Article 207 C.C.P. requires that, where an amendment is opposed, the amending party present a motion to the court for a ruling; absence of opposition by one affected party does not render the amendment partially accepted.
application: Because Damary opposed and no art. 207 motion had been presented, the amended application was not officially part of the record, a matter for the case-management judge. The Court nonetheless examined the Elmaleh-specific amendments and found they added nothing: the alleged Charter breach could not stand where she merely relayed a phone at the wife's and hospital's instruction without reading its contents, and the belated date change and blanket solidary damages conclusions were themselves indicia of abuse.
conclusion: The amendments were of no assistance and did not improve the plaintiffs' position; they did not cure the abuse.

issue: Was Elmaleh entitled to compensatory damages equal to her extrajudicial fees?
facts: Elmaleh incurred $32,652.90 in extrajudicial fees defending a claim from which the plaintiffs' counsel had, by 30 November 2020, been given all documents to file a discontinuance but refused. Her counsel's rates and hours were documented.
rule: Under arts. 51-54 C.C.P. (compensatory in nature), a finding of fault plus frivolity/abuse allows recovery of extrajudicial fees, assessed for reasonableness (importance and difficulty of the dispute, time required, conduct of the instance, reasonableness of rates, proportionality) with a causal link between the fees and the abusive fault (Greenstone Realties, 2020 QCCS 3310).
application: Elmaleh was drawn into a litigation that was never hers; the fees flowed directly from the plaintiffs' refusal to discontinue. The rates and amount were found just and reasonable given the nature and complexity of the matter.
conclusion: Both plaintiffs were condemned solidarily to pay $32,652.90 in compensatory damages with interest and additional indemnity.

issue: Were punitive damages warranted and against whom?
facts: Beyond the abusive proceeding, Dvir Bitton filed unfounded ethics complaints against Elmaleh with the Jewish General Hospital ombudsman and the Ordre des ergothérapeutes (both rejected), the second complaint (18 Dec. 2020) accusing her of reprisals for filing her dismissal motion and demanding the syndic force her to withdraw it.
rule: Article 54 C.C.P. authorises punitive damages for abuse where circumstances justify, assessed under art. 1621 C.C.Q. (preventive function; gravity of fault, patrimonial situation, etc.).
application: The Court found Dvir Bitton's conduct reckless, vindictive and malicious—using his professional-order complaints to tarnish Elmaleh's reputation and pressure her to abandon her motion—meriting an exemplary sanction. Samprêt, however, was not implicated in this malicious personal campaign.
conclusion: Dvir Bitton alone was ordered to pay $7,500 in punitive damages; provisional execution notwithstanding appeal was ordered and costs awarded against the plaintiffs.

issue: Were the society's police records, occurrence reports and hearsay affidavits admissible on the summary judgment motion?
facts: The society relied on the mother's criminal record, records of arrest, 19 occurrence reports, community inquiry reports, and affidavits of society workers that attached case notes/logs of other, non-deponent workers and recounted third-party hearsay. Counsel initially raised few objections; the court itself called counsel back to make submissions on admissibility.
rule: Police reports are admissible as business records under s. 35 of the Evidence Act where made contemporaneously, in the ordinary course of business, by a person under a business duty; only records of facts (not expert opinion or third-party hearsay) qualify (Setak Computer Services; CCAS of Toronto v. Jean L.). Actual, if not formal, notice suffices (Exhibitors Inc. v. Allen). On a summary judgment motion the judge must scrutinize the evidence, and hearsay must meet necessity and reliability and be of trial quality (subrule 16(5) FLR). Admissions of an opposing party are admissible against that party.
application: The court found the mother had two months' actual notice of the police brief, so notice was satisfied. It admitted the mother's criminal record, records of arrest, her own statements/calls to police, police observations, and the domestic-violence victim report, but excluded third-party complaints, social-worker hearsay, opinion evidence on mental health, guilty-plea synopses and community-inquiry reports. It refused to admit case notes/logs of workers who swore no affidavit, as this deprived the mother of cross-examination and was not the best available evidence. Hearsay favourable/unfavourable from third-party professionals was admitted only where the mother consented. The child's statements about being slapped were admitted for their truth as reliable (spontaneous, no motive to lie, corroborating bruise); statements of the child's views were admitted only for the fact they were said.
conclusion: Portions of the evidence were admitted and portions excluded; the court was satisfied it could adjudicate fairly on the admissible evidence without relying on inadmissible hearsay.

issue: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial that the child was in need of protection?
facts: The child, born 2008, was apprehended in May 2015 amid concerns of physical discipline (slapping, a bruise), chronic school absences, inadequate care, and the mother's repeated volatile, threatening conduct toward workers, the foster mother, school staff, police and community members. Dr. Amitay's parenting-capacity assessment found the mother lacked insight, could not control her anger and had a poor grasp of the child's developmental needs.
rule: Section 37(2)(b),(f),(f.1),(g),(g.1),(h) CFSA; the society bears the onus to prove on a balance of probabilities a real (not speculative) risk; intention to harm need not be shown, causation may be by act, omission or pattern. On summary judgment (subrule 16 FLR; Hryniak v. Mauldin) the court takes a hard look to see whether there is no genuine issue requiring a trial, and the responding party must show specific facts, not mere denials.
application: The evidence of society workers was strikingly consistent with Dr. Amitay's assessment and with the mother's own counsellor and psychiatrist. The mother's lack of insight, inability to control anger and misunderstanding of the child's needs placed the child at risk of physical and emotional harm; school non-attendance also affected the child's development. The mother offered only denials and vague explanations and articulated no genuine triable issue beyond that Dr. Amitay had not been cross-examined.
conclusion: No genuine issue for trial; the child was found in need of protection under s. 37(2)(b), (g) and (g.1). The court declined to find actual emotional harm or a condition under (f), (f.1) or (h) for insufficient evidence.

issue: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial for a disposition other than Crown wardship?
facts: The society sought Crown wardship without access for adoption. The mother sought return under supervision or a further 6-month society wardship, without specifying what would change. No family or community placement was available. Despite over a year of counselling and programs, the mother's angry, disparaging conduct in front of the child continued.
rule: Sections 57(1)-(4), 37(3) and 70(1)(a) CFSA require the least disruptive alternative consistent with the child's best interests; Crown wardship, being the most profound order, requires the highest caution and most compelling evidence after reviewing all remedies (Jill G.-T.).
application: Dr. Amitay, a neutral professional, had explained what the mother needed to do; there was 'not the slightest evidence' the assessment changed her behaviour, and no evidence her deficiencies could be remedied in the foreseeable future. The submission that this hearing was 'rock bottom' was speculative and did not create a triable issue. Extending time in care with no credible prospect of improvement was not justified.
conclusion: No genuine issue for trial; Crown wardship was the only realistic disposition consistent with the child's best interests.

issue: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to access to the Crown ward?
facts: The mother was at times loving and affectionate, but many visits had to be terminated because of her conduct; she persistently questioned the child about the foster home, criticized the foster mother, learned the foster placement's location, school and church, and made threatening comments. The child often comforted the mother rather than vice versa.
rule: Subsection 59(2.1) CFSA presumes against access to a Crown ward; the person seeking access must prove the relationship is beneficial and meaningful to the child and that access will not impair adoption prospects (CAS Niagara v. M.J. — 'beneficial and meaningful' means significantly advantageous, assessed on the existing relationship; onus on the applicant — CAS Toronto v. D.P.).
application: Access was meaningful in that the child knew and loved the mother, but the court found it was not significantly advantageous, as the mother focused on herself and the child soothed her. The mother's threats and inability to stop undermining the placement would have to be disclosed to any adoptive family and would deter adoption; further delay would only give more opportunities to undermine the placement. The mother raised no triable issue.
conclusion: No genuine issue for trial; access was neither beneficial nor meaningful and would impair adoption, so Crown wardship without access was ordered.

issue: Is the Tobacco Products Control Act within federal legislative competence under ss. 91 and 92 of the Constitution Act, 1867?
facts: Parliament enacted the Tobacco Products Control Act (S.C. 1988, c. 20), banning most direct and indirect tobacco advertising, regulating retail display, prohibiting free samples and requiring unattributed health warnings on packages. Its stated object (s. 3) was to address a grave, urgent and national public-health problem. The tobacco manufacturers argued the Act merely regulated advertising, a matter of provincial competence.
rule: The 'pith and substance' analysis identifies the true character of the law (Whitbread v. Walley). Public health is primarily a provincial matter (Schneider v. The Queen), but the residual peace, order and good government power in the opening words of s. 91 supports federal jurisdiction over matters of genuine national concern. Under R. v. Crown Zellerbach, a matter of national concern must have singleness, distinctiveness and indivisibility distinguishing it from provincial matters, assessed with the aid of the 'provincial inability' test; the criminal-law power (s. 91(27)) requires a prohibition tied to a public evil (Margarine Reference).
application: The Court of Appeal held the trial judge mischaracterized the Act as mere advertising regulation. Properly characterized, the Act's true object was the protection of public health by reducing tobacco consumption. It could not rest on the criminal-law power because it did not prohibit the (legal) activity of consuming or selling tobacco. However, tobacco use is a national—indeed worldwide—public-health scourge, analogous to the alcohol cases (Russell; Canada Temperance Federation). Because provincial advertising laws have no extra-territorial reach and cannot control cross-border media (magazines, radio, television), the provinces are individually unable to control the advertising aspect, giving the matter the required singleness and indivisibility of national concern.
conclusion: The Act is intra vires the federal Parliament under the peace, order and good government power (national concern branch). The unanimous panel agreed on this point.

issue: If the Act limits freedom of expression protected by s. 2(b) of the Charter, is the limit justified under s. 1?
facts: The Attorney General conceded the Act limits commercial expression protected by s. 2(b) (Irwin Toy; Rocket). The respondents conceded that measures genuinely aimed at reducing the tobacco scourge could be justified. The dispute was whether the ban satisfied the Oakes proportionality test, especially the rational connection between advertising restrictions and reduced consumption and the minimal-impairment requirement; government officials had recommended an undisclosed alternative measure.
rule: Under s. 1 (R. v. Oakes), a limit must serve a pressing and substantial objective and be proportionate: rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality of effects, proven on a balance of probabilities. Subsequent jurisprudence (Irwin Toy, Keegstra, Butler, Edwards Books, Cotroni, Dickason) recognized a contextual approach and a margin of appreciation for socio-economic policy choices, requiring only a reasonable basis rather than strict proof.
application: Justice LeBel (Rothman concurring) held that in a socio-economic policy matter the state need only show a reasonable basis that the measure could achieve its objective; the evidence (Pollay, Cohen, Chandler, the U.S. Surgeon General report, WHO material and internal company documents) provided a reasonable basis and the restriction on non-central commercial expression, weighed against the serious public-health interest, satisfied minimal impairment. Justice Brossard dissented on ss. 4, 5, 6 and 8: he found no preponderant proof of a real rational link between advertising and consumption (only a mere possibility, undermined by the government's own internal documents and the Norway/Finland data), and held the total advertising ban was not minimal impairment since informative and brand advertising could have been exempted and the government refused to disclose a less intrusive alternative; he would uphold only ss. 7 (sample ban) and 9 (mandatory warnings).
conclusion: By majority the limit was justified under s. 1 and the Act upheld in its entirety; Brossard J.A. dissenting would have struck ss. 4, 5, 6 and 8. The appeals were allowed.

issue: Did the superior court have jurisdiction to rule on the validity of the trust rather than deferring to the Ontario Human Rights Commission, and was such a ruling premature?
facts: The Ontario Human Rights Commission filed a formal complaint in August 1986 alleging the Leonard Foundation trust contravened the Human Rights Code, 1981. The trustee, Canada Trust Company, then applied under s. 60 of the Trustee Act and rule 14.05 for the court's advice and direction on the trust's validity. The Commission argued the questions concerning the Code fell within its exclusive primary jurisdiction.
rule: Under Seneca College v. Bhadauria, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 181, the Human Rights Code provides a comprehensive scheme that must be pursued before resort to the courts for a breach of the Code. However, superior courts retain inherent jurisdiction over the administration of charitable trusts, reinforced by s. 60 of the Trustee Act, and may determine questions of law where no facts are in dispute (Bell v. Ontario Human Rights Commission, [1971] S.C.R. 756).
application: The court distinguished Bhadauria: this was not an attempt to create a common-law tort of discrimination but the administration of a charitable trust, a matter of centuries-old inherent equitable jurisdiction invoked by the trustee itself. The Commission's remedial powers under s. 40(1) of the Code could not alter or void the terms of a trust, so recourse to the court was necessary in any event; and the matter turned on a question of law with no disputed facts. A determination before the Commission investigated was therefore not premature.
conclusion: The court had jurisdiction to determine the validity of the trust, and the determination was not premature. This preliminary objection was dismissed.

issue: Were the trust's provisions restricting eligibility, management and benefits by race, religion and sex void as contrary to public policy (or void for uncertainty)?
facts: The 1923 indenture recited the settlor's beliefs in the superiority of the 'White Race' and Christianity and restricted scholarships, committee membership and eligible institutions to white, British, Protestant Christians; a further clause capped income spent on female students at one-quarter of the total. The trust had operated for over 65 years and drew sustained public criticism.
rule: Public freedom to dispose of property (Blathwayt v. Lord Cawley, [1976] A.C. 397) is limited by public policy, to be invoked only in clear cases where harm to the public is substantially incontestable (Re Millar, [1938] S.C.R. 1). The public policy against discrimination is drawn from the Human Rights Code, 1981, the Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, other statutes, ss. 15, 27 and 28 of the Charter, and ratified international conventions (per Tarnopolsky J.A.). A charitable trust must be wholly charitable and confer a public benefit; a condition precedent defining beneficiaries is not void for uncertainty if some person can satisfy it (Jones v. T. Eaton Co.; McPhail v. Doulton).
application: Robins J.A. read the recitals together with the operative clauses, finding the trust premised on notions of racism and religious superiority patently at odds with contemporary values of racial and religious equality guaranteed constitutionally and reflected in Canada's multicultural heritage; its continued operation in that form was inimical to the public interest. Tarnopolsky J.A. held the eligibility clause was a sufficiently certain condition precedent (severing only the 'allegiance' language if needed) so the trust did not fail for uncertainty, but was void on public policy grounds to the extent it discriminated by race, religion and sex — while cautioning that not all restrictive charitable trusts (e.g. ameliorative or needs-based ones) are void.
conclusion: The provisions confining management, judicial advice, eligible institutions and benefits on grounds of race, colour, ethnic origin, creed/religion and sex were void as contravening public policy; it was unnecessary to decide the uncertainty question (Robins J.A.), and Tarnopolsky J.A. found the trust sufficiently certain.

issue: If the discriminatory provisions were void, could the cy-près doctrine be applied to preserve the charitable trust?
facts: The trust was valid when created in 1923; changed social attitudes rendered its discriminatory terms contrary to public policy. The settlor's stated object was the advancement of education/leadership through education, and para. 13 allowed alteration of objects for purposes conducive to promoting education.
rule: A charitable trust that becomes impracticable or fails will be applied cy-près where the settlor had a general (paramount) charitable intention, as distinct from a particular intention tied to a specific mode (Re Lysaght; Re Dominion Students' Hall Trust; National Anti-Vivisection Society v. IRC, [1948] A.C. 31 — 'a charity once established does not die, though its nature may be changed').
application: Both judges found the settlor's paramount intention was charitable — the advancement of education/leadership through education — and that the discriminatory scheme was merely the machinery for carrying it out, not an essential part of the paramount intention. As changing public policy had made the original scheme impracticable and offensive, the court exercised its inherent jurisdiction to bring the trust into accord with public policy.
conclusion: Cy-près was applied. The recitals and all restrictions as to race, colour, creed/religion, ethnic origin and sex (for beneficiaries, committee members, judicial advice and eligible institutions) were struck out, preserving the charitable trust; the preferences for children of clergymen, teachers, service members, etc. were left intact.

issue: Was the plaintiff illegally dismissed, or did the employment relationship end because of his own conduct in refusing to report to his reassigned position?
facts: Benarroch, a 22-year-old supervisor in laundry and sterilization services, was transferred to a supervisor position in housekeeping. He characterized the transfer as a demotion and an illegal dismissal, linking it to his discovery of alleged misappropriation of funds by a superior, Claude Bensmihen. The employer argued Benarroch had accepted the transferred position but never reported to it. Testimony from HR officer Mallet (30 years' experience), supervisor Elbas, and colleague Audrey Bennaroche established chronic lateness, poor performance, failure to cooperate, personal internet use at work, and that a co-worker often covered his duties. The employer had offered him a way to keep his job at the same salary ($38,000), which he refused.
rule: Under Quebec employment/contract law, where an employee refuses to report to a validly reassigned position after accepting it, the ending of employment may constitute a rupture of the employment relationship by the employee's own conduct rather than an illegal dismissal. Where witness versions conflict, the court assesses credibility and probability.
application: Faced with contradictory versions, the Court preferred the defendant's credible and probable account, relying particularly on Mallet's serious investigation and Bennaroche's disinterested, courageous testimony. The evidence showed Benarroch had accepted the lateral transfer, then changed his mind and reportedly said he would stay in the laundry and that they could fire him if they wished. His performance was declining and the alleged 'targeting' after the Bensmihen incident was not made out, since Bennaroche—also involved in denouncing Bensmihen—was not targeted. The Court found the end of employment resulted from the plaintiff's presumptuous conduct.
conclusion: The Court found there was a rupture of the employment relationship caused by the plaintiff's own acts, not an illegal dismissal; the claim for $48,000 in damages was rejected.

issue: Was the disputed exhibit D-9 admissible in evidence?
facts: The defendant sought to introduce exhibit D-9, a document confirming the employee's status, over the plaintiff's objection that it had not been pleaded in the proceedings and was irrelevant. The objection had been taken under reserve.
rule: Evidence that is relevant to the issues and at least indirectly alleged in the proceedings may be admitted.
application: The Court considered D-9 relevant and not foreign to the litigation, being indirectly alleged and inferable from the whole of the evidence. It confirmed the employee's status.
conclusion: D-9 was admitted; it established that at hiring the plaintiff held a temporary full-time position, not a permanent one.

issue: Should the law clerk's affidavits, sworn on information and belief and tendered as the mother's substantive evidence, be admitted and what weight should they carry?
facts: The mother filed no responding affidavit of her own. Her counsel instead relied on two affidavits sworn by counsel's law clerk purporting to set out the mother's circumstances in Dubai, her plan of care, her income, and family support. No source for the attributed statements was identified, no contact information or names of supporting relatives were given, and the exhibits (passport copies, 'medical report', employment documents) were largely unreadable and of uncertain authenticity.
rule: Rule 14(18) of the Family Law Rules expresses a preference for personal-knowledge affidavits; Rule 14(19) permits information-and-belief evidence only where the source is named and the deponent states a belief in its truth (conjunctive requirements). A judge retains discretion to refuse hearsay led for its truth (Berger v. Berger, 2016 ONCA 884). Lawyers'/staff affidavits are generally inappropriate on summary judgment except to summarize record or uncontested facts (Ferreira v. Cardenas, 2014 ONSC 7119; Children's Aid Society of Ottawa v. B.(J.), 2016 ONSC 2757). Weight is governed by the best-evidence rule, direct evidence outweighs hearsay, and the more dispositive the hearsay the more scrutiny it attracts.
application: The clerk never indicated she had communicated with the mother or why direct affidavits from the mother, her husband, or his family could not be obtained. The attributed statements were contentious and went to the heart of the mother's response, yet no source or particulars were provided, making trustworthiness impossible to assess, and the exhibits were inherently unreliable. There was no necessity shown for the clerk to give substantive evidence.
conclusion: The court gave the law clerk's evidence as to the mother's circumstances in Dubai no weight, while not striking the affidavits.

issue: Should an adverse inference be drawn from the mother's failure to lead direct evidence?
facts: The mother did not attend the motion, filed no responsive affidavit, and provided only hearsay through her counsel's law clerk. She had never sought temporary care and control and offered no direct evidence from herself or the family said to support her plan.
rule: Rule 16(5) of the Family Law Rules permits the court to draw conclusions unfavourable to a party whose evidence is not from a person with personal knowledge of the disputed facts; the rule is permissive (Jewish Child and Family Services v. S.K., 2015 ONCJ 246). A responding party must 'lead trump or risk losing' (Sweda Farms).
application: Given the absence of any direct evidence and the unexplained failure to obtain affidavits from the mother or her supporters, the circumstances supported drawing an adverse inference that the missing evidence would have harmed her case.
conclusion: The court drew an adverse inference from the mother's failure to depose direct evidence.

issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial that the child is in need of protection?
facts: R.S.A., born 2015, was apprehended at almost 10 months old, having lived only in shelters and hotels; she was developmentally delayed and later diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder, needs the mother had not recognized. The mother had a long history with child welfare agencies, chronic instability, repeated misrepresentations of her identity, occupation and whereabouts, refused mental health assessment, and left Canada, not seeing the child since January 31, 2017.
rule: On a Rule 16 summary judgment motion the moving party must show no genuine issue for trial; the responding party must set out specific facts showing a triable issue (CAS of Toronto v. T.(K.), 2000 CanLII 20578). 'No genuine issue for trial exists where there is no realistic possibility of an outcome other than that sought by the applicant' (CAS of Niagara Region v. S.C., 2008 CanLII 52309). Protection grounds under ss. 37(2)(b)(i),(ii) and 37(2)(g) of the Child and Family Services Act.
application: The mother's own June 2016 affidavit conceded instability and untruthfulness; her plan of care was predicated on remaining in Ontario, which no longer applied. The child's significant unmet needs at apprehension and the mother's departure left no realistic alternative outcome. The hearsay clerk affidavit could not raise a triable issue.
conclusion: The court found no genuine issue requiring a trial and made the protection findings under ss. 37(2)(b)(i),(ii) and 37(2)(g).

issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial for a disposition other than crown wardship?
facts: After apprehension the mother rebuffed the Society's supports, attended access sporadically, then disappeared for extended periods, relocating to Dubai. She provided no verified travel documents, no viable plan, and no kin options. The child had been in care over two years and required substantial ongoing support.
rule: Child protection timelines are paramount; a child's need for permanency planning must be respected, with a one-year statutory limit for children under six under clause 70(1)(a) of the Act. The parent's evidence must disclose an arguable notion of better prospects than at removal (CCAS of Toronto v. G.O., 2014 ONCJ 523).
application: The only proposed trial witness was the law clerk, whose information-and-belief evidence was insufficient. The mother offered no direct or reliable evidence of an improved situation, and no alternative disposition was realistically available given the timelines and permanency needs.
conclusion: The court found no genuine issue requiring a trial for any disposition other than crown wardship.

issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to whether the mother should have access to the crown ward?
facts: The mother had not seen the child since January 31, 2017 and had ceased residing in Canada. Her counsel made no submissions on access.
rule: Section 59(2.1) of the Child and Family Services Act creates a presumption against access to a crown ward; the person seeking access must prove the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and that access will not impair the child's future opportunities for adoption.
application: With no submissions and no evidence that the relationship was beneficial and meaningful or that access would not impair adoption prospects, the presumption against access was not displaced.
conclusion: The court found no genuine issue requiring a trial on access; crown wardship with no access was ordered for the purpose of adoption.

issue: Does the statement of claim disclose a reasonable cause of action for misfeasance in public office?
facts: Mr. Budgell, after losing a wrongful dismissal grievance and multiple Labour Relations Board and judicial review proceedings, sued the Attorney General, the Minister of Labour and the Crown alleging that a 1996 statutory-revision change to s. 13 of the Labour Relations Code (replacing 'prima facie' with 'sufficient evidence that the contravention has apparently occurred') was surreptitious and illegal and that ministers deceptively covered it up, causing him to lose his career.
rule: Under Rule 19(24)(a) and Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, a claim is struck only where, assuming the pleaded facts true, it is plain and obvious it discloses no reasonable cause of action. Pleadings must set out the material facts constituting each element of a recognized cause of action (Rule 19(1); Delaney; Alford). Misfeasance in public office (Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse, 2003 SCC 69) requires deliberate unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions and awareness the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff, plus causation and compensable injury. Lawmakers and officials enforcing legislation are not liable in damages for the effects of legislation (Welbridge Holdings v. Winnipeg; Guimond v. Quebec (A.G.)); the Crown is not vicariously liable for the Board's functionaries (Speckling v. Kearney).
application: The employer, union and Board alleged to have caused harm were not made parties; the Crown is not vicariously liable for the Board's functionaries. Lawmakers and officials cannot be liable in damages for enacting or implementing legislation, so even a pleading of invalidity could not ground a claim. Critically, the statement of claim failed to plead the material facts establishing the two essential elements of misfeasance in public office; the bare assertion of an 'unlawful exercise of statutory powers' was unsupported by material facts, as in A.L. v. Ontario.
conclusion: The pleadings disclose no reasonable claim; struck under Rule 19(24)(a).

issue: Are the pleadings unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious?
facts: The statement of claim mixed allegations against ministers, ministry staff, the Board's adjudicators, the union and employer, without clearly identifying who was at fault or which acts founded the claim.
rule: Rule 19(24)(b); Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress (1999) — pleadings are irrelevant/embarrassing where so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is pleaded, and unnecessary or vexatious where they do not establish a cause of action or advance a claim known in law.
application: The pleadings were confusing as to who was at fault and why, and did not establish any recognized cause of action, rendering them irrelevant, embarrassing, unnecessary and vexatious.
conclusion: The pleadings are also liable to be struck under Rule 19(24)(b).

issue: Does the action constitute an abuse of process or an impermissible collateral attack on the administrative and judicial review process?
facts: Mr. Budgell had already litigated his fair-representation complaint through the Board, reconsideration panels, two judicial review petitions and the Court of Appeal, all unsuccessfully, and now sought compensatory damages for loss of career on issues that were or could have been raised in those proceedings.
rule: Rule 19(24)(d); Young v. Borzoni, 2007 BCCA 16 (abuse of process where court used unfairly/for improper purpose or through multiple successive related proceedings). A party cannot obtain by civil action a remedy available through the statutory judicial review process; such evasion is a prohibited collateral attack (Berscheid v. Ensign; R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines).
application: Although the court accepted Mr. Budgell acted sincerely and not dishonestly, he was seeking substantially the same relief and raising the same or available issues (including the proper s. 13 test) as in the earlier Board and judicial review proceedings. This was another in a series of multiple successive related proceedings amounting to a collateral attack.
conclusion: The action is an abuse of the process of the court under Rule 19(24)(d).

issue: Were the statements in Mr. Ayoub's complaint to the Quebec Bar Association defamatory, wrongful, and productive of compensable damages?
facts: After Mr. Avrith described himself in Small Claims Court as the 'administrator' of Phillip Avrith Investments Inc., Mr. Ayoub filed a written complaint with the Syndic of the Quebec Bar alleging Mr. Avrith had falsely presented himself as an administrator. The Syndic, noting Mr. Avrith was the duly authorized representative and signatory of the lease, found he had not lied and closed the file. The complaint was confidential and known only to the parties and the Syndic.
rule: An action in defamation rests on the ordinary rules of civil liability under art. 1457 C.c.Q.; the plaintiff must prove injury, fault and a causal link. Whether remarks are defamatory is assessed objectively — whether an ordinary person would believe the remarks brought discredit on the person's reputation (Prud'homme v. Prud'homme, 2002 SCC 85). Fault may be malicious or merely negligent; a scandalmonger who makes unfavourable statements without valid reason may be liable. Compensatory damages are evaluated on the multi-factor criteria including gravity, extent of dissemination and effect on the victim (Hill; Fabien; Gagné c. Galand). Punitive damages require an intentional and illicit interference under s. 49 of the Quebec Charter.
application: The Court found the complaint's allegation impugning Mr. Avrith's honesty was defamatory. Since 'administrator' in English properly describes a manager, Mr. Avrith's statement was not false, and there was no valid reason for the complaint, so Mr. Ayoub's conduct was unjustified though not malicious. However, the complaint was confidential with no publicity or diffusion; Mr. Avrith remained a member in good standing of the Bar and showed no actual effect on his reputation. He therefore established no injury and no compensable damages, and there was no intentional illicit violation warranting punitive damages.
conclusion: Although the complaint was defamatory and unjustified, Mr. Avrith proved no damages; no compensation was awarded.

issue: Were Mr. Ayoub's statements in Small Claims Court that Mr. Avrith had lied defamatory, wrongful, and productive of compensable damages?
facts: At the February 19, 2007 Small Claims hearing, Mr. Avrith himself first raised the Bar complaint while seeking a postponement, telling the judge Mr. Ayoub had accused him of being a liar. In response to the judge's questions, Mr. Ayoub explained that Mr. Avrith had presented himself as an administrator and 'lied to the judge.' The courtroom was said to be full of unidentified litigants awaiting their own cases.
rule: Defamation arising in the course of judicial proceedings requires proof of five elements (Terreault c. Bigras, 2005 QCCA 1243; Gagné c. Galland, 2008 QCCS 5083): that the allegations are defamatory, false, not pertinent to the litigation, made without reasonable motive, and malicious or recklessly so. Witnesses must be able to speak freely without fear of subsequent liability, and unrepresented litigants in Small Claims Court are held to a lower standard, requiring particularly convincing evidence of malice or malicious recklessness.
application: It was Mr. Avrith, not Mr. Ayoub, who introduced the subject; Mr. Ayoub, whose mother tongue was not English, merely responded to the Court's questions using the same 'lied' terminology Mr. Avrith had used. He could reasonably believe the judge wanted to understand the Bar issue, and was defending himself against a legally trained opponent. No malice or malicious recklessness was shown. In any event there was no evidence identifying anyone in the courtroom or showing any impact on Mr. Avrith's employment, revenue or reputation.
conclusion: Mr. Ayoub committed no wrongful act during the hearing, and no damages were established; the claim failed.

issue: On a summary judgment motion in a Status Review application, is there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to whether the child continues to be in need of protection?
facts: The Society had been involved with the family since 2010 based on serious domestic violence by the father N.M. against the mother R.M. Over several years N.M. was convicted of assaults, breached probation and restraining terms, failed to complete the PAR domestic-violence program, showed borderline intellectual functioning and emotional volatility, made rambling and incoherent communications, was inconsistent in access, undermined the mother during visits, and failed to advance a clear plan of care. The mother had ended the relationship and was competently caring for G.M. N.M.'s affidavit did not address the ongoing concerns.
rule: Under s. 64-65 of the Child and Family Services Act and Catholic Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto v. M.(C.), [1994] S.C.J. No. 37, a Status Review involves a two-part test: (1) whether the child continues to require a court order for protection, and (2) the child's best interests (ss. 37(3)-(4)). On summary judgment under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules and Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, the court grants final judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; the responding party must put its best foot forward with specific facts.
application: The Court found no ongoing protection concern regarding R.M., who was meeting all of G.M.'s needs. However, it found numerous persisting concerns regarding N.M.: unaddressed history of domestic violence and abusive attitudes, cognitive and emotional instability, unreliable access, undermining conduct toward the mother during visits, inability to cooperate with the Society, and no viable plan of care. N.M.'s affidavit merely minimized these concerns and offered bald assertions, providing no material facts giving his case a real chance of success. The Court could make the necessary findings on the affidavit record without the enhanced fact-finding powers.
conclusion: No genuine issue requiring a trial; the Court found G.M. continues to be in need of protection because of the ongoing concerns respecting N.M.

issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial regarding the placement and access terms in G.M.'s best interests?
facts: R.M. had been G.M.'s primary caregiver since birth, addressed her historical concerns, and cared competently for him. N.M. had never been a primary caregiver, missed numerous visits, made unsettling comments to the child about coming to live with him, disparaged the mother's care, and had no consistent plan. G.M. showed anxiety and oppositional behaviour after visits.
rule: Section 57.1 of the CFSA permits a custody order to a non-foster person where it is in the child's best interests; s. 58 governs access; best interests are assessed under s. 37(3). The child-centred focus requires permanency planning within a timeframe sensitive to the child's needs (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. R.H.).
application: The evidence clearly supported granting R.M. sole custody under s. 57.1, as she was meeting all of G.M.'s needs and the child had a close, loving relationship with her. Placement with N.M. would not be in G.M.'s best interests given the serious protection concerns and N.M.'s never having been a caregiver. Access with N.M. was found contrary to G.M.'s best interests because the negatives (undermining the placement, inconsistency, anxiety-inducing comments) far outweighed the positives, and supervised access was not practicable long-term.
conclusion: No trial required; sole custody granted to R.M. under s. 57.1 with no access to N.M. except one goodbye visit; the supervision order was terminated.

issue: Is a trial required to determine whether a restraining order should issue against N.M.?
facts: N.M. had a longstanding history of domestic violence, emotional abuse and intimidation of R.M., convictions for assault, breaches of no-contact terms, cognitive/psychological concerns, and had told G.M. he would take him by force. The Society's involvement, which had buffered R.M., was ending.
rule: Section 57.1(3) of the CFSA allows a restraining order in accordance with s. 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act where the applicant has reasonable grounds to fear for his/her safety or that of a child in lawful custody; guidance in Children's Aid Society of Halton Region v. C.(C.L.) requires evidence of threats, assault, stalking or harassment and consideration of alternative protections.
application: The Court found R.M. had reasonable grounds to fear for her own and G.M.'s safety given the history of violence, breaches of no-contact orders, N.M.'s emotional instability and his threat to take the child by force. With the Society's protective involvement ending, no adequate alternative protection existed.
conclusion: No trial required; a restraining order issued against N.M. restraining contact and prohibiting him from coming within 100 metres of specified locations.

issue: In the children's best interests, should custody be granted to the father, to the mother, or remain shared?
facts: The parties, Pakistani citizens living in Montreal, agreed through mediation in 2001 to a 50/50 shared custody of their two children. In 2002 the mother repudiated the agreement and sought full custody, alleging she had left the children only because of daycare costs and denying youth-protection allegations, while the father sought custody. Youth protection had intervened, the children were entrusted to the father, and both parents signed voluntary measures recognizing the children's security or development was endangered by the mother leaving them alone, yelling and using physical discipline. The children repeatedly expressed a wish to live with their father.
rule: Under s. 16(8),(9),(10) of the Divorce Act and arts. 32, 33, 514, 599, 600, 604, 605, 612 C.C.Q., the sole criterion is the best interests of the child, not parental interests; a prior consent is strong evidence that each parent found it adequate. Gordon v. Goertz sets a two-stage inquiry (material change, then fresh best-interests inquiry); Young v. Young and W.(V.) v. S.(D.) confirm the child's-interest focus.
application: The Court found the earlier mediated agreement strong proof that both are loving, capable parents and that shared custody served the children. It found the mother exaggerated abuse, coached and pressured the children to take sides, and offered no compelling best-interests reason to abandon shared custody. It found the father credible, his parental capacity uncontested, and no evidence of alienation or bad faith. Given the impending loss of legal status in Canada, shared custody was no longer workable.
conclusion: Custody of both children was granted to the father, with extensive defined access rights to the mother; the mother's motion for full custody was dismissed.

issue: Should the father be permitted to leave Canada and take the children to Pakistan?
facts: The father's work permit, which allowed the family to remain legally in Canada, expired November 30, 2002 and would not be renewed after he lost his job; the family could not stay legally, could not access schooling or health insurance, and their immigration file through Mexico remained pending. Pakistan was the only country where the father could work legally, obtain family support, and monitor the son's latent tuberculosis, and the mother's family also lived there. The father undertook to return to Canada and to keep the mother on the immigration file, and had sought the Court's permission as required.
rule: Section 16(6),(7) of the Divorce Act permits the Court to impose terms and conditions, including notice of a change of the child's place of residence; the determining criterion remains the child's best interests (Gordon v. Goertz), the custodial parent having the right to determine the child's residence (W.(V.) v. S.(D.)).
application: The Court found no bad faith or sinister intent by the father, who had properly asked permission to relocate. Given the family's loss of legal status and the practical impossibility of remaining in Quebec, and the father's undertakings to facilitate the mother's contact and to keep her on the immigration file, relocation with the children served their best interests.
conclusion: The father was permitted, if need be, to return to Pakistan with the children; the mother and her counsel were ordered to remit the children's identity documents and passports by November 26, 2002.

issue: Should the perception of child support and spousal alimony and arrears be suspended?
facts: The father had lost his employment, faced departure from Canada, and moved to suspend perception of child support, spousal alimony, and all arrears, referring cancellation and future fixation to the trial judge on the merits.
rule: Under s. 17 of the Divorce Act and arts. 514, 605 C.C.Q., support may be varied or suspended in light of changed means, needs and circumstances, subject to the best interests of the children.
application: Given the parties' changed financial situation and the father's loss of income and imminent departure, the Court suspended perception pending the divorce on the merits and referred the questions of cancellation of arrears and fixation of support to the trial judge, reserving the parties' right to file further provisional motions.
conclusion: Perception of child support, spousal alimony and all arrears was suspended; cancellation of arrears and fixation of support were referred to the judge hearing the divorce on the merits.

issue: Was the security and development of the six children compromised under s. 38 of the Youth Protection Act?
facts: The parents, of Russian origin, immigrated to Canada from Slovakia in June 2002 with their six children (aged 4 to 15). The father regularly beat the mother, especially after drinking, and struck the children, notably A..., to discipline them, sometimes with a stick, and threatened to kill them. On 6 February 2003 he pushed and struck the mother when she wanted to take two sons to hospital following a circumcision performed by rabbis, and threatened her with death. The father, through counsel, admitted the children's situation of compromise under paragraphs g) and e) of s. 38. The Director declared it had no evidence on the ground of lack of appropriate care (para. c).
rule: Section 38 of the Youth Protection Act sets out the grounds on which a child's security or development is deemed compromised, including physical ill-treatment (para. e) and serious risk from a parent's conduct/behaviour (para. g).
application: The Tribunal accepted the evidence of the four eldest children and the mother's earlier statements describing physical abuse and threats by the father, as well as the father's own admission of compromise under paragraphs e) and g). The psychological assessment did not exclude impulsive and aggressive reactions toward the family. The Director offered no evidence on the lack-of-care ground, so that ground was not retained.
conclusion: The Tribunal declared that the security and development of the children were in danger (compromised) under s. 38.

issue: What measures should be ordered under s. 91 to end the situation of compromise?
facts: On 27 August 2003 the Director recommended returning the children to both parents, the father's active participation in an anger management program, family access to the Family Preservation Program, individual psychological therapy for both parents, and social follow-up for one year. The psychological report recommended family reunification, finding the father was not a dangerous or abusive profile and could parent adequately with therapeutic help, taking account of migratory/acculturation stress. The father, mother and children all consented to the proposed measures.
rule: Section 91 of the Youth Protection Act empowers the Tribunal, once compromise is established, to order the measures required to put an end to the situation and protect the child, guided by the child's interest.
application: Given the psychological recommendation of reunification, the strong emotional and solidarity bonds within the family, the children's wish for their father's return, and the consent of all parties, the Tribunal entrusted the children to both parents subject to protective conditions: no exposure to violence, no physical discipline, participation in an anger management program, individual psychological therapy, medical follow-up, the Family Preservation Program, full cooperation with the DYP, and aid/counsel/assistance, all for one year.
conclusion: The Tribunal entrusted the children to their parents with a suite of supervisory and therapeutic measures for one year, entrusting oversight to the Ville Marie Child and Youth Protection Centre Director.

issue: Should the mother's trial retraction of her earlier denunciations be accepted?
facts: The mother initially denounced the father's violence to police, DYP workers, JIAS workers and immigration officials, admitted all allegations at the provisional-measures hearing, and said she wanted a divorce and custody. At trial on 20 June she recanted, claiming she had denounced him only because she panicked over the children's suffering after their circumcision by rabbis rather than by a doctor.
rule: The trier of fact assesses credibility and may prefer earlier consistent statements over a later retraction where the retraction appears motivated by external considerations.
application: The Tribunal found the mother retracted solely because she wanted her husband home, as she could not manage six children alone and the children still loved and missed their father. It therefore rejected the trial retraction and retained her prior statements made to various persons at different times.
conclusion: The retraction was not accepted; the earlier statements were retained as reliable.

issue: What weight should be given to children's expressed refusal of contact where parental alienation is present?
facts: E. and G., adopted children aged 11 and 13, saw their father regularly and happily until May 1998 (holiday ski photos showed them cheerful), after which they categorically refused to see or speak to him, not even answering the dedicated phone line installed for them. The court-appointed psychologist Dr. Worenklein concluded this was a clear case of parental alienation, meeting nearly all of Dr. Gardner's criteria, with the mother tending to devalue the father despite claiming to want the relationship maintained.
rule: Under s. 16(8) of the Divorce Act the court considers only the best interests of the child, and under s. 16(10) it applies the maximum-contact principle. Article 33 C.c.Q. requires decisions to be made in the child's interest and respect of rights. Jurisprudence (Droit de la famille — 2829; — 1485; — 1242) holds that a child's expressed wish is an important factor, but where there is undue influence of a parent bordering on parental alienation, the court must assess the child's interest beyond the expressed wish.
application: The court accepted Dr. Worenklein's uncontradicted finding of parental alienation, reinforced by the children's testimony. Applying the cited case law, the court held that the children's refusal did not reflect their genuine best interests but resulted from the parental conflict and the mother's insufficiently exercised authority. The children needed to see their father regularly and frequently and had to understand they had no choice.
conclusion: The children's stated refusal was overridden; the court looked beyond it to their true best interests, which required restoring the relationship with the father.

issue: Should the court grant access to the father and order the family to undergo therapy in the children's best interests?
facts: Both parents now wanted regular, frequent access, and both, along with the children, undertook to participate in a therapeutic process. Dr. Worenklein recommended frequent access in the former family home and family therapy at the Jewish General Hospital's Multi-Family Therapy Unit, warning that a change of custody could be considered if the situation was not normalized. A therapist, Mme L.G., specialized in parental alienation, agreed to conduct the follow-up.
rule: Section 16 of the Divorce Act and art. 33 C.c.Q. authorize access orders in the child's best interests; the court may order therapeutic measures and dispense with the oath and notice requirements (arts. 418, 419 C.p.c.) for a witness therapist.
application: Finding the children's psychological stability already shaken and the mother now sincerely willing to remedy the situation, the court set a detailed access schedule (Tuesdays, Sundays, holidays), ordered the mother to facilitate and not undermine access, took note of the parents' undertakings, and mandated a ten-week therapeutic follow-up with Mme L.G., dispensing her from oath and notice under arts. 418–419 C.p.c.
conclusion: The motion for access was allowed; access rights were granted to the father and a ten-week family therapeutic process was ordered.

issue: Did the operators of an online message board 'publish' the allegedly defamatory words posted by another user?
facts: Roger Smith (a.k.a. 'Peter O'Donnell') posted the impugned words on Free Dominion, a conservative message board moderated and administered by Connie and Mark Fournier. The Fourniers did not write, edit or endorse the post but declined to remove it after Dr. Baglow complained. They argued that, like a content-neutral hyperlink, provision of message-board software should not amount to publication, and relied on Crookes v. Newton and U.S./U.K. statutory immunities.
rule: Publication requires that the defendant, by any act, conveyed defamatory meaning to a third party who received it (Crookes v. Newton, 2011 SCC 47; McNichol v. Grandy). In Crookes a mere hyperlink was held not to be publication because it is content neutral and exerts no control over content. Carter v. B.C. Federation of Foster Parents Association, 2005 BCCA 398, held a forum operator with knowledge and control could be a publisher.
application: The Court held Crookes was distinguishable — 'apples to oranges'. A message board exists precisely to provide content; the Fourniers were not passive bystanders but posted themselves, set terms of service, and had the ability to delete posts and ban users. Given that nearly all users posted anonymously, treating operators as non-publishers would leave plaintiffs with no way to correct reputational harm and would upset the balance the law of defamation strikes. Canadian legislatures have not enacted the U.S./U.K. immunity schemes.
conclusion: The impugned words were published by both the Fourniers and Mr. Smith.

issue: Were the impugned words defamatory of the plaintiff given the political-blog context?
facts: The post referred to 'Dr. Dawg', the plaintiff's pseudonym, as 'one of the Taliban's more vocal supporters', published while Canadian forces were at war with the Taliban. Dr. Baglow's identity as Dr. Dawg was widely known and had been linked to his real name repeatedly, including on Free Dominion. The defendants and the CCLA argued the rough-and-tumble, hyper-partisan blog context meant a reasonable reader would not think less of him.
rule: A plaintiff must prove the words (1) refer to the plaintiff, (2) were published, and (3) are defamatory, i.e. would tend to lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61). This is a low threshold (WIC Radio v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40). Meaning is assessed contextually including audience and manner of presentation (Crookes).
application: Reference and publication were established. Although context on partisan blogs is important, the Court rejected the notion that little could ever be defamatory in that medium; in WIC Radio even 'shock-jock' statements were defamatory. Expert evidence showed lurkers' views were unknowable and anonymous online actors could gain credibility over time. The impugned words nearly stood alone, with no prior Free Dominion debate on Khadr to supply context. The words were reasonably capable of meaning the plaintiff supported an Islamist terrorist organization and thereby tended to lower his reputation.
conclusion: The plaintiff established all three elements; the words were defamatory.

issue: Did the defence of fair comment apply?
facts: The words concerned the well-known Omar Khadr controversy, on which public opinion was split and about which Dr. Baglow had written extensively, taking the position that Khadr should be repatriated. Smith honestly believed that supporting Khadr amounted to supporting the Taliban. The post appeared in a subforum 'Opinions are Like Clymers' and was a rambling political rant.
rule: Fair comment requires: (1) the comment is on a matter of public interest; (2) it is based on fact; (3) it is recognizable as comment (which may include inferences of fact); and (4) any person could honestly express that opinion on the proved facts (WIC Radio v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Grant v. Torstar). Words appearing factual may, in pith and substance and context, be comment.
application: Public interest was easily met (the Khadr case). The factual substratum — Khadr's detention and Dr. Baglow's notorious pro-repatriation, anti-mission views — was sufficiently known. The context (a conservative opinion forum, an 'Opinions' subforum, a rambling rant, and the hyperbolic phrase 'one of the Taliban's more vocal supporters') showed the words were recognizable comment, not fact. Applying the honest-belief test (not a reasonableness test), a person could honestly hold the view that support for Khadr amounted to support for the Taliban, as Smith and others in fact did.
conclusion: The defence of fair comment was established.

issue: Was the fair comment defence defeated by express malice?
facts: Malice was alleged only against the Fourniers, based on their refusal to retract, two mocking responsive posts ('FD gets libel notice…' and 'John Baglow puts on his frilliest internet dress'), and their spoliation allegations.
rule: Fair comment is defeated only if the plaintiff proves malice was the dominant motive for the publication (Simpson v. Mair, 2004 BCSC 754; WIC Radio). Ill will or anger alone does not establish malice where the dominant purpose is a proper one.
application: The Fourniers investigated the complaint and gave non-malicious reasons for leaving the post up (the Ms. Mew sock-puppet, the ongoing debate, the public-interest nature, Dr. Baglow's own similar conduct). The responsive posts were reactions to the sock-puppet and were no harsher than Dr. Baglow's own commentary about them. Their spoliation suspicions were understandable given the disappearance of the old comments. None of this showed malice as the dominant motive. The related spoliation claim itself failed on the evidence.
conclusion: Malice was not proven; the fair comment defence stood and the action was dismissed.

issue: Should leave be granted to amend the claim to attack the validity of the expropriation despite s. 51 of the Expropriation Act?
facts: GVTA expropriated about 89 acres in Maple Ridge for the Golden Ears Bridge; the expropriation notice was filed June 21, 2005 and title vested about June 29, 2005. Camp accepted roughly $9 million in advance payments and in 2006 sued only for enhanced statutory compensation. Nearly four years after vesting Camp sought to amend to allege the taking was ultra vires and void because the notice misstated the true purpose and excess land was taken.
