rule: Amendments/pleadings are struck only where it is 'plain and obvious' the claim cannot succeed (Hunt v. T&N plc; Extra Gift Exchange; Dempsey v. Envision). Section 51(1) of the Expropriation Act provides that legal proceedings to challenge the validity of an expropriation must not be brought after land vests under s. 23, and s. 51(2) (30-day judicial review window) is subject to s. 51(1) (Rella v. Village of Montrose; Seaside Acres; Roadmaster). Adding a new cause of action after a limitation period has expired is inappropriate (City Construction Co. v. Salmon's Transfer).
application: The court found the notice stated the purpose as the Golden Ears Bridge Project Transportation System constituting a linear development; the whole/partial taking question had been canvassed between the parties beforehand. The 'no notice' and tax-sale authorities (Costello, Van Kam, Gray) did not assist Camp, and following Gray/McLachlin J.A., the legislative scheme evinces an intent that an expropriation stand after vesting notwithstanding defects. Since vesting occurred nearly four years earlier, s. 51(1) is a complete answer and any validity challenge is bound to fail; the expropriated party retains statutory compensation as redress.
conclusion: Leave to amend to challenge the validity of the expropriation was refused; those amendments raise an issue bound to fail.

issue: Are the validity amendments barred as inconsistent with the original pleading?
facts: The original statement of claim asserted the land had been expropriated and sought additional statutory compensation for an inadequate advance payment; Camp accepted the payments and stood by while the bridge was built. The proposed amendment recharacterized the taking as merely 'purported' and void.
rule: Rule 19(7) prohibits pleading a claim inconsistent with a previous pleading, subject to the right to plead alternatively (R. 19(8); Gabbs v. Bouwhuis). More significantly, the substantive law of election applies: where a person has, with full knowledge, done an unequivocal act choosing one of two inconsistent rights, he cannot later pursue the other (United Australia v. Barclays Bank; M.E.P.C. Canadian Properties v. The Queen; Molander v. Cranbrook; Erickson v. Kamloops).
application: By accepting advance payments, commencing an action for enhanced compensation within the Act's time limits, and standing by during construction, Camp made an unequivocal election to treat the expropriation as valid. Asserting the taking is now void is inconsistent and precluded by the substantive law of expropriation election, distinguishable from Gabbs where amendments were merely alternate theories on the same facts.
conclusion: The validity amendments were also impermissible as inconsistent with the position on which the action was commenced.

issue: Should leave be granted to amend to allege bad faith and breach of s. 21, and are those claims barred?
facts: Camp sought to add that GVTA failed to offer surplus land back to it as required by s. 21 of the Act, breaching a statutory duty on or before June 28, 2007, and acted in bad faith. GVTA argued no cause of action, statute-bar, and that it had not 'disposed' of the property.
rule: The 'plain and obvious' test governs (Hunt). Under the Limitation Act, 'injury to property' in s. 3(2)(a) means physical harm by external force (410727 B.C. Ltd. v. Dayhu Investments); pure economic loss falls under the six-year period in s. 3(5) (Alberni District Credit Union; Armstrong v. West Vancouver). Breach of statutory duty is a recognized tort.
application: The claim was for economic loss, so the applicable period was six years and had not expired. Camp pleaded breach of the statutory duty in s. 21, a recognized cause of action; whether a separate cause of action is needed, whether the remedy is confined to s. 21, and the meaning of 'disposed' are arguable matters properly resolved on the pleadings, not plain and obvious losers.
conclusion: Leave to amend to plead breach of s. 21 and related bad faith was granted (amendments similar to proposed paragraphs 48-52 allowed).

issue: Was it in the best interests of the children to move with their mother to Montréal?
facts: The applicant mother, the children's primary caregiver, wished to relocate the three young children (ages 8, 7 and 5) to Montréal, where her family resided, offering free accommodation and better employment and schooling prospects. The children had lived in Thornhill all their lives, attended school there, had their synagogue and most of the father's extended family in the area, and had a strong and growing relationship with their father through a well-established access regime.
rule: On a mobility application the test is the best interests of the child under s. 16(8) of the Divorce Act, applying the framework in Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27: where there is a material change, the court conducts a fresh best-interests inquiry considering, among other factors, the existing custody and access arrangements, the desirability of maximizing contact with both parents, the child's views, the reason for moving (only where relevant to parenting ability), and the disruption from a change in custody or from removal from family, school and community.
application: The court found there was no final order so the threshold step did not apply, and proceeded to weigh the Gordon v. Goertz factors. A move to Montréal would effectively cut the children off from frequent contact with their father, from whom they derived great benefit, and the applicant's proposed bi-weekly driving plan was unrealistic and would alienate the children. The children wished to see both parents (Daniel wished to see more of his father); the mother's reason for moving (financial support from her father) did not establish she could not provide adequately in Ontario; and the move would remove the children from their family, schools, friends, synagogue and community.
conclusion: The court held it was not in the children's best interests to move to Montréal; they should remain in the Thornhill area.

issue: Which parent's home should serve as the children's primary residence and what custody/access arrangement best serves the children?
facts: Both parents sought sole custody. The mother was consumed by hatred and resentment toward the father, hired a private investigator, hacked his computer, made slanderous statements to the Children's Lawyer and tried to sabotage his new relationship. The father, though initially immature, had stabilized with a committed partner (Ms. March) and his parents' support; the Children's Lawyer found the children's relationship with the father stronger and their routine more stable in his home. The three children had special needs requiring substantial attention and homework help.
rule: Custody is determined under s. 16 of the Divorce Act by reference solely to the best interests of the child; s. 24(2) of the Children's Law Reform Act provides a useful checklist including love and emotional ties, the child's views, stability of the home, each parent's ability and willingness to provide guidance, education, necessaries and to meet special needs, the parties' plans, the permanence and stability of each family unit, and the blood relationship.
application: Applying the checklist, the court found the extended-family factor even but the children looked first to the father for affection and their relationship with the mother was more distant. The father's household, aided by Ms. March and his parents, provided more stable routine, discipline, and consistent help with homework and David's learning disability, whereas the mother's home was more chaotic and she was preoccupied by the litigation. The mother's household lacked permanence (no employment, dependent on gifts). Shared custody could not succeed given the mother's persistent animosity and attempts to undermine the father. The children needed to continue seeing their mother substantially, achieved through alternate-weekend and weekly access.
conclusion: The court ordered joint custody with daily care and control to the father as primary residence, education/medical/dental decision-making to the father, and a defined access schedule for the mother including alternate weekends, weekly evenings, alternating holidays and Jewish High Holidays, and four summer weeks.

issue: Was judicial review by way of prohibition available to prevent a Human Rights Act Board of Inquiry from proceeding with its hearing?
facts: The Human Rights Commission recommended, and the Minister of Labour appointed, a Board of Inquiry to investigate Attis' complaint that School District 15 had condoned the anti-Jewish/discriminatory conduct of teacher Malcolm Ross. Before the Board's first hearing, the School Board and the Teachers' Federation obtained a stay and applied for judicial review to prohibit the inquiry; Miller, J. quashed the Minister's order.
rule: Prohibition may issue against a tribunal where there is a clear question of law, not dependent on particular facts, upon which the tribunal's jurisdiction depends (Bell v. Ontario Human Rights Commission, [1971] S.C.R. 756; Re CIP Paper Products (1978) 87 D.L.R. (3d) 609; R. v. Tottenham & District Rent Tribunal, [1957] 1 Q.B. 103). Courts must exercise curial deference and not usurp a tribunal's statutory functions (C.U.P.E. v. N.B. Liquor, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227), but have a duty to intervene where a tribunal acts without jurisdiction.
application: The Court held the three substantive grounds (interpretation of s.5, Attis' status, and sufficiency of the complaint) were questions of law that could be decided on the uncontested affidavit facts without determining the merits. Miller, J. had not decided the merits but had identified genuine legal questions. The Teachers' Federation had not acquiesced in the Board's jurisdiction, having sought party status and immediately applied for review; unlike Re Colonial Coach Lines, there was no high-handed conduct.
conclusion: Judicial review by prohibition was available; the first-instance judge properly exercised his jurisdiction to entertain the applications.

issue: Does subsection 5(1) of the Human Rights Act cover education provided by the New Brunswick public school system?
facts: Attis complained that the public school board's conduct deprived Jewish and other minority students of equal opportunity within the educational system provided as a service to the public. Miller, J. had held that school facilities and education programs are not 'accommodation, services and facilities' under s.5.
rule: Human rights legislation is quasi-constitutional and must be given a fair, large and liberal, purposive interpretation (Insurance Corp. of B.C. v. Heerspink, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 145; Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Simpsons-Sears, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536; Robichaud v. Canada, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 84; s.17 Interpretation Act). A service offered to the public need not be offered to all members of the public, and eligibility criteria do not remove it from human rights scrutiny (Re Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission and Government of Saskatchewan (1988) 52 D.L.R. (4th) 253).
application: The Court found the case law unsettled (Winnipeg School Division v. MacArthur declining coverage vs. Schmidt v. Calgary Board of Education and Rawala v. DeVry favouring it) but adopted the broad purposive approach. A narrow reading would allow a public school to refuse entry to Jewish, Indigenous or male children without contravening the Act — an absurd result. Public education under the Schools Act is a service provided to a client group meeting eligibility requirements and thus falls within s.5(1).
conclusion: Public education in New Brunswick is within the purview of subsection 5(1); Miller, J. erred on this point.

issue: Did David Attis have status as a 'person claiming to be aggrieved' and hence a valid complainant?
facts: Attis is a Jewish parent with three children enrolled in District 15. Neither he nor his children had direct contact with Ross as their teacher. Miller, J. suggested Attis was not an aggrieved party and was purporting to speak for a group.
rule: Section 17 of the Human Rights Act allows 'any person claiming to be aggrieved' to file a written complaint; the phrase is to be read broadly, especially at a preliminary stage. Whether someone is a 'victim' of a discriminatory practice is almost wholly a question of fact, looking to effects rather than intent, and may extend beyond the direct target (Re Singh (1988) 86 N.R. 69).
application: The statute speaks of a 'person claiming to be aggrieved', not an established aggrieved party; it is for the Commission and Board to assess merit. Attis filed a written complaint on the prescribed form as a parent of enrolled children. The Court declined to treat this as a prohibited representative/group action, since the Minister conceded no group-action rules apply and Attis asserted his complaint concerned discrimination against him and his own children.
conclusion: Attis met the s.17 standard and has status as a complainant.

issue: Was Attis' written complaint sufficiently precise to be a valid complaint under the Act?
facts: Attis' written statement identified himself, his children, the teacher (Ross), the School Board, the alleged conduct (racist/anti-Jewish statements, Holocaust denial, the Board's inaction and failure to condemn), the period (1977–1988) and cited s.5. Miller, J., relying on Mackin v. Judicial Council (N.B.), held it lacked the requisite specificity.
rule: 'Complaint' in s.17 must be interpreted to advance the Act's broad purposes. A valid complaint should contain elements such as identification of complainant and victim, time, location, the nature of the discriminatory practice and the relevant section (Canadian Human Rights Commission v. Bell Canada (1981) 2 C.H.R.R. D/265). The stricter standard for complaints under the Provincial Court Act (Mackin) does not govern the Human Rights Act.
application: The Attis complaint was in writing on the prescribed form and contained most of the essential Bell Canada elements. Any further detail could be obtained by demand for particulars, the Board of Inquiry having conciliation-board procedural powers (s.20(3) HRA; s.66(2) Industrial Relations Act). It is the Board's function, not the reviewing court's, to investigate the merits, and this was not a clear case of the tribunal lacking jurisdiction.
conclusion: The complaint met the statutory requirements of s.17 and was sufficient; Miller, J. erred.

issue: Is E. incapable of consenting to the required care and lodging, so that court authorization is engaged under the Civil Code of Quebec?
facts: E., aged 55, is intellectually handicapped, has chronic diabetes and paranoid schizophrenia. She is under full tutorship to the person and curatorship of property held by the Public Curator. Psychiatrist Dr. Lafontaine concluded she has no understanding of her medical condition or the need for treatment and no capacity to consent to care, lodging or her future; her refusal of placement is a direct consequence of her mother's psychotic domination ('folie à deux').
rule: Arts. 11, 12, 15, 16 and 23 C.C.Q.: no one may be made to undergo care without consent; where a person of full age is incapable, consent is given by the mandatary, tutor or curator; court authorization is necessary where an incapable person of full age categorically refuses care required by their state of health. The notion of 'care' includes the choice and supervision of lodging (CSSS Rimouski-Neigettes c. T.C., 2010 QCCA 143; CHUQ c. L.R., J.E. 2000-1984 (C.A.)).
application: The medical and psycho-social evidence established that E. does not understand her condition, cannot manage her medication or diet, and her health and safety are endangered living with her mother. She strongly opposes placement, so although the Public Curator could consent, the Court held it must intervene where the person manifests firm opposition, and authorization under art. 16 was engaged.
conclusion: E. is incapable of giving a valid consent and, because she categorically refuses the care/lodging her health requires, the matter falls within the Court's authorization jurisdiction under arts. 11–16 C.C.Q.

issue: Is placement of E. in a lodging facility, against her wishes and separated from her mother, in her best interest?
facts: E. thrived medically after being removed to a Ressource Intermédiaire (controlled diet, stable glucose, medication), whereas in her mother's care she was hospitalized with pneumonia, poorly controlled diabetes and kidney problems, and suffered physical and verbal abuse. E. nonetheless wishes to return home, largely to prevent her elderly mother from moving to Israel and to avoid being alone; the mother wants E. back mainly for her own comfort.
rule: Art. 12 C.C.Q.: a person consenting for another must act in the sole interest of that person, taking account of any wishes expressed; the court's paramount role is to decide in the person's best interest.
application: The Court found it is in E.'s best interest to stop living with her mother, whose dominance operated for the mother's benefit rather than E.'s well-being; a break in cohabitation plus controls to reduce the mother's dominance were necessary. Yet total separation would annihilate a life-long relationship both need, so protective measures had to be balanced against maintaining contact.
conclusion: Continued placement outside the mother's home is in E.'s best interest, but must be accompanied by preserved and progressively improved mother-daughter contact rather than near-total separation.

issue: Should the Court grant a permanent three-year lodging order with the strict contact limits proposed, or defer pending a progressive 'exit plan'?
facts: The CSSSM sought a three-year order effectively replacing the interim order of Peacock J., with limited, supervised telephone calls (three times weekly, 15 minutes) and supervised synagogue/community visits. The Court considered these restrictions too strict.
rule: Art. 23 C.C.Q. requires the court to obtain expert and interested-party opinions and to consider the wishes of the person concerned; the court is not an expert and should act on the recommendations of treating professionals.
application: The Court was not satisfied with simply making the interim regime permanent for three years without a progressive plan to relax supervision over six to nine months and eventually permit unsupervised calls and visits (while E. continues to reside in the facility). It declined to make a final order and instead directed the CSSSM to prepare such a plan and report back.
conclusion: Final order postponed to March 2014; Peacock J.'s interim order renewed and continued for 90 days, the motion continued pro forma, and the CSSSM requested to examine an 'exit plan' improving contact between E. and her mother.

issue: Should the impugned portions of the defendant's response to civil claim be struck under Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules?
facts: The plaintiff sued for breach of a residential tenancy agreement, seeking $180,000 in unpaid rent. Mr. Chang's response contained allegations about non-parties — that the plaintiff's principal Tariq Kassam was an unlicensed property manager who had been found by the Real Estate Council to have committed professional misconduct, that Canadian National Relocation Ltd. was his alter ego, and that Kassam's brother Khalil Kassam had been subject to regulatory orders over an earlier rental scam. The plaintiff sought to strike these as irrelevant to the contract dispute.
rule: Rule 9-5(1)(a)–(d) permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim/defence, are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial, or are otherwise an abuse of process. A pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not establish the cause of action or advance a defence known in law (Willow v. Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860). Scandalous matter is struck only if irrelevant as well as scandalous. Pleadings must state material facts concisely and must not contain evidence (Rules 3-7(1); PGT v. Johnston, 2016 BCSC 1388).
application: The Court found the underlined portions largely concerned the conduct and regulatory history of non-parties (Tariq Kassam, CNR Ltd., Khalil Kassam) with no clear connection to whether the tenancy agreement between the plaintiff and defendants was formed or enforceable. Allegations of Kassam's professional misconduct and his brother's regulatory history amounted to smearing by association and 'misconduct by association', which is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous and vexatious. Some references to Mr. Wong/CNR Ltd. as the plaintiff's agent might be relevant but were ambiguous and required clarification.
conclusion: Several impugned portions (para. 3 in part, para. 6 second/third sentences, para. 10 underlined portion, and Part 3 paras. 7 and 8) were struck; the agency references in paras. 5 and 6 (first sentence) required clarification on amendment.

issue: Was the defendant's defence of fraudulent misrepresentation and his denial of the contract adequately pleaded?
facts: Mr. Chang admitted executing the tenancy agreement and wiring or attempting to wire funds, but pleaded in Part 3 that the elements of a contract were not met and that he pleaded fraudulent misrepresentation, reciting the legal elements without tying them to specific facts.
rule: The elements of a contract are offer and acceptance, meeting of the minds, certainty, consideration and intention to be bound (Vancouver Canucks LP v. Canon Canada Inc., 2013 BCSC 866). Fraudulent misrepresentation requires a false representation of fact known to be false, intended to be acted upon, inducing the victim to contract to their detriment (Wang v. Shao, 2019 BCCA 130; Derry v. Peek). Under Rule 9-5(1)(a) a defence is struck only if it is plain and obvious it cannot succeed; material facts for every essential element must be pleaded (PGT v. Johnston).
application: Mr. Chang did not identify which elements of the contract were absent, and having admitted executing the agreement and attempting payment, did not clearly raise the absence of a valid contract. He also failed to plead the material facts needed for each element of fraudulent misrepresentation — who made the false representation, its content, reliance, and resulting loss. The pleaded misrepresentation defence was therefore deficient.
conclusion: The Court found the denial of the contract and the fraudulent misrepresentation plea deficient, but did not finally dismiss them; instead it allowed amendment.

issue: Should the defendant be granted leave to amend his response to civil claim?
facts: Counsel for Mr. Chang requested leave to amend to cure any deficiencies if portions were struck.
rule: A pleading should not be struck where, if amended, it could disclose a reasonable defence (Olumide v. British Columbia (HRT), 2019 BCCA 386; Carhoun & Sons Enterprises Ltd. v. Canada (AG), 2015 BCCA 163).
application: Because the deficiencies could potentially be cured by proper pleading of material facts, and consistent with the principle favouring amendment, the Court held Mr. Chang should be allowed to reformulate his defences, including possibly incorporating the struck elements into a properly constituted amended plea.
conclusion: Leave to amend was granted. The Court also noted the plaintiff's own amended notice of civil claim was deficient in failing to specify the basis on which it was entitled to rent the apartment. The plaintiff was awarded costs of the application, not payable forthwith.

issue: Should the corporate plaintiff be ordered to post security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act where it concedes it cannot pay a costs award if unsuccessful?
facts: Carhoun, a corporate plaintiff, sued Canada in negligence and misfeasance over delay in granting a Fisheries Act s. 35(2) authorization. Carhoun conceded it could not pay costs if it lost; none of the Carhoun companies own real estate and the plaintiff had defaulted on numerous loans leading to foreclosures. Canada sought security for costs estimated at $306,191.45.
rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 gives the Court discretion to order security for costs where a corporate plaintiff appears unable to pay the defendant's costs if the defendant succeeds. Once a defendant establishes a prima facie case of inability to pay, the onus shifts to the corporation. The discretion is guided by the seven Keary Developments Ltd. v. Tarmac Construction Ltd. factors, adopted via Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Courts Ltd. and Fat Mel's Restaurant Ltd.
application: The Court accepted that the plaintiff conceded inability to pay and that Canada had a plausible defence, satisfying the threshold. However, the residual discretion required weighing all Keary factors, several of which favoured the plaintiff. The Court found the claim not obviously doomed (per Garson J.A. in 2015 BCCA 163), that any meaningful security would stifle the claim, and that the alleged connection between Canada's conduct and the plaintiff's impecuniosity was not without merit.
conclusion: The Court declined to order security for costs; Canada's application was dismissed.

issue: Would an order for security for costs unfairly stifle the plaintiff's claim, considering the plaintiff's and its principals' inability to raise funds?
facts: Karel Carhoun deposed he was unemployed, owned no real estate or vehicle, lived rent-free, and could not borrow from friends or family; his parents would lend no more; his brother Philip (a labourer) and Philip's wife Susan (a realtor) were estranged and unwilling to assist. Canada sought an adverse inference from the absence of affidavits from Philip and Susan.
rule: Under Kropp, to show that security would stifle the action the plaintiff must show more than a lack of assets — it must show the corporation lacks any means of raising money, including from directors, shareholders, and backers. The adequacy of evidence is assessed case by case; extensive financial documentation is not invariably required.
application: The Court declined to draw the adverse inference urged by Canada, accepting that strained family relations explained the missing affidavits and that it was not left without information. It found the principals had exhausted their borrowing power and that neither the brothers nor Susan Carhoun could provide security in any amount, so any real security would stifle the claim.
conclusion: The Court was satisfied the plaintiff could not post security in any amount and that an order would stifle a legitimate claim, favouring dismissal.

issue: Does the defendant's delay in bringing the application for security for costs weigh against granting it?
facts: The claim was filed May 24, 2013; Canada did not file its security-for-costs application until January 27, 2016. By then some 2,800 and 5,000+ documents had been assembled, examinations for discovery were substantially advanced, and a 342-page notice to admit had been served. Canada attributed the delay to seeking clarity of the case and to the trial estimate doubling in September 2015.
rule: Under the seventh Keary factor (Honda Canada Inc. v. Tonka Motorcycle Sales Ltd.), the lateness of an application for security weighs against granting it, especially where the plaintiff has been lulled into a false sense of safety and prejudiced by the delay.
application: The Court found neither explanation sufficient; the magnitude and nature of the claim had not changed, and even the original 25-day trial estimate implied significant costs. Canada's near three-year delay obliged the plaintiff to address issues that an earlier application could have avoided.
conclusion: This factor weighed heavily in the plaintiff's favour and supported dismissal of the application.

issue: Should the surreptitious recording of the UDC hearing be expunged as an abuse of process, and is it otherwise admissible extrinsic evidence on judicial review?
facts: Contrary to the University's Student Discipline Appeal Procedure (s. 2.72 prohibiting recording), the UDC's express direction, and his own counsel's advice, Mr. Zaki secretly recorded his April 8, 2022 disciplinary hearing because he feared bias. He sought to rely on the recording and transcripts to show the Decision misstated the oral evidence and to support bias allegations.
rule: Court of King's Bench Rule 25.11(1)(c) permits striking documents that are an abuse of process. Judicial review is normally confined to the record before the decision-maker, with narrow exceptions (procedural fairness, gaps in the record) requiring relevance and necessity (Manitoba Metis Federation Inc. v. Pallister, 2019 MBQB 118; Bernard v. Canada (Revenue Agency), 2015 FCA 263). Courts retain inherent discretion to prevent abuse of process focused on the integrity of the adjudicative process (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E.; Prouse v. Lands Appeal Board, 2015 SKQB 66; Spiring v. Gould, 2008 MBQB 282; Law Society of Saskatchewan v. Abrametz, 2022 SCC 29).
application: The court found Mr. Zaki should have sought the UDC's permission to record before the hearing rather than unilaterally changing the terms on which the quasi-judicial proceeding proceeded. Allowing reliance on the recording would make a mockery of the tribunal's rules and directions and retroactively alter the hearing's parameters. The transcript's reliability was also doubtful (unidentified speakers, multiple versions). Balancing usefulness against the egregious manner of obtaining it, the abuse outweighed any benefit. Alternatively, the recording, though relevant, was not necessary: other participants including Mr. Zaki could depose to their recollections, and the reasonableness review could proceed on the existing record (Vavilov).
conclusion: The recording, transcripts, and all references were expunged from the Application, Affidavit #1, and Affidavit #2 without leave to amend.

issue: Should the post-hearing Abner report be expunged as inadmissible new evidence?
facts: Dr. Abner's June 10, 2022 report on Mr. Zaki's completion of ethics/professionalism instruction post-dated the April 8, 2022 hearing. At the hearing only 6 of 9 sessions were complete and Mr. Zaki filed no interim report or called Dr. Abner as a witness.
rule: Extrinsic evidence not before the decision-maker is generally inadmissible on judicial review, which is not a de novo hearing. The Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 fresh-evidence criteria do not apply to judicial review.
application: The report is precisely the kind of new evidence the exclusionary rule targets; it post-dated the Decision and could have been adduced with due diligence had Mr. Zaki completed the sessions and called the author. Admitting it would improperly make the court a fact-finder. Even under Palmer, the first criterion (unavailability with diligence) was not met.
conclusion: The Abner report and related paragraphs and exhibit were expunged from Affidavit #1 without leave to amend.

issue: Should other paragraphs of Affidavit #1 be expunged as irrelevant, duplicative, or argumentative?
facts: The University sought to expunge paragraphs 10–68, 74–75, 96–97 and 100 of Affidavit #1, describing Mr. Zaki's background, the postings, the investigation and remediation, the prior appeal, and editorial commentary.
rule: Under Manitoba Metis Federation Inc., the context/background exception only assists the reviewing court in understanding the record; affidavits must not contain spin, advocacy, argument, conclusions of law, or irrelevant statements.
application: Paragraphs 10–68 and 96–97 and 100 did not fall within any recognized exception, were duplicative of the record, and contained advocacy and editorial commentary. Paragraphs 74–75, however, recorded Mr. Zaki's observations at the hearing (including the admissible lay-opinion that the Dean appeared angry) and filled a gap in the record, so they were retained.
conclusion: Paragraphs 10–68, 96, 97 and 100 were expunged without leave; paragraphs 74–75 remained.

issue: Should leave to amend be granted to particularize a bias allegation, and should the supporting Affidavit #2 evidence be preserved?
facts: Mr. Zaki sought to amend to allege reasonable apprehension of bias because the UDC Chair, a College of Pharmacy professor, reported through the Dean of the Faculty of Health Sciences, who was involved in his expulsion and testified. He raised bias generally at the hearing but not this specific reporting relationship, which he says he discovered only in 2024.
rule: Rule 38.05.1(2) permits amendment unless uncompensable prejudice results; amendment factors include prejudice, delay/explanation, and whether the amendment raises an arguable point (Capitol Steel Corp., 2023 MBKB 76). Bias evidence may be admitted if not otherwise on the record (AOV Adults Only Video, 2003 MBCA 81), but objections available at first instance must be raised there (Bernard; Hennessey v. Canada, 2016 FCA 180).
application: Although the underlying documents were largely publicly available before the hearing, Mr. Zaki did raise potential bias at the outset of the hearing and the UDC's in camera reasons for rejecting a conflict were unknown; he accepted that conclusion in good faith. If the alleged undisclosed reporting relationship is accurate it may affect the Application, so it was not plain and obvious Affidavit #2 should be expunged. On amendment, the application was still at an early stage (no cross-examinations or briefs), so no prejudice; delay was explained by late discovery; and the amendment raised an arguable point given the Dean's involvement and the working relationship between Chair and Dean.
conclusion: The motion to expunge the balance of Affidavit #2 was dismissed and the motion to amend the Application was granted.

issue: Should third-party disciplinary decisions concerning another student be disclosed?
facts: Mr. Zaki sought two disciplinary decisions involving a College of Nursing student whose suspension for online posts (found antisemitic, discriminatory and unprofessional) was overturned despite no apology, arguing they showed differential treatment and the faculty's tolerance for expression. The student was personally served but neither responded.
rule: The court has jurisdiction to order production of relevant documents on judicial review (Jewish Community Campus of Winnipeg Inc. v. Metaser, 2013 MBQB 303); a non-party cannot be compelled to respond and the matter may proceed in their absence. Extrinsic evidence post-dating the hearing is generally inadmissible and must be relevant.
application: The decisions post-dated the hearing and were not relevant: that another student was reinstated after similar posts would not assist in determining whether the UDC was biased against Mr. Zaki. If factually similar cases decided differently by different tribunals within one institution automatically applied to one another, this would have no principled limit; the decisions had no probative value.
conclusion: The disclosure motion was dismissed and Affidavit #3 expunged in its entirety.

issue: Does s. 18 of the Yukon Occupational Health and Safety Act create a private civil cause of action for reprisal?
facts: Wood was dismissed while on probation and framed her entire action on an alleged contravention of s. 18 of the OHSA, asserting she was terminated for raising safety concerns. She had already pursued the matter before the YWCHSB, which declined to prosecute.
rule: Section 18 of the OHSA operates in a public summary conviction context, referring to an employer being 'convicted' and to 'the convicting court' (s. 18(2)); it creates the possibility of a summary conviction prosecution, not a private civil remedy.
application: The court held that the language of s. 18 signals a public prosecution framework, not a civil one. Wood was 'simply mistaken' in asserting that s. 18 'creates a civil cause of action for a prohibited reprisal.' Her claim, based entirely on s. 18, therefore disclosed no reasonable cause of action.
conclusion: Section 18 does not create a private civil cause of action; the claim founded on it cannot succeed.

issue: Should the plaintiff be permitted to add seven new YG-employee defendants under Rule 15(5)(a)(iii)?
facts: Wood sought to add seven YG employees and to raise numerous new causes of action (wrongful dismissal, breach of fiduciary/statutory duty, conspiracy, malfeasance in public office, negligent supervision, etc.), largely tied to the Ogilvie Conflict of Interest Mitigation Strategy.
rule: Rule 15(5)(a)(iii) requires (1) a real, non-frivolous issue between the plaintiff and the proposed defendant relating to the subject matter (a low threshold), and (2) that it be just and convenient to add the party: Strata Plan No VIS3578 v Canan Investment Group Ltd, 2010 BCCA 329; Letvad v Fenwick. A pleading may be frivolous/vexatious or an abuse of process (collateral attack on a tribunal decision subject to appeal): Willow v Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083; Acumar, 2014 BCSC 814.
application: None of the proposed individual defendants could grant the remedies sought (e.g., reinstatement); adding them would needlessly complicate proceedings; the Strategy was only an administrative policy creating no legal duty (Friends of the Oldman River; Arsenault); employer-employee relations are contractual, not fiduciary; government employees acting within scope cannot conspire together (Kuhn); malfeasance requires unlawful conduct (Odhavji); and the various framings did not rise above frivolousness. The action also collaterally attacked the YWCHSB and Human Rights proceedings.
conclusion: The application to add defendants was dismissed.

issue: Should the amended statement of claim be struck under Rules 20(26)(a),(b),(d)?
facts: The amended claim rested entirely on s. 18 of the OHSA and effectively sought to appeal Wood's probationary dismissal, a matter already addressed through the Public Service Act, Public Service Labour Relations Act, the Collective Agreement, and multiple tribunal proceedings.
rule: A claim is struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of action where it is plain and obvious it cannot succeed (Hunt v Carey; R v Imperial Tobacco); as vexatious where it advances no claim known in law; and as an abuse of process where it is a collateral attack on an appealable/reviewable administrative decision or relitigates decided issues (Willow; Cimaco; Toronto (City) v CUPE).
application: Since s. 18 creates no civil cause of action, the claim disclosed no reasonable cause of action. It was vexatious as an attempt to appeal a probationary dismissal for which the statutory appeal was exhausted with no further right of appeal. It was an abuse of process as the fourth forum used to relitigate the dismissal, and a collateral attack on the YWCHSB Appeal Tribunal after Wood withdrew her further statutory appeal.
conclusion: The application to strike the amended statement of claim was granted.

issue: Are the pleadings asserting Canwest's editorial bias and policies relevant to a passing-off or copyright defence?
facts: The defendants published a mock edition of the Vancouver Sun that duplicated the masthead and satirically criticized Israel's policy toward Palestinians and Canwest's Middle East reporting. Canwest sued in passing-off, breach of s. 7(b) of the Trade-marks Act and copyright. Paragraphs 2, 3 and 4 of Murray's defence alleged aggregate circulation of all Canwest papers and a centralized pro-Israel editorial bias, said to be relevant to confusion.
rule: Under Rule 19(24)(a) a defence may be struck where it is plain and obvious it will fail assuming pleaded facts true (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959); under (b) and (c) the focus is on relevance to the cause of action (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress). Passing-off requires goodwill, deception by misrepresentation, and actual or potential damage (Ciba-Geigy v. Apotex, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 120); s. 7(b) is the statutory equivalent (Asbjorn Horgard). Copyright protects original works irrespective of their truth.
application: Confusion is assessed by comparing the publications themselves, consumer/survey/expert evidence, not by the plaintiff's intentions or editorial policies. Canwest's actual policies were beside the point; at most the public's perception mattered, which is not what the paragraphs pleaded. The aggregate circulation of all Canwest papers was irrelevant since only the Vancouver Sun was in issue. Copyright likewise has nothing to do with the truth of the contents.
conclusion: The paragraphs disclosed no defence and were unnecessary and apt to delay a fair trial; properly struck.

issue: Do Charter values or the constitutional validity of the Acts make the truth of the mock paper relevant?
facts: Murray argued that the common law and the Trade-marks Act must be interpreted consistently with Charter values, that truth should factor into balancing intellectual property against free expression (analogous to the defence of truth in defamation), and that if the Acts prohibited his parody they infringed s. 2(b).
rule: Freedom of expression under s. 2(b) protects all communications conveying meaning regardless of content; courts refuse to consider the content of the expression (R. v. Zundel, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 731). Charter values are applied by balancing competing interests, as in BCAA v. OPEIU Local 378, 2001 BCSC 156.
application: The defamation analogy was inapt: defamation turns on the falsity of statements, whereas passing-off concerns misrepresenting one's goods as another's and is indifferent to truth. In BCAA the court balanced competing interests without inquiring into truth. Since s. 2(b) analysis disregards content, the truth of the parody was irrelevant to the Charter-values or constitutional-validity arguments; the same reasoning applied to the copyright claim.
conclusion: Truth of the parody's contents was not a relevant defence; the Charter and constitutional-validity pleadings failed.

issue: Should paragraph 11 attacking the plaintiff's motives be struck absent a counterclaim for abuse of process?
facts: Paragraph 11 (beyond its first sentence) alleged the lawsuit was intended to inflict harm and deter the defendants' pro-Palestinian expression, was an abuse of process, but no counterclaim for abuse of process was pleaded.
rule: The tort of abuse of process requires the elements set out in Hemming v. Newton, 2006 BCSC 1748: subjection to legal process, predominant improper collateral purpose, a definite act/threat in furtherance, and actual damage. Absent a counterclaim, a plaintiff's motives are irrelevant; courts may even stay such counterclaims (Starbucks Corp. v. Second Cup Ltd.).
application: Without a pleaded counterclaim, the plaintiff's motives were irrelevant, including to the question of special costs. Merely asserting abuse of process was an overly-polemical way of asserting the claim lacked merit and had no place in a pleading.
conclusion: Paragraph 11 (except its first sentence) was struck.

issue: Should the document production motion be granted?
facts: Murray sought documents concerning Canwest's alleged pro-Israel bias, centralized editorial policy, and motives for bringing the lawsuit, as pleaded in the struck paragraphs.
rule: Document production must relate to matters in issue in the pleadings.
application: The documents sought related solely to the paragraphs that had been struck, so they were no longer connected to any live issue.
conclusion: The production motion was denied; the appeal was dismissed with costs.

issue: Should the Bank's claims for breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, gross negligence, constructive fraud and unjust enrichment be struck under Rule 19(24)?
facts: The Bank sued two former employees, a Mortgage Specialist (Tortora) and a Financial Services Manager (Poonja), for secretly splitting commissions and for gross negligence in arranging ten 'Papas Mortgages' involving fraudulently altered appraisals, alleging breaches of the Bank's Code and Policies, breaches of employment contracts, fiduciary duty, constructive fraud and unjust enrichment.
rule: Under Rule 19(24) of the B.C. Rules of Court, pleadings may be struck where it is 'plain and obvious' that no reasonable cause of action is disclosed, assuming all pleaded facts to be true (McNaughton v. Baker; Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959). Weakness or novelty is no ground to strike (Minnes v. Minnes). Embarrassing/scandalous/vexatious pleadings (subrules (b)–(c)) must be shown certain to fail (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform). An employee below senior management may in certain circumstances owe fiduciary duties (Barton Insurance Brokers Ltd. v. Irwin). Constructive fraud may arise absent actual deceit (Nocton v. Ashburton). Unjust enrichment may be pleaded as an alternative to contract (Isaac v. Guardian Capital).
application: Accepting the pleaded facts as true, the amended statement of claim set out the elements of a fiduciary relationship (discretion/power, ability to affect the Bank's interests, and the Bank's vulnerability), so novelty of an employee fiduciary claim was no bar. The contract claims, though not drafted in the traditional way, made the gist clear (failure to follow Code/Policies plus breach of an implied duty of honesty and good faith) and were not embarrassing. The gross negligence claim adequately pleaded standard of care, breach and damages. Constructive fraud was viable since a fiduciary breach was disclosed and equity-falling conduct was alleged. The unjust enrichment claims against Tortora and Poonja pleaded enrichment, corresponding deprivation and absence of juristic reason as alternative claims.
conclusion: The applications to strike these claims were dismissed; it was not plain and obvious that they disclosed no reasonable cause of action.

issue: Should the unjust enrichment claim against Mr. Punja be struck?
facts: The Bank alleged Mr. Punja, Ms. Poonja's husband, received over $245,000 'in turn' from Ms. Tortora, but pleaded no payments made by the Bank to him and no relationship between the Bank and him.
rule: Unjust enrichment requires (a) enrichment of the defendant, (b) a corresponding deprivation of the plaintiff, and (c) absence of a juristic reason for the deprivation.
application: There was no pleaded deprivation of the Bank corresponding to any enrichment of Mr. Punja; the only funds he received came from Ms. Tortora, not the Bank, and he had no relationship with the Bank that could cause the Bank to be deprived when he received those funds.
conclusion: The unjust enrichment allegation against Mr. Punja was struck.

issue: Can a conspiracy claim under the unlawful-means branch stand against Mr. Punja, who committed no unlawful act?
facts: The Bank alleged the three defendants conspired to split commissions; only Tortora and Poonja were alleged to have breached the Bank's Code, Policies, contracts and fiduciary duties. Mr. Punja's role was receiving and transferring funds, with no unlawful act alleged against him.
rule: The tort of conspiracy requires either a predominant purpose to injure the plaintiff or, under the second branch, unlawful conduct directed at the plaintiff with constructive intent (Canada Cement LaFarge Ltd. v. B.C. Lightweight Aggregate Ltd., [1983] 1 S.C.R. 452). The tort is an anomaly not to be extended (Frame v. Smith; Normart Management Ltd. v. West Hill Redevelopment). Under the second branch each conspirator sued must be alleged to have committed the unlawful act.
application: There was no allegation of a predominant purpose to injure and none of Mr. Punja's acts were unlawful per se. To hold him liable where he neither intended injury nor committed a wrongful act would create an impermissible third category of conspirator drawn in only by his familial/business relationship. Clerk & Lindsell and Rookes v. Barnard did not assist, and Tracy (Instaloans) left the point undecided on distinguishable facts.
conclusion: It was plain and obvious that no reasonable cause of action in conspiracy lay against Mr. Punja; the claim against him was struck.

issue: Do the conspiracy claims against Tortora and Poonja survive or merge into the contract and fiduciary duty claims?
facts: The unlawful acts pleaded against Tortora and Poonja in the conspiracy claim (breach of Code/Policies, contract and fiduciary duty) were the very same acts underpinning the separate contract and fiduciary claims; actual damage from the commission splitting was pleaded.
rule: Where a tort has been committed by two or more persons, an allegation of prior conspiracy adds nothing and merges in the tort (Ward v. Lewis; Hovsepian v. Westfair Foods Ltd., 2001 ABQB 700; Napoleone v. Baraldi). A conspiracy claim survives only where the wrongful acts pleaded differ from those grounding the underlying torts (as in Hunt).
application: Although actual damage was pleaded, the wrongful acts founding the conspiracy claim were identical to the breaches of contract and fiduciary duty already alleged, so the conspiracy added nothing. This was not a Hunt situation of distinct wrongful acts. Given the Bank had already amended once with very different allegations and still failed, leave to amend was refused.
conclusion: The merger principle applied; the conspiracy claims against Tortora and Poonja were struck without leave to amend.

issue: Did the amended statement of claim comply with Rule 24(3)?
facts: Ms. Poonja and Mr. Punja sought an order requiring a paragraph-by-paragraph marked-up amended statement of claim; the Bank's amended pleading reproduced the entire original document crossed out and replaced with a 34-page version.
rule: Rule 24(3) governs the form of amended pleadings.
application: The amended statement of claim contained the entire original so changes could be discerned by comparison; the format proposed would be more difficult to read and serve no purpose, and the pleading as delivered complied with Rule 24(3).
conclusion: The Rule 24(3) application was dismissed.

issue: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial on whether the child, M-R, was in need of protection?
facts: The society had extensive historical involvement with both parents over substance abuse, criminal activity and domestic violence; the mother used marijuana, methadone, Fentanyl and morphine during pregnancy, gave inconsistent accounts of her drug use, breached supervision conditions, was incarcerated four times after the application was commenced, and filed no material on the motion. The mother did not attend the hearing and her counsel made only legal submissions.
rule: On a summary judgment motion under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules (as amended in 2015 to mirror Rule 20), the court may weigh evidence, assess credibility and draw inferences (Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7). The onus is on the society to show no genuine issue for trial; the responding party may not rest on bald denials but must set out specific facts showing a genuine issue (r. 16(4.1)). Protection under s. 74(2)(b)(i) CYFSA arises where there is a risk the child is likely to suffer physical harm from a person's failure to adequately care for, provide for, supervise or protect the child.
application: The society's affidavits established a prima facie case of risk of harm; the mother filed nothing to rebut it and provided nothing for the court to weigh. Her counsel conceded a protection finding 'might be a foregone conclusion.' The mother's ongoing drug use, repeated incarcerations and unstable lifestyle raised no material dispute, and a mere heartfelt desire to parent does not create a triable issue.
conclusion: No genuine issue for trial existed; the child was found in need of protection under s. 74(2)(b)(i) of the CYFSA.

issue: What disposition order under s. 101 was in the child's best interests, and should interim care be extended under s. 122?
facts: M-R, under six years old, had been in society care since February 2017 (14 months at the hearing, 17 at judgment). The mother had failed for a full year to complete any of the conditions of the May 2017 order (drug testing, ADSTV counselling, Heartspace, consents, punctual attendance). No parenting plan was filed; the father filed nothing and had one visit.
rule: Under s. 101 CYFSA the court must make the order in the child's best interests (s. 74(3)); options are supervision, interim society care, extended society care, or a combination. Section 122 limits interim care to 12 months for a child under six, extendable by up to six months if in the child's best interests. Permanency planning for young children should not be delayed by 'litigation drift' (Children's Aid Society (Simcoe County) v. T.D., 2012 ONSC 6737).
application: The maximum available interim-care extension was about one month, which could not realistically allow the mother to complete conditions she had failed to meet over a year. There was no evidence she was near completion or had a viable plan; the s. 74(3) factors—continuity of care with the foster family (her psychological parents), weak emotional ties, risk of harm on return, effect of delay—all favoured permanency. An extension would serve only a 'heartfelt desire to parent,' not the child's best interests.
conclusion: No genuine issue for trial on disposition; the court ordered the child placed in extended society care under s. 101 until terminated under s. 116 or expired under s. 123.

issue: Should any access to the child be granted following an order of extended society care?
facts: The mother attended access when available and was affectionate, but was frequently late, missed visits due to incarceration, and put her access at risk through her own choices. The foster family wished to adopt.
rule: Under s. 105(4) an existing access order terminates upon an extended-care order; under s. 105(5)-(6) the court may make a new access order only if satisfied it is in the child's best interests, considering whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful to the child (and, if relevant, impact on adoption prospects). 'Beneficial' means advantageous and 'meaningful' means significant; the applicant must prove the relationship brings a significant positive advantage to the child (Children's Aid Society of the Niagara Region v. J.C., 2007 CanLII 8919).
application: While access visits were pleasant and affectionate, given the child's young age, the missed and suspended visits, and the mother's willingness to jeopardize access, the relationship was not shown to be beneficial and meaningful from the child's perspective. Love and pleasant visits alone are insufficient.
conclusion: Access was not beneficial and meaningful to the child; no access order was made (making it unnecessary to consider s. 105(6)(b)).

issue: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial on whether the four children were in need of protection under s. 37(2) CFSA?
facts: C.C.A.S. became involved after Y.N.Y. disclosed his father hit him; later M.L.Y., Y.N.Y. and S.C.H.Y. disclosed repeated and severe physical and emotional abuse to multiple professionals. Three of the four children were diagnosed with PTSD, exhibited aggression, self-harm and suicidal ideation, and consistently said they feared and did not wish to return to their parents. The parents denied all abuse, claimed the children were manipulated by C.C.A.S., and alleged cultural bias and racism, offering mostly bald denials.
rule: Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules permits summary judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; the responding party may not rest on mere allegations or denials but must set out specific facts showing a triable issue (r. 16(4.1)). The court must take a 'hard look' at the merits (Children's Aid Society of Hamilton v. M.N.). A child is in need of protection under s. 37(2)(a),(b),(f),(f.1),(g),(g.1) CFSA where physical/emotional harm or the risk thereof exists.
application: The children's detailed, consistent disclosures to numerous professionals, the PTSD diagnoses, and their disturbed behaviours constituted overwhelming evidence. The court held that a protection finding did not even require proof of the alleged physical abuse — the risk of emotional harm alone sufficed. The parents' bald denials and blame of others did not raise specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial.
conclusion: No triable issue existed; all four children were found in need of protection under the enumerated subsections of s. 37(2) (M.K.Y. under (b) and (g)).

issue: What disposition was in the children's best interests?
facts: C.C.A.S. sought Crown wardship for adoption. A prior supervision order (April–November 2011) had failed. The parents refused parenting-capacity assessments and most services, rejected the PTSD diagnoses, took no responsibility, and proposed only that the children be returned to them. No family or community alternative placements were offered.
rule: Section 57(1) CFSA sets out available orders; s. 57(2)-(4) require the court to consider society efforts, less disruptive alternatives and community placements; s. 37(3) lists best-interests criteria. The test is not whether parents intend to change but whether they have in fact changed and can safely parent (CAS of Winnipeg v. R.; CCAS of Metro Toronto v. C.M.). Crown wardship is a remedy of last resort, 'the capital punishment of family law', reserved for the clearest cases.
application: The same protection concerns present at apprehension persisted; the parents showed no insight, remorse or change and had engaged in no meaningful services. A supervision order depends on trust and cooperation, which were absent, so return even with supervision would not keep the children safe. No alternative plans existed. The parents' plan had no air of reality and no chance of success at trial.
conclusion: Crown wardship for all four children was ordered as the only disposition serving their best interests and offering certainty and finality.

issue: Should the parents have access to the children as Crown wards?
facts: The parents had had no access for nearly two years; earlier access motions had been dismissed and not appealed. The three oldest children feared their parents and did not want visits, though S.C.H.Y. said she missed them and M.K.Y. asked about her father.
rule: Section 59(2.1) CFSA bars an access order for a Crown ward unless the relationship is beneficial and meaningful to the child and access will not impair future adoption opportunities; s. 59(2) presumes access is revoked. The onus is on the party seeking access, focusing on the child's experience (NB (Minister) v. L.(M.); CCAS v. M.(C.)).
application: With no access for two years and the children not wanting contact, no beneficial and meaningful relationship existed to support parental access. The parents failed to rebut the presumption or meet the s. 59(2.1) onus. Sibling relationships, however, were bonded and warranted access among the four children.
conclusion: Parental access was denied; an order for access among the four siblings (at C.C.A.S.'s discretion and later as agreed) was made.

issue: Was the respondent dismissed for cause on November 5th, and was it error to put the question of whether his conduct justified dismissal to the jury?
facts: The respondent, engaged as rabbi, slaughterer, cantor and teacher for a three-year term, refused after October 22nd to continue teaching alongside Lederman and stopped performing his teaching duties. On November 5th Mausberg, the congregation's president, personally ejected him from the school and told him he was dismissed. The jury, answering Question 6, found he had not refused 'without lawful excuse' to discharge his teaching duties and found dismissal occurred December 20th.
rule: Only questions of fact may be put to a jury under s. 60 of the Judicature Act, R.S.O. 1937, c. 100. Whether proved facts are sufficient in law to warrant dismissal is for the judge; whether the alleged facts are proved is for the jury (McIntyre v. Hockin (1889), 16 O.A.R. 498). An employee's refusal to perform duties justifies discharge (Boston Deep Sea Fishing & Ice Co. v. Ansell (1888), 39 Ch. D. 339).
application: The evidence, including the respondent's own admission, was all one way that he refused to teach after October 22nd; the jury could not consistently have found otherwise. Question 6, however, asked whether the refusal was 'without lawful excuse' — a question of law improperly delegated to the jury. The respondent received no effective notice of dismissal until he was ejected on November 5th, and that dismissal was for cause (his refusal to teach). Because the jury was misdirected, it never addressed whether the parties' conduct after November 5th amounted to a resumption of contractual relations, which alone could support a December 20th dismissal. The conflicting evidence about the respondent acting as cantor and the parties' later dealings left the matter genuinely triable.
conclusion: There was a dismissal for cause on November 5th; the real issue of whether contractual relations were resumed thereafter was untried. A new trial is ordered on the wrongful dismissal claim.

issue: Did the individual defendants conspire to procure, or maliciously induce, the congregation's breach of the respondent's employment contract?
facts: The jury found Mausberg and Lederman conspired to procure the wrongful dismissal and, apart from conspiracy, maliciously induced the breach. Lederman had quarrelled with the respondent over how he should be addressed; Mausberg acted as president in effecting the dismissal.
rule: A plaintiff alleging conspiracy bears a heavy burden of proof (Sweeney v. Coote, [1907] A.C. 221); it is damage, not the agreement, that is the gist (Mogul S.S. Co. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. (1889), 23 Q.B.D. 598). A director or officer acting within the scope of authority in causing the company to breach a contract is not liable for inducing breach (Said v. Butt, [1920] 3 K.B. 497; Henderson v. Kane and Pioneer Club, [1924] N.Z.L.R. 1073).
application: Since wrongful discharge had not been established, the conspiracy issue would in any event require retrial. But there was no admissible evidence of any combination or intention to injure. Lederman's quarrel did not establish a conspiracy and he had no shown connection with the discharge. Mausberg acted only within the scope of his duties as president, so the Said v. Butt principle shielded him from liability for inducing breach.
conclusion: The claims for conspiracy to induce, and for inducing, the breach fail and are dismissed.

issue: Were the impugned publications defamatory, and did the judge err in excluding evidence of the truth of the facts in the newspaper letter?
facts: Three publications imputed that the respondent was unqualified as a slaughterer / that his Kashruth could not be relied on: (1) Mausberg's November 6th circular ('I am not responsible for his Kashruth'); (2) Zimmerman's newspaper advertisement annulling the respondent's Kabalah; and (3) Lederman's letter to a Hebrew newspaper. For the letter the defence pleaded qualified privilege and fair comment, and the judge excluded evidence of the truth of the stated facts, holding a separate plea of justification was needed.
rule: Words must be reasonably capable of a defamatory meaning (Beswick v. Smith (1907), 24 T.L.R. 169). Where fair comment is pleaded, evidence of the truth of the facts commented on is admissible without a separate plea of justification (Boys v. Star Printing & Publishing Co., [1927] 3 D.L.R. 847, 60 O.L.R. 592; Gatley, 3rd ed., p. 675); Sutherland v. Stopes, [1925] A.C. 47 is not to the contrary. There can be no fair comment unless based on facts truly stated.
application: The Beswick argument addressed only the innocuous words about ending employment, not the defamatory Kashruth phrase, so it failed as to the circular. Mausberg was fixed with the advertisement by the statement of defence admitting its publication, and with the letter by evidence connecting him to it. On the letter, however, the judge wrongly excluded evidence of the truth of the facts; that evidence was essential to the fair-comment defence, and its exclusion caused counsel to abandon fair comment.
conclusion: The verdicts on the November 6th circular ($1,000) and the advertisement ($500) stand and those appeals are dismissed; the judgment on Lederman's letter cannot stand and a new trial is ordered on that libel because of the erroneous evidentiary ruling.

issue: Was the claim for conspiracy to libel properly established by the jury's verdict?
facts: The statement of claim alleged the defendants conspired to defame the respondent through the three publications; a general question on conspiracy to libel was answered affirmatively, but the jury assessed separate damages for each libel and awarded no damages for the conspiracy itself.
rule: It is the damage done, not the conspiracy, that is the gist of the action (Mogul S.S. Co. v. McGregor, Gow & Co.). A jury finding unsupported by an assessment of damages tied to the pleaded cause is treated as an answer 'in the air' (Thomas v. Moore, [1918] 1 K.B. 555).
application: The pleading disclosed only a joint cause of action for conspiracy to libel followed by the overt libels, not separate libel causes of action. Yet the case was tried and argued as though damages were claimed for each separate libel, and the jury assessed no damages for the conspiracy. The conspiracy finding therefore hung 'in the air.'
conclusion: The conspiracy-to-libel claim is dismissed.

issue: Did the plaintiff's verbal and sexual harassment of a subordinate constitute just cause for summary termination?
facts: Watkins, the 61-year-old Golf Course Superintendent with almost 13 years' service, developed romantic feelings for Ms. Li, his direct subordinate 32 years his junior. After she repeatedly rejected him and asked that communications remain professional, he continued sending personal texts/emails, monitored her intrusively, argued with her within earshot of staff, asked about her pornography habits, and called her a 'cunt' or 'fucking cunt'; he also berated and fired seasonal employee Ms. Kent and poisoned the department atmosphere.
rule: There is no fixed rule for summary termination; the analysis is contextual, assessing the degree of misconduct and surrounding circumstances (McKinley v BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38; Hodgins v St. John Council for Alberta, 2008 ABCA 173). Dismissal is justified where conduct violates an essential condition of the contract, is fundamentally inconsistent with the employee's obligations, or destroys the mutual faith of the relationship (McKinley at para 48). Sexual harassment is 'unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature that detrimentally affects the work environment' (Janzen v Platy Enterprises, [1989] 1 SCR 1252) and may justify summary dismissal (Geluch v Rosedale Golf Association).
application: The court found the harassment sustained over several months, escalating from unwanted romantic pursuit to hostility, and aggravated by the fact that Watkins was Ms. Li's sole direct supervisor upon whom she was economically dependent. This distinguished the case from Brazeau and placed the conduct at the upper-middle of the severity spectrum. As a senior supervisor he had a duty to provide a safe, respectful workplace and to protect the employer from liability (Bannister; Poliquin), which he not only failed but personally breached, showing no recognition his conduct was wrong.
conclusion: The plaintiff's conduct was incompatible with continued employment; summary termination was for just cause.

issue: Was the employer required to warn the plaintiff before terminating him?
facts: The employer had no respectful-workplace or harassment policy in 2011 and gave no warning before dismissal.
rule: There is no hard-and-fast rule requiring a warning; the greater the wrong, the less likely a warning is required (Leach v Canadian Blood Services, 2001 ABQB 54; Bannister v General Motors of Canada). Management employees have a duty to protect other employees and the employer from civil claims.
application: Given the severity of the harassment, the duty owed to Ms. Li and other staff, and the plaintiff's complete failure to recognize his conduct as unacceptable (indeed his immediate blanket denial), no warning was mandated before termination.
conclusion: The plaintiff was not entitled to a warning before termination.

issue: Did the employer condone the plaintiff's misconduct?
facts: The plaintiff argued his behaviour was condoned, making a warning necessary.
rule: Condonation requires more than mere delay and presupposes the employer's knowledge of the misconduct (Geluch v Rosedale Golf Association).
application: There was no evidence the Board or senior employees knew the particulars of the plaintiff's treatment of Ms. Li or Ms. Kent until the fall of 2011, after which termination followed quickly.
conclusion: No condonation was established.

issue: Did the employer's inadequate investigation defeat its claim of just cause?
facts: The employer met with the plaintiff and let him read and respond to Ms. Li's letter but never spoke directly with Ms. Li about her allegations and gave the plaintiff limited time to respond.
rule: A proper investigation can enhance, and its absence can hurt, an employer's case for summary dismissal, but failure to investigate does not automatically obviate an otherwise justified termination (Foerderer v Nova Chemicals; Leach; Kinch v Amoco).
application: The court found the investigation inadequate for failing to interview Ms. Li and rushing the plaintiff's response, but concluded that a proper investigation would only have confirmed Ms. Li's allegations and those of other employees; the admissions and evidence at trial independently justified dismissal.
conclusion: The inadequate investigation did not defeat just cause; termination remained justified.

issue: Did the plaintiff's failure to demote or fire Ms. Li amount to insubordination?
facts: Mr. Lyle told the plaintiff Ms. Li could not be 'Assistant Superintendent'; the plaintiff said he was told to terminate her, while Lyle said 'reclassify.' The plaintiff repeatedly asked to defer the decision, receiving silence, and the matter was still under discussion on October 24, 2011.
rule: Refusal to follow an unlawful or unreasonable order may not be insubordinate (Karmel v Calgary Jewish Academy, 2015 ABQB 731). Insubordination requires a clear and unequivocal direction.
application: The direction was equivocal and unresolved, and the plaintiff had general authority over hiring/firing in his department and had made deferral requests met with silence.
conclusion: The plaintiff's conduct did not amount to insubordination, though this did not affect the finding of just cause on the harassment grounds.

issue: To whom should custody of the child J.B. be granted in accordance with his best interests?
facts: J.B., 11½ years old, lost his mother at birth and his father when he was 8½. A custody-tutorship dispute arose among his paternal aunt (T.B.-C.) and her husband (M.C.), his maternal grandmother and step-grandfather (N.T.-B. and C.B.) with whom he had been living in British Columbia since January 1995, and the executrix/tutrix named in the father's will (D.F.). The paternal aunt claimed she had been cut off from the child and alienated by the grandparents; the grandparents said they had cared for the child continuously and met his needs.
rule: Articles 32 and 33 of the Civil Code of Québec: every child has a right to protection, security and attention from parents or those acting in their stead, and every decision concerning a child must be taken in light of the child's interests and the respect of his rights, considering his moral, intellectual, emotional and material needs, age, health, personality and family environment. The applicant bears the burden of proving that the proposed custody serves the child's interests.
application: Over five days of hearing, fourteen witnesses and extensive exhibits, the Court found the paternal aunt (T.B.-C.) not credible and lacking custodial capacity; her account of being prevented from returning the child to Montréal and of alienation by the grandparents was found to be false, and her failure to make any real effort to see the child between 1995 and 1997 undermined her claim. The Court rejected the expert report of Mr D'Abate as based uncritically on facts supplied solely by the aunt's family. By contrast, the maternal grandparents (N.T.-B. and C.B.) testified credibly and demonstrated through their day-to-day care that they loved the child and could meet his intellectual, religious, emotional and physical needs. D.F. withdrew her own custody request.
conclusion: The aunt's motion for custody was dismissed and D.F.'s motion was dismissed on her withdrawal; custody of J.B. was granted to the maternal grandparents N.T.-B. and C.B., with access to D.F. and no access to the aunt, uncle or paternal grandmother, subject to psychological support for any future access.

issue: Should the nomination of D.F. as tutrix to the child be confirmed?
facts: The father's will appointed C.F./D.F. as executrix and tutrix to J.B. The Public Curator of Quebec was a mis en cause on the tutorship application.
rule: Provisions of the Civil Code of Québec governing tutorship to a minor and confirmation of a testamentary tutor's nomination.
application: Having disposed of the custody question in favour of the maternal grandparents and given the father's testamentary appointment of D.F. as tutrix, the Court confirmed her nomination, ordering provisional execution notwithstanding appeal.
conclusion: The nomination of D.F. as tutrix to J.B. was confirmed, with provisional execution notwithstanding appeal, without costs.

issue: Were the defendants entitled to their costs of the motion to dismiss/stay and of the plaintiff's motion to vary, notwithstanding divided success?
facts: The defendants moved to dismiss or stay the action for non-payment of two costs orders; the court stayed the action until the first costs order was paid rather than dismissing. The plaintiff opposed both dismissal and a stay, brought three motions to vary (one withdrawn, two dismissed), and forced five attendances. The defendants argued 'clear divided success.'
rule: Costs are discretionary under s. 133(1) of the Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, and rule 57.01; a fair and reasonable award is to be made having regard to success and conduct. Rule 57.03(1) presumes costs fixed and payable within 30 days unless a different order is more just.
application: The Master rejected the 'divided success' characterization: a stay was the alternate relief the defendants sought and the plaintiff opposed both dismissal and stay. Staying only pending payment of one of two costs awards was a significant indulgence to the plaintiff, not a success for her. The plaintiff lost the motion to vary. The defendants acted reasonably while the plaintiff generated unnecessary costs.
conclusion: The defendants were substantially successful on both motions and were entitled to their costs; the remaining questions were quantum, who pays, and timing.

issue: Should the plaintiff's solicitor be ordered to pay costs personally under rule 57.07?
facts: Counsel withdrew a motion to vary before the Master to bring it before a judge (dismissed by Brown J.), then brought a third motion to vary before the Master on essentially the same grounds (also dismissed), causing repeated adjournments of the dismissal motion from January to September 2007. Counsel had been told repeatedly that the motions should be heard together by the Master who made the original order, that the proper route was an appeal, and that there were no grounds to vary under rule 59.06. The defendants gave the required rule 57.07(2) notice.
rule: Rule 57.07(1)-(2): where a solicitor causes costs to be incurred without reasonable cause or wasted by undue delay, negligence or other default, the court may require the solicitor personally to pay another party's costs, provided the solicitor has a reasonable opportunity to make representations. Per Walsh v. 1124660 Ontario Limited (2007 CanLII 4789) and Young v. Young (1993 CanLII 34 (SCC)), abuse of process/bad faith need not be shown; it is enough that the acts described in the rule occurred, but courts must be extremely cautious to protect fearless advocacy, judging reasonableness at the time expense was incurred, not with hindsight.
application: The Master found this was not hindsight second-guessing: counsel was warned in advance about the proper forum, the need to appeal, and the absence of grounds to vary, yet pursued repetitive motions to vary. This caused costs to be incurred without reasonable cause and through undue delay, negligence or other default, particularly the wasted March 8, June 7 and July 23 attendances and repeated preparation. Impecuniosity/access-to-justice arguments had already been considered and rejected. Counsel was found responsible for at least one third of the defendants' costs.
conclusion: An order under rule 57.07 was warranted; the solicitor was ordered to pay $4,000 personally within 30 days.

issue: To what extent should the impecunious plaintiff be relieved of, or allowed to defer, costs liability?
facts: The plaintiff relied on disability pensions with a monthly surplus of about $102.70 (including a $25 charitable donation). She attended every appearance, was aware of the prior costs orders and of counsel's tactical steps, and sought to have any costs paid only after trial by set-off against any recovery.
rule: Impecuniosity is a relevant but discretionary factor in awarding costs (as set out in the Master's November 2, 2007 reasons and Christian Jew Foundation v. Christian Jew Outreach, [2007] O.J. No. 2140). The court must balance access to justice against the defendants' right to compensation, and probe whether impecuniosity is invoked in good faith or as a means to avoid responsibility; modest means do not entitle a party to play by a different set of procedural rules.
application: The Master had already found the plaintiff used impecuniosity as a means to avoid her litigant responsibilities, not in good faith. Allowing full deferral to after trial would let unreasonable procedures continue without consequence and risk no recovery if she lost. Balancing her finances, the Master found she could afford $50 per month (potentially foregoing the charitable donation), with the balance payable after trial.
conclusion: Impecuniosity did not shield the plaintiff from costs but justified instalment payments; her share was payable at $50/month once the stay is lifted, with the balance on final disposition.

issue: What quantum of costs is fair and reasonable, and how should payment be allocated and timed?
facts: The defendants incurred actual costs of $28,897 and claimed $22,806 on a partial indemnity basis for the intertwined dismissal/stay and variation motions (excluding the motion before Brown J.). Counsel asserted the costs were unreasonable and sought to cross-examine on the Costs Outline but made no substantive quantum submissions.
rule: Rule 57.01 factors govern; fixing costs is not merely multiplying hours by rates but must yield a fair and reasonable amount. There is no authority to cross-examine on a Costs Outline.
