The dissent, while also finding the damages large, held it was not shown the jury was misled or actuated by improper motives, and would not disturb the jury's discretion.
conclusion: The majority found the damages excessive and a substantial wrong under s. 28, justifying a new trial.

issue: Did the appellant's failure to object at trial to the impugned evidence and jury address preclude a new trial on appeal?
facts: Trial counsel for the appellant (different from appellate counsel) did not object to the evidence or to respondent's counsel's address at the time.
rule: There is a salutary rule that objection to improper conduct of counsel or admission of evidence must be raised before the trial judge on the spot (Sornberger v. Canadian Pacific R.W. Co., 24 A.R. 263; Dale v. Toronto R.W. Co., 34 O.L.R. 104), save in exceptional cases.
application: The majority held that once substantial wrong is established, the appellant is not to be denied a new trial merely because trial counsel failed to object, relying on Gage v. Reid. The dissent (Hodgins J.A.) applied the general rule strictly, finding no protest was made and the objection was therefore not open to the appellant, and that the case was not exceptional.
conclusion: The majority held the failure to object did not bar relief; the dissent would have applied the rule to dismiss the appeal.

issue: Should the respondents be prohibited from bringing further motions without leave under Rule 37.16 on the basis that their motions are frivolous and vexatious?
facts: The proceeding originated with an in rem forfeiture application by the Attorney General under the Civil Remedies Act seeking forfeiture of $229,345.00 and a 2006 Lincoln Mark LT truck as proceeds or instruments of crime. The Direk/Direkoglu respondents launched a 'counter-application' seeking to quash the application and claiming four billion dollars, alleging a decades-long judiciary-driven conspiracy, corruption, crimes against humanity and other atrocities. They then brought an endless string of unsuccessful motions and appeals, recycling near-identical grounds, repeatedly re-litigating an unmeritorious conflict-of-interest allegation against Stinson J. and levelling scandalous accusations of fraud, forgery, sexual abuse and other crimes against every judge who ruled against them.
rule: Rule 37.16 of the Rules of Civil Procedure (together with Rule 61.16(1) applying it to appellate motions) permits an order prohibiting a party from bringing further motions without leave — a 'mini-vexatious litigant order'. The indicia of vexatious proceedings are set out in Lang Michener v. Fabian (1987), 59 O.R. (2d) 353 (H.C.J.), endorsed in Bishop v. Bishop, 2011 ONCA 211, including re-litigating determined issues, actions that cannot succeed or serve no good, proceedings brought for improper purposes such as harassment, grounds repeated and supplemented in successive proceedings, the whole history of the matter, failure to pay costs, and persistent unsuccessful appeals.
application: The Court found each Lang Michener principle plainly applicable, with 'motions' substituted for 'actions' under Rule 37.16. The respondents' motions recycled identical grounds, re-litigated the failed conflict-of-interest claim against Stinson J., added baseless allegations against every judge who ruled against them, and were unsupported by any evidence. The multiplicity of frivolous and vexatious motions was found to be brought to delay the proceedings or abuse the process of the Court; the Court considered it unnecessary to recite the many motions in detail.
conclusion: Motion granted. The respondents are prohibited from bringing further motions in the specified Divisional Court and Superior Court files (or new files raising the same or similar matters) without leave, leave to be sought only by written motion; the Registrars are not to accept material other than a written leave motion; costs of $1,500 payable forthwith; the order effective immediately without the respondents' approval.

issue: Did the Society establish on a balance of probabilities that the children suffered actual physical harm under s. 74(2)(a)(i) and (ii) of the CYFSA?
facts: The children disclosed that M.A.R. and his partner T.E. hit and yelled at them during access, sometimes leaving bruises, and that this occurred at most visits. M.R. stopped attending access in January 2017 because she could no longer tolerate being hit. E.M.T. produced photographs of bruises. M.A.R. and T.E. denied all abuse, but the court found the workers' and children's evidence credible and the respondents' evidence riddled with material inconsistencies.
rule: Actual physical harm is the foundation of grounds under s. 74(2)(a) CYFSA and must be proved on a balance of probabilities (Children's Aid Society of Algoma v. J.B., 2019 ONCJ 6). Causation may be by act, omission or pattern and intention need not be proved (Jewish Family and Child Service v. K.(R.), 2008 ONCJ 774, aff'd 2009 ONCA 903); harm must be more than trifling (CAS Niagara v. P.T.; Rainy River v. B.(C.)). Corporal punishment using objects or blows to the head is harmful (Canadian Foundation for Children, Youth and the Law v. Canada (AG), 2004 SCC 4).
application: The court accepted the strikingly similar independent disclosures of M.R., J.R. and O.R., corroborated by consistent worker testimony, over the contradictory and evasive evidence of E.M.T., M.A.R. and T.E. A consistent pattern of repeated physical discipline (slaps to the back and face, occasional bruising), coupled with yelling, swearing and alcohol use that made the children fear for their safety, represented more than trifling harm. M.A.R. failed to protect the children from T.E., and E.M.T. was aware and failed to act protectively.
conclusion: A finding of actual physical harm under s. 74(2)(a)(i) and (ii) was made out.

issue: Did the Society establish that the children are at risk of physical harm under s. 74(2)(b)(i) and (ii) of the CYFSA?
facts: M.A.R.'s home was marked by yelling, swearing, excessive alcohol use that made him angrier, exposure to T.E.'s drug use and conflict including throwing objects, and repeated police involvement. E.M.T. knew of these concerns but took no protective steps until the Society intervened in November 2017.
rule: Section 74(2)(b) CYFSA requires a real and likely (more probable than not) risk of physical harm, inflicted by, or resulting from the failure or pattern of neglect of, the person having charge (Rainy River v. B.(C.), 2006 ONCJ 458; Ottawa-Carlton v. T. and T., 2000). A child may be at risk even if conduct is not directed at that child (Catholic CAS of Metro Toronto v. O.(L.M.)).
application: The environment of alcohol-fuelled anger, exposure to T.E.'s untreated drug use which M.A.R. himself conceded was 'not good', ongoing adult conflict including thrown objects, and M.A.R.'s poor judgment in permitting T.E.'s continued contact with the children established a real and likely risk. E.M.T.'s failure to protect further supported the finding.
conclusion: A finding that the children are at risk of physical harm under s. 74(2)(b)(i) and (ii) was made out.

issue: Did the Society establish that the children are at risk of emotional harm under s. 74(2)(h) of the CYFSA?
facts: The Society called no expert to establish a risk of emotional harm. Beyond a brief reference by the intake worker that O.R. had 'significant challenges' in the classroom, there was little evidence of the children's behaviours in home, school or community demonstrating listed symptoms of emotional harm.
rule: Section 74(2)(h) CYFSA requires the Society to prove, on a balance of probabilities, a real likelihood that the child will suffer at least one listed emotional harm (anxiety, depression, withdrawal, self-destructive or aggressive behaviour, delayed development), of a serious (not minimal, mild or moderate) degree, causally connected to the parent's conduct (Algoma v. A.B., 2018 ONCJ 831; Algoma v. J.B., 2019 ONCJ 6). Expert evidence is preferred but not mandatory; risk may be established from exposure to domestic violence or a child's distressed reactions (Chukwunomso v. Ransome, 2017 ONCJ 121; CAS Toronto v. S.A.C.).
application: Although a risk of physical harm was established, that does not automatically establish a risk of emotional harm. The Society adduced no evidence from anyone with the credentials to establish the risk, and failed to show that any child was likely to suffer a listed symptom in a serious degree. The evidence was insufficient to demonstrate the required risk and its severity.
conclusion: The claim for a finding of risk of emotional harm under s. 74(2)(h) was dismissed.

issue: What disposition is in the best interests of the children given the protection findings?
facts: The children had been placed with E.M.T. since apprehension on November 16, 2017; the Society had no protection concerns with her and she complied with the interim order. M.A.R. refused to communicate consistently with workers, would not sign consents, undertake drug screens or programming, breached directions regarding contact at R.R.'s home, and behaved aggressively toward a worker. However, his access visits were generally positive and J.R. and O.R. wished for more time with him; M.R. did not wish to attend access.
rule: Sections 101 and 102 CYFSA set out available orders where a child is found in need of protection; the paramount purpose (s. 1(1)) is the best interests, protection and well-being of the child, which takes precedence over the secondary purposes in s. 1(2) (Syl Apps Secure Treatment Centre v. D.(B.), 2007 SCC 38). Best-interests factors are enumerated in s. 74(3), and s. 101(2) requires consideration of the Society's efforts and the least intrusive order.
application: The Society made significant efforts to engage M.A.R., who refused to cooperate, failed to acknowledge concerns, and did not address the protection issues; supervised access alone did not show the risks were remedied. The court weighed the children's expressed wishes (J.R. and O.R. wanting more, but content with supervised access; M.R. not wishing to attend) and M.A.R.'s warm relationship with the younger children. The least intrusive order consistent with the children's best interests was placement with E.M.T. under supervision with Society-discretion access to M.A.R.
conclusion: A six-month supervision order placing the children with E.M.T. was made, with access to J.R. and O.R. at the Society's discretion and access to M.R. subject to her wishes.

issue: Should the Society be granted summary judgment under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules, i.e. is there no genuine issue requiring a trial?
facts: The four children had all been apprehended and placed with grandparents under temporary supervision orders; statutory protection findings under s. 47(2) and s. 37(2)(b) CFSA had already been made on November 17, 2011. The mother (T.M.1) sought return of the children or expanded access and opposed the orders; she had a history of non-compliance with supervision terms, exposure of the children to domestic violence, inconsistent access, mental-health concerns and failure to complete recommended programs.
rule: Rule 16 Family Law Rules permits summary judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; the responding party may not rest on mere allegations or denials but must set out specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial (r. 16(4.1)); r. 16(6) is mandatory. The court must take a 'good hard look' at the full evidentiary record but must not weigh evidence or assess credibility (Aguonie; Guarantee Co. of North America v. Gordon Capital; CAS Waterloo v. V.L.; CAS Toronto v. R.H.). The paramount purpose of the CFSA (s. 1(1)) is the best interests, protection and well-being of children, and the strict timelines in ss. 57 and 70 must be respected.
application: Justice Zuker reviewed the plans of care and the full evidentiary record. He found the mother's material amounted to a heartfelt desire to resume care rather than specific facts showing changed parenting ability; the uncontradicted facts (R.H.'s criminal record, history of domestic violence, mother's exposure of children to that violence, non-compliance with orders, mental-health and financial instability, no kin plan for J.H.) established a prima facie case. The children had been out of parental care beyond the statutory timelines and were in stable placements. No material fact affecting best interests required a trial.
conclusion: Summary judgment was granted; the mother failed to demonstrate a genuine issue for trial.

issue: What custody disposition under s. 57.1 CFSA is in the best interests of the children?
facts: T.M.2 and A.M. had lived with the maternal grandparents (B.Y. and S.P.) for extended periods and the grandparents consented to custody with the father D.F. also consenting. E.H. and J.H. were in the care of the paternal grandmother D.H., who consented to a six-month supervision placement, with R.H. consenting to supervision. The mother opposed and sought return of all children.
rule: Section 57.1 CFSA allows a custody order to a non-foster-parent with that person's consent where it is in the child's best interests; such an order is deemed a custody order under s. 28 of the Children's Law Reform Act. Best interests are governed by the non-exhaustive factors in s. 37(3) CFSA. The disposition must be the least disruptive order consistent with best interests (s. 57(2)-(4)), and best interests take priority over parental wishes (Catholic CAS v. C.M.; Young v. Young; King v. Low).
application: The court weighed continuity of care, the children's established stable placements, and the risks the mother continued to present. The proposed placements with consenting grandparents reflected the children's special needs, importance of family relationships and continuity, and the degree of risk. The rebuttable presumption favouring parental care was rebutted by the mother's unaddressed parenting deficits.
conclusion: Custody of T.M.2 and A.M. was granted to the maternal grandparents and custody of E.H. and J.H. to the paternal grandmother subject to Society supervision, all under s. 57.1.

issue: How should the parents' access be determined, and is the request for increased or unsupervised access a triable issue?
facts: D.F. sought regular overnight and holiday access and decision-making over religious upbringing, objecting to access being delegated to the grandparents' discretion. R.H. sought unsupervised access to E.H. and J.H. T.M.1 attended less than half her scheduled visits and sought unsupervised/overnight access. The Society and grandparents proposed supervised/limited access.
rule: Access is a right belonging to the child, not the parent, and must be decided in the child's best interests; a court can prohibit access (Catholic CAS v. M.(C.)). Access questions turn on whether the relationship is significantly advantageous to the child. Future access that is speculative and hypothetical is not a triable issue where it is not susceptible of proof.
application: The court found access with the mother generally positive but held that claims for increased/unsupervised access were premised on assumptions that did not yet exist and were too uncertain, speculative and hypothetical to constitute a triable issue. Given the disposition (leading toward adoption), the court left future access to be decided by the children's future adoptive parents, while setting specified interim access terms for R.H. and T.M.1 to the boys.
conclusion: No triable issue on access existed; the access terms in the disposition orders were fixed and future access left to the children's caregivers/adoptive parents.

issue: Does an Ontario court have jurisdiction simpliciter over a proposed global class action including non-resident Absent Foreign Claimants, and did the constitutional challenge remain live?
facts: Four Bangladeshi plaintiffs commenced a proposed class action in Ontario on behalf of survivors and families of the Rana Plaza collapse. Most putative class members reside in Bangladesh and had not attorned to the Ontario court. After Airia Brands and Excalibur, the plaintiffs recast the class from opt-out to opt-in and also ran an attornment/consent program in Bangladesh; Loblaws challenged jurisdiction and raised a constitutional argument, prompting the Attorney General of Ontario to intervene.
rule: Jurisdiction simpliciter is established by the presumptive connecting factors in Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17, together with traditional attornment. Excalibur Special Opportunities LP v. Schwartz Levitsky Feldman LLP, 2016 ONCA 916 confirms an Ontario court may take jurisdiction in a global class action over non-resident members; Harrington v. Dow Corning, 2000 BCCA 605 recognizes that non-residents can attorn by opting in. The Class Proceedings Act, 1992 is procedural and does not create or alter substantive rights (Bisaillon v. Concordia University, 2006 SCC 19).
application: The court held it had jurisdiction simpliciter based on a combination of the named parties' attornment, the Van Breda connecting factors, and the opt-in class definition. Because non-resident members would attorn post-certification through a court-supervised opt-in notice program, there would be no true Absent Foreign Claimants and no need to rule on the validity of the Bangladesh consent-collection exercise. The constitutional challenge therefore became moot.
conclusion: The Ontario court has jurisdiction simpliciter; Loblaws' constitutional challenge was moot and was dismissed without a ruling on its merits.

issue: Is the choice of law for the tort and fiduciary claims Ontario law or the law of Bangladesh?
facts: Loblaws formulated its Corporate Social Responsibility standards, retained Bureau Veritas, and made purchasing decisions in Ontario, but the Rana Plaza building, the workers, the social audits, and the deaths and injuries all occurred in Bangladesh. The plaintiffs pleaded that the wrongdoing occurred in Ontario; the defendants argued Bangladesh law applied (and would statute-bar the claims).
rule: The choice of law for torts is the lex loci delicti — the law of the place where the tort occurred (Tolofson v. Jensen, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 1022), with only a narrow discretionary 'injustice' exception. The place of a tort is the jurisdiction substantially affected by the defendant's activities and their consequences and whose law was in the parties' reasonable contemplation (Moran v. Pyle; Leonard v. Houle; Éditions Écosociété v. Banro). Limitation periods are substantive.
application: The court rejected the plaintiffs' 'pleading artifice' locating the wrongdoing exclusively in Ontario. The duty, breach, causation and damage elements of the negligence claim, and the equitable claim, were centred in Bangladesh, where the collapse and all harm occurred and whose law was referenced in the CSR standards. Even treating the case as a 'thorny' one where act and consequence diverge, the consequences were felt in Bangladesh, which designates Bangladesh law. Arguments to oust Bangladesh law for failure of proof, unsophisticated jurisprudence, discriminatory Sharia succession rules, and absence of punitive damages were rejected — the offensive Sharia distribution rule could be severed and none of the grounds met the injustice exception.
conclusion: Bangladesh law governs the tort and breach of fiduciary duty claims.

issue: Are the plaintiffs' claims statute-barred under Bangladesh's Limitation Act, 1908?
facts: The action was commenced on April 22, 2015, roughly two years after the April 24, 2013 collapse. Ten foreign-law experts testified. The key authority was Bangladesh Beverage Industries Ltd. v. Rowshan Akhter and the interplay of Articles 21, 22 and 120 of the Limitation Act, 1908.
rule: Foreign law is a question of fact proved by expert evidence; where experts conflict the court may examine the sources and decide (Allen v. Hay; General Motors Acceptance Corp. v. Town and Country Chrysler). Articles 21 and 22 of the Limitation Act, 1908 impose a one-year limitation for fatal-accident and personal-injury claims; Article 120 is a six-year residual provision; s. 6 extends time for minors; ss. 7 and 13 provide limited tolling.
application: Preferring the defendants' experts, the court found the Appellate Division in Bangladesh Beverage confirmed a one-year limitation period under Articles 21 and 22 for wrongful-death and personal-injury claims (the s. 4 vacation extension only made sense on a one-year period). Sections 7 and 13 did not toll the claims; s. 13 did not apply to a corporation never present in Bangladesh, and Bureau Veritas was present throughout. Only s. 6 preserved claims of class members who were minors (born on or after April 22, 1996) at the time of collapse.
conclusion: Under Bangladesh law the tort and fiduciary claims are statute-barred, except for putative class members who were minors at the time of the collapse.

issue: Is it plain and obvious that the defendants owed no viable duty of care in negligence?
facts: Loblaws was a purchaser of garments from Pearl Global, which sub-contracted to New Wave at Rana Plaza; Loblaws did not own, construct or control the building. Bureau Veritas conducted limited 'social audits' that expressly did not cover structural integrity. The plaintiffs alleged the defendants assumed responsibility for worker safety through CSR standards and audits.
rule: Under English/Bangladesh law a duty of care requires satisfaction of the Caparo test (foreseeability, proximity, and policy), the assumption-of-responsibility test (Hedley Byrne), or incremental development; the common law generally imposes no positive duty to protect others from third-party harm (Mitchell v. Glasgow City Council; Michael v. Chief Constable of South Wales Police). Under Ontario law the Anns/Cooper v. Hobart framework applies (foreseeability, proximity, residual policy), with special caution for nonfeasance (Childs v. Desormeaux; Fullowka).
application: Preferring Dr. Goudkamp over Dr. Morgan, the court held the claims were novel and failed every test. Proximity was absent: the defendants did not create the danger, had no control over the workplace, employers or building, and the alleged wrong was nonfeasance (a failure to protect from third-party conduct). Reliance was fictional — most workers and the many non-New Wave victims knew nothing of the CSR standards or audits. Bureau Veritas' limited retainer did not extend to structural integrity. Policy factors (indeterminate liability, disproportion, floodgates, discouraging beneficial CSR practices and trade with developing countries) overwhelmed any prima facie duty. Government-inspection precedents were inapposite because they rest on a pre-existing statutory duty.
conclusion: It is plain and obvious that neither Loblaws nor Bureau Veritas owed a viable duty of care under either Bangladesh or Ontario law; the negligence claims cannot succeed.

issue: Is Loblaws vicariously liable for the negligence of Pearl Global and New Wave?
facts: Pearl Global was a supplier and New Wave a sub-supplier of garments to Loblaws; neither was Loblaws' employee or agent. The plaintiffs alleged garment manufacturing in Bangladesh was inherently dangerous and that Loblaws had a non-delegable duty.
rule: Vicarious liability attaches to employer-employee relationships and, exceptionally, where an enterprise creates a risk that materializes (671122 Ontario Ltd. v. Sagaz Industries, 2001 SCC 59; K.L.B. v. British Columbia, 2003 SCC 51). A person is generally not liable for the acts of an independent contractor absent an inherently dangerous activity ordered by the defendant (Savage v. Wilby) or a non-delegable duty grounded in statute or relationship.
application: Pearl Global and New Wave were independent businesses selling goods, not services performing Loblaws' own work; Loblaws was a retailer, not a garment manufacturer, and had no control over the workplace. Garment manufacturing is not inherently dangerous in the exceptional sense. There was no source (statutory or relational) for a non-delegable duty; Bangladesh Beverage was merely a routine employer-employee case. The plaintiffs' reasoning ran backwards from a dangerous industry to a non-delegable duty that Loblaws never had.
conclusion: It is plain and obvious there is no viable vicarious liability claim against Loblaws under either legal system.

issue: Is there a viable breach of fiduciary duty claim against Loblaws?
facts: The plaintiffs alleged Loblaws, through its CSR standards and control over the scope of audits, undertook to protect the vulnerable workers' safety and owed them an ad hoc fiduciary duty.
rule: An ad hoc fiduciary duty requires an undertaking to act in the beneficiary's best interests, a defined class vulnerable to the fiduciary's control, and interests adversely affected by the exercise of that discretion; vulnerability must arise from the relationship (Galambos v. Perez, 2009 SCC 48; Elder Advocates of Alberta Society v. Alberta, 2011 SCC 24). Fiduciary duties are rarely imposed in commercial relationships.
application: There was no legally significant relationship — only an 'association' — between Loblaws and the workers, and none at all with the many non-New Wave victims. The workers' vulnerability pre-existed and did not arise from any understanding with Loblaws; Loblaws gave no express or implied undertaking of loyalty and held no discretionary power over the class. The CSR standards operated at a commercial, not fiduciary, level. The claim was in reality a disguised negligence/limitation-avoidance claim, with no unjust enrichment.
conclusion: It is plain and obvious there is no viable breach of fiduciary duty claim under either Bangladesh or Ontario law.

issue: Should the action be certified as a class proceeding under the Class Proceedings Act, 1992?
facts: The plaintiffs sought certification of a global opt-in class of survivors and families; the defendants opposed on all five s. 5 criteria.
rule: Section 5 of the Class Proceedings Act, 1992 requires a cause of action, an identifiable class, common issues, preferable procedure, and a suitable representative plaintiff, applied purposively (Hollick v. Toronto (City), 2001 SCC 68; AIC Limited v. Fischer, 2013 SCC 69).
application: Because the plaintiffs had no legally viable cause of action (and, under Bangladesh law, statute-barred claims), the cause-of-action criterion failed and there was nothing to certify. The court nonetheless held that, had viable claims existed, the identifiable class (subject to refinement), common issues, preferable procedure, and representative plaintiff criteria would have been satisfied, and the Apology Act and prior-accident pleadings would have been struck as improper.
conclusion: Certification is refused; the action is dismissed. The impugned pleadings would have been struck had the action been certified.

issue: Did the trial judge err in his findings as to whether the impugned statements were defamatory?
facts: Dr. Cadsky, a senior psychiatrist on stress leave, described colleague Dr. Chohan as a 'paranoid Sikh' during a private discussion with Drs. Rai and Woods about who might replace the departing clinical director. Drs. Baker, Ohlhauser and Gardener later communicated concerns that Dr. Chohan 'may be paranoid' to persons responsible for his practice. Dr. Chohan alleged all these statements defamed him.
rule: A publication is defamatory if it tends to lower a person's reputation in the estimation of reasonable/right-thinking members of the community (Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada; Botiuk v. Toronto Free Press, [1995] 3 S.C.R. 3; Hill v. Church of Scientology). Whether a statement is capable of defamatory meaning is a question of law reviewable for correctness (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33); underlying credibility and factual findings attract deference.
application: The Court held the trial judge effectively found Cadsky's remark defamatory and proceeded to the privilege analysis; he declined to rule on its truth. The trial judge rejected the evidence that Cadsky had threatened to force Dr. Chohan to resign, a credibility finding supported by the evidence and not palpably wrong. For Drs. Baker and Gardener the trial judge accepted that they did not use the term 'paranoid'; the Court of Appeal found it unnecessary to resolve whether they used the word, since even if defamatory the statements were protected.
conclusion: No reversible error; the defamation findings (and the credibility findings underpinning them) stood.

issue: Were the statements made on occasions of qualified privilege, and were the limits of that privilege exceeded?
facts: Cadsky's remark was made in a private, limited discussion among three FACS psychiatrists about candidates for a supervisory vacancy. The other defendants each communicated their honest concern about Dr. Chohan's health to persons (Drs. Block, Hibbard, Gardener) responsible for his practice and well-being.
rule: Qualified privilege attaches where the person communicating has a legal, social or moral interest or duty to make the communication and the recipient has a corresponding interest or duty to receive it (Hill v. Church of Scientology, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130). Privilege may be defeated where the communication is not reasonably germane/appropriate to the occasion (Adam v. Ward; Douglas v. Tucker). Whether privilege applies is a question of law reviewable for correctness.
application: Colleagues frankly discussing another employee's qualifications for a supervisory post is exactly what qualified privilege protects; each participant had a legitimate interest even without power over the decision. Offensive or intemperate language ('Sikh') did not defeat the privilege because the statement remained relevant to the protected interest and the argument that it exceeded the limits had not been argued below. The other defendants communicated only to persons responsible for Dr. Chohan's practice, without idle gossip, and did not exceed their duty.
conclusion: All occasions were properly held to be privileged; the privilege was not exceeded.

issue: Did the appellant establish actual malice sufficient to defeat qualified privilege?
facts: Dr. Chohan argued the remark was racially motivated and that Dr. Gardener, Ohlhauser and Baker acted with ulterior purposes, pointing to later letters and the committee Dr. Gardener appointed.
rule: Qualified privilege is defeated only by proof of express/actual malice — spite, ill-will, an indirect or ulterior motive conflicting with the occasion's duty, or speaking dishonestly or with reckless disregard for the truth; the onus lies on the plaintiff (Hill). Malice is a question of mixed law and fact reviewable for palpable and overriding error (Cimolai v. Hall, 2007 BCCA 225; Housen).
application: The trial judge found Cadsky honestly believed Dr. Chohan exhibited paranoid traits and used 'Sikh' descriptively; evidence (including from Sikh colleague Dr. Rai) showed Cadsky was generous across races, so the remark, though inflammatory, was not maliciously motivated. Subsequent letters written 15 months later could not establish the speaker's state of mind at the time of publication. For Ohlhauser, Baker and Gardener, each acted on genuine concern for a colleague's health and communicated to appropriate persons; there was no evidence of predetermined bias or ulterior purpose.
conclusion: Malice was not established against any defendant; the actions were properly dismissed.

issue: Should the father's request for exclusive custody be granted, or should shared custody be maintained in the child's best interests?
facts: The parents separated in 1999 and have exercised week-on/week-off shared custody since a December 2005 consent order endorsed by Guthrie J. Their relationship is highly conflictual. The 13-year-old daughter, X, has behavioural and learning difficulties (dyslexia), told the expert, her lawyer and the court she would prefer to spend more time with her father, but insisted on maintaining regular contact with both parents. The psychologist Pérusse found both parents have parental capacity, the mother somewhat stronger, and recommended custody to the mother partly to 'send a message' to the father.
rule: Under art. 33 C.c.Q. the child's best interests, assessed through moral, intellectual, emotional and physical needs, age, health, character and family environment, govern custody. Per C.J. c. M.T. each case turns on its own facts and no form of custody is presumptively preferred. A child over twelve's wishes are significant but not determinative (A.Z. c. S.O.). Expert recommendations inform but do not bind the judge, though reasons must be given for departing from them (D.L. c. L.D.). Continuity/status quo has merit but does not bar change where the child's interest requires it.
application: The court weighed X's preference, the expert report and the evidence. It found X has a positive image of both parents, loves both, and would suffer notable harm if substantially separated from either. The court respectfully declined to follow the expert's recommendation of maternal custody, holding that X's welfare must come before any 'message' to a parent, and noting many conflicts would arise regardless of the custody mode. The father demonstrated no change in circumstances justifying a modification, and the mother herself opposed exclusive custody because X needs her father.
conclusion: The request for exclusive custody was denied; the parents continue shared custody on the alternating one-week/one-week schedule.

issue: How should the access rights for the child's Jewish holidays be fixed given the parents' disagreement over their duration and the court's role regarding religion?
facts: The 2005 agreement provided X would be raised in the father's Jewish religion (the mother is Catholic) and would share the major Jewish holidays with her father. The parents disputed which holidays were important and how long the access should last. They agreed the relevant festivals are Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur, Passover, Chanukah, Purim and Shavuot, but no evidence beyond their testimony explained their significance or observance. The mother sought shorter access to minimize lost school days given X's learning difficulties; the father sought longer access.
rule: Per Young c. Young, custody and access decisions are not based on parents' faith, but religion may be a relevant circumstance; where religion is in conflict the court does not adjudicate a 'war of religion' but examines the practice's effects on the child, with the child's interest prevailing. A court cannot arbitrate what a religion requires and must use the sincerity criterion (citing Multani), recognizing adherents observe dogma with varying rigour.
application: The court held it could not arbitrate the religious requirements and balanced the father's attachment to the festivals against X's best interests, including minimizing lost school days during a difficult academic period. It fixed specific hours of access for each of the six named holidays, giving Jewish holidays priority where they conflict with Catholic ones.
conclusion: The father's request was granted in part; detailed access schedules for the six Jewish holidays were set, with priority over conflicting Catholic holidays. Passport/health card to follow the child, and transport arrangements clarified.

issue: On a summary judgment motion, is there a genuine issue for trial regarding Crown wardship of Brittney P.?
facts: Brittney, born with severe medical problems requiring G-tube feeding and ongoing specialist care, had been in society care for over 18 months after a 2007 finding that she was a child in need of protection based on the mother's inadequate prenatal and post-natal care. The mother filed a lengthy affidavit but produced little evidence of changed circumstances, took no counselling or parenting courses, had a chaotic lifestyle, and now planned with Mr. Mohammed K., a man with a troubling history known to the society.
rule: Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules permits summary judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; the moving party bears the onus (CAS of Hamilton v. M.N.). The court takes a 'hard look' but does not weigh credibility (CAS of Nipissing v. Marielle M.). A parent must put their 'best foot forward' and show more than a heartfelt desire to parent — an arguable improvement in circumstances (CAS of Toronto v. Robin H.). On a status review the court asks 'what has changed?' (Catholic CAS of Metropolitan Toronto v. Cidalia M.), applying best-interests criteria in s. 37(3) and disposition provisions in ss. 57, 70 CFSA. No genuine issue exists where there is no realistic possibility of an outcome other than that sought (CAS of Niagara v. S.C.).
application: The mother's affidavit largely re-litigated the original protection finding (which she never appealed) and consisted of bald denials without corroborating medical or third-party evidence. The risk concerns present at apprehension persisted: instability, conflict, neglect of the children's needs, no insight, and a plan involving an uninvestigated, high-risk partner. The statutory society-wardship period for a child under six had elapsed, and no trial judge would return this high-needs child without a lengthy graduated access period that was no longer available.
conclusion: No triable issue existed; Brittney P. was made a Crown ward for the purpose of adoption.

issue: Should the mother's access to Brittney P. be reinstated?
facts: The mother's access had been suspended in September 2008 after she missed a visit following Justice Spence's order triggered by chronic missed/late visits. She moved to reinstate access.
rule: Once Crown wardship is ordered, s. 59(2.1) CFSA creates a presumption against access unless the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and access will not impair future adoption; the onus to rebut is on the respondent (CAS of Toronto v. Dora P.). Under s. 141.1 an outstanding access order must be terminated before adoption placement.
application: The mother led no evidence that access would not impair Brittney's opportunity for adoption, so she failed to rebut the presumption; it was unnecessary to decide whether the relationship was beneficial and meaningful.
conclusion: The presumption was not rebutted; Crown wardship was ordered without access and the mother's motion to reinstate access was dismissed.

issue: Are the two older children in need of protection and properly placed with the paternal grandparents?
facts: Irene (b.2001) and Christina (b.2003) had lived with the paternal grandparents since January 2008, thriving there. In the mother's care they had missed significant school, suffered grossly neglected dental needs (Christina), lapsed immunizations, and were exposed to repeated domestic conflict between the parents culminating in police involvement.
rule: Section 37(2)(b)(i)/(ii) CFSA (risk of physical harm from failure to care or pattern of neglect) and s. 37(2)(g) (risk of emotional harm). The court may find protection under an unpleaded clause where there is no surprise and full opportunity to test the evidence (Durham CAS v. R.S.; CAS of Hamilton-Wentworth v. K.R.). Past conduct is admissible (s. 50(1)); risk must be real not speculative (CAS of Ottawa-Carleton v. T.); exposure to domestic violence suffices (CAS of Niagara v. T.P.; CAS of Toronto v. Sheila Ann C.). Disposition governed by ss. 57(1),(3),(4) and 37(3) best-interests criteria.
application: The parents' neglect of Brittney, plus neglect of the older children's dental/medical needs, school absences, housing instability and exposure to domestic conflict, established no triable issue that they were at likely risk of physical harm (s.37(2)(b)) and emotional harm (s.37(2)(g)). The grandparents' home provided stability and improvement; the mother's identical, deficient plan and unaddressed concerns about Mr. Mohammed K. left no realistic chance of return. Access needed to remain supervised given the mother's inappropriate questioning and escalating unfounded abuse allegations.
conclusion: No triable issue; the children were found in need of protection under ss. 37(2)(b)(i),(ii) and (g), placed with the paternal grandparents under six months' society supervision with the mother's access supervised at the society's discretion and the father's supervised by the grandparents.

issue: Should a restraining order issue against the mother under s. 80(1) of the Act?
facts: A society worker relayed the paternal grandfather's complaint that the mother and Mr. Mohammed K. were frequently calling, hanging up, and circumventing a call block; the mother denied any recent contact.
rule: Section 80(1) CFSA permits a restraining order; given the severe consequences of breach (including imprisonment), the court must be satisfied the evidence justifies the order, especially on summary judgment.
application: The society's evidence was hearsay through the worker, without direct evidence from the grandfather or corroborating telephone records; the court could not determine on a balance of probabilities that harassment occurred.
conclusion: There was a triable issue; the summary judgment motion for a restraining order was dismissed, without prejudice to renewing it with further evidence.

issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to whether the child continues to be in need of protection?
facts: The child had been found in need of protection in 2012 and had lived continuously with the paternal grandmother since February 2013. The mother had removed the child from a supervised access visit without permission, refused to allow the Society to assess her residence or speak with her proposed support (her father), had two hospitalizations for suicidal ideation, was diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, and had not visited the child at the Society's office for over a year while showing up unannounced at the grandmother's home and the child's school. In reply the mother largely offered bald denials and self-serving assertions without third-party corroboration.
rule: Under Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules the court shall grant summary judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial (Rule 16(6)); the responding party must put its best foot forward with specific facts and cannot rest on bald denials (Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto v. A.(M.); Toronto-Dominion Bank v. Hylton). Following Hryniak v. Maulin, the court first asks whether the record permits a fair and just adjudication. In child protection the paramount consideration is the best interest, protection and well-being of the child (s. 1(1) CFSA), and courts must be cautious but need not confine summary judgment to the clearest cases (Jewish Child and Family Services v. A.(R.)).
application: The court took a hard look at the record. The concerns that led to apprehension persisted: the mother's refusal to permit assessment of her plan, her year-long failure to visit, her fixation on the child's feeding, her unresolved mental-health issues addressed only recently, and her repeated moves. Her denials were self-serving and unsupported by any third-party affidavit (including her proposed support, her father), so they did not raise a triable issue. The court found no realistic possibility of an outcome other than a continued finding of need for protection.
conclusion: No genuine issue for trial; the child continues to be in need of protection.

issue: Is a custody order to the grandmother under s. 57.1 CFSA in the child's best interests, or is there a triable issue on disposition?
facts: The child, now nine, had thrived in the grandmother's care for three years, improving academically and behaviourally, participating in community activities, and enjoying extended-family support. The grandmother committed to being a long-term caregiver and to fostering the child's relationship with both parents. The mother's plan had shifted between May and October 2015 (originally living with her father, then an undisclosed residence) and remained unverified.
rule: On disposition the court may make an order for custody under s. 57.1, guided by the best-interests factors in s. 37(3) CFSA (child's needs, development, cultural background, continuity of care, relative merits of the plans, child's views, and risk). Sections 57(2)-(4) require considering earlier efforts, less disruptive alternatives and family/community placements. The test throughout is the child's best interests (s. 65(1)).
application: Applying s. 37(3), the grandmother's plan met the child's physical, mental and emotional needs, preserved cultural connections on both sides, maintained relationships with both parents, and provided the least disruptive continuity of care. The mother's recently formulated and unverified plan posed an unjustified risk of harm if the child were removed. There was no realistic alternative outcome, so no triable issue on disposition.
conclusion: Custody placed with the grandmother under s. 57.1; no genuine issue for trial on disposition.

issue: Should access to the parents be left to the grandmother's discretion?
facts: The mother had failed to exercise supervised access for over a year and had engaged in harassing conduct at the grandmother's home and the child's school; there was a history of domestic violence between the parents.
rule: The court retains discretion to structure access consistent with the child's best interests (s. 65(1) CFSA).
application: Given the mother's conduct and the need for stability, the court found no triable issue warranting a fixed access regime and left the level, location and length of access to the grandmother's judgment.
conclusion: All access to the mother and father is at the sole discretion of the grandmother.

issue: Is an order for access between the mother and a child placed in extended society care in the child's best interests under the CYFSA?
facts: A.G., born prematurely in 2018 with significant medical needs, was found in need of protection and placed in extended society care. The mother, who has a long history with the society and lost custody of her other children, had never parented A.G., missed most of his medical appointments, and had many parenting limitations requiring fully supervised access, but had consistent, loving, positive weekly supervised visits since August 2018 and had made significant life changes (no alcohol since October 2017; no contact with the abusive father since November 2017).
rule: Under ss. 105(5) and (6) of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, an access order to a child in extended society care may be made only if it is in the child's best interests; the court must consider, as part of that analysis, whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and, if relevant, whether access will impair future adoption opportunities, weighed against the best-interests factors in s. 74(3). Per Kawartha-Haliburton Children's Aid Society v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316, the changes represent a significant shift: there is no longer a presumption against access, the burden no longer requires the parent to prove a beneficial/meaningful relationship and no impairment, and the court undertakes a holistic best-interests analysis (endorsing the flexible interpretation in Jewish Family and Child Service of Greater Toronto v. K.B., 2018 ONCJ 659).
application: The court applied the more expansive Kawartha approach. Although the child's most meaningful relationship was with his foster mother, his relationship with the mother was beneficial: she was loving, consistent, punctual, calm, and met his instrumental needs, and access preserved a connection with a biological parent, his Ethiopian culture and language, and his family/medical history, with potential future meaning as he ages. Weighing the s. 74(3) factors, access would not interfere with his secure placement (supervised visits posed no risk), was consistent with sibling access, and would not unduly delay permanency. The court also found the mother lacked the attributes that impair adoptability (aggression, undermining, dishonesty, litigiousness) and the society led no evidence that access would deter the foster mother's adoption plan, so access would not impair future adoption opportunities.
conclusion: The court held that an access order between the mother and the child is in the child's best interests.

issue: What access order is in the child's best interests?
facts: The mother had supervised visits once weekly for 90 minutes; the child is a secure member of the foster family who is his psychological parent, and permanency planning (adoption) should not be delayed.
rule: The court must balance preserving a beneficial relationship against permitting the child's mental and emotional transition toward permanency (Children's Aid Society of Ottawa v. J.B., 2017 ONSC 1194); post-extended-care access is qualitatively different from pre-care access, serving only to preserve a positive relationship (Native Child & Family Services of Toronto v. J.E.G., 2014 ONCJ 109).
application: Given the quality of the visits, the child's need for a secure, undisrupted placement, and the goal of permanency, the court reduced contact substantially from the current weekly regime to a modest schedule in the society's discretion.
conclusion: The court ordered a minimum of 6 supervised visits per year of at least one hour each, plus a recent photograph provided to the mother 4 times per year.

issue: Who should be named as access holders and access recipients?
facts: Only an access holder may bring an openness application if the society files a notice of intention to place the child for adoption; the mother has cognitive, educational and language limitations.
rule: Subsection 105(7) of the Act requires the court to name access holders and recipients; only an access holder can bring an openness application under s. 195.
application: Because the court was not confident the mother could bring a timely openness application given her limitations, it named both the mother and the child as access holders and recipients, enabling the Office of the Children's Lawyer to bring an openness application on the child's behalf if warranted.
conclusion: Both the mother and the child were named as access holders and access recipients.

issue: Is access between the father and the child in the child's best interests?
facts: The father did not file an Answer/Plan of Care, did not participate, was found in default, has a violent and extensive criminal history, and has chosen not to have a relationship with the child.
rule: Access must be in the child's best interests under ss. 105(5)-(6) and s. 74(3) of the CYFSA.
application: The father chose not to have a relationship with the child, has a violent criminal history, and access with him would be neither beneficial nor meaningful.
conclusion: The court held that access with the father is not in the child's best interests and ordered no access to the father.

issue: Does the 'creation of money out of thin air' theory disclose a reasonable cause of action under Rule 19(24)(a)?
facts: The claimants (credit-card and mortgage debtors) alleged that the defendant banks and credit unions created money 'out of thin air' by advancing credit through bookkeeping entries rather than paying out cash or hard currency, and that their loans and enforcement proceedings were therefore void. All causes of action pleaded (breach of contract, unjust enrichment, unlawful creation of money, usury, conversion, etc.) rested on this premise.
rule: Under R. 19(24)(a) a pleading may be struck where it is 'plain and obvious' that it discloses no reasonable claim, taking the pleaded facts as true and resolving doubt in favour of the pleading (Hunt v. T & N plc, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress). No evidence is admissible on such an application (R. 19(27)). 'Money' at law is not confined to cash or legal tender: any medium that fulfills the function of money and is accepted in payment of a debt is money (Reference Re Alberta Legislation, [1938] S.C.R. 100). The Bank Act, s. 409(2)(d), authorizes issuing and operating credit-card plans.
application: The Court held that Canadian law does not restrict 'money' to cash or hard currency; credit created by bookkeeping entries is money and banks are lawfully entitled to deal in it and to issue credit cards. The claimants' fundamental premise—that the banks' failure to hand over cash rendered the transactions unlawful—is therefore untenable, and every cause of action derived from it is bound to fail.
conclusion: The 'money for nothing' theory discloses no reasonable cause of action; the derivative claims are dismissed under R. 19(24)(a).

issue: Do the claims against the banks' solicitors disclose a cause of action or are they an abusive collateral attack?
facts: The plaintiffs sued the solicitors and law firms who acted for the banks in collection and foreclosure proceedings, alleging unlawful interference with contractual relations, fraud on the court, and lack of standing, and purporting to 'charge' the solicitors large sums to cease acting.
rule: A court order made within jurisdiction is binding unless set aside on appeal or lawfully quashed; a collateral attack is an attack in proceedings other than those whose specific object is to reverse the order (Wilson v. The Queen, [1983] 2 S.C.R. 594, cited in Samos Investments Inc. v. Pattison). Abuse of process may be found under R. 19(24)(d) (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E. Local 79, 2003 SCC 63).
application: The claims against the solicitors were derivative of the money-creation theory and, insofar as the banks had already obtained judgments, amounted to collateral attacks on those judgments. The debtors' proper recourse was to appeal or move to set aside the judgments, not to sue the banks' lawyers.
conclusion: The claims against the solicitors disclose no cause of action and are struck under R. 19(24)(a) and as an abuse of process under R. 19(24)(d).

issue: Should claims/counterclaims be struck as res judicata or abuse of process where prior judgments existed or the allegations could have been raised earlier?
facts: In several actions the banks had already obtained foreclosure orders or default judgments (e.g., RBC, Laurentian, Canada Trust, Envision, CIBC against Dempsey; MBNA's Ontario default judgment against Darmantchev). The claimants had not appealed and, in some cases, had raised or could have raised the same allegations in the earlier proceedings.
rule: Parties must bring their whole case forward and may not re-litigate matters that could have been raised earlier (Henderson v. Henderson (1843) 3 Hare 100; Samos Investments Inc. v. Pattison). Abuse of process under R. 19(24)(d) prevents proceedings that violate judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of justice (Toronto v. C.U.P.E.; Babavic v. Babowech).
application: Because judgments had already been obtained and no appeals taken, and because Darmantchev had chosen not to pursue the same defence in the Ontario action, re-advancing the allegations in British Columbia offended the Henderson v. Henderson principle and finality. No special circumstances existed.
conclusion: Such claims are res judicata and abusive; they are struck under R. 19(24)(d).

issue: Should the amended counterclaims be struck as unintelligible, embarrassing, or for failing to plead material facts?
facts: The Liong and Luinenburg amended counterclaims used 'accepted for value / authorized representative / nominal defendant' language, described the defendants as 'corporate/legal fictions,' and listed bare conclusory causes of action without supporting facts; some amendments also added solicitors contrary to an earlier stay order.
rule: R. 19(1) requires pleadings to state, in summary form, the material facts relied on. Pleadings that are unintelligible, confusing, or fail to state a real issue intelligibly are embarrassing and may be struck under R. 19(24)(a) and (c) (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform; Borsato v. Basra; Keddie v. Dumas Hotels Ltd.).
application: The Court found the amended counterclaims unintelligible and lacking any statement of material facts, and the original counterclaims rested on the failed money-creation theory. Amendments adding the banks' solicitors also breached the prior stay order.
conclusion: The counterclaims are struck/dismissed under R. 19(24)(a) and (c) and for breach of R. 19(1).

issue: Should the court order production to the Society under s. 130(3) of the CYFSA of the requested third-party records regarding the parents and children, and subject to what conditions?
facts: With trial five weeks away, the Society moved to compel 15 third parties (police, doctors, schools, psychologists, addiction and diversion services) to produce records on the parents and five children. The parents had signed consents over a year earlier but refused to renew them, notably refusing consent to the mother's Diversion Program records. The parents did not argue irrelevance but said the Society already had valid consents and had not first sought and been refused the records, making the motion premature and a 'fishing expedition.'
rule: Section 130(3) CYFSA permits the court, where satisfied a record 'may be relevant' and the holder has refused inspection, to order production for inspection and copying. Section 130(6) restricts disclosure of information so obtained. The 'may be relevant' test is not onerous ('semblance of relevance'); where the best interests of the child are at issue the court has a positive obligation to ensure the most helpful and relevant information is before it; police records are relevant; privacy interests are not weighed beyond those built into the section and must be supported by an evidentiary basis (Jewish Family and Child Service of Greater Toronto v. H.B.S., 2012 ONCJ 663; Catholic Children's Aid Society of Hamilton v. L.K., 2016 CanLII 15148 (ON SC)).
application: The court found the parents' procedural objections to be 'pure semantics' and counterproductive; their own refusal to renew consents caused the delay they complained of. The records were clearly relevant to whether the children need protection and the appropriate disposition, and the court would not risk them being unavailable at trial. The court nonetheless tailored the order to protect privacy in sensitive categories, excluding counselling session notes from the father's addiction records and the child B.L.'s psychological records, and limiting the mother's Diversion Program records to those confirming required programming, attendance, completion and engagement.
conclusion: Motion granted in its entirety, subject to the stated exceptions; production orders issued against all 15 third parties on the specified terms.

issue: Are the kin, added as parties solely to advance an access claim to one child (A.L.), entitled to disclosure of the Society's entire file and all records produced under s. 130?
facts: The kin, formerly caregivers of A.L. (1), were added as parties in October 2020 for the limited purpose of advancing an access claim to A.L. They cross-moved for release of the Society's complete file and all records ordered produced, relying on Catholic Children's Aid Society of Hamilton v. L.K. The parents objected that the information was irrelevant to the access claim and intruded on their privacy.
rule: Section 130 CYFSA's enhanced production power is available only to a society, not other litigants (Children's Aid Society of Algoma v. J.R., 2018 ONCJ 835). Disclosure to other parties is governed by Rules 19–22 of the Family Law Rules and turns on relevance to the claim advanced. Catholic Children's Aid Society of Hamilton v. L.K. does not stand for an absolute rule that all society records must be shared with all parties; sharing depends on relevance to that party's claim.
application: The kin were made parties only to advance an access claim to A.L., to be assessed at the disposition stage if A.L. is first found in need of protection; they have no right to participate in the protection-finding stage. If their CYFSA access claim fails they may still seek a contact order under the CLRA. Their request for the entire file was a fishing expedition, none of it relevant to the limited access claim. The kin already had access to the voluminous Continuing Record, participated in the settlement conference, and had cared for A.L. full-time until Fall 2020, giving them ample material to prepare. Only the family doctor's records regarding A.L. herself were relevant.
conclusion: The cross-motion for the full file was refused; the kin were entitled only to Dr. Bell/Appletree Medical Centre records regarding A.L. (1).

issue: Was the defendant entitled to further and better particulars of publication and distribution, to be supplied before discovery continued?
facts: The plaintiff, a group named in a Canadian Jewish Congress document as a 'white supremacist hate group', pleaded only that the document was 'widely distributed to judges, lawyers, police officials, and important decision-makers, as well as the public', without naming recipients or specifying the manner of distribution. There was no evidence the document had in fact been published, and the defendant intended to raise defences (justification, fair comment, qualified/absolute privilege) that turn on the circumstances of each publication.
rule: Under Rule 19(11) a party may obtain particulars necessary to formulate its defence. In defamation, a plaintiff must plead the names of persons to whom words were published and cannot use discovery as a fishing expedition to find instances of publication (Gatley on Libel and Slander, para. 1067, adopted in Wesson v. Royal Canadian Legion (1985), 63 B.C.L.R. 327 (BCCA); Walker v. C.R.O.S. (1993)). The discretion to postpone particulars until after discovery is much narrower in defamation actions (Esson J.A. in Wesson).
application: The court found only a bald assertion of wide distribution with no evidence of actual publication and no 'peculiar knowledge' held by the defendant. The situation was unlike Richardson, where the defendant alone knew to whom remarks were made; here the plaintiff, claiming wide distribution, could itself supply the details. Following Wesson, particulars in a defamation action should generally be furnished before discovery, and this pleading verged on speculation.
conclusion: The defendant was entitled to the particulars requested; the plaintiff must provide the names of persons to whom the document was allegedly distributed and details of how it was directed to them before discoveries continue.

issue: Should the claim against Dr. Elterman be dismissed under Rule 18A?
facts: Dr. Elterman, Chair of the Congress's Pacific Region, deposed he had no involvement in drafting, publishing or distributing the document. However, he conceded that the 'Forward', which expressly referred to and adopted the impugned document, went out under his name with his approval, though signed on his behalf by a Mr. Nest.
rule: On a Rule 18A summary trial application, dismissal requires that the matter be capable of just resolution on the affidavit evidence. A person who adopts and publishes defamatory material, with knowledge of its distribution, may attract liability.
application: The court held Elterman's affidavit denial was not sufficient in the absence of contrary material, because he admitted the Forward was in his name and adopted the impugned document. If publication and distribution can be established and the document found defamatory, he could be liable along with the Congress by reason of his adoption of the material. No submission was made that he was not a proper party. These issues could only be resolved after particulars were furnished and pleadings amended.
conclusion: The application to dismiss the action against Dr. Elterman was denied.

issue: Could the plaintiff compel Dr. Elterman to answer discovery questions and examine him as the Congress's representative?
facts: The plaintiff sought to compel answers to questions Elterman refused at his examination for discovery and to examine him as representative of the Congress. The defendant had initially objected but conceded he was a proper person to be examined in that capacity.
rule: A party is entitled to examine an opposing party to test denials made in an affidavit, subject to relevance and the state of the pleadings.
application: Despite his affidavit denials, the plaintiff was entitled to examine Elterman to test those denials. With the concession that he was a proper representative of the Congress, some questions objectionable to him personally were now unobjectionable in his representational capacity. The court declined to define the permissible questions, leaving that to counsel in light of the particulars ruling, with liberty to apply.
conclusion: The plaintiff may examine Dr. Elterman; the precise scope of questions was left to counsel to resolve, failing which the parties had leave to apply.

issue: Should the father's access rights be suspended as the mother requested, or maintained and progressively increased?
facts: Custody of X (born 2006) was granted to the mother in 2009 with the father, who is Jewish, having weekend, summer and Jewish-holiday access. X increasingly refused to see his father and reacted negatively before and after visits. The mother sought suspension of access, supported by pediatrician Dr. Hortop's recommendation of respite; the father sought increased access following psychologist Raymond David's joint expert report recommending gradual expansion of access, parental coaching and psychological follow-up.
rule: Access decisions are governed by the best interests of the child. Where individual parental capacities are not seriously in doubt, it is highly desirable for a child to maintain good relations with both parents and not be confined in a one-way allegiance (Droit de la famille – 2085, 1994 CanLII 6230 (QC CA)).
application: The court preferred Mr. David's complete, documented and corroborated opinion over Dr. Hortop's, noting that Dr. Hortop's recommendation only addressed symptoms and lacked full data on their cause. The anxiety symptoms reported by the mother appeared only in her presence and were not corroborated by the teacher, school psychologist, father, or the photos/videos. Suspending access would deprive X of a parent, which was not advisable; the experiential relationship with the father needed to be intensified rather than interrupted.
conclusion: Access was not suspended; the court granted and progressively increased the father's access (up to alternate weekends Friday to Sunday plus a Wednesday supper), ordered parental coaching, prohibited denigration and recording of the child, and recommended psychological follow-up and reassessment at the end of 2014.

issue: How does the finding of parental alienation affect the child's best interests and the weight given to his expressed wishes?
facts: Two psychologists (Gauthier and David) independently found X displayed the characteristic behaviour of a child experiencing parental alienation: categorical rejection of the father, absence of ambivalence, weak/absurd reasons, adult concepts, unconditional support for the mother, and animosity extending to the father's spouse. The mother's unconscious anxiety toward the father was radiated to and absorbed by the child.
rule: Parental alienation is a situation in which a parent, consciously or unconsciously, negatively programs and indoctrinates the child to the detriment of the other parent (Collection de droit 2011-2012, vol. 3); Dr. Gardner's eight symptoms of parental alienation apply. In such a situation, the child's expressed wish cannot be considered voluntary or in the child's interest.
application: The court found X exhibited Gardner's symptoms and that the alienation was the unconscious product of the mother's anxiety, not deliberate conduct. Because the refusal to see the father resulted from alienation, X's stated wish never to see his father could not be treated as voluntary or determinative of his interests; his interest required steps to rebuild his relationship with the father.
conclusion: The court concluded X was in all likelihood the object of parental alienation, discounted his expressed wish, and adopted measures aimed at motivating him to invest in his relationship with his father.

issue: Do the plaintiff grandparents have standing to sue for damages on behalf of the children?
facts: DM and MM, the paternal grandparents of three children taken into care by the Director of Child and Family Services, purported to bring two actions seeking damages both on their own behalf and on behalf of the children arising from the children's separation from them.
rule: Rule 2.11(a) of the Alberta Rules of Court requires that an individual under 18 years of age must have a litigation representative to bring, defend, continue or participate in an action. Standing to sue on a child's behalf requires legal guardianship or appointment as litigation representative.
application: The grandparents were neither legal guardians of the children (permanent guardianship having been awarded to the Director) nor appointed litigation representatives. They therefore had no status to advance claims on the children's behalf, and even if appointed, the actions would still fail as a collateral attack.
conclusion: The plaintiffs had no standing to bring proceedings on the children's behalf; the claims advanced for the children were dismissed.

issue: Are the plaintiffs' claims for separation damages an abuse of process amounting to a collateral attack on the custody and guardianship orders?
facts: The separation of the grandparents from the children was authorized by a series of custody and guardianship orders of the Provincial Court and Court of Queen's Bench under the CYFEA, all of which the plaintiffs had participated in and unsuccessfully appealed. Their damages actions rested on the premise that they had been wrongfully denied custody and access.
rule: The doctrine of abuse of process (Toronto (City) v C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63) empowers a court to prevent the misuse of its procedure, including relitigation of matters already determined; a collateral attack on prior court orders is an abuse of process (also Alberta v W. (B.J.), 1990 ABCA 300; ESA Holdings Ltd. v Shea Nerland Canlan LLP, 2007 ABQB 78; 644036 Alberta Ltd. v Morbank Financial Inc., 2014 ABQB 681). Rule 3.68 permits striking such claims.
application: Both the Provincial Court and the Court of Queen's Bench had determined that the plaintiffs should not have custody and should have access only as permitted by the Director; the plaintiffs' appeals had all failed. The damages actions were founded on the contrary premise that custody and access had been wrongfully denied, thereby seeking to relitigate the very issues already decided.
conclusion: The actions were an abuse of process as a collateral attack on the prior orders and were struck under Rule 3.68; summary dismissal was granted.

issue: Did the Society meet its two-part onus under the CYFSA to establish that W could not be adequately protected in KB's care subject to supervision?
facts: W is a 16-month-old, non-verbal child. His mother KB faces criminal charges for making child pornography and exposure arising from photographs in which she performed a sexual act while a young child (T) was present. KB and father OA (facing numerous serious child-pornography and sexual-assault charges) had recently separated, though KB continued to advocate for OA's virtual access. KB provided only scant evidence about the photographs, failed to disclose the separation to the Society worker, and did not return signed consents. Her instrumental care of W was not in issue and she was compliant with prior orders.
rule: At a temporary care and custody hearing the Society bears a two-part onus: (1) to establish on credible and trustworthy evidence reasonable grounds to believe a real possibility that returning the child to the pre-intervention caregiver makes it more probable than not the child will suffer harm; and (2) that the child cannot be adequately protected by terms of an interim supervision order (Children's Aid Society of Ottawa-Carleton v. T., 2000 CanLII 21157; CAS of Halton Region v. Z. (T.A.), 2012 ONCJ 231). The onus is relatively low given the statutory language of 'reasonable' grounds, 'risk' and 'likely' harm (CAS of Dufferin County v. A.T., 2011 ONCJ 52). A supervision order requires a minimum threshold of cooperation, reliability and an open, honest relationship with the Society (CCAS of Toronto v. S. (P.N.), 2015 ONCJ 164). Evidence is admitted under s. 94(10) CYFSA if credible and trustworthy.
application: The court found risk arose from KB's serious criminal charges and her relationship with OA. KB's minimal explanation of the disturbing photographs showed at best a significant lapse in judgment, and W required a caregiver alert to child-focused conduct. KB minimized the charges and, post-separation, advocated for OA's virtual access, raising concern she did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation or the risk OA could record interactions. The relationship indicators showed OA had been controlling and KB was only in the early stages of counselling and had not yet demonstrated she was impervious to his influence. On the second branch, supervision could not adequately manage the significant, largely unknown risk; KB's failure to disclose the separation and to return consents undermined the open, honest relationship a supervision order requires.
conclusion: The Society met both branches of the test. W could not be safely returned to KB even with supervision terms.

issue: Was it in W's best interests to be placed in the temporary care and custody of maternal grandmother CB, subject to Society supervision?
facts: CB had been deemed a place of safety since November 7, 2023 and W had thrived in her care. A full kinship assessment of CB was approved January 25, 2024 with no concerns, and no concerns existed about CB's compliance with the existing supervision order. CB gave positive feedback about KB and confirmed she would contact the Society if concerned.
rule: The CYFSA requires the least disruptive placement consistent with adequate protection (s. 94(2),(4),(5); CAS of Hamilton v. D. (B.), 2012 ONSC 2448). Where a child cannot be returned to the pre-intervention caregiver, the court must consider placement with a relative or extended-family member before agency care, assessed against the best-interests factors in s. 74(3) CYFSA. Supervision terms must be reasonable and proportionate to the risk (CAS of Windsor-Essex v. B. (S.), 2007 ONCJ 2700).
application: CB demonstrated an ability to meet all of W's needs, the kinship assessment was positive, and W was thriving. The supervision terms requested were proportionate and addressed specific risk concerns. Kinship placement with CB was the least disruptive option consistent with protecting W.
conclusion: Placement of W in CB's temporary care and custody, subject to Society supervision, was in W's best interests.

issue: Should KB be granted unsupervised parenting time with W?
facts: KB's Release Order prohibited contact with persons under 18 and attendance at parks and places where children are present. KB sought unsupervised time including in the community to bond with W. She resides with CB and W, is primarily responsible for W's needs while supervised, and many alternate supervisors have been approved. W remained strongly attached to KB.
rule: Access orders are made under s. 94(8) CYFSA on terms the court considers appropriate, guided by the paramount best-interests purpose and the s. 74(3) factors, and by the principle of least disruptive action consistent with the child's best interests (ss. 1(1),(2) CYFSA).
application: Unsupervised access would contradict KB's existing Release Order, and even if varied the court would not order it because it was not in W's best interests, relying on the placement risk analysis. Given W's young age and the absence of professional evidence supporting the need, the court declined. KB already had unrestricted duration and frequency of supervised time while living with W and CB, with no evidence the arrangement harmed their bond.
conclusion: KB's request for unsupervised parenting time was refused; her supervised access continued.

issue: Should the father OA be granted supervised virtual or telephone access in addition to his in-person supervised visits?
facts: OA faces multiple serious charges including making and possessing child pornography and sexual assault. His in-person supervised access at Smith Falls had gone well, he was affectionate with W, and CAST reimbursed some travel costs. He sought added virtual and phone access, partly due to transportation and cost difficulties.
rule: Access is determined under s. 94(8) CYFSA on the best-interests standard in s. 74(3), the paramount purpose being the protection and well-being of the child; orders are not made on a 'what's the harm' basis but on the best-interests factors.
application: Given the nature of OA's charges, the risk associated with virtual access was heightened; the court was not satisfied virtual access could occur safely without being recorded or photographed, and OA offered no concrete plan to allay this. Telephone access was not shown to be in a 16-month-old's best interests. An order leaving location, duration and frequency to the Society's discretion allowed the agency to expand in-person visits if appropriate.
conclusion: OA's request for supervised virtual or telephone access was refused; his in-person supervised access continued, with the Society given discretion over location, duration and frequency.

issue: Is the dismissal power under s. 21.1 of the Divorce Act available even after the civil divorce judgment has been rendered?
facts: The parties were divorced civilly on 1 August 1997. In December 2007 the wife served a fresh affidavit under s. 21.1(2) seeking removal of the obstacle to her religious remarriage (the get) and moved to dismiss the husband's pending proceedings. The husband argued s. 21.1 relief is only available before the civil divorce judgment.
rule: Section 21.1 of the Divorce Act permits the court to dismiss any application, affidavit or other pleading filed by a spouse who fails to remove a barrier to the other spouse's religious remarriage. Section 21.1(1) defines 'époux' as including an ex-spouse. The text imposes no temporal limitation.
application: The court reasoned that since the dismissal may be sought against or by an 'ex-époux', and an ex-spouse only exists after a divorce judgment, the remedy must be available after the civil divorce. The court distinguished Droit de la famille — 2296 (Tannenbaum J.), where the barrier-removal-before-completion language addressed the different factual context of a pre-judgment motion. Ordering dismissal here promotes the statutory purpose described by Ministers Lewis and Campbell.
conclusion: The court held it has the power to dismiss the husband's affidavit and proceedings even after the civil divorce, as the wife requested.

issue: Did the husband advance serious grounds founded on religion or conscience justifying his refusal to grant the get under s. 21.1(4)?
