Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860, a pleading is vexatious if it does not establish a cause of action or advance a claim known in law; scandalous allegations relevant to the proceeding will not be struck.
application: Unlike Ebrahim and Babavic, this case did not involve re-litigation of decided matters. Though the plaintiff displayed high animosity toward her parents, all her allegations, however extreme or embarrassing, were relevant to proving her claims under recognized causes of action. The court would not comment on the merits at this stage.
conclusion: The defendants failed to establish grounds to strike as vexatious or an abuse of process; the application was dismissed except as to the Charter allegation.

issue: Should the plaintiff be ordered to post security for costs?
facts: The defendants said the plaintiff had no history of steady employment and likely could not pay costs if the action failed. The plaintiff deposed she was employed as a pre-school teacher but gave no particulars.
rule: Per Bronson v. Hewitt, 2007 BCSC 1751, the court's inherent jurisdiction to order an individual resident to post security for costs should be exercised cautiously, sparingly and only in very special or egregious circumstances; poverty is no bar to access to the courts. Special circumstances include multiple prior actions (Louie v. Louie) or inability to produce any supporting evidence long after commencing (Rotvold v. Rocky Mountain Diesel).
application: No comparable special or egregious circumstances were shown, and the evidence of the plaintiff's alleged impecuniosity was entirely speculative.
conclusion: The application for security for costs was dismissed.

issue: Should the statement of defence be struck because the defendants failed to attend an examination for discovery?
facts: The defendants had not attended a scheduled examination for discovery while awaiting production of documents; defence counsel understood the plaintiff's former counsel was still assembling them.
rule: Striking pleadings for non-attendance is a discretionary remedy of last resort; the court may instead order production and rescheduling.
application: This was not an appropriate case for striking pleadings. The court had already ordered production of the requested documents at the close of argument and assumed discovery could then be arranged without difficulty.
conclusion: The plaintiff's application to strike the defence was dismissed.

issue: Does maintaining the sealing and non-publication order over the affiants' sworn declarations meet the Sherman test for a discretionary limit on the open court principle, or should it be lifted?
facts: Following pro-Palestinian demonstrations on 4 and 5 March 2024 outside Jewish institutions belonging to the plaintiffs, injunctions were obtained on the strength of affidavits, and on 15 March 2024 Masse J. issued a permanent sealing and non-publication order anonymizing the affiants because of threats and vandalism. Defendant Independent Jewish Voices Canada argued the demonstrations were peaceful, the affiants were never individually threatened, and their safety fears were hypothetical, so the order breached the open court principle; the plaintiffs and intervenors argued the affiants' physical and psychological safety was at serious risk.
rule: Under arts. 11 and 12 of the Code of procedure civile, civil justice is public but the court may make exceptions to protect the dignity or important legitimate interests of persons concerned. Sherman (Succession) v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25, sets a three-part test: (1) court openness poses a serious risk to an important public interest; (2) the order is necessary because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; and (3) the benefits of the order outweigh its negative effects. Serious risk may be established by logical inference from objective circumstantial facts (A.B. v. Bragg Communications), not mere conjecture.
application: The court held protection of persons against physical harm—and the closely linked psychological safety—is an important public interest. Although the affiants were not individually threatened, videos showed masked demonstrators blocking entrances, committing vandalism and chanting 'Mort aux juifs' and 'Mort à Israël', which the court found constituted a threat to any Jewish person. The demonstrators' later targeting of Professor Angela Campbell at her private home (graffiti, 'wanted' posters, chants) supported an inference of serious risk of reprisals if the affiants were identified. The order was necessary as no alternative would protect them, while permitting counsel and one representative per defendant to access the affidavits for the case. The benefits (reducing risk of reprisals and reassuring litigants who turn to the courts) outweighed the limited negative effects, since the file remained public in near-totality and there was no public interest in knowing the affiants' identities.
conclusion: The three Sherman conditions were satisfied; the sealing and non-publication order of Masse J. was a minimal and necessary impairment of court openness and was maintained.

issue: Was the purchasers' consent to the 12 June 1993 sale vitiated by dol arising from the defendant's failure to disclose the true content of the railway lease?
facts: Fortier and Samson bought Gagné's house, part of which sat within the railway right-of-way of the Compagnie du Chemin de Fer de Québec Central on land held under a written lease. Gagné, by hand gesture during a visit and later statements, led the buyers to believe the property line ran along the foundation and that the lease merely required annual payment of $150. He never produced the written lease (clauses 19 and 22 permitted 90-day termination and removal of buildings). A 1988 notary's letter (P-17) had already warned Gagné his titles were defective because the house sat on short-term leased railway land. The buyers only discovered the lease's real terms and the plan showing the dividing line running through the centre of the house in June 1994.
rule: Under the Code civil du Bas-Canada (applicable via s. 2 of the Loi sur l'application de la réforme du Code civil to a situation created before 1 January 1994), arts. 984, 988, 991-993 require legally-given consent; dol (art. 993) is a cause of nullity where the manoeuvres of a party are such that without them the other would not have contracted, and it must be proven. Dol includes réticence (silence/failure to disclose a determinative fact). The obligation to inform, grounded in good faith, is described in Banque de Montréal c. Bail Ltée, [1992] 2 R.C.S. 554, and by Baudouin (Les Obligations): a party who knows or should know a determinative fact must disclose it where the other cannot inform itself or legitimately relied on the cocontractant.
application: The court found the plaintiffs and their witnesses far more credible than Gagné, who damaged his credibility (e.g., denying an earlier 1988 offer contradicted by independent witnesses and by the notary's letter P-17). Gagné knew, from the 1988 warning, that the lease imposed serious constraints, yet concealed them and let the buyers believe the lease was a mere formality entailing only a $150 annual payment, even telling them to disregard the correct lines on the plan. This constituted dol by reticence and by outright falsehood. The buyers' clear testimony established the dol was determinative — they would not have signed had they known the lease's content.
conclusion: The defendant committed dol that induced the plaintiffs to sign the 12 June 1993 deed; their consent was vitiated, grounding annulment.

issue: Was the purchasers' error inexcusable, barring annulment under s. 75 of the transitional statute?
facts: The buyers did not obtain a copy of the written lease before purchasing, and the deed (clause 2.2) mentioned the lease. The defendant argued they had every opportunity to examine it and could not complain of their own negligence.
rule: Section 75 of the Loi sur l'application de la réforme du Code civil provides that nullity of a pre-reform contract can no longer be pronounced on the basis of a party's inexcusable error. The correlative obligation 'de se renseigner' (Baudouin) limits the duty to inform, but does not protect a party who provides partial or misleading information; where a party legitimately relies on the cocontractant, error remains excusable.
application: As soon as they learned of the lease, the buyers inquired of both Gagné and notary Chabot, who reassured them the lease meant only a $150 annual payment and that they could rebuild after a fire. Given these assurances — repeated by the notary — the buyers were justified in believing they were dealing with a good-faith cocontractant. Although somewhat naïve in not obtaining the lease, their error was excusable in the circumstances.
conclusion: The error was excusable, so s. 75 did not bar annulment; the plaintiffs could seek nullity and damages under art. 1407 C.c.Q.

issue: What restitution and damages are owed following annulment of the sale?
facts: The buyers paid $40,000 for the immovable, carried out renovation and maintenance works, paid transfer duties, and claimed $58,891.70 in damages including $25,000 for trouble and inconvenience. They offered to return the property.
rule: Article 97 of the transitional statute applies arts. 1699-1707 C.c.Q. to restitutions after its coming into force. Restitution is in kind (art. 1700); the owner must reimburse necessary and useful expenses of a good-faith possessor (arts. 958-959, via art. 1703). Damages for dol are available under art. 1407 C.c.Q., with legal interest and the additional indemnity of art. 1619.
application: The court ordered return of the $40,000 purchase price with interest and the art. 1619 indemnity from 13 September 1994. Relying on the admitted invoices (P-6), it awarded $16,147.93 for renovation/maintenance works and transfer duties, deducting $400 paid to Me Chabot (reserved to the companion file), $52 for a blue bin, and refusing municipal/school taxes, loan interest, bank fees and rent (expenses tied to the buyers' enjoyment of the property, causing no loss). The $25,000 claim for trouble and inconvenience was reserved for the companion file no. 350-05-000212-942.
conclusion: Sale annulled; defendant condemned to repay $40,000 and $16,147.93 with interest and indemnity; ancillary orders made regarding registration, discharge of the hypothec and cancellation of the lease assignment; counterclaim dismissed, with costs against the defendant.

issue: Should the late-filed offer-to-purchase document be admitted despite Rule 17?
facts: At trial, counsel for Me Chabot sought to file an undated, unsigned draft offer to purchase, produced after the certificat d'état de cause (filed 2 October 1996), with no explanation for the delay other than that the opposing party knew of the document.
rule: Rule 17 of the Rules of Practice of the Superior Court (R.R.Q., c. C-25, r. 8) permits filing after the certificat d'état de cause only with leave, granted only where necessary in the interests of justice; the case law (Air Saguenay; Raymond Chabot Fafard Gagnon inc. c. Latouche; Harewood; Steckmar; Licata) requires valid reasons and diligence, distinguishing situations of inadvertence or evolving circumstances.
application: Unlike Steckmar (evolving situation) and Licata (inadvertence), counsel for Me Chabot gave no valid reason for the delay, merely asserting the other party's knowledge and the interests of justice. The discretion under Rule 17 is not meant to excuse negligence.
conclusion: The objection was upheld and the late document was excluded.

issue: Was the 2007 employment agreement a fixed-term contract ending at age 55, or an indefinite-term contract?
facts: In 2007 the plaintiff, a 49-year-old unionized worker, accepted a non-unionized foreman position under a letter (P-1) guaranteeing relocation to another post 'jusqu'à 55 ans' in case of economic layoff or administrative reorganization. He had refused an earlier draft (P-6) precisely because he wanted assurance he could keep working past age 55 to complete 35 years of service for a full pension. His foreman post was abolished in May 2011 during a reorganization; he was kept on salary until August 4, 2013 (his 55th birthday), when his employment ended.
rule: The party alleging a fixed-term contract bears the burden of proving it (Commission des normes du travail c. IEC Holden Inc., 2014 QCCA 1538). Contract interpretation looks to the parties' common intention and surrounding context.
application: The defendant called no witness present at the signing and did not contradict the plaintiff's uncontradicted testimony about the negotiating context. The rejected P-6 draft confirmed the plaintiff's intent to continue working after August 4, 2013. The Court found the 55th-birthday date was not a firm end date but the outer limit of an employment guarantee. The employment link was maintained from May 2011 to August 2013 (no relocation, but salary paid, a 2.6% raise applied in 2012, and the only record of employment issued August 15, 2013 listed August 4, 2013 as the last paid day).
conclusion: The contract was of indefinite term; the defendant failed to prove a fixed-term contract.

issue: Is the plaintiff entitled to a severance/reasonable notice indemnity, and in what amount?
facts: Employment truly ended August 4, 2013 after 31 years of service. The sums paid between May 2011 and August 2013 were salary (116 weeks), not a termination indemnity, since no work was performed. A comparable foreman, M. Lamuresnu, received two weeks' salary per year of service.
rule: Article 2091 C.c.Q.: a party to an indefinite-term contract may terminate it by giving reasonable notice, taking account of the nature of the employment, its circumstances and the duration of service. The indemnity cannot be based on the collective agreement (inapplicable to the plaintiff) nor on inconsistent case-by-case practices (Canadian Jewish Congress c. Polger, 2011 QCCA 1169; Desaulniers c. General Motors, 2010 QCCS 2650).
application: Considering the plaintiff's age, functions and 31 years of service, the Court fixed a reasonable indemnity of two weeks' salary per year of service, consistent with what the defendant's representative considered payable by law and with what the comparable foreman received. The Court refused to include the disputed January 1, 2013 raise, since salaries were then tied to performance and the plaintiff had performed no work in 2012. The award: 31 years × weekly salary of $1,382.42 × 2 weeks = $85,710.
conclusion: The plaintiff is entitled to $85,710 as a severance indemnity, with interest and additional indemnity from the demand of May 16, 2013.

issue: Is the plaintiff entitled to the 2013 salary increase, availability premium and compensatory time-off?
facts: The plaintiff claimed a 2.6% raise from January 1, 2013 ($1,555.20), an availability premium ($5,750) and compensatory time-off for overtime ($2,837.90), on the basis that his employment link continued. No work was actually performed from May 2011 to August 2013.
rule: Contractual entitlements tied to actual performance (availability, overtime) are not owed where no such work was required; performance-based raises require an actual work performance to assess.
application: Because the plaintiff rendered no work during the relevant period, he neither had to make himself available outside normal hours nor perform overtime; and, salaries being performance-based from 2013, no raise could be assessed for a year in which he did not work.
conclusion: These claims were rejected.

issue: Did the mother alienate the children from the father, warranting an order that she indemnify him for 50% of the therapeutic access costs?
facts: The father alleged a 'profound' campaign of alienation beginning shortly after the June 2003 separation, based on delayed access after separation, the move to Oakville, seizure of a vehicle, repeated calls to Jewish Family and Child Services, the Halton CAS and the police, enrolment of the children in 'Safety Zone' counselling, disputes over private schooling, use of other surnames, holiday-access difficulties and threats about Cadets.
rule: Parental alienation was described by Perkins J. in C.S. v. M.S., 2007 CanLII 6240 (ON SC), where alienated children hold almost exclusively negative, demonizing views of the targeted parent and reflexively support the alienating parent. The father relied on A.G.L. v. K.B.D. (2009), 2009 CanLII 943 (ON SC) and its table of warning signs of pathological alienation.
application: Reviewing each allegation, the court found the mother generally acted to protect the children or to facilitate access. Overnight access was granted within a week of separation and a schedule proposed within 25 days; the move to Oakville had legitimate business/financial reasons; the CAS/JF&CS calls were largely substantiated (the husband was repeatedly cautioned and admitted conduct); the Safety Zone counselling addressed real exposure to violence and the husband declined to participate; the police calls did not reach the children; the surname and Cadets issues were unsupported. J. actually complained about his mother to the CAS, contradicting alienation. Unlike A.G.L., the father maintained a regular relationship and it was he who imposed a 'time out' from his daughter. At most one or two of the sixty warning signs (questioning after visits; occasionally deferring to the children's wishes) were met, and no expert evidence was led.
conclusion: The court found no parental alienation under C.S. v. M.S. or otherwise; the mother is not required to reimburse the father for therapeutic access costs.

issue: Should the mother, though granted sole custody, be required to consult the father on decisions concerning the children?
facts: The parties agreed the mother would have sole custody. J. had disclosed self-harm thoughts and had learning disabilities affecting high-school placement; the father had not been advised of counselling programs or medical concerns; R. was approaching post-secondary decisions.
rule: Decisions about custody and consultation are governed by the best interests of the children.
application: Despite the acrimony, the court found it in the children's best interests that the father be consulted on material education and medical matters, including counselling, given the history of non-communication (e.g. the father learning of J.'s self-harm thoughts and of Safety Zone only later), while leaving final decision-making with the mother.
conclusion: Sole custody to the mother, but she must consult the father on educational and medical issues, with the mother making final decisions in the event of dispute.

issue: What income should be attributed to the father, and what child support should he pay?
facts: McWatt J. had in 2004 set support on an imputed income of $42,000. The father's reported income was $31,883 (2008), $38,133 (2007) and about $17,000 (2006); he offered to continue paying on $42,000. The mother sought imputation of $60,000–$70,000, alleging concealed income, a lavish lifestyle (BMW, Hawaii trip funded by his mother) and pointing to a credit-card application stating $150,000 income and to an expert (Mr. Alksnis) who said $145,000 was needed to carry his debts.
rule: Sections 16 and 17 of the Child Support Guidelines (Ontario): annual income is determined from the T1 General 'Total income' adjusted per Schedule III, unless that would not be the fairest determination.
application: The court found no basis to impute income. The expert's calculation was undermined on cross-examination (roughly $55,000 in overstated expenses plus a $180,000 equity take-out), the lifestyle items were funded by the husband's mother, the credit-card figure was an admitted exaggeration, and the husband's employment history had always been sporadic. Section 16 was the fairest measure.
conclusion: No income imputed; the father pays child support under the Guidelines based on the $42,000 income used by McWatt J.

issue: Is the father entitled to a refund of overpaid child support, including support paid for the eldest child A. while A. was not a dependent?
facts: The father claimed $26,063.41 overpaid between separation and McWatt J.'s November 2004 order, plus support paid for A. while A. was in a group home (2003–2004) and after A. left school. Evidence included a Request to Admit, rental income from the Beaty property, and cheques the mother said repaid a family loan.
rule: The party seeking reimbursement bears the burden of proving the overpayment; a child ceases to be a dependent when no longer in full-time attendance (relevant to A.'s schooling).
application: Most claims failed for lack of proof: the Request to Admit did not characterize payments as support; rental receipts and withdrawals were unproven or explained (loan repayment, boiler replacement). Only a proven $1,507 August 2003 rent cheque supported a refund. The court accepted A. was in JF&CS care March 2003–January 2004 and, relying on the Provincial Report Card, that A. last attended school in May 2007, so support paid for A. after those dates was recoverable.
conclusion: The mother must refund $1,502.50 for the September 2003–November 2004 overpayment (no interest), plus support paid for A. after A. ceased to be a dependent; the larger $26,063.41 claim was dismissed for want of proof.

issue: Should the father be ordered to contribute to private-school and post-secondary tuition as section 7 expenses?
facts: The mother sought the father to pay 100% of A.'s final elementary-school year and 60% of R.'s future post-secondary costs. J.'s private schooling had been funded by the paternal grandmother; R.'s and J.'s post-secondary costs were unknown.
rule: Section 7 of the Child Support Guidelines (Ontario) requires assessing the necessity of the expense in the child's best interests and its reasonableness relative to the parents' means and their spending pattern during cohabitation; see Farden v. Farden, 1993 CanLII 2570 (BC SC).
application: The father was not in a financial position to fund private tuition (which had depended on the non-party grandmother), and R.'s and J.'s future post-secondary costs were unknown, making any contribution order premature.
conclusion: No section 7 order made, but without prejudice to a future application once the education costs and budgets are known.

issue: Should the court grant the father's requested orders prohibiting use of the children as 'go-betweens' and compelling communication of telephone messages?
facts: The father sought orders barring either parent from using the children as messengers on 'inflammatory' or 'contentious' matters, and requiring the mother to relay all his phone messages and encourage return calls; he suspected messages were withheld.
rule: Court orders must be precise and enforceable, not vague: Zhang v. Chau, 2003 CanLII 75292 (QC CA), and M. (A.C.) v. M. (D.) (2003), 2003 CanLII 18880 (ON CA), where a 'clean bill of health' condition was held too vague.
application: The 'go-between' order was unenforceably vague (who defines 'inflammatory' or 'well received'?). On phone messages, the court accepted the mother's evidence, supported by faxes, that she relayed messages and encouraged the children (aged 15 and 12, J. having ADHD) to return calls; an order would only invite contempt motions.
conclusion: Both requested orders were refused as unnecessary or too vague, though the court encouraged the parties to use common sense.

issue: Should the late-filed exhibits D-10 to D-14 and the related surveyor testimony be admitted?
facts: On the first day of trial the notary Julien's counsel sought to file exhibits D-10 to D-13 and later a plan (D-14) and testimony of surveyor Michel Bédard, purportedly in response to an amendment to paragraph 7 of the declaration adding mention of the 1939 servitude. Hydro-Québec objected as late and irrelevant. The scope of the 1939 servitude had, however, been raised by Julien himself years earlier, and a pre-trial conference of 12 December 1997 had required an exhaustive exhibit list by 15 January 1998.
rule: Rule 17 of the Rules of Practice of the Superior Court of Quebec in civil matters bars production of further documents after the certificate of readiness except with leave, granted only where necessary in the interests of justice; Air Saguenay (1980) inc. c. British Aviation Insurance, Raymond Chabot Fafard Gagnon inc. c. Latouche and Harewood c. Jewish General Hospital support refusing untimely filings.
application: The claimed justification (the amendment) was a false pretext because Julien had himself litigated the 1939 servitude's scope four years earlier and had certified an exhaustive exhibit list on 15 January 1998. Nothing new or unforeseeable had arisen after that date. The pre-trial agreement reinforced the exclusion.
conclusion: The objections were maintained; exhibits D-10 to D-14 and the associated Bédard testimony were not considered.

issue: Are the 1915 and 1939 servitudes valid and do they prohibit construction?
facts: A servitude registered in 1915 (P-2) for The Shawinigan Water and Power Company was granted by Elizabeth Auger, whose title to lot 207 could not be established from the registry, the lot appearing to belong to Jules Delisle. A second servitude registered 1 December 1939 (D-2) granted the company the right to erect and maintain a 69,000-volt transmission line over lot 207, with rights to trim trees and a right of way, but no express prohibition against building.
rule: Arts. 545, 548, 552, 553, 557 and the last paragraph of art. 2098 C.C.B.C. (registration of an unregistered acquirer's grant is without effect); jurisprudence Hydro-Québec c. Toutant, Hydro-Québec c. Goguen, Hébert c. Villeneuve and Johnson c. Fleck on implied prohibition of building and determination of a servitude's assiette.
application: Because Auger's ownership could not be shown, the 1915 servitude was declared without effect under art. 2098 rather than null under art. 545. The 1939 servitude, read with arts. 552, 553 and 557, implicitly prohibited construction: a two-storey house would interfere with the line's use, upkeep and repair more than trees the company could cut. Expert evidence and Hydro-Québec norm PAEL 90-150 (art. 4.5.3) confirmed the incompatibility. The assiette was fixed at 50 feet on each side of the line's centre.
conclusion: The forced-intervention action succeeded as to the 1915 servitude (declared without effect) but failed as to the 1939 servitude, which validly prohibits construction; no costs on that action.

issue: Did the vendor breach his warranty against eviction by not disclosing the non-apparent servitude?
facts: The 19 January 1988 deed of sale (P-1) declared the property free of servitudes except an 'aspect' servitude, was made with legal warranty, and included the vendor's guarantee that no other servitude existed. The offer to purchase (D-1) had excepted 'servitudes d'utilité publique'. The 1939 servitude prohibiting construction was not disclosed.
rule: Arts. 1506, 1508, 1519, 1065 and 1019 C.C.B.C.; the vendor owes warranty against undisclosed non-apparent charges (Pourcelet, La Vente); a purchaser need not search the registry for non-apparent servitudes; art. 1519 permits annulment where an undisclosed non-apparent servitude is so significant the purchaser would not have bought.
application: The clear terms of the deed of sale prevailed over the offer to purchase under the 'déclaration relative à l'avant-contrat', and the deed gave a full warranty. Even if the two texts were reconciled, the ambiguous 'servitudes d'utilité publique' exception, in a contract of adhesion, would be construed against the vendor (art. 1019) as covering only apparent servitudes. The undisclosed 1939 prohibition was a non-apparent charge the purchasers were entitled to rely on; they would not have bought had they known.
conclusion: Samson breached his warranty against eviction; the purchasers were entitled to annulment of the sale under art. 1519.

issue: Did the notary breach his professional obligations in the title search and advice?
facts: Julien conducted a 30-year title search and found nothing to report, but he had seen a 14 August 1964 deed (D-5) expressly listing servitudes including registration no. 97393 (the 1939 servitude). He did not investigate it, assuming it had disappeared with the 1975 subdivision of lot 207 or because later deeds omitted it.
rule: A notary's duty on title examination is one of means, comprising both the search and advising the client (Baudouin, La Responsabilité civile; Aquin); arts. 3.01.5 and 3.02.04 of the Code de déontologie des notaires; art. 556 C.C.B.C. (subdivision does not extinguish servitudes).
application: Subdivision does not extinguish servitudes (art. 556), so that assumption was wrong. The omission of the servitudes in the 1974 deed (D-4) should have raised suspicion of error. The offer-to-purchase exception did not relieve him of searching, for the reasons applied to Samson. Having actually seen the 1939 servitude in D-5, he failed to investigate and advise.
conclusion: Julien did not properly discharge his title-examination and advisory obligations; the principal action succeeded against him for damages.

issue: What prestations and damages are payable and by whom?
facts: The purchasers paid $9,670.05, municipal/school taxes, and claimed costs of a replacement lot, surveying, temporary lodging, a GST-related cost increase, cedar hedge, land improvements, notary's fees and general inconvenience.
rule: Art. 97 of the Act respecting the implementation of the reform of the Civil Code applies arts. 1699-1707 C.C.Q. to restitution; arts. 958-959 C.C.Q. on necessary and useful expenses; art. 1619 C.C.Q. (additional indemnity); contractual solidarity is not presumed.
application: Samson must restore the $9,670.05 price and $6,580.75 in taxes (necessary expenses, art. 958), but not the removed cedar hedge (art. 959) or unproven improvement costs. The replacement-lot, surveying, lodging and GST claims were not direct damages. The court allowed $327 for wasted notary fees and $2,000 for trouble and inconvenience, totalling $2,327 in damages, charged entirely to Julien since he caused the error; Samson never knew of the prohibition, and solidarity could not be imposed absent stipulation.
conclusion: Sale annulled; Samson ordered to repay price ($9,670.05) and taxes ($6,580.75) with interest and indemnity; Julien ordered to pay $2,327 damages; registration to be radiated; costs against both defendants.

issue: Should the child continue attending Vancouver Talmud Torah (VTT) or transfer to a West Vancouver school?
facts: The child, aged six, had attended VTT, a Jewish day school, since preschool and had completed Grade 1. The father wished her to remain there to be immersed in Jewish traditions and Hebrew, his first language; the mother wanted her to attend Collingwood School near her West Vancouver home. Both parties treated attendance casually in preschool/kindergarten. The mother had never applied to Collingwood before separation. A s. 211 report by Dr. England recommended a non-denominational school to reduce conflict, but was based largely on the mother's account. School staff described the child as happy, well-adjusted and doing well at VTT.
rule: Under s. 37(2) of the Family Law Act, S.B.C. 2011, c. 25, the court must decide the child's schooling solely on the best interests of the child, weighing enumerated factors including health and emotional well-being, the child's views (where appropriate), relationships, history of care, and need for stability; s. 37(3) requires that any order protect the child's physical, psychological and emotional safety and well-being to the greatest extent possible. The interplay of the Divorce Act and Family Law Act was explained in Hansen v. Mantei-Hansen, 2013 BCSC 876.
application: The judge found the mother not credible, rejecting her evidence of an agreement to switch to Collingwood, and concluded the parties had in fact agreed the child would attend VTT for her elementary years. Evidence from the head of school and teachers established VTT is an excellent, secure, diverse school without forced indoctrination, where the child is happy and thriving. The judge declined to follow Dr. England's recommendation, finding it rested on the mother's distorted description, that the mother's true objection was the school's location rather than religion, that both parties had abandoned reliance on the child's manipulated views, and that a change was not shown to lessen conflict while it would undermine stability.
conclusion: The child was ordered to continue attending VTT until the end of Grade 7; a transfer to Collingwood was refused.

issue: Should the father have final decision-making authority over the child's education and cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual upbringing?
facts: Both parents were granted joint custody and full parental responsibilities. The father emphasized education and Jewish cultural and linguistic heritage. Dr. England identified ongoing parental conflict, largely generated by the mother, as harmful to the child; the mother had drawn the child into disputes, made false allegations, and allowed her friends (the Florians) to fund and influence school decisions.
rule: Section 41 of the Family Law Act lists parental responsibilities, including (d) decisions respecting the child's education and (e) decisions respecting cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual upbringing and heritage, exercised in the child's best interests (s. 37).
application: The judge found the mother manipulative and likely to perpetuate conflict over schooling and upbringing if she retained input. Vesting final decision-making in the father addressed Dr. England's concern about conflict harming the child, was consistent with continued attendance at VTT, and reflected the father's genuine and beneficial pursuit of the child's Jewish cultural and linguistic heritage. The court also expressed concern that the mother's friends were improperly making decisions for the child.
conclusion: The father was granted final decision-making authority over the child's education and her cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual upbringing and heritage, though both retained full parental responsibilities otherwise.

issue: Should the six-year-old child have a cellphone?
facts: The mother justified the child having a cellphone, given as a gift by her friend Ms. Florian, on the basis that she wished to have daily contact and worried about emergencies while the child was with the father.
rule: Section 37 best-interests analysis; telephone-contact arrangements to be reasonable and to minimize conflict, consistent with Dr. England's recommendation of one call per five-day parenting span.
application: The judge found a six-year-old does not need a cellphone; parents can control telephone use through their own phones. The cellphone was another instance of the mother allowing friends to make decisions that should be made by the parents. One phone call during each five-day period the child is with the other parent was reasonable.
conclusion: The child does not need a cellphone; contact ordered as one call on the middle day of the other parent's five-day parenting time.

issue: Do the appellants hold acquired rights permitting them to use the property for maintenance and repair of their trucking company's vehicles despite the agricultural zoning?
facts: From the mid-1960s to 2000 the appellants' predecessor, Mr. Oes, used the lot as the base of a well-drilling and water-transport-by-tanker business, storing equipment, maintaining and repairing his equipment, and housing small administrative premises. The 1972 zoning by-law placed the lot in a commercial zone allowing motor-vehicle repair, but a 1986 by-law rezoned it agricultural. Since acquiring the property in autumn 2000, the appellants used it to repair and maintain vehicles of a goods-transport business. The municipality sought cessation of that use under art. 227 of the Loi sur l'aménagement et l'urbanisme.
rule: Art. 227 Loi sur l'aménagement et l'urbanisme (L.R.Q. c. A-19.1). Acquired rights cannot arise from an accessory use, and an accessory use is not protected once it becomes so extensive as to become a principal use; an owner cannot have more rights than his predecessor. The analytical framework is set out in St-Romuald (Ville de) c. Olivier, 2001 CSC 57: first characterize the purpose of the pre-existing use based on activities actually carried out on the site.
application: The trial judge found the principal use of the immovable was to serve as the home base of a specialized well-drilling and water-transport business — storage, equipment maintenance and administration — not the maintenance of road-transport vehicles, which was merely accessory. Vehicle maintenance had not been the dominant characteristic of Mr. Oes's use of the lot.
conclusion: The appellants do not hold acquired rights authorizing use of the property for maintenance and repair of their trucking fleet; the derogatory use must cease.

issue: Can the appellants' current use qualify as a reasonable evolution of the protected non-conforming use?
facts: The protected use established by Mr. Oes was as the base of a specialized construction (well-drilling) enterprise. The appellants transformed the site into a repair and maintenance facility for trucks serving their road-transport business.
rule: Per St-Romuald, the characterization of the acquired right must not be so general as to free the owner from what he actually did, nor so narrow as to deny reasonable evolution; use may evolve with market and technological changes but must remain fundamentally the same type of use that founded the acquired rights.
application: Analyzing the contemporary use flexibly, the protected use was that of a home base of a specialized construction enterprise. Converting the lot into a repair and maintenance site for trucks used in a road-transport business is not a reasonable evolution of that prior use — it is a fundamentally different type of use.
conclusion: The current use is not a reasonable evolution of the protected non-conforming use; no acquired right shields it.

issue: Can the Court of Appeal intervene in the trial judge's factual determination of the principal use of the property?
facts: The appellants argued the judge erred in characterizing vehicle maintenance as accessory, isolating that aspect of the prior use to claim it was the principal use.
rule: Appellate intervention in factual findings requires demonstrating a palpable and overriding error (erreur manifeste et dominante).
application: The appellants were in reality attacking a factual determination. The trial judge's conclusions about the principal use were supported by the evidence, and the appellants failed to establish any palpable and overriding error.
conclusion: No basis for appellate intervention; the factual findings stand.

issue: Does the Superior Court have jurisdiction over access rights and relocation when the Court of Quebec, Youth Division, has already declared the children compromised under the Youth Protection Act?
facts: The Director of Youth Protection had the children declared in danger under s. 38(c) of the Youth Protection Act; the Court of Quebec granted interim custody to the mother and postponed its merits hearing to allow the Superior Court to hear the divorce, including the relocation issue. The DYP and both parties invited the Superior Court to rule.
rule: Article 37 C.C.P. distinguishes exclusive jurisdiction in adoption, jurisdiction in youth matters under special Acts, and a third paragraph (new in the 2016 C.C.P.) allowing the Court of Quebec to rule on related custody matters when a youth-protection matter is already before it. The third paragraph omits the word 'exclusive'. Statutory interpretation per Celgene Corp. v. Canada (A.G.), 2011 SCC 1: clear words dominate, otherwise the interpretation best serving the statute's purpose applies. Jurisdiction ratione materiae cannot be conferred by party admission.
application: The Court held that the absence of 'exclusive' in the third paragraph of art. 37 shows the Court of Quebec does not have exclusive jurisdiction; there is overlapping or concurrent jurisdiction that must serve the children's best interests. Even if the words were unclear, expediency and early referral govern which court decides. Here the Superior Court held a four-day trial, heard both parents and two social workers, and the Court of Quebec had implicitly deferred to it.
conclusion: The Superior Court had jurisdiction to determine access rights and the relocation request; it assessed the matter and left the access arrangements in place pending departure, inviting the DYP to keep monitoring.

issue: How should the father's income be determined and should the child-support arrears be cancelled?
facts: The father claimed 2016 income of only $26,000, no income in 2017, and social assistance in 2018, seeking cancellation of $31,906.74 in arrears. He operated a succession of companies under changing names, handled large amounts of cash, had a cash machine, safe and firearm at home, and had earlier admitted earning up to $66,000. His credibility was poor and evidence suggested undisclosed cash-loan brokerage income; family lifestyle cost about $10,000/month.
rule: Article 446 C.C.P. permits the court to supplement incomplete or contested income information and to impute income based on assets and earning capacity. Per Droit de la famille — 162999 (QCCA), income may be imputed where information is incomplete/erroneous or where a parent fails to maximize earning capacity (job abandonment, voluntary income reduction, refusal to maximize earnings).
application: The Court found the father's tax statements had limited probative value (unaudited, cash business), his credibility doubtful, and no medical or other justification for not working full-time. Both s. 446 triggers applied: he understated real income and refused to maximize earning capacity. The Court preferred the mother's evidence of a $10,000 net monthly family budget and imputed gross annual income of $100,000 as conservative. No credible basis supported cancelling arrears.
conclusion: Income imputed at $100,000 gross; child support set at $1,729.28/month from January 2018, indexed; the motion to cancel arrears dismissed and all arrears ordered paid. The claim for $1,000/month special expenses was refused for lack of proof.

issue: Should the mother be authorized to relocate to Israel with the four children without the father's consent?
facts: The mother is an Israeli citizen with all her family in Israel, does not speak French, has only basic English, never applied for Canadian citizenship, and lives off social assistance and community support since separation. The parties had planned before separation to emigrate to Israel. She has a job offer there, free schooling, and would raise the children as Orthodox Jews near family. The father opposed on grounds of safety in Israel, loss of contact, and fear of pedophiles, but did not seek custody himself.
rule: Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27: (1) threshold of a material change in circumstances; (2) fresh best-interests inquiry considering all relevant factors, with no presumption for the custodial parent but great respect for the custodial parent's decision to live and work where they wish, absent an unjustified reason impairing parenting ability. Followed in Droit de la famille — 171821 and — 172102 (QCCA); safety abroad a relevant factor (L.S. v. G.S., 2012 BCCA 154; Droit de la famille — 152832).
application: The separation was a material change. The mother, not the father, has adequate parental capacity; the father's parental capacities were found lacking. There was no genuine alternative other than mother-with-children in Israel or children staying with the father. The Court found the children would be adequately cared for by Israeli services, the safety evidence anecdotal and general, the pedophilia allegation unsupported and illogical, and reduced contact inherent in any relocation, mitigated by generous access (two two-week periods, virtual access, visits whenever the father is in Israel) with Israel a party to the Hague Convention. The mother's decision was reasonable, in good faith, and not to punish the father.
conclusion: The mother was authorized to emigrate to Israel with the four children after the end of the 2017-2018 school year (or after June 24, 2018), granted sole custody and sole passport holder status, with defined minimal and post-emigration access rights ordered for the father.

issue: Should the corporate plaintiffs be ordered to furnish security for costs under s. 254 of the Yukon Business Corporations Act?
facts: The corporate plaintiffs (Freedom TV Inc., Masterworks 2011 TV Inc., DP1 Inc., Symphonic Vision Inc.) were not registered in the Yukon; a Receiver had been appointed for related Goldman corporations under s. 243(1) of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act; and despite the application being filed in January 2016, Mr. Goldman had filed no financial statements showing exigible assets. The action was premised on Mr. Goldman's inability to pay small invoices until financing or CRA tax credits materialized, neither of which had occurred since 2013.
rule: Section 254 of the Yukon Business Corporations Act permits an order for security for costs where it appears a body corporate plaintiff will be unable to pay a successful defendant's costs. The four-part test from 37790 Yukon Inc. v. Skookum Asphalt Ltd., 2007 YKSC 24 (adopting Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)) asks: (1) does the plaintiff company appear unable to pay costs if the action fails; (2) has it shown exigible assets sufficient to satisfy a costs award; (3) do the defendants have an arguable defence; and (4) would the order cause undue hardship preventing the case from being heard.
application: The court found the corporate plaintiffs appeared unable to pay costs, that Mr. Goldman had been unable or unwilling to file financial information showing exigible assets, and that the defendants had an arguable defence — namely that there was no agreement making payment contingent on financing and no causal connection between the corporations' financing troubles and the defendants pressing for payment. Given Mr. Goldman's professed optimism about future financing and tax credits, and the fact he travelled from Manitoba to appear, an order would not visit undue hardship preventing the action from being heard.
conclusion: All four criteria favoured an order; security for costs against the corporate plaintiffs was warranted.

issue: Should security for costs be ordered against the individual plaintiff, Mr. Goldman, given the elevated threshold applicable to individuals?
facts: Mr. Goldman resides in Manitoba, has no Yukon assets, and had unpaid costs orders elsewhere (a $30,000 partial-indemnity order from Meyers J. and a consent judgment exceeding $1.26 million to RBC). The proceeding — over roughly $3,200 in unpaid invoices and a delayed audio file — had generated more than ten case management conferences, repeated adjournment requests, a 465-paragraph affidavit, and new claims against opposing counsel, consuming excessive court time.
rule: Following Han v. Cho, 2008 BCSC 1229 and Gichuru v. Pallai, 2015 BCCA 81, the power to order security for costs against a natural person is exercised cautiously, sparingly, and only in special or egregious circumstances (e.g., a weak claim combined with impecuniosity, prior failures to pay costs, or refusal to obey court orders), because poverty must not bar access to the courts. Residence outside the jurisdiction, absence of local assets, or impecuniosity are not, by themselves, sufficient.
application: The court held the order was not based merely on Mr. Goldman's residence or impecuniosity, but on the prospect of abuse of the court's process: he had turned a minor payment dispute into a Supreme Court action, consumed excessive court time on procedural matters unrelated to the merits, repeatedly sought adjournments while professing to want a speedy trial, and his various claims were tenuous at best. Access to justice had to be balanced for the defendants, small businessmen with limited resources, against the well-resourced Mr. Goldman.
conclusion: The circumstances were egregious; a security for costs order against Mr. Goldman was appropriate. The action was stayed until $10,000 security is provided by certified cheque.

issue: Should the court continue the interim injunction restraining removal of life support until trial under the 'just or convenient' standard of s. 55(1) of the Court of Queen's Bench Act?
facts: Samuel Golubchuk, a critically ill ICU patient at the Salvation Army Grace General Hospital, was on a ventilator, tube-fed and medicated. His physicians concluded further treatment was not beneficial and proposed withdrawing life support; his family objected on the basis of a genuinely held religious (Jewish) belief and obtained an emergency without-notice injunction on November 30, 2007.
rule: Section 55(1) of the Court of Queen's Bench Act, C.C.S.M., c. C280, permits an injunction where 'just or convenient'. Pereira v. Smith, [1993] M.J. No. 469 (C.A.) sets the balancing factors: strength of the plaintiff's case, inadequacy of damages to the plaintiff and adequacy of the undertaking to the defendant, balance of convenience, desirability of maintaining the status quo, and any special circumstance.
application: The court found damages would be an inadequate remedy since the plaintiff would die if support were withdrawn; the balance of convenience favoured the plaintiff, who could otherwise be heard on his legal, religious and Charter positions during his lifetime, whereas the physicians would merely be compelled to continue treatment already in place; the status quo (patient on ventilator, placed there by the physicians) favoured continuation; and a special circumstance—the absence of any offered mediation strongly recommended by the Manitoba Law Reform Commission—supported adjudication. Schulman J. found in the plaintiff's favour on each Pereira factor.
conclusion: It was just and convenient to continue the injunction until trial; the order was continued and case management ordered to expedite trial.

issue: Is there a serious, non-frivolous triable issue as to whether physicians may withdraw a ventilator and life support without the patient's or family's consent?
facts: The proposed withdrawal, per the ICU director's affidavit, would involve reducing ventilatory support, likely administering narcotics over objection, disconnecting tubing from the tracheostomy, and would hasten death. The parties' experts disputed the plaintiff's level of consciousness and cognition; no neurologist had examined him and no CT/MRI had been done.
rule: Contrary to the defendants' position, it is not settled law that a physician has the final say on withdrawing life support. Child and Family Services of Manitoba v. R.L., 1997 CanLII 3742 (MB CA) held 'treatment' requiring consent means positive touching, distinguishing DNR omissions. Sawatzky and Jin v. Calgary Health Region, 2007 ABQB 593 recognized untested triable Charter issues. Common law must develop consistent with Charter values including freedom of religion (s. 2(a)) and respect for life and autonomy (s. 7): Hill v. Church of Scientology, 1995 CanLII 59 (SCC).
application: The court found the removal probably involves interaction with the plaintiff's body and administration of narcotics over objection, so a trial judge could find it a positive act requiring consent, distinguishable from R.L. Whether withholding and withdrawing should be treated alike, and whether the plaintiff has a right to continued treatment at common law or under the Charter, remained open. There was also a genuine, non-frivolous factual dispute about the plaintiff's cognition requiring trial.
conclusion: There were material legal and factual issues that were not frivolous, satisfying the strength-of-case component and supporting the injunction.

issue: Should the injunction be dissolved for the plaintiff's failure to disclose, at the without-notice hearing, that an emergency physician had independently examined the patient?
facts: At the ex parte hearing the plaintiff's family did not disclose that they had obtained an emergency-room physician's assessment of Mr. Golubchuk and its findings. The defendants did not bring a motion to set aside the interim injunction.
rule: Courts may dissolve an injunction, on a defendant's motion, for failure to disclose a material fact known to the party at a without-notice hearing, as a punitive response reinforcing the duty of full disclosure. Any remedy must be proportionate to the wrong.
application: Schulman J. accepted the facts should have been disclosed but doubted disclosure would have led him to refuse the injunction; the defendants had not moved to set it aside, and dissolving the injunction would be disproportionate to the wrong. The non-disclosure could instead be addressed through the costs of the proceeding.
conclusion: The injunction was not dissolved; the non-disclosure would be dealt with on costs.

issue: Is a justice of the peace's decision to receive an information under s. 504 of the Criminal Code, including administering the oath, a ministerial act not subject to judicial review?
facts: Ellis sought mandamus to compel Justice of the Peace Altobello to process private informations against a bus driver and a Crown prosecutor after the JP declined to proceed because Ellis could not produce valid identification.
rule: Receipt of an information under s. 504 of the Criminal Code is a ministerial act not subject to judicial review: R. v. Jean Talon Fashion Center Inc. (1975), 56 D.L.R. (3d) 296; McHale v. Ontario, 2010 ONCA 361, at para. 43. A justice must receive an information that alleges an offence known to law and is facially compliant. Section 9 of the Commissioners for taking Affidavits Act requires the officer administering the oath to satisfy himself of the genuineness of the deponent's signature.
application: The court held that the ministerial character of receiving an information extends to the JP's administration of the oath on the tendered information. Because verifying the informant's identity is part of properly administering the oath, all aspects of the decision to receive an information fall within the non-reviewable ministerial act.
conclusion: The JP's decision, including verification of identity when administering the oath, is a ministerial act and is not reviewable.

issue: If reviewable, did the justice of the peace commit a jurisdictional error in refusing the information for insufficient proof of identity?
facts: Ellis produced only two self-made cards — an illegible 'Anishinabe Nations of Turtle Island' card with his photo and a frayed, photoless 'Identification, Passport, Tax Exempt' card — and had no government-issued photo identification, refusing government ID as stripping his 'sovereignty'.
rule: Under s. 9 of the Commissioners for taking Affidavits Act, the officer must satisfy himself of the genuineness of the deponent's signature; independent, reliable third-party verification of an informant's identity is needed to prevent fraudulent complaints in another's name and duplicative or vexatious informations. It is for the JP to decide case-by-case whether the proffered evidence of identity is sufficiently reliable.
application: The self-prepared, barely legible cards did not provide independent, reliable verification of Ellis's identity. Identity may be proved by means other than government photo ID (e.g., a third party attesting), but that is a last resort and it remained the JP's discretionary assessment. The JP reasonably found the evidence insufficient.
conclusion: Even if reviewable, no jurisdictional error was committed; the JP was entitled to find the identification insufficient.

issue: Should mandamus issue to compel receipt of the proposed private informations?
facts: Ellis had already pursued private prosecutions against Mr. John (who pled guilty to assault) and the Crown prosecutor arising from the same events, and asked that the information be received under 'the 613 Laws and Commands as set out in the Torah' rather than the Criminal Code.
rule: Mandamus is a discretionary remedy that may be refused where an adequate alternative remedy exists or where the proceeding is vexatious or an abuse of process.
application: An adequate alternative remedy existed — returning to a JP with legible, valid identification. The proposed prosecution was vexatious because it re-charged the same individuals for the same events already prosecuted, and the request to proceed under Torah law had no basis in law. The applicant's submissions regarding the Torah were without legal merit.
conclusion: Mandamus would be denied in any event; the application was dismissed.

issue: Do the plaintiffs' pleadings for misfeasance in public office disclose a reasonable cause of action under Rule 9-5(1)(a)?
facts: FORCOMP and its principal Martin Watts alleged that FAIB employees, embarrassed by Watts pointing out errors in the Ministry's forestry data, deliberately altered contract bidding qualifications, refused to award contracts, denied data access and interfered with contracts in order to financially harm the plaintiffs.
rule: Under Rule 9-5(1)(a) a claim is struck where it is 'plain and obvious' the pleadings disclose no reasonable cause of action (Hunt v. Carey; R. v. Imperial Tobacco, 2011 SCC 42). The tort of misfeasance in public office (Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse, 2003 SCC 69; J.P. v. British Columbia, 2017 BCCA 308) requires (1) deliberate unlawful conduct by a public officer in exercise of public functions and (2) awareness the conduct is likely to injure the plaintiff, in Category A (targeted malice) or Category B (knowing lack of power and likely harm) forms.
application: Reviewing the amended notice of civil claim and particulars, the court found much of the pleading to be speculation, sentiment or conclusory statements amounting to a 'fishing expedition.' The plaintiffs failed to plead material facts that, if true, would establish deliberately unlawful conduct in the exercise of duties that the defendants knew would cause tangible harm.
conclusion: The misfeasance claim as pleaded has no reasonable prospect of success and is bound to fail.

issue: Do the plaintiffs' pleadings for civil conspiracy disclose a reasonable cause of action?
facts: The plaintiffs alleged the four FAIB employees agreed between 2002 and 2014 to exclude Watts and FORCOMP from contract opportunities and to prevent them from meeting bidding qualifications.
rule: Conspiracy in tort takes two forms—predominant purpose conspiracy and unlawful means conspiracy (Pro-Sys Consultants; Watson v. Bank of America). Pleadings alleging conspiracy must be as specific as possible, identifying the parties, dates, objects, means and overt acts (Can-Dive Services Ltd. v. Pacific Coast Energy Corp.).
application: The plaintiffs did not clearly identify which form of conspiracy was alleged (appearing to favour predominant purpose). The allegations were vague and undefined, spanned more than ten years, and failed to specify who did what, with whom and when.
conclusion: It is plain and obvious the conspiracy pleadings disclose no reasonable cause of action.

issue: Do the plaintiffs' pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action for breach of freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter?
facts: Watts alleged the defendants punished him for publicizing errors in the Ministry's data by limiting his opportunities to speak publicly and by damaging his business to silence him.
rule: Section 2(b) of the Canadian Charter guarantees freedom of expression; the Rule 9-5(1)(a) 'plain and obvious' test applies, and Charter damages may be available for punitive, arbitrary or retaliatory state conduct (Ernst v. Alberta Energy Regulator, as relied on by the plaintiffs).
application: Even taking the alleged facts as true, the court could not see how they amounted to a legitimate s. 2(b) cause of action. As with the misfeasance and conspiracy claims, the pleadings disclosed no reasonable cause of action.
conclusion: The s. 2(b) claim discloses no reasonable cause of action and is certain to fail at trial.

issue: Should the court recognize a novel tort of 'blacklisting', and if so, is it adequately pleaded?
facts: The plaintiffs asked the court to recognize a new tort of blacklisting contractors in unique fields, proposing elements including a duty of fairness, malice, inability to obtain reasonable work, and resulting damages.
rule: On a motion to strike, novelty is not determinative; the court asks whether, assuming the pleaded facts are true, there is a reasonable prospect of success, erring on the side of allowing a novel but arguable claim (Imperial Tobacco, 2011 SCC 42 at para. 21).
application: Applying the proposed elements, the plaintiffs failed to plead that the Ministry or Province had actually refused to contract with them—merely that they had been unsuccessful in obtaining contracts. That essential element, which the plaintiffs themselves deemed necessary, was missing from the pleadings.
conclusion: The proposed blacklisting tort as pleaded has no prospect of success.

issue: Are the plaintiffs' pleadings unnecessary, frivolous or an abuse of process under Rule 9-5(1)(b) and (d), and should a further amendment be permitted?
facts: This was the plaintiffs' second attempt to plead, Master Bouck having earlier struck almost all of the original claim (2017 BCSC 1157) with leave to amend. The amended pleading and particulars remained lengthy, narrative and conclusory.
rule: Under Rule 9-5(1)(b) a pleading is unnecessary/vexatious if it advances no claim known in law, cannot succeed, is confusing, prolix or embarrassing (Willow v. Chong; Johnston, 2016 BCSC 1388). Rule 9-5(1)(d) allows striking for abuse of process to protect judicial economy, finality and the integrity of justice. Pleadings must comply with Rules 3-1 and 3-7.
application: The pleadings were prolix, unstructured, short on material facts and long on conclusory statements; the supplementary particulars added only to their nebulousness. Permitting the claim would cause unwarranted expense and squander judicial resources. Given the plaintiffs had already failed twice, a third opportunity to amend would be pointless.
conclusion: The pleadings breach Rule 9-5(1)(b) and (d); the claim is struck without leave to amend and the action dismissed against all defendants, with Scale B costs to the defendants.

issue: Were declaratory relief and de bene esse judicial review procedurally available to the appellant even though the impoundment matter had become moot?
facts: After the trial judge refused to hear her while wearing a hijab and postponed the matter sine die, the appellant's vehicle was released by operation of law, mooting the s. 209.11 Highway Safety Code application. She then sought various judicial declarations plus, on a de bene esse basis, judicial review, having amended proceedings to add the Court of Québec and SAAQ. The Superior Court judge dismissed everything on procedural grounds (court decision not a 'juridical act' under art. 142 C.C.P., no genuine problem, no standard-of-review submissions, mootness).
rule: Article 25 C.C.P. and s. 24(1) of the Canadian Charter confer wide discretionary remedial power; courts favour determination of rights over their negation by procedural means (Vachon v. Attorney General (Québec), [1979] 1 S.C.R. 555). Declaratory relief lies where the court has jurisdiction, the dispute is real, the party has a genuine interest, and the respondent has an interest in contesting (Ewert v. Canada, 2018 SCC 30; Solosky). While declaratory judgment is not the proper vehicle to attack a court decision (R.B. c. R.C.), judicial review is available; the reviewing court determines the applicable standard of review.
application: The Court held the file's unique circumstances (the constitutional issue raised sua sponte by the trial judge, the unusual s. 209.11 recourse with no true defendant, and the 30-day mootness window) justified a flexible procedural approach. The appellant had filed timely hybrid proceedings; the declaratory criteria were all met and the constitutional issues remained live and important despite the impoundment mootness. The failure to plead a standard of review was no bar since the court itself fixes it — here reasonableness under Dunsmuir/Doré/Loyola/Trinity Western.
conclusion: The Superior Court judge erred; declaratory relief and judicial review were both available, and the merits had to be decided.

issue: Did the refusal to hear the appellant while wearing a hijab, under the courtroom dress code, unreasonably infringe her freedom of conscience and religion?
facts: The trial judge, treating the courtroom as a secular space and interpreting art. 13 of the Regulation of the Court of Québec ('suitably dressed') as barring religious head coverings, refused to hear the appellant unless she removed her hijab, which she wore from sincere religious belief. No competing interest was engaged.
rule: Paragraph 2(a) of the Canadian Charter and ss. 3 and 10 of the Quebec Charter protect freedom of religion, including religious expression (R. v. Big M Drug Mart; R. v. Edwards Books). State/courtroom religious neutrality does not extinguish religious practice (Loyola; Mouvement laïque québécois v. Saguenay). Courts must accommodate sincerely held religious beliefs unless they conflict with or harm an overriding public interest such as another's constitutional rights (R. v. N.S., 2012 SCC 72). Judicial discretion must be exercised consistently with the Charters.
application: The trial judge gave no consideration to the appellant's religious rights and conducted no balancing, treating an absolute conception of secularism as an overriding principle. The dress code does not prohibit religious clothing; requiring 'suitable dress' is not a bar to sincerely held religious garments. No overriding public interest (e.g., trial fairness, identification) was engaged by a face-uncovering headscarf. The decision ignored controlling authority and failed even to begin the constitutional balancing exercise.
conclusion: The February 24, 2015 decision was unreasonable and had to be quashed; the appellant was entitled to be heard wearing her hijab.

issue: What declaratory remedy was appropriate regarding the appellant's present and future right to wear a hijab in the Court of Québec?
facts: The appellant sought broad declarations affirming her right to wear a hijab in the Court of Québec generally. The Court of Québec objected that its judges must retain authority to assess sincerity of belief and overriding interests case by case.
rule: A court is not bound by the wording of the declarations sought and may reformulate them (Solosky). Inquiries into sincerity of belief must be as limited as possible and undertaken only where sincerity is genuinely at issue (Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47). Where a well-known religious garment is worn, no intrusive inquiry is generally needed.
application: An absolute, unqualified declaration would improperly override judges' authority to intervene where a practice conflicts with an overriding public interest or is unsuitable. The Court granted a tailored declaration: the appellant was entitled to be heard on February 24, 2015 wearing a hijab, and the Regulation's dress code does not forbid the hijab where the practice flows from a sincerely held religious belief and does not conflict with or harm an overriding public interest.
conclusion: Tailored declaratory relief granted, affirming the right while preserving judicial authority to intervene where circumstances warrant; the whole without legal costs.

issue: Should leave to appeal be granted from a Superior Court judgment that refused Independent Jewish Voices Canada Inc. leave to intervene as an amicus at the authorization stage of a proposed class action?
facts: David Cobrin sought authorization to bring a class action against McGill University on behalf of Jewish students to compensate for harm suffered during campus protests following the October 7, 2023 events in Israel. IJV applied to intervene amicus curiae at the authorization stage, wishing to argue, among other things, that the proposed class description wrongly assumed all Jewish students are Zionists and that Cobrin's demand to treat anti-Zionism as antisemitism threatened freedom of expression and academic freedom. The motion judge refused the intervention as not indispensable at the authorization stage. IJV sought leave to appeal that refusal.
rule: A judgment refusing a third party's voluntary intervention ends the proceeding for that party and requires leave to appeal under art. 30 al. 2(4°) C.p.c. Leave is granted under art. 30 al. 3 C.p.c. where the question is one that should be submitted to the Court (a matter of principle, a new question, or a question of law on which there is conflicting case law). Per Lamontagne c. Sani Métal ltée and Essilor (2019 QCCA 186), mere demonstration of an error is insufficient; leave is granted sparingly, guided by proportionality and the interests of justice, and only where a serious error causes a denial of justice (grave, flagrant or intolerable injustice). On amicus intervention at authorization, Abihsira c. Johnston (2019 QCCA 657) and Amnistie internationale Canada c. Environnement Jeunesse (2020 QCCA 223) hold that ordinary voluntary intervention rules (art. 187 al. 2 C.p.c.) apply but are modulated so that the usefulness criterion approaches indispensability.
application: Justice Harvie found IJV did not meet the strict criteria. The question was not truly novel: Abihsira and Amnistie internationale had already analyzed amicus intervention in the class action context, and Bich J.A. in Amnistie held that the usefulness of an intervention 'must approach indispensability' at the authorization stage. The motion judge did not merely rely on indispensability but carefully assessed the intervention's usefulness in harmony with the judge's limited role at authorization, addressing each of IJV's arguments — that the class description was vague and assumed all Jewish students are Zionists, and that the recourse threatened freedom of expression and academic freedom — and correctly held these were merits issues not to be resolved at authorization, where no right is decided except the contours of the recourse. The judge exercised her discretion, to which deference is owed; only an abusive, unreasonable or non-judicial exercise would warrant intervention, and none was shown. IJV's concern that authorization would fix the class action's structure was rejected, since amicus intervention could still be sought and art. 588 C.p.c. gives the court broad powers to modify at that stage.
conclusion: Leave to appeal was refused. No denial of justice was established; the application for leave to appeal was dismissed with costs, and the motion to stay the Superior Court proceeding was declared moot.

issue: Are the defendants civilly liable for damages arising from false criminal accusations that led to the plaintiff's arrest and acquittal?
facts: After Felsher exercised a hypothecary right against Hilel and his ex-spouse, and sold Jewish religious items left in the residence to Spiegelman for $2,000, Hilel filed a sworn complaint with the SPVM accusing Felsher of extortion and theft, corroborated by a sworn declaration from Spiegelman. Charges were laid, Felsher was arrested in March 2018, and he was acquitted of all charges in November 2018. Spiegelman conceded he supported his longtime friend Hilel and effectively acknowledged the complaint was unfounded.
rule: Civil liability under Quebec law (art. 1457 C.C.Q.) requires fault, injury and causation; lodging a false or vengeful criminal complaint knowing the information is untrue constitutes a fault engaging solidary liability.
application: The Court found Felsher's retention of items belonging to Hilel was, at most, a civil matter that could not be characterized as extortion or theft. Hilel filed the criminal complaint out of anger and vengeance rather than good faith, and Spiegelman knew the information given to police was false yet confirmed it out of friendship. Both thus committed a fault causing Felsher to incur defence costs.
conclusion: Both defendants were found solidarily liable for the fault of causing Felsher's wrongful criminal prosecution.

issue: What damages are recoverable, and may moral/punitive damages grounded in defamation be awarded in Small Claims Court?
facts: Felsher claimed $15,000: $8,123.64 in legal fees plus $6,876.36 in moral and punitive damages, alleging lost business opportunities from the false accusations. He proved payment of $5,245.75 to Me Lamarche who defended him from arrest to acquittal, but the $2,802.52 paid to another lawyer lacked a clear description tying it to this matter, and no evidence of actual business losses was provided.
rule: Damages must be proven; unproven losses are not compensable. Under article 537 of the Code of Civil Procedure, defamation claims are not admissible in Small Claims Court.
application: The Court allowed only the $5,245.75 in proven legal fees directly attributable to the criminal defence, rejecting the other legal fees as unsupported. The claim for moral and punitive damages failed both for lack of proof of actual damages and because it rested on defamation, which cannot be adjudicated in Small Claims.
conclusion: Recovery limited to $5,245.75 with interest, additional indemnity, and $205 costs; moral and punitive/defamation damages refused.

issue: Did the taxpayer present sufficient prima facie evidence to rebut the statutory presumption of validity of the assessment?
facts: Revenu Québec assessed Filion, a former MNA, on $22,918.05 of allowances paid by the National Assembly to third parties, treating the amounts as a taxable benefit in 1998 based essentially on the findings of the Superior Court that the sums were not authorized under the Assembly's rules.
rule: Under art. 1014 L.I. an assessment is presumed valid, but the taxpayer may rebut it by a prima facie case (Hickman Motors; 9027-5967 Québec inc. c. Québec; Alertpay c. ARQ). A prima facie case is evidence sufficient to establish a fact until the contrary is shown; once made, the burden shifts to the tax authority to prove the assessment on a balance of probabilities.
application: Revenu Québec's auditor relied merely on the Superior Court's conclusion that the sums were unauthorized allowances, without analyzing whether the services actually enriched the taxpayer or increased his net worth. Painting, partition work and exterior repairs to a seven-year-old constituency office did not automatically increase the property's value, and some payments compensated genuine political work. The evidence showed that, at most, only part of the assessment could constitute enrichment.
conclusion: The taxpayer rebutted the presumption; it was set aside and the dispute was decided on the balance of the evidence.

issue: Could Revenu Québec reassess 16 years after the initial assessment despite the three-year limitation?
facts: The initial assessment was made 11 May 1999; the reassessment for the 1998 year was issued 8 April 2015. In his April 1999 return the taxpayer did not report the disputed sums, which had been paid to third parties he engaged, some of whom did work on a building he owned.
rule: Art. 1010(2) L.I. allows reassessment beyond three years where the taxpayer made a misrepresentation attributable to neglect ('incurie'), wilful omission or fraud; 'incurie' is assessed objectively as negligence or lack of diligence (Chiasson; Labrosse). Delay must be tested by administrative-law principles requiring proof of significant prejudice (Blencoe; Markevich; Donaldson).
application: Objectively, the taxpayer could not ignore that these persons had done work on a building he controlled and that the costs could not be entirely attributed to an MNA's functions, so his 1999 return objectively contained a misrepresentation or wilful omission. Moreover, by suing for his transition allowance in 2001 and agreeing to suspend proceedings pending the criminal case, he effectively renounced the three-year limitation; the dispute over the allowances ran from 1999 to the 2013 Superior Court judgment, and the 2015 reassessment followed within a reasonable time.
conclusion: The reassessment was not time-barred; Revenu Québec could reassess the 1998 year in 2015.

issue: Should the tax consequences be attributed to 1998 or to 2013?
facts: The Superior Court quantified the misused amounts in its 2013 judgment; Revenu Québec taxed them in 1998 and allowed an administrative-tolerance deduction of the same amount in 2013 to reflect the compensation ordered.
rule: Under arts. 28, 36 and 37 L.I., income, including benefits and misappropriated funds, is included in the year received or realized; proceeds of fraud or misappropriation constitute income (Peek; Poynton; Zins). Economic advantage is realized in the year the benefit accrues.
application: Unlike cases where the wrongdoer retained the funds, Filion did not hold cash; the sums went to third parties. Any economic advantage—the increase in his property's value or the avoidance of personal expenses—was realized in 1998 when the work was done. 1998 was therefore the correct year.
conclusion: 1998 was the appropriate taxation year for any taxable benefit.

issue: Did the taxpayer in fact receive a taxable benefit from the improper use of the allowances?
facts: The MNA allowances were paid to third parties (Giguère, Latouche, Morin, L'Italien, others). In January 1999 the National Assembly unilaterally withheld the taxpayer's entire transition allowance ($52,617.13), an amount exceeding the misused sums, and interest was only awarded from November 2009.
rule: Under art. 37 L.I. a taxable benefit requires a real economic advantage that increases the taxpayer's net worth, assessed in concreto (Bernier c. Sous-ministre du Revenu; Beauregard; Smith c. R., 2019 FCA 173). Illegality of the conduct does not itself make the sums a taxable benefit.
application: Much of the amount (Giguère's $11,356.38) compensated genuine political work, not enrichment; painting and exterior repairs were essentially maintenance of a long-used constituency office and did not raise the property's value except in a small proportion. Only limited sums (e.g., part of Latouche's payment, the $2,500 to Morin's spouse, $1,000 to Morin, and $2,655.10 to Morrissette/Filion) reflected personal benefit. Critically, the Assembly had appropriated his transition allowance in January 1999—exceeding the misused amounts—so the compensation Revenu Québec only recognized in 2013 had in reality already occurred, depriving him of any economic benefit. When he filed his April 1999 return he held no taxable advantage.
conclusion: No taxable benefit existed; the assessment and the penalty (and interest) were annulled.

issue: Does the Superior Court have jurisdiction over parental time when the Youth Division is seized of a protection matter?
