facts: The father asked the court to decline jurisdiction in favour of the Court of Québec, Youth Division, where three hearings had occurred and the children were represented. No custody application was pending before the Youth Division, and the DPJ confirmed in writing and at the hearing that it would not participate in the Superior Court debate.
rule: The Superior Court has exclusive jurisdiction over custody (art. 33 C.p.c.) unless a clear legislative provision removes it; art. 37 para. 3 C.p.c. permits the Court of Québec to rule on custody only where it is already seized of a protection or adoption matter to which a custody request is intimately linked (Droit de la famille — 18996; Kirouack). There is no res judicata as between the two courts, and concurrent jurisdiction serves the child's best interests.
application: No custody application was pending in the Youth Division and the DPJ declined to be involved; the Youth Division was seized only of a compromission question and could rule on custody only if compromission were found. Having heard five days of evidence, the Superior Court was well placed to decide parental time in the children's best interests.
conclusion: The Superior Court retained and exercised jurisdiction to decide parental time; the father's request to decline jurisdiction was rejected.

issue: What parental-time arrangement is in the children's best interests?
facts: Three children (13, 11, 8) were caught in a bitter conflict. Evidence and DPJ reports established repeated physical violence and inappropriate discipline by the father (hitting X in the face, striking the boys with a prayer book and a lulav, throwing objects), exposure to conflict with his new partner, and the father's obstruction of and interference with the children's needed psychological therapy. A 2017 provisional order had established shared 2/2/3 custody on the recommendation of expert Dr. David (2016).
rule: Under s. 16 of the Divorce Act the court considers only the best interests of the child, giving primary consideration to physical, psychological and emotional safety and well-being, and must weigh family violence (s. 16(3)-(4)) and maximum contact (s. 16(6)). No presumption favours equal time (Droit de la famille — 14576); shared-custody criteria include stability, parental capacity, ability to communicate and absence of conflict (Droit de la famille — 091541, Bich J.A.). The trial judge is not bound by provisional orders or expert recommendations (S.M. c. A.G.).
application: The father minimized his violence, lacked introspection, denigrated the mother and her religious practices before the children, obstructed therapy, and left the children unsupervised; X reported fearing him weekly. The high conflict and the father's deficient parenting capacity meant equal time no longer served the children. The 2016 expert report was outdated and the problems were never put to the expert; maintaining the status quo was not required.
conclusion: The majority of parental time was awarded to the mother, with the father receiving alternate weekends, Wednesday evenings, and defined holiday periods; joint decision-making with anti-conflict orders was imposed.

issue: How should the parents' incomes be determined for child support?
facts: The father, employed by a family real-estate business and holding minority interests in several companies, declared modest incomes ($63,000–$127,000) inconsistent with his lifestyle. He received cash from his father, a company car and cellphone, a rent-free apartment, and support from his sister. The mother received recurring monthly gifts of $5,450 from her parents (formerly via a family trust).
rule: Art. 446 C.p.c. lets the court attribute an appropriate income reflecting true ability to pay; art. 9 of the Règlement sur la fixation des pensions alimentaires pour enfants defines annual income to include income from all sources, net rental income, and business income, with non-taxable amounts converted to taxable equivalents. Gross income is used and recurring family support may be included where regular (Droit de la famille — 121520).
application: A minority shareholder without control cannot have corporate net profits attributed as income, but the father's personal 12.5% rental income (added back for CCA), undeclared cash (~$30,000/yr), car and cellphone benefits, sister's recurring gifts, and rent-free apartment ($3,000/mo notional) were added and grossed up. The mother's declared income plus grossed-up recurring parental gifts (~$65,400 net/yr) were used.
conclusion: The father's income was set well above his declared figures ($201,504 in 2016 rising to $318,562 by 2020-2021); the mother's around $99,000–$108,000, then $103,335 for 2020-2021.

issue: How should special expenses be apportioned?
facts: The children had activity costs, psychological care, and private-school fees; a July 2020 order (Poirier J.) had required the father to pay all of X's school A fees, and the father had confirmed his intention to pay all school fees.
rule: Art. 587.1 C.c.Q. and art. 9 of the Règlement allow the base contribution to be increased for special expenses, normally shared in proportion to the parents' respective incomes.
application: Given the income proportions, special expenses were to be shared 23% mother / 77% father; psychologists' fees shared net of insurance; school fees left with the father as previously ordered and as he had accepted.
conclusion: Special expenses shared 23%/77%; the father ordered to pay all school-related fees for schools A and B.

issue: Does s. 21.1 of the Divorce Act apply where removing the barrier to Iranian Shia Muslim religious remarriage lies within the spouse's control rather than solely with a religious institution?
facts: Both parties are Iranian Shia Muslims married in Iran in 2014 who moved to Canada. Under Iranian law the right to divorce belongs to the husband; the wife cannot initiate divorce except in limited circumstances, and while a Canadian civil divorce would leave her still married in Iran, unable to leave Iran without the husband's permission and at risk of adultery charges. Competing experts addressed whether an Iranian religious divorce could be executed abroad. The defendant argued removal was not within his control under s. 21.1(6) because it depended on judicial and religious institutions.
rule: Section 21.1 of the Divorce Act gives the court discretionary power where a spouse refuses to remove a barrier to religious remarriage, but only where the barrier's removal lies within the hands of one or both spouses (s. 21.1(6)); it does not apply where the power rests with a religious body or official. The provision is not limited to the Jewish get (Bruker v. Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54) and has been applied to Iranian/Shia Muslim divorces by Quebec courts.
application: Relying on the plaintiff's expert (and experts retained by courts in similar matters), the Court found that under the 'Note' to s. 15 of the Iranian Family Protection Law, Iranians abroad may register a divorce through a licensed Imam upon written request of the husband, and the Imam has no discretion to refuse where the husband requests it and the wife is not pregnant and financial conditions are satisfied. The defendant need only grant a power of attorney or appear before a licensed Imam, provide documents, attend the virtual registration and pay his share of costs. The defendant's expert's contrary view rested on assumptions about imams' discretion unsupported by practical experience. The plaintiff met the conditions (not pregnant, renounced spousal support, accepted postponing the Mahr). Removal was therefore within the defendant's control.
conclusion: Section 21.1 applies; the barrier's removal lies within the defendant's control, so the court's discretionary power is engaged.

issue: Was the defendant's refusal based on genuine religious/conscientious grounds, or an improper bargaining tool warranting the court's exercise of power under s. 21.1(3)?
facts: The defendant refused to sign religious-divorce documents until the Canadian civil divorce and all marital issues (notably the Mahr and accessory measures) were resolved, relying on an Imam's hearsay statement (no affidavit, no testimony). His affidavits showed preoccupation with the plaintiff's Mahr claim and fear of losing his rights and facing financial consequences.
rule: Section 21.1(4) exempts refusals based on genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature. The purpose of s. 21.1 is to prevent a spouse from using refusal as a bargaining tool to extract concessions on custody, support or financial matters in the civil divorce; it levels the playing field during the instance (A.D. v. J.P.; Droit de la famille — 151954; Droit de la famille — 231185). Under s. 21.1(3) the court may dismiss the refusing spouse's applications and strike pleadings.
application: The Imam's alleged advice was inadmissible hearsay. The defendant's affidavits demonstrated that his real motivation was to settle the Mahr and other financial issues first, using the refusal as leverage — directly contradicting the objective of s. 21.1. His asserted lack of control was not made out. Following Droit de la famille — 112747, the Court granted a last delay (until May 7, 2025) for the defendant to remove the barriers, failing which his proceedings would be dismissed.
conclusion: The refusal was not based on genuine religious grounds but was an impermissible bargaining tactic; the plaintiff's s. 21.1 demand is well founded and the Court will exercise its s. 21.1(3) power, subject to a final delay.

issue: Is the plaintiff entitled to damages for the defendant's faulty refusal to remove the barriers to religious remarriage?
facts: The plaintiff had been unable to travel safely to Iran and had not seen her ageing parents and relatives for three years, living with stress, anxiety and fear of never returning or seeing her parents again. The refusal persisted from the filing of her modified application in October 2023.
rule: A former spouse's refusal to remove a barrier to religious remarriage engages personal extracontractual civil liability and may constitute a fault giving rise to damages, including punitive damages for unlawful and intentional interference with the other spouse's rights (Droit de la famille — 22187; Droit de la famille — 23260). Interest and additional indemnity run under art. 1619 C.C.Q.
application: The Court found the plaintiff undeniably suffered damages from the defendant's faulty refusal. It awarded $5,000 in compensation for suffering since the October 2023 modified application, with legal interest and the additional indemnity from service. Future compensatory damages and punitive damages were referred to the divorce judge to be assessed on all the evidence.
conclusion: The plaintiff is awarded $5,000 in compensatory damages; further and punitive damages are referred to the divorce judge. The defendant is also ordered to abide by his undertaking not to impose any travel ban.

issue: Did the Media Defendants breach the injunction so as to satisfy the test for contempt of court beyond a reasonable doubt?
facts: Lederman J. had granted the plaintiff summary judgment for libel and a permanent injunction barring the Media Defendants from publishing, or encouraging others to publish, statements suggesting (directly or by innuendo) that Senator Enverga committed criminal fraud in KCCC fundraising or was a pathological/biological liar. After judgment, Ms. Cusipag disseminated emails re-asserting the truth of the original allegations, forwarded them to third parties including a Senator, expressly noting 'I have permanent injunction', circulated a new article by Marquez repeating the $6,000 fraud allegation, and posted online comments vowing Balita would 'continue to publish the truth'.
rule: The three-part test for contempt (Carey v Laiken, 2015 SCC 17, para. 32) requires: (a) the order stated clearly and unequivocally what must not be done; (b) the alleged contemnor had actual knowledge of it; and (c) the alleged contemnor intentionally did the prohibited act. Intent means the prohibited act was done intentionally; no 'contumacious intent' need be shown (Carey, para. 29). Contempt must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt, with doubts resolved in favour of the alleged contemnor.
application: Both sides agreed para. 2 of the judgment was clear. Lederman J. had expressly found (para. 22) that the original article and Facebook posting carried the prohibited meanings, so re-asserting the truth of those publications necessarily re-published the enjoined meanings by plain meaning, innuendo and res judicata. Ms. Cusipag knew of the injunction (she cited it) and deliberately disseminated and encouraged others to spread the very allegations she had admitted, and the court had found, to be false. Her stated intent to violate the order by enlisting others made her contumacious intent plain, though only intent to do the act was required. The court distinguished Quenneville v Volkswagen, finding no ambiguity in either the order or the conduct.
conclusion: All three elements were proven beyond a reasonable doubt; the Media Defendants were found in contempt.

issue: Was the contempt criminal rather than civil?
facts: Ms. Cusipag openly, continuously and flagrantly sought to spread her defamatory message globally, enlisting media contacts and public figures, and portrayed the court's ruling as the product of a conspiracy (including a racist slur that the judge and opposing counsel 'are both jews'), continuing a malicious public campaign to destroy the plaintiff's reputation despite the court order.
rule: Per United Nurses of Alberta v. Alberta (A.G.), 1992 CanLII 99 (SCC), a mere breach is civil contempt, but where public defiance of the court's process is added, calculated to lessen societal respect for the courts, it becomes criminal contempt; the gravamen is the 'open, continuous and flagrant violation' of an order that 'transcends the limits of any dispute between particular litigants and constitutes an affront to the administration of justice as a whole' (Poje; B.C.G.E.U.).
application: The Media Defendants' conduct was an open, continuous and flagrant violation, publicly defying the injunction and impugning the legitimacy of the court's ruling, going far beyond a private breach affecting only the parties' interests.
conclusion: The contempt was criminal; Tess Cusipag, Balita Newspaper and Balita Media Inc. were found guilty of criminal contempt, with costs reserved to sentencing.

issue: Does the notice of civil claim disclose a reasonable cause of action given the s. 170 privative clause of the Securities Act, which bars actions against the Commission absent a plea of bad faith?
facts: Following a 2016 settlement, the Commission issued a notice of hearing, a Preservation Order freezing approximately $20,000, a liability decision and a $60,000 administrative penalty with a seven-year market ban. The plaintiff sued for damages flowing from the Preservation Order but pleaded no express allegation of bad faith. He argued the Court of Appeal's revocation of the Preservation Order constituted a finding of 'undue harm' supporting bad faith.
rule: Section 170 of the Securities Act provides that no action lies against the Commission for any act done in good faith in performance of its duty or exercise of power. On a strike application under R. 9-5(1)(a), material facts are taken as true, but not allegations that are incapable of proof, speculative or verifiably untrue (Young v. Borzoni, 2007 BCCA 16; Attn. Gen. of Can. v. Inuit Tapirisat, 1980 CanLII 21 (SCC)).
application: The court found the Court of Appeal had made no finding that the Preservation Order caused undue harm, so the plaintiff's asserted factual basis for bad faith was verifiably untrue and could not be taken as true. The notice of civil claim contained no plea of bad faith. Without such a plea, the claim fell squarely within the s. 170 immunity.
conclusion: As framed, it was plain and obvious the claim was bound to fail by virtue of s. 170 of the Securities Act.

issue: Is the action an impermissible collateral attack on the Commission's decisions and on the appeal/review process available under s. 167 of the Securities Act?
facts: Section 167(1) gave the plaintiff a right to appeal Commission decisions to the Court of Appeal. He did not seek leave to appeal the liability decision, his appeals of the sanction decision were unsuccessful, and his application to vary the sanctions was refused on June 25, 2024. He then filed this damages action seeking to set aside all sanctions.
rule: A claim is an impermissible collateral attack where it undermines a prior court or tribunal order and the party has not used the direct attack procedures available (Garland v. Consumers' Gas Co., 2004 SCC 25; Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63). Successive related proceedings constitute abuse of process even where the plaintiff believes earlier decisions were wrong (Ajvazi v. Century 21, 2024 BCSC 276). This applies even where damages sought would be unavailable on judicial review (Kamoto Holdings, 2020 BCSC 606; Squamish, 2017 BCSC 2177).
application: The plaintiff sought to relitigate issues already decided or reviewable through the Securities Act's appeal process. His procedural-fairness arguments were or ought to have been raised in the appeal and variation proceedings and were barred by issue estoppel. The fact that damages were not available through those processes did not save the action.
conclusion: The action was an impermissible collateral attack and abuse of process; the claim was bound to fail on this basis as well.

issue: Is the claim statute-barred under the Limitation Act?
facts: The Preservation Order was revoked by the Court of Appeal on April 8, 2022. The plaintiff's alleged losses (loss of counsel, missed payments, business and personal opportunities, emotional distress, litigation costs) arose between the order's filing in January 2021 and its revocation. The notice of civil claim was filed September 26, 2024.
rule: Section 6(1) of the Limitation Act, S.B.C. 2012, c. 13 imposes a two-year limitation period running from discoverability under s. 8.
application: The court held the actionable wrong and losses were discoverable no later than April 8, 2022, when the Preservation Order was revoked, so the limitation period expired April 8, 2024. The plaintiff's argument that damages from his inability to defend himself were not discoverable until the sanction decision was rejected: he knew of the revocation, liability submissions were not complete until May 20, 2022 and the sanction hearing occurred April 17, 2023, giving ample time to retain counsel; no appeal of the liability decision was taken.
conclusion: The claim, filed September 26, 2024, was out of time; the limitation period had lapsed and the claim was bound to fail.

issue: Should the plaintiff be granted leave to amend before the claim is struck?
facts: The plaintiff sought the opportunity to re-plead to add bad faith and negligence causes of action.
rule: A party is generally given an opportunity to re-draft an inadequate pleading, but not where it is plain and obvious a re-drafted pleading is bound to fail or where leave would offend judicial economy, consistency and finality (Ajvazi, 2024 BCSC 276, para. 54; Strata Plan LMS3259 v. Sze Hang Holdings, 2009 BCSC 473; Stein v. Keebler, 2019 BCSC 1338).
application: Because the claim was barred as a collateral attack under s. 167 and by the Limitation Act, any amendment was bound to fail and permitting it would disregard judicial economy.
conclusion: Leave to amend was refused; the notice of civil claim was struck under R. 9-5 without leave to amend, with costs to the Commission.

issue: Did the Monitor have standing/authority to bring the bankruptcy application?
facts: Ernst & Young Inc., the court-appointed Monitor of Bondfield under the CCAA, obtained a transfer-at-undervalue judgment against John Aquino and, as a judgment creditor, applied to assign him into bankruptcy. John argued the Monitor exceeded its 'eyes and ears of the court' role and needed prior court authorization.
rule: Under s. 36.1 of the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act the Monitor had authority to bring the TUV Application; conduct incidental to enforcing a judgment obtained in that capacity requires no separate authorization.
application: The Monitor obtained the TUV Judgment under its CCAA authority and now brings the bankruptcy application as a judgment creditor, which is incidental to its rights under that judgment. There was no suggestion the Monitor was abandoning its duties, and the trustee performs a distinct function (controlling the debtor's assets for creditors).
conclusion: The Monitor had authority; no further authorization was required, and the court granted authorization in any event.

issue: Were the statutory requirements for a bankruptcy order under the BIA met?
facts: John owed the Monitor and the Formacon Trustee an aggregate Net Judgment Debt of not less than $37 million on final TUV Judgments. At his examination he admitted he had no liquid assets, no income, no credit and could not pay now.
rule: Section 43(1) BIA requires a debt of at least $1,000 and an act of bankruptcy within six months; allegations must be proven on sufficient evidence (Levesque (Re), 2016 ONCA 393). Section 42(1)(j) makes it an act of bankruptcy to cease meeting liabilities generally as they become due, per the test in Howard Paul Ivany (Re), 2012 ONSC 7058.
application: John clearly owed more than $1,000. There were two unpaid judgment debts to two creditors, and John admitted he had no assets, income or credit and could not pay. He had therefore ceased to meet his liabilities generally as they became due within the preceding six months.
conclusion: The requirements of s. 43(1) and an act of bankruptcy under s. 42(1)(j) were established.

issue: Should the application be dismissed under s. 43(7) because the debtor is able to pay?
facts: John claimed he owned 50% of four companies holding valuable Ontario properties and would be able to pay once he succeeded in the Aquino Action and liquidated the properties.
rule: Section 43(7) BIA mandates dismissal if the debtor satisfies the court he is able to pay his debts, but the decision is discretionary and exercised on sound judicial reasoning and credible evidence (Medcap Real Estate Holdings Inc. (Re), 2022 ONCA 318). Ashton v. Moody (1997) requires an actual finding of present ability to pay.
application: Unlike Ashton, where the debtor was found able but unwilling to pay, John said he 'will' be able to pay only if he first succeeds in disputed litigation and then liquidates the properties—future, uncertain events, not a present ability. The onus was on John and he did not meet it.
conclusion: The court declined to exercise its residual discretion; no basis to dismiss under s. 43(7).

issue: Should the application be stayed under s. 43(10) pending trial of the Aquino Action?
facts: John argued facts were in dispute—namely whether the properties' value was sufficient and whether he owned 50% of the companies—and sought a stay pending trial of those issues in his litigation against his father Ralph.
rule: Section 43(10) permits a stay where there is a bona fide dispute between the parties, but a mere denial does not automatically require a stay (1719108 Ontario Inc. (Zoren Industries), 2024 ONSC 909; Re Bearcat Exploration, 2003 ABCA 365). Stays are granted only in clear cases (Re Axler; Tsoukalis (Re)).
application: John did not dispute the existence, validity, amount or non-payment of the TUV Judgments and asserted no claim against the Monitor; his dispute was with his father Ralph, not the petitioning creditor. As in Axler and Tsoukalis, the merits of the complex Aquino Action (involving deceit, misrepresentation, breach of fiduciary duty and credibility) could not be assessed. Balancing that delay and uncertainty against the clearly established act of bankruptcy favoured refusing a stay.
conclusion: No bona fide dispute between the parties existed; the stay under s. 43(10) was refused.

issue: Was the application an abuse of process brought for a collateral purpose?
facts: John alleged the application was designed to foreclose or compromise his claim against Ralph, pointing to Zurich's interest as DIP lender and indemnitor of the trustee's fees, and Zurich's settlement/claim positions favouring Ralph's success.
rule: A bankruptcy application may be dismissed as an abuse of process where brought for a collateral purpose such as debt collection, resolving creditor-debtor disputes, or harassment (Bankruptcy of the Jewish Foundation of Greater Toronto, 2022 ONSC 2120).
application: John adduced no evidence that Zurich could dictate whether the trustee pursues the Aquino Action; his concerns were speculative. The trustee must act in all creditors' best interests, and a creditor may pursue litigation under s. 38 BIA if the trustee declines. The Monitor is an independent court officer, and the Formacon Trustee supported the application without concern.
conclusion: No collateral purpose was established; the application was not an abuse of process.

issue: Should the Mareva order be continued as a post-judgment order in aid of execution?
facts: The Monitor obtained Mareva orders in 2019–2020 after John transferred his family home to his wife for $2 shortly after the TUV Application. John argued the Mareva order merged with the TUV Judgment and was spent.
rule: A post-judgment Mareva injunction in aid of execution is governed by a five-part test (Tabrizi v. Majesty Development Group Inc., 2022 ONSC 2665, citing Lamont v. Kent): full and frank disclosure; particulars of the claim; grounds to believe the defendant has assets in the jurisdiction; grounds to believe a real risk of dissipation; and an undertaking as to damages.
application: The court found it unnecessary to decide the merger issue. The Monitor satisfied disclosure, particulars, and assets-in-jurisdiction. Real risk of dissipation was shown by the $2 home transfer and John's uncooperativeness about his assets and income. No undertaking as to damages was required, as none was imposed originally and John could not claim damages where a Supreme Court-affirmed judgment remained unpaid.
conclusion: The Mareva order was continued as a post-judgment order in aid of execution.

issue: Was the prohibition appeal moot, and should the court hear it despite mootness?
facts: Before sentencing, Histed applied to the Court of Queen's Bench for an order prohibiting the Law Society from proceeding to sentencing (and for an apology and a compliance program). The motions judge dismissed the application, finding an adequate alternative remedy by appeal under s. 76 of The Legal Profession Act. By the time of the appeal, Histed had already been sentenced (fine of $2,500 plus $7,500 costs).
rule: A court may decline to hear a moot appeal absent exceptional circumstances (Borowski v. Canada (A.G.), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 342). Courts should be slow to intervene in an administrative process that provides an internal appeal (Mondesir). Reasons are assessed functionally (R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26).
application: Because sentencing had already occurred, the request to prohibit sentencing was moot. The motions judge's brief reasons were sufficient for meaningful review. An adequate statutory appeal existed (indeed the companion appeal), through which Charter values and any s. 24(1) remedy could be addressed. Adjudicating the matter mid-process would encourage a multiplicity of proceedings. Unlike Adelaar, there was no lengthy delay or breach of natural justice creating exceptional circumstances.
conclusion: The appeal was moot and not an appropriate case to hear despite mootness; the appeal from the denial of the prohibition order was dismissed.

issue: Did The Privacy Act render the letter inadmissible before the panel?
facts: Histed's letter was addressed to opposing counsel for the Attorney General and copied to two co-defendants' counsel. A recipient forwarded it to senior counsel, who sent it to the Law Society.
rule: Section 7 of The Privacy Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. P125 excludes evidence obtained by a violation of privacy; s. 3(d) makes use of a person's letters a violation only if done without the consent of a person in possession of them with the author's consent.
application: The recipient held the letter with Histed's consent, having been sent it directly. Passing it on therefore did not violate Histed's privacy under s. 3(d). This was sufficient to dispose of the argument, making it unnecessary to decide whether disciplinary proceedings are 'civil proceedings' or whether the Act's defences applied.
conclusion: The Privacy Act did not apply; the letter was admissible.

issue: Was the letter protected by settlement privilege?
facts: The letter, marked 'Strictly Confidential and Without Prejudice,' concerned agreeing on a list of three judges from which a case management judge would be selected ":
rule: Settlement privilege requires (a) a litigious dispute in existence or contemplated, (b) an express or implied intention that the communication not be disclosed if negotiations failed, and (c) a purpose of effecting settlement (Sopinka, Lederman & Bryant). Without-prejudice communications may still be admitted where exclusion would facilitate abuse of the privilege or another overriding interest of justice requires it (Meyers v. Dunphy, 2007 NLCA 1; Rush & Tompkins).
application: The label did not attach privilege; substance governs. Selecting a case management judge to set dates, give directions and move the action along was procedural, not an attempt to effect settlement, so the third condition failed. In any event, the public interest in the ethical practice of law and in allowing the Law Society to investigate members' conduct outweighed the interest in encouraging settlement, especially where disclosure was extraneous to the main litigation and merely exposed a potentially unprofessional communication.
conclusion: Settlement privilege did not attach, and even if it did, the letter was properly admitted.

issue: Does regulating a lawyer's allegedly political speech fall outside provincial competence?
facts: Histed argued that regulation of free political speech is a federal matter and that provincial authority to regulate the professions does not extend to members' political speech.
rule: Regulation of the legal profession falls under provincial jurisdiction over property and civil rights, s. 92(13) of the Constitution Act, 1867 (Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, 2002 SCC 65). There is a distinction between criminal laws that intrude on speech (e.g., contempt, hate speech) and professional conduct regulation (R. v. Kopyto).
application: Even assuming the comment was 'political,' the pith and substance of The Legal Profession Act is to regulate the profession and protect the public interest — a valid provincial object. Conduct not otherwise protected is subject to the Law Society's conduct process.
conclusion: The division-of-powers argument failed; any remedy lay in the Charter, not the division of powers.

issue: Did the Code and the panel's decision infringe s. 2(b), and was any limit justified under s. 1?
facts: The panel found Histed breached the Code by writing to opposing counsel that a named judge was 'a bigot.' Histed acknowledged 'bigot' imported racism, closed-mindedness and unfitness for the bench, but led no evidence that the allegation was true. He challenged both the Code provisions (as vague) and the panel's decision, and argued the Law Society led insufficient s. 1 evidence.
rule: Section 2(b) is broadly protected but not absolute; limits must be 'prescribed by law' and justified under s. 1 (R. v. Oakes; Multani, 2006 SCC 6). Vagueness fails only where a provision gives no basis for legal debate (R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society). The Charter applies to statutory bodies and their decisions (Slaight; Rocket v. Royal College of Dental Surgeons). Justification does not require empirical proof and may rest on reason, logic and self-evident matters (Sauvé; R. v. Bryan; Ross v. NB School District No. 15); expression far from s. 2(b)'s core attracts attenuated justification (RJR-MacDonald; Lucas).
application: The Law Society conceded the breach. The Code's norms ('abusive, offensive or otherwise totally inconsistent with the proper tone of a professional communication') were sufficiently intelligible to permit legal debate and constituted a 'law.' The objectives — protecting the public and the administration of justice — are pressing and substantial (Kopyto; Rocket; Pearlman). There was a rational connection, as calling a judge a bigot strikes at judicial impartiality; impairment was minimal, restricting only the manner of expression (Histed remained free to reject the judges or complain to the Judicial Council); and given the low value of gratuitous insults and the modest fine, the effects were proportionate. An attenuated evidentiary burden was satisfied by the statute, the Code, and jurisprudence on professional discipline for insulting judges.
conclusion: The infringement was justified under s. 1; the appeal on the merits was dismissed.

issue: Does s. 333.3 LSSSS infringe freedom of association under s. 3 of the Quebec Charter and s. 2(d) of the Canadian Charter?
facts: Section 333.3 requires a specialized medical centre (CMS) to operate either exclusively with physicians subject to a health-insurance agreement (participating) or exclusively with non-participating physicians, preventing the two groups from practising together in such a centre. Specialist physicians testified that the rule ended certain shared clinic arrangements (e.g., anesthesiologists assisting non-participating surgeons at private clinics), but each physician retained ongoing professional and business relationships with the same colleagues.
rule: Freedom of association (s. 3 Quebec Charter; s. 2(d) Canadian Charter) protects three categories of activity per Mounted Police Association of Ontario v. Canada, 2015 SCC 1: (1) the right to join and form associations (constitutive approach); (2) the right to associate to exercise other constitutional rights (derivative approach); and (3) the right to associate to meet, on more equal terms, the power of stronger entities (purposive approach). A breach occurs where the State targets or prohibits an activity because of its associational nature. Being regulated by a legislative regime does not itself impair a profession's freedom of association (Rombaut; Jewish Hospital of Hope). The Charters do not guarantee a constitutional right to practise a profession without constraint or to do business with persons of one's choice (Chaoulli, 2005 SCC 35; Siemens v. Manitoba, 2003 SCC 3; Black v. Law Society of Alberta).
application: The Court found s. 333.3 does not prohibit forming associations: physicians may unite in private practices, in participating or non-participating CMS, in companies owning a CMS, and in professional federations. The evidence showed only the sharing of premises and services, not a genuine association formed to pursue a common purpose; leasing an operating room and paying an anesthesiologist is a commercial and professional activity, not an association. The legislature regulated the operation of CMS, not the right to associate, so the constitutive approach was not engaged. The derivative approach failed because there is no protected constitutional right to practise medicine where and how one wishes or to make business arrangements with persons of one's choice—these are purely economic interests outside s. 7 (Chaoulli, Siemens). The purposive approach failed because physicians are not vulnerable, isolated individuals needing to face the State on equal footing, having federations to represent them. The Court rejected reliance on Kerans J.A. in Black, noting McIntyre J. had squarely rejected that broad conception of association in the Alberta Reference.
conclusion: Section 333.3 affects only the physicians' business relationships and economic interests and does not infringe their freedom of association under either Charter.

issue: If s. 333.3 infringed freedom of association, would the limit be justified under s. 1 of the Canadian Charter and s. 9.1 of the Quebec Charter?
facts: The impugned provisions form part of an integrated scheme (LAM, LAH, LSSSS) designed to guarantee universal access to insured health services based on medical need rather than ability to pay, adopted after extensive consultation following Chaoulli.
rule: Under s. 1 (Oakes) and s. 9.1, a limit must pursue a pressing and substantial objective and be proportionate: rational connection, minimal impairment, and overall proportionality. Preserving the public health-insurance regime and discouraging a parallel private system is a valid and pressing objective within provincial competence (Chaoulli, per Deschamps J.). Courts must show deference to legislative choices addressing complex social and economic problems (Hutterian Brethren, 2009 SCC 37).
application: Section 333.3 ensures the 'watertightness' of public financing so that ability to pay does not affect access, reiterates the LAM prohibition on mixed participating/non-participating status, prevents the State from indirectly subsidizing recourse to non-participating surgeons by paying participating physicians in the same centre, and avoids creating incentives for more physicians to become non-participating. These are reasonable solutions constituting minimal impairment, adopted after broad study.
conclusion: Even had a limit on freedom of association been established, it would be a reasonable and demonstrably justified limit, satisfying the s. 1 / s. 9.1 criteria.

issue: Should the court make a custody order or decline to make one and adopt a parenting plan instead?
facts: The mother sought sole custody (she already held temporary sole custody); the father asked that no custody order be made and that decision-making be shared in parallel parenting. The parties are strong-willed, high-conflict litigants who repeatedly used the child as a battleground.
rule: Section 16(1) of the Divorce Act and s. 28(1)(a) of the Children's Law Reform Act (CLRA) are permissive ('may'), not mandatory. Per M. v. F., 2015 ONCA 277, courts may adopt a 'parenting plan' without awarding 'custody' to avoid the harmful 'winner/loser syndrome.' Best interests govern (s. 16(8) Divorce Act; s. 24(2) CLRA).
application: The court found this a high-conflict case where labelling one parent 'custodial' would be perceived as a win/loss and would fuel conflict, contrary to the child's best interests. The reasoning in M. v. F. applied. The court rejected the argument that Bjornson v. Creighton requires a custody finding before deciding mobility, holding that it is the structure of the parenting relationship, not who wears the 'C' badge, that matters under Gordon v. Goertz.
conclusion: No custody order was made; the court instead ordered a detailed shared parenting plan allocating responsibilities.

issue: How should medical, religious and educational decision-making authority be allocated?
facts: The mother sought authority over major medical and educational decisions and that the child be raised Jewish to the exclusion of other faiths; the father sought shared/parallel decision-making with final say over education and activities. The father agreed the child be raised Jewish. The assessor recommended the mother have final say on medical and religious matters and that educational disputes go to a parenting coordinator.
rule: Best interests of the child under s. 16(8) Divorce Act and s. 24(2) CLRA; 'divided parallel parenting' is available in high-conflict cases (K.(V.) v. S.(T.), 2011 ONSC 4305; Young v. Young, [1993] 4 SCR 3).
application: The court agreed the mother should have final decision-making on medical and religious matters (given her managed emotions and need for timely decisions and the father's agreement on the Jewish faith), but disagreed with the assessor that education should go to a parenting coordinator, finding this would delay decisions and expose the child to conflict. The court found education and religion could be disengaged into separate spheres and gave the father final decision-making authority over education (excluding parochial school, reserved to the mother's religious authority), to preserve his meaningful role.
conclusion: Mother granted final decision-making on medical and religious matters; father granted final decision-making on education; extracurricular activities to reflect the child's preferences with mutual consent for overlapping-time activities.

issue: Should the mother be permitted to relocate with the child to San Francisco?
facts: The mother, a US and Canadian citizen who had not lived in San Francisco since 2002, wished to move there where her parents, grandparents and childhood friends live; she offered generous access to the father. The father opposed, and the assessor recommended deferring the decision until before grade one.
rule: Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 SCR 27: a fresh inquiry into the best interests of the child with no presumption favouring either parent, considering the existing custody/access arrangements, maximizing contact with both parents, the child's views, and (only in exceptional cases) the moving parent's reasons where relevant to parenting ability.
application: The court declined to defer the issue, deciding it on present circumstances. It found the mother had close friends, a good home, and realistic employment prospects (approx. $125K) in Toronto, so a move was not required to improve her parenting; her reason for moving was a preference to have extended family involved, not relevant to meeting the child's needs. Relocation would reduce the father's consistent day-to-day contact (currently 8 of 14 days) to visits, which technology cannot replace, and the court was concerned the mother might not facilitate the father's role. It also rejected the claim that the parties had intended to move permanently to the US.
conclusion: Relocation refused; it was not in the child's best interests to move to San Francisco.

issue: What parenting-time schedule serves the child's best interests, and should the father have equal time?
facts: Both parents love the child and share a strong bond; the child is happy and well-adjusted. The father sought equal shared time; the mother accepted the assessor's schedule. The father had refused to undergo a recommended psychiatric assessment and had a history of anxiety and impulsivity.
rule: Best interests of the child (s. 16(8), (10) Divorce Act; s. 24(2) CLRA); the principle that a child should have maximum contact with each parent consistent with best interests.
application: The court adopted the assessor's schedule (child with father 5 of 14 nights) rather than equal time. The dobermans safety risk had been eliminated and the father's anxiety was a minimal risk, but the father's unexplained refusal to comply with the recommended psychiatric assessment deprived the court of information relevant to his request for equal time, so the status quo should not be changed. The court permitted the mother regular travel to San Francisco but capped travel periods at seven consecutive overnights.
conclusion: Assessor's parenting-time schedule adopted, with defined travel and holiday provisions; father's request for equal time refused.

issue: Is the parties' post-separation conduct and the father's non-compliance with court orders relevant to their parenting ability?
facts: The father ignored parts of several court orders, hired a private investigator, sent a damaging corporate notice, and sent threatening communications; the mother made repeated police reports, took money from the company, and facilitated an abuse investigation. Both engaged in egregious post-separation behaviour.
rule: Section 16(9) Divorce Act and s. 24(3)-(4) CLRA: past conduct is considered only if relevant to a person's ability to act as a parent, including whether violence or abuse was committed; the Family Law Rules provide separate consequences for non-compliance.
application: The court found both parties equally blameworthy but held the conduct was not relevant to their go-forward ability to parent, as both parented responsibly and the child thrived. Non-compliance was disrespectful and could bear on costs but did not affect the father's parenting ability. The father's vulgar and threatening electronic communications, viewed in context of a bitter custody fight, did not amount to domestic violence under s. 24(4) CLRA.
conclusion: The post-separation conduct and non-compliance were not treated as relevant to either party's ability to parent; the abuse characterization was rejected.

issue: Was Zohar's September 2, 1993 shutdown and lockout an abusive breach of contract, or was it justified by the exception of non adimpleti contractus?
facts: The parties shared extrusion facilities under a three-year agreement (Exhibit P-2). Relations soured; Imaflex indicated an expected but not promised departure 'on or about September 1, 1993'. When that date passed with Imaflex still on the premises and owing about $31,000 (only about $9,224 aged 31-60 days), Zohar ceased all production, locked Imaflex out, refused re-entry, retained finished goods and clandestinely removed Imaflex's resin.
rule: Under the Civil Code of Lower Canada the exception non adimpleti contractus must be exercised proportionately to the creditor's non-performance, an application of the good-faith requirement reflected in art. 1024 C.C.L.C. (now expressly codified in art. 1591 C.C.Q., requiring substantial non-performance). Abusive exercise of contractual rights engages liability (Houle v. Canadian National Bank, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 122).
application: Imaflex had never promised to move by September 1; an expectation is not a promise. It had substantially met its payment obligations, having just paid over $5,000, with most arrears within the contractual 30-day term. Zohar did not merely suspend production after warning; it evicted Imaflex without a prior default notice, retained goods and removed resin, thereby repudiating the contract. Its reaction was disproportionate and abusive.
conclusion: Zohar's termination was premature and abusive, itself a breach of contract. Imaflex was awarded $62,300 for 89 days of lost gross profit ($700/day), plus related shutdown damages (resin removal $2,032, unauthorized Oerlikon use $8,820, Oerlikon repairs $9,208.33).

issue: Did Imaflex meet its burden of proof on its numerous contractual damage claims?
facts: Imaflex advanced claims totalling $486,735 including late start-up ($63,000), quality ($2,153.64), shipping ($5,646.75), consulting fees, missing resin ($65,524.64), excess scrap ($52,359.95), downtime from poor maintenance ($25,210.37) and loss of reputation ($100,000). The Agreement was often silent, and proof was highly technical and quantitative.
rule: Contractual obligations are measured by the Agreement and, where silent, by the parties' conduct, equity, usage and law (art. 1024 C.C.L.C.). A written notice of default was required to claim delay damages (art. 1067 C.C.L.C.); claims must be established by serious, precise and concordant presumptions (art. 2849 C.C.Q.). The obligation to return leased equipment in good condition is one of result (art. 1623 C.C.L.C.), whereas maintenance/quantity claims without a contractual standard are obligations of means.
application: Late start-up failed for absence of default notice and two years of passivity. Quality claims were granted as independent, credible proof shifted the burden to Zohar, which failed to rebut. Shipping, consulting, extraordinary communication, loss of reputation, excess scrap and downtime claims failed as speculative, after-the-fact, or lacking a proven industry standard. Missing resin was assessed on the more objective Harel Drouin methodology (pounds produced, not sold), yielding 27,897 lbs and $12,269. Oerlikon repairs succeeded partly given the result-obligation presumption Zohar did not rebut.
conclusion: Most large claims were rejected; a limited set was granted. The gross award to Imaflex was $132,201.45, reduced by Zohar's maintained account claim of $31,500.61 to a net award of $100,700.84 (plus the separate $30,000 punitive award).

issue: Were exemplary/punitive damages warranted, and against whom?
facts: Zohar excluded Imaflex and its principals from the premises, retained finished goods worth far more than the arrears with no right of retention in law, and removed Imaflex's raw materials without knowledge or consent, without segregating them.
rule: Punitive damages under art. 49 of the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms require an intentional infringement of protected rights — here the right to peaceful enjoyment and free disposition of property (art. 6) and against entry upon another's property (art. 8). Reckless disregard for a co-venturer's rights, not malice as such, warrants sanction.
application: Zohar's acts constituted an intentional and abusive infringement of Imaflex's rights under arts. 6 and 8. The individual defendants, however, may have believed Imaflex would not move and would not pay, so their conduct was not wholly devoid of colour of right; imposing punitive damages on them additionally would be unduly harsh.
conclusion: Punitive damages of $30,000 were awarded against Zohar alone. No punitive damages were imposed on the individual defendants.

issue: Should the corporate veil be lifted to hold the individual principals solidarily liable with Zohar?
facts: Jules Amar, Michel Amar and Serge Afflalo were Zohar's principals and, by common accord, caused the shutdown, denial of access, retention of finished goods and clandestine removal of Imaflex's resin, from which they, owning Zohar with their families, stood personally to gain.
rule: Under the C.C.L.C., contractual and delictual (extra-contractual) liability could be combined. Directors incur personal solidary liability where they commit a common fault causing intentional harm (art. 1053, 1106 C.C.L.C.); mere breach at the instigation of directors, absent fraud or abuse, does not pierce the veil (Lanoue v. Brasserie Labatt; Golden Harvest v. Pakis).
application: The shutdown and related abusive acts exhibited the element of abuse justifying personal liability, the individuals being 'not the servants of Zohar but its masters' with a personal expectation of gain. The other, purely operational claims did not exhibit abuse and did not justify lifting the veil.
conclusion: The individual defendants were held solidarily liable with Zohar only for the $64,332 of compensatory damages flowing from the September 1993 shutdown, and costs limited accordingly; they bore no liability for the other claims or for the punitive award.

issue: Which high school should the twelve-year-old child attend where the parents disagree between a Jewish-immersion school and a secular school?
facts: X, twelve, was raised in the Jewish faith and attended a secular school from kindergarten to grade six. Both parents identify as Jewish; the father favours School B, an immersive Jewish-culture school that meets the Quebec curriculum, while the mother favours the secular School C. X applied to and was accepted at several schools; her first choice was School B, her second School C.
rule: Under the parens patriae authority in family matters and the governing principle of the best interest of the child, the court determines contested questions of a child's education when parents cannot agree.
application: The court found X bright, mature and thoughtful, that she had done her own research, visited open houses and consulted friends. It found no proof of undue pressure by the father, addressed the mother's concerns about Hebrew preparedness (an accelerated program at School B resolves this) and about stability, but concluded X's stated priority of developing her Jewish identity in a school setting was appropriate.
conclusion: The court ordered that X be enrolled at School B for the 2021-2022 school year, with education costs declared special expenses; parents to support her integration.

issue: What weight must be given to the articulated preference of a child aged twelve or older on school choice?
facts: Through her court-appointed attorney, X clearly expressed a preference for School B, based on her desire to explore and intensify her Jewish faith and belonging, and to learn Jewish culture, values and traditions she felt she had been missing. She also cited a warmer, more diverse environment.
rule: Droit de la famille — 201310, 2020 QCCA 1139 (paras. 14-16, 20): from age twelve, a child's articulated preference on school choice should be respected and is determinative unless the court finds it not in the child's best interest; the trial judge must verify the choice is appropriate for the child and that the reasons given are rational.
application: The court verified that X's choice of School B was appropriate for her and that her reasons were rational, both parents agreeing she was bright, thoughtful and mature. It found respecting her expressed preference to be in her best interest.
conclusion: X's preference was respected as determinative; School B was chosen accordingly, with a mechanism for future review should X later wish to change schools.

issue: What was the agreement between the parties as to the services and price, and what balance remained owing to Mr. Gauvin?
facts: Ms. Gagné retained Mr. Gauvin, initially at $50/hour, to transcribe her manuscript into LaTeX; he later took a broader role (layout, corrections, photos). She admitted the total value of his work was at least $5,000 and that $4,120.70 remained unpaid.
rule: The contract is the law of the parties (art. 1434, 1385 C.c.Q.); the plaintiff bears the burden of proving the merits of the claim.
application: Ms. Gagné did not contest that Mr. Gauvin performed the work or that $4,120.70 represented the unpaid balance of the agreed price. Mr. Gauvin therefore discharged his burden of proof.
conclusion: Mr. Gauvin's claim was well founded; Ms. Gagné owes the balance, subject to set-off arising from the counterclaim.

issue: Can Mr. Gauvin recover damages for the time and effort devoted to pursuing his lawsuit?
facts: Mr. Gauvin claimed an additional $862.86 for the time and effort spent on his judicial recourse.
rule: Such costs are recoverable only where the opposing party has abused, whether on the merits or in the conduct of the litigation (Viel c. Entreprises immobilières du terroir ltée, 2002 CanLII 41120; Dawcolectric inc. c. Hydro-Québec, 2014 QCCA 948).
application: There was no abuse by Ms. Gagné, either on the merits or in the conduct of the case.
conclusion: The claim for litigation-related damages was denied.

issue: Was the service contract resiliated as a result of fault on Mr. Gauvin's part, engaging his contractual liability?
facts: After the parties disagreed over the book's font size (Taille 10 vs 11) and format, Mr. Gauvin repeatedly threatened to withdraw, issued shifting ultimatums, and concealed his intention to keep control of the LaTeX-transcribed version while reassuring Ms. Gagné otherwise. The contract ended in late November 2020.
rule: A service contract (art. 2098 C.c.Q.) may be unilaterally resiliated by the client at any time (art. 2125 C.c.Q.); a service provider may resiliate only for serious cause and not at an inopportune time (art. 2126 C.c.Q.). Every contract must be performed in good faith (art. 1375 C.c.Q.); source code has been held to belong to the client (Valade.net, 2007 QCCS 3213). Fault causing resiliation gives rise to damages.
application: The court characterized the relationship as a service contract despite Mr. Gauvin's expanded role. Regardless of who formally ended it, the resiliation resulted from Mr. Gauvin's faulty conduct: he persisted against Ms. Gagné's clear instructions, made contradictory threats, and dissembled about retaining the LaTeX version, breaching his duty of good faith.
conclusion: The resiliation resulted from Mr. Gauvin's fault, engaging his contractual civil liability.

issue: What damages are owed to Ms. Gagné, and how should the reciprocal debts be set off?
facts: Ms. Gagné had to hire a graphic designer, a photographer and an editor to complete the book, incurring $802.41, and suffered trouble and inconvenience (contacting 150 pre-sale buyers, delay, pressure) for which she claimed $3,000.
rule: Damages compensate the loss suffered and profit deprived flowing immediately and directly from the co-contractor's fault (art. 1607, 1611 C.c.Q.); reciprocal debts are extinguished by compensation (art. 1673 C.c.Q.); interest and the additional indemnity run under art. 1619 C.c.Q.
application: The $802.41 in replacement costs was justified by the invoices; the $3,000 for trouble and inconvenience was reasonable given the missed December publication and pressure caused. The counterclaim of $3,802.41 was granted in full and set off against the $4,197.47 owing to Mr. Gauvin as of notification.
conclusion: Counterclaim allowed in full; after compensation a residual $395.06 remained payable to Mr. Gauvin, with interest and additional indemnity from 19 May 2021, and Mr. Gauvin bears the legal costs on both claims.

issue: Was the dismissal justified by a serious reason under art. 2094 C.c.Q.?
facts: After 34 years of continuous service within the Desjardins Movement, the plaintiff was hired by the defendant in May 2013 as director of the personal-market and business-development division, supervising 23 employees. She was sent home on 17 April 2014 by the newly arrived general manager, Michel Truchon, who cited her authoritarian management style and the threatened departure of key employees. Before this she had received a superior performance rating and a certificate of recognition, and had never been reprimanded during her career; the only reproach was her handling of the Fabien Maltais file and the 2014 performance-management exercise, both conducted in accordance with objectives fixed by the Fédération.
rule: Art. 2094 C.c.Q. allows unilateral resiliation of an employment contract without notice for a serious reason; the burden of proving serious cause rests on the employer (Sirois c. O'Neill; Lesage c. Lama Transport). For administrative/incompetence dismissals, the employer must ordinarily give the employee notice of deficiencies, a chance to correct, support and warning of dismissal (Costco Wholesale Canada Ltd c. Laplante).
application: The Court found the defendant never advised the plaintiff of any deficiency before 11 April 2014, gave no clear reproach, imposed no corrective measures, and forced her onto vacation, undermining her authority after the board reversed course on the Maltais file. The employer met none of the five Costco prerequisites and did not prove incompetence, negligence or insubordination; at most she had a rigid, inflexible attitude consistent with her contractual mandate focused on financial objectives set by the Fédération.
conclusion: The dismissal (the sending-home of 17 April 2014 followed by termination on 16 February 2015) did not rest on a serious reason.

issue: What was the date of dismissal and the reasonable notice period, accounting for service across Desjardins entities?
facts: Truchon told the plaintiff on 17 April 2014 to leave and propose terms for ending her employment; a written termination came only on 16 February 2015. She had worked continuously for three different Desjardins caisses from 1980 to 2015, about 35 years, but only about 22 months for the defendant. She was 52, in a senior position.
rule: Under art. 2091 C.c.Q. an indeterminate contract may be ended with reasonable notice, assessed globally by factors such as age, nature and level of the position, length of service and difficulty of finding new work (Industries de Caoutchouc Mondo; Nurun c. Deschênes). The dismissal date is a factual question fixed at the moment the employee unequivocally knows she is dismissed.
application: The 17 April 2014 statement invited negotiation and left open reassignment within the Movement, so it was not an unequivocal termination; no salary suspension or administrative measures followed. Termination occurred only on 16 February 2015. Continuous service across Movement entities counts (contrasting Boyer, where service was interrupted, and following Vallières). Given her age, senior rank, 35 years of service and greatly reduced re-employment prospects, notice of 24 months was warranted.
conclusion: Dismissal took effect 16 February 2015; the plaintiff was entitled to a 24-month notice period.

issue: Must disability benefits be deducted and did the plaintiff mitigate?
facts: The plaintiff received disability benefits of $163,280.51 over 853 days (22 April 2014–22 August 2016) under a group plan funded 80% by the employer (65% before 2004) and 20% by the employee. She began new, lower-paid work in August 2016 and later started a business.
rule: Art. 1608 C.c.Q. provides that benefits from a third party do not reduce damages except to the extent of subrogation; where the employer funds the disability plan, the employer-funded portion of benefits received during the notice period is deducted (Sylvester c. British Columbia). The employer bears the burden of showing failure to mitigate.
application: The Court prorated benefits to the notice period ($105,854.77, being 70.58% of the total), then applied the employer's funding proportions (65% pre-2004, 80% post-2004), yielding $73,475.66 to be deducted. The plaintiff's job-search efforts were reasonable given her illness and age, so no failure to mitigate was shown; but income earned during the notice period ($31,317.61) was deducted.
conclusion: Deductions reduced the severance indemnity to $129,709.14; no failure to mitigate.

issue: Was the plaintiff entitled to additional moral damages for abusive dismissal?
facts: Truchon sent her home abruptly and laconically, expressing loss of confidence without explaining reasons, offering no chance to respond or correct, and no Movement support; he then remained silent for weeks. The plaintiff fell into a serious depression and her reputation in the financial sector suffered.
rule: Arts. 6, 7 and 2087 C.c.Q.; moral damages beyond the notice indemnity require a distinct fault—negligence, bad faith or an identifiable fault—causing harm beyond that normally flowing from termination (Standard Broadcasting c. Stewart; Bristol-Myers Squibb c. Legros; Structures Lamerain c. Meloche). A brutal or intempestive dismissal can constitute abuse of right even absent bad faith.
application: The Court found the dismissal intempestive, cavalier and brutal, humiliating and lacking respect for the plaintiff's dignity, and that it seriously and durably injured her reputation in a small financial market. This negligent conduct was a distinct fault causing harm exceeding the notice indemnity, though the claimed $500,000 was grossly exaggerated.
conclusion: Abuse of right established; $75,000 in non-pecuniary damages awarded.

issue: Was the plaintiff entitled to punitive damages under the Quebec Charter?
facts: The plaintiff claimed $500,000 for unlawful/intentional interference with reputation and dignity and a further $500,000 for being dismissed while suffering a handicap (major depression) on 16 February 2015.
rule: Art. 1621 C.c.Q. and arts. 4, 49 and 10 of the Quebec Charter; punitive damages require the unlawful interference to be intentional, meaning the author wanted the consequences (St-Ferdinand). Art. 7 C.c.Q. requires an intent to harm.
application: The Court found the conduct abusive but no intent to harm the plaintiff's reputation—it was driven by fear of losing employees. As the employer believed it had dismissed her on 17 April 2014 (before the depression arose), no unlawful intent to dismiss for handicap could be formed; and there was no evidence of the employer's knowledge of her medical condition on 16 February 2015.
conclusion: Punitive damages refused; the $1,000,000 claim was excessive.

issue: Was legal cruelty proven of the kind required to entitle the petitioner to a decree of judicial separation?
facts: The petitioner, about 56 and already suffering from serious high blood pressure and albumen when she married the respondent in 1936, was subjected to frequent violent outbursts of temper, obscene language, vile epithets, orders to leave the house, a false accusation that she was poisoning him, opening of her trunk, and repeated demands that his difficult daughter Ida be brought into the home. Medical evidence showed her health progressively deteriorated during cohabitation.
rule: Legal cruelty need not depend on physical violence but may arise from conduct operating on the mental condition of the aggrieved spouse where it creates mental distress sufficient to impair health or a well-founded apprehension of worse treatment (Lovell v. Lovell (1906) 13 O.L.R. 569). There must be 'danger to life, limb or health, bodily or mental, or a reasonable apprehension of it' (Russell v. Russell [1895] A.C. 315, aff'd [1897] A.C. 395).
application: The court accepted the petitioner's account as substantially true and disbelieved the respondent where his evidence conflicted. The respondent's conduct created a reasonable apprehension that continuance would injure her health, and the medical evidence established her health was in fact seriously impaired. The court was convinced that a forced return would make his conduct worse and might materially hasten her death.
conclusion: Legal cruelty was proven with respect to conduct occurring before 25 March 1940.

issue: Did the petitioner condone the cruelty by returning to and remaining in the marital home, and was that condonation revived?
facts: After first leaving on 25 March 1940 the petitioner returned on 13 April 1940 following a reconciliation meeting and lived as a wife in the home until 20 August 1940. The respondent soon breached the reconciliation agreement (dismissing the maid, renewing outbursts because Ida was not invited to a dinner, abusing a mutual friend, and accusing her of poisoning him).
rule: Restoration of conjugal cohabitation, even apart from sexual intercourse, carries condonation with it, but condonation is always conditional and is wiped out if the respondent's subsequent conduct revives the original wrong (Cramp v. Cramp [1920] P. 158).
application: By resuming cohabitation as a wife until 20 August 1940 the petitioner condoned the earlier cruelty. However, the respondent's renewed abusive conduct recreated conditions deleterious to her health similar to those before, thereby wiping out the condonation.
conclusion: The plea of condonation based on the resumption of cohabitation from April to August failed; the condoned cruelty was revived.

issue: Did the parties' association after the petitioner's final departure amount to a fresh condonation barring relief?
facts: After leaving on 20 August 1940 the petitioner did not return to the marital home but dined and stayed overnight with the respondent at the 'Rio Vista' auto camp on seven or eight occasions, on the strength of his promise of a 'scheme' that would end their troubles. The scheme was never disclosed or fulfilled, and he ultimately used the association to argue she could no longer succeed in court.
rule: For a husband, sexual intercourse is conclusive evidence of condonation, but the rule is less strict where the wife is petitioner; condonation is conditional and is established only if the condition on which cohabitation is resumed is fulfilled (Cramp v. Cramp).
application: Although the court inferred sexual intercourse occurred, there was no restoration of conjugal cohabitation since the petitioner never returned to the home. The intercourse was allowed only on the strength of the respondent's promise of a resolving scheme; that condition was never fulfilled, so no condonation arose whether the promise was a genuine hope of reconciliation or a plot to defeat her claim.
conclusion: No fresh condonation was established; the petitioner remained entitled to relief.

issue: Do the incapable adult's repeated fugues constitute a categorical refusal of care under art. 16 C.c.Q.?
facts: The adult, declared incapable of consenting to or refusing care and under public curatorship since 2010, periodically leaves the hospital or residence. Her treating psychiatrist and occupational therapist attribute the absences to her mental illness and cognitive impairments, not a desire to avoid treatment; she generally returns on her own and accepts all treatment without resisting.
rule: Under art. 16 C.c.Q., a 'categorical refusal' must result from an organized will to refuse to receive the proposed care (Kouri and Philips-Nootens); it need not be express and may be inferred from circumstances such as strategic feigned acceptance, but the objective of avoiding the care must be established.
application: The court found the adult flees only to obtain gratifications unavailable in hospital, not to avoid treatment, and appears incapable of forming such a design. Her current conduct at the residence, where she returns on her own, confirmed the earlier finding. No organized will to refuse care was shown.
conclusion: The fugues do not amount to a categorical refusal of care, so they cannot confer jurisdiction on the court in place of the substituted consent the legislator favours.

issue: May the court order peace officers to assist in returning the adult, characterizing such assistance as 'care'?
facts: The Hospital sought orders authorizing recourse to peace officers 'sans autre formalité' to transport the adult back for treatment. The Curateur public neither consented to nor opposed this conclusion. The Hospital argued police would refuse to act without such orders; no police representative testified, and police had in fact cooperated when the residence raised concerns.
rule: 'Soins' under art. 11 C.c.Q. is generic, covering examinations, treatments and interventions of a medical, psychological or social nature, including preliminary lodging (M.B. c. Centre hospitalier Pierre-Le Gardeur, 2004 CanLII 29017). Police intervention is instead an accessory order meant to give effect to a care authorization (P. Deschamps). A court cannot make care orders without jurisdiction to do so.
application: The court held that treating police intervention as a 'social intervention' required by the adult's health would be exorbitant; it is an accessory order to a care authorization. Since the court had no jurisdiction to authorize care (no categorical refusal and consent given), it could not grant the accessory order, and no Civil Code provision authorized it. The factual premise that police would refuse to act was unproven and contradicted by events.
conclusion: The court declined to issue the peace-officer orders; the Hospital withdrew that part of its demand and the remainder was dismissed.

issue: Does the court have jurisdiction to authorize the proposed care where the adult does not categorically refuse and the substitute decision-maker consents?
facts: The Curateur public, curator to the person and property since 2010, accepted the treatment plan. Evidence showed the Hospital had been treating the incapable adult since 2008, apparently without substituted consent or judicial authorization, and had confirmed her incapacity to the Curateur public by 2012.
rule: Under art. 16 C.c.Q., care may be given to an incapable adult with the consent of the person authorized to consent, or, where that person is prevented or unjustifiably refuses, with court authorization; outside emergencies (art. 13 C.c.Q.) no treatment may be given without such authorization. The court also emphasized the Curateur public's protective duties (art. 263 C.c.Q.) and notification duties toward it (art. 270 C.c.Q.; C.p.c. art. 395).
application: Because valid substituted consent existed and there was no categorical refusal, the statutory conditions for judicial authorization were absent. The court noted the Hospital had improperly treated the adult without authorization for years and that the Curateur public should have intervened in the care plan from its appointment.
conclusion: The court lacked jurisdiction to hear the care authorization demand and dismissed it (without costs given the consents).

issue: Should the court grant the Curateur public interim custody of the incapable adult via a safeguard order?
facts: At the November 28 hearing, counsel for the Curateur public confirmed a mandate to seek custody (garde) of the adult, fearing that police in other sectors might not cooperate if she left her current residence, but had not been authorized to file the demand owing to a lawyers' strike.
rule: Article 272 C.c.Q. permits the court, even before the instance, to designate the Curateur public to protect the person of the adult; article 263 C.c.Q. excludes custody when the Curateur public is named tutor or curator, requiring a separate application. A safeguard order may issue for urgent protection.
application: The court characterized the anticipated custody demand as part of the protection regime, akin to opening such a regime, and found urgency requiring rapid intervention to ensure the adult's health and safety pending a final ruling.
conclusion: The court issued a time-limited safeguard order (valid until December 22) entrusting custody of the adult to the Curateur public, without costs.

issue: Was Feldman in contempt of the non-dissemination injunction issued by Desfossés J. when he repeated the defamatory allegations in a plea, cross-demand and exhibits filed in the related Lande file?
facts: Desfossés J. had ordered Feldman, a lawyer, not to disseminate defamatory allegations (that the Plaintiffs benefited from gold bars stolen from Holocaust victims) found in three paragraphs of his Long Form Affidavit, and had ordered certain exhibits sealed. Shortly after service of that judgment, Feldman's firm filed a plea, cross-demand, a revised long-form summary and similar exhibits repeating the allegations in the Lande defamation file without sealing them.
rule: Contempt in civil proceedings is governed by arts. 57–62 C.c.p.; proof must be beyond a reasonable doubt (art. 61 C.c.p.). Per Carey v. Laiken, 2015 SCC 17, the plaintiff must prove three elements beyond a reasonable doubt: (1) the order states clearly and unequivocally what must and must not be done; (2) the alleged contemnor had actual knowledge of it; (3) the party intentionally did the prohibited act. Per Morasse v. Nadeau-Dubois, 2016 SCC 44 and Daigle c. St Gabriel de Brandon, ambiguity or multiple reasonable interpretations of the order must benefit the accused; contempt is an enforcement power of last resort.
application: The court found the injunction covered only 3 of the 7 requested paragraphs, so allegations in other unprohibited paragraphs covered the same ground, making the order susceptible of at least two reasonable interpretations. Read as the Plaintiffs urged, the order would impermissibly deprive Feldman of his right to a full and complete defence and the audi alteram partem rule in two defamation actions where truth/fairness of his comments was in issue (art. 99 C.c.p.). The sealing order named only specific exhibits and did not extend to the Lande file. While Feldman had actual knowledge (served by bailiff by email on June 14, 2021) and intentionally directed the filings, the lack of clarity of the order defeated the contempt charge.
conclusion: Feldman found not guilty; the order lacked sufficient clarity to sustain a contempt finding beyond a reasonable doubt.

issue: Was Feldman in contempt for failing to communicate all documents and remarks made concerning the Estate and the Plaintiffs, as ordered?
facts: Feldman provided nothing after the Desfossés J. order, but testified that all such information had already been provided following an earlier case-management order of Bélanger J.; no evidence of the earlier communications was filed.
rule: The court has discretion to find contempt (arts. 57–62 C.c.p.). Per Morasse v. Nadeau-Dubois, 2016 SCC 44, contempt is an exceptional, last-resort power to be used only where genuinely necessary to safeguard the administration of justice. Sections 49 and 158 C.c.p. give courts broad powers, including alternative case-management remedies.
application: A doubt subsisted because some documents had been provided under Bélanger J.'s order and Feldman swore they constituted all the information he was required to communicate. Because contempt is a last resort and the court has broad alternative powers likely more efficient, the issue should be addressed by other means.
conclusion: Feldman found not guilty on this charge as well.

issue: Do the pleadings disclose a reasonable cause of action against the 49 independent CAS Defendants?
facts: Each of the 49 CAS Defendants is a separately incorporated, independently governed entity that issued Birth Alerts on its own discretion, without top-down direction from the Ministry or coordination with other CASs. The plaintiffs relied on shared membership in the OACAS, the OACAS-authored Eligibility Spectrum, and the inter-governmental PT Protocol to allege concerted action.
rule: Under s. 5(1)(a) CPA the test mirrors a motion to strike: a claim survives unless it is 'plain and obvious' it discloses no reasonable cause of action (Cloud v. Canada). Unlawful means conspiracy requires pleading, with particularity, each conspirator's overt acts and a meeting of the minds, not mere parallel conduct (Normart; Carcillo; Lilleyman/Bumblebee). In a class action there must be a representative plaintiff with a claim against each defendant — the Ragoonanan/Hughes v. Sunbeam problem.
application: The plaintiffs pleaded no meeting or agreement among the CASs; membership in the OACAS and common use of the Eligibility Spectrum amounted only to conscious parallelism (analogous to lawyers following a CBA code), and the PT Protocol was a government-to-government agreement, not one among CASs. The independent, non-hierarchical structure meant there was no collective or concerted-action liability, so negligence, intrusion upon seclusion and misfeasance could not attach to the group. G.G. and W.W. each had a claim only against the one CAS that harmed them, not against the other 47-48.
conclusion: It is plain and obvious that none of the common-law causes of action meets the s. 5(1)(a) threshold against the CAS Defendants; the conspiracy and other tort claims fail.

issue: Do the plaintiffs have standing to bring Charter s. 7 and s. 15 damages claims against CAS Defendants that did not issue a Birth Alert affecting them?
facts: The plaintiffs sought individual declarations and monetary damages under s. 24 of the Charter against all CAS Defendants; each named plaintiff was affected by only one CAS (Native Child and Family Services Toronto for G.G.; Chatham-Kent Children's Services for W.W.).
rule: CASs are government actors under s. 32(1) of the Charter (H.(T.); Chatham-Kent). A personal Charter damages claim under s. 24, as opposed to a s. 52 declaration of invalidity, 'can only be made by the person whose Charter rights have been infringed' (R. v. Edwards); standing is tied to causation (Snell v. Farrell), and cannot be acquired 'through the back door of a class action' (Allee v. Medrano; Bailey v. Patterson).
