application: This was a private-interest, compensation-seeking claim, not a challenge to legislation (Birth Alerts had already been cancelled). Absent a causal link, G.G. had no standing against Chatham-Kent and W.W. had none against Native Child and Family Services Toronto; the other CASs were strangers to each plaintiff's claim. The same Ragoonanan defect infected the Charter claims.
conclusion: It is plain and obvious the Charter claims against the CAS Defendants fail for lack of standing/causation and do not meet s. 5(1)(a).

issue: Is the negligence claim against Ontario tenable or barred by policy-decision immunity?
facts: The Ministry has extensive oversight, funding, directive and takeover powers over CASs (CYFSA ss. 4, 34, 42-44) but does not deliver services or direct individual cases. It was aware of Birth Alerts yet never assessed whether CASs stayed within jurisdiction; it terminated the practice by Policy Directive CW 005-20 on July 14, 2020 only after the MMIWG Report flagged them as discriminatory and ultra vires (fetuses are not legal persons: Tremblay; Winnipeg CFS).
rule: Ontario is not vicariously liable for CASs (CYFSA s. 34(5)-(6)); liability must rest on the Crown's own wrongful conduct. A duty may arise from a statutory oversight mandate where no conflicting overarching duty exists (Syl Apps; Papassay; Dilico; Reilly). Section 11(4) CLPA immunizes good-faith 'policy matter' decisions (Bowman v. Ontario), but operational conduct is not immune (Francis v. Ontario).
application: Ontario argued its non-action was a policy decision, yet it also insisted Birth Alerts were never a provincial policy but an operational/administrative practice at CAS level; the cessation directive was a policy decision (immune), but the failure to end a known, unauthorized and harmful practice was not. The alleged tort of omission — failing to keep regulated entities within their statutory bounds — did not attract immunity, and the commission/omission line was too fine to resolve on a pleadings motion.
conclusion: It is not plain and obvious the negligence claim against Ontario fails; it passes s. 5(1)(a).

issue: Must the Charter s. 7 and s. 15 claims against Ontario fail?
facts: Birth Alerts intruded into pregnancy and the parent-child relationship, compelled disclosure of health information, and disproportionately impacted Indigenous, racialized and disabled parents, deterring prenatal care. The Ministry knew of the practice for years and acquiesced until 2020.
rule: Section 7 protects liberty, security of the person and privacy in the pregnancy/child-protection context (Dobson; Cheskes; KLW; G.(J.)), and requires conformity with fundamental justice (arbitrariness, overbreadth, gross disproportionality: Bedford). Section 15 is engaged by pregnancy-based and adverse-impact discrimination (Fraser; Taypotat). Government actors are individually responsible under s. 32 (Eldridge), and Ontario is generally not liable for CAS conduct (C.R.; Selkirk).
application: Because Ontario stood in the same relationship to all class members, the Ragoonanan problem did not apply. Although Ontario's role was passive acquiescence, its personnel knew or should have known Birth Alerts targeted fetuses beyond CAS jurisdiction and disproportionately harmed protected groups; the distinction between active discrimination and tolerated ongoing discrimination may be one without substantive difference. The alerts were arguably arbitrary, overbroad and disproportionate and not saved by s. 1.
conclusion: It is not plain and obvious the s. 7 and s. 15 claims against Ontario fail; both pass s. 5(1)(a).

issue: Are the s. 5(1) certification criteria met against Ontario?
facts: The plaintiffs proposed a class of pregnant persons subject to Birth Alerts since May 10, 2007 (plus a Family Class and an Indigenous/racialized/disabled subclass), 20 common issues, and both named plaintiffs as representatives.
rule: Section 5(1) CPA requires a cause of action, an identifiable class, common issues (some basis in fact: Pro-Sys; Hollick), preferable procedure viewed through judicial economy, behaviour modification and access to justice (AIC v. Fischer), and a suitable representative plaintiff with a workable litigation plan.
application: Against Ontario a viable cause of action existed, the class and subclass were objectively defined, and common issues (reworded to remove the word 'scheme' and to target Ontario alone) had a basis in fact, including aggregate/aggravated/punitive damages questions. A class action was preferable to numerous individual actions given Ontario's resources and the behaviour-modification interest in its oversight failures. The representatives were suitable; the premature notice-mailing provision was struck from the litigation plan. Against the CASs, no cause of action meant no class, no common issues and no preferable procedure.
conclusion: Certification is granted against Ontario on negligence and Charter ss. 7 and 15, with the modified common issues; the motion is dismissed against the CAS Defendants, with liberty to bring separate CAS-by-CAS actions.

issue: Was it in the children's best interests to continue the suspension of the respondent father's access?
facts: Following an interim support order, the father repeatedly disparaged the mother to the three boys, discussed the litigation with them, used them as 'pawns', and encouraged them to spend more time with him to reduce the mother's support entitlement. Professionals resigned as mediators, an intake for a reunification program failed because the children refused to attend, and the JFCS found the children were at risk of emotional harm. The father filed little proper evidence, failed to appear at later motions, and refused to cooperate with the JFCS.
rule: Custody and access turn entirely on 'the best interests of the child', particularly the child's needs and circumstances: Children's Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12, s. 24.
application: The court found the father continued to disregard orders not to disparage the mother or discuss the litigation, used even his one hour of weekly telephone access to disparage the mother, refused to meet the JFCS or affirm compliance with a parenting plan, and delayed reconsideration of the suspension. The evidence, including JFCS findings that the children were in need of protection and 'safe with intervention' only because of the suspension, reinforced that continued suspension served the children's best interests.
conclusion: The suspension of the father's access was maintained, subject to structured, recorded telephone contact and the Family Bridges framework.

issue: Should the applicant mother be granted temporary sole custody to enable participation in the Family Bridges Program?
facts: The parties had joint custody and equal parenting under a 2015 Partial Separation Agreement, but the children resisted therapeutic intervention and the father would not compel their participation or cooperate. The Family Bridges Program typically requires temporary sole custody to the non-favoured parent and a no-contact period; the mother sought sole custody to enrol the children in the program and in schooling for 2018-2019.
rule: Best interests of the child under s. 24 of the Children's Law Reform Act; standard provisions of reunification interventions requiring temporary sole custody to facilitate the program.
application: Given the father's continuing conflict, non-compliance and refusal to cooperate, and the JFCS's protection concerns, the court concluded that granting the mother temporary sole custody was necessary to compel the children into appropriate therapy and to make educational decisions, and was in the children's best interests.
conclusion: The mother was granted temporary sole custody until December 10, 2018, with the parties to comply with the Family Bridges Program terms and telephone calls to be recorded.

issue: Did the Commissioner and Labour Court exceed their jurisdiction by denying the intervening employee the right to know and refute the evidence relied on?
facts: Iacovelli, an employee and member of the bargaining unit, was allowed to intervene in the employer's petition to revoke the Union's accreditation. She requested the names of employees who had withdrawn their resignations, but the Commissioner refused; the Commissioner instead ordered a survey with sworn declarations and based his dismissal of the revocation petition on that additional evidence, verified privately.
rule: Under Art. 846 C.C.P. the Superior Court's superintending power survives the privative clause of the Labour Code where there is an excess of jurisdiction. Natural justice includes the right to be heard, which encompasses the right to be informed of the evidence used and to correct or refute it (Pépin & Ouellette; Harelkin v. University of Regina, 1979 CanLII 18 (SCC)).
application: The Commissioner evidently relied on the renunciations of resignation and survey forms without disclosing them to the petitioner, depriving her of any opportunity to refute or correct that pertinent and fundamental information. The invitation merely to call witnesses did not cure this. Such a breach of natural justice constitutes an excess of jurisdiction under Art. 846(1) C.C.P.
conclusion: The failure to disclose the evidence violated the petitioner's right to be heard and amounted to an excess of jurisdiction.

issue: Does the Art. 36 secrecy rule extend to revocation proceedings?
facts: The employer argued that Art. 36 of the Labour Code, which forbids revealing a person's union membership, authorized withholding the names.
rule: Art. 36 imposes secrecy only 'au cours de la procédure d'accréditation'. Exceptions to the general right to know and refute proof must be narrowly construed. The Court of Appeal in Vassart v. Robert Simpson's affirmed the primacy of public debate even in certification.
application: The Court held the secrecy condition applies only during certification proceedings, not to revocation/cancellation proceedings under Art. 41; extending it was not warranted by the express text. Being an exception, it must be read narrowly and could not justify the secret evidence.
conclusion: Art. 36 did not authorize withholding the information in a revocation proceeding.

issue: Did failure to send the second certification report and acceptance of late membership cards constitute an excess of jurisdiction?
facts: After the May 11, 1981 hearing the Commissioner obtained a further report from the certification agent but did not send a copy to the interested parties, and appeared to accept membership cards dated after the February 20, 1981 filing of the revocation petition.
rule: Art. 41(3) of the Labour Code requires the Commissioner to send a copy of the agent's report to the parties, who may contest it within ten days. Art. 36.1 fixes the representative-character assessment as of the date of filing of the petition. An erroneous interpretation contrary to common sense or giving the text an unsupportable meaning justifies intervention (Bradburn v. Wentworth Arms Hotel, 1978 CanLII 44 (SCC)).
application: The Commissioner's failure to transmit the second report breached more than a simple preliminary rule, and acceptance of adherences posterior to February 20, 1981 misapplied Art. 36.1, denying the petitioner her right to refute the proof. Both errors reached the magnitude of an excess of jurisdiction.
conclusion: These procedural and interpretive errors amounted to an excess of jurisdiction warranting evocation.

issue: Is the mother entitled to child support arrears and, if so, in what amount and on what basis?
facts: The father paid the $575/month ordered in the 2004 Roy judgment only two or three times and contributed nothing to the child's needs from 2004 onward, despite working 2000-2004, 2006-2010 and 2012-2014. The mother raised the child, now 23, alone and paid all expenses. She offered two calculation scenarios: scenario A applying the $575 order indefinitely ($152,429.70), and scenario B using the father's actual income, federal guidelines and periods without income ($75,272.16).
rule: A support order cannot be maintained as if a safeguard/interim order for 14 years (C.p.c. art. 158(8)); retroactivity of support requires a contextual approach in the best interests of the child (Droit de la famille — 17122, 2017 QCCA 107). Interest is permitted (Droit de la famille — 3235).
application: The Court rejected the father's position that he owed nothing and refused to perpetuate the interim order indefinitely. It adopted the mother's scenario B as consistent with the evidence, reflecting the father's real income and unemployed periods, with interest.
conclusion: Arrears fixed on the scenario B basis ($75,272.16 with interest); this obligation is compensated through the unequal partition of the family patrimony.

issue: Is the claim for child support arrears prescribed under arts. 595 and 2904 C.C.Q.?
facts: The father argued only arrears since 15 August 2015 (three years before the cross-application) were recoverable. He was abroad for years, gave no address, hid his return and full-time work in City B (2012-2014), behaved violently and unpredictably, and the mother had precarious health, no job security and periods without counsel.
rule: Art. 595 C.C.Q. limits child support for past needs to three years unless the debtor parent behaved reprehensibly; art. 2904 C.C.Q. suspends prescription where a person is in fact unable to act. Blameworthy conduct is interpreted broadly (D.B.S. v. S.R.G., 2006 SCC 37, para. 106; Droit de la famille — 122743, 2012 QCCS 5164), including deliberately ignoring the obligation.
application: The Court found the mother was in fact unable to act throughout: reconciliation attempts, the father's whereabouts unknown abroad, two foreign addresses, his concealed return and full-time employment, a default dismissal she did not consent to, and her exhaustion and lack of representation. His conduct was reprehensible.
conclusion: The prescription argument was rejected; the arrears are not prescribed.

issue: Is the mother entitled to a 20% increase in parental contribution for non-exercise of access?
facts: The father did not exercise access for most of the child's life; the mother carried a heavy economic burden alone for 18 years.
rule: A court may account for a parent's conduct and burden when fixing support, but has discretion on increases.
application: Rather than granting the 20% increase, the Court chose to reflect the mother's heavy sole economic burden through the partition of the family patrimony.
conclusion: No 20% increase awarded.

issue: Is the father entitled to spousal support for himself?
facts: The father, remarried and on welfare, amended his support claims three times (from $1,500/month, to $727/month, to $1,500/week). He worked until 2014, received EI, and his medical work restriction was only for six months (to 1 May 2019).
rule: Bipolar disorder, when treated, is not in itself an impediment to work capacity (Y.A. c. M.B., 2004 CanLII 11044 (QC CA)).
application: The Court found the escalating claims unfounded; the father had earning capacity and had never paid support while employed.
conclusion: The father's application for spousal support is dismissed.

issue: Is either party entitled to a provision for costs under art. 588(2) C.C.Q.?
facts: The father sought a provision for costs but filed no counsel invoices or fee agreement and had never paid support while working; the mother sought $10,000 but there was no evidence of the father's ability to pay.
rule: Art. 588(2) C.C.Q. governs provisions for costs, requiring consideration of the parties' means and conduct.
application: The father could not seek a provision while having refused support and reactivated litigation; the mother's claim failed for lack of evidence of the father's ability to pay.
conclusion: Both applications for a provision for costs are dismissed.

issue: Should the family patrimony be partitioned unequally, and is the City A apartment an acquest?
facts: The co-owned family residence was the only property to partition; the father lived there six years, made an $11,000 down payment and contributed nothing for over 15 years, while the mother paid over $400,000 in home expenses and $70,000 in tuition and incurred ~$160,000 in debt. The City A apartment was bought by the mother's mother in the mother's name to facilitate an inheritance; no money passed to the mother and the couple never lived there.
rule: Art. 422 C.C.Q. permits unequal partition where equal partition would be unjust, tied to the failure of the economic partnership and a spouse's failure to contribute (M.T. c. J.-Y.T., 2008 SCC 50). Art. 450(2) C.C.Q. excludes property received by gift or succession from acquests.
application: The father's total failure to contribute to the marriage's economic partnership justified departing from equal partition; the mother is declared sole owner of the residence, also compensating the unpaid child support arrears. The apartment, received gratuitously through inheritance, is not an acquest.
conclusion: Unequal partition ordered; mother declared sole owner of the residence; the City A apartment is not an acquest.

issue: Did the TAQ have jurisdiction to add to the roll the contributory value of immovables not accounted for by the assessor at deposit, absent a complaint?
facts: Impérial had filed complaints contesting the value inscribed on the roll, including the mechanical systems. The TAQ added the contributory value of energy-producing systems (steam and chilled water) that the assessor had not initially computed, without a formal demand by a party.
rule: Under the Loi sur la fiscalité municipale, for 'new generation' rolls the assessor and the TAQ must determine the value of the 'unité d'évaluation dans son entier' (art. 145 LFM), the value 'telle qu'elle aurait dû être portée au rôle' (art. 34 LFM), and may fix a value higher or lower than proposed (art. 147 LFM). Distinguished from 'old generation' rolls (Atlific, Shell Canada, Talisman) where the BREF could not add ultra petita. Jurisdiction is a question of law reviewed on correctness (Pushpanathan).
application: Because Impérial had filed a complaint contesting the inscribed value, it conferred jurisdiction on the TAQ to review the entirety of the unit's value. As this is a new-generation roll governed by art. 34 LFM, the TAQ had to consider the whole evaluation unit under art. 145 LFM (Hewquip). The prior jurisprudence Impérial relied on concerned old-generation rolls and was inapplicable.
conclusion: The TAQ had jurisdiction to take into account the contributory value of any property forming part of the evaluation unit within the meaning of art. 34 LFM, even where the assessor had not accounted for it. No error.

issue: Are the palletization and materials-handling equipment excluded from the roll under s. 65 LFM as machinery used principally for industrial production?
facts: Impérial's plant modernization ('Montréal 2001') automated central palletization. Cigarettes cannot be sold until fiscal control stamps (SAP) are affixed, which occurs at the end of the conveyor before removal by forklift. The equipment (palletizers, wrappers, conveyors) had a depreciated cost of $2,216,189.
rule: s. 65(1) LFM excludes from the roll machinery, apparatus and accessories used or destined principally for industrial production. Industrial production is a continuous, integrated process ending when the marketable product is ready for storage; it is not complete until the product is saleable per applicable law (Irving Oil, Cie pétrolière Impériale, Société d'énergie Talisman, RJR MacDonald). This qualification question is a mixed question not within the TAQ's core specialization (Vigi Santé; Charny v. Alex Couture), reviewable for error of law/qualification.
application: Since the product cannot be sold before the fiscal stamps are affixed, industrial production is not complete until that operation. The palletization equipment therefore forms the last integrated step of production, distinguishable from Procter & Gamble where no fiscal stamping was required. The TAQ erred in applying Procter & Gamble and in treating the equipment as post-production.
conclusion: The TAQ erred; the equipment described at pp. 47-48 of report I-32F must not be entered on the roll (s. 65 LFM). Appeal allowed on this point.

issue: Could the TAQ set aside the parties' agreement/admissions on the base cost of the mechanical and electrical systems?
facts: The parties had agreed by written admissions on the base 1972 cost of the mechanical/electrical systems, expressly noting the sums represented only the portion corresponding to building services, excluding production services, and that nothing constituted an admission on whether these should be on the roll under s. 65.
rule: An admission is a question of fact revocable only for error of fact (art. 1245 C.C.; Adricon; Gulf Canada). However, deciding whether an immovable is inscribed or excluded under s. 65 is a question of law which parties cannot derogate from by consent; a tribunal is not bound by such an agreement on a legal question. Jurisdiction question reviewed on correctness.
application: The agreement was only on base cost, not an admission that the contributory value of the systems must (or must not) be on the roll. Whether to inscribe a mixed system is a legal question the TAQ had to decide; the agreement could not be a pretext to avoid inscribing the full related costs. The cited jurisprudence (Adricon, Gulf Canada) was inapplicable because there the party sought to revoke an admission on facts outside the res gestae.
conclusion: The TAQ did not err; it could decide the s. 65 question notwithstanding the base-cost agreement. Appeal rejected on this point.

issue: Are the integrated electrical and mechanical systems (electrical, plumbing, heating, air-conditioning/humidification) principally used or destined for industrial production, so as to be excluded from the roll under s. 65 LFM?
facts: The complex had a single high-voltage electrical entry distributed throughout; ~77% of electricity served production. Plumbing had a 14-inch water entry, ~81% consumption for production. Heating/cooling/humidification maintained a constant 72°F and 62% humidity essential to tobacco production. Impérial argued single integrated systems principally serving production; Montréal argued multiple discrete systems (per panel); the TAQ invented a third theory (23 electrical systems by 'artère de moyenne tension') excluding only 13% (the electrical entry).
rule: Since the 1993 amendment, s. 65(3)-(4) LFM: an integrated mechanical/electrical system is not part of the construction and, if used principally for industrial production, is entirely excluded (all-or-nothing rule; art. 2 proportionality excluded). Whether a system serves principally production or building is a mixed question outside the TAQ's core specialization (Charny v. Alex Couture; Vigi Santé), reviewed on correctness/error of law; the audi alteram partem rule requires notice where a tribunal adopts a theory not advanced by any party (Pétromont). Teleological interpretation of tax legislation (Notre-Dame de Bon-Secours; Ciment Québec).
application: By adopting, without expert support or notice to the parties, the 'artère de moyenne tension' theory and rejecting both experts, the TAQ breached audi alteram partem. Limiting exclusion to 13% (the entry) contradicted the all-or-nothing rule of s. 65 and effectively re-applied art. 2 proportionality via the outdated 1972 Manuel. The proportion of consumption and connected loads is a relevant indicator for a mixed integrated system, and the 'destination' element was ignored. The installations form single integrated systems principally used/destined for production (electricity ~77%, plumbing ~81%, heating/gas ~99%/62%, chilled water ~74%, ventilation ~78%).
conclusion: The TAQ erred; the electrical and mechanical systems (plumbing, heating, air-conditioning/humidification) are principally used or destined for industrial production and their contributory value must not be entered on the roll under s. 65 LFM. Appeal allowed on these points.

issue: Did the TAQ err in relying on institutional coherence rather than the preponderant evidence to fix the local adjustment factor (Factor F) for the 1995 roll?
facts: Impérial's expert (Caumartin) study yielded Factor F of 0.80; Montréal's expert (Lévesque) study yielded 1.05, and Montréal, for the first time, submitted a genuine Factor F study and critique (32 days of testimony, 86 exhibits). The TAQ acknowledged numerous deficiencies in Caumartin's study but retained 0.80 'par souci de cohérence institutionnelle.'
rule: Institutional/decisional coherence is desirable but not absolute; decisional autonomy and appreciation of the specific evidence prevail (Domtar; Tremblay; Consolidated Bathurst; CSST v. Fontaine; ABI; Investissements Canpro). Each case must be decided on its own evidence on the balance of probabilities; whether to prefer coherence over new evidence is a question of law (correctness).
application: Montréal's new, different evidence had never been before the TAQ in prior cases. The TAQ, having found Caumartin's study deficient, could not use coherence to grant it de facto res judicata. It had to weigh the two contradictory studies on the balance of probabilities or, if both deficient, neutralize the factor. Analyzing the evidence itself, the Court found Montréal's methodology preferable (indexation to reference date via Statistics Canada, homogeneous comparables), but both studies had deficiencies (dated/old-generation data). Accordingly the factor should be neutralized to 1.0, which enjoyed a presumption of accuracy at deposit.
conclusion: The TAQ erred in law; Factor F is neutralized at 1.0 for the 1995 and 1995-modified rolls. Montréal's appeal allowed in part on this point.

issue: Did the TAQ err in its treatment of the various heads of depreciation?
facts: Impérial claimed curable physical/functional obsolescence on four elements, precariousness of public-domain occupation (tunnels/passageways revocable on 30 days' notice), decline of the tobacco market, supply/snow-removal difficulties, and building configuration/multi-level layout (prior BREF decision had allowed 20%; TAQ allowed 10%).
rule: Depreciation lies at the core of the TAQ's specialized jurisdiction; review is limited to patently unreasonable error. Contributory value of refurbishment must be netted against its cost (General Motors; Camco; Schering; SIQ). One cannot depreciate for missing elements not in the reproduction cost (CAE; Camco). Institutional coherence does not bind where evidence differs.
application: On curable obsolescence, the TAQ correctly followed doctrine (Desjardins) and jurisprudence by accounting for added value of refurbishment (de Grandpré method); no reviewable error. On public-domain precariousness, uncontradicted evidence showed Montréal never revoked such permissions and the past is guarantor of the future; the reasonable risk over 10 years' remaining life was too small to quantify. On tobacco-market decline, the TAQ erred factually in saying no evidence was led, but Impérial itself claimed no economic obsolescence and provided no quantum, so no operative error. Supply/snow-removal issues duplicated configuration and reflect age-related obsolescence captured by age-life tables; missing storage cannot depreciate. On configuration (10% vs prior 20%), the evidence had materially changed (Montréal 2001 project, primary processing moved to Aylmer, layout changes); the TAQ's finding was defensible and within its expertise; institutional coherence did not bind because the evidence differed.
conclusion: Save for the factual misstatement on tobacco-market evidence (without operative effect), the TAQ did not commit patently unreasonable error on depreciation. Impérial's appeal on depreciation rejected.

issue: Did the TAQ err on the rental-value parameters (inclusion of the non-residential immovables surtax and the property value used in decapitalization)?
facts: For the 1995 rolls, the TAQ used 1993 reference-date tax rates (including a 1% water tax and 2.06% surtax that replaced water/business taxes for 1993 only) and applied them to the property value inscribed at the reference date. The assessor had not included the surtax when depositing the 1995 rental-value roll, so complainants like Impérial bore an added burden.
rule: s. 69.5 LFM: rental value is the most probable gross annual rent including property taxes; s. 1 LFM defines the non-residential immovables surtax as a property tax (Germain v. Montréal, SCC). The tax amount included is that effectively expended in the reference year, requiring combination of reference-date rates with the value then inscribed (Hewquip; General Motors). These parameter questions are within the TAQ's core specialization; review for patently unreasonable error. The TAQ must render the decision the assessor should have made.
application: The surtax is a property tax and must be included under s. 69.5; the TAQ correctly included it and rendered the decision the assessor should have made, despite the resulting unequal treatment of complainants. On the value to use, only combining reference-date tax rates with the value inscribed at the reference date respects the LFM requirement that the tax reflect the effective expenditure in the reference year.
conclusion: The TAQ did not commit patently unreasonable error; inclusion of the surtax and use of the reference-date inscribed value are upheld. Impérial's appeal rejected on these points.

issue: What is the applicable standard of appellate review of a trial judge's factual and mixed fact-and-law findings, and was it met?
facts: The grandmother appealed a Crown Wardship order made after a nine-day trial, alleging errors of fact and mixed fact and law, including undue weight on the foster-parent relationship.
rule: Factual findings attract significant deference and may only be reversed for a 'palpable and overriding error' — one plainly seen on the face of the record (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33; Van de Perre v. Edwards, 2001 SCC 60). An appeal court cannot substitute its own view merely because it would weigh the evidence differently.
application: The court found the trial judge's factual findings — including the assault, the credibility assessments, the acceptance of Dr. Kershner's parenting-capacity assessment, and the weighing of the children's relationships — were overwhelmingly supported by the evidence. The trial judge properly balanced the children's relationships with both foster parents and grandparents and correctly stated the legal framework, which the appellant did not dispute.
conclusion: No palpable and overriding error was shown; deference to the trial judge's findings was warranted.

issue: Did the trial judge err in finding that the children's best interests required Crown Wardship with no access for adoption?
facts: The three children had lived with the grandparents since birth under supervision; the grandmother assaulted a child in 2007 (guilty plea) leading to apprehension; a consent parenting-capacity assessment found the grandparents unable to meet the children's psychological, social, medical and academic needs and unable to improve despite supports and parenting classes.
rule: On a status review the sole issue is disposition, determined by the child's best interests under the criteria in s. 37(3) CFSA, from a child-centred perspective; good intentions are not enough — parents must have actually changed and be able to provide adequate care (Jewish Child and Family Services v. R.K.). The court must consider less disruptive alternatives (ss. 57(1), 57.1 CFSA).
application: The trial judge considered the full evidence — expert assessments, support-worker observations, the children's low cognitive functioning and improvement in foster care, and the grandparents' inability to learn new parenting skills — and reasonably concluded the earlier voluntary placement reflected inadequate supervision rather than adequate parenting. Crown Wardship for adoption was in the children's best interests.
conclusion: No error; the disposition was amply supported by the evidence.

issue: Did the trial judge err in denying the grandparents access after making the children Crown Wards?
facts: Once children are made Crown Wards, access is automatically terminated; the grandparents sought access. Evidence showed visits were difficult, the children had little attachment to the grandparents and strong attachment to their foster mother of three years; fresh evidence on appeal confirmed this.
rule: Under s. 59 CFSA the person seeking access to a Crown Ward bears the onus of showing the relationship is beneficial and meaningful to the child and that access will not impair future adoption opportunities (s. 59(2.1); Children's Aid Society of the Niagara Region v. M.J.).
application: The trial judge correctly placed the onus on the grandparents and found, on the totality of evidence and confirmed by fresh evidence, that access was not beneficial or meaningful and the children lacked strong attachment to them.
conclusion: No error; the denial of access was properly grounded in the statutory test and the evidence.

issue: Did the foster/adoptive parents' notice, attendance and testimony violate the appellant's right to an unbiased hearing held in the absence of the public?
facts: The foster parents received notice, attended and testified at the protection hearing.
rule: Section 39(3) CFSA entitles a foster parent who has continuously cared for a child for six months before the hearing to notice of and presence at the hearing; it is common practice for foster parents to testify.
application: Because the statute expressly authorizes foster parents to receive notice and attend, they are statutorily mandated participants, not 'members of the public,' and their participation could not create bias or interference or breach the appellant's right to a hearing in the absence of the public.
conclusion: This ground had no merit.

issue: Did the trial judge's findings or the CFSA disposition infringe the appellant's Charter rights under ss. 7, 12 or 15?
facts: The appellant argued the trial judge's characterization of her as intellectually and emotionally limited breached s. 15, that denial of custody/access breached s. 7, and that 'deprecatory' comments breached s. 12.
rule: Section 7 guarantees life, liberty and security of the person; s. 12 prohibits cruel and unusual treatment or punishment; s. 15 addresses equality. A constitutional challenge to legislation requires joining the Attorney General under s. 109 of the Courts of Justice Act.
application: The s. 15 argument failed because the characterization was a factual finding supported by evidence, not a breach of fundamental justice. Any challenge to the constitutionality of the CFSA access provisions could not be entertained as the Attorney General was not joined; treated as a challenge to the access ruling, the onus was correctly applied. The s. 12 argument was unsupported by authority and the court found no deprecatory comments were made.
conclusion: The Charter grounds were rejected.

issue: Should the release signed on June 3, 1991 be set aside as an unconscionable bargain?
facts: After a July 1990 T-bone collision (liability admitted), Gindis, a Russian émigré with limited English and no meaningful assessment of his claim, negotiated directly with ICBC adjuster Larry Laws while financially destitute and effectively unrepresented. Laws instigated settlement talks knowing Gindis was desperate, relied selectively on Dr. Richards' October 17, 1990 report, refused to disclose that report, remained wilfully blind to other medical information showing ongoing problems under investigation, and secured a $25,000 global release (net cheque $16,054) for less than the claims committee's own reserves.
rule: A bargain is presumptively unconscionable where (1) there was inequality of bargaining position due to ignorance, need or distress of the weaker party, and (2) there is proof of substantial unfairness; the onus then shifts to the stronger party to show the bargain was fair, just and reasonable: Morrison v. Coast Finance Ltd. (1965), Harry v. Kreutziger (1978), Smyth v. Szep (1992), Cougle v. Maricevic (1983). A Crown corporation exercising a monopoly (ICBC) is held to a high standard of commercial morality and must at least disclose to an unrepresented claimant all medical and other information underlying its settlement offer.
application: Gindis was clearly the weaker party — naive, unsophisticated, without documented medical information, medically unassessed, and financially ruined after his wife left. Laws' refusal to disclose Dr. Richards' report and his deliberate failure to obtain available medical information (Dr. Ciszak's file, ongoing neurological assessment) left Gindis unable to make an informed decision. Laws' goal was to limit coverage and obtain a quick, cheap settlement, ignoring that a work-hardening program had been recommended. The settlement was premature and unfair; the court deferred final determination until it assessed proper compensation and, having found the injuries far exceeded the settlement, concluded the bargain was not fair, just and reasonable.
conclusion: The release was set aside.

issue: Did the accident cause the plaintiff's chronic pain syndrome and consequent losses?
facts: Gindis suffered a mild concussion and soft-tissue injuries and, with pre-existing low back pain and paranoid/narcissistic personality traits, developed chronic pain syndrome (CPS) causing physical, cognitive and emotional impairment. Most specialists diagnosed CPS; none found malingering or exaggeration. He was not dysfunctional before the accident.
rule: Causation in tort applies to psychological as well as physical injuries. The plaintiff must show the defendant's unlawful act was a cause-in-fact ('but for') and a proximate cause of the symptoms: Maslen v. Rubenstein (1993), Skelton v. Stewart (1994), Yoshikawa v. Yu (1996). A defendant takes the victim as found — the thin skull / 'eggshell personality' rule — and need only have materially contributed to the injury; the defendant is not excused because other causal factors also contributed: Athey v. Leonati, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 458.
application: The court found Gindis' pre-existing personality traits and low back pain were aggravated and exacerbated by the accident's soft-tissue injury, and that the resulting interplay produced CPS which would not have occurred but for the defendant's negligence. The eggshell-personality principle applied; genuine, non-organic psychological symptoms are compensable. ICBC's failure to arrange an early work-hardening program contributed to his deconditioning, though Gindis' own refusal to exercise also contributed.
conclusion: Causation was established; the CPS and related losses were compensable.

issue: What quantum of damages is appropriate and how should it be reduced for failure to mitigate?
facts: Gindis had a limited, intermittent work history (approx. $15,000/year combined employment and UI), was capable of light sedentary work from January 1991 but did not pursue it (later choosing to stay home to care for his son), and failed to follow medical advice to exercise.
rule: Damages are assessed under distinct heads; awards may be reduced for a plaintiff's failure to mitigate: Janiak v. Ippolito, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 146; Watters v. Rose.
application: Non-pecuniary damages assessed at $75,000, reduced 10% for failure to mitigate to $67,500. Past income loss (projected $90,802 based on ~$15,000/year) reduced 50% to $45,401 for his ability to do light work not pursued. Future income loss (projected $240,234) reduced 50% to $121,200 for residual earning capacity. Future care $15,000; special damages $88.
conclusion: Total awards granted, less the $25,000 already received under the release, with court-ordered interest on past income loss and special damages and costs to the plaintiff.

issue: Does a person served with or put 'on notice' of a petition who files a response automatically become a full party to the petition proceeding?
facts: Mr. Rashid designated the Langley School District and Trish Kolotyluk as 'on notice' without naming them as parties in the style of cause and sought no relief against them. When they applied to be removed, he argued their filing of responses made them 'parties' who were participating unlawfully.
rule: Under Rule 1-1 a 'party' is a person named in the style of the proceeding. Kitimat (District) v. Alcan Inc., 2006 BCCA 562, holds that filing a response does not confer full party status; a person must apply to be added under Rule 6-2(7) or apply to intervene. Case law is unsettled (Kellogg, Delta Sunshine, Pierce, Louis), but Delta Sunshine implicitly applied Kitimat to petitions under Rule 16-1.
application: The Court reviewed the conflicting authorities and followed the notation in Pierce (para. 39) that Delta Sunshine implicitly concluded Kitimat applies to Rule 16-1 petitions. Merely being served and filing a response makes a person a party of record but not a full party. The applicants had not been named in the style of cause and had not applied under Rule 6-2(7).
conclusion: Ms. Kolotyluk and the Langley School District were not made full parties merely by filing responses; the Petitioner's assertion that they participated unlawfully was without merit.

issue: Should the pleadings referring to the 'on notice' entities be struck and those entities removed from the proceeding?
facts: The petition contained bald Charter allegations and factual assertions against the Langley School District, and referred to a letter by Ms. Kolotyluk, an Alberta employee who had provided no information about the Petitioner. No relief was sought against either and no facts supported any claim.
rule: Rule 9-5(1) permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim (a), are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious (b), or are otherwise an abuse of process (d). A pleading is vexatious where it would serve no useful purpose and waste court resources (Willow v. Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083; Nevsun Resources Ltd. v. Araya, 2020 SCC 5); abuse of process engages the court's inherent jurisdiction (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63).
application: Charter relief was not available in a proceeding brought by petition; the allegations lacked any factual foundation; Edmonton Public Schools and Ms. Kolotyluk, being Alberta entities, could not be the subject of relief in British Columbia; and no order could be made against either applicant. The impugned paragraphs were scandalous, frivolous or vexatious and served no useful purpose.
conclusion: The Court ordered the applicants have no role in the petition, struck the identified paragraphs without leave to amend, and removed all references to the applicants from the style of cause and elsewhere.

issue: Should the Petitioner be declared a vexatious litigant and prohibited from bringing further proceedings without leave?
facts: Mr. Rashid had pursued judicial reviews, a Human Rights Tribunal complaint (dismissed as premature), reconsiderations and appeals, an Alberta action against the RCMP (struck as disclosing no reasonable claim and abusive), and this petition, all repeating unsupported allegations of discrimination and conspiracy. He had been warned by the Alberta Court and by Edelmann J. (upheld by the Court of Appeal).
rule: Section 18 of the Supreme Court Act permits an order barring further proceedings without leave where a person has habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds instituted vexatious proceedings. Proceedings must be vexatious/without reasonable grounds and there must be a knowing, deliberate repetition, assessed objectively (British Columbia (Public Guardian and Trustee) v. Brown, 2002 BCSC 1152). Indicia of vexatiousness are set out in Holland v. Marshall, 2010 BCCA 243, and Pearlman v. ICBC, 2010 BCCA 362 (from Re Lang Michener and Fabian).
application: Mr. Rashid repeatedly rolled forward the same unsupported claims across multiple forums despite clear warnings, and brought this 'on notice' proceeding against an Alberta employee over whom the Court had no jurisdiction, amounting to harassment. No reasonable litigant could expect relief by repeating such claims. The whole history showed habitual and persistent vexatious conduct without reasonable cause.
conclusion: The Court declared the Petitioner a vexatious litigant, prohibited him under s. 18 from instituting further legal proceedings without leave of the Court, and awarded the applicants special costs payable forthwith after assessment.

issue: What effect does Ferras have on the assessment of sufficiency of evidence for extradition committal, and did the extradition judge apply the correct standard?
facts: Italy sought Seifert's extradition on murder charges arising from alleged tortures and killings at the Bolzano Transit Camp in 1944-45, presenting its case by way of a Record of the Case. The committal judge decided the case in 2003, several years before Ferras, relying on the limited role of the judge described in Shephard, and committed on seven of nine counts.
rule: Under United States of America v. Ferras; Latty, 2006 SCC 33, an extradition judge must be satisfied the requesting state's evidence is both reliable and available, and has discretion to engage in a limited weighing of the evidence to determine whether it is sufficient to enable a properly instructed jury, acting reasonably, to convict — thereby overruling a key element of United States of America v. Shephard (as the Court explained in United States of America v. Graham, 2007 BCCA 345).
application: The judge took a careful look at all the evidence and even discharged on two counts, but framed his role in the narrower Shephard terms and could not be said to have anticipated the Ferras development, so his sufficiency assessment did not conform to the current standard and a reassessment was required.
conclusion: A reassessment of the evidence under the Ferras standard was necessary.

issue: Should the matter be remitted for a new committal hearing or should the Court of Appeal itself reassess the evidence, and does the evidence meet the Ferras test?
facts: Seifert sought a new hearing, arguing credibility issues from his four days of oral testimony denying every allegation. The Record of the Case contained eyewitness statements from former prisoners, gathered through Italy's inquisitorial process and certified as available and admissible.
rule: Following the approach in Ferras and Graham, an appellate court may review the evidence in light of the new rule to avoid delay; credibility is 'pre-eminently a jury question' (Hall J.A. in Graham), and evidence is examined 'through the lens of judicial experience' (R. v. Biniaris, 2000 SCC 15). Committal remains a prima facie determination.
application: A new hearing would cause intolerable delay in an already protracted case; extradition partners are entitled to swift determinations. Seifert's testimony was a series of denials going to credibility, not to the reliability or availability of Italy's evidence. On a count-by-count review the eyewitness accounts (e.g., on counts 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9) were sufficient to put the case to a jury; the alleged defects (hearsay, age of allegations, deceased witnesses, possible collaboration, leading questions) went to credibility and did not render committal unjust.
conclusion: The Court reassessed the evidence itself, found it sufficient on all committal counts under Ferras, and dismissed the appeal from committal.

issue: Did the Minister of Justice's background give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias in exercising the surrender discretion?
facts: The surrender decision was made by Minister Irwin Cotler, who as a law professor and advocate for the Canadian Jewish Congress and B'nai Brith had campaigned against impunity for Nazi war criminals. Seifert argued a reasonable person would doubt the Minister could bring an open mind to whether surrender of an elderly, long-blameless resident would be unjust or oppressive.
rule: The test is the reasonable apprehension of bias held by a reasonable, right-minded, informed person viewing the matter realistically (Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board; Wewaykum Indian Band v. Canada, 2003 SCC 45). Impartiality does not require a decision-maker to have no opinions, only to keep an open mind (Arsenault-Cameron v. P.E.I.); the surrender decision is political, at the extreme legislative end of the administrative continuum (Idziak v. Canada).
application: The Minister's record reflected the uncontroversial theme that there must be no impunity for war crimes — an international norm Canada embraced through the Rome Statute and the Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act. Nothing showed he advocated punishment regardless of the merits or that he would negate the s. 44(1)(a) discretion, and he affirmed he brought an open mind. As a Minister he leaves behind the advocate's role but need not abandon his convictions.
conclusion: No reasonable apprehension of bias was made out; the petition for judicial review was dismissed on this ground.

issue: Would surrender be unjust or oppressive under s. 44(1)(a) of the Extradition Act?
facts: Seifert was 83 during the appeal, had health problems, and had lived a peaceful, law-abiding life in Canada for over 50 years, working, raising a family and attaining citizenship. The offences were nine murders accompanied by extreme cruelty at the Bolzano camp.
rule: Under s. 44(1)(a) the Minister must refuse surrender if it would be unjust or oppressive having regard to all relevant circumstances; the leading authority is United States of America v. Burns, 2001 SCC 7. The standard of review of this determination is correctness (Ganis v. Canada, 2006 BCCA 543).
application: The Minister weighed Seifert's age, health, family and community ties, and Canada's interest in not being a safe haven for fugitives. The gravity of the crimes overwhelmed the personal circumstances; denying surrender would let Seifert escape justice and deny Italy's legitimate treaty request.
conclusion: Surrender was not unjust or oppressive; the Minister was correct, and this ground of review was dismissed.

issue: Is the action prescribed, and when did the three-year limitation period begin to run?
facts: The plaintiff claims ownership of 238.50 shares of Les Transports Spécialisés du Saguenay inc. evidenced by certificate no. 16 (1982). A 1984 sale contract (P-4) to Jean-Claude Roy was allegedly a simulation. Roy's heir, Danielle Boutin, allegedly sold all the company's shares to Autobus Laterrière inc. around 1998; the company was struck off in 2000. The plaintiff says he only learned of the sale in October 2009 by reading a local newspaper. The action was filed 9 June 2011. Defendants argued prescription running from 1984, 1998 or 2000.
rule: Art. 165(4) C.p.c. (irrecevabilité) and art. 54.1 C.p.c. (rejet); on a motion to dismiss all alleged facts are taken as true and courts act with prudence, dismissing only where clearly the allegations cannot give rise to the relief sought (Entreprises Pro-Sag inc. c. Groupe Olson Construction inc.). Prescription runs from the day the right of action arises, or in cases of gradual/late damage from its first manifestation, when the plaintiff knew of fault, damage and causation (Gervais, La prescription); art. 2904 C.c.Q. suspends prescription where it is impossible to act.
application: The court characterized the action as a personal recourse to recover the value of a good sold without right by a third party (Boutin), the transaction dating to 1998, more than three years before suit. However, the plaintiff alleged he learned of the sale only in 2009 and, on a motion to dismiss, these allegations must be taken as true. Whether his prior ignorance amounts to an impossibility to act under art. 2904 C.c.Q. is a question of fact or mixed fact and law to be resolved at trial after a full contradictory debate. Accordingly the action appears, on its face, to be within time.
conclusion: The prescription argument cannot be upheld at this stage; the motion in irrecevabilité on that ground is dismissed.

issue: Does the plaintiff have a sufficient legal interest and cause of action against Autobus Laterrière inc. and against the dissolved company?
facts: The pleadings contain no allegation of fault against Autobus Laterrière and only paragraph 27 seeks to link it, asking to be declared a shareholder of Autobus Laterrière because Boutin struck off Les Transports Spécialisés and refused to revive it. Les Transports Spécialisés du Saguenay inc. was dissolved 7 December 1999 (certificate MC-1).
rule: Sale of another's property gives the true owner only a restricted remedy: art. 1714 C.c.Q. allows annulment and revendication against the buyer, not a personal claim, and may require reimbursing the buyer. A simulation/contre-lettre cannot be set up against a third party without consent (arts. 1451, 1452 C.c.Q.). Under the Canada Business Corporations Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, s. 226(4)) a creditor's recourse lies against former shareholders; a company dissolved more than two years cannot be sued without first being reconstituted (Martel, La compagnie au Québec). Arts. 55, 216 C.p.c. require sufficient interest and necessity of a party; art. 152 C.p.c. requires an apparent right for injunctive relief.
application: The plaintiff's claim against Boutin and 2786362 Canada inc. (declaration of simulation being an accessory that shares the principal action's apparent non-prescription, and opposable to Boutin as continuator of the co-contractant's juridical personality) is not manifestly unfounded. But against Autobus Laterrière the contre-lettre is not opposable, art. 1714 gives no personal money claim against the buyer, and the refusal to revive the dissolved company confers no right to shares in Autobus Laterrière. The company being dissolved, no action lies without reconstitution — a public-order issue the court may raise proprio motu. The injunction-type conclusion (production of the sale contract) rests on no apparent right (art. 152 C.p.c.) and is premature (art. 402 C.p.c.).
conclusion: The plaintiff shows no sufficient legal interest against Autobus Laterrière inc. or the dissolved Les Transports Spécialisés du Saguenay inc.; the originating application is declared irrecevable and rejected as against both, with costs to Autobus Laterrière. The motion of Boutin and 2786362 Canada inc. is dismissed.

issue: Is the plaintiff's proceeding abusive under art. 54.1 C.p.c.?
facts: Autobus Laterrière sought a declaration of abuse and extrajudicial costs, characterizing the proceeding as improper.
rule: Art. 54.1 C.p.c. permits sanctioning abusive proceedings.
application: Although the pleading is poorly articulated and deficient in several respects, a plaintiff who believes he owns a right in a good he knows to be held by the mise en cause cannot be said to act in bad faith merely by attempting a flawed procedural route against it.
conclusion: The proceeding is not abusive; the request for extrajudicial fees/costs on that basis is refused (the rejet motion is granted only in part).

issue: What standard of review applies to the ATA Appeal Committee's decision?
facts: The ATA's hearing and appeal committees, composed of teaching professionals, found Ms. Eggertson guilty of unprofessional conduct. The Teaching Profession Act contains no right of appeal but preserves judicial review (s. 56).
rule: The pragmatic and functional approach in Pushpanathan v. Canada (1998) requires weighing the privative clause, tribunal expertise, purpose of the Act and provisions, and whether the question is one of fact or law; expertise is the most important factor.
application: There was no full privative clause but a demonstrated legislative intent of limited court intervention. The committees possessed particular expertise to assess whether conduct was unprofessional and were acting within the Act's purpose. These factors weighed toward a patently unreasonable, or at least reasonableness, standard for the factual determinations, while disclosure (mixed fact and law) and the Charter question (pure law) attracted correctness.
conclusion: Reasonableness applied to the committee's factual and unprofessional-conduct findings; correctness applied to the disclosure and Charter issues.

issue: Was the finding of unprofessional conduct reasonable where the statements were made off-duty as a parent?
facts: At school meetings Ms. Eggertson allegedly criticized two former teachers to Ms. Campbell-Davies, who was not a 'proper official', without informing the criticized teachers, contrary to the ATA Code. She denied making the comments; the committee found she did.
rule: A teacher's conduct is evaluated on the basis of position rather than location (Ross v. New Brunswick School District No. 15, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 825); a teacher cannot choose which 'hat' to wear (Re Cromer v. B.C. Teachers' Federation (1986)). Unprofessional conduct may encompass off-duty conduct.
application: The committee heard the witnesses, assessed credibility and had a reasonable basis for its finding; the court would not substitute its view. Ms. Eggertson could advocate as a parent but, as an experienced teacher whose criticism carries enhanced impact, she had to follow the Code's procedure. Deferring to the committee's expertise, the finding that the comments criticized other teachers and were unprofessional was reasonable.
conclusion: The finding of unprofessional conduct was reasonable and would not be disturbed.

issue: Did the failure to disclose the investigator's complete file breach any disclosure duty?
facts: Ms. Eggertson requested all of the investigator's notes; she received formal witness statements, interview summaries, the complaint letter and the investigator's report, but not the complete file (including notes of the principal's interview).
rule: Sections 30(3) and 37 of the Teaching Profession Act require reasonable particulars and provide for issuance of notices to witnesses, but do not impose full pre-hearing disclosure. The Stinchcombe level of disclosure does not apply to professional discipline (Kullman v. Borbridge (1995); Anderson v. Twin River School District (1994)); only fairness is required.
application: The statutory provisions did not require production of all evidence, only sufficient particulars. The common law duty of fairness did not require full disclosure. Ms. Eggertson received adequate particulars, was not prejudiced, and was told the principal had no recollection of events.
conclusion: There was sufficient disclosure; no breach of statutory or common law obligations occurred.

issue: Does the Charter apply to the ATA Code of Ethics, and if so was freedom of expression infringed?
facts: Ms. Eggertson argued the Code, made under the Act, was provincial legislation subject to the Charter and that her s. 2(b) freedom of expression was breached.
rule: Section 32(1) Charter applies to government action. Authorities conflict: Re Cromer assumed application; Tomen v. Federation of Women Teachers of Ontario and Re Westerlund (relying on Stoffman v. Vancouver General Hospital (1990)) held such internal-management rules are outside government action. Reasonable and justified limits do not infringe s. 2(b).
application: The court held the Code constitutes directives of internal management, not government action, so the Charter did not apply. Even if it applied, the Code's limits are reasonable and justified: it does not prohibit criticism but requires it be made to proper officials after notice, promoting professional standards and harmony, demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
conclusion: The Charter did not apply to the Code, and in any event any limit on expression was reasonable and justified.

issue: Should the court order sole custody to the mother rather than joint custody, given the parents' conflict and history of one parent's exclusionary conduct?
facts: The parents never married and share a week-about schedule for their daughter AB. The father obtained an ex parte custody order in June 2016 through significant misrepresentations to the court, imposed a racial bar on nanny selection, repeatedly made unilateral decisions about medical care, religion (enrolling AB at Temple Sinai over objection), schooling and activities without consulting the mother, and failed to facilitate the mother's relationship and the child's contact with her Irish family. The mother consistently consulted the father before making decisions.
rule: Under s. 20 of the Children's Law Reform Act (CLRA) both parents are equally entitled to custody; sole custody requires justification (Rodriguez v. Guignard, 2013 ONSC 146). Joint custody principles are set out in Jackson v. Jackson, 2017 ONSC 1566: there is no default in favour of joint custody, effective communication and cooperation must be achievable, and where one parent is the major source of conflict or cannot put the child's needs first, joint custody is inappropriate. Past conduct is relevant only where it bears on the ability to parent (CLRA s. 24(3)).
application: The court found the father deliberately misled the court on the ex parte motion, engaged in controlling and exclusionary behaviour, could not freely acknowledge the mother as a caring parent, refused to accept medical recommendations, and repeatedly resorted to counsel over minor disputes. An objective review showed the parties had never been able to cooperate or communicate effectively and that the father would not put AB's needs ahead of his desire for control. The mother, by contrast, consulted and facilitated the father's role. Joint decision-making would produce continued conflict contrary to AB's best interests.
conclusion: Sole custody was granted to the mother, with an obligation to consult the father and give serious consideration to his views on major medical and educational decisions, but with final decision-making authority.

issue: Is it in the child's best interests to have her primary residence with her mother in Buffalo, with generous access to the father in Toronto?
facts: AB, age three, had lived week-about between Buffalo and Toronto since 11 months old. Both parents are physicians with uncertain future locations: the mother on a J1 visa in Buffalo (fellowship to ~2021), the father bound by an International Medical Graduate Return-of-Service Agreement requiring five years' work in a Ministry-approved underserviced community after 2020. AB thrived in both homes but faced continual cross-border commuting and duplicated medical providers.
rule: CLRA s. 24(2) best interests factors (love and emotional ties, stable home, ability to provide guidance, plan of care, permanence and stability, ability to parent, familial relationships). The maximum contact principle is expressed through the best interests lens (Lemon v. Lemon, 2018 ONCA 684; Jackson v. Jackson, 2017 ONSC 1566). Proposed place of residence is a relevant factor (Terris v. Terris). Proceedings should be concluded with dispatch (Appiah v. Appiah).
application: Both parents are loving, but the mother demonstrated the ability to parent independently and to foster the father's relationship, while the father lived with his parents with no certain future plan and drew an adverse inference for not calling the nanny. As AB ages, the two-country, two-school week-about arrangement is not sustainable; a single home base and school better serve stability. The father's proposals depended on speculative assumptions about remaining in Toronto and invited continued litigation, disadvantaging the mother given financial disparities. Primary residence with the mother in Buffalo, with generous weekend/holiday access to the father, best served AB's stability while maintaining her bond with her father and paternal grandparents.
conclusion: AB's primary residence was ordered to be with the mother in Buffalo, with a detailed access, holiday and travel schedule for the father; the mother must obtain a further order to relocate outside the Buffalo-Niagara Falls area; Ontario retains jurisdiction for five years.

issue: How should child support and section 7 special or extraordinary expenses be allocated?
facts: The father's reported income was $76,134.12 and the mother's $66,726.11. The mother sought table support; the father sought set-off. Claimed expenses included JCC pre-school tuition, swimming lessons, toddler yoga, and uninsured medical/dental costs.
rule: Federal Child Support Guidelines: s. 9 (shared custody threshold) and s. 7 (special or extraordinary expenses shared in proportion to incomes, with 'extraordinary' defined in s. 7(1.1)).
application: Because the final order matched neither party's proposal, the parties had not calculated the residency percentages needed to determine whether the s. 9 shared-custody threshold was met; the court left this to be recalculated. On the claimed expenses, swimming lessons and toddler yoga were not 'extraordinary' within the Guidelines, whereas daycare/pre-school tuition and uninsured medical/dental costs qualified as special expenses.
conclusion: The parties are to share eligible s. 7 expenses (JCC pre-school tuition and uninsured medical/dental) proportionate to income; table support and the shared-custody calculation were reserved for further submissions.

issue: Does s. 4 of the Oleomargarine Act infringe s. 15 equality rights, and can corporations claim s. 15 protection?
facts: Three of the applicants were corporations (two margarine manufacturers and a trade association); the fourth was an individual consumer. Section 4 requires margarine to be coloured lighter or darker than butter, disadvantaging margarine producers relative to butter producers and limiting consumer colour choice.
rule: Section 15(1) of the Charter guarantees equality to 'every individual.' Authorities (Re Aluminium Co. of Canada; Milk Board v. Clearview Dairy Farm; Surrey Credit Union v. Mendonca; Re Homemade Winecrafts) hold that s. 15 protects the dignity and worth of human beings and does not extend to corporations, distinguishing Big M Drug Mart (which concerned the unqualified freedoms in s. 2). Discriminatory inequality is assessed under the framework in R. v. Ertel and R. v. Century 21 Ramos Realty: identify the class, determine whether classes are similarly situated, and apply the 'pejorative' approach requiring the complainant to show the differential treatment is unfair or irrational.
application: The word 'individual' in s. 15 does not include the corporate applicants; unlike the unqualified s. 2 freedoms, s. 15 inherently requires a differentiation in treatment tied to human dignity. Even assuming s. 15 applied, applying the Ertel steps, butter and margarine producers form part of a general class of edible-oil producers and are similarly situated, and the corporate applicants suffered an inherent disadvantage, but they failed to show the differential treatment was unfair or irrational given the legitimate objective of protecting the economic stability of the dairy industry. For the consumer applicant, any advancement of the consumer-protection objective was minor, and consumers' objections to colour were of minor importance next to the dairy-stability objective, since no one is barred from buying (or self-colouring) margarine.
conclusion: Section 4 does not offend s. 15(1); corporations are not protected by s. 15, and in any event no unconstitutional discrimination was established.

issue: Does s. 4 infringe s. 2(b) freedom of expression, and if so, is it saved by s. 1?
facts: Section 4 prevents margarine producers from colouring their product a wholesome, appetizing (butter-like) colour, thereby restricting how the product is presented to the public.
rule: Section 2(b) protects freedom of expression, construed broadly and not limited to particular kinds of expression; commercial advertising, including product presentation, is protected. A limit must be justified under s. 1 as a reasonable limit demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
application: The colour and presentation of a product constitutes a form of advertising and expression, so s. 4 infringes the corporate applicants' s. 2(b) rights. However, protection of the dairy industry is of substantial economic and social importance, and although s. 4 detrimentally affects margarine production methods and market share, the restriction is not disproportionate to that important legislative objective.
conclusion: Section 4 infringes s. 2(b) but is a reasonable limit justified under s. 1; the challenge fails.

issue: Does s. 4 violate s. 7 by regulating economic or commercial rights?
facts: Applicants argued the s. 7 right to liberty protects the commercial right to market and purchase products in a colour of one's choice.
rule: Section 7 guarantees life, liberty and security of the person, subject to the principles of fundamental justice. Economic/commercial rights fall outside the ambit of s. 7 (Re Malartic Hygrade Gold Mines; Re Aluminium Co. of Canada; Re Gershman Produce; R. v. Video Flicks/Edwards Books).
application: Economic rights such as the right to market or purchase a product in a chosen colour are not protected by s. 7. Moreover, s. 4 was enacted for rational social and economic purposes and no evidence showed any breach of the principles of fundamental justice.
conclusion: Section 4 does not violate s. 7; the argument was rejected.

issue: Did the newspaper article defame the plaintiff by lowering his reputation in the eyes of right-thinking members of the community?
facts: The Globe and Mail published an article about how any Canadian can create a charity and channel tax-subsidized dollars abroad, using the plaintiff's newly registered charity for Rwandan children as an illustration. The plaintiff complained of several statements: that he was described as inexperienced, that he alone could administer the charity, that no one would require him to account for the money, that the charity's name was inaccurate, that his floor of residence was wrong, and that he could give money to 'the most vicious murderers in Rwanda.'
rule: To be defamatory, a statement must contain a misstatement of fact or comment that would lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of right-thinking members of the community.
application: The court found the article described the plaintiff as 'good-hearted and well intentioned' and 'above reproach.' The identified errors (11th versus 15th floor, the charity's name) were trivial misstatements not capable of lowering his reputation. The description of him as the spearhead and spokesperson accurately reflected the situation, since his son was a minor and his mother-in-law's signature was affixed on her behalf. The statement about lack of accountability was a true comment directed at the government system, not the plaintiff, and the 'vicious murderers' passage was a true statement of legal possibility with no suggestion the plaintiff would act on it. Read as a whole, the article was thoughtful, well-researched investigative journalism about government charity policy.
conclusion: The article did not lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of right-thinking people and was not libellous.

issue: Was the article published with malice arising from an alleged grudge against the plaintiff's family?
facts: The plaintiff alleged his father was a wealthy Ontario figure who owned a polluting disposal dump, that the Globe and Mail had written articles about the father in the 1980s, and that the article about him was motivated by mala fides against the Goodhead name. The author, Mr. Matas, testified he had never heard of the plaintiff's father, never seen any such articles, and knew nothing of the dump.
rule: An allegation of malice must be supported by evidence establishing bad faith or improper motive on the part of the publisher.
application: The court accepted Mr. Matas' evidence, finding no evidence from which it could conclude he was not telling the truth, and determined the article was written in good faith.
conclusion: There was no malice; the article was written in good faith and without malice.

issue: Do the facts alleged, taken as true at the filtering stage, justify issuing a special order requiring the mise en cause (an attorney of record) to appear to answer a charge of civil contempt for failing to redact an affiant's name from a transcript excerpt sent to the Barreau's syndic, contrary to Justice Masse's non-disclosure order of 15 March 2024?
facts: Justice Masse's order of 15 March 2024 (subparagraph C.d)) prohibited disclosure, publication or dissemination of the names of various affiants. The mise en cause, counsel of record, filed a complaint with the syndic of the Barreau du Québec against opposing counsel concerning conduct during an out-of-court examination of an affiant, and attached an unredacted excerpt of the transcript in which the affiant's name appeared in the header. The plaintiffs applied ex parte for a special order to appear for contempt.
rule: On an application for an order to appear for contempt the judge exercises a filtering role, taking the alleged facts as true (Droit de la famille — 122875, 2012 QCCA 1855, para. 26). A civil contempt finding is exceptional and should be pronounced only where genuinely necessary to protect the administration of justice, especially in litigation between private parties (Morasse c. Nadeau-Dubois, 2016 CSC 44; Centre commercial Les Rivières ltée c. Jean bleu inc., 2012 QCCA 1663). The role of a professional order's syndic requires a complete picture of the facts, and information given to the syndic enjoys various protections (Pharmascience inc. c. Binet, 2006 CSC 48; Code des professions, arts. 114, 122, 124; Loi sur le Barreau, art. 76).
application: Although the facts, taken as true, showed the mise en cause was aware of Justice Masse's order, the mere failure to redact a name in the header of a stenographic transcript in a communication addressed solely to the syndic did not amount to any obstruction of the normal course of justice or any attack on the court's authority or dignity. Given the syndic's need for a complete factual picture and the confidentiality protections surrounding complaints, the conduct could not support a contempt conviction. The Court further found the application reflected misplaced rigorism and served merely to inflame already acrimonious litigation.
conclusion: The facts, even taken as true, could not give rise to a contempt conviction; the application for a special order to appear was dismissed, without costs.

issue: Did the original or amended statement of claim plead the constituent elements of a s. 130 prospectus-misrepresentation claim so as to interrupt the limitation period?
facts: The original claim (July 29, 2009) and the amended claim (November 17, 2009) alleged negligence and negligent misrepresentation in Manulife's 'disclosure documents' (annual reports, financial statements, MD&As) and foreshadowed a secondary-market claim under Part XXIII.1. Neither pleading mentioned a prospectus, s. 130, or deemed reliance; the plaintiffs purchased only in the secondary market. Specific prospectus allegations appeared for the first time in the proposed fresh as amended statement of claim served May 18, 2010.
rule: A pleading must contain a concise statement of the material facts (rule 25.06); no particular formula is required (Almas v. Spenceley), but to assert a cause of action and give fair notice the pleading must state its constituent elements. A s. 130 claim requires pleading (a) the existence of a prospectus, (b) a misrepresentation in it, (c) purchase of a security offered by the prospectus during distribution, and (d) that the defendant was the issuer or a signer/director/expert. Section 130 is a complete statutory code dispensing with reliance (McKenna v. Gammon Gold). Compared with McCann v. CP Ships Ltd.
application: Read fairly, generously and as a whole, the pleadings could only be understood as alleging negligence and misrepresentation in statutory 'disclosure documents' plus a foreshadowed secondary-market claim. None of the four constituent elements of a s. 130 claim was pleaded: no prospectus was mentioned, no purchase under a prospectus was alleged, and the incorporation of MD&As by reference into a prospectus was not pleaded. Given experienced securities counsel (who had run McCann), the certification notice and factum describing the s. 130 claim as an 'addition', it was inconceivable the existing pleading was understood to assert s. 130. McCann was distinguished because its pleading was broad enough to encompass a primary-market claim.
conclusion: Neither the original nor the amended statement of claim contained a s. 130 claim; the limitation period was not interrupted.

issue: Was the s. 130 claim time-barred when first raised on May 18, 2010?
facts: The proposed fresh as amended statement of claim acknowledged the 'truth was revealed' on February 12, 2009, when Manulife announced its increased reserves and its share price fell. The s. 130 claim was first advanced when that pleading was delivered on May 18, 2010.
rule: Section 138 of the Securities Act imposes a limitation of the earlier of 180 days after the plaintiff first had knowledge of the facts giving rise to the cause of action or three years after the transaction. A limitations issue may be decided on a pleadings-amendment motion where it is plain and obvious no additional facts could show the period had not expired (Beardsley v. Ontario).
application: February 12, 2009 marked both the end of the class period and the date the plaintiffs had knowledge of the facts; the plaintiffs did not dispute this. May 18, 2010 was well more than 180 days later. Claims tied to 2005–2006 prospectuses were in any event outside the three-year cap and were withdrawn.
conclusion: The s. 130 claim was time-barred as of May 18, 2010.

issue: Does the court have jurisdiction to extend the s. 138 limitation period through the 'special circumstances' doctrine given the Limitations Act, 2002?
facts: The Securities Act limitation period is listed in the Schedule to the Limitations Act, 2002 and thereby preserved. The plaintiffs invoked the special-circumstances doctrine (Basarsky v. Quinlan) to save an otherwise time-barred amendment.
rule: Under Joseph v. Paramount Canada's Wonderland the Limitations Act, 2002 abolished the common-law special-circumstances doctrine for claims and rule 26.01 amendments governed by its general period. Under Guillemette v. Doucet, Giroux Estate and Bikur Cholim, s. 20 preserves extension/variation mechanisms where a scheduled statute contains its own discretionary provision or has a pre-existing common-law gloss (e.g., Solicitors Act, Trustee Act s. 38(3)).
application: The court reasoned it made little sense for the legislature to preserve the relatively short s. 138 period, with its built-in discoverability regime, only to erode it through a doctrine it does not historically carry. The special-circumstances rule should be confined to existing statutory exceptions or pre-existing common-law exceptions engrafted on a scheduled limitation period, unlike s. 138.
