conclusion: The court doubted the doctrine applied to the Securities Act period, favouring confining it to statutes with existing exceptions; but it did not need to decide the point definitively because it would refuse relief in any event.

issue: If the doctrine were available, should the court exercise its discretion to extend the limitation period?
facts: The defendants were named in the original pleading; the s. 130 claim arose from the same events and documents; pleadings had not closed and no discoveries had occurred; refusal would affect putative class members. Experienced securities counsel possessed the material facts and consciously restricted the claim to the secondary market.
rule: The expiry of a limitation period creates a presumption of prejudice that is determinative unless rebutted by special circumstances (Frohlick v. Pinkerton). Rule 26.01 does not contemplate adding unrelated statute-barred claims. Special circumstances are typically procedural or informational mistakes that did not mislead the opposing party.
application: The s. 130 claim is an extraordinary, distinct cause of action (no reliance required), not incidental to or subsumed by the common-law and Part XXIII.1 claims. There was no procedural error; rather, informed counsel made a conscious tactical choice to plead only a secondary-market claim, as in Bikur Cholim and Meady. Allowing the amendment would defeat the purpose of the 180-day period and promote uncertainty in securities markets.
conclusion: Even if available, the discretion would be declined; no special circumstances existed beyond the ordinary hardship of an expired limitation.

issue: Does a Superior Court judge have jurisdiction to rule on a vexatious litigant's request for authorization to bring proceedings before another court (the Court of Québec)?
facts: The appellant had been declared a vexatious and quarrelsome litigant on 10 June 2011, and was prohibited from taking any proceeding connected with the settlement of her parents' estates without prior authorization from the Chief Justice of the Superior Court or a designated judge. The underlying action she wished to attack by a motion in retraction (before the Court of Québec) stemmed from that estate litigation. She sought authorization from a Superior Court judge to present her retraction motion in the Court of Québec.
rule: Articles 46 and 54.5 C.p.c. and the Superior Court's inherent power of control and supervision permit it to prohibit an abusive litigant from bringing proceedings before any tribunal subject to that supervisory power (Barreau du Québec c. Srougi; Dubé c. CRT; Joad c. Journal La Voix; Production Pixcom inc. c. Fabrikant, 2005 QCCA 703; Tremblay c. Charest, 2006 QCCA 204). The power to prohibit proceedings before another court carries with it the correlative power to authorize them.
application: The Court of Québec file was directly covered by the 10 June 2011 prohibition order because it arose from the estate-settlement dispute. In ruling on an authorization request the Superior Court exercises its own jurisdiction, not that of the court where the right may be exercised. Since it can prohibit proceedings before another tribunal within its supervisory jurisdiction, it can equally authorize them—especially where the prohibition targets a well-defined dispute known to the Superior Court. The fact that the Court of Québec may itself issue quérulence orders under art. 54.5 C.p.c. does not oust the Superior Court's general supervisory jurisdiction.
conclusion: Yes; the Superior Court had jurisdiction to entertain and refuse the authorization request.

issue: May a Superior Court judge evaluate the prospects of success of the proposed proceeding and refuse authorization accordingly?
facts: The appellant failed to appear on the dates set to fix a timetable, transmitted an unauthorized and unserved defence and counterclaim, and had default judgment of $6,500 rendered against her. She then sought authorization to file a motion in retraction, which the designated judge (Déziel, j.c.s.) refused, finding it had no chance of success.
rule: A vexatious litigant seeking authorization to file a proceeding bears the burden of demonstrating prima facie the seriousness of the request; there is a form of presumption that his proceedings are vexatious (Pixcom). The authorizing judge must conduct a preliminary analysis of the value of the asserted right (art. 88 R.P.C.).
application: The Superior Court was not persuaded of the seriousness of the retraction motion. On the reported facts, the appellant did not demonstrate any error in that assessment—she had obtained leave to appear and set a timetable but failed to act diligently, allowing default judgment to be rendered.
conclusion: Yes; the assessment was proper and the appeal was dismissed with costs.

issue: On a motion to set aside an arbitral award, is the court confined to errors on the face of the award?
facts: The parties referred 'all matters in dispute between us' to the Canadian Jewish Congress Court of Arbitration under a submission that made the award final and not subject to appeal. The employer moved to set the award aside as defective on its face and wrong in law.
rule: On a motion to set aside an award the court is limited to errors appearing on the face of the award, or corruption, fraud, excess of jurisdiction, or like matters; it may not go into the evidence (Re Grant v. Eastwood (1875), 22 Gr. 563). The submission and a letter of the arbitrators may be examined to ascertain the subject-matter dealt with (Attorney-General for Manitoba v. Kelly, [1922] 1 A.C. 268).
application: Rose C.J.H.C. treated the matter strictly as a motion to set aside, not an appeal, since the submission excluded appeal. He accepted he was confined to what appeared on the face of the award but could look at the submission and the arbitrators' letter of 26 June 1942.
conclusion: The court's review was confined to errors on the face of the award; the evidence could not be examined.

issue: Did the award disclose an error of law on its face given the finding of a weekly hiring and an award made 'in good conscience'?
facts: The submission did not expressly define the matters referred; it covered 'all matters in dispute'. The arbitrators found the hiring was weekly, not yearly, but concluded the employee was entitled 'in good conscience' to $200 covering his convalescence and re-establishment, more than legal damages on a weekly contract.
rule: An award is not lightly set aside; it must be supported by the submission. Absent an express provision to the contrary, an arbitrator is to decide according to the legal rights of the parties, not according to what he considers fair and reasonable (Russell on Arbitration and Award, 13th ed., p. 332; Jager v. Tolme & Runge, [1916] 1 K.B. 939).
application: Rose C.J.H.C. held that because the submission was undefined, it was possible the dispute submitted was what the employee should receive 'in good conscience' rather than his strict legal entitlement; the court could not determine the nature of the disputes without examining evidence it was not entitled to consider. The Court of Appeal, assuming arbitrators were confined to legal rights, nonetheless found no error of law on the face.
conclusion: No error of law appeared on the face of the award; the award stood.

issue: Was the arbitrators' assessment of the employee's entitlement a question of law or of fact?
facts: Beyond the finding of a weekly hiring, the court knew nothing of the terms of the contract, the nature of the employment, the rate of pay, or the circumstances leading to the $200 conclusion.
rule: Absent custom or an express or implied contractual provision, an employee is entitled to reasonable notice of termination, and what is reasonable notice is a question of fact (Payzu, Limited v. Hannaford, [1918] 2 K.B. 348; Carter v. Bell & Sons (Canada) Ltd., [1936] O.R. 290).
application: Robertson C.J.O. held that even assuming the arbitrators were confined to legal rights, the matter on which error was alleged was reasonable notice on a weekly hiring, which is a question of fact. With no knowledge of the contract terms or surrounding circumstances, the arbitrators' conclusion was a finding of fact.
conclusion: The conclusion was a finding of fact and, whether right or wrong, afforded no ground for setting aside the award; appeal dismissed with costs.

issue: What standard of review applies to the CMQ's decision recognizing (or refusing) a property-tax exemption under the LFM?
facts: B'Nai B'Rith sought judicial review of the CMQ's decision granting exemption for only part of its building. The City argued the CMQ was protected by a privative clause (relying on arts. 21 LCM and 94.2 C.p.c., and on Centre communautaire juridique de l'Estrie) and that the patent-unreasonableness standard applied; B'Nai B'Rith argued correctness.
rule: The pragmatic and functional approach governs the choice among correctness, reasonableness simpliciter and patent unreasonableness (Southam; Pushpanathan; Dr Q; Ryan; Voice Construction Ltd), weighing four contextual factors: presence/absence of a privative clause or appeal right, relative expertise, the purpose of the statute and the provision, and the nature of the question.
application: The Court found no privative clause in the LFM or LCM (arts. 21 LCM and 94.2 C.p.c. belong to civil procedure, not protection from judicial review; at most a 'timid' clause given the absence of an appeal), no special CMQ expertise in municipal taxation (its members need not be jurists), a fiscal statute whose exemption criteria involve little discretion, and a question that is mixed fact and law but turns essentially on interpreting art. 243.8 LFM applied to uncontested facts. The Estrie and Mont Baldy authorities declined to fix the standard because the decisions were patently unreasonable anyway.
conclusion: The weighted analysis pointed to the correctness standard; the legislature required little or no deference to the CMQ on exemption recognition.

issue: Did B'Nai B'Rith's building satisfy the conditions of art. 243.8 LFM for a full property-tax exemption?
facts: B'Nai B'Rith, a non-profit society serving Jewish post-secondary students near McGill, used the 3460 Stanley building for courses, conferences, Holocaust education, cultural and social activities, community Shabbat meals, kosher food, transitional housing for young foreign students (17-18) with no family in Montréal, moral/psychological/legal/economic support, and a student newspaper. Commissioner Hamelin recognized only the first-floor library, applying a room-by-room (partitionist) analysis.
rule: Under art. 243.8 LFM the user must, for a non-profit purpose, carry on one or more admissible activities such that this constitutes the principal use of the building; admissible activities include informative/educational activities (para. 2) and activities to promote/defend the interests of a group, combat discrimination, assist or prevent persons from falling into difficulty (para. 3, read with art. 243.11); exemption may be partial (arts. 2, 243.2), and accessory spaces cannot be dissociated from qualifying activities (Cinémathèque québécoise; YM-YWHA).
application: The Court held the Commissioner erred by compartmentalizing the building instead of assessing its overall vocation and 'principal use.' His findings were also unreasonable on the merits: treating university students without family in Montréal as not socially vulnerable was arbitrary (they fall within art. 243.8(3)(a) and (d)); the caretaker's lodging, rabbi's office and accountant's office were accessory; refusing exemption for the kosher kitchen while proposing to tax its operator (not a party) was illogical; and characterizing a student newspaper as not informative was irrational. Prior CMQ decisions (Building a Jewish Tomorrow, Institut A. Reisen) granted full exemptions for materially similar buildings.
conclusion: The building as a whole was used principally for admissible activities and qualified for exemption; the decision was quashed and, since the CMQ was to be abolished, the Court itself granted a full exemption effective 1 January 2001, with costs against the City.

issue: Did the TAQ have jurisdiction to add to the roll the contributory value of components the municipal assessor had not taken into account when the roll was deposited, absent a complaint on that point?
facts: Impérial contested the roll inscriptions for its industrial complex. The TAQ, at paras 219-237, took into account the contributory value of steam and chilled-water energy-producing systems that did not appear on the roll. Impérial argued a formal demand was indispensable to confer jurisdiction. The rolls in issue were 'new generation' rolls governed by the concept of unité d'évaluation.
rule: For 'new generation' rolls under the Loi sur la fiscalité municipale (LFM), art. 34 defines the unité d'évaluation and arts. 144, 145 and 147 require the tribunal to consider the unit 'dans son entier' to assess real prejudice and permit fixing a value higher or lower than the parties propose. Jurisdictional questions attract the correctness standard (Pushpanathan v. Canada (MCI), 1998 CanLII 778 (SCC)). Leading authority: Pointe-Claire (Ville de) c. Hewquip Holdings, 1997 CanLII 6578 (QC CQ).
application: The Court distinguished old-generation cases (Atlific, Shell Canada, Sedaz Parking, Talisman) which barred adding items absent a complaint, from new-generation rolls. Because Impérial filed a complaint contesting the roll value, it conferred jurisdiction on the TAQ to revise the entire value of the unit, including contributory value of components omitted by the assessor, since art. 145 requires considering the unit in its entirety.
conclusion: The TAQ did not err; it had jurisdiction to consider the contributory value of any property forming part of the unité d'évaluation under art. 34 LFM even if the assessor had not taken it into account at deposit.

issue: Are the palletizing and materials-handling equipment excluded from the roll under s. 65 LFM as machines used principally for industrial production?
facts: Impérial's modernization ('Montréal 2001') centralized automated palletizing at AC-1. Cases of cigarettes are conveyed, robotically palletized, wrapped, and labelled with excise (SAP) labels before removal by forklift; the total value at issue was $2,462,432 (new) / $2,216,189 (depreciated). Products cannot be sold until required fiscal labels are affixed.
rule: Section 65(1) LFM excludes from the roll machines, appliances and accessories used or destined principally for industrial production. Whether a good is used for industrial production is a mixed question of fact and law on which the TAQ has no privileged position (Vigi Santé c. Montréal, 1999 CanLII 13626 (QC CA); Charny c. Alex Couture). Industrial production is a continuous, integrated process ending when the marketable product is ready (Irving Oil, 1980 CanLII 176 (SCC); Cie pétrolière Impériale; Société d'énergie Talisman; R.J.R. MacDonald).
application: The product cannot be marketed until the fiscally required labels are affixed at the end of the conveyor, so production is not complete before that step. The case is analogous to Irving Oil/Talisman (regulatory requirement completes production) and distinguishable from Procter & Gamble (no such fiscal requirement). Production is integrated and continuous, ending after affixing fiscal labels.
conclusion: The TAQ erred; the palletizing/handling equipment is part of industrial production and is not to be entered on the roll under s. 65 LFM.

issue: Could the TAQ set aside the parties' agreement/admissions on the base cost of the mechanical and electrical systems?
facts: The parties filed written admissions (P-79, P-80) agreeing on the 1972 base costs of plumbing, heating, air-conditioning, ventilation, electricity and fire protection, expressly stating these represented only the portion corresponding to service to the building, and that nothing constituted an admission on whether the items were to be on the roll under s. 65.
rule: Whether an immovable is entered or excluded under s. 65 LFM is a question of law; parties cannot derogate from it by agreement and the tribunal is not bound (correctness standard). Adricon Ltée c. East Angus, 1977 CanLII 197 (SCC) and Gulf Canada distinguished (those involved revoking admissions on facts within the res gestae).
application: The admissions concerned only base cost, not whether contributory value must be on the roll. The determination of inscription/exclusion under s. 65 is legal; the TAQ was not bound and could decide whether to include the contributory value. The Adricon/Gulf jurisprudence was inapplicable since evidence and exhibits were led on the point.
conclusion: The TAQ did not err; it could decide the s. 65 question notwithstanding the cost admissions, which did not admit inclusion or exclusion from the roll.

issue: Are the integrated electrical and mechanical (plumbing, heating, air-conditioning, ventilation, humidification) systems used principally for industrial production and excluded under s. 65 LFM, and did the TAQ breach audi alteram partem?
facts: About 77% of electricity and large proportions of steam (62%), chilled water (74%) and air (78%) served production; systems were hybrid/integrated. The TAQ rejected both parties' expert theories (one system vs 266 systems) and, on its own, held there were as many systems as 'medium-voltage arteries,' excluding only 13% (the main electrical entrance).
rule: Section 65 LFM (as amended 1993) treats an integrated mechanical/electrical system as an immovable analyzed on the 'all or nothing' rule of the 4th paragraph: entirely excluded if used/destined principally for industrial production, otherwise entirely on the roll; art. 2 proportionality is excluded. Qualification is a mixed question (correctness/reasonableness simpliciter). Audi alteram partem requires notice where the tribunal adopts a theory not advanced by parties (Pétromont c. Varennes). Guiding cases: Aluminerie Alouette; Manac; Aluminerie Bécancour; PCI Chimie; Domco Tarkett.
application: The TAQ breached audi alteram partem by adopting an 'arteries' definition no expert proposed, without inviting submissions, in a domain (electrical systems) outside its evaluation expertise. It also erred by limiting exclusion to 13% contrary to the all-or-nothing rule and by ignoring the 'destination' branch and the proportion of use. On the evidence, the complex has a single integrated hybrid electrical system principally used/destined for production; similarly the plumbing and the heating/air-conditioning/humidification/ventilation systems are principally used/destined for production.
conclusion: The TAQ erred; the electrical and mechanical systems (plumbing, heating, air-conditioning, ventilation) are principally used or destined for industrial production and their contributory value is not to be entered on the roll under s. 65 LFM.

issue: Did the TAQ err by resolving the local adjustment factor (Factor F) for the 1995 rolls on institutional coherence rather than on the balance of the evidence?
facts: Impérial's expert (Caumartin) produced a Factor F study yielding 0.80; Montréal, for the first time, led a genuine competing study (Lévesque) yielding ~1.05, over 32 days and 86 exhibits. The TAQ found numerous deficiencies in Caumartin's study yet retained 0.80 'by institutional coherence,' while acknowledging Lévesque's study was more reliable.
rule: Institutional coherence is desirable but not absolute; decisions must be based on the evidence adduced and the balance of probabilities (Tremblay c. Québec, 1992 CanLII 1135; SITBA c. Consolidated Bathurst, 1990 CanLII 132; Domtar c. CALP, 1993 CanLII 106; CSST c. Fontaine, 2005 QCCA 775; Aluminerie Bécancour). Whether to prefer coherence over prevailing evidence is a question of law (correctness).
application: With two contradictory studies (one new), the TAQ was required to weigh the evidence, not defer to prior results. Montréal's method (indexing construction costs to the reference date via Statistics Canada and using the same conversion factor as the buildings assessed) was scientifically preferable, but its study also had deficiencies (BABN/Reban data, time lag), as did Caumartin's (non-contemporaneous, agrandissements, autoconstruction, non-homogeneous sample, indexation anomaly, asymmetry). Neither study was probative enough.
conclusion: The TAQ erred in law; its 0.80 finding is null. On the record, no reliable Factor F was established, so a neutral factor of 1.00 is retained for the 1995 and 1995-modified rolls (Montréal's appeal allowed in part).

issue: Did the TAQ err in its treatment of the various heads of depreciation/obsolescence?
facts: Impérial claimed curable physical/functional obsolescence on four items, precarious occupation of the public domain (tunnels/passerelles revocable on 30 days' notice), decline of the tobacco market, supply/snow-removal difficulties, and functional obsolescence from multi-storey, multi-building configuration (prior BREF decision had granted 20%; TAQ granted 10%).
rule: Depreciation lies at the core of the TAQ's specialized expertise; the reviewing court intervenes only for a patently unreasonable error. Contributory value of repairs must be netted against repair cost (Desjardins, Traité de l'évaluation foncière; General Motors; Camco; Schering; SIQ c. Montréal). A building cannot be depreciated for missing elements not in its cost (CAE; Camco). Each roll is decided on its own evidence.
application: The TAQ correctly applied doctrine/jurisprudence on curable obsolescence (netting contributory value) and reasonably found the public-domain revocation risk too remote to quantify (uncontradicted evidence the City never revoked). On the tobacco-market decline, the TAQ wrongly stated there was 'no particular evidence,' but Impérial itself claimed no economic obsolescence and gave no quantum, so no error in result. Supply/snow-removal overlapped with configuration and reflected age-related obsolescence captured by the age-life table. On configuration/agencement, given significant factual changes since 1989 (Montréal 2001 project), the 10% finding was defensible and within the TAQ's expertise; institutional coherence did not compel following the 1989 20% because the evidence differed.
conclusion: The TAQ's depreciation conclusions stand; no reviewable (patently unreasonable) error was established, so this branch of Impérial's appeal is dismissed.

issue: Did the TAQ err on the rental-value parameters (inclusion of the non-residential immovables surtax and the property value used for decapitalization)?
facts: For 1995, the assessor had not included the non-residential surtax in rental value; the TAQ included it. The TAQ also used the property value at the reference date (with reference-date tax rates) to compute the taxation component in the decapitalization method.
rule: Rental value is the most probable gross annual rent including property taxes (s. 69.5 LFM). The non-residential immovables surtax is a property tax (Germain c. Montréal, 1997 CanLII 393 (SCC)). The tax amount included is that actually expended in the reference year, combining reference-date rates with the value then on the roll (Hewquip; General Motors). These parameters lie at the core of the TAQ's expertise (patently unreasonable standard).
application: Because the surtax is a property tax, s. 69.5 requires its inclusion; the TAQ must render the decision the assessor should have. Although this disadvantages a complaining taxpayer relative to non-complainants, the TAQ and Court must apply the law. Using reference-date rates with the reference-date roll value is the only method respecting the LFM requirement that the tax reflect an actual reference-year expenditure.
conclusion: The TAQ did not err (no patently unreasonable error); inclusion of the surtax and the use of reference-date value for the taxation component are upheld; Impérial's appeal on rental value is dismissed.

issue: Was there a material change in circumstances since the July 22, 2005 final order sufficient to justify varying the joint custody arrangement?
facts: The parties held joint custody of Olivia under a detailed 2005 consent order. The mother sought sole decision-making, alleging chronic high conflict largely caused by the father; the father sought equal residential time, relying on his 2007 remarriage, his stepdaughter's presence, and Olivia's stated wishes. Extensive evidence and a psychological assessment by Dr. Weinberger showed persistent conflict over medical care, counselling, school, extracurricular activities, holidays and the weekend rotation, with Olivia drawn into the conflict.
rule: Under s. 17(5) of the Divorce Act a custody order may be varied only if there has been a change in the condition, means, needs or circumstances of the child. Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27, requires a change that materially affects the child and that was not foreseen or reasonably contemplated when the original order was made. Montgomery v. Montgomery held that cumulative unrelenting stress on the child can itself constitute a material change.
application: The court found the parents never established an effective co-parenting regime; the joint decision-making and conflict-resolution clauses had broken down, and the parents could not even agree on a process to resolve disputes. Olivia had been exposed to and negatively affected by ongoing conflict, aligned by her father against her mother. This breakdown was not reasonably foreseeable in 2005. By contrast, the father's remarriage, the stepdaughter's presence and Olivia's (influenced) views did not meet the threshold with respect to the residential arrangements.
conclusion: A material change in circumstances was established warranting a change from joint to sole decision-making, but no material change justified altering Olivia's residential schedule.

issue: Does the best interests of the child require sole custody to the mother rather than the joint custody with equal residential time recommended by the assessor?
facts: Dr. Weinberger recommended continued joint custody with equal alternating-week residence, a mandatory arbitration clause, and counselling. He nonetheless found this a high-conflict case with the father largely responsible, harsh in his treatment of the mother, lacking self-insight, and improperly involving Olivia. The mother sought sole custody; she did not seek to reduce the father's time.
rule: Once a material change is shown, the court considers the matter afresh with the child's welfare as the only issue (Gordon v. Goertz). Joint custody requires evidence of historical cooperation and an ability to communicate and agree on a dispute-resolution process (Kaplanis v. Kaplanis; Roy v. Roy; Lawson v. Lawson); it is inappropriate where conflict causes visible stress to the child (Montgomery; Wreggitt v. Belanger). A court cannot impose mandatory binding arbitration without consent.
application: The court accepted Dr. Weinberger's factual findings but rejected his recommendations, finding them unsupported by his own observations and incapable of reducing conflict. A conflict-resolution clause had already failed, and the court could not order binding arbitration absent consent. The best approach was to remove areas of uncertainty by imposing a fixed, inflexible schedule and granting sole custody to the mother, who contributed less to the conflict and was less likely to marginalize the father. Increasing the father's time was found not to be in Olivia's best interests given his influence over her.
conclusion: Sole custody was awarded to the mother (subject to limits on dentist, Jewish upbringing and residence in Ottawa), the existing residential schedule was maintained in a fixed inflexible form, and counselling was ordered for both parents and Olivia as a condition of custody and access.

issue: Should income be imputed to the father and child support and s. 7 expenses recalculated, and from what date?
facts: The father, a Bachelor of Commerce graduate, earned $30,000 working for his father's company since 2000, received a regular $1,061 monthly gift, had his $266 child support paid directly by the company, and enjoyed an employer health plan and annual family cruises. He had previously earned $50,000. The 2005 consent order fixed support at $266/month on a $30,000 income despite his 40%+ access. Both parties' incomes had since changed.
rule: Section 14 of the Federal Child Support Guidelines defines a change of circumstances giving rise to variation. Income may be imputed where a parent is underemployed (Bak v. Dobell, 2007 ONCA 304). Where shared custody exists (40%+ access), s. 9 of the Guidelines requires consideration of the table amounts, the set-off, increased costs of shared custody, and the conditions, means and needs of each parent and child (Contino v. Leonelli-Contino, 2005 SCC 63).
application: The court found the father underemployed and imputed $50,000 (grossing up his non-taxable $15,924 in gift and support payments plus health benefits). A material change under s. 14(a) was established as both incomes had changed. Variation was allowed only from April 1, 2007, midway between the parties' notices of motion. Applying s. 9 and Contino, and giving weight to the reliance factor and the father's failure to pay his share of activities, no change was warranted from April 2007 to September 2009. From October 1, 2009, given the mother's new cohabitant sharing expenses and the income shift, support was fixed at $150/month, with s. 7 expenses shared 54.55/45.45; the father owed $295 for the school uniforms.
conclusion: Income of $50,000 was imputed to the father; child support remained $266/month to September 2009 and was reduced to $150/month from October 1, 2009, with proportionate sharing of specified s. 7 expenses.

issue: Does EGALE have a sufficient direct interest in the subject matter of the proceeding to qualify for intervention as an added party under rule 13.01(1)(a)?
facts: EGALE, a national organization dedicated to legal equality for gays and lesbians with membership in every province and territory, moved for added-party status in an application by same-sex couples seeking marriage licences and a declaration that any law prohibiting same-sex marriage offends the Charter. It relied on its lobbying record, its Executive Director's witness experience, and its accumulated legal knowledge and research on equality rights.
rule: Rule 13.01(1)(a) of the Rules of Civil Procedure requires a genuine and direct interest in the subject matter, over and above that of the general public (Gould Outdoor Advertising v. London (City); John Doe v. Ontario (Information & Privacy Commissioner)). Greater latitude is afforded in Charter challenges, but a direct interest and useful contribution must still be shown (Ontario Federation of Anglers & Hunters). A lobbyist's or witness's interest is insufficient (Ward v. Canada (A.G.)).
application: The court held that EGALE's lobbying experience and its director's role as a witness could not ground intervention, since courts interpret rather than change law and expert evidence can be led through the applicants. However, EGALE's longstanding institutional legal knowledge, extensive legal research, and its representation of a broad spectrum of gays and lesbians who would be directly affected by the outcome gave it a genuine and direct interest beyond that of the general public.
conclusion: EGALE satisfied the 'interest in the subject matter' requirement of rule 13.01(1)(a).

issue: Can EGALE make a useful contribution beyond repeating the applicants' perspectives so as to warrant added-party status?
facts: The applicants were 16 individuals in same-sex couples all seeking marriage licences, supported by up to 10 expert affidavits presenting a broad factual and expert record. EGALE proposed a series of legal arguments about the social reality of gays and lesbians and the dignity interest in choosing to marry.
rule: An intervenor must offer something more than repetition of the parties' evidence and argument or a slightly different emphasis (Stadium Corp. v. Toronto (City); Schofield). The court weighs the likely useful contribution against injustice to the immediate parties (Peel (Regional Municipality) v. Great Atlantic & Pacific Co.; M. v. H.), and lack of a party's resources or the option of a separate proceeding are irrelevant.
application: The court found much of EGALE's proposed argument duplicated the applicants' broadly-based record. However, EGALE could bring genuinely distinct perspectives: that of gays and lesbians who do not wish to marry but seek the freedom to choose whether to marry (the relationship-option/diminishment perspective), and a non-Toronto, national perspective reflecting diverse communities across Canada. These were perspectives the couple-applicants could not present.
conclusion: EGALE could make a useful contribution on those limited, unique perspectives, justifying added-party status confined to those issues.

issue: What terms should be imposed to prevent undue delay or prejudice under rule 13.01(2)?
facts: EGALE sought unrestricted rights to file material, cross-examine and conduct the proceeding as a full party at a stage when the record was still being built; the Attorney General of Canada opposed, urging friend-of-the-court status limited to argument. EGALE undertook to work cooperatively and avoid duplication.
rule: Under rule 13.01(2) the court must consider whether intervention will unduly delay or prejudice the parties' rights and 'may make such order as is just', typically specifying conditions; intervention at first instance where the record is being formed carries greater potential for delay than appellate intervention (M. v. H.; Little Sisters).
application: To balance useful contribution against delay, the court restricted EGALE's role to its unique perspectives, requiring it not to repeat the applicants' arguments, to adhere to case-management timetables, to file no more than two affidavits, to cross-examine only on affidavits touching the designated issues, to file a factum limited to 20 pages, and to present oral argument only if later ordered, with liberty to vary the terms as circumstances changed.
conclusion: Intervention was granted as an added party under rule 13.01(1) on specified, limiting terms, with no costs of the motion or proceeding for or against EGALE.

issue: Was A.B. a child in need of protection under s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
facts: A.B. was apprehended by the Durham CAS at four months of age from a YWCA shelter amid concerns about her half-brother's behaviour, the presence of the violent M.C., a cigarette burn, and a kidney condition. The mother, R.B., had a history of poverty, substance abuse, poor decisions and repeated flight from child-protection authorities, largely tied to her destructive relationship with M.C.
rule: Section 37(2)(b)(ii) CFSA: a child is in need of protection where the child has suffered physical harm resulting from the caregiver's pattern of neglect in caring for, providing for, supervising or protecting the child; s. 37(2)(e): where the child needs medical treatment the parent fails to provide. A protection finding is assessed on the facts from the time of apprehension forward.
application: The s. 37(2)(e) allegations failed: the cigarette burn was an accident, the tissue damage minor, and no inadequate medication of the kidney condition was proven. However, under s. 37(2)(b)(ii), R.B. had repeatedly exhibited poor judgment — fleeing authorities, entangling herself in the criminal justice system, and prioritizing the violent M.C. over her children — a pattern that re-emerged in the unplanned move to Ontario.
conclusion: The court found A.B. to be a child in need of protection under s. 37(2)(b)(ii), though based on a low level of risk.

issue: What disposition was in A.B.'s best interests — Crown wardship for adoption or placement with the biological family?
facts: A.B. had been in the same foster home since four months of age due to an inordinate three-year delay; the CAS sought Crown wardship with no access so she could be adopted. R.B. had turned her life around over the past year, moved in with her sister C.B., ended contact with M.C., and secured employment. C.B. committed to permanent care of A.B. whether or not R.B. succeeded. Dr. Berman assessed R.B. as capable of parenting and questioned anxiety in the foster attachment.
rule: Sections 57 and 1(2) CFSA, with best-interests criteria in s. 37(3): the court must consider less disruptive alternatives (s. 57(3)), the biological family's plans (s. 57(4)), continuity of care, effects of delay, risk of harm, and the paramount purpose of protecting the child, supported by the autonomy and integrity of the family unit.
application: The court could not place A.B. with R.B. alone because her lifestyle changes were too recent and unproven. However, C.B. had the skills, fortitude and commitment to permanent care to provide a stable placement, working with R.B. The finding rested on low risk, and the CAS had made little effort to assist R.B. or preserve access, funnelling energy into its Crown-wardship position. With best interests balanced between adoption and family placement, the additional purpose favouring the autonomy and integrity of the biological family tipped the scales.
conclusion: The court ordered A.B. placed with C.B. and R.B. under CAS supervision with detailed conditions (including no contact with M.C.), with sole care reverting to C.B. if R.B. breached or the cohabitation broke down, and ordered therapeutic reintegration assistance funded by the CAS.

issue: Should the court appoint a litigation administrator for the estate of a defendant who died before the action was commenced?
facts: G.B. sued Etienne Fortin and institutional defendants in April 2009 for historical sexual abuse alleged to have occurred in 1969–1970 at St. Joseph's Training School. Fortin had died on February 22, 2002, unknown to the plaintiff, and his estate was administered by the provincial executor. Les Frères opposed appointment, arguing there was no estate and the appointment was unreasonable.
rule: Under rule 9.02 the appointment of a litigation administrator is discretionary, and rules 9.03(3) and (5) provide that a proceeding commenced against a person who died before its commencement is not a nullity but may be continued against a litigation administrator with the title amended accordingly.
application: The court found the appointment reasonable because the plaintiff was motivated not by the existence of an estate to satisfy damages but by the possible existence of records, which is not an unreasonable litigation approach. Because live limitation arguments meant it was not clear the action was out of time, appointment was warranted.
conclusion: The court ordered that a litigation administrator be appointed, with terms of appointment adjourned to be settled by the parties before June 30, 2011.

issue: Is it plain and obvious, for the purpose of the appointment, that s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act bars the action against the deceased defendant?
facts: The alleged assaults occurred in 1969–1970 while Fortin was in a position of trust/authority over the 15–16 year old plaintiff. Fortin died in 2002; the action began in 2009, more than two years after death. The plaintiff pleaded permanent incapacity and reliance on the sexual-assault provisions of the Limitations Act, 2002.
rule: Section 38(3) of the Trustee Act imposes a two-year limitation for actions against estates, preserved by s. 19(1)(a) and the Schedule of the Limitations Act, 2002. However, s. 24(7)(2) transition provision provides there is no limitation period where s. 16(1)(h) (sexual assault by a person in a position of trust or authority) would apply, and s. 10(3) creates a presumption of incapacity. Doctrines of fraudulent concealment (Giroux Estate) and special circumstances (Bikur Cholim) may toll s. 38(3). Camarata v. Morgan and Swain Estate address the interplay of the periods; B.L. (P.T.) held it was not plain and obvious such a claim was statute-barred.
application: The court held the motion required only a preliminary, non-final analysis akin to summary judgment. Distinguishing Bikur Cholim and Kramarz (which did not consider s. 24(7)(2)), the court found several live arguments could defeat the limitation: fraudulent concealment, special circumstances, application of s. 16(1)(h), the incapacity defence, and the transition provisions. Because these were all arguable, it was not clear the action was time-barred.
conclusion: The court declined to make a final limitations determination and found that, given the live arguments, it was not clear the action was out of time, supporting appointment.

issue: Is the plaintiff's proposed individual an appropriate litigation administrator?
facts: The plaintiff proposed Mr. Jerome Gardner, a local lawyer. Les Frères objected, believing him to be a unilingual Anglophone whereas les Frères operated in French.
rule: Rule 9.02 gives the court discretion over the appointment and its terms.
application: The court did not resolve the objection but invited counsel to propose mutually acceptable terms and a name, failing which submissions could be made before the judge.
conclusion: Terms of appointment, including the identity of the administrator, were adjourned to be settled by the parties before June 30, 2011.

issue: Should the plaintiffs be granted leave to appeal an interlocutory judgment concerning security for costs?
facts: The plaintiffs, Allan Gladstone and Jennifer Bradshaw, sued Dr Jerry Dankoff and the Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital, with the Attorney General of Quebec as mis-en-cause. They brought a motion bene esse for leave to appeal an interlocutory judgment (relating to security for costs). They did not contend that requiring them to post security for costs would deny them access to the courts for lack of means.
rule: Leave to appeal an interlocutory judgment under arts. 29, 494 and 523 C.P.C. requires that the interests of justice warrant appellate intervention.
application: The Court noted that the plaintiffs did not argue that posting security for costs would bar their access to the courts because of inability to pay, and concluded that the interests of justice did not require that leave be granted.
conclusion: Leave to appeal was refused.

issue: Was there a binding $15,000 agreement, and could it be proven by testimony absent a writing?
facts: Goikhberg alleged that during a November 2014 telephone call Mankovitz admitted giving false information to authorities and agreed to pay him $15,000. Mankovitz admitted the call but denied any promise to pay, saying Goikhberg was distraught and she was merely empathetic. There was no writing evidencing the alleged deal.
rule: Art. 2862 C.C.Q.: proof of a juridical act by testimony is not permitted between parties where the value in dispute exceeds $1,500, except where there is a commencement of proof in writing or the act was done in the ordinary course of an enterprise's business. The plaintiff bears the burden of proof (arts. 2803, 2804 C.C.Q.).
application: Goikhberg had no writing, could not invoke the ordinary-course-of-business exception, and offered no commencement of proof in writing. In any event the Court accepted Mankovitz's version: it made no sense for a lawyer to promise such a sum over a single phone call, there was no prior contractual relationship, the call came years after the impugned statements, and any claim would have been handled by her liability insurer.
conclusion: No agreement for payment of $15,000 existed; that part of the claim fails.

issue: Can the lawyer be liable in extracontractual damages for statements made for her client in immigration proceedings?
facts: The impugned statements were made in July 2009 and reiterated in a September 2010 Federal Court proceeding on behalf of Ms. Dakhova. Criminal charges against Goikhberg followed by September 26, 2011. He sued Mankovitz on December 14, 2015, claiming impossibility to act during his incarceration and late discovery of her involvement.
rule: Art. 2925 C.C.Q.: a personal action is prescribed after three years. Incarceration does not, absent special circumstances, constitute impossibility in fact to act (Olivier v. Canada, 2013 QCCA 70). A lawyer is an officer of the court and enjoys immunity for allegations made within the scope of her mandate; immunity ends only where bad faith and absence of reasonable and probable cause begin (Juneau c. Taillefer; art. 1457 C.C.Q.).
application: The action was instituted more than three years after both the statements and the resulting charges. Neither incarceration nor Goikhberg's failure to locate the Board decision earlier (obtained through disclosure over three years before) amounted to an impossibility to act. Alternatively, no fault was shown: Mankovitz acted in good faith and reasonably relied on her client's account, especially given Goikhberg's convictions.
conclusion: The extracontractual claim is prescribed and, in any event, discloses no fault; it is dismissed.

issue: Is the plaintiff's action abusive under arts. 51 ff. C.C.P.?
facts: Mankovitz argued Goikhberg was a vexatious litigant and the suit abusive. The action arose out of Goikhberg's grievance over criminal convictions in which Mankovitz played no role.
rule: Arts. 51-53 C.C.P.: the court may declare a judicial application abusive where it is clearly unfounded, frivolous, vexatious, quarrelsome, or defeats the ends of justice.
application: Having dismissed the action for tardiness and absence of legal basis, the Court found it sufficient to note that the suit against Mankovitz defeated the ends of justice as retaliation for a criminal conviction in which she had no part.
conclusion: The action is characterized as defeating the ends of justice; it is dismissed with court fees against Goikhberg.

issue: Was Richard Jr. a child in need of protection under s. 37(2) of the Child and Family Services Act?
facts: Richard Jr., born November 2007, was apprehended in December 2007. His parents had a persistent history of domestic violence, unaddressed drug-testing concerns, and failure to complete counselling. His two older siblings had already been found in need of protection in November 2006. The CAS's amended application initially omitted the CFSA section relied on, which was corrected by amendment at trial under rule 26.01.
rule: Section 37(2)(b) and (g) of the CFSA: a child is in need of protection where there is a risk of physical harm resulting from a parent's failure to adequately care for or protect the child, or a pattern of neglect, and where there is a risk of emotional harm from the parent's actions or neglect. Rule 26.01 of the Rules of Civil Procedure permits amendment of pleadings unless non-compensable prejudice results.
application: The court permitted the pleadings amendment as no party was prejudiced. Although Richard Jr. had been little parented by the couple, their ongoing physical and verbal confrontations, frequent police intervention and criminal charges posed a risk that the child would be physically harmed during disputes or emotionally harmed by witnessing violence. The parents had shown minimal effort to address the issues that led to the original protection finding for the siblings.
conclusion: Richard Jr. was found to be a child in need of protection under s. 37(2)(b) and (g) of the CFSA.

issue: Should the children be returned to their parents or made Crown wards for adoption, considering the statutory time limits and best-interests factors?
facts: Alizeah and Anthony had been in CAS care since July 2006, Richard Jr. since December 2007 — all well beyond the s. 70 statutory limits. The parents had ten to twenty separations marked by documented domestic violence, repeated breaches of no-contact court orders, unfulfilled promises regarding counselling and drug testing (R.B. never provided drug results after a positive cocaine test three years earlier), and no stable housing. Kinship placement with grandmothers was investigated and not recommended.
rule: Section 70 of the CFSA caps society wardship duration (12 months for a child under six), leaving only return or Crown wardship where the limit is exceeded. Section 1 declares the paramount purpose to be the best interests, protection and well-being of children. Section 37(3) lists best-interests factors including the child's needs, cultural background, relationships, merits of the CAS plan, effects of delay, and degree of risk. Courts recognize that exposure to domestic violence harms children (Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S.A.C., 2005 ONCJ 274; Jewish Family and Child Service v. R.K., [2008] O.J. No. 1940; CAS of Peel v. A.O., 2006 ONCJ 149).
application: Only the factors of blood relationship and cultural background favoured the parents. Neither parent presented a viable plan: both lacked suitable housing after three years, and their unresolved domestic violence continued, with the same conditions persisting as justified the original 2006 protection finding. The children needed stability and could wait no longer; each was a good adoption candidate with no special needs. The court criticized both the CAS (for seeking adjournments contrary to time guidelines) and the parents for the inexcusable delays.
conclusion: The children were made Crown wards for the purpose of adoption; return to the parents was not a viable option.

issue: Should the Crown wardship be with no access, and what safeguard protects the parents' status-review rights?
facts: The CAS sought Crown wardship with no access for adoption. The parents had attended most access visits and the hearing, showing some commitment. Under s. 65.1 a parent may seek status review, but s. 65.1(9) bars applications once a Crown ward is placed for adoption, and parents might not learn of placement.
rule: Section 65.1 of the CFSA governs status-review applications by a parent, subject to timing and leave restrictions; s. 65.1(9) bars applications where the ward has been placed for adoption and still resides in that home.
application: To preserve the parents' meaningful ability to exercise status-review rights before adoption placement forecloses them, the court ordered the Society to inform each parent in writing within seven days of the children being placed for adoption; this also served to discourage further delay by the Society.
conclusion: Crown wardship with no access was ordered, coupled with a direction that the Society notify the parents in writing when the children are placed for adoption.

issue: What parenting and decision-making arrangement is in the best interests of the two oldest children, given allegations of parental alienation?
facts: Following the parents' 2018 divorce, the three children initially resided primarily with the mother (Ms. D). The two oldest children (16 and almost 14) ceased contact with her in 2019 and 2020 respectively and now live full-time with the father (Mr. B), while the youngest (11) has continued shared week-on/week-off parenting with both parents. Ms. D alleged Mr. B alienated her from the older children and sought a reversal of parenting; Mr. B claimed the children were merely exercising their own choices. Expert reports (Wilkinson, Torres) and Counsel for the Children documented alienating and estranging conduct.
rule: Section 16 of the Divorce Act, RSC 1985, c 3 (2nd Supp), requires the court to consider only the best interests of the child, giving primary consideration to physical, emotional and psychological safety, weighing the enumerated s. 16(3) factors, family violence under s. 16(4), and the s. 16(6) maximum-contact principle subject to the child's welfare (Young v Young; SS v AS, 2020 ABQB 810). A court may find parental alienation on the facts alone without conclusive expert evidence (Malhotra v Henhoeffer, 2018 ONSC 6472; VMB v KRB, 2014 ABCA 334). Four post-alienation options exist (RMB v DTB, 2019 ABQB 826 at para 112; JLZ v CMZ, 2021 ABCA 200).
application: The court found that although Ms. D engaged in some estranging behaviour, Mr. B engaged in a far more troubling campaign of alienation, encouraging the children to reject their mother, over-involving them in litigation, making unsubstantiated abuse allegations (an unfounded PN5), a public 'Go Fund Me' page vilifying the mother, and severing the children's Jewish faith and maternal family ties. The older children exhibited classic alienation behaviours. However, given the children are teenagers who 'vote with their feet' (unlike the younger children in RMB), the proposed transitional caregiver (Ms. X) was a stranger and unsuitable, and a full custody reversal would likely cause the children to run away, the court concluded neither 'doing nothing' nor an immediate reversal served their best interests. Reunification therapy while the children remained with the father, aimed at restoring shared parenting (as already worked for the youngest child), was appropriate.
conclusion: The two older children are to remain with the father while reunification therapy continues for six months with the goal of returning to shared parenting; failure to attend therapy without reasonable excuse triggers a return to court to show cause why custody should not be reversed.

issue: What consequences should follow from Mr. B's contempt of court?
facts: Mr. B admitted knowing about and consenting to the March 19, 2021 Consent Order but largely refused to follow it — failing to arrange or pay for the children's counselling, breaching the prohibition on further applications by commencing PN5 abuse allegations and obtaining restraining orders, and failing to obtain counselling for AB. He had previously been warned and even held in contempt with unpaid costs by other judges.
rule: Rule 10.52(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court permits a declaration of civil contempt where a person without reasonable excuse does not comply with an order of which they have knowledge; Rule 10.53 sets out sanctions including imprisonment. Civil contempt requires (1) a clear order, (2) knowledge of it, and (3) intentional act/omission breaching it (Carey v Laiken, 2015 SCC 17). Its dual goals are securing compliance and protecting the integrity of the administration of justice (United Nurses of Alberta, [1992] 1 SCR 901). Family-law contempt sentences have ranged from 2–90 days, often suspended for future compliance (Rea v Rea; Holt v Holt; Skalitzky v Skalitzky).
application: Mr. B knew the order's terms and deliberately disobeyed them without reasonable excuse, so contempt was proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Monetary fines would only add pressure to a toxic family situation and were insufficient given the contumacy; prior threats, findings and costs awards had not curbed his behaviour. Some incarceration was necessary to protect respect for the administration of justice, but proceeding in civil rather than criminal contempt avoided a criminal record.
conclusion: Mr. B was found in contempt and sentenced to six days' gaol, suspended for six months pending his cooperation with reunification therapy and capable of indefinite suspension based on future compliance; costs reserved for six months.

issue: Was the proceeding properly commenced by a Notice of Application rather than by a Statement of Claim?
facts: Hamza, a lawyer facing LSO complaints over offensive LinkedIn posts, launched a Notice of Application seeking to stop the investigation, various declarations, and substantial damages. He relied only on Rule 1.04(1) (liberal construction) when asked for authority to proceed by application.
rule: Rule 14.02 requires every proceeding to be by action unless a statute or the Rules provide otherwise; Rule 14.03 makes a statement of claim the originating process for an action; Rule 14.05(3) lists limited exceptions permitting an application. Declaratory relief under 14.05(3)(g) must be ancillary to relief properly claimed by application, and damages claims cannot be pursued by application (Hefford v. Charpentier, 2009 CanLII 21761).
application: None of the 14.05(3) exceptions applied: the declaratory relief was not ancillary to a properly commenced application, the catch-all 14.05(3)(h) was unavailable because the 1,000+ pages contained numerous disputed 'facts', and the substantial damages claims had to proceed by action. The manner of commencement matters because it affects a defendant's rights to counterclaim, discovery, jury notice and trial. Hamza had been warned of this defect by Leach J. yet took no corrective step.
conclusion: The Rules did not authorize commencement by application; the application was dismissed on that basis.

issue: Should the Charter challenges to the Law Society's investigative powers be heard by the court or deferred to the Law Society Tribunal?
facts: Hamza alleged that being required to submit to an interview under s. 49 of the Law Society Act, and other investigation procedures, violated ss. 8, 11(b), 13 and s. 2 of the Charter, and sought orders reforming the investigation process. He refused to cooperate with the ongoing LSO investigation.
rule: Absent exceptional circumstances a court should not interfere in an administrative proceeding until it has run its course; an administrative tribunal can consider a Charter challenge and decline to apply an impugned provision, and only a s. 52 Constitution Act declaration of invalidity must await the courts (DioGuardi Tax Law v. Law Society of Upper Canada, 2015 ONSC 3430, aff'd 2016 ONCA 531; Okwuobi).
application: The court found the reasoning applied even more forcefully here, since every remedy sought (other than a s. 52 declaration, which was not requested) could be granted by the Law Society Tribunal. The Charter challenge to the LSO's investigative powers should be deferred to the Tribunal.
conclusion: The court declined to exercise jurisdiction over the Charter claims; subrule 14.05(3)(g.1) therefore gave no authority to proceed by application.

issue: Should the applicant's pleadings be struck out in their entirety under Rule 25.11 without leave to amend?
facts: Hamza's Notice of Application, affidavit and 131-page factum, with hundreds of pages of exhibits, contained racist and misogynist attacks on the respondents and the judiciary (including repeated use of the term 'red Indian'), attacks on Leach J. and the judiciary as 'corrupt', and demands such as recusal of any non-Indigenous judge and referral to a 'Muslim Arab arbitrator'.
rule: Rule 25.11 permits striking pleadings that may prejudice a fair trial, are scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or are an abuse of process; Rule 38.12 applies it to applications and Rule 14.09/21.01(1)(b) allow striking originating process disclosing no reasonable cause of action. Carney Timber Co. v. Pabedinskas (2008) sets out when pleadings are scandalous/vexatious, and Jaffer v. York University, 2010 ONCA 654 allows striking where a claim is untenable.
application: The pleadings met almost every Carney Timber example: they were replete with opinion, inflammatory attacks, irrelevant 'historical' references and abuse of the judicial process to air the applicant's views. The remaining substantive claims were 'nonsense', untenable at law with no chance of success, so no amendment could cure them.
conclusion: Had the application been properly before the court, the pleadings would have been struck in their entirety, with prejudice and without leave to amend.

issue: Are the damages claims barred by statutory immunity and are the complaints protected by qualified privilege?
facts: Hamza sought large damages against the LSO and the individual complainants, who were lawyers, a law student and one member of the public who reported his LinkedIn posts to the LSO in good faith.
rule: Section 9 of the Law Society Act immunizes the LSO and its officials from damages for acts done in good faith; bad faith must be pleaded with precision and full particulars (Potis Holdings Ltd. v. Law Society of Upper Canada, 2019 ONCA 618; Edwards v. Law Society of Upper Canada, 2001 SCC 80). Qualified privilege protects communications made by a person with an interest or duty to make them to a recipient with a corresponding interest (Beach v. Freeson, [1972] 1 Q.B. 14).
application: Nothing in the materials pleaded bad faith with the required precision, so s. 9 immunity applied to the LSO. The complainants each had a social or moral interest in reporting conduct unbecoming of a lawyer, and the LSO had an interest in receiving the complaints, so the complaints were protected by qualified privilege.
conclusion: The damages claims against the LSO were barred by statutory immunity and the complaints were protected by qualified privilege, reinforcing dismissal.

issue: What parental-time arrangement is in the best interest of the parties' 7-year-old son, X?
facts: X, aged 7, suffers from severe ADHD, oppositional defiance disorder and anxiety, requires a full-time shadow at school, and needs stability. The Mother has been his primary caregiver and provides structure; the Father sought 50/50 shared parenting time. A court-appointed psychosocial expert (Mr. De Wit) had recommended progressive shared parenting conditional on the Father resuming punctual contact, obtaining psychological therapy and reducing conflict. The Father had unilaterally suspended his access for months, did not follow the recommendations, and engaged in persistent conflict and post-separation abuse.
rule: Section 16 of the Divorce Act requires the court to consider only the best interest of the child, giving primary consideration to the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being, weighing the enumerated non-exhaustive factors including stability, parental capacity, family violence, and ability to communicate/cooperate. Article 33 C.C.Q. is to the same effect. Shared parenting is assessed by factors including parental capacity, availability, stability, communication and absence of conflict, and the child's expressed wishes.
application: Though it valued the expert's insights, the Court found the 18-month-old expertise outdated and rendered without knowledge of the Father's combative and coercive conduct. Stability favoured the Mother, the child's principal caregiver; the Father was more fluctuating in presence, had suspended access, minimized the child's condition, failed to pursue therapy or co-parenting support, escalated litigation (including a defamation suit) and engaged in domestic abuse making him a poor role model. The persistent parental conflict made shared parenting contrary to X's interest, but the child's expressed wish to see his father more, and the Father's strengths, justified enlarging access beyond what the Mother proposed.
conclusion: Shared parenting was refused; the Mother retained principal parenting time, with the Father granted enlarged parental time (alternating Thursday-to-Monday weekends plus vacation and holiday periods) starting May 1, 2023, and joint exercise of parental authority.

issue: What notional income should be imputed to the Father for support purposes?
facts: The Father, a lawyer operating a boutique firm through several corporations, declared low personal incomes ($41,450 in 2020; $75,152 in 2021) but used his law firm's bank accounts and credit cards to pay extensive personal expenses (car rental, restaurants, retail, travel to Florida, tens of thousands on trading cards). His declared position on income shifted repeatedly during litigation.
rule: Art. 9 of the Regulation respecting the determination of child support payments defines annual income broadly to include income from any source; art. 446 C.C.P. authorizes the court to complete or establish a party's income, considering assets and income they generate. The burden lies on the party contesting the declared revenue; where disclosure is not fulsome, the court may fix income approximately in the manner it considers reasonable.
application: The Court accepted the Mother's painstaking analysis showing the Father used his firm as a 'personal piggy bank'. Rejecting the claim that trading-card spending was a business, it grossed up identified personal expenses year by year to determine notional revenues, finding the Father's disclosure misleading and untransparent.
conclusion: Notional annual income was fixed at $167,894 (2020), $298,145 (2021), and $315,255 for both 2022 and 2023.

issue: Is the Mother entitled to spousal support, and in what amount and duration?
facts: This was a traditional marriage; the Mother, an HR specialist, put her career on hold for roughly seven years to care for the special-needs child, losing employment and suffering post-traumatic symptoms and post-separation abuse. She lives modestly with a monthly deficit of about $4,000; the Father's income and lifestyle grew substantially.
rule: Section 15.2 of the Divorce Act permits an order of periodic or lump-sum support that is reasonable, considering the condition, means, needs and other circumstances, the length of cohabitation and functions performed, and pursuing the four objectives in s. 15.2(6) (recognizing economic advantages/disadvantages, apportioning child-care consequences, relieving economic hardship, and promoting self-sufficiency), none paramount.
application: The Father gained economically while the Mother sacrificed her career and suffered economic disadvantage and hardship, exacerbated by the Father's withholding of resources. Her expenses were reasonable and her situation precarious, while the Father could afford the requested support despite his understated Form III.
conclusion: The Father was ordered to pay spousal support of $3,500 per month retroactively to May 1, 2020, continuing until May 1, 2025, indexed annually.

issue: Is the Mother entitled to a provision for costs?
facts: The Mother incurred some $360,000 in legal fees. The Father, himself a lawyer, retained six successive lawyers, filed abusive procedures, withheld support and financial disclosure, launched a defamation suit and abuse claims, and submitted false financial portraits; prior judges had already sanctioned him, including a $30,000 award by Justice Davis.
rule: Arts. 502 and 588 C.C.Q. allow the court to order a spouse to pay a provision for the costs of proceedings, to ensure the less fortunate party can be heard without financial constraint. Criteria (per the Court of Appeal): nature/importance of the case, means of and disparity between the parties, respective conduct, amount of support, and protection of the child's rights.
application: The case was made complex by the Father's opaque corporate finances and abusive, conflictual conduct; he had greater means; his conduct 'perverted justice' and breached the duties of good faith and cooperation; and the Mother's fees were largely alimentary in nature. Some $46,500 had already been paid in prior costs/abuse awards.
conclusion: The Father was ordered to pay a provision for costs of $150,000 within 30 days.

issue: Is the Mother entitled to a lump sum payment?
facts: The Mother sought a lump sum (reduced to $200,000) to relocate and pay down debts, having sacrificed her career. After partition of the family patrimony ($275,000), child and spousal support and the provision for costs, the Father claimed no remaining capacity.
rule: Section 15.2(1) of the Divorce Act allows a lump sum; a lump sum is alimentary, awarded according to the debtor's means and the creditor's needs, considering the advantages and disadvantages of the marriage (Droit de la famille – 121300, 2012 QCCA 1017).
application: Although the Mother presented a valid claim, once the patrimony partition, support and provision for costs were accounted for, the Court was unconvinced the Father had sufficient assets and revenue to pay a further sum; his true financial situation remained murky with no evidence of additional means.
conclusion: No lump sum was awarded.

issue: Should paragraphs 15 to 28 of the statement of claim be struck under Rule 19(24) as disclosing no reasonable cause of action?
facts: The plaintiff, a lawyer whose articles were terminated by Mr. Smith, pleaded facts about the defendants hiring other articled students/associates after his dismissal (paras. 15-20) and about the defendants' conduct in the earlier Small Claims proceedings (paras. 21-28). The defendants sought to strike these as irrelevant and disclosing no cause of action.
rule: Under Rule 19(24), a pleading may be struck only where it is 'plain and obvious' that it discloses no reasonable cause of action; any doubt is resolved in favour of allowing the pleading to stand, all pleaded facts are assumed true, and a pleading disclosing a triable issue, as framed or as may be amended, should not be struck (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform; Hunt v. T & N plc; Helman v. Brown). Special costs may be awarded for reprehensible conduct leading up to and during litigation (Marchen; Stanton v. Stanton Estates; Benekritis; Garcia).
application: For paras. 15-20, the court found the pleadings could conceivably disclose a cause of action if read with the breach of fiduciary duty claim (i.e., that Mr. Smith terminated the plaintiff to hire others), so they raise a triable issue that may be cured by amendment. For paras. 21-28, the court found the alleged conduct leading up to and during the litigation could support a claim for special costs and that some alleged misconduct, if true, might be worthy of rebuke; weakness of the case is not a ground to strike.
conclusion: The application to strike paragraphs 15 to 28 was dismissed; the plaintiff was permitted to amend.},{},{},{}]},{},{},{}]

issue: Should the plaintiff's claim for punitive damages be struck or dismissed?
facts: The plaintiff sought punitive damages but pleaded no conduct at the time of the breach that was high-handed, malicious, arbitrary or highly reprehensible, and filed no affidavit to contradict Mr. Smith's sworn statement that he could not recall acting arbitrarily, wrongfully or in a callous or malicious manner.
rule: Punitive damages require an actionable wrong independent of the breach of contract, arising from high-handed, malicious, arbitrary or highly reprehensible misconduct departing markedly from ordinary standards of decent behaviour at the time of the breach (Whiten v. Pilot Insurance Co.; Marchen v. Dams Ford Lincoln Sales Ltd.). On a Rule 18(6) summary judgment application the defendant may adduce evidence, and the claim may be dismissed where the plaintiff is bound to lose.
application: No facts pleaded, even if assumed true, met the Whiten standard, and the plaintiff filed no evidence to rebut Mr. Smith's affidavit. There was thus no bona fide triable issue on punitive damages.
conclusion: The claim for punitive damages was dismissed under Rule 18(7).

issue: Should the action against Mr. Smith in his personal capacity for breach of contract be dismissed, and should the corporate veil be pierced?
facts: The plaintiff admitted he was employed by Howard Smith & Company (the law corporation) and articled to Mr. Beuhler, not Mr. Smith. He did not plead a contract of employment with Mr. Smith personally, but argued during submissions that the corporate veil should be pierced because Mr. Smith was the sole operating mind of the corporation. This fact was not pleaded or supported by affidavit.
rule: Officers and directors are protected from personal liability absent fraud, deceit, dishonesty, want of authority, or tortious conduct exhibiting a separate identity or interest from the company (Montreal Trust Co. of Canada v. ScotiaMcLeod Inc.; 607730 B.C. Ltd. v. Quay Realty). On Rule 18(6) the court may consider evidence and dismiss where the plaintiff is bound to lose.
application: The plaintiff had no contractual relationship with Mr. Smith personally; the original articled student agreement was void for illegality or superseded by the Beuhler agreement. The bare, unpleaded assertion that Mr. Smith was the sole operating mind was insufficient to pierce the corporate veil, as none of the recognized circumstances were present.
conclusion: The claim for breach of contract against Mr. Smith personally was dismissed under Rule 18(6) and (7).

issue: Should the claim against Mr. Smith for breach of fiduciary duty be struck or dismissed?
facts: The plaintiff alleged Mr. Smith was his de facto principal who directed and supervised his work, and that abruptly terminating the articles breached fiduciary duties. Mr. Smith deposed the plaintiff worked only for his corporation under his direction, but stated he knew of no facts supporting a breach of fiduciary duty; the plaintiff filed no responding affidavit.
rule: Under Rule 19(24)/18(6), a claim is struck only if it is plain and obvious it discloses no reasonable cause of action or is bound to fail; on Rule 18(6) the judge does not weigh evidence but determines whether a bona fide triable issue exists; deficient pleadings that can be amended should be allowed to be amended rather than struck (Skybridge Investments; Immocreek Corp.).
application: Read most favourably, the statement of claim pleaded a de facto principal relationship and, via paras. 15-20, that termination to hire others breached fiduciary duties. Unlike Immocreek, the pleading at minimum pleaded the necessary facts, raising a bona fide triable issue that could be cured by amendment.
conclusion: The application to strike the breach of fiduciary duty claim was dismissed; the plaintiff was ordered to amend to properly set out the cause of action.

issue: Are the plaintiffs entitled to a prohibitive interlocutory injunction restraining allegedly defamatory statements under the heightened test applicable in defamation cases?
facts: Dr. Andrew Feifer and Jonathan Feifer, members of the Jewish community and liquidators of their late mother's estate, were accused by Mr. Feldman — a lawyer and former business partner of their uncle Irwin — of having inherited and profited from billions of dollars in gold bars allegedly stolen from Holocaust victims by the Nazis. Feldman disseminated these allegations through a 'Long Form Affidavit' sent to a judge and through disturbing videos communicated to third parties, and vowed to continue his 'mission.' He admitted several allegations of the demand, including that his statements were fictitious, and threatened further litigation. He filed no evidence supporting the truth of the allegations.
rule: Article 511 C.C.P. permits an interlocutory injunction where the applicant appears to have a right and it is necessary to prevent serious or irreparable prejudice. In defamation cases the ordinary test is modified: per Prud'homme c. Rawdon (2010 QCCA 584) and Champagne c. Cégep de Jonquière (1997 CanLII 10001), the discretion must be exercised with great prudence, reserved for the clearest and rarest cases where the words are clearly defamatory, the harm irreparable, the order targets precise statements, and the author's justification defence appears bound to fail. Defamation is assessed by whether an ordinary citizen would find the statements discredited the plaintiff's reputation (Prud'homme c. Prud'homme; Radio Sept-Îles). Comparing a person of Jewish faith to a Nazi is highly defamatory (case law cited). Reputation once tarnished by libel can seldom be restored (Hill v. Church of Scientology, 1995 CanLII 59).
application: The Court found the allegations clearly defamatory: they were extremely serious, unsupported by any evidence in the record, Feifer denied inheriting such sums, and Feldman himself admitted the allegations were fictitious, undermining his credibility as a practising lawyer. His intent was punitive — to punish the plaintiffs for siding with his enemy Irwin. On serious or irreparable harm, being accused of profiting from a fortune criminally taken from Holocaust victims is among the most detrimental allegations imaginable for a member of the Jewish community; potential moral and punitive damages could not fully repair a tarnished reputation, and an injunction would prevent worsening harm while the allegations had not yet reached the plaintiffs' communities. The balance of inconveniences favoured the plaintiffs, who faced grave prejudice while Feldman suffered little from abstaining pending trial.
conclusion: The plaintiffs established a right to the interlocutory injunction. The Court granted the application in part, ordering Feldman not to communicate the specified defamatory affirmations or information about the estate and plaintiffs, sealing certain exhibits, dispensing with security, and ordering provisional execution notwithstanding appeal.

issue: Should the Law Society's Response to Civil Claim be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(a) as disclosing no reasonable defence?
facts: Heller, a Victoria lawyer, sued the Law Society for defamation arising from a September 10, 2024 press release he says imputed racism to him after he sponsored a resolution to alter Indigenous Intercultural Course materials about unmarked burial sites at the former Kamloops residential school. The Law Society's Response denied the press release was defamatory and, in the alternative, pleaded fair comment, qualified privilege and responsible communication. Heller argued each defence was doomed for failure to plead material facts (e.g. due diligence, justification for publication to the world).
rule: Under Rule 9-5(1)(a) SCCR, a pleading is struck only where, assuming the pleaded facts true, it is plain and obvious it discloses no reasonable claim or defence (Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse, 2003 SCC 69; Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959); no evidence is admissible (Rule 9-5(2)); a pleading is struck only for a 'radical defect' and if it cannot be amended. Defamation defences of fair comment (WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40), responsible communication (Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61) and qualified privilege (Pressler; Smith BCSC/BCCA) each have established elements requiring pleaded material facts (Rule 3-3(2)).
application: The court found the Law Society pleaded facts capable of supporting each defence: the historical/contextual background (2015 TRC Report, TSN statements, Dr. Beaulieu's radar findings, Canadian Archaeological Association statement, the portal discussion) could establish public interest and comment honestly held for fair comment; the Law Society's role as provincial regulator communicating to the bar supported qualified privilege; and the steps taken before publication supported diligence for responsible communication. Whether scope of publication defeated the defences and whether the Law Society knew the materials were inaccurate were matters for trial, not radical defects.
conclusion: The Response was not plainly and obviously deficient; the application to strike under Rule 9-5(1)(a) was dismissed.

issue: Should the Response be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b), (c) or (d) as unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, vexatious, embarrassing or an abuse of process?
facts: Heller argued the Response contained gratuitous smears (calling him 'offensive', attacking his competence), was ideologically driven and filed for the collateral purpose of advancing Indigenous social-justice issues, was prolix and confusing, and improperly relied on R. v. Dick which he said had already validated his use of the word 'potential'.
