application: The Master correctly set out the test, reviewed the evidence and authorities, and found at para. 22 that the Merchant GSA created a priority claim over the appellant's cash such that there was a real possibility no cash would remain to pay the respondent's costs if the action failed. Read as a whole, her reasons clearly found that a prima facie case had been made out; the appellant's argument ignored her reasons in their totality and recast a factual/discretionary assessment as legal error, as in Beta.
conclusion: The Master applied the law correctly and made the necessary prima facie finding; the first ground of appeal fails.

issue: Was the Master's finding that the appellant's assets were at risk of dissipation clearly wrong or based on mere speculation?
facts: Uncontroverted evidence established a GSA over all the appellant's assets in favour of Merchant, whose particulars the appellant chose not to disclose; the appellant relied on cash holdings and ongoing income but produced no accountant-prepared financial statements.
rule: Once a defendant establishes a prima facie case that a plaintiff lacks sufficient assets, the plaintiff must provide evidence of exigible assets (WestCorp Solutions Ltd. v. Collins, 2014 BCSC 1606; New Home Warranty of B.C. v. 462146 B.C. Ltd., 2000 BCSC 143). A discretionary risk assessment involving judgment is not 'mere speculation' (Beta Properties Ltd. v. 4301 Hastings Development Ltd., 2018 BCSC 103).
application: The Master accepted that the appellant's assets were encumbered by the Merchant GSA and that the appellant failed to rebut the prima facie case with evidence of exigible unencumbered assets. WestCorp and New Home were distinguishable because there no GSA existed and the plaintiffs had sufficient unencumbered assets. The Master's risk assessment was a proper exercise of judgment on the evidence, not speculation.
conclusion: The Master exercised her discretion judicially and was not clearly wrong; the second ground of appeal fails.

issue: May a custodial parent relocate the children out of the province without the other parent's permission absent special circumstances?
facts: Following a consent divorce decree granting joint legal custody but placing day-to-day care and the right to select the children's place of residence with the father (petitioner), the father proposed to move to California for about one year for business reasons. The mother (applicant) sought an order restraining removal of the children or varying the decree so the children would reside with her.
rule: In the absence of special circumstances, a parent who has custody has the right to remove the children without the permission of the other parent, absent some specific agreement to the contrary or access terms clearly indicating the parties intended the children to remain in close proximity: Wright v. Wright (1973), 1 O.R. (2d) 337 (C.A.); Re Dube (1956), 3 D.L.R. (2d) 421; Beck v. Beck, [1949] 2 W.W.R. 1175. The welfare of the children is the paramount consideration.
application: The decree expressly assigned to the father responsibility for the children's day-to-day care and decisions including their place of residence. Although the father's move was voluntary rather than employer-compelled, the governing authority permits a custodial parent to relocate. Considering the whole decree and, paramountly, the children's welfare, the court concluded the father should be permitted to have the children reside with him in California, and the relocation would not unreasonably deny the mother access.
conclusion: The custodial father is permitted to take the children to California; the application to restrain removal or to vary custody is refused.

issue: Did the detailed access provisions, including Jewish-holiday and Florida-visit terms, evidence an intention to keep the children in close proximity to both parents so as to prevent relocation?
facts: The decree gave the mother alternate-weekend access, access on specified Jewish holidays (with an obligation to take the children to synagogue services), a portion of the summer, and a right to take the children to Florida annually. The mother had no permanent Ontario residence, spent considerable time in Florida and elsewhere, and was a woman of independent means.
rule: Access terms bar relocation only where they clearly indicate the parties must have intended the children to remain in close proximity for the access right to be effective (Wright v. Wright); the children's welfare remains paramount.
application: The court found the consent decree, read against the parties' way of life, disclosed no such intention. The mother's wealth and mobility meant she could readily visit the children in California; the Florida-visit clause lost its force as an indicator of an intention to keep the children nearby. Only the Jewish-holiday/synagogue clause gave slight difficulty, but such detailed provisions would need revision once relocation was permitted. Minor formal variations to visitation and birthday-party clauses were ordered.
conclusion: The access terms did not indicate an intention to keep the children in close proximity; the application was dismissed subject to specified variations, without costs.

issue: Were the security and development of the children compromised under the Youth Protection Act given the parental conflict, domestic violence, and the elder child's behavioural difficulties?
facts: The Director of Youth Protection filed petitions alleging that the parents' behaviour and way of life created a risk of moral or physical danger. The father had a history of verbal and physical abuse toward the mother and children and faced an assault charge; both parents had pending assault/harassment charges. The elder child J... was aggressive toward his mother, had expressed suicidal ideations, threatened her with a knife and struck her with a broom, and admitted difficulty controlling his anger. Both parents admitted the majority of the allegations, and the children had witnessed violent outbursts.
rule: Under the Youth Protection Act, security and development may be declared compromised where the parents' behaviour or way of life creates a risk of moral or physical danger (s. 38), and where a child has serious behavioural problems the parents cannot resolve (s. 38 h)). Section 90 requires the court to give reasons.
application: The Court accepted the parents' admissions, the testimony of the Youth Protection Delegate Ms. Linda Murphy, and the Director's reports. The evidence showed an ongoing conflictual and violent relationship witnessed by the children, persisting tension, and an impact on the children's behaviour. This satisfied the statutory threshold.
conclusion: The Court declared that the security and development of both children were compromised and granted the Director's petition.

issue: What protective measures best served the children's interests, particularly regarding custody and contact with the father?
facts: The mother had interim custody from the Superior Court and agreed with the Director's proposed measures. The Director recommended the children be entrusted to the mother with aid, counsel and assistance, and that the father's contacts be supervised. The father sought unsupervised visits, cited difficulty finding a supervisor, and said he saw no need for anger management or therapy.
rule: Measures ordered under the Youth Protection Act must serve the children's protection and best interests; the court may entrust the child to a parent, order supervised contacts, order psychiatric assessment and treatment, and provide aid, counsel and assistance.
application: Given the persisting tension, the Court found the parents must prioritize their children's needs and follow therapy at least to help the children cope. It maintained custody with the mother, ordered supervised paternal contacts until December 31, 2002, continued psychiatric follow-up and assessment at the Jewish General Hospital, and recommended therapy for both parents.
conclusion: The Court ordered custody to the mother, supervised paternal contact, psychiatric assessment and follow-up, recommended parental therapy, and ordered one year of aid, counsel and assistance under the Director's supervision.

issue: Was summary judgment appropriate in this child protection proceeding, or was there a genuine issue requiring a trial?
facts: FACS moved for summary judgment under r. 16 of the Family Law Rules for protection findings and placement of the two children with their Mother. The Father opposed, alleging genuine credibility issues (coaching by the Mother and half-sister) requiring a trial. The record included multiple affidavits from FACS workers, the Mother, the Father and his family, and OCL submissions reflecting the children's consistent wishes.
rule: Rule 16(4)-(6) of the Family Law Rules permits final judgment where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial; the moving party bears the burden. Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7 sets the fairness/proportionality test, and rr. 16(6.1)-(6.2) allow weighing evidence, assessing credibility and drawing inferences unless the interests of justice require a trial. Kawartha-Haliburton Children's Aid Society v. M.W., 2019 ONCA 316 adapts Hryniak to child protection, requiring caution and application of the CYFSA objectives, including the child's best interests.
application: The court screened the evidence, applied the state-of-mind hearsay exception to the children's statements (used to show their state of mind, not the truth of contents), and found the children's views consistent and non-suspicious despite the Father's coaching allegations. It concluded the record was sufficiently comprehensive to make the necessary findings of fact and apply the law proportionately, expeditiously and less expensively than a trial, while recognizing the Charter implications for vulnerable litigants.
conclusion: There was no genuine issue requiring a trial for the s. 74(2)(h) and (k) grounds; summary judgment was the just, proportionate means of resolution.

issue: Were the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(k) because the Father was unavailable to exercise custodial rights?
facts: The Father was subject to bail conditions barring contact with the children arising from sexual offence charges involving their half-sister G.S. He had not sought to vary those conditions, offered no explanation, and had not seen the children in over two years. The care arrangements were made by FACS, and he proposed instead that the children live with his sister without explaining why that served their best interests.
rule: Section 74(2)(k) CYFSA: a child is in need of protection where the parent is unavailable to exercise custodial rights and has not made adequate provision for the child's care. Unavailability is an objective determination independent of subjective intention (Children's Aid Society of Kingston (City) v. H.); incarceration or comparable constraints can trigger the analogous predecessor provision, s. 37(2)(i) CFSA (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. C.T.).
application: Although not incarcerated, the Father's unremedied bail conditions rendered him unable to exercise custodial rights for over two years, and he had made no adequate provision for the children's care beyond arrangements FACS itself made. The court rejected his explanation blaming the Mother and G.S., noting he and his family had done little to promote a relationship with the children.
conclusion: The children were found in need of protection under s. 74(2)(k).

issue: Were the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(h) due to a risk of serious emotional harm caused by the Father?
facts: The children reported the Father's degrading treatment of their half-sister G.S. (calling her a 'slut', 'ho', 'liar'), his stalking behaviour, involving them in that conduct (creating social media accounts, filming with a dashcam), erratic and frightening driving, appearing naked before S.R.S., and fear that he would 'turn on' them as he did with G.S. No expert report on emotional harm was filed.
rule: Section 74(2)(h) CYFSA requires a risk of serious emotional harm (of the kinds in s. 74(2)(f)) causally connected to the parent's conduct (Children's Aid Society of Algoma v. A.B.). A clinical diagnosis or expert evidence is not mandatory; the court may draw inferences and take judicial notice from a panoply of evidence (Chukwunomso v. Ransome; Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S.A.P., 2020 ONCA 208). The children's statements are admissible under the state-of-mind hearsay exception (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. N.N.).
application: The court relied on the children's consistent statements to show their state of mind — fear of the Father, experience of him as unstable and erratic — and found the risk of serious emotional harm, including anxiety, causally connected to his conduct. Having not seen him in over two years and being clearly frightened, the children would likely suffer emotional harm if returned.
conclusion: The children were found in need of protection under s. 74(2)(h).

issue: Were the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(d) due to a risk of sexual abuse or exploitation?
facts: FACS relied on the Father's prior sexual assault conviction, the pending charges involving G.S., his statements about G.S., and his appearing naked before S.R.S. The children denied being touched. The only evidence of the details of the alleged offences against G.S. was worker D.W.'s account of witnessing G.S.'s police interview; G.S. swore an affidavit but declined to detail the assaults.
rule: Section 74(2)(d) CYFSA: a child is in need of protection where there is a risk of sexual abuse or exploitation as described in s. 74(2)(c). Hearsay must satisfy the principled exception (necessity and reliability) of R. v. Khan, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 531.
application: D.W.'s recounting of G.S.'s allegations, if offered for their truth, was hearsay; because G.S. had sworn an affidavit, the evidence was not 'necessary' and the Khan exception did not apply. There was thus no admissible direct evidence of the alleged offences. The Father and his supporting deponents raised sufficient disputed material facts that this ground could not be resolved summarily.
conclusion: The court declined to find the children in need of protection under s. 74(2)(d) on the summary judgment motion.

issue: What disposition and access orders were in the children's best interests?
facts: The children consistently expressed wishes to remain with their Mother, to have no forced contact with the Father, and to maintain a relationship with their half-sister G.S. The Mother was described as protective and supportive; FACS raised no protection concerns about G.S. The Father remained subject to no-contact bail conditions.
rule: Sections 101-102 CYFSA govern disposition where a child is in need of protection, with best interests (s. 74(3)) as the governing principle; s. 105(2) requires an access order unless contact is not in the child's best interests, and s. 104(1) permits sibling access orders. The child's views and wishes must be given due weight per s. 74(3)(a) and Article 12 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (Ontario (Children's Lawyer) v. Ontario (IPC), 2018 ONCA 559).
application: Weighing the s. 74(3) factors — the children's consistent mature wishes, the Mother as a protective factor, their need for stability and continuity, the risk of harm if returned to the Father, and the effects of delay — the court placed the children with the Mother under s. 102. Access to the Father was ordered in accordance with the children's wishes and at the Mother's discretion; sibling access to G.S. was likewise ordered.
conclusion: Final order placing the children with the Mother under s. 102, with access to the Father and to G.S. governed by the children's wishes and the Mother's discretion.

issue: Did Aldo Occhionero have the mental capacity required to make a valid will on February 25, 2014?
facts: Aldo, aged 76 and dying of terminal stomach cancer, signed a will three months before his death leaving everything to his sister Rina, with whom he had recently gone to live. Evidence from his wife, son, a domestic aide and a friend described marked cognitive and behavioural deterioration through 2013-2014 (disorientation, hiding, self-harm, incoherence). His hospital chart (CH Verdun, Feb. 5-14, 2014) recorded confusion and disorientation as to time, place and person on Feb. 5 and Feb. 11, needing full assistance to dress. The expert geriatric physician, Dr. Brock, opined Aldo probably suffered moderate-to-severe dementia and lacked capacity. The notary who prepared and took the will spent only 10-15 minutes with Aldo and did not verify capacity or know of his health history.
rule: A testator must have sufficient memory, comprehension and judgment to understand the nature and consequences of the act — knowing the nature and extent of assets, the nature of the deed, the identity of and relationship with beneficiaries, and being able to relate and remember these factors (criteria drawn from Barette/Duguay). Capacity is presumed, but once that presumption is rebutted the party upholding the will bears the burden of proving capacity (Caron c. Forest (Succession de), 2010 QCCS 2604).
application: The medical records and corroborated lay testimony rebutted the presumption of capacity. Dr. Brock's uncontradicted expert opinion, consistent with the CH Verdun chart, established probable dementia with an estimated MMSE score of 8-15 even on good days. Rina produced no contrary expertise, and her account of a normal, healthy Aldo conflicted with the medical file and was found not credible. The notary's brief, uninformed meeting could not establish capacity. Rina failed to prove that Aldo had regained sufficient capacity by February 25.
conclusion: Aldo lacked the capacity to make a valid will; the will is null on this ground.

issue: Was the will the product of undue influence exercised by the sister/sole beneficiary?
facts: After Aldo moved in with Rina on February 3, 2014, Rina concealed his hospitalization and terminal diagnosis from his wife and children, refused Francesca's requests to see or speak with him, threatened Francesca ('my family will destroy yours'), and had a lawyer's letter sent demanding Francesca cease contact. Rina and her family were constantly at his bedside while his wife and children were kept away. She repeatedly denigrated Francesca, Lisa and Gianni to the social worker and medical staff in Aldo's presence. The will, made through Rina's son contacting the notary, named Rina sole heir and liquidator, despite Aldo never having excluded his family over the prior 30 years.
rule: The party alleging undue influence bears the burden of proof. Undue influence is akin to fraud — reprehensible manoeuvres aimed at orienting a person toward a gift or legacy not otherwise granted; the court must be satisfied such conduct determined the testator's intentions. The situation is assessed globally, considering the testator's age, health, isolation, denigration of loved ones, and the circumstances of execution; it may be proven by presumption (Gatti c. Barbosa Rodrigues, 2011 QCCS 6734).
application: The evidence showed Rina deliberately isolated a sick, frail and vulnerable Aldo, kept his family in ignorance, and fed him and third parties false, denigrating accounts of his wife and children. That Aldo never excluded his family across three decades but did so only once Rina took control of his affairs supported the inference that the will reflected her influence rather than his true intentions. The court was convinced Rina exercised undue influence to become sole beneficiary.
conclusion: The will is also null on the ground of undue influence.

issue: Did the June 1980 letter of commitment and subsequent discussions create a binding fixed-term contract requiring no notice, or an indefinite hiring requiring reasonable notice?
facts: When the three Jewish schools were amalgamated under the defendant Board in 1980, Mr. Gilman, principal of the I.L. Peretz School, received a letter dated June 26, 1980 stating a 'Term of Contract' from September 1, 1980 to June 30, 1983 with set salaries, but expressly noting a formal contract would follow. Gilman accepted the letter subject to negotiation of a formal written contract covering benefits, notice of termination and renewal (like the contract later given to principal Cohen). No formal contract was ever negotiated or signed; Gilman continued as principal and drew the stated salaries until June 30, 1983.
rule: Where documents relied on as a contract contemplate execution of a further contract, it is a question of construction whether that further contract is a condition of the bargain or merely a desire as to how an agreed transaction will proceed (Von Hatzfeldt-Wildenburg v. Alexander, [1912] 1 Ch. 284 (C.A.)). An agreement leaving critical terms to future negotiation is no contract or only an agreement to agree (May and Butcher v. R., [1929] All E.R. 679 (H.L.); National Bowling and Billiards v. Double Diamond Bowling Supply (1961), 27 D.L.R. (2d) 342 (B.C.S.C.)). Acceptance by conduct must be absolute and unequivocal, judged by what a reasonable person would believe (Welton Tool Rental Ltd. v. Douglas Aircraft Co.). A contract of service of indefinite duration contains an implied term of reasonable notice negatived only by clear words (Bagley v. Gustavson International Drilling Co.; Chadburn v. Sinclair Canada Oil Co.).
application: The Court found Gilman's acceptance of the letter of commitment was conditional on negotiation of a formal contract containing additional substantive terms (pension, insurance, notice of termination and resignation). That condition was never fulfilled, so no binding fixed-term contract on the letter's terms arose. Continuing to work and accepting the salaries did not amount to an absolute and unequivocal acceptance, because Gilman had made clear his acceptance was conditional and never withdrew that condition, and Dr. Isler acknowledged the Board intended to draw up the formal contract but 'never got around to it'. What existed was a contract of service of indefinite duration carrying an implied term of reasonable notice.
conclusion: There was no fixed-term contract; Gilman was employed under an indefinite hiring and was entitled to reasonable notice of termination.

issue: What was the appropriate length of reasonable notice and the resulting damages?
facts: Gilman, 41, held a B.A. and B.Ed., had been principal since 1977. The predecessor school board had a practice of giving about ten months' notice due to the difficulty of finding work in the Jewish school system. The comparable principal, Mr. Cohen, was given a contract terminable on six months' notice, and Gilman said he wanted a contract like Cohen's. Gilman ultimately sought and obtained work outside the Jewish system (Winnipeg School Division). Clear notice of dismissal came May 20, 1983, effective at the end of the school year (June 30, 1983); he received just over one month's notice. His 1982-83 salary was $43,200.
rule: Reasonable notice is assessed by asking what the parties would have agreed to had they addressed the notice question at the time of hiring (Lazarowicz v. Orenda Engines, [1961] O.R. 141 (C.A.)).
application: Applying the Lazarowicz test, the Court reasoned the Board, having given Cohen only six months, was unlikely to agree to more for Gilman, who himself wanted terms similar to Cohen's. The rationale for the predecessor board's ten-month practice (scarcity of parochial-school work) was diminished because Gilman was willing to and did look outside that system. Six months' notice was reasonable. Gilman received just over one month's notice, so he was short about five months. Five months of his $43,200 salary is $21,600, rounded to $21,000 given he received slightly more than one month.
conclusion: Reasonable notice was six months; damages were assessed at $21,000 plus costs.

issue: Did the Facebook post constitute actionable defamation?
facts: On June 21, 2017 Mr. Jamieson posted on his Facebook wall (with roughly 600 friends, many in the same industry) a 'hypothetical' statement that his 50/50 business partner had been stealing from the company and walked off with a hundred grand in receivables. Three acquaintances of Mr. Hawkins swore they immediately understood the post to refer to him.
rule: Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61: a plaintiff must prove (1) the words were defamatory (tend to lower reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person), (2) the words referred to the plaintiff, and (3) they were published to at least one other person; falsity and damage are then presumed. Reference/identification test from Grant v. Cormier-Grant, 2001 CanLII 3041 (ON CA); defamatory meaning from Botiuk v. Toronto Free Press, 1995 CanLII 60 (SCC); publication of a Facebook post established per Mueller v. Livingstone, 2019 NBQB 28.
application: Although the post did not name Mr. Hawkins, Mr. Jamieson admitted referring to him and three acquaintances identified him, satisfying the reference element. Alleging theft imputes criminal/dishonest conduct that lowers the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society, satisfying the defamatory element. The post to some 600 Facebook friends, several of whom read and reacted, satisfied publication.
conclusion: All three Grant v. Torstar elements were met; the post was defamatory and actionable, shifting the onus to Mr. Jamieson to establish a defence.

issue: Was the allegation of 'stealing' (charitable donations and the Alma Club membership) substantially true?
facts: The 'stealing' allegation rested on a sharp 2016 increase in charitable donations ($21,765 committed in the last three months) and a $2,000 Alma Club membership purchased with XYZ funds but held personally by Mr. Hawkins. The donations were not concealed and Mr. Jamieson learned of them from the books; the Alma Club membership was known to Mr. Jamieson for over two years and required personal (not corporate) ownership.
rule: Grant v. Torstar (justification requires proof the statement was substantially true); Jones v. Barton, 2014 NBQB 42 citing R.E. Brown, The Law of Defamation in Canada (substantial truth, must meet the 'sting'); Ross v. Beutel, 2001 NBCA 62 (a sufficient substratum of fact).
application: Mr. Hawkins may have benefited from the donations, but they also benefited XYZ and Mr. Jamieson, were openly recorded and not pocketed. The Alma Club membership was openly known, required personal ownership, and warranted only a financial adjustment. Neither matter amounted to theft.
conclusion: Justification failed as to the 'stealing' allegation; there was no substantial truth supporting the imputation of theft.

issue: Was the allegation that the plaintiff 'walked off' with the receivables substantially true, given the Buy-Sell Agreement?
facts: Throughout negotiations both parties operated on the understanding that XYZ's net profits/receivables would be split 50-50 regardless of the share sale, with Mr. Hawkins repeatedly estimating each side's share at around $40,000. After Mr. Jamieson triggered the Buy-Sell (shotgun) Agreement and Hawkins agreed to buy his shares for $10,000, Hawkins delayed invoicing until after the May 1 closing, kept the company operating to at least October 2017, and asserted the shares were worth nil and that no profit distribution was owed.
rule: Grant v. Torstar (substantial truth); Bhasin v. Hrynew, 2014 SCC 71 (duty of honest performance / organizing principle of good faith); parol evidence rule and the collateral-contract exception per Michta v. Stewart, 2016 ONSC 5989 and Guttierrez v. Tropic International.
application: The Buy-Sell Agreement contained no 'entire agreement' clause and addressed only the purchase price and closing, not distribution of profits, so it did not extinguish the parties' collateral, non-inconsistent agreement to share net profits. Hawkins acted contrary to good faith by delaying invoices, keeping profits, and asserting a nil valuation he knew was false. There was substantial truth that Hawkins walked away with receivables he was not entitled to keep.
conclusion: Justification succeeded for this portion of the post; that statement was not defamation.

issue: What damages should be awarded?
facts: Mr. Hawkins, a 40-year communications professional and community leader, sought general damages around $50,000 plus aggravated and punitive damages up to the Rule 79 cap of $75,000, alleging threatening/extortionate conduct. He was not named in the post, which was removed the next day; Jamieson acted out of frustration over the profit dispute and was not cross-examined.
rule: Defamation Act, R.S.N.B. 2011, c.139, s. 2 (damage presumed); Hill v. Church of Scientology, 1995 CanLII 59 (damages at large; list of factors); Leenen v. CBC, 2000 CanLII 22380; comparators including Mueller v. Livingstone ($2,500), White v. Zed ($35,000), Boudreau v. McGraw ($14,000); aggravated damages require malice increasing injury and punitive damages require outrageous conduct (Whiten v. Pilot Insurance; Delphinium).
application: Given that Hawkins was not named, the post was removed the next day, and Hawkins's own refusal to honour the profit-sharing agreement provoked the outburst, a modest award was appropriate. No malice or genuinely threatening conduct was shown, and general damages sufficed; extortion was not established.
conclusion: General damages of $7,500 awarded; aggravated and punitive damages refused.

issue: Can Mr. Jamieson recover his share of the receivables from Mr. Hawkins personally by piercing the corporate veil?
facts: Jamieson counterclaimed for about $40,000 (his 50% of receivables), plus donations and the Alma Club amounts (share-price claim dropped). The profits were XYZ's to distribute; Jamieson held his interest through his numbered company, 621947 N.B. Inc.
rule: Salomon v. Salomon & Co.; Estate of Michael Burke v. Royal & Sun Alliance, 2011 NBCA 98 and Transamerica (corporate veil lifted only where those in control use the corporation as a shield for fraudulent or improper conduct); Shoppers Drug Mart v. 6470360 Canada Inc., 2014 ONCA 85 (distinguished); Business Corporations Act, S.N.B. 1981, c. B-9.1, s. 166 (oppression remedy).
application: The claim for profits was in reality a claim against XYZ, not Hawkins personally. Hawkins's conduct was a breach of contract/good faith, not fraud or misappropriation, so the veil could not be lifted merely to reach an equitable result. Jamieson did not plead unjust enrichment or veil-piercing, had an oppression remedy he did not use, and held his interest through his numbered company, which was the proper claimant.
conclusion: The corporate veil was not lifted; the counterclaim was dismissed.

issue: What is the meaning of 'place of worship' in s. 3(1), para. 3(i) of the Assessment Act, and what test governs the exemption?
facts: FLK, a religious organization, sought exemptions from property tax for various properties. The Assessment Act exempts land owned by a religious organization that is 'a place of worship and the land used in connection with it', but does not define 'worship' or 'place of worship'.
rule: Under s. 3(1), para. 3(i) of the Assessment Act, a place of worship is exempt. 'Worship' has been defined (Re Singh and City of Sudbury) as reverence or veneration paid to a being or power regarded as supernatural or divine, displayed through appropriate acts, rites or ceremonies. Whether a location qualifies is determined by the 'primary purpose' test — an objective determination of the principal purpose for which the land is used and occupied (Buenavista on the Rideau; Diocese of Toronto Camps v. MPAC). The interpretive threshold is a question of law reviewed for correctness; the characterization of activities on the properties is a question of mixed fact and law reviewable only for palpable and overriding error.
application: The court accepted the dictionary-based definition of 'worship' (which FLK did not contest) and the agreed 'primary purpose' test. It confirmed that whether the disputed properties are places of worship is a question of mixed fact and law attracting appellate deference on the factual findings. The court rejected FLK's suggestion that the courts below had applied an unduly narrow, Judeo-Christian or 'strict construction' definition, finding the Divisional Court correctly used 'strict construction' as a contrast term describing the rigour of the primary purpose test rather than a rule of statutory interpretation.
conclusion: The governing framework is the ordinary meaning of 'worship' combined with the objective 'primary purpose' test; the application judge did not err in the legal test she applied.

issue: Do FLK's tai chi classes at the satellite sites constitute 'worship' making those sites exempt places of worship, and is the inquiry focused on participants or organizers?
facts: The 19 satellite sites are predominantly used for tai chi classes that look virtually identical to secular tai chi, taught by volunteers who need not be Taoists, with no prayer or chanting in beginner instruction, though sites contain some religious iconography and are also used for Taoist chanting. MPAC conceded FLK sincerely believes the practice of FLK Taoist Tai Chi at its consecrated properties is worship.
rule: Per Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47, courts assess only the sincerity of a claimant's religious belief and do not judge its validity. However, whether an activity is 'worship' under the Assessment Act is a legal question, and not every religiously motivated activity is 'worship'. The dictionary definitions focus the inquiry on the intentions of the participant; the burden lies on the applicant to establish the primary purpose of the property is worship (analogy drawn to Keewaydin Camps, assessing purpose from campers' perspective).
application: The court accepted that persons who sincerely believe their own performance of tai chi is a spiritual act are worshipping, but rejected FLK's proposition that participants worship regardless of their own awareness simply because organizers view the classes as religious. The definition of 'worship' focuses on the participant's intention. Given evidence that the classes were indistinguishable from secular tai chi, that instructors were not required to be Taoists, and that religious character would not be apparent to ordinary attendees, the application judge was entitled to be unsatisfied that participants predominantly attended for worship. Her finding that the sites were used in an 'evangelical' (promotional) way was supported by the record. These were factual findings entitled to deference.
conclusion: The satellite sites are not 'places of worship'; the appeal on this issue fails.

issue: Are the Contemplative Garden and sales area at the International Centre exempt as places of worship or land used in connection with worship?
facts: The Contemplative Garden contains religious statues and is used for private prayer, with organized public ceremonies held only three times a year. The sales area is a retail store selling FLK materials, logo merchandise, honey and maple syrup.
rule: The primary purpose test governs; land is exempt if primarily used for worship or, for connected land, if sufficiently closely linked to worship occurring elsewhere (s. 3(1), para. 3(i)). Grounds used for private prayer but not formal public worship are not places of worship (Holy Theotokos Convent; Les Sœurs de La Visitation D'Ottawa).
application: The Contemplative Garden was not primarily used for organized worship — thrice-yearly ceremonies fell short, and the application judge properly treated it as analogous to convent grounds used for private prayer in Holy Theotokos Convent. The sales area's primary purpose was commercial selling, which is not worship, and many items (e.g., honey) had no connection to worship, so it was not 'land used in connection with' worship. These fact-specific determinations disclosed no reversible error.
conclusion: Both the Contemplative Garden and the sales area are taxable; the appeal on these issues fails.

issue: On a motion under art. 165(4) or art. 54.1 C.C.P., may the plaintiff's action be terminated at a preliminary stage?
facts: Following the water-ski boating accident and examinations on discovery before defence, the defendant conjointe de fait and the defendant insurance broker each moved to dismiss the plaintiff's $2,000,000 claim as unfounded in law and to have it declared abusive.
rule: On a motion to dismiss under art. 165(4) C.C.P. the judge confines analysis to the facts alleged and exhibits, exercises great restraint, and dismisses only where the situation is 'clear, evident and unequivocal' (Le Breton v. Dubé, 2008 QCCS 5225; Grenier v. Ladouceur). Prescription-based dismissal is granted only where the ground is clear and precise. Under art. 54.1 C.C.P. the court may consider examinations on discovery, but must exercise heightened prudence, particularly where dismissal of the demand is sought, and requires 'blameworthy conduct' (Acadia Subaru c. Michaud, 2011 QCCA 1037).
application: The court stressed that a plaintiff may cure gaps in discovery at trial and that the evaluation of contested facts must be left to the trial judge. Because key questions of law and fact remained live on each ground raised, none of the moving parties met the demanding threshold for terminating the action prematurely.
conclusion: The preliminary-motion framework did not permit dismissal; the motions were assessed against these standards and ultimately failed.

issue: Is prescription governed by Canadian maritime law or the Civil Code of Québec, and if maritime law applies, which limitation period applies and from when?
facts: The accident occurred July 4, 2008 on the Rivière-des-Prairies, a navigable inland waterway; the defendant drove the plaintiff's water-ski boat and struck him in the water after he fell from a towed surf board. The action was instituted June 13, 2012.
rule: Tort liability from negligent operation of a pleasure craft on Canadian inland navigable waters falls within Canadian maritime law and exclusive federal jurisdiction; provincial statutes of general application (incl. art. 2925 C.C.Q.) do not apply (Whitbread v. Walley, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1273; Ordon v. Grail, [1998] 3 S.C.R. 437; Frugoli, J.E. 2009-1312). The Marine Liability Act ss. 6, 14 and 23 govern only dependants' claims and vessel-to-vessel collisions. Section 140 M.L.A. (in force Sept. 21, 2009) imposes a three-year limitation for all other maritime claims. Limitation provisions are procedural and any ambiguity is resolved in favour of the plaintiff (Jumbo Motors; Sullivan on the Construction of Statutes).
application: Because this was neither a dependants' claim nor a vessel collision, ss. 6, 14 and 23 did not apply (following Lebel and Beaulne v. Martel, 2010 QCCS 5550; disagreeing with Deschambault, Lemieux and the s. 39 Federal Courts Act approach in Lebel). Before s. 140 came into force no maritime limitation applied to such a claim; a court cannot impose one where Parliament had not. From Sept. 21, 2009 the three-year s. 140 period ran, fairly giving the plaintiff three years and the defendants a limitation where none had existed.
conclusion: Canadian maritime law governs; s. 140 M.L.A.'s three-year limitation ran from Sept. 21, 2009 to Sept. 21, 2012.

issue: Is the plaintiff's action prescribed?
facts: The action was instituted June 13, 2012, within the three-year period running from September 21, 2009.
rule: Section 140 Marine Liability Act; procedural nature of new limitation provisions.
application: Since the s. 140 three-year period ran from Sept. 21, 2009 to Sept. 21, 2012 and the action was filed June 13, 2012, it was timely. The court added that even if a limitation had run from the accident, whether an 'impossibility to act' (akin to art. 2904 C.C.Q.) suspended it was a mixed question of fact and law: the plaintiff alleged (supported by neuropsychologist Simard's July 15, 2010 report and discovery) that his cognitive injuries prevented him from comprehending fault, prejudice and their linkage (Christensen v. Roman Catholic Archbishop of Quebec, 2010 SCC 44), giving an arguable case for the trial judge.
conclusion: The claim was not prescribed; prescription could not support dismissal.

issue: Does the alleged renunciation (Exhibit R-1) bar the action on a preliminary motion?
facts: The plaintiff gave contradictory discovery evidence about signing a document renouncing his right to sue the defendant; he later contested his signature by art. 89 C.C.P. affidavit and alleged in his Re-Amended Introductory Motion that R-1 was invalid, that he did not sign it or was incapable, and that he was exploited.
rule: Under art. 165(4) and art. 54.1 C.C.P., dismissal requires that the plaintiff's case clearly have no chance of success; a plaintiff's right to lead evidence supporting pleaded explanations cannot be prematurely terminated.
application: Although defence counsel argued the plaintiff's responses were 'invraisemblables et incompatibles,' the plaintiff pleaded facts (para. 21.8 ff.) which, if believed, could invalidate R-1. The validity of the renunciation was a serious issue requiring a full hearing of witnesses before the trial judge.
conclusion: Renunciation could not ground dismissal; the motions failed on this basis.

issue: Do the pleadings and discovery disclose a possible fault by the insurance broker?
facts: The broker placed a JEVCO policy (2007) then an AVIVA policy in force at the time of the accident but delivered four days after it; both excluded personal injury to the insured and limited water-sports coverage. The plaintiff, a self-described insurance neophyte, alleged the broker failed to advise him and obtain coverage adapted to his water-sports needs.
rule: Article 28 of the Loi sur la distribution des produits et services financiers imposes a duty to describe the product, relate it to identified needs and explain exclusions. An insurance broker is a professional with a duty to inform and counsel, must proactively raise questions the client does not, and cannot simply act as a conduit (Fletcher v. MPIC, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 191; 125057 Canada Inc. c. Rondeau, 2011 QCCS 94).
application: The broker argued the plaintiff received the civil-liability coverage he requested (art. 2500 C.C.Q. reserving it for injured third parties). But what advice was actually given, and whether the broker could shift responsibility onto the insured via its letters, were mixed questions of fact and law for trial; the second policy's letter was received only after the accident. The broker had not shown the pleadings disclosed no fault or abuse.
conclusion: The broker failed to establish an absence of cause of action; its motions were dismissed.

issue: Should the statement of claim be amended under rule 26.01 to accord with the jury verdict, where the jury awarded more than the amounts pleaded?
facts: The plaintiff had pleaded $350,000 in general damages and $250,000 in punitive damages. The jury awarded $400,000 in general and aggravated damages and $1,000,000 in punitive damages against the Estate. On consent, no range for punitive damages had been put to the jury. The Estate opposed increasing the punitive claim to match the verdict.
rule: Rule 26.01 of the Rules of Civil Procedure is mandatory: an amendment 'shall' be permitted unless it causes prejudice that cannot be compensated by costs or an adjournment. A pleading may be amended to accord with a jury verdict (Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto (1992); Padfield v. Martin, 2003 CanLII 36239 (ON CA)). A verdict higher than the amount claimed does not, by itself, establish prejudice.
application: The court found Hill controlling: the fact that the award exceeded the pleaded amount was not itself prejudice, and the parties had jointly left the punitive quantum to the jury without a range. No cognizable prejudice was shown; the remainder of the Estate's argument went to the appropriateness of the award, addressed under the punitive-damages motion. C.O. v. Williamson was distinguished as a judge-alone case with no pleading issue.
conclusion: Leave to amend the relief sought for both general and punitive damages was granted.

issue: Should the jury's $1,000,000 punitive damages award against the Estate be set aside or reduced?
facts: The abuser, Peter Kaczmarczyk, was dead; he had been criminally charged with sexual assault and released on bail with conditions, but the case never went to trial and there was no conviction. Expert Dr. Klassen testified it was the worst case of child sexual abuse he had encountered. The Estate argued deterrence was moot given the abuser's death, that charges and bail conditions amounted to punishment, and that the amount was out of step with comparable awards.
rule: A trial judge may disregard a jury's answer only where there is no evidence to support it or where the answer cannot in law found a judgment (Hill; McLean v. Knox, 2013 ONCA 357; CNR v. Lancia, [1949] S.C.R. 177; rule 52.08). Punitive damages serve retribution, deterrence of the wrongdoer AND of others, and denunciation (Whiten v. Pilot Insurance, 2002 SCC 18); the criminal law is the primary vehicle of punishment, but a conviction does not bar punitive damages (Victims' Bill of Rights, s. 4(4)). Appellate, not trial, courts adjust quantum, and only where it is a wholly erroneous estimate (Koukounakis v. Stainrod).
application: Deterrence of others and denunciation still applied despite the abuser's death; P.M. v. Evangelista was unpersuasive for lacking analysis. Charges and bail conditions, absent any finding of guilt or public denunciation, were not 'punishment,' and in any event were never put to the jury to weigh. There was ample evidence—repeated abuse of a young child by a person in a parental role, characterized by the expert as the worst he had seen, with no punishment or acknowledgement—to support the award. Even if the judge thought it too high, adjusting quantum was the Court of Appeal's role. The award compensates the victim and does not 'punish' heirs, who take only the residue after debts.
conclusion: No basis to interfere; the punitive damages award was upheld.

issue: Should CCAST be held only severally (or 0%) liable rather than jointly and severally liable with the Estate?
facts: The jury found both defendants liable and apportioned 75% to the Estate and 25% to CCAST (punitive damages being solely the Estate's). CCAST argued the Negligence Act applies only to fault or negligence and not to Kaczmarczyk's intentional/deliberate conduct, and that the heinous nature of the abuse should eclipse its own negligence entirely.
rule: Section 1 of the Negligence Act makes concurrent tortfeasors jointly and severally liable to the plaintiff (Martin v. Listowel Memorial Hospital). Tortfeasors are concurrent where their acts 'run together to produce the same damage' (Lawson v. Viersen, 2012 ONCA 25). 'Fault' includes intentional wrongdoing, not just negligence (Bell v. Cope, adopted in Bell Canada v. Cope (Sarnia) Ltd., 1980 CanLII 1868 (ON CA); cf. Blackwater v. Plint, 2005 SCC 58). Apportionment is primarily for the trier of fact (Ingles v. Tutkaluk Construction, 2000 SCC 12).
application: Although the defendants' conduct differed and was separated in time, the jury accepted CCAST's negligence was causative of the plaintiff's psychological and physiological harm, making them concurrent tortfeasors. Hollebone v. Barnard's narrow reading of 'fault' was rejected in Ontario; intentional torts fall within 'fault,' so CCAST could be jointly liable with an intentional tortfeasor. The obiter suggestions in Rabideau and Gerling Global that one tortfeasor's conduct might eclipse another's were not fully developed and not determinative. Reducing CCAST to 0% would set aside the jury's apportionment, which had a factual and legal foundation.
conclusion: CCAST remains jointly and severally liable; no reduction to several liability or to 0%.

issue: What rate and commencement date apply to pre-judgment interest on the general damages and past-income-loss awards?
facts: Pre-judgment interest applied to the $400,000 general award and the $940,000 past income loss (not to punitive or future-care awards). The plaintiff sought interest from 1964; the defendants argued for 2010 or 2019, sought to reduce the 5% non-pecuniary rate and to halve the 2% pecuniary rate, and relied on CCAST's finances, late commencement (2019), and offers to settle.
rule: Courts of Justice Act s. 128 governs pre-judgment interest, running from when the cause of action arose; s. 128(2)/rule 53.10 set 5% for non-pecuniary personal-injury damages; s. 128(3) requires six-monthly calculation on past pecuniary loss at the bank rate when the action was commenced (2% in 2019); s. 128(4)(a) excludes punitive damages. Under s. 130 the court may vary interest only where 'just,' the presumptive rate governing absent evidence of market rates (Henry v. Zaitlen, 2024 ONCA 614; Aubin v. Soloway JCC, 2024 ONCA 615; MacLeod v. Marshall, 2019 ONCA 842). In historical assault cases the cause of action arises when the plaintiff connects the abuse to the harm, presumptively on first seeking therapeutic assistance (M.(K.) v. M.(H.), [1992] 3 S.C.R. 6; C.O. v. Williamson; L.R. v. S.P., 2019 ONSC 1737).
application: Because the pre-1989 Judicature Act required written notice (none given) and no interest ran on unliquidated damages before 1977 (Heeney v. Best), interest could not run from 1964. The cause of action arose when Ms. Evans first sought therapeutic help—June 1992, when she was hospitalized and disclosed the abuse. The defendants produced no evidence of market interest rates (only the published pre-judgment rates), so no downward adjustment was warranted; there was no advance payment, no relevant medical-disclosure or delay issue, CCAST's charitable finances were no basis to deviate, and delay in commencing the action does not reduce compensatory interest (Royal Bank v. Roband). Borland v. Muttersbach did not require halving the pecuniary rate.
conclusion: Interest was set at 5% on the general damages and 2% on the income loss, both commencing June 1992, calculated bi-yearly on the income loss (at 71% of the expert's figure). The verdict was endorsed and judgment granted.

issue: Should third-party service providers and assessors be added as parties to a concluded family law proceeding and compelled to disclose information?
facts: After a seven-day trial and a final judgment released April 26, 2010, Mr. Katz served an 'Enforcement Motion' on Jewish Family & Child Services, the assessor Linda Chodos and Family Solutions, Associated Hebrew Schools, Jewish Vocational Services and TanenbaumCHAT, seeking to add them as parties and compel disclosure and written explanations of their conclusions.
rule: A children's aid society or similar service provider should not be added as a party to a family law proceeding, to avoid fettering its discretion to act freely and without fear in matters concerning the protection of children (L. v. L., 1990 CanLII 12276 (ON CTGD), 31 R.F.L. (3d) 320). Service providers and assessors must be free to act without fear of retaliation by an unsuccessful litigant.
application: The court found the relief was either outside the statutory framework or, as to adding the named respondents as parties, wholly without merit. Permitting a disgruntled party to relitigate lost issues by attacking those who tendered evidence or services would bring the administration of justice into disrepute. The named organizations were not parties and there was no jurisdiction to make orders against them.
conclusion: The request to add the parties and compel disclosure was refused; the motion failed on the substantive analysis.

issue: Was the motion procedurally deficient for want of an originating process and case conference?
facts: Mr. Katz brought the motion without an originating process or case conference, did not seek a variation of the prior final order, and served the organizations only about seven working days before the hearing.
rule: Rule 14(4) of the Family Law Rules requires a case conference before certain steps; a motion must be founded upon an application in which the relief claimed can be grounded.
application: There was no application before the court in which the relief claimed could be founded, and no case conference had been held per Rule 14(4). On this basis alone the motion could be dismissed.
conclusion: The motion was procedurally defective and dismissed on that ground as well.

issue: Should the respondent be restrained from bringing further motions without leave of the court?
facts: This was Mr. Katz's fifth motion in five months following the final judgment, comprising basket motions blaming solicitors, the assessor and the children's physician, and using the court process for an improper purpose against non-party, largely not-for-profit organizations.
rule: Rule 14(21) of the Family Law Rules permits the court, where a party makes numerous motions without merit to delay the case, add to costs, or otherwise abuse the court's process, to order that the party bring no further motions without the court's permission.
application: Given the repeated meritless motions and misuse of the process, the court found it entirely appropriate to make such an order to protect the applicant, the remaining minor child, and the not-for-profit respondents from spurious litigation.
conclusion: The court ordered that Mr. Katz take no further steps in the proceeding without leave of the court, and awarded costs to the responding organizations.

issue: Can a court strike select alleged defamatory meanings under Rule 19(24)(a) where the words are not reasonably capable of bearing the pleaded meanings?
facts: The plaintiff, a Regional Director of the Capital Regional District, sued over letters, a newspaper article and a circular authored by defendants Wehmann, Thornton and Harlow criticizing his handling of land-use voting procedures. The plaintiff pleaded numerous defamatory meanings/innuendoes for each publication. The defendants applied to strike only select alleged meanings, not the entire claims.
rule: Rule 19(24)(a) permits striking the whole or any part of a pleading that discloses no reasonable claim; the test is whether it is 'plain and obvious' the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action (Hunt v. Carey; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress). Whether words are capable of a defamatory meaning is a question of law (Lions Gate Marketing v. Used Car Dealers Assn.). The court assesses whether reasonable persons of ordinary intelligence would read the words as lowering the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society (Sturdy v. Canada). Facts pleaded are assumed true, but the court still determines the legal question of capacity to bear the alleged meaning.
application: The court held Rule 19(24) authorizes culling select meanings without striking an entire claim, consistent with the object of the Rules (Rule 1(5)) and Hemming v. Newton. Rejecting the plaintiff's argument that capacity must be presumed or reserved for a Rule 34 hearing, the court analysed each publication. Wehmann's 'conjecture' and prospective/speculative wording could not support meanings that Lund was uninformed, exercised influence for campaign supporters, or committed a s. 122 Criminal Code breach of trust. Thornton's warnings of future harm, references to unrelated events, and political criticism could not bear meanings of causing economic strife, unfitness for office, deceitful/fraudulent use of office, lying about a map, or criminal breach of trust. Harlow's criticism of political manoeuvring could not bear meanings of deceit, political corruption, self-interest, or arbitrary/capricious conduct.
conclusion: The court struck subparagraphs 17 a and c, 19 e, 21 b and c, 23 a and b, 25 b, and 27 a–d as disclosing no reasonable claim, leaving the remaining meanings to proceed.

issue: Does paragraph 32 plead special damages requiring particulars under Rule 19(16)?
facts: Paragraph 32 alleged the statements 'disparage the Plaintiff in his trade and calling and have caused a loss of custom in the Plaintiff's private business.' In response to a demand for particulars, the plaintiff gave only the name and nature of the business, relying on Brown v. Cole and Pressler to argue particulars were unnecessary where economic loss cannot be proven.
rule: Special damages must be specifically pleaded and proven (Botiuk v. Toronto Free Press; Pootlass v. Pootlass) and are defined as any material or temporal loss capable of being estimated in money. General economic loss may be an independent head of general damages where loss lacks the precision needed for special damages (WeGo Kayaking v. Sewid). Rule 19(16) allows the court to order particulars.
application: Although the plaintiff did not use the words 'special damages', paragraph 32 alleged pecuniary loss related to his business, which the court found amounted to a claim for special damages. Accordingly the defendant was entitled to particulars.
conclusion: The court ordered the plaintiff, under Rule 19(16), to provide within 10 days the amount of loss, dates, names of customers, and which losses were caused by each publication, failing which paragraph 32 would be struck — noting the plaintiff could still seek general damages for unprovable business loss.

issue: Does the plaintiff's claim fall within the two-year limitation period in s. 38 of the Trustee Act as a 'wrong to another in respect of his or her person'?
facts: Ms. Laljee claimed $750,000 (or the value of the estate) for care she provided to her late sister, Yasmin Peerwani, in reliance on promises that she would be compensated by the estate. She pleaded constructive trust and unjust enrichment, proprietary estoppel, quantum meruit and breach of contract.
rule: Section 38(2)-(3) of the Trustee Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. T.23 permits an action against a deceased's estate for a 'wrong to another in respect of his or her person or to another person's property' but bars it after two years from death. In Smallman v. Moore, [1948] S.C.R. 295 the Supreme Court held it is the nature of the injury, not the form of action, that governs; Roth v. Weston Estate (1997), 36 O.R. (3d) 513 (C.A.) and Ethier v. Raspberry applied this to care-for-compensation claims focused on the deceased's personal conduct.
application: Herman J. found the essence of Ms. Laljee's claim to be personal in nature, focused on the deceased's conduct, the personal duty allegedly owed to the plaintiff and the resulting personal consequences — mirroring Ethier, where identical restitutionary and contractual claims were held to be captured by s. 38.
conclusion: The claim is a 'wrong to another in respect of his or her person' within s. 38(2) and is therefore subject to the two-year limitation period.

issue: Is the s. 38 Trustee Act limitation displaced by the Limitations Act (former or new)?
facts: Ms. Peerwani died on April 22, 2003, when the former Limitations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.15 (six-year period) was in force; the new Limitations Act, 2002 came into effect afterward.
rule: Smith Estate v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (1998) held that death reduces an otherwise longer limitation to two years from death under s. 38; English Estate v. Tregal Holdings and Kramarz v. KMH Cardiology confirmed that s. 38 was not altered by the Limitations Act, 2002 and that its transition provisions do not apply to a limitation that pre-existed the new Act.
application: Applying this authority, the court held that the death of Ms. Peerwani engaged the two-year window in s. 38 rather than the general six-year period, and the new Act's transition rules did not revive a longer period.
conclusion: The two-year limitation period in the Trustee Act applies.

issue: Does the court have discretion to extend or suspend the s. 38 limitation, and can it be decided on this motion?
facts: Ms. Laljee sued more than three and a half years after death. She said she was ill and that her uncle, estate trustee Mr. Virani, led her to believe she would be compensated, telling her not to spend money on lawyers, and that a copy of the will was withheld from her father for three years. Mr. Virani deposed she knew the will's contents at all relevant times.
rule: In Waschkowski v. Hopkinson Estate (2000), 47 O.R. (3d) 370 (C.A.) the discoverability rule does not extend s. 38; the only period is two years. However, per Bikur Cholim v. Langston and Giroux Estate v. Trillium Health Centre, the equitable doctrine of fraudulent concealment can suspend the clock where (a) the parties are in a special relationship, (b) the defendant's conduct is unconscionable given that relationship, and (c) the defendant concealed the plaintiff's right of action. It prevents a limitation from operating as an instrument of injustice.
application: Discoverability could not assist Ms. Laljee, but fraudulent concealment might. On the conflicting affidavit evidence, the court could not determine whether a special relationship existed, whether Mr. Virani's conduct was unconscionable, or whether he concealed the right of action by assurances of compensation or by withholding the will. These were genuinely contested factual questions.
conclusion: Whether fraudulent concealment applies is a triable issue; the court could not find the action statute-barred, and the motion to dismiss was dismissed.

issue: Was there a genuine issue requiring a trial that would preclude summary judgment placing the children in extended society care?
facts: The children R.B. and M.B. had been in the society's care since August 2016, over two years and beyond the statutory timeline. The mother suffered repeated mental health crises, hospitalizations (some involuntary), and diagnoses of amphetamine-induced psychosis; she declined or failed to follow through with numerous supports offered by JFCS. The mother opposed summary judgment, arguing genuine issues (particularly her mental health diagnosis) required a trial.
rule: Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules; the two-step test in Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, as applied to child protection in Kawartha-Haliburton Children's Aid Society v. M.W., 2018 ONSC 2783. The court asks whether it can make necessary findings of fact, apply law to facts, and achieve a just, proportionate result summarily. Disposition governed by s. 101 CYFSA and best interests criteria in s. 74(3), preferring the least disruptive alternative.
application: The court found the uncontested and only baldly-denied evidence sufficient to decide disposition without resorting to the expanded fact-finding powers in subrule 16(6.1). Although the mother's precise diagnosis was disputed, the court focused on her undisputed behaviours and repeated hospitalizations rather than the cause; the mother offered only explanations and justifications for her conduct. Her plan lacked any air of reality given she had not seen the children since September 2017 and showed no insight or improvement. JFCS had made extensive, uncontested efforts to assist her, and no viable community/family placement existed. Extended society care was the least disruptive alternative serving the children's best interests.
conclusion: No genuine issue required a trial; summary judgment was granted placing R.B. and M.B. in the extended care of JFCS.

issue: If extended society care is ordered, is there a genuine issue requiring a trial regarding the mother's access to the children, and is such access in their best interests?
facts: The children love their mother, enjoyed visits, and consistently expressed a wish to return to her care, but access had been suspended since September 2017. Past visits featured the mother coaching the children against the foster parents, arguing with staff, attending in a distressed state, and other conduct causing the children anxiety. The mother sought reciprocal access.
rule: Sections 104 and 105(5)-(6) CYFSA: once a child is in extended society care, existing access orders terminate unless the person seeking access shows access is in the child's best interests, considering whether the relationship is beneficial and meaningful and whether access would impair future adoption opportunities; best interests factors in s. 74(3). The court reviewed post-CYFSA interpretations (T.S., 2018 ONCJ 411; C.H., 2018 ONCJ 453) adopting a flexible best-interests approach.
application: The court found the relationship meaningful to the children but not beneficial, because each contact carried a significant risk of emotional harm given the mother's unaddressed mental illness, her undermining conduct, and her breaches of orders. The mother possessed multiple attributes (poor impulse control, undermining alternate caregivers, dishonesty, litigiousness) recognized as likely to impair the children's future adoption. The children's wish to see their mother was outweighed by the risk to their stability and wellbeing.
conclusion: No trial was required; access was not in the children's best interests and no access order was made in the mother's favour (access to the maternal uncle S.B. was ordered at the society's discretion).

issue: Is there a genuine issue requiring a trial regarding the society's claim for a restraining order against the mother?
facts: The mother had obtained the foster home address, sent emergency services there, attended the foster home in breach of a restraining order (leading to a criminal charge), attended the children's school causing a lockdown, and repeatedly posted identifying information about the case online in violation of the CYFSA publication ban.
rule: Section 137 CYFSA permitting restraining orders; summary judgment principles under Rule 16 and Hryniak.
application: The court relied on the uncontested evidence of the mother's persistent breaches and concerning conduct, finding it justified a restraining order without a trial.
conclusion: A restraining order was granted restraining the mother from contact with the children and from attending specified locations except with the society's prior written approval.

issue: Did the plaintiffs prove a valid oral trust created in 1996 and payment of their capital contributions?
facts: In 1996 Mr. Cheema bought the Surrey property for $690,000. The three men agreed Cheema would hold legal title in trust with Mand and Gill each holding a 10% beneficial interest, conditional on paying 10% of the price and 10% of ongoing expenses. Gill produced a bank draft proving his $40,537.67 contribution; Mand had no documentation, and Cheema disputed that Mand paid.
rule: The onus of proving a valid trust lies on the party asserting it (Larochelle v. Soucie Estate). A trust requires the three certainties—intention, subject matter and objects—plus constitution by transfer of title (Warde v. Slatter; Larochelle). Certainty of intention may be inferred from surrounding circumstances and conduct. A plaintiff may prove a fact by reasonable inference from circumstantial evidence (Paguio v. Fraser; Angel Acres). Adverse inferences may follow from failure to produce material documents (Youyi; Le Soleil).
application: The parties agreed on the essential terms, satisfying the three certainties, and legal title vested in Cheema, constituting the trust. Although all three principal witnesses lacked credibility and Mand had no direct proof, the court drew an adverse inference from Cheema's failure to produce the September/October 1996 Vancity statements (which would have shown Mand's deposit) and relied on the parties' subsequent conduct—Mand's inclusion as a named beneficiary in all trust deeds, his ongoing involvement with the property, matching $2,500 payments in 2004, and Cheema's later delivery of financial statements—to infer Mand had paid.
conclusion: A validly constituted oral trust was created in September 1996 with Cheema as trustee and Cheema (80%), Mand (10%) and Gill (10%) as beneficiaries; both Mand and Gill satisfied the capital-contribution condition precedent, leaving only the ongoing condition subsequent to pay their share of expenses.

issue: When were Trust Agreement #2 and the Modification Agreement executed, and did they extinguish the plaintiffs' beneficial interest?
facts: Trust Agreement #1 was executed March 30, 2005. The defendants claimed Trust Agreement #2 and a Modification Agreement 'nullifying' the trust were signed the same day, extinguishing the plaintiffs' interest for non-payment. The plaintiffs said those documents were executed in 2016. None of the deeds recorded execution dates. The 2016 Binpal & Associates file, a June 17, 2016 reporting letter, a 2014 draft addendum, and Gill's 2016 email archive were key.
rule: A trustee is a fiduciary owing duties of good faith, loyalty, record-keeping and accounting (Boe v. Alexander; Pirani v. Pirani; Trustee Act). Where a trust arises from contract the two are indissociable (N-Krypt; Waters' Law of Trusts). A condition subsequent divesting a vested interest must be clearly identified in the instrument or the parties' intention, including the divesting event and consequence (Jack Estate; Canada Trust Co. v. Ontario (HRC)). Reasonable inferences may be drawn from proven facts; adverse inferences may be drawn for failure to call a material witness (Singh; Angel Acres).
application: Rejecting the evidence of Cheema, Mand, Gill and the interested family members, the court relied on the credible evidence of Ms. Mand and Mr. Binpal, the contemporaneous Binpal File and Gill email archive (including an identical misplaced signature block in the Modification Agreement) and drew an adverse inference from Cheema's failure to call Mr. Saini, finding Trust Agreement #2 and the Modification Agreement were executed after June 17, 2016. Even if signed in 2005, an out-of-order execution would not 'nullify' the trust. The deeds did not create a clear condition subsequent with a divesting event, and as fiduciary Cheema bore the duty to account and seek reimbursement; he could not rely on non-payment to divest the beneficiaries.
conclusion: Trust Agreement #2 and the Modification Agreement were executed after June 17, 2016 and did not nullify or extinguish the plaintiffs' beneficial interest; the plaintiffs retained a collective 20% beneficial interest.

issue: Was the plaintiffs' claim barred by the Limitation Act?
facts: The action was commenced in 2020. In their 2020 responses the defendants admitted Cheema held the property in trust for the plaintiffs; that admission was withdrawn with leave in June 2023 (Admissions RFJ). Cheema argued discovery occurred in 2005 or 2014.
rule: The basic limitation period is two years from discovery (s. 6, Limitation Act, S.B.C. 2012, c. 13). For a trust claim, discovery occurs when the beneficiary is fully aware injury has occurred, and the trustee bears the onus of proving discovery (s. 12; Ali v. Ali). The limitation period runs from an act by the trustee inconsistent with the beneficiary's interest (Ghag; Lennox v. Lennox).
application: The court did not accept that Cheema proved he told the plaintiffs in 2005 they were no longer participants, nor that they were fully aware of their claim in 2014 (Gill still received the 2016 appraisal). Because the defendants admitted the trust until the June 2023 withdrawal of admissions, the plaintiffs could not be found fully aware of a denial of the trust before then.
conclusion: The limitation period began to run only in June 2023; the claim was not time-barred and the Limitation Act defence failed.

issue: What remedies are the plaintiffs entitled to, including partition/sale and equitable compensation for the undisclosed leases?
facts: Cheema, without the plaintiffs' informed consent, leased the property to his company Transport Ltd. on triple-net leases from 2012 (renewed 2017 and 2022) at low rents, using it for truck parking that was not permitted under the property's agricultural zoning. The plaintiffs sought a declaration of trust, sale under the Partition of Property Act and equitable compensation based on market rents.
rule: A trustee needs the beneficiaries' informed written consent to deal with property (trust deed clauses 2(d),(h); Pirani). Equitable compensation is a loss-based, restitutionary remedy restoring the beneficiary's lost opportunity, assessed with hindsight; the presumed 'most favourable use' must be realistic (Southwind v. Canada). A co-owner/beneficiary with an immediate possessory interest may compel sale under ss. 2, 7 and 8 of the Partition of Property Act unless there is good reason to the contrary (Zackariuk; Pallot; Chung).
application: Cheema breached his fiduciary duty by leasing to his own company without informed consent, but the plaintiffs' claim to market truck-parking rents was not a realistic 'most favourable use' because truck parking was unauthorized and no arm's-length lease could be obtained. The court awarded the plaintiffs 20% of the gross lease payments Transport Ltd. should have paid, plus 20% of rental income from the home (July 2004–June 2007), less their 20% share of reasonably incurred expenses (to be quantified by a Registrar's reference), less mortgage/line-of-credit amounts and tax consequences. Because the trust deed gave the beneficiaries an immediate right to demand conveyance, they had standing to seek sale; holding less than 50%, they showed sale was more beneficial than partition given the parties' animosity.
conclusion: A declaration of trust was granted (each plaintiff 5%, Cheema 80%); the property is to be sold under the Partition of Property Act; the plaintiffs receive 20% of net proceeds and defined equitable compensation, subject to a Registrar's reference on expenses; costs deferred.

issue: Is correspondence passing between the solicitors for the parties subject to discovery in a libel action?
facts: In a $250,000 libel action arising from a newspaper article accusing the plaintiff of directing the killing of Slovakian Jews and likening him to Hitler, the plaintiff sought discovery of a series of letters exchanged between the parties' solicitors between October 1963 and July 1964. The Senior Master had refused to compel the defendants to reattend and answer questions about the correspondence.
rule: Discovery of correspondence between solicitors may be allowed where it is relevant (Rule 326). In a libel action the conduct of the defendants from publication to the moment of verdict may be considered by the jury (Gatley on Libel and Slander, 6th ed.). Any fact rationally probative of a material proposition is admissible unless caught by an exclusionary rule.
application: The court found the correspondence was potentially evidence of a refusal to apologize, of malice, motive and aggravation of damages — all relevant in a libel action where conduct up to verdict counts. Allowing discovery lets the parties explore the facts and circumstances surrounding the letters and determine whether any admissions were hypothetical or statements of the litigant's real position, ensuring the trial judge has all relevant facts.
conclusion: Discovery of the correspondence should be permitted; the appeal was allowed with costs.

issue: Does marking a letter 'without prejudice' conclusively protect that correspondence, and subsequent letters, from discovery and later use as an admission?
facts: Only the first letter of the series bore the words 'without prejudice.' The Senior Master had held that this stamped the entire chain as privileged. The letters showed settlement was at times contemplated, but also that the plaintiff's solicitor was skilfully developing his case to secure a refusal to apologize and evidence of malice, motive and aggravation.
rule: The 'without prejudice' shibboleth does not automatically protect a letter from later use as an admission (4 Wigmore, 2nd ed., paras. 1060-2). The exclusion rests on the notion of a hypothetical concession made to secure settlement, which does not represent the party's true belief. Under the rule of multiple or alternative admissibility, evidence inadmissible through one gateway may be admissible through another; 'without prejudice' correspondence may be admissible in various circumstances (Williston and Rolls, Civil Procedure, c. 16), such as where it is not a genuine settlement attempt but a repudiation, or where its main purpose is to threaten or malign. The trial judge retains discretion under the common law, the Evidence Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 151, and the Rules of Practice to admit or reject such statements.
application: The court held that the label was not conclusive; the real question is whether a party intended to concede a fact hypothetically to effect settlement or to declare a fact as really existing. Reading the letters, the court found sufficient material that a trial judge might allow to go to the jury, in whole or part, as admissions as to malice, motive or aggravation of damages, to be determined after hearing evidence in the jury's absence. Obtaining an answer on discovery gives no absolute right to read it to the jury, as admissibility remains within the trial judge's discretion.
conclusion: The 'without prejudice' designation did not bar discovery; the correspondence was discoverable, with admissibility left to the trial judge's discretion.

issue: Does the 'New Construction Commercial' space qualify for exemption under paragraph 5 of s. 3(1) of the Assessment Act, given that the owner (the Village) could only satisfy the exemption through hypothetical future changes to its nature and operations?
facts: The Village owns a 3.33-acre property at 536 Huron Street, London. A roughly 10,000 sq. ft. addition built in 2008 was purpose-built for and leased (at $1/year) exclusively to the London Community Hebrew Day School, a non-profit seminary of learning. MPAC assessed the whole property as fully taxable. The Village did not itself currently occupy or use the space for any exempt purpose; it relied on a stated intention that, if the School ever left, it 'would' use the space for 'relief of the poor.'
rule: Section 3(1) of the Assessment Act makes all real property liable to taxation subject to enumerated exemptions. Paragraph 5 exempts land 'leased and occupied' by a non-profit philanthropic, religious or educational seminary of learning 'if the land would be exempt from taxation if it was occupied by the owner.' Exemptions are construed under the modern (Driedger) principle of statutory interpretation as adopted in Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes and applied to tax statutes in Stubart and Notre-Dame de Bon-Secours; the primary/principal-use test is objective, and the taxpayer bears the onus of bringing itself clearly within the exemption. Courts must not read words into the statute that are not there (R. v. McIntosh).
application: The Court held the ordinary and grammatical meaning of 'if the land would be exempt from taxation if it was occupied by the owner' contemplates only a single hypothetical — notional occupation by the existing owner as it exists and operates in the relevant tax year — not a 'hypothetical upon a hypothetical' in which the owner is also notionally transformed into a differently-organized entity.
