Twist & Go Power Sports Inc., 2014 ONSC 2469).
conclusion: All three elements were established on a balance of probabilities for each publication.

issue: Did the defences of justification, qualified privilege and fair comment succeed, or were they defeated by malice?
facts: Mr. Hanna pleaded justification and fair comment; Mr. Jackman, Mr. Paine and VTS pleaded qualified privilege. Hanna's justification particulars concerned the Granville Island Hotel, dealings with Martin Chambers, employment of Brian Slobogian, Ms. Chun's origins, acquisitions, and alleged statements including the 'rubber gloves' warning. The defendants intended to damage the plaintiffs' reputation to gain a competitive advantage on the BC Hydro and Telus work.
rule: The defendant bears the onus of proving substantial truth of the sting (Brown on Defamation; Taseko Mines Ltd. v. Western Canada Wilderness Committee, 2016 BCSC 109). Malice — spite, an indirect or ulterior motive, or speaking dishonestly or with reckless disregard for truth — defeats qualified privilege and fair comment (Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto, 1995 CanLII 59 (SCC); WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40).
application: The Court accepted Mr. Malak's evidence and found none of Hanna's particulars justified the stings; a general charge of bad conduct cannot be proven by isolated instances, and Hanna himself testified he did not believe the Follow-Up Notes to be true, deflating his truth plea. The 'rubber gloves' and 'dirty Jew' allegations were rejected. All defendants were found to have acted with malice, intending to destroy the plaintiffs' reputation for competitive advantage, which defeated the qualified privilege and fair comment defences.
conclusion: Justification failed; qualified privilege and fair comment were defeated by malice. The defences failed.

issue: Were the defendants jointly liable on the basis of a common design?
facts: Following the Ansan Group's termination of acquisition negotiations, on May 1, 2012 Mr. Hanna sent Mr. Jackman a list of 'Raoul's lawsuits', shared with Mr. Paine. Hanna's remuneration from VTS was purely contingent on winning the BC Hydro (and possibly Telus) work, and its terms were never documented or disclosed.
rule: Concurrent tortfeasors acting in furtherance of a common design are jointly liable, without needing to realise they are committing a tort (Botiuk v. Toronto Free Press Publications Ltd., 1995 CanLII 60 (SCC), citing Fleming, The Law of Torts).
application: Because Hanna was 'Jim Arthur', and Jackman and Paine knew this yet took no steps to disassociate, and given shared financial motive and non-disclosure of documents, the Court found a common design to destroy, diminish or undermine the plaintiffs' reputations existed by May 1, 2012. The 'Mike Flagger' September 19, 2012 email was also part of that common design.
conclusion: Mr. Hanna, Mr. Jackman, Mr. Paine and VTS acted in furtherance of a common design and are jointly liable.

issue: Was Valley Traffic Systems Inc. vicariously liable for Mr. Hanna's conduct?
facts: VTS engaged Mr. Hanna (through Advanced Traffic, which had no assets, operations or other employees) to help prepare and front the BC Hydro tender under VTS's name, on a contingency basis. Hanna took a high-profile role communicating with BC Hydro on behalf of 'the team', with Jackman's approval, and represented that the parties were 'in partnership'.
rule: Vicarious liability turns on whether the wrongful act is sufficiently related to authorized conduct and whether there is a significant connection between the creation/enhancement of risk and the wrong (Bazley v. Curry, 1999 CanLII 692 (SCC)), with control being key (Sagaz Industries, 2001 SCC 59). A principal may be liable for slanders uttered by an agent engaged to solicit legal relations on its behalf (Colonial Mutual Life Assurance Society Ltd. v. Producers and Citizens Co-Operative, applied through Bazley/Sagaz).
application: The Court found Hanna was VTS's agent with considerable authority to represent VTS to BC Hydro, and that VTS controlled whether he made representations on the team's behalf. Applying the Bazley factors, VTS afforded Hanna the opportunity to abuse his power, his wrongful acts furthered VTS's aims and were incentivized by the contingency arrangement, and the plaintiffs were vulnerable to such internet 'hit pieces'.
conclusion: VTS is vicariously liable for Mr. Hanna's defamatory conduct, including where Jackman or Paine shared or sent the material.

issue: Is there a lien de droit between the plaintiff and each defendant, and can they be held solidarily liable for the 2011 sale transaction?
facts: Only Béram was named as vendor/co-contractant in Lauzon's offer to purchase the undivided half of the farmland. Marco Folini signed for Béram, while Guy Noël (through Les Vallons and J.-G. Noël et fils) drafted and signed the fictitious $500,000 offer that induced Lauzon to raise his bid. Lauzon sued all defendants solidarily.
rule: Arts. 1457 and 1458 C.c.Q. distinguish contractual from extracontractual liability; art. 1521 C.c.Q. governs solidarity where several persons' faults cause a single injury. Corporate veil-piercing rules apply where individuals participate personally in the wrongful conduct.
application: Béram, as Lauzon's lessor and vendor, was in a contractual relationship and bound by a duty of good faith. Noël, Folini and Les Vallons had no contract with Lauzon but participated personally and knowingly in preparing and presenting the sham offer, engaging their extracontractual liability. Noël signed both the $500,000 offer and the documents directing the $50,000 to J.-G. Noël et fils, so his own liability, not merely his company's, was engaged.
conclusion: All defendants are liable — Béram contractually, the others extracontractually — and the criteria of art. 1521 C.c.Q. are met, permitting a solidary condemnation for the first claim.

issue: Did the defendants commit a fault by failing to disclose the parallel $50,000 agreement, and does the conduct amount to civil fraud?
facts: The $500,000 offer presented to Lauzon secretly included a $50,000 payment to Noël's holding company to settle Rudy Folini's alleged old debt; Béram in fact kept only $450,000 for the land. Lauzon, unaware, matched the offer to keep land he had farmed for years, then learned the truth weeks later when Noël refused an exchange, saying the land was worth only $450,000.
rule: Art. 1375 C.c.Q. imposes good faith in negotiation and performance; art. 1399 C.c.Q. requires free and enlightened consent. Good faith is presumed (art. 2805) and bad faith/fraud must be proved on a balance of probabilities by the party alleging it (arts. 2803-2804). Civil fraud (dol) requires proof at a higher threshold than mere fault, per the case law on dol.
application: A reasonable co-contractant would have been influenced by disclosure of the side agreement; the parallel deal was a relevant fact that Béram, as lessor and prospective vendor, was obliged to disclose. By concealing it, all defendants induced Lauzon to overpay by $50,000. However, the object of the scheme was to offload Rudy's supposed debt onto Lauzon, not to defraud him as such; the evidence did not meet the higher bar for civil fraud, especially since it was not clear Lauzon would have declined at $500,000 given his own plan to swap the land.
conclusion: The defendants committed a fault (breach of good faith / failure to secure enlightened consent) but not civil fraud; the $50,000 claim is well founded.

issue: Were the clandestine audio recordings and their transcriptions admissible and probative once the whole of the evidence was heard?
facts: After being advised by the SQ to record the suspects, the Lauzons secretly recorded hours of conversations with the defendants in 2012. The recordings were admitted 'sous réserve' at the start of trial; the defendants challenged their integrity, authenticity and probative value, noting gaps and missing 'bips'.
rule: Admissibility of clandestine recordings is governed by the criteria set out in Cadieux c. Service de gaz naturel Laval Inc. (1991) and the court's own interlocutory judgment (2018 QCCS 3903); the outstanding criterion was probative value, to be assessed against the whole record.
application: The recordings and transcriptions contained sufficient reliable content to be contextualized against the balance of the evidence; the defendants were sophisticated businessmen not obliged to speak as they did, had received disclosure well in advance, and had a full opportunity to explain discrepancies. No party was deprived of a full defence. The gaps were not on sensitive points and did not suggest tampering; the disputed laugh was found to be Roger Lauzon's, not Noël's.
conclusion: The reservation is lifted; the recordings and transcriptions (P-13 and P-13a to P-13n) are admissible and probative, though they were not strictly necessary for the first claim, which was established independently.

issue: Should the $50,000 award be reduced by the $25,000 the plaintiff received in 2012, under the duty to mitigate?
facts: In 2012, Béram paid Lauzon $25,000 to suspend his right of first refusal so Les Vallons could buy the second undivided half. The defendants argued this offset the 2011 loss under the mitigation principle (art. 1479 C.c.Q.).
rule: Art. 1479 C.c.Q. requires a victim to minimize damages; recoverable contractual damages are limited to foreseeable loss (arts. 1611, 1613 C.c.Q.).
application: The $25,000 arose from a separate contract with different consideration (suspension of the right of first refusal) and a different context; Marco Folini himself testified the two payments were unrelated. It caused no negative consequence to Béram or Noël, unlike the 2011 payment, and was Lauzon's legitimate gain.
conclusion: No reduction; the $25,000 is not connected to the 2011 loss. The separate $15,000 damages claim was dismissed for lack of a direct, foreseeable link and insufficient proof.

issue: Did the plaintiff and Les Vallons agree to share the drainage costs of their co-owned land, and is Les Vallons liable?
facts: After Les Vallons became co-owner in May 2012, Noël stated he would pay his share of drainage if he became owner and the lease was respected. Noël participated in choosing the contractor, negotiated drain and fitting prices, received explanations, and told the contractor to begin 'when you can'. Lauzon paid the entire $107,443.55 bill; Les Vallons denied any agreement.
rule: Art. 2862 C.c.Q. bars testimonial proof of a contract over $1,500 absent a commencement of proof (art. 2865); admitted recordings can supply that commencement. Arts. 1018-1019 C.c.Q. impose common expenses on co-owners; unjust enrichment provides an alternative basis.
application: The admitted recordings and Noël's own testimony supplied both a commencement of proof and direct evidence that Noël's two conditions (becoming co-owner and the lease continuing) had materialized and that he had actively participated in implementing the drainage. Alternatively, as co-owner Les Vallons would owe its share under the co-ownership rules, and unjust enrichment applied since Noël admitted the works increased the land's value. Additional works were refused for lack of preponderant proof.
conclusion: Les Vallons is condemned to pay its just share, fixed at $52,759.28, with interest and additional indemnity.

issue: On a temporary motion, should the father be granted equal decision-making and an equal (2/2/3) parenting schedule with the children spending time at his separate residence?
facts: The parties married in 2016, separated in January 2020, and continued to live in the matrimonial home. They have two young children (born 2017 and 2019). Since a February 2020 consent order of Akbarali J., the parents shared decision-making and equal parenting under one roof, but the arrangement became tense and unworkable. The father rented a separate home nearby and sought a 2/2/3 equal schedule; the mother opposed, claiming to be the primary parent and alleging poor and dangerous parenting, seeking sole decision-making and roughly 4 of 14 days for the father.
rule: The sole test for custody and access is the best interests of the child: Divorce Act, s. 16(8); courts often consider the factors in s. 24(2) of the Children's Law Reform Act. Section 16(9) directs the court not to consider past conduct unless relevant to parenting ability, and s. 16(10) requires effect be given to the maximum contact principle. Best interests are assessed from the child's perspective (Young v. Young, [1993] 4 S.C.R. 3). On interim motions, stability and maintenance of the status quo are paramount unless there is a compelling reason to disturb it (Kimpton v. Kimpton, 2002 CanLII 2793).
application: The court found the status quo was the February 2020 consent order providing equal parenting and joint decision-making, entered into with counsel. What had changed was that co-parenting under one roof had become unworkable, not the shared nature of parenting. The court declined to resolve conflicting credibility, noting the mother's numerous allegations (car seat, chin laceration, hygiene, food) largely reflected ordinary daily parenting disagreements and were exaggerated, detracting from her credibility (Alsawwah v. Afifi). Breastfeeding was not a trump card (Holomey v. Hillis) and the medical evidence was dated. The nannies' evidence was of limited value. The young age of the children did not preclude equal parenting (Schmidt v. Haley). Separating the parties physically would reduce conflict; the s. 24(2) CLRA factors favoured the father's plan as the only one giving equal time, though a graduated schedule (Schedule B) was preferred to ease adjustment.
conclusion: The father's motion for equal decision-making and a revised, graduated equal-time parenting schedule (Schedule B, commencing February 1) was allowed.

issue: Should the mother be granted temporary exclusive possession of the matrimonial home?
facts: The mother sought exclusive possession citing need for privacy, non-interference during her parenting, and protection from her allegedly abusive (psychologically violent) husband. The father undertook not to return to the matrimonial home but opposed exclusive possession as prejudicial to a potential future sale, given his significant equity was tied up in the home. No motion to sell was pending.
rule: Section 24(1) of the Family Law Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.3 sets out the criteria for ordering exclusive possession, including the best interests of the children and any violence (Mohajeri v. Stroedel; Pinto v. Pinto).
application: The s. 24(1) factors did not favour the mother. Given the order for equal decision-making and parenting, the best interests of the children were not advanced by granting exclusive possession, which could be seen as tilting the field toward the mother. The relief was unnecessary in light of the father's undertaking not to return, and inadvisable at the outset of a new parenting arrangement. Exclusive possession should not be used pre-emptively to block a possible future sale motion. The father categorically rejected the allegations of violence, and the court was not satisfied the alleged psychological violence warranted an order; the case was distinguishable from Pinto v. Pinto.
conclusion: The mother's cross-motion for temporary exclusive possession of the matrimonial home was dismissed.

issue: Was the matter suitable for summary disposition under Rule 18A of the Supreme Court Rules?
facts: The CBC broadcast about Canada's hate movement referred to the plaintiff, wife of Aryan Nations leader Terry Long, including a statement that the Longs dressed their children in 'pint sized Klan uniforms' for a cross burning. The plaintiff sued in defamation and opposed proceeding by Rule 18A, arguing viva voce and expert evidence were needed. She adduced no evidence of her own, relying essentially on an insufficiency-of-evidence position.
rule: On a Rule 18A application the court must decide whether it can find the facts necessary to decide the issues and whether it would be unjust to do so, weighing sufficiency of evidence, amount involved, complexity, urgency, prejudice from delay, cost of a conventional trial and the course of proceedings (Inspiration Management Ltd. v. McDermid St. Lawrence Ltd. (1989), 36 B.C.L.R. (2d) 202 (C.A.)).
application: There were no issues of credibility or conflicting evidence. Examinations for discovery were complete and the plaintiff's own admissions supplied ample evidence. The likely damages were modest since the plaintiff's alleged losses predated the broadcast, and a ten-day trial would impose unnecessary expense for little gain given the six-year lapse since the statement.
conclusion: The issues were appropriate for disposition under Rule 18A and the court could and should give judgment.

issue: What was the natural and ordinary defamatory meaning (the sting) of the impugned statement?
facts: The plaintiff variously characterized the sting as association with her husband's public racist activities, insinuation that her children were KKK members, and forcible indoctrination of her children in racist ideology. The defendants pleaded a lesser meaning—that with her husband she exposed her children to a racist ideology to which she was sympathetic—or substantial justification.
rule: A defendant may plead any defamatory meaning the words are capable of bearing and prove it true or fair comment, so long as it does not act oppressively (Pizza Pizza Ltd. v. Toronto Star Newspapers Ltd. (1998), 167 D.L.R. (4th) 748; Polly Peck Holdings v. Trelford, [1986] 2 All E.R. 84). The trier of fact determines the natural and ordinary meaning, including reasonable innuendo, as what the words convey to the ordinary reasonable viewer reading between the lines (Rubber Improvement Ltd. v. Daily Telegraph Ltd., [1964] A.C. 234; Lucas-Box v. News Group Newspapers Ltd., [1986] 1 All E.R. 177), and is not bound by either party's interpretation.
application: Viewing the statement in the context of the whole broadcast and the other references to the plaintiff and the Long children, the court found the sting was neither as mild as mere exposure to racist beliefs nor as strong as forcible indoctrination, but that notorious racist Terry Long had involved his wife and children in his expression of racist ideology as 'a family affair.' The literally untrue detail about the Klan uniforms was simply another insinuation to that effect.
conclusion: The sting of the libel was that the plaintiff was involved with, and involved her children in, her husband's expression of racist ideology.

issue: Did the defendants establish justification (truth or substantial truth) of the defamatory meaning?
facts: On discovery the plaintiff admitted she never publicly opposed her husband, was proud of his positions in the movement, attended some five or six annual Aryan Nations congresses at Hayden Lake with her children where cross lightings occurred with people in Klan and Nazi-style dress, helped with children's activities, took no steps to disassociate from the beliefs expressed, and recorded a telephone message for the Canadian Liberty Net referring critically to Jewish people as controlling society.
rule: Truth (justification) is a complete defence to defamation; the defendant need only prove the impugned meaning is true or substantially true on a balance of probabilities, and minor inaccuracies of detail that do not alter the substance are immaterial.
application: The plaintiff's uncontradicted admissions proved she and her children were involved with Terry Long's racist beliefs and activities. Sub-paragraphs (a) through (e) of the defence were made out, and the immaterial and literally untrue detail about how the children were dressed did not defeat the defence because what the viewer took away—that the Longs supported Long's proclamation as a racist leader as a family—was true and would shock the ordinary reasonable person.
conclusion: The defamatory statement was justified in fact and at law; the substantial truth defence succeeded.

issue: Should a provisional injunction be granted to ban demonstrations within 100 metres of McGill's 154 buildings and to enjoin nuisance, intimidation, harassment and obstruction of access?
facts: Two McGill students sought a quia timet provisional injunction after a pro-Palestinian encampment was set up on campus on 27 April 2024. They alleged fear for their safety, discomfort, perceived antisemitic and violence-inciting slogans, and McGill's failure to enforce its student code of conduct. Their affidavits and those of nine others contained much hearsay and largely subjective fears; no one established blocked access to buildings or missed exams arising from the current encampment. McGill considered the encampment illegal, had tried to negotiate, issued warnings, and called police, but took no position on the injunction.
rule: Provisional injunction under the Code de procédure civile requires urgency, plus a colour of right (apparence de droit), irreparable harm, and the balance of convenience. The remedy is discretionary. Universities are special places where freedom of expression and peaceful assembly carry significant weight (R. v. Whatcott, 2012 ABQB 231; UAlberta Pro-Life v. Governors of the University of Alberta, 2020 ABCA 1).
application: The Court found no urgency: no affidavit showed access to exam venues was blocked or exams missed; fears of blockage stemmed from earlier, distinct protests, and past conduct does not guarantee future conduct; McGill had acted proactively within only five days. On colour of right, a content-neutral ban on all demonstrations within 100 metres of 154 buildings was far broader and more restrictive of freedom of expression and peaceful assembly than dismantling the encampment, and contrary to McGill's own policies. The nuisance/harassment order raised serious but discretionary concerns and would be difficult to enforce. On irreparable harm and balance of convenience, the plaintiffs' evidence was fragile and largely subjective; they had not personally suffered harassment, violence or threats; the balance favoured protecting the protesters' fundamental freedoms.
conclusion: The provisional injunction was dismissed for failure to demonstrate urgency, though McGill and the plaintiffs may return to court if circumstances deteriorate; the Court invited protesters to reconsider words perceived as calls to violence or antisemitic.

issue: Should the plaintiffs' affidavits be placed under seal?
facts: The plaintiffs asked that the affidavits they filed be sealed.
rule: Sealing orders are governed by the criteria in A.B. c. Robillard, 2022 QCCA 959, and Sherman (Succession) c. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25.
application: The allegations in the record were insufficient to meet those criteria.
conclusion: The sealing request was dismissed.

issue: Was there non-disclosure or delayed disclosure by the society or the mother that prejudiced the father?
facts: The father sought a mistrial partly on the ground that Jennifer Shneer's therapeutic notes (mother's Woman Abuse counsellor, employed by JFCS) were disclosed only in February 2014, after 20 trial days. The society maintained a 'wall' between its child-protection and Woman Abuse therapeutic functions and had no access to those records absent mother's consent or a court order; it saw the notes at the same time as the father. The mother disclosed the notes once she decided to call Shneer as a witness. The father argued Shneer had actively participated in child-protection decisions, but the notes/emails he produced concerned only mother's safety during access transfers.
rule: A children's aid society, as a quasi-state actor, has a continuing obligation to make reasonable disclosure of documents in its possession so respondents know the case to meet (Catholic Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. S. (A.), 2007 ONCJ 596). The onus is on the moving party to prove on a balance of probabilities that disclosure was withheld and that the party was misled/prejudiced.
application: The society could not access the Woman Abuse records without consent or court order, and the father never brought a production motion despite being invited to by Justice Sherr. The notes the father tendered did not show Shneer making or influencing child-protection decisions; they showed her addressing mother's safety concerns, consistent with her counselling role. The father failed to establish he was misled. The court also declined to fault the mother, noting the father himself was in continuing breach of a production order (his Utah psychiatric/criminal records) and thus came with unclean hands.
conclusion: No breach of disclosure obligations by the society, and the mother's February 2014 disclosure did not prejudice the father's ability to meet his case.

issue: If the father was prejudiced, must a mistrial be declared or can lesser measures cure any prejudice?
facts: The father argued the prejudice was irreparable and that recalling three society witnesses would create confusion. The trial had run 20+ days, was to resume April 28, 2014, and was scheduled to continue intermittently for 43 more days; the society's case was still ongoing and the father's case had not begun.
rule: A mistrial is a last resort; a decision to proceed must be 'consistent with the interests of justice and the maintenance of public confidence in the fairness of the trial' (R. v. M.Q., 2012 ONCA 224). Courts must canvass any conceivable way to save the trial before ordering a mistrial (Tupper v. Van Rooy; Carey v. Ontario). The inquiry is fact-driven (Onuselogu v. Okeke; Carbone v. De La Rocha).
application: The evidence in this trial had not been confusing or disjointed (distinguishing Onuselogu, where a mistrial was ordered on already-confused evidence). Substantial time remained before the father's case in chief, and if genuine prejudice appeared, the court could recall witnesses or grant a brief adjournment. Declaring a mistrial would add roughly a year of delay, contrary to the remedial, timely-resolution objectives of the Child and Family Services Act and harmful to the children's interests — and ironic given the father's own delay-based Constitutional Motion.
conclusion: Even assuming prejudice, any prejudice could be remedied by orders short of a mistrial; no basis to declare a mistrial at this stage.

issue: Does the judge's distant familial connection to a proposed witness create a reasonable apprehension of bias requiring recusal?
facts: The judge disclosed before trial that Shneer 'may be a distant relative' and invited any concerns by 14B form; none were raised until after 20+ trial days. The judge explained Shneer would, if related, be his step-second cousin — not a blood relative, friend, social contact, or someone he had seen in decades. Father argued any familial relationship, however remote, creates apprehension of bias.
rule: The test is whether a reasonable, informed person would think it more likely than not the judge would not decide fairly (Committee for Justice and Liberty v. Canada (NEB); R. v. S. (R.D.) — high threshold, strong presumption of impartiality; Bailey v. Barbour). Consent of parties cannot cure a genuine apprehension of bias, and the recusal decision rests with the judge alone (Lacey-House v. Lambert). Mechanical 'connection rules' are rejected in favour of a realistic, fact-based assessment (Boardwalk Reit LLP v. Edmonton; CAS of Waterloo Region v. B.(L.-A.); recusal on trifling grounds wastes resources and risks injustice).
application: The father's position rested on a 'mechanical rule' that any relationship disqualifies, which the case law rejects. The connection was highly tenuous — a 'step-second cousin' label with no real relationship. Weighed against the strong presumption of judicial impartiality and the enormous waste of resources and year-long delay recusal would cause, a fully informed reasonable person would not perceive a real likelihood of bias.
conclusion: No reasonable apprehension of bias would arise from Shneer testifying; recusal not warranted.

issue: Does the Superior Court have jurisdiction under art. 16 C.C.Q. to authorize medical treatment where the defendant is alleged to be incapable of consenting?
facts: A 30-year-old man was admitted to the Jewish General Hospital in a psychotic, paranoid state and was refusing psychiatric medication. The hospital's experts recommended a court-ordered 36-month regime of long-acting injectable antipsychotic medication. The expert report answered only one of the five incapacity sub-questions; the treating physician (Dr Geagea) did not testify, and the psychologist who testified could not address the nature, purpose, risks or benefits of the treatment.
rule: Article 16 C.C.Q. requires court authorization where a person of full age incapable of giving consent categorically refuses care. Per Centre universitaire de santé McGill (Hôpital Royal-Victoria), 2015 QCCA 1139, the court must first verify two essential jurisdictional conditions: (1) incapacity to consent, assessed through five sub-questions (understanding of the illness, nature and purpose of treatment, risks/benefits of undergoing it, risks of refusing it, and whether capacity to understand is affected by the illness); and (2) a categorical refusal.
application: The Court found the defendant did not understand his illness (he believed his only problem was high blood pressure) and that his capacity to understand was impaired by his illness. However, the evidence failed to answer the remaining incapacity sub-questions: the report was silent on whether he understood the nature and purpose of the treatment, the risks and benefits of undergoing it, and the risks of not undergoing it, and no witness could fill these gaps.
conclusion: The evidentiary gaps prevented the Court from being satisfied of full incapacity, and combined with the failure to prove categorical refusal, the jurisdictional threshold was not met.

issue: Did the plaintiffs establish a categorical refusal of the proposed care?
facts: Following the earlier confinement order of Justice Lewis (June 9, 2016), the defendant accepted to take oral medication, though he stated it was 'because he was blackmailed.'
rule: Under art. 16 C.C.Q. and the McGill (Hôpital Royal-Victoria), 2015 QCCA 1139 analytical grid, the court may only intervene where there is proof of a categorical refusal; the treatment must have been offered, considered and discussed and then refused.
application: Because the defendant had accepted oral medication after the Lewis judgment, the Court could not conclude that a categorical refusal existed, notwithstanding his stated reluctance.
conclusion: No categorical refusal was proven; a further essential condition for jurisdiction was absent.

issue: Did neither parent in fact assume the care, maintenance or education of the children for at least six months under art. 559(2) C.c.Q.?
facts: Both children, M... (born 2001) and R... (born 2002), were placed in foster care from birth by court order. The father never appeared, ceased attending a violence-intervention program, and stopped contacting the agency after July 2002. The mother attended some parenting-support programs but participated poorly, denied her difficulties, disappeared for long periods, and the children's severe distress at contact forced the director to suspend visits.
rule: Art. 559(2) C.c.Q. allows a child to be declared eligible for adoption where 'ni les père et mère ni le tuteur n'ont assumé de fait le soin, l'entretien ou l'éducation depuis au moins six mois.' Case law (Droit de la famille — 1544, 1992 CanLII 3971 (QC CA)) requires the court to assess, in light of the particular circumstances of a placed child, whether the parent nonetheless assumed the essential parental burden through concrete, materially identifiable acts, including efforts to eliminate the causes of the placement.
application: Although both parents were kept from the children's daily life by judicial placement orders, the court examined whether they nevertheless assumed their parental role through concrete acts. The father did nothing and abandoned intervention. The mother's efforts were superficial and 'apparents' only; she failed to acknowledge her difficulties, did not correct the situation that led to placement, ended her relationship with the father only belatedly, and went long periods without inquiring about the children. Neither made the tangible efforts the jurisprudence demands.
conclusion: The court found that neither the father nor the mother had in fact assumed the care, maintenance or education of M... and R... during the last six months.

issue: Did the parents rebut the presumption under art. 561 C.c.Q. of improbability of resuming care?
facts: Psychological assessments found the father had an antisocial personality disorder with marked aggression and the mother had significant cognitive limits, affective dependency, denial of her problems and a poor prognosis. The children reacted with acute distress to the mother; M... showed anguish and R... entered crisis on seeing her.
rule: Art. 561 C.c.Q. presumes it improbable a parent will resume care once art. 559 is met; the probability of resumption is assessed from the standpoint of both the parent and the child, including whether a significant attachment bond can be created (Droit de la famille — 1741, 1993 CanLII 3555 (QC CA)).
application: The parents' conduct since the children's birth, their failure to correct the situation, and the children's negative reactions to the mother demonstrated no realistic prospect of a significant bond. The mother's more insistent requests to see the children were not matched by genuine interest or change. The presumption was reinforced rather than rebutted.
conclusion: The parents did not rebut the presumption; it was improbable either would resume care of the children.

issue: Is a declaration of eligibility for adoption in the best interests of the children?
facts: M... and R... had lived in their foster families essentially since birth, were developing normally, had formed secure attachment bonds and a sense of belonging in those homes, while showing distress toward their biological mother.
rule: The best interests of the child is a relevant criterion throughout the adoption-eligibility process and adoption cannot be pronounced if contrary to the child's interest (Droit de la famille — 1544; Droit de la famille — 1914).
application: The children had taken root in stable foster families that met their needs, and the attachment bonds served their development. Breaking these consolidating bonds would be harmful. An adoption project was manifestly in their interest.
conclusion: The declaration of eligibility for adoption was in the best interests of the children.

issue: Did Dr. Lee breach the standard of care in his emergency-room treatment of the plaintiff on November 21, 2014?
facts: The plaintiff attended the Scarborough Hospital E.R. with a seven-day history of perianal pain described as a hemorrhoid flareup, a mild fever and slightly elevated pulse. Dr. Lee, an emergency physician of over 40 years' experience, took a history, conducted visual and physical examinations, diagnosed a likely perianal abscess in the early stages of infection, performed an incision and drainage, arranged home nursing wound care and (per his usual practice) advised follow-up with a primary care practitioner within two weeks. He did not order an ultrasound, perform a digital rectal exam (DRE), or chart the follow-up instruction. The plaintiff, whose evidence the court found unreliable, denied being told to follow up.
rule: A physician must exercise the degree of skill and care of a normal prudent practitioner of the same experience and standing (ter Neuzen v. Korn, [1995] 3 S.C.R. 674; Crits v. Sylvester; Gent v. Wilson). The standard is measured against a reasonable practitioner in similar communities, assessed through the eyes of a physician of the same background (Wilson v. Swanson), and expert evidence from the same care setting carries greater weight (Stepita v. Dibble; Bogdan v. Folman). A physician need not order every test, only usual tests (Watson v. Soon; Wade v. Nayernouri), and honest, properly-founded clinical judgment satisfies the standard (Tacknyk; Williams v. Bowler). Usual practice is good evidence of what occurred where records are incomplete (Turkington v. Lai; Power v. Carroll). A differential diagnosis is required only where a patient presents with non-specific complaints.
application: The court preferred the defence expert Dr. McMillan, whose community-hospital and CPSO assessment experience more closely matched Dr. Lee's setting than the plaintiff's expert Dr. Kingsley, who practised only in a tertiary academic centre. The court found Dr. Lee's assessment, working diagnosis of perianal abscess, and incision and drainage reasonable and consistent with the plaintiff's specific presentation (low-grade fever, elevated pulse). Because the complaints were specific, no differential diagnosis of serious conditions was required; nothing suggested cancer, and there was no life-threatening emergency requiring imaging. Declining an ultrasound and DRE were reasonable clinical judgments (Kingsley conceded the DRE call belonged to the treating physician). The discharge plan, including home nursing and a two-week follow-up instruction, met the standard; the absence of a chart entry did not mean the advice was not given (Turkington; Power v. Carroll).
conclusion: Dr. Lee met the standard of care of an emergency physician practising in Ontario in 2014; no breach.

issue: Did Dr. Chiu breach the standard of care in his general-surgery consultation of the plaintiff on December 31, 2014?
facts: Called to consult in the E.R., Dr. Chiu, a general surgeon of 30 years' experience, took a history, performed a full physical examination including a DRE, diagnosed a prolapsed mucosa and hardened incision area, recommended sitz baths, stool softeners and laxatives, and directed follow-up at his office in two weeks (or a return to E.R. if symptoms worsened), recording this in a note dictated about 2½ hours later. He did not provide a community CT requisition or refer to a colorectal surgeon/oncologist. Neither Scarborough nor comparable community hospitals had a colorectal surgeon on staff. The plaintiff's pain was rated 3/10 and there was no palpable rectal mass.
rule: Same standard-of-care framework (ter Neuzen; Crits v. Sylvester). Expert evidence from the same specialty and care setting is preferred; a specialist opining critically about a physician outside the expert's own setting is given less weight (Williams v. Bowler; Stepita; Bogdan).
application: The court preferred defence expert Dr. Hagan, a community-hospital general surgeon, over the plaintiff's expert Dr. Vasilevsky, a tertiary-centre colorectal surgeon who conceded Dr. Hagan was better placed to assess a community general surgeon's scope and who was unfamiliar with Ontario inter-hospital referral and imaging procedures. Vasilevsky conceded a community CT requisition would have met the standard and that admission/transfer was not required; her contrary opinions rested on incorrect assumptions (e.g. that the plaintiff was in severe pain preventing a DRE). Given the absence of a rectal mass, low pain score and no life-threatening emergency, there was no requirement to requisition hospital imaging or refer out, and the two-week office follow-up was reasonable. The court preferred Dr. Chiu's account, supported by his contemporaneous note, over the plaintiff's unreliable memory.
conclusion: Dr. Chiu met the standard of care of a community general surgeon in Ontario in 2014; no breach.

issue: Would the need for an ileostomy have been avoided but for any breach (causation)?
facts: The plaintiff developed a recto-vaginal fistula and underwent an ileostomy in April 2015, with anal cancer (squamous cell carcinoma) confirmed weeks later. The plaintiff argued the defendants' failure to requisition imaging created an evidentiary gap warranting an adverse inference.
rule: Causation is determined by the 'but for' test: the plaintiff must show on a balance of probabilities that the injury would not have occurred but for the defendant's negligence (Clements v. Clements, 2012 SCC 32). Causation must be linked to the specific act said to breach the standard (Chasczewski). Speculation or mere possibility is insufficient (Rothwell v. Raes; Salter v. Hirst). A defendant may rebut by showing the injury would have occurred regardless (Clements).
application: Because no breach was found, causation did not arise and the court's comments were obiter. Even so, no expert evidence connected any alleged breach by Dr. Lee to an earlier diagnostic pathway. As to Dr. Chiu, even a community CT requisition would have yielded a diagnosis no earlier than mid-March 2015, and by January 2015 the plaintiff already had indications for an ileostomy (incontinence, obstruction, pain). No imaging was clinically warranted in November/December 2014, so no adverse inference was drawn.
conclusion: Causation not established; the ileostomy could not have been avoided even had the diagnosis occurred earlier. Issue moot given no breach.

issue: Would the plaintiff have been contributorily negligent had liability been established?
facts: The plaintiff did not follow Dr. Lee's two-week follow-up instruction, did not attend Dr. Chiu's office follow-up, delayed three days after Dr. Feldman advised her to go to the E.R., declined a nursing re-assessment (ending wound care), and did not seek further medical attention until April 8, 2015, a week after stool began passing through her vagina.
rule: A plaintiff who fails to take reasonable care for her own health may have damages apportioned for contributory negligence.
application: The court found the plaintiff repeatedly failed to follow medical advice and follow-up instructions. Had negligence and causation been established, this conduct would have justified an apportionment.
conclusion: Obiter: the court would have found the plaintiff 40% contributorily negligent, had liability otherwise been established.

issue: Should the father be granted interim access to the child where allegations of abuse and a police investigation exist but remain unsubstantiated?
facts: The parties are in an ongoing matrimonial dispute; the mother has custody and the father has access. A court-ordered s. 15 psychological assessment by Robert Colby found the father posed no risk to the child and recommended gradually increased overnight visitation. After the report, the mother refused unsupervised access, relying on letters from a police detective and a social worker recommending suspension of visits pending a criminal investigation into an abuse disclosure. The nature, date, time, place and source of the allegation were not identified, and prior similar complaints had been investigated to no effect.
rule: On interim access applications the governing principle is the best interests of the child; parents ought to have as much contact with their children as is good for them. The court weighs the risk of harm against the benefit of parental contact, and evidence advanced (here hearsay letters) must rise to a threshold creating a realistic concern of actual danger to the child.
application: The court found the complaint 'inchoate, so amorphous, so poorly documented' that, given the context of prior unsubstantiated complaints and the timing after a favourable psychological report, it did not create a realistic concern of actual danger. The hearsay letters could have been presented in a more reliable form. Balancing the principle of maximum beneficial contact against the unsubstantiated concern, the material failed to reach the threshold justifying denial of access, though the court noted access could be revisited if better evidence emerged.
conclusion: Access reinstated on a defined schedule (Tuesday/Wednesday and Saturday periods, with monthly overnight), pick-up and drop-off arranged, and unrestricted telephone contact with the mother facilitated.

issue: Should the father be ordered to pay for the child's continued play therapy?
facts: An earlier judge (Kirkpatrick J.) had noted the need for play therapy was nearly at an end; Mr. Colby recommended it continue as valuable. The parents disagreed on its value and the mother sought an order that the father pay for it.
rule: An expense will not be imposed on a parent where, on the evidence, the activity does not amount to a necessity and the parents disagree as to its value.
application: The court found play therapy was not, on the evidence, the sort of activity amounting to a necessity, and given the parents' disagreement about its value, the father should not be required to pay, though he was encouraged to support and participate in the therapy.
conclusion: No order made requiring the plaintiff to pay for the play therapy.

issue: Should the interim spousal support order be reviewed and reduced given the defendant's failure to seek employment?
facts: Spousal support was fixed at $2,200. Kirkpatrick J. had directed a review and firmly recommended the defendant seek part-time work, recognizing a disability preventing full-time work. Little or nothing had been done to seek employment, and the defendant said her involvement with the child left no time, a burden aggravated by her cutting off the father's access.
rule: Interim spousal support may be adjusted on review; a recipient spouse is expected to make efforts toward self-sufficiency where able, and the court may set a graduated reduction to allow adjustment to a lesser income stream.
application: The court signalled, in stronger terms than Kirkpatrick J., that efforts to obtain employment were required. To avoid a sudden income drop, it ordered a graduated reduction from $2,200 (through 2001) down stepwise to $1,500 by May-June 2002, with liberty to seek a review thereafter, expecting the defendant to produce evidence of her employment efforts.
conclusion: Spousal support ordered reduced on a graduated schedule to $1,500, with a review mechanism and mutual income-disclosure directions.

issue: Did the solicitor breach the retainer agreement by refusing to continue unless a guardian ad litem was appointed?
facts: Waldock was retained under a written contingency agreement to 'obtain an offer ... or, if necessary, proceed to a trial'. Midway through the personal injury jury trial he insisted a guardian ad litem be appointed for Kent and declared he would not proceed without it; both Kent and his father were adamantly opposed, and Kent then discharged him, leading to a mistrial.
rule: A contingency retainer to prosecute a claim to settlement or judgment is 'an entire contract to conduct the action to the end' (Underwood, Son & Piper v. Lewis, [1894] 2 Q.B. 306; Gray v. Firm of Solicitors (1979), 17 B.C.L.R. 392; Trainor v. Deverell, Harrop (1980), 22 B.C.L.R. 322). Counsel may only withdraw in a civil case with leave of the court, and cannot refuse to proceed on his own terms.
application: The court found that Waldock's true position throughout was that he 'refused to proceed further without the appointment of a guardian' — a condition he was not entitled to impose, since under Rule 6 the appointment is for the court. This refusal was a repudiation of the entire contract, or at least an anticipatory breach, entitling Kent to discharge him.
conclusion: Waldock unilaterally breached (or anticipatorily breached) the retainer agreement; Kent was entitled to discharge him.

issue: Was the proposed guardian ad litem appointment in the client's interests under Rule 6(10)?
facts: Waldock told the trial judge his client was not mentally incompetent but 'under a disability as to this case'. He had advised the Kents in writing to appoint a committee, adjourn, obtain a mistrial and appeal the rulings, and admitted he was suggesting they 'orchestrate a mistrial'. He discussed 'tactical' benefits of keeping Kent out of the jury's view.
rule: Rule 6 of the Supreme Court Rules governs guardians ad litem; Rule 6(9) requires appointment where a party becomes mentally incompetent, and Rule 6(10) permits appointment 'if it is in the interest of a party who is under disability'.
application: Assuming an appointment could have been made under Rule 6(10) on grounds short of incompetency, the evidence compelled the conclusion it was not in Kent's interest: it was tied to Waldock's plan to orchestrate a mistrial and re-open the excluded evidence, to purported tactical advantages unrelated to the client's need, and to Waldock's inability to obtain the single instruction the client refused — consent to a guardian. The trial had gone 'off the rails' because of the judge's evidentiary rulings, not Kent's conduct.
conclusion: The proposed guardian ad litem appointment was not in the client's interests and was not intended for that purpose.

issue: Is the solicitor entitled to fees, a solicitor's lien, and disbursements?
facts: Waldock counterclaimed for 25% of the $325,000 settlement plus taxable costs and a solicitor's lien, and alternatively quantum meruit. Kent had settled his ICBC costs claim for $95,000, and roughly $31,700 in Waldock disbursements were outstanding; earlier disbursements of $32,261.10 had been paid.
rule: Having undertaken an entire contract on a contingency basis, a solicitor who breaches by withdrawing/refusing to continue receives no remuneration (Trainor v. Deverell, Harrop). Disbursements may nonetheless be recoverable from sums received.
application: Because Waldock breached the entire contract, he was not entitled to any fee or solicitor's lien. Disbursements were allowed subject to taxation, but the court disallowed disbursements connected to the mistrial-related conduct — witness fees, trial-filing and per diem fees, and expenses for the mislabelled x-rays and erroneous special-damages list.
conclusion: Declaration that Waldock has no claim for fees or a solicitor's lien; disbursements allowed subject to taxation, with specified deductions.

issue: Is the client entitled to punitive damages for the solicitor's misconduct?
facts: Kent claimed punitive damages for misconduct causing the mistrial, including Waldock failing to correct the court after Dr. Hendler repeatedly denied having his clinical records, and wrongly telling the court Dr. Stevens had never examined Kent.
rule: Punitive damages in contract are rare, require an actionable wrong, and are reserved for harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious conduct (Vorvis v. Insurance Corporation of British Columbia, [1989] 4 W.W.R. 218).
application: Although Waldock should have corrected the record about Dr. Hendler, wrongly represented Dr. Stevens' examination, and orchestrated the mistrial, the court held these did not amount to an actionable wrong toward Kent of the character warranting punitive damages. Kent's remedy lay in the declaration denying fees.
conclusion: No punitive damages awarded.

issue: Is it plain and obvious that the impugned portions of the response to civil claim should be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b) or 9-5(1)(c)?
facts: The plaintiffs, an estate executor/trustee and an amalgamated company, sue Isachsen (former sole director of the deceased's companies) and Wolf Consulting for breach of fiduciary, contractual, statutory and common-law duties. The RTCC pleads that the deceased, Mr. Johansson, retained ultimate control, was engaged in tax evasion and 'deception', and caused the losses. The plaintiffs applied to strike numerous passages as inflammatory attacks on the deceased's reputation.
rule: Rule 9-5(1) SCCR permits striking pleadings that are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious (b) or that may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial (c). Per Willow v. Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083 and Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860, a scandalous allegation is struck only if irrelevant as well as scandalous; the 'plain and obvious' standard applies to all branches (Huang v. Silvercorp; B.C. (Director of Civil Forfeiture) v. Lam). Pleadings are read generously and as a whole (Lee v. G.Y. Lee & Associates).
application: The court found the RTCC generally responsive to the claim: a key plank of the defence was that Johansson retained ultimate control and his own mismanagement and tax evasion caused the losses. Allegations of his mismanagement, tax-evasion practices and deception were relevant and material to a bona fide defence. Though the pleadings could have been more carefully drafted, they were not, in general, a gratuitous attack on reputation, and the presumptive-language argument (Bari Cheese) was rejected where the words related to a genuine defence.
conclusion: But for a narrow exception, it was not plain and obvious that the pleadings were unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, vexatious, prejudicial or embarrassing; the application was largely dismissed.

issue: Do the pleadings about uncollected cash rents (paras. 70, 73, 74) and the Petra Capital dealings (paras. 109-119) remain relevant and material to the defence?
facts: The plaintiffs had removed from the Amended Claim the allegations that Isachsen failed to collect, deposit and account for rents. They argued the corresponding response paragraphs were now irrelevant, and that the Petra gold-investment paragraphs were an irrelevant strawman requiring extra disclosure.
rule: A pleading is not struck merely for being superfluous; it must be irrelevant and materially prejudicial (Huang; Carr v. Cheng). Relevance is assessed against the bona fide defence advanced.
application: The court held the rent allegations remained relevant because they supported the respondents' theory that Johansson personally collected cash rents and used improper accounting to avoid tax. The Petra paragraphs (his signing a $1.5M gold purchase, ordering Carlton funds to repay his RBC loan, investing $2.6M) were relevant because they demonstrated Johansson's continuing control over the Companies and assets after Isachsen became director and offered a defence to the capital-gains claim regarding Carlton's property sale.
conclusion: Paras. 70, 73, 74 and 109-119 were relevant and material and were not struck.

issue: Should the sweeping allegations of 'illegality', 'bad acts for decades' and 'lifelong efforts to avoid paying taxes' be struck?
facts: Paragraphs 7, 10 and 17 of the RTCC alleged the deceased was 'engaged in illegality' and 'bad acts…for decades', 'long been…intent on avoiding taxes', and made 'lifelong efforts to avoid paying taxes'.
rule: Under Rule 9-5(1)(b)/(c), pleadings so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is pleaded, or so disconnected in time as to be irrelevant and to involve the parties in a dispute apart from the issues, may be struck (Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform; Willow v. Chong).
application: The court found the sweeping words suggested other unspecified 'illegal' activities and 'bad acts' whose nature, scope and relevance were unclear, and that terms like 'decades' and 'lifelong' obscured the relevant time period. The pleadings were confusing and appeared to encompass allegations too disconnected in time to be relevant, creating prejudice.
conclusion: The identified portions of paras. 7, 10 and 17 were struck, with leave to amend by April 15, 2026 to clarify the nature and scope of the allegations.

issue: Did the defendants prove, on a balance of probabilities, that they held acquired rights to operate an outdoor commercial parking lot on the lots?
facts: The defendants operated an outdoor parking lot facing the Centre Bell, admitting the essential elements of the offences but pleading acquired rights. The zoning history showed no prohibition before 1 December 1960, then progressive prohibitions on outdoor parking (by-laws 2583, 5415, 5591) subject to narrow exceptions. Evidence (aerial photographs, land-use plans, occupancy permits, resolutions) was led about the actual use of lots P-594, P-595, 1925, 604, 605 and 596-2 over time.
rule: The party invoking acquired rights bears the burden of proving them on a balance of probabilities; the conditions are set out in Huot c. L'Ange-Gardien (1992) — the prior derogatory use must have been legal, actually exercised (not merely intended), continued without significant interruption, and attaching to the immovable. Acquired-rights regimes are interpreted restrictively (Frelishburg c. Sibeca). Existence of a permit or payment of taxes does not create acquired rights; only the legality of the actual use matters.
application: The court found that P-595 held acquired rights only to an indoor 'garage public' (lost on demolition — see issue 2); P-594 was a gas station never used for parking before 1995-96; lot 1925 had parking before 1960 but the use was abandoned for over ten years during a prolonged excavation, extinguishing the rights; lots 604 and 605 were within the 150-foot/45 m prohibited strip and were never legally used for outdoor parking; only the southern strip of lot 596-2 (4.25 m wide, outside the 45 m band) was proven to have acquired rights. The permits and personal, non-transferable authorizations were not sources of rights.
conclusion: Stationnement Populaire and 9090-6421 Québec inc. failed to prove acquired rights on any of the former lots; Masdev proved acquired rights only on the southern portion of lot 1851392.

issue: Does demolition of a building housing an indoor parking garage extinguish acquired rights so they cannot extend to a later outdoor parking use?
facts: The two-storey garage on lot P-595 was demolished in 1995-96 and immediately replaced by an outdoor parking lot under a personal, non-transferable authorization granted under s. 649a of the Charter of the City of Montréal, since the zoning by-law (94-077) did not permit that use.
rule: The municipal legislator has always distinguished indoor parking (requiring a building) from outdoor parking as distinct uses; acquired rights attached to a building are lost upon its demolition (St-Denis-de-Brompton c. Courtois; Hoppenheim c. Ville de Montréal), and by-law 94-077 art. 704 expressly provided that a destroyed derogatory construction must be rebuilt in conformity with current norms. A personal, non-transferable authorization does not create rights (2630-2042 Québec inc. c. Ville de Montréal).
application: The commercial activity remained 'public parking,' but the regulatory scheme treated indoor and outdoor parking as different uses. The acquired right protected an indoor 'garage public'; its demolition extinguished that right and the protection could not be transferred to outdoor parking, which was then prohibited in the sector.
conclusion: Demolition of the garage in 1995-96 extinguished the acquired right to indoor parking, and that protection could not extend to the newly established, prohibited outdoor parking use.

issue: Is the City precluded (préclusion/forclusion) from prosecuting given delay, taxes and permits?
facts: Over many years the City tolerated the parking activity, collected various taxes, and issued occupancy permits (one containing a gross error later corrected); several applications by the defendants had, however, been refused since 1972.
rule: The préclusion theory (per Rochon J.A. in Montréal (Ville de) c. Chapdelaine) allows courts, in exceptional and rare circumstances, to refuse a municipality's remedy where all listed factors are present (exceptional circumstances, interests of justice, diligent good-faith contravenor unaware of the breach, no serious consequences, unreasonable and inexcusable delay usually over 20 years, positive municipal act, no danger to health/safety). Public-law estoppel cannot prevail against a clear statutory provision (Mont-Sinaï). In statutory penal matters the court has no discretion once the essential elements are proven beyond reasonable doubt and the defence rejected.
application: Although the City tolerated the situation, collected taxes and issued permits, these do not confer rights. The defendants were not without fault, having known since 1972 that the use was prohibited and having had numerous requests refused. In a statutory penal proceeding the court has no discretion to refuse to convict where the offence is made out and the defence fails.
conclusion: The préclusion/forclusion theory does not apply to bar the prosecution.

issue: Must the defendants be acquitted if only a portion of the described location enjoys acquired rights?
facts: The offences described the location as new lot 1851391 (with the former lots enumerated) and lot 1851392; defendants argued the location was an indivisible whole so acquired rights on any former lot required acquittal.
rule: The prosecution must describe the offence location as precisely as possible to allow full answer and defence; where a single new lot regroups former lots, mention of the former lots is for precision only and does not add to the prosecution's burden. Once illegal occupation of the lot is established, the offence is proven regardless of the proportion occupied illegally.
application: The court held that once it was satisfied there was illegal occupation of lot 1851391 (or 1851392), whether on 10%, 50% or 100% of the lot, the offence was proven; the defendants had admitted all essential elements on the offence dates.
conclusion: The indivisibility argument was rejected; partial acquired rights do not require acquittal.

issue: Did the defendants breach the standard of practice by not resorting to aCGH or a targeted FISH 4p- probe that might have identified Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome before birth?
facts: The fetus showed significant, early and unexplained intrauterine growth restriction that worsened over the last 13 weeks, but was otherwise vigorous, symmetrical, without structural malformation, facial dysmorphism or the usual markers of Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome. Standard screening (trisomy screen, TORCH, general FISH, cystic-fibrosis testing) and the amniocentesis karyotype of 7 October 2011 were all negative. The syndrome (a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4, prevalence 1:50,000) was masked because a similarly sized duplication of chromosome 2 translocated onto the deleted portion of chromosome 4, rendering the karyotype normal. It was diagnosed only about 11 months after birth.
rule: A physician's obligation is one of means, not of result: liability requires proof that the physician did not act as a reasonably prudent and diligent specialist placed in the same circumstances, assessed in abstracto and according to the standards of practice in force at the relevant time (St-Jean c. Mercier, 2002 SCC 15; Ter Neuzen c. Korn, [1995] 3 SCR 674; Lapointe c. Hôpital Le Gardeur, [1992] 1 SCR 351). The plaintiff bears the burden of proving fault (art. 2803 C.c.Q.); the court must rely on expert evidence and must avoid reasoning backward from the known outcome (second-guessing).
application: The Court preferred the geneticist expert Dr Maranda and fetal-medicine expert Dr Morin over the plaintiffs' experts (Dr Gekas and Dr Gouin), who reasoned a posteriori from the result and offered their own practice as the standard. The evidence, including CCGM/SOGC guidelines (2005–2013), showed that in 2011 aCGH was standard postnatally but only exploratory prenatally, appropriate only where ultrasound revealed fetal structural anomalies — none of which were present here. A targeted FISH 4p- probe would only be ordered given a high index of suspicion for Wolf-Hirschhorn, but the fetus displayed none of its markers (the dolichocephaly, cardiac axis, amniotic fluid level and echogenic bowel relied on by Dr Gekas were not structural anomalies or markers of the syndrome). Earlier amniocentesis would have changed nothing since the karyotype was normal.
conclusion: No fault: it was consistent with 2011 standards of practice to rely on standard cytogenetic testing; the plaintiffs failed to prove a breach on this ground.

issue: Did the defendants breach their duty to inform the parents of the genetic risk and possible outcomes so the mother could choose whether to continue the pregnancy?
facts: From the first detection of growth restriction (29 August 2011), Dr Girard explained the possible etiologies (placental, infectious, genetic/chromosomal, or constitutionally small baby), gave an example of a genetic anomaly (cri-du-chat), and told the parents an abortion remained available at any time. The same message was repeated by Drs Hall, Khalifé, Klam and by genetic counsellor Maria Lalous; Dr Klam's detailed contemporaneous notes recorded discussion of 'abnormal baby', increased morbidity/mortality and the limits of the karyotype. The educated parents researched the issues and repeatedly questioned the physicians. The mother said she would seek an abortion if a serious handicap were revealed but set no risk threshold.
rule: The duty to inform is assessed first on a subjective standard (the patient's testimony and all circumstances) tempered by a test of rational subjectivity (Chouinard c. Landry; Pelletier c. Roberge; Ferland c. Ghosn). A physician cannot guarantee results (Code de déontologie des médecins, art. 83); where the pregnancy is not itself a medical condition, the duty is to inform the parents of the possible outcomes and that termination remains an option and to leave the decision to the patient (art. 29 C.déont.; Hopp c. Lepp).
application: The Court found, on the balance of probabilities and relying on the physicians' credible testimony and contemporaneous records (presumed truthful), that the parents were repeatedly warned that a genetic/chromosomal cause could not be excluded despite the normal karyotype and that outcomes ranged from a healthy small baby to a severely handicapped child. Because no percentage could honestly be attached to any outcome and the fetus retained the potential to be born normal, physicians were not required in 2011 to recommend abortion. Applying rational subjectivity, the birth resulted from the informed decision of the parents; there was no basis for the 'more dramatic warning' Dr Gekas said was owed.
conclusion: No fault: the defendants adequately informed the parents; the claim fails on this ground as well.

issue: Can the defendants be held collectively and solidarily liable for a 'collective fault' under art. 1480 C.c.Q. for compartmentalized (silo) practice?
facts: The plaintiffs argued each physician committed at least a minor fault that others should have caught, and that as members of a care team they engaged in a collective wrongful act and operated an organized economic activity (art. 1525 C.c.Q.), justifying solidary liability.
rule: Article 1480 C.c.Q. addresses the apportionment, not the conditions, of liability; civil liability requires proof of a fault by each person (act or omission). Hébert (Hôpital de l'Enfant-Jésus), 2011 QCCA 1521, applied a traditional obligation-of-means analysis and did not impose collective liability. Solidarity under art. 1525 requires an integrated economic chain and regularity of services (Ceracaise c. Catalfamo).
application: The Court rejected 'liability by association': merely being part of a care team does not make each member liable, and the conditions of art. 1525(3) were not met (no economic integration or regularity). Each defendant had to be, and was, assessed individually; none committed a fault, and the physicians in fact communicated diligently among themselves and with consultants.
conclusion: No collective or solidary liability; since no individual fault was established, the collective-fault theory cannot succeed.

issue: Does the statement of claim disclose a reasonable cause of action under Rule 19(24)(a)?
facts: The self-represented plaintiff's one-page statement of claim alleged that ICBC, its claims representative and defence counsel infringed her Charter rights (ss. 2, 7 and 12), and committed intimidation, defamation, professional misconduct, breach of trust, abuse of power and conspiracy to suborn perjury, arising from a dispute over her account of a motor vehicle accident and a warning about breach of insurance coverage.
rule: On a Rule 19(24)(a) application the applicant must show the action has no chance of success and is certain to fail; the court assumes the pleaded material facts are true (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959). Rule 19(1) requires a statement in summary form of the material facts relied upon.
application: The court found no material facts pleaded to support the ss. 7 and 12 Charter claims, and that mere disbelief of the plaintiff's account could not infringe freedom of thought or expression under s. 2(b). No material facts supported defamation, professional misconduct, breach of trust or abuse of power, which were subsumed by the intimidation and conspiracy allegations. However, the court found it arguable that the claim could be amended to allege conspiracy to suborn perjury, as the outline of the alleged wrongdoing and its purpose was present.
conclusion: The statement of claim failed to disclose reasonable causes of action for the Charter and most tort claims; only the conspiracy/intimidation allegations were potentially amendable.

issue: Can the Charter apply to private-party defendants and to ICBC absent any pleaded reliance on a statute or regulation?
facts: The law firm and Mr. Bajpai were private parties; ICBC was assumed for argument to be a governmental entity. No pleading alleged reliance on any statute, regulation or common-law rule to justify infringing the plaintiff's rights.
rule: The Charter does not generally apply to private litigation (R.W.D.S.U. v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 573); Charter application requires government action, such as reliance on a statute or regulation.
application: As against the firm and Mr. Bajpai, the Charter had no application as they were private parties and no statutory reliance was pleaded. Even assuming ICBC were governmental, no material fact alleged that it invoked any statute or regulation to justify an infringement, and disbelief of an insured's account could not itself infringe freedom of expression.
conclusion: No viable Charter claim lay against any defendant.

issue: Should the action be summarily dismissed under Rule 18(6)?
facts: The plaintiff's affidavit evidence never asserted that Bajpai or Turner asked her to change her story, nor that she was told coverage would be cancelled if she did not do so; she maintained she consistently gave one account. She did not allege she was induced to make a false statement or that she suffered damage.
rule: On a Rule 18(6) summary judgment application the defendants must establish the plaintiff is 'bound to lose' — that there is no bona fide triable issue (Serup v. School District No. 57 (1989), 54 B.C.L.R. (2d) 258 (C.A.); Skybridge Investments Ltd. v. Metro Motors Ltd., 2006 BCCA 500).
application: The plaintiff's evidence disclosed only her subjective belief that the defendants wanted her to change her story; beliefs are not evidence. Defence counsel and ICBC acted properly under ss. 73 and 74.1 of the Insurance (Vehicle) Regulation in reviewing her account and controlling the defence. The evidence could not support intimidation or conspiracy to suborn perjury, and no loss was shown, so the plaintiff was bound to lose even if the claim were amended.
conclusion: Summary judgment was warranted; the claims were bound to fail.

issue: Does s. 30(3) of the Insurance Corporation Act bar the claim against the ICBC claims representative?
facts: Ms. Turner sent a defective 'breach of coverage' warning letter after settling Mr. Knight's claim, which she should not have sent, but the plaintiff alleged Turner acted in bad faith.
rule: Section 30(3) of the Insurance Corporation Act bars any action against a person for acts or omissions done in good faith in the administration or carrying out of the Act, regulations or an insurance plan.
application: The facts deposed by the plaintiff could not support a finding that Ms. Turner acted in bad faith; her evidence supported good faith despite the erroneous letter sent after settlement.
conclusion: The statutory immunity provided a further ground for dismissing the claim against Ms. Turner.

issue: Should the insolvent corporate plaintiff be ordered to post security for costs under s. 236 of the Business Corporations Act, and in what amount?
facts: KSW, an insolvent recreational-vehicle dealer, sued its insurers over a December 31, 2008 fire loss. The insurers, more than two years into the litigation, sought security for costs of over $200,000 (later argued at $100,000) plus a stay until security was posted. KSW conceded its insolvency, which was at least partly linked to the fire and the insurers' refusal to pay.
rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 permits the court to require a corporate plaintiff to give security where it appears it will be unable to pay a successful defendant's costs, and to stay proceedings until security is given. The court applies the discretionary factors endorsed in Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd. (1997) and affirmed in Galaxy Sports Inc. v. Umbro Holdings Ltd., 2004 BCCA 208: complete discretion on all circumstances, balancing oppression against unfair pressure, avoiding the merits unless obvious, timing/lateness of the application, and the amount lying in the judge's discretion. The staged test in Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform / Scotford asks whether the plaintiff can pay costs, whether it has exigible assets, whether the defence is arguable, and whether an order would visit undue hardship stifling the claim.
application: The court found the plaintiff insolvent, the defendants having at least an arguable (not obviously winning or losing) defence, and that the defendants could not recover costs if successful. It weighed against ordering security the fact that the application came late, after the plaintiff was heavily invested in a two-year-old action, and the link between the fire loss and the insolvency. Balancing these, the court declined the full amount sought and fixed a reduced sum of $40,000.
conclusion: Security for costs of $40,000 was ordered; the claim and counterclaim were stayed pending its posting.

issue: Did the plaintiff establish that an order for security for costs would stifle a genuine claim?
facts: Mr. Streichert's affidavit stated KSW had exhausted its resources, had borrowed from family, sold property, faced foreclosure and debt litigation, and that any more-than-nominal security order would bar KSW from advancing its fire claim.
rule: Under Kropp and Galaxy, to show an order would stifle the action the plaintiff must do more than assert impecuniosity; it must lead evidence that it has no means of raising money for security, including from third parties. The court must be satisfied it is probable the claim would be stifled before refusing security on that ground.
application: The court accepted the plaintiff's evidence of insolvency and the connection between the fire loss and its impecuniosity, and treated the stifling concern as a genuine consideration weighing toward a reduced order rather than a refusal or full award. It concluded that a reduced amount appropriately balanced the risk of stifling a legitimate claim against the defendants' inability to recover costs.
conclusion: The stifling concern justified reducing the security to $40,000 rather than declining an order or awarding the full amount sought.

issue: Do the signed employment letters limit the plaintiff's reasonable notice, and what notice period (with retention bonuses) is appropriate?
facts: Lalonde, a 62-year-old (56 at dismissal) journeyman millwright, worked for the defendant continuously from April 2008 until his dismissal in July 2012. He signed an April 2008 employment letter and a February 2011 letter after ownership changed. The April 2008 letter's termination clause limited entitlement to statutory minimums except where termination was for 'willful or professional misconduct, conflict of interest, disobedience or willful neglect of duty.' The defendant purported to dismiss him for disobedience/professional misconduct (later withdrawn). His compensation included short- and long-term retention initiative payments.
rule: Reasonable notice is assessed on the Bardal factors — character of employment, length of service, age, and availability of similar employment (Bardal v Globe & Mail; Wallace v United Grain Growers, 1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)); the factors are non-exhaustive and assessed prospectively (Nelson v Champion Feed Services, 2010 ABQB 409). Damages must place the employee in the position he would have occupied had proper notice been given, including bonuses that are an integral part of compensation (Paquette v TeraGo Networks, 2016 ONCA 618).
application: The court found the April 2008 letter applicable but held that because the plaintiff was dismissed for alleged disobedience and professional misconduct, the clause's carve-out meant his entitlement was not limited to statutory minimums (and the 2011 letter would not have limited notice either). Applying Bardal — length of service (just over 4 years), age (56), technical tradesman role with occasional minor supervisory duties, and difficulty finding comparable millwright work — the court set reasonable notice at 6 months, within a 4–8 month range drawn from comparable cases. The retention initiative, expressly payable pro rata on release without cause, was an integral part of compensation, so 6 months of the retention bonus was added to 6 months' salary, less mitigation earnings.
conclusion: The employment letters did not limit notice. Reasonable notice fixed at 6 months' salary plus 6 months of short- and long-term retention bonuses, less amounts earned in mitigation.

issue: Is the plaintiff entitled to aggravated (moral) damages for the manner of his dismissal?
facts: The plaintiff was summarily accused of serious safety violations and insubordination, given little chance to respond, suspended, and escorted off the site in front of co-workers. The defendant made up its mind to terminate within days, ignored a supporting letter from co-worker Larry Dakin, maintained cause allegations (framed in the Statement of Defence as dishonesty, serious misconduct, insubordination) for nearly five years until withdrawing them on the eve of trial. His EI was delayed, rumours of theft circulated in his small community, and his wife's uncontradicted letter described depression, humiliation and family strain.
rule: Damages for the manner of dismissal are available where the employer's conduct during dismissal is 'unfair or in bad faith by being untruthful, misleading or unduly insensitive,' and the mental distress was within the reasonable contemplation of the parties (Wallace; Honda Canada v Keays, 2008 SCC 39; Fidler). Such moral/aggravated damages reflect actual damages, not an arbitrary extension of notice (Elgert v Home Hardware, 2011 ABCA 112). Attacking the employee's reputation and misrepresenting reasons for dismissal are compensable examples.
application: The court found the defendant 'shot first and asked questions later': the investigation ignored the plaintiff's side and Dakin's supporting account and was 'at best incompetent and unfair and at worst a sham.'
