conclusion: The anti-Semitic threats were treated as an aggravating factor increasing the accused's blameworthiness.

issue: What emotional harm and property loss from the victim impact statements may properly be considered as aggravating?
facts: The Grossmans and their daughter filed detailed victim impact statements, updated two years later, describing ongoing psychological harm and listing stolen items including jewelry and documents. The defence argued only the two stolen artworks could be linked to the October 24, 2021 break-in and that harm from an earlier October 21 break-in (not charged) could not be counted.
rule: Victim impact and loss considered on sentencing must be connected to the offences of which the accused was convicted; the court may only consider emotional harm, property damage or economic loss flowing from the commission of the proven offence.
application: The court accepted that the accused was not charged with the October 21 break-in and considered the continuing psychological harm from the October 24 offences as aggravating, while the defence's submissions on limiting property loss to the recovered/linked artwork informed the analysis. The psychological harm to the victims two years later was expressly recognized.
conclusion: The court relied on the continuing psychological harm from the proven offences as aggravating, consistent with the constraint that only harm connected to the October 24 offences be counted.

issue: Do the accused's post-offence rehabilitation efforts constitute a significant mitigating factor warranting a reduced sentence?
facts: After submissions, the accused made a lengthy statement showing he appeared a changed man: he had completed university-level courses, addressed severe addiction issues through programming and reflection while in pre-trial custody, apologized to the victims and expressed insight into the harm caused.
rule: Sentencing must give weight to rehabilitation and the overarching principles of restorative justice; genuine rehabilitative efforts and insight are mitigating factors (s. 718 et seq.).
application: The court found the specificity and extent of the accused's rehabilitation went much further than the standard often seen, and combined with his relatively young age, constituted an unusual and significant mitigating factor not captured in the pre-sentence report or submissions, leading the court to accept the defence's proposed sentence.
conclusion: The rehabilitation was found to be a significant mitigating factor justifying the 3.5-year global sentence.

issue: Did R v. McFarlane bar the imposition of a conditional discharge for this weapons-related offence of violence?
facts: Ms. T., a first offender with no record, drew a knife and threatened its use while in a psychotic episode caused by paranoid schizophrenia. The sentencing judge considered himself bound by R v. McFarlane to refuse a discharge and imposed a suspended sentence with two years' probation instead.
rule: R v. McFarlane (1976), 55 A.R. 222 (Alta. S.C.A.D.) generally speaks against a conditional discharge for offences of violence or those committed with a weapon, save in exceptional circumstances.
application: Justice Martin agreed McFarlane counsels against discharges for violent or weapons offences, but held that its reasoning was not intended to apply to a first offender so mentally ill as to be completely out of touch with reality at the time of the offence. Such a situation fell within the exceptional circumstances contemplated by McFarlane.
conclusion: McFarlane did not preclude a conditional discharge in these exceptional circumstances.

issue: Was the suspended sentence with a criminal record a fit sentence, or should a conditional discharge be substituted?
facts: Ms. T. committed the offence during a psychotic state; she had no prior record, was responsive to anti-psychotic medication, and posed minimal continuing risk if medicated. The Crown opposed a discharge, characterizing the offence as a racist act involving threats with a weapon; defence showed she held no anti-Semitic views when well. A discharge was in her best interests and not contrary to the public interest.
rule: A conditional discharge is available where it is in the best interests of the accused and not contrary to the public interest; sentencing must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender. Serious mental illness attracts more lenient dispositions reflecting diminished responsibility (R. v. Taylor (1975), 24 C.C.C. (2d) 551 (Ont. C.A.); R. v. Moreau (1992), 76 C.C.C. (3d) 181 (Que. C.A.)); see also the s. 16 and Part XX.1 regime and Winko v. British Columbia (1999).
application: The offender's blameworthiness was nominal because she was in a full psychotic state; no one was injured. A conditional discharge coupled with a probation order requiring her to attend her physician and take her prescribed medication achieved the same protective safeguard as the suspended sentence while sparing her a criminal record. Nothing was to be gained by fixing her with a record.
conclusion: The suspended sentence and resulting record were unfit; appeal allowed and a conditional discharge with a two-year probation order substituted.

issue: Did the refusal to continue employing Sharon McEvoy after her maternity leave amount to discrimination based on sex under s. 9(1) of the Human Rights Code?
facts: McEvoy was a home care worker for 80-year-old Vincent Dalton from April 2000 until she began maternity leave in August 2001. Patricia Power was hired as a temporary replacement. During the leave Dalton had gallbladder surgery, requiring bathing and washroom assistance, and became more comfortable with Power (whom he had long known) and preferred her cooking. When McEvoy was ready to return in March 2002, Dalton decided to keep Power permanently, citing a higher level of care. There were no complaints about McEvoy's prior performance.
rule: Section 9(1) of the Human Rights Code, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. H-14 prohibits refusing to continue to employ a person because of sex. Discrimination on the basis of pregnancy is a form of sex discrimination (Brooks v. Canada Safeway Ltd., [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1219), and the test is one of effect, not intention (O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd., [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536; Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143). A tribunal must consider all circumstances and ask whether it is reasonable to infer that maternity leave was a causative factor in the refusal to continue employment.
application: Unlike Hazelwood, Dorvault, Parry and Vestad, Dalton did not decide to retain Power permanently while McEvoy was on leave; his decision was made on March 1, 2002 when McEvoy was ready to return and could compete for the position. The uncontradicted evidence showed the reason was Dalton's greater familiarity and comfort with Power providing new personal-care duties arising from his surgery, plus his preference for her cooking — reasons unrelated to a prohibited ground and rebutting any inference of discrimination. There was no evidence of any unintended discriminatory effect within the Andrews definition.
conclusion: The refusal to continue McEvoy's employment was not based on her pregnancy or maternity leave; the Board's finding of sex discrimination was unreasonable. The Trial Division was correct and the appeal was dismissed.

issue: Can a client's personal preference for a particular caregiver support the refusal to employ following maternity leave without constituting discrimination?
facts: Dalton, the client whose home care was funded, expressed a preference for Power over McEvoy. The Board treated this as mere customer preference incapable of defending discrimination.
rule: Customer or client preference cannot justify a discriminatory act where the preference relates to a prohibited ground (Middleton v. 491465 Ontario Ltd. (1991), 15 C.H.R.R. D/317; Berry v. Manor Inn (1980), 1 C.H.R.R. D/152). However, a client's preference may still be considered in determining the actual reason for a refusal to employ.
application: Dalton never said he declined to employ McEvoy because she had been pregnant; he gave valid reasons unconnected to any prohibited ground (familiarity, comfort with intimate personal care post-surgery, meal preferences). Because the preference was not tied to a prohibited ground, the employer's acting on his instructions did not discriminate. The timing at the end of the leave, though a factor to weigh, did not make an inference of discrimination reasonable given Dalton's legitimate stated preferences.
conclusion: The client's preference here was grounded in legitimate, non-prohibited reasons; it did not establish discrimination, and no prima facie case was made out on the effect analysis either.

issue: Did either party repudiate the millwork contract, and with what consequences?
facts: NGW almost completed the millwork by mid-December 2016; only minor touch-ups (kitchen handles to be supplied by the owner, filler pieces) remained. Arviv complained about design features not in the contract, stopped paying after paying about 59%, denied NGW access, ceased all communication, and stated he would not pay 'a penny' until satisfied. NGW repeatedly sought access to complete the work and later registered and perfected its lien.
rule: Contractor 'abandonment' requires cessation of work plus a lack of intention to complete (Baeumler Quality Construction Inc. v. Pirraglia, 2018 ONSC 7610; Nigeco Contracting Ltd. v. Aizenstros, 2019 ONSC 3364; Heyday Homes Ltd. v. Gunroj, 2004 CanLII 34324). Repudiation occurs where 'the very thing bargained for has not been provided' (Guarantee Co. of North America v. Gordon Capital Corp., 1999 CanLII 664 (SCC)), assessed on the five factors in 968703 Ontario Ltd. v. Vernon, 2002 CanLII 35158 (ONCA). The innocent party may elect to end or continue the contract.
application: NGW did not abandon the contract, having shown a continuing intention to complete through nine unanswered requests for access and handles. Arviv, by ceasing payment, refusing access, complaining only about design (which was not NGW's responsibility) and cutting off communication, repudiated the contract in December 2016/January 2017. NGW elected to accept the repudiation by perfecting its lien and commencing the action on February 21, 2017, which excused NGW from performing deficiency correction work.
conclusion: Arviv repudiated the contract; NGW did not abandon it and was excused from further deficiency correction obligations.

issue: Was NGW entitled to payment of its contract and extras invoices despite incomplete work?
facts: Only about $1,500-$2,000 of work (roughly 1% of the $183,767.28 price) remained, undone because Arviv failed to deliver handles and refused access. NGW invoiced $56,250 for the contract balance and $17,517.28 for authorized extras (girls' closets, laundry cabinetry, wall frame). The expert Walker independently valued the extras at $17,993.93, close to the invoice.
rule: A contractor is entitled to payment upon 'substantial completion'; minor defects do not prevent fulfilment of the condition precedent (Heyday Homes Ltd. v. Gunroj, quoting Goldsmith on Construction Contracts). 'Completion' is deemed under Construction Act s. 2(3) when the cost to complete is the lesser of 1% of the contract price or $1,000. An owner alleging quality deficiencies must notify the contractor and allow correction (Turano's Home Improvement Inc. v. Stern, 2018 ONSC 201).
application: The value of outstanding work was about 1% of the price, so NGW substantially completed the contract and was entitled to the full $56,250. The extras were outside the contract scope but authorized by Arviv ('just make it the same...I trust you') at a reasonable fixed price confirmed by the expert. The Scott Schedule 'deficiencies' were largely design changes, owner-caused issues, or wear and tear; at most a few items totalling roughly $675 might have succeeded had the counterclaim not been struck, and Arviv had not spent money correcting them.
conclusion: NGW was entitled to be paid the full $73,767.28 for the contract and extras invoices.

issue: Did NGW preserve and perfect its lien within the statutory time?
facts: NGW registered its claim for lien on January 27, 2017, commenced the action on February 21, 2017, and registered a certificate of action on February 28, 2017. The value of work remaining when it ceased was $1,500-$2,000.
rule: Under the pre-July 2018 Construction Act, a contractor's lien must be preserved within 45 days and perfected within 90 days of 'completion' or 'abandonment' (ss. 31(1)(b), 36). 'Completion' is deemed under s. 2(3) when the remaining cost is the lesser of 1% of the price or $1,000.
application: Since the value of remaining work ($1,500-$2,000) exceeded the $1,000 threshold, the contract had not been 'completed' by December 12, 2016, and NGW did not abandon it. As NGW did no further work, the 45-day and 90-day periods had not begun to run, so registration and perfection were timely.
conclusion: NGW properly preserved and perfected its lien; the lien is $73,767.28, with priority over the CIBC mortgage to the extent of the unpaid $18,376.72 holdback and full priority over the NHE second mortgage.

issue: Should the defendant's set-off and counterclaim be struck and adjournment denied for non-compliance?
facts: Arviv failed to deliver any of his seven fact-witness affidavits despite directions, cycled through five lawyers, walked out of a settlement conference, barred NGW's principal from a consented site visit, and admitted being 'too busy' and that the case was 'a waste of his time.' On the eve of the summary trial he sought an adjournment to retain counsel.
rule: Rule 60.12(b) allows striking a defence for non-compliance with an interlocutory order; striking is not a first resort and requires consideration of the merits of the defence, the context of the misconduct, and whether the lawyer rather than the party was at fault (Koohestani v. Mahmood, 2015 ONCA 56; Rock Precast Erectors Ltd. v. Canadian Precast Ltd., 2012 ONSC 5924). Rule 50.01(2)(b) permits dismissing a counterclaim where a defendant fails to appear at trial.
application: Arviv's defence appeared blatantly unmeritorious, his non-compliance was entirely his own doing and part of a delay strategy, and an eight-month adjournment would prejudice NGW whose trial evidence was already filed. The master struck the set-off and counterclaim but preserved the defence so Arviv could cross-examine, and denied the adjournment.
conclusion: The set-off and counterclaim were struck and the adjournment denied; the defence was preserved.

issue: Should the master recuse himself for a reasonable apprehension of bias?
facts: Arviv, an Israeli Jew, alleged the master said 'you're one of those people,' creating an apprehension of anti-Semitic or anti-elitist bias. The audio recording showed the master actually said 'so you were one of those people who were travelling abroad,' referring to the COVID-19 controversy about foreign travel.
rule: The test for reasonable apprehension of bias is whether an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically and having thought it through, would conclude the judge would not decide fairly (R. v. S. (R.D.), 1997 CanLII 324 (SCC); R. v. Richards, 2017 ONCA 424). There is a presumption of judicial integrity and a high onus on the moving party; stereotyping may raise an apprehension. Recusal on trifling or invalid grounds wastes resources and risks injustice (Jewish Family and Child Service of Toronto v. J.Z., 2014 ONCJ 165).
application: The statement actually made concerned travelling abroad contrary to public-health advice during the pandemic, not Arviv's ethnicity or name, and would not lead a reasonable person to perceive anti-Semitic or anti-elitist bias. The complaint was invalid, and recusing on such grounds would waste resources and cause delay.
conclusion: The recusal motion was denied.

issue: Should the New Claim be struck under Rule 9-5(1) as disclosing no reasonable claim, as vexatious, or as an abuse of process?
facts: Mrs. Nayyar's original 2004 disability benefits claim against Costco and Manulife was ultimately dismissed by the Court of Appeal, and costs and execution proceedings (including sale of her home) were concluded. The Nayyars repeatedly attempted to re-litigate, including a Judicial Review Petition dismissed by consent on their undertaking not to re-advance the same issues. They then filed the New Claim (February 22, 2016), an almost incomprehensible pleading citing unrelated rules, statutes and cases, claiming 43 heads of loss, and apparently asserting Mr. Nayyar's unregistered one-half interest in the sold property and re-asserting the benefits claim.
rule: Rule 9-5(1)(a),(b),(d) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules permits striking a pleading that discloses no reasonable claim (plain and obvious test: Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959), that is frivolous or vexatious, or that is otherwise an abuse of process. Abuse of process is a flexible doctrine, an adjunct of res judicata, protecting judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the administration of justice (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63). Under the Family Law Act ss. 81, 82, 103(2) and Land Title Act s. 29, an unregistered spousal interest in land is unenforceable against a third-party judgment creditor.
application: The New Claim was incoherent and could not be saved by redrafting because its deficiencies were fundamental. Any claim by Mr. Nayyar to a one-half interest failed: Registrar Cameron's unappealed report confirmed Mrs. Nayyar was sole registered owner, and under the FLA/Land Title Act an unregistered interest is unenforceable against creditors like Costco and Manulife. To the extent the claim revisited the Benefits Claim and the Execution Proceedings, those matters had been fully litigated and were res judicata, making relitigation an abuse of process.
conclusion: The whole of the New Claim was struck under Rule 9-5(1).

issue: Should Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar be declared vexatious litigants under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act?
facts: The New Claim was the fourth proceeding in which the Nayyars sought to challenge the outcomes of the Benefits Claim and/or Execution Proceedings. They had been told by both the Supreme Court and Court of Appeal that their claims had no merit, had repeatedly failed to pay costs orders (one still outstanding), continued to demand $99 million, and sent rude and threatening communications to opposing counsel. Mr. Nayyar was found throughout to be the directing mind driving the litigation.
rule: Section 18 of the Supreme Court Act permits an order that a person who has habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds instituted vexatious proceedings may not institute proceedings without leave. The non-exhaustive Fabian factors (Re Lang Michener v. Fabian (1987), 59 O.R. (2d) 353), affirmed in Harrison, 2016 BCCA 210 and Pearlman, 2010 BCCA 362, guide the analysis, including relitigating decided issues, hopeless actions, improper purpose, rolling forward grounds, the whole history, failure to pay costs, and persistent unsuccessful appeals.
application: Virtually all hallmarks of vexatious conduct were present: repeated relitigation of conclusively determined matters despite express warnings, hopeless claims, improper demands, rolling forward of grounds, failure to pay costs orders, and threatening/abusive communications. Simply striking the claim would not deter the Nayyars given their relentless, unceasing pattern. Because Mr. Nayyar was the directing mind even where earlier proceedings named only Mrs. Nayyar, courts may declare an assisting spouse a vexatious litigant (Daniel v. I.C.B.C., 2003 BCSC 475; Griffith, 2004 BCSC 1443).
conclusion: Both Mr. and Mrs. Nayyar were declared vexatious litigants, precluded from instituting any proceeding against Costco or Manulife and related persons without leave of the court.

issue: Was the respondent the successful party presumptively entitled to costs?
facts: The respondent's motion for summary judgment was granted, dismissing the applicant's entire claim.
rule: Rule 24(1) of the Family Law Rules creates a presumption that a successful party is entitled to costs.
application: Having obtained summary judgment dismissing the whole claim, the respondent was clearly successful within the meaning of r. 24(1) and presumptively entitled to costs of the motion and proceeding.
conclusion: The respondent was the successful party and presumptively entitled to costs.

issue: What was the impact of the offer to settle that did not strictly satisfy r. 18(14)?
facts: The respondent made an offer to settle dated March 20, 2024 that complied with most r. 18 requirements but included a condition restricting the applicant from further litigation without leave — a condition not obtained on the motion.
rule: Rule 18(14)-(16) governs costs consequences of failing to accept an offer; r. 24(12)(a)(iii) lists written offers as a factor; Mattina v. Mattina, 2018 ONCA 867 identifies encouraging settlement as a fundamental costs principle.
application: Because the respondent did not obtain an order as favourable as the offer (he got no litigation-restriction condition), he did not satisfy r. 18(14). However the offer was reasonable, timely, and differed from the outcome only on ancillary relief, so it still carried significant weight under r. 24(12)(a)(iii) and the settlement-encouragement rationale.
conclusion: The offer did not trigger the r. 18(14) consequence but weighed significantly in favour of the respondent's costs.

issue: Did the applicant act in bad faith, triggering full recovery costs under r. 24(8)?
facts: The applicant repeatedly accused the respondent of pedophilia, sexual assault, incest, human trafficking and kidnapping, used racist, xenophobic and homophobic language, attacked opposing counsel as a stalker and pervert, and made settlement contingent on withdrawal of criminal charges — all while her application sought to grant the respondent unsupervised parenting time.
rule: Rule 24(8) requires full recovery costs where a party acted in bad faith. Kumar v. Nash, 2024 ONCJ 16 (citing Scipione, S.(C.) v. S.(M.), Stewart v. McKeown) sets a high threshold: bad faith involves conscious, intentional duplicity, obstruction or obfuscation, distinct from unreasonable conduct or poor judgment.
application: The meritless parenting claim alone would only show poor judgment, and the child-support claim was arguable. But the court found the applicant engaged in a duplicitous campaign of harassment to which her legal claims were secondary. Her baseless, vile attacks on the respondent and his counsel, and conditioning settlement on withdrawal of criminal charges, met the high bad-faith threshold and permeated the whole proceeding.
conclusion: The applicant acted in bad faith and the finding applied broadly to the litigation, engaging full recovery costs under r. 24(8).

issue: What amount of costs was reasonable and proportionate?
facts: The respondent claimed $23,730 for 70 hours at $300/hour (counsel called in 2020), inclusive of HST.
rule: Even on a full recovery basis, the court must screen for unreasonable or disproportionate claims: Kumar v. Nash, 2024 ONCJ 16; Jackson v. Mayerle, 2016 ONSC 1556; r. 24(12) proportionality factors.
application: While the applicant's attacks warranted a thorough response, 70 hours was not proportionate to the complexity of the litigation. The court reduced the recoverable time to 40 hours at counsel's rate.
conclusion: Costs fixed at $13,560 inclusive of fees, disbursements and HST, payable immediately.

issue: Should the portions of the counterclaim relating to CPL #2 be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b)-(d) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules?
facts: OTBEC filed two certificates of pending litigation (CPL #1 and CPL #2) against the defendants' development Lands during litigation over OTBEC's $1 million subscription investment. After both CPLs were cancelled, Promintory filed a counterclaim alleging CPL #2 was registered for an improper purpose and caused loss. OTBEC applied to strike the CPL #2 portions of the counterclaim.
rule: Rule 9-5(1)(b)-(d) permits striking pleadings that are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, that may prejudice/embarrass/delay a fair hearing, or that are an abuse of process. A pleading is frivolous/vexatious if it advances no claim known in law or cannot succeed (Willow v. Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083); embarrassment and abuse of process are described in Sahyoun v. Ho, 2015 BCSC 392 and Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860. A common law claim for wrongful filing of a CPL requires proof of malicious or unlawful purpose amounting to abuse of process (Liquor Barn Income Fund v. Becker, 2011 BCCA 141).
application: The court found the damages claim for wrongful filing of CPL #2 is a recognized common law cause of action, requiring proof that OTBEC had a malicious or unlawful purpose amounting to abuse of process. Damages could include increased cost of funds, construction delay and legal costs. This is not a summary judgment application, so Promintory was not required to adduce evidence at this stage. The claim was neither confusing nor obviously bound to fail.
conclusion: The court saw no merit in the application; the CPL #2 portions were not frivolous, vexatious or prejudicial and remain to be determined on the merits.

issue: Does the Consent Order preclude Promintory's damages claim relating to CPL #2 through res judicata, issue estoppel or waiver of costs?
facts: A December 23, 2022 Consent Order recorded that the ANOCC did not adequately disclose an interest in land to sustain CPL #2, dismissed OTBEC's claim for a CPL 'without costs', and adjourned generally Promintory's remaining application including its constructive trust dismissal request and costs. OTBEC argued the Counterclaim was res judicata or a collateral attack, and that Promintory had waived any CPL #2 claim.
rule: Court orders are interpreted by examining the pleadings, the order's language and the circumstances (Yu v. Jordan, 2012 BCCA 367). Res judicata can apply to consent orders (Spender v. Spender, 1999 CanLII 6548) but requires that the same questions were determined (Danyluk v. Ainsworth Technologies Inc., 2001 SCC 44). Costs are distinct from damages claims (Basha Sales Co. v. Adera Equities Inc., 2017 BCSC 1715).
application: The Consent Order only determined the inadequacy of the pleading for registering a CPL under s. 215(1) LTA; it did not adjudicate the substantive constructive trust claim (adjourned generally) or any damages arising from CPL #2, which had not even been pleaded at that time. The 'without costs' term addressed costs only, distinct from the damages claim, and showed no intention to release CPL #2 claims. Whether OTBEC's acknowledgement bears on its motive remains to be seen.
conclusion: No res judicata, issue estoppel or waiver arose from the Consent Order; the damages claim is not barred.

issue: Was the filing of the counterclaim an abuse of process because it was allegedly intended to delay or cloud the summary trial?
facts: Promintory filed the counterclaim on August 23, 2023, days before OTBEC's scheduled summary trial. OTBEC alleged this was a tactic to delay or cloud the issues. The summary trial did not proceed due to an insufficient time estimate and outstanding pre-trial matters, and OTBEC had served amended documents only after hours the Friday before.
rule: Abuse of process under R. 9-5(1)(d) is a flexible doctrine protecting judicial economy, consistency, finality and integrity of the administration of justice (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63).
application: The court found the summary trial was not ready to proceed for multiple reasons unrelated to the counterclaim. Moreover, the counterclaim advanced many claims beyond CPL #2 (subscription agreements, misrepresentation, trust over Units), yet OTBEC sought to strike only the CPL #2 portions. The court found no logic in alleging abuse of process while attacking only part of the pleading — it must be all or nothing.
conclusion: The filing of the counterclaim was not an abuse of process; the application was dismissed with costs payable in any event of the cause.

issue: What is the appropriate quantum of costs on the successful contempt motion?
facts: The applicant obtained a finding that the respondent was in contempt of a March 18, 2020 access order after repeatedly being denied access to the parties' 10-year-old son. He sought full recovery costs of $2,119.88; the respondent proposed $500 contingent on a future breach.
rule: Costs are discretionary and governed by the Family Law Rules, principally subrule 24(12) factors (behaviour, time, offers to settle, legal fees), guided by reasonableness and proportionality (Mattina v. Mattina, 2018 ONCA 867; Beaver v. Hill, 2018 ONCA 840; Berta v. Berta, 2015 ONCA 918). Quantum reflects what the unsuccessful party could reasonably expect to pay (Arthur v. Arthur, 2019 ONSC 938). Costs sanction conduct that increases the expense of litigation (Okanagan Indian Band, 2003 SCC 71).
application: The applicant was the successful party who acted reasonably, having attempted lesser enforcement options and to restore access through counsel before resorting to contempt, which is the court's last resort (Hefkey v. Hefkey). The respondent acted unreasonably, was openly defiant and undermined the child's relationship with the applicant and the administration of justice. The absence of an offer to settle was not a discounting factor since there was no reasonable element of compromise. The time and rates claimed were reasonable and proportionate, and receipt of legal aid is not a factor in setting costs (Ramcharitar; Alvarez; Loncar; S.G. v. A.S.).
conclusion: Costs were fixed at $1,800 inclusive of fees, disbursements and HST — a reduction from the full recovery amount sought.

issue: How should the respondent's limited financial circumstances affect the costs award and payment terms?
facts: The respondent is on public assistance and is primarily raising the child; she argued costs should be reduced or unenforceable and pointed to her impecuniosity.
rule: A party's limited finances are considered on quantum but are not a shield against liability for costs (MacDonald v. Magel; Snih v. Snih; Beaulieu v. Diotte). Those who can least afford to litigate should be most motivated to settle (Mohr v. Sweeney; Balsmeier v. Balsmeier). A party cannot be in contempt and then hide behind impecuniosity; payment terms may be structured to preserve the purposes of costs (E.K.B. v. Jewish Family and Child Services, 2020 ONSC 2924; Sang v. Suteu, 2016 ONCJ 160).
application: The court weighed the respondent's public-assistance status and caregiving role against her repeated breaches despite warnings, the harm to the child's relationship with the applicant and the distress and system costs caused. Rather than reduce liability, the court accommodated her circumstances through extended payment terms, with a mechanism to accelerate payment if she breaches the access order again.
conclusion: The costs of $1,800 are payable at $50 per month starting March 1, 2021, subject to acceleration on any future breach of the access order.

issue: Does the child's security and development remain compromised so as to warrant a review of the protection order under art. 95 of the Youth Protection Act?
facts: A prior order of 6 July 2015 had placed the nine-year-old child in a foster home (his maternal grandparents) with social follow-up. The DPJ applied on 12 February 2016 to review it. The child presents an oppositional disorder, an insecure attachment disorder and relational problems, and is at risk of developing a personality disorder without intervention. His parents separated in mid-July 2015.
rule: Article 95 of the Loi sur la protection de la jeunesse (L.R.Q., c. P-34.1) allows review of a protection order where the child's situation requires it; the analysis is governed by the principles of the Act, with the child's interest as the guiding standard.
application: The evidence (social study D-9 and Dr. Guzder's letter D-8) established most of the alleged facts. The child's fragile psychological state and continuing need for specialized services, together with the change in the family situation, satisfied the Tribunal that the situation required revision of the order.
conclusion: The Tribunal found the security and development of the child remained compromised and granted the review application.

issue: What corrective measures serve the child's best interest — should the child be entrusted to the father rather than placed in shared or maternal custody?
facts: Since 15 February 2016 the child had been entrusted to the father, who successfully completed anger/impulsivity therapy and now manages the child's behaviour with a clear framework. Ongoing conflict persisted between the parents. The mother, though loving, still had work to do on her sensitivity to the child's needs and had only attended three of 21 group sessions. Specialists said the child could not benefit from services until his living situation stabilized.
rule: Measures under the Youth Protection Act must be ordered in the best interest of the child; stability and freedom from parental conflict are central where the child's psychological health is fragile.
application: Given the child's need for a stable environment to access specialized pediatric psychiatric services, the father's demonstrated capacity, and the risk that shared custody would expose the child to ongoing parental conflict, the Tribunal found entrusting the child to the father, while favouring contact with the mother and maternal grandmother, best served the child. It also ordered health services, co-parenting workshops, non-denigration, and social follow-up.
conclusion: The Tribunal ordered the child entrusted to the father with favoured contacts with the mother and grandmother and required health services, until 23 June 2017.

issue: Were the statements comparing the plaintiffs' political nationalism to Hitler's defamatory?
facts: In its January 1993 confidential investment bulletin, Lafferty, Harwood, directed by Richard Lafferty, characterized the nationalism of PQ leader Parizeau and Bloc Québécois leader Bouchard as tribalism inevitably leading to dictatorship, 'no different from what Hitler did', invoking Nazi tactics of fear. A Le Devoir journalist obtained the bulletin and published extracts under the headline 'Bouchard, Parizeau, Hitler: même combat'. Lafferty reiterated the remarks in a February 16 letter copied to the media.
rule: Under art. 4 of the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms everyone has a right to the safeguard of their dignity, honour and reputation, a limit on freedom of expression (art. 3). Defamation (Radio Sept-Îles; Le Devoir inc. c. Centre de psychologie) requires fault assessed by the reasonable-person test, whether committed with intent to harm or through recklessness/negligence; the meaning of published words is judged objectively by the ordinary reasonable reader, not the author's intended sense.
application: The reasonable reader would understand the article to mean that the plaintiffs are nationalists whose politics inevitably lead to dictatorship as under Hitler, that their demagoguery instills fear so no one dares criticize them, and that they use Hitler's fear tactics. When asked to give concrete examples justifying the comparison, Lafferty could offer none; the uncontradicted evidence (party program, speeches, articles) showed both plaintiffs were deeply committed to democratic values and minority rights. Editorialists at The Gazette and La Presse and B'nai Brith's League for Human Rights all condemned the analogy as unfair and false. A politician does not lose the right to reputation.
conclusion: The statements were false and defamatory of both Parizeau and Bouchard; the defendants committed a civil fault, and Lafferty, Harwood, as publisher, is also liable.

issue: Does the defence of fair comment (commentaire loyal) apply?
facts: The defendants argued their remarks were an honest expression of opinion on a matter of public interest. Lafferty admitted he had never read a biography of Hitler or Mein Kampf, did not know Hitler was democratically elected, had not read the PQ program (only newspaper summaries), and had read no material on the plaintiffs' positions on rights and minorities before publishing.
rule: The fair-comment defence (Steinhaut c. Vigneault; Picard c. Gros-Louis) requires three elements: (1) a matter of public interest; (2) an honest intention to serve a just cause; and (3) a conclusion reasonably supportable on the facts reported.
application: The first condition (public interest) was admitted. The court accepted the second condition, finding Lafferty sincerely believed what he wrote and felt obliged to share it with clients. However, the third condition failed: Lafferty conducted no research, no verification, and no inquiry before drawing the Hitler comparison, relying on decades-old impressions. He did not discharge his burden of showing the remarks were reasonably supportable.
conclusion: The fair-comment defence fails because the comparison was not reasonably supportable on the facts.

issue: What moral and exemplary damages are payable?
facts: Each plaintiff claimed $100,000 in moral damages and $50,000 in exemplary damages. The bulletin nominally went to 275 corporate/financial clients, but Lafferty had no control over redistribution and reiterated the remarks to the media. Evidence showed the plaintiffs were hurt and indignant but did not establish long-lasting injury; both were soon electorally successful. Lafferty refused to retract even at trial and attached a caricature of the plaintiffs giving a Nazi salute to his February letter.
rule: Damages in defamation vary with the gravity of the words and the harm suffered; the judgment itself is a primary form of reparation (case law survey). Exemplary damages under art. 49 of the Quebec Charter require an unlawful and intentional interference, i.e. conduct done with knowledge of its immediate, natural or at least extremely probable consequences (St-Ferdinand). Quantum factors (West Island Teachers' Association c. Nantel) include prevention/deterrence, the offender's conduct, extent of harm, ability to pay, and compensatory quantum.
application: The court found the plaintiffs, seasoned politicians accustomed to criticism, were not long affected, and the crude, obviously false comparisons likely influenced few readers. It fixed moral damages at $10,000 each. On exemplary damages, although Lafferty sincerely intended to serve clients, he acted with knowledge of the probable consequences, confirmed and reiterated the remarks to the media, refused to retract, and appended a mocking caricature; ability to pay was admitted. The court awarded $10,000 each in exemplary damages.
conclusion: Action allowed in part: defendants condemned solidarily to pay each plaintiff $10,000 in moral damages and $10,000 in exemplary damages, with interest and additional indemnity as specified, and costs.

issue: Should the trial be adjourned on the eve of hearing because the defendant claimed to be without counsel?
facts: Mr. Arviv had hired and dismissed five lawyers, admitted being 'too busy on other matters' to prepare ordered trial evidence, accepted his last counsel's resignation less than a month before trial, and repeatedly sought adjournments to retain new counsel while refusing to name prospective lawyers. New Generation's trial evidence was already on the record as ordered. A lawyer appeared on the trial's second day retained only to seek an adjournment of at least eight months, giving no assurance Mr. Arviv would comply with future directions.
rule: A court exercises discretion over trial adjournments, weighing the reasons for the request, the requesting party's conduct, and the prejudice to the opposing party; an adjournment may be refused where the representation problem is self-created and part of a delay strategy.
application: The Master found Mr. Arviv had ample resources to retain counsel, that his 'without counsel' predicament was self-inflicted and part of a deliberate delay strategy including breach of directions to deliver affidavit evidence, and that an adjournment (effectively at least eight months) would significantly prejudice New Generation, whose evidence was already filed. Nothing at the January 13-14 hearing altered the earlier January 7 refusal.
conclusion: The renewed request to adjourn was refused; the January 7, 2021 ruling denying the adjournment stood.

issue: Did the presiding Master's remark give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias requiring recusal?
facts: Mr. Arviv, an Israeli Jew residing in Miami, alleged the Master said 'you're one of those people,' which he interpreted as anti-Semitic (and 'anti-elitist') bias. The audio recording showed the Master had actually said 'so you were one of those people who were travelling abroad,' referring to the COVID-19 controversy over unnecessary foreign travel, in the context of Mr. Arviv's failure to attend a December 23, 2020 teleconference. Mr. Arviv took no exception at the time.
rule: The test for reasonable apprehension of bias (R. v. S. (R.D.), [1997] 3 S.C.R. 484 at para. 111): whether an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically and having thought it through, would conclude the decision-maker would not decide fairly. Per R. v. Richards, 2017 ONCA 424 (paras. 43-50), there is a presumption of judicial integrity, the threshold is high but not insurmountable, the onus is on the moving party, and stereotyping reasoning may found an apprehension of bias. Recusal on trifling or invalid grounds wastes resources and may prejudice other parties (Children's Aid Society of Waterloo Region v. B.(L.A.), 2004 ONCJ 235; Jewish Family and Child Service of Toronto v. J.Z., 2014 ONCJ 165).
application: The statement actually made concerned foreign travel during the pandemic, not Mr. Arviv's name, origin or ethnicity, and would not lead a reasonable person to perceive anti-Semitic bias. The 'anti-elitist' characterization also failed: the remark was on its face a statement of fact carrying no value judgment, and travel abroad was unrelated to the construction dispute. The grounds were 'invalid,' and recusing would waste resources and cause unnecessary delay.
conclusion: The recusal motion was denied.

issue: Did the appeal judge err in ordering a new trial on the basis that the trial judge failed to consider relevant evidence on the intent element of wilfully promoting hatred under s. 319(2)?
facts: Mr. Ahenakew, a prominent First Nations politician, made comments rationalizing the Holocaust during a brief, confrontational three-minute interview initiated by a newspaper reporter after a conference speech. He was convicted at trial under s. 319(2) on the basis of certain statements made during that interview. The defence position was that the statements were made spontaneously in anger, only once, in response to the reporter's questions, that Ahenakew ended the interview himself and hung up on a follow-up call, and that he did not intend to promote hatred.
rule: Section 319(2) of the Criminal Code criminalizes wilfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group. Under R. v. Keegstra, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697, 'wilfully' requires that the accused subjectively desired or foresaw as substantially certain the promotion of hatred, and 'promotes' means active support or instigation (French 'fomenter'). Per Mugesera v. Canada, 2005 SCC 40, the trier of fact must consider the speech objectively but with regard to the circumstances, manner, tone, and audience. A trial judge must have regard to all relevant evidence when determining guilt (Macdonald v. The Queen, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 665; Harper v. The Queen, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 2).
application: The Court examined the structure of the trial judge's reasons. On every other issue — the speech, the 'private conversation' question, and 'hatred' — the trial judge laid out or referenced all the significant relevant evidence, yet on 'wilful promotion' he referred only to the 'fury and passion' in the delivery. The evidence going to intent (the abrupt confrontational nature of the interview, its spontaneity, its brevity, that Ahenakew ended it) was mentioned only under the 'private conversation' analysis, not the intent analysis. Compared to the rest of the reasons, this omission revealed a substantive failure to take that evidence into account, not a mere failure to record it.
conclusion: The appeal judge made no error in concluding the trial judge failed to consider relevant evidence and in ordering a new trial; the Crown's appeal was dismissed. The Court added that on retrial the interview's context is also relevant to whether Ahenakew 'promoted' (not merely 'wilfully' promoted) hatred.

issue: Is inadequacy of a trial judge's reasons, by itself, a ground of appeal, and did the reasons here reveal a substantive error of law?
facts: The appeal judge relied in part on R. v. G.(R.M.) to suggest a trial judge sitting alone must, like a jury charge, set out the defence theory and the evidence bearing on it. The Crown argued this imposed an erroneous duty to give jury-style reasons.
rule: Per R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26, and R. v. Braich, 2002 SCC 27, a trial judge sitting alone is not required to give the equivalent of a jury instruction; adequacy of reasons is assessed functionally, and inadequate reasons ground reversal only where they prevent meaningful appellate review. However, a failure to consider (as opposed to merely record) relevant evidence is a substantive error of law.
application: The Court agreed the appeal judge erred insofar as he suggested a trial judge sitting alone must produce jury-charge-style reasons. But it read the appeal judge's decision as finding a substantive failure to consider relevant evidence, consistent with Macdonald and Harper (approved in Sheppard), rather than a mere deficiency in the reasons. The trial judge's reasons positively revealed that intent evidence was not taken into account.
conclusion: Despite the appeal judge's unfortunate reference to R. v. G.(R.M.), his basic approach was sound; the trial judge committed a substantive error of law by failing to consider relevant intent evidence, so the new trial order stands.

issue: Does the seizure-and-forfeiture regime in s. 12 of the Wild Life Act violate s. 15(1) of the Charter by producing unequal or discriminatory treatment?
facts: An RCMP/wild life officer stopped Brown for a seat-belt check and observed an uncased, unwrapped .303 rifle and ammunition in his vehicle while he was in a closed hunting area. He was convicted under s. 82(1) of the Wild Life Regulations and fined $100, but the trial judge refused to confirm forfeiture of the rifle under s. 12 of the Act, holding that provision unconstitutional; the summary conviction appeal court (Barry J.) upheld that ruling relying on R. v. Hillyard, finding s. 12 unfair and discriminatory because officers have unfettered discretion to seize, guns vary in value, forfeiture under s. 12 is automatic while s. 11 forfeiture is discretionary, and owners not in possession have no recourse under s. 12.
rule: Section 15(1) of the Charter guarantees equality before and under the law and equal protection and benefit without discrimination. Under Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143, the 'similarly situated' test is rejected; discrimination means a distinction based on grounds relating to the personal characteristics of an individual or group that imposes burdens or withholds benefits. Section 15(1) protection is confined to the enumerated grounds and analogous grounds (Reference Re Workers' Compensation Act (Nfld.), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 922; R. v. Turpin, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1296). Differential treatment is permitted provided it is 'without discrimination'; only discrimination on enumerated or analogous grounds engages s. 15(1).
application: The Court accepted that s. 12 may produce differential treatment—seizure is discretionary, guns vary in value, s. 12 forfeiture is automatic unlike discretionary s. 11 forfeiture, and non-possessing owners have no recourse. However, applying the post-Andrews/Turpin framework unavailable to the courts below, the Court held this was 'differential treatment without discrimination.' Section 12 and s. 82(1) of the Regulations make no distinction based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age, or disability, nor on any analogous personal characteristic; they apply to all would-be hunters. No individual or group identifiable by an enumerated or analogous ground was set apart. Flawed or piecemeal legislation producing unequal impact does not amount to Charter-prohibited discrimination.
conclusion: Section 12 does not infringe s. 15(1) of the Charter; the seizure and forfeiture were not discriminatory. Consideration of s. 1 therefore did not arise. Leave to appeal granted, appeal allowed, and the order returning the firearm set aside; forfeiture is complete upon entry of the conviction without any further order.

issue: Do the plaintiff's pleadings against the realtor defendants disclose a reasonable cause of action such that they should survive an application to strike under Rule 19(24)?
facts: Ng, self-represented, alleged that real estate agents Chan and Tse breached fiduciary and statutory duties by failing to disclose they were 'business associates' with the builder Parmar and by leading him into a failed April 2008 sale contract and failing to arrange the buyers' inspection. The pleadings were vague and did not identify any specific misrepresentation or plead that Tse owed a duty to disclose the associations.
rule: Rule 19(24) of the Rules of Court permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim. The test under Rule 19(24)(a) is whether, assuming the pleaded facts can be proved, it is 'plain and obvious' that no reasonable cause of action is disclosed (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959). The court examines whether the material facts, if proved, would complete all constituent elements of a cause of action known in law (Budgell v. British Columbia, 2007 BCSC 991). Doubt is resolved in favour of allowing the pleading to stand.
application: Reading the pleadings in the light most favourable to Ng, the court found no material facts establishing that Tse owed him any duty of care or duty to disclose, and no identified misrepresentation or pleaded damages flowing from non-disclosure. Against Chan, the disclosure-based claim likewise failed to plead the necessary duty and any damages independent of the failed transaction. The essential elements of the asserted causes of action were not pleaded.
conclusion: The pleadings failed to disclose a reasonable cause of action against either realtor; combined with the abuse of process findings, the statement of claim was struck in its entirety.

issue: Do the plaintiff's claims constitute an abuse of process because they seek to relitigate issues already finally determined in prior proceedings between related parties?
facts: In the earlier Manjit Action, Wedge J. found after trial that Ng had not overpaid Manjit, that the $20,000 deposit was never received by Manjit, and that the April 2008 offer was not a legitimate purchase — the purported buyer 'John' was likely Ng himself attempting to pressure Parmar. Ng's evidence was found to be fabricated. That judgment was substantially upheld on appeal (2009 BCCA 429). Ng's new claims against Chan and Tse rested on the same factual allegations.
rule: Rule 19(24)(d) codifies the court's inherent jurisdiction to strike claims amounting to abuse of process. The doctrine focuses on the integrity of the adjudicative process and precludes relitigation of issues already decided even where strict issue estoppel requirements of privity/mutuality are not met (Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79, 2003 SCC 63; Skender v. Farley, 2007 BCCA 629). Relitigation may be permitted only where the first proceeding was tainted by fraud, fresh conclusive evidence emerges, or fairness so dictates.
application: Both the escrow claim and the realtor claims depended on findings 'at complete variance' with Wedge J.'s conclusions. The first proceeding was not tainted by fraud other than Ng's own, no new evidence was advanced, and fairness did not favour reopening. The escrow claim was an abuse Wedge J. had expressly warned against. Allowing relitigation of the legitimacy of Ng's fraudulent conduct would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
conclusion: The claims were dismissed as an abuse of process; relitigation would not enhance but would impeach the integrity of the judicial system.

issue: Can the plaintiff maintain a claim for breach of fiduciary duty against his listing agent where he pleads no damages independent of the impugned transaction and comes to equity without clean hands?
facts: Assuming Ng could show Chan failed to disclose a material business relationship amounting to a breach of a fiduciary duty of loyalty and disclosure owed by a listing agent, Ng claimed no damages other than those said to arise from the failed April 2008 transaction, and the alleged breach arose in a listing context marked by Ng's own deception and false testimony.
rule: On breach of a fiduciary duty a plaintiff may seek prophylactic or restitutionary damages measured by benefit to the defendant or loss to the plaintiff (Strother v. 3464920 Canada Ltd., 2007 SCC 24); a mere breach of duty yields no damages absent benefit or loss (Canson Enterprises v. Boughton & Co., [1991] 3 S.C.R. 534). Equitable relief may be denied where there is an immediate and necessary relation between the plaintiff's own blameworthy conduct and that alleged against the defendant (clean hands doctrine; Canson; Parnell v. Viger).
application: Ng pleaded no viable actual damages independent of the failed transaction that had already been found illegitimate, and his alleged loss was inseparable from his own fraudulent conduct. Without pleaded loss the breach would generate no damages, and the clean-hands bar precluded equitable relief given the immediate connection between his deception and the impugned dealings.
conclusion: The residual fiduciary claim could not proceed; permitting it would be an abuse of process and threaten the integrity of the adjudicative process, so it too was struck.

issue: Does an owner with a right of entry who forcibly enters premises wrongfully held over acquire lawful possession sufficient to prove the plea of justification and to justify removing the occupant?
facts: John Ferguson Jr., who had acquired Napier's interest through a chain of conveyances under the Insolvent Act of 1869, demanded possession of the St. Peters dwelling occupied by Mrs. Napier, who held over and refused to leave. In the husband's absence Ferguson broke open the locked door, removed the daughter and furniture, and when Mrs. Napier returned and re-entered he put her out by force, injuring her. He pleaded that he 'was possessed' of the dwelling in which she was trespassing.
rule: An owner entitled to possession may enter on his land and use no more force than necessary to remove a wrongdoer; possession follows title so that where two are in apparent possession the law adjudges possession in the one with title (Jones v. Chapman; Butcher v. Butcher). A forcible entry exposes the owner to indictment under 5 Rich. II, c. 7, but not to a civil action by the wrongful occupant, who has suffered no legal injury (Harvey v. Brydges per Parke B.; Blades v. Higgs per Erle C.J.; Taylor v. Cole; Taunton v. Costar; Lowe v. Telford).
application: Per Allen C.J. (Fisher and Wetmore JJ. concurring): Ferguson had a superior title to the plaintiffs, entered, and was in actual possession de facto; the assault on Mrs. Napier occurred not while making entry (she being absent when he broke in) but in preventing her wrongful re-entry and continuation. Having the right and being in actual possession, he had the legal possession; she was a trespasser whom he could remove using no more force than necessary. No question of excess was left to the jury. The majority declined to follow Newton v. Harland on this point, preferring Harvey v. Brydges and Blades v. Higgs, and saw no difference in principle between defending possession and regaining it.
conclusion: The majority held the plea of possession was, or should have been treated as, made out; the trial judge misdirected the jury, and a new trial was ordered.

issue: Does a forcible entry contrary to 5 Rich. II, c. 7, prevent the owner from acquiring lawful possession, so that the plea of possession is negatived?
facts: The entry was effected by breaking the locked door with a plank while the daughter, left expressly to keep possession, was inside — a forcible entry within the statute. The defendants relied only on the constructive/legal possession said to accrue eo instanti on entry, not on any completed actual possession.
rule: 5 Rich. II, c. 7 forbids entry 'with strong hand' even where entry is given by law; a right cannot be acquired through the commission of a wrong, and a lawful possession cannot be derived from an unlawful act (Newton v. Harland per Tindal C.J. and Bosanquet J.; Blades v. Higgs (H.L.); Lowe v. Telford distinguishing actual from constructive possession).
application: Per Duff J. (Weldon J. concurring, dissenting): the plea alleged possession, not a completed entry under title; the defendants had only a forcible entry plus a claimed constructive possession, since the furniture removal was unfinished and the daughter was in actual occupation when the door was broken. To make out possession they had to invoke a legal fiction to enlarge an indictable act, which the law will not do. Applying Lowe v. Telford, the defendants had neither actual nor lawful possession at the time of the assault, and had not even properly pleaded or proved a freehold title.
conclusion: The dissent would have upheld the verdict for the plaintiffs, holding the plea of possession not proved; but the dissent did not prevail.

issue: Had the defendant established a sufficient title through the insolvency conveyances?
facts: Napier assigned under the Insolvent Act 1869; the official assignee transferred to the creditors' assignee (DesBrisay), who under a composition deed reconveyed to Shireff, thence to Kelly, thence by sale to Ferguson. Objection was taken that conditions (preferential rent/costs) were not shown satisfied.
rule: Under ss. 95–96 of the Insolvent Act of 1869 the insolvent's interest passes through the assignee; a condition (payment of the assignee's costs) imposed for the assignee's benefit may be waived by him, and a stranger cannot object after conveyance that costs were unpaid.
application: Allen C.J. found no evidence of preferential rent claims, held the assignee could waive his costs, and concluded whatever title Napier had vested in Ferguson. Duff J., dissenting, was not satisfied the freehold title was proved and noted the plea did not even allege ownership of the freehold. The point had not been squarely raised at trial.
conclusion: The majority treated the title as sufficient (at least a superior leasehold interest) to support the right of possession; this reinforced the order for a new trial.

issue: May a public-interest group be granted leave to intervene in a criminal appeal to support the Charter/civil-liberties grounds already advanced by the appellant?
facts: Jacinthe Caron was convicted under s. 338 of the Criminal Code of welfare fraud for allegedly cohabiting maritally with a spouse within the meaning of the Loi sur l'aide sociale (L.R.Q. c. A-16) while receiving benefits between June 1984 and March 1986. Her notice of appeal raised, among other grounds, that the trial judge's interpretation and application of s. 338 infringed ss. 7, 8 and 15 of the Canadian Charter by employing differentiated standards of criminal intent that discriminated on the basis of sex and economic condition (para. 5k)1 and 2). LEAF sought leave to intervene solely on those civil-liberties questions.
rule: Article 59 of the criminal appeal rules incorporates the Code de procédure civile, notably art. 208 (intervention by a person having an interest before judgment). While a strict reading of art. 208 and the criminal-law jurisprudence (Ogg-Moss v. R., [1984] 2 R.C.S. 173; Morgentaler v. The Queen (1975), 20 C.C.C. (2d) 449) would bar a third party from adding grounds of appeal against an accused, courts possess a fundamental residual power to control their own procedure to ensure justice (Fishing Vessel Owners Assn. of B.C. v. A.G. Canada (1985), 57 N.R. 376; Canadian Labour Congress v. Bhindi (1985), 17 D.L.R. (4th) 193). Standing rules have been liberalized in constitutional matters (Thorson; McNeil; Borowski), and granting intervention on genuine constitutional/civil-liberties issues is discretionary, guided by whether the intervenor can usefully assist the court and represents affected social interests.
application: Unlike Ogg-Moss and Morgentaler, LEAF did not seek to add new grounds of appeal but to support a civil-liberties argument the appellant had already raised, so no unfairness to the accused arose and a genuine justiciable dispute already existed. The appeal squarely raised systemic discrimination in the application of the Loi sur l'aide sociale and, through it, of s. 338 C.Cr. — a question affecting significant segments of the Quebec population. LEAF had repeatedly demonstrated its capacity to assist Canadian courts, up to the highest levels, in constitutional debates, and open intervention providing its own perspective was preferable to merely assisting counsel. The court found subparagraphs 1) and 2) raise substantially the same legal question: whether the definition of spouse in the welfare legislation entails a necessarily discriminatory application of the fraud concept to single mothers receiving social assistance. The intervention was strictly limited to those constitutional civil-liberties questions.
conclusion: The motion was allowed. LEAF was granted leave to intervene limited to the questions in para. 5k)1) and 2) of the notice of appeal and given 45 days to file a memorandum on those questions.

issue: Is the Mahr an enforceable pre-nuptial contract or is it governed by the Matrimonial Property Act's formal requirements?
facts: Just before their Muslim marriage ceremony, the parties entered, through negotiating uncles, into a Mahr under which Mr. Nasin agreed to pay Mrs. Nasin $10,000 upon marriage breakdown. There was an offer, acceptance and consideration but no written agreement, no s. 38 acknowledgment and no independent legal advice. The husband argued the Mahr was a purely religious obligation not enforceable by the courts, or alternatively a factor under s. 8.
rule: A dispute's religious dimension does not make it non-justiciable; parties can convert moral obligations into legally binding ones (Bruker v. Marcovitz, 2007 SCC 54). A pre-nuptial agreement made in contemplation of marriage falls under s. 37(2) of the Matrimonial Property Act and is enforceable only if it meets the mandatory formalities of s. 38 — a written acknowledgment by each spouse, made separately before independent counsel, of awareness of the agreement's nature, of possible property claims being given up, and of executing it freely. Canadian authority on Mahr agreements is divided (Nathoo, Amlani, N.M.M. in B.C. enforcing them; Kaddoura and Khan in Ontario).
application: The Court found the Mahr was a contract — a genuine exchange of promises intended to bind — properly characterized as a pre-nuptial agreement, and that its religious context did not bar enforcement. However, it met none of the s. 38 requirements: it was not in writing, there was no certificate of acknowledgment, and the parties received no independent legal advice. As a matter of legislative public policy protecting parties from unequal bargaining power, such agreements are enforced only when the statutory formalities are satisfied.
conclusion: The Mahr, though a contract, is unenforceable for failing to comply with s. 38 of the Matrimonial Property Act; the property must be divided under Part 1 of the Act.

issue: How should the matrimonial property be identified, valued, exempted and divided in this short marriage?
facts: The nine-month marriage produced a house (bought by the husband before marriage), a defunct wedding-decor business (Y & S Event Decor), RRSPs, stock options, furnishings, a car, cash wedding gifts and various debts. Property values, exemptions and division of post-separation gains were disputed; the trial occurred about 15 months after separation, during which the husband alone paid the mortgage and lived in the home.
rule: Under Hodgson v. Hodgson, 2005 ABCA 13, matrimonial property is valued at the date of trial through the four-step process in ss. 7 and 8 of the Matrimonial Property Act: (1) determine all property at trial; (2) identify s. 7(2) exemptions (property brought into marriage, valued at acquisition/marriage); (3) divide s. 7(3) property (gains on exempt property) justly and equitably per s. 8 factors; (4) divide remaining s. 7(4) property equally unless unjust. Debts brought into the marriage are generally exempt. Dissipation requires bad faith or neglect (Metz v. Metz, 2004 ABQB 528).
application: The Court valued the house at $475,000 at trial but, given the very short marriage and complete financial separation for the longer post-separation period, declined to share the fortuitous post-separation appreciation, dividing equally only the $47,000 in-marriage increase. RRSP gains ($5,155) were shared equally. Property brought in (car, stock options, pre-marriage RRSPs, pre-marriage debts, pre-wedding gifts and engagement/wedding costs borne by custom) were exempt. The husband had to account for the $14,000 cash wedding gifts (improperly used to pay his pre-marriage line of credit) and could not shift his pre-marriage debt onto the wife. The business equity ($20,500 after an $8,500 exemption) and $3,000 furnishings were divided equally; only $3,342 of debt qualified as matrimonial. No dissipation was established regarding the lost business contracts.
conclusion: Total property divided: $52,155 under s. 7(3) and $34,158 under s. 7(4), for $86,313; the husband keeps the house, his RRSPs and the business materials, and pays the wife an equalization payment of $43,156.

issue: Does a civil court have jurisdiction to interpret the Kethubah and adjudicate a claim rooted in Jewish religious marriage practice?
facts: The respondent challenged the Court's jurisdiction to interpret the Kethubah or to interfere in what he characterized as essentially matters of religion. There was, however, no conflict of dogma; the parties agreed on a statement of Jewish law, and orthodox Judaism was not divided on the subject.
rule: Civil courts will not adjudicate disputes turning on the preferment of one religious doctrine over another (Hofer v. Hofer; Dunnet v. Forneri; A.G. v. Ripon Cathedral), but will hear cases where the consequences go beyond religious dogma and affect temporal or patrimonial interests (Brown v. Curé of Montreal; Davis v. Jenkins; Gold v. Maldaver). Freedom of religion is affirmed by s. 1(c) of the Canadian Bill of Rights, 1960.
application: Wilson J. held there was no conflict of dogma to resolve and no personal religious conviction of the respondent forbidding the act sought. The Kethubah was an instrument in writing, signed by the parties and intended to have effect, so it fell within Queen's Bench Rule 536, and its interpretation was not barred merely because it touched religious belief, particularly where the parties agreed on its meaning. The disabilities attaching to the applicant's status in her community engaged temporal consequences justifying the Court's intervention.
conclusion: The Court had jurisdiction to interpret the Kethubah and to hear the claim.

issue: Is the applicant entitled to a declaration that the respondent must deliver a Get under the Kethubah?
facts: The parties married in traditional Jewish form with a Kethubah; their civil marriage was dissolved but, in the eyes of orthodox Judaism, remained subsisting until the husband delivered a Get. Without the Get, the applicant could not remarry in her faith and any children she bore would be regarded as Mamzerim.
rule: The law will give effect to a formal antenuptial marriage contract to the extent it is not contrary to public policy or otherwise invalid; execution and delivery of the Kethubah is tantamount to a prenuptial contract.
application: On the uncontradicted evidence, including the expert statement of Jewish law endorsed by several rabbis of the Winnipeg Beth Din, the applicant's rights under the Kethubah included the delivery to her of a Get. The respondent offered no evidence and did not cross-examine.
conclusion: The applicant was entitled to a declaration that, under the Kethubah, she is entitled to the preparation and delivery of a Get by the respondent.

issue: May the court issue mandamus compelling the respondent to present himself before the Beth Din and institute proceedings for the Get?
facts: The respondent had himself filed a cross-petition for divorce, so was not opposed to divorce in principle. The applicant had no other means of compelling delivery of the Get. Rabbinical courts can no longer impose physical sanctions and Jewish law authorizes them to seek civil-court assistance in enforcing their orders.
rule: Under s. 58 of The Queen's Bench Act, R.S.M. 1970, c. C280, and the prerogative writ jurisdiction, mandamus may issue to command fulfilment of a duty where the applicant is personally interested, has no other remedy, acts bona fide, and the act is consonant with right and justice (R. v. Inland Revenue Commissioners; Re Nathan). The court retains a residual power to enforce fundamental values (Shaw v. DPP), and the discretion is to be exercised liberally (Re Winnipeg Charter).
application: The order would merely oblige the respondent to complete what he had voluntarily set out to do by cross-petitioning for divorce. The act would not offend his conscience, as orthodox Judaism was not divided and he advanced no personal religious objection. The applicant had no other means of relief and acted in good faith. The absence of prior precedent (as in Koeppel v. Koeppel and Brett v. Brett, which recognized the wife's interest in the Get) was no bar.
conclusion: Mandamus granted: the respondent must present himself before the Beth Din to inquire whether a Get is necessary and, if so determined, institute proceedings for it.

issue: Should the self-represented plaintiff's statement of claim be struck out in its entirety under Rule 19(24) of the Rules of Court?
facts: Tammy Peacock, operating a tourist facility, sued Tourism British Columbia and various officials after her blue-and-white highway sign was removed following a failed 2008 inspection, alleging economic loss. She filed a writ and statement of claim on October 26, 2009. The defendants applied to strike the claim as prolix, confusing and disclosing no reasonable cause of action.
rule: Rule 19(24) permits the court to strike out pleadings that (a) disclose no reasonable claim, (b) are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, (c) may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial, or (d) are an abuse of process. Rule 19(1) requires pleadings to be brief and to contain material facts in summary form. The test is whether it is 'plain and obvious' that the claim discloses no reasonable cause of action (Budgell v. Oppal, 2007 BCSC 991); a claim should not be struck if there is a chance of success, and neither novelty nor the strength of the defence should bar it. The court examines whether the material facts pleaded, if proved, would complete all the constituent elements of causes of action known in law.
application: The court found the statement of claim failed to plead material facts. Allegations of conspiracy and malicious discrediting did not state what each defendant did, with whom, or when. Certain paragraphs were merely descriptive or critical of government policy with no cause of action; others related to an irrelevant judicial review; and paragraphs 27–30 were embarrassing and scandalous while paragraphs 24–25 were unnecessary and vexatious contrary to Rule 19(24)(b) and (c). Rather than dismiss outright, the court gave the plaintiff leave to file a fresh statement of claim within 60 days and stayed pre-trial discovery until re-filing.
conclusion: The statement of claim was struck out in its entirety with costs in the cause, with leave to file a new statement of claim within 60 days.

issue: Did the statement of claim plead the material facts necessary to make out misfeasance in public office, defamation, and negligence?
facts: The claim was headed 'Misfeasance in public office' and sought damages for misfeasance, negligence in performance of a public duty, acting without authority, plus punitive damages, an apology and a declaration. Allegations included that Wanda Hook conspired to 'maliciously discredit' the facility and communicated 'slanderous un-truths.'
rule: Misfeasance in public office (Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse, 2003 SCC 69) requires (i) deliberate unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions, (ii) awareness the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff, plus proof of causation and compensable injury. Defamation requires pleading the defamatory words, who spoke them, to whom, and when. Negligence requires pleading a duty of care, its basis, the breach of the standard of care, and resulting damage.
application: The misfeasance allegations did not identify the offending defendants, the acts exceeding authority, or when they occurred, so material facts were missing. The defamation allegations failed to plead the actual words spoken, by whom, to whom, or when. The negligence claim did not assert any duty of care owed, its basis, or how the standard was breached. None of the torts were adequately pleaded.
conclusion: None of the causes of action were made out on the pleadings, supporting striking the claim, though with leave to re-plead.

issue: Should the conspiracy paragraphs of the statement of claim be struck under R. 19(24) on the basis that it is plain and obvious the claim is bound to fail because the Crown cannot conspire with itself?
facts: Northland Road Services Ltd. sued the Province (through the Minister of Transportation and Highways) and several named individual officials, alleging two conspiracies—a 'Maintenance Services Conspiracy' and a 'Tender Process Conspiracy'—involving unlawful means (defamation, fraud, deceit, negligence, abuse of power, breaches of agreement) and, alternatively, a predominant purpose to injure the plaintiff. The defendants applied to strike paras. 95–102, arguing that since the individual defendants were all Crown agents/employees acting within the scope of employment, the Province was effectively alleged to have conspired with itself.
rule: R. 19(24) permits striking a pleading that discloses no reasonable claim; no evidence is admissible (R. 19(27)). The test is whether it is 'plain and obvious' that the claim is bound to fail assuming the pleaded facts are true (Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., 1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)). The tort of conspiracy requires (a) an agreement/common intention, (b) an overt act, and (c) resulting damage; it arises where defendants use lawful means with a predominant purpose to injure, or where defendants use unlawful means directed at the plaintiff knowing injury is likely. A corporation or the Crown cannot conspire with itself where agents act within the scope of their employment (Kuhn v. American Credit Indemnity Co.; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress, 1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)).
application: The court distinguished the authorities relied on by the defendants. Critically, the defence itself denied para. 9 (that the individuals were all agents/employees for whom the Crown was vicariously liable), so that question was in issue and could not be assumed in the defendants' favour on a strike application. The pleaded acts against the individuals included malice, bad faith, deceit, fraud, abuse of power, negligence, breach of warranty and conspiracy. The conspiracy allegations transcended the named individuals ('other persons presently unknown'), the aim was broadly defined, and there was an allegation of unjust enrichment. In these circumstances the court could not conclude it was plain and obvious the conspiracy claims must inevitably fail.
conclusion: The application to strike paras. 95–102 was dismissed; the plaintiff may pursue its asserted rights at least to the examination for discovery stage. The plaintiff was awarded costs of the application in any event of the cause.

issue: Should leave to amend under Rule 26.01 be granted where the proposed new claims may be untenable at law?
facts: N.H.B. sought leave to deliver a fresh as amended statement of claim converting a five-page defamation action into a thirteen-page pleading adding intentional infliction of mental distress, conspiracy to injure, malicious prosecution and a Family Law Act s. 61 claim, after the action had been set down for trial.
rule: Rule 26.01 is mandatory ('the court shall grant leave to amend') unless the amendment causes non-compensable prejudice; however, leave will not be granted where the pleading is untenable at law such that, even if all pleaded facts are proven, they do not make out the legal conclusion. Rule 25.06(8) requires full particulars where malice or intent is alleged (AGFA Inc. v. Partners Prepress).
application: The Master reviewed each proposed new cause of action against its constituent elements and the pleaded facts, granting leave only for the claim that satisfied the legal test and was unopposed, while refusing amendments that were untenable or improperly pleaded.
conclusion: Leave granted only in part; amendments untenable at law were refused.

issue: Was the tort of conspiracy to injure properly pleaded?
facts: N.H.B. alleged that L.B. and her daughter L.M.C. conspired to injure her by harming her son A.B., but L.M.C. was not named as a defendant, and the pleading referred only to L.B.'s motive and did not allege that L.M.C. agreed to injure.
rule: Conspiracy requires two or more persons using lawful or unlawful means for the predominant purpose of injuring the plaintiff, an agreement to injure, acts in furtherance, and resulting damages (Harris v. GlaxoSmithKline Inc., 2010 ONSC 2326; Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., 1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)). Rule 25.06(8) requires full particulars of malice.
application: Only one defendant was sued, no case law supports a single-defendant conspiracy, and merely naming L.M.C. in the body of the claim deprived her of a voice while insulating the plaintiff from cost consequences. No agreement to injure was alleged, and malice against L.M.C. (who McWatt J. found was 'trapped' in her mother's camp) could not simply be inferred from the acquittal.
conclusion: Essential elements were absent; the conspiracy claim could not stand and leave was refused.
