application: The court held the amendments did not end the abridgment: the burden on Saturday-observing consumers remained; the exemption protected only owners and co-religionists, leaving employees of differing faiths unprotected (e.g., a Jewish employee of a corporation naming no religion); and non-Christian retailers still had to close on Christian holy days plus their own. The B.C. Court of Appeal's reasoning in Canada Safeway confirmed customers and employees must be considered.
conclusion: The amended Act infringes freedom of conscience and religion under s. 2(a).

issue: Is the s. 2(a) infringement justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
facts: The Act's objective was a common pause day for retail workers. New evidence included attitudinal surveys favouring Sunday shopping and testimony about retail worker vulnerability. The new s. 4 municipal option gave municipalities near-unrestricted power to permit or require holiday openings/closings.
rule: The Edwards Books/Oakes test: the objective must relate to a pressing and substantial concern, and the means must be proportional—rationally connected, minimally impairing, and not disproportionate in effect. The onus is on the party seeking to uphold the limit on a balance of probabilities.
application: The court accepted the common pause day as a valid objective and found the new sabbatarian exemption a reasonable constitutionally valid trade-off. However, the new municipal option failed both branches: by empowering municipalities to nullify the objective completely, the Legislature showed it did not regard the objective as pressing and substantial; and a scheme letting each municipality set (or omit) criteria had no careful design or rational connection to the objective—a 'carte blanche'. The new evidence gave some support but the decision rested primarily on the municipal option.
conclusion: The infringement is not justified under s. 1; the applicants failed to demonstrate justification.

issue: Does the Act violate the right to liberty under s. 7?
facts: Store owners and employees argued the prohibition on Sunday retail business deprived them of liberty.
rule: Per Edwards Books, 'liberty' in s. 7 is not an unconstrained right to transact business whenever one wishes; regulation of business is distinguishable from complete deprivation of the right to practise a profession (Wilson v. B.C. distinguished).
application: Following Edwards Books, the court found prohibiting Sunday retail operation and Sunday work is business regulation, unlike the total exclusion from professional practice in Wilson.
conclusion: The Act does not violate s. 7.

issue: Does the Act infringe equality rights under s. 15?
facts: The Act's effect burdens religious minorities who observe rest days other than Sunday.
rule: Section 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds including religion; discrimination that cannot be justified under s. 1 renders legislation invalid.
application: The court found the Act's effect discriminates against members of minorities on the ground of religion, and for the same reasons the s. 1 justification failed for the religious-freedom infringement, it failed here.
conclusion: The Act infringes s. 15 and is not saved by s. 1.

issue: Was granting a discharge in the best interest of the accused?
facts: Mr. Feldman, a 67-year-old lawyer with no criminal record, pleaded guilty to criminally harassing his long-time friend and business partner Mr. Lande over a nine-and-a-half-month period. He still owns real estate in California and had been refused entry to the United States three times because of the pending case, and had also advised the Barreau du Québec of his guilty plea.
rule: Under s. 730 of the Criminal Code, where the offence carries no mandatory minimum and is not punishable by 14 years or life, the Court may discharge the accused absolutely or on conditions if it is in the best interest of the accused and not contrary to the public interest. Per Corbeil-Richard c. R., 2009 QCCA 1201 and R. v. Fallofield, the best-interest condition presupposes an accused of good character without prior conviction where a conviction is unnecessary for deterrence/rehabilitation and would have significant adverse repercussions.
application: The prosecution conceded, and the Court agreed, that a discharge was in Mr. Feldman's best interest. He needed to remove obstacles to travelling to the United States to manage his property, and a conviction would carry significant professional and personal repercussions.
conclusion: The best-interest criterion was met.

issue: Would granting a discharge be contrary to the public interest?
facts: The prosecution emphasized Mr. Feldman's lack of remorse and failure to take full responsibility, pointing to his testimony before the Barreau's disciplinary committee where he maintained the truth of his Holocaust-gold allegations and said he 'could not let go'. A criminological evaluation nonetheless concluded that the harassment was an isolated act in an emotionally charged context and that the risk of recidivism was low.
rule: The public-interest analysis considers general deterrence, seriousness and frequency of the crime, public attitude toward the offence and public confidence in the justice system (R. c. Rozon). A discharge is not exceptional and general deterrence, even for serious crimes, is not itself a bar (Harbour c. R., 2017 QCCA 204). Absence of remorse is not an aggravating factor.
application: The Court held that Mr. Feldman's continued belief in his allegations did not mean he lacked regret for his conduct; his comment that Mr. Lande did not fear for his safety could not be considered given the guilty plea. His respect for all bail conditions, his admission to the criminologist that he had gone too far, his 12 psychology sessions, his lifelong productive law-abiding history, family support, and the low recidivism risk reassured the Court. The collateral consequences (arrest, border refusals, professional discipline, career upheaval) were relevant to whether the public interest required a conviction.
conclusion: A discharge was not contrary to the public interest.

issue: Should an absolute or conditional discharge be imposed?
facts: The defence sought an absolute or conditional discharge; the prosecution sought a suspended sentence with two-year probation prohibiting contact with Mr. Lande and his family. Protecting Mr. Lande required continued no-contact conditions.
rule: A conditional discharge, like a suspended sentence, carries a probation order and requires the accused to earn the discharge (R. v. Meneses). It permits imposition of protective conditions, whereas an absolute discharge would not.
application: Because protective conditions prohibiting communication with and presence near Mr. Lande were an essential component of the sentence, an absolute discharge was inappropriate; a conditional discharge with two-year probation achieved the necessary conditions while avoiding a criminal record.
conclusion: The Court granted a conditional discharge with a two-year probation including no-contact and no-mention conditions.

issue: Does sexual harassment constitute discrimination on the basis of sex under the Manitoba Human Rights Act?
facts: Two waitresses at Pharos Restaurant were subjected to unwanted touching, kissing, pats and suggestive remarks by the cook, Tommy Grammas. The adjudicator and the Court of Queen's Bench (Monnin J.) held this was sex discrimination under s. 6(1) of the Act. Another waitress testified the cook was merely friendly toward her, suggesting the complainants were singled out for personal characteristics.
rule: Section 6(1) of The Human Rights Act (C.C.S.M. c. H175) prohibits an employer or person acting on behalf of an employer from discriminating in employment 'because of ... sex' among other grounds. 'Discriminate' means differentiation on a categorical/generic basis (per Re Board of Governors of University of Saskatchewan (1976); distinguished from Bell and Korczak v. Ladas (1980) and Brennan v. Robichaud (FCA)). The Manitoba statute, unlike the amended federal, Ontario, Quebec and Newfoundland legislation, contains no express prohibition of sexual harassment.
application: Huband J.A. held that discrimination under the Act means treating a class (e.g., women as a group) differently, whereas sexual harassment targets a person for individual/personal characteristics, not gender as such; the Manitoba legislature, unlike Parliament and other provinces, had not enacted a harassment prohibition. Twaddle J.A. agreed that harassment is an act while discrimination is a method of categorical selection; for harassment to be discrimination it must occur by reason of categorical selection of the complainants because they were women. On the evidence (the cook did not harass all female staff), the complainants were chosen for characteristics peculiar to them, not their sex.
conclusion: Sexual harassment as it occurred here is not sex discrimination under the Manitoba Act; the complaints must fail on this ground.

issue: Is Platy Enterprises Ltd. liable, vicariously or personally, for the cook's conduct?
facts: Platy, the corporate owner, had no discriminatory policy and did not condone the cook's conduct. Grammas was an hourly evening-shift cook who could send waitresses home early but had no authority to hire or fire, though staff were left to believe otherwise. Philip, a director and manager, was the directing mind of the restaurant.
rule: Under s. 6(1) only an 'employer or person acting on behalf of an employer' can be liable, and s. 28(2) permits orders only against 'the party' or 'person who contravened the Act'. Vicarious liability requires express statutory authority (Re Nelson v. Byron Price & Associates (BCCA 1981); Brennan v. Robichaud (FCA); Dakota Ojibway Tribal Council v. Bewza (MBCA 1985)). The organic/'directing mind' theory (Lennard's Carrying Co. v. Asiatic Petroleum [1915] A.C. 705) attributes liability where the actor is the directing mind and acts in the course of employment.
application: The Court found no statutory basis for vicarious liability, and s. 28(2)'s penalty/exemplary damages power made imposing liability on a faultless employer manifestly unjust. The cook was not 'acting on behalf of' the employer, was not the directing mind of the corporation, and his conduct was not within the course of his employment — 'Patting the buttocks of a waitress is dehors his job as a cook.' There was no substantial risk that cooking duties would generate such acts.
conclusion: Platy is not liable, whether on vicarious or organic-theory grounds.

issue: Does the board of adjudication under the Act violate s. 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867?
facts: Platy argued the provincially-appointed adjudicator exercised a function reserved to federally-appointed s. 96 judges.
rule: The three-step test from Reference Re Residential Tenancies Act (1981) (historical inquiry; judicial function within institutional setting; function as a whole).
application: Because ordinary discrimination is a new statutory concept unknown to s. 96 courts in 1867, adjudicating discrimination does not offend s. 96. However, sexual harassment involving unwanted touching/kissing is analogous to assault, a matter within 1867 superior/civil-criminal courts; a board deciding harassment claims would operate like a s. 96 court. Since the Manitoba Act contains no harassment prohibition, no constitutional infirmity arises.
conclusion: The board is intra vires as to discrimination; no s. 96 violation on the facts.

issue: Were the damages properly reduced?
facts: The adjudicator awarded lost wages and exemplary damages; Monnin J. reduced them; the complainants cross-appealed to restore the original awards.
rule: Assessment of exemplary damages under s. 28(2)(c), guided by Dakota Ojibway Tribal Council v. Bewza.
application: Because the appeal was allowed on liability, the damages issue was largely moot; nonetheless the Court agreed Monnin J. was right to reduce the awards.
conclusion: Cross-appeal dismissed; the reductions were upheld.

issue: Does the reverse-onus truth defence in s. 281.2(3)(a) infringe the presumption of innocence under s. 11(d) of the Charter?
facts: Keegstra, a high school teacher, was convicted of wilfully promoting hatred against the Jewish people through statements made while teaching. Section 281.2(3)(a) provides a defence where the accused 'establishes' the truth of the statements, which the Supreme Court has held means proof on a balance of probabilities.
rule: Section 11(d) guarantees the presumption of innocence; per R. v. Oakes it is breached where an accused must disprove a presumed fact. Following R. v. Holmes (SCC), any burden on the accused that dictates conviction despite a reasonable doubt—whether it relates to an essential element or to an element extraneous but essential to the verdict—contravenes s. 11(d).
application: The court rejected the Crown's argument that s. 281.2(3)(a) merely creates a 'defence' outside s. 11(d). A defence proven only on a balance of probabilities means a jury must convict even where it retains a doubt about the truth of the statements, contrary to s. 11(d). The purpose of avoiding a Crown burden to prove a negative justifies shifting only an evidentiary burden, not the persuasive burden.
conclusion: The reverse-onus provision infringes s. 11(d) of the Charter.

issue: Does s. 281.2 infringe freedom of expression under s. 2(b) of the Charter?
facts: The impugned offence criminalizes wilful promotion of hatred against identifiable groups; s. 281.2(3)(c) offers a defence where the accused, on reasonable grounds, believed his statements true, thereby criminalizing 'imprudent' speech (innocent of knowledge of falsehood but blameworthy for failing to verify).
rule: Section 2(b) protects freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression. Internal limits to s. 2(b) spring from the nature and purpose of the right; competing claims are addressed under s. 1 (Edmonton Journal; Grier). Calculated lies may be unprotected (Zundel), but the toleration of some error and imprudent expression forms part of the tradition of free speech.
application: The court held that s. 2(b) protects both innocent error and imprudent speech, not merely careful or true expression. Because s. 281.2 makes a crime of imprudent speech that is not a conscious lie, it limits protected expression. Competing concerns about harm are properly analysed under s. 1.
conclusion: Section 281.2 limits freedom of expression under s. 2(b).

issue: Is s. 281.2 a reasonable limit demonstrably justified under s. 1 of the Charter?
facts: Parliament enacted s. 281.2 following the Cohen Committee's recommendations to combat hate propaganda. The provision requires only the wilful promotion of hatred; it does not require that anyone actually come to hate a target group, nor any communal acceptance of, or serious risk from, the message.
rule: Under R. v. Oakes, a limit must serve a sufficiently important objective and be proportionate: rationally connected to the objective, minimally impairing, and not so severe that its effects outweigh the objective. 'Broad-brush' legislation that fails to distinguish culpable from non-culpable conduct fails proportionality (Motor Vehicle Reference; Smith; Vaillancourt).
application: The court accepted that protecting target groups from serious reputational and non-physical injury—which arises when the hate-monger gains an audience—is a sufficient objective, and that s. 281.2 is rationally connected and clear enough. However, the section is overbroad: it permits conviction of a person who causes no serious harm or risk of harm, even where nobody believes or is likely to believe him. Reliance on prosecutorial discretion (the Attorney General's fiat), which is not subject to judicial review, is an inadequate protection of a Charter right (Smith). The section therefore fails minimal impairment and proportionality.
conclusion: Section 281.2 is not demonstrably justified under s. 1 because its sweep is too broad.

issue: What remedy follows from the finding that s. 281.2 is inconsistent with the Charter?
facts: Keegstra was convicted at trial; the constitutional challenge was renewed on appeal.
rule: Section 52 of the Charter provides that laws inconsistent with the Constitution are 'of no force and effect'; declarations may exceptionally be withheld where the offending application is remote or speculative, and remedies such as reading down or constitutional exemption may be available (Edmonton Journal; Jahelka).
application: The court found the overbreadth could not be cured by reading down or a constitutional exemption, since the section catches the harmless crank and heated hyperbole in public debate. The defect was not remote or speculative.
conclusion: Section 281.2 is declared of no force and effect; the appeal is allowed, the conviction set aside and the charge quashed.

issue: Did the defendant make the alleged discriminatory and insulting statements to his passenger, proven beyond a reasonable doubt?
facts: Passenger Lisa Bering testified that during a 12-minute taxi ride Mr. Khan, unprompted, disparaged Jamaicans, police officers, a Jewish taxi driver, Canadian women (as only wanting money), credit-card users, and the city of Mumbai (which he called 'dirty', knowing her father was from there). Mr. Khan denied the comments and called a character witness. He contradicted himself on whether he recognized the passenger and on his comments about credit-card users and Mumbai.
rule: The prosecution must prove a strict liability regulatory offence beyond a reasonable doubt (R. v. P.G., 2013 ONCA 520; R. v. Starr, 2000 SCC 40). Credibility is assessed under the framework in R. v. W.(D.), 1991 CanLII 93 (SCC).
application: The court found Ms. Bering's testimony clear, cogent and consistent with her contemporaneous email, while Mr. Khan's evidence contained material inconsistencies and contradicted his earlier statement to Officer Bosley. Applying the third branch of W.(D.), the court was not left in doubt and accepted the complainant's account.
conclusion: The court found beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Khan made the statements as alleged.

issue: Did those statements contravene the requirement that a licensed taxi driver be 'civil and well-behaved' under s. 545-148 H of the Toronto Municipal Code?
facts: The Toronto Municipal Code requires every licensed driver while operating a cab to 'be civil and well-behaved.' The phrase is undefined. Khan's comments included disparagement of ethnic groups, women, and a passenger's ancestral city.
rule: Words are read in their entire context and ordinary sense (Bell ExpressVu v. Rex, 2002 SCC 42; Greater Essex County DSB, 2012 ONCA 482). Dictionary meanings: 'civil' = polite, obliging, not rude; 'well-behaved' = demonstrating good manners or conduct. The offence is one of strict liability (R. v. Sault Ste. Marie, R. v. Pontes). The Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19, s.1 has primacy and must inform the whole law (Tranchemontagne, 2006 SCC 14); civility standards may proportionately limit expression (Doré v. Barreau du Québec, 2012 SCC 12).
application: Khan's remarks were impolite and offensive, intersecting enumerated Human Rights Code grounds (race, ancestry, place of origin, sex, creed) and the right to equal treatment in services. Chastising a customer about spending habits and calling a passenger's father's city 'dirty' were neither civil nor well-behaved. Such conduct was inappropriate for a licensed taxi driver on any lawful standard.
conclusion: The statements contravened the 'civil and well-behaved' licensing requirement; the offence was made out and a conviction was entered.

issue: Were the security and development of the adolescent still in danger, justifying an extension of the protective order under s. 95 of the Youth Protection Act?
facts: The adolescent, born in 1988, had been entrusted to his mother in March 2003 with corrective measures. His behaviour deteriorated in December 2003: he missed school, violated curfews, failed to disclose his whereabouts, associated with negative peers and adults, threatened his younger brother with a knife on about January 16, 2004, and the mother found marijuana residue and drug paraphernalia in his room. The mother requested placement. Provisionally, the child was ordered into mandatory placement in a rehabilitation centre for up to 30 days.
rule: Section 95 of the Loi sur la protection de la jeunesse permits the Director to seek an extension of an order where the child's security or development remains compromised; the tribunal decides in the interest of the child and with respect for the child's rights.
application: The Director alleged continuing behavioural problems endangering the child. Both the adolescent (through counsel) and the mother admitted the behavioural troubles and consented to the measures sought. Considering the allegations, admissions, consents, the reports filed, and the interest of the child, the Court found the security and development of the child still in danger.
conclusion: The Court declared the child's security and development still in danger and granted the extension of the order.

issue: What corrective measures were appropriate given the parties' admissions and consent?
facts: The mother agreed to continued care of her son, proposing to use the maternal grandmother for respite rather than a rehabilitation centre, but reserved the right to seek long-term placement if measures failed. The child consented to substance-abuse testing, education/treatment sessions, and weekly family therapy at the Jewish General Hospital.
rule: Under the Youth Protection Act, the tribunal orders measures tailored to the child's interest and rights, entrusting supervision to the Director of Youth Protection.
application: The Court entrusted the child to his mother's care and ordered a package of measures: attendance at substance-abuse education/treatment, submission to substance-abuse testing on request, weekly group family therapy, compliance with rules at home/school/community, refraining from aggression, and accounting to the mother for his whereabouts, with aid and counsel from the Ville Marie Child and Youth Protection Centre, for six months.
conclusion: The Court ordered the corrective measures for a six-month period and entrusted execution to the Director of Youth Protection.

issue: Should the impugned paragraphs referencing the surgeon's prior complaints and proceedings be struck under Rule 19(24)?
facts: In a medical/dental negligence action against oral surgeon Dr. Wittenberg, the plaintiff pleaded that the defendant had been the subject of prior founded and unfounded complaints and court/College of Dental Surgeons proceedings by former patients, and that he therefore knew or should have known he was not competent to treat the plaintiff. The defendants applied to strike paragraphs 12, 18(c) and 18(d).
rule: Rule 19(24) permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim (subrule (a)), are unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious (b), may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial (c), or are otherwise an abuse of process (d). Under Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, a claim is struck only where it is 'plain and obvious' it discloses no reasonable cause of action, assuming the pleaded facts true. Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress and Dempsey v. Envision Credit Union set out when pleadings are irrelevant, scandalous, unnecessary or an abuse of process.
application: The court found the pleadings were framed very broadly, sweeping in both founded and unfounded prior complaints with no limitation as to their nature, and provided no particularity from which the court could assess similarity to the treatment of the plaintiff. There was no nexus to the procedure performed on the plaintiff and no evidence of specific or pervasive problems, so the paragraphs could not stand in their present form.
conclusion: The impugned paragraphs (and specified phrases) could not stand and were ordered struck.

issue: Do the impugned pleadings satisfy the requirements for pleading similar fact evidence, and are they saved by the punitive damages claim?
facts: The plaintiff argued the pleadings were needed to prove negligence through similar fact evidence and to support aggravated and punitive damages, and that striking was premature before discovery. The plaintiff relied on D.M.M. v. Pilo, Sinclair v. March and Williams v. Wai-Ping.
rule: Similar fact evidence is admissible only where acts are 'so strikingly similar that the similarity is not attributable to coincidence' with a 'nexus apparent to an issue in the action' (Sinclair v. March; R. v. C.(M.H.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 763). Under Williams v. Wai-Ping and Prism Data Services, similar-fact allegations are proper only where the added complexity does not outweigh probative value and there is a sufficient, provable degree of similarity.
application: Unlike Pilo (striking pattern of common characteristics) or Sinclair v. March (request confined to same procedure and same complication creating a nexus), the present pleading contained no particulars establishing a sufficient degree of similarity and no nexus to the procedure performed on the plaintiff. The defendants did not contest that punitive damages or similar fact evidence could be available in an appropriate case; but these deficiencies were not cured by adding a punitive damages claim.
conclusion: The pleadings did not conform to the requirements for pleading similar facts and were not saved by the punitive damages claim; they were struck.

issue: Was a sentence of probation with community service, rather than incarceration, a fit sentence for antisemitic wilful damage?
facts: Two young respondents, aged 19 and 20 with no criminal records, spray-painted crude antisemitic slogans, swastikas and Nazi symbols on a Calgary building they believed to be a synagogue, causing about $1,000 in damage. They had unremarkable backgrounds, were initially reluctant, and were led by a third accused. They were convicted of wilful damage and sentenced to probation with $500/$501 restitution and 200 hours of community service, plus being held over the noon break to taste incarceration. The Crown appealed as inadequate.
rule: On a Crown sentence appeal, an appellate court considers the fitness of sentence, weighing aggravating factors and sentencing principles including deterrence and denunciation. Racial/hateful motivation is a significant aggravating factor (cf. R. v. Lelas (1990), 58 C.C.C. (3d) 568 (Ont. C.A.)).
application: The majority held that the obvious and disgusting racism in the messages was a major aggravating factor warranting a period of incarceration less than one year, or its equivalent. However, Lelas was distinguishable because that offender was a member of a racist organization who deliberately targeted the Jewish community, whereas these respondents had unremarkable backgrounds, no prior involvement, and were reluctant participants led by another. The majority found 200 hours of community service, a very high number, could serve as the equivalent of the appropriate custodial range.
conclusion: The majority found the sentence fit and dismissed the Crown appeal; Shannon J., dissenting, found it inadequate.

issue: Can community service substitute for a short custodial sentence to satisfy general deterrence and denunciation for a hate-motivated offence?
facts: The Crown argued 200 hours of community service was inadequate because neither the community nor potential offenders view it as equivalent to jail, and that general deterrence and society's denunciation required imprisonment for conduct terrorizing a long-vilified segment of society.
rule: Sentencing must reflect deterrence and denunciation; the sentencing court balances these objectives against the utility and visibility of the punishment.
application: The majority reasoned that community service can serve justice better than a short gaol term: jail is expensive, invisible, and imposes further loss on society, whereas community service gives something back and is visible in the community. While accepting deterrence is important and that such racial assaults breed emulation, the majority found the prospect of serving victims or those in need had deterrent value, and recommended the service be performed for the Calgary Jewish community. Shannon J. dissented, holding the sentences were sufficient to deter these respondents but failed to provide general deterrence and to express society's denunciation of conduct aimed at insulting and terrorizing a group meriting special protection.
conclusion: The majority upheld community service as an adequate equivalent and dismissed the appeal; the dissent would have allowed the appeal and imposed imprisonment.

issue: Was the accused the person who created, controlled and maintained the Exterminance website and made the impugned postings?
facts: Police executed a search warrant on the apartment occupied solely by Noble in Fort St. John, seizing a computer connected to the Internet whose hard drive held files, images and website-building software matching content on www.exterminance.org. A 'who is' printout listed Noble's name, address and phone as registrant, with organization 'Aryan Resistance Movement' and email adolfhitler@shaw.ca. Postings under the name 'Exterminance' on stormfront.org and ypenterprise.net carried an avatar bearing Noble's picture, and a FAQ page identified 'Bill Noble, age 28.'
rule: Identity is a question of fact to be proven by the Crown beyond a reasonable doubt on the whole of the evidence.
application: The court found the accumulation of evidence — the computer contents, the registration data, the avatar photo, the self-identifying FAQ, and the software capable of maintaining the site — left no reasonable doubt that Noble created and maintained the Exterminance website from the seized computer and was the 'Exterminance' who authored the postings on the various forums.
conclusion: The court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused controlled the website and made the impugned postings.

issue: Did the Internet communications fall within the 'private conversation' exception in s. 319(2)?
facts: The impugned statements were posted openly on publicly accessible websites and discussion forums requiring only a computer, Internet connection and web browser to access. No password protection or access restrictions were used, and no accident or negligence was suggested.
rule: Section 319(2) criminalizes wilful promotion of hatred 'other than in private conversation.' Per R. v. Keegstra, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697, private conversation is excluded and s. 183 defines private communication as one made in circumstances where the originator reasonably expects it will not be intercepted by anyone other than the intended recipient; R. v. Elms (2006, ON CA) holds the issue is whether the statement is made 'other than in private conversation', not merely the private setting; the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt the statements were not made in private conversation (R. v. Ahenakew).
application: While technology can create secured areas allowing communications to be treated as private, no such precautions were taken here. The postings were 'wide open and accessible to anyone who had the technology and chose to look,' and no issue of accident or negligence arose. The content and circumstances did not bring the communications within the exception.
conclusion: The communications were not private conversations; the exception did not apply.

issue: Did the accused 'wilfully promote hatred' against the named identifiable groups?
facts: Over roughly two years the accused posted Holocaust-denial and antisemitic material (e.g. the 'Final Solution' post, 'inherent nature of the Jew: it is irredeemably a parasite'), racist content including a 'rhyming dream' invoking lynching of a Black man, hosted David Lane's works Misdirected Hate and the novella KD Rebel, distributed Project Schoolyard/Panzerfaust CDs aimed at children, promoted the '88 precepts' advocating race war, and recruited skinheads.
rule: Under s. 319(2), 'wilfully' requires the accused subjectively desire the promotion of hatred or foresee it as substantially certain (Keegstra, adopting R. v. Buzzanga and Durocher); 'promotes' means active support or instigation (fomenter). The speech must be assessed objectively but in context — the circumstances, manner, tone and audience (Mugesera v. Canada, 2005 SCC 40; R. v. Ahenakew, 2008 SKCA 4). 'Identifiable group' is defined in s. 318(4).
application: Unlike Ahenakew, where words spoken in anger required consideration, the evidence unequivocally established that the accused pursued a sustained, calculated course of conduct to express and advance his white-supremacist beliefs. The representative postings, hosted tracts, recruitment and distribution materials were writing calculated to vilify and deliberately promote hatred against Jews, Blacks, homosexuals and other identifiable groups. Hatred is broader than violence.
conclusion: The accused wilfully promoted hatred against the identifiable groups; each element of the offence was proven.

issue: Did the British Columbia court have jurisdiction given the website was hosted on U.S. servers?
facts: The Exterminance website appeared to be hosted on servers in Texas, and the accused argued his website was on an American server and outside the court's jurisdiction.
rule: Jurisdiction over the offence depends on where the impugned conduct originated.
application: The court was satisfied that the accused's actions — creating, maintaining and posting the content — originated from the computer in his apartment in Fort St. John, British Columbia, notwithstanding the physical location of the hosting servers.
conclusion: The court had jurisdiction; the jurisdictional submission was rejected.

issue: Did the preliminary inquiry judge exceed his jurisdiction by balancing competing Charter values?
facts: Although the preliminary inquiry judge said he was deciding an evidentiary issue about the manner in which the complainant would testify, his reasons expressly started from the accused's fundamental right to make full answer and defence and to face their accuser, and he weighed that against the complainant's freedom of religion before ordering her to remove her niqab.
rule: A preliminary inquiry judge is not a court of competent jurisdiction and therefore has no jurisdiction to hear and determine whether a Charter right has been infringed (R. v. Mills, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 863). Certiorari lies to cure an excess of jurisdiction (R. v. Forsythe, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 268).
application: By reconciling the accused's s. 7 fair-trial interests with the complainant's freedom of religion, the judge in substance adjudicated competing Charter values, a task he had no jurisdiction to perform. His characterization of the ruling as merely evidentiary did not save it.
conclusion: The judge exceeded his jurisdiction; certiorari was available to quash the ruling.

issue: Was the complainant denied procedural fairness?
facts: When the defendants withdrew their admission of the sincerity of the complainant's belief, the judge immediately questioned the unrepresented complainant himself, on an 'informal basis,' without an oath or affirmation, and refused to let her obtain the independent counsel the Crown was seeking; he then relied on her answers to conclude her belief was weak and comfort-based.
rule: Procedural fairness requires that a person whose interests are affected be able to consult counsel and to have contentious factual determinations made on a proper evidentiary footing; a procedural error causing prejudice can result in loss of jurisdiction.
application: Requiring the complainant to answer questions about her religious reasons without independent counsel (the Crown being conflicted) and without an oath was clearly prejudicial, and the impugned order was based in part on those answers. This procedural defect tainted the decision.
conclusion: The complainant was prejudiced by the denial of an opportunity to consult counsel; the order was quashed on this ground as well.

issue: What procedure should govern whether a witness may testify while wearing a niqab at a preliminary inquiry?
facts: The complainant wished to testify veiled; the accused sought her unveiling to observe demeanour on cross-examination. The judge had powers under s. 537(1) to regulate the inquiry and a mandatory duty under s. 540(1) to permit cross-examination.
rule: A preliminary inquiry judge may conduct a hearing within the inquiry (R. v. Pickett) and may order removal of a veil under s. 537(1). Freedom of religion requires the claimant to show a practice or belief with a nexus to religion and sincerity, without judicial inquiry into the belief's validity (Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem, 2004 SCC 47; R. v. Big M Drug Mart). Section 540(1) guarantees a full, careful cross-examination (R. v. Durette).
application: The judge should hold two hearings within the inquiry, with the complainant testifying veiled and on oath: first to determine, on the complainant bearing the onus, whether she wears the veil for a religious or other valid reason (exploring limits, exceptions, and possible dispensation, and matters such as her driver's licence photograph); and second, if the belief is established, whether she can be cross-examined within the meaning of s. 540(1) while veiled, with the substantive testimony videotaped to permit meaningful judicial review. If no valid reason is shown, s. 537(1) permits an order to unveil; if cross-examination cannot occur, the evidence is inadmissible.
conclusion: The matter was remitted to the preliminary inquiry judge with detailed directions, including that the veil-related hearing be videotaped.

issue: Should the Superior Court itself grant s. 24(1) relief permitting veiled testimony?
facts: The applicant asked the Superior Court to order that she be allowed to testify veiled at the preliminary inquiry. The record contained no photograph, description, or videotape of the complainant, and no established competing-rights foundation.
rule: A Superior Court judge granting prerogative relief has jurisdiction to grant an additional remedy under s. 24(1) of the Charter (R. v. Mills). A genuine conflict of Charter rights must be established on evidence before balancing (Dagenais v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp.).
application: Deciding the issue in the abstract, without seeing and hearing the complainant's substantive testimony, would be mere speculation and would in effect have two judges conduct one preliminary inquiry. The evidentiary record needed to balance the competing rights should be built at the preliminary inquiry, not on this motion.
conclusion: The Court declined to exercise its s. 24(1) jurisdiction; the request to permit veiled testimony was refused.

issue: Should the charges have been stayed for unreasonable delay under s. 11(b) of the Charter, and could the trial judge reject the accused's uncontradicted affidavit evidence of prejudice?
facts: Nineteen and one-half months passed between charge and trial, 15.5 months of which the trial judge attributed to Crown/institutional delay. The accused filed unchallenged affidavits asserting actual prejudice from strict house-arrest bail terms (loss of work, education, income and social life).
rule: Section 11(b) of the Charter guarantees trial within a reasonable time; the Morin framework (R. v. Morin, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 771) governs, and prejudice concerns liberty, security of the person and the ability to make full answer and defence (R. v. Godin, 2009 SCC 26). A trier of fact is not obliged to accept any evidence tendered, even if uncontradicted (R. v. Mathisen, 2008 ONCA 747).
application: The trial judge gave reasons for disbelieving the affidavits (no educational plan, no details of work forgone, one accused had breached bail) and was entitled to require proof of asserted actual prejudice. He nonetheless inferred a 'moderate degree' of prejudice from the restrictive bail terms and factored it into the Morin analysis, concluding the delay fell within guidelines. The later-discovered prejudice from Yii's absence was not raised on the s. 11(b) motion and was properly addressed under the s. 715(1) analysis instead.
conclusion: No reversible error; the trial judge did not err in finding the delay was not unreasonable and refusing a stay.

issue: Did the trial judge err in admitting the key witness's preliminary inquiry testimony under s. 715(1) of the Criminal Code?
facts: Ritchie Yii was the only witness who said the accused attacked the victim and that Lau used a lead pipe. The police did not attempt to subpoena him until shortly before trial, by which point he had left Canada. The trial judge first refused to allow read-in for lack of due diligence, then reconsidered after the police confirmed Yii would not return even if his airfare was paid. Yii had asked police whether his evidence could be given some other way.
rule: Section 715(1)(d) permits reading in prior testimony of a witness absent from Canada, subject to a residual discretion to exclude to prevent unfairness (R. v. Potvin, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 525). The principled approach to hearsay (R. v. Starr, 2000 SCC 40; R. v. Khelawon, 2006 SCC 57) informs its application, and necessity requires that hearsay be the only means of obtaining the evidence, considering alternatives such as teleconference or commission evidence (R. v. O'Connor; R. v. Finta). Sections 714.2 and 714.4 authorize video and audio testimony from abroad. A ruling may be reconsidered on a material change of circumstances (R. v. La, [1997] 2 S.C.R. 680).
application: Reopening the ruling was proper because the witness's confirmed unwillingness to return was a material change. However, the trial judge treated the principled approach as irrelevant to s. 715(1) and considered only commission evidence, ignoring the possibility of taking Yii's evidence live by teleconference or videoconference — options made more pertinent because Yii himself had asked if his evidence could be heard another way, suggesting he might have cooperated. The Crown had not taken the minimal effort required, so the necessity/minimal-effort criteria remained unmet and there was no basis to change the original ruling.
conclusion: The trial judge erred; as the Yii evidence was crucial, the proviso (s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) did not apply, and a new trial was ordered on this ground alone.

issue: Was the caution to the jury regarding the read-in evidence insufficient or misleading?
facts: After ruling the transcript admissible, the trial judge cautioned the jury but declined defence's requested instruction on the different purposes of preliminary-hearing cross-examination. In the charge he told the jury that read-in required, and there had been, a 'full opportunity' to cross-examine Yii.
rule: A trial judge has discretion as to the extent of a caution (Potvin; R. v. Kerr; R. v. B. (A.)). Under s. 715(1), 'full opportunity' to cross-examine is a legal precondition ruled on by the judge, and tactical reasons may explain limited cross-examination at a preliminary inquiry.
application: Declining the requested instruction was within discretion. But telling the jury, without elaboration, that there had been a 'full opportunity' to cross-examine risked leaving them to believe a full cross-examination had actually occurred, when a full opportunity does not mean full cross-examination and admissibility rulings are not normally communicated to the jury.
conclusion: The trial judge erred in this respect, contributing to an unfair trial.

issue: Did the trial judge err by discharging the eleventh juror who was ill for one day?
facts: After the holiday break the jury was already down to eleven; one juror had the flu but expected to recover the next day. To avoid losing a sitting day and to accommodate scheduling (including an Orthodox Jewish juror who could not sit past Friday afternoon), the judge discharged the ill juror over one accused's objection.
rule: Section 644(1) of the Criminal Code allows discharge of a juror who cannot continue by reason of illness or other reasonable cause, and s. 644(2) permits continuation with ten jurors; an accused should not lightly be deprived of a jury of twelve and counsel should be heard (R. v. Chambers; R. v. Basarabas).
application: The judge heard counsel and exercised his discretion based on timing exigencies after the break. Although he could have waited a day, he was not obliged to do so, and the Code expressly permitted the discharge.
conclusion: No error; this ground of appeal was dismissed.

issue: Did the trial judge err by giving the jury only selected written portions of the charge several hours into deliberations?
facts: Without any jury question, the judge sent into the jury room three written portions ('A', 'B', 'C') — including the six routes to party liability and the use of co-accused/non-accused statements — but omitted the presumption of innocence and burden of proof. Written portion 'B' also omitted that only evidence directly admissible against a particular accused may be used to determine common-purpose membership.
rule: Portions of a charge may be provided in writing to assist with complex instructions, but such portions must be complete, accurate, fair and balanced, and should include the fundamental instructions on presumption of innocence and reasonable doubt (R. v. Poitras, 2002 CanLII 23583 (ON CA)).
application: Delivering only party-liability and statement-use instructions late in deliberations tended to emphasize the Crown's perspective without the balancing fundamental instructions. The inaccuracy in written portion 'B' added to the complexity and, had the jury noticed the discrepancy with portion 'A', they could not have known which was correct. Given the legal complexity, the timing and the omissions, the proviso could not cure the errors.
conclusion: The trial judge erred; the procedure rendered the trial unfair, supporting the order for a new trial.

issue: Was the evidence on the G.-sisters counts sufficiently similar to the other counts to be admitted as similar fact evidence, thereby also defeating the severance motion?
facts: Shearing, leader of the Kabalarian Philosophy, was charged with sex offences against eleven complainants over 1965-1990. The defence sought to sever the counts involving the resident G. sisters (whose abuse began younger and was more serious) from the other complainants, arguing the acts differed in timing, nature, frequency and the character of consent, and that the G. evidence was so prejudicial it required the highest degree of probative similarity.
rule: Similar fact evidence is admissible where its probative value outweighs its prejudicial effect; a high degree of deference is owed to the trial judge's assessment of the facts absent an error of law or jurisdiction (R. v. B.(C.R.), [1990] 1 S.C.R. 717; R. v. Arp, [1998] 3 S.C.R. 339).
application: The trial judge acknowledged real dissimilarities but found significant and multiple similarities constituting a pattern of predatory sexual conduct within a religious group, all complainants being members dominated by the leader who cloaked the acts in spiritual purpose. He instructed the jury they had to find 'substantial and significant similarities' amounting to a pattern before cross-using the evidence for credibility and honest belief in consent, and twice warned against propensity reasoning. Although it would have been preferable to list the dissimilarities, counsel canvassed them thoroughly and they were obvious to the jury.
conclusion: The similar fact ruling disclosed no error; the imperfection in the charge did not amount to reversible error. The ground failed, and the severance ground failed with it.

issue: Did limiting cross-examination of complainant K.W.-G. on the absence of any reference to abuse in her personal diary infringe the appellant's right to full answer and defence?
facts: The defence possessed K.W.-G.'s eight-month diary from the period she alleged ongoing abuse and wished to cross-examine on its silence about the abuse. The complainant asserted a privacy interest. The trial judge weighed probative value against privacy, found the questioning premised on a discriminatory myth that a child would record abuse, assigned it minimal probative value, and barred that line of questioning.
rule: Cross-examination is a core element of full answer and defence under ss. 7 and 11(d) (R. v. Osolin, [1993] 4 S.C.R. 595) but is not unlimited; defence evidence may be excluded only where prejudice substantially outweighs its value (R. v. Seaboyer, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 577). Complainant privacy and equality rights (s. 15) must be weighed, and there is no right to information that would only distort the search for truth (R. v. O'Connor, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 411; R. v. Mills, [1999] S.C.J. No. 68).
application: The Court held Mills shifted the balance to give weight to complainant privacy and equality rights and confirmed the accused has no right to information serving only to distort truth-seeking. The trial judge did not undervalue the evidence: given the complainant's confinement, control and humiliation, and the diary's style, it was unlikely she would record abuse, so its probative value was minimal, while a personal diary attracts a very high privacy interest and the questioning would open the whole diary. Barring discriminatory questioning fell within the principled balance approved in Mills.
conclusion: The restriction was proper; the ruling conformed with the governing principles and the ground was dismissed.

issue: Did the failure to distinguish the pre-1983 law from the post-amendment law on authority as a factor vitiating consent constitute reversible error, and on which counts?
facts: The trial judge instructed the jury for all counts that the exercise of authority could vitiate consent, though 'the exercise of authority' (now s. 265(3)(d)) was only added by the 1983 amendment. Several counts pre-dated the amendment. The Crown conceded the error but argued it did not affect the outcome.
rule: Under R. v. O'Connor (BCCA, 1998) and now s. 265(3), for pre-amendment counts authority is relevant only to whether consent was in fact given, not as an element that renders consent invalid; a blanket instruction is an error of law. R. v. Jobidon, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 714 was distinguished. The curative proviso (s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) applies only where the error could not have affected the result.
application: The Court declined to reconsider O'Connor. The error affected only the pre-amendment indecent assault counts for C.K. (count 10) and J.V. (count 12), where consent and its vitiation were live issues. For the G. sisters consent was never a real issue, so the misdirection did not contaminate those verdicts, and the jury, presumed to follow instructions, would not have used vitiation of C.K./J.V.'s consent to prove the G. offences. Because consent and fraud may have been entangled, fraud could not be shown to be the sole basis of the C.K./J.V. verdicts, so the proviso could not save them.
conclusion: The error was reversible only as to counts 10 (C.K.) and 12 (J.V.); the convictions on those counts were set aside and a new trial ordered, the appeal otherwise dismissed.

issue: Should the Court, pursuant to s. 672.31 of the Criminal Code, find the accused unfit to stand trial?
facts: Weekes was charged with criminal harassment (s. 264(2)(b)) and uttering a threat (s. 264.1(1)(a)) against a Calgary radio personality. Before any election or plea, the Crown applied under s. 672.23 to have the Court determine fitness. Dr. Xie, a forensic psychiatrist, testified the accused suffers from chronic, treatment-resistant paranoid schizophrenia with grandiose and persecutory delusions.
rule: Under s. 2 of the Criminal Code, an accused is 'unfit to stand trial' if, on account of mental disorder, unable to understand the nature or object of the proceedings, understand the possible consequences, or communicate with counsel. On a Crown application the burden is proof on a balance of probabilities (s. 672.23; s. 672.31). The 'limited cognitive capacity' standard applies (R. v. Whittle, 1994 CanLII 55 (SCC)).
application: The Court accepted the accused had a mental disorder but distinguished R. v. Iyoho, 2009 ABPC 262. Weekes did not disrupt the hearing, quietly consulted with defence counsel, instructed counsel to admit Dr. Xie's qualifications, and elected to call no evidence. He understood the charges and procedure (harassment and threats against the radio personality), maintained his innocence and intended to plead not guilty, and understood consequences (believing he would be acquitted or the charges dropped). Evidence showed he had only fired one lawyer and communicated with counsel without apparent difficulty. Delusions alone do not equate to unfitness.
conclusion: The Court found the accused fit to stand trial; the Crown failed to meet its burden.

issue: Does a serious mental disorder with delusions render an accused unfit where he can still understand and instruct counsel?
facts: Dr. Xie diagnosed severe, treatment-resistant paranoid schizophrenia with persecutory and grandiose delusions, yet conceded that a person may have delusions and still be fit, and that lack of insight is common with untreated schizophrenia.
rule: Per R. v. Rooney (1994) P.E.I.J. No. 82 (PEISC), an accused is not unfit if able to recount the necessary facts to present a defence; unfitness arises only where that ability is presently blocked by delusions. Analytical reasoning to accept counsel's advice or make optimal decisions is not a prerequisite (R. v. Whittle).
application: The Court was not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the accused's ability to recount facts was blocked by delusions, nor that he lacked the limited cognitive capacity to understand the process and communicate with counsel. His loose or disorganized thought process and inability to exercise optimal analytical reasoning did not render him unfit.
conclusion: The mental disorder did not render the accused unfit; the limited cognitive capacity standard was met.

issue: Did a terrorist group within the meaning of s. 83.01 of the Criminal Code exist?
facts: Ahmad and Amara led overlapping Scarborough and Mississauga cells. Loaded handguns were smuggled from the U.S. on Ahmad's credit card; Ahmad sought training to bomb government buildings and power grids; the Washago Camp involved paramilitary training and firearms use; Ahmad's videotaped exhortation declared 'Rome has to be defeated' and that 'we already started striking'; the group scouted a safe house at Opasatika, discussed storming Parliament and beheading politicians, and Amara built a remote-control bomb detonator and researched ammonium-nitrate explosives.
rule: Section 83.01(1)(b) defines 'terrorist activity' as an act for a political, religious or ideological purpose intended to intimidate the public or a government and to cause death, serious harm or destruction; s. 83.01 defines a 'terrorist group' as an entity with a purpose or activity of facilitating or carrying out terrorist activity. The Carter test (R. v. Carter; R. v. Barrow; R. v. Mapara) requires the trier first to be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the group/conspiracy existed.
application: The evidence, largely admitted or otherwise incontrovertible (intercepts, seized videos, agreed facts), overwhelmingly established a group headed by Ahmad and Amara pursuing violent, ideologically-motivated goals against Canadian targets. The court rejected the defence that Ahmad's plans were mere 'musings and fantasies' or that amateurish execution negated danger: the charge is participation in terrorist activity, not on an epic scale, and the political/religious/ideological motivation was explicit.
conclusion: A terrorist group consisting of at least Ahmad, Amara, Chand, Durrani and Dirie existed, proven beyond a reasonable doubt (Carter step one satisfied).

issue: Were co-conspirators' statements admissible against N.Y. under the Carter/common-design exception, and was N.Y. probably a member?
facts: The Crown relied on Ahmad's and Amara's out-of-court statements (that N.Y. removed a surveillance camera, shoplifted walkie-talkies 'for me', and stole camping gear at Canadian Tire). Directly admissible evidence against N.Y. included his attendance at both camps, his shoplifting, his close association with and deference to Ahmad, and admissions to Sergeant Tost.
rule: Under the three-step Carter analysis (R. v. Carter; R. v. Barrow; extended beyond conspiracy in R. v. Falahatchian), once the group is proven, the trier reviews evidence directly admissible against the accused to decide on a balance of probabilities whether he was a member; the accused's acts may be viewed against the acts of co-conspirators (R. v. Gagnon). Only at step three may in-furtherance declarations be used against him (R. v. Lynch; R. v. Yanover). Vetrovec caution applies to Ahmad's unsavoury statements.
application: Making full allowance for N.Y.'s youth, limited education, rudimentary grasp of Islam and world politics, and the fact that many Muslims distrust CSIS, the court found that after Ahmad's Washago exhortation N.Y. understood the group's terrorist intent yet continued his close association, shoplifted for the group's purposes, and attended the Rockwood Camp. Ahmad's statements were made to trusted associates in furtherance of the group's security and were confirmed by admitted facts.
conclusion: On a balance of probabilities N.Y. was knowingly a member of the terrorist group (Carter step two satisfied), and the co-conspirator statements were admissible against him.

issue: Did N.Y. know of the existence of the terrorist group?
facts: N.Y. attended the Washago Camp where Ahmad delivered a forceful 'call to arms', stated the group 'shared the principles and methods' of Al-Qaeda, and had a loaded handgun N.Y. fired. N.Y. maintained a six-to-seven month friendship in which Ahmad was his mentor, and attended the Rockwood Camp where Durrani spoke of 'missions' in the U.S. In April 2006 Ahmad told Shaikh the 'smaller guys' (including N.Y.) 'know we were gonna do something here.'
rule: The Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused knew of the group's existence, but not that he knew any specific planned terrorist activity (s. 83.18(2)(c)). Where based on circumstantial evidence, guilt must be the only reasonable inference (R. v. Rhee). Exculpatory statements are assessed under R. v. W.(D.).
application: The court disbelieved N.Y.'s statement that any terrorist intent was lost on him, noting he lied about the Rockwood Camp and was evasive. Given Ahmad's openness, the compulsory exhortation, the propaganda materials, and Ahmad's own confirmation that the 'smaller guys' knew the group planned something in Canada, knowledge was the only reasonable inference.
conclusion: The Crown proved beyond a reasonable doubt that N.Y. knew of the existence of the terrorist group.

issue: Did N.Y. participate in or contribute to an activity of the terrorist group and intend to enhance its ability to carry out a terrorist activity?
facts: After the Washago Camp N.Y. removed a surveillance camera outside Ahmad's apartment, shoplifted walkie-talkies and camping supplies used or intended for the camps, and attended the Rockwood Camp participating in marching and the masked video.
rule: Section 83.18(1) makes it an offence to knowingly participate in or contribute, directly or indirectly, to any activity of a terrorist group for the purpose of enhancing its ability to facilitate or carry out terrorist activity; s. 83.18(3) includes receiving training and providing a skill; s. 83.18(2) removes any requirement that a specific terrorist activity be foreseen or carried out. Only reasonable inference standard (Rhee) applies.
application: The court found N.Y.'s shoplifting was justified and directed by Ahmad (permissible only as theft from 'disbelievers' harming the government) and that the camps were training for a terrorist purpose. His participation and contribution, made with knowledge of the group's terrorist aims, permitted the inference that he intended to enhance its ability, there being no innocent explanation for continued involvement.
conclusion: Proven beyond a reasonable doubt; the participation, contribution and requisite intent were all made out.

issue: Should the minor-injury defence be struck as unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process under Rule 9-5(1)(b)-(d)?
facts: The plaintiff, injured in a September 2020 motor vehicle accident, amended her claim to allege only serious injuries (bilateral adhesive capsulitis, a C6-7 nerve root injury, and a pain syndrome causing serious impairment) and adduced medical opinion that the injuries fall outside the minor-injury regulation. She sought to strike the defendants' pleading that the injuries were minor injuries under the Insurance (Vehicle) Act, arguing it would sideline her action for 15-18 months before the CRT and cause prolonged stress.
rule: Rule 9-5(1)(b)-(d) permits striking pleadings that are unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, that prejudice or delay a fair trial, or that are an abuse of process; on such applications evidence is admissible but the court does not weigh the merits (Delaney & Friends Cartoon Productions Ltd. v. Radical Entertainment Inc., 2005 BCSC 371; Willow v. Chong, 2013 BCSC 1083; Canadian Federation of Students v. Simon Fraser Student Society, 2010 BCSC 1816; Rossner v. Nystrom, 2019 BCSC 583). Under s. 133(1)(b) CRTA the CRT has exclusive jurisdiction to determine whether an injury is a minor injury.
application: The court held it could not, without assessing the merits and medical evidence (which it must not do), find the pleading obviously unable to succeed or serving no useful purpose. The minor-injury defence was a bona fide defence whose consequence is to place the minor-injury question within the CRT's exclusive jurisdiction, not an irrelevant pleading that strays from the issues. It might resolve the action without trial and did not amount to a plain and obvious abuse of process bringing the administration of justice into disrepute.
conclusion: The plaintiff's application to strike was dismissed.

issue: Was the court required to stay the action under s. 16.1(2) CRTA pending a CRT minor-injury determination?
facts: The defendants sought a stay relying on s. 16.1(2) CRTA. Their response to civil claim pleaded only that any injuries were 'minor injuries as defined by the Insurance (Vehicle) Act and regulations'; it did not plead the jurisdiction of the CRT or cite the CRTA.
rule: Section 16.1(2)(a) CRTA requires the court to stay a proceeding where 'a party alleges that a matter in a proceeding before the court relates to a minor injury within the jurisdiction of the tribunal under section 133(1)(b)' — i.e. the party must allege both a minor injury and the tribunal's jurisdiction. Provisions limiting a plaintiff's right to bring an action are construed strictly with ambiguity resolved in the plaintiff's favour (Brar v. Feng, 2022 BCSC 1719; Berardinelli v. Ontario Housing Corp, 1978 CanLII 42 (SCC)); every word is presumed meaningful (Sullivan; Wormell v. ICBC, 2011 BCCA 166). Mandatory stays were granted in Madden v. Ampabeng and Carter v. Uytterhagen where the defendants pleaded both minor injury and CRT jurisdiction.
application: Unlike the pleadings in Madden and Carter, the defendants' response failed to allege the CRT's jurisdiction as required by s. 16.1(2). Construing the section strictly against a limit on the right of action, the pleading did not meet the statutory criteria triggering a mandatory stay. Horvath v. Thring was distinguishable as a Workers' Compensation absolute statutory bar not requiring a defence to be pled.
conclusion: The defendants' stay application was dismissed, with leave to renew upon amending their pleadings; costs in the cause.

issue: Was the bomb aboard Air India Flight 182 located in the baggage area containing the Vancouver-checked 'M. Singh' bag, as the Crown's theory required?
facts: Only about 5% of the aircraft was recovered from the ocean floor. Crown expert Professor Peel placed the device at Body Station 2020 in Baggage Area 52 Left (the M. Singh bag area); defence experts Dr. Trimble and Mr. Taylor placed it roughly five feet forward in Baggage Area 51 (Toronto-loaded luggage). Both agreed the device was in the left aft cargo hold and was four to five times larger than the Lockerbie bomb.
rule: The Crown must prove each essential element beyond a reasonable doubt (R. v. Lifchus; R. v. Starr), and the evidence must be considered as a whole (R. v. Morin). Competing expert opinions are weighed with regard to the specialized expertise most relevant to the precise question in issue.
application: The Court preferred Professor Peel's opinion because his specialized expertise in physical metallurgy and the effects of internal detonations on aircraft structure was more suited to pinpointing the device's location than Dr. Trimble's broader accident-investigation experience, the cause and general location not being in dispute. Peel's location was internally consistent across Targets 26, 1011 and 656, whereas Trimble's analysis fluctuated between BS 1960-1980 and BS 1920 and rested on misapprehensions. Peel's conclusion also cohered with the ticketing/check-in evidence: the M. Singh and L. Singh tickets were booked and paid for together, both interlined to Air India flights, neither passenger boarded, and the L. Singh bomb (Narita) was forensically linked to Reyat.
conclusion: The Court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the explosive device detonated in Baggage Area 52 aboard Flight 182, in the M. Singh bag that originated in Vancouver as part of a single conspiracy that also produced the Narita explosion.

issue: Did the Crown establish beyond a reasonable doubt that Malik was a conspirator or party to the offences?
facts: No forensic evidence linked Malik to either bomb. The case rested on: Mr. B's account that Malik asked him in 1985 to carry a suitcase to India; Mr. A's account of a 1984 solicitation to place a bomb-laden attaché case at the airport; and Ms. D's evidence of a detailed 'Newspaper Confession' and other admissions. Evidence of association, motive and post-offence conduct (financial support to the Reyat family; alleged witness tampering via Joginder Gill) was also led.
rule: Guilt must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt on the whole of the evidence (R. v. Morin; R. v. Starr). Where the Crown's case relies on out-of-court statements of the accused, the court must be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the statements were made and were true (R. v. Kyllo; R. v. McKenzie). Motive is circumstantial evidence only and insufficient standing alone (R. v. Lewis; R. v. Yebes). Suspect witnesses attract Vetrovec cautions requiring confirmatory evidence (R. v. Vetrovec; R. v. Brooks).
application: Mr. A's account was found impossible (the location he described did not exist until 1986 renovations) and implausible, and he came forward only after hearing of Mr. B's evidence. Mr. B was found not credible: 12-year delay, powerful motive for revenge after financial ruin, disclosure immediately after threatening Malik, prior false sworn statements, and internal inconsistencies. Ms. D's protestations of ongoing love were disbelieved; her delayed disclosure, feigned memory loss about her CSIS/RCMP dealings, and above all the migration of four public-domain factual errors into her 'Newspaper Confession' led to the conclusion that she fabricated it. Association evidence was neutral and post-offence conduct carried no weight as it was equally consistent with innocent explanations.
conclusion: The Crown failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt; Malik was found not guilty on each count of the Indictment.

issue: Did the Crown establish beyond a reasonable doubt that Bagri was a conspirator or party to the offences?
facts: The Crown relied on motive (the Madison Square Gardens and Panthak Conference speeches), association with Parmar, Mr. C's evidence of several inculpatory statements ('We did this'; 'walls have ears'; etc.), and Ms. E's hearsay statements to CSIS agent Laurie describing Bagri's late-night request to borrow her car to take baggage to the airport the eve of the bombings. Ms. E professed memory loss at trial.
rule: Proof beyond a reasonable doubt on the whole of the evidence; motive alone is insufficient (Lewis; Yebes). Suspect witnesses require Vetrovec cautions and confirmatory evidence (Vetrovec; Brooks; Kehler); witnesses seeking or receiving benefits attract heightened scrutiny (Dikah; Bevan). Hearsay admitted for its truth as the core of the Crown's case must be shown ultimately reliable beyond a reasonable doubt (R. v. McKenzie; R. v. Kyllo; R. v. Harvey), assessed on all the evidence including opportunity for cross-examination (R. v. B.(K.G.); R. v. U.(F.J.)).
application: Motive, though established, was shared by countless Sikhs and was not unique to Bagri; association evidence showed opportunity but Parmar's suspicious dealings were with others, making Bagri's prominent involvement less likely. Mr. C was found driven by self-interest (immigration lies, accessory conduct after the New Orleans incident, $300,000 payment and a last-minute demand for a further $200,000) and his accounts were internally and externally inconsistent, with the pivotal gas-station conversation contradicted by Bagri's work records and the timing evidence; his evidence was rejected even absent a Vetrovec caution. Ms. E's hearsay was unsworn, given under a promise of confidentiality, lacked a full record, could not be effectively tested because of her feigned memory loss, and was uncorroborated on the material 'core conversation' (which she associated at trial with the June 9 visit, not the eve of the bombings).
conclusion: A reasonable doubt arose as to the ultimate reliability of Ms. E's statements and Mr. C's evidence was not credible; the Crown failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt and Bagri was found not guilty on each count.

issue: Does the petitioners' freedom of religion encompass the right to erect eruvin whose wires cross city streets, so as to entitle them to accommodation from the City of Outremont?
facts: The petitioners are Orthodox Jews residing in Outremont who wish to string barely visible wires (an eruv) between private buildings, traversing city streets, to permit carrying objects outside the home on the Sabbath and holidays. Without an eruv, observant Jews are effectively housebound on those days. The City dispatches employees to dismantle eruvin, having dismantled one on the eve of Rosh Hashana. Rabbi Merling's affidavit material established that the eruv is firmly rooted in Orthodox Jewish precepts and facilitates communal worship.
rule: Freedom of religion under the Canadian Charter and the Quebec Charter must be given a generous, purposive interpretation without overshooting the right's purpose (R. v. Big M Drug Mart; R. v. Edwards Books); it protects the practice and manifestation of religion; and where a Charter right conflicts with a public or private interest, reasonable accommodation up to the point of undue hardship must be provided. Laws limiting Charter rights on public property must be interpreted to facilitate the right where its use is not unreasonable (Ramsden; Committee for the Commonwealth of Canada).
application: The Court found on the record that the erection of an eruv is essential to enable Orthodox Jews to attend Sabbath services and participate in related activities, distinguishing Rochon J.'s finding in Amselem (where the succah practice was held optional). Recognizing the right does not overshoot the guarantee; that the eruv also enables secular activities like pushing a stroller is beside the point. The City is asked only to tolerate barely visible wires over its streets, not to fund or endorse Orthodox Judaism, comparable to tolerating Christmas decorations or church bells.
conclusion: Yes; the petitioners' freedom of religion includes the right to erect eruvin and entitles them to accommodation, subject to reasonable regulation by the City.

issue: Does the City's duty of religious neutrality, or other residents' claimed freedom from religion, bar accommodation or establish undue hardship?
facts: The City argued it had to remain strictly neutral and that Quebec law mandated absolute religious neutrality, so it could not permit anything on religious grounds. The Mouvement laïque québécois and four residents asserted a right to freedom from religion and objected to living within a religious enclave. The only concrete inconvenience identified was one affiant's inability to fly a kite; no hardship arose from Gomery J.'s interim order permitting eruvin during Passover.
rule: The State must not establish an official religion or discriminate among religions, but Canadian and Quebec law is not strictly neutral (Charter preamble recognizing supremacy of God; Code of Civil Procedure art. 6 non-juridical Christian holidays; Municipal Taxation Act tax exemptions for religious institutions). Accommodation is part of the constitutional fabric (Woehrling), and the State must accommodate religious practices that do not cause undue hardship.
application: The Court held the City's position that the law required absolute neutrality was wrong in law; the City instead has a constitutional duty to accommodate religious practices that do not impose undue hardship. The area within an eruv is a religious zone only for those who believe it to be one, i.e. Orthodox practitioners, not other residents. No evidence of inconvenience, hardship, or havoc from eruvin in neighbouring municipalities (Mount Royal, Ville St-Laurent, Côte St-Luc, etc.) was adduced, defeating the "floodgates" argument.
conclusion: No; neutrality does not bar accommodation and no undue hardship was shown. The City may regulate but not prohibit eruvin.

issue: Should provisional execution notwithstanding appeal be ordered?
facts: The petitioners sought provisional execution. The record showed a continuing infringement of their religious freedom and no demonstrable harm from eruvin elsewhere on the Island of Montreal or from Gomery J.'s interim order.
rule: Under the penultimate paragraph of art. 547 C.C.P., the Court has discretion to order provisional execution for any sufficient reason, notably where an appeal is likely to cause serious or irreparable injury; the party seeking it must establish a special reason justifying an exception to the general rule that an appeal suspends execution (165440 Canada Inc. v. Hull).
application: The Court found the ongoing infringement of the petitioners' freedom of religion, coupled with the absence of any demonstrable harm from permitting eruvin, constituted a sufficient special reason.
conclusion: Yes; the judgment was ordered executory notwithstanding appeal.

issue: Did Ms. A. have the legal capacity to sign the protection mandate of April 26, 2016?
facts: Ms. A. signed her protection mandate before Notary Lamarre on April 26, 2016. The first observed cognitive problems appeared in September 2017; a dementia diagnosis followed in 2018. D. contested the mandate, alleging his mother lacked capacity to sign it, but led no evidence on the point and made no submissions on it at trial.
rule: Capacity is presumed (art. 4 C.C.Q.). The party alleging incapacity bears the burden of establishing an habitual state of insanity or mental weakness, on a balance of probabilities; a simple doubt is insufficient (Bertrand c. Opération Enfant Soleil; S.P. c. V.P., 2022 QCCS 495; Brusenbauch c. Young).
application: D. adduced no evidence — not even a doubt — as to his mother's cognition in April 2016. There was no sign of cognitive impairment before September 2017. Notary Lamarre testified she had no doubt as to Ms. A.'s capacity to understand the mandate.
conclusion: Ms. A. had the capacity to sign the protection mandate.

issue: Did R. exercise undue influence (captation) over Ms. A. in her appointment as mandatary?
facts: R. was already assisting her mother and was present for most of the notary meetings. D. was under a restraining order following a supermarket altercation and was not appointed. D. alleged undue influence and 'elder abuse' but gave only vague testimony about events occurring in 2019, after the mandate was signed.
rule: The party alleging undue influence bears the burden (Savoie c. Savoie). Captation is akin to fraud vitiating consent, characterized by alienation of the person from relatives and abuse of the influencer's position; the manoeuvres must be determinative of consent (Stoneham and Tewkesbury v. Ouellet, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 172). It may be proved by serious, precise and concordant presumptions (arts. 2846, 2849 C.C.Q.).
application: D. produced no probative evidence of undue influence. Ms. A. initiated the change to add a living-arrangement clause, was not shown to be vulnerable in 2016, chose R. because R. already helped her, and reasonably declined to name D. given the restraining order. The notary noted no concern about R.'s presence. Ms. A. expressed no fear of R.
conclusion: R. did not exercise undue influence; the mandate reflected Ms. A.'s free choice.

issue: Is homologation of the protection mandate in Ms. A.'s interest and does it safeguard her autonomy, wishes and preferences?
facts: Ms. A.'s total and permanent incapacity was established and uncontested. The psychosocial report recommended homologation and R.'s appointment. R. had long managed her mother's affairs and acted promptly when cognition declined.
rule: The mandatary must ensure the moral and material well-being of the person, taking account of her condition, needs, faculties and circumstances (art. 2167.3 C.C.Q.), respecting her wishes and preferences as expressed before incapacity.
application: Ms. A. had set out her wishes (remaining at home) in the mandate. The social worker, after consulting the family and physician, concluded homologation and R.'s appointment were in Ms. A.'s best interest. R. demonstrated attentive, appropriate care and a commitment to her mother's well-being.
conclusion: The protection mandate is homologated and R. is confirmed as mandatary to Ms. A.'s person and property.

issue: Must D. reimburse the $48,000, and is he entitled to restitution for work he performed?
facts: Between September and November 2018, D. received $48,000 from his mother's accounts after she offered him money. By June 21, 2018, medical evidence showed Ms. A. was incapable of administering her property. D. claimed the money was a gift and that he did equivalent work on her properties, producing dubious backdated receipts totalling $45,000 for 2018-2020.
rule: A gift is a contract by gratuitous title (arts. 1806, 1381(2) C.C.Q.). A contracting party must have capacity (art. 1398). Acts before homologation may be annulled on proof the incapacity was notorious or known to the other party (art. 2170 C.C.Q.); this may be shown by serious, precise and concordant presumptions (arts. 2846, 2849).
