The applicant did not show the respondents knew or ought to have known the facilitated activity was unlawful, so nothing gave colour to the fraud or knowing-receipt charge, even assuming the exception could extend beyond fraud.
conclusion: The crime-fraud exception does not apply; privilege stands.

issue: Have the respondents waived privilege by putting their state of mind in issue, or does fairness require waiver?
facts: The applicant argued the respondents' state of mind was central to the knowing-receipt claim and that, because counsel drafted the APA and gave advice to complete the purchase, the respondents had relied on legal advice and put their state of mind in issue; alternatively, fairness required disclosure. The applicant conceded it was itself who raised the respondents' state of mind.
rule: Evidence justifying waiver must be clear and unambiguous (Maximum Ventures). A party waives privilege only by an affirmative allegation voluntarily injecting its own state of mind and relying on the legal advice received (Fraser v. Houston), and must have simply adopted counsel's advice without independent reflection (Freyberg 2007 ABQB 80). Fairness may compel waiver where a party did not voluntarily place its state of mind in issue only in rare, compelling cases (Ed Miller); privilege's importance otherwise prohibits broader release (Refco).
application: The applicant led no evidence that the respondents put their legal knowledge in issue, and admitted it was the applicant who raised the respondents' state of mind — a party does not waive privilege when the opposing party makes such an allegation. There was no evidence the respondents adopted counsel's advice without independent reflection; merely obtaining legal advice is insufficient. The fairness grounds were neither compelling nor exceptional.
conclusion: There was no waiver; fairness did not require disclosure. The application was dismissed with costs to the respondents.

issue: What custody order is in the child's best interests given a finding of deliberate irrational parental alienation, and may the court order a change of custody, therapeutic intervention and a no-contact period?
facts: The father SGB deliberately alienated the two sons from their mother SJL over several years; the arbitrator and appeal judge both found irrational alienation. The younger son JB (16, with Klinefelter's Syndrome and a learning disability) refused all meaningful relationship with his mother. Expert psychiatrists (Dr. Goldstein, Dr. Fidler, Dr. Warshak, and even the father's expert Dr. Korenblum) agreed that in severe irrational alienation the child must be removed from the favoured parent. The mother sought sole custody, authority to enrol JB in the 'Family Bridges' Workshop, and cessation of contact with the father, older brother LB, the father's friend and JB's therapist.
rule: Under s. 16(8)-(10) of the Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), custody is determined solely by the best interests of the child, past conduct is considered only if relevant to parenting ability, and the maximum-contact principle applies subject to best interests. Courts have ordered changes of custody coupled with the Workshop in comparable alienation cases (e.g., A. (A.) v. A. (S.N.); L. (J.K.) v. S. (N.C.)).
application: The court found that doing nothing would not repair the relationship, that all experts agreed JB must be separated from the alienating parent, and that intensive therapy alone required the father's participation, which he refused. The Workshop coupled with a change of custody was the only remedy with a chance of success. JB's special needs and separation from his brother did not outweigh the benefits (LB was leaving home anyway). The father's past conduct showed he would not foster contact and could not meet JB's needs, while the mother could parent appropriately and put JB's interests first. JB, though 16, was not mature enough to decide to sever ties with a parent.
conclusion: The mother was awarded sole custody of JB with authority in her sole discretion to obtain treatment/intervention including the Workshop; for three months the father, LB, the father's friend Nila and Dr. Harman were prohibited from contacting JB and vice versa, with enforcement and travel/passport provisions.

issue: How is the mother's income determined under the Federal Child Support Guidelines, and had she overpaid or underpaid support?
facts: The mother was beneficiary of a family trust owning an investment corporation (SJIL). On the 2005 sale of the Hopedale Mall she received a one-time taxable dividend of about $2 million in 2006 and SJIL received a one-time non-taxable capital dividend; those funds became SJIL's only asset and generated her ongoing income. The father argued her income should be imputed based on lifestyle (~$375,000) or a five-year average (~$854,405). The mother had paid $119,469 in support since LB moved to the father in 2004.
rule: Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175: income is determined from line 150 (s. 16), adjusted by Schedule III (dividends replaced by actual amount), with power under s. 17(1) to depart where line 150 is not the fairest determination given non-recurring amounts, and s. 19(1) imputation only in enumerated circumstances. Capital is not income.
application: None of the s. 19(1) imputation grounds applied; the mother was not underemployed, exempt or diverting income, and lawfully encroached on capital. Averaging or depleting capital has no basis in law. The 2006 one-time taxable and non-taxable dividends were non-recurring capital forming her ongoing income source, so they were excluded and her 2006 income fixed at $74,499. Computing table amounts for each year (2004-June 2010) yielded a total obligation of about $99,968 against $119,469 paid.
conclusion: The one-time dividends were excluded from 2006 income; the mother had overpaid by roughly $19,500 but did not seek reimbursement. Her obligation to pay the father ended July 1, 2010; the father's undue-hardship circumstances meant no order against him, and support for adult child LB would be arranged directly between LB and his mother under s. 3(2).

issue: Must a sentencing court disclose to the convicted person the prejudicial contents of a probation officer's pre-sentence report so that the offender may respond to them?
facts: The appellants pleaded guilty to attempted armed robbery and were sentenced to five years. The magistrate had before him a pre-sentence report prepared by a Provincial Probation Branch officer and appears to have considered it, but its contents were never disclosed to the accused, who were unrepresented at sentencing.
rule: Following R. v. Campbell (1911), 6 Cr. App. R. 131, R. v. Van Pelz (1942), 29 Cr. App. R. 10, R. v. Butterwasser, [1948] 1 K.B. 4, and the Canadian authorities R. v. Piluk (1933), R. v. Markoff, [1937] 1 D.L.R. 77, R. v. Lim Gim, and the Court's own unreported decisions (Tolmie & Rambo, Nahanee), prejudicial factual material placed before a sentencing court must be disclosed to the accused; if denied, proof should be given in open court subject to cross-examination, or the material must be ignored. Justice must be seen to be done (R. v. Sussex Justices, Ex p. McCarthy). A probation officer's pre-sentence report stands on no higher footing than a police officer's pre-sentence statement.
application: The Court held that a pre-sentence probation report, insofar as it contains factual allegations prejudicial to the prisoner, cannot be placed in a different category from a police officer's pre-sentence statement; the same principles apply. The convicted person must be informed of the substance of the detrimental portions so he may agree, explain, or deny; if denied and considered material, the allegation must be proved in open court or ignored. The Court distinguished Williams v. New York (1949), 337 U.S. 241, reading it narrowly and refusing to adopt any principle permitting secret prejudicial information to found a sentence, while accepting Goddard L.C.J.'s caution in R. v. Dickson that undisclosed psychiatric/mental-condition material may sometimes properly be withheld.
conclusion: A convicted person must be informed of the substance of a probation officer's report insofar as it is detrimental to him, with an opportunity to concur, explain, deny, and test it by cross-examination.

issue: Does the non-disclosure of the report in this case warrant appellate interference with the sentences?
facts: The magistrate considered the undisclosed pre-sentence reports, which the Court reviewed on appeal.
rule: An appeal against sentence will succeed only where the appellant has suffered a substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.
application: Although the Court found a violation of the disclosure principle, it concluded that the reports contained so little prejudice to the appellants that the magistrate could have placed little if any reliance on them as factors influencing him against the accused. No other ground justifying interference was advanced.
conclusion: No substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice resulted; leave to appeal was granted but the appeals were dismissed.

issue: Should leave to intervene be granted to the moving party on the case-specific issues (defence counsel's jury address and the charge to the jury)?
facts: The Canadian Holocaust Remembrance Association, a non-profit organization founded to preserve the memory of Holocaust victims and to support prosecution of Nazi war criminals, sought leave to intervene in the Crown's appeal against Finta's acquittal on war crimes and crimes against humanity charges. Two of the three issues on which it sought to intervene were case-specific: the propriety of defence counsel's remarks to the jury and the trial judge's charge on the lack of medical evidence as to cause of death during train transports.
rule: Under Rule 28 of the Rules respecting Criminal Proceedings the court has discretion to grant leave to intervene, but the right to intervene where the liberty of the subject is involved should be granted sparingly (R. v. Seaboyer; R. v. Zundel). Under s. 7(3.75) of the Criminal Code the prosecutor is the Attorney General of Canada. Both fairness and the appearance of fairness in the criminal process are paramount.
application: An accused obliged to respond to submissions of more than one prosecutor lacks the appearance of fairness, which alone justified refusing intervention on these issues. Further, case-specific issues whose resolution has no ramifications beyond the appeal itself are not the kind of issues on which leave to intervene is usually granted, unlike issues affecting the state of the law generally.
conclusion: Leave to intervene on the case-specific issues was refused.

issue: Should leave to intervene be granted on the constitutional challenge to ss. 7(3.71) and 7(3.74) of the Criminal Code?
facts: The respondent intended to argue that ss. 7(3.71) and 7(3.74) were void as inconsistent with ss. 7, 11(a), (d), 12 and 15 of the Charter. The moving party wished to assist the court, particularly on justification under s. 1, given its interest and experience in the fair prosecution of war criminals.
rule: A constitutional issue affects the state of the law and warrants the court knowing all bases on which the issue may be decided. Leave to intervene is granted where the intervener can offer assistance different from that of the existing parties; the Attorney General has both an interest and a duty to defend challenged legislation on every relevant basis, including s. 1 evidentiary considerations (following R. v. Zundel over R. v. Seaboyer).
application: Although the moving party had a profound interest in the effective and fair prosecution of such proceedings, it was not shown how its perspective would translate into submissions different from those the Attorney General of Canada would make. Any factual or evidentiary material relevant to s. 1 justification would be placed before the court by the Attorney General, who would obtain the moving party's assistance if needed. The case resembled Zundel (intervention refused) more than Seaboyer (intervention granted).
conclusion: Leave to intervene on the constitutional issue was refused; the motion was dismissed.

issue: Was the plaintiff dismissed for just cause?
facts: Rivard, a clerical/terminal-operator employee hired in 1981, was terminated at the end of October 1985 after a period of illness she attributed to a lacquer spray near her workstation. On the termination form the employer initially gave no reason (marking 'other') and only weeks later asserted she was discharged for her 'attitude and difficulties to work with fellow workers.' The company witness could not substantiate this at trial, and the specific allegations in the statement of defence had little or no evidentiary support.
rule: An employer may terminate employment, but a dismissal without just cause entitles the employee to reasonable notice or pay in lieu; the employer bears the burden of proving cause.
application: The court found neither the illness up to the end of October 1985 nor the inconclusive allegations of unsatisfactory performance amounted to just cause. Hitachi was entitled to dismiss Rivard for its own reasons, but had not established cause.
conclusion: The dismissal was without just cause, so the only remaining question was whether the pay in lieu of notice was reasonable.

issue: What period of reasonable notice (or pay in lieu of notice) was the plaintiff entitled to?
facts: Rivard was about 27 when hired, worked roughly four years in an average, non-supervisory clerical role, earning $325/week at termination. There was a contract of employment but no written agreement addressing duration, notice, or benefits. Hitachi paid four weeks in lieu of notice (double the Employment Standards Act minimum); Rivard demanded six times that amount. Because of illness she did not seek work for about six months but found a job quickly once she did.
rule: Reasonable notice is determined objectively, having regard to the intention of the parties, not by a purely comparative or subjective approach (Yosyk v. Westfair Foods Ltd. (1988), 51 Man.R.(2d) 191, per Twaddle, J.A., referring to Lazarowicz v. Orenda Engines, Gilman v. Winnipeg Board of Jewish Education, and Balchin v. Diecast Morwest); courts may read a missing notice term into an unwritten employment contract where supported by the evidence. Employment Standards Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. E-110.
application: The court rejected the argument that no contract existed and the argument that inferring intention was mere speculation. Considering Rivard's young age, short service, non-professional/non-managerial clerical role, stable but unremarkable employment with only incremental raises, and the ease with which she found new work, the court inferred the parties would have agreed to a modest notice period. Her attempt to recover lost earnings from her lacquer-related illness (barred to her under Workers' Compensation) through the notice claim was rejected as an improper 'backdoor' approach with no bearing on notice.
conclusion: Eight weeks was reasonable notice. Having already received four weeks' pay in lieu, Rivard was awarded a further four weeks' salary, i.e. $1,300, plus Class I costs.

issue: Should the plaintiff have sole custody, or should the parents share joint custody and guardianship of the children?
facts: Both parents were found to be capable and loving parents with complementary parenting styles; the s. 15 assessor (Dr. Elterman) recommended sole custody to the plaintiff owing to conflict and poor communication. The plaintiff sought sole custody based on communication difficulties; the defendant sought shared parenting and opposed sole custody. Communication problems flowed largely from the manner of separation and the plaintiff's intrusive monitoring of the defendant.
rule: Custody must be decided on the best interests of the child, guided by the non-exhaustive criteria in s. 24 of the Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 128 and s. 16 of the Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.); the analysis is wide-ranging and free of presumptions for or against joint custody (J.S. v. G.J.S., 2005 BCSC 1373; Young v. Young; King v. Low; Robinson v. Filyk; Gordon v. Goertz). Where both parents are able and loving, arrangements should maximize each parent's contact with the children.
application: The court found the communication levels were not as poor as the plaintiff portrayed; the parties had adjusted access by consent without court intervention, the conflict stemmed from the mode of separation rather than differing parenting philosophies, and the defendant deferred to the plaintiff's directions. Sole custody would not eliminate the need for communication. Both parents were capable of meaningful dialogue once a parenting routine was set.
conclusion: Joint custody and joint guardianship (on the Joyce Model) were ordered, with the plaintiff having primary care and the final decision-making power on disputed major decisions, subject to the defendant's right to seek court review under s. 32 of the Family Relations Act.

issue: What parenting schedule serves the children's best interests, and should the defendant be restricted from removing the children from Canada?
facts: The children (T.M., born April 2005, and I.A., born January 2007) were young; I.A. had never spent an overnight with the defendant. The defendant worked nights Sunday through Wednesday, making 50/50 shared parenting impractical. The plaintiff feared the defendant, whose family lived in Brazil, might not return the children if allowed to take them abroad. The plaintiff wished the children exposed to their Jewish heritage and holidays.
rule: Best interests of the child under s. 24 FRA and s. 16 Divorce Act; contact with each parent should be maximized where both parents are fit, with due regard to practical constraints and the children's need for stability.
application: The court set an expanding week-to-week schedule with graduated overnight transitions for I.A., allocated statutory and cultural holidays (including making Jewish holidays such as Passover and Yom Kippur available to the plaintiff with make-up time to the defendant, and preserving the plaintiff's Chanukah time), rejected splitting the siblings' time, and found the children not ready for international travel. It ordered that neither party change the children's residency from Kamloops without consent or court order and that the defendant not remove the children from Canada until I.A. turns five (January 2012), thereafter permitting travel with consent not to be unreasonably withheld.
conclusion: A detailed alternating parenting schedule was ordered with holiday allocations; travel outside Canada by the defendant was barred until I.A. is five, and residency was fixed in the Kamloops area absent consent or court order. The court remained seized of parenting matters for two years.

issue: How should the modest family assets and debts be divided, and is reapportionment warranted?
facts: The matrimonial home was appraised at $660,000 but was subject to roughly $700,000 in mortgages; there was additional debt to the plaintiff's father and on the defendant's vehicle. Refinancing had discharged about $90,000 of the plaintiff's pre-marriage student loan. The plaintiff had brought about $30,000 in RRSPs into the marriage and sought reapportionment; the defendant sought a lump sum to fund accommodation for the children.
rule: Family assets are presumptively divided equally under s. 56(2) of the Family Relations Act, subject to reapportionment; pre-marriage student debt discharged with family-home equity is not family debt.
application: The court noted the home's value was exceeded by roughly $55,000 in family debt and that the plaintiff had benefited from using home equity to retire her non-family student loan (notionally leaving about $35,000 in equity). Balancing that benefit against the plaintiff's pre-marriage RRSP contribution, the court ordered the defendant to transfer his interest in the home to the plaintiff, who would retain it and indemnify him on the mortgages and the father's loan, and ordered the RRSP divided equally by spousal rollover.
conclusion: The defendant transferred his home interest to the plaintiff (who indemnifies him on the mortgages and the father's loan); the plaintiff's RRSP was divided equally by rollover; each party kept and remained responsible for their own vehicle and individually held debt.

issue: What income should be imputed to the parties for support purposes?
facts: The defendant's undisputed income was $33,000 annually. The plaintiff, an anaesthesiologist, claimed income of $173,300 based on three days' work per week after expenses; her work history was interrupted by maternity and disability leaves, and 2006 (net income $179,130) best reflected her earning capacity. Full-time work would yield in excess of $300,000; her part-time choice was not driven by the children's care needs.
rule: Income for support is determined under the Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175, and a court may find income greater than declared where business expenses have personal components and part-time work is not justified by childcare needs.
application: The court accepted the defendant's $33,000, yielding a Guidelines table amount of $515/month for two children. For the plaintiff, it found her declared $173,300 understated, discounted the personal component in claimed expenses (notably automobile), and took account of upcoming call shifts and additional shifts available when the defendant has the children, fixing her income at $225,000 net.
conclusion: The defendant's income was $33,000 (child support $515/month); the plaintiff's income was set at $225,000 net for support and proportionate sharing of the children's extraordinary expenses.

issue: Is the defendant entitled to spousal support and should the award depart from the SSAG range?
facts: The defendant gave up a secure Club Med career and career advancement to move to Canada and marry the plaintiff, who had far greater earning capacity; he faced language barriers and limited transferable skills. The marriage was brief. The plaintiff proposed SSAG-range support of $300–$450/month for 1.5 to 3 years.
rule: Section 15.2(6) of the Divorce Act sets the objectives of spousal support; Moge v. Moge, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 813, holds the primary purpose is to redress the economic consequences of marriage breakdown with no single objective paramount. The SSAG are advisory 'useful tools' (Redpath v. Redpath, 2006 BCCA 338; McEachern v. McEachern, 2006 BCCA 508) from which departure is justified for reasons on the facts, including where a non-custodial parent needs support to fulfil a parental role (Petit v. Petit, 2008 CanLII 705).
application: The court found the defendant's economic disadvantage disproportionate to the short marriage, that slavish adherence to the SSAG would unfairly place the whole financial burden of the breakdown on him and undermine his ability to house the children during his parenting time. Applying the Petit reasoning and a means-and-circumstances analysis, and considering tax consequences, it awarded well above the SSAG range.
conclusion: Spousal support of $2,200/month was ordered for 48 months, to be reviewed de novo thereafter as to entitlement and quantum; the defendant remains obliged to pursue self-sufficiency. A divorce was pronounced. Costs: each party to bear their own, absent further submissions.

issue: What is the fit and appropriate sentence for a racially motivated assault causing bodily harm together with the related offences to which the accused pleaded guilty?
facts: The 22-year-old accused, intoxicated and in breach of probation, singled out three young Black men, used a racial slur, struck one in the face with a mug causing a laceration requiring three sutures, threatened all three, and poured his drink over a young woman. He had 25 prior Criminal Code convictions, including many breaches of court orders, showed no remorse, and had an outburst in court.
rule: Sentencing must consider the objectives of denunciation, deterrence (specific and general), protection of the public, and public confidence in the administration of justice, together with the principle of totality (R. v. Crocker). Precedents include R. v. Ingram & Grimsdale (1977) 35 C.C.C.(2d) 376, R. v. Lelas (1990) 58 C.C.C.(3d) 568, and R. v. Miloszewski.
application: The court found the accused was sliding from property offences into violent hate crimes, lacked insight and remorse, and posed continuing danger. Applying the denunciatory approach in the precedents, the court imposed cumulative sentences: six months for the assault causing bodily harm (concurrent six months for the racially motivated threats), thirty days consecutive for the assault on the girl, three months consecutive for breach of probation by committing assault, sixty days consecutive for breach of probation by consuming alcohol, and time served for causing a disturbance—totalling one year.
conclusion: The accused was sentenced to a total of one year in jail, with a DNA order, a ten-year firearms prohibition, and the victim fine surcharges waived due to impecuniosity.

issue: How must racial motivation be treated in the sentencing analysis?
facts: The accused targeted the victims solely because of the colour of their skin, calling them 'niggers' and telling them they did not belong in Canada, while committing the assault and threats.
rule: Section 718.2(a)(i) of the Criminal Code expressly mandates that motivation by bias, prejudice or hate based on race be considered an aggravating factor. Case law (Ingram & Grimsdale, Lelas, Miloszewski) holds that racially motivated offences are more heinous and call for sentences expressing public abhorrence.
application: The court treated the race-based motivation as a serious aggravating factor, characterizing the crimes as 'ignorant, cowardly, racially motivated, unprovoked,' and stressed the need to denounce such conduct in the strongest terms to specifically and generally deter such behaviour.
conclusion: Racial motivation was applied as a significant statutory aggravating factor, driving the emphasis on denunciation and deterrence and supporting a custodial sentence.

issue: Was a community-based sentence or further probation an appropriate disposition?
facts: The accused had breached court orders more than a dozen times, lacked insight into his substance abuse, refused Addictions Services, showed no remorse, and the pre-sentence report—unlike an earlier 2002 report—no longer supported him as a candidate for community supervision. His proposed supervisor was over 50 kilometres away.
rule: A sentence must promote rehabilitation where realistic but must not undermine public confidence in the administration of justice; probation is inappropriate where an offender has a demonstrated record of non-compliance (R. v. Hendrix, G.E.R., Lewis).
application: Given the repeated breaches, deterioration from suitable to unsuitable for community supervision, and lack of insight, the court found probation and a community-based sentence would be an affront to good sense and would not aid rehabilitation, leaving imprisonment as the only appropriate tool.
conclusion: Both a community-based sentence and further probation were rejected; a custodial sentence was imposed.

issue: Was the fine imposed for wilfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group manifestly inadequate given that the offender was a teacher who repeatedly inflamed his students against the Jewish people?
facts: Keegstra taught social studies at Eckville High School from 1978 to 1982 and repeatedly vilified the Jewish people as historical fact, propounding conspiracy theories and denying the Holocaust. He was convicted by a jury of unlawfully promoting hatred contrary to the Criminal Code. The trial judge imposed a $3,000 fine, treating repudiation and deterrence as paramount but concluding the sentence was adequate because the students became productive members of society and the hate promotion was confined to a small group.
rule: For an offence where general deterrence and denunciation are the paramount sentencing factors, the sentence must express society's unconditional rejection of the conduct. The promotion of hatred is a serious crime; committing it in a position of trust over impressionable young people is an aggravating, not mitigating, factor, and lack of demonstrated success or harm does not mitigate the offence.
application: The Court held that despite the accused's previous good record the crime deserved imprisonment to express society's rejection of hatemongering and to deter others. Promoting hatred to students over several years in breach of a teacher's trust was aggravating. The absence of proven harm did not count in the accused's favour; some students admitted a lasting negative impact. Free speech is not absolute and hate law is a bulwark of a free society. A one-year custodial term was warranted.
conclusion: The fine was manifestly inadequate; the appropriate sentence was one year of imprisonment.

issue: Did the sentencing judge err by treating the accused's lack of success, loss of reputation, career and public scorn as mitigating factors?
facts: The trial judge remarked that the accused had 'fought the good fight', had been 'ground through' the court system, and had suffered loss of his teaching certificate, reputation and public scorn, implying these consequences reduced the need for further punishment.
rule: Natural public reaction to a crime, and consequences flowing from the criminal's own conduct, do not make the offender a victim and are not proper mitigating factors; the seriousness of hate promotion is not diminished by absence of proven harm.
application: The Court found the 'good fight' comment unfortunate: the accused was not fighting a good fight but attempting to twist young minds, and showed no remorse. Scorn and loss of reputation were natural consequences of his crime, not mitigating circumstances. The accused was not a harmless eccentric but knowingly defied his employers, the courts and Parliament.
conclusion: The sentencing judge erred in relying on these matters as mitigation; they did not reduce the gravity of the offence.

issue: Could the exceptional 12-year litigation history justify suspending an otherwise appropriate sentence of imprisonment?
facts: The indictment was preferred in 1984 and the matter came before the courts through nine major proceedings over 12 years, including two Supreme Court of Canada decisions and multiple new trials, none of which was the fault of the Crown or the accused.
rule: Mere delay in sentencing where not the Crown's fault is not mitigating (A.B.C., 1991 ABCA 337), nor is pre-charge delay significant where deterrence and denunciation are paramount (Spence, 1992 ABCA 352). However, a protracted prosecution with an unusually long record of litigation steps can be a mitigating factor because of added expense and extended anxiety for the accused and his family (Cooper No. 2; Zundel No. 2).
application: The Court found the litigation history 'quite remarkable and, fortunately, unique' and almost without precedent, and the fault of nobody. In light of these special circumstances, and for no other reason, the Court suspended the one-year sentence it would otherwise have imposed, releasing the accused on probation with 200 hours of community service preferably serving victims of racial, religious or ethnic hatred, and a term prohibiting any preaching of hatred against the Jewish people.
conclusion: The extraordinary procedural history justified suspending the custodial term; the accused was placed on one year's probation with community service, but this was not a vindication.

issue: Is a restrictive covenant prohibiting the sale of land 'to Jews, or to persons of objectionable nationality' void as contrary to public policy?
facts: Drummond Wren owned York County land subject to a covenant he had assumed and agreed to exact from his assigns providing that the land was 'not to be sold to Jews, or to persons of objectionable nationality.' He applied for a declaration that the covenant was invalid; no one appeared to oppose.
rule: Any agreement injurious to the public or against the public good is void as contrary to public policy (7 Halsbury, 2nd ed.); public policy varies with the circumstances of the time (Naylor, Benzon & Co. v. Krainische Industrie Gesellschaft, [1918] 1 K.B. 331, aff'd [1918] 2 K.B. 486). Courts may look to Dominion and Provincial statutes and public documents as an aid in determining public policy (Walkerville Brewing Co. Ltd. v. Mayrand, 1929 CanLII 368 (ON SCAD), 63 O.L.R. 573).
application: MacKay J. reasoned that sanctioning such a covenant would permit the segregation and confinement of religious and ethnic groups to particular areas, deepening divisions in a province and country of minorities. Prevailing public opinion, reflected in the San Francisco (UN) Charter, the Atlantic Charter, The Racial Discrimination Act, 1944, s. 99 of The Insurance Act, and The Community Halls Act regulations, plus international declarations condemning racial and religious discrimination, all confirmed a public policy against such discrimination. Applying (not inventing) established public-policy doctrine to these facts, the covenant was injurious to the public good, made especially poignant given anti-semitism as a weapon of the recently defeated enemies.
conclusion: The covenant is void as offensive to public policy.

issue: Is such a covenant void as an unlawful restraint on alienation?
facts: The covenant restricting sale to certain classes was not limited in time or to the life of the immediate grantee.
rule: At common law land should be freely alienable; a limited class of partial-restraint exceptions has been recognized (In re Macleay (1875), L.R. 20 Eq. 186), though doubted in In re Rosher; Rosher v. Rosher (1884), 26 Ch. D. 801, and contrary to Attwater v. Attwater.
application: MacKay J. found it unnecessary to challenge In re Macleay because the covenant here was unlimited in time and not confined to the immediate grantee, unlike the partial restraints enforced in decided cases. The long-established principle of free alienation, reinforced by his public-policy conclusion, precluded recognizing so novel a limitation.
conclusion: The covenant is void as an unlimited restraint on alienation.

issue: Is such a covenant void for uncertainty?
facts: The covenant barred sale to 'Jews, or to persons of objectionable nationality.'
rule: A covenant is void where its terms are too uncertain for a court to give them legal meaning (Clayton v. Ramsden, [1943] A.C. 320, holding 'of Jewish parentage' and 'of the Jewish faith' uncertain).
application: The phrase 'persons of objectionable nationality' was hopelessly vague, incapable of legal meaning. Bound by Clayton v. Ramsden, MacKay J. held that the term 'Jews' admitted of no more certainty than the phrases there condemned, and he would have so held even if the matter were open.
conclusion: The covenant is void for uncertainty.

issue: Did the Crown rebut the presumption of diminished moral blameworthiness of the young person under s. 72(1)(a) of the YCJA?
facts: M.G. was less than a month shy of his 18th birthday when, over four nights in November 2016 while on youth probation, he spray-painted swastikas and hateful antisemitic, anti-Black and anti-Muslim messages on six places of worship in Ottawa. The offences were planned and researched online, the targets carefully chosen, and he acted independently. He had a prior youth record for assault, robbery and failing to comply.
rule: Under s. 72(1)(a) of the YCJA the court must be satisfied the presumption of diminished moral blameworthiness is rebutted. Per R. v. S.B., 2017 ONCA 22, the Crown must show the young person demonstrated the maturity, moral sophistication and capacity for independent (and mature) judgement of an adult. The Crown's onus falls below proof beyond a reasonable doubt but requires careful consideration (R. v. A.O., 2007 ONCA 144).
application: The court found the offences were planned, deliberate, independently carried out and researched online; M.G. knew the acts were illegal and would cause community distress; he was nearly 18 with a prior record. Although his motivation rested on crude racial stereotypes reflecting immature judgement, that was not enough to overcome the evidence rebutting the presumption.
conclusion: The presumption of reduced moral culpability was rebutted; the first branch of the s. 72(1) test was met.

issue: Did the Crown establish that a youth sentence would not be sufficient to hold the young person accountable under s. 72(1)(b), justifying an adult sentence?
facts: M.G. had already spent almost nine months in custody at a secure youth facility, where he obtained his high school diploma, took paid work and skills training, engaged in weekly psychotherapy, and agreed to ongoing counselling through youturn and mental health treatment on release. Dr. Federoff assessed him at high risk to reoffend (VRAG-R) but noted incarceration in an adult facility would likely increase his risk of adopting criminal attitudes.
rule: Section 72(1)(b) requires the court to find a youth sentence would be insufficient to hold the young person accountable per s. 38. Accountability means meaningful consequences promoting rehabilitation and reintegration, not accountability to society at large or deterrence (R. v. A.O.), and mirrors retribution with restraint (R. v. S.B.; R. v. M.(C.A.)). Section 38(2) requires the least restrictive, proportionate sentence not exceeding what an adult would receive for the same offence. Comparison drawn to R. v. Lelas (1990) where an adult received one year for similar synagogue vandalism.
application: The court rejected the Crown's argument that a high-risk youth must be held as long as he poses a risk, finding it contrary to the principle of restraint. The best protection for the public was the intensive counselling and support in place, which would be lost if M.G. moved to the adult system. The available three-year youth sentence range (with up to nine further months' custody and 18 months' supervision) was a considerable sanction that adequately held M.G. accountable; an adult sentence would be disproportionate given Lelas and contrary to s. 38.
conclusion: The court was not satisfied a youth sentence would be insufficient; the second branch failed, so the adult sentence application was dismissed.

issue: Does an appeal lie to the Court of Appeal from the dismissal of an application for habeas corpus in extradition proceedings?
facts: After Evans C.J.H.C. committed Rauca for extradition and dismissed his habeas corpus application, an appeal was launched to the Court of Appeal. The respondents suggested no appeal lay, relying on Ex parte Johnston (1959), which had held there was no jurisdiction to hear such an appeal.
rule: Section 719 of the Criminal Code (as amended in 1965, subss. (2)-(6)) provides a right of appeal to the Court of Appeal from the refusal of a writ of habeas corpus ad subjiciendum and from a judgment on the return of such a writ.
application: Reviewing the legislative history — the confusion identified in Ex parte Shane and the responsive 1965 amendment — the Court held that s. 719 was intended to create a general right of appeal in habeas corpus proceedings, including those arising out of an extradition claim, and is not confined to habeas corpus under the Criminal Code. The Court also rejected the suggestion that the application was premature, since a warrant of committal had issued and been executed and the fugitive had been advised of his right to seek habeas corpus.
conclusion: The Court held it had jurisdiction to hear the appeal.

issue: Does committing a Canadian citizen for extradition infringe s. 6(1) of the Charter, and if so, is the limit justified under s. 1?
facts: Rauca, a naturalized Canadian citizen since 1956, was ordered committed for surrender to the Federal Republic of Germany to face charges of murdering roughly 11,584 persons in Nazi-occupied Lithuania. He argued the Extradition Act and treaty were inoperative under s. 52 because they conflicted with his s. 6(1) right to remain in Canada.
rule: Charter s. 6(1) guarantees every citizen the right to enter, remain in and leave Canada; s. 1 subjects guaranteed rights to reasonable limits prescribed by law demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. Analysis proceeds in two steps (infringement, then justification), and the party supporting the limit bears the onus on a balance of probabilities (following Re Southam Inc. and the Queen (No. 1)).
application: The Court agreed the committal order prima facie interfered with the citizen's right to remain in Canada, and rejected the respondents' argument that the onus lay on the appellant. On justification, it considered the rationale and lengthy history of extradition in free and democratic societies, Canada's obligations to the international community, the principle that crime should not go unpunished, and comparative material (International Covenant, European Convention protocols) showing no bar to extraditing one's own nationals. The executive discretion to refuse surrender operated only in the fugitive's favour and was not arbitrary; Germany's constitutional refusal to extradite its own nationals was offset by its undertaking to prosecute them, giving equivalence in substance. There was no present ability to prosecute Rauca in Canada, and even if there were, it would not render the limit unreasonable.
conclusion: The limit imposed by the Extradition Act and treaty on s. 6(1) was reasonable and demonstrably justified; the Charter argument failed.

issue: Were the offences committed within the 'territory' of the Federal Republic of Germany within the meaning of the extradition treaty?
facts: The murders were alleged to have occurred in Lithuania in 1941-1943. Lithuania was a sovereign state occupied and under de facto control of Germany at the relevant time, administered as part of the 'Ostland' Reich Commissariat under German law. Article 1(1) of the treaty permits extradition for an offence 'committed within the territory of the requesting state.'
rule: Under the treaty, 'territory' concerns the area in which territorial jurisdiction is exercised, not de jure sovereignty; de facto jurisdiction suffices to found extradition (Schtraks v. Government of Israel, [1964] A.C. 556; Re Ryan (1973), 360 F. Supp. 270, aff'd).
application: Evans C.J.H.C. found Germany was in de facto occupation and control of Lithuania in 1941, applying German law and courts there. Following Schtraks and Ryan, the Court of Appeal held that recognizing jurisdiction under the treaty did not mean recognizing German sovereignty or the wartime regime; 'territory' includes areas occupied and under de facto German control during the Second World War. Germany had also acknowledged its obligation to prosecute its nationals for such crimes wherever committed.
conclusion: The Requesting State had jurisdiction to seek extradition; the appeal on this ground also failed, so it was unnecessary to consider art. 1(2).

issue: Did the defendant establish that he was exercising a constitutionally protected Métis aboriginal right to trap under s. 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982?
facts: The defendant, a self-identifying Métis raised in Hinton, admitted trapping squirrels on his uncle's trapline without a licence and without permission, saying he did so to teach his children to trap in his family's tradition. His family had trapped for at least three generations, though the historic trapping was near Lac St. Anne and the Berland/Red River area, not shown to be near Hinton.
rule: Section 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 recognizes and affirms existing aboriginal rights, and s. 35(2) includes the Métis. R. v. Powley, 2003 SCC 43 sets out the ten-step test for Métis rights, requiring identification of a historic and contemporary rights-bearing community and site-specific, community-based rights; R. v. Van der Peet, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 507 places the onus on the claimant to prove the right on a balance of probabilities.
application: The court accepted that the defendant is a self-identifying Métis and a member of a contemporary Métis community in Hinton, and that trapping is integral to his family's culture with intergenerational continuity. However, the evidence failed to establish the existence of a historic rights-bearing Métis community in or around Hinton before effective European control, and no relevant time frame for European control was proven. Because aboriginal rights are communal and site-specific, the absence of a proven historic and contemporary rights-bearing community with a right to trap in this area was fatal.
conclusion: The defendant did not establish that he was exercising a s. 35 aboriginal right; the Powley test was not satisfied, so this defence failed.

issue: Can the Interim Métis Harvesting Agreement operate as a defence to the Wildlife Act charge?
facts: Alberta entered into IMHAs with two Métis organizations purporting to allow members to hunt, trap and fish throughout the province on harvesting lands for subsistence purposes. The Crown conceded the agreements are neither legislation nor regulation, and para. 4 reserved Alberta Justice's authority to prosecute.
rule: Under the Constitution Act, 1982 (Powley and R. v. Blais, 2003 SCC 44), Métis harvesting rights are restricted to members of a present-day community ancestrally tied to a historic community in a specific area. R. v. Catagas (1977), 38 C.C.C. (2d) 296 (Man. C.A.) holds that the Crown cannot by executive action grant a blanket dispensation from the law in favour of a particular group. Charter equality rights (s. 15) and the Alberta Bill of Rights guarantee equality before the law.
application: The IMHA purports to extend to all Métis, everywhere in the province, rights broader than those defined in Powley, without regard to the site-specific community-based criteria. As a non-legislative policy formalized in an agreement, it cannot override the equality guarantees of the Charter or the Alberta Bill of Rights, and it amounts to an impermissible executive dispensation as condemned in Catagas. Para. 12 of the NRTA applies only to Indians and, per Blais, cannot be extended to Métis. The court rejected the Crown's reliance on the prosecution-reservation clause but held the IMHA still could not confer a valid defence.
conclusion: The IMHA cannot operate as a defence; to the extent it conflicts with or extends s. 35 rights it has no effect. The defendant was convicted and, given he may have been misled and was acting to teach his children, a nominal fine of $25 was imposed.

issue: Did the Crown prove criminal harassment under s. 264 of the Criminal Code beyond a reasonable doubt, including harassment and objectively reasonable fear?
facts: After the complainant ended their romantic relationship on July 8, 2002, Mandell repeatedly followed her, communicated with her directly and indirectly, watched her residence, phoned and visited her friends and relatives to locate her, and on October 19, 2002 pursued her by car through traffic and threw himself onto the hood of her moving vehicle. The defence argued the complainant was not harassed, was not credible, continued to associate with him voluntarily, and that any fear was objectively unreasonable.
rule: Section 264(1) and (2) of the Criminal Code. Per R. v. Sillipp (1997 ABCA 346), the mens rea is knowledge or recklessness/wilful blindness that the complainant is harassed; the Crown must prove the prohibited conduct, that the complainant was harassed, the requisite knowledge, that the conduct caused the complainant to fear for safety, and that the fear was reasonable in all the circumstances. Harassment means being tormented, troubled, worried continually, plagued, bedevilled or badgered (R. v. Kosikar; R. v. Ohenhen; R. v. Kordrostami; R. v. Lamontagne). The judge applied R. v. W.(D.), Lifchus and Starr on credibility and reasonable doubt.
application: The judge rejected Mandell's evidence as making 'no sense' and preferred the complainant and independent civilian witnesses, who confirmed her car was stopped when Mandell was sprawled on the hood. Although the complainant continued contact after July 8, she did so under Mandell's psychological and emotional control (analogized to the dynamics discussed in R. v. Lavallee) and while avoiding him. Mandell repeatedly followed, communicated with and watched her contrary to s. 264(2)(a),(b),(c); he knew or was wilfully blind to the fact she was harassed; her fear, crystallizing on October 19, 2002, was genuine and reasonable.
conclusion: The Crown proved criminal harassment beyond a reasonable doubt; a finding of guilt was entered.

issue: Did the accused have an operating mind and the intent required to breach the conditions of his recognizance under s. 145(3)?
facts: While bound by a recognizance to abstain from communicating with the complainant, Mandell phoned her on November 12 and twice on November 13, 2002, including from a school and a public phone booth, seeking her help. He argued a mild concussion from the October 19 accident left him impaired and unaware of what he was doing.
rule: Section 145(3) of the Criminal Code requires proof of intent to fail to comply with a condition; a defence exists where the accused lacked an operating mind. Medical and neuropsychological expert evidence was considered.
application: All four doctors agreed Mandell suffered only a mild concussion, was never hospitalized, and his judgment, memory, concentration and orientation were intact. His judgment was as poor before as after the accident. He had the presence of mind to lie to his doctors and wife, to have his mother lie about his whereabouts, and to call from locations that would conceal his identity — showing a clear operating mind and deliberate contact.
conclusion: Mandell knew exactly what he was doing and had the requisite intent; findings of guilt were entered on all breach counts.

issue: Should the complainant's parallel civil action for damages be taken into account in the criminal trial?
facts: During and after submissions, defence counsel sought to put before the court, by agreed statement, that the complainant had issued and later amended a civil statement of claim alleging stalking, harassment, assault and related torts arising from the same events.
rule: The rule in Hollington v. Hewthorn ([1943] K.B. 587) makes a criminal conviction inadmissible in later civil proceedings; the civil and criminal standards of proof differ (R. v. W.(D.); Lifchus; Starr). Civil proceedings between the complainant and accused are res inter alios acta relative to the Crown's prosecution.
application: The judge noted every offence against the person gives rise to a civil right of action (ubi jus, ibi remedium) and that the complainant had to file within the two-year limitation period under the Limitations Act, 2002. The statement of claim was merely an unproven pleading not drafted by her, and the civil action was res inter alios acta as regards the criminal case.
conclusion: The court declined to take the civil proceedings or the amended statement of claim into consideration.

issue: Does a judge in chambers under article 550 C.C.P. have jurisdiction to grant the ancillary conclusions (removal of credit/internet information and an order restraining opposing counsel) contained in the motion?
facts: Saraffian's motion sought, beyond suspension of provisional execution, orders directing the Hospital to remove allegedly libellous and derogatory information from her credit rating and from jurisprudence websites, and to order counsel to cease 'fomenting hatred' against her reputation.
rule: A judge in chambers acting under article 550 C.C.P. is limited to determining whether to suspend provisional execution ordered by the trial judgment; the provision does not confer authority to grant substantive ancillary relief.
application: Hilton J.A. found that, as a chambers judge under art. 550 C.C.P., he had no authority to grant the conclusions in paragraphs B), C) and D) of the motion; at most he could suspend the provisional-execution order in paragraph [100] of the Superior Court judgment.
conclusion: The chambers judge lacked jurisdiction to grant the ancillary relief; only the suspension request could be entertained.

issue: Should the provisional execution of the vexatious-litigant order be suspended pending the appeal?
facts: The Superior Court declared Saraffian a vexatious/quarrelsome litigant under the Rules of Practice, barred her from instituting proceedings without prior judicial authorization, and ordered provisional execution notwithstanding appeal. A panel had earlier allowed her to prosecute her own appeal without authorization but refused to let her freely institute other proceedings. She argued she was held 'hostage', faced looming prescription deadlines for actions against the Public Curator and regarding asbestos, and that the authorization system was ineffective.
rule: Per article 550 C.C.P. and the case-law (e.g. Procureur Général du Québec c. Produits de l'Érable Bolduc et fils inc., J.E. 2002-1239 (C.A.)), an applicant to suspend provisional execution must show the order results from a flawed exercise of the trial judge's discretion; the judgment enjoys a presumption of validity and the applicant bears the burden of demonstrating its apparent weakness. Article 86 of the Rules of Practice provides a mechanism to seek authorization to bring proceedings; article 84 defines quarrelsome conduct.
application: Hilton J.A. declined to suspend the order: the Court had already refused, in the earlier motion, to permit Saraffian to institute proceedings elsewhere, and a chambers judge should not effectively revise a panel judgment; article 86 offered a working mechanism she had not used, and being told to write to the Chief Justice did not render the system ineffective; her prescription concerns lacked adequate detail and no draft proceedings were attached; and the trial judge's careful reasoning (reviewing the Rules of Practice, doctrine on quérulence, and the factual record) showed no apparent weakness rebutting the presumption of validity.
conclusion: The motion to suspend provisional execution was dismissed, with costs.

issue: Does s. 164 of the Criminal Code target the mailing of a periodical to subscribers, or only individualised objectionable mailings?
facts: Pink Triangle Press, publisher of The Body Politic (a newspaper serving the gay community), and three of its directors used the mails to send subscribers the December 1977–January 1978 issue, which contained the article 'Men Loving Boys Loving Men.' They were charged under s. 164; the Crown had proceeded summarily under s. 165(b) and, at the outset, was refused leave to add 'obscene' to the charge.
rule: Section 164 makes it an offence to make use of the mails to transmit or deliver anything obscene, indecent, immoral or scurrilous. Section 159 separately targets the publisher who makes, prints, publishes, distributes or circulates obscene written matter, including by mail.
application: The court reasoned that s. 159 was designed to catch the broadcast distributor of objectionable periodicals, while s. 164 was aimed at the 'sick individual' who anonymously mails obscene or scurrilous matter to shock a victim — the 'invisible exhibitionist.' Where the Crown was unwilling to charge directly under s. 159, it should not be allowed to reach the same conduct indirectly through s. 164, which would otherwise operate as little more than a post-office regulation.
conclusion: Section 164 was not aimed at the mass mailing of a periodical to subscribers, though this did not necessarily mean the conduct could not fall within its words.

issue: Did the Crown establish beyond a reasonable doubt, on the community-standard test, that the publication was indecent, immoral or scurrilous?
facts: The Crown called police, clergy, a psychiatrist and a columnist; the defence called journalists, academics, psychologists and ministers. Witnesses variously found the article distasteful, immoral, or acceptable, but no scientific public-opinion survey of the Canadian community was tendered.
rule: The community-standard approach used for obscenity (R. v. Brodie; Dominion News & Gifts v. The Queen; R. v. Prairie Schooner News) applies equally to indecency, immorality and scurrility; the objective standard of community tolerance must be proved, and admissible opinion-survey evidence requires a properly selected national 'universe.' The onus of proof beyond a reasonable doubt is on the Crown.
application: The witnesses — professors, journalists, a police officer, psychiatrists and ministers — were not representative of the community and disagreed among themselves; several addressed only the single article, not the whole issue. No competently conducted national opinion survey was offered. The court also noted the article was the third in a series, none of the others being in evidence, making an informed assessment of the whole difficult.
conclusion: The Crown failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the publication as a whole exceeded the community standard of tolerance.

issue: Applying the ordinary meaning of the terms, is the publication 'immoral,' 'indecent' or 'scurrilous'?
facts: The publication and its central article discussed pedophilia largely as reportage and advocacy for non-condemnation; the language was crude but the treatment was not lascivious, prurient or titillating. The individuals described (Simon, Peter, Don, C.J. Atkinson) may have been fictitious, as no evidence of their existence was led.
rule: 'Immoral' is undefined and, absent a statutory definition, too vague to found a criminal conviction. Indecency depends on the treatment/handling of the subject-matter, not the subject-matter itself (R. v. Close, approved in Brodie). 'Scurrilous' denotes mean or vicious, coarse or foul abuse and requires an identifiable object. The court favoured tolerance in borderline cases (Dominion News).
application: Morality is generally the stuff of ethics and religion, not legislation, and the term was too imprecise to guide conduct. On the indecency 'handling' test, the material — reportage and commentary comparable to press coverage of the Jaques case or accounts of Nazi atrocities — was not proved indecent; describing indecent acts does not make the description indecent, and intention does not determine decency (R. v. St. Clair). Scurrility failed for want of any proven object, since the persons attacked or defended might be fictitious and one cannot insult a fictitious person or find 'scurrility in the air.' The court found no clear incitement to unlawful action, only a plea for understanding to a limited subscriber audience.
conclusion: The publication was neither legally immoral, nor indecent, nor scurrilous.

issue: Does s. 9.4 of the Non-Smokers Health Protection Act, which exempts lands reserved for Indians from the smoking prohibitions, discriminate against off-reserve, non-Aboriginal proprietors contrary to s. 15(1) of the Charter?
facts: Mr. Jenkinson and his corporation operated a licensed hotel in Treherne with drinking and VLT gaming. They were convicted of failing to prevent smoking, failing to remove ashtrays and failing to post signage. Section 9.4 exempted businesses on reserve lands (competitors, essentially all Aboriginal-operated) from the same prohibitions, producing a proven detrimental financial impact on the accused.
rule: Section 15(1) of the Charter guarantees equal protection and benefit of the law without discrimination on enumerated or analogous grounds. The three-stage test from Law v. Canada, Andrews and Egan asks whether there is (1) differential treatment, (2) based on an enumerated or analogous ground, and (3) amounting to substantive discrimination that harms human dignity (Law, para. 53). Corbiere v. Canada recognized aboriginality-residence as an analogous ground.
application: The court held the Act was a law of general application despite the exemption. Although the Legislature did not intend it, the effect of s. 9.4 was to subject the accused to differential treatment in the conduct of their lawful business on the analogous ground of aboriginality-residence, analogous to Corbiere. The exemption denied off-reserve proprietors the equal economic benefit of the law while denying on-reserve persons equal health protection. On a subjective-objective basis, the interference with the right to conduct a lawful business and compete on a level playing field harmed Mr. Jenkinson's human dignity and self-worth; unlike taxation legislation, this exemption served no s. 15(2) ameliorative purpose and rested only on the Legislature's erroneous belief that it lacked jurisdiction to regulate smoking on reserves.
conclusion: Section 9.4, by exempting reserve lands, discriminated against the accused and others similarly situated contrary to s. 15(1) of the Charter.

issue: Do the accused, including the corporation Creekside, have standing to challenge the constitutional validity of the Act?
facts: The Crown argued s. 15 does not apply to a corporation and that the accused were improperly asserting equality rights on behalf of Aboriginal people.
rule: Under R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., no individual or corporation may be convicted of an offence under an unconstitutional or invalid law, regardless of whether s. 15 itself applies to the corporate accused.
application: Relying on Big M, the court held that neither Mr. Jenkinson nor Creekside could be convicted under a law that offends the Charter. The accused were not seeking relief on behalf of Aboriginal people; the effect of the Act on Aboriginal persons was merely a relevant fact in assessing whether the accused's own s. 15(1) rights were breached.
conclusion: The accused had standing to raise the invalidity of the Act and to obtain relief.

issue: Is the s. 15(1) infringement justified under s. 1, and what remedy is appropriate?
facts: The legislative purpose of the Act was to protect the health of Manitobans from second-hand smoke. No evidence explained the reserve-lands exemption beyond a mistaken jurisdictional assumption.
rule: A limit on Charter rights must be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society (s. 1). Remedial tailoring must preserve the statutory objectives within constitutional boundaries without unnecessary intrusion into the legislative sphere (Baril v. Obelnicki; Baron v. Canada).
application: There was no evidence or submission showing the discriminatory restriction was justified; the exemption in fact undermined the Act's health objectives. Rather than retroactively reading down or convicting the accused under the discriminatory provision, the court directed acquittals. Applying the Baril approach, it concluded striking s. 9.4 (as it relates to reserve lands) preserved the Act's health-protection objectives within constitutional limits, subject to a reasonable transition period for on-reserve proprietors to comply.
conclusion: The infringement was not justified under s. 1; the appeals were allowed, acquittals directed on all charges, and s. 9.4 struck out with the balance of the Act preserved.

issue: Does the defendants' third party claim for contribution or indemnity satisfy Queen's Bench Rule 29.01?
facts: The plaintiff sued the defendants (Asper and CanWest) in defamation over a letter Asper wrote replying to an earlier allegedly defamatory letter Schultz had sent to Asper. The defendants issued a third party claim against Schultz and his companies claiming contribution and indemnity, relying on Rule 29.01.
rule: Queen's Bench Rule 29.01 permits a third party claim against a non-party who (a) is or may be liable to the defendant for all or part of the plaintiff's claim, (b) is or may be liable for an independent claim arising out of a transaction or occurrence involved in or related to the main action, or (c) should be bound by determination of an issue between plaintiff and defendant.
application: The master found insufficient nexus between the plaintiff's claim and the third party claim: the facts the plaintiff relied on did not arise from any relations between the defendants and the third parties, and the alleged defamation of the defendants occurred after (and was a separate transaction from) the alleged defamation of the plaintiff. The chambers judge concurred with the master's thorough review.
conclusion: The third party claim does not satisfy Rule 29.01; the master's disposition striking it out was upheld.

issue: Can the defendants recover contribution from the third parties under s. 2(1)(c) of The Tortfeasors and Contributory Negligence Act?
facts: The 'damage' at issue is the injury to the plaintiff caused by Asper's allegedly defamatory letter. The plaintiff never sued the third parties and the pleadings disclose no cause of action she could have against them.
rule: Under s. 2(1)(c) of The Tortfeasors and Contributory Negligence Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. T90, a tortfeasor may recover contribution only from another tortfeasor 'who is, or would if sued have been, liable in respect of the same damage.' As Fleming notes, that person must have been sued and held liable, or be someone who, though not sued, would have been liable for the same damage.
application: The third parties were not held liable to the plaintiff, were not sued by her, and the pleadings suggest no cause of action she could assert against them for defamation. The third party claim merely alleges Schultz defamed Asper and that Asper's reply was made to defend himself — which could be a defence, but does not make the third parties liable for the same damage suffered by the plaintiff.
conclusion: Section 2(1)(c) has no application; contribution is not available.

issue: Have the defendants pleaded any basis for indemnity from the third parties?
facts: If the defendants are found liable, it will be because of their own blameworthy conduct in defaming the plaintiff. There is no employment, agency, contractual or warranty relationship pleaded between the defendants and the third parties regarding the plaintiff's claim.
rule: Per Fleming, indemnity (a complete shifting of loss) is allowed where a blameless party is held liable for another's tort — e.g., vicarious liability, bona fide execution of orders, fraud/misrepresentation, or contract/implied warranty (as in Allan v. Bushnell T.V. Co. Ltd., 1968 CanLII 330).
application: There is no vicarious or strict liability and no contractual liability. Unlike Allan v. Bushnell, where defamatory content was based on information the third parties had contracted to supply, there was no such relationship here. The pleadings spell out no cause of action for indemnity.
conclusion: No basis for indemnity is pleaded; indemnity is unavailable.

issue: Do the defendants have a viable independent claim under Rule 29.01(b) despite the limitation period?
facts: The defendants argued their claim against the third parties could have been brought as an independent claim for damages arising from the same transactions as the main action, since the third parties' defamation of the defendants is intrinsic to the defence.
rule: Rule 29.01(b) permits a third party claim for an independent claim for damages arising out of a transaction or occurrence involved in or related to the main action; Rule 29.01(c) applies where the third parties should be bound by determination of an issue between plaintiff and defendant.
application: The defendants could once have sued the third parties in defamation for Schultz's letter, but that claim is now statute-barred except for special damages. The only special damages available would be contribution or indemnity on the plaintiff's claim, which the court held are unavailable. Given those conclusions, Rule 29.01(c) also has no possible application.
conclusion: The defendants no longer have an independent claim; Rules 29.01(b) and (c) cannot save the third party claim.

issue: Was the Independent Review of the Motherisk laboratory admissible on the certification motion, and for what purpose?
facts: The Ontario government appointed the Hon. Susan Lang to conduct an Independent Review, which concluded the laboratory's hair-test results were unreliable but expressly disclaimed any finding of civil liability. The plaintiff sought to rely on it; the defendants argued it was inadmissible hearsay produced by a non-adjudicative process.
rule: Evidence on a certification motion must meet the usual admissibility standards (Robb Estate v. St. Joseph's Health Care Centre). Out-of-court statements are admissible where non-contentious, where not hearsay for the issue to be decided, or under recognized exceptions such as admissions by a party (R. v. Evans) or business records (Ares v. Venner; Ontario Evidence Act, s. 35).
application: The court found both sides overstated their positions. Many facts in the Review were common ground, drawn from the defendants' own documents, or admissible under party-admission or business-record exceptions, and some were admissible merely for having been said. The Review could not prove the merits of the claim nor ground any issue estoppel.
conclusion: The Independent Review was admitted for the limited purposes of the certification motion; it was not necessary to decide whether the public-document or principled hearsay exceptions applied.

issue: Did the proposed systemic-negligence class action satisfy the preferable procedure criterion under s. 5 of the Class Proceedings Act, 1992?
facts: Ms. R.G. alleged all 18,463 laboratory tests were unreliable and sought $200 million in negligence damages plus $250 million in punitive damages for a class defined by positive test results, plus a family law class. Compensable harm (loss of parental rights, distress) depended on each individual's test being not merely unreliable but also false and adversely influential to the outcome of that person's court proceedings; 328 plaintiffs were already pursuing individual or joinder actions.
rule: Preferability (AIC Limited v. Fischer) is assessed through judicial economy, behaviour modification and access to justice, in both its procedural and substantive dimensions, and requires a fair, efficient and manageable procedure preferable to alternatives such as individual actions or joinder. Where individual issues overwhelm the common issues the action fails the criterion (Dennis v. Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corp.); by contrast systemic-negligence classes are viable where the common wrong meaningfully advances every claim (Rumley v. British Columbia; Gay v. New Brunswick).
application: The court found a 'design defect': proving class-wide unreliability would yield little or no compensation, because damages flowed only from an individual test being false and adversely influential — matters requiring complex individual trials on liability, causation, apportionment and defences. This mirrored Dennis and was distinguishable from Rumley and Gay, where the common finding substantially advanced each claim. Individual trials were inevitable and would swamp any advantage from a common issues trial; ss. 12 and 25 could not fairly compress them without sacrificing the defendants' due-process rights on a multi-million-dollar claim. Individual actions (which could also join other defendants) were the more efficient route.
conclusion: The preferable procedure criterion was not satisfied.

issue: Did the proposed common issues satisfy the common issues criterion, including aggregate and punitive damages?
facts: Six common issues were proposed: breach of duty, Family Law Act entitlement, aggregate damages, quantum, punitive damages entitlement, and punitive quantum.
rule: A common issue must be a substantial ingredient of each class member's claim whose resolution avoids duplication (Hollick; Western Canadian Shopping Centres v. Dutton). Aggregate damages under s. 24(1) require an antecedent finding of liability with no remaining questions other than assessment (Pro-Sys v. Microsoft). Punitive damages alone cannot justify certification.
application: Common Issue No. 1 (breach of duty) was technically certifiable but did not avoid duplication or extrapolate to each member, and the duty of care of the individual defendants appeared individual, not common. Aggregate damages failed because liability and damages required individual trials and there was no base amount common to the class. Punitive damages were peripheral, could not alone support certification, and were realistically remote against a children's hospital funded by taxpayers and philanthropists.
conclusion: None of the six proposed common issues satisfied the common issues criterion.

issue: Did the plaintiff satisfy the representative plaintiff criterion through a workable litigation plan?
facts: Ms. R.G.'s plan proposed, after a common issues trial, an 'Impact Interview' panel and a two-hour 'Damages Hearing' before a referee, limited to a joint report and three-page expert statements, with the defendants given no meaningful disclosure or right to be heard on causation.
rule: The representative plaintiff must produce a litigation plan that corresponds to the complexity of the case and addresses how individual issues remaining after the common issues trial will be resolved (Carom v. Bre-X; Caputo v. Imperial Tobacco). Sections 12 and 25 of the CPA are not meant to sacrifice a defendant's due-process rights.
application: Ms. R.G. was personally qualified, but the litigation plan was unfeasible and procedurally unfair: it assigned the most difficult forensic work — causation and damages — to a truncated individual phase that aborted the defendants' rights to defend a $450 million claim. Unlike Lundy v. VIA Rail (small class, admitted liability, quantum-only dispute), this case could not be managed under ss. 12 and 25.
conclusion: The representative plaintiff criterion was not satisfied.

issue: Does the liquidator act in the hospital's own right for prescription purposes, or as an independent 'interested person'?
facts: Raymond Chabot inc. was appointed liquidator of the Hôpital général de Lachine in October 1996. It argued it exercised a personal right as a 'personne intéressée' under art. 265 LSSSS, so prescription ran only from its appointment; alternatively that prescription ran only from discovery of the illegality.
rule: Under arts. 451.11 and 451.12 LSSSS the liquidator is seised of the institution's property and acts as administrator of the property of others with full administration; art. 360 C.c.Q. and the winding-up jurisprudence (Coopérants (Les) c. Dubois, 1996 CanLII 242 (SCC); McCarter v. York County Loan Co.) treat the liquidator as the statutory representative of the entity, not a third party. The 'interested person' in arts. 264 and 265 LSSSS is a third party such as the regional board, the Minister, or a s. 139 member.
application: The Court held the liquidator is neither the Minister's nor the regional board's representative but the person designated to exercise the hospital's rights and settle its liabilities. Its powers are those of the hospital, not those of an independent interested person, so prescription applicable to the hospital continued to run and no new period began on appointment.
conclusion: The liquidator exercises the hospital's rights; the hospital's prescription applies, not a fresh one from appointment.

issue: Were the transfers illegal and null for lack of prior regional board authorization?
facts: In June 1995 the hospital transferred its ~$2.7M endowment fund to the Foundation, and in February 1996 reimbursed $65,426 in donations, without any proven prior authorization from the regional board. The Foundation invoked the exception in art. 262.1 LSSSS.
rule: Art. 265(1)(4) LSSSS bars a public institution from gratuitously disposing of property except with prior authorization of the regional board; art. 264 LSSSS renders contracts made without required authorization absolutely null (art. 1417 C.c.Q.). The art. 262.1 exception applies only to corporations designated by the Minister under art. 139 LSSSS.
application: No immovable had been alienated, so art. 262.1 para. 2 did not apply. The para. 4 exception for pre-1992 member-administered funds applies only to art. 139-designated corporations; interpreting 'la corporation' in light of parliamentary debates and the surrounding provisions, and given that the hospital never obtained art. 139 designation, the exception was unavailable. Prior regional board authorization was therefore required and absent. As to the reimbursement, the trial judge preferred the regional board official's testimony that no authorization had been given, an unassailable finding.
conclusion: Both transfers were illegal and absolutely null for lack of the mandatory prior authorization.

issue: What prescription period governs a public-law action in nullity, and had it expired?
facts: The transfers occurred on 29 June 1995 and 8 February 1996; the action was instituted 8 October 1999. The trial judge applied the three-year period of art. 2925 C.c.Q. and dismissed the action as prescribed.
rule: A public-law direct action in nullity does not enforce a personal right; historically it prescribed by 30 years (art. 2242 C.c.B.-C.) and now by 10 years under art. 2922 C.c.Q. (Mignault; Côté c. Corporation County of Drummond; Comité des citoyens de la Presqu'île-Lanaudière c. Québec). The Superior Court retains a discretion to refuse relief for excessive delay.
application: The Court held the liquidator's recourse, though imprecisely drafted, was an action in nullity of the transfers for illegality with restitution as an accessory conclusion (art. 1422 C.c.Q.). It did not enforce a personal right — it could equally have been brought by the Minister, regional board, or any interested person — so the ten-year period, not the three-year period of art. 2925 C.c.Q., applied. The action was thus timely. The delay after appointment was explained by discussions and the Foundation's 1996 undertaking not to use the funds, causing no prejudice, so no discretionary refusal was warranted.
conclusion: The ten-year period applied; the action was not prescribed and had to be allowed, with restitution ordered.

issue: Did the Foundation prove the 1980s donations were conditional and returnable?
facts: By cross-appeal the Foundation claimed reimbursement of donations allegedly made in the 1980s specifically for renovation of the hospital's Dawes wing, a purpose rendered impossible by closure.
rule: To overturn factual findings an appellant must point to a palpable and overriding error (H.L. c. Canada (Procureur général), 2005 SCC 25). Under art. 134 of the former Act, contributions for special purposes had to be placed in a special fund.
application: The Court found no reviewable error: no contemporaneous writing evidenced a conditional purpose, the funds were not segregated into a special fund, some donations in the period were unrelated to the Dawes project, and the Foundation's own 1996 letter tied the gifts generally to 'projects related to its immovables'. The trial judge's conclusion that the alleged condition was 'revisionist history' stood.
conclusion: The Foundation failed to establish conditional donations; the cross-appeal was dismissed.
