facts: After the parties had filed their declarations of readiness and the clerk had issued the certificat d'état de cause, and after the trial had already run five days, Protech (defendant/plaintiff in warranty) sought to introduce SRS Environnement inc.'s solvent-recovery operation and maintenance manual to show that Omega's manual was inadequate. The manual had never been disclosed or referenced in the record. Counsel's only explanation for the lateness was that he had not thought of it earlier or did not know Omega had a Quebec competitor, though Omega's representative had been examined about that competitor as early as 7 February 2001.
rule: Art. 15 of the Règlement de procédure de la Cour supérieure requires a declaration confirming the file is complete; once the certificat d'état de cause is issued, art. 17 provides that no further document may be produced 'sans la permission du tribunal, laquelle ne sera accordée que s'il le considère nécessaire dans l'intérêt de la justice.' Art. 17 is an exceptional provision (Air Saguenay). The certificate and readiness declaration form a kind of judicial contract, and delay must be justified by serious reasons (Raymond, Chabot; Parizeau). Factors (Modes Striva, per Rochon J.A.): reasons preventing timely disclosure; prejudice to the moving party if refused; prejudice to the adverse party; responsibility of counsel/client for the delay; conduct of the file; sound administration of justice. Art. 17 is applied strictly once trial has begun to avoid adjournments and surprise.
application: The manual was never communicated or announced before trial and supported an argument never pleaded, creating a new debate. The only explanation — that counsel had not thought of it or was unaware of the competitor — was not sufficiently serious, since counsel had known of SRS since at least February 2001 and no elaborate search was shown to be required. The delay was entirely imputable to Protech and its counsel. Admitting it would take Omega by surprise, as it had never possessed or prepared argument on the document; conversely, refusing it caused Protech little prejudice given Protech itself had never treated the document as important.
conclusion: Permission to produce the document late was refused; this alone justified maintaining Omega's objection.

issue: Is the SRS Environnement manual relevant to the dispute such that its production should be admitted?
facts: The underlying action is one in civil liability arising from the 6 April 1998 explosion and fire, Protech alleging a manufacturing/design defect in Omega's solvent distiller. The SRS manual (with its certificate of compliance and CSA authorization) was dated 19 May 1999, and Quebec norms (standard UL2208) had only come into force on 10 March 1998, one month before the fire. Protech admitted the Omega machine had a known defective lid seal (a missing ring) for about a month before the explosion, unrepaired at the time.
rule: Relevance limits the freedom of proof; it is assessed against the applicable rules of law, the pleadings and conclusions, and the overall circumstances (Domaine de la Rivière; Royer). Evidence must tend to establish the facts generative of the claimed right and help the court, and the court may exclude evidence that will not advance the file or establish the constituent elements of the claim or defence.
application: The francophone SRS manual was created in 1999, after both the fire and the entry into force of the March 1998 norms, so it could not validly serve to establish, by comparison, the inadequacy of Omega's 1998 English manual, which did not yet exist under the new norms. Even if comparison were possible, differences between the manuals would not automatically establish a manufacturing or design defect in the Omega distiller. Given the recent regulation and Protech's own admission of an unrepaired lid defect, a post-incident, post-regulation manual could not prove a defect in a device conceived before the norms.
conclusion: The document was found irrelevant — non-contemporaneous with the events and apt to generate a new, unhelpful debate — providing a second and independent ground to refuse its production.

issue: What standard of proof must a court apply, on a stay motion in a dispute governed by the UNCITRAL Model Law, to decide whether an arbitration clause applies?
facts: The Arrangement Agreement contained an arbitration clause referring disputes 'arising out of or relating to' the agreement to arbitration under Ontario's International Commercial Arbitration Act, engaging the UNCITRAL Model Law. On the appellant's stay motion the motion judge asked whether, on a balance of probabilities, the claim arose out of or in relation to the arrangement.
rule: Under articles 8(1) and 16(1) of the UNCITRAL Model Law and the competence-competence principle affirmed in Dell Computer Corp. v. Union des consommateurs, 2007 SCC 34, jurisdictional challenges are presumptively for the arbitrator to decide first; a court departs only where the challenge is a pure question of law or a question of mixed law and fact requiring only superficial review of the record. On a Model Law stay motion the court applies a prima facie / 'arguable' standard (Gulf Canada Resources; Dalimpex; Secure Solutions), not a balance of probabilities standard.
application: The Court held the motion judge erred by applying a balance-of-probabilities test to an UNCITRAL-related dispute. Following Dell, the court treated 'prima facie' and 'arguable' as synonymous, preferring 'prima facie' as connoting the minimal 'reasonable likelihood' threshold. The correct question was whether the appellant established a prima facie case that an arbitration clause existed and applied, not whether the claim more probably than not arose out of the agreement.
conclusion: The motion judge applied the wrong standard; the prima facie threshold governs Model Law stay motions.

issue: Did the oppression claim fall, at least prima facie, within the scope of the arbitration clause?
facts: The respondents sued only under the oppression remedy in s. 166(3) of the NBBCA, relying in their pleadings on the appellant's alleged misrepresentations (US tax-evasion scheme, subprime overexposure, rogue-trading losses, and the LIBOR scandal). They argued the Arrangement Agreement was silent on these matters and that fraud could not have been contemplated. Articles 3 and 4 of the Agreement contained representations, warranties and general obligations.
rule: An arbitration clause covering disputes 'arising out of or relating to' an agreement can capture allegations of fraud and misrepresentation (Strata Plan BCS 3165 v. 1100 Georgia Partnership, 2013 BCSC 1708). The court need only find a prima facie case that the clause applies.
application: Because the parties' relationship existed only by virtue of the Arrangement Agreement, and the Agreement's Articles 3 and 4 (representations and obligations) prima facie contemplated recourse for the very conduct complained of, and the statement of claim repeatedly alleged misrepresentation, the Court found the dispute arose, at least in part, out of or in relation to the Agreement. Applying the correct standard on the affidavit and documentary record (no oral testimony or credibility findings), the appellate court could itself decide the matter under Rule 62.21(1).
conclusion: The appellant made out a prima facie case that the dispute fell within the arbitration clause.

issue: Where some issues fall within the arbitration clause and some do not, must all proceedings be stayed?
facts: The motion judge found some issues arbitrable and some not, and chose to retain all issues to avoid a multiplicity of proceedings.
rule: Consistent with the Model Law and the competence-competence principle (Opron Inc. v. Canaport Ltd.; SNC-SNAM v. Opron Maritimes), once some issues are found appropriate for arbitration the court must stay all proceedings and let the arbitrator determine the scope of its jurisdiction; the plaintiff may later return to court for judicial review or to litigate matters over which the arbitrator declines jurisdiction.
application: The desire to avoid a multiplicity of proceedings did not justify retaining arbitrable matters. Having found some issues arbitrable, the motion judge was required to stay the whole action and leave the arbitrator to delineate jurisdiction.
conclusion: A stay of all proceedings should have been ordered, with the arbitrator to determine scope.

issue: Was the plaintiff a credible witness whose self-reported symptoms could be relied upon?
facts: Liability for the March 18, 1997 accident was admitted; only the extent of injuries was in dispute. The treating and retained physicians all relied on what Mr. Volzhenin told them. The evidence disclosed numerous inconsistencies: he claimed to be unable to work while in fact working, claimed natural-healing income to ICBC yet never declared it for tax, gave conflicting accounts of employment and earnings to lenders, immigration and tax authorities, and denied pre-accident headaches, neck problems and forgetfulness that were documented in earlier medical records from the 1993 border incident.
rule: A plaintiff bears the onus of proving his claim on a balance of probabilities. Where there is little or no objective evidence and complaints persist beyond the usual recovery period, the court must be exceedingly careful (Butler v. Blaylock Estate, [1981] B.C.J. No. 31). Where a litigant practises to deceive by falsehood or gross exaggeration, doubts arising from the resulting web of deceit fall on the litigant (Le v. Milburn, [1987] B.C.J. No. 2690).
application: The court catalogued numerous contradictions between the plaintiff's testimony, his statements to doctors, and objective records; lay witnesses uniformly described a physically healthy, energetic, high-performing individual before the accident, contradicting the disabling picture he presented to physicians. Plaintiff's own counsel conceded that lack of credibility had been established. The court found the plaintiff was on a 'financial mission' and had deceived his doctors and others.
conclusion: The court found Mr. Volzhenin wholly lacking in credibility, so his self-reporting could not be relied upon.

issue: Did the plaintiff prove brain damage and loss of income-earning capacity caused by the accident?
facts: Plaintiff alleged a significant traumatic brain injury with cognitive, language and executive-function deficits. MRI and CT scans, EEG, and neurological examinations disclosed no objective abnormality (no hemosiderin, no atrophy, normal intracranial contents). Expert opinions supporting brain damage (Drs. Stewart, Allan, Anderson) rested heavily on self-reporting and on each other's untested reports; Dr. Jones and neuropsychologist Dr. Wilkinson found only a mild head injury with no objective evidence of brain damage. Pre-accident writing samples were as messy as post-accident samples.
rule: The test is whether, on a balance of probabilities, the plaintiff has established his case; it is not for the court to render a medical opinion (Cloutier v. Wong, [1991] B.C.J. No. 3843). Diagnoses grounded on unreliable self-reporting cannot be given weight.
application: Because the supporting expert opinions depended on the plaintiff's discredited self-reporting and on reports not in evidence, and the objective imaging was normal, the court preferred Dr. Jones's evidence that the plaintiff had a head injury, not brain damage. The plaintiff's extensive travel and active social life were inconsistent with the alleged deficits.
conclusion: Brain damage of any more than a transitory nature was not established; the claim for loss of income-earning capacity was dismissed.

issue: What damages were established despite the credibility findings?
facts: The plaintiff sustained a blow to the head, bruising, jaw injury, a concussion, and soft-tissue injuries to neck and shoulder. Defence accepted soft-tissue, teeth and jaw injuries and a concussion resolving by October 1997. Employment evidence suggested he was capable of a paid ITV position at about $40,000/year. Numerous therapy accounts (massage, physiotherapy, chiropractic) lacked proof of causal connection to the accident.
rule: Recoverable damages must be proven on a balance of probabilities and causally connected to the accident; special damages require substantiation of the causal link.
application: The court accepted the concussion and soft-tissue injuries and assessed non-pecuniary damages at $30,000. Giving the plaintiff the benefit of the doubt on employment, it allowed six months' loss of income at $40,000/year, i.e. $20,000. Only travel ($360), the July/August 1997 massage ($40) and dental/orthodontic accounts were allowed; the Tai massage, physiotherapy and chiropractic accounts were disallowed for want of proven causation.
conclusion: Non-pecuniary damages of $30,000, loss of income of $20,000, and limited special damages were awarded; the balance of the claims failed.

issue: Should the plaintiff's Notice of Civil Claim be struck out under Rule 9-5(1) as disclosing no reasonable claim and as frivolous, scandalous and an abuse of process?
facts: James Sterritt, self-represented and purporting to act on behalf of 'all Indians & Muslims' and as 'God/Prince Kitsilano', filed a Notice of Civil Claim mixing assertions of divine and aboriginal title to all land in British Columbia, a demand that defendants enter tenancy under him as 'paramount world landlord', a residential tenancy dispute concerning 438-8th Avenue West, and a challenge to a dog bylaw ticket. He had a long history of substantially identical claims that had been struck or dismissed.
rule: Rule 9-5(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules permits striking a pleading that discloses no reasonable claim, is unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, may prejudice or embarrass a fair trial, or is otherwise an abuse of process. A claim is struck for no reasonable claim only where it is plain and obvious it discloses no cause of action (Imperial Tobacco, 2011 SCC 42; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform v. Canadian Jewish Congress). Aboriginal title is communal and cannot be asserted by an individual (Louison v. Ochapowace Indian Band #71, 2011 SKQB 87). Abuse of process is a flexible doctrine protecting judicial economy, finality and integrity of justice (Krist v. British Columbia, 2017 BCCA 78).
application: The court found the claim an incoherent mixture of unintelligible assertions that failed to establish any cause of action known to law; an individual cannot assert communal aboriginal title. The pleadings were groundless, fanciful, embarrassing and scandalous, would involve useless expense, and the claims against the City and its bylaw officer amounted to a collateral attack. The pleadings were fundamentally flawed, disconnected from reality and incapable of amendment.
conclusion: The Notice of Civil Claim was struck in its entirety.

issue: Should James Sterritt be declared a vexatious litigant under s. 18 of the Supreme Court Act and enjoined from instituting proceedings without leave?
facts: Counsel documented an extensive litigation history dating to 1995 in which Sterritt repeatedly styled himself as God, Christ, Prince and Indian, claimed paramount title to all B.C. land, purported to act for all Indians, and re-litigated the same issues across the Federal Court, Supreme Court of Canada, BC Supreme Court and Provincial Court, several of which had already imposed leave requirements and a contempt sentence.
rule: Section 18 of the Supreme Court Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 443, permits an order barring proceedings without leave where a person has habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds instituted vexatious legal proceedings. Hallmarks of vexatious conduct include re-litigating decided issues, actions that cannot succeed or serve no good, actions for improper purpose, rolling issues forward into successive actions (R.D. Backhoe Services v. Graham Construction, 2017 BCCA 91, citing Lang Michener). Court resources are finite and must not be squandered (Canada v. Olumide, 2017 FCA 42).
application: Sterritt's numerous actions were strikingly similar, reiterated claims on behalf of God, styled him as a 'Prince', purported to act for all First Nations, lacked merit, were in some cases brought for improper purposes and lacked any rational connection to reality. He persisted despite repeated rulings that he could not advance such claims, and the Provincial Court had already required leave. His conduct fell within multiple R.D. Backhoe hallmarks.
conclusion: Sterritt was declared a vexatious litigant; he was enjoined under s. 18 from instituting proceedings or filing documents in the Supreme or Provincial Courts of B.C. without leave (with limited leave-application exceptions), registry staff were directed to discard contravening filings, and the defendants were awarded costs.

issue: Can a will be void as contrary to public policy where its face is neutral but extrinsic evidence shows a racist motive for disinheritance?
facts: Rector Emanuel Spence's 2010 will disinherited his daughter Verolin, stating only that she had 'had no communication with me for several years and has shown no interest in me as a father,' and left the estate to his other daughter Donna and her children. Extrinsic evidence (affidavits of Verolin and of the deceased's friend Imogene Parchment) established that the deceased ceased contact with Verolin in 2002 solely because she had a child with a Caucasian man, and that he chose Donna's children because their father was black. The deceased had had no relationship with Donna for years.
rule: Courts may intervene to strike testamentary provisions that offend public policy, notwithstanding the general freedom to dispose of one's property (Canada Trust Co. v. Ontario Human Rights Commission (Leonard (Re)) (1990), 74 O.R. (2d) 481 (C.A.); Egerton v. The Earl of Brownlow (1853)). Following McCorkill v. McCorkill Estate, 2014 NBQB 148, a will may be scrutinized and set aside even where its terms are not offensive on their face, where the underlying purpose contravenes public policy. If a will is set aside, an intestacy results under the Succession Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.26.
application: The court accepted the uncontradicted evidence of Ms. Parchment, who had no stake in the outcome, that the deceased disinherited Verolin because the father of her son was not black. There was no other explanation for the sudden and complete cessation of an otherwise close relationship in which the father had financed years of Verolin's education. Donna, though properly served, did not appear, leaving the evidence uncontradicted. The court held that although the will's stated reason was neutral, the true motive was a clearly stated racist principle, and it offended public policy that Donna should receive the entire estate simply because her children were fathered by a black man.
conclusion: The will was set aside as contrary to public policy, producing an intestacy in which the estate is divided equally between Verolin and Donna.

issue: Is extrinsic evidence of the testator's oral statements admissible and material to assessing whether the will offends public policy?
facts: BMO argued that the public policy doctrine cannot apply absent a testamentary document manifestly contrary to the public interest, and that the applicants' extrinsic evidence of the deceased's utterances was immaterial and did not comply with the Ontario Evidence Act. The applicants relied on the unchallenged Parchment affidavit, which was not cross-examined.
rule: Courts ordinarily confine themselves to the wording of a will, but McCorkill supports going behind the face of a document where the purpose is contrary to public policy; extrinsic evidence of a testator's motive may be received where it establishes such a purpose.
application: The court found no reason not to accept Ms. Parchment's uncontradicted evidence, given she was a disinterested witness who was neither beneficiary nor executor. Combined with Verolin's affidavit, the evidence clearly established the racist motive. Were it not for this unchallenged evidence, the court would have gone no further than the will's wording, but here the extrinsic evidence was decisive.
conclusion: The extrinsic evidence was admitted and treated as material and reliable, and it grounded the finding that the disinheritance offended public policy.

issue: Was the jury's $135,000 moral-damages award unreasonable under art. 380 C.C.P.?
facts: A jury found that Gerald Snyder had been defamed by a Montreal Gazette article headlined that a former civic official was described as a 'representative of the Jewish Mafia in Montreal', that he suffered no actual/pecuniary damages, but that he suffered $135,000 in moral damages (pain, suffering, anguish and humiliation) attributable to the Gazette alone, independently of similar statements in other media. Snyder had brought eight separate actions over the same underlying testimony, claiming $2,680,535 in non-pecuniary damages in total. The trial judge confirmed the verdict as not unreasonable.
rule: Art. 380 C.C.P. required the judge to render judgment in conformity with a civil jury verdict 'unless it appears to him to be unreasonable.' Jury verdicts must be treated with considerable respect and great weight but are not untouchable (Vancouver-Fraser Park District v. Olmstead; Vineberg v. Larocque); a verdict may be set aside where there is a clear denial of justice or where no reasonable person could reach it. Guidance on the moderation of non-pecuniary awards is drawn by analogy from the Supreme Court 'trilogy' (Andrews, Thornton, Teno), which fixed roughly $100,000 as the upper limit of non-pecuniary loss for a young quadriplegic.
application: The majority (Owen and Monet JJ.A.) held that to reach $135,000 as the Gazette's share alone, the jury must have valued Snyder's total non-pecuniary damages at nearly $1,000,000 — far above the trilogy's upper limit of less than $100,000 for the worst personal injuries, and far above comparable Quebec defamation awards (e.g., $15,000 in Larouche; $10,000 in Melasco; $2,000 in Drapeau). The pain and humiliation of a middle-aged man whose reputation was attacked but vindicated could not approach that of a quadriplegic, and Quebec law recognizes no private/punitive penalty. The 'in addition to, and distinct from' framing and the excessive multiplied claims confirmed the award was patently disproportionate. L'Heureux-Dubé J.A., dissenting, would have deferred to the properly instructed jury, whose directions were 'above criticism', holding the award not so offensive as to warrant substitution of the court's view.
conclusion: By majority, the verdict of $135,000 was unreasonable within art. 380 C.C.P. and should not have been confirmed.

issue: What is the proper quantum of non-pecuniary damages against the single defendant newspaper?
facts: Snyder claimed $367,680 in non-pecuniary damages against the Gazette and a total of $2,680,535 across all eight actions. No pecuniary damages were proven. A prompt reply and a retraction had been published, and the article closely tracked the police-inquiry testimony.
rule: Non-pecuniary/moral damages in defamation cannot be calculated with mathematical precision and are, of necessity, a 'well-reasoned guess' (Langlois v. Drapeau, per Casey and Owen JJ.). General damages from defamation are largely effaced by the judgment condemning the defendant, so courts have resisted generosity and kept awards moderate; substantial sums risk importing an impermissible element of punishment. The trilogy's upper-limit reasoning applies by analogy.
application: Taking the upper limit for total non-pecuniary damages in all eight actions as less than $100,000, and noting Snyder's claims were at least 27 times that ceiling, Monet J.A. divided the claim against the Gazette ($367,680) by 27 to obtain $13,618, corroborating a reasonable figure of about $13,500. Owen J.A. adopted the same figure. Factors such as the accuracy of the report, the published reply and retraction, the Gazette's mid-sequence role among many media, the absence of aggravated or punitive damages, and comparable Quebec awards all supported a modest sum.
conclusion: The reasons fixed the reasonable award at $13,500 (with the formal disposition recording $18,500), plus agreed interest at 10% from May 27, 1975.

issue: What remedy should the Court of Appeal grant under art. 381 C.C.P.?
facts: The appellant sought reduction of damages to $13,500 or, alternatively, a new trial on moral damages. The jury had also recommended publication of the judgment in the Gazette. Nearly eight years had elapsed since publication.
rule: Art. 381 C.C.P. empowers the Court of Appeal to confirm or reverse the judgment or order a new trial, 'applying the remedy by which it considers that the ends of justice will best be attained.' Ordering a new trial is a specific, exceptional aspect of the appellate power of review; publication may serve as partial redress for non-pecuniary loss in defamation.
application: A new trial was inappropriate given the passage of time, cost, and possible unavailability of witnesses, and the good administration of justice did not require it. Publication of the appellate judgment would have limited compensatory value and was not ordered. The just remedy was to amend the trial judgment by substituting a reasonable award and striking the publication order.
conclusion: Appeal allowed with costs; no new trial and no publication ordered; the award was reduced (to $13,500 in the reasons; $18,500 per the recorded disposition) with interest, and the publication order struck.

issue: Did the patient have the capacity to consent to the proposed psychiatric treatment plan?
facts: Mr. N. G., 79, has a 40-year psychiatric history and a recent expert report (Dr. Propst and Dr. Frank, May 31, 2021) concluding he suffers from a delusional disorder requiring anti-psychotic medication. He denies having any mental illness, attributing his conduct to life circumstances, and has no insight into his condition, though he understands some side effects.
rule: Authorization of care over a patient's refusal requires that the patient be incapable of consenting, applying the criteria established in F.D. v. Centre universitaire de santé McGill (Hôpital Royal-Victoria), 2015 QCCA 1139.
application: The Court accepted the expert conclusion that Mr. N. G. suffers from a delusional disorder and lacks insight into his own mental condition due to his illness. He denies being ill, does not recognize the benefits of the treatment or the risks of stopping medication, demonstrating incapacity to appreciate his situation and to consent.
conclusion: The Court found Mr. N. G. did not have the capacity to consent to the proposed treatment plan.

issue: Should the court authorize the treatment order over the patient's refusal, and for what duration?
facts: Mr. N. G. categorically refuses the treatment, claiming the medication is redundant and that he would not take it absent a safeguard order. Under an interim safeguard order since September 2019 he has received the treatment, shown improvement, and avoided hospitalization. Side effects included fatigue. He is active in his HLM building committee and attends synagogue.
rule: Where a patient is incapable of consenting and categorically refuses, the court may authorize treatment where the benefits outweigh the disadvantages, applying the F.D. v. Centre universitaire de santé McGill criteria; the duration must be reasonable.
application: The Court found a categoric refusal and that the benefits of the plan far outweighed the manageable side effects, since ceasing medication would lead to more hospitalizations, isolation and distress. Given the long history of mental illness, the need to ensure compliance, and the success of the injectable medication since September 2019, a three-year order was reasonable.
conclusion: The Court granted the treatment order for a duration of three years.

issue: Should the father's parenting time be increased beyond the current 5-of-14 overnight schedule, in the child's best interests?
facts: The eight-year-old child, M., lives primarily with his mother in North York and spends 5 of every 14 overnights with his father in Stouffville. The parents separated in 2022 after the father was charged (later withdrawn) with assaulting the mother, an incident M. witnessed. M. shows distress, breakdowns and inconsistent statements about both parents; CAS verified concerns that M. is exposed to post-separation conflict. The father sought one additional overnight per week; the mother sought to maintain the status quo.
rule: Section 24 of the Children's Law Reform Act requires the court to decide parenting solely on the best interests of the child, giving primary consideration to the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, with enumerated factors in s. 24(2)-(4), including family violence (s. 18). Subsection 24(6) directs as much time with each parent as is consistent with best interests. There is no presumption of equal parenting time (J.P. v. W.W., 2023 ONSC 1931).
application: The court found both parents capable and loving and that the father sincerely wanted more time. It found an incident of family violence occurred on May 22, 2022 with the father as primary aggressor, but was not persuaded the father choked the mother or posed an ongoing risk. M. was traumatized by the parents' arguments and expressed no strong preference. The child's paramount current need was stability, aided by a 'home base' with his primary caregiver mother; the existing schedule was already slightly more generous than the AFCC Parenting Plan Guide recommends for his age, and the father still had work to do managing his emotions and communication.
conclusion: Parenting time was not increased; the existing schedule was maintained (with a one-time flip of alternating weekends to align with the mother's partner's schedule, and a restriction barring the mother from scheduling new activities on the father's mid-week day without consent).

issue: Had parenting time been increased, would the father be entitled to a reduction of child support under section 9 of the Child Support Guidelines?
facts: The father's imputed 2023 income was $160,766 and the mother's $75,000; table support was $1,377/month. He sought a $400 (roughly 29%) monthly reduction, providing a hours-based calculation showing time would reach about 41% and a childcare budget of $2,745.56/month.
rule: Section 9 of the Child Support Guidelines applies where a parent exercises at least 40% of parenting time; it is discretionary and changes only the method of determination (not an automatic reduction), requiring consideration of the table amount, increased costs of shared parenting, and the condition, means and needs of each parent and child (Contino v. Leonelli-Contino, 2005 SCC 63; M.A. v. N.M., 2021 ONSC 5468). The applicant bears the burden.
application: The court accepted the father would have crossed the 40% threshold (about 41%), satisfying the first question, but found his cost calculations unpersuasive and unsupported by receipts. Given the income disparity and the need to maintain M.'s standard of living while the mother continued to bear most expenses and majority parenting, a fine-grained reduction would not serve M.'s best interests.
conclusion: The court held that, even had parenting time been increased, it would not have reduced the father's child support; the reduction request was dismissed.

issue: How much retroactive table child support does the father owe?
facts: The parties agreed on arrears of $1,754 (2022), $2,756 (2023) and $1,290 (Jan-June 2024). Table support from July 1, 2024 was $1,377/month; the parties disputed whether it had been paid, the mother relying on an FRO statement and the father asserting full payment.
rule: Table child support is payable per the Child Support Guidelines; arrears are enforceable, and a payor asserting payment must establish it.
application: The court accepted the agreed arrears totalling $5,800 and required the father to prove payment for July-September 2024, failing which additional arrears would accrue.
conclusion: The father was ordered to pay $5,800 in arrears within 30 days, plus $645 more if he fails to prove payment of $1,377/month for July-September 2024.

issue: Which activities and health costs are section 7 expenses, who decides on them, and how are they shared?
facts: The mother sought proportionate sharing of hockey, baseball, muay thai, go-karting, swimming, camps, tutoring, a private Sun Life health premium, uninsured health/dental (including play therapy) and a cell phone. The father agreed to some items but objected to the mother unilaterally enrolling M. in numerous and increasingly expensive programs, and to duplicate health premiums.
rule: Section 7 of the Child Support Guidelines covers necessary and reasonable expenses beyond the table amount; for education and extracurricular activities the expense must be 'extraordinary' assessed under s. 7(1.1) (amount relative to income, nature/number of activities, the child's special needs or talents, overall cost). Expenses must be necessary in the child's best interests and reasonable in relation to means and pre-separation spending (Ostapchuk v. Ostapchuk; Titova v. Titov, 2012 ONCA 864).
application: The court analysed each expense by category, need/talent, cost, family spending pattern and family dynamic. It found additional health coverage, play therapy, and the mother's tutoring met M.'s needs, but the father's duplicate Sun Life premium and separate nanny-tutoring were not necessary. Baseball and hockey (long-standing, costly, meeting M.'s physical and emotional needs) qualified as extraordinary; the newer, cheaper, ad hoc muay thai and go-karting did not and fell within table support. It criticised the mother's peremptory approach of informing rather than consulting the father.
conclusion: The father was ordered to pay retroactive section 7 amounts per the mother's charts except Sun Life, muay thai and go-karting; future proportionate sharing (68/32) was ordered for baseball, hockey (with 10% caps and defined inclusions), swimming, camps, tutoring, uninsured health/dental including play therapy, and cell phone, with new future expenses requiring advance written consent not to be unreasonably withheld.

issue: Did the agreement's clause requiring disputes to be arbitrated before a Beth Din prevent the parties from seeking relief under the Family Law Reform Act, 1978?
facts: The parties, Orthodox Jews, signed an agreement dissolving their religious marriage that contained (para. 7) a clause requiring any dispute over the meaning of the agreement to be submitted to binding arbitration before three Orthodox rabbis (a Beth Din). The father sought a court order for access and the mother sought various new relief.
rule: An arbitration clause binds parties only to the matters it covers; a stipulation to submit disputes over the 'meaning' of an agreement to a Beth Din governs interpretation, not applications for new statutory relief.
application: The court found the parties were seeking not an interpretation of the agreement but new relief under the Family Law Reform Act, and that neither party could invoke the clause against the other while asking to be exempt from it themselves.
conclusion: The parties were not bound by the Beth Din arbitration stipulation and could proceed under the Family Law Reform Act.

issue: Could the mother's waiver of spousal support in the domestic contract be set aside under s. 18(4)(a) or (b) of the Family Law Reform Act?
facts: The August 1979 agreement was a 'separation agreement' and thus a 'domestic contract'; in para. 6 the mother released the father from all claims arising from the marriage and birth of the child. She was receiving municipal welfare assistance, alleged she signed under duress and while unwell, and chose not to work in order to care for the child. The marriage's cohabitation lasted only about ten months.
rule: Family Law Reform Act, 1978, s. 18(4): a court may set aside a support provision where (a) the provision for support or the waiver of the right to support results in unconscionable circumstances, (b) the provision for support is to a spouse who qualifies for a public-money allowance, or (c) default in payment. Courts should not lightly interfere with contracts freely entered into (Re Stevenson; Dal Santo v. Dal Santo; MacNeill v. MacNeill). Interpretation Act, s. 10; expressio unius est exclusio alterius.
application: Section 18(4)(b) conspicuously omits the words 'waiver of the right to support' found in (a); the court held it could not read those words in, since the omission was deliberate, and it was not for a judge to correct a legislative deficiency. Under (a), it is the results flowing from the agreement, not circumstances at signing, that must be unconscionable; the mother's position was essentially unchanged from before the short marriage except that she chose not to work to care for the child (for whom she received support), and the father was not wealthy. There was no fraud, duress, undue influence or public-policy invalidity.
conclusion: The waiver could not be set aside under either s. 18(4)(a) or (b); the mother remained bound by her waiver of support for herself.

issue: Was the mother entitled to reimbursement of obstetrical/hospital expenses and the cost of the child's ritual circumcision despite the release?
facts: The mother sought her semi-private hospital room cost, an uncovered obstetrical bill, and a $200 fee for the child's ritual circumcision, which the father had unilaterally arranged by bringing a mohel from Montreal without consulting her or explaining why a local person could not be used.
rule: Family Law Reform Act, s. 55(1): in determining matters respecting a child, the court may disregard any provision of a domestic contract where doing so is in the best interests of the child; s. 19(1)(h) (birth-related expenses).
application: Having upheld the mother's waiver, the court could not consider the obstetrical and semi-private room expenses, as these were incurred for her own sake. The circumcision, however, related to the child; under s. 55(1) the court disregarded the waiver of claims concerning the child's birth and, given the father's unexplained arrangement of a costly out-of-town mohel, held him responsible for the full expense.
conclusion: Reimbursement of obstetrical and hospital room expenses refused; the mother awarded $200 for the circumcision cost.

issue: What access should the father be granted, applying the best-interests-of-the-child standard?
facts: The father lived in Brooklyn with a net income under $10,000, could afford to come to Toronto only about once every two months by bus, and stayed in inexpensive hotels unsuitable for meeting the child. He sought four hours' access per day away from the mother; she offered supervised visits of 1–1½ hours in her presence. Relations between the parties had deteriorated.
rule: Family Law Reform Act, s. 35(1): access is determined in accordance with the best interests of the child; access is a right of the child, not the parent (M. v. M.; Knudslien v. Rivard). Custodial parents must facilitate access (Jones v. Jones; Tassou v. Tassou; Woodburn v. Woodburn; Re Petryczka).
application: To develop a genuine father-son relationship, access each day the father is in Toronto (up to three days at a time) for four hours was found reasonable and desirable; shorter visits would not achieve this. Weekday visits were to occur at Jewish Family and Child Services with a worker supervising until the child was comfortable; when that agency was closed, the mother was to arrange use of a friend's or relative's property, on a week's written notice. The court emphasized both parents' duty to protect the child's right to know his father.
conclusion: The father was granted access of four hours on each day (up to three days) he is in Toronto, with supervision and notice arrangements; both parents were reminded of their obligation to facilitate the child's contact with his father.

issue: Should Singer's re-amended claim against Lett and the Bunzl entities be dismissed under art. 168(2) C.p.c. for want of legal basis?
facts: Singer, a business broker, contacted GF Inc.'s principals in 2012 offering to find a buyer for a 3% finder's fee payable by the seller, and separately contacted Bunzl (through Lett) as a potential buyer. He never obtained a signed mandate and never had any agreement with Lett or the Bunzl entities. When GF was later acquired by a Bunzl entity, Singer sued all defendants solidarily for the fee and punitive damages, alleging Lett acted in bad faith and circumvented him.
rule: Art. 168(2) C.p.c. allows summary dismissal, in whole or part, of a claim that is unfounded in law even if the alleged facts are taken as true. Under Boucher c. Pitre (2001 QCCA) and Constructions Serafini inc. c. Gold Coin Development Corp. (2000 QCCA), a corporate fault in performing a contract does not by itself engage the personal liability of an administrator; lifting the corporate veil requires specific alleged facts of fraud or abuse.
application: Even taking the facts as true, no juridical link existed between Singer and Lett or the Bunzl entities; they never engaged Singer or promised any commission. Any commission owed would be payable by the seller, never the buyer, as Singer himself acknowledged. The extracontractual allegation that Lett 'circumvented' Singer disclosed no breach of any obligation, since the buyer never undertook to deal exclusively through Singer. Lett acted only as an officer of Bunzl USA and no facts justified lifting the corporate veil. The punitive-damages claim under arts. 6 and 49 of the Quebec Charter failed because a mere refusal to pay an (unowed) debt is not an unlawful and intentional interference with peaceful enjoyment of property.
conclusion: The claim against Lett and the Bunzl entities was wholly unfounded in law and dismissed.

issue: Is Singer's proceeding against Lett and the Bunzl entities abusive under art. 51 C.p.c., warranting reimbursement of extrajudicial fees under art. 54 C.p.c.?
facts: Singer's out-of-court examinations confirmed he had no written or verbal agreement with Lett or Bunzl, never participated in the negotiation, and always understood his commission was payable by the seller. On the eve of the hearing he re-amended his pleading to add an extracontractual bad-faith theory against those defendants.
rule: Art. 51 C.p.c. defines abuse of process, which may result, regardless of intent, from a claim that is manifestly unfounded, frivolous or dilatory (art. 51(2)); Royal Lepage commercial inc. c. 109650 Canada Ltd. sets the standard of what a reasonable and prudent person would do. Art. 54 C.p.c. permits ordering reimbursement of extrajudicial fees.
application: Given the total absence of any juridical link and the admissions in Singer's examinations, suing Lett and Bunzl reflected a reckless disregard a reasonable person would not have shown, and the last-minute re-amendment revealed an attempt to keep these defendants in the case solely to pressure Alberta/the Martins. The claimed fees ($56,070.83 taxes included) were reviewed and found reasonable, and Singer's counsel had agreed to proceed on the filed exhibits without contesting the amounts.
conclusion: The proceeding against Lett and the Bunzl entities was declared abusive, dismissed, and Singer was ordered to reimburse $56,070.83 with interest and the additional indemnity from 25 November 2016.

issue: Which claims against Alberta, Greg and Doug Martin are inadmissible, and is that proceeding abusive?
facts: Singer alleged a verbal mandate from Greg Martin, sought punitive damages of $2,200,000 and personal condemnation of the officers, and claimed $100,000 for an alleged antisemitic remark by Greg Martin ('when a Jew buys a company, he makes sure that every pen and pencil remains in the desk'). Singer had lost family in the Holocaust.
rule: Art. 168(2) C.p.c. (partial inadmissibility); Quebec Charter arts. 6 and 49 and the intentionality standard from Québec (Curateur public) c. Syndicat national des employés de l'hôpital St-Ferdinand (1996 SCC) for punitive damages; Boucher c. Pitre and Serafini for officer/corporate-veil liability; art. 51 C.p.c. for abuse.
application: The punitive-damages claim and the personal claims against Greg and Doug Martin failed for the same reasons as against the Bunzl group — a refusal to pay a commission is no unlawful, intentional Charter breach, and no characterized fault was alleged to pierce the corporate veil. However, the antisemitic-remark claim, taken as true, could support damages including punitive damages and could not be dismissed at this stage. The abuse claim regarding the commission failed because credibility of the alleged verbal mandate required a trial, so the proceeding against Alberta was not abusive.
conclusion: The punitive-damages claim and the personal claims against Greg and Doug Martin were declared inadmissible; the antisemitic-remark claim against Greg Martin and the commission claim against Alberta were held admissible; no abuse declaration or fee reimbursement was ordered against these defendants.

issue: Was the Tribunal's discretionary decision to refuse to accept the petitioner's human rights complaint for filing patently unreasonable?
facts: The petitioner, a self-identified Pastafarian and member of the Church of the Flying Spaghetti Monster, was denied a driver's licence photo showing him wearing a pirate's tricorn hat, and filed a s. 8 Human Rights Code complaint alleging religious discrimination by ICBC. The Tribunal refused to accept the complaint for filing on the basis that Pastafarianism satirizes religion and the facts alleged, if proven, could not contravene the Code.
rule: Under s. 27(1)(b) of the Code the Tribunal acts as gatekeeper and may decline to accept a complaint that fails to allege facts which, if proven, could contravene the Code (Rule 12(2); McCulloch; Goddard). On judicial review the court may only intervene if the discretionary decision was patently unreasonable (ATA s. 59(3); Code s. 32(q)), meaning arbitrary, in bad faith, for an improper purpose, based predominantly on irrelevant factors, or ignoring statutory requirements (ATA s. 59(4)), or 'clearly irrational' (Francescutti; Ryan). Gatekeeping decisions attract high deference (Mzite; Edgewater Casino). Religion under the Code requires practices/beliefs with a nexus to religion (Amselem, 2004 SCC 47).
application: The court held it could not reweigh the evidence. Canadian courts have recognized Pastafarian practices as satirical (Narayana; Unrau), and the petitioner himself conceded there 'may be some elements of satire'. A decision based on allegedly insufficient evidence is not patently unreasonable (Auyeung; O.S.S.T.F.). The Tribunal reasonably concluded that accommodating a practice satirizing religion in a public service would not further the Code's purpose of promoting mutual respect and dignity (s. 3).
conclusion: The Decision was neither clearly irrational nor so flawed that no deference could save it; it was not patently unreasonable.

issue: Did the Tribunal's Decision give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias or rest on false assumptions?
facts: The petitioner argued the Decision was biased because it assumed the Church of the Flying Spaghetti Monster mocks religious beliefs and used the word 'colander', which did not appear in his complaint. He filed lengthy submissions comparing his beliefs to other religions.
rule: Fresh material not before the Tribunal is inadmissible on judicial review (Albu v. UBC). A finding must be shown to be biased or founded on false assumptions to be impugned.
application: The petitioner's own submissions, describing Pastafarianism as valuing 'humour, self-deprecation and silliness' and being 'atheistic to all gods other than the one we believe in', reinforced rather than undermined the Tribunal's view that the practices were at least partly satirical. His reconsideration letter did not deny a satirical purpose, only that no bylaw mandated mocking religion. The material not before the Tribunal was inadmissible.
conclusion: No reasonable apprehension of bias or false assumption was established; the submissions buttressed the Tribunal's conclusion.

issue: Did the employer have just cause to summarily dismiss the employee for alleged incompetence and deception?
facts: Tipon, a safety officer of four years' service responsible for maintaining the company's COR certification, became seriously ill with lichen planus in early 2014. His helpful supervisor Mr. Johns left the company; his replacement supervisor in Calgary had minimal contact and conducted no performance reviews; his essential assistant Ms. Jurace was dismissed on the employer's direction over Tipon's objection. The company was rapidly expanding, doubling its Alberta branches, increasing Tipon's workload. The COR certification lapsed after an extension request was refused, and Tipon was dismissed for 'non-performance' with one month's pay.
rule: An employer dismissing summarily must prove just cause on a balance of probabilities. Under McKinley v. BC Tel, 2001 SCC 38, a contextual approach applies: misconduct alone does not establish cause; the question is whether the behaviour was such that the employment relationship could no longer viably subsist (para. 29). What constitutes just cause depends on the nature of the employment and status of the employee (Blackburn v. Victory Credit Union, 1998 CanLII 6089 (NSCA)). Conduct must go to the root of the contract (Panton v. Everywoman's Health Center, 2000 BCCA 621).
application: The court found no incompetence or deception. Tipon performed well before his illness. The employer effectively repudiated the contract by dismissing the indispensable assistant Ms. Jurace over Tipon's protest and by failing to replace the departed mentor Johns with competent supervision — Tipon met Palma only three or four times in 14 months and received no performance reviews. The employer, having minimal involvement, could not fairly judge Tipon's competence. Tipon had disclosed as early as September 18, 2014 that COR recertification was in jeopardy, and was only definitively refused an extension on March 27, 2015. At worst he was naïve in believing he could obtain an extension, and naiveté is not dishonesty.
conclusion: The employer failed to prove just cause; the dismissal was wrongful.

issue: Could the employer rely on after-acquired cause to justify the dismissal?
facts: After dismissing Tipon, Bzeta reviewed Tipon's emails, including a December 11, 2014 email disclosing the company could not submit an internal audit, and asserted Tipon deceitfully withheld information about the COR deadlines.
rule: After-acquired cause requires evidence of dishonesty or dishonest intent, per Nelson v. Champion Feed Services Inc., 2010 ABQB 409.
application: Following Nelson, the court found no evidence of dishonesty or dishonest intent. At worst Tipon did not do his job perfectly, but there was no wilfulness or bad intent. The emails showed Tipon was openly communicating difficulties and seeking an extension, not concealing them.
conclusion: The employer could not rely on after-acquired cause; it failed to discharge its onus.

issue: Did the employer dismiss the employee in bad faith so as to warrant aggravated damages?
facts: Bzeta's termination letters cited 'non-performance' and 'mistakes' that 'could not be corrected'; the reasons given were inaccurate and the employer took no responsibility. The dismissal occurred amid company-wide austerity, office closures and staff reductions during economic contraction.
rule: Employers must be candid, reasonable, honest and forthright and not act in bad faith (Wallace v. United Grain Growers, 1997; Honda v. Keays, 2008 SCC 39); a duty of honest performance and good faith applies (Bhasin v. Hrynew, 2014 SCC 71; Potter v. NB Legal Aid, 2015 SCC 10). Aggravated damages compensate for intangible injuries from insulting conduct (Fidler v. Sun Life, 2006 SCC 30; Vorvis, 1989) and require conduct akin to intent, malice or blatant disregard (Merrill Lynch v. Soost, 2010 ABCA 251); mere sloppy conduct does not suffice.
application: Although the stated reasons were inaccurate and clumsy, the employer's conduct was not calculated or directed solely at Tipon, unlike in Karmel. This was an employer caught in a 'perfect storm' of expansion followed by contraction, focused on cost-cutting rather than deliberately making Tipon's work life miserable. The conduct did not display blatant disregard amounting to intent or malice.
conclusion: No aggravated damages were awarded.

issue: What is the appropriate reasonable notice period and damages?
facts: Tipon was 4+ years of service, earning $82,400/year ($6,866/month) with benefits; he found new work in 4.5 months at $57,000/year during difficult economic times; he had received one month's pay in lieu.
rule: Reasonable notice is assessed on the Bardal v. Globe and Mail, 1960 CanLII 294 (ONHCJ) factors: character of employment, length of service, age, and availability of similar employment.
application: Applying Bardal, the court set reasonable notice at six months. Tipon reasonably mitigated by finding new work in 4.5 months. Damages were six months' wages ($41,200) plus $1,500 benefits, less credit for the one month already paid ($6,866) and 1.5 months' alternate income differential ($7,125). No bonus was awarded as no evidence of entitlement for 2015 was led.
conclusion: Judgment for the plaintiff of $28,709 plus judgment interest from May 27, 2015 and costs.

issue: Was the removal and retention wrongful, and did the father consent or acquiesce within the meaning of s. 21(1) of the Act?
facts: The mother abruptly left the father at a Cambridge hotel with the two children and drove to Montreal without allowing him to say goodbye. She set conditions for her return (address, bed, telephone), which the father promptly satisfied, and later induced him to write on a restaurant placemat that he did 'for the time being' not object to the children being in Montreal, without disclosing that she had already consulted counsel and intended not to return. She falsely claimed she had been denied entry to the U.S. for lack of birth certificates.
rule: Sections 3 and 21(1) of the Act respecting the civil aspects of international and interprovincial child abduction (R.S.Q. c. A-23.01) implementing the Hague Convention; a court may refuse return only where the applicant consented to or acquiesced in the removal or retention. Consent must be freely and voluntarily given and, per A.M.I. v. D.T.L., [2001] R.D.F. 221 (C.A.), a conditional or non-permanent statement does not amount to unqualified consent.
application: The father's conduct throughout — sending money, arranging housing, contacting border officials, coming to Montreal, and obtaining an ex parte custody order in Los Angeles on October 31 — was consistent only with seeking to reunite the family, not with consent. The placemat note was neither unconditional nor permanent, and any apparent consent was vitiated because the mother did not make full and accurate disclosure. Justifications based on the father's financial difficulties are not defences enumerated in the Act.
conclusion: The removal of the two children to Montreal was wrongful under s. 3, and the father neither consented to nor acquiesced in the removal or retention under s. 21(1).

issue: What was the children's habitual residence, and could the court order their return to Los Angeles though removal occurred from Cambridge?
facts: The children were born and had always lived in Los Angeles. They left with their parents on October 1 for a planned academic-year stay in Cambridge, arriving late October 10, and were removed by the mother on October 12 after fewer than 48 hours and two nights in hotels.
rule: Neither the Act nor the Convention defines habitual residence; courts determine it case-by-case focusing on the child's reality at the time of removal, not the parents' intentions (Droit de la famille – 2454, [1996] R.J.Q. 2509 (C.A.); Freidrich v. Freidrich, 983 F.2d 1396). Per Droit de la famille – 3713, [2000] R.D.F. 585 (C.A.), an appreciable period must elapse, with a real and active connection and a certain degree of continuity, before a new habitual residence is acquired.
application: The children had spent their entire lives in Los Angeles and less than 48 hours in Cambridge with no integration, connection, or continuity there. Their reality remained in Los Angeles. Allowing removal from a transient location to defeat the Convention would frustrate its purpose, so the court retained the power to order return to the place of habitual residence.
conclusion: The children's habitual residence was Los Angeles; the court ordered their return there with their father.

issue: Should the mother be ordered to reimburse the father's expenses under s. 39 of the Act?
facts: The father incurred substantial legal and travel expenses initiating proceedings in Montreal and Los Angeles; the mother is unemployed, was the children's primary caregiver, and has limited means, with further legal costs ahead.
rule: Section 39 of the Act allows the court, 'where appropriate,' to order reimbursement of expenses; it is a discretionary deterrent power to be exercised judicially.
application: Although the removal was wrongful, ordering the impecunious mother to reimburse the father would ultimately harm the children by diverting scarce resources. The costly custody battle in Los Angeles had only begun and both parents wanted the best for the children.
conclusion: The court declined to order reimbursement of expenses, but awarded costs in favour of the father's counsel as an adequate, non-burdensome deterrent.

issue: Who bears the onus on the 'arguable defence' element of a security-for-costs application, and did the insurers establish an arguable defence?
facts: The corporate plaintiff conceded it could not pay costs and lacked exigible assets, so the inquiry turned on whether the insurers had an arguable defence and whether an order would cause undue hardship. The insurers' evidence of a meritorious fraud defence was set out only in the affidavit of Ms. Haines, a legal assistant, reciting the advice and representations of counsel (Mr. Neen), while the plaintiff tendered direct affidavits from its two principals denying involvement and challenging the reliability of the witness (Mr. Madonna) and the Senez engineering report.
rule: Section 236 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 confers a discretionary jurisdiction to order security. Per Fat Mel's Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co. (1993) the burden lies on the defendant and the order is discretionary; Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress (1999) sets four factors (inability to pay, exigible assets, arguable defence, undue hardship). Per Citizens and Spartans Canadian Football Association of BC v. McAvoy, 2001 BCSC 1305, the onus first falls on the defendant to show a bona fide/reasonable defence, then shifts to the plaintiff; an arguable defence requires 'some evidence' beyond a bare denial.
application: The Court held that a plaintiff, ignorant of the defendant's case, should not bear the onus of proving the negative; the defendant must first show an arguable defence. Because the insurers had completed their investigation and denied coverage for fraud seven months before suit, this was not an early-stage case where a solicitor's outline would suffice — admissible evidence existed and could have been tendered. Offering only a legal assistant's recitation of counsel's opinion, which also shielded the position from cross-examination, was insufficient once the plaintiff answered with direct evidence and exposed uncertainties in the Madonna statement and undisclosed interviews.
conclusion: An arguable defence was not made out; alternatively, even if the bare assertion sufficed, the Court would exercise its discretion to refuse security.

issue: Should security be refused because it would stifle a claim whose viability is tied to the defendants' own denial of coverage?
facts: The plaintiff's affiants swore that requiring $50,000 security would prevent it from pursuing a meritorious claim, and that its financial difficulties flowed from the insurers' refusal to pay, the fraud allegations, and the insurers' insistence that documents would only be produced once litigation was commenced. Pre-litigation correspondence from Mr. Hilliker warned that the coverage refusal was harming the business.
rule: Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd. (1997) and Keary Development v. Tarmac Construction warn against security being used as an instrument of oppression to stifle a legitimate claim; Scotford Electrical v. Blue Mountain Log Sales, 2005 BCSC 538 and Grant v. Henderson Development, 2003 BCSC 1473 permit the Court to decline or reduce security where the plaintiff's impecuniosity is linked to the cause of action. Insurers owe a duty of good faith and fair dealing (Alexander v. Great West Life, 2004 NBQB 285).
application: The evidence showed the plaintiff's financial predicament was tied to the insurers' denial of coverage, and the pre-existing creditor disputes were minimal against its gross sales. The insurers' pre-litigation position — that they would disclose documents only if sued — breached their duty of transparency, and it would be unfair to let them capitalize on a situation of their own making by then erecting a security-for-costs roadblock.
conclusion: Security for costs was refused outright, with costs to the plaintiff payable forthwith in any event of the cause.

issue: Did filing an affidavit by a member of defence counsel's firm representing the substance of the defence waive solicitor-client privilege?
facts: Ms. Haines, a legal assistant at defence counsel's firm, swore an affidavit on information and belief detailing the evidence the insurers 'will show' at trial and asserting a meritorious fraud defence. The plaintiff sought a declaration of waiver and production of Mr. Neen's file up to the date of the affidavit.
rule: Where a solicitor 'enters the fray' by providing affidavit evidence on a matter of substance, the client is taken to have waived privilege (Casino Tropical Plants Ltd. v. Rentokil, 1998; Murao v. Blackcomb Skiing Enterprises, 2003 BCSC 558). Privilege cannot be used as a sword (Cheung v. 518402 BC Ltd., 1999); waiver may be implied where fairness and consistency require and extends to the whole communication (Pacific Concessions, Inc. v. Weir, 2004 BCSC 1682; Wigmore on Evidence). The principle applies equally to affidavits on information and belief (Re Mannix Resources Inc., 2004 BCSC 1315).
application: Counsel's representations conveyed through the legal assistant could only be the product of everything known to counsel when made, and could not be segregated into privileged and non-privileged. Having chosen to represent the merits of the defence rather than tendering a party's evidence, the insurers could not disclose as much as they pleased while withholding the rest; using a legal assistant to shield counsel from cross-examination did not temper the waiver.
conclusion: Privilege was waived over defence counsel's file concerning the matters in paras. 10–12 of Ms. Haines' affidavit; the parties were to return to address whether production of the file should be ordered. The cross-examination application was dismissed as moot with no order as to costs.

issue: What parenting arrangement (residence and parenting time) is in the best interests of the child?
facts: The 9-year-old child has lived primarily with the Applicant mother since the parties separated when he was three months old. The Respondent father had inconsistent contact, relocated repeatedly (British Columbia, Mexico, Miami), had no in-person parenting time since 2023, made harassing social media posts, livestreamed the child, and was convicted of criminal harassment. The child expressed a preference not to have contact with the father at present.
rule: Under the Children's Law Reform Act, s. 24(1)-(3), the court considers only the best interests of the child, giving primary consideration to the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being, weighing enumerated factors including need for stability, strength of relationships, willingness to support the other parent's relationship, history of care, the child's views and preferences, and any family violence (s. 24(4)).
application: The court found the child needs stability and has thrived as primary caregiver with the mother and her spouse. Although the child currently opposes contact, the child is young, had positive past visits, and an order of no parenting time for a father is rare. The father's harassing conduct and lack of a stable plan meant parenting time must proceed through a supervised, therapist-led reintegration/reunification plan.
conclusion: The child shall reside primarily with the Applicant; the Respondent is to have parenting time through a reintegration/reunification plan with therapeutic support and supervised video calls, moving to regularized parenting time on the therapists' recommendations.

issue: What decision-making regime is in the best interests of the child?
facts: The Applicant had held temporary sole decision-making since July 2020, and the child was thriving. The Respondent has had only limited day-to-day decision-making during sporadic in-person time and is largely absent from the child's life, with serious communication difficulties between the parties.
rule: Best interests of the child under the Children's Law Reform Act, s. 24; joint decision-making requires the ability to communicate and cooperate.
application: Given the father's absence and the parties' inability to communicate and cooperate, joint or consultative decision-making was not practical or feasible; the status quo of sole decision-making by the mother should not be disrupted.
conclusion: The Applicant is granted sole decision-making responsibility for major decisions (health, education, religion, extra-curriculars), and may obtain/renew the child's travel and government documents without the Respondent's consent.

issue: What amount of child support, including imputed income and retroactive support, should the respondent pay?
facts: The Respondent was a healthy 45-year-old capable of working multiple jobs, reported $35,000 income in 2023, and provided no financial disclosure. He claimed to have paid some support historically but produced no evidence.
rule: Family Law Act, s. 31(1) obliges parents to support their children. Income may be imputed to an underemployed or unemployed parent under the Guidelines s. 19(1)(a) (Drygala v. Pauli, 2002 CanLII 41868 (ON CA)). The applicable table amount is set under the Ontario Child Support Guidelines, s. 3(1), with disclosure required under s. 21.
application: The court imputed income of $35,000, yielding a table amount of $304 per month. In the absence of disclosure of past payments, retroactive support from separation to January 31, 2025 was calculated at $17,024.
conclusion: The Respondent shall pay $304/month table support (part of a fixed $500/month), plus $17,024 in retroactive child support, and provide annual financial disclosure.

issue: What proportionate share of section 7 special and extraordinary expenses should each party bear?
facts: The Applicant claimed full-time nanny childcare of $32,780/year; the Respondent's imputed income was $35,000 and the Applicant's income was $350,000.
rule: Ontario Child Support Guidelines, s. 7(1)-(2): the court may order special/extraordinary expenses shared in proportion to the parties' respective incomes.
application: Proportionate shares were 9.1% (Respondent) and 90.9% (Applicant). The Respondent's share of the nanny expense was $228/month, but the Applicant accepted $196/month so the combined monthly payment totalled $500.
conclusion: The Respondent's share of section 7 expenses is 9.1% ($196/month accepted); no arrears of section 7 expenses were claimed.

issue: What penalty should be imposed for the respondent's failure to remove social media posts contrary to court orders, and does his conduct constitute family violence?
facts: The Respondent repeatedly disobeyed numerous court orders (2020-2024 and the January 14, 2025 order) requiring removal of social media posts denigrating the Applicant and Mr. Binns and referencing the litigation. He called them 'child abusers,' published identifying information, and encouraged followers to contact them, causing them to fear for safety and move house; he was criminally convicted of harassment.
rule: Family Law Rules, s. 1(8) permits the court to make any order necessary for a just determination where a person fails to obey an order, including a penalty/fine (s. 1(8)(a.1)). 'Family violence' is defined in the Children's Law Reform Act, s. 18(1)-(2) to include harassment, psychological abuse and threats; social media posts can constitute family violence (S.B. v. J.I.U., 2021 ONCJ 614; Rubio v. Leigh, 2024 ONSC 6215).
application: The court found the posts were harassment, psychological abuse and threats amounting to family violence, and that the Respondent's non-compliance was deliberate, wilful and flagrant despite many opportunities. A monetary penalty of $100/day until removal, plus the ability to pause the reintegration plan on any breach, was reasonable; a further restraining order barring future proceedings was unnecessary.
conclusion: The Respondent shall pay $100/day until all offending posts are removed, and the Applicant may pause the reintegration/reunification plan on any breach; the social media conduct was found to be family violence.

issue: Should a mis-trial be declared (or the application dismissed) for alleged misconduct in the tendering of the loan agreement exhibit?
facts: When the application was filed, the affidavit of verification (First Robson Affidavit) appended an incomplete 'Short Version' of the loan agreement missing Schedules D and E. At trial, counsel marked as Exhibit 2 the complete 73-page 'Long Version' (with the schedules) and identified it as the same document, and later failed to comply with the court's Direction to replace Exhibit 2 with exactly what had been Exhibit A. Grillone alleged evidence tampering (spoliation), perjury by Robson and suborning of perjury by counsel, contempt, and bad faith under s. 4.2 BIA.
rule: A mis-trial is a last resort granted only in the clearest cases where an irregularity fatally wounds the trial process and prevents a party from presenting its case or securing a fair adjudication (Forsythe v. Tone, 2018 ONSC 3598; van Ooyen v. Carruthers, 2018 SKQB 73; R. v. Khan, 2001 SCC 86). Spoliation requires destruction of evidence (Catalyst Capital v. Moyse); perjury requires a false statement made with intent to mislead (Criminal Code s. 131; R. v. Hebert, [1989] 1 SCR 233); contempt requires intentional breach of an order (BDC v. Cavalon Inc., 2017 ONCA 663); the s. 4.2 BIA good-faith duty forbids conducting proceedings for an improper purpose or misleading as to the loan status (CWB Maximum Financial v. 2026998 Alberta Ltd., 2021 ABQB 137).
application: The court inferred the Short Version was appended in error, that the mis-description of Exhibit 2 was inadvertent (attributable to too many lawyers marshalling evidence in a virtual trial), and Robson lacked intent to mislead. No evidence was destroyed (no spoliation), the requisite intent for perjury and contempt was absent, and Grillone showed no prejudice — he had signed the Long Version in 2018, received it again in May 2022, admitted its authenticity, and could have examined witnesses on Schedules D and E. The mis-description did not go to the status of the loan or lender-borrower relationship and was not connected to any purpose of avoiding the Counterclaim. Although counsel failed to follow proper exhibit-correction procedure and the court's Direction, this did not fatally wound the trial.
conclusion: Mis-trial motion (and alternative request for dismissal) dismissed; the irregularities were addressed through costs rather than a mis-trial.

issue: Were the s. 43(1) BIA requirements (debt ≥ $1,000 and an act of bankruptcy within six months) satisfied?
facts: Grillone and his law firm borrowed litigation-disbursement funding under a December 2018 loan agreement and he gave a $1M guarantee. Bluecore claimed principal of $1,332,462.58, updated at trial (through bookkeeper Ms. Lau) to a net Indebtedness of $2,479,960 at the filing date and $3,773,553 by trial. The alleged act of bankruptcy was ceasing to meet liabilities as they came due by failing to pay Bluecore (s. 42(1)(j)).
rule: Under s. 43(1) BIA the applicant must prove a debt of at least $1,000 and an act of bankruptcy in the preceding six months, on the civil balance of probabilities but with strict proof of every allegation (Re Levesque, 2016 ONCA 393; Re Holmes (1975); Re Ivany, 2012 ONSC 7058). Section 42(1)(j) captures a debtor who 'ceases to meet his liabilities generally as they come due.'
application: The single executed Long Version loan agreement, together with Robson's and Lau's testimony, strictly proved a debt far exceeding $1,000 at both the filing date and trial, net of payments and inclusive of contractual default interest. The precise amount need not match the affidavit; trial evidence could supplement it. Grillone's challenges (accounting impairment note, funding by Bluecore affiliates, the $1M guarantee cap) did not undermine his contractual liability as 'Borrower'.
conclusion: The s. 43(1) monetary threshold and, subject to the special-circumstances analysis, the act of bankruptcy were established.

issue: Were 'special circumstances' required and demonstrated for a single-creditor bankruptcy application?
facts: The act of bankruptcy rested solely on non-payment of Bluecore. Bluecore pursued the Bluecore Civil Action from June 2020 through the six-month period; the Indebtedness (c. $2.48M) was large relative to Grillone's roughly $500,000–$650,000 in realizable assets; a Mareva injunction had earlier been granted on findings of asset dissipation; and more than 25 claims/counterclaims involved Grillone, with several creditors testifying in support of a streamlined bankruptcy process.
rule: Failure to pay a single creditor can constitute an act of bankruptcy under s. 42(1)(j) only where special circumstances exist, recognized in Valente v. Courey, 2004 CanLII 8018 (ON CA) in three categories: (a) repeated demands in the six-month period; (b) a significantly large debt with fraud or suspicious circumstances in handling assets; (c) admitted inability to pay creditors generally. Confirmed in Levesque (Re), 2016 ONCA 393. Categories may not be closed (ATB Financial v. Coredent, 2020 ABQB 587).
application: Category 1 was met: Bluecore's continued prosecution of the civil action evidenced persisting demands; the unproven Counterclaim did not negate this. Category 2 was met (or a new analogous category): the debt was large relative to available assets, and Grillone's litigious, counter-suing conduct against a large class of creditors, together with the earlier Mareva findings, required the BIA processes to be set in motion. A single forum was needed to ensure orderly distribution and no unfair advantage among creditors.
conclusion: Special circumstances were established; the single-creditor act of bankruptcy was proven.

issue: Did the secured creditor provide a satisfactory estimate of the value of its security under s. 43(2)?
facts: Bluecore's security comprised assigned receivables from the Funded Files, after-the-event insurance policies (later rescinded by DAS), and the personal guarantee. The First Robson Affidavit called value 'de minimis'; at trial Robson estimated recoveries at zero to about $100,000, given transferred files, unknown recoveries, and competing BNS security.
rule: Section 43(2) BIA requires a secured creditor either to offer up its security or give an estimate of its value; a secured creditor may set its own estimate, and unless absurdly small or a sham the court need not determine true value (Hugh M. Grant Ltd. (Re) (1982); the estimate may be provided during a contested proceeding before the order is made).
application: The estimate could properly be supplied at trial in a contested application. Robson's estimate of nil to $100,000, supported by the collapse of the insurance security and uncertainty over the Funded Files, was neither absurdly small nor a sham.
conclusion: A satisfactory estimate was provided; s. 43(2) was satisfied.

issue: Should the court refuse the order under s. 43(7) for improper purpose or lack of good faith?
facts: Grillone argued the application was brought to avoid defending his $16M Counterclaim via the automatic stay, and that Bluecore acted in bad faith. Robson acknowledged wanting an orderly wind-up of the litigation but also cited a large class of creditors and multiplicity of proceedings.
rule: Section 43(7) confers a residual discretion to dismiss an otherwise proven application for sufficient cause (Medcap Real Estate Holdings (Re), 2022 ONCA 318; Buth-Na-Bodhaige v. Lambert (2002); Diena (Re), 2012 ONSC 5849), and s. 4.2 requires good faith. Using bankruptcy to collect a debt or gain remedies unavailable outside bankruptcy is not improper (First City Trust v. Omni-Stone (1991); 0757376 B.C. Ltd. (Re), 2011 BCSC 1268).
application: Avoiding the Counterclaim was not the sole purpose; streamlining a multiplicity of claims and counterclaims for the benefit of all creditors is a legitimate purpose. Grillone did not prove he could pay his debts, and none of the recognized improper-purpose categories were established.
conclusion: The court declined to exercise its s. 43(7) discretion; the bankruptcy order was granted.

issue: Were the occasions on which Despard made the defamatory statements occasions of qualified privilege?
facts: Despard, assistant branch manager of a car-financing company, made disparaging remarks about the car dealer Taylor to three prospective buyers (Lachance, Boy, Franklyn) who had approached the company for loans secured by chattel mortgages on cars they intended to buy from Taylor, when explaining why the company would not finance those purchases.
rule: Per Lord Atkinson in Adam v. Ward, [1917] A.C. 309 at 334, a privileged occasion exists where the person making a communication has an interest or duty (legal, social or moral) to make it and the recipient has a corresponding interest or duty to receive it; this reciprocity is essential.
application: The finance company had an interest in communicating to each applicant its reasons for refusing a loan on a car bought from Taylor, and each applicant had a corresponding interest in learning those reasons; both parties also had a vital interest in the title they would respectively acquire as purchaser and chattel mortgagee. As the company could only speak through its employees, Despard was entitled to the same protection as his employer.
conclusion: The Court held the trial judge was right: all the occasions were occasions of qualified privilege.
