facts: Burnaby City Council, by resolution adopting the City Manager's recommendations, approved The Gavel Historical Society's request to build a $600,000 replica of a 1914 Masonic Lodge on City land at the Burnaby Village Museum; the City would own and control the building. Watson argued the building would be used for religious purposes and that spending public money to support a religion was not authorized.
rule: Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 290, ss. 679(1) (acquire and hold property for museum uses), 682(1) (construct and maintain buildings for such purposes), 223 (powers exercisable by resolution unless a bylaw is expressly required) and 287 (power to do anything incidental or conducive to an allotted power).
application: The Court found the essential purpose of the replica lodge, as shown in the City Manager's report, was historical — an integral part of the museum with full public ownership and access. The 'Points for Consideration' relied on by Watson, read in context (including the express prohibition on promotional or recruiting activity and on use as a clubroom), did not support an inference of religious use. Approving the project by resolution was incidental or conducive to the museum power and did not require a bylaw.
conclusion: The resolution was a valid exercise of Burnaby's powers under the Municipal Act; the first ground failed.

issue: Did the resolution violate freedom of religion under s. 2(a) of the Charter?
facts: Watson, a member of the Christian Reformed religion, contended that funding a project connected with Masonry indirectly infringed his freedom of religion by devoting tax dollars to support a religion not his own.
rule: Charter s. 2(a); R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295; Jones v. The Queen, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 284 — legislative or administrative action whose effect on religion is trivial or insubstantial is not a breach; s. 2(a) does not bar every burden touching religion.
application: The resolution did not prevent or hinder anyone from holding or practising religious beliefs, so there was no direct violation. On the effects-based argument, the true purpose was to provide an historical museum, not to promote religion, and any incidental call on the public purse had no substantial impact on anyone's freedom of religion.
conclusion: No violation of s. 2(a); the second ground failed.

issue: Did the resolution violate equality rights under s. 15(1), and if so was it justified under s. 1?
facts: Watson argued it was discriminatory for Burnaby to let the Masons use city land for the replica lodge when the same benefit was not extended to his Protestant Reformed religion.
rule: Charter s. 15(1); Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143 (discrimination is a distinction based on personal characteristics imposing burdens or withholding benefits); R. v. Turpin; Haig v. Canada. Section 1 justification per Andrews (McIntyre and La Forest JJ.) and the Oakes/proportionality approach.
application: There was no evidence that Watson or his religion had been denied any benefit based on a personal characteristic; Burnaby merely approved a historical project on its merits without excluding other proposals. Even if s. 15(1) were engaged, preservation of history is a desirable social objective, law-makers must have reasonable scope for such choices, the Society bore construction costs, the building became City property, and use to promote Masonry was prohibited — making the resolution reasonable and proportional.
conclusion: No breach of s. 15(1); alternatively, the resolution was justified under s. 1. The third ground was rejected.

issue: Was the Mason councillor disqualified from voting for conflict of interest or bias?
facts: Councillor Young, a Mason, seconded and voted for the motion (passed 7–2). He had no financial interest and was not a member of The Gavel Historical Society; the objection rested solely on his being a Mason.
rule: Common law on disqualifying interest: In Re L'Abbé and Corporation of Blind River (1904), 7 O.L.R. 230; Old St. Boniface Residents Association v. Winnipeg, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1170 — a councillor is disqualified where the interest is so related to the public duty that a reasonably well-informed person would conclude it might influence the vote; the interest must be substantial and peculiar to the councillor, beyond a community-of-interest. Municipal Act s. 225(7)-(8) (1993 amendment) addresses pecuniary interest but does not codify or displace the common law on non-pecuniary interests.
application: Councillor Young had no pecuniary or personal interest beyond that shared with other Burnaby residents; the project was historical, not religious, and benefited all residents. Applying L'Abbé, Elliott, Casson and Old St. Boniface, his interest was merely a community of interest, not a disqualifying substantial personal interest. The Court tested this by analogy to Christian councillors voting on a replica church, reaching the same result.
conclusion: No conflict of interest or reasonable apprehension of bias; the fourth ground was rejected.

issue: Was the resolution invalid for failure to notify an opponent of the meeting?
facts: Ms. Starr claimed the City Clerk had promised to notify her when further action would be taken; the Clerk denied any such promise. Both Starr and Watson had already made presentations against the proposal on March 7 and were in attendance on March 14 when the motion was lifted from the table and passed.
rule: Subject to any statutory requirement, a municipal council need not notify or grant a hearing to persons affected by exercise of its legislative powers: Rogers, The Law of Canadian Municipal Corporations; Laurie's Caterers Ltd. v. North Vancouver (1985), 30 M.P.L.R. 145 (B.C.C.A.); Re Vancouver Charter; Re Wheatley (1957), 24 W.W.R. 323 (B.C.S.C.).
application: The disputed promise was immaterial because both opponents attended the March 14 meeting and observed the vote, and had already presented their views on March 7. No provision of the Municipal Act required notice of intention to pass such a resolution.
conclusion: Watson and Starr received more than their legal rights; the notice ground was rejected.

issue: Should an interim safeguard order be issued authorizing treatment and hospitalization pending the full hearing on the application for authorization of care?
facts: Mr. N. G., a 78-year-old man diagnosed with schizophrenia and narcissistic personality disorder, was confined in the Hospital under a 30-day court order. The Hospital sought authorization to administer a three-year antipsychotic treatment plan. Mr. N. G. requested a three-month postponement to obtain a counter-expertise and contest the application; the Hospital agreed but sought interim safeguard measures. He had been non-compliant with medication since November 2018, his mental state had deteriorated, and the confinement order was about to expire.
rule: Under arts. 11, 12 and 16 C.C.Q., no person may undergo care without consent except with court authorization. The seven-step analysis mandated by F.D. c. Centre universitaire de santé McGill (Hôpital Royal-Victoria), 2015 QCCA 1139, and the criteria in Institut Philippe Pinel de Montréal c. A.G., 1994 CanLII 6105 (QC CA), govern applications for authorization of care. A safeguard order requires: (1) urgency; (2) a serious question to be tried; (3) serious or irreparable harm if relief is refused; and (4) a balance of inconvenience favouring the applicant.
application: The Court found urgency because Mr. N. G.'s condition was deteriorating into psychotic decompensation and the confinement order was expiring imminently. There was a serious question to be tried given the strong evidence of incapacity and the medical necessity of treatment. Serious or irreparable harm would result from leaving his psychosis untreated, given his intimidating and harassing conduct impairing his functioning. The balance of inconvenience favoured a temporary, limited pharmacological treatment over an absence of treatment that would leave him in delusion, paranoia and distress. The order was limited to three months to allow him to retain an expert and contest the application on December 16, 2019.
conclusion: The Court issued the safeguard order, valid until December 16, 2019, authorizing administration of the antipsychotic treatment plan and continued hospitalization until a safe discharge plan is in place.

issue: Is Mr. N. G. incapable of consenting to the proposed treatment plan?
facts: Mr. N. G. denies his schizophrenia diagnosis and does not believe he is mentally ill; he understands the nature of the treatment but not its benefits or the risks of refusing it. He has categorically refused antipsychotic medication since November 2018. Dr. Roy, his treating psychiatrist, testified that his inability to understand his diagnosis and consequences stems from his illness.
rule: Article 16 C.C.Q. permits court authorization of care where a person of full age is incapable of giving consent and refuses categorically; incapacity is assessed under the criteria concerning ability to understand the nature of the illness, the treatment, its benefits and risks, and whether the refusal is a product of the illness.
application: The evidence and Mr. N. G.'s own testimony established that although intelligent and articulate, he denies his illness and cannot appreciate the benefits of treatment or risks of refusing it, an incapacity resulting from his disorder. The Court found the Hospital presented a strong case of incapacity to consent.
conclusion: The Court confirmed Mr. N. G.'s incapacity to consent to the proposed treatment plan.

issue: Can a lawyer's undertaking bind the client?
facts: During the June 3, 2016 stay hearing before Myers J., Bentworth's counsel Pinckard "undertakes to allow the applicant to attend and remove his goods." Pinckard filed no evidence on the motion about the nature of the undertaking or her discussions with Bentworth, and Bentworth argued the undertaking was Pinckard's personal one.
rule: Whether an undertaking is given personally by counsel or on behalf of the client as agent is a question of fact; only if given on the client's behalf can it bind the client.
application: Myers J.'s wording that counsel undertook to "allow" removal could suggest it was not a personal undertaking, since Pinckard did not operationally control the storage facility, but the endorsement was not clear on whether it was personal or given as Bentworth's agent. Pinckard adduced no evidence to resolve the ambiguity.
conclusion: The issue could not be resolved on the record; a trial is needed to determine whether the undertaking binds Bentworth.

issue: Is the summary enforcement procedure for lawyers' undertakings available against a non-lawyer party?
facts: Waugh sought to invoke against Bentworth, a corporate non-lawyer party, the summary procedure normally used to compel lawyers to honour undertakings.
rule: Thomas Gold Pettingill LLP v. Ani-Wall Concrete Forming Inc., 2012 ONSC 2182: the court's summary jurisdiction to enforce lawyers' undertakings is rooted in securing higher standards of conduct, honesty and integrity from its officers.
application: Because the summary jurisdiction depends on a lawyer's status as an officer of the court, it cannot be extended to a non-lawyer party such as Bentworth.
conclusion: The extraordinary summary procedure is not available against Bentworth.

issue: Was the undertaking sufficiently clear to enforce?
facts: Waugh argued Myers J. ordered that he be allowed to retrieve all belongings, including vehicles, taking as long as he needed. Bentworth argued the undertaking, read in context, required prompt removal and did not permit indefinite delay; evidence conflicted on whether it covered all vehicles.
rule: An undertaking must be clear in content and scope before it can be enforced.
application: Read in the context of Myers J.'s endorsement—which stressed that Waugh had "stalled" for months, that Bentworth's business was at risk, and that Waugh must remove his goods promptly under supervision—the undertaking clearly did not permit indefinite delay, but it was unclear whether it extended to all of Waugh's vehicles, and the evidence on this point conflicted.
conclusion: The scope of the undertaking could not be confidently determined on the motion record.

issue: Was the undertaking breached?
facts: Between June 3 and 23, 2016 Waugh repeatedly failed to attend to remove his goods; Bentworth eventually retained Saulnier to tow vehicles on June 22–23. Waugh alleged some vehicles and contents were removed without consent; Hirshberg deposed Waugh was allowed to keep whatever he wished and directed Saulnier as to what to discard. Saulnier filed no evidence.
rule: Whether a clear undertaking has been breached is a fact-driven inquiry requiring assessment of the parties' conduct.
application: The affidavit evidence was sharply conflicting on what happened on June 22–23 and whether Bentworth prevented Waugh from retaining vehicles he wished to keep. The court could not resolve these credibility-laden factual disputes on the paper record.
conclusion: A trial is required to determine whether the undertaking was breached.

issue: Should the summary declaratory and damages relief be granted?
facts: More than three years after the undertaking and two years after issuing his statement of claim (which did not plead breach of undertaking or seek declaratory relief), Waugh sought an immediate declaration and $180,963 in damages, supported only by his own list and valuation of goods, against defendants who were not all before the court.
rule: Courts retain discretion to refuse declaratory relief (Harrison v. Antonopoulos, 2002 CanLII 28725). Partial summary judgment is a rare procedure reserved for issues readily bifurcated and dealt with expeditiously; it is inappropriate where it risks duplicative proceedings and inconsistent findings (Hryniak; Butera v. Chown, Cairns LLP, 2017 ONCA 783; Mason v. Perras Mongenais, 2018 ONCA 978; Avila v. Couto, 2019 ONSC 400).
application: The relief sought was in substance an advance ruling and partial summary judgment. Any damages had crystallized long ago; Waugh delayed three years; the valuation was disputed ($183,963 vs. $8,100); and the motion would not dispose of the action, since claims against other defendants (including Saulnier) and other causes of action would proceed, raising the risk of duplicative and inconsistent findings.
conclusion: Granting the relief would be inappropriate and contrary to the interests of justice; the motion was dismissed.

issue: Does the zoning by-law prohibiting a place of worship near the resort unjustifiably infringe freedom of religion?
facts: The Chabad Lubavitch organization bought a building on Chemin Desmarais in the TO 820 zone, where places of worship are not permitted, knowing this was a prohibited use. Its worshippers, Orthodox Jews, cannot use motor vehicles on the Sabbath and must pray in a quorum at a synagogue reachable on foot. Some 80% of the worshippers are tourists staying at the Station Mont-Tremblant resort. The by-law authorizes places of worship in 25 zones, several within walking distance of lodging establishments, but none within walking distance of the resort's recreational facilities.
rule: Freedom of religion is protected by s. 2(a) of the Canadian Charter and s. 3 of the Quebec Charter (Big M Drug Mart; Amselem). It includes the right to a place of worship (Congrégation des témoins de Jéhovah de St-Jérôme-Lafontaine v. Lafontaine). To engage the right, a claimant must show a sincere religious belief/practice and that the impugned conduct interferes with it in a more than trivial or insubstantial way (Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem). The right is not absolute; zoning limits necessary to preserve safety, order and the proper use of the territory do not violate freedom of religion (Lafontaine, per LeBel; Val-Morin; Église de Dieu Mont de Sion).
application: The Court accepted that the worshippers sincerely believe they must walk to a synagogue for group prayer on the Sabbath, so the first two Amselem requirements were met. However, the by-law does not prevent that practice: it permits places of worship in numerous zones with lodging within walking distance. What the defendant truly sought was a place of worship near the resort's recreational installations so its adherents could enjoy the ski/vacation site while walking to prayer. That is a personal, recreational choice, not a religious precept, and is not protected by the Charters. The by-law reflects legitimate urban-planning objectives derived from the MRC land-use scheme and the municipal plan (concentrating community uses in the urban and village cores, reserving the resort zones for recreational/tourist uses).
conclusion: The zoning by-law does not infringe the freedom of religion of the defendant or its worshippers.

issue: If there were interference, would it be more than trivial or insubstantial?
facts: Adherents would still have to lodge temporarily near a permitted place of worship or forgo enjoying the resort on the Sabbath; alternative sites within walking distance of lodging exist.
rule: Legislative or administrative action whose effect on religion is negligible or insubstantial does not violate freedom of religion (R. v. Jones; R. v. Edwards Books; Amselem). Churches and members are not exempt from all effort or sacrifice.
application: Even assuming interference, it would merely make the exercise of the religious practice more difficult—requiring worshippers to lodge near a permitted zone—without compromising it. Any such burden is negligible.
conclusion: Any interference would be negligible and would not trigger Charter protection.

issue: Was the municipality obliged to amend the by-law, and is the by-law inopposable to the defendant?
facts: The defendant bought the building knowing the use was prohibited and never sought to relocate, insisting only on a zoning change for Chemin Desmarais. The City repeatedly refused but consistently offered to help the organization relocate to a permitted zone and to consider regulatory amendments elsewhere; the defendant did not pursue this.
rule: Land-use planning decisions fall within municipal expertise and courts will not intervene absent an established, unjustified infringement of freedom of religion assessed under s. 1 of the Canadian Charter/s. 9.1 of the Quebec Charter (Oakes). Positive municipal intervention is required only in exceptional cases where worship would otherwise be impossible on the territory (Lafontaine, per LeBel).
application: Because the by-law provided ample permitted locations within walking distance of lodging, this was not an exceptional case requiring positive intervention. The defendant's intransigence, its purchase without verification, and the City's genuine relocation offers confirmed there was no duty to amend the by-law and no basis to declare it inopposable.
conclusion: The municipality had no obligation to amend the by-law; the request for a declaration of inopposability is dismissed.

issue: Should the mother's access to the children continue to be supervised?
facts: In 1994 TMG made allegations that AAG physically and sexually assaulted the children; an interim trial judge (Braidwood J.) found the allegations wholly untrue and deliberately made, granted custody to AAG, and ordered supervised access. The children's treating child psychiatrist, Dr. Braunstein, testified that supervised access remained essential because the children had lost trust in their mother, who continued to deny responsibility for the false allegations and her substance abuse.
rule: Under the Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 128 and the Divorce Act, access and its conditions are determined by the best interests of the children; a trial judge is not bound by interim findings but cannot ignore well-supported ones.
application: The court accepted Dr. Braunstein's expert opinion that unsupervised access could be very damaging while the mother remained in denial about the harm caused by her false allegations and her substance abuse. The court found TMG not credible, that she continued to spread the allegations, and that the preliminary protective orders had proven to be in the children's best interests. The evidence was insufficient to justify any change to the status quo.
conclusion: Supervised access was continued, with the only addition being supervised telephone contact on birthdays or special occasions.

issue: Should an order of joint guardianship be made?
facts: TMG sought joint guardianship; the record showed her continued denial, lack of insight, and inability to co-parent constructively.
rule: Joint guardianship should only be ordered where it accords with the best interests of the children.
application: Given the findings regarding TMG's conduct and the lack of trust, the court concluded this was not an appropriate case for joint guardianship, but ordered AAG to provide report cards, an annual written medical report, and notice of any medical conditions requiring a physician.
conclusion: Joint guardianship was declined, subject to limited information-sharing obligations on AAG.

issue: Should the order restraining removal of the children from the jurisdiction be continued?
facts: The 1994 order of Dohm J. restrained both parties from removing the children from British Columbia; AAG had to seek variations to take the children to visit his parents in Ontario or vacation out of province.
rule: A restraining order limiting a custodial parent's movement of children should be maintained only where necessary.
application: AAG had custody and no intention of leaving British Columbia, so the restriction served no purpose.
conclusion: The order of Dohm J. was varied to delete the removal restriction.

issue: How should the family assets and liabilities be divided?
facts: At separation, at the time of the s. 57 order (May 1996), and at trial, the family's liabilities consistently exceeded its assets (assets approx. $1.98M, liabilities approx. $2.43M, plus over $500,000 in income tax owing). AAG was near bankruptcy. TMG argued for a half interest in most assets while leaving the debt to AAG.
rule: Family assets and liabilities under the Family Relations Act are to be identified and valued; where liabilities exceed assets there is nothing to distribute, and the burden should not fall disproportionately on one spouse.
application: The court accepted the business valuator's opinions, found several corporate interests had nil value, and determined liabilities exceeded assets at all times. TMG's proposal ignored the staggering debt and lacked foundation. To allow AAG to reduce the debt and avoid bankruptcy, the court ordered corporate assets transferred to AAG, the Qualicum Beach property and both apartments sold, the West Vancouver home declared AAG's with no interest to TMG, and RRSP trust funds applied to liabilities.
conclusion: There were no net assets to distribute; the court made a series of orders to sell properties and apply proceeds to debt, leaving each party to pay debts in their own name.

issue: What amount of spousal maintenance should be ordered?
facts: AAG had net income of about $240,000 but a monthly deficit of nearly $14,000 given his debt servicing, private school, and nanny costs. TMG had received $3,500/month (said to be net of tax) plus an $874/month disability pension and lived rent-free at the Butterball property; she sought $6,000/month retroactive to 1996.
rule: Spousal maintenance is fixed having regard to need, means, and the circumstances of the parties; a disability pension does not itself establish inability to work.
application: The court found no reason to change the existing arrangement given TMG's rent-free accommodation and AAG's crushing debt, and that her work capacity could not be assessed until she relocated after the Butterball property sold.
conclusion: Spousal maintenance was continued at $3,500 per month, subject to being revisited once the Butterball property was sold and family liabilities addressed.

issue: Does an individual strata lot owner have standing under the Strata Property Act to sue on matters belonging to the strata corporation or against council members outside the conflict-of-interest provisions?
facts: Mr. Wong, a co-owner of a unit in Strata Plan LMS 2461, brought numerous claims against the property manager, individual council members, and the strata corporation alleging mismanagement of common property, records, funds, parking, cameras and other affairs. The strata corporation did not authorize the action.
rule: Under the Strata Property Act, s. 2 creates the strata corporation as a separate legal entity, s. 3 makes it (not individual owners) responsible for common property, and s. 171 requires a ¾-vote resolution for the corporation to sue. Section 164 permits an owner to sue only where the corporation's conduct is 'significantly unfair' to that owner in particular (Ang v. Spectra Management Services, 2002 BCSC 1544); Hamilton v. Ball, 2006 BCCA 243 allows an owner to sue a third party only for injury to the owner's proportionate share of common property; ss. 32–33 (per Dockside Brewing Co. v. Strata Plan LMS 3837, 2007 BCCA 183) allow an owner to sue a council member only for breach of the conflict-of-interest provisions.
application: An individual owner's standing is confined to (1) a s. 164 claim of conduct 'significantly unfair' to him particularly, (2) the Hamilton v. Ball exception for his proportionate share of common property injured by a third party, and (3) s. 32 conflict-of-interest claims against council members. Most of Mr. Wong's claims concerned losses to the strata corporation, enforcement of the corporation's management contract, or grievances not framed as significantly unfair to him or as council conflicts of interest, so he lacked standing.
conclusion: The owner lacked standing to advance the great majority of the claims, which belonged only to the strata corporation or fell outside ss. 32–33.

issue: Does filing a response to civil claim preclude a later Rule 9-5(1) application to strike?
facts: The defendants had filed a response to the civil claim before applying to strike; the plaintiff argued this barred the application.
rule: Rule 9-5(1) permits an application to strike 'at any stage of a proceeding,' meaning up to and including trial and entry of judgment (R&J Siever Holdings v. Sunridge, 2007 BCSC 632; Hundal v. Border Carrier Ltd., 2011 BCSC 1703).
application: The Court found no authority in the Rules or case law prohibiting a strike application after a response is filed; Hundal shows such an order may be made even on the first day of trial.
conclusion: The plaintiff's preliminary objection failed; the application to strike was properly brought.

issue: Which claims should be struck as disclosing no reasonable claim or as unnecessary/vexatious, and which may proceed or be amended?
facts: The 48-page notice of civil claim (and a second action, No. 145263) advanced claims about ash bins, common-property alterations, water ingress in another unit, security/surveillance cameras, records access, reimbursement of payments, parking, council hearings, defamation, assault, AGM voting, keyfob deactivation and more.
rule: Rule 9-5(1) allows striking where a pleading discloses no reasonable claim, is unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, or is an abuse of process; the test is whether it is 'plain and obvious' the claim must fail (Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse, 2003 SCC 69; Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., [1990] 2 SCR 959), with doubt resolved in favour of allowing the pleading to stand (BC (Director of Civil Forfeiture) v. Flynn, 2013 BCCA 91).
application: Applying the standing limits, the Court struck and dismissed nearly all claims as either belonging to the strata corporation, outside ss. 32–33, or disclosing no cause of action. Exceptions: the disbursement/reimbursement payments to Eddie Chu (NOCC paras. 98–99, $727.80) could arguably be an unreasonable/unfair conflict transaction under ss. 32–33 and were not dismissed; the defamation claims (March 16 and August 27, 2011 minutes) and the assault claim against Eddie Chu could proceed only if properly amended to comply with the Rules and plead injury.
conclusion: The application was largely granted: most claims in both actions were struck and dismissed, with the Eddie Chu payment claim preserved and the defamation and assault claims left open to amendment. Defendants awarded costs, with submissions on scale to follow.

issue: What quality and sufficiency of evidence is required on a summary judgment motion in a child protection case seeking Crown wardship without access?
facts: The society moved for summary judgment for Crown wardship without access of a 4½-year-old child already found in need of protection, relying on affidavits of a family services worker; neither the mother nor the maternal grandparents appeared, making the motion effectively unopposed.
rule: Rule 16 of the Family Law Rules makes summary judgment available in child protection cases, but the remedy must be invoked with caution, especially for Crown wardship without access (CAS of Halton Region v. A.; CAS of Hamilton v. W.). Subrules 14(18)-(19) require affidavit information to be within the deponent's personal knowledge, with a narrow hearsay exception requiring the source be named and believed true; subrule 16(4)-(5) requires 'admissible' evidence setting out specific facts and permits the court to draw unfavourable conclusions from non-personal-knowledge evidence. Evidence on summary judgment should be of a level and quality that could withstand the rigour of trial (Huron-Perth CAS v. C.H.).
application: The court synthesized the divergent case law (paras 52) and held it must act as gatekeeper: affidavits should be concise, within personal knowledge, contain the full trial-worthy evidentiary record, and any hearsay must satisfy necessity and reliability (the 'MacKenzie' approach) with the source named and believed true. Summary judgment, particularly for Crown wardship, demands the highest standard of admissible evidence and procedural fairness.
conclusion: The court articulated a thirteen-point framework for the evidence required on a summary judgment motion, emphasizing caution and admissibility for Crown wardship without access.

issue: Was the society's affidavit evidence admissible and sufficient to support Crown wardship without access?
facts: The supporting affidavit incorporated an earlier affidavit and exhibits, contained multiple layers of hearsay, opinion evidence from unnamed or anonymous sources (e.g., 'Susan Sorrell', 'Safe Kids', 'Dr. Roy'), attached third-party reports without a basis for admission, included an inadmissible mental-health report the parties had agreed not to rely on, and lacked focus or thematic organization.
rule: Merely attaching third-party reports to an affidavit does not make their contents admissible; hearsay requires compliance with subrule 14(19) and the necessity/reliability test; affidavits must avoid conclusions, opinion, and scandalous or irrelevant material (Lisanti; Evans v. Evans and Finkenzeller; CAS of Toronto v. S.). The record must address the mandatory statutory inquiries under ss. 56, 57(2)-(4) and 59 of the Child and Family Services Act.
application: The court found the affidavit was 'a jungle of inadmissible and multiple hearsay observations,' inadmissible opinion from unnamed sources, with no attempt to establish a basis for admission (e.g., business records) and no compliance with subrule 16(5). It failed to include a statutory plan of care under s. 56 and offered no evidence on the mandatory inquiries under ss. 57(2)-(4) and 59. The information was unfocused, making it impossible to draw a line from the material to a finding of Crown wardship.
conclusion: The evidence was inadmissible, deficient, and insufficient; the record was 'an unfortunate constellation of errors' that could not support the relief.

issue: Should the motion be granted simply because it was unopposed?
facts: Society counsel argued that because the relief was unopposed the court should simply make the order sought; the mother did not oppose and the grandparents had not appeared since July 2010.
rule: Even on an unopposed motion, the court retains a gatekeeping role and must be satisfied that a sound admissible evidentiary basis exists; procedural fairness demands the record reveal a sound basis for the relief, and best interests of the child require caution for Crown wardship.
application: The court declined to make the order on the deficient material, instead adjourning for a 'better' affidavit and confirmed service on the grandparents, rejecting the submission that the unopposed nature of the motion cured the evidentiary shortcomings.
conclusion: The court refused to grant Crown wardship on the record and adjourned the motion for proper evidence and confirmed service.

issue: Does the statement of claim disclose a reasonable cause of action under s. 7 of the Charter arising from a professional licensing examination requirement?
facts: Shaulov applied for a licence to practise law, failed the Barrister Licensing Examination four times, and was deemed to have abandoned his application. He pleaded that the psychometric Licensing Examinations breached his liberty and security of the person, including his psychological integrity, and impaired his ability to upgrade his profession as a tax auditor.
rule: On a Rule 21.01(1)(b) motion a pleading is struck only if it is plain and obvious it discloses no reasonable cause of action (Potis Holdings; McCreight). Section 7 requires pleading a deprivation of life, liberty or security of the person contrary to fundamental justice (Ogiamen). Liberty protects fundamental personal choices, not economic interests, and s. 7 does not protect the right to practise a profession (Malmo-Levine; Siemens; Mussani; Tanase). Security of the person requires a serious and profound effect on psychological integrity greater than ordinary stress (G.(J.); Blencoe).
application: The court held the pleaded s. 7 violation was in substance about the right to practise a chosen profession, which is not protected. Writing a licensing examination, even a psychometric one, is undertaken voluntarily to pursue a profession and does not interfere with fundamental personal choices or constitute a serious psychological incursion assessed objectively. Any stress from voluntarily writing the exams does not amount to state interference with security of the person.
conclusion: The s. 7 claim discloses no reasonable cause of action and is struck without leave to amend.

issue: Does the s. 15 Charter claim disclose a cause of action and does the plaintiff have standing to allege discrimination on grounds of cognitive disability, perceived disability, and racial/ethnic/cultural background?
facts: The plaintiff, a naturalized Canadian of West Asian (Persian/Russian/Uzbek Jewish) origin, alleged the exams discriminate based on cognitive disability, perceived cognitive disability, and racial/ethnic/cultural background. In particulars he confirmed he does not have a cognitive disability.
rule: A s. 15 claim requires material facts showing (1) a distinction based on an enumerated/analogous ground and (2) that it reinforces, perpetuates or exacerbates disadvantage (Meekis). Private interest standing requires a personal, direct interest (Carroll); public interest standing is assessed on the Downtown Eastside factors (serious justiciable issue, real stake, reasonable and effective means).
application: On cognitive disability, the plaintiff lacks private interest standing (he has no such disability) and public interest standing is declined under the Downtown Eastside factors. The 'perceived disability' claim is circular and unsupported—he does not plead anyone believed him disabled or that he was treated differently on that basis. The racial/ethnic/cultural claim pleads no material facts on differential impact or perpetuation of disadvantage, but it is not a clearest case for denying amendment since he may plead further true facts.
conclusion: The disability and perceived-disability s. 15 claims are struck without leave; the racial/ethnic/cultural s. 15 claim is struck with leave to amend, limited to characteristics the plaintiff shares. The court rejected the s. 15(2) argument as unsuited to a no-evidence motion.

issue: Should the Human Rights Code claims be struck, including as against the private Non-LSO defendants?
facts: The plaintiff claimed breaches of ss. 6, 10(3) and 11(1) of the Code against the LSO and against PAG and its directors (private actors), and sought monetary compensation under s. 46.1(1).
rule: A Code discrimination claim requires a protected characteristic, adverse impact, and the characteristic being a factor (Anoquot). Section 46.1(2) bars a civil action based solely on an infringement of a Part I right. Under s. 32 of the Charter, private actors not performing governmental functions are not bound by the Charter (Eldridge).
application: The disability-based Code claims are struck for the same reasons as under s. 15. The racial/ethnic/cultural Code claim is struck with leave to amend against the LSO only, but is viable only if a s. 15 cause of action also survives, because s. 46.1(2) bars a stand-alone Code action. Against the Non-LSO defendants, no valid Charter claim can lie and the only claim is under the Code, which s. 46.1(2) bars; they are also not necessary parties merely to obtain discovery.
conclusion: Code claims against the Non-LSO defendants (and those defendants) are struck without leave; the racial/ethnic/cultural Code claim against the LSO is struck with leave to amend contingent on a viable s. 15 claim.

issue: Does the Superior Court have jurisdiction over the plaintiff's non-Charter claims that the Licensing Examinations are ultra vires the Law Society Act and other judicial-review-type relief?
facts: The plaintiff sought declarations that the exams were ultra vires and unreasonable, an order setting aside the October 1, 2020 decision, and orders compelling an assessment interview and issuance of a licence—relief in the nature of certiorari, mandamus and declaratory review of a statutory power.
rule: Section 6(1) of the Judicial Review Procedure Act requires applications for judicial review to be made to the Divisional Court, absent urgency. The Divisional Court has exclusive jurisdiction over challenges to the exercise of a statutory power and ultra vires declarations (Alford; Di Cienzo; J.N. v. Durham; Bard).
application: The non-Charter claims seek mandamus, certiorari and declaratory relief regarding the LSO's exercise of a statutory power and are properly the subject of judicial review in the Divisional Court. Despite Justice Corbett's earlier transfer directing a statement of claim within Superior Court jurisdiction, these claims fall outside that jurisdiction; the plaintiff again misunderstood the available procedure. The court declined to strike them for want of a cause of action, instead convening a case conference regarding a possible transfer.
conclusion: The Superior Court lacks jurisdiction over the non-Charter claims; the Divisional Court has exclusive jurisdiction. A case conference was scheduled to address next steps.

issue: Does the Freeholders top lease breach the rule against perpetuities on its proper construction?
facts: On 7 August 1950 Taylor Senior granted Freeholders a lease of the minerals 'UPON AND IN THE EVENT OF the termination, cancellation, avoidance or expiration' of the prior Imperial Oil lease, to have and enjoy for 99 years. There was no life in being, so the interest had to vest within 21 years of the grant. The Imperial lease might have continued indefinitely 'so long thereafter as' substances were produced, so the top lease might vest more than 21 years after 1950.
rule: The modern rule against perpetuities (Gray): 'No interest is good unless it must vest, if at all, not later than twenty-one years after some life in being at the creation of the interest.' Validity is tested by possibilities at the date of the instrument, not actualities; the instrument is construed by ordinary rules of construction, favouring early vesting, before the rule is applied (Anger and Honsberger; Canadian Long Island Petroleums v. Irving Industries).
application: The trial judge and the dissent (Jackson J.A.) read the words 'upon' and 'in the event' as connoting time and condition, so that no interest was granted until the Imperial lease terminated — an uncertain event that might occur outside the 21-year period. The 99-year 'to have and to enjoy' clause fixed only a maximum duration, not immediate vesting, and the recitals, ss. 3-4 (payment on the 'effective date') and the 1961 agreement confirmed future, contingent vesting. American authorities (Peveto v. Starkey; Hammans) held similar wording void. The majority proceeded on the assumption that a mechanistic application of the rule would void the lease and did not decide the construction point, expressly preserving it.
conclusion: The dissent held the top lease offends the rule and is void; the majority assumed, without deciding, that a rigid application of the rule would void it, leaving the interpretation grounds for possible future appeal.

issue: May the court decline to apply the rule against perpetuities to a commercial top lease that does not offend the policy behind the rule, or must reform be left to the legislature?
facts: Top leases are an accepted and widespread practice in the Saskatchewan oil and gas industry (hundreds of leases, hundreds of thousands of acres). This top lease had been relied on for 50 years and, on the trial judge's finding, encouraged rather than fettered commercial development. The Saskatchewan Law Reform Commission recommended abolition of the rule; a bill to abolish it died on the order paper in 1995.
rule: Courts may make incremental changes to judge-made common law to keep it in step with changing social and economic conditions, but complex changes with uncertain ramifications should be left to the legislature (R. v. Salituro; Watkins v. Olafson; Winnipeg Child and Family Services; Tolofson v. Jensen; Morguard; Arthur J.S. Hall v. Simons). The rule against perpetuities rests on public policy against fettering alienability of property (Halsbury's; Cheshire).
application: The majority (Tallis and Sherstobitoff JJ.A.) held that the socio-economic conditions that spawned the rule no longer exist, that top leases promote drilling and alienability rather than tying up land, and that the rule was never intended to reach such commercial transactions; the genius of the common law lies in its adaptiveness, so an exception could be made where a rigid application would defeat the rule's purpose. Jackson J.A., in dissent, held the rule is a firmly embedded rule of property whose modification could affect hundreds of leases and raise unmanageable issues of retrospectivity; given the legislature's deliberate inaction, such a change should be left to Parliament, not the courts.
conclusion: By majority, the court intervened and held the top lease was not rendered void by the rule against perpetuities; the appeal was allowed and the action for a declaration of voidness dismissed. Jackson J.A. would have dismissed the appeal.

issue: Did Maxx breach a duty of confidence, and what remedy is warranted?
facts: Tarragon disclosed to Maxx the only available copy of the 1950 top lease for the limited purpose of Maxx's due-diligence review under a proposed farmout. Maxx instead used the document to conclude the lease was void and negotiated its own lease with Taylor, to Tarragon's detriment.
rule: Breach of confidence requires (1) confidential information, (2) communicated in confidence, and (3) misused by the recipient (Lac Minerals Ltd. v. International Corona Resources Ltd.). Remedies include constructive trust, accounting of profits and damages; damages require causation restoring the confider to its 'but for' position (Cadbury Schweppes v. FBI Foods).
application: The trial judge found all three elements met and imposed a constructive trust, an accounting and damages. On the cross-appeal, Jackson J.A. held damages were unavailable because Tarragon's lease was void in any event, so Maxx did not cause its loss; a constructive trust was inappropriate given Taylor's freedom to contract with Maxx and the low value of the interest. An accounting of profits to trial adequately denounced the wrong without over-penalizing Maxx. The majority found the cross-appeal moot given its disposition on the perpetuities question but preserved it for future consideration.
conclusion: Per Jackson J.A., the cross-appeal was allowed to set aside the constructive trust and damages, leaving only an accounting of profits to trial; on the majority's disposition the cross-appeal was moot but preserved.

issue: Should the action be dismissed under rule 2.1.01 as frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process?
facts: The self-represented plaintiff sued Food Basics (and its parent Metro) and His Majesty the King (RCMP and CSIS) for damages for 'attempted murder; pain and suffering; mental trauma and torture.' He alleged that after consuming two cans of Caribbean non-alcoholic beer and two nutritional supplements purchased at Food Basics his beverages had been 'spiked with crystal meth' by the RCMP and CSIS as part of a 41–43 year campaign of surveillance, home invasions and harassment against him, with grocery store staff acting as 'proxies.' The registrar referred the matter under rule 2.1.01(7); the plaintiff was given notice and filed a ten-page written submission.
rule: Rule 2.1.01 of the Rules of Civil Procedure permits the court to stay or dismiss a proceeding that appears on its face to be frivolous or vexatious or otherwise an abuse of process. Per Gao v. Ontario (WSIB), 2014 ONSC 6100 and Scaduto v. Law Society of Upper Canada, 2015 ONCA 733, the rule is not for close calls but is to be robustly applied to nip clearly meritless proceedings in the bud. A frivolous proceeding lacks legal basis or merit and will inevitably fail (Van Sluytman; Gill v. MacIver, 2023 ONCA 776; Lavallee v. Isak, 2022 ONCA 290; Pickard); a vexatious proceeding is one taken to annoy or embarrass or conducted in a vexatious manner.
application: The court found the statement of claim confusing, devoid of material facts, and resting on conclusory assertions incapable of belief — essentially a 'wild conspiracy theory' of state agents spiking his drinks and invading his home for over 40 years. The formatting (full caps, bold, underlining, rhetorical questions, attached photos and an email to himself) was typical of frivolous proceedings. The plaintiff's written submissions, alleging a transgenerational campaign by CSIS/RCMP/Mossad tied to 'Zionist' interests, did not persuade the court otherwise and instead confirmed the action was both frivolous and would be conducted in a vexatious manner. The action lacked legal basis and would inevitably fail while consuming disproportionate court resources.
conclusion: The court was satisfied the action was frivolous and vexatious and dismissed the proceeding under rule 2.1.01(1), without costs.

issue: Did the plaintiff and the estate abuse the judicial process, entitling the defendants to reimbursement of fees and punitive damages under arts. 51-54 C.p.c.?
facts: Following her father's death, Rhonda Sofaer, a residuary trust beneficiary and later co-liquidator, launched proceedings in 2013 based on an erroneous legal opinion that the trusts could be wound up in her favour. Over nearly ten years she obtained two seizures before judgment (both quashed for insufficiency), amended her claim five times, generated an 18-page docket requiring over 15 judges, filed multiple rejected expert reports, and ultimately refused to attend the trial after making grave fraud and theft accusations against the liquidators and professionals. Numerous forensic accountants she retained found no fault with the defendants.
rule: Articles 51-54 C.p.c. permit a court to declare proceedings abusive and, under art. 54 C.p.c., to condemn a party to pay damages including the other party's fees and disbursements, and where warranted punitive damages. Article 1621 C.c.Q. governs the assessment of punitive damages (preventive function, gravity of fault, patrimonial situation, avoidance of double indemnity); the Supreme Court in Cinar Corporation c. Robinson, 2013 SCC 73, cautions that punitive damages be awarded with restraint.
application: The court found the length of the docket, the persistence of serious unproven accusations, the repeated quashed seizures and rejected expertises, and the ultimate refusal to appear at trial (after the claim was already dismissed for lack of evidence) established abusive conduct by both Mme Sofaer and the estate acting at her behest. Analogizing to the Jetté/Rosenbloom/Groupe Sutton c. Blouin line, the court ordered reimbursement of the defendants' defence fees, while noting Mme Sofaer's limited means. Because the proceedings that led to Mr. Mashaal's removal as liquidator were justified (per Justice Roy's findings), his abuse recovery excluded the destitution-related account.
conclusion: The conduct was declared abusive; Rhonda Sofaer and the estate were condemned solidarily to reimburse the professional defence fees of Wiener (18,745$ + 89,450.69$), Benchimol (102,639.60$), Vitaro (55,117.74$), Schrier (54,811.84$) and Mashaal (97,007$), with punitive damages addressed individually.

issue: Did Mme Sofaer defame the defendants and injure their reputations through unfounded complaints and publications, and what damages result?
facts: Mme Sofaer filed complaints with the Ordre des CPA against Wiener and with the Barreau syndic against Benchimol, both dismissed after investigation, accusing them of fraud and misappropriating about $1 million using blank cheques she had signed. She also complained to police against Benchimol and Vitaro and was the evident source of defamatory internet publications ('Frank Report') attacking Benchimol, Vitaro and Mashaal, containing intimate details only she could have supplied, read by relatives in Europe.
rule: Defamation in Quebec requires fault, injury and causation (art. 1457 C.c.Q.). Article 193.1 of the Code des professions grants immunity for good-faith complaints to a syndic, codifying the requirement of proof of bad faith (Bélair c. V.B.; Hert c. Dufour); liability arises where the complainant acted with intent to harm, unjustified recklessness or gross negligence. Punitive damages under the Quebec Charter require an intentional interference (Québec (Curateur public) c. Syndicat national des employés de l'hôpital St-Ferdinand), assessed per art. 1621 C.c.Q.
application: The court found the fraud and theft accusations were never substantiated, that Mme Sofaer persisted (even seeking review of the syndic's decision) and was therefore in bad faith, defeating any immunity. The complaints and internet publications caused reputational harm and moral prejudice to Wiener, Benchimol, Vitaro, Schrier and Mashaal, and the attacks were deliberate and intended to harm, satisfying the criteria for punitive damages. Awards were calibrated by reference to comparable cases (Brunet c. Segal; Blank c. Blank; D.H. c. I.D.) and moderated given the difficulty of quantifying moral damages and doubts about deterrence given Mme Sofaer's means.
conclusion: Defamation established; Rhonda Sofaer was condemned to pay moral and punitive damages: Wiener 25,000$/10,000$; Benchimol 35,000$/15,000$; Vitaro 35,000$/15,000$; Schrier 10,000$/5,000$; Mashaal 25,000$/10,000$. The estate was also condemned to pay outstanding professional fees to Wiener (54,791.34$) and Vitaro (23,973.70$).

issue: Does the referee have jurisdiction to decide post-separation adjustments incurred before trial, or are such claims barred by res judicata?
facts: Paragraph 10 of Justice McLean's order (after an eight-day 2013 trial of all issues) directed a $493,000 NFP adjustment and provided that jointly owned property that could not be divided or transferred in kind 'shall be sold in the normal course with directions to be given by the master.' A consent order of October 23, 2014 sent issues about jointly owned property and division of sale proceeds to the reference. The parties sought numerous credits, many for expenses paid before trial.
rule: Res judicata prevents relitigation of claims that were or could have been raised in an earlier proceeding, absent clear language carving out an issue for later determination. Post-separation adjustments are typically decided at trial (Lazarevic v. Lazarevic, 2014 ONSC 7348; Laing v. Mahmoud, 2011 ONSC 4047). A referee's jurisdiction is limited to that conferred by the order of reference; clear language is required to preserve pre-trial adjustments for later determination by someone other than the trial judge.
application: The referee held that paragraph 10 empowers him to oversee the sale of jointly owned properties and to adjudicate claims and adjustments for costs to preserve, maintain and carry joint assets, but only for costs incurred after trial, since the power to give directions implicitly includes post-trial adjustments. Costs incurred before trial should have been raised at the 2013 trial; nothing in Justice McLean's order clearly carved them out for later determination, so they are caught by res judicata. He left open the possibility of the parties seeking clarification from Justice McLean within four months.
conclusion: Post-separation adjustments for costs incurred before June 3, 2013 are subject to res judicata; the referee's jurisdiction extends only to post-trial adjustments and division of sale proceeds, subject to any clarification from Justice McLean.

issue: Is the Applicant entitled to a credit for the post-separation carrying costs of the matrimonial home?
facts: The parties separated June 6, 2010; the Respondent left the matrimonial home with the five children July 1, 2011. The Applicant remained in the home until its court-ordered sale closed January 29, 2015, paying occupational expenses but stopping mortgage payments June 2014, prompting the bank's power-of-sale proceedings. He sought credits for mortgage, insurance and municipal taxes; the Respondent never claimed occupational rent, understanding it was offset by the Applicant's payments.
rule: Factors governing occupational rent in Rezel v. Rezel, 2007 CanLII 12716 (ON SC) apply by analogy; occupational rent is exceptional relief, and carrying costs and living expenses may offset one another, including any occupational-rent claim (Lazarevic v. Lazarevic, 2014 ONSC 7348 at para. 123).
application: Weighing the Rezel factors, the referee found several favoured the Respondent: the children resided primarily with her, the Applicant paid essentially no child support, and the occupying Applicant did not preserve or increase the home's value (it sold well below the 2013 appraisals). The Respondent would likely have succeeded in claiming occupational rent, which was foregone in lieu of the Applicant's carrying costs. Applying Lazarevic, these costs and any occupational rent essentially offset one another.
conclusion: The Applicant is not entitled to any credit for the post-separation carrying costs of the matrimonial home; the claim is offset by the unclaimed occupational rent.

issue: How should the proceeds of sale of the jointly owned properties be accounted for and adjusted between the parties?
facts: Ms. Huggan, the court-appointed real estate lawyer, sold the matrimonial home and paid tax arrears, mortgage, the Applicant's personal legal-fee executions (Gowlings, SullivanLaw), commissions and other amounts from the proceeds, leaving $122,247.27 in trust. Other jointly owned assets included the Aerolite trailer (conditional sale contract and RBC loan in both names) and the 9 Birchview rooming house, managed and occupied by the Applicant who kept all rental income.
rule: Amounts paid from sale proceeds that are properly the obligation of only one owner must be adjusted so that the balance reflects the parties' true entitlements; a joint owner who declines to use a jointly owned asset is not thereby relieved of the loan and carrying costs; expenses of a solely managed income property should be borne by the managing owner.
application: The referee ordered numerous adjustments to Dr. Silver's 50% share to ensure Mr. Silver alone bore taxes, mortgage, his personal legal executions and Enbridge arrears, while sharing genuine joint costs (commissions, mortgagee's legal fees). The trailer was found jointly owned; half of post-trial payments made by Mr. Silver were subtracted from Dr. Silver's share. As Mr. Silver managed and occupied the rooming house rent-free and kept its net income (exceeding his imputed support income per Silver v. Silver, 2015 ONSC 3816), he was made responsible for all its post-separation expenses, roof repairs and tax arrears, with corresponding adjustments. Outstanding costs orders were credited to or subtracted from the NFP adjustment.
conclusion: The referee ordered a detailed schedule of credits added to and subtracted from Dr. Silver's 50% share of the proceeds, allocating one-owner obligations to Mr. Silver, and directed Mr. Silver to continue managing and funding the rooming house pending sale, with final accounting to follow.

issue: Was the T.A.Q.'s decision refusing reimbursement manifestly unreasonable so as to justify judicial review under arts. 846 ff. C.C.P.?
facts: Stein was diagnosed with colon cancer that spread to his liver. The recommended liver surgery scheduled at St-Luc Hospital in Montréal was repeatedly cancelled between January and April 1996 as 'elective', past the 4–8 week safe window unanimously recognized by the medical experts. Stein obtained treatment in New York; two years later he was cancer-free. The T.A.Q. upheld the Régie's refusal to reimburse.
rule: The Superior Court exercises restraint and deference toward specialized tribunals such as the T.A.Q. and intervenes only where the decision is patently unreasonable — 'clearly irrational' (A.G. Canada v. P.S.A.C., [1993] 1 S.C.R. 941; Domtar; Pezim; Southam). A decision is reviewable where there is no rational link between the evidence retained and the conclusions drawn (Paccar; Tremblay v. C.A.L.P.).
application: The T.A.Q. acknowledged (para. 72) that all experts agreed the liver surgery had to be performed within 4–6 weeks, yet concluded the Régie acted reasonably because Stein only requested New York treatment in April. This ignored that the April request arose precisely because Montréal surgery was repeatedly cancelled and the danger increased daily. The Court found this conclusion irrational and unsupported by, indeed contrary to, the proof and the purpose of the Health Insurance Act.
conclusion: The decision was patently unreasonable; the Court intervened and annulled it.

issue: Did the T.A.Q. err in finding the treatments were available in Canada or experimental under the Health Insurance Act?
facts: The first operation (liver resection) was available in Montréal but not performed in time. The second operation combined cryosurgery and the insertion of an Infusaid pump for intra-hepatic chemotherapy; all parties admitted these treatments were not available together anywhere in Canada, and the Régie's own doctor acknowledged the pump was unavailable in Canada owing to cost.
rule: Section 10 of the Health Insurance Act (R.S.Q. c. A-29) permits reimbursement of insured services obtained outside Québec only where not available in Canada; s. 3 covers services that are 'medically required', excluding experimental procedures.
application: The T.A.Q. treated the Infusaid pump as experimental merely because it was unknown to and had no standard within the Canadian medical community. The Court held this reasoning tautological: any procedure not performed in Canada would automatically be 'experimental' and 'unknown', which is irrational and would defeat coverage of all procedures regularly performed abroad. The follow-up surgery necessarily had to be done by Dr. Daly, and the treatments were uncontradictedly life-saving and unavailable in Canada.
conclusion: The T.A.Q.'s findings on availability and the experimental nature of the treatments were irrational and unsupported by the evidence.

issue: Did the T.A.Q. breach the rules of natural justice?
facts: The T.A.Q. relied on hearsay medical opinions referenced in Dr. Vigeant's April 1996 letters, treating the referenced doctors as 'witnesses', and after taking the matter under advisement rejected Stein's account of the April 2nd cancellation based on the St-Luc file without calling his surgeon, Dr. Roy.
rule: Administrative tribunals must respect the rules of natural justice; a decision resting on hearsay and on rejecting sworn testimony without affording an opportunity to address contradictory material may be reviewable.
application: The Court found the T.A.Q. relied on hearsay medical evidence and, without hearing Dr. Roy, concluded Stein's testimony about the cancellations was false — a conclusion incomprehensible given the tribunal's own earlier acknowledgement (paras. 18–19) that the surgery had been repeatedly postponed.
conclusion: These failings reinforced the conclusion that the decision could not stand.

issue: What remedy is appropriate?
facts: Stein sought either a substituted order for monetary reimbursement or referral back to the Régie for reassessment.
rule: On judicial review under arts. 846 ff. C.C.P., the Court may annul the impugned decision and remit the matter for reassessment rather than substitute its own valuation where quantification falls within the administrative body's function.
application: Though sympathetic to Stein, the Court held it was not in a position to substitute a monetary condemnation against the Régie; instead it ordered the Régie to accept the claim and reassess its value under the law and regulations.
conclusion: Motion in evocation granted; decision annulled; Régie ordered to accept and assess the claims, with costs.

issue: Were the defendant's allegations of family violence in divorce proceedings and her police complaints actionable defamation, or protected by relative immunity?
facts: Following two altercations during child pick-ups on February 20 and 27, 2012, A.M. described violent conduct by V.S. in an Access Revocation Motion and made police complaints; V.S. later gave an undertaking to keep the peace under s. 810 and admitted his ex-wife had reason to fear him. He alleged she intentionally portrayed him as violent to gain leverage in the divorce.
rule: Under the doctrine and jurisprudence reviewed in Bureau c. Bouchard, defamatory allegations made in legal proceedings are actionable only where they are false, irrelevant to the dispute, and made maliciously or at least without reasonable and probable cause; a witness/party enjoys a relative immunity (Gagné c. Galand; Baudouin & Deslauriers) so that participants may speak frankly without fear of suit.
application: The Court found A.M.'s version of the February 2012 events more credible than V.S.'s, that her allegations were relevant to the access issue and supported by reasonable grounds (including his own admission and the video consistent with an assault on her). V.S. produced no palpable evidence of fault or malice; his own sincerity in the divorce was doubtful, and the Superior Court had found his conduct abusive.
conclusion: The statements were protected by relative immunity and not actionable; V.S. failed to prove their malicious character, so the defamation claim failed.

issue: Was the part of the claim based on the criminal accusations prescribed?
facts: V.S. learned of A.M.'s police complaint immediately during her February 27, 2012 911 call and was arrested that evening; he instituted the action on March 5, 2013.
rule: Defamation actions are subject to a one-year prescription running from the day the person became aware of the defamation (art. 2929 C.C.Q.; Gille c. Placements Diar inc.).
application: Because V.S. was aware of the alleged defamatory complaint on February 27, 2012, prescription began then and expired before the March 5, 2013 institution of proceedings.
conclusion: That part of the claim was prescribed.

issue: Did the defendant assault the plaintiff, entitling him to damages for bodily harm and moral prejudice?
facts: V.S. alleged A.M. struck his forearm with a car door on February 27, 2012 and later attributed injuries also to a strip-search and assault by a Neo-Nazi co-detainee while in police custody. A low-resolution silent surveillance video showed the car-door altercation ambiguously.
rule: The plaintiff bears the burden of proving fault, injury and causation on the balance of probabilities.
application: The video was consistent with A.M. having been pushed back by the larger V.S. and returning to protect her child, and did not adequately prove an assault by her; any injury from detention could not be causally linked to the February 27 event.
conclusion: The plaintiff did not discharge his burden; the assault claim failed.

issue: Was the plaintiff's action abusive, warranting extrajudicial costs and punitive damages on the cross-demand?
facts: V.S. sued A.M. for her participation in legitimate divorce proceedings and police complaints; the divorce was conducted in camera, and a Superior Court judgment had found V.S.'s conduct in the divorce abusive.
rule: Legal proceedings taken to silence an opponent asserting rights may constitute abuse (arts. 54.1 and following C.C.P.; Viel c. Entreprises immobilières du terroir Ltée), permitting recovery of extrajudicial costs and punitive damages, notably where a suit functions as a SLAPP ('poursuite bâillon').
application: The Court found the defamation and false-complaint aspects proceeded from an obvious intention to discourage A.M. from maintaining positions she had every right to take, amounting to a private SLAPP; the assault claim, though not frivolous on its face, was inseparable from and used to prosecute this improper objective, rendering the proceedings a misguided nuisance.
conclusion: Cross-demand allowed in part: V.S. condemned to pay $15,000 in extrajudicial costs as abuse-of-process damages and $5,000 in punitive damages.

issue: Do the balcony restrictions in the declaration of co-ownership infringe the respondents' freedom of religion and equality rights under the Quebec Charter?
facts: The respondents, Orthodox Jewish co-owners in a luxury Montréal condominium (the 'Sanctuaire du Mont-Royal'), erected succahs on their balconies to celebrate Soukot. The declaration of co-ownership (arts. 2.6.3, 6.5, 6.16, 9.3) barred any construction, closure, decoration or placement of objects other than usual outdoor furniture on balconies, which are common portions reserved for exclusive use. Two rabbis testified: Rabbi Levy said Jewish law imposes no obligation to own one's own succah or to place it at a particular location — proximity is a matter of convenience; Rabbi Ohana emphasized a more subjective view tied to the 'spirit' of the festival.
rule: Under the Quebec Charter (arts. 3, 10, 13) discriminatory contractual clauses, including indirect/adverse-effect discrimination (O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears), are without effect. Freedom of religion (R. v. Big M Drug Mart) protects sincerely held beliefs and the observance of essential practices demanded by one's religion; a court may not assess the validity of a belief but must verify its sincerity and the existence of a genuine religious precept (Jones v. R.; R. v. Edwards Books — trivial or insignificant burdens are not infringements). The claimed practice must retain a rational, reasonable and direct link to the religious teaching, not a purely subjective conception.
application: The court found the restrictions clearly prohibited erecting a succah and were validly justified by the destination, characteristics and situation of the building under art. 1056 C.c.Q., and were applied uniformly (no discriminatory application established). On religion, the court preferred Rabbi Levy's evidence: there is a consensus that Jewish law imposes no obligation to build one's own succah on one's own balcony; location is a matter of convenience. The respondents' past conduct (using others' succahs, travelling elsewhere) corroborated this. Rabbi Ohana's subjective 'spirit of the festival' approach could not ground a religious freedom claim because the rite is externally imposed by religious teaching, not by each individual's subjective conception.
conclusion: The restrictions do not infringe the respondents' freedom of religion or equality rights, because prohibiting a succah on the balcony does not prevent them from fulfilling their religious duties.

issue: If freedom of religion were infringed, was the duty of reasonable accommodation met and the restriction justified under s. 9.1?
facts: The syndicate met repeatedly with the respondents, allowed them to be heard at meetings, and proposed erecting a common succah on adjacent grounds at the co-owners' collective expense, resolving technical issues (security system, electrification, access). The Canadian Jewish Congress endorsed the compromise. The respondents kept raising new objections and, except for one, insisted on a succah near their own units. The declaration also created emergency passage servitudes over the balconies; succahs could obstruct fire-escape routes.
rule: For adverse-effect discrimination the party must offer reasonable accommodation up to the point of undue hardship (Simpsons-Sears; Central Okanagan v. Renaud; Chambly v. Bergevin), and the complainant must in turn demonstrate willingness to accommodate. Section 9.1 of the Quebec Charter permits justified limits; competing fundamental rights — peaceful enjoyment of property (art. 6) and security of the person (art. 1) — must be reconciled harmoniously without hierarchy.
application: The court held, subsidiarily, that the restrictive clauses were rational (part of an architectural concept), the syndicate's common-succah proposal was reasonable, and the respondents failed to show any genuine willingness to compromise, particularly given that the restriction arose from an individually accepted contract. The co-owners' collective right to enjoyment of property and the safety concern of unobstructed emergency passage further justified the limit as reasonable under s. 9.1.
conclusion: Even assuming an infringement, the syndicate discharged its duty of reasonable accommodation and the restrictions constituted justified, reasonable limits.

issue: Does art. 1080 C.c.Q. bar a permanent injunction unless serious and irreparable harm is proven?
facts: The syndicate sought a permanent injunction ordering the respondents to refrain from erecting succahs and to dismantle those installed. Whether a 15-day-a-year succah caused serious harm was doubtful, raising the effect of art. 1080 C.c.Q.
rule: Art. 1080 C.c.Q. allows a co-owner/syndicate to seek an injunction where a co-owner's refusal to comply with the declaration causes 'serious and irreparable prejudice', with a possible further sanction of forced sale. In civil law, specific performance (execution in nature) is the rule (Baudouin); the notion of 'serious and irreparable harm' is normally an interlocutory concept (art. 752 C.p.c.).
application: The court reasoned that art. 1080 must be read as a whole and interpreted to give effect to all provisions; the 'serious and irreparable prejudice' requirement governs the additional remedy of forced sale for transgressing the injunction, not the availability of the injunction to enforce compliance. Reading it otherwise would create chaos by suspending the rule of law until harm became serious and irreparable. Specific performance remained available under arts. 1590, 1601–1603 C.c.Q.
conclusion: Art. 1080 does not preclude the injunction; a permanent injunction enforcing the declaration was granted, with orders to dismantle and restore the balconies at the respondents' expense, with costs.

issue: Did the master have authority to determine the referred issues and issue a report without proceeding to a formal hearing before another master, given the respondent's repeated non-compliance?
facts: Allen J. referred three narrow issues (wedding presents, household possessions, pension) to the master for an accounting under The Family Property Act. The Winnipeg masters' practice uses a two-stage process: preliminary/pre-trial hearings before one master, then a formal hearing before another. The respondent repeatedly failed to comply with directions to produce proper lists and valuations, insisted on calling many witnesses and taking two to three weeks, made irrelevant and disparaging comments, and was impervious to cost orders.
rule: Queen's Bench Rule 55.01(1) requires a master to 'devise and adopt the simplest, least expensive and most expeditious manner of conducting the reference' and permits dispensing with unnecessary procedure; Rule 55.02(3) allows directions as to evidence; Rule 55.02(11) makes directions binding without a formal order; Part XIII references rules and Rule 70.25 govern Family Property Act references. By analogy the master relied on the case-conference rules (Rule 70.24(25),(27),(30)) permitting a judge to make any appropriate order, including striking pleadings, where a party fails to comply.
application: The master found the respondent's 'free-wheeling fishing-expedition approach' abusive of process, a waste of time and unfair to the cooperative petitioner. The master has no contempt power and cost orders were ineffective. Because the confidential 'without prejudice' settlement discussions were not being relied upon, and given the wide discretion under Rule 55.01(1) and the analogy to case-conference powers, the master concluded there was discretion to determine the matters at the preliminary stage and short-circuit the normal process. Continuing to a formal hearing would be an abuse of process, and the only credible evidence would be the petitioner's documentary disclosure.
conclusion: The master had discretion to determine the referred issues and issue a report at the preliminary stage without proceeding to a formal hearing before another master.

issue: What were the shareable values of the wedding presents, household possessions, and pension?
facts: The petitioner provided detailed lists and a professional appraisal (D.A. Stevens) valuing shareable wedding presents at $3,500 and household possessions at $480, plus documentation valuing the shareable Israeli pension (Radview Software) at $35,956.21 with certified Hebrew translations. The respondent claimed roughly $45,000 in wedding gifts, $50,000 in household items and 'about' $100,000 for the pension, but produced no appraisals or supporting documentation and was precluded from adducing further evidence.
rule: Under The Family Property Act, only jointly acquired items retained by the petitioner at the date of separation (March 9, 2003) are shareable, valued as of the reference-order date (July 30, 2007) per Allen J.'s clarification; the Act provides for sharing of value, not return of specific items. Expert reports must comply with Rule 53.03. The pre-nuptial agreement upheld by Allen J. excludes property it covers.
application: The respondent's claimed vehicles were shown to be 2001 models bought by the petitioner's father in 2002, not wedding gifts; his other claims lacked appraisals or documentation; his lists used wrong valuation dates and included clothing and excluded property. His pension theory rested on a bank statement the petitioner credibly explained as a bank error, with no link to the pension, and his objection to the certified translations (without producing his own or specifying errors) was frivolous. The petitioner's documented, appraised valuations were the only credible evidence.
conclusion: Shareable wedding presents $3,500 (respondent entitled to $1,750); household possessions $480 (respondent entitled to $240); pension $35,956.21 (respondent entitled to $17,978.10).

issue: Should costs be awarded against the respondent?
facts: The petitioner was largely self-represented, complied fully with directions, and asked that the respondent's non-compliance be sanctioned. The respondent repeatedly disregarded directions and made disparaging remarks about the petitioner, her family, friends and the Jewish community despite warnings.
rule: The court's discretion as to costs on a reference; conduct and non-compliance are relevant factors.
application: The respondent's refusal to comply with directions, without more, justified costs; his conduct reinforced the award. The petitioner, though self-represented, was awarded costs plus disbursements.
conclusion: Costs of $800 plus reasonable disbursements awarded to the petitioner.

issue: Was Mr. T. incapable of consenting to the proposed care and placement, so that court authorization was required under article 16 C.C.Q.?
facts: Mr. T., admitted to the Hospital since March 18, 2021, suffers from a major cognitive disorder (formerly 'dementia') aggravated by alcohol, causing serious aggressivity. He was subject to prior Court of Quebec confinement judgments and charged with uttering death threats against his wife. He repeatedly expressed his wish to 'go home' but could not appreciate the risks, including breaching his criminal conditions. Experts in geriatric medicine (Dr. Popescu-Crainic) and social work (Ms. Bolofer) opined he lacked capacity; he intermittently seemed open to placement but refused to sign documents and changed his mind.
rule: Article 16 of the Civil Code of Québec requires court authorization where a person of full age incapable of giving consent categorically refuses required care (except hygienic or emergency care), or where the person who may consent is prevented or unjustifiably refuses; see also F.D. c. Centre universitaire de santé McGill, 2015 QCCA 1139.
application: Relying on the expert reports and testimony, and on its own exchanges with Mr. T. at the hearing (in English and through an interpreter), the Court found he could not understand why returning home was problematic given his aggression toward his wife and the pending charges. His inability to comprehend the consequences flowed from his cognitive disorder. He was refusing the placement plan, and his family chose not to attend. His incapacity and the family's absence triggered the Court's role to decide.
conclusion: The Court confirmed Mr. T.'s incapacity to consent to the placement plan, so court authorization under article 16 C.C.Q. was required and the Court would step in to decide.

issue: Was the proposed two-year placement plan in Mr. T.'s best interests, justifying an order authorizing care despite his refusal?
facts: Expert social worker Ms. Bolofer identified numerous risk factors against returning to the community: cognitive decline, short-term memory problems, complications from pending criminal proceedings, family's inability to provide care, inability to perform daily living tasks (feeding, bathing, dressing), and access to alcohol leading to aggressivity. The Hospital sought a two-year placement order, executory notwithstanding appeal.
