rule: Abuse of the right to litigate is a fault committed on the occasion of a legal action (Viel v. Entreprises immobilières du terroir ltée, 2002 QCCA); a court should not find abuse merely because a party's theory is weak without being abusive (Industries Lassonde).
application: While Seggie's claims were weak, the Court declined to treat the mere pursuit of a weak theory as abusive conduct sufficient to award extrajudicial fees, distinguishing this from the malicious defamatory allegations already sanctioned.
conclusion: The claim for reimbursement of extrajudicial professional fees was not granted as an abuse-of-process remedy.

issue: Should a permanent injunction be issued restraining the defendant from sending harassing, insulting and defamatory communications to the university?
facts: Following a dispute over a research mandate and unpaid sums, Côté sent nearly a hundred emails and faxes over 2004–2005 to the university's rector, deans, administrators, professors and employees, accusing the administration of corruption, banditry and criminal conduct, some labelled 'Communication de Presse – pour distribution immédiate'. A safeguard order in December 2005 had stopped the communications.
rule: Under art. 7 C.c.Q. no right may be exercised with intent to injure another or in an excessive and unreasonable manner contrary to good faith. Freedom of expression is not absolute. For a permanent injunction the criteria of irreparable harm and balance of convenience do not apply; the court decides on the merits whether the right to the injunction is established (Ferron, Piché-Messier, Poitras). Defamation is judged objectively by whether an ordinary citizen would find the words discredited the reputation of another (Prud'homme c. Prud'homme; Radio Sept-Îles); good faith of the defendant is irrelevant (Baudoin; Fondation Le Corbusier).
application: The evidence clearly established that Côté sent massive, threatening and injurious communications that paralyzed the university's communications and impugned the dignity and reputation of its members. Although Côté genuinely felt wronged and was in great personal distress, his writings were objectively defamatory and exceeded the limits of legitimate expression. The right to an injunction was established, following authorities such as Doré c. Turmel and CSSS de la Vallée de l'Or c. A.
conclusion: The demand for a permanent injunction was granted in part; the defendant was ordered to abstain from sending communications relating to the 2002–2005 conflict similar to the offending exhibits, the order to remain in force notwithstanding appeal.

issue: Was the defendant's cross-demand prescribed, or was it saved by connexity with the principal demand?
facts: The injunction proceeding was instituted in October 2005; Côté filed his cross-demand in September 2007 seeking unpaid salary, damages for sabotage of his mandate and damages for defamation of his reputation. The university argued prescription under arts. 2925 (3 years) and 2929 (1 year, defamation) C.c.Q.
rule: Article 2896 C.c.Q. provides that interruption of prescription by a judicial demand has effect for all rights flowing from the same source. Under art. 172(2) C.p.c. a cross-demand must arise from the same source as, or a source connected to, the principal demand, requiring a close link or relationship of dependence or similarity (Ferland & Emery; F.N.G. Gibraltar c. Aziz; Cabba c. American Express).
application: The court found a close and visible connection between the university's demand (based on Côté's harassing communications) and Côté's claims (the unpaid sums and alleged attack on his reputation), which all stemmed from the same 2002–2003 dispute. It was therefore a single problem, and prescription of the contractual claim was interrupted. Since no evidence supported the delictual (defamation) claims, whether their prescription was interrupted need not be decided.
conclusion: The cross-demand was found connected and not barred as to the contractual claim; the delictual claims failed for lack of proof.

issue: Is the defendant entitled to unpaid remuneration under the August 2002 research mandate?
facts: Dean Vinay offered Côté a three-month mandate at $5,000/month to study researchers' careers. Côté worked from August 2002, delivered a synopsis in October, and a cheque of $5,000 (24 October 2002) was withheld/never received. The mandate was not renewed after the faculty committee found the synopsis unsatisfactory; Côté's 31 October 2002 email was misread as ending the mandate.
rule: Contractual obligations must be honoured; damages bear interest and the additional indemnity under art. 1619 C.c.Q. from the date of the reconventional demand.
application: The court found the mandate ended around 15–22 November 2002 and that one amount had not been fully paid on the 8 August 2002 contract. In equity the university had to pay the outstanding sum, but the other claims (large damages, mea culpa, defamation damages) were unproven and rejected.
conclusion: The university was ordered to pay $5,000 with interest and the additional indemnity under art. 1619 C.c.Q. from the service of the cross-demand (25 September 2007, per the corrected judgment); each party to bear its own costs.

issue: What evidence is required to satisfy the third step of the prima facie test for discrimination under s. 8 of the Code, and did the Tribunal apply too onerous a standard?
facts: The Tribunal accepted that a disproportionate number of the street-homeless Class were Aboriginal or had disabilities and that Class members suffered adverse treatment under the Ambassadors Program, but dismissed the complaint because there was no direct evidence of a 'nexus' between the adverse treatment and protected grounds; there was statistical/demographic evidence and expert evidence from Dr. Miller but no testimony from an affected homeless individual of Aboriginal descent or with a disability.
rule: Under Moore v. British Columbia (Education), 2012 SCC 61 at para. 33, a claimant must show (1) a protected characteristic, (2) an adverse impact regarding the service, and (3) that the protected characteristic was 'a factor' in the adverse impact. The Code is quasi-constitutional and must be interpreted broadly and purposively (Tranchemontagne, 2006 SCC 14); evidentiary requirements must be sensitive to the evidence likely available and statistical evidence is helpful but not essential (Radek v. Henderson Development, 2005 BCHRT 302). Standard of review is correctness under s. 59(1) ATA.
application: The court held the Tribunal misstated the test by requiring a 'causal connection' (drawn from Coast Mountain, 2010 BCCA 447) and evidence that the group was 'treated or affected differently,' which is stricter than the 'a factor' standard in Moore. Requiring a causative connection elevates the burden and risks importing intention. The court found the Tribunal misread Chapdelaine and Meiorin, where statistical evidence alone established the nexus, and that Radek confirms inference, judicial notice and common sense may prove systemic discrimination. On the whole of the evidence—the demographics, the ambassador data, and Dr. Miller's unrejected expert evidence—the protected characteristics were a factor; no 'something more' was needed.
conclusion: The Tribunal erred in law by applying too strict an evidentiary standard; applying the correct 'a factor' test, all three steps of the prima facie test were established.

issue: Did the Tribunal err in its characterization of the comparative analysis?
facts: The Tribunal reasoned that there was no evidence Ambassadors were more likely to remove Aboriginal than non-Aboriginal individuals 'in similar circumstances,' comparing protected and non-protected members within the Class.
rule: Per Moore (paras. 29-30) and Withler, 2011 SCC 12, the comparator should not be defined so as to descend into a 'separate but equal' formalism; the comparison is with the general public who enjoy the service, not with a sub-group defined by the impugned treatment.
application: The court found the Tribunal made the same error the Court of Appeal made in Moore—comparing dyslexic special-education students to other special-education students. The correct comparison is between Class members subjected to adverse treatment and the general population who have unrestricted access to downtown public space. Framing the comparison within the Class was a legal error.
conclusion: The Tribunal erred in law in its comparative analysis, vitiating its conclusion that prima facie discrimination was not proven.

issue: Did the Tribunal err by importing an intention requirement into the analysis?
facts: The Tribunal used the language of 'systemically targeted' and 'selectively targeted,' and the respondents argued the Program aimed only at illegal behaviours, not at people with protected characteristics.
rule: Section 2 of the Code states intention to discriminate is not required; discrimination is defined by effect/impact (Andrews, 1989; Action Travail, 1987). Adverse effect, not intent or design, is the focus.
application: The court accepted the Program was not intentionally discriminatory but held that lack of intent does not eliminate discrimination. The 'targeting' language reflected a focus on the Program's intent/design rather than its impact, which flowed from the same error of applying too strict a nexus test. The proper focus is disproportionate impact.
conclusion: By focusing on targeting and requiring stricter proof of disproportionate impact, the Tribunal effectively imported an intention element, an error of law.

issue: Is a remedy available against the City of Vancouver despite its mootness argument?
facts: The City funded overnight operation of the Program for one year under a contract that was not renewed; it also promoted the Program, provided some training, and owned the data collected. It argued no live dispute remained.
rule: Mootness (Borowski v. Canada, 1989) bars adjudication where a decision would have no practical effect on the parties' rights.
application: The court found the issues were not abstract: the City funded, promoted and was involved in the Program, and its funding directly enabled overnight ambassador interactions with more rough-sleeping homeless people. A finding of discrimination could stand against the City, but only for the one-year period it funded the Program.
conclusion: Relief is available against the City for the one year it funded the Program; the matter is not moot.

issue: Can the Court rectify the approved class action settlement to correct indemnity miscalculations caused by inadvertent error?
facts: After the settlement was approved, Joseph Élie Ltée discovered its computer software ('Minifuel') had been mis-encoded, creating duplicate transactions that inflated the diverted volume by about 20% (60 million vs. 49 million litres) and the customer count by 400. Independent forensic accountants (Navigant Consulting) confirmed the error was inadvertent human error and validated the corrected figures. Class counsel verified the correction caused no prejudice to members and did not oppose.
rule: Art. 475 C.C.P. permits the Court to correct a judgment containing a miscalculation (Potvin v. Gagnon, [1967] B.R. 300). Under arts. 1036, 1037 and 1040 C.C.P. the judge has broad discretion and acts as administrator of the settlement's execution (St. Lawrence Cement Inc. v. Barrette, 2008 SCC 64).
application: The Court engaged forensic accountants who confirmed the error resulted from inadvertence, not bad faith, and that customers had in fact been properly indemnified for the actual volume diverted. The Court accepted the corrected Net Indemnity of $3,268,195.08 and Total Indemnity of $3,570,488.03. Because the miscalculation relied on by both the parties and the Court was inadvertent and its correction prejudiced no class member, it fell squarely within art. 475 C.C.P.
conclusion: The Court rectified the May 28, 2009 judgment to establish the corrected Total and Net Indemnity amounts.

issue: Is a private agreement reducing the Fonds d'aide aux recours collectifs' contribution enforceable, or must the statutory percentage apply?
facts: The parties and the Fonds had agreed (letter of March 30, 2009) that the Fonds would receive 20% up to a maximum of $20,000. The Fonds later moved to rectify, asserting its statutory entitlement of 60% of a reliquat between $100,000 and $200,000, i.e. $89,790.60 on a reliquat of $149,651.
rule: Arts. 38 and 42 of the Loi sur le recours collectif, R.S.Q. c. R-2.1, and the Règlement sur le pourcentage prélevé par le Fonds d'aide fix the Fonds' entitlement on a reliquat or liquidated claim; regulations once adopted have the force of law (Ruel v. Québec (Éducation), 2001 CanLII 27967; Le Fonds d'aide v. Syndicat des employés d'entretien, [1995] R.J.Q. 2002).
application: The Court held the Fonds' entitlement is statutorily determined and is a matter of public order; the parties and the Fonds could not agree to a lesser amount than that prescribed by regulation. Sixty percent of the corrected reliquat of $149,651 equalled $89,790.60.
conclusion: The March 30, 2009 letter was declared unenforceable as contrary to law; the Fonds was awarded its statutory entitlement of $89,790.60, without costs on its motion since it had contributed to the error.

issue: How should the remaining reliquat be distributed under art. 1036 C.C.P., and can it go to Measurement Canada?
facts: After indemnifying members and paying the Fonds, a reliquat of $59,860.40 remained representing funds intended for members who could not be located. The parties proposed distribution to hospitals and their respiratory departments and to local community charities/United Way. Measurement Canada's inspections had originally uncovered the fraudulent flow-meter tampering.
rule: Art. 1036 C.C.P. gives the Court broad discretion to dispose of the balance 'taking particular account of the interest of the members,' after hearing the parties and any designated persons. Execution must be 'practical and rational' (Comité de citoyens de St-Césaire, [1986] R.J.Q. 1061); the compensatory function and correspondence between victim and beneficiary must be respected (Lafond); cy-près-type distributions must reasonably benefit class members (cf. Ontario Class Proceedings Act, s. 26(4)).
application: The Court found the hospitals, respiratory departments and general charities lacked a sufficiently direct 'interest' connection to the class, there being no evidence heating oil posed a respiratory health risk. It corrected its own omission of the word 'Government' from the recipient categories and heard the Attorney General. Because Measurement Canada's inspections uncovered and deter the very tampering that caused the loss, funding it serves the interest of all heating-oil consumers, including the overcharged members. The Court recommended the funds be added to (not replace) Measurement Canada's budget, respecting that only Parliament allocates federal funds.
conclusion: The Court ordered the reliquat of $59,860.40 be paid to the Receiver General of Canada with a strong recommendation that it be allocated to the fuel-oil inspection section of Measurement Canada in Greater Montreal.

issue: Did Michael and Nikki procure the October 2018 Wills by undue influence through testamentary fraud with respect to Tracy's inheritance?
facts: Carol-Sue Shapiro, whose estate of roughly $7 million derived from the 'Swedlove Legacy' left by her father, progressively reduced her daughter Tracy's inheritance over successive wills from 2013 to 2018, culminating in the October 2018 Wills that left Tracy only specific jewelry and made her son Michael the sole residuary beneficiary. Carol-Sue was preoccupied by fear that Tracy's husband, Jo Corcos, would gain access to the family wealth. Tracy alleged Michael and his wife Nikki fraudulently fed Carol-Sue false beliefs (Jo's mafia/criminal ties, that Tracy and Jo were back together) to disinherit her.
rule: The party attacking a will bears the onus of proving undue influence, whether by coercion or fraudulent means, on a balance of probabilities (Vout v. Hay, 1995 CanLII 105 (SCC)). Testamentary fraud is a species of undue influence: inducing a testator, by a program of falsehood and manipulation, to make a gift she otherwise would not make (Poyser, Capacity and Undue Influence; Patterson Estate (Re), 2017 NSSC 221; Mayrand v. Dussault, 1907 CanLII 94 (SCC); Anderson v. Walkey, 1961 CanLII 112 (ON CA)). Evidence is usually circumstantial; indicators include dependence, social isolation, recent family conflict, bereavement, wills inconsistent with prior wills, and substantial pre-death transfers of wealth (Gironda v. Gironda, 2013 ONSC 4133; Tate v. Gueguegirre, 2015 ONSC 844).
application: The court reconstructed the family history from Carol-Sue's perspective, principally through her emails. Most alleged 'falsehoods' were not manifest lies: Jo's romantic involvement with another woman, his interest in the money, and that Tracy remained with Jo were substantiated or reasonably believed, and Tracy admitted the Fall 2018 sighting was true. Only the belief that Jo was a mafia member/criminal was false, but there was no evidence Michael and Nikki manufactured it. Applying the Gironda/Tate indicators, Carol-Sue was not dependent on Michael and Nikki (she used her financial power to try to force them to reconcile with Tracy), was not socially isolated (she had many advisors and friends who reported on Tracy and Jo), and the family conflict was not exploited (Michael and Nikki urged Tracy to leave Jo, which would have preserved her inheritance). The October 2018 changes were consistent with Carol-Sue's stated intentions dating to 2013-2016, and pre-death gifts to Michael's family were explained by tax planning, income disparity, travel assistance and keeping money from Jo. Jo's own threatening conduct was the strongest catalyst.
conclusion: Undue influence through fraud was not established; Carol-Sue made up her own mind gradually to protect the Swedlove Legacy. Tracy's objection was dismissed.

issue: Was the reduction of Jack's inheritance the product of undue influence through fraud?
facts: Jack, Carol-Sue's husband, had his bequest reduced across successive wills to $250,000 plus a life interest in the condominium. He alleged Michael and Nikki convinced Carol-Sue falsely that he had ample savings and would pass any inheritance to Tracy (and thus to Jo).
rule: Same rule: the objector must prove undue influence by fraudulent means on a balance of probabilities, supported by direct or circumstantial evidence (Vout v. Hay; Gironda; Tate).
application: While it was untrue that Jack had a million dollars in savings, the court found this was Carol-Sue's own erroneous assumption (the spouses kept separate finances) rather than a lie planted by Michael and Nikki. Carol-Sue's belief that Jack would share money with Tracy reflected his genuinely more trusting attitude toward Jo, not a fabrication. There was no evidence, direct or circumstantial, that Michael or Nikki induced these beliefs.
conclusion: Jack's claim of undue influence through fraud was dismissed.

issue: Should the derivative claims be struck where the plaintiff never obtained leave under s. 232 of the Business Corporations Act?
facts: The plaintiff, a founder, shareholder, director, officer and creditor of Epoch, pleaded numerous claims, some of which sought recovery for losses to the company itself (e.g. failure to collect receivables, misappropriation, transfer of assets to Vanstar rendering Epoch insolvent). She intended these to form a derivative action on behalf of Epoch but had not applied for or obtained leave of the court.
rule: Section 232 of the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 requires leave of the court to bring a derivative action on behalf of a company. Claims that are fundamentally derivative — for loss to the company rather than a personal loss — must be struck unless leave is granted (Hoet v. Vogel; Robak Industries Ltd. v. Gardner, 2007 BCCA 61). A shareholder has no personal cause of action for loss of investment or share value arising from a wrong to the corporation (Foss v. Harbottle; Hercules Management Ltd. v. Ernst & Young).
application: The plaintiff wished to pursue both personal and derivative claims but had not distinguished them and had not sought the required leave. The pleadings blended losses personal to her with losses to Epoch (e.g. under the defined 'Harmful Acts'). To the extent the claims were derivative, they could not proceed without leave; and the plaintiff was simultaneously suing Epoch while proposing to sue on its behalf.
conclusion: The derivative claims must be struck; if the plaintiff wishes to pursue a derivative action she must first bring an application for leave under s. 232.

issue: Should the Notice of Civil Claim be struck under Rule 9-5 for failing to disclose a reasonable claim and for being confusing?
facts: The NOCC and proposed amended NOCC asserted a plethora of causes of action (conspiracy, intentional interference, deceit, fraud, negligence, misrepresentation, breach of fiduciary duty to the plaintiff and to Epoch, breaches of contract, oppression, and derivative claims) against multiple defendants occupying overlapping capacities, based on events spanning several years. It was often unclear which claims were made against which defendant, in which capacity, and on what facts.
rule: Rule 9-5(1)(a),(b),(d) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules permits striking pleadings that disclose no reasonable claim, are unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious, or are an abuse of process. The 'plain and obvious' test governs (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42; Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.). Pleadings must clearly define the issues of fact and law and plead the material facts for each cause of action (Rule 3-1(2); Stoneman v. Denman Island Trust Committee). Prolix, confusing pleadings that prevent the opposing party from knowing the case to meet may be struck (Gateway Building Management Ltd. v. Randhawa; Canfor Pulp Limited Partnership v. Siemens).
application: The pleadings failed the basic purpose of defining issues: they lumped defendants together, did not identify the capacity in which each party was liable, and did not tie material facts to particular causes of action. Complexity did not relieve the plaintiff of the duty to plead properly; she could not rely on discovery to supply facts she was obliged to plead. However, the NOCC did set out facts that could potentially support viable causes of action.
conclusion: The NOCC is struck out in its entirety under Rule 9-5, but outright dismissal is not warranted because viable claims may exist.

issue: Should the action be dismissed, or should leave to amend be granted, and should discovery precede repleading?
facts: The plaintiff asked that the application be adjourned to permit discovery, arguing she lacked information because she had been ousted and blocked from the company's records.
rule: A claimant must plead the material facts on which the claim relies whether or not able to prove them at the pleadings stage (Imperial Tobacco). Pleadings define the issues and therefore the scope of discovery; discovery cannot precede adequate pleadings (SunOil Ltd. v. Big Snowy Resources L.P.). Where a defect can be cured by amendment the court may grant leave to amend rather than dismiss (Henry v. British Columbia (AG)).
application: Because the NOCC contained facts capable of supporting viable non-derivative claims, dismissal was inappropriate; the appropriate remedy mirrored Stoneman. The plaintiff could not obtain discovery before filing intelligible pleadings.
conclusion: The NOCC is struck with leave to amend to plead non-derivative causes of action within 90 days; the action is stayed meanwhile; if no amended NOCC is filed the defendants may apply to dismiss, and may later apply to strike any amended pleading. The defendants, being substantially successful, were awarded costs payable in any event of the cause.

issue: Should the individual defendants be ordered to produce further documents said to be material to proving malice under Rule 7-1?
facts: The plaintiff, a physician suing BCMA directors and officers for defamation arising after her 2008 electoral defeat, sought the individual defendants' own agendas, minutes, handwritten and electronic notes, arguing defamation cases can turn on candid but damaging notes and that malice could be inferred from them. Affidavit evidence showed several defendants had deleted emails, suffered hard-drive failures, or had no relevant documents; others had disclosed all documents.
rule: Rule 7-1(1) of the Supreme Court Civil Rules limits initial production to documents that could be used to prove or disprove a material fact, consistent with the proportionality principle in Rule 1-3(2) (Biehl v. Strang, 2010 BCSC 1391). Materiality focuses on the material issues in dispute; the material fact here is malice, which may be proved by extrinsic evidence of the defendant's conduct and state of mind (Brown on Defamation; Simpson v. Mair, 2004 BCSC 754; Turner v. MGM Pictures).
application: The court found the individual defendants had produced their documents and that the only potential source of further disclosure was deleted or lost emails of Appleton, Cavers, Fritz and Vance. Whether recoverable emails exist could be explored at the upcoming examinations for discovery. Rather than order production now, the court would permit the plaintiff to renew the application before the case-managing judge if discovery revealed that relevant documents exist or could be recovered.
conclusion: The application to compel the individual defendants to produce additional documents was dismissed, with liberty to renew after examinations for discovery.

issue: Should the BCMA be ordered to produce further meeting minutes, agendas and post-litigation audio recordings, or are they privileged?
facts: The plaintiff demanded all BCMA board and executive audio recordings from June 2008 to October 2011. The BCMA had already produced digitized recordings from June 2007 to February 2009 (which the plaintiff refused to pay for). In-house counsel Cathy Cordell swore that the plaintiff was referred to only on a small number of occasions, always in the context of legal advice, litigation strategy or costs.
rule: Documents whose dominant purpose is seeking or giving legal advice, or relating to litigation strategy and instructions to counsel, are protected by privilege. Production still requires materiality to a material fact under Rule 7-1.
application: The court accepted Ms. Cordell's evidence that the vast majority of meeting content concerned the ordinary business of the BCMA and that references to the plaintiff arose only in privileged contexts. It saw no meaningful distinction between the parties' claimed purposes for recording meetings (accuracy) and concluded the plaintiff's name arose only in privileged discussions.
conclusion: The application for further minutes, agendas and audio recordings was dismissed; the court would not order production of the recordings.

issue: Are the BCMA's communications with counsel on governance and the special committee, and drafts of the president's letters, privileged?
facts: The plaintiff sought pre-February 2008 communications with internal/external counsel on governance, process and procedure, communications about the ad hoc special committee struck to investigate her alleged breach of the code of conduct, and drafts of the president's letters/bulletins. Cordell's affidavit stated the letters were prepared or edited by the BCMA's external counsel and reflected confidential legal advice. The plaintiff was in acknowledged conflict with the board, had retained counsel, and had earlier litigated the special committee (2008 BCSC 1559; 2010 BCCA 43).
rule: Solicitor-client privilege belongs to the corporation (BCMA), not its individual members, and a director-litigant in conflict with the corporation cannot negate that privilege (Dublin v. Montessori Jewish Day School of Toronto, 2007 CanLII 8923 (ON SC)). Legal advice must also be material to a fact in issue to be producible.
application: The court held the plaintiff was in conflict with the board and not entitled to its solicitor-client communications. The advice on process, procedure and governance of the special committee, and the counsel-prepared drafts of the president's letters, did not tend to prove whether the impugned communications were defamatory or whether the BCMA breached its contract with her — questions for the court, not counsel.
conclusion: The communications with counsel and drafts of the president's letters were held privileged and need not be disclosed; those parts of the application were dismissed.

issue: Should each defendant be required to swear an affidavit verifying their list of documents under Rule 7-1(8)?
facts: The plaintiff sought verifying affidavits from each of the 15 defendants. The broadened disclosure demand was only served on October 17, 2011; the action had been stayed pending payment of outstanding costs paid on the last day (September 6, 2011); and no examinations for discovery had yet occurred, the trial being set for January 2012.
rule: Rule 7-1(8) permits an order that a party verify its list of documents by affidavit; the court exercises discretion having regard to fairness and the proportionality principle.
application: The court found it would be unfair to order verifying affidavits given the late broadening of the demand and the plaintiff's own delay in conducting discoveries, which she bore responsibility for. Whether such affidavits were warranted would be better assessed after the examinations for discovery.
conclusion: The application for verifying affidavits was adjourned, with liberty to bring it before the trial management judge if the plaintiff determined it was required after discovery.

issue: Were the words complained of in the two newspaper articles defamatory of the plaintiff?
facts: The plaintiff, a Member of Parliament, used his franking and 'ten percenter' mailing privileges to distribute materials supporting a party leadership candidate. The StarPhoenix published two articles (March 4 and 5, 2002) quoting party members and MPs criticizing this use, including statements that it was 'crooked' to send such mail by franking and that MPs were 'put in office ... not to steal from us', plus references to the Bakkers and to 'abusing' privileges and not passing 'the smell test'.
rule: A plaintiff must prove the words were defamatory (would tend to lower reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person), referred to the plaintiff, and were published: Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61. Words are judged objectively by the standard of an ordinary, right-thinking, reasonably informed person, avoiding the worst possible meaning: Color Your World Corp. v. CBC (1998); Lund v. Black Press Group Ltd., 2009 BCSC 937. Criticism of public officials is not automatically defamatory, but words imputing moral fault or criminality cross the line: Wells v. Puddister, 2007 NLCA 25.
application: Reference and publication were conceded. The court found most passages, though harsh, were legitimate criticism of a politician. However, the Ballantyne quote calling the conduct 'crooked' and the Fyfe quote suggesting the plaintiff was 'stealing' from the public imputed moral fault/criminality and would lower reputation in the eyes of a reasonably informed reader; these two passages in the Bernhardt article were defamatory. The Bakker comparison was mere hyperbole, and none of the four impugned passages in the Parker article were defamatory.
conclusion: Two passages in the first article were defamatory; the second (Parker) article was not, so the action against Parker was dismissed outright.

issue: Did the defence of responsible communication on matters of public interest protect the defendants?
facts: Both articles concerned a federal party leadership race and an MP's use of publicly funded communication allowances. Reporters interviewed multiple named sources, obtained copies of the mailouts, sought the plaintiff's response (obtained by Bernhardt, unsuccessfully attempted by Parker who reiterated prior comments), and an expert testified the articles met best journalistic practices.
rule: Grant v. Torstar Corp., 2009 SCC 61 and Quan v. Cusson, 2009 SCC 62 establish the defence of responsible communication: the publication must be on a matter of public interest, and the publisher must have acted responsibly, assessed against the eight factors in Grant (seriousness, public importance, urgency, source reliability, whether the plaintiff's side was sought, justifiability of inclusion, reportage, and other circumstances).
application: The leadership race, internal party strife, and use of taxpayer-funded privileges were matters of genuine public interest. Applying the Grant factors, the allegations did not seriously impute criminality, the matter was publicly important, sources were named and reliable, the plaintiff's side was sought and prominently reported, inclusion of the impugned statements was justifiable, and the repetition qualified as reportage. The defendants met and exceeded the standard, and there was no malice.
conclusion: The defence of responsible communication succeeded and the claim was dismissed on this basis.

issue: Did the defence of qualified privilege protect the defendants?
facts: The articles reported on infighting during a national leadership race and the propriety of an elected official's use of communication allowances, disseminated to the public through the newspaper.
rule: Qualified privilege attaches to an occasion where the maker has a duty or interest to communicate and the recipient a corresponding interest to receive; it presumes bona fides and is defeated only by proof of malice: Adam v. Ward, [1917] A.C. 309; Hill v. Church of Scientology, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130; Brown, The Law of Defamation. Courts have recognized the media's legitimate interest in reporting on the conduct of governments and elected officials (Loos v. Robbins; Stopforth v. Goyer; Parlett v. Robinson).
application: The public had a real interest in the leadership race and in whether elected representatives spent their allowances properly, and the media had a corresponding interest in publishing it. There was a sufficient nexus between the defendants' publication and the public interest to establish a privileged occasion, and no malice was proven.
conclusion: Qualified privilege availed all defendants and provided an alternative basis for dismissal.

issue: Did the defence of fair comment protect the defendants?
facts: The impugned 'crooked' and 'steal' statements were opinions expressed by third parties about the plaintiff's admitted use of his franking privilege to support a leadership candidate, reported in the context of a leadership race.
rule: Fair comment protects prima facie defamatory words that are recognizable as comment, based on true facts, on a matter of public interest, that any person could honestly express on the proven facts, absent proof of express malice: WIC Radio Ltd. v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Myers v. CBC (1999); Cherneskey. The objective test is not a high threshold and protects obstinate, prejudiced or offensive opinion.
application: The 'crooked' and 'steal' statements were recognizable as opinion/characterizations rather than fact, rested on the true and admitted underlying facts (the franked mailouts supporting a candidate, ultimately at public expense), concerned a matter of public interest, and were comments an honest person could make on those facts. No malice was established.
conclusion: The defence of fair comment also availed the defendants, and the action was dismissed on this basis as well, with costs to the defendants on Column 4.

issue: Was the wife's Workers' Compensation award excluded from matrimonial assets, and should the matrimonial assets be divided equally?
facts: The parties, married in 1983, separated in 1989 with two young children. The husband, a veterinarian with a 1/4 partnership interest, and the wife, a former nurse now working in day care, disputed the treatment of a $15,000 Workers' Compensation Appeal Board award received by the wife, and whether assets should be split equally. A $10,000 sum from the husband's parents was found to be a repayable loan.
rule: Section 4(1)(b) of the Matrimonial Property Act, 1980 excepts 'an award or settlement of damages in court in favour of one spouse' from matrimonial assets; s. 4(2) qualifies this for awards paid in respect of a matrimonial asset. Section 13 authorizes an unequal division of matrimonial assets where an equal division would be unfair, having regard to factors including s. 13(b) and (h).
application: The Court held a Workers' Compensation Board award is not the equivalent of an award or settlement of damages 'in court', so it is not exempt; and in any event it was paid in respect of lost income which, if accumulated, would be a matrimonial asset. The partnership interest was found to be a business asset, not a matrimonial asset. Because the wife would have custody of the children with attendant needs, and given the difficulty of dividing the partnership interest, an equal division would be unfair.
conclusion: The compensation award was a matrimonial asset. The Court ordered a 70%/30% division of matrimonial assets in favour of the wife, allocating the specific assets accordingly and directing sale of the matrimonial home to give effect to the split.

issue: What maintenance should be ordered given the parties' means and needs?
facts: The husband earned about $5,750/month with a projected deficit driven partly by business debts of some $47,000; he had voluntarily paid $1,800/month without prejudice. The wife earned about $305/month in day care plus family allowance, and could not resume nursing because of a lumbar disc protrusion for which she reasonably declined surgery.
rule: Sections 15(5), (7) and (8) of the Divorce Act, 1985 require consideration of the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of each spouse and child, promotion of economic self-sufficiency so far as practicable, and apportionment of the joint obligation to maintain children according to relative abilities to contribute.
application: The Court accepted the wife was doing her best and could not resume nursing, but found the husband could not sustain $1,800/month while repaying business debts essential to preserving his income; requiring the present level short-term would harm his long-term ability to pay. The long-term interests of the children and wife should prevail.
conclusion: Maintenance was reduced to $1,400/month for two years to allow debt reduction, after which the husband is to resume the current level or such level as a court then orders.

issue: Should the Court order that the two boys become bar mitzvah at age 13 as an incident of custody/access?
facts: The husband is Jewish (though non-observant) and wanted the boys, who were circumcised according to Jewish rites, to become bar mitzvah to know Jewish tradition and understand anti-Semitism. The wife, a convert to Judaism who returned to Catholicism, intended to raise them Catholic but agreed to expose them to Judaism; she opposed compelled bar mitzvahs. The parties had agreed the wife would have custody with liberal access to the husband.
rule: Under the Court's inherent parens patriae jurisdiction and s. 16 of the Divorce Act, 1985, custody/access orders are governed solely by the best interests of the child. Courts do not choose between faiths (In re J.M. Carroll; Re Custody of Pamela A.) and a custodial parent generally directs religious upbringing (Henderson; Gunn; Brown; Fougere), while a non-custodial parent's religion may be exposed to the children (Pfeifer).
application: The Court held it had jurisdiction to make the order. Assessing the children's condition, means, needs and circumstances, it found exposure to both faiths would not be damaging and would foster understanding and tolerance; it doubted the wife's commitment to expose them to Judaism given the secret baptism. Delaying the decision would in effect favour the mother's position, so an immediate decision was preferable. The decision was framed not as choosing a religion but as giving the children the opportunity to know both faiths and eventually choose.
conclusion: The Court directed both parents to encourage and give the two children the opportunity to study and celebrate their bar mitzvahs, with liberty to apply to Family Court for directions if the parents cannot agree.

issue: Was the Director's determination that the Discriminatory Business Practices Act did not apply because the University was not 'engaging in business' in relation to the impugned Provision reasonable?
facts: The University of Windsor entered into two agreements with student groups to resolve protest encampments, including a Provision that the University would not pursue institutional academic agreements with Israeli universities until Palestinian self-determination was realized, unless supported by the Senate. CIJA complained to the Director under the Act, who concluded in a December 23, 2024 letter that the Act was not engaged because the University is a public academic institution whose primary purpose is education and research, not profit.
rule: The standard of review is reasonableness (Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65); the court assesses whether the Director's statutory interpretation is reasonable, not conducting a de novo interpretation. The Act (Discriminatory Business Practices Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. D.12) aims at business relationships; s. 2 targets discrimination against 'persons employed in or engaging in business', and s. 4 deems certain 'discriminatory business practices'. Whether an entity carries on business turns on the 'preponderant purpose' test: if profit-making is the preponderant purpose it is a business (Ontario (Regional Assessment Commissioner) v. Caisse Populaire de Hearst, [1983] 1 S.C.R. 57). Beauchamp v. North Central Predators AAA Hockey Assn. (2004 CanLII 48698) is the leading interpretation of the Act.
application: The Court held that the analysis could be resolved on the specific facts of the Provision. The Provision concerned the University's institutional academic partnerships with Israeli universities — a core non-business, academic purpose. Reading s. 4(1)3(ii) in the context of the Act's title, purpose and wording (all directed at 'business' relationships), it was reasonable for the Director to conclude the University was not engaging in business in relation to this Provision. Reliance on Beauchamp (hockey associations not businesses due to non-profit preponderant purpose) was not unreasonable, and the 1991 Ontario Science Centre 'assurance of voluntary compliance' — a profit-generating contract with Oman — was distinguishable and had little precedential value.
conclusion: The Director's conclusion that the Act did not apply to the Provision in the student agreements was reasonable.

issue: Was the Director's alternative finding that the agreements did not meet the requirements of s. 4(1)3(ii) of the Act reasonable?
facts: CIJA argued the Provision meant Israeli academics could not teach or research at the University and that University faculty would be precluded from opportunities at Israeli universities affecting their advancement. The Provision was subject to Senate approval and expressly stated it did not prevent individual academics at the University from working or collaborating with academics in Israel.
rule: Section 4(1)3(ii) requires a contract that includes a provision that a party 'will refuse or fail to employ or promote or will dismiss or suspend from employment' a second person on account of an attribute. The modern principle of statutory interpretation requires reading the plain language in light of purpose and context (Vavilov, para. 118).
application: The Court found the Provision was not mandatory — it was subject to the Senate's statutory role under the University of Windsor Act and by-laws, not a device to evade the Act. Any uncertainty about impact on professors was addressed by the Provision's express carve-out allowing individual academics to collaborate with Israeli academics. As for Israeli professors, the applicant did not demonstrate any employment relationship between the University and those professors that would engage the 'refuse to employ/promote/dismiss/suspend' language of the Act.
conclusion: The Director's conclusion that the requirements of s. 4(1)3(ii) were not met was reasonable.

issue: Must Manitoba produce an unredacted Final Licence Record where the redactions withhold confidential consultation and funding information relating to non-party Indigenous communities?
facts: Tataskweyak Cree Nation (TCN) seeks judicial review of the Minister's decision to issue a Final Licence to Manitoba Hydro for the Churchill River Diversion, alleging breach of the Crown's duty to consult. Manitoba redacted portions of the Final Licence Record containing budget/funding tables, a consultation participation table, information provided in confidence by other Indigenous communities, and financial figures relating to the Augmented Flow Program.
rule: The Crown has a common law duty to provide the record of proceedings on judicial review (Kalo v. Winnipeg, 2019 MBCA 46). Redactions may be justified where the redacted portion is clearly irrelevant and the redaction is necessary to protect an important interest or prevent significant harm; the onus rests on the party seeking to maintain the redaction (WSIB Investments v. Plenary Group, 2022 MBQB 145; Duhamel, 2018 BCSC 601; McGee, 2010 ONSC 1408). Adequacy of consultation is a group-specific factual inquiry, not a comparative exercise (Haida Nation, 2004 SCC 73; Bigstone Cree Nation, 2018 FCA 89; Tsleil-Waututh, 2018 FCA 153). Confidential commercial and third-party interests can constitute an important interest (Sierra Club, 2002 SCC 41; Sherman Estate, 2021 SCC 25).
application: The Court found the redacted funding, consultation-table and community information clearly irrelevant because the adequacy of consultation with TCN must be judged only on TCN's own consultation record, not by comparison to other communities; TCN's premise that Manitoba rejected its work plans over funding amounts was unsupported. The AFP financial figures were only one reason for incorporating the AFP and were irrelevant. Disclosure would harm Manitoba Hydro's confidential commercial interests and, more significantly, undermine the confidentiality that Indigenous communities reasonably expect, threatening the free, open, reconciliatory dialogue essential to Crown-Indigenous consultation (relying on the uncontested Silva affidavit and Métis Nation of Alberta, 2021 ABQB 282). The proposed sealed-filing alternative would not avoid the harm because confidential community information would still be disclosed to a third party.
conclusion: Order #1 refused; Manitoba need not produce an unredacted Final Licence Record.

issue: Should the Court order Manitoba to include six additional documents in the Consultation Record?
facts: TCN sought to add to the Consultation Record letters between TCN and the Deputy Minister about the AFP, an open letter and Winnipeg Free Press op-ed by TCN and OPCN, and correspondence to the Minister from religious organizations (the Interchurch Council and the Mennonite Church Manitoba).
rule: The Administrative Record consists of the material that was before the original decision-maker, and evidence not before the decision-maker is generally inadmissible on judicial review (Kalo, 2019 MBCA 46). Extrinsic material may be introduced only through the applicant's own affidavit evidence establishing a proper foundation, within recognized exceptions (Pimicikamak, 2018 MBCA 49 and 2014 MBQB 143; Manitoba Métis Federation Inc. v. Pallister, 2019 MBQB 118).
application: The Court found TCN conflated the Administrative Record with the Consultation Record and cited no authority requiring the Crown's affiant to swear a new affidavit attaching documents the Crown does not regard as part of the consultation process. The proposed documents were not related to the Final Licence consultation process, and the proper route for TCN was to adduce its own extra-record affidavit evidence.
conclusion: Order #2 refused.

issue: Should the Court order production of internal government deliberative documents that informed the recommendation to the Minister but were never before her?
facts: TCN sought production of internal input from technical experts, the Wildlife and Fisheries Branch, and correspondence between Manitoba Conservation and Climate and Manitoba Hydro concerning the proposed licence terms — documents acknowledged not to be part of the Final Licence Record or Consultation Record.
rule: Discovery is generally unavailable in applications (Jewish Community Campus of Winnipeg v. Metaser, 2013 MBQB 303); a court may order production only of documents actually or potentially admissible as extrinsic evidence, judicial review not being a hearing de novo (Pimicikamak (QB), 2014 MBQB 143). A decision-maker's internal files do not form part of the Administrative Record if they were not before the decision-maker (Waverley v. Nova Scotia, 1993 NSCA; Manitoba Métis Federation Inc., 2018 MBQB 131). The Gitxaala Nation (2016 FCA 187) participatory right arose from a specific statutory step under the National Energy Board Act with no equivalent under The Water Power Act.
application: The documents were prepared internally to give ministerial advice and consider options, were never before the Minister, and were irrelevant to the adequacy-of-consultation issue. Ordering their production would transform the application into a de novo hearing of public servants' deliberations. Gitxaala's participatory-rights holding was distinguishable because it depended on a statutory recommendation step absent here, and Manitoba Métis Federation Inc. supported treating such deliberative advisory documents as irrelevant and normally not subject to access; disclosure would also harm free and open internal deliberation.
conclusion: Order #3 refused; the motion is dismissed in its entirety.

issue: Did the moving-party defendants establish that the action arises from an expression relating to a matter of public interest under s. 137.1(3)?
facts: Volpe, publisher of the Italian-Canadian newspaper Corriere Canadese, wrote articles attacking TCDSB trustees and the LGBTQ2S+ community, including calling an LGBT YouthLine link a 'recruitment site' and 'smut site.' City councillors (Wong-Tam, Ainslie) and TCDSB trustees responded with tweets, a City Council motion, a joint letter and press-conference statements describing the plaintiffs as homophobic, transphobic and anti-LGBTQ2S+; Yahoo published an article stating Volpe had 'well documented anti-LGBTQ+ views.'
rule: Under s. 137.1(3) the moving party must show on a balance of probabilities that the proceeding arises from its expression and that the expression relates to a matter of public interest, defined broadly and without qualitative assessment (1704604 Ontario Ltd. v. Pointes Protection Association, 2020 SCC 22; Grant v. Torstar, 2009 SCC 61; Grist v. TrueGrp Inc., 2021 ONCA 309).
application: All impugned statements were communications ('expressions') from which the action arose. The expressions related to the TCDSB's removal and reinstatement of the LGBT YouthLine link, the use of public taxpayer funds for City advertising, and the councillors' and trustees' statutory duties (CTA s. 131, HRAP; Education Act s. 169.1) to represent constituents and ensure a safe, inclusive school environment. These are quintessential matters of public interest, not private disputes or attempts to 'censor' the newspaper.
conclusion: The defendants met the s. 137.1(3) threshold; the burden shifted to the plaintiffs under s. 137.1(4).

issue: Did the plaintiffs establish substantial merit of their causes of action under s. 137.1(4)(a)(i)?
facts: The plaintiffs advanced defamation, misfeasance in public office (and abuse of authority), inducing breach of contract, and wrongful interference with economic relations, seeking over $30 million; the impugned statements characterized the plaintiffs as homophobic, transphobic and anti-LGBTQ2S+.
rule: The plaintiff must show a 'real prospect of success' that tends to weigh more in its favour (Pointes, paras. 49-50). Defamation requires publication, reference to the plaintiff, and words tending to lower reputation (Bent v. Platnick, 2020 SCC 23). Misfeasance requires a deliberate unlawful act in bad faith intended to harm (Odhavji Estate; Catalyst v. Dundee Kilmer). Inducing breach of contract requires a breached contract known to the defendant (Drouillard). Interference with economic relations requires unlawful means against a third party (A.I. Enterprises v. Bram).
application: Calling the plaintiffs homophobic/transphobic/anti-LGBTQ2S+ would tend to lower reputation, so defamation had substantial merit; the court declined to take a 'deep dive' into existing reputation. However, there was no evidence of bad faith, unlawful acts, an existing City advertising contract (advertising was 'buy-as-we-need'), knowledge of any contract, or intent to injure economic interests; councillors and trustees acted within their statutory duties. The other torts therefore lacked a real prospect of success.
conclusion: Only the defamation claim had substantial merit; the remaining claims failed s. 137.1(4)(a)(i).

issue: Did the plaintiffs establish that the defendants had no valid defence under s. 137.1(4)(a)(ii)?
facts: Defendants relied on fair comment (all), qualified privilege (councillors and trustees), justification (councillors, Li Preti, Yahoo), statutory immunity under CTA s. 391 (councillors), and responsible communication (Yahoo Defendants). The impugned characterizations were grounded in Volpe's own published articles.
rule: The plaintiff must show a real prospect of success that none of the defences would succeed. Fair comment requires public-interest comment, a factual basis, recognizability as comment, an opinion any person could honestly hold, and absence of express malice (WIC Radio v. Simpson, 2008 SCC 40; Awan v. Levant; Mondal v. Evans-Bitten). Qualified privilege attaches to reciprocal duty/interest communications, including elected officials and their electorate (Hill; Prud'homme; Stopforth; Parlett). Justification requires truth of the sting (Bent). Responsible communication requires public interest and diligence (Grant v. Torstar). CTA s. 391 immunizes good-faith acts of councillors.
application: Calling someone homophobic is recognizable as comment, was based on Volpe's own inflammatory articles (a 'sufficient launching pad'), could be honestly held (others including Pizza Nova and LGBT YouthLine reached the same view), and showed no malice, being made in good faith in a public debate the plaintiffs initiated. Qualified privilege applied to the councillors' and trustees' communications made under their duties to constituents on the HRAP and public spending, within appropriate scope and without malice. Justification could succeed if the statements were facts. The Yahoo Defendants reported diligently on a public-interest matter. The plaintiffs failed to show any defence lacked a real prospect of success.
conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to establish no valid defence; the fair-comment finding alone was sufficient to dismiss the action.

issue: Did the plaintiffs establish that harm was sufficiently serious to outweigh the public interest in protecting the expression under s. 137.1(4)(b)?
facts: Volpe asserted lost advertising and reputational harm but produced no contracts, no revenue figures and no financial records; Pizza Nova had withdrawn advertising on November 17, 2020, before any impugned statement.
rule: The plaintiff must show on a balance of probabilities that harm is causally connected to the expression and sufficiently serious that the public interest in continuing the proceeding outweighs the public interest in protecting the expression (Pointes, paras. 61-82; Levant v. DeMelle, 2022 ONCA 79; Armstrong v. Corus, 2018 ONCA 689). Bald assertions are insufficient.
application: There was little or no evidence of monetary harm and no causal link, since Pizza Nova's earlier withdrawal preceded the statements. Against negligible harm stood strong public-interest expression: political speech by elected officials protecting the LGBTQ2S+ community, oversight of public spending, and free-press reporting, all lying at the core of s. 2(b). The plaintiffs had injected themselves into a heated public debate and should expect forceful rebuttal; permitting the claim would chill public debate.
conclusion: The plaintiffs failed the weighing test; the balance strongly favoured protecting the expression.

issue: Did the arbitration board err in law by not treating the collective agreement as amended by the Individual's Rights Protection Act?
facts: The company agreed with Olympia (cl. 46) not to work from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset or on Jewish holidays. Union members were consequently limited to fewer than the normal 35–36 weekly hours. The union grieved a breach of art. 5.05 of the collective agreement, arguing the agreement should be read as amended by s. 6 IRPA.
rule: Under the Alberta Labour Act, 1973, s. 138(4) model clause para (f), an arbitration board 'shall not alter, amend or change the terms of the collective agreement.' Article 5.05 guarantees no less than 35 hours pay for an employee 'working' the complete normal hours in the pay period.
application: Moore J. held the key word in art. 5.05 is 'working': the guarantee applies only to days actually worked. A day on which no work is scheduled because the company could not work under its Olympia contract is not a 'working day'. Nothing in the collective agreement precluded the company from scheduling fewer than five days, and the union had not challenged the board's finding that the agreement guaranteed no weekly or daily hours. The agreement did not conflict with the IRPA.
conclusion: The board did not err in law; its interpretation of the collective agreement was correct.

issue: Did the closure of the site on Jewish holidays amount to employment discrimination under s. 6 IRPA, and can the owner fall within 'any other person'?
facts: The company argued the arrangement flowed from the owner's contract; no one worked on the specified days. The union argued the company was an employer under s. 6(1) and that Olympia fell within 'any other person' in s. 6(1)(b).
rule: Section 6(1) IRPA prohibits an employer from refusing to employ or discriminating in terms of employment because of religious belief of that person 'or of any other person.'
application: The board found no differentiation against these employees over and above others, since no one worked on the specified days. Moore J. agreed and further held that Olympia, the owner, could not properly fall within the words 'or any other person', as the section addresses discrimination by an employer against someone working for him, not the religious observance driving the site closure.
conclusion: No discrimination under s. 6 was established; the owner did not fall within 'any other person'.

issue: Could the court amend the collective agreement in light of the statute, and was the grievance the appropriate remedy?
facts: The union sought certiorari and mandamus asking the court to read the agreement as entitling members to pay for work not done on Jewish holidays.
rule: The Alberta Labour Act prohibits altering the terms of a collective agreement; a complaint of statutory discrimination must be pursued under the IRPA's own procedure.
application: The court held it could not amend the agreement, as doing so would contravene the Alberta Labour Act. If the union had a genuine discrimination complaint, the proper course was to file proceedings under the IRPA rather than to seek amendment of the agreement through arbitration/judicial review.
conclusion: The court would not amend the agreement; the IRPA route was the proper remedy. Application for certiorari and mandamus dismissed with costs to the company.

issue: Do mandatory Christian opening exercises in public schools infringe s. 2(a)?
facts: Sudbury Board schools opened daily with O Canada and the Lord's Prayer, with Scripture readings in some; the Board had not exercised its s. 28(1) option to use non-Christian prayers/readings. The three appellants were parents (one Jewish, one Muslim, one non-religious) of public-school pupils.
rule: s. 2(a) Charter. Per R. v. Big M Drug Mart (1985), freedom of religion means freedom from coercion (direct and indirect), protects minorities from the 'tyranny of the majority', and protects non-believers' right to abstain. First step of Charter analysis is prima facie interference (Oakes).
application: Reciting the Lord's Prayer (a Christian prayer) and reading Christian Scriptures imposes Christian observances on non-Christian pupils and religious observance on non-believers. Judged from the standpoint of religious minorities in the sensitive public-school setting, s. 28(1) compels conformity to majority practice; peer pressure on children is real and pervasive. The infringement is not trivial or insubstantial (Jones; Edwards Books).
conclusion: On its face s. 28(1) infringes s. 2(a) (conceded by the respondents).

issue: Does the exemption provision cure the infringement?
facts: s. 28(10)-(12) and s. 50(2) allow a pupil/parent to seek exemption; the appellants declined, to avoid singling out their children.
rule: Coercion includes indirect control (Big M); Abington School District v. Schempp (Brennan J.) — an excusal procedure can itself coerce by stigmatizing dissenters.
application: Requiring pupils to seek exemption penalizes them by stigmatizing them as non-conformists, compels a religious statement, and discriminates against minorities (adopting the Mackay Committee). Its chilling effect discourages use of the exemption.
conclusion: The exemption does not mitigate but aggravates the infringement.

issue: Can the s. 2(a) breach be justified under s. 1?
facts: The AG/Board asserted secular educational and moral objectives; appellants argued the purpose was religious.
rule: s. 1 / Oakes proportionality. Where a law's purpose is to compel religious observance it is incapable of s. 1 justification (Big M; A.-G. Que. v. Quebec Ass'n of Protestant School Boards). Purpose, not effect, fixes constitutional character.
application: After reviewing the Act, Regulations and history (Ryerson; Hope Commission; Mackay Report), the Court found the purpose of s. 28(1) religious, its moral/educational effects merely derivative — so s. 1 is unavailable. In any event it fails minimal impairment: the Toronto Board's multi-faith book of readings shows less intrusive means exist.
conclusion: Incapable of s. 1 justification, and would fail s. 1 (minimal impairment) even if available.

issue: Do s. 28 / s. 50 violate s. 15(1) equality rights?
facts: Appellants also sought declarations under s. 15(1), the Religious Freedom Act, and the Ontario Human Rights Code.
rule: s. 15(1) Charter; a court need not decide issues unnecessary to disposition.
application: Having found s. 28(1) of no force or effect under s. 2(a) + s. 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982, the majority held it unnecessary to address the s. 15/statutory claims. Lacourciere J.A., dissenting, would have held s. 28 does not violate s. 15, but the Board's exclusively Christian practice did.
conclusion: Not decided by the majority; addressed only in dissent.

issue: Were the housing and employment questions within a “census of population” under ss. 18 and 20(1) of the Statistics Act, or ultra vires the Order in Council?
facts: The 1981 census, ordered by Order in Council P.C. 1980-477 (Feb. 8, 1980) under ss. 18 and 20(1) of the Statistics Act, used a long form (Qq. 1–46) delivered to one-fifth of households and a short form (Qq. 1–13) for the rest. Qq. 13–22 concerned housing (age and type of dwelling, rooms, heating equipment and fuel, state of repair, payments) and Qq. 39–46 concerned employment and income. The trial judge held these were not part of a “census of population” and were ultra vires.
rule: Sections 18 and 20(1) authorize a “census of population,” which is undefined in the Act; in its ordinary meaning it is an official enumeration of the population (14 C.J.S. 101; Webster’s Third). Section 20(1) requires the Governor in Council to prescribe the census questions; s. 7.1 lets the Minister authorize the obtaining of non-census information on a voluntary basis; s. 8(2) empowers the Minister (not the Governor in Council) to authorize sampling; s. 21 lets the Governor in Council request statistics on a particular subject from the Minister. A discretionary delegated power must be exercised only by the delegate to whom it is committed: delegatus non potest delegare (de Smith, Judicial Review of Administrative Action, 4th ed.).
application: The court doubted that questions such as the state of repair of a house (Q. 19) or its fuel bill (Q. 20) fell within any reasonable meaning of a “census of population.” More significantly, it disagreed with Meyer J. in R. v. Churchill (1978), 45 C.C.C. (2d) 312: the Order in Council purported to act solely under ss. 18 and 20(1), yet by confining Qq. 13–46 to one-fifth of households the Governor in Council had used the sampling power (s. 8(2)) and the voluntary/compulsory-designation power (s. 7.1) that the Act delegates only to the Minister. Such statistics ought to have been sought by a s. 21 request directing the Minister, who alone could authorize sampling and designate voluntary questions.
conclusion: The Order in Council, insofar as it folded sampling and extraneous housing/employment questions into the exercise of the census power, was ultra vires; the court concurred in the trial judge’s result, though on this different (delegatus non potest delegare) footing.

issue: Can an unreasonable intrusion upon the respondent’s right to privacy constitute a “lawful excuse” under s. 29(b)?
facts: Otto refused to complete the form as a matter of principle, considering it an invasion of privacy. The long form sought, among other things, information on common-law relationships, the number of children ever born to a married woman (Q. 37), ethnic or cultural origin, religion, language, education and income.
rule: A “lawful excuse” must rest on a legal principle usable as a shield against the statutory power. No Canadian enactment or judgment had yet formulated a general right to privacy, but privacy — “the right to be let alone” (Warren & Brandeis; Prosser; Katz v. United States; Hunter v. Southam Inc.; Motherwell v. Motherwell) — falls within the residuum of human rights and fundamental freedoms preserved by s. 5 of the Canadian Bill of Rights and s. 26 of the Charter, and the Statistics Act is not excepted from the Bill of Rights. The protected interest is a “reasonable expectation of privacy” (Hunter v. Southam), so only an unreasonable intrusion engages it. Charter s. 8 was held not to apply retrospectively, so the Canadian Bill of Rights governed events in 1981.
application: Most census questions, though intrusive, were reasonable and required no justification beyond the form’s “Message to All Canadians.” But questions touching religion, ethnic origin, common-law relationships and children born to a married woman concern deeply private matters — especially for members of minorities who have experienced repressive state action — and the Census Guide offered no explanation of their necessity. Reasonableness is the handmaiden of necessity; absent a factual basis demonstrating that such sensitive inquiries were necessary, they were unreasonable intrusions.
conclusion: To the extent the form contained questions of that sensitive genre, it was an unreasonable intrusion on Otto’s reasonable expectation of privacy, which furnished a “lawful excuse” for not responding.

issue: Was the respondent “the occupant” liable under s. 31 to fill in and return the form?
facts: The census taker left one long form at the Otto dwelling (4931 Cedar Crescent, Delta) without addressing it to any named person, relying on s. 31 rather than a s. 22 form addressed to a named person. The household had at least two adult occupants — Mrs. Otto and Mr. Otto — and each refused to complete it; Mr. Otto was never charged. The charge alleged refusal “between” June 2, 1981 and Feb. 27, 1982 rather than on census day, June 3, 1981.
rule: Section 31 provides that leaving a form at a house bearing a notice to fill it in and sign it is, “as against the occupant, a sufficient requirement” for the occupant, or in his absence some other member of the family, to do so, even though the occupant is not named. Read with s. 26(7) of the Interpretation Act (singular includes plural), “the occupant” is properly construed in the singular; where only one construction is feasible, it prevails (R. v. Noble, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 632). Refusing to fill in a form under s. 31 is a distinct offence from refusing to furnish information.
application: Because only one form was left and it named no one, only a single person could be “the occupant” made liable by s. 31; the alternative reading (“the occupants”) would render the section’s “or in his absence … some other member of the family” meaningless. With at least two adult occupants each refusing, the Crown could not prove that Otto rather than her husband was “the occupant.” The charge’s timing was also defective, since liability arose on census day (June 3, 1981), not over the alleged range.
conclusion: Otto was entitled to the benefit of the doubt as to whether she was “the occupant” required to complete the form under s. 31, providing a further reason to dismiss the appeal.

issue: May the court extend any deference to the parties’ separation agreement in the s. 44(4) best-interests analysis?
facts: The parties’ 2018 separation agreement contained a “School Provision” requiring the children to attend school on the North Shore as of September 2022. The mother sought to enforce it; the father cross-applied under s. 44(4) of the FLA to vary it. The parties disputed whether the Agreement itself could be a factor in the s. 44(4) analysis; the mother relied on Dosch v. Wimmer, 2021 BCSC 2167 (citing Leiding v. Leiding, 2016 BCSC 2567), for extending deference to the agreement on Miglin contractual principles.
rule: FLA s. 44(4) requires the court to set aside or replace all or part of a parenting-arrangements agreement if satisfied the agreement is not in the best interests of the child. FLA s. 37(1) makes the best interests of the child the only consideration on a Part 4 application, and s. 37(3) reinforces that focus. In the case law, Leiding para. 29 (deference / material-change reluctance, drawing on Miglin v. Miglin, 2003 SCC 24) is obiter dictum; B.A.C. v. K.C., 2018 BCSC 2111 (Gomery J.), adopting Niijar v. Gill, 2017 BCSC 1362, and S.C.B. v. K.M.B., 2018 BCSC 1148, rejects any reluctance to change an agreement absent a material change and treats the existence of an agreement as a background fact, not a factor.
application: The court held Leiding para. 29 to be obiter, and Dosch’s citation of it (even if read as approval) likewise obiter. Section 37’s word “only” precludes giving weight to the parties’ contractual expectations in the guise of “deference”; the agreement is a background fact, not a factor. It remains relevant only insofar as it assists the court in identifying and assessing the children’s needs and circumstances. Where, after a fresh and full best-interests assessment, the options are a “dead heat,” the tie goes to the agreement — not because of any deference, but because the s. 44(4) applicant has then failed to discharge the onus to satisfy the court that the agreement is not in the best interests of the child.
conclusion: Section 37 does not permit extending any deference to the Agreement in the s. 44(4) analysis; best interests governs, with the onus on the party seeking to set the agreement aside and any true tie resolved in the agreement’s favour.

issue: Is enforcing the School Provision (schooling on the North Shore) rather than varying it (schooling in Gibsons) in the children’s best interests?
facts: The status quo — split school-week parenting enabled by the mother home-schooling on Fridays — could not continue once O. entered high school, as the children must attend school five days a week in one place. The competing options were North Shore schools (mother) and Gibsons (father). There were no family-violence issues; the parents were capable and able to co-operate. Evidence included Dr. Bolgar’s s. 211 Views of the Child report, the children’s relationships with step-siblings A., B. and M. and partners K. and T., the children’s Jewish cultural/community involvement, their academic ability and O.’s interest in film-making, and O.’s Crohn’s disease.
rule: FLA s. 37(1) makes best interests the only consideration; s. 37(2) requires all of the child’s needs and circumstances to be considered, including the child’s health and emotional well-being (a), the child’s views unless inappropriate (b), the nature and strength of relationships with significant persons (c), and the need for stability given age and stage (e). Section 37(3) requires an arrangement to protect the child’s physical, psychological and emotional safety, security and well-being to the greatest extent possible. A child’s expressed views may be given little weight where the conditions of their elicitation undermine reliability.
application: The children’s expressed preference for Gibsons was given little weight: they were asked to compare a vague hypothetical (unknown schools, residence and route) to the familiar, the report did not address whether their views had been influenced, and the father had disregarded a witness-exclusion order; their views were fairly neutral. The children were resilient and adapted well to change (separation, moves, blended families). The father overstated the impact of a North Shore schedule on the children’s relationships with A., B., M. and K.; overlap would continue, and O. and A. could gain weekend time. Fuller participation in the Vancouver Jewish community, education and culture — and connection to extended family in Israel — was beneficial. O. (bright, studious, keen on film-making) would be better served by an academically focused school offering advanced courses and specialized extracurriculars, and N. would benefit similarly and from a schedule matching O.’s. O.’s Crohn’s disease was well managed by the physician-father, and health-care continuity in Gibsons could be maintained if needed.
conclusion: Enforcing the School Provision — the children attending school on the North Shore — is in the children’s best interests.

issue: Who should have custody of the six-year-old child on the best interests of the child?
facts: A.J.K. (born 2000) is the daughter of Y.T. (from Japan) and J.K.1 (from Poland), who married in New York and immigrated to Toronto in 2002. The mother was the full-time primary caregiver from birth; the father worked and studied and (as the court found) overstated his early involvement, and the child’s first language is Japanese with limited English. The mother alleged controlling, obsessive and intimidating conduct; the father kept 120–180 pages of intensely emotional access journals and sought a shared residency / joint decision-making arrangement, while the mother sought sole custody.
rule: Children’s Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12, s. 24: custody is determined by the best interests of the child, with s. 24(2) factors including (a) love, affection and emotional ties, (b) the child’s views, (c) stability of the home environment, (d) each applicant’s ability to provide guidance, education and the necessaries of life, (e) the proposed parenting plans, (f) the permanence and stability of the family unit, and (g) the blood relationship. A joint-custody order requires evidence that the parents can communicate effectively (Kaplanis v. Kaplanis, 2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)); the maximum-contact principle (Divorce Act s. 16(10)) applies by analogy (Woodhouse v. Woodhouse).
application: The mother had most consistently cared for A.J.K. and had the more substantial connection; at six the child was too young for meaningful views; the mother provided stability despite the post-separation move, which was prompted by her fear of the father. Both parents could provide the necessaries, but the father’s practices (always carrying the child, never refusing her, aspiring to be her “friend,” and sobbing publicly at an exchange) offered poorer guidance. Joint custody / shared residency was unworkable because the parties could communicate only through a written book and the mother feared the father. A.J.K. had stronger ties to her extended maternal family (Japan) than to her paternal relatives; the blood-relationship factor was neutral.
conclusion: It is in A.J.K.’s best interests to be in the sole custody of her mother, with access to her father.

issue: Should the custodial mother be permitted to relocate with A.J.K. to Japan?
facts: The mother, as custodial parent, sought to move to Japan for family support, employment and emotional stability, and would not move without the child; the father opposed, citing reduced contact, loss of exposure to the child’s Polish heritage, an alleged risk of discrimination in Japan, and that Japan is not a signatory to the Hague Convention.
rule: Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27: there is no legal presumption in favour of the custodial parent, though that parent’s views merit great respect; the only issue is the child’s best interests, not the parents’ rights. The court considers, inter alia, the existing custody and access relationships, the desirability of maximizing contact, the child’s views, the custodial parent’s reasons for moving (only in the exceptional case where relevant to that parent’s ability to meet the child’s needs), and the disruption of a change in custody or removal from family, school and community. Maximum contact is important but not absolute (Young v. Young).
application: The mother’s views as custodial parent merited great respect, whereas the father improperly focused on his own rights. This was an exceptional case in which the custodial parent’s reasons for moving were relevant to her ability to meet A.J.K.’s needs: she had no family or close friends in Canada, feared the controlling father, and would obtain employment, financial independence and family support in Japan, where A.J.K. speaks Japanese, holds citizenship and has close maternal relatives. The maximum-contact principle was tempered by the father’s obsessive fixation (though there was no evidence of sexual misconduct). Disruption was limited: A.J.K. was six, had lived in Toronto only about 3½ years across two neighbourhoods, and her young friendships were not yet significant (distinguishing Bartlett v. Bartlett); the discrimination concern was unsubstantiated for the relevant area.
